After lunch, we went on a hike, and I stayed at the very back the whole time, as if I wanted to cut myself off from everyone. When I got home, I was utterly exhausted and collapsed onto the bed. A few days passed, yet the uneasiness still seemed impossible to fully shake off. Every time I thought about what happened that day, I felt a heaviness in my chest. My mother noticed that I was troubled and couldn’t help asking, “How was your day?” I simply shook my head, not knowing how to explain. Although it was over, its shadow still lingered in my heart.

The sun was just right, not too glaring. Mom moved the big basin onto the balcony, and I followed with a small one, which held a few of my clothes. The balcony floor was a little hot, and when my feet stepped on the tiles it felt like stepping on sun-warmed sand, with a bit of heat. Mom always liked having me do housework with her. She said habits should be formed from a young age. I wasn’t very happy about it, but I didn’t dare say so, and could only keep my head down and wash my own clothes.

The water in the basin reflected the sunlight with a slightly dazzling glare. I rubbed the clothes with my hands, and my palms had a wrinkled feeling. Mom would occasionally glance at me, probably to make sure I wasn’t being lazy. “Don’t just scrub the edges of the clothes. Focus on the dirty spots, like here at the cuffs.” She pointed at the cuff of the T-shirt in my hands. I looked and saw it really was a bit yellowed.

The clothesline on the balcony swayed slowly in the wind, and the few clothespins on it lightly knocked against each other, making a faint ticking sound. I stared at them for a while and actually thought it was kind of fun. Every time Mom asked me to hang clothes, I had to tiptoe and stretch hard to reach the highest line. Sometimes I couldn’t reach, so I would use the clothes hanger instead. For me, this process felt like completing a small challenge, though my arms always ended up sore.

“Wring the water out a bit more before you bring it over, or the clothesline will drip,” Mom reminded me. I nodded and twisted the clothes hard. Water squeezed out of the fabric and ran down my wrists, feeling a little cold. I carried the nearly wrung-out clothes to the line, draped them over it, and secured them with clothespins. When the clothespin clamped down on the clothes, it made a click.

Sunlight filtered through the hanging clothes and spilled down; the clothes on the line cast shadows of different colors. I looked up at those shadows for a while, spacing out, and Mom smiled and shot me a glare, saying, “Don’t be lazy. There are still quite a few clothes left to wash!” I quickly ran back and kept washing.

The whole afternoon passed like that. By the time the last piece of laundry was hung up, my hands had grown a little stiff. Mom patted me on the shoulder. “All right, go wash your hands.” I ran to the sink and scrubbed my hands hard. When I rinsed away the foam, it felt a little refreshing.

That night, during dinner, I secretly glanced at the balcony. The wind had stopped, and the clothes hung quietly there, like rows of little flags. I thought to myself that by tomorrow, these clothes would be dry, and they would smell a little like sunshine.

Today was an activity day, and we were on the school playground. The sunlight was harsh, and I squinted as I watched everyone choosing game partners. I hoped someone would take the initiative to ask me, but everyone seemed busy, gathering in threes and fives. I stood off to the side, and unease began to creep into my heart.

Suddenly, Xiaoming came over and said, “Hey, we’re going to play hide-and-seek. Come join us!” I felt a surge of joy and nodded, saying, “Okay!” I tried to make my voice sound cheerful, but I still couldn’t hide my nervousness. Xiaoming turned and walked away, and I followed behind him.

The sandy ground on the playground gave off a warm feeling under the sunlight, and it felt soft beneath my feet. I tried not to seem too excited, so I wouldn’t look silly.

But soon I realized everyone had already found places to hide, and no one told me where I should hide. I stood there, my heart pounding, feeling my cheeks growing red and my palms getting sweaty. I muttered softly, “Did they forget about me?”

I finally mustered the courage to ask Xiaoli, who was hiding, “Where should I hide?” But she only replied vaguely, “Just find some place.” Then she hurried off. I looked at her retreating figure and felt a wave of disappointment, as if the whole playground were mocking me.

The game began, and I had no choice but to hide in a small corner at the edge of the playground, where there were a few stones. I curled up, feeling my heartbeat grow faster and faster, like a drum beating beside my ear. Xiaoli’s answer kept echoing in my mind: “Just find some place.”

After the game ended, I slowly walked back to the classroom, feeling heavy all over, while the same question repeated in my mind: “Does no one want to play with me?” The air in the classroom felt stifling, and the smell of chalk dust made me feel oppressed.

On the way home from school, I kept thinking about it, full of self-doubt. That night, when Mom asked how things had gone at school, I just kept my head down and said, “It was okay.” Then I quickly ran back to my room.

Lying on my bed, I stared at the ceiling, feeling a little sad and ashamed, wondering whether all of this happened because I had done something wrong. A few days later, although the incident gradually faded, I still often reflected to myself: what should I do so I won’t be overlooked?

I stood in a toilet stall, gripping the hook on the stall door so tightly that my fingertips had gone white. The walls of the stall were painted a dull yellow, and it felt as if they were about to swallow me whole. I could smell the pungent scent of disinfectant mixed with some damp, moldy odor, making my stomach churn even more. My heartbeat started racing again, and my ears were filled with that thudding “thump—thump—thump” sound, as if each beat were reminding me of what had just happened.

During the break, I accidentally knocked over the pencil case of the classmate sitting next to me in the classroom, and all the pencils rolled onto the floor. He stood up and said harshly to me, “Why are you so stupid? You always bump into my things!” His voice stabbed into my ears like needles, and my face burned at once. I whispered an apology: “I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to.” But he didn’t listen at all and kept shouting, “You say sorry every time, but you never change! Is there something wrong with your brain?”

His words shattered the last bit of self-respect I had managed to piece together. I felt the whole room suddenly go quiet, as if all the classmates were staring at me and laughing. A crazy image flashed through my mind: they were gathered in a circle, pointing at me and laughing, saying I was an idiot, someone who should never have come to school. I wasn’t sure whether they were really laughing, but my vision was already blurring, and I didn’t dare look up anymore.

I ran out of the classroom and hid in the toilet stall. My heart was pounding so hard it felt like it might burst my chest open, and my stomach was burning as if there were a ball of fire inside it. I looked down at my feet and saw that my shoelaces were untied, but I had no strength to tie them. I could hear the noise of break time outside, someone shouting, “Let’s play rock-paper-scissors!” and girls laughing, but those sounds felt very far away, as if they didn’t belong to my world.

The scene I had just experienced kept replaying in my mind, and every detail cut at my heart like a knife. I thought: he must hate me now, and everyone will side with him. They’ll talk about me behind my back, saying I’m a troublemaker, saying I don’t belong with them at all. I gripped the hook on the toilet stall door, my nails digging deep into it, trying to stop myself from crying, but the tears still fell. I kept whispering “I’m sorry,” though I didn’t know who I was saying it to.

Soon the bell rang, and break time was over. I heard everything quiet down outside, but I still didn’t have the courage to walk out. Staying in the toilet made me feel a little safer, but I also knew that when the teacher called roll, the whole class would realize I wasn’t there. Would someone guess I was hiding here? Would they make fun of me, or say I was throwing a childish tantrum again? These thoughts made me even more tense, leaving me almost breathless. I wiped my face, trying hard not to look too embarrassed, and only then slowly made my way back to the classroom. My feet felt as heavy as if they were filled with lead, and each step was laborious.

Over the next few days, I became very careful, always standing farther away in advance and trying my best to avoid touching other people’s things. But I kept feeling that the way they looked at me had changed—or was that just my imagination? In any case, that feeling of being isolated weighed on my chest like a stone, making it hard for me to breathe.

The classroom was quiet, with only the rustle of pencils on paper breaking the silence, as everyone nervously worked on the math quiz. I sat by the window, sunlight spilling across my desk and making the paper seem a little glaring. I stared at the last big problem, growing more and more anxious; my heartbeat seemed louder than the sound of the pencil rubbing against the page. I read the problem over and over, trying to figure out what was wrong, but I had no idea where to begin. My palms started to sweat, and it was even hard to hold my pencil.

Suddenly, the teacher walked over to my side and glanced at me, then asked softly, “Is there anything you don’t understand?” I quickly lowered my head and pretended to be thinking, but inside a voice kept telling me, “You can’t do it. You must have done it wrong.” I forced out a smile and said, “No, it’s just a little difficult.” The teacher nodded slightly and walked away. Her expression didn’t seem unusual, but I kept feeling that it meant disappointment.

I began imagining the worst-case scenario: would not doing this problem well make the teacher think I was stupid? My hands unconsciously clenched the hem of my clothes, and my stomach ached faintly. Time passed little by little, and I knew I had to hand in my paper, so I reluctantly put down my pen.

After the test, I walked out of the classroom, hearing my classmates talking as they discussed their answers. My friend asked me, “How did you do?” I gave a self-mocking smile. “I barely understood the last question. I probably got it all wrong.” She patted me on the shoulder. “It’s okay. Everyone runs into difficult questions.” But I thought to myself, “If I were a smart kid, I shouldn’t be stumped by this.”

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning. Scenes of the teacher’s expression when she looked at me, along with my classmates’ cheerful voices, kept replaying in my mind. I felt I was worse than all of them, and I even began to doubt whether I could keep up with everyone else. It wasn’t until a few days later, when the papers were handed back, that I discovered I had actually gotten all the other questions right and only missed the last one. My mood improved a little. Yet that moment of shame remained deeply etched in my mind.

I stood by the edge of the playground, the soles of my shoes slowly tracing circles in the sandy ground. The sunlight was blinding, and the plastic track on the ground reflected a bit of glare, so I had to squint to see clearly into the distance. The team leader said we were going to discuss class activities after morning exercises, but I wasn’t sure whether she was targeting me specifically or just making casual arrangements. When I walked over, there was a trace of impatience in her voice, and she said to me, “Hurry up, don’t hold us back!” The look she gave the other classmates made me feel like I was someone unnecessary.

“I’m not holding anyone back,” I said softly, my voice almost drowned out by the noisy crowd around us. But she had already turned away, as if she didn’t want to continue the conversation with me. I froze in place, my palms heating up and my heartbeat starting to quicken. I began to wonder: had I just not walked fast enough? Did I look awkward? Did they... not want me to join at all? My stomach suddenly tightened. I wanted to leave, but if I walked away now, I felt like I would seem too cowardly.

A little boy beside us suddenly cut in: “Why aren’t you saying anything? Are you scared?” His voice carried a hint of mockery, and I immediately flushed red. I managed to force out, “No, I just...” But before I could finish, the other kids interrupted again; they had already started enthusiastically talking among themselves, completely without me. I felt as though my voice had come from inside a cave, weightless and insignificant. I stood there, feeling like my feet had been nailed to the ground.

My mind kept replaying what had just happened: was she angry? Did she think I wasn’t good enough, which was why she didn’t want to listen to me? My legs were a little shaky, and my palms were now soaked with sweat. I sneaked a look at her expression; there didn’t seem to be anything special on her face, but that only made me more nervous. I felt like she was deliberately ignoring me. “What do I need to do to make people notice me?” I thought, but I had no idea how to do it.

When the activity finally ended, I quickly ran off toward the restroom. I put my hands under the faucet, and the cold water washed the sweat from my skin. My stomach was still faintly aching. I wondered, why is my reaction always so strange whenever I encounter something like this? Why do I always feel like other people have a problem with me? When I walked back to the classroom, my head was lowered as far as it could go. I tried to tell myself that this was just an ordinary misunderstanding and that they weren’t really targeting me, but my mind still wouldn’t stop.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed the team leader’s tone over and over in my head. That “don’t hold us back” felt like a thorn piercing my heart. I kept wondering: if I could have been a little quicker, or acted more confident, would she have liked me more? But the more I thought about it, the tighter and more uncomfortable my chest felt. I tried to turn over and force myself not to think about it, but even with my eyes closed, her face and her words still echoed in my mind.

On a bright afternoon, the school playground was buzzing with noise as we were split into teams for a soccer match. The air was filled with the smell of grass and earth, and every so often a breeze would blow by, bringing a hint of coolness. I felt both excited and nervous. Standing in the middle of the field, I clenched my fists, my palms slightly sweaty.

Not long after the game began, my teammate Xiaoming passed the ball to me, and it rolled quickly toward me. My heart raced, and I kept repeating to myself, “Don’t mess up, don’t mess up.” Just as the ball was about to reach me, I felt my foot slip. I lost my balance, my toe missed the ball completely, and it slid past my foot and rolled straight to the opposing team.

“Hurry, get the ball back!” Xiaoming shouted from behind, his voice somewhat urgent. I quickly chased after that seemingly deadly ball, filled with regret and panic. Why was I always like this? Why did I always ruin things?

The other team counterattacked quickly and scored an easy goal right in front of my defensive line. I stood there, my cheeks burning, as if countless eyes were fixed on me. My heartbeat quickened, and the tension surged over me like a tide.

“What’s wrong with you? That ball was crucial!” Xiaoming said with some dissatisfaction, his tone carrying a hint of blame. I lowered my head and stared at my sneakers, not knowing how to explain. All I could hear was the stream of criticism and shame inside me.

For the rest of the match, I was completely dazed, trying my hardest but always feeling inadequate. Whenever I heard my teammates whispering among themselves, I suspected they were blaming me. That mistake seemed to magnify all my other small errors. I felt like a heavy stone, dragging down the whole team.

After the match, I silently walked back to the classroom, with the scene still replaying in my mind. On the desk was the homework sheet the teacher had just handed out, but I had nomood to look at it. I kept holding a pen in my hand, yet I didn’t know where to start. That night I tossed and turned in bed, and even that small mistake gave me stomach pain, leaving me unable to sleep peacefully.

The next day, I sat silently at the breakfast table. My mother noticed my mood and asked, “What’s wrong? Are you okay?” I just shook my head, wanting to hide my unease and shame. I knew I was just too easily affected, unable to let even a small mistake go.

Although this incident wasn’t a big one, it made me feel even more insecure, always sensing that if I wasn’t good enough, I would be disliked or abandoned.

Sunlight streamed through the window and fell across the classroom floor. Quietly, I sat beside a wooden desk, holding colored pencils in my hands, with a clean sheet of white paper spread out before me. The classroom was filled with a faint smell of chalk and the fresh scent of paper. I began to look around; everyone was busy with their own work, and the murmur of voices and the sound of paper rustling intertwined, creating this quiet yet noisy moment.

Today the teacher said there would be a drawing competition, with the theme “My Dream.” I wanted to draw a star-filled night sky, with me and my little dog out on an adventure. My heart was pounding, and I didn’t know whether I could draw well. I slowly began to sketch lines on the paper, my heart filled with a small expectation for the unknown outcome.

After a while, I heard classmates talking beside me, their voices carrying a relaxed confidence.

“What are you going to draw?” one classmate asked.

“I want to draw a huge spaceship,” another replied.

A wave of unease rose in my heart, and I felt that my idea was not as good as theirs. The pencil in my hand grew heavy, as if an invisible force were preventing me from going on. I bit my lip and tried hard to focus.

When I finally finished my drawing, I looked up and saw that the classmates around me had almost all finished too. The teacher came over, smiling as he looked at our work. My heart beat even faster, and my palms began to sweat.

“Child, your drawing is interesting,” the teacher said, then turned to continue looking at the other children’s drawings. I let out a sigh of relief, feeling a little calmer.

But just then, I heard a classmate nearby mutter, “The stars look a bit messy.”

Those words were like a needle, quickly piercing my heart. I looked at my drawing and suddenly felt that my stars really were a little disordered, that the picture was not as beautiful as I had imagined. I began to wonder whether my dream itself was not good enough.

That afternoon, after I got home from school, I couldn’t stop thinking about those words, and the classmate’s muttering kept replaying in my mind. When I went to bed at night, I lay there wondering whether I should give up drawing, because I still couldn’t shake the unease in my heart. My heart was filled with shame and helplessness, and with those feelings, I slowly fell asleep.

Over the next few days, every time I saw that drawing, I couldn’t help but remember that comment. Waves of emotion would still rise in my heart, and my urge to tear up the paper was gradually suppressed. I tried to tell myself that different stars might also be a form of individuality.

This experience made me understand that, no matter what, my work could never satisfy everyone, but at the very least, I should have the courage to try.

I was sitting in the last row of the classroom, with a freshly drawn pencil sketch on the desk—a little bird with its wings spread. Sunlight poured through the window onto the drawing paper, making the pencil lines stand out sharply. Looking at my own work, I felt a little proud, but also a little uncertain. I decided to let the classmate next to me take a look at my drawing; maybe she would think it was pretty? I turned around, pinching the corner of the paper, and carefully handed it to her, asking in a low voice, “What do you think of this drawing?”

She looked up and glanced at it. Her expression seemed casual, and there was also some emotion I couldn’t explain. She said offhandedly, “Oh, it’s okay, I guess.” Then she turned away and kept chatting with the classmate in front of her. In that instant, I felt as if something had lightly struck my chest. I forced myself to manage a smile, lowered my head to look at the paper, and tried to convince myself that she just hadn’t looked carefully, not that she thought my drawing was bad.

But suddenly, all sorts of images seemed to surge through my mind: Was I not good enough at drawing? Should I not have bothered her? Did she think I was annoying? The more I thought about it, the more my stomach felt tight, as if a knot had been tied there. I could hear the other students in the class talking and laughing, but those sounds seemed distant, somewhat blurry. All I could hear was my own heartbeat, fast and a little hot in my chest.

I secretly glanced up at her and found that she wasn’t looking in my direction at all, as if that moment just now had been completely meaningless. I quickly lowered my head, my fingers pinching the edge of the paper, and without realizing it, I scraped tiny marks into it with my nails. Over and over in my mind, I asked myself: Why doesn’t she like my drawing? If it were someone else, would I be ignored like this too? Maybe I’m just not good at drawing at all; maybe I shouldn’t be bothering other people.

For the rest of lunch break, I kept my head down, doodling in my sketchbook, but I couldn’t draw anything decent anymore. I always felt that the lines I drew were crooked and lifeless. There was a strange heaviness in my chest, as if it were being pressed down, and my breathing became shallow. I heard the classmates in front of me talking and laughing, and wanted to lift my head and join them, but I was afraid I would say something wrong and make them think I was awkward.

That evening at home, I sat at my desk flipping through my sketchbook, wanting to tidy up that bird drawing again. I tried drawing some new feathers, thinking I should make it prettier. But no matter how I changed it, I still felt it wasn’t good enough, as if every stroke were being weighed down by her comment, “Oh, it’s okay, I guess.” After drawing a few lines, I finally closed the sketchbook, feeling a little sore inside, even wondering whether I would ever be able to draw something that others truly liked. Before going to sleep, I lay in bed, and my mind kept replaying her expression and that remark, feeling as if they were a needle, piercing my heart—lightly, perhaps, but persistently there.

I was sitting on the grass in the yard, surrounded by the laughter and chatter of the adults. They were talking about things I didn’t understand, and I tried to join in, but it seemed like no one noticed me. I saw Mom standing with a few uncles and aunts, her head gently shaking, her expression seeming a little displeased. My heart sank at once. Was she unhappy with what I had just said?

“Little one, come help us carry the drinks, okay?” one of the uncles waved me over. I quickly ran over, feeling a little excited—finally, someone was calling me. But when I handed him the drink, he just gave a faint smile and turned back to continue talking with Mom.

My heart started racing, and my palms were sweaty. I felt tense all over. Why weren’t they paying attention to me? Had I done something wrong? I felt a dull pain in my stomach, as if something were twisting inside. The noise in the yard grew louder and louder, and my face grew hotter and hotter. All I could think about was whether they disliked me, whether my expression was too strange, or whether I had said something wrong just now.

After a while, Mom finally noticed me. She came over, patted my head, and said softly, “Why are you staying by yourself? Go play with the other kids.” Her tone sounded calm, but I couldn’t help interpreting it as a kind of distance. I bit my lip, trying hard not to let my tears fall. “I’m tired. I don’t want to play,” I replied in a low voice.

That night, I lay in bed, my mind replaying over and over the image of Mom slightly shaking her head and everyone’s casual disregard of me. My stomach still felt uncomfortable, and I wrapped the blanket tightly around myself, trying to find even a little bit of safety. I felt abandoned; none of them cared about me, and I couldn’t fit into their world. Had I done something wrong? Was I not good enough? The feeling clung to me and kept me awake all night.

The next day, Mom didn’t seem to notice anything unusual about me, and I kept trying to act normal. But the shadow in my heart seemed to grow bigger and bigger. I started to fear showing myself in front of my family, afraid that they wouldn’t like me.

The classroom was filled with noise, as everyone discussed the upcoming class performance auditions. I stood in the middle of the room, nervous, and although the sun was shining brightly outside the window, I couldn’t feel its warmth. I looked at the teacher’s face; she seemed to be smiling, but my mind was flooded with images of failure. The teacher began calling names. My palms were sweaty, and I could feel my heartbeat speeding up. When my name was called, I tried to look confident and stood up, but inside, one voice kept circling in my head: “You’re going to embarrass yourself. They’re all going to laugh at you.”

Standing at the front of the classroom felt like standing in the center of a huge whirlpool, with every gaze converging on me, pressing so hard that I could hardly breathe. I took a deep breath and began to perform. I only had to sing a simple children’s song, something that should have been easy for me. But just as I started singing, my mind suddenly went blank, and I forgot the lyrics. I froze in place, and it seemed as though I could hear people whispering nearby. “Why are you so stupid!” I shouted at myself inwardly, trying hard to remember the words, but the more anxious I became, the more I couldn’t recall them.

The classroom fell silent, frighteningly so. I could hear my heartbeat growing louder and louder, my body began to feel hot, and my cheeks were burning. I felt ashamed, as if everyone were laughing at me. I forced out a smile and said, “Sorry, I forgot the lyrics,” my voice barely audible. The teacher’s gentle voice came from the front, saying it was okay and that I could try again, but I shook my head, trying not to let my tears fall. Just then, I saw one classmate whispering to another and smiling, and my heart sank. They must be laughing at me, I thought.

I returned to my seat, tears streaming down my face, and quietly wiped them away with the back of my hand. I felt utterly defeated and ashamed, and the teacher’s comforting words became a blur. That night, lying in bed, I replayed that moment over and over, my heart full of regret and pain. Why do I always make mistakes? Why can’t I be as composed as everyone else? The next day, I still didn’t have the courage to face my classmates, afraid they would bring up what happened yesterday. Even if they didn’t mention it again, that small voice inside me kept blaming me without end: “If only I didn’t make mistakes anymore. If only I could be perfect.”

A few days later, these feelings gradually faded, but every time I stood before a crowd, that moment would surface in my mind, filling my heart with fear—afraid of being stared at again, afraid of making a mistake once more.

The living room at home was decorated with colorful balloons hanging from the ceiling. I could clearly smell the scent of cake mixed with cream, sweet and rich. Low voices from my parents echoed through the room. Although they seemed to be trying not to let me hear, I could still feel the tension filling the air. I sat on the floor, fiddling with the ribbon in my little hands, trying not to pay attention to those unsettling sounds. A foreboding feeling welled up inside me, like the heavy oppressive stillness before rain.

“I told you, I don’t want to repeat what happened yesterday!” Mom’s voice suddenly rose. I gripped the ribbon tightly, my heartbeat instantly quickening. I could feel tears welling in my eyes, just from fear and unease. “Don’t do this in front of the child,” Dad said softly, but I could hear the fatigue and helplessness in his voice. “You think the child can’t feel it?” Mom responded emotionally.

I buried my head between my knees, trying to make myself disappear. Why were they like this on my birthday? Had I done something wrong? I didn’t know how to make them happy, so I could only keep asking myself over and over. At last, tears slipped down my cheeks, and I quickly wiped them away with my sleeve, not wanting them to see.

There was always a voice inside me saying it was because I wasn’t good enough. So in their argument, I felt like I was unnecessary. Like an unwanted existence. I wanted to shout for them to stop, wanted them to know how much I wanted a happy birthday, a home without fighting. My stomach began to ache faintly, though I knew it wasn’t from hunger, but from fear.

A few minutes later, Mom hurried out the door, leaving Dad and me alone. I stared at the doorway, hoping she would come back and tell me that it had all been a dream. Dad came over and gently patted my shoulder, his palm warm yet slightly trembling. “I’m sorry, kid,” he said softly. “Today may not go very well, but we’ll make it up to you, okay?” I nodded, yet felt that those words could not erase the shadow in my heart.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, the events of the day flashing through my mind from time to time. Although my father had tried to comfort me, I still felt profoundly lonely and uneasy. When I woke the next day, life had returned to normal, but the sense of being ignored and abandoned still would not leave me. One evening a few days later, I looked up at the starry sky outside the window and swore that one day I would prove I was worthy of being loved, and that I would never feel so helpless again.

That afternoon during the elementary school class spring deep-cleaning, sunlight poured through the spotless classroom windows, filling the room, while the air was thick with the fresh scent of detergent. I was assigned to clean the windows, so I carefully wiped each pane, afraid of leaving any dirt behind. My classmates were busy sweeping and mopping the floor, and the classroom was a scene of lively yet orderly activity.

“Hey, watch out!” my deskmate’s voice suddenly rang out. “You almost splashed water on me.” I looked up and realized he was standing right beside me, wiping the edge of the blackboard. I hurriedly apologized, but inside I suddenly felt a wave of panic, and my palms began to sweat slightly. I kept wondering whether he was angry because of it, whether he was secretly blaming me.

I went back to the window and carefully wiped the water marks from the glass, but I still felt uneasy, as if I were being watched. At last, without meaning to, I heard a few classmates whispering, occasionally glancing in my direction. In an instant, I felt they were talking about me, because I am always like this—easily imagining that everything has something to do with me.

“Are they talking about me?” I couldn’t help asking myself. My heart racing, I tried to hide my anxiety with a smile, only to feel my cheeks growing hot.

After the cleaning was over, I sat in the corner of the classroom with my forehead pressed against my knees, trying to steady my rapid breathing. The other students left amid laughter and chatter, but in my ears the whispers and the words “You almost splashed water on me” still echoed on and on.

At dinner, I ate absentmindedly, and my mother noticed something was off. “What’s wrong? Did something happen today?” she asked.

“Nothing, I’m just... just a little tired,” I said vaguely, unwilling to bring it up, afraid I would be accused of making a mountain out of a molehill. But deep down, I was overwhelmed with grievance and unwillingness, feeling as though everyone was against me, yet I couldn’t explain why.

That night, I lay in bed clutching my stomach, the pain in my belly keeping me tossing and turning, unable to sleep. Moonlight spilled softly through the window, but I still couldn’t calm my mind. Again and again, I replayed the events of the day in my head, feeling as though my thoughts were tied in knots that I could never untangle. The next day, I still went to school weighed down by the gloom that had not yet lifted; my whole body felt weak when I walked, my vision seemed hazy, and I was especially afraid of running into my deskmate again.

A few days later, through a small collaborative homework activity, I finally forced myself to talk to my deskmate again. He seemed not to remember anything unpleasant, and that finally put my mind at ease. I realized that I had overinterpreted many trivial details, though my sensitivity was not something that could be changed overnight.

This is one moment I can never quite erase, and even in the many years that followed, whenever I faced similar situations, I would still instinctively worry about being misunderstood. But gradually, I also began to learn to tell myself to relax, and that an unintentional act need not be worried over too much.

The soup on the dinner table was steaming, mingled with the aroma of stir-fried dishes and the smell of fish. I accidentally brushed against the edge of the table, and a glass slid off and shattered on the floor with a sharp crash. The sound exploded through the air, and my breath stopped in an instant. Father put down his chopsticks, his brows tightening as if tied in a knot. His gaze was like a searchlight of judgment, shining straight at me. “Why are you so careless?” he said, his voice low but cutting. My cheeks burned at once, and a buzzing filled my ears; it felt as if everyone in the room was looking at me. I hurried to crouch down and pick up the shards, and when my fingers touched the glass edge, I accidentally cut myself a little, but I didn’t care about the pain at all. All I could think about was ending this embarrassment as quickly as possible.

“Can’t you be more careful? You can’t even do something this simple!” Father’s voice rose again, even louder than before. The shards in my hand slipped from my grip, and tears were already welling up in my eyes, but I held them back hard. Mother tried to ease the tension. “The child didn’t mean it.” But Father cut her off: “This is a matter of attitude. You don’t even know the basics of manners!” Mother’s voice gradually fell silent, and my stomach twisted into a knot. Beads of sweat began to form in my palms, and waves of numbness spread across the soles of my feet. I kept my head down, not daring to look at him, nor at anyone else, only staring at the broken glass on the floor as if it were an escape route that could save my life. The images flashing through my mind were all his dissatisfaction with me, the possibility that he would never like me again, that no matter how hard I tried I would always be a failure.

After dinner, I hid in my room. The moment I closed the door, it felt as if I had finally escaped that oppressive atmosphere, but my heart was still racing so fast it wouldn’t calm down. I sat on the edge of the bed, staring at the floor, while Father’s voice kept echoing in my ears. He must be disappointed in me, right? Am I really that bad? Is everything I do wrong? These thoughts were like black insects, crawling all over my mind and leaving me unable to stop thinking. The discomfort in my stomach grew worse. I pressed a pillow over my face and cried softly for a while, but then I was afraid Mother might hear me, so I quickly held back my tears.

The next morning, when I got up, my eyes were still a little swollen, but I deliberately didn’t let myself look in the mirror. At breakfast, I was desperately careful; even my hand trembled slightly when I picked up the dishes. I tried my best to show Father how I was behaving, hoping he would give me a slightly gentler look, but he only finished quickly and left. I tried to tell myself not to think about it anymore, but my emotions, like that shattered glass cup, could no longer be restored.

The classroom was filled with the restlessness that follows an exam. Bright sunlight poured in through the window, but I felt as though I were wrapped in shadow. The test paper on my desk still gave off the smell of ink, and the teacher had just announced the scores; I had done especially badly that time. A few classmates gathered together discussing the questions, and their voices grew clearer and clearer, but every sentence felt like mockery stabbing at my ears.

“Did you see so-and-so’s answer? She got it so ridiculously wrong!” came a boy’s voice, followed by bursts of laughter. I froze. I had gotten that question wrong too, and in exactly the same “ridiculous” way. I lowered my head and looked at the paper, and the red Xs seemed to be laughing at me. I didn’t dare look up, afraid they would turn and notice me. My stomach began to tighten, and my palms grew wetter and wetter.

“What’s wrong?” The girl next to me gently poked my arm. She sounded concerned, but I felt an undertone of blame. Had she already noticed that I had made such a basic mistake too? Was she laughing at me in her heart? I immediately shook my head and said in a voice so soft I could barely hear it myself, “Nothing.” She didn’t seem to ask further, but I thought her expression looked a little unnatural. Did she actually already know what was wrong with me?

My mind kept replaying that question over and over, and the huge “wrong” marked on the paper seemed to keep growing larger. Suddenly I felt like a complete failure. Why couldn’t I even do such a simple question? If I got something this easy wrong, would no one ever see any value in me again? If everyone knew I had missed that question, would they think I was an idiot? The more I thought, the more frightened I became. I even started to wonder whether the “so-and-so” the boy had just mentioned actually referred to me, only he didn’t dare say my name directly.

The cicadas outside the window seemed to be mocking me too. Their cries were shrill and noisy, and my scalp tingled. My hands and feet gradually grew cold, but at the same time my heartbeat raced like a galloping horse. To hide it, I pretended to flip through the paper, only to find my hands trembling constantly, the handwriting blurring. I even felt as if the red X were a pool of blood, about to swallow me whole.

When the bell rang, everyone began packing up to head to the playground, but I deliberately dawdled, pretending to put my books away, trying to delay leaving the classroom. I was afraid to go out, because I felt everyone’s eyes would sweep over me and mock my clumsiness in their hearts. In the end, I still trailed slowly behind the last student, keeping my head down as I hurried through the corridor and fled to a corner beside the flowerbed. I sat there alone. The sunlight fell on me, yet I only felt cold. I began blaming myself: How can you be so stupid? Why do you always make mistakes? They must think you’re hopeless.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw the red X on the exam paper. Even after my mother came in and turned off the light, it still seemed to flicker in the darkness. I kept thinking: if I hadn’t gotten that question wrong, if no one had noticed my mistake, would I be able to feel a little better? But the answer could not be changed. I could only sink into endless regret and shame. For the entire first week, I tried my best to avoid saying much to anyone in the class. Even though they no longer seemed to be talking about the exam, I felt that I could be exposed at any moment, seen through at any moment as a complete failure.

The sun was blazing, spilling over the paths through the fields. From the grass at times came the sharp chirping of cicadas. I used a branch to push aside the wild grass under my feet, feeling the soles of my shoes already tightly stuck with crushed blades and mud. Our class picnic was nearing its end, and most of the students were gathered around a large pot of the “stone soup” we had cooked. What had originally been a fun activity somehow turned into one of the most painful memories in my mind.

When it was my turn to ladle out the soup, I noticed there was hardly any left in the pot. There were probably still five or six people who hadn’t gotten any. I weighed my bowl in my hand, wondering whether I should take a little less so there would be some for the people behind me. At the same time, I realized I was starving too; my stomach had been growling nonstop, as if reminding me that if I didn’t take enough, I would have to endure unbearable hunger for the next few hours.

“Come on, hurry up!” a boy in the back urged. His tone wasn’t especially harsh, but it instantly made my heart race, and my face burned as if it were being scorched by fire. I couldn’t help but begin guessing what he really meant: Was he thinking I was deliberately stalling? Had he already taken issue with me?

I explained, “I was thinking I shouldn’t take too much, or there won’t be enough for the people behind me.” Unexpectedly, he said, “Who cares? It doesn’t taste like anything anyway.” The students around us burst out laughing, seeming to mock my unnecessary fussing as well. My face flushed red and then pale; I hurriedly scooped up a ladle of soup and quickly moved away from the pot, even forgetting to look at the expressions of the people behind me.

I sat on the edge of the field ridge, looking down at the thin soup in my bowl. A few leaves floated on the surface, and a small piece of radish drifted in the middle. After taking a sip, I only felt emptiness in my stomach; it did nothing to satisfy my hunger. But I didn’t dare go back for a second serving. What if someone said I was selfish again? I heard a girl beside me mutter, “I should’ve taken more, sigh.” My nerves tightened, and tears suddenly welled up in my eyes. I knew she was complaining about herself, but—was she also blaming me for being petty? Did she think I was the one responsible for the unfair division of the soup?

For the rest of the time, I couldn’t bring myself to drink another sip. The emptiness in my stomach gradually turned into a suffocating pressure in my chest, and I couldn’t tell whether I was hungry or just upset. Fighting back tears, I tried hard to act as if nothing had happened. A friend beside me handed me a steamed bun. “I took an extra one, here.” Almost instinctively, I refused: “No need! I’m not hungry!” But right after that, I regretted it. I wanted nothing more than to rush back and take the bun. Being hungry was simply too painful.

On the bus back to school, I sat by the window, pretending to enjoy the fields flashing past outside, yet I couldn’t stop replaying the scene of ladling out the soup just now. Had I upset someone again today? Why was it that even such a routine little thing, I could still mess it up? Why was I always not good enough? The emptiness in my stomach gradually spread into an all-pervading discomfort throughout my body, and even my ears were ringing.

That night, when I got home, my mother asked how the picnic had gone. I lowered my head and said vaguely, “It was fine,” then fled to my room and buried myself under the blankets. The words “Who cares?” kept echoing in my ears. The more I thought about it, the more useless I felt, unable even to distribute a bowl of soup properly. I secretly vowed that next time there was an activity like this, I would not overthink it, and I absolutely would not make trouble for myself again.

The classroom lights buzzed overhead as I sat at the group’s round table, my palms already damp, the mind map I had drawn on the paper a complete mess, so tangled I couldn’t even make sense of it myself. The teacher asked each group to choose one person to summarize the discussion and speak, and everyone in my group fell silent, turning their eyes on me. That silence was suffocating, as if they were quietly blaming me. “Then you do it. Didn’t you always want to show off?” the group leader said under his breath, with a hint of mockery. I answered softly, “Okay, I’ll try.” But my voice was as weak as a mosquito’s buzz. 

When it was our group’s turn to present, I stood up, clutching the draft paper in my hand; the edge of it had already gone soft from my sweaty grip. I began to explain, but soon realized I had gotten the order wrong. The more I spoke, the more confused I became, until my words were broken and scattered. The classroom was far too quiet, and everyone’s gaze stabbed into my skin like needles. I wanted to explain, but my throat was so dry I couldn’t make a sound. 

“What are you even saying? You didn’t listen to the key points of our discussion at all!” A boy in the group suddenly interrupted me, his voice not loud but full of impatience. I froze, and in an instant my mind flashed with familiar scenes: they were angry, I had done something wrong again, I was going to be abandoned. “I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’ll start over!” I stammered, my face burning red. The teacher also frowned, seeming ready to speak. I hurriedly lowered my head and frantically searched the paper for the content, only to find I had no idea where to begin. 

I felt as if I were trapped in a nightmare that would never end. My heart was pounding like a hammer, sweat began to bead on my forehead, and my stomach clenched in pain. I wanted the floor to crack open and swallow me whole. My groupmates’ eyes grew colder and colder, and they began whispering to one another. I heard someone say, “How is she so bad?” “What a waste of time.” Those words sliced through my head like knives. I gasped for breath, trying hard not to let the tears fall, but my mouth kept trembling uncontrollably. 

“Alright, sit down for now. We’ll talk after class,” the teacher finally said. I sat back down as if fleeing for my life, but my legs were shaking. I heard my groupmates whisper behind me, “She’s really embarrassing.” After class, I tried to apologize, but no one paid any attention to me. Everyone left in a hurry, leaving only me sitting at my desk. I stared at the messy drawings on the tabletop, as if they were mocking my incompetence. I kept thinking over and over: if I hadn’t been so rash, if I could have been smarter, would they have liked me? But I had already ruined it. 

When I got home, I didn’t say a word to my family. I just hid in my room, spacing out. The stomach pain hadn’t gone away, and the tightness in my chest only grew stronger. I replayed that day over and over in my head, every tiny expression, every sentence, each one like a needle prick I couldn’t stop reliving. The light before bed reminded me of the fluorescent tubes in the classroom, and I tossed and turned until deep into the night. The next day, I made up an excuse and didn’t go to school, afraid of facing those people again.

I had been staring at the words on the blackboard until they were almost blurring, but I couldn’t remember a thing the teacher had just said. When he called my name, my stomach lurched as if someone hadfiercely grabbed it, and all my attention snapped back to the classroom. “Look at this yourself. What is this about?” His voice was low and cold, like a bucket of ice water poured over me. I slowly stood up, my legs feeling a little weak. I saw my workbook in his hand, with several red crosses glaring especially brightly, like flames burning.

“These problems—we just went over them yesterday, didn’t we? How could you get them so completely wrong?” He held my book up for the whole class to see. In that moment, I felt the air turn thick, making it hard to breathe. A few of the students around me started to laugh quietly. I heard someone whisper, “I knew they’d be like this.” My face began to burn, a scorching sensation spreading from my neck to my cheeks. I tried to lower my head, but found I couldn’t move at all, standing there like a wooden dummy.

“What kind of attitude is this?” he shouted at me. “You don’t care about studying at all, do you?” My mouth opened slightly, but not a single word came out. I wanted to explain instinctively, but my mind felt tied up with ropes, and I couldn’t say anything. I could hear my heartbeat pounding in my ears, my palms already soaked with sweat, my fingertips cold.

“Sit down.” His tone was full of disappointment, as if I had made some irreparable mistake. I sat down mechanically, but my legs were still trembling slightly. The other students seemed to quickly turn their attention back and keep listening, but my head was full of the scene from just now. I kept seeing his frowning face and cold eyes replaying over and over in my mind, like a broken videotape. I felt so ashamed, as if I had been stripped bare all over, with nowhere left to hide.

During lunch break, I heard two classmates talking in low voices: “It’s them. They can even get such an easy problem wrong. Who knows how they got into this school.” I wanted to pretend I hadn’t heard, but those words stabbed into my ears like needles. I felt my stomach churning, and even the lunch tasted bitter. I tried hard to hold back my tears, but my nose still stung.

When I got home, I slammed the workbook onto the desk. Not wanting my family to see my expression, I immediately crawled under the blanket, hugged my pillow tightly, and wondered why I always disappointed people. Was I really that stupid? Would I never be able to change? I clenched my teeth, pressing the pillow over my face, trying not to let the tears fall.

Over the next few days, whenever I went to the classroom, I tried my best to hide in the back row, afraid of being called on again. Every time I heard the teacher’s voice, my shoulders would involuntarily shrink, and my heartbeat would start to go out of rhythm. I began spending more time checking my homework, staying up until eleven at night, but every time I turned it in, the voice in my head saying “what if it’s wrong again” still wouldn’t go away.

The sunlight in the playground was a bit dazzling, and I squinted as I kicked at the small pebbles on the ground. After class, everyone poured outside, and a few classmates called me over to play dodgeball. While we were playing, a sandbag suddenly slammed hard into my head. I let out a muffled groan and instinctively covered my head, tears almost instantly welling up. In my ear, I faintly heard someone let out a light laugh. I turned around and saw Xiaoli standing not far away. There was no expression on her face, but I felt certain she must have been laughing at me.

“Why did you hit me?” I shouted at her. My voice was a little shaky, sounding less angry than coquettish, which only made me feel more ashamed. She looked confused. “It wasn’t me, it was Xiaowei!” She pointed to the boy standing beside her, but I only felt that she was lying. I stared at her and muttered, “You did it on purpose.”

The air seemed to freeze. After a second of silence, a few classmates around us froze too, then began whispering among themselves. I heard someone say softly, “Why is she so sensitive?” Another person laughed and said, “Who told you to stand there?” My face burned at once, as if I had been stripped naked in front of everyone. I wanted to explain that I hadn’t meant it, but the words seemed stuck in my throat, and I couldn’t get them out no matter what.

Xiaoli stared at me and curled the corners of her mouth downward. “Forget it, I’m not playing anymore.” She turned and walked away. I reflexively reached out to grab her, but her back disappeared into the crowd, my hand frozen in the air. Then I heard people laughing, as if at me, or at something else—I couldn’t tell at all.

All day long, I kept thinking about her expression at the end. After school that day, I didn’t go home with everyone else as usual, but walked at the back of the line with my head down, silently counting the bricks on the ground. “One, two, three...” My head felt swollen and painful, and my chest felt as though something was pressing down on it, making it hard to breathe. I remembered that that morning she had still been discussing with me whether we should go to her house on the weekend to do homework together. How had everything changed so suddenly? Had I acted strangely somewhere, or was I making too much of a fuss?

When I got home, I sat at my desk and stared blankly at my textbook for a long time. In my head, over and over again, was her expression from earlier, along with the looks the others had given me. At dinner, Mom asked me what was wrong, and I vaguely said it was nothing, but I couldn’t hold my chopsticks steadily, and grains of rice spilled all over the table. I quickly put down my bowl and ran back to my room, with only one thought in my mind: did she start hating me?

The next morning, when I got to school, I deliberately arrived early to the classroom, wanting to say something to Xiaoli. I wanted to say “I’m sorry,” but then I felt that she had been the one who hurt me first—why should I apologize? But if I didn’t apologize, would she never speak to me again? Just as I was struggling with this, she walked into the classroom, glanced at me casually, and said nothing. I didn’t speak either, but my head started buzzing, and I couldn’t even make out the class bell.

Today I was busy arranging the seats in the classroom to prepare for the upcoming parents’ meeting. The classroom windows were half open, and from outside came the rustling sound of wind moving through the leaves, making the room feel a little chilly. I tried hard to concentrate and lined up the desks neatly. I could smell the faint woody scent coming from the storage cabinet in the corner and the smell of chalk dust. Apart from the wind, the classroom was eerily quiet; I could even hear my own heartbeat, each beat seeming to strike heavily against my eardrums.

Then my good friend walked into the classroom. She smiled and said to me, “You’ve arranged this pretty well. Your parents will definitely like it.” Her tone was light and cheerful, but I always felt there was something else hidden beneath it. I paused my work and asked tentatively, “Do you think my parents might have any opinions?” She was clearly caught off guard by my question. “Uh, no way, they’re both pretty easygoing.” I felt a trace of unease, and my heartbeat quickened. She turned and walked away, and I watched her back as my mind filled with all sorts of things she might have been thinking. I began to reflect on my own behavior just now, wondering whether I had seemed overly nervous.

As time passed, my physical reactions became even stronger. My hands began to sweat slightly, and my stomach felt uncomfortable too. I tried taking deep breaths to calm my nerves, but it did little good. I started rehearsing all kinds of possible problems in my mind: if the parents thought the classroom setup wasn’t good enough, how should I explain it? Would I be blamed by the teacher? These thoughts surged over me like a flood, making it almost impossible to think about anything else.

After the parents’ meeting ended, I remained restless. Even after I got home, I still couldn’t shake off that sense of anxiety. All night long I kept agonizing over whether I had done enough, going back over every detail and wondering whether I had unintentionally offended any parent. This feeling continued into the next day. Even though there was no negative feedback at all, I still felt the worry in my heart would not go away. I tried to focus on other things, such as my schoolwork, but I was always quickly interrupted by those uneasy thoughts.

After a few days, although my emotions had calmed somewhat, I knew that as soon as any potential negative trigger appeared, I could once again fall into this whirlpool of excessive rumination.

The cafeteria was always so lively, with the clatter of plates and the sound of people talking all mixed together like a noisy sea. As I carried my tray to a seat, I heard a classmate sitting nearby whisper, “Why is she always so slow?” They said it very softly, but I still heard it. I wasn’t sure if they were talking about me, but I immediately felt a sharp sting in my heart. In that instant, it felt like my face had suddenly caught fire, burning as if by flames. I sat down with my head lowered, gripping my fork tightly, too afraid to look up and meet their eyes.

“What’s wrong?” a classmate suddenly asked me. “Your face is red like a tomato.” It sounded like concern, but in my mind a harsher explanation immediately sprang up: they’re all making fun of me. I hurriedly shook my head and said, “I’m fine.” My voice was so low it was almost inaudible, even drowned out by the sound of a plate crashing behind me.

My heart was pounding so fast, and it felt as if a huge stone were pressing down on my chest. I stuck my fork into the mashed potatoes on my tray, but I couldn’t swallow a bite. I kept thinking back to what I had just heard: were they talking about how slow I was? Was it because I was always dragging my feet that they were getting impatient with me? My mind was like a broken machine, endlessly replaying those scenes and possible conversations. Had they been glaring at me in secret? Was their tone deliberately sarcastic? Had I done something wrong that made me seem especially annoying?

My stomach began to ache, as if an invisible hand were squeezing it. I tried to calm myself and focus on the plate in front of me, but out of the corner of my eye I kept catching their movements. They were eating with their heads down, occasionally saying a few words, seemingly paying no attention at all to my embarrassment. Maybe they didn’t care at all why I wasn’t speaking, but I still couldn’t escape my own thoughts. I felt as though I were trapped in a glass cage, with the world outside moving on normally while I remained stuck in my own shame and fear, unable to break free.

When lunchtime ended, I rushed out of the cafeteria, feeling the need to get away from all that noise. I hid in a bathroom stall and slid down against the door, listening to the faint footsteps coming from outside. I told myself they must be out there talking about how awkward I had been. In my mind, I even began constructing a scene: they were in the hallway laughing, saying, “Did you see how she looked just now?” Even though I knew it was only my guess, it sounded so real. I covered my face with both hands, hoping to shut myself off from these thoughts, but they kept flooding in like a tide.

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t stop thinking back over every detail of the afternoon. I tried to convince myself that maybe “Why is she always so slow?” hadn’t been about me at all, maybe I had misunderstood. But it was useless—I still felt as if my head were about to explode. Later, I even started listing my own “problems”: I’m too slow, I’m too sensitive, I’m too easily awkward. I felt like a jigsaw puzzle taken apart, impossible to put back together no matter how hard I tried. Over the next few days, I always avoided sitting in the same seat, and even deliberately took a longer route to the cafeteria, hoping not to have to sit with them again.

The track beneath my feet was already covered with deep spikes marks, and the orange-red lanes looked glaringly bright under the sun. I stood at the starting line, my palms slick with sweat, my running shoes feeling so heavy they seemed impossible to lift. The noise all around made my scalp tingle and my ears ring; it felt as if everyone was waiting to see me make a fool of myself.

“Ready—” The referee’s whistle pulled my attention back. I stared at the starting line, trying hard to focus on what lay ahead, repeating to myself the form I had practiced at home: relax the knees, push off with the toes, keep breathing. But inside, it felt as if ants were gnawing at me, a dull, nagging pain.

Bang! The starting gun went off, and I instinctively drove off the ground, only to find my stride nothing like what I had imagined. My right foot stepped on the heel of my left foot, and my body lurched forward violently. A sharp pain shot through the sole of my foot. I put my hand down to steady myself, quickly got back up, and kept running, but I was already behind. One by one, my classmates passed me; their backs looked like walls moving away from me. I gritted my teeth and desperately tried to catch up, but my breathing grew short and chaotic, my throat felt scorched by fire, and my chest heaved violently.

Scattered cheers came from the bleachers, but I couldn’t tell who they were for, nor did I dare look back, let alone wonder whether those voices were mocking me. My vision gradually blurred into a haze. By the time I looked up again, the finish line was right ahead, but everyone had gotten there before me. In the end, I crossed it second to last.

I bent over, hands on my knees, gasping for breath, my legs trembling from soreness. The scrape on my knee burned, but I didn’t have the courage to look at it. Amid the laughter of some students in the stands, my ears began to buzz, and my cheeks felt as though they had been scalded. Tears welled up without my noticing, but I fought hard to keep them from falling. A classmate came over and patted my shoulder. “It’s okay. Try harder next time.” His tone sounded casual, even a little perfunctory.

“Thanks,” I replied softly, but in that moment I felt as if he were comforting a complete loser. A tide of inferiority surged through me, crushing me until I could barely breathe. I looked up and saw the referee handing the score sheet to another student, apparently confirming the results. I lowered my head and stared at a small knot in my shoelace, unable to stop blaming myself for making such a stupid mistake at the most crucial moment.

I quietly slipped away from the crowd and walked to the shade of a tree at the edge of the field. Sitting on the ground, I buried my face in my hands, and at last the tears came uncontrollably. Again and again I replayed the moment I fell, as if the projector of my mind had gotten stuck on that single second. How could I be so stupid? Everyone must be laughing at me. Cramping pain rolled through my stomach, and I even felt like I was going to vomit.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, unable to sleep, my mind endlessly churning over the events of the day. I imagined whether those classmates would be talking about me behind my back, whether they would equate my name with failure. The next day, I deliberately detoured around the sports meet results board, too afraid to look at the records posted there, and I didn’t even have the courage to greet my classmates.

The lights in the multipurpose classroom were bright yet gentle, and the floor had been polished spotless, reflecting a faint sheen. I sat in the back row, palms sweating, my knees pressed tightly against my legs under the desk. I noticed my shoelaces had come undone, but now was not the time to bend down and tie them. Up front, the screen was displaying the rules of the psychology game, and the teacher stood at the podium with a beaming smile, explaining, “Each student needs to answer one question. We’ll go one by one, and if you answer incorrectly, you’ll have to accept a random punishment.” Her tone was relaxed, but my heartbeat grew faster and faster, as if someone had clenched it tightly in their hand.

When it was my turn, my eyes swept over the question on the screen—“If there are three colors of balls, the number of red balls is twice the number of green balls, and the number of green balls equals the number of blue balls, what percentage of the total are red balls?” My head felt hot, and I couldn’t think at all, as if someone had pulled an alarm inside my brain. I struggled to save myself, quickly trying to calculate, repeating formulas over and over in my mind, but I found my fingers drumming wildly on the desk, making it impossible to concentrate.

“Come on, hurry up!” Xiao Ming in the front row turned around to urge me on, his voice clearly impatient. I froze for a moment and blurted out an answer: “One-third?” The teacher paused, frowned slightly, and said, “Not quite. The correct answer is—fifty percent.”

Laughter immediately broke out around me. Although almost everyone was only chuckling softly, those laughs felt like little hammers pounding on my eardrums. I clenched my teeth, my nails digging into my palm, eyes fixed tightly on the patterns on the desk, my cheeks so hot they seemed about to smoke. The punishment was decided quickly: I had to go onstage and perform a funny dance. My mind went blank in an instant, and all I could feel was the sweat on my back growing more and more, even the feeling of my pants sticking to the chair becoming sticky and uncomfortable.

I forced myself onto the stage, each step feeling as heavy as lead. The teacher smiled encouragingly at me and even made a cheer-up gesture. But to me, her smile had thorns, as if she were subtly mocking how stupid my answer was. The classmates below the stage stared at me without blinking, and I felt like an insect trapped in a glass jar, where even breathing was suffocating. The music started, and I mechanically swung my arms, forcing out a stiff smile. I tried to imitate the dance moves I’d seen on TV, but my clumsy motions only made me look even more ridiculous. Sure enough, the laughter started again, growing louder and louder, and I felt as if my stomach had been twisted into a knot.

After that, I lost all interest in taking part in the rest of the activities. I could only fix my gaze on my knees, replaying the scene of my dancing over and over in my head. When I left the classroom, it wasn’t until the cool breeze hit my face that my tight chest eased a little. But that night, lying in bed and staring at the ceiling, I could still hear those laughs echoing in my mind. Even when I closed my eyes, the image of myself standing onstage remained, tormenting me again and again. I even started worrying whether, when I got to school the next day, some classmates would bring it up again.

The air in the classroom felt as if something were pressing down on it. The chirping of insects outside kept seeping in through my ears in waves, making it impossible to sit still. I shrank into the back row, staring at the scratch across my desk made by a ballpoint pen, my heartbeat already starting to quicken out of control. On the blackboard, today’s suddenly added debate topic was written in chalk—“Is it reasonable to ban the shops around the school?”—the crooked handwriting seemed to be mocking me.

“Okay, let’s go group by group, and share your views one by one.” The teacher’s voice was clear and bright, bouncing around the classroom.

I counted: our group was third. There was still time. I told myself there was still time to figure out what to say.

But there wasn’t enough time at all. The group leader’s gaze swept over me, paused on my face for a second, then motioned with their chin—meaning, you.

I felt a loud scraping sound between the chair legs and the floor, as if the whole classroom were watching me stand up. The eyes around me pressed in like physical weight; my ears started to burn, and my palms were already damp with sweat.

“Uh… I think the shop can actually stay, but it should… be limited…”

The words got stuck. Right there, motionless.

A faint laugh came from the back row, and I didn’t know whether it was directed at me, but my face burned in that instant. I heard my own voice turn thin and dry: “I mean… the snacks they sell could be reduced a bit, like spicy strips and stuff…”

The teacher frowned.

That frown lasted less than a second, but I saw it clearly. They said, “Pay attention to your logic and make your point clear.”

My fingers clenched the edge of the textbook so tightly that my nails dug into the pages. My mind was a complete mess; every word I wanted to say kept crashing into the others, and in the end I only sped up, pouring out the rest like dumping out trash: “Anyway… I just think they shouldn’t be completely shut down.”

Then I sat down.

The clothes on my back were pressed against my skin, damp and cold. My legs felt weak, as if I had just finished running a very long distance. A classmate leaned over and said in a low voice, “You were too nervous. I couldn’t even tell what you were saying.”

They meant no harm; I knew that. But the words were like a fine needle, stabbing precisely into the place that had just started to scab over. My stomach gave a sudden jolt, and the heaviness of lunch suddenly became very real.

I began replaying the scene in my head frame by frame. What did that frown mean? Did the teacher think I had no logic at all? Was the laugh from the back really laughing at me? Had my wording made the whole group lose points?

The bell rang. The others had already rushed into the hallway, chatting and laughing as if nothing had happened. I stayed in my seat a little longer, glancing out of the corner of my eye and seeing the teacher still tidying things up on the podium. I wanted to go over and explain, or apologize, or say something—but then I thought, they probably wouldn’t even remember this detail, and going over would only make me even more embarrassed.

I did nothing. I just walked out of the classroom.

That incident clung to me like a wet cloth for the entire following week. Every time I heard someone speaking in class, I would first rehearse the worst possible outcome for myself: trembling voice, incoherent words, quiet laughter from below. Little by little, I started lowering my head before the teacher’s gaze even swept over me, and I began to feel that being invisible was a kind of safety.

I don’t know exactly what I lost after that day. I only vaguely felt that a door had quietly closed before I even had the chance to walk through it.

On Thursday afternoon, in art class, the light in the art room always seemed especially soft. The walls were covered with colorful paintings, and the air was filled with the smell of paint. Everything seemed to remind me that creativity was the driving force here. I stood in front of the worktable, staring at the gray lump of clay waiting to be shaped, my heart full of unease. I tried to mold a simple shape with my fingers, but the clay at my fingertips was cold and slippery, making me feel as if I couldn’t control it. In my ear, I heard the teacher’s voice: “Remember, every work of art is an extension of your imagination. Don’t be afraid to try.” Her words circled in my mind, making the pressure on my shoulders feel even greater. The other students all seemed deeply absorbed, their low conversations filled with enthusiasm for creating. But I felt as though my hands were bound; no matter how hard I tried, the piece in front of me always looked dull and stiff.

The atmosphere gradually grew more complicated, and the occasional chatter of my classmates only made me more nervous. “Wow, that one’s really good!” exclaimed a classmate suddenly. I couldn’t help looking up and saw the teacher admiring another student’s sculpture—a delicate little animal model, lifelike and vivid. Jealousy and shame surged through me. I quickly lowered my head, trying to hide my messy work. My heartbeat began to race, and before I knew it, my palms were sweating.

“Are you okay?” my deskmate asked softly, as if noticing my unease. I nodded hard, though inside I was thinking, “Why can’t I do it?” Yet deep down, a voice kept roaring over and over: “Everyone else is doing so well—what about me?” This feeling of being abandoned seemed innate, constantly reminding me how inadequate I was.

I struggled to suppress the urge to give up, took a deep breath, and tried again. At that moment, the teacher came over to my side and asked gently, “Do you need help?” I forced a smile and shook my head, but my mouth was so dry I couldn’t say anything. She nodded and continued on to the next student.

After class, I packed up my tools, picked up my backpack, and left. On the way home, even the rustling of the leaves by the roadside made me anxious. I kept worrying that after this lesson the teacher would think I was terrible, or would talk to other teachers behind my back about how I wasn’t trying hard enough. Small doubts rolled around in my mind like a stone lodged in my heart.

That night, I tossed and turned and couldn’t fall asleep. The scenes from art class kept replaying in my mind. I imagined the worst possible outcome, my heart pounding violently and a dull pain rising in my stomach. In the end, I decided I had to work harder and show a better piece in next week’s art class, so that I could finally feel at ease.

A few days later, I started practicing at home, trying as much as possible to improve my skills. Although the anxiety inside me still remained, I hoped that through effort, I could show everyone a better version of myself in the next art class.

Sunlight streamed through the classroom windows onto the floor, and the art supplies were neatly arranged on the tables. The air was filled with the smell of earth and paint, feeling like the standard setup for every art class. The teacher came over to my desk, preparing to show my clay piece: a carefully sculpted little cat. My heartbeat began to race, and I felt a little nervous. After all, this was a piece I had spent weeks making, full of hope that I would get some recognition.

“This little cat is absolutely adorable,” the teacher said, her voice echoing through the classroom. But just as she reached for it, her fingers slipped, and the cat fell to the floor, breaking into several pieces. I froze, feeling as if I had been struck hard in the heart, my face heating up rapidly, as though it were burning. Tears instantly welled up, and I struggled to keep them from falling. “Oh, I’m so sorry!” the teacher exclaimed, bending down to pick up the fragments, but all I could see was dust and broken clay on the floor. A voice in my head kept repeating, “They’re going to think I’m stupid and that I made something terrible.” I didn’t know how to react, and could only stand there, feeling as though the entire classroom’s eyes were on me. I wanted to escape this disaster scene that had become mine.

The teacher tried to comfort me, gently patting my shoulder. “We can make a new one. Would you like that?” she asked softly. I couldn’t answer, so I just nodded, trying not to look like I was about to cry. My body tensed up, my hands began to sweat, and it felt as if something were stuck in my throat. When I got home that afternoon, everything felt bleak. That night, I lay in bed, replaying the scene of the clay cat breaking over and over in my mind, unable to shake it even in my dreams. Days later, whenever I thought about it, a strong wave of shame and sadness still rose in my heart, as if it were a wound that could never fully heal.

In the hallway, the long fluorescent lights stretched my shadow out for a long way. I could hear the low conversations and laughter of my classmates coming from the classroom not far behind me. A strange sense of tension and unease filled my heart, like a tangled mess of threads twisted together. I slowly paced back and forth on that familiar floor, the soles of my shoes brushing lightly against the ground with a faint hissing sound.

The group activity today made me feel extremely anxious. I knew that in a little while I would have to go up and present what I had prepared. It wasn’t complicated, but I always worried that I would make mistakes. In my mind, I seemed to have already begun rehearsing possible scenes of failure. I thought, if I were to stand at the podium later, would my voice tremble? And how would I handle the embarrassment if I forgot my lines halfway through?

My heartbeat thudded against my chest so fast that it nearly left me breathless. My palms began to grow slightly sweaty, and I could even feel a faint trembling in my fingertips. Just then, a classmate passed by at the end of the hallway, saw me standing there, and asked with a smile, “Are you okay? Are you ready?”

I forced out a smile, nodded, and kept repeating, “Mm, I’m fine.” Yet inside I was terribly uneasy, afraid that the smile would fail to hide the panic in my heart. During that brief exchange, I kept reading the microexpressions on his face, trying to catch any hint of doubt or displeasure.

At last, it was time for the activity to begin, and everyone filed into the classroom one after another. As the footsteps of the other students drew closer, I felt my stomach churn violently, and that familiar shame quietly welled up inside me. It was always like this—why could I never pull myself out of this kind of anxiety?

After the activity ended, I walked home alone, passing through the sky painted with the colors of sunset, my mood still heavy. From time to time, I could hear my classmates cheering in my ears, but I still couldn’t feel myself becoming part of it. When I got home, I lay on my bed, over and over replaying every detail from the classroom, magnifying every tiny mistake, and anxiously worrying about how my classmates would look at me tomorrow.

After a few days, that fear finally began to fade, replaced by a kind of helpless fatigue. I knew this cycle of emotions would eventually happen again, but there was nothing I could do. I could only hope that when it came next time, I would be strong enough to face it.

The laboratory was filled with an atmosphere of anticipation and tension. Sunlight fell across the tables, casting a faint shimmer, and the students were all focused on their own experiments. I nervously held a test tube, my palms already slightly sweaty, while the lab instructor explained the procedures at the front. I listened carefully, but panic began to creep in: What if I made a mistake? Would he scold me? My heart started racing, and the sounds around me gradually became blurred.

The student in front had already started the experiment, and I stared aimlessly at their actions, hoping to learn something from them. Suddenly, a classmate turned around and asked me, “Do you need help?” I immediately felt my face grow hot and quickly shook my head. “No, I can do it.” But a trace of unease flashed through my mind: Did he think I couldn’t do this experiment?

Then it was my turn to begin. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself. The sweat on my palms made the test tube feel slippery in my grip. I carefully poured the solution into the beaker, but because I was so nervous, my hand shook and some of the solution spilled out. The liquid in the beaker began to bubble, and I instantly sensed something was wrong. My heart sped up, and my stomach churned. “It’s over, my experiment has completely failed. Will they laugh at me?” For a moment, I felt as though everyone was staring at me, and the whole laboratory’s gaze was like sharp arrows aimed at me.

The teacher came over to check what had happened, and I closed my eyes, waiting to be criticized. Unexpectedly, the teacher did not blame me, but patiently demonstrated the correct method instead.
