I could feel nearly every pair of eyes behind me staring at me, and I even felt as if the projector on the classroom wall were mocking my embarrassment. For the entire class, I couldn’t concentrate; my mind kept replaying the fall and those possibly imagined remarks over and over.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, feeling my heart pound so fast it seemed about to burst out of my chest. Every time I closed my eyes, the scene of the fall flashed before me, tormenting me again and again. I even began blaming myself for not watching my step, for not being more careful, for making such a fool of myself. I knew it wasn’t something worth obsessing over, but I couldn’t stop myself from replaying it and regretting it again and again.

The next day, I didn’t have the courage to talk to any classmates on my own, and even when the teacher encouraged me to try again, I only nodded and didn’t dare say a word. I felt that saying anything at all might expose the shame inside me, and I couldn’t bring myself to believe that I could still perform well on stage. The closer the day of the speech contest got, the more frequently my stomach hurt.

Sunlight streamed through the bookstore’s floor-to-ceiling windows, slanting across the wooden floor and filling the place with a warm, cozy feeling, as if honey had been mixed into the air. I stood in front of the shelf for humanities and social sciences, holding a book that looked quite interesting from the cover, but after opening it, I soon found that its contents were not quite what I had expected. I casually closed it and put it back, then turned to look at the fiction section beside me. In my ear, I heard a clerk ask in a soft voice, “Can I help you find anything?” I shook my head and said quietly, “No, thank you.” She said nothing more, only continued arranging the books beside her, her movements light, unhurried, and calm. My gaze moved to the shelf, where I saw a cover depicting a person standing by the sea, with the title Kafka on the Shore. I had never heard of it before, so I casually pulled it out and flipped through a few pages. The typeface was delicately printed, and the paper carried a faint scent of ink. I couldn’t help leaning down to smell it more clearly, so I could take in that fragrance more distinctly. To me, everything here felt so quiet and gentle, as if it were a world entirely separate from the bustle of the street outside. There weren’t many people in the bookstore, and when someone did walk by, they made footsteps so soft and scattered they seemed like leaves being lightly stepped on. I stood by the shelf and browsed for a while, then felt a little tired, so I found a chair by the window and sat down. Sunlight fell on the back of my hand, warm and pleasant, and I suddenly noticed that my nails were a little uneven, and the skin at the edges seemed to have been torn off a bit. I touched my fingertips, feeling a slightly rough texture. After sitting for a while, I finally set down the book in my hands, closed my eyes, and quietly felt the warmth of the sunlight and the atmosphere around me. Outside the window, cars occasionally passed by, their sounds like low breathing, only to vanish suddenly into the distance. I didn’t know how much time had passed until I began to feel a little hungry, and only then did I stand up, put the book back on the shelf, and walk toward the exit. As I left, I looked back at the bookstore, thinking that next time, perhaps I could choose a book I truly loved and sit here reading for a little longer.

The lab table was covered with all kinds of equipment: power supplies, wires, small bulbs, and several neat rows of resistors. Outside the window, raindrops slapped against the glass; the ticking patter mixed with the students’ hushed whispers inside. The air was filled with a metallic smell and the dampness of a place long left uncleaned, making me feel both excited and uneasy. I kept staring at the circuit diagram the teacher had drawn on the blackboard, trying to understand the order of connections, but the more I looked, the more confused I became. My heartbeat seemed to quicken, and the overhead lights began to feel harsh and glaring.

“After assembling the circuit, test it. Each group must finish within fifteen minutes,” the teacher said in a steady voice, but to me it sounded almost like an alarm bell. Two classmates and I divided up the work. They were in charge of connecting the wires, while I was assigned to adjust the resistance. I held the tiny sliding rheostat in my hand, my palm already slightly sweaty. I kept silently repeating the steps to myself: slide the contact to the left, adjust it to 10 ohms... but even so, my finger trembled, and I moved the slider too far. By the time I realized it, the circuit was already connected. The bulb suddenly lit up blindingly bright, then went out with a faint pop.

“What happened? Did you do something wrong?” The boy in my group frowned and asked quietly. His tone wasn’t loud, but in my ears it sounded like a reprimand. I hurriedly lowered my head to check, but my sweaty fingers slipped, and the rheostat let out another squeaking sound.

“Sorry, maybe I adjusted it wrong,” I said softly, trying to sound less panicked. But a dull pain had started in my stomach, as if my mistake had become a real weight and dropped into it.

“Ten minutes left!” the teacher reminded us from the front. His tone wasn’t especially harsh, but I immediately felt my whole body tense up, my shoulders almost aching. I imagined the teacher walking over to inspect it, and a chain of scenes flashed through my mind: him frowning at the burnt-out bulb, then announcing, “This group failed.” Would my classmates think I was just dragging everyone down? That possibility kept magnifying in my head, and my heartbeat sounded like a drum pounding in my ears. I even found myself unable to help saying to the others, “Do you want to reconnect the circuit? Don’t use the rheostat I adjusted.”

“Calm down. Let’s see where the problem is first,” another classmate replied in a somewhat impatient tone. They checked the connections again, while I let go of the rheostat and pretended to tidy up the wires. My fingers dug hard into the tabletop, as if I could release a little of the pressure through that small motion.

For the rest of the experiment, I couldn’t focus at all. Even after my classmates reassembled the circuit and the bulb successfully lit up, I still couldn’t stop the thoughts looping in my head: “If only I had let someone else adjust it just now,” “Why can I even break something this simple?”

When I got home, the rain had stopped, but the damp air still felt oppressive. I flung my backpack into a corner of the room and collapsed onto my desk, yet the moment the bulb went out kept lingering in my mind. My classmate’s expression and the teacher’s reminder kept replaying again and again; I even wondered if they were still secretly laughing at me. The stomach pain seemed to grow more noticeable, and I had no choice but to curl up in my chair, pressing my hand against my belly in an attempt to ease the discomfort.

During lunch break, the classroom was noisy and bustling, with sunlight streaming in through the windows and speckled light reflected on the floor. I sat in a corner seat, holding a sandwich in my hand, but I had no appetite. A few classmates nearby were laughing loudly, and I could only catch fragments of their conversation, from “can’t find any friends” to “so pitiful.” I kept trying to tell myself it had nothing to do with me, but the sharper their laughter sounded, the faster my heartbeat became. My stomach began to ache faintly, and my palms started to sweat. After thinking for a while, I decided to swallow my unease along with the ham in my sandwich and join their conversation.

I walked over, trying to smile, and said, “What are you talking about?” I only got a casual glance. “Nothing, just chatting,” one of them said with a shrug, turning back to someone else. I felt like a transparent person, like a drop of water that vanished the instant it fell into fire. I stood there awkwardly smiling, then quickly added, “Okay, then I won’t interrupt.”

Just as I turned back toward my seat, my foot caught the edge of a desk, and an empty bottle rolled to the floor with a harsh clattering sound. Instantly, the whole class focused on me. Someone burst out laughing, and another person whispered in surprise, “How can you be so clumsy!” My face flushed red, my lips went dry, and a flood of images suddenly rushed through my mind: my loneliness in the group, the moments of being ignored again and again, and several arguments with friends. I felt as if these images were like labels stuck onto my bones, telling me, “You’re awful. You don’t fit in.”

After sitting back down, I noticed that Xiaowei, who had always been very close to me, wasn’t laughing. Instead, she gave me a cold, indifferent glance. Gathering my courage, I asked her softly, “Did you think I was really annoying just now?” She replied a little impatiently, “You’re overthinking it.” That sentence stabbed into my heart like a needle. “Yeah, I really do overthink things.” I forced out a faint smile, but my body felt heavier and heavier, as if filled with lead. Her words kept repeating in my mind, “You’re overthinking it,” as though all my reactions were wrong, all proof of my incompleteness, my not being good enough.

The next morning, when I woke up, I could still feel that sense of shame, like a damp cloth pressed tightly against my face. No matter how hard I tried to distract myself with textbooks, those voices and expressions still lingered like echoes. I began avoiding Xiaowei and also tried to reduce my interactions with the others in class, always feeling that they were talking behind my back about my shortcomings. I kept asking myself, “Why do I always embarrass myself in front of others? Why can’t I just be a little more normal?” This feeling lasted for several days, making my stomach pain even worse and making it hard to eat. I even started to worry that every time I walked into the classroom, everyone would be ready to laugh at me.

On an autumn afternoon, the small grove beside the school playground made me feel an inexplicable loneliness. I walked along the leaf-covered path, the ground rustling beneath my feet. A cool breeze swept through the treetops, and the air was filled with the faint scent of earth and leaves. I had gone for a walk there with a few classmates, originally hoping to relax after a soccer game.

“Do you still remember your exam scores from last time?” one of them suddenly brought up, in a casual tone. My heart tightened, and my pulse quickened; I could feel a slight sheen of sweat on my forehead. I tried hard not to let my panic show, and kept walking, pretending to be focused on the leaves on the ground.

“I heard someone got every single application problem wrong,” another classmate added with a smile, sounding offhand, but the words stabbed into me like a needle. I forced myself not to think that they might be talking about me, but I could not completely suppress the suspicion in my mind. I began to feel a slight cramping in my stomach, my breathing grew faster, and countless images of past exam failures flooded into my head.

“Are you talking about me?” I couldn’t help blurting out, my voice sharper than I had expected. I could feel heat rising quickly to my face, and all the classmates stopped and looked at me. Panic surged through me, and I felt their gazes piercing through my surface like searchlights.

“Oh, don’t be nervous, I was just speaking casually,” the first classmate hurried to explain, wearing an awkward smile.

Some corner deep inside me told me they meant no harm, but my self-attacking mechanisms had already kicked in. I wanted to avoid this topic and this situation, and wished I could leave there quickly. My hands clenched involuntarily, my nails digging into my palms, but the pain made me feel slightly reassured.

A few minutes later, we returned to casual conversation, but I still felt down and detached. That night, lying in bed, I kept thinking over their words and my reaction. Sleep would not come for a long time, and my mind was filled with fear of failing exams, dissatisfaction with my own performance, and worry about being left out.

A few days later, I tried to reconnect with those classmates, telling myself that I had simply been too sensitive. Even so, whenever I recalled that conversation, I still felt uneasy and self-reproachful, telling myself that I needed to be more mature and steady, and not be so easily shaken.

The sound of shoe soles scraping against the stairs echoed through the empty hallway, as if mocking me on purpose. With my backpack on, I walked down the stairs step by step, feeling my eyes grow hot, my nose ache, and something lodge in my throat, so tightly that I could hardly breathe.

Just now in the classroom, I had wanted nothing more than to find a hole in the ground and crawl into it. During the group activity, it had clearly been agreed that I would be in charge of content planning, but when I put my ideas forward, the expressions on everyone’s faces made half my heart turn cold. That self-important group leader lightly nudged the person next to him with his elbow, then drawled, “Hmm, this direction isn’t impossible, but it’s kind of... ordinary?”

Ordinary? I had clearly spent so much time researching, and even used some unique ideas from the internet. This was not ordinary at all! But they all ignored my explanation and started chattering about an entirely different proposal, even rejecting mine without so much as drafting anything. What was most infuriating was that when I later suggested we divide the work more clearly, he actually said, “Ah, just revise this part a bit more. Anyway, what you do is good enough.”

He deliberately dragged out the words “good enough,” as if mocking me. The whole group burst into laughter, and I felt my face burning, my eyes so hot it felt as though they were on fire. I wanted to argue back, but my throat was blocked, and for a long time I couldn’t force out a single word. The few seconds of silence around me were even more piercing than any loud ridicule.

“Forget it, I’ll handle it myself.” I snapped my notebook shut, my voice much louder than I expected, as if I were trying to force myself to believe it. I threw my backpack on and hurried out. Low murmurs came from behind me. I walked faster, but my steps felt unsteady.

The light at the stairwell corner was dim, tinted with a faint yellow flicker. I leaned against the cold, hard wall; the strap of my backpack dug painfully into my shoulder, but I didn’t even have the strength to loosen it. My mind was filled with the echo of that word “ordinary,” and the more I thought about it, the worse I felt. My heart was beating chaotically, my chest felt weighed down by something, and I couldn’t catch my breath. I heard my breathing turn rapid, and tears suddenly fell like a broken string, hitting the back of my hand.

“Are you okay?” a voice sounded beside me, and I instantly froze. It was a classmate from another class, peeking at me, with what looked like an opened bottle of mineral water in his hand. Panicking, I turned away, wiped my face blindly with the back of my hand, and mumbled, “I’m fine. I just ate something bad.”

“Oh, okay. Do you need any help?” he asked. I shook my head without turning back, and only heard his footsteps gradually fade away. Once it fell quiet again, my face burned even hotter, and tears started falling again. This time it wasn’t because I was angry, but because I was ashamed, as if someone had discovered my emotions and all my vulnerability had been laid bare.

It wasn’t until the sky outside the stairs had grown completely dark that I finally left that corner. After I got home, I threw my backpack onto the sofa, pulled the blanket over my head, and buried my face in a pillow. I wanted to curse myself a few times, but when I opened my mouth, all that came out were hoarse gasps.

That night, I didn’t even feel like doing my homework. My head was full of that word “ordinary” from the team leader, and the expressions on everyone’s faces. In the end, I still forced myself to finish my homework, but the next day, when I looked up at them, my heart still ached in sharp little waves. It was as if if they said even one more thing, I might break down on the spot.

The school hallway was always so lively, with crowds surging through it and the faint humming from the computer lab weaving together. The air carried an indescribable stale smell, which I suspected came from the floors that had been used for so long. That noon, I was walking to class with several heavy books in my arms, feeling a little weighed down. Not far ahead, I saw a classmate leaning against the wall, head down, scrolling on his phone. I wanted to pass by him and didn’t notice that his backpack took up more space than I had expected.

Just as I stepped aside, he suddenly looked up, and our eyes met briefly. “Ah, sorry, I didn’t notice,” I said quickly, feeling a sudden rush of nervousness. My heartbeat seemed to speed up, and beads of sweat began to form on my forehead. He glanced at me, gave a slight nod, and said nothing, only shifting his backpack inward a little. I felt relieved, but also a bit uneasy. “Is he angry?” I kept replaying that look of his in my mind.

The noise in the hallway seemed even louder, and with mixed feelings I kept walking toward the classroom. The corners of the books lightly bumped against my forearm, leaving a faint sting. I tried to steady my breathing and did my best not to think about the small incident that had just happened. But those thoughts were like stubborn shadows that wouldn’t leave me alone, and I kept feeling that my behavior had been clumsy; self-critical thoughts would surface from time to time.

After entering the classroom, I tried to focus on the lesson, with the teacher’s voice lingering in my ears. But I kept drifting off, occasionally glancing out the window in an attempt to relax myself. Even after it was over, until that night, my mind would still occasionally drift back to what had happened during the day. I began to wonder if I was being too sensitive. Didn’t everyone bump into others unintentionally? It wasn’t a big deal at all. Thinking this way, I gradually felt a little more at ease.

A few days later, everything seemed to be back on track. I ran into that classmate in the school cafeteria, and he smiled at me as if nothing had happened. I let that little incident go, feeling that I didn’t seem to care about it so much anymore. Before going to bed that night, I tried to clear my mind and not sift through those trivial memories. I knew that such things might still happen in the future, but so what?

Outside the window, the rain fell without stopping, droplets sliding down the glass and forming lines of transparent tear stains. I sat in a corner of the library, holding a heavy novel in my hands, forcing myself not to think for the moment about the book-sharing session I would soon have to face. Around me were bookshelves, countless books standing quietly as if comforting me. The sound of rain in my ears mingled with hushed discussions, and I tried hard to focus on reading, but I could not shake off the anxiety that clung to me like a shadow. The sound of my heartbeat grew clearer in my chest, and my hands turned cold and damp.

“Next it’s your turn. Are you ready?” A classmate came up to me, his voice carrying a gentle reminder. I managed to force out a smile and nodded. The walk to the front seemed endlessly long, and my footsteps sounded especially abrupt in the quiet library. The teacher sitting in the front row was smiling at me, and the other classmates leaned back in their chairs, waiting for my share-out.

Countless thoughts flashed through my mind: “What if I say something wrong? What if everyone dislikes what I share?” Each thought was like countless needles piercing my already fragile heart. The tension spread rapidly, the sweat in my palms dampening the book. I tried to regulate my breathing, only to find my throat seemed blocked.

“Hello everyone, I’m…” My voice trembled slightly. Trying to steady myself, I took a deep breath and continued, “Today I want to share this book. It has made me think a lot about the relationship between myself and others.” The cover of the book carried a faint scent of paper and ink. I lowered my head, doing my best to avoid the others’ gazes.

I could feel my classmates’ eyes sweeping over me like searchlights, and even a few people whispering to one another. This made my heartbeat even more rapid, and in my mind I rehearsed countless possible reactions from them: ridicule, indifference, coldness. I began to regret today’s sharing, feeling as though I were exposed before everyone, with no protection at all.

Yet, during my sharing, I noticed almost inadvertently that the teacher in the front row was giving me an encouraging smile. That calmed me a little and helped me find my voice. After each pause, the tension in the air was released like the heavy moisture after a long rain. By the time I finished, I breathed a sigh of relief, and my tense body finally had a moment of relaxation.

After the meeting, a classmate came over to me and said with a smile, “Your sharing was great. I really like that book too.” In that moment, I felt the stone in my heart ease down a little. Though I was still somewhat uneasy, those words of praise undoubtedly gave me a bit of comfort.

After returning home, my thoughts were still occupied by that day’s sharing session, as if both my body and mind were still trapped in that stressful moment. I tried to avoid thinking about being laughed at, telling myself to remember those positive responses. That night, my stomach still ached faintly, and my mind kept replaying my performance and others’ reactions. Although the process left me exhausted, I knew that this experience had given me a little more confidence for future sharing, even if only a tiny bit.

During rehearsals for the school arts festival, I stood on the stage with the lights shining on my face, feeling a little dazzled. The students around me were all nervously practicing their lines and movements, while I was somewhat absentmindedly thinking about my own part. Suddenly, the stage director walked over and said softly to me, “Can you be a little more serious?” I froze. My heart suddenly sped up, and I felt my face begin to heat up slightly. Had I done something wrong? Did everyone think I wasn’t performing well? These thoughts kept replaying in my mind, and there was a tight knot in my stomach.

I tried hard to steady my heartbeat and forced a smile, replying, “Oh, okay, I’ll pay attention.” But in fact, I had already started blaming myself, feeling that I must not be good enough somewhere. I didn’t dare look at the expressions of the students around me, afraid of seeing disappointment or dissatisfaction on their faces. The conversation continued: “It’s fine, just pay a bit more attention.”

I tried to keep focusing on the rehearsal, but my mind was filled with all kinds of doubts and anxiety. It felt as though my ears were stuffed with a buzzing noise, and everyone else’s voices seemed to be filtered out. Although the warm yellow stage lights made me feel somewhat comforted, waves of pounding in my chest still made me feel suffocated, as if every breath was difficult.

After the rehearsal ended, I quickly fled backstage, trying to avoid everyone’s gaze. On the way home, I kept replaying the director’s tone in my mind. Was he really criticizing me? Had everyone else also noticed my failure? My heart was full of anxiety and shame, and there was always a voice inside me blaming me. I couldn’t help thinking, “If only I could have done better.” At dinner, I had almost no appetite and just sat there silently staring at the food on my plate.

A day later, I was still repeatedly thinking about my performance, trying to figure out what I could improve. Although the next day the teacher and my classmates didn’t mention the matter at all, my mood remained low because of that conversation. I felt an indescribable pressure, as if the eyes of the people around me were silently judging me. Even though everyone was busy with their own things, I still couldn’t shake off that feeling of being criticized.

After the group activity ended, I sat alone in a corner of the playground. The glow of the setting sun had turned the playground gold, and the air was filled with a faint scent of grass, yet my heart felt unusually heavy. Then several classmates walked over, and one of them, with whom I usually got along fairly well, said to me, “Hey, why are you always by yourself? You look so lonely.”

“I’m not lonely at all,” I retorted immediately, my voice far sharper than I had expected. Amid their laughter, I felt my cheeks burn, my heart race, and every muscle in my body tense up. My stomach began to ache faintly, as if those words had just struck me like fists.

“Don’t be mad, we’re just joking.” As they spoke, they started discussing plans to go to the movies, but they didn’t invite me. Their backs grew farther and farther away, leaving me alone on the empty playground, with only the sound of the wind brushing past my ears. That sentence kept echoing in my mind over and over, as if they had simply spoken the truth I had always refused to face: I was always being left out.

I kept blaming myself, wondering why I couldn’t blend in with them like everyone else, why I was always the target of such thoughtless jokes. Tears welled up in my eyes without warning, and I lowered my head, not daring to let anyone see. Images kept flashing through my mind of being overlooked in class, as if no matter how hard I tried, I would always be forgotten or misunderstood.

On the way home, I could not calm down. In my mind, I kept rehearsing what might happen next: perhaps tomorrow they would distance themselves from me even more, perhaps this was how everyone truly saw me. Even the slightest touch seemed to trigger a chain reaction of emotional earthquakes.

That night, I lay in bed staring at the ceiling, unable to sleep. The classmate’s words kept ringing in my ears like an endless echo, and my frustration at my own helplessness grew stronger and stronger. The next day, I put on a heavy coat, trying to wrap myself up tightly as if that could protect me from being hurt. At school, I deliberately avoided those classmates and tried to keep my distance, afraid of being hurt again.

When we first arrived at the library, sunlight streamed through the windows and fell across the bookshelves, with dappled patches of light and shadow on the floor. I like sitting near the window because there is always a bit of warmth there. Although the winter sun is not strong, it has a calming effect. My classmate walked in front of me and said softly as we went, “I’m still completely confused by those chemistry formulas we studied today.” I smiled and pretended to be confident as I replied, “You’ll get it if you do the problems a few more times.” In fact, I wasn’t sure myself either. The examples the teacher used in chemistry class that morning had left me unable to keep up at first, and even now they still felt a little hazy.

We found a table by the side and sat down, each with our pencil case and textbook beside us. The surrounding noise was very light, only the rustling of pages and the occasional low conversation. I opened my chemistry textbook, turned to those problems, and tried hard to remember the methods the teacher had taught us. I don’t know why, but I was always worried that I wasn’t learning well enough, afraid that I’d be a mess during the exam. I picked up my pen and began writing formulas on scratch paper, trying to solve one problem.

“Look at this formula—shouldn’t it be substituted like this?” the classmate sitting next to me suddenly asked. I turned and glanced at her scratch paper, and found that she had used the wrong variable. “The one you’re plugging in should actually be another value,” I said, my voice just soft enough for her to hear. She nodded and rewrote the formula. “As expected, you’re faster than me!” She smiled and kept working on the problems. Hearing her praise me, I didn’t say anything, but I still felt a faint sense of relief inside—maybe I really could help a little.

The details of the library made me especially focused. My eyes would occasionally fall on the little desk lamp, and its soft yellow light made me feel at ease. Time passed slowly. My fingers had grown a little dry, and when they brushed against the scratch paper now and then, they made a faint sound. I could feel that the chair beneath me was a bit hard, and my lower back was slightly sore, probably because I had been sitting too long. A classmate nearby stood up and walked to the bookshelf to pick out a book, and I heard her footsteps clacking on the wooden floor. Someone else coughed quietly not far away. The library made me feel very still, but not completely silent.

When I finally finished the last problem, I felt a sense of relief, as if a stone had been lifted from my chest. I stretched, put my pen back on the table, and took out my English textbook to look over the vocabulary list, thinking about the dictation we might have in the next class. My classmate also stopped, rubbed her wrist, and said to me, “These problems today were really tough!” I nodded in agreement, but didn’t continue the conversation, just lowered my head and kept checking the vocabulary.

We stayed for about two hours, until the sky grew dark and the streetlights outside came on. When I walked out, I felt the winter chill blowing in through the library entrance, and I pulled my scarf tighter. My classmate waved goodbye to me. After that, I slowly walked home, feeling that everything today had been peaceful, with just a small sense of fulfillment.

The classroom was filled with the busy sound of footsteps and the chatter of classmates as I fiddled with an electronic model on the lab table, preparing for the upcoming science and technology fair. The air around us carried a faint smell of wires and plastic, and it was precisely that which made me feel that we were truly creating something. Suddenly, a small bulb on the model short-circuited and a puff of smoke rose at once; the pungent smell of burning instantly filled my nose. My heart seemed to speed up all of a sudden, pounding as if it were about to leap out of my chest, and my palms began to sweat. I hurriedly pulled the bulb out, filled with worry—if this problem couldn’t be solved, my project would not succeed. My partner looked at me and said, “It’s okay, we can replace the bulb. I’ll handle the circuitry—just focus on the other parts.” His voice was especially clear amid the chaos. I nodded, yet I couldn’t suppress the panic and frustration rising in me. That small mistake quickly turned in my mind into a disaster that could cause me to lose everything. My inner voice kept repeating, “Why does something always go wrong? Why can’t I get it right the first time?” Clinging to those thoughts, I began checking the circuit over and over, afraid of making another mistake. My fingers unconsciously clenched the tool tighter, the muscles on the back of my hand tensing as I felt deep shame over that brief moment of failure. Even though my partner reassured me, the feeling of self-doubt still would not go away. After class, I walked along the corridor toward the cafeteria, with the laughter and chatter of classmates in my ears. By contrast, my mood was as heavy as an overcast sky. I kept replaying that moment, wondering whether I should have been more careful, smarter. Even though the bulb had been replaced and the problem solved, I still felt as if my abilities had been rejected by some invisible hand. That night, lying in bed, my thoughts were in a tangled mess as I kept turning over everything that had happened during the day. The next morning, I decided to ask my teacher for advice about the circuit after class, hoping to find some comfort or guidance.

In the classroom, the leaves on the trees outside the window were swaying gently in the breeze, and I sat by the window, feeling a little dazed. The teacher was lecturing, explaining the material on the blackboard while pacing back and forth. I couldn’t really focus; I felt restless inside and kept sensing a note of dissatisfaction in the teacher’s tone. I secretly wondered if he was angry because I hadn’t finished my homework after class yesterday. My heartbeat began to quicken, and my body felt tense. The blackboard in front of me was covered with formulas, which left me confused and helpless. Suddenly, the teacher asked a question, his voice echoing through the whole classroom. After a few seconds of silence, I gathered my courage and answered softly. But as soon as the words left my mouth, a classmate beside me gave a quiet laugh. I froze instantly, my cheeks burning, sweat beading on my palms. Had I said something wrong? Had I exposed my stupidity? I realized I might have mixed up one of the formulas. The teacher’s expression quickly shifted from surprise to indifference. He was silent for a moment, then continued explaining, seeming to offer little criticism, yet I felt he was disappointed in me. The world outside the classroom seemed to drift farther and farther away, leaving only me and my embarrassment. In my mind, I kept replaying that mistake over and over, sinking into relentless self-attack. I shouldn’t have answered so rashly; I should have double-checked before speaking. All afternoon, I couldn’t shake the thought. My heartbeat sped up and slowed down, and there was a slight pain in my stomach. After the bell rang, I struggled to pack up my bag, and the sound of my classmates’ chatter echoed in my ears, as if it were laced with mockery directed at me. On the way home, I walked very slowly, the laughter of my classmates and the teacher’s expression constantly surfacing in my mind, each scene making me feel ashamed and powerless. After I got home, I sat at my desk and tried to redo my notes, but found I couldn’t focus at all, because that moment kept haunting me. That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to let go of my emotions. The next day, I still went to school with a heavy heart, secretly hoping that something like that wouldn’t happen again. It took several days before I calmed down a little, but that scene still often replayed in my mind, making me afraid of speaking up in class.

The sun was shining just right on the court, and the basketball bounced rhythmically on the floor, making a thumping sound. My friends and I split into two teams, moving quickly across the court, the scrape of sneakers against the floor and the cheers intertwining in the air. The ball was passed to me. I stared at it, my heart racing, tightened my grip, and prepared to dribble forward. Just as I took a step, I suddenly heard someone behind me shout, “Watch out!” I froze, the ball slipped from my hand, and rolled off to the side. A teammate nearby immediately picked it up and kept the offense going.

“What was that just now?” a friend asked me, half joking and half reproachful. I smiled, trying to hide my embarrassment, but a wave of unease rose inside me. Why had I made a mistake? It was only a small slip-up, so why did I feel so uncomfortable?

I stood at the sideline, watching my teammates run across the court, my throat feeling slightly hot, my heartbeat seeming to still follow the rhythm from just moments ago. The sunlight in front of me was glaring, sweat slid down from my forehead, and I wiped it away with the back of my hand, only to feel my palm a little sticky.

“Don’t worry about it, you’ll definitely make the next one,” another friend said, patting my shoulder and encouraging me with a smile. I nodded and tried to relax, but the trace of frustration in my heart did not fade away.

The game went on, and I gradually focused my attention, trying not to think about the mistake I had just made. As time passed, I slowly got back into the game, the cheers once again surrounding my ears, as if what had happened just now was not such a big deal.

After the game, we sat on the sideline, drinking water and chatting. The air was filled with the smell of sweat and the freshness of grass. “We had a good time today,” someone said.

On the way home, I walked alone on the sidewalk, my mind still replaying the scene from earlier. That moment flashed through my mind, as if I could hear that “Watch out!” again. With the rhythm of my footsteps, I slowly began to accept that it had only been a small mistake, not something worth worrying about so much.

That night, lying in bed, I thought back to the game that afternoon, and my mind was no longer so restless. Gradually, I realized that perhaps I had magnified those small details too much, and that I should enjoy the process of taking part more, rather than being led around by those trivial mistakes. The next day, when I walked into the classroom, my mood was no longer affected by yesterday’s little incident.

The afternoon in the music room is always so quiet. Sunlight pours through the tall windows onto the light wood floor, and I can catch a faint scent of chalk in the classroom mixed with the woody fragrance of the instruments. As the teacher’s voice echoes through the room, my fingers tap unconsciously on the desk. It is an ordinary music lesson, until the teacher suggests that each of us perform a short solo piece. I have never liked putting myself on display in front of others. Even though I can sing, standing in the music room and facing the whole class feels like a weight pressing down on my shoulders.

The teacher’s voice interrupts my thoughts: “Who wants to go first?” Silence blankets the classroom, as if everyone is waiting for someone else to speak first. My heart races, and my palms begin to sweat. The teacher’s gaze searches the room and finally lands on me. The very thing I feared most happens—he calls my name. “Come on, believe in yourself.” His tone is gentle, but I suspect it’s because class is about to end and he wants someone to stand up quickly.

“Uh, okay.” I hear my own weak voice reply. The moment I stand up, it feels as if all eyes are on me. My ears burn, and my mind goes blank. Stepping onto the platform at the front of the classroom, I can feel the floor tremble slightly, as if it too is nervous for me. I take a deep breath, trying to calm my violently pounding heart.

When the first line of the song comes out of my mouth, my voice rises a note higher than usual. Whether from nerves or because the classroom air is too dry, my voice carries a faint tremor. Several notes go off-key, and I hear a low laugh from somewhere among my classmates, which only makes me more flustered. Sweat slides down my forehead; I quickly raise my hand to wipe it away, only to forget the next note.

Standing on the platform, I feel the rustling sounds around me crash in like huge waves, and my stomach clenches painfully. The whole classroom feels like a magnified lens, with every expression enlarged beyond measure. Suddenly, I remember how I used to protect myself from being hurt by attacking myself first, so I blur out in a hurry, “I guess my lung capacity just isn’t enough today. How embarrassing.” A round of snickers ripples through the classroom. I try to smile, but it feels as though every muscle in my face is protesting.

At last, the brief performance ends. I sit back down, my heart still pounding wildly. I hear the teacher praising me from the front of the class for being brave enough to try, but all that keeps replaying in my mind are my classmates’ smiling faces and that suffocating pressure. For days after class, I practice the song over and over alone in my room, chewing over the reason for this mistake again and again, hoping I can do better next time.

In the dream that night, I am still standing in that music room, the air filled with the scent of chalk and wooden instruments, and I am still trying to find the next correct note.

The air in the classroom seemed to be mixed with the smell of chalk dust and the cool breath of the air conditioner. I could feel the back of the seat pressed uncomfortably against my back—maybe because my whole body was already tensed too tightly. Our group was discussing the topic for the semester project. We sat in a circle, with draft paper spread across the table and several reference books opened but not yet closed. I was interested in literary topics, so when it was my turn to speak, I brought up an idea related to a classic novel. My voice was a little shaky, but I tried to sound more confident: “I think we could use The Lonely City to explore the alienation of modern relationships. That would not only be meaningful, but also make the project more engaging.”

As soon as I finished, the group leader smiled, but didn’t respond to me. Instead, she turned to the classmate sitting across from her: “What do you think? Maybe we should still do a tech topic—after all, that direction is easier to score well in.”

The attention focused on me dispersed. I heard a few quiet words of agreement, as if my suggestion were just a breeze in the air, passing by and disappearing. I forced a smile on my face and tried to look unconcerned, but my fingers tightened harder and harder under the table, my nails nearly digging into my palm.

“Tech is still more practical. Literature is kind of abstract,” someone else added.

“But literature can…” I tried to interject, but for some reason my voice got stuck in my throat and came out so faintly it was almost inaudible. They had already started discussing the tech topic, and no one was looking at me anymore. I lowered my head and pretended to look through the draft paper, but the words before my eyes began to blur. I could clearly feel a sharp, knotted pain in my stomach, and my heartbeat was pounding in my ears.

“Do they think I’m stupid?” The thought suddenly surfaced, like an unbearable thorn. I began to replay every detail of my speech just now—was my voice too soft? Was my explanation too messy? Should I not have brought up this topic at all? Why did I have to voice an opinion? If I had stayed quiet, would that have been better?

They were talking enthusiastically, while my body seemed frozen in place. I felt an overwhelming loneliness, as if there were an invisible pane of glass between me and them. I tried to take deep breaths, but my throat felt blocked by something, and I couldn’t calm down at all. I started pretending to write in my notebook, trying to make myself look busy rather than ignored.

“Okay, then it’s settled.” The group leader tapped the table. I looked up and saw their smiling faces, and suddenly felt like a complete outsider. When the bell rang, I stood up stiffly, quickly gathered my things, and walked out of the classroom. The fluorescent lights in the hallway were harsh enough to make my eyes dizzy. I almost ran back to my seat with my head down.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mind full of the scene from the group meeting. I tried to recall every one of their words, and kept blaming myself for being incapable and stupid. “If I had been more confident, that would have been better—I should at least have tried to fight for it.” But at the same time, another voice said: “Even if you had tried, so what? Wouldn’t you have been ignored anyway?”

A few days later, I still tried to avoid talking to the group members. When they smiled and discussed their progress, I only nodded along. I didn’t want to make myself seem any more unnecessary.

As school was about to let out, only a few classmates were still tidying up their books in the classroom. I dragged my feet out of the room, but stopped at the end of the hallway. The light coming through the window at the end of the hall was a little harsh, and I squinted, not noticing the few classmates beside me. They muttered to each other in low voices, then suddenly burst into laughter. My heart raced, a light sweat broke out on my forehead, and my palms turned damp. I couldn’t help thinking that they were laughing at me.

“Hey! Did you fall asleep in class just now?” came a familiar voice; it was one of my classmates. His tone sounded like a joke, but I felt as if it were hinting at something. Had I done something wrong today? I tried hard to remember, but all I felt was a headache.

“Not really...” I forced out a smile, trying to hide my unease.

“Really not?” he pressed again. A few other classmates were also standing there, as if waiting for my answer. I felt my face burning, as though all the blood in my body had rushed to it. My mind went blank, with only one thought echoing over and over: “They must think I’m so stupid.”

I don’t remember how I made it back to the classroom; it was as if I mechanically walked back to my seat. I lowered my head, my heartbeat pounding so loudly it was like a drum. I started blaming myself—why was I always so nervous, always not knowing how to respond? Those sharp bursts of laughter wouldn’t leave my mind, and it felt as if a stone were pressing down in my stomach. That familiar sense of tension came surging back.

After school that day, I stayed alone in the classroom, pretending to organize my bag just to wait until everyone had left. I was afraid of being seen looking so miserable, afraid they would be whispering about me again behind my back. Outside the classroom window, the sky held a faint glow of twilight, and the evening sun cast long shadows across the floor. I stared at those shadows, wondering whether I really wasn’t needed.

When I got home that night, I lay on my bed, replaying everything that had happened that day over and over in my mind. I felt angry, ashamed, and above all, helpless. I hated how sensitive I was, hated how I always seemed unable to keep up with everyone else’s pace. Even after trying every way I could think of to calm myself down, my heartbeat still would not settle.

A few days later, I began to avoid those classmates as much as possible at school, afraid of feeling that same sense of exclusion and ridicule again. I buried it all deep inside and didn’t even mention it to my closest friend. I only felt that whenever I thought of what happened that day, an indescribable pain would spread through my heart.

I sat in the art classroom, surrounded by the smell of paint, with paintings of different colors hanging on the walls. On the table were all kinds of art supplies and sheets of paper strewn about. I was working hard to finish an abstract painting, secretly hoping to get the teacher’s praise. At that moment, I heard a classmate sitting next to me say, “This painting of yours looks a little strange. Did you mean to paint it like that?” His tone didn’t seem malicious, but I immediately felt a wave of discomfort. “Of course I meant to,” I replied lightly on purpose, though the turmoil inside me would not settle down. Was my painting really that bad? Why can’t I ever paint well?

My heart started racing, my palms began to sweat, and my brow unconsciously furrowed. The noise around me grew louder, as if everyone’s attention were focusing on my unfinished work. I kept replaying that sentence in my head, and even felt that everyone passing by was staring at my painting and pointing at it. I kept painting, but my hand began to tremble and the colors went on crookedly. I had never wanted so badly to leave a place immediately.

“Hey, are you okay?” another classmate asked, pulling me back to reality. I forced a smile. “I’m fine, I’m just a little tired.” But my mood had already been badly affected; even a tiny comment seemed more than I could bear. When the class bell rang like salvation, I hurriedly packed up my art supplies and fled the classroom.

That afternoon, after I got home, I remained gloomy. Sitting in my room, I kept going over every detail of what had happened in class. I remembered similar situations from before; whenever someone made even a slight comment about my work, I would become incredibly sensitive and feel that I wasn’t good enough. My stomach began to ache slightly, as if some indescribable pressure were weighing on it. I pressed hard against my stomach, trying to ease the discomfort.

The next day, when I walked into the classroom, I deliberately avoided the gazes of those classmates. Over the following days, I kept dwelling on my shortcomings, always feeling that painting was mocking my incompetence. What was even more discouraging was that I lost confidence in my interest and even began to wonder whether I should keep painting. However, a few days later, the teacher returned our assignments. Beside my work, he wrote: “Your use of color is unique. Keep it up.” Seeing those words, I finally felt a little relieved, as if they proved I still had some value.

The sound of piano keys danced briskly through the classroom, and the teacher stood at the front of the lectern announcing today’s assignment: “Next, work in groups to create a two-minute melody.” I heard rustling around me as my classmates began gathering into groups of three or five. A little nervously, I looked to my right and wanted to smile to signal that we could form a group, but they didn’t seem to notice me and simply turned around to join another table.

“Why don’t we work with the few students in the front row?” a voice came from behind me. Turning around, I saw it was the class monitor, slightly bent over as he spoke to me. I paused, then nodded and forced out a “Sure. Anything’s fine.” But my voice was so faint it seemed like it might disappear at any moment.

After we sat together, the class monitor suggested that everyone take turns offering ideas. I thought for a long time, then finally gathered the courage to say, “We could try starting in C major, so the melody would sound more... um, brighter.” As soon as I finished speaking, I felt the girl on my right turn her head and glance at me, her mouth tightening a little. I didn’t know if it was my imagination, but she seemed to mutter, “That’s way too ordinary.”

My palms started sweating, and my heartbeat instantly went off rhythm. She probably didn’t mean it on purpose, right? But why say “ordinary”? Did she think I was uncreative? I tried hard to calm myself down, clasping my hands over my knees, but my body only grew stiffer. The class monitor picked up on what she said: “It’s okay if it’s not ordinary. We can make some changes, for example, add a chord transition.” He spoke in a very natural tone, but I could hear a subtle note of “soothing” in it, as if he were trying to smooth over my embarrassment.

For the rest of the time, I basically didn’t speak up on my own again. Everyone else was discussing things; I nodded, occasionally chiming in with a laugh, but my gaze kept drifting to the tabletop or the floor, trying to avoid making direct eye contact with anyone. That phrase “too ordinary” kept replaying in my mind, and the more I thought about it, the more it hurt, like a label stamped right on my forehead.

When the bell for class ended rang, the class monitor patted my shoulder and said, “You did pretty well today.” At that moment, my mouth opened slightly, but I still couldn’t manage a complete reply. Was he really praising me, or just being polite? In an instant, I couldn’t quite tell.

That night, lying in bed, I tossed and turned, with the girl’s pursed-lip expression and the class monitor’s tone replaying over and over in my head. I even tried imitating her voice, whispering “too ordinary” at the ceiling, changing the intonation several times—what exactly had she really meant? By midnight, I started to feel a burning sensation in my stomach, as if an invisible hand were twisting something inside it. I turned over to face the wall, buried my head under the blanket, and told myself not to think about it anymore, but my chest still felt heavy, as if a wet cotton pad were pressed down over it.

The sun filtered down through the treetops, and that warm feeling made me not want to walk too fast, so I slowed my pace and listened to the faint crunching sound of my shoes on the stone pavement. My friend beside me was enthusiastically talking about a new drama she liked, her voice tinged with excitement: “Do you know what? The villain ended up not being the bad guy after all! The twist was so huge it made me cry!” I nodded and smiled too: “Really? Sounds kind of interesting. But I still haven’t been watching many dramas lately.” Honestly, I wasn’t particularly interested in the plot she was describing, but I figured it would be rude not to respond. She kept talking, and I would occasionally murmur “mm” and “yeah,” while my eyes drifted more toward the snack stalls along the roadside.

We passed a stall selling sugar-roasted chestnuts, and a wave of heat hit us, carrying a sweet caramel aroma. Suddenly I remembered that the last time I had sugar-roasted chestnuts was in winter, when my hands were red from the cold and I held a warm bag of chestnuts, feeling incredibly happy just from the smell. I stopped walking. “How about we buy some of this? I kind of want some.” My friend smiled and said, “Sure, but I don’t really like peeling them. Can you peel them for me?” I laughed and rolled my eyes: “Sure, two yuan per chestnut.” Then we went and bought a small bag. I carried it in my hand; the bag was warm, and I couldn’t help covering it with my other hand.

As we walked and ate on the way, the chestnut shells really were hard to peel. I struggled quite a bit before finally peeling one whole chestnut and holding it straight up to my friend’s mouth. “Here, this one’s for you.” She bit off half and mumbled, “I’ll waive your two yuan this time. It tastes pretty good.” We both laughed. Later we passed a stall selling grilled cold noodles. The vendor’s movements were especially skilled, the sauce brushed on neatly and evenly, the egg mixture spread thin and uniform. I watched, mesmerized, and my friend nudged my shoulder. “Are you getting hungry from watching?” I quickly shook my head. “No, no, I just think watching them make these things is kind of fun. Being a street food stall owner seems pretty interesting too.”

After wandering around for a while, we returned to the bench at the street corner and sat down. It always felt like I still carried the smell of all the snack stalls on me—the mix of charcoal smoke, oil fumes, and sweet, cloying spices always seemed to remind you of this street. The sun was nearly touching the rooftops along the street, and I looked up to see the sky turning a little orange-yellow. My friend took out her phone for a selfie. “Don’t move, I’m getting the scenery.” After she took it, she showed me the photo. My expression looked a little stiff, my smile not natural enough, but I said nothing and just casually remarked, “It looks pretty good.”

After that, we went our separate ways home. On the way, I took out a few leftover chestnuts and peeled and ate them as I walked, still wondering whether I always smiled a little unnaturally, and whether she would post the photo just taken. Thinking of that, I felt a little nervous, but soon that feeling was covered over by a simple, carefree sense of contentment. All in all, it was a very ordinary afternoon, but maybe this kind of ordinariness is pretty good too.

The art classroom always had a special softness to its light. The walls were covered with students’ work, and the air seemed to carry a faint smell of paint and paper. Today the teacher asked us to make crafts using various materials, and my heart was filled with unease. I was unsure whether my work would be as good as everyone else’s. On the table were all kinds of colored paper, scissors, and glue, and I began to prepare the materials. “Try to let your creativity shine as much as possible!” the teacher said with a smile. I forced a smile in return, but inside I was full of doubt and anxiety.

I tried hard to focus on the task in front of me and not think about these troubling feelings. However, the laughter and chatter of my classmates from time to time still distracted me. “Are you okay? Have you finished?” a classmate beside me noticed my silence and asked casually. “I’m still thinking about how to make it look better,” I replied, forcing out a smile, trying to hide my anxiety.

My heartbeat began to quicken, and my palms grew slightly sweaty; my fingers trembled involuntarily. I worried that my work would be laughed at by everyone. Even though I knew it was only a classroom activity, my body kept reminding me that I might be criticized. In order not to be judged a “failure,” I began to blame myself, accusing myself of not being smart enough or creative enough.

As time passed, my stomach began to ache faintly, and each time that feeling came over me, I knew I was close to breaking down. In the end, I finished a piece that I was somewhat satisfied with, but I was still afraid of how others would react. “I’m done,” I said softly, trying to find an outlet for my effort in my heart. The teacher came over, looked at my work for a while, and then nodded slightly. “Not bad, kid,” she said.

Although the teacher’s praise should have comforted me, the anxiety in my heart did not ease. I returned to my seat and looked at the other students’ work. Their carefree expressions made me both envious and ashamed. I always felt as if there was an invisible wall between them and me, making it impossible for me to truly blend into their joy and excitement.

That night, lying in bed, I kept going over every detail of the class, unable to stop blaming myself. It seemed that every glance and every word magnified my fear and unease. The next day, when I woke up, I still felt tired and worried, as if nothing had changed. The invisible pressure from art class still hung over me, making it difficult to face each day ahead with ease.

“Although this essay is fairly fluent in language, its viewpoint is somewhat vague, especially in the second paragraph…” The teacher’s voice cut through the silence of the classroom, clear in everyone’s ears and piercing into my head. I sat rigidly in my seat, and it seemed as if everyone around me had turned to look at me. Though no one was really looking, I distinctly felt those gazes fall on my back like needles, carrying scrutiny and hiding contempt. My palms began to sweat, my ears burned as if they were about to smoke, and my heart was pounding so violently it seemed ready to burst out of my chest at any moment.

“Look at this—doesn’t this expression seem a bit redundant?” Standing on the platform, the teacher pointed at my name with a red pen and looked straight at me. My lips moved, but not a single word came out. “Um… maybe.” I forced out a reply, my voice as tiny as a mosquito’s buzz. The classroom fell silent, with only the teacher’s continuing comments floating in the air. I lowered my head and pretended to flip through my textbook, but I couldn’t make out a single word on the page. My fingernails dug hard into the edge of the desk, nearly embedding themselves in the wood.

“In fact, the biggest problem with this essay is still its theme; it lacks depth. You all need to pay attention—writing like this won’t let people truly remember it.” The teacher’s tone was flat, as if he were discussing something trivial. But my mind had already started racing, images sliding past frame by frame: Had I smiled too stiffly when I handed in my essay yesterday? Did the teacher misunderstand me as not caring? Or was my handwriting so ugly that it made people think I was careless at first glance? Was my deskmate mocking me in his head? Would the boys in the back joke after class, saying, “You really have no talent”?

A dull pain spread through my stomach, like a stone there about to drop at any moment. I tried to take a deep breath, but the more I breathed, the tighter my chest felt. Isecretly glanced at the teacher; he was still slowly turning the pages of my essay notebook. At last, the critique ended. He gently placed the notebook back on my desk and said, “You can go back and think again about how to revise it.” Then he turned and continued commenting on the next student’s work.

I quickly reached out and closed the notebook, as if that could cover up all the shame it had brought me. I glanced at my deskmate; he was head down, scribbling on a draft sheet, seemingly completely unaware of what had just happened. I secretly looked around the classroom again and found everyone’s attention on their own seats. Reason told me that no one was actually paying attention to me, but my emotions were utterly beyond control. My neck felt stiff as stone, and I sat there afraid to move, like a criminal about to be exposed.

That afternoon, after I got home, I opened my essay notebook and looked at the teacher’s comments, the red writing stabbing painfully at my eyes. “Confused viewpoint,” “unclear logic,” “pile-up of expressions”... every word was like a hammer blow to me. The scene kept replaying in my mind—the teacher’s voice, the classmates’ gazes, my embarrassment with nowhere to hide. I sat at my desk for a long time, trying to begin revising the essay, but the moment my hand touched the pen, the violent pounding of my heart made me give up again.

Over the next few days, I kept brooding over this matter, and even whenever I saw the Chinese teacher, it felt as though I could hear him talking to someone else about my clumsy writing. I began to doubt whether I had any real chance of ever writing well at all, whether everything I did would, like this essay, only disappoint people. Although no one brought it up again, I kept feeling some invisible weight pressing on my chest, forcing me to the brink of breathlessness.

On a Friday afternoon, the classroom was filled with the lingering smell of chalk dust after the lesson, and the slanting sunlight from outside poured in, falling across our messy desktops. Not long after the group discussion began, the other three members quickly leaned in together and started exchanging ideas intensely. “How about making it into a survey questionnaire?” the girl on the left suggested, her voice crisp and clear, instantly drawing the attention of the other two. I tried to cut in, “I think…” but before I could finish, another boy eagerly continued, “Yeah, if it’s a questionnaire, we can ask the other students in the class!”  
  
My voice was completely drowned out, and I wasn’t even sure if anyone heard me. A tightness rose in my chest, as if something was stuck there, making it hard to breathe. I lowered my head and looked at my notebook, forcing myself to write something, but my fingers had started to tremble slightly from nervousness. My palms were a little sweaty, and the slick feeling of holding the pen made me even more uncomfortable. I tried to tell myself this was nothing, that maybe they were just too excited and hadn’t heard me clearly. But then another thought shot through me like an arrow: “They don’t care about me at all, do they? Do they think I’m completely worthless?”  
  
Their discussion grew more and more heated, and I felt as though I were sealed inside a glass case, with the noise and excitement having nothing to do with me. My heart was beating faster, my ears were buzzing, and I couldn’t even make out what they were saying anymore. I secretly glanced at the girl sitting opposite me; she was waving her arms, describing some idea, a look of excitement on her face. I instinctively lowered my head, not daring to let her notice my gaze. I felt my presence was unnecessary, and I even began to regret why I had joined this group.  
  
“What do you think?” the boy suddenly looked up and asked me. I froze, my mind blank like a kite with its string cut loose. For a full three seconds, I couldn’t say a word. “Uh, I think... maybe...” My voice was so faint that I could barely hear it myself. He didn’t seem to care about my answer, nodded, and turned back to keep talking and laughing with the others. I forced out a smile, as if I were taking part in their discussion, but in fact my mind was a mess, repeating only one sentence over and over: “Do they think I’m useless?” The more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt, and the heat on my face shot up quickly, as if all the sunlight in the classroom had fallen on me alone.  
  
The bell rang. My deskmate looked at the incomplete plan, frowned, and asked me, “Try to participate a bit. Don’t zone out all the time.” His words were not harsh, but they stabbed into my heart like a knife. I hurriedly nodded and mechanically apologized, “Sorry, I’ll improve.” My stomach began to ache faintly, as if I had just swallowed a stone that couldn’t be digested, but on the surface I tried hard to stay calm.  
  
That night, lying in bed, I kept hearing my deskmate’s words over and over again in my ears: “Try to participate a bit. Don’t zone out all the time.” I kept turning it over in my mind: would he never want to be in a group with me again because of this? Would the others also think I was a burden? I tossed and turned, unable to sleep, and in the end could only hug my pillow and tell myself that tomorrow I would definitely speak up proactively, but deep down I was inexplicably afraid of tomorrow’s arrival.

Sunlight streamed through the library windows and spilled across the floor, while the air was filled with drifting dust particles. I sat in a corner of the library, trying to focus on finishing an essay, but the surrounding noise kept me from concentrating. Students’ whispered conversations, the rustle of turning pages, and footsteps intertwined, making me feel restless and uneasy. I could feel my heartbeat growing faster, my palms beginning to sweat, and an unbearable knot forming in my stomach.

“Be quiet, this is a library!” I couldn’t help muttering under my breath, hoping the noisy sounds would disappear because of my annoyance. A classmate sitting next to me heard me, turned around, and said in a teasing voice, “You’re not the only one here, don’t make such a fuss.” His tone wasn’t exactly mean, but to me it felt like a heavy blow.

“I just want it a little quieter,” I replied softly, but inside I was full of irritation and unease. I could feel the heat rising in my face, as if everyone was looking at me and thinking I was the troublemaker. My eyes began to sting, and that familiar feeling of anxiety filled my nose.

At that moment, my inner monologue became unbearably loud: Why am I always so sensitive? Why do other people’s simple words always hurt me? I hate this feeling, hate the helplessness of being unable to control my emotions. Tears welled up in my eyes, and I hurriedly lowered my head, trying to hide my vulnerability.

I quickly gathered my books and notes and practically fled the library. The air outside was cold and fresh. I took a breath and tried hard to calm my racing heart. Yet the tension in my body did not completely disappear, and even my steps felt heavier than usual.

For several hours after getting home, I was still unsettled. I kept thinking back to what happened in the library, chewing over the conversation and my own reaction again and again. I felt ashamed of my sensitivity. Why do I always overreact like this? Tossing and turning in bed, I feared being mocked and gossiped about when I returned to school the next day. I kept reminding myself to learn to be strong, to learn not to be driven by my emotions. Yet these self-reminders seemed futile. Even so, I still tried to meditate briefly in my room, hoping to calm myself down a little.

That night, I remained restless in bed until the early hours of the morning, finally drifting off into a dazed sleep. My dreams were filled with all kinds of blurred scenes, yet there was always a sense of being isolated. Still, I knew I had to learn to face situations like this, because they are part of my life, and also the darkness in my heart that I must eventually step out of.

In the classroom, sunlight filtered through the windows and cast dappled patterns of light and shadow across the desks. Our class was holding a group discussion, and the teacher had assigned us a topic about environmental protection. All around me was the hum of my classmates talking, along with the occasional burst of overlapping laughter. Sitting in the group, I felt somewhat out of place.

The student next to me was pouring out his ideas nonstop, his voice even drowning out the low buzz in the classroom. I tried to cut in and share my thoughts, but every time I spoke, he would interrupt me and continue with his discussion. A wave of unease began to rise in me, as though something were churning in my stomach.

“Maybe we could start by talking about reducing plastic use?” I finally found a gap to slip in a sentence.

“Yes, but I think we should focus more on reusing resources…” He immediately took over the topic and kept talking, as if my suggestion wasn’t even worth mentioning.

Did the way he said that mean my idea was really that bad? Self-doubt surged through me. I began to feel a little angry at his attitude, but more than that, I felt discouraged. I couldn’t help glancing sideways at the other students’ expressions, trying to find any sign of approval or disapproval of my suggestion in their faces. But they all seemed more interested in what he was saying.

My heartbeat quickened, and I could feel sweat in my palms. Every time I tried to speak again, it felt as if my throat were blocked. I didn’t dare interrupt him anymore, afraid I would be even more openly ignored or mocked. My thoughts spiraled: Did they all dislike me? Did they think everything I said was nonsense?

The bell rang, and the meeting ended. I quickly gathered my things and wanted to leave the classroom as soon as possible. On the way from the classroom to the hallway, I felt as though I were shrouded by an invisible shadow, unable to let go of the scene that had just played out, turning it over in my mind again and again.

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t stop thinking about the discussion. I kept replaying my classmates’ expressions and tone of voice, blaming myself over and over for not being more confident when I spoke. I even started to doubt my abilities, feeling that maybe, in my classmates’ eyes, I was just an unimportant presence.

The next day, I walked into the classroom still carrying those thoughts, silently deciding that in the future I would try my best to avoid joining such discussions again, because I couldn’t face another round of disappointment and being ignored.

Before the bonfire party began, my classmates and I sat in a circle on the grass, feeling the crisp autumn air. The firelight reflected on our faces, warm and gentle. Laughter and cheerful voices rose all around us, and someone was strumming a guitar, its music drifting through the night sky. I looked around, forcing a smile, but deep inside I felt a profound sense of loneliness and unease. “Why do I always feel like I don’t fit in?” I thought to myself.

Suddenly, Xiao Ming waved at me. “Come over! Everyone’s about to start telling jokes!” I walked over, trying to blend into the group. Xiao Ming told a joke about the teacher, and everyone burst into laughter. I laughed too, but I kept doubting whether my laugh sounded natural. My heart began to race, my palms started to sweat unconsciously, and I felt a slight stomachache—physical reactions that had been troubling me for a while. Thoughts kept creeping into my mind: “If they realize my laughter is fake, will they stop inviting me to events?” That frightening possibility would not leave me alone.

“What’s wrong? You seem a bit distracted,” a classmate beside me asked with concern. I shook my head as if it were nothing. “I’m fine, just thinking about some things.” In truth, I was thinking about how to avoid drawing their attention so I could feel at ease. Then Xiao Li began preparing to perform a little magic trick. Everyone gathered around excitedly, while I stood at the back, wanting to fit in yet afraid of losing myself.

After the party ended, I wandered home aimlessly, replaying the scene over and over in my mind. I felt as if I had been abandoned, even though no one had truly shown me any hostility. The night was dark and heavy, and I felt a trace of desolation. When I got home, I lay on my bed, trying to relax, but my mood never settled down. I kept overanalyzing my behavior at the party and worrying about how my classmates saw me. A few days later, I still felt anxious. Every time I met my classmates, I tried hard not to bring up what had happened that night, so as not to make the awkwardness worse.

Although I knew these worries had no real basis, my emotions still tugged at every nerve, leaving me unable to free myself from them.

The backstage lighting was dim, and the air was thick with the mingled scent of sweat and tension. I sat in a corner, gripping my sheet music tightly, my mind in chaos. From the stage came my classmates’ laughter and applause, as if reminding me of the performance soon to come. My heart pounded like a drum, sweat began to bead on my forehead, and it felt as though a small insect were writhing in my stomach.

“Little one, are you ready?” The teacher’s voice broke through my thoughts. I jerked my head up and forced myself to nod.

“You have to do your best, okay? Everyone’s looking forward to you.” She smiled and patted my shoulder, but I felt a wave of unease.

The moment I stepped onto the stage, the lights were blinding, making it almost impossible to keep my eyes open. I took a deep breath, and my fingers found the first note on the keys. The silence below the stage made me feel my own heartbeat even more clearly, like rolling thunder.

The performance began, and I tried hard to suppress my trembling hands. But halfway through, my fingertips suddenly slipped, and the notes came out in a jumbled mess that assaulted my ears. I heard whispers from the audience below, as if a bucket of cold water had been poured over me. My face flushed bright red, and all I wanted was to disappear at once.

“How could you mess it up like that!” After the performance, the leader of the girls’ group scolded me in a low voice backstage. “All our hard work was wasted, you know?”

“I’m sorry...” I murmured, my voice so soft I could barely hear it myself.

“It’s okay, everyone makes mistakes sometimes.” Another classmate comforted me gently, but what I felt was a sense of isolation, of not being understood. My heart raced, my palms were sweaty, and I wanted to flee this place.

That night, after I got home, I lay in bed tossing and turning, my mind replaying those embarrassing scenes over and over. The cramps in my stomach seemed impossible to ease. When I got up the next morning, my mood was still heavy, as if bound by invisible chains.

A few days later, when I faced those classmates again, I still couldn’t let it go, couldn’t face those sharp accusations and the gossip behind my back. I realized that my fear of rejection and isolation was not something that would easily fade, like a shadow forever wandering in my heart.

The classroom is always noisy. During breaks, almost all the students are chatting and laughing loudly. I tried to focus on organizing the notes I had just taken, when I suddenly heard a bright laugh behind me. Then someone called out, “Look at this, it’s so funny!” I turned around and found them staring at my desk, pointing at some small marks I had made with a blue highlighter.

“What’s wrong?” I asked, trying hard to keep my voice calm, though my stomach had already begun to tighten slightly. They exchanged glances, and one classmate said with a smile, “Nothing, your note-taking style is pretty special—kind of an artistic creation!” Though the smile looked friendly, I couldn’t hear any warmth in it; all I felt was a hidden malicious meaning behind the words.

“I just wrote them that way so they’d be easy to look at,” I hurried to explain, my voice carrying a trace of haste even I could hear. I forced myself to stay composed and lowered my head, flipping through my notes again, but their laughter kept echoing in my ears, almost like mockery. That phrase kept replaying in my mind: “An artistic creation!” Each word was like a small knife, carving tiny wounds into my heart.

My hand began to grip the highlighter nervously, and sweat slowly seeped into my palm, making it slightly slick. I noticed my heart beating faster and a slight heaviness in my chest. I tried to breathe in, but it felt as if the air were blocked in my throat. Suddenly I felt my face growing hot; maybe I was already blushing. I murmured softly, “Why are they always like this? Why is their laughter so harsh?” Then I started blaming myself: “Was I really not good enough? Are these marks really that childish?”

After the break ended, I realized I hadn’t absorbed any of the rest of the lesson at all. My mind was a tangled mess, filled with echoes of those conversations and their expressions. I kept rehearsing all kinds of possible scenarios in my head: What if they laughed at me again later? What if other classmates also thought my notes were strange? Those thoughts surged in like a tide, pressing down on me until I could barely breathe.

When I got home and packed up my schoolbag, I saw the notes again. My first reaction was to tear them up on the spot, but then I thought: if I did that, wouldn’t that be admitting I really was useless? I started flipping through the notes while using a red pen to circle my “flaws,” as if trying to find where exactly the problem was. The more I circled, the more upset I became, until I finally closed the notebook. There was a voice in my heart telling me, “Maybe next time don’t use a highlighter; switching to pencil would be safer.” But another voice was mocking me: “What a failure, brought down by just a few words.”

The next day in class, I chose to sit near the window, hoping to reduce that group of classmates’ attention. I felt a bit like someone avoiding a battlefield, yet at the same time I kept pushing myself inwardly: “Why can’t you just be tougher and fight back? Are you really that weak?”

The classroom lights were always a little harsh, the white fluorescent lamps bleaching the desktops into a blank glare. I sat in the back row, a thin layer of sweat beading in my palms. Today’s group activity had just been assigned, and I had been placed in a group, but the leader seemed somewhat hesitant about how to arrange me. As they discussed my task, I kept feeling a restless tension hanging in the air. The group leader stared at my worksheet for a while, then looked up and said to me, “Well... you can handle this part, right?” His tone sounded casual enough, but I suddenly felt there was some hidden meaning in it. Did he think I wouldn’t do well? Or did he simply not want me involved at all? I nodded and forced out, “Sure, no problem.” My voice sounded stiffer than I expected, as if I were deliberately trying to hide something.

From that moment on, I kept turning over that sentence in my mind: “right?” What did it mean? Was it doubting my ability? Or did he think I was only barely acceptable? My fingers kept tapping on the desktop, and I could feel my stomach starting to feel uncomfortable, twisted tight. The seats around me were quiet, with only the occasional chirp of birds drifting in from outside, and that silence made my own heartbeat sound especially clear.
