I recalled their tones and expressions, trying to find more clues to prove that my own judgment was correct, but the more I thought about it, the more I felt like a complete failure. I kept asking myself: Why does it turn out like this every time? Is there really something wrong with me?

The next day, I really didn’t want to face my groupmates again, but I still went to school, bracing myself. All morning, I avoided making eye contact with those few members, and even when answering their questions, I kept my voice very low. My mind was still replaying yesterday’s scenes, like an old movie that couldn’t be stopped.

Walking down the school hallway, I kept my gaze fixed ahead, my ears filled with the noise of students chatting after class. It wasn’t until I saw her—my former best friend—that the familiar wave of anxiety surged back. She was laughing and talking with a group of classmates, apparently not noticing me at all. Her laughter seemed magnified in my mind, as if every note were mocking me. My heart raced, and I could feel my palms starting to sweat.

“Hey,” I said as I walked up to her, filled with doubt and unease. She turned around, froze for a moment, then smiled. “You seem really busy lately. You hardly ever contact me anymore.” I tried to make my tone sound casual, but there was still a trace of blame in my voice. She clearly noticed it, and her smile stiffened instantly.

“Oh, I... schoolwork has been pretty busy,” she said, running a hand through her hair, her eyes shifting uneasily.

In that instant, the defenses in my heart collapsed. The feeling of being abandoned was so intense that I began to doubt whether every one of her actions and expressions was hinting that our friendship was already over. “Too busy to even reply to a message? Or do you just not care about our friendship anymore?” My voice trembled slightly, and I suddenly felt as though I were standing on the edge of a cliff.

Her expression gradually shifted from surprise to anger, and the curious glances of passersby fell on us. I felt even more pressure and humiliation. “It’s not like that! I just...” she tried to explain, but I could no longer listen. The torrent inside me swept away the little reason I had left, and I heard my own sharp voice echoing through the hallway.

For the next few minutes, we argued fiercely, her voice rising with her emotions as well. My face burned, my breathing quickened, and my stomach felt heavy, as if a huge stone had settled in it.

After the argument ended, I stood there frozen. The people in the hallway gradually dispersed, leaving only me alone, facing the empty corridor and the emptiness in my heart that I couldn’t shake. My heartbeat was still racing, my fingers trembling slightly as I tried to calm my agitated emotions.

That night, lying in bed, I tossed and turned, my mind replaying the argument from earlier over and over again. Regret and self-blame wrapped tightly around me like two enormous hands. I began to wonder whether I was really worthy of having friends, or whether I was simply a flawed person who always made a mess of everything.

A few days later, I tried to contact her and sent an apology, hoping to mend the relationship. Her reply was brief and distant, and it stung like I had lost a part of myself. That fear of abandonment surged back once again, and I realized that although I didn’t want to admit it, I was still deeply trapped in it.

I stood by the beverage vending machine in the gym, and the line was moving forward as slowly as a snail. My palms were a little sweaty. Sunlight slanted in through the windows, making the floor gleam, but it was heating up my back. I couldn’t help sneaking another glance toward the front of the line. Two girls were standing by the machine, chatting on their phones, not the least bit in a hurry to choose a drink. I felt as if a ball of fire were burning in my stomach, and my heartbeat seemed a few beats faster than before. I began weighing whether I should just walk over and remind them, but I was also afraid they’d roll their eyes or say something nasty.

“Could it get any slower?” I heard a boy behind me mutter softly. His voice wasn’t loud, but it was definitely clear enough. I turned my head slightly and caught him frowning, his eyes seeming to seek my agreement. I didn’t respond. I just lowered my head and pretended to check my wallet. Honestly, I had no desire to form some kind of “revolutionary friendship in the line” with a stranger, because I didn’t know whether it would turn into an argument.

At last it was my turn. I quickly pressed a few buttons and chose the orange juice I knew best, and then it felt as if a stone in my heart finally dropped away. The machine clicked, the orange juice fell into the slot, and when I reached for it, I realized my fingers were a little cold. I grabbed the drink and didn’t dare linger by the line, practically fleeing out of the gym, still feeling damp across my back.

Back in the classroom, I took a sip of the orange juice. It still tasted like the usual sweet-tart flavor, but this time it somehow seemed a little bitter going down. I kept replaying the boy’s expression in my head—did he think I should have said something too, to hurry the line along? Or did those girls think I was a coward, someone who didn’t dare stand up for her rights, because I stayed silent? These little thoughts tormented me until the evening self-study session ended, and only then did I start to feel a little less awful.

The next morning, when I passed the gym, I had a strange urge to take a detour, but then I felt that would be a bit unnecessary. I told myself that what happened yesterday was only a trivial matter—no one would remember it, and no one would care. But I still felt a faint uneasiness in my heart. In front of the gym entrance, I took a deep breath and hurried into the teaching building.

The classroom was filled with rustling sounds as the teacher wrote a math problem on the blackboard. I stared nervously at the podium, my palms starting to sweat. The teacher called my name and asked me to stand up and explain how to solve the problem. I tried hard to remember, but my mind was a mess. My heartbeat sounded like a drum, pounding through my body one beat after another. The eyes of the whole class were fixed on me, and an invisible pressure hung in the air. I could hear the soft snickering of the students in the front row. “Go on, say it,” the teacher urged. My lips were dry, and my voice was weak and unsteady: “I... I don’t know.” At that moment, the classroom was so silent it felt suffocating, and the muffled laughter that followed stabbed into my heart like needles.

“How embarrassing,” I blamed myself inwardly, my cheeks burning as if all the heat in my body had gathered there. I sat down in a panic, head lowered, not daring to look at anyone again. Every second dragged on so slowly, and my stomach felt knotted, with a dull ache spreading through it.

When the bell for class dismissal rang, I hurriedly packed my bag, wanting to escape that suffocating place. In the hallway, my steps were quick, but an inner voice kept echoing: “Why am I always so useless? They must all be laughing at me.” I couldn’t help but think back to all the similar situations in the past; every mistake felt like a new wound carved into my heart. I felt utterly ashamed and frustrated, as if I had been abandoned alone on a deserted island.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to fall asleep. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw the classmates’ mocking laughter and the teacher’s disappointed gaze. The next day, I delayed going to school for a long time, afraid of facing them again. I rehearsed countless times in my mind the scene of myself being laughed at, and the more I thought about it, the more hopeless I felt.

After a few days, I began avoiding speaking in class. I often pretended I was taking notes, while deliberately avoiding eye contact with the teacher and my classmates. At night, I stood in front of the mirror practicing over and over, trying to improve the way I spoke, but the fear and shame in my heart never truly faded.

The classroom lights were a little dim and yellowish, and the glass by the window was coated with moisture, faintly reflecting the darkening sky outside. The debate competition was starting in half an hour, and my group members and I were gathered around a table near the front, urgently discussing the final points of our speeches. The air was thick with the smell of draft paper, and everyone’s discussion mixed with the low murmurs of other groups nearby, making the classroom feel slightly noisy.

“We need to make our position clear, or the audience will think our response is weak!” said the boy sitting next to me in a somewhat louder voice. His tone sounded a little rushed, as if he were subtly blaming someone for not preparing enough. I lowered my head and looked at the draft on my desk, a wave of unease rising in me. I kept feeling that his tone was directed at me. “Does he think I missed something important again? Do they all think I’m not capable enough?” In my mind, I immediately replayed the previous few meetings. I remembered them seeming to frown at some of my suggestions, and now that I thought about it, maybe they had been thinking I wasn’t professional enough.

“What do you think?” another girl sitting in front turned to ask me. I jerked my head up and found everyone’s eyes on me. My heart sped up, the tips of my ears grew hot, and my palms began to sweat, yet my mind was blank. The air felt thick, and breathing became difficult. Feeling guilty and uncertain, I lowered my voice and replied, “I think... maybe... we could start with the relevant data.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I regretted them. How worthless that sounded! My face felt like a furnace, and I no longer dared meet anyone’s gaze, staring instead at the pen on the desk.

“Yes, data is important.” Another girl nodded and added, “We can first list the supporting evidence, then summarize it into a strong conclusion.” Her voice was very calm, but I still felt a chill. Was she saying that just to ease my embarrassment? Why wasn’t anyone else speaking up? Were they silently thinking I was terrible? I tried hard to steady my breathing, but my stomach had already started to cramp, and I could only press it gently with my hand.

The discussion continued, and I felt myself gradually being pushed to the edge. The voice in my head grew louder and louder: “What I just said was really childish, wasn’t it? Was it not going to be taken seriously at all? They all think I’m a burden, don’t they?” I even began to suspect they might directly have someone else speak in my place. The tension in my body grew stronger and stronger; my shoulders and neck felt as if they had been tied up, and my fingers unconsciously tightened around the pen.

In the end, the discussion was over, and I didn’t even speak once more. Everyone split up to prepare their own parts, and I walked to the window to calm myself down. The cold glass touched my fingers, as if offering a slight comfort. I stared at the dark, heavy sky outside, filled with self-blame and shame. During the competition, I performed at the bare minimum, trying hard to control my speaking pace and expression, yet I felt my clumsy voice squeezing out of my throat, every word seeming to be put on trial. After the competition, I didn’t even dare make small talk; I hurriedly packed up my things and left.

After I got home, I lay on my bed, unable to stop my thoughts. My mind replayed every detail like a movie, obsessing over whether I had dragged down everyone’s efforts. I clearly could have answered the other side’s questions much better, but there was nothing I could do to change it now. My stomach still ached dully from time to time, so I curled up under the blanket, hoping to fall asleep as soon as possible and forget all of it, but the boy’s urgent voice still echoed in my head, lingering long after.

I stood on the stage in the school auditorium, looking out at the densely packed students below, so nervous I could almost suffocate. The lights shone down from above, illuminating every glance with piercing clarity. I could hear quiet conversations and a few soft laughs by my ears, and a wave of fear of being mocked surged through me. My palms began to sweat, my throat went dry, as if an invisible hand were tightly gripping it. “I won’t mess this up. They won’t laugh at me,” I kept telling myself, hoping to calm the anxiety flooding in.

“Come on, you can do it,” a classmate beside me said softly. I nodded, but the unease in my heart only grew stronger. I began to wonder whether he was truly encouraging me or just being perfunctory. When it was my turn to speak, I could hear my heartbeat quickening. I stiffly walked up to the microphone, my fingers unconsciously clutching the script. The words I had not yet spoken kept turning over in my mind, as if I could already foresee myself mispronouncing every single one. I tried to swallow, then finally began. “Hello everyone, today I want to share with you...” I tried to keep my voice steady, but there were still a few moments when it trembled slightly.

By the third paragraph, I felt a sharp cramp in my stomach, like a clenched fist striking me hard. A thought even flashed through my mind: “What would happen if I fainted here?” and the situation instantly felt a little out of control. My lips began to tremble, as if confirming my inner doubts about my own ability. I heard my voice catch for a second or two, and immediately a wave of self-attack surged through my mind: “How can you be so useless? Everyone is watching you make a fool of yourself.” At that moment, a teacher below the stage gently said, “It’s okay, take your time.” I nodded slightly and did my best to keep going.

After the speech ended, I walked off the stage stiffly, my mind filled with embarrassment and regret. I hardly dared look anyone in the eye, afraid I would see disappointment or ridicule. The whole afternoon, I was immersed in my own inner monologue, repeatedly reviewing every detail of the speech. That night, lying in bed, I was still overwhelmed by feelings of failure and shame, my mind full of the faint laughter from below the stage and the students’ gazes. When I woke up the next day, I decided to go to my teacher first thing in the morning to confirm whether he was truly not angry, and to ask whether he had any criticism of my performance. I found that I was always seeking affirmation from others to dispel my inner self-doubt; even a mild word of comfort could make me catch a glimmer of security.

The moment the test tube hit the floor, it felt as if my brain had been hit with a pause button. Glass shards scattered everywhere, flashing with a cold light, and my hand was still frozen in midair. The tongs I had been holding the test tube with suddenly felt impossibly heavy. I heard a brief gasp from the classmates around me, then the sound of chairs scraping back, followed quickly by the teacher’s voice: “Be careful, there’s broken glass over there!” It carried a note of urgency and warning. I nodded mechanically, my heart already pounding so fast it felt like it might burst through my chest. My face burned in waves, as if every gaze around me were piercing into my back.

“Are you okay? Did you cut your hand?” A girl came closer, her tone much gentler. I think she was only being polite. But I couldn’t help imagining that she was mocking me in her head for not even being able to handle a simple lab procedure. “I’m fine.” My voice was as dry as a wind blowing out of the desert. I lowered my head, trying hard to avoid everyone’s eyes. The glass shards on the floor seemed to be accusing me of my clumsiness, and my stomach began to twist with a dull ache.

The teacher brought over a broom and dustpan and didn’t say much more, only quietly saying, “Don’t move so fast next time.” That reminder stabbed into my heart like a needle. I nodded desperately and hurried to help clean up the fragments, but my fingers trembled so badly on the tongs that I could barely control them. I knew that in truth no one was really paying that much attention to me, but in my mind it was as if a concert had started, with every negative comment shouting at full volume: “How can you be so useless?” “Everyone’s watching you make a fool of yourself!” “Who would still want to be in a group with you after this?” The voices grew louder and louder, almost crushing me.

The faint smell of disinfectant in the lab had once made me feel safe, but now it felt pungent and suffocating. I heard classmates nearby whispering, “Wow, it dropped the moment they touched it.” “Maybe the tongs weren’t held steady?” Their tone carried no malice, but I still felt as if each word were a heavy blow landing on my chest. I tried to pretend I was focused on the equipment on the table, tried to pretend I couldn’t hear them, but my hearing had become terrifyingly sharp. Even the slightest snicker felt magnified tenfold. I began to feel sweat all over my body, and my palms were so slippery I could barely hold the tongs.

That night I sat alone in my room, replaying the scene of the test tube falling over and over in my head, like an old film reel stuck on repeat. I could even hear the sound of the glass shattering again and again—the sharp cracking sound of something bursting from within—which once more tightened my stomach into a knot. I imagined myself walking into the lab the next day, and wondered whether the teacher would look at me with disappointment. If something like this happened again, would people really laugh out loud this time? My mind felt trapped in an endless pit; every attempt to climb out became another round of attacks against myself. I wondered if I would never be able to do these things properly.

A few days passed, and I avoided alltake the initiative socializing, spending even the breaks sitting at my desk in a daze. I tried my best to ignore my classmates’ greetings because I was afraid they would bring up what happened in the lab. Even when they didn’t, I still couldn’t stop stealing glances at their expressions, trying to find any possible hint—was someone still talking about how clumsy I was? But in reality, the “attention” toward me had long since disappeared from their minds, and those malicious stares were nothing more than the phantoms conjured by my own inner demons.

Outside the window, the sky was overcast and gray. Fine raindrops struck the glass, leaving long streaks of water behind. The classroom lights were a bit harsh, reflecting off the desks in a pale, glaring white. I sat at one end of the long table, frantically sorting through the papers in front of me. The air was filled with my classmates’ laughter and discussion, each syllable piercing my ears like needles. I tried hard to focus on the materials, but the sweat on my palms made it impossible to hold my pen steady.

“Next, please come to the front and put on the microphone to prepare your speech.” The judges’ teacher’s voice came from the podium. As soon as I heard it, it felt like I’d been whipped by a sharp voice, and I couldn’t help straightening my back. It was my turn. When I stood up, I could clearly feel my legs were stiff, my steps unsteady, like I was walking on cotton.

The few seconds it took to walk to the podium seemed stretched out infinitely. I could feel everyone’s gaze burning against me, my back feeling as if it had been scorched by a hot iron. I told myself to keep looking straight ahead, but low snickers kept drifting into my ears, as if they were aimed at me. Had someone already criticized my posture for not seeming confident enough? Or did they think I was dressed too casually today? I unconsciously tugged at my hem, only to feel even more awkward all over.

Standing in the center of the podium, I gripped the microphone tightly, my fingers trembling slightly from the force. But the first sentence I spoke came out with a faint quiver. This was bad. I shouldn’t be like this, my mind raced. My gaze inadvertently swept across the judges’ faces; one teacher was lowering his head to take notes, and the corner of his mouth seemed to curl slightly. Had my opening been too plain, making him think I wasn’t professional enough? In an instant, countless scenes flashed through my mind: the judges complaining over tea about some contestant’s poor performance in this selection round, everyone exchanging knowing smiles when that person’s name was mentioned, and me becoming the butt of the joke.

My stomach clenched, and I hurriedly adjusted my breathing. “Next, I’d like to analyze three important aspects of this debate topic.” I went on, but suddenly realized I couldn’t remember one section of my argument no matter how hard I tried. I had clearly recited it countless times just back in my seat—how had it evaporated now? I could feel the judges’ gaze sliding over my shoulder. I looked up instinctively and saw another judge raise an eyebrow. He’s dissatisfied with me, I concluded quickly. It was as if a bucket of cold water had been splashed onto my face; my whole body went cold, but sweat had already started beading on my back. My clothes clung to my skin, wet and sticky.

“So, my point is this…” My voice involuntarily rose, only to tremble at the end. I hurriedly finished my speech, even forgetting the closing remarks I was supposed to say, and then lowered my head and quickly walked back to my seat. Sparse applause sounded here and there, and I felt as if I were in a dream, the sound distant and dim. The moment I sat down, my limbs went weak, yet my heart was pounding so hard it felt like it might burst.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed the afternoon scene over and over in my head. Why had my opening been so flat? Did the judges’ expressions mean I had lost my chance? If I had prepared a little more thoroughly, would everything have been different? It felt as if a stone were pressing on my chest, and the more I thought about it, the harder it was to breathe. I tossed and turned, unable to sleep until after midnight. When I woke the next day, my eyelids were badly swollen, but my thoughts were still stuck in the unfinished rumination from the day before.

During the break, we sat in the classroom. The group discussion had just ended, and I was feeling anxious. Around me was a noisy buzz—desks and chairs scraping, a few people laughing and chatting about something—but all my attention was on the discussion we’d just had. I held a pen and drew circles on my scratch paper, yet my mind kept replaying the same fragments over and over: what I said, their expressions, their tone of voice. When the group leader wrapped up at the end, he glanced at me and simply said, “Mm, not bad.” I nodded and smiled at the time, but doubts filled my mind. What did he mean by that? Was he just brushing me off, or was it genuine approval? Was there something cold in his eyes? Did he think I performed terribly? 

My palms were already a little damp, and the pen pressed harder and harder against the paper. I started reviewing my performance frame by frame, like an interrogation video. Was I speaking too quickly? Was my voice a little shaky? I clearly thought I had prepared for a long time, but suddenly I began to wonder whether the examples I chose were too ordinary. I started to regret not picking a more impactful story. Why didn’t they respond to my joke? Or was I never supposed to say those lighthearted things in the first place? Was that person’s tone really just “not bad”? Was it praise, or criticism? 

“What are you spacing out for?” A student from the neighboring group tapped my desk and pulled me back from my thoughts. I looked up and forced a smile. “Nothing, just doodling.” He said, “You did pretty well just now.” I nodded quickly, but I didn’t quite buy it. Why did he say “pretty well” instead of “great”? Did “pretty well” actually mean just so-so? Was he only trying to comfort me? I even started to suspect that maybe he thought I talked too much, so he deliberately said something nice to brush me off.

My stomach started to feel a little unsettled, as if a stone had been shoved inside. I didn’t want to talk to anyone anymore, so I lowered my head and kept drawing circles. At that moment, I didn’t even know what I was drawing—I just needed something to do to escape the doubts flooding into my head. When I spun my pen, my fingers were damp, and I felt an indescribable sense of suffocation, as if someone were standing beside me, staring at me and smiling the whole time.

A few days later, those memories would still resurface. Sometimes when I was washing my face, or when I saw the group leader walk past in the hallway, I would involuntarily start thinking about that discussion again. How exactly had he judged me? If I had been less impulsive and spoken in a more composed way, would I have earned more recognition? But I knew I shouldn’t keep dwelling on such a small thing, so I kept telling myself that “not bad” might really have been nothing more than an ordinary comment, with no deeper meaning at all. Those words calmed me a little, but my mind would still drift back from time to time, as if trapped in a vague memory.

I walked into the school science lab. The cold, gloomy weather outside seeped in through the windows, and the air was filled with a faint smell of disinfectant. I took a deep breath and silently cheered myself on. The lab tables were covered with all kinds of equipment, and the teacher was explaining today’s experiment up front, with the sound of the cold wind howling constantly outside as background noise. I stared at the teacher’s lips, trying hard to keep up with every word, but my mind kept flashing with scenes of what might go wrong.

The child sitting next to me gently nudged me. “Hey, are you okay?” I nodded, trying to appear calm, but my heartbeat was silently speeding up, and my palms were sweating. I was always afraid I would make a mistake and then be publicly called out by everyone, so I often harshly criticized myself several times beforehand in my mind. The teacher handed out some reagents, and I took them carefully, my fingers trembling slightly, my gaze falling on the transparent liquid. I wiped the sweat from my forehead with the back of my hand, trying to make myself look more normal.

After the experiment began, everyone around me seemed so confident, carrying out each step with ease. When I used the dropper to draw up the reagent, I could feel the stiffness in my fingers and the uncontrollable trembling, as if any mistake could lead to serious consequences. “Don’t make a mistake, don’t make a mistake,” I kept telling myself over and over. Suddenly, a little liquid splashed out of the mouth of the reagent bottle and landed on the lab table. I froze instantly, my heart pounding wildly.

“Be careful, it’s okay,” a classmate reminded me at just the right moment. I forced out a smile, but shame and panic surged through me. I felt a dull ache in my stomach, as if all those emotions had erupted in this tiny mistake. For the rest of the time, I was especially careful with every step, afraid of making another mistake.

When the experiment was over, I put away the equipment, trying not to look too embarrassed. As I left the lab, the wind outside was still bitterly cold, and I shoved my hands into my coat pockets, trying to find some warmth. That night, lying in bed, I replayed every detail in my mind, repeatedly blaming myself for not being able to perform better. A few days later, I still kept thinking back to that moment of embarrassment and fear, feeling as though I always did my worst when it mattered most.

Even in conversations with friends, I would sometimes recall the scene in the lab, with a faint sense of self-reproach weighing on my heart. I realized that my fear of failure and rejection was so strong that every small mistake was magnified into a disaster in my mind, becoming a shadow I could not escape.

Today the kindergarten’s little playground was covered in green everywhere. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the leaves, and the dappled light and shadows on the ground swayed gently with the wind. My palms were sticky and still had a little sand on them. We were building a tiny castle woven out of blades of grass. Suddenly, while picking up a very long branch, a little classmate pushed me, and my elbow slammed hard into the gritty ground. I immediately felt a sharp sting. “Ouch, what are you doing!” I cried out loudly, my voice a little shaky. She stopped, froze for a moment, then chuckled and said, “Sorry, I didn’t mean it.” I lifted my arm and saw a red scratch had already appeared on it, and I felt terribly wronged. My mind churned with suspicion: had she done it on purpose? Did she not like me? But there was no malicious look on her face.

I pouted, refusing to talk to her out of spite, and grumbled to myself: maybe I should go somewhere else and play with other kids? But then I thought, if I left, maybe no one would keep building this pretty castle with me.

At that moment, I felt my heart beating a little faster, my face was getting warm, and my palms were sweaty too. Then the teacher came over and asked me softly, “Are you uncomfortable anywhere, little one?” I said quietly, “I hurt my hand.” The teacher examined my elbow carefully, touched it gently, and said, “It’s okay, it didn’t break the skin. It’s just a little red; it’ll be fine after a while.”

I nodded, looking at the teacher’s calm face, and felt a little better. After she left, I hesitantly said to that child, “I’m not angry, it just hurts a little.” She nodded and said, “Then let’s keep playing.”

When we left kindergarten in the afternoon, it had started to rain. The raindrops hit the ground with a pattering sound. I looked out the window and saw that the place where we had just played in the sand was already pooling with water. Leaning back in my seat, I felt that what had happened today might not have been such a big deal after all. That night, lying in bed, I touched my elbow, and the redness and swelling had already gone down. I thought that perhaps she really hadn’t meant it. Maybe everyone has moments of carelessness; it was just that at the time it felt hard to get over, and I felt a bit sulky inside.

The next day when I arrived at kindergarten, that child greeted me again, as if nothing had happened. My heart felt warm, and I thought that this friendly little episode perhaps didn’t really count after all.

In the kindergarten hall, the teachers were handing out craft materials. I stood in line, feeling the excitement and chatter of the children around me. In the distance, sunlight streamed in through the window, casting bright patches on the floor, and the air was filled with a faint smell of paper and glue. The teacher smiled and said, “Come on, kids, today we’re going to make a little house with our own hands.”

I received a pair of scissors, several sheets of colored paper, and a bottle of glue, then sat down on the floor and started working. The voices of the children around me rose and fell: “Poke you!” “Look at mine!” I felt a little nervous, and my palms began to sweat slightly. My heartbeat seemed faster than usual, thumping like a little drum, and I was afraid I would do a bad job and be laughed at by the other children.

“Are you going to use this color?” a child beside me asked, leaning over. I nodded, but I didn’t dare look at him, afraid of reading some bad hint from his eyes. I began to cut the paper carefully, my fingers trembling a little, and the glue on my fingertips felt sticky.

Various worst-case scenarios kept replaying in my mind: what if my house turned out crooked, and the teacher called me to the front to demonstrate? Or what if someone said the colors I chose didn’t look good together? These thoughts made my stomach feel heavy, as if it were filled with stones. I tried hard to concentrate, but I found myself constantly thinking the wrong way.

After the activity ended, the teacher asked everyone to place the little houses they had made on the table for display. I set my little house at the edge of the table, my heart beating even faster, feeling as if someone might point out my mistakes at any moment. “Your house has such interesting colors!” the teacher praised with a smile. Only then did I feel a little relieved, but the uneasiness in my heart still would not completely fade.

That night, I told my mother at home about the little house I had made in kindergarten, and she praised me for being very creative. Although I felt somewhat comforted, I still couldn’t help reflecting, thinking about how I could do better, worried that I would have to face similar challenges again the next day. Lying in bed, I watched the moonlight spill in through the curtains outside the window, and my mood calmed down a little, but I still hoped I could care less about what others thought of me.

The walls of the stairwell felt a little cold, and the patter of raindrops could still be heard overhead. The window was half open, and a few drops of water splashed onto the back of my hand, so cold it made me shiver. I crouched in the corner, hugging my knees, trying hard to steady my breathing and keep my sobs quiet, afraid that a teacher or classmate passing by would hear me. What had just happened kept replaying in my head over and over—the split second when I slipped, the harsh sound of my shoe sole against the floor, and the way I fell to the ground, the icy feel of the floor and how everything around me suddenly went quiet. I could feel everyone looking at me. Were they laughing? Someone must have been laughing! I didn’t dare look up, only heard someone ask, “Are you okay?” but there were more murmurs, as if they were talking about me.

“Why did I slip? I was being so careful going downstairs!” I tried to reconstruct every detail in my mind. Was there water on one of the steps? Or had I been walking too fast? No, I heard laughter—they must have been laughing at how clumsy I was! My eyes stung a little, my nose started to sting too, and tears came falling down before I could stop them. I tried to wipe my eyes with the back of my hand, but the more I wiped, the blurrier everything became, and my nose started running too. All I could do was curl up tighter and bury my face in my knees.

“If someone comes by and sees me crying here, they’ll definitely think I’m so embarrassing, right? What will they say then? Will they tell the other students?” The more I thought about it, the more afraid I became. My heart beat faster and faster, and my throat tightened as if I had swallowed a huge rock. I clenched my fists, my nails digging into my palms, trying to use the pain to calm myself down. The stairwell smelled a little strange, like damp floors that had been mopped and still weren’t completely dry. I could hear footsteps upstairs, and from the classroom next door someone called out, “Teacher,” the word drawn out.

“No, I can’t let anyone see me. If someone sees me crying here, it’ll be even more humiliating.” I sniffled hard, wiped away my tears, took a deep breath, and stood up. I put my hand on the railing, wondering whether I should just run straight back to class. But at the thought of walking in and possibly running into the classmates who had seen me fall, my feet seemed to freeze on the spot.

After a while, the stairwell grew quieter and quieter, with only the rain still tapping on the window intermittently. I gathered my courage and slowly walked back to the classroom, my palms still sweaty, my fingers even a little sticky. When I pushed the door open, hardly anyone in the classroom paid attention to me. Only one boy casually asked, “Hey, why did you take so long?” I pretended not to hear him and walked straight back to my seat with my head down. Was he laughing at me too? Was he still telling others about the way I had just fallen?

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t help thinking about that moment. Every time I closed my eyes, the sound of the fall and my classmates’ gazes came back to me. I turned over, pulled the blanket tighter around me, and my heart began to beat fast and hard again—were those whispers really about me?

The kitchen was filled with the sweet scent of vanilla. I stood on a stool, looking down at the cake ingredients on the table. My mother stood beside me, smiling as she handed me an egg and let me try to crack it. Sunlight poured through the window and fell on us, making the kitchen feel especially bright. Carefully, I picked up the egg and tapped it lightly against the edge of the bowl, hoping it would crack without shattering into a mess like last time. Just then, my mother reminded me from the side, “Be careful, take it slow.” Her voice was gentle and encouraging. But I could feel the egg slipping restlessly in my hand, and a wave of nervousness suddenly rose in me. My palms began to sweat. What happened next was too fast: with a crack, the egg burst in my hands, and the egg white and yolk splattered all over the table, leaving a terrible mess. My heart sank at once. Why am I always so bad at these little things? My mother quickly handed me some tissues and said with a smile, “It’s okay, we still have lots of eggs. Just try again.” My cheeks burned, and my heartbeat quickened, as if everyone in the kitchen were watching me, even though only my mother was there. I hurriedly wiped the table clean, my eyes a little wet, trying not to let my mother see. I lowered my head and thought: Why do I always mess up these little things? At that moment, my mother gently patted my shoulder. “Don’t worry, this is part of the learning process.” Hearing her comforting words, I felt a little better. Later, I finally managed to crack an egg successfully; the yolk lay obediently in the bowl, intact and unbroken. At that moment, I let out a long sigh, and my whole body seemed to relax. A few days later, during lunchtime at school, I talked with my friends about making a cake, and they all said they wanted to try it. My mood brightened, and I realized that making a cake was actually quite fun. Although I was nervous at the beginning, I had learned something in the end.

The sunlight outside the classroom window was blinding. I held a book up to my face, but I could still feel the heat baking my shoulders. The Chinese teacher stood at the front of the platform, holding a thick storybook, talking about a scene in which an adult conversed with a monster. My heart was pounding. One hand was secretly gripping the edge of my desk, while the other was raised high, almost pressed against my face. I knew the answer. I knew the monster had agreed to the adult’s terms. I had already been putting my thoughts into words in my head, imagining how I would say them clearly and earn praise. This would have been the most rewarding moment of my day. But the teacher’s gaze swept across the classroom and didn’t land on me. “Xiaoming, tell us—what happens next?” She called on the classmate behind me.

My arm froze in midair, and my heart dropped into my stomach, as if it had tumbled around in panic a couple of times.

I slowly lowered my hand and pretended to keep listening, but I couldn’t make out a word of what Xiaoming was saying. I stared at the cover of my textbook in my hands and pressed it against my face again, as if that could hide me. Why didn’t she choose me? Was my hand-raising posture too strange? Or did the teacher think what I was going to say wasn’t interesting enough? Did she simply not want to let me speak? My eyes started to sting, and there was a lump blocking my throat. Don’t cry, don’t cry. I lightly pressed the edge of the book against my nose and sniffed, my palms already soaked with sweat.

My deskmate suddenly nudged my arm and asked me in a low voice, “What’s wrong? You were raising your hand so hard just now, and she still didn’t pick you?” I froze for a moment and forced a casual look: “It’s nothing. Maybe she didn’t see me.” But my voice came out so soft that hardly anyone could hear it. Feeling my deskmate’s eyes still on me, I pulled the book down a little more to cover my face, not wanting him to keep staring.

After the story ended, the teacher told us to copy sentences on our own. I shrank back behind my desk, and the pencil in my hand kept writing wrong characters. Every time I made a mistake, I couldn’t help cursing myself for being stupid in my heart. I even secretly pinched my palm with my fingernails, hoping it would help me focus. But that scene from earlier kept replaying in my mind: my raised hand ignored by everyone, even noticed by my deskmate. Was I acting too hard, too eager? Maybe the teacher deliberately ignored me because she thought I looked ridiculous.

When the bell rang, I was still staring at the words in my notebook, with no desire at all to go out and play. My mind started replaying what had just happened again, like an endless movie on loop that I couldn’t stop. The shouts and laughter of my classmates outside the window only made my stomach begin to ache faintly, as if someone were stirring it little by little with a small spoon. On the way home, I kept thinking about it over and over—wondering whether I had done something wrong, whether the teacher had a problem with me, whether my deskmate would tell others about my embarrassing performance. I didn’t want people to think I was trying too hard, yet I also couldn’t control my excitement and anticipation every time I had a chance to speak.

That night, lying on my bed, I couldn’t help turning the events of the day over and over in my mind. Tears quietly soaked into the pillow, giving off a damp, warm smell. I secretly resolved that if I had another chance tomorrow, I definitely wouldn’t rush to raise my hand again. But then I thought: if I got too scared to raise my hand again, would everyone think I was useless? My mind was like a tangled ball of yarn, impossible to sort out no matter how I thought about it.

The sky was a bright blue, and sunlight filtered through the leaves, casting dappled patches of light and shadow. I stood on the path in the neighborhood park, playing hide-and-seek with a few little kids. We decided to take turns being the one who searched, and I always hoped to be the seeker rather than the one hiding.

“I’ll count to ten, so hurry and hide!” My voice, carried along by my excitement, rose a little louder.

As the numbers climbed one by one, my heartbeat grew faster too. My palms were slightly sweaty, and this feeling of nervousness and excitement made me both look forward to it and feel a little flustered. After counting to ten, I opened my eyes and started looking around. The area was filled with children’s laughter and the rustling sound of running feet.

A light breeze blew by, and the leaves made a soft rustling sound. I walked carefully along the path. Suddenly, I noticed some movement behind a bush. A little boy was hiding there, and I quickly ran over and shouted, “I found you!” He laughed and ran off. I chased after him, but accidentally tripped and fell to the ground, a sharp pain shooting through my knee.

“Are you okay?” A little girl stopped, crouched beside me, and spoke with concern.

“I’m fine.” I held back my tears and stood up, but a voice in my heart kept saying, “How could you be so clumsy? Everyone saw you fall.”

A wave of shame rose from deep inside me, as if everyone was staring at me, judging my mistake. Even though they continued the game, I was no longer as happy. All I could think about was hiding well so I wouldn’t be found.

When it was my turn to hide, I chose a very concealed spot and squeezed into a small clump of bushes, where there was the damp smell of earth. The branches were a little rough against my arms, and I tried hard to stay still, my breathing slowing and becoming cautious. Time passed second by second, and the sound of my heartbeat seemed to reverberate in my ears, as if everyone had forgotten about me. Suddenly, a fear of being left behind surged up, and I began to think, “Did they all leave and abandon me here?”

“Hey, where are you?” I heard the children calling from far away, but I didn’t answer. My anxiety grew heavier and heavier, and tears began to stream down my face.

“Here!” I finally shouted, rushing out of the bushes. My nose stung, and I threw myself into an auntie’s arms. She gently patted me and said, “It’s okay, it’s just a game.”

That night, back home, I lay in bed, my heart still uneasy from what had happened during the day. Although my parents spent a long time talking with me and comforting me, saying it was only a game, the feeling of being forgotten and the anxiety lingered for a long time. For several days afterward, I kept wondering whether next time I should run out faster, or choose not to play this kind of game that so easily made me panic.

When the puzzle competition began, I stared at the pieces on the table, trying to find the edge pieces, but the more I looked, the more I felt they simply didn’t fit. My palms were slightly sweaty; every time I picked up a piece, my fingers felt cold and slippery, and I dropped pieces twice. I heard my deskmate beside me say, “Can you go a little faster?” His tone was flat, but in my mind a voice exploded: “He must think I’m so stupid! Everyone is watching me, thinking I’m the fool in this competition!” I stared at his expressionless face, desperately trying to find some trace of approval in his eyes, but his gaze simply swept calmly over me and the tabletop.

My ears started to burn, and the sounds around me flooded into my head like a deluge—the teacher’s footsteps back and forth, other people’s whispers, the soft clatter of puzzle pieces hitting the table—everything became harsh and unbearable. I clenched my fists hard, trying to focus, pressing the corner of a piece with my fingertips, but it still wouldn’t slot into place. I tried several times, and each time I got stuck, the sweat in my palms grew worse.

My deskmate sighed and said, “Give it to me. I’ll help you do the border.” I froze, pushed the pieces toward him, and struggled to hold back the guilt rising in my throat. “I can do it myself…” I said softly, but he replied, “Let me finish the border first and then give it back to you. That’ll make it easier.” He worked on it with concentration, while I could only sit there staring at the table, my eyes stinging, my head buzzing, as if I were waiting for some unavoidable verdict.

After the competition ended, he returned the puzzle with the border completed. I wanted to smile and thank him, but my mouth felt stiff, and I could only say in a low voice, “Thank you…” He nodded and said nothing more. The bell from the school building rang, and I felt as though I were trapped in an invisible pincer, my shoulders tight, a dull ache in my stomach. I put the puzzle back into the box, carefully avoiding letting others see my movements, because I felt I still wasn’t nimble enough, and that would only prove my failure.

After I got home, I didn’t dare tell my family about the competition for a long time, and only said, “I didn’t do well in the puzzle competition today.” My mom nodded and asked, “Do you want to practice more on your own next time?” Hearing that, my heartbeat sped up again, as if something vulnerable and shameful had been struck. I didn’t answer, and just walked back to my room with my head down, staring for a long, long time at the puzzle box on my desk, while in my mind the deskmate’s sigh and the slippery feel of my sweaty hands kept echoing. The whole evening, I kept thinking about that line, “Can you go a little faster?” Even after the sun rose the next day, I still felt that sentence was reminding me that I wasn’t good enough, not smart enough.

The warm autumn sunlight spilled over my face, and the park was covered with golden fallen leaves. I sat on a swing, with a few friends beside me, chasing and laughing nearby. The swing rocked gently, and I could feel the breeze brushing across my cheeks, bringing a hint of coolness. In the distance, Mom and the other adults were chatting on a bench. She would glance over here from time to time. Though I couldn’t hear their words, I knew they were talking and laughing happily.

“Push me higher!” I heard one of my friends call from the side, signaling for the swing to be pushed. I dug my feet into the ground, trying hard to make the swing arc higher. Suddenly I felt a little nervous, but even more excited. As the swing swayed, I could see the view changing constantly—sometimes blue sky and white clouds, sometimes grass and trees. My mood rose and fell with the rhythm of the swing, as if I were about to fly.

“Let’s go play by the slide!” one of my friends suggested loudly. We all jumped down from the swing and ran toward the slide, our legs a little weak. The slide gleamed in the sunlight, as if inviting us. I touched its surface; it was a bit cool. The slope looked rather steep, but I still couldn’t resist climbing up. The other friends waited below, urging me on from time to time.

Sitting at the top of the slide, I took a deep breath and then slid down. A wave of nervousness rose in my stomach, but it was swept away by the rush of wind as I descended, leaving only a smile on my lips. At the bottom, my feet felt the softness of the grass. I turned around and saw my friends applauding me, and I felt a little shy.

Lying on the grass, I felt the sunlight spill over me, heard the rustling of leaves stirred by the wind, and the birdsong coming from afar. I didn’t know how long it had been since I had felt so relaxed, thinking of nothing, my heart full of simple happiness. After a while, Mom came over to call us home. She said softly, “It’s getting late. Say goodbye to your friends.”

“Goodbye. Can we come again tomorrow?” I asked reluctantly. Mom nodded, smiling as she took my hand, and I could feel the warmth of her palm.

That night, lying in bed, swings, slides, and my friends’ smiling faces kept flashing through my mind. I thought that tomorrow would bring even more games and adventures waiting for me.

When I was eating lunch, I had deliberately brought apple slices that my mom had cut for me and put them in a small plastic container. After I opened the lid, a sweet apple scent drifted out, and I especially loved that smell. Sitting next to me was my deskmate, who always brought a plain sandwich and a bottle of milk. She glanced at my apple slices and held her gaze there for a few seconds. I immediately felt a kind of tension, as if someone had noticed a secret of mine. She asked, “Can you share some with me? They look really good.” I froze for a moment, and my mind suddenly started calculating whether I had enough apple slices, whether I would be hungry in the afternoon, and whether I should refuse her. I looked down at the container; there were about ten slices left, but I felt like my stomach needed them even more urgently than I did.

Out loud, I said, “Okay, you can have one slice.” At the same time, I was already regretting it, feeling that this decision might leave me hungry, or even make my mom think I had wasted her effort. I pushed the container toward her a little. She took a slice, bit into it, and said with a smile, “It’s really delicious, thank you!” I felt a complicated mix of emotions, a little pride because my apple slices had been appreciated. But more than that, I felt uneasy. Would she think I was too stingy? Was she genuinely happy in her tone, or was she secretly a little displeased? As I kept thinking about it, I noticed my hand had tightened around the edge of the container, as if I were trying to stop her from taking any more.

After lunch, she chatted with me as usual about trivial things, like what was in today’s textbooks and the music class we would have in the afternoon. Yet I started to feel an inexplicable emptiness in my stomach; losing one apple slice seemed to have taken away some of my energy too. I suddenly felt that maybe I had done something wrong. Whether I shared too much or too little, I could never feel satisfied. When I got home, I tried to ease my afternoon hunger with snacks. My mom asked, “How were the apple slices today?” I casually replied, “Pretty good.” But inside, I felt a pang of bitterness. I didn’t dare tell her that I had shared one slice with someone else, and I didn’t dare bring up how conflicted I had felt, as if I had done something wrong and refused to admit it. By the time I went to bed at night, I was still thinking about that question: was I really a stingy person? Why could one apple slice bother me so much?

The sun was gradually sinking, and the sky was tinted with a pale violet dusk. I was playing with a few neighborhood kids in the community park, with laughter, running footsteps, and the rustling of autumn wind in the leaves filling my ears. We were playing a game that required quick running and agile reactions: tag. I felt a mix of nervousness and excitement, eager to win the challenge yet afraid of becoming the one being chased.

Not long after the game started, I felt my shoelaces come loose, so I hurriedly stopped and crouched on the grass to tie them. The kids nearby didn’t notice and kept running ahead. I quickly tied my shoelaces and did my best to catch up with them. My heart was beating fast, thumping in my chest, and my palms began to sweat as I nervously swung my arms to speed up.

Suddenly, I heard one of the kids say loudly, “You’re always so slow. You should have tied your shoelaces earlier!” His voice rang out through the air, as if every tiny leaf were carrying the message along. I stopped in my tracks, feeling as though my stomach had beenfiercelyly twisted. It seemed like everyone was staring at me. My face felt hot, as if it were burning, and I wanted to explain immediately, but the words got stuck in my throat.

“I... I just didn’t notice...” I murmured, my voice so faint it was almost carried away by the wind. But they had already gone on with the game and didn’t respond. I felt pushed to the margins, suddenly unbearably lonely. I began to wonder whether they were deliberately excluding me. I stood there motionless, staring at their backs, a wave of helplessness and unease rising within me.

A minute later, maybe longer, they came back and said to me, “Come on, come play with us!”

“You... you’re really not angry?” I asked cautiously, my voice tinged with fear and hope.

He smiled and replied, “Of course not, we were just joking.” Hearing that, my heartbeat slowly settled down. Even though they had explained, I still felt uneasy, as if I had accidentally exposed my own flaws. I took a deep breath and tried to blend into their laughter, but I was still a little unsettled inside.

After I got home, I sat on the edge of my bed, replaying that sentence over and over in my mind. I felt as if I was always so clumsy, always letting others down. That night, I tossed and turned, unable to fall asleep, and just thinking about seeing those kids again the next day brought back my anxiety.

A few days later, I brought a gift to one of the kids’ homes to apologize, hoping to make up for my mistake. Although they didn’t think I had done anything wrong, I needed to confirm it. I felt like an easily troubled child, trying to ease the unease in my heart through an apology. Even so, I still could not forget that moment of loneliness.

On an autumn afternoon, I sat on the swing in my grandmother’s backyard and rocked gently back and forth. The leaves rustled in the breeze, and I could smell the faintly sweet scent of fruit in the air. The neighborhood children were running around in the yard, playing hide-and-seek, and I felt a little nervous, unsure whether I should join them. My heart began to beat faster, and my palms grew slightly sweaty.

“Come play with us!” one of the children called to me excitedly. I hesitated, wondering whether they might not like me. Slowly, I walked over, stepping on a few fallen leaves that made a soft crunching sound beneath my feet. After joining the game, I tried hard to seem cheerful, but deep down I kept worrying that I might do something wrong.

We decided to take turns hiding. I hid first behind a bush, clutching my hands tightly together. After a few seconds, I began to imagine what would happen if they couldn’t find me. Would they stop playing with me because I wasn’t smart enough? My stomach started to feel uneasy, and I tried to take deep breaths to stay calm.

One of the children found me quickly. He smiled and said, “You hid well!” A flicker of relief passed through me, but it was quickly followed by doubt: was he only saying that to be polite? I tried to smile back, but my smile didn’t quite come through, which made me even more nervous. Not long after, we moved to another spot and kept playing, and I tried to suppress the unease in my heart.

At dinner, I sat at the table while Grandma had prepared my favorite food, but I still felt overwhelmed with anxiety. After dinner, I tossed and turned in bed, thinking about every detail of the hide-and-seek game earlier that day and worrying about what others thought of me. I tried to remember the laughter and the friendly words, but there always seemed to be a lingering shadow in my heart.

The next day, I returned to the backyard as usual, and the birdsong around me made me feel a little more at ease. I saw the same children playing, and I found myself unable to resist wanting to join them again. This constantly rising sense of unease made my time at my grandmother’s house a somewhat complicated season: on one side, the laughing playmates; on the other, my own repetitive, overthinking self.

Today was game day at the kindergarten, and sunlight streamed through the windows, casting a golden glow over the room. Our classroom was filled with the sound of children’s laughter, rising and falling all around us. In one corner of the classroom, I set my eyes on a little red car, shining in the light. I walked over, and just as I reached out to take it, I found that another child wanted the car too. My hand froze in midair, and I felt a little upset inside. “I saw it first!” I said quickly. She ignored me and only held onto the toy tightly. My heartbeat began to quicken, and I could feel sweat forming in my palms. At that moment, my cheeks also started to feel hot.

Neither of us was willing to give in, so we began to argue. I could hear the usual noise beside us, mixed with our quarrel. “We can take turns playing with it,” she suggested. I didn’t want to compromise, after all, I had seen it first. My uneasiness kept growing, and I worried that if I gave in, I might never get another chance to play with that toy again.

Our argument drew a teacher’s attention. “Children, what happened?” the teacher came over and asked gently. My fingers tensed up involuntarily. Holding up the toy, I said, “I want to play with this first.” My voice was almost choking. The teacher looked at us, then smiled and suggested that we play together. She said, “How about letting the little car run on the floor? You can both push it.”

I thought for a few seconds, let out a deep breath, and put the toy down. The uneasiness in my heart seemed to ease a little. The other child and I sat down and pushed the little car back and forth on the floor. The wheels rolled lightly across the floorboards, making a rustling sound, and I gradually felt my mood calm down.

After school, when I got home, my mom asked me what had happened at kindergarten. I briefly described how I had fought with the other child over the toy. She smiled, patted my head, and said, “Sometimes arguments are unavoidable, but learning to share will make you happier.” That night, lying in bed, I thought back on what had happened today and felt a little embarrassed, wondering why I had been so stubborn.

A few days later, I found myself playing with that same child again. She seemed to have forgotten that argument, and I no longer minded either. We were still happily running around as before, as if nothing had ever happened.

During art class, the teacher handed each of us a sheet of colored paper and asked us to cut out an animal. I chose yellow paper and wanted to make a little chick. Sunlight filtered through the curtains and fell across the desk, giving the paper a warm, soft sheen. I held the scissors, but my palms had already started to sweat, because I kept feeling as if the teacher’s eyes were on me, even though she was over on the other side helping the others. As the scissors sliced through the paper, a jagged, uneven edge appeared. I froze for a moment and began to think I must be making it look terrible. Sure enough, in less than two minutes, I had cut the paper into several strange shapes, like broken wings, nothing like the little chick I had imagined. My heart started racing, and my face felt a little hot. Isecretly glanced at the desk beside me, where a boy was intently cutting out a beautiful bunny, his movements so smooth and practiced. Suddenly I felt so stupid, my eyes growing wet, but I didn’t dare cry. When the teacher passed by me, she paused, looked at my work, and asked gently, “Is this a chick? Why don’t you try again?” Her expression was kind when she spoke, but I felt sure she must think I was really bad at this. I nodded and lowered my head, not daring to look at her again. The girl next to me also turned and glanced at my paper-cutting, muttering, “Hmm... it looks a bit like a bunch of scraps flying around.” Hearing that, I immediately felt a knot twist in my stomach, as if someone had stabbed me. I said nothing, but in my mind I kept replaying what she had just said, and the more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt. Later, I pretended I was still carefully cutting something, but the scissors had already pinched my fingertips, and my movements had become mechanical. One thought kept rising in my mind: why do I always mess up such simple things? When class ended, I secretly stuffed the mess of a paper cutout into my backpack, as if hiding some embarrassing secret. That afternoon I hardly spoke at all, and when I got home I didn’t dare tell my mother about art class. I just sat dazedly by my desk. Whenever I remembered my classmate’s muttering and the teacher’s gaze, my stomach would still ache faintly—as if they had never left.

The classroom lights were always so stark and bright that they stung my eyes. The “scritch-scritch” of chalk on the blackboard, mixed with the sound of desks and chairs shifting and the classmates’ low laughter, seemed magnified countless times, filling my ears completely. I placed both hands on my knees, my fingernails digging tightly into the fabric of my pants, my heart pounding so fast it felt like drumsticks beating against my chest. I knew the teacher had been staring at me for several seconds already. “You, come answer this question.” Her gaze locked onto me, her voice carrying a coldness that left me nowhere to hide.

I stood up, my legs weak, as if I were stepping on a swaying plank. I couldn’t make out the writing on the blackboard, and my mind was a blank. I heard my own voice, very small, forcing out only a few words with trembling: “...It’s... it’s four.” As soon as I finished, a few children in the classroom couldn’t help laughing. I could hear their laughter stabbing into my ears like needles. “Four?!” The teacher repeated with drawn-out emphasis. “Are you joking? You can’t even answer such an easy question—were you even paying attention?” She tapped the blackboard hard with her chalk, the sound cracking through the air like a whip. I hurriedly lowered my head, my face burning hot as if it were about to smoke.

“Everyone look—this is what happens when you don’t pay attention in class!” The teacher swept her gaze across the room, and all my classmates’ eyes shot toward me at once. I stared desperately at the floor, not daring to look up, feeling my ears burning red. A scratch on my shoe suddenly became incredibly clear, and I stared at it with all my might, as if that alone could help me escape everything. I felt waves of nausea rising in my stomach, my chest as if it were pressed under a massive boulder, my breathing growing rapid.

When the bell finally rang, I felt like a sheet of paper soaked in cold water, not even having the strength to stand up. The classmates around me gathered in twos and threes to chat, but I could only stare at their backs, my mind filled with thoughts: “Why did she laugh at me just now?” “Do they think I’m really stupid?” “Should I never have answered the question in the first place?”

When I got home, the teacher’s voice and the classmates’ laughter were still echoing in my ears. I hid in my room, shut the door, and wrapped myself tightly in the blanket, trying to block out every sound from outside. That feeling of shame was like a wet cloth, pressed over my face again and again, crushing me until I could hardly breathe. I couldn’t help wondering whether it would have been better if I had never stood up to answer that question. But there was no answer to that at all.

That evening, Mom knocked on my door and asked why I hadn’t eaten dinner. I really didn’t want to talk, so I just shook my head. She asked a few more times, and I could only force out a “It’s nothing.” She looked at me for a while and then left. As I heard the door close, my heart clenched again, as if it were being bound by a thin rope. I even thought that maybe they didn’t want to hear me speak at all; even if I said anything, no one would really care.

The noise on the playground made my whole body tense up. The sun was glaring, sweat slid down my forehead, and my back was sticky with sweat against my T-shirt. I stood in the jump-rope competition lineup, clutching the rope in my palm, feeling its plastic surface cold and slippery. “It’s almost your turn!” a classmate next to me whispered. I managed to force out a faint smile, but it quickly stiffened on my face. I caught a glimpse of the referee teacher’s expression, which seemed a little stern, and I started wildly guessing—maybe she didn’t like me, maybe she thought I wasn’t good enough at jumping. I knew I always thought too much, but that voice wouldn’t obey and kept worming into my head; the more I thought, the more annoyed I became. My heart pounded like a drum, and my hands started to shake.

Then it was my turn. I walked to the center of the field, avoiding everyone around me and staring only at the ground beneath my feet. The rope felt heavy in my hands. I took a deep breath and told myself, “Relax, relax, it’s just jump rope.” The teacher’s whistle sounded like a thunderclap, and I jumped up abruptly. The rope passed under my feet, but on the third jump, my toe actually got caught.

The rope cracked against the ground with a slap, and whispers broke out around me. “They’re really bad at this.” “They even tripped.” Some voices even carried a laugh. My face burned instantly, as if it were on fire, and my eyes grew a little blurry—I couldn’t tell whether it was sweat or tears about to fall. One thought kept surging over and over in my mind: they must think I’m a failure. Why am I always like this?

I looked up at the teacher, hoping for a little comfort, but she only made a gesture telling me to continue. I lowered my head and started again. Every jump felt unbearably heavy, and the sound of the rope was magnified in my ears, piercingly loud. I counted each jump, repeating silently to myself, “Hurry and end, hurry and end.” At last, after barely holding on until the whistle blew again, I turned and walked back to the line, head down, afraid to look at anyone.

My classmates’ comments still lingered in my ears, impossible to shake off like flies buzzing nearby. My stomach suddenly twisted painfully, my palms grew even sweatier, and my grip on the rope felt weaker. I forced myself to stand in line and pretend nothing was wrong, but inside it felt like a whirlpool, constantly pulling me toward negativity.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the moment my foot caught on the rope and the sound of my classmates’ comments, and the more I thought about it, the sadder I felt. I kept blaming myself: why couldn’t I just do a little better? Those voices seemed to keep mocking me, and the more I remembered, the more ashamed I felt. For several days after that, whenever I passed the playground, I felt a sense of suffocation, and I even started finding excuses to avoid PE activities.

Sunlight spilled across the yard, and a gentle breeze swayed the swing. I sat on the swing, holding a shiny glass marble in my hand, one I treasured dearly. The marble refracted rainbow-like glimmers in the sunlight. I carefully placed it on the ground, then gave it a hard flick, and it rolled and tumbled across the ground. I could hear my mother busying herself in the kitchen, a sound that always made me feel safe.

Suddenly, the marble rolled into the grass. I ran over to look for it right away, but I couldn’t find it no matter how hard I searched. My heart started racing, sweat broke out on my forehead, and my palms grew damp and slippery. I panicked, and before I knew it, tears were streaming down my face, because I knew that if Mom found out I had lost my beloved marble, she would surely be angry.

Just then, Dad came out of the house. Seeing me pawing through the grass, he raised his voice and asked, “What are you doing? Causing trouble again?” His voice exploded in my ears, and I instantly felt fear and shame. The tears kept flowing, and a small voice in my heart kept echoing: They’re going to say I’m careless again, that I can’t do anything right.

“I’m sorry, I just want to find my marble,” I sobbed softly, but Dad’s expression did not soften. He sighed. “Why are you always so careless?” Those words stabbed into my heart like needles, as if I were a child who was always making mistakes and could never satisfy them, no matter how hard I tried.

Mom came out of the kitchen and, seeing the scene, added her reproach: “Why are you making such a mess again? Hurry up and go inside.” I lowered my head, my stomach aching faintly, my heart filled with the panic of being abandoned and a sense of failure. Why was I always like this? Why couldn’t I make them happy?

At night, I lay in bed, staring at the ceiling, my heart still refusing to calm down. That tiny marble seemed to have turned into a huge monster, blocking my chest. For days after, I kept replaying what had happened, feeling like a child who was always doing things wrong. I couldn’t let them down. I was afraid of losing their love, afraid that I simply wasn’t worthy of it.

That fear and self-blame felt unbearably real; even in sleep I had nightmares, and in them I always heard my parents’ disappointed voices. It took me days before I could finally force myself not to think about it, but whenever I saw the grass or the swing, I still felt an inexplicable tension and unease.

The warm sun spilled over the school playground, where I was playing hopscotch with a few classmates. We drew several lines on the ground with white chalk. I tossed a small stone, and it landed right in square number three. I was overjoyed, sure that today would go smoothly.

As I hopped from square to square, I noticed the classmates nearby whispering to each other in low voices. “Impossible, they definitely stepped on the line.” My heart tightened, and the easy rhythm of the game suddenly felt heavy. Hadn’t I stepped on the line? I needed to check again. My heartbeat sped up, and tiny beads of sweat appeared on my forehead.

So I stopped and looked at the chalk lines on the squares, feeling as if the lines might disappear. “No, I didn’t step on it,” I said nervously, trying to hold back the unease inside me. The classmates all gathered around, speaking in hushed tones.

“Come look here,” one classmate said, pointing to the edge of the line, their voice calm. But my heart was thudding like a drum. I stared at the ground, trying hard not to show even the slightest hint of unease, while thinking: If I really did step on the line, would I be blamed? Would everyone ignore me?

A light breeze blew by, carrying the scent of the playground’s sandy ground, and in an instant it brought me back to reality. The feeling of friction came from the soles of my shoes, seeming to remind me that every step had to be taken with care. In the end, we decided to start the game over, and I no longer dwelled on the argument from before.

I tossed the stone again, trying to forget the little conflict. When I got home, I told my mom about what had happened on the playground that day. While preparing dinner, she smiled and said, “Don’t worry too much about these small things. What matters is having fun.”

I felt relieved and thought that I really shouldn’t be troubled by such trivial matters. A few days later, I found myself still joyfully playing on the playground, trying as much as possible not to pay too much attention to what other people thought.

The living room was filled with voices and laughter. I was squatting on the corner sofa, eating an orange and fiddling with a toy car. The orange was sweet with a slight tang, and my hands were left sticky from peeling it. The adults were gathered around the coffee table chatting, which was covered with fruit platters and several delicate porcelain vases. Suddenly, a sharp crash cut through the noise, and all the voices were severed, as if someone had pressed pause. A white vase had fallen to the floor, its shards scattering everywhere. In an instant, all eyes turned to me, the child nearest to the vase.

An aunt frowned and walked over. “Did you knock over the vase?” I hurriedly shook my head. “It wasn’t me, I was on the sofa and didn’t move!” But the crease between her eyebrows only deepened. “Children should be honest. If you broke it, you broke it—why won’t you admit it?” Several adults nearby chimed in too: “That vase was expensive,” “We’ll have to teach proper manners better in the future.”

My face started to burn, and my stomach felt tightly squeezed. I turned to my mother for help, but she was talking to relatives on the other side and didn’t seem to notice what had happened here. Clenching my teeth, I shouted again, “It wasn’t me!”

“Then who did it?” The aunt’s tone grew harsher, like a wall pushing toward me, and my whole body stiffened. “I don’t know!” I cried, my voice trembling, tears beginning to well up. At that moment, a cousin a little older than me came over and said, “I just saw them standing over there.” My heart sank even further, and my tears poured out uncontrollably, like a dam breaking.

“All right, all right, stop arguing. The child’s crying like this already.” Finally, an uncle stepped in to smooth things over, but the aunt was still sighing, saying, “If something like this isn’t corrected early, it’ll be hard to deal with when they grow up.” I wanted to speak, but not a single word came out. It felt as if a hard stone had been stuffed into my stomach; my breathing turned rapid, and my vision began to darken.

Later, when my mother finally came over, she asked, “What happened?” Just as I was about to speak, someone beside me had already answered for me: “They broke the vase and still won’t admit it.” I could feel my mother’s gaze fall on me, carrying a trace of confusion and slight irritation. I suddenly lowered my head, too afraid to look into her eyes, and my body began trembling uncontrollably.

That night, at dinner, I barely touched my chopsticks. The smell of the dishes on the table made me a little nauseous, and my heart felt blocked, making me think, “Why does no one believe me?” My mother asked if I was still sulking over what happened today. I opened my mouth, but nothing came out. After returning to my room, I hugged a pillow and curled into a ball, burying myself under the blanket. My tears soaked the comforter, my eyelids ached from swelling, and it was nearly midnight before I drifted into a dazed sleep.

Over the next few days, whenever I ran into that aunt or cousin, I would unconsciously lower my head or keep my distance. I felt as if I had really done something wrong. Even though I knew full well I hadn’t, the heaviness and shame in my chest never went away.

The instant the glass hit the corner of the table, that sharp crack was like a needle piercing the noise of the entire room. Juice spread out, the orange-yellow liquid creeping along the pattern of the white tablecloth, carrying a cloying sweet smell. I stood frozen, as if time had suddenly stopped—every voice and laugh around me seemed to have been muted, leaving only the sound of juice dripping, drop by drop, onto the floor.

My face began to burn, from the roots of my ears all the way down my neck. My heart was beating so fast it felt unnatural, as if something were thrashing around inside my chest. I knew everyone was looking at me; I could feel those gazes, like thin threads wrapping around me, tighter and tighter.

“How could you be so careless!”

My mother’s voice was the first to break the silence. There was something she couldn’t quite hold back in her tone; every word landed like a heavy blow. I wanted to explain, my lips moved, but no sound came out. My throat felt blocked by something hard and cold, something I couldn’t swallow and couldn’t spit out. I looked instinctively at my father—he frowned and waved me aside, signaling me to stand somewhere else.

I tried to catch my cousin’s eye for help. She lowered her head and took a sip of water, as if she hadn’t seen anything at all.

My uncle, sitting across from me, said with a teasing tone, “Kids are always like this. When will they ever stop making people worry?”

Laughter rippled again around the table. But it sounded as if there were a layer between it and me, like glass—I was inside, they were outside. My stomach began to churn, my palms were covered in sweat, and I hid my hands behind my back, clutching my fingers tightly.

“Go get a rag and wipe it up!”

I ran toward the kitchen, my legs weak, nearly slipping. My hands trembled as I grabbed a dishcloth, only to find it was dirty, so I switched to another one. By the time I ran back, my mother had already wiped away most of it, still muttering, “You can’t even do something this small properly. When will you ever stop making people worry?” Her gaze swept over me, and I felt as if something had been jabbed into my chest—cold and painful—but I still couldn’t say a word.

Then, just like that, it was over.

New dishes were brought out, everyone kept talking, kept laughing, as if nothing had happened at all. I stood by the dining table, feeling like something transparent—existing, but not belonging here. I didn’t dare move, not knowing whether I should sit back down or keep standing, while in my head I replayed the moment the glass tipped over again and again.

Why couldn’t I have been more careful? Why wouldn’t my hands ever listen to me? Why was I just incapable of making everyone happy?

That night, I lay alone in bed, wrapped tightly in the blanket as if I wanted to hide my whole self inside it. My stomach still ached faintly, my palms were still warm and damp. I bit my finger to keep myself from crying out, but my mind wouldn’t stop—the look in my mother’s eyes, my uncle’s words, the way my cousin had lowered her head. I pulled apart every detail and looked at it again and again, trying to find where I had gone wrong, trying to figure out what exactly was wrong with me.

There was a stone pressing on my chest, and I couldn’t catch my breath.
