I thought that maybe I was the kind of person who was bound to make mistakes. Maybe everyone had already thought so too, and today I had finally proven it myself.

In the morning, a few soft white clouds floated in the sky, and there was a hint of chill in the air. A little child from next door came to play at my house. We sat on the living room floor, surrounded by the wooden floor my mother had just mopped that morning, faintly scented with lemon. I excitedly showed her my toys, and in front of us was a brand-new toy car with a shiny red body.

Just as we were focusing on loading blocks into the toy car, she accidentally knocked over a glass of juice on the table. The orange liquid quickly spread across the floor, like a watercolor painting expanding before our eyes. I froze for a moment, my heart began to race, and my palms started to sweat. My mind flashed to my mother’s stern face; she always demanded that the floor stay clean, and I knew she would be angry.

She hurriedly stood up and kept saying, “I’m sorry, I’m sorry!” Her eyes were full of panic and apology. I quickly stood up too, wanting to grab a tissue to wipe it up, but I couldn’t find any tissues anywhere. The juice glistened golden in the sunlight, stinging my eyes, and my head began to buzz.

“It’s okay, it’s not your fault. I’ll help you clean it up too,” I said hurriedly, hoping she wouldn’t blame herself too much, and hoping I would have less trouble myself. But the corners of my mouth were trembling involuntarily, worrying about the scolding I would have to endure next.

My mother heard the noise and came out from the kitchen. Her expression changed from shock to reproach in an instant, her brows tightly furrowed. “What’s going on with you two?”

I quickly explained, “She accidentally bumped it over, I didn’t do it on purpose.” I could feel the skin on my scalp tightening, and a rumbling sound seemed to echo in my ears. I longed for my mother to understand that I had done nothing wrong.

“You need to be more careful. Watch out next time,” my mother said, still sounding reproachful, though I could tell she was already holding back her emotions. I nodded, feeling my breathing gradually settle down.

That night, I lay in bed staring at the patterns on the ceiling, and the moment the juice spilled kept replaying in my mind. My stomach hurt faintly, and I worried about whether I would still be able to play happily with her in the future. I didn’t dare go find her to play anymore, afraid something similar would happen again. The next day, I noticed that even during lunch break at school, I was still restless, my fingers tightly intertwined, and I barely ate any lunch.

A few days later, I finally gathered the courage to go see her. As soon as we met, I asked, “Are you okay? It’s all right about that day, isn’t it?” She smiled and nodded, and at that moment, I finally felt a weight lift from my heart. Sure enough, some things just need to be talked through.

During nap time, the room was dimly lit, the curtains swaying slightly and casting dappled shadows. I lay on the little bed, surrounded by quiet breathing and the occasional rustle of a child turning over. The air was filled with a faint mix of milk and disinfectant, and I still couldn’t fall asleep. Suddenly, I felt an inexplicable tension in my heart.

All at once, I heard the teachers’ voices outside the door. A gentle female voice said softly, “What if this child stays overnight at kindergarten tonight?” Another teacher replied in a low voice, “That could be a good opportunity for her, to help her become a little more independent.” My heartbeat suddenly quickened, and my ears rang. It felt as though every word struck my heart with a heavy blow, almost unbearable. I held my breath, trying to hear more clearly. Their voices gradually faded, but they left behind a lingering shadow in my heart.

I began to let my imagination run wild. What if my parents didn’t want me anymore? Did staying overnight at kindergarten mean they didn’t love me anymore? My heart beat faster and faster, my palms grew sweaty, and my stomach churned violently, as if I were about to vomit. I squeezed my eyes shut hard, hoping these sensations would disappear quickly.

Lying in bed, I kept imagining the worst outcome: being left at kindergarten forever, never seeing my family again, with them perhaps never appearing again. I clenched my blanket tightly, trying to find a little sense of safety in its familiar texture. But these thoughts kept churning in my mind, impossible to calm.

After nap time ended, I mechanically walked out of the sleeping room. When I saw the teacher’s kind face, I still couldn’t calm myself down. She smiled and greeted me, “Did you sleep well? You look a little tired.” I forced a smile, but my mind was still filled with those harsh words.

Over the next few days, I kept wondering whether the teacher would bring up that terrible plan again. I became even more anxious, and every time the teacher called me over, I would panic, afraid of hearing her mention the decision for me to stay overnight. Each night before falling asleep, I repeatedly checked that the familiar sounds in the room were there, and only then did I feel slightly reassured.

At home, I kept asking my parents, “Will you pick me up at night? Will you still come for me tomorrow?” Although they always answered firmly, “Of course we will. How could we not come?” I still felt uneasy, always afraid that a tiny detail could change everything.

During lunch break, I walked to the swing set on the playground, hoping to have a turn on the swings. Sunlight streamed through the gaps in the leaves, scattering dappled patches of light and shadow across the ground. I could hear my classmates laughing and playing in the distance, and birds chirping all around me. Not far away, a few children were fighting over a hula hoop, their laughter ringing out nonstop. I hesitated, feeling uneasy, and only wanted to swing quietly by myself for a while.

“Hey, kid, are you alone?” A boy walked over, the sunlight shining on his face as he smiled with squinting eyes. I nodded, too nervous to look up at him. “Why aren’t you playing with everyone else?” he asked. I opened my mouth, but I didn’t know how to answer. I just lowered my head and kicked at a small pebble on the ground.

“Maybe they don’t want to play with us, haha,” came the voice of another little girl from beside us. Her words stabbed my heart like a needle. My stomach lurched, and I felt my cheeks burning hot. “That’s not true!” I couldn’t help protesting softly, but my voice was so faint I could barely hear it myself.

Then came a burst of laughter, as if the whole playground were mocking me. My chest felt tight, my heart raced, and my palms began to sweat. Everything around me seemed blurred, and all I could see were vague shadows surrounding me. I wanted to say something to explain, but no words would come, and tears began to fall despite my efforts to hold them back.

It seemed as if the air carried a smell of earth and grass, mixed with the warmth of the afternoon sun. I struggled to keep from crying, but my emotions surged up like a tide. “Stop bullying them.” At last, another voice cut in. It was a little girl with a ponytail. She came over to my side and shielded me, saying, “They’re just shy.”

I kept my head down and wiped away my tears with the back of my hand, feeling grateful and even more embarrassed. Even though she was helping me, I still felt like a strange, out-of-place person. “Sorry, I…” I murmured, my voice drowned out by the noise around us. She patted my shoulder and said gently, “It’s okay, don’t mind them.”

That afternoon, after I got home, I kept thinking about what had happened. At dinner, I sat at the table feeling like something was stuck in my throat, making it hard to swallow. Mom asked me what was wrong, and I shook my head and just said I wasn’t hungry. She didn’t ask any further; she simply poured me a cup of warm water in silence.

A few days later, I went back to school. Though I was no longer as afraid of the playground, I was still somewhat cautious. I started trying to play with the other children. Even though I still felt a little uneasy inside, sometimes laughter could also make me feel at ease. That experience made me more aware of how sensitive I was to what others thought, and it also helped me slowly learn how to face and deal with those feelings.

The classroom was filled with the chatter of little children; craft class was always lively like this. That day, we were making clay animals. I gently pinched a piece of clay with my fingers and slowly shaped it into a little cat. I made it two pointed ears and a curled-up tail, and finally used a thin bamboo skewer to carve in its whiskers. I adored it and couldn’t bear to put it down, as if it were my own treasure.

“Your little cat turned out so well!” a classmate beside me said as they looked at my work. I felt my cheeks grow warm, but inside I was filled with delight.

Just as I was about to paint the little cat, a classmate accidentally bumped into my desk. The little cat fell off the desk and broke into several pieces. It felt as if time had stopped. I stared blankly at the fragments on the floor, my heart tightening over and over again. In that moment, it felt as though something were pressing on my chest, making it hard to breathe.

“I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to...” the one who caused it said quietly, but I couldn’t take it in at all. My mind was completely filled with the shattered image of that little cat.

“It’s okay, I’ll try making another one,” I forced out a smile, but my voice couldn’t hide my heartbreak. My heart raced, and sweat began to form on my back. Tears welled up in my eyes, and I struggled to hold them back.

After class, I went home, and my mother asked me what was wrong. I just shook my head, my throat tight with emotion, too afraid to speak. At dinner, my stomach hurt a little, and I had no appetite at all. I kept replaying that scene in my mind: the little cat falling off the desk, the sound of it breaking into pieces seeming to echo in my ears.

That night, I sat in my room for a long time. Looking at the clay in my hands, I made another little cat, but it still didn’t seem as good as the first one. I kept blaming myself inside: Had I not placed it carefully enough? Had I not protected it well enough?

A few days later, I finally told my teacher about it. She comforted me gently and said, “There are always times when things don’t go as we hope, but we can learn from them.” She helped me repair the little cat, and I finally felt relieved. Although it still had some cracks, I felt that the little cat had become stronger.

Through this experience, I realized that I always tend to turn small things into the end of the world. My sensitivity made me feel ashamed, and yet I was unable to stop blaming myself. But I also began to learn to be a little gentler with myself, and to try to find courage and strength in failure.

Today it was very windy at kindergarten, and the sand on the playground was blown everywhere. After the teacher finished playing games with us, I walked to a corner and started building a little castle out of sand. As I lowered my head, I heard the children’s shouts mixed into the wind—happy and noisy. Suddenly, I felt a grain of sand hit my face, and the sting made me squint. I instinctively wiped the sand away with my hand, feeling a little uncomfortable. Around me were the laughter of the children, yet I felt as if someone was staring at me.

“Why did you hit me?” Xiaoming stood in front of me with an unhappy look on his face, tilting his head, his eyes full of accusation.

“I didn’t!” I protested immediately, panicking inside, and quickly waved my hands to explain. But Xiaoming turned and ran to the teacher, shouting that I had hit him.

Watching Xiaoming’s back as he ran off, my heart sank, and it felt like there was a stone in my stomach. My palms started to sweat, and I could even hear my own heartbeat. “I’m done for now. Will the teacher punish me?” I asked myself, my mind filled with the worst possible outcomes.

After a while, the teacher came over, knelt down gently, and asked me, “Did you hit Xiaoming?”

I shook my head, but tears began to flow uncontrollably. “I didn’t. I really didn’t.” My voice trembled with hurt and nervousness. The teacher patted my shoulder and said nothing more, only letting out a soft sigh, as if thinking about something.

That night, lying in bed, I kept hearing Xiaoming’s accusation echo in my head. Tears seemed to well up for no reason; clearly I had done nothing wrong, yet it felt like everything was my fault. I thought of that moment—though the teacher hadn’t blamed me, I still felt a deep unease. The next morning, when Mom saw how listless I was, she asked me what was wrong. I shook my head, too afraid to tell her what was on my mind.

A few days later, when Xiaoming came to play with me again, it seemed he had already forgotten about that day. But I remained careful and cautious, afraid of being misunderstood again. There was always a voice in my heart reminding me: if someone misunderstood me again, how would I explain it?

After this incident, I began paying attention to every little movement. Each time a friend came near, I would unconsciously step back, worried that I might be misunderstood again by accident. That stone in my heart seemed never to have been set down; I always felt that Xiaoming’s eyes were still closely following me from behind.

The notes of the piano echoed through the classroom, and music class began. The cloudy sky outside cast a soft light into the room. I sat on a small stool, looking forward to the music teacher leading us in a new song. The teacher walked to the piano and played a lively melody, and we clapped along to the beat. “Children, today we’re going to learn a new song,” the teacher said with a smile. I felt a little nervous, worried that I might sing it wrong. When it was my turn to stand up and sing solo, my heart was pounding, and my voice trembled with the scales. Halfway through my song, the teacher suddenly stopped playing and said to me, “Pay attention to your pitch, and sing on the beat.” I froze, feeling the blood rush to my face, and my heart beat even faster. I felt like I had done terribly, like they were all looking at me. “Did I sing out of tune? Are they all laughing at me?” My mind was filled with such thoughts, and I couldn’t stop blaming myself. The air in the music room seemed to freeze. I felt hot all over, my palms were sweating, and it was as if I were trapped in an invisible cage.

As the music teacher continued the lesson, I kept replaying what had just happened in my mind, and every syllable became a reason to blame myself. I noticed the children nearby whispering, and I was certain they were talking about me singing out of tune. Even when the teacher kept encouraging everyone, I couldn’t take it in; my mind was entirely occupied with my own mistake. At last the bell rang, and everyone rushed off to play, while I followed slowly behind.

That afternoon, I didn’t play with my friends. Instead, I sat on the kindergarten swing, gently rocking back and forth. I tried hard to calm myself down, but what had just happened hovered above me like a dark cloud. “Why do I always do things badly?” The voice of self-blame kept echoing in my heart. The ropes of the swing felt cold in my hands, and I felt lonely and helpless.

When I got home, I sat on the rug in my little room and told my mom in a low voice about what had happened in music class when she came to ask me. She comforted me and told me that everyone makes mistakes sometimes, so I shouldn’t take it too much to heart. I knew she was trying to reassure me, but the shame of being criticized by the teacher still wouldn’t fade.

Over the next week, music class became the lesson I least wanted to attend, and I kept worrying that I would make the same mistake again. During recess, I also paid even closer attention to every word the teacher said, afraid of hearing criticism again. For little me, that music class seemed to foreshadow a burden I could never put down, something I would keep reliving in the days to come.

On a bright afternoon, the playground was filled with the scent of grass and earth. I was playing and laughing with a few other children beside the slide, my heart full of anticipation for the game. But when it was my turn to go down, a boy taller than me suddenly cut in line and shoved me aside. I froze, panic rising in my chest, my face growing hot.

“Hey, that’s my spot!” I shouted, but my voice was so small it was almost carried away by the wind. The boy paid no attention to me; he was already getting ready to slide down. I felt as if I had been ignored, and something like a little bug was restlessly crawling inside my heart. I looked around, hoping to find a teacher, but she was far away, attentively watching other children play.

My heartbeat quickened, and my palms began to sweat slightly. Seeing the other children laughing, with no one stepping forward to speak up for me, a sense of loneliness quickly took over my heart. I forced out an ugly smile, pretending that none of this mattered to me.

“It’s okay, I can wait a little longer,” I whispered to myself, though my heart was full of unease. A breeze blew from the top of the slide, carrying a hint of chill. I shrank back, looking down at the ground below, feeling as if there were a big hole inside me.

After a while, it was finally my turn. I struggled up the slide, but I kept thinking about what had just happened. When I slid down, my body remained stiff, and I didn’t feel any of the joy the slide should have brought. I only felt as if I were sliding into a heavy shadow.

When I got off the slide and tried to rejoin the other children, my steps slowed down involuntarily. I kept thinking, “Do they all dislike me? Did I do something wrong?” Those thoughts surged like waves, pounding at my heart.

That night, lying in bed, the image of that boy cutting in line still flashed through my mind. His face was blurry yet vivid, and my mood grew even heavier. I pulled the blanket up a little higher, hoping it could hide that unease and shame.

The next day, I was still afraid to go play by the slide. I chose the sandbox on the side and sat there alone, hoping in my heart that someone would come over and ask what was wrong with me. But when the entire afternoon passed quietly and nothing happened, I gradually realized that perhaps no one would notice my silence. That made me even more certain that maybe I should just be alone, so I wouldn’t have to feel that pain of being ignored again.

The autumn sun spilled across the kindergarten playground, and the golden light made everything feel warm and cozy. Yet my mood was shrouded in a shadow. I stood in a corner of the playground, watching the other children play happily on the slide, their laughter filling my ears. But tears were welling up in my eyes, and my heart was in a panic.

I remember it was just an ordinary playtime, when the teacher let us go off and play freely. I had wanted to play in the sand with my good friend Xiaoli, but she said, “I’ve already made plans with Xiaoming. Go find someone else.” My heart sank at once, as if I had been pushed hard. I forced out a smile: “Oh, okay.” But inside, I couldn’t help but start overthinking. Was she angry with me? Was it because I had accidentally torn her drawing yesterday? I wanted to go ask her clearly, but my feet felt nailed to the ground and wouldn’t move.

The other children ran around, and the swings on the playground made a creaking “squeak, squeak” sound, while I could only stand there blankly, as if the whole world had forgotten me. Images kept flashing through my mind of Xiaoli and Xiaoming having so much fun together, and I felt a wave of jealousy and frustration. My palms started to sweat, my heart beat much faster than usual, and my stomach felt a little upset.

Just then, the teacher came over and gently asked me, “What’s wrong, little one?” I wanted to say I was fine, but I couldn’t hold back my tears, and my voice trembled: “Xiaoli won’t play with me anymore.” The teacher smiled slightly and patted my head. “It’s okay. Maybe she just wants to try a different game. Everyone has times like this.” Half-believing her, I nodded, though my heart was still a little sore. Still, her words gave me a tiny bit of comfort, and I tried talking to another child.

On the way home after school that day, my mom held my hand, and I gathered my courage to tell her what had happened. She said with a smile, “Friendship can be like small waves sometimes, with ups and downs. It’s okay.” The next day, I went to kindergarten feeling uneasy, only to find Xiaoli running up to me on her own, taking my hand, and going to play in the sand together. Although the worry in my heart had not completely faded, I understood that perhaps everything was much simpler than I had imagined.

It was still raining, not heavily, but enough to turn the kindergarten playground into a muddy mess that was hard to walk through. The rain mixed with the smell of earth, filling the air with dampness and mud. I stood at the edge of the playground, my feet on the slippery ground, watching my companions laugh and play in front of me. I felt torn—wanting to join their game, yet worrying that my clothes would get dirty with mud. “Come on, play with us!” my friends called to me. I hesitated as I moved closer, silently telling myself not to fall.

Just then, my foot slipped, and I fell hard onto the muddy ground. Mud and water splashed up, soaking my clothes. The others around me suddenly fell silent for a moment, then burst into laughter. “Haha, he fell—so stupid!” someone shouted, the words stabbing my ears. Sitting there in the mud, my hand touching the slick muck, I felt a wave of shame and anger. Why were they laughing at me? Why was I always the one making a fool of myself?

My heartbeat quickened, and my face burned as if everyone’s eyes were fixed on me. I tried to stand up, but my body seemed not to obey; my hands and feet felt stuck to the slippery mud. “Are you all right?” A gentle voice came from beside me. I looked up and saw the teacher standing there, concern on her face. I forced out a smile, but the mud on my face made even my expression feel stiff. She helped me up and patted the mud off my clothes. My heart was full of shame—why was I always so clumsy? It felt as if the whole world were watching my embarrassment.

Back in the classroom, my wet clothes clung sticky to my body, and the air was filled with the musty smell of damp fabric. I sat in a corner, trying not to meet the other children’s eyes. I kept thinking: why am I always like this? Why can’t I be as at ease as everyone else? The resentment and shame inside me were tightly knotted together, impossible to shake off.

That night, even at home, I could still feel that gaze surrounding me, as if something inside had been locked away forever. It was as if a voice kept telling me that I wasn’t good enough, that I shouldn’t have let myself fall, that I should have done better. I prayed that I could forget it by tomorrow, but a deep mark had already been left in some corner of my heart, as if it could be reopened at any moment.

Sunlight streamed into the classroom through the blinds, scattering bright white patches across the floor. Standing at the podium, the teacher said that today we would make a three-dimensional paper crane. I heard almost all the children in the classroom let out soft gasps of wonder, and everyone seemed excited. I lowered my head and looked at the sheet of colored origami paper on my desk; I had chosen pink. My fingertips pinched one corner of the paper, whose texture was smooth and soft. I felt a little nervous, because origami was not easy for me. I often couldn’t fold accurate shapes and always felt that the paper wouldn’t obey me.

The teacher began demonstrating the folds step by step, saying we should first make an exact square, then fold in from the corners. I tried to follow along, but my hands trembled slightly, and each time I folded, it was always a little off. My breathing gradually grew quicker, and it felt as if the air in the whole classroom had suddenly become thick. Isecretly glanced at the classmate beside me; she had already folded half of her crane, her movements smooth, the edges of the paper neat as if cut by a knife. My heart sank. I quietly turned the paper in my hands, only to find that the creases I had just made were completely wrong.

“You’re folding it wrong,” the classmate beside me suddenly said, her voice carrying a hint of unintentional amusement. “Look here, you need to fold along the center line again, otherwise it’ll be crooked.” She reached out to help adjust it, which made me feel especially embarrassed. I quickly snatched the paper back and said hastily, “I know how to fold it!” But my voice sounded sharp and tense. She withdrew her hand, and the smile on her face stiffened slightly. A burning sense of shame surged up in me, and I felt that I was doing terribly.

Even though the teacher was still explaining patiently, I couldn’t hear a word of it. I looked down at the paper in my hands, now covered in messy creases. My palms began to sweat, my fingertips felt cold, and my stomach ached faintly. Images flashed through my mind of how the other students might be looking at me—would they think I was so stupid that I couldn’t even make a paper crane? Was someone secretly paying attention to me, thinking I was a joke? The more I thought about it, the more panicked I became; my hands shook even more, and I could hardly continue working with the paper. In the end, I simply crumpled it into a ball and pushed it aside, pretending not to care.

“You didn’t make one?” When the teacher walked over to me, my heart tightened. “Where’s your paper crane?” she asked, and I felt my face grow hot as if it were about to burn. I stared at the crumpled waste paper on the desk and stammered, “I… can’t do it.” The teacher sighed and said, “It’s okay, we’ll try again next time.” But even though her tone was gentle, I still felt as if a huge spotlight had been turned on me, leaving me nowhere to hide. I heard the students around me whispering, and my ears seemed to grow hotter and hotter; even sitting there felt uncomfortable.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mind repeatedly replaying the crumpled pink origami paper and the brief, stiff smile of my classmate. I kept wondering whether she was secretly making fun of me, or even telling others that I was stupid. I tried to fall asleep, but my heartbeat kept pounding against my chest like a drum, until eventually I grew so exhausted that I drifted off without realizing it. The next day, when I saw that classmate, she nodded at me as if nothing had happened. But that didn’t completely ease my mind; I still felt that she might have some opinion of me behind my back, and that guesswork kept me in a subtle state of unease.

The scissors in my hand slipped, and the colored paper was cut into a crooked edge; clearly, the pattern was supposed to be a complete star. I lowered my head and looked at thattoo horrible to look at sheet of paper, panic burning in my heart like fire. Before I could try to fix it, the teacher’s gaze had already locked onto me. Her voice sounded especially harsh in the empty classroom: “What’s wrong with you? You can’t even manage such a simple pattern!” I felt everyone’s eyes gather on me, and sweat started pouring down my back, itching unbearably.

“Sorry…” I said softly, my voice almost inaudible. My face felt as if it were on fire, tears swelled in my eyes, but I forced myself not to let them fall. I heard someone behind me chuckle quietly, and that sound stabbed into my ears like a sharp knife. I secretly glanced at the children beside me; their paper-cuttings were all neat and beautiful, while only my desk was a mess, like a failed experiment. I felt as though I had been thrown into a transparent cage—no matter how badly I wanted to escape, I couldn’t get out.

The teacher’s criticism continued: “Have you not been putting any effort into practicing at all? If you’re this careless, what will you ever be able to do in the future?” Her tone cut into my chest like a knife. I lowered my head and stared at the desk, trying to hide myself. But I realized my hands were trembling slightly, and every movement of the scissors became more difficult. I didn’t dare look up at her, and I didn’t dare look at my classmates. I was afraid of seeing the expressions on their faces, afraid they would look at me with ridicule.

After the craft class ended, I hurried to a corner and hid the failed paper-cut deep inside my schoolbag. My heart kept racing, and it felt as if my stomach were clenched tight. Only one voice echoed in my head: “Am I really that bad? Why is it always like this?” I tried to remember whether I hadn’t worked hard enough somewhere, whether there was something I could have done better in advance to keep all this from happening. But no matter how I thought about it, I couldn’t find an answer. I only felt that I could never do anything well, that I would always be worse than everyone else.

When I got home, I said nothing. Mom asked me what was wrong, and I said, “I don’t want to talk about it.” I was afraid that telling her about the teacher’s criticism would disappoint her. I barely ate dinner, and in my head, I kept replaying every detail of that class, as if I were watching a movie over and over again. I even started imagining that if the teacher had been gentler with me, if my classmates hadn’t laughed, would I not have felt this awful? I spent the whole evening immersed in this endless self-reflection until I was finally so exhausted that I fell asleep. When I woke up the next morning, my chest still felt painfully tight, and I didn’t want to face the new day. Those images and sounds followed me like a broken tape recorder. I had a faint feeling that something like this would keep happening in the future, and that I would never be able to do anything right. Touching the edge of that paper-cut, I could still feel how ruined it was, and I didn’t even dare take it out to show anyone.

During recess, most of the students were playing and chatting in the classroom. I sat at my desk, listening to the birds outside the window and the sounds of my classmates laughing and talking. Sunlight streamed through the window and fell on the desk, forming a warm square patch of light. I tried to join in everyone’s conversation, but I always felt a little nervous. My deskmate, a lively girl, was arguing with another classmate about something, with a smile on her face that I couldn’t decipher.

“Do you think I’m right?” she suddenly turned to me and asked. My heart seemed to beat faster; I was a little sweaty, my palms slightly damp. “Um, I think that might not be the case,” I answered cautiously, but she only smiled. That smile made me feel as if she were mocking me, and I immediately felt a surge of being ignored or looked down on.

I began to overthink her smile again and again in my mind. Did she think I was stupid? That thought made me uneasy. I tried to find more clues in her expression, but she looked away and kept smiling. My stomach ached faintly. Feeling irritated, I wanted to escape the situation, so I turned around to look out the window.

Even after recess ended, my mood remained low. Whenever I thought of her smiling face, I felt excluded by everyone. After school, I sat on the bus ride home, and the bumping of the vehicle only made me more agitated. When I got home, her laughter was still echoing in my ears. I began to doubt whether I had really said something wrong. That night, lying in bed, my thoughts still wouldn’t stop, my heart was still racing, and my hands clenched the blanket tightly. The next day, I became even quieter at school, trying to avoid any conversation that might put me in an embarrassing situation again.

A few days later, I noticed my deskmate talking to me as usual, seemingly completely unaware of my earlier inner struggle. I breathed a sigh of relief, but that unease and self-doubt still often resurfaced deep inside me.

The scorching sun hung overhead, and the playground was bustling with activity. The laughter and cheers of the elementary school students rose and fell in waves, while the fresh scent of grass and the smell of sweat filled the air all around. I stood at the starting line, my heart pounding, my palms breaking into a thin layer of sweat. The PE teacher announced in a loud voice, “Ready... go!” I threw myself forward with all my strength. My steps were quick, but after only a few strides I stumbled, and everything spun as I felt a sharp pain shoot through my knees and palms. I lay on the ground, the smell of earth filling my nose, and tears welled up and fell without my meaning to. The sound of my classmates’ laughter came to my ears, stabbing at my eardrums like needles. “Are you okay?” A taller boy bent down and reached out his hand to help me up. I gave no response, only lowered my head and dared not look at him. I was afraid he would see the tears in my eyes—symbols of shame and incompetence. My face burned as though it were on fire, and I said in a low voice, “I’m fine.” I got up, my knees trembling slightly, and hobbled to the side. Sitting by the track, I watched the other children continue the race, cheering and jumping with excitement, while I felt like an outsider. I kept replaying the moment in my head: why did I fall? What did I do wrong? If only I had run more carefully. My stomach began to ache faintly, which was my body’s reaction whenever I felt anxious. That night, I lay in bed, and the chirping of crickets drifted in from outside the window from time to time. I closed my eyes, but I kept thinking about what had happened that day, about the hand the boy hadstretch out, which I had lacked the courage to take. I wondered whether my classmates would think I was stupid, and whether anyone would mention it when I went to school the next day. I barely slept the whole night, and when I went to school the next day, I was extremely cautious, avoiding eye contact with others, afraid of seeing mockery or pity in their eyes. A few days passed, and although no one mentioned the fall again, that embarrassing feeling of being watched by everyone still surfaced in my mind from time to time. I began to feel tense before every run, worried about embarrassing myself again, so I always hesitated, making myself seem even clumsier.

The sun hung high over the playground, casting down searing golden light. I stood among a group of children, feeling the heat radiating up from the ground. Sweat trickled down my cheeks, sticky and prickly, and seeped into my collar. We were playing a game called “The Big Wind Blows.” My heart was pounding so fast I felt I could be chosen at any moment. The teacher was nowhere nearby; only gusts of wind and sand blew past from time to time, bringing a little coolness. Suddenly, a boy beside me walked over, looking somewhat irritated. “You’re standing too close. Move farther away!” His voice was sharp, tinged with impatience. I froze, feeling my cheeks burn even more, as if the ground beneath my feet had suddenly become unsteady. I hurriedly stepped back a few paces, my heart beating even faster, my palms damp with sweat.

Laughter and chatter rose around me. Someone said, “She’s always like that.” Another voice chimed in, “Yeah, always in the way.” My face went pale, as if all the blood in my body had stopped flowing. I wanted to explain, to tell them I meant no harm, but my throat seemed blocked. I could only hear my own heartbeat and the wind and sand howling past my ears. I looked down at my shoes and felt as though they were mocking me too. My stomach suddenly clenched, and a wave of pain hit me.

“Am I really that bad?” I asked myself in my heart. I thought of all the times I had been excluded before, every time I tried to fit in but always failed. I clenched my fists hard, hoping to ease the pain, but it was still there, like a stubborn stone. A girl nearby walked over. She said nothing, only looked me over and frowned slightly. I instantly felt even more ashamed, lowered my head, and didn’t dare look at her.

“What’s wrong with me? What exactly is wrong with me?” My mind was in chaos, like churning waves, wanting to break free from this feeling but unable to do anything about it. A few minutes later, the bell for class rang. I stood there in a daze until all the other children had left before I moved. When I got home, I was still replaying my friends’ voices and expressions in my mind. All evening, I felt abandoned and rejected. The cool bedsheets offered me no comfort, and I couldn’t understand why I was always misunderstood.

The next day, I saw them again during recess, and a nameless fear made me want to run away immediately. I began to wonder whether I shouldn’t show up in front of them anymore, not wanting to endure that embarrassment again. I was like a shadow on the playground, afraid to go near anyone, afraid of becoming the center of attention again.

The classroom air was a little stuffy and hot. I sat by the window, and sunlight filtered through the glass onto my textbook, making the words look a bit dazzling. The teacher stood in front of the blackboard, explaining a math problem. Her voice was steady and clear, like a gentle stream flowing through the classroom. I clenched my pencil tightly, my heart beating a little faster, and sweat quietly began to form on my forehead.

“Who can tell me the answer to this problem?” the teacher asked, her gaze sweeping across the classroom. At that moment, my heart tightened suddenly, as if a mixture of anticipation and fear was surging within me. I wanted to raise my hand, but I was afraid of making a mistake and being laughed at by my classmates. My palm was a little slick, and I unconsciously gripped my pencil even tighter.

I heard whispered voices behind me, as if everyone else knew the answer and only I was hesitating. “If I’m wrong, will they laugh at me?” I thought to myself, once again feeling a slight discomfort in my stomach.

“What do you think?” the teacher suddenly asked me. Her voice was gentle, but I felt an invisible pressure. I tried hard to calm myself down, slowly stood up, and said in a trembling voice from nervousness, “Is it fifteen?”

The teacher smiled and nodded. “That’s right, it’s fifteen.” At that moment, the heavy stone in my heart finally fell away. I let out a long breath, feeling the whole of my chest relax quite a bit.

After I sat down, a classmate beside me whispered, “You’re always so nervous.” Their voice seemed to drift lightly past my ear. My face felt a little hot, and a sense of shame quietly welled up. I looked out the window, trying to relax myself.

That afternoon, I kept thinking about my answer. Although it was correct, I still felt an inexplicable anxiety, afraid that the answer had been right only by chance. In the dormitory, the feel of the bedsheets seemed especially soft, but there was still a trace of unease in my heart, fearing the next mistake.

A few days later, I took part in an extracurricular activity at school, and the teacher even praised my performance that day, saying I had been very brave. A wave of warmth instantly rose in my heart, as if all my anxiety and worry had found a little comfort. But I still could not completely shake off those subtle feelings of unease, always afraid of being abandoned and rejected.

On a sunny afternoon, the park was filled with laughter and cheerful voices. Several children and I were playing by the sandbox, building sandcastles. This is one of my favorite activities; watching the grains of sand sparkle in the sunlight always makes me feel happy. A gentle breeze blew by, carrying the scent of grass and earth. I carefully piled up sand towers with a small shovel and cautiously built up the sand walls. Suddenly, a boy next to me pushed the sandcastle I had built, and the sand spilled everywhere. I froze for a moment, and a wave of unease rushed over me. “Why did you do that?” I asked, my voice a little tense. The boy curled his lip and said, “I just wanted to see how you’d react.” His words made me feel like he was mocking me, and my chest tightened with discomfort.

It felt as if the air had frozen in an instant. I could hear my own heartbeat and began to panic a little, even my hands trembling slightly. Some of the children nearby were smiling and watching, as if waiting to see how I would respond. I felt pressured inside, as though everyone was judging me. Instinctively, I wanted to cry, but I held back my tears. “Don’t cry, don’t cry,” I told myself in my heart.

To make myself seem stronger, I awkwardly gathered the scattered sand back together, trying not to look at the boy’s face. But a voice kept repeating in my mind: “Why are they doing this? Why don’t they like me?” A trace of hurt crept into my heart. I tried hard not to think about it, focusing only on quickly rebuilding the sandcastle, as if nothing had happened.

Although it was a small matter, the feeling of being rejected lingered in my mind. After a while, I gradually began to feel my palms grow slightly sweaty, and my temples felt hot. I lowered my head so no one could see the expression on my face.

This little friction didn’t last long; soon everyone moved on to running and playing chase. But my heart never fully settled down. On the way home, the sunlight was still just as bright, and the leaves were rustling in the breeze, but I had no mood to enjoy any of it. After I got home, I shut myself in my room and tried hard to think about what I should have done at the time so I wouldn’t have felt so uncomfortable. My mother came in and asked me what was wrong. I paused for a moment and replied, “Nothing, I’m just a little tired.” Then I sat at my desk and quietly drew pictures, slowly covering over that unease with color.

Although it was just a small incident, it made me realize that even minor unpleasantness during play can stir up strong emotions inside. For the next few days, I kept thinking about that sandcastle and that boy’s laughter, and I always felt a bit upset.

Outside the library window, rain tapped softly against the glass, accompanied by occasional low rumbles of thunder. I sat by a small table near the window, an illustrated fairy tale open in front of me, though my attention was not on it. I rested my hand on the book, feeling the slight coolness of the pages, while my heartbeat quickened over something so small. My deskmate, Xiao Ming, had accidentally dropped one of my favorite books while borrowing books. When he hastily and apologetically said he was sorry, I felt an inexplicable shame, as if I had done something wrong rather than him. Although Xiao Ming had already said he did not mind, I was still deeply worried, as if I could already see the teacher’s reproachful face. I nervously rubbed my hands together, my palms slightly damp with sweat. Over and over in my mind I thought: “What if the teacher finds out? Would she think I was careless? Or believe I’m a child who likes to lie?” Xiao Ming’s voice beside me interrupted my thoughts: “What are you thinking about? I really didn’t mean it.” His voice was sincere, yet I only felt too ashamed to face him. I forced out a smile and said, “It’s okay, don’t worry about it.” But I knew how strained that smile was. My stomach tightened, and the damp, cold sound of rain made me feel even colder. Even though this little library usually always made me feel safe, today’s tension left me with nowhere to hide. Around me, some of the children were speaking softly, some were reading with their heads down; in the quiet atmosphere, only the sound of turning pages could be heard, yet I felt my own heartbeat was unbelievably loud. After leaving the library and returning home, I was still shaken, replaying the scene from the library over and over in my mind. I set down my schoolbag and hid in my small room, trying to distract myself by drawing, but the rough feel of the paper could not compare with the irritation in my heart. I thought of the teacher’s smiling face and hoped she would still be the same tomorrow. By night, that unease was still clinging to me; the rain sounded like a spell cast upon me, keeping me awake for a long time. It took several days for those feelings to slowly fade, but they left a deep mark in my heart, and whenever I heard thunder, I would involuntarily think of that small incident.

Sunlight streamed through the window and spilled onto the balcony, leaving a few bright patches on the floor. I lay on the mat, feeling warm and comfortable. The air was filled with the sweet scent of the cake Mom had just baked, and from time to time I could also catch the fragrance of flowers outside the window. I felt as if every breath I took was easy and light. Mom sat down beside me, holding a book in her hand, but she didn’t open it; she only smiled and looked at me. She said, “Little one, would you like to hear a story from when Mom was young today?”

I nodded. Though the sunlight was a little dazzling, I still tried hard to keep my eyes wide open. “Yes, I want to hear it!” Mom laughed softly, and her laugh sounded as pleasant as bells.

“When Mom was as old as you are now, I also especially liked basking in the sun on the balcony,” Mom began. I stared at her mouth as her voice was gentle, making me feel especially at ease. “Once, my little friends and I played house on the balcony. We spread some old newspapers together as a carpet and sat on them drinking tea.”

I imagined what Mom looked like as a child, playing house with her little friends. I asked, “You didn’t have real tea, you were just pretending, right?”

“That’s right, we only put water in little teacups, but in our hearts that was tea,” Mom replied with a smile.

As I listened, I couldn’t help laughing, feeling especially warm inside. The sunlight shone on my back, and I felt myself growing sleepier and sleepier, as if I were being gently wrapped in sunshine. I closed my eyes and listened closely to Mom’s voice. Before I knew it, it seemed as though I had returned to that time too, becoming part of the story.

“Maybe it was because that game of house was so much fun that we didn’t want to stop all day,” Mom continued. “Until evening, when my mom—your grandma—came out to call us for dinner, and only then did we reluctantly pack up and go back inside.”

The balcony was quiet, with only the soft sound of the wind. I felt like I was about to fall asleep, but the scenes Mom described still lingered in my mind.

“I want to play house with my little friends too,” I told Mom.

She patted my head and said softly, “When you’re a little older, you can play with your friends.”

The sunlight fell gently, and in the breeze I felt a reassuring warmth, my heartbeat slow and steady.

A few days later, I thought again of that afternoon on the balcony. Mom’s story was like a lullaby, echoing in my mind from time to time, making me miss that peace and warmth very much. This memory made me feel happy and at ease.

When I leapt over the first obstacle, I could feel that the sand beneath my feet was a bit loose, and the soles of my shoes couldn’t get a firm grip. I heard the shouts of my classmates around me as they cheered others on; their voices sounded faint and distant. The sunlight was blinding, and a thin layer of sweat formed on my forehead. Sweat trickled along my hairline into my eyes, stinging so much that I blinked quickly a few times. A classmate ahead of me had already cleared the second obstacle. I gritted my teeth and tried to quicken my pace, when a voice suddenly popped into my head: “Whatever you do, don’t fall. If you do, everyone will laugh at you.”

That thought only made me rush even more. As I neared the second obstacle, I quickly rehearsed the move in my head: push off hard, lift my knee high, and just get over it. But the moment I jumped, my left foot caught on a small rock sticking out of the sand. My center of gravity shifted instantly, and I pitched forward onto the ground—my knee slammed hard against the firm pavement. At that moment, the sounds around me seemed to be pulled away all at once. All I could hear was my own heartbeat, pounding loudly.

“Are you okay?” came a boy’s voice from beside me. He looked like a referee and came over to help me up. I froze for a second, then hurriedly shook my head. “I’m fine. I can keep running!” My voice even sounded a little shaky. I noticed the gazes of other classmates around me; some seemed to be looking at me and whispering to each other. I didn’t dare lift my head. I quickly got up, brushed the sand off my knee, and found that my right knee had scraped open, with a faint stinging pain. Sweat, mixed with fine grains of sand, slid into the wound, and the pain made me draw in a sharp breath.

“Slow down! Don’t rush so much!” the referee standing nearby seemed to be saying something else, but all my attention had already turned inward. “They must think I’m so stupid, falling even in an obstacle race.” I kept running with my head down, my mind in complete turmoil. “What if everyone laughs at me behind my back? Will everyone who sees me from now on bring up the fact that I fell today?” These thoughts spun around at top speed, tightening my stomach into a knot.

For the rest of the race, I finished almost mechanically. The cheering by my ears was still there, but it felt as if there were a thick veil between us. I barely even remembered how I got over the remaining obstacles. All I knew was that after I crossed the finish line, the referee handed me a bottle of mineral water and said, “You okay? Your knee may not look serious, but remember to put some medicine on it when you get back.”

I nodded, feeling the cool plastic surface of the water bottle. I didn’t dare look him in the eye and quickly walked over to the rest area, where I sat down on a bench. My legs started to go weak, and the burning pain in my knee grew even more obvious. I lifted my pant leg to examine the wound carefully, and the small swollen patch made my heart sink. Suddenly, I heard a few classmates laughing nearby, and my mind immediately jumped to the idea that they were talking about me. “They must be saying how ridiculous I looked when I fell just now...” It felt as if a little hammer wascontinuously tapping inside my head, and my face began to grow hot.

When I got home, I tried very hard to act as if nothing had happened. The pain in my knee kept me from completely ignoring it, but compared with the pain, the deep sense of shame inside me was even harder to bear. I curled up in the corner of my room, hugging my legs, and kept replaying the moment I fell over and over in my head. Every scene was magnified, especially the looks others gave me. I began to blame myself: “Why couldn’t I have been more careful? Why did I have to rush so much?” That night, I tossed and turned, unable to fall asleep.

I remember that art class when we had to make a house model out of colored paper and glue. The classroom was filled with the smell of glue and the faint rustling of paper. My desk was piled with paper in all kinds of colors—red, yellow, and green. When I first started cutting out the windows, my hands were still a little shaky, because I always felt that something would go wrong with my work. The children around me were talking and laughing, and Teacher Liu was walking around at the front of the room, occasionally reminding us in a low voice, “Be careful not to get glue on your clothes.” Her tone made me inexplicably nervous, and I kept feeling as if she were speaking to me.

When I tried to glue the window frame onto the house, I accidentally used too much force and tore the frame in half. I froze, my hand hanging stiffly in the air, my heart suddenly pounding as if someone were beating a drum right next to my ear. I hurriedly picked up another sheet of paper and cut a new piece, but the color was different and it looked awkward and out of place. Looking at it, I kept repeating in my head, “They’re definitely going to think mine looks ugly,” “The teacher might think I’m useless.”

Sure enough, when Teacher Liu came over to me, she frowned and said in a low voice, “Why are your hands so unsteady? How is a window frame like this supposed to stick on?” Her voice wasn’t loud, but I felt like the whole class heard it, and I even sensed someone sneaking looks at my desk. My face instantly grew hot, as if something were burning my cheeks. I lowered my head and stared at the desktop, trying hard not to let my tears fall, while my mind kept repeating, “She must think I’m the worst.”

My deskmate, Xiaoqing, noticed how embarrassed I was and gently nudged me, saying, “Do you want to try wrapping the edge with tape? That way it won’t fall apart.” Her words made me relax a little, but I still didn’t dare look up, afraid that if I saw the expression on her face, there would be even a trace of mockery.

Later, I barely managed to finish the house model, but no matter how I looked at it, I still felt it was worse than everyone else’s. After class, I stuffed it into a paper bag, thinking that next time I must be more careful and more serious. I worried all afternoon about whether Teacher Liu would tell my mom that my craftwork was too poor, and by evening I couldn’t even eat dinner. Before bed, I secretly hid the house deep in the closet, afraid it would be discovered.

A few days later, the class held a display of our work, and some students’ houses were placed in the classroom display case. I saw that my house wasn’t there, and my feelings were mixed and complicated. On the one hand, I felt relieved, because no one would see my “failed work.” On the other hand, I felt ignored, and the thought kept running through my head: “I’ll never be good at these things.”

The classroom lights were always so glaring, and the cartoon posters on the walls were bright and colorful. I sat in the back row of the classroom, my palms sweating, because the teacher was calling on us one by one to answer questions. I kept silently praying that the teacher wouldn’t call on me, and my heartbeat grew faster and faster. I stared at the words in the textbook, as if they might suddenly become clearer and tell me the right answer.

“Please answer this question,” the teacher’s voice came from the front, and my name was called. My stomach tightened into a knot, and I knew the other students were all looking at me. I stood up, trying to remember what the question was, but my mind was blank. All I could hear were the ticking of the clock and the students’ whispered voices around me. I thought I heard someone say, “They definitely can’t answer it.”

“Uh, it... it...” I tried to speak, but my voice was so soft I couldn’t even hear myself. My whole body started to sweat, the textbook in my hands felt slick, and the warm air seemed like a heavy weight pressing on my chest. The teacher stood quietly waiting in front, and I felt more and more embarrassed.

“Ha, they’re so stupid!” a classmate laughed out loud, and others began to laugh too. I could feel my cheeks burning red, as if a gust of hot wind had swept over them.

“Enough. They’re just nervous,” the teacher said sternly, but the laughter still didn’t stop. At that moment, I felt all my shortcomings laid bare before everyone, as if an invisible hand had pushed me out of the crowd.

After class, I lowered my head and hurried out of the classroom. The wind blew over the grass on the playground, carrying a fresh scent of green grass. But I couldn’t care less; I just wanted to hide quickly in a toilet stall, pull the door shut, and deal with that feeling of being abandoned on my own. I couldn’t help sobbing softly, feeling as if the whole world were mocking me.

That night, back home, lying in bed, I could still hear the classmates’ laughter echoing in my ears, like a nightmare that would never end. The next day, I didn’t want to go to school, afraid I would be called on again and mocked again. I told my mom I wasn’t feeling well, but she only said, “You’re just a little nervous. It’s nothing serious.”

After a few days, I still went to school as usual, but even sitting in the classroom, as soon as the teacher’s gaze lingered on me for even a moment, my heartbeat would unconsciously quicken. During every activity class, I tried my best to avoid the classmate who had mocked me, and I didn’t even dare to meet the other students’ eyes, afraid they would again discover how “stupid” I was.

The playground was filled with the sound of voices, and the autumn sunlight fell on our running figures. My classmates and I were in the middle of a tense chasing race, with everyone desperately trying to catch up to the child holding the relay baton. I could feel my heart pounding like a drum and my breathing growing short. I could smell the dirt and sweat in the air, and beneath my feet was the rough plastic track.

“Go! Hurry up!” my classmates shouted beside me, their voices carried to my ears by the wind. I gripped the baton tightly and sprinted forward with all my strength. A voice kept warning me in my head: Don’t fall, don’t make a fool of yourself. But the more I thought that, the more nervous I became, as if every nerve in my body were stretched tight, almost ready to snap.

Suddenly, panic washed over me. Something caught my foot, and I lost my balance; the whole world spun before my eyes. At the moment I fell, I could hear the dull thud of my knee hitting the ground, a burning pain shot through it, and my face pressed against the cold track.

The noise around me gradually grew distant, and my mind went blank except for the self-blame repeating over and over. This time I’d definitely ruined the race. Why is it that I can never do anything perfectly, without mistakes? Why am I always so easy to embarrass myself?

A classmate stopped and helped me up, asking, “Are you okay? Don’t be afraid, we can keep going.” His voice was gentle, but I still couldn’t help wondering: Did he think I was stupid?

“I’m fine...” I forced out the words, my voice trembling slightly, not daring to look him in the eye. My knee still hurt, and the shame in my heart was impossible to hide. I could feel my heartbeat quicken, fine sweat breaking out all over me, my stomach churning. The cheerful laughter on the playground felt completely at odds with how I felt.

The race went on, but I was distracted, still worrying about the mistake I had just made. Even after I returned to the classroom, I still couldn’t shake off that feeling. The teacher noticed something was wrong, came over, and asked me what had happened. I could only lower my head, feeling dull and heavy inside: “Nothing, I just fell down.” Yet inside, I was full of frustration, as if a thorn had been stuck in my heart all along.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the scene on the playground and couldn’t fall asleep. I tossed and turned restlessly, and it seemed I could still hear the classmates’ cries of surprise when I fell. The next morning, the scrape on my knee was glaringly obvious, and my caution couldn’t hide the worry in my heart. It was like a scar, reminding me of the insecurities and shame that had yet to heal.

The wind on the playground was chilly, and the sleeves of my school uniform were blown up a little. I ran back to the classroom with the class line, my steps a bit hurried because I was afraid of being late. I hated it most when people watched the way I ran; I always felt like my legs were two stiff sticks, especially clumsy. After I got to the classroom, the teacher was writing on the blackboard, and the white chalk left a line on the green board: “What is beyond the mountain?” I sat down and tried to focus, but I was a little nervous because I knew the teacher might ask us to raise our hands and answer later. My palms were a little sweaty, so I gently held the edge of the desk, trying to stay quiet and make myself less noticeable.

“Next, who knows the answer?” The teacher suddenly looked around the classroom, and my heart tightened. When her gaze fell on my row, I felt like her eyes were shining on me like a searchlight. A few answers flashed through my mind, but none of them felt certain. To avoid being called on directly, I gathered my courage and raised my hand, hoping to end this torment sooner. I stood up and said, “I think it should be a stretch of tall grass?” After I finished speaking, the brief silence in the classroom made me feel terribly awkward, as if a wave of heat were burning from my neck all the way to my cheeks.

The teacher smiled, but not the encouraging kind of smile I had expected. Instead, she said in a somewhat correcting tone, “No, the correct answer is the ocean in the distance.” She continued explaining, and when I sat down, I felt as if my back had become heavy and stiff. I lowered my head and looked at the textbook, not daring to look up at the classmates around me, not daring to confirm whether they were laughing at me. My mind kept replaying my own words: “Tall grass, tall grass—what kind of nonsense answer was that?” My heartbeat was fast, each beat like a drum strike, and my fingers unconsciously gripped the edge of the textbook hard.

After class, I heard a classmate behind me whisper, “How could they think it was grass?” Although the voice was soft, every word felt like a needle stabbing into my heart. Suddenly, it felt as though everyone around me was looking at me sideways, as if anyone might be laughing at my wrong answer, my answer, my stupidity. I quickly packed my bag, left the classroom with my head down, and didn’t want to speak to anyone.

When I got home, I told my mom about it, hoping she would comfort me. But she only patted my shoulder and said, “It’s okay. If you don’t want to raise your hand next time, then don’t. Just listen carefully to the teacher.” Her tone was very calm, even a little indifferent, completely failing to understand the upheaval inside me. I sat alone at my little desk and wrote the words “the ocean in the distance” on a sheet of white paper with a pencil, then desperately imagined that there really was an ocean beyond the mountain. It was such a beautiful answer, but unfortunately it wasn’t my answer. All night long I kept thinking about why I hadn’t thought of the ocean at the time. It was such an obvious thing—why had grass come into my mind instead? Was I stupid? Was I worse than the other students? These questions wrapped around me like coiled wire and didn’t stop even when I fell asleep.

The community activity center was bustling with excitement on the weekend. Outside, a gentle breeze brushed against my face, and the air was filled with the fresh scent of grass. As I walked into the hall, bright banners and colorful balloons filled the surroundings, and noise came from every corner. My eyes swept across the room, where many parents and children were waiting to go on stage to perform. Anxiety began to well up inside me; my small palms were sweating, and my stomach felt as if a little worm were wriggling nonstop. Ever since long ago, I had always been wary and terrified of situations like this.

"Are you ready?" a kind staff member crouched down and asked me, her smile making me feel a little calmer. I nodded, yet I couldn’t stop imagining myself forgetting the lines and embarrassing myself under everyone’s gaze. I tried not to look at the audience, but a voice kept reminding me in my ear: “Everyone is watching you. Don’t do anything wrong.”

I started taking deep breaths, hoping to slow my racing heartbeat, but it didn’t help at all. My body was tense, as if wrapped all over in waves of heat. In that state, with my heart pounding, the staff member led me toward the stage. The lights shone brightly, and I was almost swallowed up by that brilliance. “I must not make a mistake in front of them,” I kept telling myself over and over.

When I stood in the center of the stage, my ears were filled with soft whispers and applause. The swaying lights made me slightly dizzy, and my legs trembled faintly. I forced out a smile and began reciting my little poem in a trembling voice. My mind was in chaos, and my tongue seemed to move on its own inside my mouth. As time passed, the words came awkwardly out of my mouth, and I held my breath, afraid I would miss a line.

At last, I stumbled through the final sentence and hurriedly bowed. The moment I stepped off the stage, I felt as if I had been released from a state of tension, and a sigh of relief rose in my heart. A few seconds later, a faint sense of pride slowly welled up inside me—“I did it. Not perfectly, but I did it.”

Back in my seat, my heartbeat gradually slowed, and the tension in my body slowly faded away. Mom gently hugged me. “You did very well!” she said, her tone full of encouragement. Although I knew my performance was far from perfect, at that moment I seemed to feel a little warmth and brightness, the comfort that comes from having tried.

That night, when I got home, the room was warm and quiet, and I could hear the soft ticking of rain outside the window. Lying in bed, images of the day kept flashing through my mind. Although I still felt a little uneasy inside, this experience taught me that I was not as likely to embarrass myself as I had imagined. Perhaps next time, I will do even better.

The classroom was filled with a tense atmosphere. Sunlight streamed through the window onto the floor, casting mottled shadows. Sitting at my desk, I felt my palms sweat slightly, and a sense of unease rose in my heart. I knew it would soon be my turn to go up and tell the story. The teacher stood at the podium, flipping through the list in her hand over and over, and finally called my name. My heartbeat instantly quickened, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. I slowly stood up, feeling my legs tremble uncontrollably.

The students around me were whispering to one another, and their faint murmurs reached my ears, making me even more anxious. As I walked toward the podium, every step felt unbearably heavy. The moment I stepped up, my gaze swept across the entire class, whose eyes were all fixed on me. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself.

“Today I’m going to talk about...” I began to stammer out the prepared story, my voice sounding urgent and strained. I tried hard to keep smiling, but it felt like the corners of my mouth were twitching uncontrollably. As I told the story, many images flashed through my mind. I worried I would forget my lines, and I feared they would laugh at me. I kept repeating to myself, “Don’t make a mistake, don’t let them down.” However, halfway through the story, I really did forget the next part.

My mind suddenly went completely blank, and I felt a suffocating tension in my chest; my palms began to sweat. I paused for a moment. The room was utterly silent, as if even the clock on the wall had stopped ticking. Isecretly glanced at the teacher’s expression, hoping for help, but all I saw was a slight frown. The inner voice grew more intense: “They must think I’m stupid. They must be laughing at me.”

Finally, I remembered what came next and managed to finish the story. My voice was slightly hoarse from nervousness. When I finished, there was scattered applause in the classroom. My face began to burn, and my heartbeat was still racing. Back at my seat, I kept replaying every detail from just now, trying to find where I had gone wrong.

That night, my parents asked me how the competition went. I tried to act relaxed and told them it was nothing special, but inside I still couldn’t shake off that feeling of shame. Over the next few days, I tried my best to avoid discussing it with my classmates, afraid they would bring it up again. I even began to wonder whether I should take part in similar activities in the future.

In the classroom, incandescent lights were on, and the hard edge of my chair dug into my thigh. The teacher stood at the front of the room, holding a paper-cutting piece in her hands, looking like a butterfly spreading its wings. “Today, everyone will be doing paper cutting—cut out a pattern you like.” Her voice was gentle, but to me it felt a little condescending. My palms began to get sweaty. I looked around and saw that everyone seemed excitedly opening their colored paper. I wasn’t sure I could do it well, but I still picked a sheet of yellow paper from the materials box on the desk.

The scissors felt heavy in my hands, and the cold metal edges pressed against my fingers. I tried to cut out a heart, but the paper kept tearing in the wrong direction, leaving the edges rough and ragged. My lips unconsciously clenched tight. I didn’t dare look at what the classmate beside me was doing, but from the corner of my eye I could see his paper cut already vaguely taking on the shape of a flower. I tried hard to concentrate, but the more I wanted to cut out a perfect shape, the more my hands shook. Suddenly, I made a mistake and cut off one corner; one side of the heart broke off completely, and inside me it felt as if something had crashed to the floor. I couldn’t help lowering my head to look at the desk, feeling my cheeks grow hot and my breathing become rapid.

“Ha ha, look at what they’re cutting!” I heard two boys in the back row speaking in low voices and laughing, but my ears instantly magnified the sound, as if it were directed straight at me. I jerked my head up to look, and their gazes brushed past me before turning back to their own desks. But I bit my lip, and the laughter kept replaying in my mind over and over. “They must think I’m so stupid,” the thought crept into my chest like a cold wind. I wanted to hide the botched piece on the desk with my elbow, but the yellow paper was still exposed there. My stomach began to feel a little off, as if it had been twisted.

The teacher walked over and glanced down at my desk. “Scissors are hard to control, aren’t they? Try not to use too much force.” Her tone was very light, but in my ears it sounded like a silent sigh. I nodded, too afraid to look up at her. She turned to other students, and I felt relieved, yet also strangely empty from being ignored. I lowered my head and picked up the scissors again, the muscles in my wrist stiff and tight, not knowing why I was still continuing.

In the end, my work was a “broken heart,” all its edges unevenly curled up. The teacher had us put our finished pieces on the classroom display wall. I shuffled over and stuck mine in a corner. I felt as if there were eyes on my back, always sensing someone spying on my work. I buried my head and sat back down, clenching my hands tightly under the desk, my sweaty palms making my fingertips sting.

That night in bed, I kept thinking back to the two boys’ laughter. I seemed to be able to hear them talking at home about my awful paper cutting, even making exaggerated gestures of mockery. My heart beat fast, and each time the scene replayed in my mind, I felt more and more incapable. Even after several days, when I saw the works on the display wall, I still didn’t dare look directly at my yellow “broken heart.”

The kitchen air was a little warm, and orange-yellow light spilled across the floor through the curtains. The pan was making a sizzling sound—it was Mom frying eggs. I stood beside her on tiptoe, watching the yolk in the pan slowly develop golden edges, while the whites were as soft as snow. As I breathed in the aroma drifting through the air, I felt my stomach start to rumble.

Mom gently flipped the egg with a spatula. “Watch closely. This way, it won’t break when you turn it,” she said. I nodded, my eyes fixed firmly on her movements, wanting to memorize this “secret trick,” even though I still wasn’t sure when I would ever use it.

Mom handed me an egg. “Go ahead and try.” A little nervous, I took it, feeling that it was cool in my hand. I tapped it lightly against the rim of a bowl, and the tiny crack let me see the yolk slowly spilling out. But then the shell broke a little more than I had expected. I panicked. “Mom, is this okay?” Mom smiled. “It’s fine. We’ll just fry it and eat it.” She used the spatula to help me pick out the broken bits of shell. The pan kept steaming, and the kitchen was filled with the smell of hot oil and eggs. Suddenly, my mistake didn’t seem so important anymore.

“This egg is almost done. Add a little salt,” Mom said. I picked up the salt shaker and tried to sprinkle a little onto the egg, but my palms were sweating a bit, as if each grain of salt determined the flavor. I held my breath, feeling like a magician performing a wondrous ritual. Seeing how tense I looked, Mom patted my head. “Actually, cooking isn’t that hard. Just do your best and put your heart into it.” I looked down at the egg in the pan and felt it gently sizzle, as if it were saying, “It’s okay. You’re already doing great.”

After breakfast was served, I saw that my fried egg was a little less neatly shaped than Mom’s, but I still thought it was especially delicious. I picked up my fork and poked the yolk. It slowly flowed out, like a reward for my efforts. “This egg was fried by me!” I said proudly, my voice carrying a hint of satisfaction. Mom smiled and nodded. “That’s right. Give it a try.” I took a bite, and the flavor carried a familiar warmth. Although I knew Mom may have helped me a little, I still felt that this egg was almost entirely made by me.

After breakfast that day, I kept wandering around the kitchen, looking for other things I could “try,” like cutting fruit or setting out bowls and chopsticks. It was a long time before I went back to the living room to play with building blocks, but in my heart, the kitchen always felt like a place full of possibilities. Even in the days that followed, whenever Mom fried eggs, I would run over to watch and couldn’t help saying, “Let me try again!”

The floor of the music classroom felt a bit chilly, and I sat in the chair by the window, rubbing my fingers together with a slight tremble. The cold wind outside made the glass faintly shiver, and my gaze moved past row after row of staff notation to the big clock behind the teacher. The hands moved second by second, and my heartbeat quickened along with them, as if the ticking were striking my heart. Today I was going to play a piano solo in front of the whole class, and I was terribly nervous.

"Next, please come up one by one and perform the pieces you’ve prepared," the teacher said, her voice gentle yet firm, like an echo coming from afar. I tried to nod slightly and do my best to look confident, but my stomach tightened further with nerves.

When my name was called, a wave of heat surged up from the soles of my feet, and I stiffly walked forward, feeling my palms slick with sweat. Sitting down on the bench, my fingertips touched the piano keys, and the icy sensation made me shiver. I secretly took a breath, but after only a measure, I stumbled because of a careless mistake and lost the rhythm.

"It’s all right, take it slowly," the teacher encouraged me gently, but my face felt burning hot, and my ears were filled with my classmates’ whispered voices. In my mind, it was as if there were a little figurecontinuously repeating, "Everyone is making fun of you." I tried again, but my fingers, too tense, felt as though they were touching scorching flames, and I managed to finish the piece only in fragments.

I hurried away from the piano, and when I returned to my seat, I felt utterly drained, with waves of tingling crawling over my scalp and my cheeks flushed red. I buried my face in my hands, trying to shut out the sounds around me, while I kept blaming myself inside: "How could this happen? Why couldn’t I play properly?"

After class, I walked home with the messed-up melody still echoing in my ears. The wind swept up fallen leaves, and the branches creaked, as if mocking my failure. I desperately tried to throw off those embarrassing memories, but the scene kept replaying itself in my mind, and my fingers were still trembling slightly.

That night, lying in bed, I kept turning over my performance in music class. It felt as though a stone were pressing on my heart, making it hard to breathe. I rehearsed it over and over in my mind, trying to imagine a flawless ending. Though these efforts were useless, I still couldn’t stop.

A few days later, I was still repeatedly dwelling on those details, and whenever I thought that someone might laugh at me because of my mistake, it felt as if millions of tiny insects were crawling in my chest. Even in my dreams, I would suddenly wake up, as though that endless sneering laughter were sounding again in my ears.

As the pencil slid across the paper, that delicate scratching sound was drowned out by the whole classroom’s rustling of pages and quiet chatter. I sat at the desk near the window, sunlight slanting through the glass and falling along the edge of the desk, but my attention was completely drawn to the lines on the paper. After drawing for a few minutes, I suddenly realized that I had just drawn one line wrong. A line that was supposed to be a downward branch had accidentally veered to one side, like a crease bent by the wind. My heart began to race, and tiny beads of sweat started forming on my forehead.

“What are you drawing?” a classmate beside me asked softly.

“Um, a tree,” I replied in a low voice, trying to sound calm. But my eyes stayed fixed on that wrong line, as if with every glance it became more glaring.

I tried to erase it with the eraser, but it left a gray smudge on the paper. The more I erased, the worse it got. I felt as if an invisible hand had clutched my stomach, and my breathing grew rapid. I lowered my head and covered the paper with my palm, afraid that others would notice my “mistake.”

“Look, I’m drawing a little cat!” the classmate across from me said excitedly, holding up her picture. I forced out a strained smile, but before I could praise her, tears suddenly welled up uncontrollably. I hurriedly lowered my head and wiped my eyes with my sleeve, but the tears blurred my vision and the drawing on the paper began to fade into indistinctness.

“What’s wrong?” another desk mate asked quietly.

“It’s nothing, I just... didn’t draw it well.” My voice trembled slightly as I tried to hold back my crying.

At that moment, the teacher walked over, bent down, and looked at my drawing. “Oh, is this a tree? You’ve drawn it quite nicely. Why are you crying?”

Her tone was very gentle, but I felt a sour ache in my chest, and more tears came spilling out. “I drew one line wrong...” I said softly, my voice so low it was almost inaudible.

The teacher seemed to freeze for a moment, then gently patted my shoulder and said, “Everyone makes mistakes. Art doesn’t really have absolute right and wrong. Maybe the wrong part can become something special. How about trying to turn that line into something else? Like a leaf?”

I nodded, but I still felt sad—in my mind, that line had already ruined the whole drawing, and even all my effort. I tried to follow the teacher’s suggestion and turn the wrong line into a leaf, but it seemed even more out of place. The sounds around me grew louder and louder, and I felt like I was transparent, with everyone’s gaze examining my mistake. In fact, they probably hadn’t even noticed my drawing at all.
