That afternoon after I got home, I kept staring blankly at the drawing. I tried picking up the pencil and continuing, but my hand paused in midair and never came down. In the end, I tucked the drawing into a book, closed it, and put it into my backpack. For some reason, I felt that hiding it away would make me feel a little better.

In the next few days, I tried my best to avoid talking about the art class. Every time I saw the book with the drawing tucked inside, my heart would start racing, as if it were some forbidden thing. It wasn’t until a week later, when I accidentally opened the book and saw the drawing, that the sadness in my heart eased a little. Although that wrong line was still glaring, I began to think that it really did look a bit like a strange leaf.

That day, the sunlight was fierce.

I remember the light striking the concrete of the playground, reflecting a blinding white. I was sitting on the edge of a bench, turning a little plastic toy in my hands—the kind everyone in class wanted to touch, with movable joints and a bright orange-red color. I was just waiting, waiting for someone to come and call me to run along with them.

Then that voice came.

“It was you who broke it, wasn’t it!”

I looked up, and before I could even make out who it was, my heartbeat had already slipped out of rhythm ahead of me. It felt as if something in my chest had suddenly gone taut. I looked down at the toy in my hands—it was intact, the joints were still there, the color was still there, nothing was broken.

“I didn’t break it.”

My voice came out much softer than I had expected. Hearing it, I felt as though it had drifted from far away, light, without any weight.

Footsteps gathered from all around. I could feel eyes settling on me, layer by layer, like something pressing down. My palms started to sweat. I gripped the toy tighter, my knuckles turning a little white, a little painful, but I didn’t let go—letting go would have meant admitting to something.

“You did it on purpose!”

I wanted to explain. I arranged words frantically in my mind, trying to find a sentence that would make everyone listen, but nothing came out. I glanced toward where the adults were standing; there were teachers there, people chatting, and no one was looking this way.

Then came that sentence.

A classmate I usually got along with turned around and said to the others, “Don’t bother with them anymore. They just like to cause trouble.”

I heard footsteps leaving. One step, two steps, farther and farther away.

I didn’t go after them. Not because I didn’t want to, but because my legs wouldn’t obey me. I just stood there. The sounds of the playground were still there, the laughter was still there, but everything had become distant, as if separated by some kind of barrier. I stared at the toy in my hands, trying hard not to let the tears in my eyes fall, because I knew that if I cried, it would only get worse.

When the bell rang, I followed at the very back of the line back to the classroom, head lowered, footsteps light, as if I were practicing how to disappear.

When I got home, the sound of my backpack hitting the floor was louder than usual. Someone asked me how my day was, and I said it was fine. I didn’t mention what happened on the playground, not because I didn’t want to, but because I didn’t know where to begin, and I wasn’t sure whether saying it out loud would only lead to, “Are you sure you didn’t really break it?”

I lay face down on the bed alone, and when the tears came, they came without a sound. There was a dull, heavy pressure in my chest, as if something was stuck there, unable to be coughed up or swallowed down.

For several days after that, whenever I ran into classmates in the hallway, I would lower my head first. Not because I didn’t want to greet them, but because I didn’t know how they saw me now. I kept replaying that afternoon in my head, thinking that if I had spoken louder then, if I had handed the toy over immediately, if I hadn’t been sitting on that bench—

But the toy had clearly been fine.

I knew it was fine.

The classroom was filled with the faint smell of chalk dust, and the occasional sound of car horns drifted in from outside the window, distracting me from time to time. The teacher was standing in front of the blackboard, writing the new lesson with white chalk, each stroke making a crisp sound in the air. I gripped my pencil tightly, my heart beating a little too fast, always afraid the teacher might suddenly call my name. Whenever she paused and looked over the class, I felt an invisible pressure, as if her gaze could see straight through me.

“Be sure to listen carefully in class and don’t get distracted,” the teacher reminded everyone. I immediately straightened up. But just then, I suddenly heard her say in a slightly stern tone, “Some people, if they don’t pay attention in class, will eventually fall behind everyone else.” In an instant, my heart seemed to leap into my throat. “Is she talking about me? Did I do something wrong again?” I thought, my forehead starting to sweat, my palms feeling icy.

I quickly reviewed how I had behaved in class just now—had I turned to talk to the classmate beside me? Had I missed the teacher’s questions? I tried hard to search my mind for any possible detail, but the more I looked, the more all the details seemed to blur, as if they belonged to another lifetime. It felt like standing at the edge of a cliff, with a bottomless sense of unease constantly rushing in.

“If the teacher criticizes me in front of everyone, will my classmates start to dislike me too?” My mind raced through a string of worst-case scenarios, and the fear of being isolated kept growing, like a huge stone pressing on my chest. I clenched the pencil in my hand even tighter, as if it were my only lifeline.

At that moment, all the other sounds in the classroom seemed to fade away, leaving only the sound of my own heartbeat echoing in my ears. My stomach felt strangely tight, as if it had been bound up, and I didn’t dare move even a little.

When the bell rang, I walked hesitantly to the teacher’s desk and asked tentatively, “Teacher, the thing you just said—did I do something wrong?”

The teacher lifted her head, and instead of the reproach I had imagined, she smiled in mild surprise and said, “Oh, dear, I was talking about the whole class, not anyone in particular. You’ve always done very well.” “Really?” I asked, half believing her, and the stone in my heart eased a little.

That night, the teacher’s gentle words still echoed in my mind, and my mood gradually relaxed. Even so, that small unease still seemed like a shadow hidden deep inside me, always emerging at some quiet moment and making me repeatedly scrutinize every little thing I did.

Even when it was only a misunderstanding, I still couldn’t easily erase that shadow of worry, as if it had taken root and begun to grow, lingering in my heart.

Today was a special event for our class—a recitation contest. The teacher said it could help improve our expressive ability, but I felt incredibly nervous. I stood at the front of the classroom. The lights on the ceiling were a little dazzling, as if they were shining on me and magnifying every flaw. The chalk dust on the blackboard gave off a faint, pungent smell, and my palms began to sweat. I couldn’t help imagining the worst-case scenario: if I got stuck, would everyone laugh at me? The nightmares I had had before came flooding back, and my heart started beating faster, as if it were about to leap out of my chest.

The teacher smiled and signaled for me to begin. I swallowed, my throat feeling as if something were blocking it. I started reciting, pushing out each word one by one, only to hear my own voice echoing in the classroom. In the pauses, the echo sounded even lonelier. My voice seemed to tremble, and I heard classmates whispering in my ear. I desperately wanted to hear what they were saying, but all I could hear was my own heartbeat growing louder and louder. My speaking pace kept getting faster as I tried to finish this ordeal as quickly as possible.

The teacher across from me said in a gentle voice, “Slow down, take a breath, keep it up.” I tried to slow down, but I accidentally got stuck. My face began to burn, and that feeling of embarrassment made me too afraid to look directly into the eyes of those looking at me. I kept asking myself: were they making fun of me? Was I about to embarrass myself again? A wave of shame surged through me.

After the contest ended, I silently returned to my seat. A classmate beside me gave me a comforting smile, but inside I kept belittling myself: how could I be so miserable? I don’t want to go through such failure again. Although the teacher praised every student who participated at the end, I still felt it was only meant as consolation. I couldn’t believe I could also be called a brave person.

That afternoon, I could no longer concentrate in class, and my mind kept replaying the embarrassing moments from the morning. At night, lying in bed, I tried hard not to think about it, but every time I closed my eyes, that moment was like a shadow that would not go away.

A few days later, I still felt unsettled because of that recitation. Every time I walked into the classroom, there was a dull pain in my stomach, as if I were ready to make a mistake again at any moment. But I knew that if I kept sinking into these emotions, I would only make myself more miserable. Silently, I told myself that next time, I must be a little more confident, even if it only meant not letting my inner demons win.

The classroom air was thick with the smell of paint and glue, and sunlight streamed through the lattice windows onto the floor. I sat on my little stool, staring at the crumpled paper and a few broken straws in my hands, trying to piece them together into something that resembled a tree. The art teacher came over and stood behind me. “Hurry up, it’ll be time to present soon,” she said in a calm voice, but I felt my ears burn and my throat tighten. “Almost done,” I heard myself whisper, but my hands had already started to tremble, my glue-covered fingers sticking together in a lump, and there was only one thought in my mind: this looks terrible, so ugly.

By the time it was my turn to present at the front, my palms were already drenched in sweat. The other students’work were bright and colorful—some were flowers made of strips of cloth, others were little animals molded from clay—while the “tree” in my hands looked like a heap of messy trash. Standing at the podium, I felt the classroom suddenly go very quiet, with only the pounding of my own heartbeat thumping in my ears. A few boys nearby were covering their mouths and laughing. “What is that?” a girl’s voice clearly drifted over. I tried hard to swallow and forced out, “This is a... tree.” But before I had even finished, the whole classroom erupted into laughter.

My face started burning, tears welled up in my eyes, but I bit my lip hard and refused to let them fall. “Alright, alright, everyone quiet down. Next person,” the teacher cut off the laughter, but I could feel a hint of perfunctoriness in her tone. I hurried back to my seat, not daring to look at anyone else, only staring at the tips of my shoes, my heart pounding so fast it felt like it was about to burst out of my chest.

It wasn’t until the end-of-class bell rang that I finally breathed a little easier. I pretended to rummage through my backpack, and when most everyone else had left, I slowly stood up. I don’t remember how I got home; I only remember that all the way there my head was filled with that laughter and the image of myself standing at the podium like a joke. It felt as if a stone had been lodged in my chest the entire time, and my stomach had started to ache dully as well.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mind filled with those laughs and that girl’s voice—“What is that?” I kept replaying my appearance on the podium, and the more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt. I even started hating myself for not being able to do better. I felt like I must have been the stupidest person in the whole class, unable to even make the simplest craft. Later, Mom knocked on my door. “Are you asleep?” she asked. I hesitated and said, “Not yet.” She came in, touched my forehead, and asked, “What’s wrong? Were you unhappy today?” I shook my head. “Nothing.” But I noticed my voice was still a little hoarse.

It took several days before I gradually recovered from that embarrassment, but every time I thought about that day, my face would still burn. After that, in art class, I always tried to sit in the corner, afraid of being noticed by anyone.

I stood on the elementary school playground, the morning chill seeping from the ground into my toes. Around me, I could hear other children talking and laughing, mixed with the teacher’s whistle, sounding especially clear in the crisp air. I rubbed my hands together hard, hoping to warm up a little, but the tension in my heart seemed to lower my body temperature. The teacher walked to the front and began leading us in morning exercises. Her voice was very clear, and I could hear her commands one after another: “One, two, three, four!”

As I raised my hands, I felt my stomach tighten and my heartbeat quicken. I looked down at my feet, worried that my movements weren’t coordinated enough or that I was half a beat slower than everyone else. Beside me, the sounds of my classmates’ breathing mingled together like a chaotic piece of music. I tried hard to keep up with the rhythm, and out of the corner of my eye I glimpsed a child nearby. He lightly kicked his shoe to show he was bored, but I felt as if he were hinting that I wasn’t doing well enough.

“Don’t you find it boring?” he asked me softly.

“Not really,” I forced out with a smile.

My heart was pounding even harder, like a drum. Cold sweat slid down my forehead, and I quickly wiped it away with the back of my hand, worried someone would notice. Suddenly, the thought flashed through my mind that the teacher might come over and point out the imperfections in my movements, and the feeling of being watched by everyone terrified me.

Only when we finished the last movement did I finally breathe a little easier. When the teacher announced that we could go to the classroom, my legs were trembling. On the way back, every step felt especially heavy. The other children were chatting and laughing, sharing the amusing things that had happened these past few days, but I had no mind to join them at all.

That night, lying in bed with my eyes closed, I kept replaying every movement from morning exercises in my mind. I worried that if it happened again tomorrow, I would still disappoint everyone. I tossed and turned until late at night before finally drifting into a dazed sleep. After a few days, that feeling gradually faded, but I knew that next time morning exercises came around, I would fall into the same pattern again.

On a hot afternoon, sunlight streamed through the iron windows of the repair shop, scattering mottled patches of light across the floor. The air was thick with the smell of engine oil, and all kinds of tools lay strewn about. Grandfather was busy in the corner repairing an old bicycle, the sound of a hammer striking metal echoing through the small space. I always liked lingering here, watching him work with such focus. This time, though, I felt uneasy, because Grandfather had been cold to me that morning. My heart was pounding, my palms a little sweaty, afraid I might do something wrong and make him angry.

“Grandpa, can I help you?” I asked cautiously, swallowing hard and trying to make my voice sound more confident.

He looked up, wiped his hands with a cloth, and said expressionlessly, “No, you need to stay focused on your own work. Go play.”

Those words pierced my heart like a thorn. I walked outside the shop and sat on the steps, filled with confusion and bitterness. Why wouldn’t Grandpa ever let me help? Had I done something wrong? I began to go over every interaction I’d had with Grandpa over the past few days, trying to find the reason. It was as if everything was my fault, as if I were so incapable.

A breeze blew by, carrying the earthy scent of the distant rice fields. I looked up and found Grandpa chatting with a man I didn’t know. Their voices drifted over faintly. “That child is too sensitive, always thinking they’re not good enough.” Grandpa’s voice carried helplessness and disappointment, and it made my heart tighten.

I felt a sharp pain in my stomach, and tears began to fall uncontrollably. So Grandpa thought I was a nuisance. I lowered my head and stared at my shoes, thinking about what I could do to keep Grandpa from being disappointed. Maybe I should find my own way to prove myself.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed. Grandpa’s words kept echoing in my mind. Although I understood that Grandpa meant well, the feeling of being inadequate would not let me go. I looked at the stars outside the window and told myself that one day I would make Grandpa proud. The next day, I ran to the repair shop early in the morning and secretly tried to fix an old bicycle, only to end up with my hands covered in black grease while the bike still wouldn’t move. I sat on the floor, looking at my filthy hands, and tears welled up again.

A few days later, I worked hard to learn every detail about bicycles, determined to learn how to repair them. Although Grandpa didn’t show any obvious change, I gradually got used to meeting my inner unease and sense of inadequacy with effort.

The sunlight on the playground made my face feel a little hot, and the smell of sweat mixed with the rubbery scent of the ground, which was a bit pungent. Everyone was gathered around for jump rope, and when it was my turn, my heart was pounding and my ears were buzzing. I stared at the long rope glinting in the sun and tried my best to look calm. One classmate shouted, “Hurry up, don’t waste time,” dragging out the words with a hint of impatience. I immediately felt like he was saying I was holding everyone back, even though he hadn’t called me out by name. I suddenly became nervous, my mind in complete chaos, and my feet seemed nailed to the ground.

“Jump already!” another voice interrupted my thoughts. I forced myself to step forward and tried to match the rhythm of the rope, but I nearly stepped on it with the very first move. I heard a few quiet snickers from behind me, and they stabbed into my back like needles. “Why are you so slow? Honestly…” a girl said next, and although her tone wasn’t very harsh, to me it already felt like confirmation: they thought I was a nuisance. I gritted my teeth, stared at the rope’s swing, and tried hard not to make a mistake, but my knees grew stiffer and my movements more awkward. In the end, I still tripped over the rope, my whole body jerking forward as if yanked by something, and I barely managed to steady myself.

“See, I told you!” someone said softly. I didn’t dare turn around; I could only stare at my shoes, feeling my face burn. In my mind, it felt as if someone was constantly stabbing me with thoughts: Did they think I was stupid? Did they not want me to play with them at all? No one had said anything like that directly, but I felt that meaning in every word. I couldn’t help thinking: Am I not good enough? Is there always something I do wrong, making people dislike me? At that moment, I desperately wanted somewhere to hide.

When the game ended, I made an excuse that I needed to get water and hurried away. I ran to the small pavilion by the playground, braced my hands on the table, and tried to calm my breathing, but the heaviness in my chest wouldn’t go away. I tried to tell myself that maybe I was overthinking, but those snickers and tones kept replaying in my mind. My stomach started to ache faintly, my palms were sweaty, and in the end I didn’t even drink any water—I simply squatted in the corner and blanked out.

That night, lying in bed, I was still thinking about what that girl had meant. Was it accidental, or intentional? I even thought further: Did everyone actually have a problem with me, just too embarrassed to say it directly? These thoughts kept me tossing and turning, unable to fall asleep, until very late, when I finally drifted off in a daze.

On the playground, colorful balloons swayed in the breeze, and laughter and chatter filled the whole space. We sat around a table covered with a bright yellow tablecloth, with all kinds of snacks and a big cake on it. The cake was my favorite chocolate flavor, and the thick layer of cream made it impossible not to want to lick a bit of it. The classmates around us were buzzing with excitement, making the atmosphere lively beyond measure. I sat there and felt someone looking at me. I looked up and saw the little girl sitting across from me glance at me with what I thought was a very strange look. In that instant, my heart sank, as if something bad was about to happen.

“Does she hate me?” My brain started racing, and my heartbeat quickened too, like countless little drums were being beaten in my ear. That familiar sense of unease came rushing back, and my palms began to sweat. I kept trying to smile, but panic kept gnawing away at my confidence. “Is she mocking me?” I lowered my head and stared at the pattern on the tablecloth, trying to find something else to distract myself.

The birthday party went on, music started playing, and everyone began standing up to dance. But I felt as if my legs were nailed to the floor, unable to move. The feeling that everyone was staring at me made me utterly embarrassed. I struggled to raise a hand and wipe the sweat from my forehead, thinking: if someone asks me why I’m not dancing, what should I do?

“What’s wrong?” A classmate patted me on the shoulder, and I was startled, my heart skipping a beat. “Nothing, I’m fine, just a little hot.” I forced out a smile, trying to hide the turmoil inside.

After the party ended, I went home, still unable to calm down. I kept replaying the little girl’s expression, trying to figure out the meaning behind that look. That night, lying in bed, I kept reliving what had happened on the playground that day in my head. I imagined all kinds of conversations and scenarios, wishing I had been able to respond more naturally then.

The next day, when I returned to school, I noticed the little girl walking toward me, and another wave of unease rose in my heart. She smiled and told me that she only wanted to ask whether I had brought back the book I had lent her last time. It turned out that there had been absolutely nothing unfriendly in her look that day, nothing at all like what I had imagined. Hearing her say that, my tension finally eased.

Although the misunderstanding was resolved, I still felt that I was far too sensitive, and this habit of overinterpreting other people’s emotions always left me exhausted.

Colored pencils brushed across the paper, making a faint rustling sound. The classroom was filled with the mixed smell of wood shavings and paint, and from the playground outside came the occasional shout, separated from us by thick glass into another world. I sat in the back row, looking down at my half-finished work—a ship, pitching on the waves I had tried so hard to draw. I thought it was pretty good. But the moment those three words—“pretty good”—landed in my mind, they began to loosen.

“Your waves look so weird. They look like marshmallows.”

A classmate in the front row turned around and glanced at my drawing. Their tone was light, like they were just saying it offhandedly, with even a hint of a smile at the corner of their mouth. But the instant those words reached my ears, I felt each one bounce against my skin. My hand froze in midair, the brush suspended without moving.

*Are they serious? Or are they making fun of me?*

“Is it really that weird?” I asked in a low voice, my words almost swallowed by the surrounding noise.

“Yeah. The boat doesn’t even look like a boat. It looks like a big egg.” They shrugged and had already turned back to keep drawing their own picture.

My face flushed at once, as if something inside me had been set on fire. I didn’t dare look up, afraid of meeting anyone’s eyes. Images began replaying automatically in my head: the teacher walking over, stopping at my desk, frowning; classmates turning sideways and whispering; everyone wondering how I could draw like this. My chest tightened, my stomach felt as if someone had grabbed it and twisted, leaving a dull ache. Sweat broke out in my palms, making the brush slippery in my grip.

“I was just doodling. I drew it casually,” I blurted out, my voice rushed, as if trying to block something.

They didn’t say anything else.

I stared at the ship on the paper, and the more I looked, the stranger it felt. The colors suddenly seemed dirty, the lines like twisted snakes. I wanted to tear the whole page apart, but my hand didn’t move—if I tore it up, someone would see, and they’d know I was falling apart. I tried fixing a few strokes, only to find that the more I changed it, the worse it became. My fingers trembled slightly, and the tip of the pencil left an unintended mark on the paper.

For the next ten minutes, I hardly drew at all. The voice in my head kept looping: *Will everyone think I’m terrible? Do I really not have any talent for drawing? Why do I always make everything so bad?*

When the bell rang, my scalp was already tingling, and my palms were slick with sweat.

After school, I folded the drawing up and stuffed it into the very bottom of my backpack, underneath everything else. During dinner I stayed silent, pushing my chopsticks around in my bowl. Someone asked me what was wrong, and I said nothing. But that sentence kept replaying in my head, and I even started to feel like I could hear someone laughing—though no one was laughing at all.

I turned on my desk lamp, wanting to draw another picture. After only a few strokes, I felt it was pointless, pushed the pencil aside, climbed into bed, and stared at the ceiling.

In the art classes over the next few days, I began sliding my paper toward myself, trying not to let the person next to me see it. I also started sneaking glances at other people’s work, trying to find some place, some stroke, where I might measure up. But no matter how I looked, I always felt like my drawing was something a younger child had scribbled at random, separated from everyone else by a distance I couldn’t put into words.

I didn’t know what that distance was called back then. I only knew that it had always been there.

The sunlight fell on our faces as we stood in a golden field of sunflowers. The teacher divided us into groups, and I was put with several classmates. We ran through the field, and I could smell the mix of earth and flowers in the air. Suddenly, the classmates gathered together and started whispering. I heard them mention my name, and my heart began to race. “Do you hear what they’re saying?” I couldn’t help asking one of them. He just said softly, “Nothing, don’t worry about it.” But my mind was still in turmoil. I kept imagining that they might be talking about something I had done badly, or mocking some embarrassing moment of mine. My palms began to sweat, and my stomach churned uneasily. I forced myself to act relaxed and smile, but the smile felt stiff. My body tensed, and I tried not to look at their faces, afraid I might see some kind of hint again. I felt the lushness of the sunflowers around me, yet it seemed as if I were being pressed down by that vitality.  

At lunchtime, we sat on the grass, and I kept my distance from the other students, avoiding eye contact. My inner voice kept blaming me: Why do I always care so much about what others think? Why can’t I just relax? Why do I always have to act so stupid? When they joked around, I couldn’t help but joke about myself as well: “Am I really such a joke?” I managed a forced smile, trying to ease the shame inside me.  

After lunch, we went on a hike, and I stayed at the very back the whole time, as if I wanted to cut myself off from everyone. When I got home, I was utterly exhausted and collapsed onto the bed. A few days passed, yet the uneasiness still seemed impossible to fully shake off. Every time I thought about what happened that day, I felt a heaviness in my chest. My mother noticed that I was troubled and couldn’t help asking, “How was your day?” I simply shook my head, not knowing how to explain. Although it was over, its shadow still lingered in my heart.

The sun was just right, not too glaring. Mom moved the big basin onto the balcony, and I followed with a small one, which held a few of my clothes. The balcony floor was a little hot, and when my feet stepped on the tiles it felt like stepping on sun-warmed sand, with a bit of heat. Mom always liked having me do housework with her. She said habits should be formed from a young age. I wasn’t very happy about it, but I didn’t dare say so, and could only keep my head down and wash my own clothes.

The water in the basin reflected the sunlight with a slightly dazzling glare. I rubbed the clothes with my hands, and my palms had a wrinkled feeling. Mom would occasionally glance at me, probably to make sure I wasn’t being lazy. “Don’t just scrub the edges of the clothes. Focus on the dirty spots, like here at the cuffs.” She pointed at the cuff of the T-shirt in my hands. I looked and saw it really was a bit yellowed.

The clothesline on the balcony swayed slowly in the wind, and the few clothespins on it lightly knocked against each other, making a faint ticking sound. I stared at them for a while and actually thought it was kind of fun. Every time Mom asked me to hang clothes, I had to tiptoe and stretch hard to reach the highest line. Sometimes I couldn’t reach, so I would use the clothes hanger instead. For me, this process felt like completing a small challenge, though my arms always ended up sore.

“Wring the water out a bit more before you bring it over, or the clothesline will drip,” Mom reminded me. I nodded and twisted the clothes hard. Water squeezed out of the fabric and ran down my wrists, feeling a little cold. I carried the nearly wrung-out clothes to the line, draped them over it, and secured them with clothespins. When the clothespin clamped down on the clothes, it made a click.

Sunlight filtered through the hanging clothes and spilled down; the clothes on the line cast shadows of different colors. I looked up at those shadows for a while, spacing out, and Mom smiled and shot me a glare, saying, “Don’t be lazy. There are still quite a few clothes left to wash!” I quickly ran back and kept washing.

The whole afternoon passed like that. By the time the last piece of laundry was hung up, my hands had grown a little stiff. Mom patted me on the shoulder. “All right, go wash your hands.” I ran to the sink and scrubbed my hands hard. When I rinsed away the foam, it felt a little refreshing.

That night, during dinner, I secretly glanced at the balcony. The wind had stopped, and the clothes hung quietly there, like rows of little flags. I thought to myself that by tomorrow, these clothes would be dry, and they would smell a little like sunshine.

Today was an activity day, and we were on the school playground. The sunlight was harsh, and I squinted as I watched everyone choosing game partners. I hoped someone would take the initiative to ask me, but everyone seemed busy, gathering in threes and fives. I stood off to the side, and unease began to creep into my heart.

Suddenly, Xiaoming came over and said, “Hey, we’re going to play hide-and-seek. Come join us!” I felt a surge of joy and nodded, saying, “Okay!” I tried to make my voice sound cheerful, but I still couldn’t hide my nervousness. Xiaoming turned and walked away, and I followed behind him.

The sandy ground on the playground gave off a warm feeling under the sunlight, and it felt soft beneath my feet. I tried not to seem too excited, so I wouldn’t look silly.

But soon I realized everyone had already found places to hide, and no one told me where I should hide. I stood there, my heart pounding, feeling my cheeks growing red and my palms getting sweaty. I muttered softly, “Did they forget about me?”

I finally mustered the courage to ask Xiaoli, who was hiding, “Where should I hide?” But she only replied vaguely, “Just find some place.” Then she hurried off. I looked at her retreating figure and felt a wave of disappointment, as if the whole playground were mocking me.

The game began, and I had no choice but to hide in a small corner at the edge of the playground, where there were a few stones. I curled up, feeling my heartbeat grow faster and faster, like a drum beating beside my ear. Xiaoli’s answer kept echoing in my mind: “Just find some place.”

After the game ended, I slowly walked back to the classroom, feeling heavy all over, while the same question repeated in my mind: “Does no one want to play with me?” The air in the classroom felt stifling, and the smell of chalk dust made me feel oppressed.

On the way home from school, I kept thinking about it, full of self-doubt. That night, when Mom asked how things had gone at school, I just kept my head down and said, “It was okay.” Then I quickly ran back to my room.

Lying on my bed, I stared at the ceiling, feeling a little sad and ashamed, wondering whether all of this happened because I had done something wrong. A few days later, although the incident gradually faded, I still often reflected to myself: what should I do so I won’t be overlooked?

I stood in a toilet stall, gripping the hook on the stall door so tightly that my fingertips had gone white. The walls of the stall were painted a dull yellow, and it felt as if they were about to swallow me whole. I could smell the pungent scent of disinfectant mixed with some damp, moldy odor, making my stomach churn even more. My heartbeat started racing again, and my ears were filled with that thudding “thump—thump—thump” sound, as if each beat were reminding me of what had just happened.

During the break, I accidentally knocked over the pencil case of the classmate sitting next to me in the classroom, and all the pencils rolled onto the floor. He stood up and said harshly to me, “Why are you so stupid? You always bump into my things!” His voice stabbed into my ears like needles, and my face burned at once. I whispered an apology: “I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to.” But he didn’t listen at all and kept shouting, “You say sorry every time, but you never change! Is there something wrong with your brain?”

His words shattered the last bit of self-respect I had managed to piece together. I felt the whole room suddenly go quiet, as if all the classmates were staring at me and laughing. A crazy image flashed through my mind: they were gathered in a circle, pointing at me and laughing, saying I was an idiot, someone who should never have come to school. I wasn’t sure whether they were really laughing, but my vision was already blurring, and I didn’t dare look up anymore.

I ran out of the classroom and hid in the toilet stall. My heart was pounding so hard it felt like it might burst my chest open, and my stomach was burning as if there were a ball of fire inside it. I looked down at my feet and saw that my shoelaces were untied, but I had no strength to tie them. I could hear the noise of break time outside, someone shouting, “Let’s play rock-paper-scissors!” and girls laughing, but those sounds felt very far away, as if they didn’t belong to my world.

The scene I had just experienced kept replaying in my mind, and every detail cut at my heart like a knife. I thought: he must hate me now, and everyone will side with him. They’ll talk about me behind my back, saying I’m a troublemaker, saying I don’t belong with them at all. I gripped the hook on the toilet stall door, my nails digging deep into it, trying to stop myself from crying, but the tears still fell. I kept whispering “I’m sorry,” though I didn’t know who I was saying it to.

Soon the bell rang, and break time was over. I heard everything quiet down outside, but I still didn’t have the courage to walk out. Staying in the toilet made me feel a little safer, but I also knew that when the teacher called roll, the whole class would realize I wasn’t there. Would someone guess I was hiding here? Would they make fun of me, or say I was throwing a childish tantrum again? These thoughts made me even more tense, leaving me almost breathless. I wiped my face, trying hard not to look too embarrassed, and only then slowly made my way back to the classroom. My feet felt as heavy as if they were filled with lead, and each step was laborious.

Over the next few days, I became very careful, always standing farther away in advance and trying my best to avoid touching other people’s things. But I kept feeling that the way they looked at me had changed—or was that just my imagination? In any case, that feeling of being isolated weighed on my chest like a stone, making it hard for me to breathe.

The classroom was quiet, with only the rustle of pencils on paper breaking the silence, as everyone nervously worked on the math quiz. I sat by the window, sunlight spilling across my desk and making the paper seem a little glaring. I stared at the last big problem, growing more and more anxious; my heartbeat seemed louder than the sound of the pencil rubbing against the page. I read the problem over and over, trying to figure out what was wrong, but I had no idea where to begin. My palms started to sweat, and it was even hard to hold my pencil.

Suddenly, the teacher walked over to my side and glanced at me, then asked softly, “Is there anything you don’t understand?” I quickly lowered my head and pretended to be thinking, but inside a voice kept telling me, “You can’t do it. You must have done it wrong.” I forced out a smile and said, “No, it’s just a little difficult.” The teacher nodded slightly and walked away. Her expression didn’t seem unusual, but I kept feeling that it meant disappointment.

I began imagining the worst-case scenario: would not doing this problem well make the teacher think I was stupid? My hands unconsciously clenched the hem of my clothes, and my stomach ached faintly. Time passed little by little, and I knew I had to hand in my paper, so I reluctantly put down my pen.

After the test, I walked out of the classroom, hearing my classmates talking as they discussed their answers. My friend asked me, “How did you do?” I gave a self-mocking smile. “I barely understood the last question. I probably got it all wrong.” She patted me on the shoulder. “It’s okay. Everyone runs into difficult questions.” But I thought to myself, “If I were a smart kid, I shouldn’t be stumped by this.”

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning. Scenes of the teacher’s expression when she looked at me, along with my classmates’ cheerful voices, kept replaying in my mind. I felt I was worse than all of them, and I even began to doubt whether I could keep up with everyone else. It wasn’t until a few days later, when the papers were handed back, that I discovered I had actually gotten all the other questions right and only missed the last one. My mood improved a little. Yet that moment of shame remained deeply etched in my mind.

I stood by the edge of the playground, the soles of my shoes slowly tracing circles in the sandy ground. The sunlight was blinding, and the plastic track on the ground reflected a bit of glare, so I had to squint to see clearly into the distance. The team leader said we were going to discuss class activities after morning exercises, but I wasn’t sure whether she was targeting me specifically or just making casual arrangements. When I walked over, there was a trace of impatience in her voice, and she said to me, “Hurry up, don’t hold us back!” The look she gave the other classmates made me feel like I was someone unnecessary.

“I’m not holding anyone back,” I said softly, my voice almost drowned out by the noisy crowd around us. But she had already turned away, as if she didn’t want to continue the conversation with me. I froze in place, my palms heating up and my heartbeat starting to quicken. I began to wonder: had I just not walked fast enough? Did I look awkward? Did they... not want me to join at all? My stomach suddenly tightened. I wanted to leave, but if I walked away now, I felt like I would seem too cowardly.

A little boy beside us suddenly cut in: “Why aren’t you saying anything? Are you scared?” His voice carried a hint of mockery, and I immediately flushed red. I managed to force out, “No, I just...” But before I could finish, the other kids interrupted again; they had already started enthusiastically talking among themselves, completely without me. I felt as though my voice had come from inside a cave, weightless and insignificant. I stood there, feeling like my feet had been nailed to the ground.

My mind kept replaying what had just happened: was she angry? Did she think I wasn’t good enough, which was why she didn’t want to listen to me? My legs were a little shaky, and my palms were now soaked with sweat. I sneaked a look at her expression; there didn’t seem to be anything special on her face, but that only made me more nervous. I felt like she was deliberately ignoring me. “What do I need to do to make people notice me?” I thought, but I had no idea how to do it.

When the activity finally ended, I quickly ran off toward the restroom. I put my hands under the faucet, and the cold water washed the sweat from my skin. My stomach was still faintly aching. I wondered, why is my reaction always so strange whenever I encounter something like this? Why do I always feel like other people have a problem with me? When I walked back to the classroom, my head was lowered as far as it could go. I tried to tell myself that this was just an ordinary misunderstanding and that they weren’t really targeting me, but my mind still wouldn’t stop.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed the team leader’s tone over and over in my head. That “don’t hold us back” felt like a thorn piercing my heart. I kept wondering: if I could have been a little quicker, or acted more confident, would she have liked me more? But the more I thought about it, the tighter and more uncomfortable my chest felt. I tried to turn over and force myself not to think about it, but even with my eyes closed, her face and her words still echoed in my mind.

On a bright afternoon, the school playground was buzzing with noise as we were split into teams for a soccer match. The air was filled with the smell of grass and earth, and every so often a breeze would blow by, bringing a hint of coolness. I felt both excited and nervous. Standing in the middle of the field, I clenched my fists, my palms slightly sweaty.

Not long after the game began, my teammate Xiaoming passed the ball to me, and it rolled quickly toward me. My heart raced, and I kept repeating to myself, “Don’t mess up, don’t mess up.” Just as the ball was about to reach me, I felt my foot slip. I lost my balance, my toe missed the ball completely, and it slid past my foot and rolled straight to the opposing team.

“Hurry, get the ball back!” Xiaoming shouted from behind, his voice somewhat urgent. I quickly chased after that seemingly deadly ball, filled with regret and panic. Why was I always like this? Why did I always ruin things?

The other team counterattacked quickly and scored an easy goal right in front of my defensive line. I stood there, my cheeks burning, as if countless eyes were fixed on me. My heartbeat quickened, and the tension surged over me like a tide.

“What’s wrong with you? That ball was crucial!” Xiaoming said with some dissatisfaction, his tone carrying a hint of blame. I lowered my head and stared at my sneakers, not knowing how to explain. All I could hear was the stream of criticism and shame inside me.

For the rest of the match, I was completely dazed, trying my hardest but always feeling inadequate. Whenever I heard my teammates whispering among themselves, I suspected they were blaming me. That mistake seemed to magnify all my other small errors. I felt like a heavy stone, dragging down the whole team.

After the match, I silently walked back to the classroom, with the scene still replaying in my mind. On the desk was the homework sheet the teacher had just handed out, but I had nomood to look at it. I kept holding a pen in my hand, yet I didn’t know where to start. That night I tossed and turned in bed, and even that small mistake gave me stomach pain, leaving me unable to sleep peacefully.

The next day, I sat silently at the breakfast table. My mother noticed my mood and asked, “What’s wrong? Are you okay?” I just shook my head, wanting to hide my unease and shame. I knew I was just too easily affected, unable to let even a small mistake go.

Although this incident wasn’t a big one, it made me feel even more insecure, always sensing that if I wasn’t good enough, I would be disliked or abandoned.

Sunlight streamed through the window and fell across the classroom floor. Quietly, I sat beside a wooden desk, holding colored pencils in my hands, with a clean sheet of white paper spread out before me. The classroom was filled with a faint smell of chalk and the fresh scent of paper. I began to look around; everyone was busy with their own work, and the murmur of voices and the sound of paper rustling intertwined, creating this quiet yet noisy moment.

Today the teacher said there would be a drawing competition, with the theme “My Dream.” I wanted to draw a star-filled night sky, with me and my little dog out on an adventure. My heart was pounding, and I didn’t know whether I could draw well. I slowly began to sketch lines on the paper, my heart filled with a small expectation for the unknown outcome.

After a while, I heard classmates talking beside me, their voices carrying a relaxed confidence.

“What are you going to draw?” one classmate asked.

“I want to draw a huge spaceship,” another replied.

A wave of unease rose in my heart, and I felt that my idea was not as good as theirs. The pencil in my hand grew heavy, as if an invisible force were preventing me from going on. I bit my lip and tried hard to focus.

When I finally finished my drawing, I looked up and saw that the classmates around me had almost all finished too. The teacher came over, smiling as he looked at our work. My heart beat even faster, and my palms began to sweat.

“Child, your drawing is interesting,” the teacher said, then turned to continue looking at the other children’s drawings. I let out a sigh of relief, feeling a little calmer.

But just then, I heard a classmate nearby mutter, “The stars look a bit messy.”

Those words were like a needle, quickly piercing my heart. I looked at my drawing and suddenly felt that my stars really were a little disordered, that the picture was not as beautiful as I had imagined. I began to wonder whether my dream itself was not good enough.

That afternoon, after I got home from school, I couldn’t stop thinking about those words, and the classmate’s muttering kept replaying in my mind. When I went to bed at night, I lay there wondering whether I should give up drawing, because I still couldn’t shake the unease in my heart. My heart was filled with shame and helplessness, and with those feelings, I slowly fell asleep.

Over the next few days, every time I saw that drawing, I couldn’t help but remember that comment. Waves of emotion would still rise in my heart, and my urge to tear up the paper was gradually suppressed. I tried to tell myself that different stars might also be a form of individuality.

This experience made me understand that, no matter what, my work could never satisfy everyone, but at the very least, I should have the courage to try.

I was sitting in the last row of the classroom, with a freshly drawn pencil sketch on the desk—a little bird with its wings spread. Sunlight poured through the window onto the drawing paper, making the pencil lines stand out sharply. Looking at my own work, I felt a little proud, but also a little uncertain. I decided to let the classmate next to me take a look at my drawing; maybe she would think it was pretty? I turned around, pinching the corner of the paper, and carefully handed it to her, asking in a low voice, “What do you think of this drawing?”

She looked up and glanced at it. Her expression seemed casual, and there was also some emotion I couldn’t explain. She said offhandedly, “Oh, it’s okay, I guess.” Then she turned away and kept chatting with the classmate in front of her. In that instant, I felt as if something had lightly struck my chest. I forced myself to manage a smile, lowered my head to look at the paper, and tried to convince myself that she just hadn’t looked carefully, not that she thought my drawing was bad.

But suddenly, all sorts of images seemed to surge through my mind: Was I not good enough at drawing? Should I not have bothered her? Did she think I was annoying? The more I thought about it, the more my stomach felt tight, as if a knot had been tied there. I could hear the other students in the class talking and laughing, but those sounds seemed distant, somewhat blurry. All I could hear was my own heartbeat, fast and a little hot in my chest.

I secretly glanced up at her and found that she wasn’t looking in my direction at all, as if that moment just now had been completely meaningless. I quickly lowered my head, my fingers pinching the edge of the paper, and without realizing it, I scraped tiny marks into it with my nails. Over and over in my mind, I asked myself: Why doesn’t she like my drawing? If it were someone else, would I be ignored like this too? Maybe I’m just not good at drawing at all; maybe I shouldn’t be bothering other people.

For the rest of lunch break, I kept my head down, doodling in my sketchbook, but I couldn’t draw anything decent anymore. I always felt that the lines I drew were crooked and lifeless. There was a strange heaviness in my chest, as if it were being pressed down, and my breathing became shallow. I heard the classmates in front of me talking and laughing, and wanted to lift my head and join them, but I was afraid I would say something wrong and make them think I was awkward.

That evening at home, I sat at my desk flipping through my sketchbook, wanting to tidy up that bird drawing again. I tried drawing some new feathers, thinking I should make it prettier. But no matter how I changed it, I still felt it wasn’t good enough, as if every stroke were being weighed down by her comment, “Oh, it’s okay, I guess.” After drawing a few lines, I finally closed the sketchbook, feeling a little sore inside, even wondering whether I would ever be able to draw something that others truly liked. Before going to sleep, I lay in bed, and my mind kept replaying her expression and that remark, feeling as if they were a needle, piercing my heart—lightly, perhaps, but persistently there.

I was sitting on the grass in the yard, surrounded by the laughter and chatter of the adults. They were talking about things I didn’t understand, and I tried to join in, but it seemed like no one noticed me. I saw Mom standing with a few uncles and aunts, her head gently shaking, her expression seeming a little displeased. My heart sank at once. Was she unhappy with what I had just said?

“Little one, come help us carry the drinks, okay?” one of the uncles waved me over. I quickly ran over, feeling a little excited—finally, someone was calling me. But when I handed him the drink, he just gave a faint smile and turned back to continue talking with Mom.

My heart started racing, and my palms were sweaty. I felt tense all over. Why weren’t they paying attention to me? Had I done something wrong? I felt a dull pain in my stomach, as if something were twisting inside. The noise in the yard grew louder and louder, and my face grew hotter and hotter. All I could think about was whether they disliked me, whether my expression was too strange, or whether I had said something wrong just now.

After a while, Mom finally noticed me. She came over, patted my head, and said softly, “Why are you staying by yourself? Go play with the other kids.” Her tone sounded calm, but I couldn’t help interpreting it as a kind of distance. I bit my lip, trying hard not to let my tears fall. “I’m tired. I don’t want to play,” I replied in a low voice.

That night, I lay in bed, my mind replaying over and over the image of Mom slightly shaking her head and everyone’s casual disregard of me. My stomach still felt uncomfortable, and I wrapped the blanket tightly around myself, trying to find even a little bit of safety. I felt abandoned; none of them cared about me, and I couldn’t fit into their world. Had I done something wrong? Was I not good enough? The feeling clung to me and kept me awake all night.

The next day, Mom didn’t seem to notice anything unusual about me, and I kept trying to act normal. But the shadow in my heart seemed to grow bigger and bigger. I started to fear showing myself in front of my family, afraid that they wouldn’t like me.

The classroom was filled with noise, as everyone discussed the upcoming class performance auditions. I stood in the middle of the room, nervous, and although the sun was shining brightly outside the window, I couldn’t feel its warmth. I looked at the teacher’s face; she seemed to be smiling, but my mind was flooded with images of failure. The teacher began calling names. My palms were sweaty, and I could feel my heartbeat speeding up. When my name was called, I tried to look confident and stood up, but inside, one voice kept circling in my head: “You’re going to embarrass yourself. They’re all going to laugh at you.”

Standing at the front of the classroom felt like standing in the center of a huge whirlpool, with every gaze converging on me, pressing so hard that I could hardly breathe. I took a deep breath and began to perform. I only had to sing a simple children’s song, something that should have been easy for me. But just as I started singing, my mind suddenly went blank, and I forgot the lyrics. I froze in place, and it seemed as though I could hear people whispering nearby. “Why are you so stupid!” I shouted at myself inwardly, trying hard to remember the words, but the more anxious I became, the more I couldn’t recall them.

The classroom fell silent, frighteningly so. I could hear my heartbeat growing louder and louder, my body began to feel hot, and my cheeks were burning. I felt ashamed, as if everyone were laughing at me. I forced out a smile and said, “Sorry, I forgot the lyrics,” my voice barely audible. The teacher’s gentle voice came from the front, saying it was okay and that I could try again, but I shook my head, trying not to let my tears fall. Just then, I saw one classmate whispering to another and smiling, and my heart sank. They must be laughing at me, I thought.

I returned to my seat, tears streaming down my face, and quietly wiped them away with the back of my hand. I felt utterly defeated and ashamed, and the teacher’s comforting words became a blur. That night, lying in bed, I replayed that moment over and over, my heart full of regret and pain. Why do I always make mistakes? Why can’t I be as composed as everyone else? The next day, I still didn’t have the courage to face my classmates, afraid they would bring up what happened yesterday. Even if they didn’t mention it again, that small voice inside me kept blaming me without end: “If only I didn’t make mistakes anymore. If only I could be perfect.”

A few days later, these feelings gradually faded, but every time I stood before a crowd, that moment would surface in my mind, filling my heart with fear—afraid of being stared at again, afraid of making a mistake once more.

The living room at home was decorated with colorful balloons hanging from the ceiling. I could clearly smell the scent of cake mixed with cream, sweet and rich. Low voices from my parents echoed through the room. Although they seemed to be trying not to let me hear, I could still feel the tension filling the air. I sat on the floor, fiddling with the ribbon in my little hands, trying not to pay attention to those unsettling sounds. A foreboding feeling welled up inside me, like the heavy oppressive stillness before rain.

“I told you, I don’t want to repeat what happened yesterday!” Mom’s voice suddenly rose. I gripped the ribbon tightly, my heartbeat instantly quickening. I could feel tears welling in my eyes, just from fear and unease. “Don’t do this in front of the child,” Dad said softly, but I could hear the fatigue and helplessness in his voice. “You think the child can’t feel it?” Mom responded emotionally.

I buried my head between my knees, trying to make myself disappear. Why were they like this on my birthday? Had I done something wrong? I didn’t know how to make them happy, so I could only keep asking myself over and over. At last, tears slipped down my cheeks, and I quickly wiped them away with my sleeve, not wanting them to see.

There was always a voice inside me saying it was because I wasn’t good enough. So in their argument, I felt like I was unnecessary. Like an unwanted existence. I wanted to shout for them to stop, wanted them to know how much I wanted a happy birthday, a home without fighting. My stomach began to ache faintly, though I knew it wasn’t from hunger, but from fear.

A few minutes later, Mom hurried out the door, leaving Dad and me alone. I stared at the doorway, hoping she would come back and tell me that it had all been a dream. Dad came over and gently patted my shoulder, his palm warm yet slightly trembling. “I’m sorry, kid,” he said softly. “Today may not go very well, but we’ll make it up to you, okay?” I nodded, yet felt that those words could not erase the shadow in my heart.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, the events of the day flashing through my mind from time to time. Although my father had tried to comfort me, I still felt profoundly lonely and uneasy. When I woke the next day, life had returned to normal, but the sense of being ignored and abandoned still would not leave me. One evening a few days later, I looked up at the starry sky outside the window and swore that one day I would prove I was worthy of being loved, and that I would never feel so helpless again.

The small garden outside the classroom was always so lively. It was a sunny morning, and sunlight filtered through the gaps in the leaves, casting dappled patterns on the ground that danced as the leaves swayed. I sat on the bench by the garden, staring at the lush thicket of bushes. In my ears came the sound of my classmates laughing and chatting, and the air was filled with the fresh scent of earth mixed with flowers and grass.

Not far from me, a few classmates had gathered in a small circle, chatting cheerfully. Their voices were not loud, but I could hear a boy suddenly burst into laughter, and that laugh instantly pierced my ears. My heart suddenly sped up, as if all the blood in my body had rushed straight to my head. “Are they laughing at me?” I thought, and memories of past ridicule came flooding back.

“Hey, what are you talking about?” I forced myself to stay calm and stepped forward, trying to join their conversation. But my voice trembled a little, and I could feel my palms were already sweating.

“Oh, we were talking about something funny from gym class just now,” one of the classmates said, turning around to me with a friendly smile.

Even so, I was still filled with unease. I forced out a smile. “Oh, really? I thought you were talking about me,” I said jokingly.

“Of course not! You’re overthinking it,” the classmate said with a wave of the hand, smiling even more brightly, and the others chimed in as well.

They didn’t mind, but I felt an inexplicable wave of embarrassment, and my heartbeat still hadn’t settled. I smiled and nodded, pretending I hadn’t been affected, then turned and walked away, though I couldn’t calm down inside. Back on the bench, I sat down and let my gaze fall on the bushes again, trying to distract myself, but the laughter in my ears still refused to fade.

That night, lying in bed, I was still thinking about it. Why was I always so sensitive, always taking other people’s simple laughter as if it were directed at me? Silently, I promised myself that next time I would be more firm and not so easily made uneasy. But unease was like an invisible chain, binding me at every moment.

The next day, at school, I paid even more attention to my behavior, trying to relax and make an effort to interact with my classmates. I told myself that I had to learn to distinguish friendliness from hostility, and that I could no longer let the illusion of misunderstanding trouble me so easily.

I sat in the second row of the classroom. Sunlight streamed through the window and spread across the floor, while a faint dusty chalk smell filled the room. The teacher was explaining a math problem, her voice light and energetic. “Next, let’s hear what you think,” she suddenly asked. My heartbeat instantly sped up, as if I could hear every beat clearly. I tried hard to look at the problem on the blackboard; the writing was clear, yet somehow seemed distorted and blurry. My palms started to sweat, and the fingertips of my hands tingled slightly.

My classmates turned to look at me, and I felt countless eyes on me, which made me even more nervous. “What do you think of this problem?” the teacher asked with a smile, her tone kind, but I still felt a hint of pressure. I couldn’t help swallowing, and my words got stuck in my throat. “Uh, I…” I stammered, my voice so weak it was almost inaudible. As my heartbeat quickened, I felt my stomach begin to churn slightly.

“It’s okay, take your time. You can do it,” the teacher encouraged me, her smile seeming to bring a little comfort. But I still felt anxious, silently blaming myself over and over for why I couldn’t simply say the answer. In my mind, I began rehearsing the worst possible outcomes again, worried that I would be laughed at or criticized.

I lowered my head and looked at the problem again carefully. After taking a few breaths, I nervously gave my answer, my voice still weak but at least completing the response. The teacher nodded and praised me, saying, “Very good, you’re right.” In that instant, I felt a great sense of relief, and the tension throughout my body gradually eased. Although my heart was still beating a little fast, it was nowhere near as intense as before.

When the bell rang for class to end, the crisp “ding-a-ling” sound instantly brought the classroom to life. I quietly let out a breath and sat in my seat, regaining my composure. My deskmate turned to me and said, “You answered pretty well just now!” His tone was sincere, and I nodded, though I kept replaying the experience in my mind. I had been nervous, but at least I hadn’t made a mistake.

That evening, after returning home, I was still brooding over what had happened that day. I asked my mom, “Why am I always so nervous?” My mom crouched down slightly and answered gently, “Everyone has things they’re not good at. You’ve already done very well.” Though I still felt a little uneasy, her words brought me some comfort.

Over the next few days, I still kept reflecting on my performance in that class, silently promising myself that I would do better next time. A bit of anxiety still lingered, but at least I had the courage to face it.

I was standing in the corner of the field at the time, with a faint earthy smell drifting through the air. The sunlight was harsh, and I squinted as I watched the other children play, while all I wanted was to hide myself away. I tried hard to remember the long jump movement the teacher had told us to practice, but when I ran forward with all my strength and prepared to jump, my foot caught on a pothole in the ground and I fell. I heard the laughter around me turn shrill, like bursts of piercing buzzing. A boy shouted, “TA can’t even do the long jump, what an idiot!” The others laughed along. My face suddenly grew hot, burning like fire, and tears welled up in my eyes at once. I blinked hard, not wanting to cry.

The teacher walked over, and I thought she would comfort me, but she frowned and said in a somewhat impatient tone, “Why are you being so careless? You fell again.” Those words stabbed into my chest like a knife. I instinctively felt that she was making fun of me too. My mind started racing wildly, filled with all kinds of terrifying thoughts: Did everyone think I was useless? Was even the teacher disappointed in me? Should I never have come to school at all? My stomach felt as if someone had squeezed it hard, hurting so much I could barely stand straight. After I got up, I didn’t dare look anyone in the eye. I just wanted to leave quickly, to get away from that horrible place.

When I got back to the classroom, I shrank into my seat and pulled my backpack zipper tight, my palms covered in sweat. The others kept chatting and fooling around, while I kept thinking about that word “idiot” and the teacher’s frown. The scene of me falling kept replaying in my mind, clearer each time. I felt my body growing heavy, as if even breathing had become difficult. Isecretly glanced at the teacher. She was grading papers at the podium, expressionless, but I felt as though she might be deliberately avoiding looking at me because I had embarrassed her.

That night, I lay in bed, staring at the ceiling. Mom came in and asked if I was tired. I didn’t dare tell her the truth, so I just nodded. In fact, I wasn’t tired at all; I just felt like I was a broken thing. Why could everyone else play happily while I was so stupid and so humiliating? I was a problem. It seemed like I would never be liked. When I closed my eyes, the laughter on the field and the teacher’s words surfaced again in my mind, and my heart ached in waves, as if being pricked by needles. After that, I didn’t want to go to the field anymore. From that day on, I always found excuses to avoid PE class.

My grandparents’ kitchen was always warm and cozy, especially when it was time to start preparing dinner. A pot of soup simmered on the gas stove, and the air was filled with a rich aroma. I stood on a small stool beside it, carefully washing some leafy greens in water. My grandmother was busy next to me, a gentle smile on her face. In her low, soothing voice, she said, “Separate the leaves and wash them one by one, and that way they’ll get cleaner.” I nodded eagerly, though my movements were still a little clumsy.

Suddenly, my grandfather came in from outside and said to my grandmother in an urgent tone, “There’s a fly in the kitchen. Hurry up and chase it out.” The moment I heard that, my heart sank—had I failed to close the door properly and let the fly in? My face started to burn, my heart pounded violently, and my hands froze. I didn’t even notice the drops of water falling from the leaves onto the floor.

“You didn’t check carefully, did you?” my grandfather went on. I tensed up immediately and felt that he was speaking to me, even though he wasn’t looking at me. It must have been me, it had to be my fault; I should have been more careful. Worry and shame surged over me like a tide. I put down the vegetables and lowered my head, apologizing softly, “I-I’ll pay more attention next time.”

“Oh, no, I’m not talking about you, little one,” my grandmother said with a smile, patting my head. “We’re looking for that fly. You can keep washing the vegetables—you’re doing a great job.” Her voice was as warm as spring sunshine, and I relaxed a little, but the unease in my heart still lingered. I kept washing the vegetables, but I couldn’t help glancing toward the corners of the room, as if that fly might appear at any moment and expose my incompetence.

At dinner, I sat by the table, and although delicious food was spread before me, I found it utterly tasteless. I kept worrying about that so-called fly, imagining over and over how everyone would make fun of me the next day for being so careless. The soft light from the dining table fell gently on everyone’s faces, and the sound of my family chatting drifted in my ears, but I felt as though I were surrounded by an invisible barrier.

That night, I tossed and turned and couldn’t sleep properly. I kept feeling that it must have been because of me that the fly got into the kitchen, and that made me feel guilty; the feeling followed me like a ghost. Over the next few days, whenever I passed the kitchen door, I was always extra cautious, afraid something else might go wrong.

Even after my grandmother repeatedly reassured me a few days later, explaining that it had only been an accident, I still found myself thinking about that little episode from time to time. The feeling of being blamed and tense lingered in my heart for a long time, as if reminding me that even the smallest lapse could turn into a disaster.

I was sitting in a corner of the school library, sunlight streaming through the window and spilling onto the pages of the book in front of me, forming warm, gentle patches of light. The cover of the book glowed faintly in the sunlight, and the rustle of the pages as I turned them was almost silent, as I slowly read page after page. It was very quiet around me; I could hear only the occasional sound of pages turning and the distant ticking of a clock.

Just as I was lost in the book, a sudden voice broke the silence. “Hey! What are you reading?” A male classmate’s voice came from behind me, startling me so much that my hand slipped, and I accidentally dropped the book on the floor.

“Uh, I...” I hurriedly bent down to pick it up, feeling flustered inside. His voice echoed in my ears, as if he were questioning me about something. It made my heart beat faster, and my fingers trembled slightly.

“Why do you always look so easily startled?” he said with a smile, his tone carrying a hint of teasing. I forced out a smile. “Oh, I was just concentrating on reading, so I got startled.” But he seemed to find it amusing, and then turned and left, while my mood felt as though something heavy had pressed down on it.

I sat back down and tried to keep reading, but I could no longer calm myself. The scene kept replaying in my mind: his tone, his smile, and my own embarrassment when I dropped the book. My cheeks felt warm, and I had an indescribable sense of shame in my heart.

That afternoon, after leaving the library, my emotions were still tossing about like waves. I wondered if everything would have been different if I weren’t so easily startled. I began quietly blaming myself: “I’m really too fragile, always like this.”

When I got home, I still couldn’t pull myself away from what had happened that afternoon. Mom asked with concern, “How was school today?” I managed to say, “It was okay.”

That night, lying in bed, the unease in my heart still would not go away. Even under the blankets, I could still feel my heart pounding like a drum, and it seemed as though the male classmate’s voice was still echoing in my ears. After a few days, I gradually began to let go of that little incident, but deep down, that sensitivity and unease seemed never to have truly disappeared.

On a weekend afternoon, my family and I decided to go into the city for a stroll. We walked to the nearby bus stop, waiting for the green bus to arrive. The sun was high in the sky, and from time to time one or two white clouds drifted by lazily. In the flowerbed near the stop, a few sparrows were hopping about, their chirping mingling with the sound of the occasional passing car. At last, the bus appeared, and I quickly grabbed my mother’s hand and slowly boarded with the crowd. The air inside the bus was a little stuffy, but I was thrilled, looking around for a window seat. Luckily, there was an empty seat in the very back, and I sat down happily, pressing close to the window, eager to take in every detail outside. Accompanied by the engine’s low hum, the bus slowly pulled away, and my heartbeat seemed to quicken slightly along with the increasing speed. The scenery outside kept changing; the shop signs looked especially vivid in the sunlight, and pedestrians came and went, each seeming to have their own destination. I tried hard to make out the words on those uncommon signs, and sometimes I would quietly read them aloud. As the bus entered the city center, the roads grew busier. The buildings gradually became taller, and occasionally one could see a brand-new high-rise, its glass curtain wall flashing with a blinding brilliance in the sunlight. “Look at that building, it’s so tall!” I said to my mother, pointing out the window. “Yes, it’s beautiful,” my mother replied with a smile. The fan inside the bus gave off a faint creaking sound, blowing waves of warm air and, from time to time, a trace of some unexplained gasoline smell. I gently nudged my mother with my elbow, signaling her to look at every interesting thing I saw outside the window, though some of them she may have already seen many times before. As the trip went on, I felt a slight nervousness in my stomach, perhaps because of the bus’s bumps and jolts, or perhaps because of the excitement and anticipation of soon reaching the city center. At last, the bus entered the square in the heart of the city, and the driver lightly stepped on the brakes as the passengers began standing up to get off. We followed the crowd slowly out of the carriage. The sunlight shone harshly on my face, yet I couldn’t help squinting as I adjusted to the brightness. After a whole afternoon of sightseeing, when I got home, my heart was still full of impressions of the scenery outside the window. That night, lying in bed, I recalled those moments on the bus, and it seemed I could still feel the vibration beneath the wheels, while the echo of my heartbeat had not yet fully subsided.

The classroom was a little dim, probably because the curtains hadn’t been opened. The teacher said that today we would be showing our drawings, and I felt both nervous and excited. I had drawn a forest, with lots of animals in it, including my favorite pony. I filled the whole sheet with crayons, thinking that I would soon get praise from the teacher. However, when the teacher began walking around to look at everyone’s work, my palms started sweating and my heartbeat quickened a lot. Whenever the teacher lingered a little longer at someone else’s desk, I worried that she was looking for mistakes in my drawing. She finally came to me, smiled, and said, “Your picture is so full of life; the little animals look like they’re dancing happily.” Hearing that, I felt a surge of joy, but then I immediately started wondering whether someone else’s drawing might be better than mine. The teacher was going to take my picture to the front to display it, and I saw her carefully pick up the paper, but just then, because of the pulling, a corner of the page got torn a little. I froze at once, my heart sinking. I felt my face start to burn, my ears getting hot, and a stinging feeling in my chest. I couldn’t help thinking: was it because I drew badly that the paper got damaged? If I had drawn better, the teacher wouldn’t have torn it. I lowered my head, tears welling up in my eyes, and looked fearfully at the torn part. The teacher looked up at me and said, “I’m very sorry, I’ll help you fix it.” But all I wanted was to snatch the picture back and not let anyone see that hole anymore. I returned to my seat, and my mind kept replaying the scene from just now, wondering how I should explain it to my mom when I got home. I even started imagining that I would never take art class again. For the whole afternoon, I sat in my seat, too afraid to look up at the front, and too afraid to let my classmates see the tears about to fall from my eyes. When I went home, I rolled up the drawing and hid it in my backpack, wanting to leave quickly and get away from this embarrassing place. Over the next few days, whenever I saw the teacher walk into the classroom, that torn feeling rose up in my heart again, and that sheet of paper seemed to have become a small scar in my heart.

On the balcony there is a small rocking chair, my secret base. Every time I sit there, I always feel like a little explorer, able to see all the changes of autumn. This afternoon, sunlight streamed through the glass window and fell on my face, warm and gentle. I sat in the rocking chair, my legs swingingcontinuously, my toes lightly touching the railing. I rocked the chair hard, feeling as if I were on a swing. The little birds nearby chirped in the branches, and from time to time fallen leaves drifted down with a rustling sound. Yellow, orange, and red leaves spun in the wind, looking like a colorful dance performance.

“What are you looking at?” came Mom’s voice from the kitchen. I didn’t answer; I just kept watching the leaves. I wanted to tell her that those leaves were as light and fluffy as cotton candy, but I knew she was busy making dinner. The soup in the pot bubbled away, the smell of my favorite potato stew with meat, and I could catch its aroma.

The rocking chair swayed gently, and my heart relaxed along with its rhythm. A little cat would also jump onto the balcony from time to time, lazily lying down by my feet. Its furry body pressed against me, and I reached out to stroke its soft fur, feeling the warmth and softness through my fingertips.

“Come in quickly, it’s almost time to eat,” Mom reminded me again. I felt that time had passed so fast; I hadn’t even looked enough. I stood up, brushed the bits of leaves off my clothes, and got ready to go inside. My heartbeat was normal, and everything felt very peaceful. I turned around and closed the balcony door, looking back wistfully at the view outside. Autumn was so beautiful.

At dinner, I sat with Mom and Dad around the table, talking about things at school. Mom chatted about something amusing she had encountered at the market today, while Dad talked about the challenges he faced at work. On the table was my favorite potato stew with meat, and I ate big mouthfuls, the tip of my tongue tasting the tender meat and rich broth, my heart full of warmth and satisfaction.

That night, the autumn insects chirped outside the window. I lay in bed, and my mind was still filled with the falling leaves on the balcony that afternoon. The shadows of the leaves by the window swayed in the moonlight, and I felt as if I were that leaf, moving with the wind, free and light. Closing my eyes, I gradually drifted into sleep, and in my dream there were still dancing leaves and a gentle breeze.

The classroom was filled with children’s voices, and the teacher was playing a simple melody on the piano. The moment I feared most had arrived: everyone was going to stand up one by one and sing that melody. Sitting in my chair, my palms began to sweat as I gripped the hem of my clothes tightly. When it was my turn, the eyes of the whole class were fixed on me. I stood up, my heart pounding so fast it felt like it might burst out of my chest. When I began to sing, the notes in my mouth seemed to be deliberately working against me, refusing to cooperate at all. I knew I had sung several notes wrong, and soft snickers and whispered comments came from around me.

“That’s not the note!” a classmate suddenly shouted, his voice carrying obvious mockery. My face turned hot in an instant, as if I had been burned by fire.
