I didn’t dare look up, terrified of seeing those sneering eyes. “Try again,” the teacher said in a calm tone, but I could still feel his disappointment. My hands and feet felt heavy as if they had been filled with lead. I took another deep breath and tried once more to sing those damn notes. But I failed again, and this time it was worse; I heard someone laugh even louder.

The teacher motioned for the next student to begin, and I seemed to be pushed out by the air itself. Sitting in my chair, I felt as though my body were sinking into a bottomless darkness, my mind filled with shame and helplessness. That phrase, “That’s not the note!” kept echoing in my head, and I began to wonder whether I had no business standing there at all. Why could other people do what I couldn’t? Was I really worse than them? Tears welled up in my eyes. I forced myself not to cry, but my throat was tight and raw.

After class, everyone went out to the playground to play. I stood to the side, watching them laugh and roughhouse, each burst of laughter stinging me. I wanted to join them, but I couldn’t bring myself to move. I kept feeling that they were watching me, as if waiting for me to do something ridiculous. In the end, I found a corner to sit in, hoping to escape everyone’s gaze. When I got home at night, my mother asked how school had been that day. I only vaguely said, “It was okay,” not wanting her to know about the embarrassment I had felt during the day.

For the next few days, I kept making excuses not to practice singing, always feeling that my voice was so useless. Every time I thought of that music class, my heart would involuntarily tighten, and I felt shut out from everyone else’s happiness. That feeling of loneliness and inadequacy kept me tossing and turning at night, unable to fall asleep for a long time.

That day in class, we were learning to write a new Chinese character. After the teacher demonstrated it on the blackboard, she told us to practice it in our own exercise books. The classroom was filled with the rustling sound of pencils moving across paper, but my attention kept being broken by the constant muttering coming from Xiaoming, who was sitting next to me. “What kind of weird thing are you writing?” His words made my heart skip a beat, and I felt a wave of embarrassment as my cheeks began to burn. I looked down at my crooked, awkward handwriting. I had only wanted to try writing it more neatly, but no matter how I looked at it, something was wrong. “Am I just useless?” I thought, my palms starting to sweat, and the pencil slipping slightly in my hand. My heartbeat quickened, as if a little drum were pounding fiercely inside my chest.

I tried to ignore Xiaoming’s voice and focus on my own notebook, but his snickering kept ringing in my ears. It seemed as though every word he said only magnified the unease inside me. Just then, the teacher walked over to our row and asked gently, “Is something wrong?” I looked up and saw her kind gaze, then quickly looked away again, answering in a low voice, “No, it’s nothing.” But inside I was thinking, “Will they think I’m incompetent?”

After class, I sat at my desk in a daze, Xiaoming’s words replaying over and over in my mind. My stomach began to ache faintly, as if it were caused by those taunting sounds echoing again and again—like the smell of spray paint dissolving into the air—making me want to escape from that place. The other students left the classroom one by one, but I felt as if my feet had been nailed to the floor, unable to move.

On the way home, I followed behind my mother, head down, kicking at small stones. She asked me, “How was your day, kid?” I only gave a soft “Mm,” afraid she would keep asking and discover that little shame I did not want anyone to know about.

That night, I lay in bed, replaying the scene from class over and over in my mind. It felt as if a stone were pressing down on my heart, heavy and suffocating. I imagined the teacher and my classmates whispering behind my back, and my heart ached again and again. Even though I tried to cover my head with the blanket and escape that choking feeling, I still couldn’t fall asleep. It took several days before the feeling gradually faded, but every so often, when I heard laughter in class, that sudden panic of being excluded would still flare up in my heart.

I was sitting on the living room carpet, the rain tapping softly against the window, the light looking especially dim and yellow. My math test lay in the center of the coffee table, and the red Xs and the score of 56 were like thorny vines, tightly wrapping around my heart. My mother was sitting on the sofa, glancing at me sideways. She picked up the test paper and, in a deliberately lowered voice, said, “Is this all you’re capable of? You got these simple problems wrong—what kind of brain do you have?” Her tone was like fine needles, pricking into my chest little by little. I kept my head down, trying hard not to let my tears fall, my fingers absentmindedly picking at the carpet fibers. 

Dad turned around from beside the TV and chimed in impatiently, “All you know how to do is play! When are you going to learn to be more responsible?” I heard his voice rise, and my heartbeat instantly sped up; it felt as if a tiny pebble had been thrown into my stomach. I looked up and whispered in protest, “I was taking it seriously. It’s just that problem was really hard.” But my voice was so faint it was almost drowned out by the sound of the rain outside. They still wouldn’t let it go. My mother stood up, pointing at the test paper as she said to me, “Taking it seriously? You call this serious? What exactly do you want us to do with you! Is it because we don’t care enough about you that you did so badly?” Another round of stinging pain hit me. I felt the skin on my face grow hot, and my tears finally began to flow uncontrollably. 

Her words flashed through my head at lightning speed: Was she disgusted with me? Did they think I was a burden? It was over now—I definitely wasn’t the child she wanted. She would surely be even more disappointed, even angrier. I tried to swallow, but my throat was so tight it felt as if someone were squeezing it shut. My hands started to tremble, like pipes about to burst. I lowered my head and said softly, “I’m sorry.” Then I quickly ran back to my room and shut the door. The moment the door closed, I felt the whole world grow heavier. The air in the room felt like a thick layer of cotton, and I could hardly breathe. 

I curled up beside my bed, burying my head in my knees. Before my eyes were the vivid red Xs on the test paper, as if they were mocking me. I kept asking myself: Why do I always let them down? Are only good children loved? That night I barely slept, and my ears kept ringing with my mother’s words: “We don’t care enough about you?” It was like a radio that couldn’t be turned off, playing on and on. I began imagining them finally losing their patience and sending me away, with the reason: “This child is too awful. We can’t manage them.” 

The next day I got up in a daze, my eyes swollen like walnuts. I walked to the dining table, and my mother handed me a glass of milk. She said, “Don’t dwell too much on what happened last night. Just do better next time.” I nodded unconsciously, but I felt no comfort at all; instead, I felt even more alone. Her tone was lifeless, like a puppet’s voice. I thought: She’s just too lazy to deal with me anymore. The milk in that glass tasted bitter to me, and even its milky fragrance seemed to have faded. 

Over the next few days, I became even quieter. I no longer dared to answer questions proactively in class, always fearing that others would notice my flaws. The criticism from them kept circling in my mind, and I couldn’t shake off that searing sense of humiliation. It seemed as though everyone secretly thought I was incompetent, and I began to fear talking to any adult. Whenever they asked about my grades, my heart would leap into my throat, and my stomach would start to ache faintly, as if reminding me not to cross the line. That deep self-doubt became a shadow, following me everywhere I went.

The playground was always full of noise, with children’s laughter, running footsteps, and the teacher’s calls from afar all mixed together. That afternoon during nap time, I gathered with a few classmates in a corner of the playground, discussing who was best at playing soccer. I wanted to join in, but they didn’t seem to notice me. They said, “The game is for good players, not for little kids.” I wasn’t sure whether they were joking, but I felt a little upset. To act indifferent, I blurted out, “You’re not even as good as I am!” Their laughter stopped abruptly, and every eye turned to me. I could feel my cheeks growing hot, my heart racing, and my palms sweating. One boy quickly shot back, “Then prove it!” He handed me a soccer ball with a challenging look. I took the ball, but my palms were so slippery I could hardly hold on. A voice inside me was blaming me—why had I said something like that? I clearly knew I wasn’t good at soccer. Under everyone’s gaze, I felt my legs trembling as I tried to kick the ball, but it barely moved. The ball rolled only a short distance, and my classmates began to snicker under their breath, with contempt and mockery. I could hear their quiet taunts: “See, they can’t do it at all.” I felt utterly humiliated, as if I had been completely left out and abandoned by them. After nap time ended, I sat in a corner of the classroom, silently watching everything around me. Those words kept echoing in my mind—“can’t do it,” “for little kids”—like shadows that wouldn’t go away. My chest felt tight, as if all my unease and shame were pressing down there. That night, I lay in bed, repeatedly reliving every detail of what had happened on the playground. My mind was filled with their expressions, their tones of voice, and my ridiculous performance. I kept worrying that the next day they would mock me again, or even isolate me from the whole class. The next morning, I kept looking at myself in the mirror, trying to seem less bothered, struggling to hide the shame and unease inside me. At school, I tried hard to avoid eye contact with them, pretending everything was normal. However, whenever I heard laughter, I couldn’t help feeling that they were talking about me again. After a few days, that feeling eased a little, but I was still afraid of going through it all over again.

The clatter of plates and cups echoed in the kitchen sink. Sitting in my own room, I pressed my ear against the door and listened to that familiar sound, feeling a dull ache begin in my stomach. At dinner, my mother mentioned my math grades, her voice carrying a cold disappointment: “Your scores have gone down again this week. What’s going on?” I nodded dazedly, trying hard to swallow the last bite of rice, but my throat had tightened, as if even air were hard to swallow.

Later she came into my room, and I was sitting on the edge of the bed in a daze. She began in a reproachful tone, “Are you even putting any effort into studying? Why are you always like this?” I looked at her, trying not to avert my eyes, but the tightness in my throat kept me from answering. She went on, “Do you know how disappointed your father is in you? If you keep this up, who will even like you?” The words hit my chest like a heavy blow, and in an instant I felt not good enough, not smart enough, not even worthy of being loved.

I tried to explain, “I am putting in effort. I really have been trying…” But my voice sounded so faint it was like a mosquito’s buzz, and even I didn’t believe it. My mother sighed, turned, and walked to the window, pulling back the curtains. Light stabbed in from outside; I squinted, but I couldn’t tear my gaze away from her. She looked back at me, and the subtle expression on her face made me feel like a complete failure.

My heart suddenly began to race; sweat beaded on my forehead, and my fingers started unconsciously pinching at my pants. The air in the room seemed to grow thick, pressing down on me until I could hardly breathe. I whispered, “I know I’m useless, but could you please not say things like that?” She paused, as if startled by my words, then shook her head hard. “Isn’t that the truth?”

In that moment, it felt like the world had collapsed. I was afraid I might cry, so I bit down hard on my lip. When my mother left the room, I heard the door shut, the sound sharp as a knife scraping across glass. I wrapped my arms around my knees and sat on the bed, tears slipping from my eyes, my fingers curled stiffly, cold sweat pouring down my back. In my mind I kept repeating her words over and over: “Who will even like you? Isn’t that the truth?” They closed over my entire mind like a net.

That night I hardly slept. I stared at the ceiling, trying to count the cracks in it to calm myself down, but the more I counted, the worse I felt. The next day at school, my chest still felt heavy, as if a huge stone were pressing on it. In class, when the teacher asked a question, I didn’t even dare raise my hand, feeling as though everyone was waiting to laugh at me. I even avoided looking my deskmate in the eye, because I kept feeling that she knew what kind of failure I was.

The classroom windows were open, and the sunlight from outside slanted in, spilling across the desks. I remember sitting on the side by the wall. The group discussion topic was related to science class, and we needed to decide on an answer together and hand it in to the teacher. I always felt that the seats near the window were more popular than the ones by the wall, and sitting there gave me a sense of being pushed to the margins.

The other three students in my group began discussing the question, their voices a little noisy. “I think the answer is ‘photosynthesis,’” one of them said. I looked down at the textbook in my hands, not quite sure of the answer, but feeling that I should take part in the discussion. So I said softly, “I think it might be ‘transpiration.’”

As soon as I said it, one of the students beside me frowned immediately. “How could transpiration be a process of absorbing energy? You’ve got it wrong, haven’t you?” Her tone wasn’t especially sharp, but in that instant my face flushed red, as if I had been pricked. I swallowed, my mouth dry, my heart seeming to speed up; I could even hear my own heartbeat. My fingers instinctively tightened around the edge of the textbook, afraid to say anything wrong again.

Another student chimed in, “Yeah, it should be photosynthesis, not transpiration.” They kept discussing, while I gradually fell silent, staring at the words in the textbook and pretending to read carefully, though my mind was actually a mess. The scene kept replaying in my head: the moment they frowned and corrected me ran through my mind over and over, as if my mistake had been magnified infinitely.

I remembered similar situations before: being corrected for speaking incorrectly, or having a teacher point out problems in my homework. Each time, those scenes brought me a very particular kind of shame—like I was always getting things wrong, always somehow not good enough. I began to wonder whether I simply wasn’t suited to expressing my own thoughts, and even whether I shouldn’t participate in discussions at all. That sense of defectiveness felt like a heavy stone in my chest.

In the end, the answer for that group activity was confirmed as “photosynthesis,” and my “transpiration” was completely ignored. When we handed in the answer, I kept my head down, trying not to draw attention to myself, afraid that mocking remarks would suddenly reach my ears. I felt a tightness in my stomach, as if I had eaten something that didn’t agree with me. I did my best to control myself and not show how uneasy I was, but my palms had already started to sweat.

Even after the whole activity was over, I was still caught in the embarrassment and shame of that moment. During the break, for reasons I couldn’t explain, I didn’t go out to play with the others but stayed at my desk flipping through the textbook, trying to find the difference between transpiration and photosynthesis. It was as if I needed some reason to prove that I wasn’t completely wrong. That night, I took the textbook home and repeatedly read the relevant chapters, trying to memorize every detail.

The next day, I made notes in the textbook, clearly marking the definitions of photosynthesis and transpiration. Although no one mentioned that moment again, I was still afraid that I would make a similar mistake the next time I joined a discussion. That expression and tone of correction seemed to have been etched into my memory.

Today, the school held a special event called Nature Theme Day. The classroom was filled with the children’s laughter, and the walls were covered with pictures of all kinds of forest creatures. Everyone was excitedly talking about the details of the event. The teacher stood at the front of the classroom, her voice bright and warm: “Children, today we are going on a forest adventure. During the adventure, you must pay attention to the songs of the birds and the rustling of the leaves.” When I heard the teacher’s words, my heart filled with anticipation, but at the same time, I felt a trace of unease. I was worried that I would not perform well during the activity and would disappoint the teacher and my classmates.

The activity began, and we were divided into several groups. My friends and I walked out of the classroom and came to a small grove behind the school. Sunlight filtered through the leaves and fell on the ground, and the air was filled with the scent of grass and earth. Everyone wore explorer hats made of paper and held the “Little Explorer’s Guide” handed out by the teacher. As we walked along the path, I heard birdcalls in the distance, just as the teacher had said—light and pleasant.

“Wow, look at that big tree hollow!” a classmate suddenly shouted, pointing at a large tree ahead. A few of us gathered around and marveled at it. I touched the rough bark with my hand, thinking about its growth rings and the passage of time. As the group moved on, I noticed the ground was scattered with golden sunlight, and in the grass there were the occasional snails and ants. I thought to myself: this really is like a tiny magical world.

“Come quick, we found a new kind of mushroom!” another classmate called out. I ran over, my heart racing, excitement mingling with a certain unnamed anxiety. I didn’t want to miss any detail, but I was also afraid I might see something wrongly or step on something. I bent down to look closely. The mushrooms were vividly colored, like magical props from a fairy tale. I heard the chatter and laughter of the classmates around me, and couldn’t help nervously thinking: if the teacher asks me the names of these mushrooms, will I be able to answer?

After the activity ended, everyone returned to the classroom, and the teacher began summarizing the day’s discoveries. My heart was full of self-reproach, afraid that I had failed to notice some important details. When the teacher mentioned the mushrooms, my heart pounded, worried that I had missed something crucial. But the teacher simply said softly, “Today everyone performed wonderfully and discovered many interesting things.” I breathed a sigh of relief, and wiped away the sweat that had formed on my forehead from nervousness with my sleeve.

After returning home, I reflected on the activity. I tried to put the leaves and small flowers I had collected into the little frame I had made in art class. After a few days, my mood gradually calmed down. I realized that although I had felt uneasy during the activity, there were also many happy moments. The forest adventure made me pay more attention to the details of nature, and it also taught me that enjoying the process is more important than worrying about the outcome.

The art classroom was filled with the smell of paint, and a fine dust drifted through the air, giving it a strangely enveloping feel. Sunlight poured in through the window, casting bright patches on the floor. I stood beside my desk, feeling as if a little deer were running wildly in my chest, nervously staring at my own painting. Today was the day we were to present our work, and for some reason I felt an inexplicable fear about this display, as though every detail were waiting to be judged.

The teacher walked over. “Are you ready, child?” Her voice was gentle, but my heartbeat instantly quickened, as if every word carried scrutiny. I tried to straighten my painting, but my fingers trembled slightly without my realizing it. “Mm, I… almost am,” I said, trying to make my voice sound calm, though inside I was already in turmoil.

The classmates nearby had already started showing their work, and whenever they received praise, I couldn’t help blaming myself inwardly: Would my painting be too ordinary? Would it disappoint everyone? My stomach began to ache faintly, as if it had already sensed the criticism to come. I tried to breathe deeply, hoping to calm the anxiety inside me, but my body wouldn’t cooperate, and sweat had already begun to slide quietly down my forehead.

When it was my turn, I could barely hear anything, only felt that I had become the center of attention, with everyone looking at me. I lowered my head, trying to hide my nervousness. “This is… my painting.” As soon as I spoke, I heard a classmate beside me mutter something under their breath, and I immediately guessed whether they were talking about me. In that instant, an image flashed through my mind of them laughing at me, and my heart beat even faster, as if it wanted to burst out of the classroom.

After the presentation ended, my mind was still crowded with those voices and faces, as if every expression on them were judging my worth. That night, I tossed and turned in bed and could not fall asleep. Even the warm lights at home and the voices of my beloved family could not dispel the fear in my heart of being cast out. The next day at school, I was even more careful, afraid of becoming the center of attention again.

A few days later, I decided to talk to the teacher about my unease. After listening, she smiled and said, “You have to believe in your work. They carry your unique expression.” Her words made me breathe a sigh of relief. Although my anxiety had not completely faded, at least I understood that creating art was not about meeting other people’s expectations, but about expressing what was in my heart.

I stood in a corner of the school playground, surrounded by laughter and friends running around, with bright sunshine and a blue sky that made people feel cheerful. On the playground, several classmates were playing a game I rarely joined in, cheering and waving me over. I hesitated as I walked toward them, my mind churning with all kinds of thoughts. “What if they’re only laughing at me?” My heart started racing, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. I joined them, trying to act natural.

“Hey, kid, come over here!” one of the classmates called to me, and I noticed the smile on her face. In an instant, I began analyzing every detail of that expression. “Is she just joking and not really welcoming me?” I forced a smile back, hoping to hide my nervousness.

The game went on, and we had to run all over the playground. I tried to relax, but every time I stepped onto the dirt ground, my stomach twisted with unease. Suddenly one classmate shouted, “Look at that kid, he’s running so slow!” The other kids laughed, and in my mind I immediately magnified the meaning of those words. Were they making fun of me? My face flushed, and my heart beat even faster. I wanted to argue back, but the words got stuck in my throat.

I rehearsed in my head what it would be like if they stopped playing with me, fearing that I would be isolated. I tried to stay calm, and although I was smiling, the shame inside me almost made me give up continuing the game. After it ended, I walked alone to a large tree at the edge of the playground and sat down, trying to collect myself. I kept replaying what had just happened, ruminating over that moment; that joke felt like a thorn piercing my heart.

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t stop thinking about the day. I imagined how everyone would distance themselves from me the next day and whisper when I passed by. Even though I knew it was just my imagination, my heart still refused to settle down. I considered whether I should explain things to them the next day. “Maybe they didn’t mean it that way at all; maybe it was all just the result of my own overinterpretation.” My emotions swelled like surging waves, impossible to control. A few days later, I noticed those classmates were still greeting me, and it seemed my fears had not come true at all. That made me breathe a little easier, but my vigilance had still not lessened.

I realized that I always tend to catastrophize small things, overread other people’s expressions and tone of voice, and then sink into a mire of self-criticism. Even when I knew many things might just be the result of my own repeated overinterpretation, I often still found myself trapped in that cycle of thoughts.

The jump rope competition was about to begin. The playground was filled with shouts and laughter, and the sun beat down on the ground, the heat making my scalp tingle a little. I stood in the class lineup, clutching my jump rope tightly, my heart feeling like a little rabbit was trapped inside, jumping around nonstop. Beside me was a girl from my class. She was usually very warm and enthusiastic, but one thing she had just said made me feel uneasy. She looked at me and said, “Don’t get too nervous, or if you end up jumping too few times later, it’ll be really embarrassing.” She seemed to be smiling when she said it, but I always felt like she was mocking me. In an instant, all kinds of thoughts flooded my mind: “Does she think I’m really bad? Does she think I can’t jump at all?” I didn’t dare keep looking at her. I lowered my head and stared at my shoes, and a sour feeling spread through my chest.

When it was my turn, I stepped onto the starting line. The sunlight was so harsh I could barely open my eyes, and the shouting in my ears became even louder. I kept telling myself, “Don’t mess up, don’t jump too few times, everyone will be watching me.” As soon as the referee blew the whistle, I started jumping rope. The sound of the rope hitting the ground mixed with my breathing. I tried to focus, but that sentence kept replaying in my mind. Halfway through, my foot suddenly caught and the rope snagged. I heard a soft laugh from nearby, and my face instantly burned; even my ears tingled with heat. I desperately tried to start again, but after every two or three jumps I would trip over the rope again. In the end, I stumbled through almost the entire time.

On my way back to the lineup, I felt as if everyone’s eyes were fixed on me, scrutinizing my failure. I forced out a smile, trying to act like nothing had happened. The girl came up to me again and said, “Are you okay? I think you actually jumped pretty well.” But her words sounded so casual that I couldn’t bring myself to believe them. That sentence kept repeating in my head, and each time it did, I felt more and more like an unlikable fool. I nodded without answering, pressed my lips together, and stood at the end of the line as if I wanted to hide.

That night, after I got home, I lay in bed, and the image of me tripping over the rope kept replaying in my mind. I could even hear the sound of the rope getting caught on the ground. My stomach felt sour, and I thought I was too useless, too terrible. I told myself, “She’s definitely going to tell the others how embarrassing I was. Everyone will laugh at me.” That thought made it hard to fall asleep, and it wasn’t until very late that I finally drifted off in a daze. Over the next few days at school, I kept avoiding talking to her first, afraid she would say something else that made me uncomfortable. But every time I saw her, her words “Don’t get too nervous” would ring in my head, making my heart race and my palms sweat.

The warm sunlight fell gently on the sandbox in the neighborhood park, and a few of my friends and I lay in the sand digging tunnels. As my fingers stirred through the fine sand, I could feel the grains slipping through them like a stream of warm quicksand. A puppy ran back and forth not far away, wagging its tail happily. Suddenly, a friend next to me shouted, “You can’t pile the sand like that—it’ll collapse!” I looked up and saw him pointing at the little sandcastle I had just built. It really did seem a bit shaky, and my heart sank. 

“But I like it this way,” I said softly, hearing a slight tremor in my own voice. My hands slowed, and a sense of unease welled up inside me, as if something bad were about to happen. My heartbeat unconsciously quickened too. 

“If you don’t change it, then I’m not playing!” He pouted, his face showing obvious displeasure. I knew he always liked to do things his own way, but his words left me a little at a loss, and fine beads of sweat began to form in my palms. I stopped what I was doing and stared down at the sandcastle, wondering over and over whether he was angry. 

The sounds of other children laughing drifted over from the playground, yet I felt the area around me had grown strangely quiet. Had I done something wrong? What if he really stopped playing with me? That thought kept turning over and over in my head. I glanced at him; there was no sign of his expression softening, and his eyes were still fixed on my sandcastle. The tension in my body kept building, and my stomach began to feel a little uneasy. 

“Sorry, I just wanted to try it,” I said, gathering my courage and hoping it would improve his mood. Sure enough, he didn’t say anything else and turned away to grab his shovel. My heart eased a little, though I was still uneasy, afraid he might really be upset. 

“What are you playing?” came a grown-up voice from afar—it was Mom. I turned around and saw her standing not far away with a smile. The sunlight poured down behind her, bringing me a hint of warmth and comfort. I quickly stood up and ran over, taking her hand and asking, “Can we go to the slide over there?” 

She smiled, patted my head, and nodded in agreement. A comforting warmth flowed through my whole body, washing away the tension from earlier. If she could stay by my side all the time, all those troubles would be chased away. 

That night, lying in bed, I thought about the sandbox incident and still felt a little annoyed, but when I thought of Mom’s warm smile, I stopped caring so much. The next day, when I saw him again, we both acted as if nothing had happened and went on happily playing together in the sandbox.

The heat had pressed the air in the little theater into something heavy and dense. Outside the window, cicadas called one after another, and sunlight slanted in through the side window, etching a pale strip of light across the wooden floor. I sat at the edge of the stage, the back of my shirt already stuck to my skin, sweat slowly creeping down from my temples. A few classmates on stage were running through their lines, their voices drifting and wavering, as if half of them had been evaporated by the heat.

The teacher sat in the front row, tapping a notebook rhythmically with a fingertip. I noticed TA frown.

“Okay, hold on,” TA’s voice bounced around the empty little theater. “The voices need to be louder, especially the student playing the flower fairy.”

My heart clenched hard.

I was the one playing the flower fairy.

TA’s gaze swept across the room and finally landed on me, lingering for a second—maybe only half a second—but in my mind, that second stretched out into a very long time. My face started to burn, and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my palms. *It’s definitely aimed at me. TA thinks I’m terrible. TA has been waiting for a chance to say this.*

“Again?” TA asked.

I nodded and stood up, my legs a little weak.

I tried to make my voice sound steady, cleared my throat, and started to recite my lines. But all through it, half my attention was fixed on TA—Had TA frowned again? Was TA writing something in the notebook? Was the corner of TA’s mouth pressed down a little? After every line, I rapidly replayed everything in my head, as if I were examining every word under a magnifying glass.

After I finished that section, I hurried backstage and stood with my back against the wall, my chest heaving.

*I must have disappointed everyone. On Open Day, I’ll stand onstage and forget my lines, everyone will be watching me, and the teacher will lower their head in disappointment...*

My stomach tightened faintly, as if something inside it were slowly twisting.

Just then, a classmate came over and asked in a low voice, “Are you okay?”

“I don’t think I should be playing this role,” I heard myself say, my tone harsher than I’d intended.

TA said I’d actually done well just now and told me not to worry. I nodded, but the words seemed to land on a sheet of glass without really getting through.

On the bus ride home, every jolt made my stomach clench. The smell of food drifted in, but I had no appetite. That night, lying in bed and staring at the ceiling, I kept seeing the teacher’s frown over and over again. *I must have been really bad.* I said it softly into the dark, as if confirming something already settled.

The next day during break, I found the teacher in the hallway. My heart was racing, and my voice trembled a little. “Teacher, yesterday’s rehearsal... was I doing something wrong?”

TA looked up, expression calm. “No. Rehearsal is for making adjustments. You did very well. I just wanted everyone to be a little more invested.”

I stood there, listening as the words slowly sank into my mind.

Something in my chest eased just a little, like a string that had been pulled tight for a long time finally slackening by a notch.

A few days later, when I stepped onto that stage again, I was still nervous, still sneaking glances at the teacher’s expression in the pauses between lines. But I started asking myself one more question in my head: *Is this real, or am I scaring myself again?*

Sometimes there was no answer. But being able to ask was already a little better than before.

The sun was glaring, and I stood at the edge of the playground squinting, holding an old volleyball that had faded with age. The teacher asked us to practice passing in groups, and I was put in a group with three other classmates. I was never very good at sports, especially volleyball, which required hand-eye coordination. When it was my turn to receive the ball, my palms touched it, but it still slammed hard onto the ground, bounced a few times, and rolled away. The chubby boy beside me laughed and said, “Why are you so stupid?” His voice wasn’t loud, but to me those words seemed to fall from the sky and crush the breath out of me. The other classmates said nothing, but I felt they must have silently agreed with him in their hearts.

“Sorry, my hand slipped,” I said softly, trying to sound relaxed, but my voice was trembling. The teacher came over and told everyone to keep practicing. I wanted to concentrate, but my heartbeat grew faster and faster, and the whole top of my head felt numb and tingly. In the following passing drills, my movements became stiffer; I just mechanically sent the ball back, not even daring to look up at the others’ expressions. Were they disappointed in me? Did they think I was holding the group back?

After a while, it was my turn to receive again. When the ball came flying toward me, my hands were not ready, and it once again dropped to the ground. This time no one laughed, but the chubby boy frowned and let out a sigh. “Can’t you be a little more serious?” he said calmly, but to me it felt like a sharp knife slicing through my defenses. I wanted to say something in response, but it felt as if a stone were stuck in my throat, and I could only stand there dazed.

I began to obsess over their expressions, especially that boy’s sigh and frown. Did they think I was terrible? Did they not want me in the group at all? My stomach felt a little upset, as if a hand were tightly gripping it. I lowered my head and stared hard at the cement floor, trying not to cry.

After practice ended, when I walked back to the classroom, I deliberately kept my distance from the other classmates. I didn’t want to walk with them, and I didn’t want to hear anything they might say about me. The scene from earlier kept replaying in my mind, especially “Why are you so stupid?” and the later “Be more serious.” At dinner, I barely ate anything, only drank a little soup. When Mom asked if I was feeling unwell, I casually made up an excuse and brushed it off. That night in bed, I kept thinking about missing the ball, and I felt like I was truly useless. If I had done a little better, would those classmates have liked me more?

The next morning, I still had a dull stomachache, and my hands felt stiff as if frozen. I didn’t want to go to school, and I even wished I could suddenly come down with a high fever so I wouldn’t have to face them. But in the end, I still put on my school uniform and dragged myself to class. I tried to avoid the classmates in my group and kept from making eye contact with them.

The choir rehearsal began, and the classroom filled with the rising and falling voices of my classmates. The teacher stood at the front, waving her hands to conduct us so we could sing the notes correctly. The piano melody echoed through the room, my palms began to sweat, and my heartbeat sped up to twice its normal pace. I was afraid the teacher would notice me, and I always felt my voice wasn’t pleasant enough. Suddenly, the teacher stopped, looked around, and then called my name. “Little one, it’s your turn to try singing this line solo.” That sentence hit me like a heavy blow. I felt every muscle in my body tense at once, and a sharp pain twisted in my stomach. I walked to the front, trying to stand as far from the teacher as possible, silently telling myself not to embarrass myself.

The piano started again. I opened my mouth, but it felt as though every syllable was stuck in my throat. The classroom was completely silent, as if everyone were holding their breath and waiting for my voice. I took a deep breath and began to sing, but my voice seemed to tremble. I could feel the heat in my face rising nonstop, and I could almost feel sweat sliding down my forehead. The teacher nodded encouragingly, and I tried hard to keep myself calm. From the back of the room, I heard a faint snicker, like a tiny needle piercing my heart.

When I finally finished the solo, the teacher gave me a comforting smile. “You did well. Next time will be better.” I knew she meant it kindly, but in my heart I still couldn’t stop hearing those snickers. Back at my seat, I gripped my pencil tightly, hoping it would help me calm down.

After class, on my way home, I kept replaying what had just happened in my mind. Every note felt like a mistake echoing in my ears. I thought my voice was awful and worried that my classmates would laugh at me. That night, lying in bed, I kept thinking about what had happened today, worrying about how my classmates would look at me the next day and whether anyone would bring it up. I tried to shift my attention to other things, but I just couldn’t shake it off.

A few days later, although no one brought up the solo again, I still kept replaying that moment in my mind, worried that I would repeat such embarrassment in other classes. I began to fear being asked to do anything that stood out, and even when the teacher encouraged me again, I always felt unable to bear it.

The classroom was somewhat noisy, and sunlight from outside fell on the floor in mottled patches. The teacher assigned us to discuss a Chinese language question in groups. I sat with three classmates; they all looked very relaxed, pointing at a passage in the textbook and saying something. I tried to make myself look less nervous, but I could feel the sweat in my palms had made the pencil slippery and damp. I lowered my head and looked at the book, but nothing sank in. I could only force myself to raise my head and suggest, “Could this be because… it’s a ‘metaphor’?” As soon as the words left my mouth, one of the classmates burst out laughing. His laugh was sharp and grating, stabbing my eardrums like the sound of stepping on glass. In an exaggerated tone, he repeated my answer: “A metaphor! Are you serious? You don’t even know this?” Another classmate beside him laughed along, and their eyes seemed to be scrutinizing some kind of monster.

“I…I thought that was it…” I tried to defend myself, but my voice grew so low that I could barely hear it myself. My face started to burn, as if scorched by fire, and my ears rang. I gripped the pencil in my hand tighter and tighter, as if it were the only thing keeping me from fainting. “You’d better not say anything. Let us discuss it, so we don’t make mistakes,” another classmate said in a tone that sounded casual but was laced with mockery. I froze there, too afraid to move, feeling as if I were trapped inside a transparent glass jar, with everyone outside staring at me, yet no one reaching out a hand to pull me out.

My mind began rapidly replaying every humiliating moment from before: that time I stammered and said the wrong word while reading aloud in front of the class, the time I fell during PE and was laughed at—those memories surged up like a flood and drowned me. I was terrified. My heart was pounding like a drum, my stomach felt tightly knotted, as if a stone were pressing down on it, and I almost wanted to throw up.

“Why is your face so red? Are you angry?” The classmate who had laughed the loudest stared at me, with an expression of mockery I couldn’t understand. I didn’t know how to answer. I could only lower my head and bite my lip to keep from crying. How I wished I could leave this place, run to a corner where no one was around, and make all those voices disappear. I was frantically repeating in my mind: “Don’t cry, absolutely don’t cry. They’ll think you’re even more ridiculous.”

In the end, the teacher came over, noticed that our group hadn’t been discussing anything, and asked, “What’s going on?” Those classmates suddenly became especially well-behaved, and one of them said, “We were waiting for her to give the answer.” I kept my head down and said nothing, only nodding mechanically. Their hypocrisy made me feel even more disgusted, but at the same time I felt powerless. I really didn’t know what to do.

After I got home, I said nothing, just sat at my little desk in a daze. That feeling of shame was like a hand tightly clutching my throat, making even breathing difficult. At night, I tossed and turned in bed, and their laughter kept replaying over and over in my head. If I hid myself away and never went to school again, would none of this happen?

Sunlight filtered through the leaves and fell across the playground, while the air was filled with the fresh scent of grass. The school organized a class event, and everyone enthusiastically split into different groups to compete. I stood off to the side, watching them run and laugh, feeling my heartbeat quicken and my cheeks grow warm. Although everyone was eagerly discussing competition strategies, I was only busy silently analyzing each person’s reactions and expressions, trying to find some sign that would let me fit in.

“Do you want to join us?” a classmate suddenly turned to ask me, with a hint of uncertainty in their voice. I forced out a smile, nodded, and then walked with them to the designated starting line. But the voice inside me kept whispering: they’re only asking because they need enough people; maybe they don’t really want me to join. I noticed a few people whispering to each other, and I couldn’t help but start wondering whether they were talking about me.

The competition began, and I tried hard to keep up with everyone else’s pace, but my steps felt heavy and clumsy. My stomach started to feel a little uneasy, and my muscles tensed up. The sounds of footsteps mixed together in my ears, and I was afraid I would drag the whole group down. In the end, our group lost the game, and I immediately felt a deep sense of shame and disappointment, as if the whole world were blaming me.

After the competition, I quietly left the playground and sat under the shade of a tree nearby. I kept replaying what had happened in my mind, while the laughter and cheers of those classmates still echoed in my ears. “What’s wrong?” another classmate came over and asked me, concern in their voice. I shook my head, trying not to let the tears fall, and said with difficulty, “I’m fine, just a little tired.” But deep inside, a voice kept asking: if I had done better, would I not have been ignored? Would everyone have liked me more?

That night, I lay in bed, closing my eyes but unable to fall asleep, my mind filled with images and sounds from the day. I thought of the smiles on my classmates’ faces, and my heart ached faintly. Although they hadn’t blamed me directly, I still felt isolated. A few days later, I finally forgot about it, but that feeling of being left out still left a mark deep in my heart.

I was standing on the playground, and the scene before me was somewhat blurry. That day the sunlight was especially glaring, shining on the area where we were playing, and the ground was covered with golden flecks of light. I accidentally took a step back and stepped on my classmate Xiaoming’s handmade craft—a paper boat he had spent several recess periods making. The paper boat was crushed out of shape under my shoe, instantly causing an uproar. The classmates around us gathered in, their faces full of anger and blame. Someone said, “Why did you step on and ruin his work?” Another classmate added, “Xiaoming worked so hard on it for so long!” I wanted to explain, but the words seemed stuck in my throat. My heart began to race, and my palms started to sweat. In my mind, I quickly flashed on their angry expressions, as if rehearsing how much they would hate me, and even a fear of being abandoned welled up inside me. My body trembled slightly, and I felt an empty ache in my stomach. Xiaoming’s face was full of disappointment; he lowered his head and would not look at me. I desperately tried to find an appropriate way to apologize, but every word felt pale and powerless. In a low voice I said, “I’m sorry, I didn’t mean to.” However, no one responded; I only heard everyone murmuring among themselves. I felt as though I were trapped inside an invisible circle, with all eyes fixed on me. I wanted to escape, but I couldn’t move. This incident left me with no mood to stay on the playground any longer; I just wanted to leave. When I got back to the classroom, I sat at my desk, still unable to calm down. For the entire day, I kept thinking about my mistake, with Xiaoming’s disappointed expression and the other classmates’ reproaches playing over and over in my mind. My stomach cramped painfully, as if protesting my helplessness. A few days later, although no one mentioned the matter again, I still felt a heavy weight in my heart, as if I could never escape that moment of being misunderstood and blamed.

The day it was my turn to go up and recite, the air in the classroom seemed to grow heavy. Bright patches of sunlight streamed through the windows, but all I could feel was a glaring, searing heat. I stood at the front of the classroom, clutching the small card in my hand so tightly that my palms were already damp with sweat. Around me were the students’ low, scattered murmurs, and their gazes made my skin prickle with discomfort. “Don’t be afraid, relax a little,” the Chinese teacher said softly, patting my shoulder. I nodded and forced out a smile, but it felt like drawing a stiff mask onto my face. My heart was pounding so fast it felt like it was about to burst out of my chest, and my legs were starting to go weak. 

The recitation began. I looked down at the card and read the first sentence in a soft voice, but by the second sentence my voice suddenly caught. My mind went completely blank, and I couldn’t remember what came next no matter how hard I tried. I froze there, and the card in my hand seemed suddenly unbearably heavy. I heard a few snickers and whispers from below, and quickly looked up, only to find several classmates whispering to one another. One of them even turned away, as if unwilling to meet my eyes. A wave of shame surged up in my chest. Were they laughing at me? Did they think I was humiliating myself? The thought snowballed until it became overwhelming, pressing down on me so hard I could barely breathe. 

“Keep going, don’t be nervous,” the teacher’s voice came again, but I felt as though those words were an inadvertent reproach. I tried hard to swallow my nerves and regain my rhythm, but the words on the card suddenly blurred, as if they had turned into unfamiliar symbols. I stammered through a few lines, my voice growing softer and softer, until I finally finished in a rush. In that moment, I wanted nothing more than to vanish from the classroom and dissolve into the air. 

On the way back to my seat, my legs felt as if they were filled with lead, every step dragging along a heavy sense of disappointment. After sitting down, I felt my stomach begin to twist and my chest tighten painfully. I took a sip of water from my cup, only to realize that even my lips were trembling slightly. “I’m such a failure,” I thought, lowering my head and pretending to read, while the scene of forgetting my lines replayed over and over in my mind. With each detail that returned, I felt even more embarrassed, as though the whole class’s attention had become fixed on my shame. 

That night, I barely slept at all. Lying in bed, I kept replaying my performance on stage, even beginning to wonder whether those classmates had continued talking about me afterward. Even the teacher’s words of comfort turned into questions: Did she feel disappointed in me? Did she think I had no future? My mind was like an endlessly running movie, magnifying everything and reprocessing it all. The next morning, on the way to school, my stomach still felt tight and unsettled, but I pretended nothing was wrong and walked into the classroom, trying my best to avoid contact with anyone. All week long, I avoided meeting the teachers’ and classmates’ eyes, and even their laughter reminded me of that day’s embarrassment.

The classroom was a little dim, and faint birdsong drifted in from outside the window, mixed with the rustling sound of leaves swayed by the wind. I sat in the last row of the classroom, gripping the report in my hands while trying hard to control my trembling fingers. Today was the day our group had to present, and the teacher had given us a full week to prepare. Now it was my turn to speak. My heart was racing, pounding in my chest like a drum, and my palms were already damp with sweat.

I stood up and tried to keep my voice from shaking so much. “Everyone, I... today we’re going to talk about the solar system...” Before I even finished, I heard a faint burst of laughter. I wasn’t sure if it was directed at me, but panic instantly began to spread through me. The group members opposite me seemed to be exchanging glances, and I couldn’t tell what they meant. I only felt that I might have said something wrong.

“What are you afraid of? You can do it, keep going!” A group member beside me quietly encouraged me. I forced a smile and continued with what I had prepared. But in my mind, thoughts kept popping up: “They’re laughing at me,” “Did they not hear me clearly?” “I think I said something wrong.”

My breathing grew faster, my stomach began to ache faintly, and I tried hard to focus. But every time I wanted to speak more smoothly, the chaotic thoughts in my head became tangled like a mess of yarn. After the presentation ended, the teacher smiled at me and said, “You did well. Next time, you can relax a little more.” Yet my heart still sank, and I felt that I hadn’t done my best.

That night the wind was strong, and the leaves outside the window rustled noisily. Before bed, I kept replaying the presentation in my mind, over and over, with my mistakes and the classmates’ laughter looping through my head. “I should have been more careful,” I kept blaming myself, filled with disappointment and unease. After tossing and turning for a long time, I finally fell into a deep sleep.

The next day, the teacher praised our group again in class, but I still felt that I didn’t deserve it. Although the other group members were all happy, I remained nervous and uneasy, worried that they would be affected by my performance. A few classmates came over to comfort me and said I had done well. I tried to smile at them, but the doubt inside me still would not go away.

The classroom was filled with the smell of paint and paper, and sunlight streamed through the window onto our desks, making the colorful pencils look even brighter. Today was the school drawing contest, and the theme written above was “My Dream Home.” My heart raced, and my palms began to sweat. I felt as if I were standing on a stage, ready to face the judges’ and audience’s scrutiny. The children beside me were all busy coloring and drawing lines on their paper. They seemed so focused, oblivious to everything else. But I kept thinking about last year’s mistake, when my drawing was criticized by the teacher for having an incomplete composition and brushstrokes that were too immature. That scene kept replaying in my mind, as if it were mocking my immaturity. My chest tightened again and again, and my stomach began to feel uneasy.

“Come on, kids, keep it up!” the teacher said gently yet firmly. I tried hard to find a beautiful image in my mind. My heart was pounding wildly, and the brush made mistakes on the paper several times. I quickly reached for the eraser, trying to rub away those marks, but faint shadows still remained. I regarded these mistakes as more important than anything else, as if my whole world depended on how this sheet of paper turned out.

At that moment, I couldn’t help but stop and stare out the window. The leaves swayed in the wind, and I imagined that as my own mood. The children in class were whispering to one another, and I began to wonder whether they were discussing my drawing. I could feel my breathing growing faster and faster, so I tried to take deep breaths and calm myself down. When I came back to my senses, I kept asking myself over and over: “Is this dream too childish?” “Will the teacher see that I’m not good enough?” I drew a few strokes intermittently, each one with extreme caution, as if I were afraid of touching some irreversible line.

As the class was about to end, the teacher began collecting our work. Trembling with fear, I handed my drawing to her, my heart full of anxiety and dread. I told myself that I should preemptively admit my shortcomings, so I wouldn’t be rejected by the teacher or my classmates. So I said softly, “Teacher, I didn’t draw this very well. It probably isn’t anything special.” The teacher smiled slightly. “Every drawing has its own unique beauty. Don’t worry.” I forced a smile, but doubts still filled my heart. A few days later, the results were announced. Although my work didn’t win a prize, the teacher praised our efforts in class, and the panic in my heart eased a little.

That week, I kept imagining my drawing, thinking about how I would change my attitude if I could go back to the moment of the contest. My mind was filled with the voice of “I must do better next time,” piled high with doubts about my own abilities, as if every choice I made needed to have its value proven. I learned to question everything and tried to anticipate my mistakes in advance.

Raindrops kept tapping against the window, their sound soft and dense. The air in the classroom was thick with dampness, mixed with the smells of chalk dust and books. Science class began, and the task the teacher assigned was a simple group experiment: using a small battery to power a light bulb. As the teacher drew diagrams on the blackboard and explained how current flowed, I listened. Even though it was a simple experiment, I still felt uneasy, because I had a nagging feeling that things would not go smoothly.

“So you need to connect it like this,” the teacher said, pointing to the rough circuit sketch on the board. My heartbeat quickened, and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my palms. I imagined the wires not being connected to the right terminals, the battery leaking, or the bulb exploding outright. These worries quickly filled my mind.

The experiment began, and each group started busily working. I carefully picked up a wire, my fingers trembling slightly, and exchanged an uncertain glance with a classmate in my group. “Hey, do you think this connection is okay?” he asked, his voice mingling with the rain, faint but clear.

“Maybe,” I forced out. My brows were tightly knit, and in my mind I kept hearing illusory sounds, as if I were saying to myself, “It definitely won’t work; something must be wrong.”

We checked the wire positions over and over, carefully inserting them into the metal clips. I gripped the wires hard, my fingers turning white with tension. As the last wire was connected to the battery, the bulb flickered faintly, then went out. The unease in my heart quickly turned into fear, as if the whole world had gone silent and only the drumbeat in my chest remained.

In an instant, I felt a wave of heat sweep through my body, and my face began to burn. “Did we do something wrong?” a classmate’s quiet reminder pulled me out of my thoughts. I immediately began retracing every step, trying hard to figure out where the mistake was.

“Did we connect it wrong?” I muttered to myself. “No, that’s not right… maybe the battery is dead.” I said this while checking the battery’s positive and negative terminals again. “What if…” Before I could finish the thought, the teacher had already come to our table. “Is there a problem?” he asked, his voice as gentle as the rain.

I reluctantly looked up, realizing my face was hot as a furnace, and could only force out a faint smile: “We… we’ll try again.” Inside, though, I was silently criticizing myself for never being good enough.

After the teacher walked away, my classmates also began helping me check each connection again. Once my heartbeat calmed down, we tried again, and this time the bulb finally lit up. Looking at the light, I felt a little more relaxed, but deep down the shame still would not fade away.

For a while after science class ended, I kept thinking about it, worrying about what the teacher and my classmates would think of me. That night, after I got home, I lay in bed replaying every scene from class over and over until my consciousness gradually blurred. It took several days before I could let go of that worry a little and tell myself that next time I would try to stay calmer.

The school fair had been in preparation for a long time, and our whole class was full of excitement that day. As I stepped into the event area, the colorful balloons and the sound of music all around me made me feel as if I had suddenly been immersed in a sea of joy. Yet deep down, I still felt a sense of heaviness. Our teacher assigned us to different activities, and I was told to help at a booth for a throwing game. Seeing my classmates around me busily making preparations in high spirits, an uneasiness kept welling up inside me: what if I made a mistake, what would everyone think of me? Just thinking about it made my heartbeat quicken, and my palms began to sweat slightly.

The event began, and the place was buzzing with noise. The laughter and cheers of children mixed together, making it hard for me to concentrate. I forced myself to smile, trying to make myself look as if I belonged there. One group of children after another came to play the game, and I was responsible for keeping score for them. Every time they finished a throw, they would turn around and look at me expectantly, while my fingers trembled uncontrollably on the paper. My shoulders were stiff as stones, and I kept thinking, I mustn’t miscalculate; everyone is watching me.

Suddenly, a boy came up to me and said, “You made a mistake, didn’t you? I clearly hit three, but you only marked two.” His tone was dissatisfied and firm. I froze for a moment, and my face turned bright red. My heart pounded so hard I almost thought the whole crowd could hear it. I quickly lowered my head to check again, only to find that the mark I had made just now was indeed a bit unclear. In my mind, a scene flashed by of my classmates laughing at how careless I was, and I felt as if there was nowhere to hide.

“I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’ll correct it right away,” I explained repeatedly, my heart like a rabbit jumping wildly inside me as I hurriedly fixed the mistake. The laughter and music around me seemed to be mocking my blunder. After that, I became even more nervous. Every score I recorded had to be checked again and again, terrified that I might make another mistake.

After the activity ended, my head felt a little dizzy, and I subconsciously rubbed my sore neck. On the way home, a wave of helplessness washed over me, and I shrank into the bus seat, the scenery outside the window blurred and indistinct. The boy’s words kept echoing in my ears, and I kept replaying the scene over and over, blaming myself for not being more careful.

When I got home that night, my emotions still hadn’t calmed down. Even though I was already lying in bed, I was still shaken. My mother knocked and came in, and seeing that I didn’t look very cheerful, she asked with concern about the day’s activities. I briefly said a sentence or two, not daring to mention the mistake, just hoping she wouldn’t press further. That night I tossed and turned, thinking that I must be more careful in the future and absolutely must not make the same mistake again.

I sat in a corner of the school library, listening to the rain outside softly tapping against the windowpane, the drip-drop sound seeming to tell a quiet story. The room was filled with the faint scent of wooden bookshelves and old books. Beside the shelves, one student was speaking quietly with another; they seemed to be looking through an interesting picture book. My heart suddenly began to beat faster, and my hands grew slightly sweaty. I started worrying that they would notice me sitting there all alone.

“Look, that book is really interesting,” I heard one of the students say softly.

I lowered my head and pretended to be deeply absorbed in the fantasy adventure book in my hands. But my attention was nowhere near the page; my thoughts began to wander, imagining that they might be talking about me, or laughing at me for sitting there by myself. The thought made my heart race with panic. I felt my cheeks growing hot, my heart pounding harder and harder, as if it might leap out of my chest.

“Are they laughing at me?” I asked myself uneasily, and many similar awkward moments from the past came flooding back. I couldn’t help remembering the last time I slipped and fell in a puddle in the hallway, and my classmates laughed for a while. I felt that same shame return.

I closed my eyes, trying to steady my breathing. But the whispering in my ears seemed to grow louder and louder, and my stomach began to feel uneasy. My gaze drifted toward the window, hoping the sound of the rain would help free me from these nagging worries. Yet the rain sounded like an endless melody, continuing my anxious tune without pause.

After a while, I tried to convince myself that maybe they were just interested in the book’s content and that it had nothing to do with me. I made an effort to find some balance in my heart, though it seemed to be of no use. I reminded myself: they don’t know me; they may not even have noticed me sitting in this corner. But a voice inside kept questioning my very presence, and my tension refused to ease.

In the quiet of the library, I felt a sense of loneliness amplified. Every time I looked up and noticed someone glancing in my direction, my fear of being laughed at or misunderstood grew stronger. Finally, I decided to close my book, stand up, excuse myself to the restroom, and leave the space that made me feel so uneasy.

After I got home, I kept replaying every detail of the library in my mind. I told myself that this anxiety wasn’t worth paying attention to, and tried to keep myself occupied with things I enjoyed to take my mind off it. But the lingering worry in my heart still left me feeling somewhat unsettled.

I was standing in line at the school cafeteria, staring at the people ahead one by one as they handed over their trays, not knowing why, but every time I queued up, time seemed to pass especially slowly. I could smell the food today, with a hint of chicken and a faint but rich curry aroma. My stomach had started to rumble a little, but I was more focused on the people in front of me. Just as I was spacing out, a boy in school uniform walked over from the side, went straight in front of me, and even pulled another girl in to cut in line with him. I froze for a moment. My lips moved, my throat was dry, and I wanted to say something, but I shrank back. In the end, I only frowned and stared at their backs. My heartbeat sped up, my face felt a little hot, and my chest felt tight. I didn’t dare look at the expressions of the people around me, afraid someone would think I was cowardly.

“You cut in line!” I finally blurted out, my voice higher than usual, though it sounded a little shaky. The boy who had cut in line turned back to look at me, apparently not taking it too seriously, and casually said, “Hey, it’s just for a moment. What’s the big deal?” Then he turned back around and kept talking to the girl. I clenched my teeth, feeling my eyes burn, as if something were stuck in my chest. I thought, how could he do that? Was cutting in line really something he took for granted? But no one around me stood up to support me, and even the classmate behind me seemed to just want to avoid trouble. I felt a strong sense of frustration, as if I were completely powerless, and I was afraid that if I said anything else, I’d be laughed at, so I shut my mouth tightly, lowered my head, took a step back, and let them go ahead.

When I finally got my lunch, I still felt uncomfortable. The tray in my hands was a little hot, but I could hardly taste the food. After lunch was over, I went back to the classroom, but my mind kept replaying what had just happened. Why couldn’t I have been more resolute? If I had been a little braver, could I have made them get back in line? But then I thought that maybe they wouldn’t have listened to me at all, and I felt even more discouraged. I sat at my desk, feeling gloomy the whole time, unable to concentrate on what the teacher was saying.

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning, unable to fall asleep. My mind kept replaying the scene of that boy cutting in line. I even thought that if I had shouted louder back then, would the outcome have been different? But another voice told me it would have been pointless—they wouldn’t care about what I said. In the end, I hugged my pillow and buried my face in it, still unable to stop the uneasy, regretful thoughts.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves and scattered across the park path, casting dappled patterns of light and shadow on the ground. I sat on the swing, lightly kicking the ground and feeling the gentle touch of the wind glide past my ears. The swing’s chains made a soft creaking sound with each movement. The trees around me rustled in the breeze, a few birds chirped in the distance, and children’s laughter drifted over. I liked listening to these sounds; they made me feel that the world was full of life and vitality. I closed my eyes, and images flashed through my mind: yesterday at school, playing with my friends, laughing and chatting, my heart feeling warm. My stomach felt slightly tense, but that feeling was quickly carried away by the relaxed atmosphere. Suddenly, I felt a slight wave of dizziness, perhaps because the swing had gone too high. I quickly gripped the swing’s chains tighter, my heartbeat quickening a little, but soon I relaxed, adjusted my posture, and let the swing slow to a stop. I opened my eyes and saw my mother, seated on a bench not far away, waving at me. Beside her was a woven bag containing freshly bought fruit, and a faint sweet fragrance drifted over. “Little one, are you tired from playing?” my mother asked with a smile. I shook my head; in truth I was a little tired, but I still wanted to play a while longer. So I kept swinging gently, enjoying the quiet afternoon. After a while, we went home. The sun was gradually setting, and the whole park was bathed in gold. My mother and I chatted along the way about amusing things that had happened at school, and I felt very happy. When we got home, I washed my hands and sat at the dining table while my mother cut up some fruit for me. After dinner, I lay on my bed, thinking about the time I’d spent on the swing in the park that day, feeling an indescribable calm and peace. A few days later, I went to the park again, and the scene from that day replayed in my mind, bringing a familiar sense of reassurance.

The smell from the dinner table still hadn’t faded. The fish soup’s savory fishiness mingled with the soft fragrance of tofu, drifting through the living room like the last warmth left by dinner. I curled up in the corner of the sofa, arms wrapped around my knees, staring at the untouched bowl on the coffee table—the rim had a tiny chip. I don’t know how long I’d been staring at it.

The voices came from the kitchen. They weren’t loud, but they were taut with tension.

“Look at these grades again! Dead last in the whole class! What have you been doing with them all this time?”

The tone was like a blunt instrument—not cutting, but smashing. I felt my shoulders draw inward, as if instinctively trying to make myself smaller.

“And it’s all my fault? What did you do all this time? Besides yelling, what else can you do?” The other voice shot back, trembling, straining to hold something back.

My heartbeat started to sound loud, so loud I thought they might hear it. A sticky layer of sweat broke out on my forehead. I didn’t dare move, didn’t dare let the sofa make any noise. I was afraid that if they turned around and found me listening, they’d dump all their anger on me too.

*Don’t let them see me. Don’t let them see me.*

“I knew it—you had a useless kid. Always daydreaming, grades this bad. What can you even do when you grow up?”

My stomach clenched suddenly, as if a hand had reached in and grabbed it, twisting hard. I bit my lower lip and shut my eyes, trying to force the word out of my ears. But it wouldn’t go away. It landed somewhere and began to sink.

“She’s only ten—”

“Ten is exactly when you should know better! It’s not like there’s something wrong with her brain!”

I stood up, my legs a little weak, ran back to my room, and pulled the door shut.

Then I slid down to the floor.

The tears came quickly, so quickly I didn’t even have time to feel ashamed. I hugged my head and heard myself let out a very low, almost soundless sob. Something felt like it was pressing on my chest; with every breath, that weight sank a little deeper.

*It’s my fault. I didn’t do well enough. If I were smarter, if I weren’t so bad, they wouldn’t be fighting.*

The thought circled once and came back, and each time it grew more solid, like hammering nails into something. I couldn’t make it stop. I even started to wonder: did they really think I was useless? Would they not want me anymore in the future? The thought was too big for me, and I didn’t dare think it through, but it was there, blocking everything.

Outside, the voices gradually died down, until finally there was silence.

I didn’t go out.

That night, I lay in bed, my hands and feet cold, my body as if soaked in something icy that wouldn’t warm up no matter what. The ceiling was black. I stared at it, while that word kept turning in my head—useless, useless, useless—like a song without melody, playing on repeat with no end.

I tried to fall asleep. I couldn’t.

I tried to think about something else. I couldn’t.

What if the next exam was the same? What if I failed again? I didn’t even dare finish the question in my head, because I already knew what the answer would be, and that answer made my stomach hurt again.

All night long, I never closed my eyes. Now and then a car passed outside, and light and shadow swept across the wall before disappearing. I just lay there, holding on to that feeling that still had no name—later I would learn that it was called shame.

I was sitting in a corner of the school library, with several books spread out on the table, their pages slightly yellowed at the edges in the afternoon sunlight. A faint smell of paper hung in the air, and the quiet surroundings were calming, yet they also made me feel even more nervous. To prepare for the class speech contest, I was here searching for materials.

“How’s your preparation going?” my classmate asked in a low voice. When he leaned over, I could smell a faint aroma of modeling clay on him.

“I’m still working hard to find materials…” I forced a smile, trying to hide my unease.

My heart began to race quickly, like a little deer desperately running through a silent forest. I started worrying whether my preparation was enough, afraid that I would stammer during the speech or say the wrong thing. Every time I thought about standing at the podium with all eyes on me, my stomach would churn with a dull ache.

I closed one book and tried to focus on the others. Outside the library window, the pleasant chirping of birds eased my anxiety a little. I tried to calm myself with deep breaths, but it seemed to make little difference.

“Don’t get too nervous. Just keep a good pace,” my classmate said reassuringly, patting my shoulder before going back to his own materials.

His encouragement put me slightly at ease, but the tension inside me still wouldn’t go away. My hands were faintly damp with sweat, and the fingertips holding my pen seemed barely under my control. Seeing my classmates all absorbed in preparing at their own desks, I reminded myself to stay calm and not lose my composure in front of them.

A few minutes later, I stood up and decided to choose more related books. As I walked between the library shelves, my fingers lightly brushed the spines, drawing comfort from the books’ solid presence. Even so, that fear of being judged remained right behind me.

That night, after I got home, I tried to keep rehearsing my speech. I paced back and forth in my room, determined not to let my mind wander. A few days later, the speech contest was held as scheduled. Although my heart was still pounding with nervousness, I told myself that even if I failed, at least I had tried. In the week that followed, I often found myself thinking back on that moment, unable not to feel a strange sense of pride in my courage.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves and fell across the playground, where specks of dappled light danced beside me. I stood at the edge of the playground, holding a blue rubber ball in my hand, yet I felt an uneasy knot in my heart. The teacher said we would be divided into teams for a competition, but I always worried that I would hold everyone back. Just as I was trying to figure out how to do better, I heard a few classmates whispering behind me. “TA is definitely going to mess it up again.” “Last time TA didn’t even kick the ball.” A wave of shame flooded over me. I gripped the rubber ball tightly, my heart beginning to race, as if it might leap out of my chest.

I tried to ignore their voices, but their words stung my heart like needles. I turned around, wanting to find somewhere quiet, but my feet seemed glued to the ground and wouldn’t move. “Hey, why aren’t you over here yet?” one classmate called to me, her voice tinged with impatience. I slowly shuffled forward, trying not to notice the heat on my face. I could feel sweat trickling down my forehead, and the sweat on my back had soaked through my clothes.

The game finally began. My palms were sweating from nervousness, and the ball kept slipping from my hands. Under the classmates’ gaze, I felt myself growing more and more clumsy, as though every movement were being magnified. I heard the cheering and criticism from around me mix together like a nightmare. Every time I made a mistake, the mocking grew louder. I began to doubt myself: why was I always so bad at this?

After the match ended, I slowly walked back to the classroom, trying hard to look as though I didn’t care. But once class began, I could still hear those harsh comments echoing in my ears. My stomach started to ache, as if someone had mercilessly twisted it. Sitting at my desk, I unconsciously lowered my head and focused on the words in my textbook, trying to hide my unease. By afternoon, my emotions had finally calmed down a little, but there was still a deep sense of disappointment in my heart.

That night, lying in bed, I closed my eyes and hoped to fall asleep quickly, but my mind kept replaying the scenes from the day. My clumsiness and my classmates’ ridicule kept surfacing again and again in my head. I kept asking myself why I always did so poorly at something so simple. As if afraid of being abandoned, I struggled to win everyone’s approval. It took several days before the turmoil in my heart slowly subsided, but I knew that seed of unease had already been planted, and it would occasionally remind me of my own shortcomings.

Rain beat against the classroom windows, the steady ticking of drops creating a tense atmosphere. Around me were the classmates’ hushed conversations and the teacher’s instructions from the podium. I sat at my desk, facing a science experiment setup that wasn’t really all that complicated. The teacher was explaining how to create a simple chemical reaction in a bottle. My heart was beating a little fast, and my palms were slightly sweaty. I tried to keep up with the steps, occasionally looking up at the blackboard.

“Be careful, don’t spill it,” the teacher reminded us. I took a quiet breath and carefully poured the reagent into the bottle. My hand trembled slightly, and images of the experiment failing and causing chaos kept flashing through my mind. I tried hard to focus, to keep my attention on the small mouth of the bottle, but all I could think about was the bottle suddenly exploding, liquid splashing everywhere, the whole class in an uproar.

Just as I was lost in my wild thoughts, a classmate next to me suddenly shouted, “Look, it’s smoking!” I jolted, my heart suddenly racing. In an instant, the thick smoke billowing out of the bottle made me panic a little. Sure enough, that dreadful thought had come true. The bottle began shaking violently, as if it were about to explode. “No, no, no, don’t do this...” I murmured unconsciously, flustered, trying to stop the chaos that was about to unfold.

“Back up, now!” the teacher’s urgent command rang in my ears. I hurriedly stepped back, the legs of the chair behind me scraping sharply against the floor, my heartbeat pounding like a drum.
