A dull thud came from inside the bottle, and in that instant, the liquid inside splashed out, a few drops landing on my hands with a slight burning sensation. Fear surged through me; my scalp tingled and my whole body stiffened, as if I had been frozen in place.

“Are you okay?” The teacher rushed over to check what had happened, and the other students gathered around as well, some curious, others uneasy. I quickly pulled my hands back, forcing myself to resist the urge to wipe off the liquid, shame flooding over me as if all the mistakes made under everyone’s watchful eyes were my responsibility.

After school, I walked home alone. The rain had turned into a light drizzle, and a cold wind brushed across my face. I kept my head down, the raindrops tapping lightly on my umbrella, as if repeating the sound of the failed experiment. The scene kept replaying in my mind; I kept wondering whether there had been some way to avoid all of this. When I got home, I tried to calm myself down, but the unease in my heart lingered for a long time, and I still felt as though those accusing eyes were fixed on me.

The next day at school, I was still a little uneasy, worried that my classmates would bring up what happened yesterday. But fortunately, no one seemed to remember it much; only occasionally would someone mention it, and I would do my best to act as if nothing had happened. That night I had a dream that I was once again doing an experiment in science class and failing, but this time, in the dream, I was no longer panicking. Instead, I slowly learned to ignore those scattered noises and to bring my attention back to my own actions.

Sunlight filtered through the lush leaves and scattered across the playground, and the air was filled with a faint earthy smell, surrounded by the laughter and chatter of children. In the center of the playground, a few of us classmates were playing a catching game. At first, I stood off to the side, watching my friends pass the ball, which traced graceful arcs through the air. I felt a sense of anticipation, hoping the ball would come my way. I really wanted to join them and experience that feeling of being accepted.

“Pass it to me, quick!” a classmate shouted from across the way. I hesitated for a moment, then finally gathered my courage and shouted, “Pass it to me, pass it to me!” But the ball whooshed past me and flew toward another classmate. I froze, as if something had pricked me in the heart.

Why didn’t they pass it to me? Do they not like me? I stood still, pretending to stretch, trying to hide my disappointment. The sunlight seemed to grow harsh, and my eyes stung a little, but I didn’t dare rub them, afraid someone would notice. I began thinking over and over: was it because I answered the wrong question in Chinese class last time, and they thought I was stupid?

A classmate nearby noticed me and called out loudly, “Why are you just standing there? Come on over!” I forced an awkward smile, though inside I was in complete turmoil. My heart started racing, my palms sweating, as if countless eyes were fixed on me. I hurried over, trying to act indifferent, but I kept wondering: did they really want me to join, or did they just think saying that was funny?

The game went on, and I began to move more actively, trying to blend into their rhythm. I paid attention to where the ball was flying each time and did my best to dive toward its path. Even so, the feeling of not being accepted never really went away. It was as if I could hear a voice in my head: They must think I’m weird.

After the game ended, I wandered alone along the edge of the playground, with the sound of other classmates talking and laughing in my ears. I kept telling myself it was nothing, nothing to worry about, but my body was still unconsciously tense, and tears welled up in my eyes.

That night, I couldn’t sleep. The scene on the playground kept replaying in my mind, and I kept feeling that I wasn’t good enough, not smart enough, while all sorts of past mistakes came back to me. This mood lasted for several days, and I became more silent in class, no longer daring to take part much in interactions with my classmates.

During PE class, the weather was clear and the sunlight on the playground was bright and glaring. I sat on a bench at the edge of the field, my eyes occasionally drifting toward my classmates who were moving around on the playground. They were running and laughing, waving their arms as if the whole world belonged to them. “Come on, join us!” one classmate noticed me and waved. My heart immediately sped up, my palms began to sweat, and I felt a dull pain in my stomach. I barely managed to raise my hand in greeting, but then I lowered my gaze and pretended I hadn’t heard him clearly. I thought to myself that if I went over, I would embarrass myself, because I definitely couldn’t run as fast as they could, and I was afraid of being laughed at. Sitting on the bench felt safest, so I pretended to be absorbed in the notebook in my hand, as if I were taking notes.

“Why aren’t you joining in? It’s just running today; anyone can do that.” A female classmate walked over to me and sat beside me, her voice like the morning sun. I looked up and forced a smile. “I’m just a little tired and want to rest.” But that wasn’t what I really felt; in my mind, I had already rehearsed a hundred possible embarrassing scenarios. I thought she must find me strange for not taking part in everyone’s activities. I felt a wave of unease. She went on, “You don’t usually take part in sports much. It’s okay; this is free time anyway.” I nodded, but deep down I was thinking that everyone must be talking about me behind my back, saying I was too scared to join in. My heart was beating so fast it seemed to make the bench tremble slightly.

After PE class ended, I returned to the classroom, still replaying everything that had just happened in my mind. I felt as if I were separated from them by an invisible sheet of glass, unable to truly become part of their circle. Even though PE was over, I still couldn’t stop thinking: my reaction just now was terrible; maybe I should have stood up and tried to join in, even if only for a little while. I wanted to know how they would judge me, whether anyone was saying behind my back that I was timid. My thoughts crawled through my mind like ants, making it impossible for me to focus on the next class.

That night, lying in bed, I was still thinking about the PE class that afternoon. I felt annoyed with myself, and a flood of thoughts surged through my head. I seemed to relive every expression and tone that might have been misunderstood, repeatedly analyzing whether I should have acted more positively, more bravely. But the more I thought about it, the more I felt trapped in this cycle, unable to break free. After a sleepless night, when I walked into the classroom the next day, I still felt heavy inside, as if I were carrying yesterday’s failure. Maybe I need to change something. Maybe only by trying to participate can I break this deadlock.

The atmosphere in science class always makes me nervous. When the teacher announced that we would be using microscopes to observe onion epidermal cells today, my heart started pounding immediately. Our group gathered around a table, with textbooks, microscopes, and transparent slides laid out in front of us. At the podium, the teacher explained how to adjust the focus on the microscope, her voice sounding like a series of rumblings in my ears.

“Be careful when placing the slide, and gently turn this adjustment knob.” The teacher’s words still echoed in my mind, but I kept staring at the microscope, worried I would make a mistake. My palms grew sweaty, and my hands trembled slightly.

The student sitting next to me whispered, “Why don’t you try?” His encouragement only made me more anxious. What if I accidentally broke something? I could almost hear the snickering of the other students, as if they were already mocking my clumsiness. Forcing out a smile, I stiffly took the microscope.

“All right, go ahead!” my deskmate encouraged me, apparently not noticing how tense I was inside.

I carefully placed the slide under the microscope, trying not to let the sweat on my hands get on it. The view was magnified beyond expectation, and I could see those tiny cells. I should have been focused on adjusting the knob, but all I felt was my stomach turning and my heart beating even faster.

“Well, can you see it?” my deskmate asked. I nodded, not daring to express what I really felt.

For the rest of the experiment, I was tense almost the entire time. Whenever it was my turn to operate, it felt as though countless eyes were fixed on me, waiting for me to make a mistake. Several times I failed to adjust the focus properly, and all I could do was awkwardly step aside and let my deskmate take over.

When the bell rang, I let out a long sigh of relief. My palms were covered in sweat, and my body felt slightly weary. On the way home, I kept replaying the afternoon’s events in my mind, waves of shame and frustration surging through me. Lying in bed, the image under the microscope kept flashing before my eyes, along with those imagined laughs and judgments.

That night, I tossed and turned, filled with unease. Whenever I closed my eyes, I would remember my classmates surrounding me, watching as I clumsily handled the microscope. I kept telling myself that next time I must do better, and absolutely must not make another mistake.

I like going to the park on weekends, especially when the weather is nice. This afternoon, the air was filled with a faint scent of fresh grass, and a few friends and I were playing ball on the park lawn. The sun shone warmly on us, and I could feel its warmth passing through my clothes; that feeling always makes me happy. We played ball and laughed at the same time. Around us, other people were jogging, and families were picnicking on the grass. The sound of children’s laughter and conversation mingled together, while the wind gently brushed past my ears, making it feel like a happy song.

“Catch it!” a friend threw the ball toward me. I hurried over; though my movements were a little awkward, I still managed to catch it. My friends cheered for me, as if I had done something remarkable. “Well done!” they said, and I felt a little proud. We kept playing, needing little more than actions and laughter to communicate. Several hours passed like that, and time seemed to fly by in happiness.

I sat on the grass, looking through the leaves at the dappled sunlight, and felt that this moment was especially beautiful. I had no worries in my heart; I only wanted to keep this peace in my mind. The sounds of the park surrounded me, bringing an indescribable feeling, a kind of calm that felt merged with the world.

On the way home, my friends and I discussed whose ball skills were the best. We talked and laughed, as if the game had never ended. My heartbeat was steady, my body pleasantly tired, yet filled with a joyful mood.

On a weekend evening, I lay in bed thinking about the day. Although nothing especially remarkable had happened, this simple happiness still left a smile on my face. When I fell asleep, my heart felt light, with no anxiety or unease, only the thought that perhaps tomorrow could be spent the same way. Although I had no special plans for the next day, I knew that even a casual stroll could bring its own pleasures.

The classroom was so hot and stuffy it was hard to breathe, and even the buzzing of the fan blades seemed to be urging us to finish the discussion quickly. The cicadas chirping in the trees outside the window were even more piercing, making my attention drift constantly. The Chinese class group task was to discuss the theme of a text, and our group was assigned “The Water’s Lament.” As our leader Xiaoya stood in front of the blackboard assigning tasks, I subconsciously lowered my head and prayed she wouldn’t mention my name.

“You, you’ll be in charge of writing the summary.” She pointed at me. Before I could refuse, the other group members were all nodding in agreement. “All right then, it’s settled. Everyone send your part to TA before next class.”

My throat felt dry, as if something were stuck in it. “Okay…” My voice was so faint it was almost inaudible; probably no one noticed. I gripped the edge of my chair tightly, my palms already starting to sweat.

For the rest of the time, I kept thinking about how to write it, but all that kept flashing through my mind were the worst possible scenes: What if I wrote it badly and got laughed at by the whole class? What if the teacher criticized me? It was as if every possible outcome proved that I would definitely fail.

Sure enough, things soon moved in the direction I had feared. Some of the sections submitted by my group members were too fragmented, and some of the viewpoints even contradicted each other. I tried to organize them into a clear summary, only to find that no matter how I connected them, they still seemed awkward. “They’ll definitely blame me for being useless,” I muttered to myself as I tore up the draft paper that was already filled with writing.

The next day, it was time for our group presentation. I tried to keep my voice as low as possible while desperately staring at the desk, too afraid to make eye contact with anyone. When I finished, the teacher was silent for a few seconds before saying, “Your summary doesn’t highlight the main points, and the logic is a bit muddled. It seems you need to work harder.”

In that instant, it felt as if my face were burning. I could feel the back of my neck heating up too, sweat rushing over my whole body, my fingers stiff as I clutched the seam of my pants and dared not move. I didn’t dare look up at my classmates’ reactions, afraid of meeting their gazes. All I heard were a few soft sighs, as if they were mocking me. The feeling was like a thousand-pound weight pressing on my chest, leaving me unable to breathe.

After class, I carried my backpack alone to a bench beside the playground, pretending to organize my books, when in fact I just wanted to avoid the crowd. The teacher’s comments and those vague sighs kept replaying in my mind, and the more I thought about them, the more irritated I became. I even started blaming myself: Why didn’t I prepare earlier? Why wasn’t I more proactive in getting everyone to work together? “I must be too useless…” That thought was like a huge net, tightly entangling me.

That night, when I got home, Mom asked me how school was. I only gave a vague “It was okay.” But while doing homework in my room, my palms were still sticky, and the words in my notebook had become distorted and ugly.

The doorbell rang once, small and crisp, like some kind of warning.

It was a cloudy afternoon. The light in the little town was already faint, and after we stepped into that antique shop, even that little bit was swallowed up. The air smelled of wood, old paper, and something I couldn’t quite name, as if time itself were rotting. I followed behind my parents, quietly hooking a finger around the hem of one of their coats and gripping it tightly, as though that piece of fabric could keep me anchored somewhere safe.

There was too much stuff on the shelves. Porcelain, bronze, framed paintings, wooden carvings—each piece stood there, still, yet somehow as if it might move at any moment. On the table near the entrance was a wooden mannequin, its joints stiff, its face wearing an expression I couldn’t decode at all—not a smile, not a cry, just hanging somewhere in between, staring at me. I looked away, but everywhere I looked there were more things like it.

My heart started racing. First my palms grew cold, then a thin layer of sweat seeped out.

“Come look at this antique clock. Isn’t it interesting?” Mom pointed to a huge standing clock in the corner. The shop owner followed her gesture and looked over, his eyes landing on me as he gave a friendly smile. “What do you think, kid?”

I opened my mouth, but nothing came out; I only nodded once.

In that moment, my mind was racing: Did they think I was weird? Why couldn’t I even say a single word? Had I already embarrassed my parents? Then the clock chimed. A deep hum rolled out from the corner, vibrating through the air like it was striking directly in my chest. I felt my stomach drop.

“Are you okay?” Mom came over, her voice lowered.

I nodded. I knew I was lying when I nodded, but I didn’t know what else to do. “We’re almost done looking. Don’t worry,” she said. I kept nodding, but my eyes were uncontrollably drawn back to the wooden mannequin. It was still there. Its eyes were made of glass, but I still felt like it was looking at me.

The tears came all at once, with no warning. I didn’t even have time to feel ashamed before I started sobbing. I grabbed Mom’s hand, my voice choked: “Can we leave?”

She froze for a moment, then nodded and went to find Dad. I heard her tell the shop owner, “Sorry, they’re not feeling very well today.”

When we walked out of the shop, the doorbell rang again. The air outside was cool. I took a deep breath, tears still hanging on my face, and the knot in my stomach loosened a little.

But that was only the physical part.

That night I lay in bed and went over the whole thing from beginning to end, again and again. Why had I cried? That doll hadn’t even done anything. The owner was just smiling; it was a normal smile. Why had I been so scared? I had embarrassed my parents so badly, and Mom even had to apologize for me—was I too fragile? Did I always react like this whenever I was somewhere unfamiliar?

For several days after that, the wooden mannequin’s face would still appear in unguarded moments. Not in dreams, but in the daytime, when I was spacing out. I started fearing passing by places like that again, fearing I would lose control again, fearing that next time no one would be there to say, “They’re not feeling well today.”

What bothered me most wasn’t the shop. It was me. It was that feeling of clearly knowing it wasn’t a big deal, yet still falling apart anyway. It was the helplessness of no matter how hard I tried, I still couldn’t hold on to my own emotions.

In the classroom, sunlight streamed through the windows onto the desks, and the air was filled with a faint smell of chalk dust. The teacher was explaining how to make a volcano eruption model using simple materials, and my heartbeat began to quicken. Today it was my group’s turn to present our experiment results, and my palms were already a little damp. When the teacher told us to begin, I stood up, clutching the small box containing the experiment model tightly in my hands. The pounding of my heart roared in my ears, as if everyone could hear how nervous I was. I struggled to recall the details we had practiced, only to find my mind completely blank. “Can you tell everyone the principle behind this volcanic eruption?” the teacher asked, her voice so gentle, yet I still felt an invisible pressure. I swallowed and began to explain haltingly. “Um... it’s just... this... this volcano, it erupts...” As I spoke, I could feel the heat in my face rising steadily. “Come on, you can do it,” a classmate beside me whispered encouragingly. I tried to steady my trembling hands, poured the baking soda into the model, and then slowly added vinegar, silently praying that everything would work properly. As the mixture began to bubble, the knot in my stomach tightened even more. I started to scold myself inside: Why am I so nervous? Why can’t I just relax? The experiment finally ended, and I could barely remember how I made it back to my seat. My heart was still racing, and I tried to take deep breaths to ease the tension in my face. The teacher smiled and said, “Well done. Next time, try to be more confident during your presentation.” That brought me a wave of relief, but before long, self-doubt filled my mind again. That afternoon after school, I lay in bed, still unable to stop replaying my stammering explanation during the experiment. The shame of feeling exposed made me miserable; it seemed that if I closed my eyes, I could hear my classmates whispering about me. Over the next few days, I kept promising myself that next time I would do better and never embarrass myself like that again. I began silently rehearsing the scene for the next science class in my mind, trying to anticipate every possible conversation, hoping to avoid falling into embarrassment again.

Sunlight streamed through the classroom windows onto our lab table, reflecting in clear bands of light. A few classmates and I sat around the table while the teacher guided us through a simple experiment—observing the stomata on plant leaves. The classroom was filled with the fresh scent of plants, along with the occasional rustle of paper and murmured whispers. My palms had already started to sweat; I gripped my pen tightly, my heart racing, though I did my best not to show it.

“Come on, take a look here—this is where the stomata are,” the teacher said, pointing to the image of the leaf under the microscope. I leaned closer to the table, hoping I could make sense of those jumbled patterns. “Hmm, this looks great. You all did an excellent job,” the teacher said with a smile. My cheeks instantly flushed. Praise like that often made me feel awkward; I would always wonder whether the teacher truly meant it or was simply being polite.

“What do you think? Can you see it clearly?” a classmate asked softly. I nodded, but I wasn’t sure myself whether I really understood. I focused again on the microscope, worried that if the teacher came over and asked me something, I wouldn’t be able to answer and would end up disappointing everyone.

My stomach began to ache faintly, as if anticipating an embarrassing moment that was about to arrive. I could hear my heartbeat quickening. I tried to concentrate on my classmates’ discussion, but every word seemed to fade into an echo, leaving only the sound of my own worry about making a fool of myself.

After the experiment ended, I walked out of the classroom, trying to shake off that unease. But the feeling lingered around me like a shadow and would not go away no matter how hard I tried. That night, lying in bed, I replayed the teacher’s praise over and over, thinking about the true meaning behind those words, afraid that in everyone else’s eyes I was a joke.

A few days later, the teacher mentioned our experiment results again in front of the whole class. Her praise made that uneasiness rise up in my heart once more, but I decided to prove through effort that I was not merely someone who received compliments without substance. I prepared carefully for the next experiment, hoping I could find some confidence in the process and gradually become less easily shaken by outside voices.

On a Saturday afternoon, the house was very quiet, with only the steady ticking of the clock in the living room. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains, spilling onto the coffee table and the floor, creating a warm glow. I sat by the dining table with an open sketchbook in front of me and a full set of my favorite colored crayons beside it. There was a faint, pleasant fragrance in the air—the lemon-scented air freshener Mom had sprayed before she went out. I thought it smelled really nice, like freshly cut lemon slices in summer, with a calming feel to it.

My hand moved casually across the sketchbook, and today I decided to draw a rabbit. Though I had originally wanted to draw a cat, I found that no matter what I did, I couldn’t get the shape of the cat’s ears right, so I changed my mind at the last minute. Rabbit ears were much easier; I only had to draw two long curves. I drew a round body, then picked up a pink crayon and colored its ears. Pink was the cutest color in my opinion, and I carefully gave it a heart-shaped nose. By then, I suddenly felt that this rabbit looked a little like a character from a cartoon, but I couldn’t remember the name at the moment. So I stopped and stared at it in a daze for a while.

From outside came the soft rustling of leaves, as if the wind were whispering to them. I looked up at the window, and although it was a little backlit, I could faintly see a few sparrows hopping on the branches, chirping. The whole world seemed wrapped in a warm blanket, and even time had slowed down. I stretched and felt a bit sore in my shoulders from drawing for too long. I got up and went to the kitchen to pour myself a glass of water. The kettle was made of transparent glass, and when sunlight shone through it, a small rainbow appeared on the table. I couldn’t help reaching out to poke at the rainbow, but of course, I touched nothing.

After drinking the water, I sat back down and continued drawing the rabbit. But when I started drawing its eyes, I suddenly felt a little conflicted: if I made them too big, it would look like a frightened little animal; but if I made them too small, it would seem lifeless. I tried drawing one slightly larger eye, and as expected, it looked a bit silly. I immediately erased it with the eraser, feeling a little disappointed. Still, I comforted myself: “It’s just a doodle anyway. It’s not like I’m going to show it to anyone.”

Later, I drew some grass and little flowers beside it, filling the page completely, and it looked like a spring landscape painting. I couldn’t help laughing a little, suddenly feeling that today’s time had passed very slowly, but very pleasantly too. The first thing Mom said when she got home was, “Oh, not bad—you drew pretty well. Got some new inspiration again?” I quickly hid the picture and replied casually, pretending not to care: “Just doodling.” But inside, I was still a little proud.

That night, lying in bed, I was still thinking about the impression that rainbow had left on me, feeling that it was magical. This tiny discovery made me inexplicably happy, and it also made me look forward to the next sunny afternoon.

The classroom of the science class always carried a mixed scent of chalk dust and old books, but that day there was also a strange hint of plants and grass. It was a set of insect specimens that the teacher was preparing to display. The teacher gently lifted off the glass cover, and a beetle specimen appeared before my eyes. Its pitch-black shell glinted eerily under the light. I pinched the edge of the desk with my fingertips, a thin sweat breaking out in my palms, and my heartbeat began to quicken. “Class, this is the specimen we’ll be observing today. I hope you can record its features in detail,” the teacher’s voice echoed between the classroom walls. I tried hard to stare at the beetle, but all that remained in my gaze was fear. The curious whispers of the other students, along with the rustling sound of their writing on paper, blended into a noisy hum in my ears.

“Are you okay?” the student sitting next to me asked softly, lightly touching my arm. I forced out a faint smile and nodded, though inside I was thinking how much I wished I could hide somewhere. I felt a slight churning in my stomach, as if I were about to throw up. I thought that if I really did vomit, everyone would laugh at me, and from then on, every time I walked into this classroom, everyone would look at me with that kind of expression. I couldn’t shake the thought, and I gripped the desk edge even tighter, as if that piece of wood were my only salvation.

As the lesson went on, I kept imagining the beetle coming to life, crawling down from the specimen stand and across the desk toward me. I knew that was impossible, but I couldn’t stop those thoughts from flooding my mind. Sweat soaked my pen in my palm, and my heart was beating almost out of control, each thump seeming to remind me of this hopeless embarrassment. “Come on, everyone can come a little closer to observe its wings,” the teacher’s voice seemed to have a kind of magic, drawing the other students to crowd around it one after another. I remained at my seat, my eyes avoiding the beetle as if wary of a beast. I sat rigidly until the bell rang, and only then did I finally let out a slight breath of relief.

That afternoon, I sat alone at home while my mother was busy in the kitchen. I looked out the window, sunlight streaming in and spilling across the floor. I began silently chewing over today’s fear. Why couldn’t I be as curious about beetles as the other students? Was I really that timid? These questions echoed in my mind. I pinched my fingers hard, trying to wake myself up, but it was no use. That night, I had a nightmare: the beetle crawled onto my face, and I could even feel its cold antennae. After I woke up, I couldn’t fall asleep for a long time, and the sounds from the classroom during the day still echoed in my ears.

The wooden bench in the music classroom creaked softly, while shafts of sunlight streamed through the cracks in the curtains and fell on the yellowed music textbooks. The students around me were chatting quietly, but I kept staring at the lyrics in my book, my heart pounding faster and faster. The teacher stood at the front, her lips pressed into a tight line, her gaze moving among us as if searching for the next person to call up to sing. My palms began to sweat, and the words on the page seemed to tremble. I tried hard to review every line, yet I still felt certain I would forget the lyrics in front of the whole class.

Suddenly, the teacher called my name. I almost held my breath; all the sounds around me seemed to disappear, leaving only my own heartbeat. As I slowly stood up, my legs were trembling slightly. I did my best to calm myself, parting my lips and trying to force the lyrics out from memory. Just as I was about to speak, my mind went blank—the words had vanished completely. The air in the music classroom grew thick, as if much hotter than usual, and all I could hear was my own rapid breathing.

At last, the teacher broke the silence. “Don’t be nervous. Sing slowly.” Though her tone was calm, I still felt as if I were being scolded. I looked around; the students’ gazes made my face burn, as though everyone were judging me. I managed to begin, but my voice became broken and halting along the way. “Sorry, I—I forgot.” My voice was so small it was barely audible. The teacher sighed and gently shook her head. “It’s okay, it’s okay. Try again next time.”

After I sat down, my body gradually relaxed, but my stomach twisted in pain. There was only one thought in my mind: I was such a failure—why had I embarrassed myself in front of everyone? When I left the classroom, my steps were hurried, wanting to get away quickly from that suffocating place. That night, I lay in bed unable to sleep, though I was utterly exhausted. Scenes from the day kept replaying in my mind like a slideshow, filling me with shame and regret.

A few days later, although the incident gradually faded among my classmates, I still found it hard to forget. Every time music class drew near, I felt tense and anxious, afraid of going through that humiliation again. I began spending more time reviewing the lyrics in advance, imagining myself doing better in such a situation next time, and trying to ease my inner unease through these efforts.

The wind was especially strong that day. The branches in the playground were swaying violently, and the dust it kicked up was like a thin veil, stinging my eyes. I hunched my neck and stood by the edge of the playground behind the school building, trying as hard as I could not to be blown around by the wind. A few classmates were gathered nearby playing hopscotch, and their laughter and chatter were blown apart by the wind.

“Hey, do you want to play?” one classmate called to me. I froze for a moment and pointed at myself. “Me?” Seeing her nod, I immediately ran over, feeling a little secretly pleased: finally, someone had noticed me.

As soon as I stood beside them, a gust of wind blew and sent my scarf whipping into my face. While I hurriedly pulled it down, I accidentally bumped into the little wooden peg holding the elastic rope. With a snap, the elastic bounced off the peg and looped around a little boy’s foot. He cried out and fell to the ground.

“What are you doing?” he shouted at me after getting back up. “Are you blind or what?”

“I—I didn’t mean to...” I quickly stepped back and raised my hand to explain, but my mouth wouldn’t cooperate, and I couldn’t get the words out clearly. Tears welled up before I could stop them; I didn’t know whether it was the wind or the hurt.

“You’re just stupid! You cause trouble every time you come!” He angrily tugged at his shoelaces, and the few girls around us looked at me awkwardly, as if waiting for me to apologize.

“Sorry...” I lowered my head, my voice so soft it was almost blown away by the wind. “I really didn’t mean it...”

“Hmph, forget it!” The boy shook his head and ran off without another word. The others didn’t look at me again, as if I had suddenly become invisible. I stood there dazed as a cold wind made me shiver all over. The warmth from just moments ago was long gone, leaving only a sour, bitter feeling in my stomach.

I didn’t dare move closer again. I could only stand at the side and watch them rehang the elastic and keep playing. Their laughter seemed separated from me by a pane of glass, and no matter how I listened, I still felt I didn’t belong there. I kept replaying what had just happened in my mind, thinking that if my scarf hadn’t fallen, maybe I wouldn’t have bumped the peg; if I had apologized sooner, maybe they wouldn’t have gotten angry.

On the way home from school, the cold wind was even more biting, but I couldn’t help looking down at my shadow, blaming myself over and over for being so stupid that I could even mess up just standing there watching others play. When I got home, I pretended nothing was wrong and quickly ran back to my room to hide. The house was very warm, but my whole body still felt frozen, my nose bright red.

That night, I lay face down under the covers, and that boy’s expression when he yelled at me still wouldn’t leave my mind. My throat felt blocked. Several times I wanted to tell Mom, but I was afraid that saying it out loud would make me seem even more “stupid,” so I kept biting the corner of the blanket and said nothing. Even after lying down in bed, the tears kept coming.

Sunlight streamed through the balcony’s glass door, warmly spreading across the floor, and the air carried a faint dusty scent. Several potted plants sat along the edge of the balcony, and on their leaves, droplets left by the watering can still sparkled in the sunlight. I sat in a small wicker chair with a cotton cushion under my feet, holding an old book that had already turned a little yellow. The corners of the cover had curled up, and I carefully smoothed them down, but they still stubbornly sprang back.

Several pages in the book bore the impressions of dried flowers I had picked up from the garden and accidentally pressed between the pages; by now they had completely shriveled. I gently touched the dried flowers with my fingertips, and they felt brittle and thin, as if they would crumble at the slightest touch. I didn’t know whether I should keep them or throw them out, but in the end I closed the book and pretended nothing had happened.

From far away came the sharp, clear chirping of sparrows. “Chirp chirp!” I looked up out the window and saw two tiny sparrows perched on the wire across from the balcony. Now and then they would hop to another spot, and then lower their heads to preen their feathers, looking as though they cared nothing about the rest of the world. I couldn’t help wondering whether they never had to stockpile food for winter. After all, being so small, how much could they possibly need to eat?

“Chirp—chirp!” The sound suddenly grew louder, as if they had spotted something. I looked around the balcony to make sure I hadn’t left any breadcrumbs behind, but I still felt they might think I was scattering food. Very quickly, though, they flew away, leaving the empty wire gently swaying in the breeze.

The book slid back onto my lap, and I tried to keep reading. There were many parts of this book I couldn’t understand, so I flipped through the illustrations, which showed some strange machines. One page was especially thin, and I almost tore it. My heart suddenly beat faster, as if I had been caught red-handed, but after I turned it over, the page seemed fine. I let out a sigh of relief.

From the other side of the balcony came my mother’s voice. “What are you doing?” Her voice was a little muffled because of the glass door. I turned and looked at her, shouting through the glass, “Nothing, just reading!” Sunlight shone on the glass, reflecting my face and her shadow, overlapping into a blur. She nodded and went back into the room, and I heard the faint sound of slippers on the floor.

After a while, the sun began to tilt a little, and shadows slowly crept from beside my feet up my legs. The air also grew a bit cooler, and I gave a small shiver, grumbling that I had forgotten to bring another jacket. The little cat by my feet woke up, lazily stretched, then yawned, showing its tiny teeth. It looked up at me, then lowered its head and licked its front paw.

I closed the book and decided to go back inside. When I stood up, my knees were a little sore, but thankfully not too uncomfortable. I bent down and picked up the dried flowers that had been pressed under the book, carefully tucking them back into the pages. I felt they shouldn’t be thrown away, after all, I had picked them up. As I went into the room, I looked back at the balcony once more; everything was quiet. The cat followed behind me, its tail brushing lightly against my calves.

That night, I put the book back on the bookshelf and specially marked the page with the dried flowers. I thought to myself that maybe I would come back and flip through it again, but then I felt it might be a long time before I remembered.

The classroom was filled with the noisy chatter of children, covered with colorful drawings on the walls, with sunlight streaming in from outside the window. I sat in my seat, clutching the script paper in my hand, my heart pounding fast and my palms sweaty. I knew it was almost time for me to go up and recite. The teacher walked over and said with a smile, “Are you ready, little one?” I nodded, though I was far from certain inside. I didn’t want to disappoint the teacher, but I was truly so nervous. I even started imagining the worst-case scenario: what if I forgot my lines? What if everyone laughed at me?

The classmate sitting beside me nudged me with his elbow. “Hey, are you okay? You look a little nervous.” He grinned. I forced a smile, thinking to myself, why am I the only one this nervous? Everyone else looks so confident. I really wished I could be like them.

At last it was my turn. I stood up, my hands and feet a little stiff, and walked toward the podium at the front of the classroom. Every step seemed heavy, and the laughter and conversation around me seemed to grow farther and farther away, until all I could hear was my own heartbeat. Standing at the podium, I met everyone’s gaze and felt as if I had been placed under a spotlight, unable to escape all those eyes on me.

Taking a deep breath, I began to recite. At first it went fairly smoothly, until I reached that particularly long sentence. My mind went blank, and I suddenly forgot what I was supposed to say. I paused, and the whole classroom seemed to fall silent; I could even hear the rustling of leaves outside the window. A classmate whispered something below, and my face began to burn. Sweat slid down the bridge of my nose, and I could almost feel it dripping onto the floor.

“Don’t be afraid, take it slowly.” The teacher’s gentle reminder helped me calm down a little. I tried hard to recall that passage and continued reading, but the unease and embarrassment in my heart never really went away. After I finished, I walked back to my seat with my head down, not daring to look at anyone.

That afternoon, I kept thinking about this mistake. Even after I got home from school, I was still replaying the moment I had paused, feeling as if the heat on my face had never faded. That night, lying in bed, I told myself that I absolutely couldn’t embarrass myself like this again next time; I had to do better. But the fear in my heart made me wonder whether I could really do it.

Only after a few days did I gradually calm down. Although every time I thought of that recitation, my heart would still tighten a little, I told myself that perhaps it had only been a small mistake and did not mean I couldn’t become better.

Sunlight streamed through the windows into the stairwell of the school building. My footsteps tapped lightly on each step as I climbed, while my heart fluttered like a little deer. The scene before my eyes was somewhat blurred, and the sunlight was so blinding that I could hardly open them. When I reached the second floor, I pushed open the small door leading to the balcony. A gentle breeze brushed across my cheeks, bringing a hint of coolness. The balcony was empty, with only a few small plants planted by the teacher quietly basking in the sun. The railing felt a little cold to the touch. I leaned lightly against it and looked down at the playground below. My classmates were running around on the field, their laughter carried to my ears by the wind. 

Just then, the homeroom teacher’s voice came from the hallway. “Are you here? Have you been waiting long?” I turned back and answered uneasily, “I just got here not long ago.” She walked over with a smile. “Don’t worry, I just want to talk about how your studies have been recently.” I nodded hard, but I didn’t know what to say. 

I felt a little nervous inside, always feeling that no matter how well I did, there would still be something that made the teacher dissatisfied. I had heard the teacher talk with other students at the podium before, and it always seemed to involve criticism and reminders. I took a deep breath and felt my palms growing a little damp, my heartbeat quickening and quickening. 

“Do you have any thoughts about your homework lately?” the teacher asked gently, trying to ease my nerves. Thoughts of recent assignments flashed through my mind. I remembered accidentally spilling paint while making a poster, and the paper was all wrinkled. I had truly felt ashamed then. “Some assignments I may not have done very well. I’ll pay more attention,” I said, subconsciously blaming myself as I recalled that time I spilled the paint. 

In the sunlight, her expression was earnest yet gentle. “It’s okay. Learning is a process; don’t put too much pressure on yourself. If you run into difficulties, be sure to speak up in time.” I nodded, and the stone in my heart lifted a little. 

She went on to ask a few more questions, and I answered them one by one. Although I was still somewhat nervous, I gradually felt that this kind of conversation wasn’t as frightening as I had imagined. After talking with the teacher, she gently patted me on the shoulder. “Go play with your classmates. Don’t always stay by yourself.” 

I smiled faintly and turned toward the stairs. I felt much more relaxed than when I came. When I returned to the playground, my friends were still playing games. The heat rising from the concrete mixed with the cool breeze, giving me a rare sense of comfort. That evening, I thought of the teacher’s words, and there was a little less anxiety in my heart and a little more courage. The next day in class, I decided to raise my hand and answer questions on my own, trying to make my voice sound more confident.

Standing on the stage of the school auditorium, I nervously adjusted my posture and let out a soft breath. Before me were the glittering lights and the audience watching in silence. I tried my best not to focus on the crowd in the seats, keeping my gaze fixed on the elegant black piano in front of me. Just as I was ready to strike the first note, my hands suddenly began to tremble, and my heartbeat sped up, as if the bright stage lights were magnifying the anxiety inside me. I could feel sweat starting to bead on my forehead, my fingers growing sore and even a little stiff. Silently, I kept telling myself over and over, “No matter what, I have to keep going. I can’t embarrass myself.”

As the music began to flow, I tried to keep my movements natural and concentrate on the performance, but my heart kept racing; I could almost hear it pounding violently in my chest with every keystroke. Just when I thought I was starting to steady myself, an unexpected noise suddenly made my fingers freeze, and the piece broke off. I looked toward the audience, trying to see what had interrupted me. Someone had accidentally tipped over a chair, making a loud crash. My heart sank, and it felt as though everyone’s eyes were fixed on me, waiting for my reaction. All at once, I felt a tight, sickening knot in my stomach, and my mind went completely blank.

I took a deep breath and adjusted my posture again, trying to continue playing, but my hands were still trembling slightly. The music went on, and I worked hard to pour emotion into it, letting the notes rise into the air again. Yet the pressure of being watched still hung over me, making it impossible to fully focus on my performance. I hastily finished the solo, politely bowed to the audience, and quickly left the stage. My heart was still pounding, and the sweat in my palms felt sticky against the piano keys.

After the competition ended, I hid in a corner outside the auditorium, staring gloomily at my hands. “Why did I get so nervous?” I kept asking myself, beginning to attack myself mentally and blaming myself for not handling the unexpected situation well. “People must think I’m not good enough, that I’m a cowardly child.” Suddenly, I felt waves of discomfort in my stomach and had no choice but to go to the restroom in the auditorium, trying to sort out my chaotic thoughts.

Over the next few days, whenever someone mentioned that competition, I became extremely sensitive, as if terrified that others would question or mock me. In my mind, I kept replaying every detail of that piano competition, wondering whether I could have done better, whether I could have performed more steadily. In the days that followed, I began avoiding discussions about the competition with my classmates, afraid of being questioned or judged. Whenever someone brought up what had happened during the competition, I always felt it was criticism directed at me, even when that was not at all their intention.

Sunlight streamed through the laboratory windows onto the floor, and I sat in the front row, feeling uneasy. The classroom was filled with the smell of chemical reagents, making my nose sting slightly. The clock in the corner ticked away, and my classmates’ whispers rose and fell around the room. Today, the teacher had us do a simple chemistry experiment, but my palms were already starting to sweat. The teacher was handing out the lab equipment at the podium, and I rubbed my hands together hard, hoping to calm myself down.

“Everyone be careful, don’t panic,” the teacher said, demonstrating by gently pouring the chemical reagent into a test tube in front of us. I followed his movements closely, afraid of missing a single detail. When it was my turn, I took the test tube, my palms damp with sweat. I took a deep breath and carefully poured the reagent into the measuring cup, trying to imitate the teacher’s actions.

“Are you okay? Do you need help?” my deskmate asked softly.

“I... I’m fine, thank you.” I forced out a smile, my heart pounding fiercely as if it were about to leap out of my chest. I wiped the sweat from my forehead with my sleeve and continued the experiment as if nothing were wrong.

However, when I tried to pour the reagent into the beaker, my hand shook, and a few drops splashed onto the tabletop, hissing as they fell. I froze, frantically looking for a tissue to wipe it up, while countless worst-case scenarios surged through my mind at once: the tabletop would be corroded, the teacher would be angry, my classmates would laugh at me, and I would be criticized.

“Here, use this wet tissue to wipe it off quickly.” My deskmate handed me a wet tissue. I hurriedly took it, my hands shaking even more, and the tissue nearly slipped to the floor.

Seeing this, the teacher came over to check what had happened. He looked down at the tabletop, then looked up at me. “It’s all right. Just be more careful.” His tone was calm, which made me feel a little more at ease.

The atmosphere in the lab gradually returned to normal, but my heartbeat remained rapid. My friend’s comfort and the teacher’s understanding gave me some reassurance, but I still felt deeply guilty. I looked out the window, where sunlight fell on the grass of the campus and the autumn breeze brushed the leaves, making them rustle softly. That small mistake replayed again and again in my mind, and I silently told myself that next time I must be more careful.

Over the next few days, I would involuntarily think back to that moment in science class, and my heart still felt uneasy. Although it was already over, the feeling of sweating palms and a racing heartbeat would not leave me. I kept trying to remind myself that it was only a small mistake and that everyone has moments like this, so I shouldn’t blame myself too much. Even so, that little incident became a memory that kept echoing in my heart, reminding me of the importance of caution and effort.

The lights in the dining room were so bright they stung my eyes, making them ache a little. I sat at the corner of the long table, holding my chopsticks, staring at the grains of rice in my bowl, feeling a thin layer of sweat on my palms. The table was piled high with dishes, red and green, all glistening with oil. Around me were everyone’s laughter and chatter; someone told a joke, and a burst of guffaws followed. I forced a smile too, but soon lowered my head and tried hard not to draw attention.

“Why are you eating so slowly?” a relative sitting across from me suddenly said. His voice wasn’t loud, but it was aimed straight at me. I froze at once, my chopsticks hanging rigid in midair. “Look at you—eating so slowly, dragging around like a turtle. It’s really frustrating.” A few people nearby started laughing too, and someone added, “She’s always like this, so slow.”

My face began to burn, as if someone had struck a match beside my ear. I wanted to say something, but when I opened my mouth, I closed it again; my throat felt blocked. I lowered my head and stared at the rice in my bowl, trying to pretend I hadn’t heard, but those words burrowed into my ears like needles and stabbed at my chest.

“Hey, don’t always be so careful, like you’re afraid of doing everything wrong,” the relative added again, his tone full of contempt and impatience. My stomach started churning, as if everything I’d just eaten was about to come back up. I held my breath, trying to calm myself, but my fingers disobeyed and clenched tightly under the table, my knuckles going numb. My ears buzzed, and the others’ laughter seemed amplified several times over, every burst crashing into my heart.

“Enough!” a voice inside me screamed, but I still didn’t move, as if I were a stone trapped in my chair. I stole a glance at Dad. He said nothing, only kept picking up food, not even lifting his head to look. My chest suddenly felt empty, as if I had fallen into a bottomless abyss. “Why is no one standing up for me?” That question spun around in my mind again and again. All at once, I felt that they weren’t laughing at how slowly I ate, but at the “me” who never should have existed in the first place.

For most of the meal, I barely touched my chopsticks again, keeping my hands hidden under the table, my nails digging hard into my palms. Everyone seemed to forget what had just happened very quickly and went back to talking and laughing, but the sounds at the table became a blurred background noise. All I could hear was my own heartbeat, thudding one beat after another like drumsticks against my eardrums, so fast it left me breathless.

Back in my room, I shut the door and crawled straight under the blankets, burying my face and trying to calm myself down, but tears still poured out uncontrollably. I felt like trash, the kind no one would notice no matter where it was thrown, let alone care about. That sense of shame was like a huge curtain, pressing down on me completely. I thought a lot—about what those people had been laughing at just then, about why Dad hadn’t said a single word for me, about whether things would have been different if I could have been a little faster, a little better.

The next day, I deliberately got up early and secretly avoided running into that relative. But the tightness in my chest was still there, and my stomach hurt as if it had been twisted into a knot. I didn’t dare speak to anyone, always feeling judgment hidden in their eyes, as if they could see through me and know just how terrible I was with one glance.

Sitting in the classroom, I stared at the blackboard in front of me while the teacher was explaining today’s math homework. My classmates around me were all discussing the problems in low voices, but I felt a wave of anxiety spreading from my stomach. My heart began to race, and I seemed to be able to hear it beating. I looked at the student beside me and tried to join their conversation. She glanced at me, frowned, and then continued talking with another classmate. Her brows were tightly knit, and I immediately felt uneasy. Had I said something I shouldn’t have? Or had I somehow offended her with the way I behaved? This uneasiness surged over me like a tide, making it impossible to concentrate on the lesson.

I tried to insert myself into their conversation: “How hard do you think this problem is?” I tried to make my voice sound relaxed and natural. However, she frowned again and said, “It’s okay, not especially hard.” There seemed to be a trace of impatience in her tone, and I immediately felt ashamed. My palms began to sweat, and the thought kept churning in my mind: “Do I look really stupid?”

During the break, I tried to sort out my thoughts, but instead I fell into even deeper rumination. I kept replaying that expression on her face, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt she might dislike me. I even began to suspect that she was talking about me behind my back with other classmates. A voice inside me said, “If you’re not smart enough, others will abandon you.” I sat in my seat, gripping my textbook tightly, repeatedly rehearsing these negative scenarios in my mind.

That night, I lay in bed and still couldn’t shake off the troubles of the day. My stomach still ached faintly, and that classmate’s furrowed brow remained in my mind. The next morning, I still felt heavy-hearted, and I kept thinking that my relationship with my classmates had become tense. I began to be afraid of going to school, afraid of seeing their subtle reactions to me again. Even at home, I didn’t dare talk to my parents about these things, worried they would think I was too sensitive.

A few days later, I was still trying hard to fit into the class, although those feelings still surfaced from time to time. I began trying not to overinterpret my classmates’ expressions, but this habit still made it hard for me to relax.

The classroom was always noisy, especially right after recess activities ended. My seat was by the window, and sunlight streamed in, spilling across the desktop. On the old wooden desk were a few scratches carved by pencils. I sat there fiddling with my eraser, my ears filled with my classmates’ laughter and chatter. Suddenly, I heard the boy behind me say loudly, “Hey, why is the craft you made so ugly?” He laughed loudly, and several students around him laughed along with him. I turned around and looked at him; there was a mocking expression on his face.

“I think it’s pretty good,” I said softly, so quietly that even I could barely hear myself. But he kept going: “You think this looks good? It’s so rough, and the colors aren’t even painted on properly!” He almost shouted it, and more people around us started turning to look.

My face instantly grew hot, as if it were burning. My heart sped up, and my chest felt so tight it was as if something were pressing down on it. I lowered my head and stared at the desktop, wanting to find a hole in those pencil scratches to crawl into. I reached out and gripped the eraser tightly, my fingertips trembling a little. My mind raced: “Does he hate me?” “Does everyone think I’m terrible?” “Am I never good enough at anything?” These thoughts surged over me like a flood.

“So boring,” I heard another classmate say from the side. “Why would you say that? She didn’t do anything to you.” I looked up and saw her frowning at the boy. Although she didn’t speak up for me directly, her attitude made me feel a little less alone. I wanted to say something, but my throat felt blocked, so I could only lower my head weakly and keep playing with my eraser.

At the time, my stomach hurt a little. I wasn’t sure whether it was from nerves or because I had eaten too many snacks during recess. I tried to make myself look calm, as if those words hadn’t affected me, but my hands were quietly sweating. Isecretly glanced at that group of people; they had already started talking about something else, but the boy’s words kept replaying in my mind. I began to wonder: if I could do a little better, would I not be laughed at? Would it have been better if I hadn’t made that craft at all?

The next day, I decided not to leave that handmade item on my desk anymore. I stuffed it into my backpack and even briefly wanted to throw it away. I didn’t want it to become the center of attention again, and I didn’t want to endure any more comments. But at the same time, I felt a little reluctant to part with it, because I had spent so long making it.

A few days later, I found myself instinctively avoiding staying in the classroom after recess activities. I would try to delay until it was almost time for class before walking into the classroom, as if that would reduce the chances of being noticed. But even so, the worry that others would say my work looked ugly still hung in my heart like a taut string.

The classroom lights were a little too harsh, and the white fluorescent tubes cast scattered reflections across the blackboard. I stood in front of the board, gripping the crumpled speech tightly in both hands. The classroom was terrifyingly quiet; aside from the occasional faint cough, all eyes were fixed on me, like countless searchlights exposing every detail of me with nowhere to hide. I licked my chapped lips. Before I had even started speaking, my palms already felt soaked with sweat.

“Hello everyone, I…” As soon as the words left my mouth, I realized how shrill my voice sounded, like a crumpled piece of paper suddenly being torn apart. I cleared my throat and tried to calm myself down, continuing to read from the script. But when my eyes swept over the students in the first row, I caught the barely concealed raised eyebrows and sneaky smiles on their faces.

“I… today the topic of my speech is…” My tongue seemed bound by some invisible force, making even a simple sentence come out haltingly. A few muffled laughs rose from below the stage, like a thin needle stabbing straight into my ears. My mind raced: “What are they laughing at? Did I say the sentence wrong, or does my voice sound weird? Is my clothes stained? Or is my hair a mess?” A familiar sense of shame spread from my chest, burning through my whole body like wildfire.

My heart was beating faster and faster, and my chest felt as if it were pinned down by a huge rock, making it hard to breathe. Cold sweat began to form on my forehead. The speech paper shook in my hands like a leaf in the wind. I tried to focus on the words on the page, but they began to blur, as if mocking me. I couldn’t help stumbling and skipping a sentence, trying to get this nightmare over with quickly.

“Speak louder, and put more feeling into it!” the teacher suddenly interrupted from the side. It was like a sudden alarm bell ringing in my head, and I froze instantly. My ears were buzzing, and the sheet of paper fell to the floor. I hurriedly crouched down to pick it up, but my fingers couldn’t manage to grasp it. At that moment, I heard a few students in the back row break into laughter. I don’t know who it was, but someone suddenly said softly, “Is she about to cry?”

My stomach began to convulse violently, as if an invisible hand were twisting it hard from inside. I kept my head down, not daring to look at anyone, with only one thought in my mind: “Hurry up and end, hurry up and end.” In the end, I forced myself through the last two lines and ran back to my seat as if fleeing for my life. I stared at the desktop, while inside me it felt like thousands upon thousands of voices were roaring: “I’m so useless! Why is everyone laughing at me? Has there never really been anyone who liked me?”

That afternoon after school, I walked home alone with my head down. Along the way, it seemed as if the laughter I had heard in the classroom was still echoing in my ears, and the more I thought about it, the tighter my heart clenched. I felt like a complete failure, unable to even do something this simple. After I got home, my mother asked me what was wrong. I wanted to say something, but in the end I just lowered my head and slipped back into my room. Sitting on my bed with my knees pulled to my chest, tears blurred my vision, and all my self-blame and shame weighed down on me until I could hardly breathe.

Over the next few days, every time I walked past the classroom door on my way to school, I felt as if it were a giant black hole, waiting to suck me in and expose all my ugliness to be laughed at. Whenever I heard my classmates talking or laughing, I instinctively felt they were talking about me, laughing at me. The tightening in my stomach became almost a daily state, and I began to avoid drawing any attention at all, wanting only to hide away.

On a bright afternoon, the playground was filled with laughter and chatter. I was in the middle of a heated soccer match with a group of classmates. All around me were their shouts and the sound of shoes scraping against the ground, and the air was mixed with the fresh smell of sweat and grass. On the field, I ran desperately, trying to win the ball and score a point. Suddenly, a classmate kicked the ball toward me. My heart raced as I nervouslystretch out my foot to receive it. But the next second, a sharp pain shot through my right leg, and I fell to the ground. The laughter on the playground instantly turned harsh and piercing. My cheeks burned, beads of sweat began to form, and it felt as if a heavy stone were pressing on my chest, making it hard to breathe.

My classmates gathered around me. “Are you okay?” one of them asked with concern in his voice. I struggled to prop myself up, trying to smile, but inside I felt a little unwilling to accept it. “I’m fine, I just fell.” The truth was, my leg hurt a bit, and I felt that I had performed terribly in the game. That feeling was like the shame of being abandoned. I began to wonder whether I just wasn’t good enough, whether everyone was secretly laughing at how clumsy I was.

“Are you really okay?” a classmate asked again. I nodded, but my heartbeat still hadn’t slowed down. I was afraid they would lose patience with me because of my mistake. Overanalyzing their expressions and tone, I seemed to hear hidden criticism: “You’re so stupid, you can’t even catch a ball.” At that moment, I felt a dull ache in my stomach, and my steps slowed as well.

After the game ended, I walked alone to the edge of the playground, feeling a wave of regret. I kept replaying the moment of my mistake and imagining how my classmates might have reacted. I even pictured them talking about my incompetence behind my back. That afternoon, I remained trapped in those negative emotions and couldn’t focus on class.

When I got home, I lay on my bed, and the scene from the game kept replaying in my mind. I kept blaming myself, thinking that if I had tried a little harder, maybe I could have avoided all this. Even when my mom asked what was wrong, I only said nothing, because I didn’t want to worry her. Over the next few days, I tried to avoid taking the initiative to join any sports activities, so I wouldn’t make mistakes again. I even imagined that if I stopped participating in games, maybe I wouldn’t be laughed at anymore. Even so, I still longed for my classmates’ approval, but I was also afraid of being rejected again.

The classroom lights were always a little harsh, shining on my essay paper so that the black words on the white page looked messy and disordered. I sat in my seat, gripping the cuffs of my clothes tightly with both hands, feeling an inexplicable nervousness inside. I knew the teacher was about to comment on my essay, and like a prisoner waiting for judgment, I felt even my breathing become unnatural. “This essay still has problems with language use. For example, here, ‘I am very happy’—a sentence like that is too simple and not very expressive.” The teacher’s tone was calm, but every word stabbed into my heart like a needle. I didn’t know why, but my eyes began to sting and my palms grew damp. There was only one thought in my head: Does she think I’m an idiot? Does she think I’m not good enough?

The classmates around me were whispering, their voices like ants crawling by my ears. “Wasn’t she usually pretty good at writing?” a voice drifted over. I instinctively lowered my head and hid my face behind my textbook. My face felt burning hot, as if countless eyes were staring at me. At that moment, my chest tightened as if it had been bound with ropes, my fingers unconsciously picking at the desk surface, and it felt as though a knotted rope were tugging at my stomach.

The teacher continued commenting on other people’s essays, and I tried to calm myself down, but I failed. I started replaying her words from earlier over and over in my mind: “too simple,” “not expressive,” like a broken record stuck on one groove. I even remembered the scene the night before when I was writing the essay. Why hadn’t I read it carefully once more before handing it in? Why hadn’t I added more descriptive words? I bitterly blamed myself, feeling that I was a complete mess and had no hope at all.

“Are you okay?” My deskmate beside me poked my arm. I suddenly looked up and felt that my eyes were already wet. I shook my head. “I’m fine.” But my voice was so faint it sounded like a mosquito buzz. I was afraid that if I said one more word, I would burst into tears right there. My deskmate glanced at me again and said nothing more. I lowered my head and stared at the paper on my desk, trying to doodle in the blank spaces with my pen, but my hand was shaking so badly that even the pen tip made a creaking sound.

That night, I lay in my bedroom and went over the whole thing again and again. I opened that essay paper, trying to find exactly what had gone wrong, but it seemed as if every sentence was mocking me. In the end I couldn’t hold back any longer and cried, lowering my voice so much that even my pillow could hear my sobs. I kept asking myself: Why am I always like this? Why am I always so easily discouraged? Is it possible that I’m just not suited to writing essays at all? That feeling of being rejected was like a flood, instantly swallowing me whole.

The next day, I tried to act as if nothing had happened when I went to school, but I still felt heavy inside. The teacher never mentioned my essay again, and I didn’t dare ask on my own. It felt as if some fact had already been stamped and sealed: I was the person who “wasn’t good with language.” I told myself that from now on I had to be more careful and not let others have the chance to criticize me again. But at the same time, I was afraid—afraid to write essays again, afraid to face comments again, because that might prove that my shortcomings were real.

The wooden floor of the dance studio looked a little slick in the sunlight, so bright it nearly made me squint. We were rehearsing for the class performance. I stood in front of the mirror, nervously watching myself, afraid of missing even one instruction from the teacher. “Everyone pay attention to your steps—keep them neat, and don’t forget to smile!” the teacher’s voice echoed through the room. I tried to keep up with the rhythm, but with every kick and every turn, I felt clumsy and slow compared with the other students. My heart beat faster and faster, and sweat began to bead on my forehead. My palms were slick with moisture, as if I could no longer hold onto anything; I could even feel my stomach tightening with nerves.

“Hey, I think you’re in the wrong spot,” a classmate beside me whispered. Her tone was gentle, but it hit me like a thunderclap. Instantly, countless thoughts rushed through my mind: Would the whole performance fail because of my mistake? Would everyone end up hating me for it? I felt utterly uneasy, as if I would be abandoned by the whole class in the next second. I squeezed my eyes shut hard, trying to calm myself down, but it was useless.

As the music continued, I forced myself to keep smiling, trying not to let anyone notice my panic. But my breathing grew rapid, as though each inhale was harder than the last. I remembered the moments in previous rehearsals when I had messed up, the scenes of being criticized by the teacher still vivid in my mind, making me even more insecure. I could almost hear my own heartbeat in my ears, and I was so tense I felt like I might faint.

“It’s okay, just practice more,” the teacher said, stopping the music. She walked over to me and gently patted my shoulder. “Next time, you can count the rhythm silently in your head first; that will make it easier to keep up.”

I nodded, doing my best not to cry. The teacher’s gentle tone didn’t relax me; instead, it made me feel even more powerless. Maybe she had lost confidence in me? The shadow of being abandoned surfaced again. I couldn’t help pressing my fingers hard against my thigh, trying to force myself to concentrate.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, the details of the day’s rehearsal echoing endlessly in my mind. Even the warm blanket couldn’t drive away the anxiety in my heart. I kept wondering if I wasn’t good enough, if I should give up on the performance. But if I did, what would my classmates think of me?

The next day, I went to school with dark circles under my eyes, determined to try again. I had to overcome this fear. “Today, I’m going to do it for sure,” I silently vowed to myself. Though I was still uneasy, I stepped into the dance studio to face another day’s challenge.

Sunlight streamed through the balcony’s glass door, wrapping warmly around my arms and face. I sat in the small wicker chair on the balcony, a novel with a slightly worn cover spread open on my knees. As I turned the pages, I could feel the paper’s faintly rough texture and catch a hint of its old book smell. Outside the balcony was the garden below; the breeze brushed gently through the leaves, making a rustling sound. Now and then I looked up, watching the leaves sway in the wind, like some kind of soft dance. In the distance, I could faintly hear children laughing, along with the occasional ring of a bicycle bell, mingling with the sound of the wind to form a strange sort of background music.

I was reading a particularly interesting chapter, where the protagonist in the novel was trying to escape a complicated predicament. I stared at the words on the page, already completely immersed in that fictional world. I tried to guess what the protagonist would do next, but couldn’t help looking forward to an unexpected twist from the author.

Suddenly, the wall clock in the room chimed twice, quite crisply. I was startled, my heart tightening slightly, and then I realized it was only reminding me that it was 2:30 in the afternoon. I stretched, placed the book on my lap, and casually picked up the water glass beside the chair for a sip. The water was cool as it slid down my throat, bringing a soothing feeling. I remembered my mom saying this morning that she would be back later today, so I probably wouldn’t see her until dinnertime.

In a corner of the balcony, a few small plants grew in an old flowerpot that I always forgot the names of, their leaves carrying a thin green hue. I reached out and gently touched one of the leaves; it felt smooth, but there were a few slightly rough veins running through the middle. I always felt that the plants in these pots were a kind of silent companionship. They grew there very slowly, yet always gave me a feeling of being wrapped in reassurance.

After a while, I heard the neighbor’s puppy barking outside the door, the sound short and sharp, as if answering something. I looked up and around, imagining that the little dog might be chasing a toy in the yard. That bark pulled me slightly away from the book, and I suddenly felt the reality of the surroundings around me. Then I turned my gaze back to the pages and continued reading.

Time slipped away quietly, and the sunlight changed from warm to somewhat dazzling. I got up and pulled one side of the balcony curtain closed to soften the light. After sitting back down, I realized I had already finished two whole chapters of the novel. The characters in the book had gone through new adventures, while I felt that these two hours had melted slowly in the sunlight into something gentle and barely perceptible.

The whole afternoon, I remained calm, with nothing particularly special happening. I simply sat there, feeling the sunlight and warmth, listening to the wind and the birds, and letting time drift by softly.

The classroom was filled with the smell of paper and glue, and craft class always made me nervous. The assignment the teacher gave us was to make a pinwheel out of colored paper. I held the scissors, my palms already a little damp. Every time the blades snapped shut, the sound felt especially harsh, as if the whole classroom were staring at me. I kept checking my paper pieces, afraid I would cut too much or cut crooked. Finally, I finished cutting the pieces, but when I started putting them together, one side just wouldn’t line up no matter what I did. My heart began to race, and my ears were buzzing, as if all the sounds in the room were rushing into my ear canals.

“Wow, your color combination looks really nice!” My deskmate suddenly leaned over to look at my pinwheel, and I froze. He was one of the most popular boys in class, and he usually didn’t say much. When I heard him praise me, my first reaction wasn’t happiness but suspicion. Why was he saying this all of a sudden? Was he making fun of me? I looked down, and even my own pinwheel seemed like a complete mess—what was pretty about it?

“Don’t force the compliment,” I blurted out, my tone sharper than I had expected. He raised his eyebrows and said, sounding a little innocent, “No, I really do think it looks nice.” He paused, as if afraid I wouldn’t believe him, and added, “You chose the colors in a really imaginative way.”

I lowered my head, and another emotion began churning inside me. Was he really praising me? Or being sarcastic about how bad I was at crafts? Or did he just feel sorry for me and pick something random to comfort me? I glanced at his expression out of the corner of my eye, but couldn’t read much. He had already gone back to his own project and was busy working on it, looking perfectly unconcerned. But I couldn’t keep making the pinwheel anymore; every movement felt clumsy. I put on too much glue, and the paper pieces stuck to the desk; the twisting pin also went in crooked. I had a strong urge to crumple the whole thing into a ball, but I didn’t dare, afraid the teacher would see.

In the end, when everyone put their finished pinwheels on the podium, mine looked especially ugly—its edges were crooked, and the colors had bled because of the glue. I stood in line, watching the teacher comment on everyone’s work. Every time her gaze swept over me, I unconsciously clenched my back teeth and my shoulders tensed, as if bracing against some invisible weight.

After class, while I was packing my bag, I secretly glanced at my pinwheel a few times. For a moment, I really wondered if I was just being too sensitive. Maybe my deskmate really had only meant well when he complimented me, but why did I feel like he had ulterior motives? The more I thought about it, the more annoyed I became, as if a small stone were pressing on my stomach. On the way home, I couldn’t help replaying that moment over and over, the words he said and the expression on his face constantly popping up in my mind, only for me to keep overturning my own guesses. Even after I got home, I still couldn’t shake the voices in my head, and dinner tasted like wax.

Before bed, I stared at the pinwheel’s crooked shape on my desk, overwhelmed by shame and self-blame. Silently, I made up my mind that if I ever ran into something like this again, I would find a way to hide it better—at the very least, I wouldn’t let others see how embarrassed I was.

During a club activity, we were gathered on the playground, crowding around to watch our teacher demonstrate the new telescope that had just arrived. Sunlight sparkled all around us, and a gentle breeze brushed my cheeks, yet my mood felt like a tightly strung violin string. The teacher stood nearby, patiently explaining how to use the telescope, his voice carrying a mix of excitement and pride. “This telescope can even show you the craters on the moon!” he said, full of anticipation. My heart gave a sudden jolt. I raised my hand and, my voice trembling slightly, asked, “If we look through it for too long, will our eyes get hurt?”

The classmates around me all turned to look at me at once, and I could feel my cheeks heating up quickly. I had thought it was a reasonable question, but in an instant I realized I might have been overthinking it. The teacher’s brows knitted slightly, and his voice rose before he could stop it. “Are you joking? There’s no need to worry about that.” His laughter drew a wave of laughter from the others, and it felt as though my heart had been struck hard. A tightness began to build in my chest, my breathing grew rapid, and I could feel my heartbeat pounding wildly in my throat as beads of sweat slid down my temples.

I lowered my head, not daring to meet anyone’s eyes, my mind filled with that one sentence. Had I messed things up again? Had I asked another question I shouldn’t have asked? Those doubts surged in like a tide, and my fingers clenched into fists in unease. “Are you okay?” a classmate gently touched my shoulder. “That’s not what the teacher meant.” His tone was comforting, but inside me everything was churning. I forced out a smile and nodded, yet I still couldn’t dispel the shadow in my heart.

After the activity ended, I walked back to the classroom alone, my body a little weak and my stomach roiling with discomfort. I sat at my desk, staring blankly at my textbook. In my mind, the scene of me asking that question kept replaying over and over, and the more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt, as if the whole world were mocking me.
