That night, I tossed and turned in bed and couldn’t fall asleep. Even the sound of the wind outside seemed to be laughing at my foolishness.

Over the next few days, I tried my best to avoid raising my hand in class, afraid I would say the wrong thing again. I kept warning myself to be careful, but in doing so I also missed many things I wanted to understand. That experience made me even more sensitive to my own performance, especially in public, and I found myself unconsciously shrinking back and refusing to speak up. Although my classmates had long since forgotten that little incident, I couldn’t stop blaming myself, as if the shadow in my heart had only grown deeper.

Under the gray-white sky, the school’s reading corner looked especially gloomy. I crouched in the corner, holding a storybook I couldn’t get into. The bookshelves beside me were piled with books scattered everywhere, and several had been thrown onto the floor, as if telling some secret story.

“Come here, let’s look at this together!” one classmate called to me excitedly. I looked up and tried hard to force a smile, but I could feel the muscles in my face starting to stiffen. They were a few girls from the class, and they seemed a little curious about me, but I knew that most of the time, they treated me like part of the background.

I nodded and slowly moved over to sit beside them, my whole body tense. They were looking at a fairy tale book with beautiful illustrations. I tried to focus, but I just couldn’t concentrate.

Suddenly, a little bug crawled out from between the pages. I screamed instinctively and jerked backward, dropping the book in my hands to the floor. The classmates were all startled, then burst into laughter. My face burned hot, my heart raced, and it felt as if the whole world was mocking how helpless I was.

“You’re such a coward!” one classmate said with a laugh, trying to comfort me. I forced a smile and pretended not to care, but the humiliation made me want to find a hole to crawl into.

My palms turned cold and damp, and my stomach began to spasm. It seemed as though everyone could see through the fear in my heart. I knew they probably didn’t really care, but I couldn’t help imagining that every look and every word from them carried some deeper meaning.

“It’s fine, this bug isn’t scary at all!” another classmate said, patting my shoulder. I gave a reluctant nod, but the fear deep inside me still hadn’t gone away.

When I got home, I shut myself in my room and kept replaying that moment over and over. That night, the whole incident kept looping in my head, and I couldn’t fall asleep. My heartbeat sounded especially clear in the silent night. The next day at school, I didn’t even dare walk into the reading corner again, afraid of having to go through that socially awkward moment all over once more.

The classroom was left with only a few scattered students. The light was dim, and the shadows of the desks and chairs stretched long across the floor. I sat in my seat, holding my textbook and pretending to read, but my ears were straining to catch the whispers of the few classmates in the back row. Every so often they let out a soft laugh, and almost every few seconds someone would murmur, “Why is she so weird?” Then came another burst of laughter. I didn’t dare turn around, but I could see their expressions in the reflection—their deliberately lowered voices clearly meant for me to hear, making my fingers tremble slightly.

My stomach began to ache dully, as if a stone were pressing down on it. I tried hard to act as if I hadn’t heard a thing, but the letters and numbers on the page started to blur. I heard a boy say, “Did you notice how fast she ate lunch today? Like she was starving.” My face suddenly burned, and my mind raced: Were they all watching everything I did? What did I do wrong? Why were they even bringing up lunch! I thought back to how I had wolfed down my food at noon; I had only done that because I was so hungry. But now that I thought about it, had my behavior seemed weird, rude? Had I embarrassed myself in front of everyone?

I couldn’t help doing something I would come to regret deeply. I stood up and casually glanced their way, wanting to see whether their expressions were as malicious as I imagined. Sure enough, they stopped talking. A girl turned her head and looked at me expressionlessly, though her eyes carried a condescending, appraising look. I hurriedly turned away, too afraid to keep looking, but in that instant I felt her eyes saying, “You’re a joke.” My body froze, my heartbeat pounding so hard it seemed ready to burst out of my chest, but I was still trying to keep up a calm facade.

“Is something the matter?” she finally asked, her voice cool and detached. I was momentarily speechless, my lips trembling, and in the end I only managed to say, “No.” Then I quickly sat down. A deep sense of shame and pain washed over me, and my stomachache grew worse, while a buzzing filled my ears. I lowered my head hard and covered my face with my hands, trying to shut out the outside world. But in my mind, their laughter kept reappearing, echoing in my thoughts like footsteps. I began to believe there really was something wrong with me: Was I too weird? Did I not belong here at all? If I disappeared, would they stop laughing?

That night, I hid in my room and didn’t want to eat. My parents called for me outside the door, but they didn’t come in. Whenever I closed my eyes, all I could hear was their muffled laughter in the classroom, and that girl’s icy expression kept flashing before me. It felt like a brick was pressing on my chest, making it hard to breathe. I was filled with self-loathing, convinced that anything I did would only be mocked. I even started to fear going to school the next day, fear facing their eyes again. Until midnight, I was still lying in bed, completely unable to sleep. Those words were like needles stabbing into me, impossible to pull out, and the pain kept getting worse. The entire weekend, I didn’t dare speak to anyone on my own, afraid that something I said would become the joke of their tea-time chatter once again.

Ribbons hung from the ceiling, and colorful balloons floated in the corners of the classroom. The teacher had us rehearse a performance for the birthday party, and I was assigned to a group where I was in charge of leading everyone in singing “Happy Birthday.” At first, everyone was pretty cheerful, and I tried to blend into the atmosphere too, but I kept feeling uneasy, as if everyone’s eyes were fixed on me. When it was my turn to sing the first line, my voice suddenly turned hoarse, as if it had caught in my throat. I saw a few classmates in the class exchange glances, then burst into giggles. My face immediately burned bright red, and it felt like my eyelids were so hot they were about to catch fire.

“Can you at least sing properly?” a voice came from the back row. I turned and saw the group leader frowning at me. “Everyone’s waiting for you. Don’t hold us back.”

It felt like a stone was lodged in my throat, and I could only nod and keep singing, but even I could tell my pitch was off. People started murmuring among themselves, and some didn’t even bother hiding it, laughing out loud. In that moment, a thought flashed through my mind: they’re all laughing at me. Why did I mess up? Why am I never good enough? I tried to focus on the lyrics, but tears were welling up in my eyes, and I was afraid that if I blinked, they would spill out.

“Don’t cry, little kid.” A boy exaggeratedly mimicked my hoarse voice, drawing a wave of laughter from those around him. I froze in place, as if nailed there, my arms and legs going weak. I could even feel the insole of my shoe getting damp beneath me, sweat soaking through into my socks.

After the rehearsal ended, I quietly hid in a corner of the classroom, leaning against the wall, my heart pounding so fast it felt like it was about to burst out of my chest. I kept replaying every detail from earlier in my mind—the laughter, those words, those expressions. Why did they do that? Was I really that terrible? Did I simply not belong here? I gripped the hem of my shirt tightly, my fingernails nearly tearing through the fabric, and the tight ache in my chest made it hard to breathe.

That night, I lay in bed staring at the ceiling, my mind racing nonstop. Every time I tried to close my eyes, those scenes played over and over like a movie, until my heartbeat sped up again. I even started imagining whether the next class event would be just as bad. Did the teacher think I wasn’t good enough too? The next day, I hesitated for a long time before walking into the classroom, keeping my head down the whole time and trying to avoid eye contact with anyone. When I sat down at my desk, I heard two classmates in the front row talking. Though they were speaking very softly, I still sharply caught the words, “She was so embarrassing yesterday.” My stomach suddenly cramped, so badly I felt like I was going to throw up my breakfast.

Sunlight streamed through the library’s large windows and spilled onto the floor, casting mottled patches of light and shadow. I stood between the bookshelves, my fingers lightly tracing the spines as I looked for a book I had long wanted to read. The library was so quiet that all I could hear was the rustling of pages and the occasional whisper. Suddenly, my eyes stopped on a novel with an exquisite cover. Just as I was about to reach for it, the librarian happened to walk over, her gaze somewhat sharp.

“Classmate, are you looking for something?” she asked coldly, sounding as if she suspected my motives.

“No, I was just... um, trying to find this book,” I answered carefully, my heartbeat quickening and my palms beginning to sweat.

She stared at me as if I had done something I shouldn’t have. Immediately, all kinds of negative scenarios flashed through my mind: she would call my parents and criticize me, say I was handling the books recklessly, or even suspect I was hiding something. Each thought struck like lightning, leaving me with a wave of stomach pain.

“This book hasn’t been processed yet; you can’t borrow it!” she said somewhat brusquely, then turned and left. I stood frozen there, my face burning red, feeling misunderstood, as if the whole world were watching me make a fool of myself.

I withdrew my hand, hardly daring to look at the book again. I only wanted to leave quickly, but my legs seemed fixed in place. For the next few minutes, I kept replaying her words and expression in my mind, every detail magnified infinitely. Why was she so suspicious of me? What had I done wrong? Was I a problem child? These thoughts swirled around like shadows I couldn’t shake off.

That night, lying in bed, I was still embarrassed by what had happened. I tried several times to let it go, but the librarian’s distrust and my own panic kept resurfacing. In the silence of the night, my heartbeat seemed even louder, and the feeling of being misunderstood and criticized lingered for a long time.

A few days later, I tried going back into the library, but I still felt uneasy. I didn’t dare go near that bookshelf, afraid of being suspected again. So I chose a book that looked safe, one with a plain cover that seemed to put my mind at ease. Even so, I kept carefully reviewing every move I made, making sure not to upset anyone.

The classroom lights were a little harsh, and through the window one could faintly see the sunlight on the playground and a few leaves swaying in the wind. I sat in the last row of the classroom, with a black plastic electronic keyboard in front of me. There were a few worn spots on the keys; it lacked texture, yet it carried a cold, hard presence. The teacher stood beside the podium, lightly tapping the edge of the blackboard with a pointer, signaling us to begin practicing with the metronome. Her voice was calm, but carried an unmistakable sense of pressure: “Pay attention to the rhythm. Everyone must take turns playing through the piece completely. Don’t make mistakes.” My heart tightened; it seemed that every time it was my turn to perform, I would make a mistake.

When it was my turn, I took a deep breath and placed my fingertips on the keys, feeling their slight chill. The first part of the melody went fairly smoothly, but when the metronome quickened, I began to panic. My fingers unconsciously sped up, and I hit a high note by mistake, producing a jarring sound. The whole classroom fell silent for a second, and then a few classmates sitting in the front row laughed out loud. A boy turned back to look at me and said teasingly, “Did the keyboard explode, haha.” His words felt like a needle piercing my skin. My face burned at once, and my ears seemed to start ringing.

I lowered my head and stared at the keys, trying not to look at their faces. Thoughts flashed rapidly through my mind: Did they always think I was clumsy? Even such a simple melody couldn’t be played well; they must be thinking that. My hands began to sweat uncontrollably, my fingertips were already a little slick, and my heart was pounding wildly in my chest. I wanted to say something to explain, but I felt that whatever I said would only make it more awkward. The teacher walked over and said in a somewhat stern voice, “Try again. Don’t panic.” Her finger pointed toward the keys, her movement somewhat mechanical. I nodded, but my voice was barely audible.

I tried hard to start playing again, but the boy’s laughter kept echoing in my head. I tried to press each key correctly, but to my surprise, I missed two notes in a row. Laughter rose again, louder this time, as if the whole classroom was staring at me with malice. My mouth felt dry, and I took a deep breath, but it turned into a short sigh. I wanted to tell myself it was no big deal, but I couldn’t convince myself no matter what.

After the bell rang, the students began to leave the classroom in twos and threes. As I packed up the electronic keyboard, I moved very slowly, trying to delay leaving, but from the corner of my eye I still noticed a few classmates glancing at me with expressions of mockery. I seemed to hear them whispering, “Why is she so stupid?” Every possible remark felt like a stone pressing on my heart. I felt as if I had nowhere to put my hands and feet; my body was stiff like a broken machine.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the wrong notes and the laughter in my head. The shame of being mocked felt like a heavy blanket covering my chest, making even breathing difficult. I kept thinking, why couldn’t I play as easily as the other students? Was there something wrong with me? I even began to doubt whether I was fit to study music at all. Outside the window, the wind gently swayed the branches, but I felt trapped in an inescapable loneliness. It wasn’t until deep into the night that I finally closed my eyes in exhaustion, yet the shrill wrong notes and laughter from class still lingered in my mind like a tape that could not be turned off. The next day, the walk to school felt especially long, and my steps grew slower and slower, afraid of becoming the center of attention again.

The water in the pot bubbled gurglingly, and white steam shrouded the kitchen window, blurring the view in the distance. I sat on a low stool with an old piece of cotton cloth spread over my knees, peeling the outer skin off a carrot with a kitchen knife in my hand. The orange-yellow shavings of carrot skin kept falling to the floor, making soft rustling sounds. I could smell the aroma of boiling bone broth in the air, along with the fresh scent of vegetables, carrying a hint of damp earth. The children’s shouts outside the window drifted in intermittently, as if they were chasing and playing, but I didn’t pay much attention.

“Be careful not to cut your hand,” Mom said, looking over from beside the stove, a ladle in her hand as she stirred. Her voice carried a trace of reproach, yet it was gentle too.

I nodded, turned the carrot over to the other side, and continued peeling carefully. I glanced at Mom; steam shrouded her face, making her look a little hazy, but her busy movements gave off a reassuring feeling. The kitchen light was a bit dim and yellow, and in that atmosphere, I felt as if the whole world had suddenly become calm and steady.

“This one’s done,” I said, holding up the carrot in my hand, a little proudly.

When Mom heard me, she turned and looked at it. “Mm, not bad, but there’s still a bit of peel left on this side. Be more careful.” She lightly tapped the edge of the pot with the spoon in her hand, making a clear, crisp sound. In the small space of the kitchen, that sound was so distinct, as if it had melted all the noise away along with the steam from the pot.

“Alright, alright, I’ll do it again.” I pouted and checked the carrot carefully once more. Only after confirming I hadn’t missed anything did I set it aside. The action gave me a little sense of accomplishment, small but very real.

The tile floor in the kitchen felt cold underfoot, and a little slippery. My toes curled unconsciously inside my slippers. Occasionally, a few droplets of water would fall from the edge of the stove, landing on the floor with tiny splatters. I nudged those droplets with my toe, watching them slide across the floor like a little game.

“Next, help me pick some cilantro. It’s in that basket over there,” Mom said, pointing to the vegetable basket by the sink. I stood up from the stool, and on the way over I accidentally bumped into the rice cooker placed nearby, making the lid go “clang.”

“Oh dear, watch it,” Mom said, turning to glance over, but there was no reproach in her tone. She only shook her head and went on stirring the soup.

I picked up the cilantro and smelled its distinctive, strong fragrance. The scent reminded me of the times before when our family chopped cilantro while making dumplings, and an idea naturally arose in my mind: “There should be cilantro in today’s soup too, right?”

“Mom, how much cilantro are you putting in the soup this time?” I asked while picking the leaves.

“Just eyeball it. Don’t use too much—save some for cold dressing tomorrow.”

After picking for a while, my fingers were covered in cilantro juice, my fingertips slightly cool. Suddenly, I felt a deep sense of peace. This quiet time seemed to have some invisible magic, making one relax without realizing it. The tension in my body slowly faded, and even my heartbeat seemed to settle down quite a bit. Even if the wind outside the window suddenly grew louder, the warmth in the kitchen still wrapped around me steadily.

After dinner, I helped carry the bowls and chopsticks into the kitchen. Mom washed the dishes while humming an old song I couldn’t understand, the tune softly echoing in the small space. At that moment, an unnamed feeling rose in my heart—perhaps because of this calm, or perhaps because, deep down, I felt that such days were simple and beautiful.

The classroom was filled with noisy chatter. My classmates ran excitedly back and forth, getting ready to present their science projects. I stood in front of the teaching podium, my mind in complete chaos, clutching my project display board so tightly that my heart felt like it was about to burst out of my chest. I looked down at the board; the words and pictures on it seemed a total mess. I started sweating, my palms were slippery, and the board was beginning to slip from my grip. I silently prayed that no one would come over and look closely at my work.

The teacher walked over and said with a smile, “Alright, kids, it’s time for your presentations now.”

I took a deep breath and tried my best to calm myself, but it felt as if my vocal cords were being pulled tight, and my voice would only circle around in my throat. I heard a classmate behind me whisper, “Their presentation isn’t anything special.” A sharp sting pierced my heart, as if someone had slashed it with a knife.

“My project is about how plants adapt to environmental changes…” I struggled to begin speaking, but my words came out haltingly and broken. A few classmates nearby started whispering to each other, and I could hear every word, each one like a needle stabbing into my ears. My face felt hot, my whole body began slowly to stiffen, and it felt as if a heavy stone had dropped into my stomach.

The teacher’s voice seemed to drift from a great distance: “You can talk about why you chose this topic.”

I froze, my mind completely blank; everything I had prepared seemed to have been swallowed by a black hole. Stammering, I said, “Because… because I think it’s important.” The sentence was short and weak, and I didn’t even believe it myself.

After the presentation ended, I quickly gathered up everything and fled the noisy classroom. The laughter and snickering from behind me still echoed in my ears. I ran all the way to a corner of the playground, struggling to breathe, my heartbeat still refusing to settle. I felt unbearably ashamed and lost, as if the whole world had abandoned me.

A few days later, that sense of shame still lingered, occasionally making my stomach hurt before school. The self-attacks in my mind began to batter me relentlessly over and over: “If only I could have done better.” But that thought only made me even more miserable.

I stood at the edge of the community swimming pool, sunlight glaring off the water. The cool scent of the water mixed with the sharp smell of chlorine hit me, and the sounds of other children laughing and splashing filled my ears. I took a deep breath, planning to try a new skill in today’s swimming lesson: diving.

“Ready?” the swimming coach asked in his usual gentle but firm voice. At first I nodded, but then my heart suddenly began pounding violently, as if sounding an alarm for the challenge ahead. The coach went on, “Relax, take it slowly.” His voice was as calm as the blue depths of the pool.

I put my foot into the water, and the icy sensation immediately spread through my body. Silently, I told myself, “This time I have to succeed. I can’t embarrass myself again.” I closed my eyes, trying to ignore the mental scenes I was about to stage underwater—choking, struggling, and not being able to get back up. I pinched my nose tightly and braced myself to dive in.

But when I finally went under, the sound of the water suddenly grew deafening, as if the whole world had been submerged. I tried hard to open my eyes, but my nerves kept me from focusing on my movements. My chest tightened, and my breathing became rapid. Before I could stop myself, I surfaced, flailing helplessly at the water, which drew a burst of laughter from the children not far away.

“Are you okay?” a classmate beside me asked with a smile. I nodded, pretending not to care, though my face burned. I could feel my heartbeat speeding up even more, sweat and pool water running down my cheeks. At that moment, I was filled with disappointment and shame. It felt as though every pair of eyes around me was fixed on me, mocking me.

After class ended, I sat silently at the edge of the pool, wrapped tightly in a damp towel. Water dripped from my hair, and I felt like one of those tiny drops falling onto the concrete floor—utterly insignificant. The coach came over and sat beside me. “You did great. Don’t be discouraged. Practice a few more times and you’ll definitely succeed.”

His encouragement made me feel a little better, but I still couldn’t shake the humiliation of being watched. On the way home, I remained silent, replaying the awkward moments in my mind again and again. Even after several days, that embarrassment still kept me from taking the initiative to go to swimming class.

During that time, whenever I wanted to try something new, that fear always stayed close behind, reminding me of the possibility of making a fool of myself. Although the encouragement from my coach and classmates mattered to me, I still couldn’t get rid of the faint self-doubt and anxiety deep inside.

I was standing in the queue at the little shop in front of the school, the air around me thick with the damp, earthy smell left after the rain. Ahead of me were a few older boys, talking about a soccer game, their voices so loud it felt like they wanted the whole line to hear. I kept clutching the coin in my hand, a thin layer of sweat forming on my palm, and I had a vague sense of unease.

My eyes kept scanning the line in front of me, calculating how much longer it would be before my turn. Just then, someone squeezed in from the side and cut straight in front of me. I instinctively took a step back, and my nose bumped into the little girl standing behind me. She let out a sound in protest, and I hurriedly apologized, but she still shot me a fierce glare. I had no choice but to look away, while an unnamed anger started churning in my head: why did he cut the line? Didn’t he see me standing here? Why did he get to just ignore me like that?

“You cut in line,” I finally mustered the courage to say, but my voice was so small it was like a mosquito’s hum, barely audible even to myself. The person turned back to look at me; it was a big boy, at least a head taller than I was. He raised his eyebrows and said carelessly, “I just took a spot. It’s not a big deal.”

My face burned instantly. I let my gaze drift around, too afraid to meet his eyes, and could only tighten my grip on the coin. My palm was so sweaty it felt like it might slip out. “But... but everyone’s lining up. That’s not... not fair,” I heard myself say haltingly.

The others heard the commotion and all turned to look. I could feel my neck and ears growing hot too, my heartbeat pounding like someone drumming right beside my ear. I started regretting saying anything, thinking: what if he sneers and says, “People like you think you can meddle?” What if he shoves me in a fit of anger? Would I just fall flat on the ground? Everyone would laugh at me, wouldn’t they?

“Tsk, fine, what a pain,” he muttered, then turned and stepped back to his place behind me. I felt as if I’d just been pulled out of water, completely drenched, my face still burning. The little girl behind me muttered softly, “Should’ve done that long ago.” I wasn’t sure if it was praise or sarcasm, and my heart was still all over the place.

When I got to the counter, I almost mechanically handed over my change and grabbed a random snack to toss into the bag, without even looking at what it was. My throat felt dry as a desert, and even my hand holding the plastic bag was trembling slightly. On the way home, I kept replaying what had just happened in my head. The boy’s raised eyebrows, that “what a pain,” and the looks from the people around me all kept flashing through my mind.

When I got home and opened the snack I’d bought, I realized I’d picked up the wrong thing. The fruit-flavored gummies I usually loved had turned into a bag of spicy strips. When the heat hit my mouth, tears suddenly welled up. A voice in my heart kept blaming me: why did you have to speak up? Why couldn’t you just stay quiet? Why did you have to make trouble? If you hadn’t said anything, you wouldn’t have bought the wrong thing later. But another voice pushed back: what if everyone cut in line casually like he did?

I stayed gloomy all evening, even doing my homework half-heartedly. The next day, when I went to school, I deliberately took a different route and avoided that little shop, thinking I’d never go there again so I wouldn’t run into that kind of awkward scene anymore.

Sunlight spilled across the school playground, and the shadows on the ground crossed and shifted with our running steps. The air was filled with the smell of dust and soil, along with the faint rustling of leaves in the distance. A few of us formed a small circle and began our afternoon soccer match, laughter rising one after another. The ball was kicked back and forth across the grass, sometimes fast, sometimes slow. As I ran, I felt a breeze brush my face, and the grass beneath my feet was slightly rough, yet full of life.

“Pass it to me!” a friend shouted. I quickly passed the ball out, watching it roll swiftly toward him. He caught it, turned, and sprinted toward the goal. We all stayed close behind him, trying to stop his attack. My heartbeat began to quicken, not out of nervousness, but from the pure excitement of sports. I felt sweat start to seep from my forehead, and the slight stickiness made me realize the day was a bit hot.

“Hurry up, stop him!” another friend yelled, his voice echoing through the air. I kept right behind him and finally managed to intercept the ball, just in time to win our team a scoring chance. Everyone was laughing, high-fiving each other in celebration. I looked up at the sky, where a few white clouds drifted across the blue expanse, perfectly matching the joyful atmosphere of the moment.

After the match ended, a few of us sat at the edge of the playground, panting, smiles of satisfaction on our faces. My heart felt utterly calm, as if all my worries had been carried away by the game. I looked at my friends beside me and felt the pleasant mood brought by their laughter. In that brief moment, it seemed as though the whole world was smiling.

On the way home, the cheerful sounds from the playground still echoed in my mind. That night, lying in bed, I thought back on the afternoon’s game and still felt my heart full of happiness. Our teamwork gave me a sense of belonging and the warmth of friendship. The whole experience was like fragments of beautiful memories, gently settling into my heart.

The sunlight was a little blinding, and I squinted at the basket, while the students’ screams and the rustling sound of shoes scraping against the floor echoed in my ears. I was dribbling the ball, getting ready to shoot, when suddenly a classmate rushed over from the side, trying to snatch the basketball away. I failed to react in time, and he slapped the ball away; it rolled off to the side. He turned to me and said, “Why didn’t you keep an eye on the ball again?” His tone carried a hint of impatience. I felt a wave of embarrassment, my face heating up, as if all the attention around me had focused on me. My heart raced, and it seemed I could even hear my heartbeat in my ears.

I said softly, “Sorry, I didn’t see you.” But inside, I felt wronged; clearly he had come so suddenly that I had no chance to react. My palms began to sweat, and I wiped them hard, pretending nothing had happened. For the rest of the game, I was somewhat distracted, my attention constantly drifting, always worried I would make a mistake again. Every time I got the ball, I didn’t dare pass it casually to others, afraid that if the pass was inaccurate, everyone would blame me.

After the game ended, I sat alone on the sidelines, watching the others laugh and chat about the game just now, feeling distant inside. I felt as if I had been enclosed on a tiny island, far away from them. I tried to join their conversation, but inside I kept replaying the earlier argument, and my emotions remained hard to calm.

“Hey, what are you thinking about?” A classmate came over and patted me on the shoulder, smiling as he said, “It’s no big deal. Everyone knows you did your best just now.” Hearing that, I relaxed a little, but the moment when I had been blamed still wouldn’t leave my mind.

That night, I lay in bed and closed my eyes, and the scene from the day appeared again in my mind. I felt somewhat unwilling to accept it, always thinking that if I had reacted a little faster, perhaps I wouldn’t have been criticized. Even so, after thinking it over and over, the tension and grievance in my heart were gradually washed away by exhaustion, and I slowly fell asleep.

A few days later, I played basketball with my classmates again. This time, I passed the ball very carefully, afraid of making a mistake again. Although none of them showed any sign of minding it, I still felt a faint unease, as if that little friction could happen again at any moment.

The sun hung in the sky, shining brightly on the little stalls at the school gate, making even the shadows on the ground look crisp and clear. A few of my classmates and I had just gotten out of school, and everyone said we should go buy popsicles to cool off. I stood at the back of the line. The line in front was pretty long, shoulder to shoulder, looking tightly packed and tense. In my ears were the classmates’ conversations and the roar of cars starting up on the nearby road, mixed with the ice pop vendor’s calls recommending different flavors. The air was especially stifling and hot. The sun had soaked my back with sweat, my scalp felt a little itchy, and sweat had started to gather under my feet, making my shoes feel sticky. I tried standing on tiptoe to see how the line was moving ahead, but it only made me more irritated.

One classmate suddenly turned back and glanced at me, the corners of his mouth lifting as he said, “You’re buying one too? You don’t usually seem to like these.” I froze for a moment, not knowing how to answer. Was that just something he said offhand, or was he hinting at something? I started to feel uneasy, replaying his expression over and over in my mind—did he think I was weird, or had he been watching me all along? I heard my heartbeat begin to quicken, and my chest gradually felt tight. I lowered my head and pretended to fiddle with my backpack zipper, trying to distract myself.

When it was my turn, I heard the popsicle vendor ask, “What flavor would you like, kid?” I suddenly froze, and a flurry of thoughts popped into my head: “If I choose the expensive one, will people think I’m showing off? If I choose the really cheap one, will I seem stingy?” I hesitated for a moment and felt the people behind me waiting. My ears began to burn, and it felt as if everyone was staring at me. “Um, blueberry flavor... thank you,” I stammered. When the vendor handed me the popsicle, my hand was trembling a little and I almost dropped it. I hurriedly gripped it tightly and pulled on the wrapper, afraid of making another mistake.

On the way back, I chatted casually with my classmates, but all my attention was on the popsicle in my hand. I even wondered if they were secretly watching me, and even a laugh made me suspect it was mocking how I had just acted. The popsicle had already begun to melt a little, and its sugary sweetness drifted into my nose. I licked it once; the moment my lips touched it, it was still pleasantly cold, but soon I felt irritated again and wanted to finish it quickly, as if that would make the chaos in my mind disappear.

After I got home, I threw the wrapper into the trash and sat at my desk to do my homework, but from time to time the scene of buying the popsicle would flash through my mind: Did I look really foolish? What exactly did other people’s looks mean? Even until bedtime, these thoughts would still occasionally surface, leaving me with an inescapable embarrassment and a subtle sense of unease.

I was sitting in the corner of the living room, clutching an orange peel in my hand, not knowing where to look, so I pretended to lower my head and peel the orange. The living room was brightly lit, the air conditioner hummed softly, and the relatives gathered around the sofa were talking about adult matters. I couldn’t join in, and felt like an alien. Suddenly, I heard a harsh laugh. An aunt’s voice cut through everyone else’s conversation: “Hey, look, why has **she** gotten fat again? Her face has turned so round. No wonder she doesn’t like to talk!” As soon as she finished, laughter burst out in the living room, as piercing as firecrackers in winter. And I froze instantly.

My ears felt hot, and my face began to flush red. I tried to force myself to stay calm, but the orange peel in my hand suddenly slipped and fell onto the carpet. I bent down to pick it up, but my fingers were trembling nonstop, like a loose wire. I heard someone nearby chiming in in a low voice, “She really has gotten fat. She was so thin when she was little, I guess she hasn’t been paying attention lately.” A sudden sour ache rose in my nose, like being pricked by a needle.

I wanted to say something, to defend myself, even to argue back, but my throat felt blocked, and not a single word came out. All I could do was clutch the orange tightly and dig my nails into its peel. My heart was like a boiling pot, steam rising nonstop: Were they all laughing at me? Was my face really that strange? Why was I so stupid that I couldn’t even say one sentence? Did they not like me at all and think I was a burden? More and more voices tangled together in my head until I couldn’t even hear my own breathing.

My aunt suddenly leaned over and patted my shoulder with a smile. “Oh, don’t be upset, we’re just joking. Kids get a little fat, and it’s pretty cute.” Her words stabbed into my heart like a needle again. I nodded desperately and forced out a stiff smile. “It’s okay.” But inside, I was already about to explode. I couldn’t help but feel my stomach twist, as if someone were clutching my insides. The sweat that had broken out on me started sticking to my palms; I lowered my head and wiped them quickly, afraid of being noticed. I was scared of being exposed—not only afraid they would see me blushing, but also afraid they would know how humiliated I felt inside.

After the gathering ended, I fled back to my room, locked myself in, and sat on the edge of the bed in a daze. My aunt’s voice kept echoing in my head, and those laughs lingered like reverberations that would not fade. I grabbed a pillow and covered my ears, only to realize that the more I did that, the more impossible it was to escape. I began blaming myself: Why hadn’t I paid attention to my appearance sooner? Why couldn’t I even react normally? Was there something fundamentally wrong with me? These fragmented thoughts made it almost impossible for me to breathe.

For the next few days, I didn’t want to leave my room, always feeling that other people would stare at my face. I started refusing to look in the mirror, and even at mealtimes I felt as if the food in my bowl was guilty. I lay in bed imagining people talking about me behind my back. Every time such an image appeared, my heart would feel gripped by someone, beating wildly out of control.

The lights on the podium were dazzlingly bright, and I almost felt waves of dizziness. The Chinese teacher casually called my name from the seating chart and asked me to go up and complete an impromptu response task. When her eyes swept over me, it felt as if even the air had grown heavy. The moment my name was called, my face flushed red, and my hands instinctively gripped the edge of the desk. My classmates were all staring at me, and I could feel their gazes like needles stabbing into my back.

“Come up quickly, don’t dawdle,” the teacher urged again. Her tone sounded emotionless, but I could hear a trace of impatience.

Standing in the middle of the podium, my palms began to sweat, and my fingers clung tightly to the edge of the teacher’s desk, afraid I might accidentally fall. My heart was beating fast, like a small drum in my chest. I tried my best to steady my breathing, but my voice still sounded shaky. The “click-clack” of chalk on the blackboard sounded as if it were exploding right beside my ear, and my mind went completely blank.

“You can begin,” the teacher reminded me, her tone seeming to carry a hint of contempt. I didn’t know whether I was imagining it, but in that moment, I really felt she was mocking my slowness.

I began to recite the text haltingly, trying to organize my thoughts, but my mouth wouldn’t cooperate and I made several mistakes. My breathing became more and more rapid, my voice growing weaker, until it seemed the whole classroom was silent except for my heartbeat. Occasionally, when I turned my head, I could see students in the front row whispering, with obvious smiles on their faces. I thought to myself: they must be making fun of me, thinking I’m ridiculous, right?

“Don’t be nervous, take your time,” the teacher’s voice rang out again, but by then it sounded more like she was just being perfunctory or trying to hide her disappointment. I gave an awkward smile and tried to force out a few words, but my voice was hoarse, as if something were blocking it. My cheeks felt even hotter, and my ears began to burn too, as if I were being scorched by fire. I could only lower my head and stare at my shoes, trying not to burst into tears on the spot.

“All right, you can go down now.” Finally, the teacher cut me off, and I also let out a sigh of relief. I hurried back to my seat, while small snickers rippled through the classroom. Though they were not loud, each one felt like a nail driving into my mind. I started blaming myself: why could I memorize so fluently at home, but become a completely different person once I got on stage? Was it because everyone was laughing at me that my mind went blank?

That night, I couldn’t sleep no matter what I did. Lying in bed, I kept replaying my stammering on the podium, and it seemed I could still hear my classmates’ laughter in my ears. Even counting sheep to 100 didn’t help; my eyelids only felt heavier and heavier. My stomach hurt a little, and I knew it was because I had been too anxious about what happened during the day.

The next day, I deliberately slowed my pace and didn’t walk into the classroom until the last few minutes. I was afraid to meet anyone’s eyes, and even more afraid of hearing them talk about what happened yesterday afternoon. Fortunately, they seemed to have forgotten, or perhaps were just too lazy to bring it up, but in my mind, the scenes from yesterday kept replaying over and over. It was truly suffocating.

That afternoon during the elementary school class spring deep-cleaning, sunlight poured through the spotless classroom windows, filling the room, while the air was thick with the fresh scent of detergent. I was assigned to clean the windows, so I carefully wiped each pane, afraid of leaving any dirt behind. My classmates were busy sweeping and mopping the floor, and the classroom was a scene of lively yet orderly activity.

“Hey, watch out!” my deskmate’s voice suddenly rang out. “You almost splashed water on me.” I looked up and realized he was standing right beside me, wiping the edge of the blackboard. I hurriedly apologized, but inside I suddenly felt a wave of panic, and my palms began to sweat slightly. I kept wondering whether he was angry because of it, whether he was secretly blaming me.

I went back to the window and carefully wiped the water marks from the glass, but I still felt uneasy, as if I were being watched. At last, without meaning to, I heard a few classmates whispering, occasionally glancing in my direction. In an instant, I felt they were talking about me, because I am always like this—easily imagining that everything has something to do with me.

“Are they talking about me?” I couldn’t help asking myself. My heart racing, I tried to hide my anxiety with a smile, only to feel my cheeks growing hot.

After the cleaning was over, I sat in the corner of the classroom with my forehead pressed against my knees, trying to steady my rapid breathing. The other students left amid laughter and chatter, but in my ears the whispers and the words “You almost splashed water on me” still echoed on and on.

At dinner, I ate absentmindedly, and my mother noticed something was off. “What’s wrong? Did something happen today?” she asked.

“Nothing, I’m just... just a little tired,” I said vaguely, unwilling to bring it up, afraid I would be accused of making a mountain out of a molehill. But deep down, I was overwhelmed with grievance and unwillingness, feeling as though everyone was against me, yet I couldn’t explain why.

That night, I lay in bed clutching my stomach, the pain in my belly keeping me tossing and turning, unable to sleep. Moonlight spilled softly through the window, but I still couldn’t calm my mind. Again and again, I replayed the events of the day in my head, feeling as though my thoughts were tied in knots that I could never untangle. The next day, I still went to school weighed down by the gloom that had not yet lifted; my whole body felt weak when I walked, my vision seemed hazy, and I was especially afraid of running into my deskmate again.

A few days later, through a small collaborative homework activity, I finally forced myself to talk to my deskmate again. He seemed not to remember anything unpleasant, and that finally put my mind at ease. I realized that I had overinterpreted many trivial details, though my sensitivity was not something that could be changed overnight.

This is one moment I can never quite erase, and even in the many years that followed, whenever I faced similar situations, I would still instinctively worry about being misunderstood. But gradually, I also began to learn to tell myself to relax, and that an unintentional act need not be worried over too much.

The soup on the dinner table was steaming, mingled with the aroma of stir-fried dishes and the smell of fish. I accidentally brushed against the edge of the table, and a glass slid off and shattered on the floor with a sharp crash. The sound exploded through the air, and my breath stopped in an instant. Father put down his chopsticks, his brows tightening as if tied in a knot. His gaze was like a searchlight of judgment, shining straight at me. “Why are you so careless?” he said, his voice low but cutting. My cheeks burned at once, and a buzzing filled my ears; it felt as if everyone in the room was looking at me. I hurried to crouch down and pick up the shards, and when my fingers touched the glass edge, I accidentally cut myself a little, but I didn’t care about the pain at all. All I could think about was ending this embarrassment as quickly as possible.

“Can’t you be more careful? You can’t even do something this simple!” Father’s voice rose again, even louder than before. The shards in my hand slipped from my grip, and tears were already welling up in my eyes, but I held them back hard. Mother tried to ease the tension. “The child didn’t mean it.” But Father cut her off: “This is a matter of attitude. You don’t even know the basics of manners!” Mother’s voice gradually fell silent, and my stomach twisted into a knot. Beads of sweat began to form in my palms, and waves of numbness spread across the soles of my feet. I kept my head down, not daring to look at him, nor at anyone else, only staring at the broken glass on the floor as if it were an escape route that could save my life. The images flashing through my mind were all his dissatisfaction with me, the possibility that he would never like me again, that no matter how hard I tried I would always be a failure.

After dinner, I hid in my room. The moment I closed the door, it felt as if I had finally escaped that oppressive atmosphere, but my heart was still racing so fast it wouldn’t calm down. I sat on the edge of the bed, staring at the floor, while Father’s voice kept echoing in my ears. He must be disappointed in me, right? Am I really that bad? Is everything I do wrong? These thoughts were like black insects, crawling all over my mind and leaving me unable to stop thinking. The discomfort in my stomach grew worse. I pressed a pillow over my face and cried softly for a while, but then I was afraid Mother might hear me, so I quickly held back my tears.

The next morning, when I got up, my eyes were still a little swollen, but I deliberately didn’t let myself look in the mirror. At breakfast, I was desperately careful; even my hand trembled slightly when I picked up the dishes. I tried my best to show Father how I was behaving, hoping he would give me a slightly gentler look, but he only finished quickly and left. I tried to tell myself not to think about it anymore, but my emotions, like that shattered glass cup, could no longer be restored.

The classroom was filled with the restlessness that follows an exam. Bright sunlight poured in through the window, but I felt as though I were wrapped in shadow. The test paper on my desk still gave off the smell of ink, and the teacher had just announced the scores; I had done especially badly that time. A few classmates gathered together discussing the questions, and their voices grew clearer and clearer, but every sentence felt like mockery stabbing at my ears.

“Did you see so-and-so’s answer? She got it so ridiculously wrong!” came a boy’s voice, followed by bursts of laughter. I froze. I had gotten that question wrong too, and in exactly the same “ridiculous” way. I lowered my head and looked at the paper, and the red Xs seemed to be laughing at me. I didn’t dare look up, afraid they would turn and notice me. My stomach began to tighten, and my palms grew wetter and wetter.

“What’s wrong?” The girl next to me gently poked my arm. She sounded concerned, but I felt an undertone of blame. Had she already noticed that I had made such a basic mistake too? Was she laughing at me in her heart? I immediately shook my head and said in a voice so soft I could barely hear it myself, “Nothing.” She didn’t seem to ask further, but I thought her expression looked a little unnatural. Did she actually already know what was wrong with me?

My mind kept replaying that question over and over, and the huge “wrong” marked on the paper seemed to keep growing larger. Suddenly I felt like a complete failure. Why couldn’t I even do such a simple question? If I got something this easy wrong, would no one ever see any value in me again? If everyone knew I had missed that question, would they think I was an idiot? The more I thought, the more frightened I became. I even started to wonder whether the “so-and-so” the boy had just mentioned actually referred to me, only he didn’t dare say my name directly.

The cicadas outside the window seemed to be mocking me too. Their cries were shrill and noisy, and my scalp tingled. My hands and feet gradually grew cold, but at the same time my heartbeat raced like a galloping horse. To hide it, I pretended to flip through the paper, only to find my hands trembling constantly, the handwriting blurring. I even felt as if the red X were a pool of blood, about to swallow me whole.

When the bell rang, everyone began packing up to head to the playground, but I deliberately dawdled, pretending to put my books away, trying to delay leaving the classroom. I was afraid to go out, because I felt everyone’s eyes would sweep over me and mock my clumsiness in their hearts. In the end, I still trailed slowly behind the last student, keeping my head down as I hurried through the corridor and fled to a corner beside the flowerbed. I sat there alone. The sunlight fell on me, yet I only felt cold. I began blaming myself: How can you be so stupid? Why do you always make mistakes? They must think you’re hopeless.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw the red X on the exam paper. Even after my mother came in and turned off the light, it still seemed to flicker in the darkness. I kept thinking: if I hadn’t gotten that question wrong, if no one had noticed my mistake, would I be able to feel a little better? But the answer could not be changed. I could only sink into endless regret and shame. For the entire first week, I tried my best to avoid saying much to anyone in the class. Even though they no longer seemed to be talking about the exam, I felt that I could be exposed at any moment, seen through at any moment as a complete failure.

The sun was blazing, spilling over the paths through the fields. From the grass at times came the sharp chirping of cicadas. I used a branch to push aside the wild grass under my feet, feeling the soles of my shoes already tightly stuck with crushed blades and mud. Our class picnic was nearing its end, and most of the students were gathered around a large pot of the “stone soup” we had cooked. What had originally been a fun activity somehow turned into one of the most painful memories in my mind.

When it was my turn to ladle out the soup, I noticed there was hardly any left in the pot. There were probably still five or six people who hadn’t gotten any. I weighed my bowl in my hand, wondering whether I should take a little less so there would be some for the people behind me. At the same time, I realized I was starving too; my stomach had been growling nonstop, as if reminding me that if I didn’t take enough, I would have to endure unbearable hunger for the next few hours.

“Come on, hurry up!” a boy in the back urged. His tone wasn’t especially harsh, but it instantly made my heart race, and my face burned as if it were being scorched by fire. I couldn’t help but begin guessing what he really meant: Was he thinking I was deliberately stalling? Had he already taken issue with me?

I explained, “I was thinking I shouldn’t take too much, or there won’t be enough for the people behind me.” Unexpectedly, he said, “Who cares? It doesn’t taste like anything anyway.” The students around us burst out laughing, seeming to mock my unnecessary fussing as well. My face flushed red and then pale; I hurriedly scooped up a ladle of soup and quickly moved away from the pot, even forgetting to look at the expressions of the people behind me.

I sat on the edge of the field ridge, looking down at the thin soup in my bowl. A few leaves floated on the surface, and a small piece of radish drifted in the middle. After taking a sip, I only felt emptiness in my stomach; it did nothing to satisfy my hunger. But I didn’t dare go back for a second serving. What if someone said I was selfish again? I heard a girl beside me mutter, “I should’ve taken more, sigh.” My nerves tightened, and tears suddenly welled up in my eyes. I knew she was complaining about herself, but—was she also blaming me for being petty? Did she think I was the one responsible for the unfair division of the soup?

For the rest of the time, I couldn’t bring myself to drink another sip. The emptiness in my stomach gradually turned into a suffocating pressure in my chest, and I couldn’t tell whether I was hungry or just upset. Fighting back tears, I tried hard to act as if nothing had happened. A friend beside me handed me a steamed bun. “I took an extra one, here.” Almost instinctively, I refused: “No need! I’m not hungry!” But right after that, I regretted it. I wanted nothing more than to rush back and take the bun. Being hungry was simply too painful.

On the bus back to school, I sat by the window, pretending to enjoy the fields flashing past outside, yet I couldn’t stop replaying the scene of ladling out the soup just now. Had I upset someone again today? Why was it that even such a routine little thing, I could still mess it up? Why was I always not good enough? The emptiness in my stomach gradually spread into an all-pervading discomfort throughout my body, and even my ears were ringing.

That night, when I got home, my mother asked how the picnic had gone. I lowered my head and said vaguely, “It was fine,” then fled to my room and buried myself under the blankets. The words “Who cares?” kept echoing in my ears. The more I thought about it, the more useless I felt, unable even to distribute a bowl of soup properly. I secretly vowed that next time there was an activity like this, I would not overthink it, and I absolutely would not make trouble for myself again.

The classroom lights buzzed overhead as I sat at the group’s round table, my palms already damp, the mind map I had drawn on the paper a complete mess, so tangled I couldn’t even make sense of it myself. The teacher asked each group to choose one person to summarize the discussion and speak, and everyone in my group fell silent, turning their eyes on me. That silence was suffocating, as if they were quietly blaming me. “Then you do it. Didn’t you always want to show off?” the group leader said under his breath, with a hint of mockery. I answered softly, “Okay, I’ll try.” But my voice was as weak as a mosquito’s buzz. 

When it was our group’s turn to present, I stood up, clutching the draft paper in my hand; the edge of it had already gone soft from my sweaty grip. I began to explain, but soon realized I had gotten the order wrong. The more I spoke, the more confused I became, until my words were broken and scattered. The classroom was far too quiet, and everyone’s gaze stabbed into my skin like needles. I wanted to explain, but my throat was so dry I couldn’t make a sound. 

“What are you even saying? You didn’t listen to the key points of our discussion at all!” A boy in the group suddenly interrupted me, his voice not loud but full of impatience. I froze, and in an instant my mind flashed with familiar scenes: they were angry, I had done something wrong again, I was going to be abandoned. “I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’ll start over!” I stammered, my face burning red. The teacher also frowned, seeming ready to speak. I hurriedly lowered my head and frantically searched the paper for the content, only to find I had no idea where to begin. 

I felt as if I were trapped in a nightmare that would never end. My heart was pounding like a hammer, sweat began to bead on my forehead, and my stomach clenched in pain. I wanted the floor to crack open and swallow me whole. My groupmates’ eyes grew colder and colder, and they began whispering to one another. I heard someone say, “How is she so bad?” “What a waste of time.” Those words sliced through my head like knives. I gasped for breath, trying hard not to let the tears fall, but my mouth kept trembling uncontrollably. 

“Alright, sit down for now. We’ll talk after class,” the teacher finally said. I sat back down as if fleeing for my life, but my legs were shaking. I heard my groupmates whisper behind me, “She’s really embarrassing.” After class, I tried to apologize, but no one paid any attention to me. Everyone left in a hurry, leaving only me sitting at my desk. I stared at the messy drawings on the tabletop, as if they were mocking my incompetence. I kept thinking over and over: if I hadn’t been so rash, if I could have been smarter, would they have liked me? But I had already ruined it. 

When I got home, I didn’t say a word to my family. I just hid in my room, spacing out. The stomach pain hadn’t gone away, and the tightness in my chest only grew stronger. I replayed that day over and over in my head, every tiny expression, every sentence, each one like a needle prick I couldn’t stop reliving. The light before bed reminded me of the fluorescent tubes in the classroom, and I tossed and turned until deep into the night. The next day, I made up an excuse and didn’t go to school, afraid of facing those people again.

I had been staring at the words on the blackboard until they were almost blurring, but I couldn’t remember a thing the teacher had just said. When he called my name, my stomach lurched as if someone hadfiercely grabbed it, and all my attention snapped back to the classroom. “Look at this yourself. What is this about?” His voice was low and cold, like a bucket of ice water poured over me. I slowly stood up, my legs feeling a little weak. I saw my workbook in his hand, with several red crosses glaring especially brightly, like flames burning.

“These problems—we just went over them yesterday, didn’t we? How could you get them so completely wrong?” He held my book up for the whole class to see. In that moment, I felt the air turn thick, making it hard to breathe. A few of the students around me started to laugh quietly. I heard someone whisper, “I knew they’d be like this.” My face began to burn, a scorching sensation spreading from my neck to my cheeks. I tried to lower my head, but found I couldn’t move at all, standing there like a wooden dummy.

“What kind of attitude is this?” he shouted at me. “You don’t care about studying at all, do you?” My mouth opened slightly, but not a single word came out. I wanted to explain instinctively, but my mind felt tied up with ropes, and I couldn’t say anything. I could hear my heartbeat pounding in my ears, my palms already soaked with sweat, my fingertips cold.

“Sit down.” His tone was full of disappointment, as if I had made some irreparable mistake. I sat down mechanically, but my legs were still trembling slightly. The other students seemed to quickly turn their attention back and keep listening, but my head was full of the scene from just now. I kept seeing his frowning face and cold eyes replaying over and over in my mind, like a broken videotape. I felt so ashamed, as if I had been stripped bare all over, with nowhere left to hide.

During lunch break, I heard two classmates talking in low voices: “It’s them. They can even get such an easy problem wrong. Who knows how they got into this school.” I wanted to pretend I hadn’t heard, but those words stabbed into my ears like needles. I felt my stomach churning, and even the lunch tasted bitter. I tried hard to hold back my tears, but my nose still stung.

When I got home, I slammed the workbook onto the desk. Not wanting my family to see my expression, I immediately crawled under the blanket, hugged my pillow tightly, and wondered why I always disappointed people. Was I really that stupid? Would I never be able to change? I clenched my teeth, pressing the pillow over my face, trying not to let the tears fall.

Over the next few days, whenever I went to the classroom, I tried my best to hide in the back row, afraid of being called on again. Every time I heard the teacher’s voice, my shoulders would involuntarily shrink, and my heartbeat would start to go out of rhythm. I began spending more time checking my homework, staying up until eleven at night, but every time I turned it in, the voice in my head saying “what if it’s wrong again” still wouldn’t go away.

The sunlight in the playground was a bit dazzling, and I squinted as I kicked at the small pebbles on the ground. After class, everyone poured outside, and a few classmates called me over to play dodgeball. While we were playing, a sandbag suddenly slammed hard into my head. I let out a muffled groan and instinctively covered my head, tears almost instantly welling up. In my ear, I faintly heard someone let out a light laugh. I turned around and saw Xiaoli standing not far away. There was no expression on her face, but I felt certain she must have been laughing at me.

“Why did you hit me?” I shouted at her. My voice was a little shaky, sounding less angry than coquettish, which only made me feel more ashamed. She looked confused. “It wasn’t me, it was Xiaowei!” She pointed to the boy standing beside her, but I only felt that she was lying. I stared at her and muttered, “You did it on purpose.”

The air seemed to freeze. After a second of silence, a few classmates around us froze too, then began whispering among themselves. I heard someone say softly, “Why is she so sensitive?” Another person laughed and said, “Who told you to stand there?” My face burned at once, as if I had been stripped naked in front of everyone. I wanted to explain that I hadn’t meant it, but the words seemed stuck in my throat, and I couldn’t get them out no matter what.

Xiaoli stared at me and curled the corners of her mouth downward. “Forget it, I’m not playing anymore.” She turned and walked away. I reflexively reached out to grab her, but her back disappeared into the crowd, my hand frozen in the air. Then I heard people laughing, as if at me, or at something else—I couldn’t tell at all.

All day long, I kept thinking about her expression at the end. After school that day, I didn’t go home with everyone else as usual, but walked at the back of the line with my head down, silently counting the bricks on the ground. “One, two, three...” My head felt swollen and painful, and my chest felt as though something was pressing down on it, making it hard to breathe. I remembered that that morning she had still been discussing with me whether we should go to her house on the weekend to do homework together. How had everything changed so suddenly? Had I acted strangely somewhere, or was I making too much of a fuss?

When I got home, I sat at my desk and stared blankly at my textbook for a long time. In my head, over and over again, was her expression from earlier, along with the looks the others had given me. At dinner, Mom asked me what was wrong, and I vaguely said it was nothing, but I couldn’t hold my chopsticks steadily, and grains of rice spilled all over the table. I quickly put down my bowl and ran back to my room, with only one thought in my mind: did she start hating me?

The next morning, when I got to school, I deliberately arrived early to the classroom, wanting to say something to Xiaoli. I wanted to say “I’m sorry,” but then I felt that she had been the one who hurt me first—why should I apologize? But if I didn’t apologize, would she never speak to me again? Just as I was struggling with this, she walked into the classroom, glanced at me casually, and said nothing. I didn’t speak either, but my head started buzzing, and I couldn’t even make out the class bell.

Today I was busy arranging the seats in the classroom to prepare for the upcoming parents’ meeting. The classroom windows were half open, and from outside came the rustling sound of wind moving through the leaves, making the room feel a little chilly. I tried hard to concentrate and lined up the desks neatly. I could smell the faint woody scent coming from the storage cabinet in the corner and the smell of chalk dust. Apart from the wind, the classroom was eerily quiet; I could even hear my own heartbeat, each beat seeming to strike heavily against my eardrums.

Then my good friend walked into the classroom. She smiled and said to me, “You’ve arranged this pretty well. Your parents will definitely like it.” Her tone was light and cheerful, but I always felt there was something else hidden beneath it. I paused my work and asked tentatively, “Do you think my parents might have any opinions?” She was clearly caught off guard by my question. “Uh, no way, they’re both pretty easygoing.” I felt a trace of unease, and my heartbeat quickened. She turned and walked away, and I watched her back as my mind filled with all sorts of things she might have been thinking. I began to reflect on my own behavior just now, wondering whether I had seemed overly nervous.

As time passed, my physical reactions became even stronger. My hands began to sweat slightly, and my stomach felt uncomfortable too. I tried taking deep breaths to calm my nerves, but it did little good. I started rehearsing all kinds of possible problems in my mind: if the parents thought the classroom setup wasn’t good enough, how should I explain it? Would I be blamed by the teacher? These thoughts surged over me like a flood, making it almost impossible to think about anything else.

After the parents’ meeting ended, I remained restless. Even after I got home, I still couldn’t shake off that sense of anxiety. All night long I kept agonizing over whether I had done enough, going back over every detail and wondering whether I had unintentionally offended any parent. This feeling continued into the next day. Even though there was no negative feedback at all, I still felt the worry in my heart would not go away. I tried to focus on other things, such as my schoolwork, but I was always quickly interrupted by those uneasy thoughts.

After a few days, although my emotions had calmed somewhat, I knew that as soon as any potential negative trigger appeared, I could once again fall into this whirlpool of excessive rumination.

The cafeteria was always so lively, with the clatter of plates and the sound of people talking all mixed together like a noisy sea. As I carried my tray to a seat, I heard a classmate sitting nearby whisper, “Why is she always so slow?” They said it very softly, but I still heard it. I wasn’t sure if they were talking about me, but I immediately felt a sharp sting in my heart. In that instant, it felt like my face had suddenly caught fire, burning as if by flames. I sat down with my head lowered, gripping my fork tightly, too afraid to look up and meet their eyes.

“What’s wrong?” a classmate suddenly asked me. “Your face is red like a tomato.” It sounded like concern, but in my mind a harsher explanation immediately sprang up: they’re all making fun of me. I hurriedly shook my head and said, “I’m fine.” My voice was so low it was almost inaudible, even drowned out by the sound of a plate crashing behind me.

My heart was pounding so fast, and it felt as if a huge stone were pressing down on my chest. I stuck my fork into the mashed potatoes on my tray, but I couldn’t swallow a bite. I kept thinking back to what I had just heard: were they talking about how slow I was? Was it because I was always dragging my feet that they were getting impatient with me? My mind was like a broken machine, endlessly replaying those scenes and possible conversations. Had they been glaring at me in secret? Was their tone deliberately sarcastic? Had I done something wrong that made me seem especially annoying?

My stomach began to ache, as if an invisible hand were squeezing it. I tried to calm myself and focus on the plate in front of me, but out of the corner of my eye I kept catching their movements. They were eating with their heads down, occasionally saying a few words, seemingly paying no attention at all to my embarrassment. Maybe they didn’t care at all why I wasn’t speaking, but I still couldn’t escape my own thoughts. I felt as though I were trapped in a glass cage, with the world outside moving on normally while I remained stuck in my own shame and fear, unable to break free.

When lunchtime ended, I rushed out of the cafeteria, feeling the need to get away from all that noise. I hid in a bathroom stall and slid down against the door, listening to the faint footsteps coming from outside. I told myself they must be out there talking about how awkward I had been. In my mind, I even began constructing a scene: they were in the hallway laughing, saying, “Did you see how she looked just now?” Even though I knew it was only my guess, it sounded so real. I covered my face with both hands, hoping to shut myself off from these thoughts, but they kept flooding in like a tide.

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t stop thinking back over every detail of the afternoon. I tried to convince myself that maybe “Why is she always so slow?” hadn’t been about me at all, maybe I had misunderstood. But it was useless—I still felt as if my head were about to explode. Later, I even started listing my own “problems”: I’m too slow, I’m too sensitive, I’m too easily awkward. I felt like a jigsaw puzzle taken apart, impossible to put back together no matter how hard I tried. Over the next few days, I always avoided sitting in the same seat, and even deliberately took a longer route to the cafeteria, hoping not to have to sit with them again.

The track beneath my feet was already covered with deep spikes marks, and the orange-red lanes looked glaringly bright under the sun. I stood at the starting line, my palms slick with sweat, my running shoes feeling so heavy they seemed impossible to lift. The noise all around made my scalp tingle and my ears ring; it felt as if everyone was waiting to see me make a fool of myself.

“Ready—” The referee’s whistle pulled my attention back. I stared at the starting line, trying hard to focus on what lay ahead, repeating to myself the form I had practiced at home: relax the knees, push off with the toes, keep breathing. But inside, it felt as if ants were gnawing at me, a dull, nagging pain.

Bang! The starting gun went off, and I instinctively drove off the ground, only to find my stride nothing like what I had imagined. My right foot stepped on the heel of my left foot, and my body lurched forward violently. A sharp pain shot through the sole of my foot. I put my hand down to steady myself, quickly got back up, and kept running, but I was already behind. One by one, my classmates passed me; their backs looked like walls moving away from me. I gritted my teeth and desperately tried to catch up, but my breathing grew short and chaotic, my throat felt scorched by fire, and my chest heaved violently.

Scattered cheers came from the bleachers, but I couldn’t tell who they were for, nor did I dare look back, let alone wonder whether those voices were mocking me. My vision gradually blurred into a haze. By the time I looked up again, the finish line was right ahead, but everyone had gotten there before me. In the end, I crossed it second to last.

I bent over, hands on my knees, gasping for breath, my legs trembling from soreness. The scrape on my knee burned, but I didn’t have the courage to look at it. Amid the laughter of some students in the stands, my ears began to buzz, and my cheeks felt as though they had been scalded. Tears welled up without my noticing, but I fought hard to keep them from falling. A classmate came over and patted my shoulder. “It’s okay. Try harder next time.” His tone sounded casual, even a little perfunctory.

“Thanks,” I replied softly, but in that moment I felt as if he were comforting a complete loser. A tide of inferiority surged through me, crushing me until I could barely breathe. I looked up and saw the referee handing the score sheet to another student, apparently confirming the results. I lowered my head and stared at a small knot in my shoelace, unable to stop blaming myself for making such a stupid mistake at the most crucial moment.

I quietly slipped away from the crowd and walked to the shade of a tree at the edge of the field. Sitting on the ground, I buried my face in my hands, and at last the tears came uncontrollably. Again and again I replayed the moment I fell, as if the projector of my mind had gotten stuck on that single second. How could I be so stupid? Everyone must be laughing at me. Cramping pain rolled through my stomach, and I even felt like I was going to vomit.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, unable to sleep, my mind endlessly churning over the events of the day. I imagined whether those classmates would be talking about me behind my back, whether they would equate my name with failure. The next day, I deliberately detoured around the sports meet results board, too afraid to look at the records posted there, and I didn’t even have the courage to greet my classmates.

The lights in the multipurpose classroom were bright yet gentle, and the floor had been polished spotless, reflecting a faint sheen. I sat in the back row, palms sweating, my knees pressed tightly against my legs under the desk. I noticed my shoelaces had come undone, but now was not the time to bend down and tie them. Up front, the screen was displaying the rules of the psychology game, and the teacher stood at the podium with a beaming smile, explaining, “Each student needs to answer one question. We’ll go one by one, and if you answer incorrectly, you’ll have to accept a random punishment.” Her tone was relaxed, but my heartbeat grew faster and faster, as if someone had clenched it tightly in their hand.

When it was my turn, my eyes swept over the question on the screen—“If there are three colors of balls, the number of red balls is twice the number of green balls, and the number of green balls equals the number of blue balls, what percentage of the total are red balls?” My head felt hot, and I couldn’t think at all, as if someone had pulled an alarm inside my brain. I struggled to save myself, quickly trying to calculate, repeating formulas over and over in my mind, but I found my fingers drumming wildly on the desk, making it impossible to concentrate.

“Come on, hurry up!” Xiao Ming in the front row turned around to urge me on, his voice clearly impatient. I froze for a moment and blurted out an answer: “One-third?” The teacher paused, frowned slightly, and said, “Not quite. The correct answer is—fifty percent.”

Laughter immediately broke out around me. Although almost everyone was only chuckling softly, those laughs felt like little hammers pounding on my eardrums. I clenched my teeth, my nails digging into my palm, eyes fixed tightly on the patterns on the desk, my cheeks so hot they seemed about to smoke. The punishment was decided quickly: I had to go onstage and perform a funny dance. My mind went blank in an instant, and all I could feel was the sweat on my back growing more and more, even the feeling of my pants sticking to the chair becoming sticky and uncomfortable.

I forced myself onto the stage, each step feeling as heavy as lead. The teacher smiled encouragingly at me and even made a cheer-up gesture. But to me, her smile had thorns, as if she were subtly mocking how stupid my answer was. The classmates below the stage stared at me without blinking, and I felt like an insect trapped in a glass jar, where even breathing was suffocating. The music started, and I mechanically swung my arms, forcing out a stiff smile. I tried to imitate the dance moves I’d seen on TV, but my clumsy motions only made me look even more ridiculous. Sure enough, the laughter started again, growing louder and louder, and I felt as if my stomach had been twisted into a knot.

After that, I lost all interest in taking part in the rest of the activities. I could only fix my gaze on my knees, replaying the scene of my dancing over and over in my head. When I left the classroom, it wasn’t until the cool breeze hit my face that my tight chest eased a little. But that night, lying in bed and staring at the ceiling, I could still hear those laughs echoing in my mind. Even when I closed my eyes, the image of myself standing onstage remained, tormenting me again and again. I even started worrying whether, when I got to school the next day, some classmates would bring it up again.

The air in the classroom felt as if something were pressing down on it. The chirping of insects outside kept seeping in through my ears in waves, making it impossible to sit still. I shrank into the back row, staring at the scratch across my desk made by a ballpoint pen, my heartbeat already starting to quicken out of control. On the blackboard, today’s suddenly added debate topic was written in chalk—“Is it reasonable to ban the shops around the school?”—the crooked handwriting seemed to be mocking me.

“Okay, let’s go group by group, and share your views one by one.” The teacher’s voice was clear and bright, bouncing around the classroom.

I counted: our group was third. There was still time. I told myself there was still time to figure out what to say.

But there wasn’t enough time at all. The group leader’s gaze swept over me, paused on my face for a second, then motioned with their chin—meaning, you.

I felt a loud scraping sound between the chair legs and the floor, as if the whole classroom were watching me stand up. The eyes around me pressed in like physical weight; my ears started to burn, and my palms were already damp with sweat.

“Uh… I think the shop can actually stay, but it should… be limited…”

The words got stuck. Right there, motionless.

A faint laugh came from the back row, and I didn’t know whether it was directed at me, but my face burned in that instant. I heard my own voice turn thin and dry: “I mean… the snacks they sell could be reduced a bit, like spicy strips and stuff…”

The teacher frowned.

That frown lasted less than a second, but I saw it clearly. They said, “Pay attention to your logic and make your point clear.”

My fingers clenched the edge of the textbook so tightly that my nails dug into the pages.
