My mind was a complete mess; every word I wanted to say kept crashing into the others, and in the end I only sped up, pouring out the rest like dumping out trash: “Anyway… I just think they shouldn’t be completely shut down.”

Then I sat down.

The clothes on my back were pressed against my skin, damp and cold. My legs felt weak, as if I had just finished running a very long distance. A classmate leaned over and said in a low voice, “You were too nervous. I couldn’t even tell what you were saying.”

They meant no harm; I knew that. But the words were like a fine needle, stabbing precisely into the place that had just started to scab over. My stomach gave a sudden jolt, and the heaviness of lunch suddenly became very real.

I began replaying the scene in my head frame by frame. What did that frown mean? Did the teacher think I had no logic at all? Was the laugh from the back really laughing at me? Had my wording made the whole group lose points?

The bell rang. The others had already rushed into the hallway, chatting and laughing as if nothing had happened. I stayed in my seat a little longer, glancing out of the corner of my eye and seeing the teacher still tidying things up on the podium. I wanted to go over and explain, or apologize, or say something—but then I thought, they probably wouldn’t even remember this detail, and going over would only make me even more embarrassed.

I did nothing. I just walked out of the classroom.

That incident clung to me like a wet cloth for the entire following week. Every time I heard someone speaking in class, I would first rehearse the worst possible outcome for myself: trembling voice, incoherent words, quiet laughter from below. Little by little, I started lowering my head before the teacher’s gaze even swept over me, and I began to feel that being invisible was a kind of safety.

I don’t know exactly what I lost after that day. I only vaguely felt that a door had quietly closed before I even had the chance to walk through it.

On Thursday afternoon, in art class, the light in the art room always seemed especially soft. The walls were covered with colorful paintings, and the air was filled with the smell of paint. Everything seemed to remind me that creativity was the driving force here. I stood in front of the worktable, staring at the gray lump of clay waiting to be shaped, my heart full of unease. I tried to mold a simple shape with my fingers, but the clay at my fingertips was cold and slippery, making me feel as if I couldn’t control it. In my ear, I heard the teacher’s voice: “Remember, every work of art is an extension of your imagination. Don’t be afraid to try.” Her words circled in my mind, making the pressure on my shoulders feel even greater. The other students all seemed deeply absorbed, their low conversations filled with enthusiasm for creating. But I felt as though my hands were bound; no matter how hard I tried, the piece in front of me always looked dull and stiff.

The atmosphere gradually grew more complicated, and the occasional chatter of my classmates only made me more nervous. “Wow, that one’s really good!” exclaimed a classmate suddenly. I couldn’t help looking up and saw the teacher admiring another student’s sculpture—a delicate little animal model, lifelike and vivid. Jealousy and shame surged through me. I quickly lowered my head, trying to hide my messy work. My heartbeat began to race, and before I knew it, my palms were sweating.

“Are you okay?” my deskmate asked softly, as if noticing my unease. I nodded hard, though inside I was thinking, “Why can’t I do it?” Yet deep down, a voice kept roaring over and over: “Everyone else is doing so well—what about me?” This feeling of being abandoned seemed innate, constantly reminding me how inadequate I was.

I struggled to suppress the urge to give up, took a deep breath, and tried again. At that moment, the teacher came over to my side and asked gently, “Do you need help?” I forced a smile and shook my head, but my mouth was so dry I couldn’t say anything. She nodded and continued on to the next student.

After class, I packed up my tools, picked up my backpack, and left. On the way home, even the rustling of the leaves by the roadside made me anxious. I kept worrying that after this lesson the teacher would think I was terrible, or would talk to other teachers behind my back about how I wasn’t trying hard enough. Small doubts rolled around in my mind like a stone lodged in my heart.

That night, I tossed and turned and couldn’t fall asleep. The scenes from art class kept replaying in my mind. I imagined the worst possible outcome, my heart pounding violently and a dull pain rising in my stomach. In the end, I decided I had to work harder and show a better piece in next week’s art class, so that I could finally feel at ease.

A few days later, I started practicing at home, trying as much as possible to improve my skills. Although the anxiety inside me still remained, I hoped that through effort, I could show everyone a better version of myself in the next art class.

Sunlight streamed through the classroom windows onto the floor, and the art supplies were neatly arranged on the tables. The air was filled with the smell of earth and paint, feeling like the standard setup for every art class. The teacher came over to my desk, preparing to show my clay piece: a carefully sculpted little cat. My heartbeat began to race, and I felt a little nervous. After all, this was a piece I had spent weeks making, full of hope that I would get some recognition.

“This little cat is absolutely adorable,” the teacher said, her voice echoing through the classroom. But just as she reached for it, her fingers slipped, and the cat fell to the floor, breaking into several pieces. I froze, feeling as if I had been struck hard in the heart, my face heating up rapidly, as though it were burning. Tears instantly welled up, and I struggled to keep them from falling. “Oh, I’m so sorry!” the teacher exclaimed, bending down to pick up the fragments, but all I could see was dust and broken clay on the floor. A voice in my head kept repeating, “They’re going to think I’m stupid and that I made something terrible.” I didn’t know how to react, and could only stand there, feeling as though the entire classroom’s eyes were on me. I wanted to escape this disaster scene that had become mine.

The teacher tried to comfort me, gently patting my shoulder. “We can make a new one. Would you like that?” she asked softly. I couldn’t answer, so I just nodded, trying not to look like I was about to cry. My body tensed up, my hands began to sweat, and it felt as if something were stuck in my throat. When I got home that afternoon, everything felt bleak. That night, I lay in bed, replaying the scene of the clay cat breaking over and over in my mind, unable to shake it even in my dreams. Days later, whenever I thought about it, a strong wave of shame and sadness still rose in my heart, as if it were a wound that could never fully heal.

In the hallway, the long fluorescent lights stretched my shadow out for a long way. I could hear the low conversations and laughter of my classmates coming from the classroom not far behind me. A strange sense of tension and unease filled my heart, like a tangled mess of threads twisted together. I slowly paced back and forth on that familiar floor, the soles of my shoes brushing lightly against the ground with a faint hissing sound.

The group activity today made me feel extremely anxious. I knew that in a little while I would have to go up and present what I had prepared. It wasn’t complicated, but I always worried that I would make mistakes. In my mind, I seemed to have already begun rehearsing possible scenes of failure. I thought, if I were to stand at the podium later, would my voice tremble? And how would I handle the embarrassment if I forgot my lines halfway through?

My heartbeat thudded against my chest so fast that it nearly left me breathless. My palms began to grow slightly sweaty, and I could even feel a faint trembling in my fingertips. Just then, a classmate passed by at the end of the hallway, saw me standing there, and asked with a smile, “Are you okay? Are you ready?”

I forced out a smile, nodded, and kept repeating, “Mm, I’m fine.” Yet inside I was terribly uneasy, afraid that the smile would fail to hide the panic in my heart. During that brief exchange, I kept reading the microexpressions on his face, trying to catch any hint of doubt or displeasure.

At last, it was time for the activity to begin, and everyone filed into the classroom one after another. As the footsteps of the other students drew closer, I felt my stomach churn violently, and that familiar shame quietly welled up inside me. It was always like this—why could I never pull myself out of this kind of anxiety?

After the activity ended, I walked home alone, passing through the sky painted with the colors of sunset, my mood still heavy. From time to time, I could hear my classmates cheering in my ears, but I still couldn’t feel myself becoming part of it. When I got home, I lay on my bed, over and over replaying every detail from the classroom, magnifying every tiny mistake, and anxiously worrying about how my classmates would look at me tomorrow.

After a few days, that fear finally began to fade, replaced by a kind of helpless fatigue. I knew this cycle of emotions would eventually happen again, but there was nothing I could do. I could only hope that when it came next time, I would be strong enough to face it.

The laboratory was filled with an atmosphere of anticipation and tension. Sunlight fell across the tables, casting a faint shimmer, and the students were all focused on their own experiments. I nervously held a test tube, my palms already slightly sweaty, while the lab instructor explained the procedures at the front. I listened carefully, but panic began to creep in: What if I made a mistake? Would he scold me? My heart started racing, and the sounds around me gradually became blurred.

The student in front had already started the experiment, and I stared aimlessly at their actions, hoping to learn something from them. Suddenly, a classmate turned around and asked me, “Do you need help?” I immediately felt my face grow hot and quickly shook my head. “No, I can do it.” But a trace of unease flashed through my mind: Did he think I couldn’t do this experiment?

Then it was my turn to begin. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself. The sweat on my palms made the test tube feel slippery in my grip. I carefully poured the solution into the beaker, but because I was so nervous, my hand shook and some of the solution spilled out. The liquid in the beaker began to bubble, and I instantly sensed something was wrong. My heart sped up, and my stomach churned. “It’s over, my experiment has completely failed. Will they laugh at me?” For a moment, I felt as though everyone was staring at me, and the whole laboratory’s gaze was like sharp arrows aimed at me.

The teacher came over to check what had happened, and I closed my eyes, waiting to be criticized. Unexpectedly, the teacher did not blame me, but patiently demonstrated the correct method instead. I felt a warm shock, and my body gradually relaxed. The teacher patted my shoulder encouragingly and said, “It’s okay, just be a little more careful.” This made me focus on the experiment again.

After school, I was still uneasy, always feeling as if my classmates were talking about me behind my back. When I got home, I sat down at my desk in low spirits, and it seemed as if I could still hear my classmates’ muffled laughter. That night, I kept replaying the moment over and over in my mind—the instant the solution spilled. I felt ashamed of my mistake and feared it would happen again in the future.

However, a few days later, when my classmates were discussing other activities together, I realized they had not cared about what happened that day. Some even took the initiative to invite me to work with them on a new science project. This gradually helped me put down the burden in my heart and begin to believe that making mistakes while trying new things is normal.

Rain beat against the classroom windows. In the practice room of the music classroom, piano notes rose and fell all around me as I sat before the piano. The air was filled with the scent of the instrument’s wooden body, and with every strike of the keys, it felt as though I were pounding against my own heartbeat. I began to play a piece, but one chord in my left hand was wrong, and the notes jolted out harshly. “Could you try again?” my teacher said softly behind me. A chill ran down my back, as if a cold wind had passed through. I struggled to steady my anxiety and played that passage again. However, my fingers had grown stiff from tension, and I made the mistake again. I could hear my own heartbeat, a drumbeat born of nerves, and a sticky layer of sweat broke out over my body. My teacher’s sigh felt like a thin needle stabbing into my heart. In that instant, I felt that all my mistakes were beyond repair, that I would surely be seen as utterly untalented, with no chance left to earn my teacher’s approval. “Are you all right?” my teacher asked, seeming to notice my unease. I nodded, trying to smile, but my mouth froze. TA gently patted my shoulder, and for some reason that made me feel even more ashamed. One scene after another of my past mistakes began to surface in my mind, as if mocking me. I stole a glance outside the window; the rain showed no sign of letting up, and the whole world lay under a gray pall, as if reflecting my inner state. When class ended, the teacher handed me a score for the next practice session. I took it mechanically, trying hard not to let my hand tremble. As I left the classroom, raindrops struck the umbrella with a clear, cold sound. I felt powerless, as though the world had abandoned me in this endless rain. That night, I sat collapsed at the edge of my bed, replaying every detail of the lesson over and over. Every note seemed like a jagged mark etched into my mind. Silently, I told myself, “If I’m not good enough, maybe sooner or later everyone will find out that I’m actually insignificant.” I resolved to practice twice as hard so that at least next time, in front of my teacher, I wouldn’t disappoint him again. A few days later, the rain stopped, and I walked into the classroom once more. Sunlight poured through the glass windows, and though unease still remained in my heart, what filled me more was anticipation—of whether I could regain my confidence under this light.

The lighting in the chemistry lab was somewhat harsh. I sat by the window, where sunlight streamed through and fell onto my lab table, blindingly bright. The table was covered with test tubes and bottles of various colors, and a faint smell of disinfectant lingered in the air. The teacher was carefully drawing out the experiment steps on the blackboard, and I tried hard to memorize the key points, silently praying that I wouldn’t make any mistakes.

“This experiment requires everyone to handle things carefully, especially when it comes to the proportions of the reagents,” the teacher said, turning around to emphasize the point.

I nodded, but my heartbeat inexplicably sped up. I began preparing the materials, repeating to myself over and over not to mess up. Yet when I picked up the test tube, my hand began to tremble slightly on its own. Just as I was adding the reagent, my hand jerked, and I poured in too much liquid. Instantly, a pungent smell rushed toward me.

“Ah!” I cried out softly, quickly stepping back as my heart pounded even faster. My face burned red in an instant, and fine beads of sweat began to form on my forehead. The other students all stopped and looked at me.

“What happened?” The teacher hurried over to my side. I lowered my head, too embarrassed to meet her eyes.

“I accidentally added a little too much reagent. Sorry,” I managed to say, my voice trembling slightly.

The teacher checked my experiment and, after putting the situation right, patted my shoulder. “It’s okay. Just be more careful next time.” She said it lightly, but the whispers from the students around me were far less kind. I could feel the heat on my face keep rising, as if I were being watched in some humiliating spectacle, and shame flooded my heart.

When I returned to my seat, my hands were still shaking slightly. For the rest of the class, I didn’t even dare to look up. I could only try to force my attention back to the textbook, yet my thoughts kept drifting back to what had just happened. When class ended, I was the last one to leave the lab, deliberately lingering in hopes of avoiding the other students’ stares.

That night, I lay in bed still unable to calm down. The scene from the afternoon kept replaying in my mind, and I kept blaming myself for being so stupid. Although I knew anyone could make a mistake, the feeling of being watched by everyone, along with the shame that followed, stayed with me for a long time and would not let go.

In the days that followed, I felt cautious in every class, afraid of making another mistake. It was as if every move I made was magnified, and any small slip-up could become fodder for other people’s idle gossip. Even though no one mentioned the incident again, my nerves remained taut, and I couldn’t fully relax even on the weekend.

The library lights were a little dim, and the air was filled with a faint smell of paper and books. I was sitting at a table with a few classmates, each of us with a book spread open in front of us. My book was a novel I had just borrowed recently; the cover showed a lonely little girl, which I found very appealing. Everyone was discussing their reading list, and I casually recommended this novel. “I think The City of Glimmer is quite interesting. It’s about a very lonely girl who tries to find a space of her own,” I said. My voice was absorbed by the surrounding silence of the library, making it stand out all the more.

The classmate sitting to my left rolled his eyes, his expression mixing indifference and contempt. “A lonely little girl? That sounds so cliché,” he said, with a hint of mockery in his tone. I froze for a moment, feeling my face grow warm and my heartbeat suddenly quicken. I forced a smile. “Maybe you think it’s cliché, but I think this kind of story has a lot of depth.”

Another classmate chimed in. “I just read a mystery novel, and it felt much more interesting than this kind of emotional story.” Her tone was casual, but to me every word seemed to imply that my recommendation was too shallow. I sat there, unconsciously rubbing my fingers against the pages, and noticed that my fingertips were a little damp. I started to wonder whether my choice really was too childish, or whether everyone actually thought I was a strange person who always liked odd things.

These thoughts snowballed in my head, and I even began to regret coming to the library today to discuss this topic with them. I quickly ran through some scenarios in my mind: would they laugh at me behind my back? Should I leave this table sooner? “I think everyone has different preferences,” I said, trying to sound as steady as possible. “This kind of story might be more suited to people who like subtle emotions.” My heart was still racing, and I even felt as if it were syncing with the library clock.

The atmosphere never really became tense, but I kept feeling an invisible pressure. I began to avoid looking them in the eye and shifted my gaze to the pile of books on the table. My stomach felt slightly tight, as if a small stone were stuck inside it. Although we later talked a little more about other books, my attention remained fixed on that dismissive remark. When I left the library, my book was still tucked under my arm, but it seemed to weigh several times more all of a sudden, and I felt stiff all over.

That night, I opened The City of Glimmer and tried to keep reading, but the words on the page seemed to blur. I kept thinking about their expressions and tone, repeatedly wondering whether they had been subtly making fun of me. In the end, I had to put the book down and lie on my bed staring at the ceiling, feeling an indescribable unease. It took me two days before I gradually pushed those feelings out of my head and started to find my reading rhythm again.

The classroom lights were a little harsh. I sat in the back row, staring at the notebook in front of me. It was filled with drafts I had prepared for my speech. The wind outside and my classmates’ conversations mingled together, making me even more restless. The teacher had said the class speech contest would be in a few days, and I should use this opportunity to do well, but I couldn’t stop imagining all the ways things might go wrong.

I murmured the speech to myself, trying to imitate the tone I should use in a formal presentation, but it still felt like something was off. A classmate beside me leaned over and glanced at my script, then said softly, “You wrote it well, but the opening could be a little more engaging.” His words kept echoing in my mind. My heartbeat began to quicken, and my palms grew sweaty.

“Really? How should I change it?” I asked eagerly, almost pleading. To put me at ease, he began offering suggestions, but there was always a voice in my head saying: What if I make a mistake then? What if everyone thinks I’m terrible?

On the way home, I kept replaying my classmate’s words over and over, even simulating the speech day scenario repeatedly in my mind. Every time I imagined myself standing at the podium, my stomach would churn. Late at night, the air in my room was so quiet that I could only hear my own heartbeat. I lay in bed, gripping the blanket tightly, trying hard not to think about those possibilities anymore.

The next day, I ran into several classmates at the school gate. They were discussing their own speeches. I stood nearby, forcing a smile, trying to seem less nervous. “How’s your preparation going?” one classmate asked me.

“Pretty good, I guess. I’m just a little worried I’ll mess it up,” I replied, trying to downplay the anxiety in my heart.

“No way, you’re so talented.” Their reassurance made me feel slightly more at ease, but I knew it was only temporary comfort.

A few days later, it was my turn to give the speech. From the podium, I looked out at the classmates and teachers below; every eye was fixed on me. My palms were slightly sweaty, and I tried to steady my breathing. I began speaking, trying my best to follow the way I had practiced, but my voice trembled a little.

After the contest, I kept looking for feedback from my teachers and classmates. Even when they said I did well, I kept wondering whether they were saying that just so I wouldn’t feel hurt. That weekend after the competition, I couldn’t stop thinking about every detail of the speech. Doubt and unease surged over me like a tide, and in the end I still couldn’t be sure how well I had done. This uncertainty left me with even more complicated feelings about such activities next time.

In the last ten minutes of math class, the teacher suddenly announced a challenge problem and said that whoever could solve it correctly the fastest would earn extra points for the group. Although I was anxious, I still wanted to try so I wouldn’t hold everyone back. The math problem on the blackboard didn’t seem too difficult. I tried hard to remember the formulas the teacher had taught before and sort out my thoughts. The classroom was so quiet that only the sound of chalk tapping on the blackboard could be heard.

But my thoughts began to drift uncontrollably: What if I got it wrong? Would my classmates think I was stupid? If I couldn’t solve it, what would the teacher think of me? My heartbeat started to speed up, and my palms grew sweaty. I glanced around and noticed a few classmates whispering; I wasn’t sure whether they were talking about me. Some of them kept turning back to look at me, with faint smiles on their faces, as if waiting to see me make a fool of myself. I bit my lip and tried hard to calm myself down.

The teacher called my name, and I stood up stiffly, taking the chalk and walking toward the blackboard. Suddenly I heard a snicker in the classroom. I turned and looked; it was the two boys in the back row laughing, with a hint of mockery in their expressions. That made me even more uneasy. Sweat was running down my forehead, sticky and uncomfortable. I forced myself to focus and looked over the problem on the blackboard once again.

My hand trembled slightly, and the words I wrote on the blackboard were crooked and messy. I tried to solve the problem using the formulas in my head, but my mind was a tangled mess. Just after I wrote one step, I heard a low voice behind me: “Doesn’t he really not know this problem?” In an instant, I felt a rush of heat surge to my face, and my heart was beating so fast it felt like it would burst out of my chest.

“Come on, hurry up, don’t drag it out,” the teacher’s voice suddenly rang out. I felt at a loss and became even more panicked. Time seemed to slow down infinitely. In those brief minutes, I could barely hear anything except my own heartbeat and the roaring heat in my ears. In the end, I forced myself to write down an answer and turned to look at the teacher.

“Wrong.” The teacher shook her head, her tone carrying a trace of disappointment. Then she turned and pointed to another student. “You try.” I stood rigidly at the blackboard and heard the snickering behind me grow more obvious. I could even hear a few classmates whispering, “How could he get it so wrong?”

After returning to my seat, I wanted nothing more than to crawl into my desk. The backs of those two boys made me feel suffocated, as if they might turn around at any moment and keep laughing at me. I lowered my head and pretended to read the textbook carefully, but my eyes were blurry and I couldn’t make out a single word. Over and over, I replayed the steps from earlier, trying to find my mistake, but the more I thought about it, the more stupid and useless I felt. My stomach began to clench, as if gripped by a cold hand.

After school, I trudged home, my mind still replaying that conversation again and again: “Doesn’t he really not know this?” Those words felt like a thorn stuck in my heart. As I walked, I muttered to myself, “I should never have stood up.” The wind on the road messed up my hair, but even the cold breeze couldn’t calm my frustration.

That night, I hardly slept at all. My mind was filled with the classmates’ laughter and the teacher’s disappointed expression. The tension felt like a net that had me tightly trapped, making even breathing seem difficult. I even began to dread the next math class, afraid of being called to the blackboard again. The next day, I spent the entire morning redoing that problem five times, but I still couldn’t calm my heart.

After school that afternoon, as the sky gradually darkened, I followed a group of classmates into the school planetarium. The lights inside were dim, creating a mysterious atmosphere. A map of the starry sky was projected onto the walls, and the stars seemed to twinkle. I sat in the back row, trying to find a trace of calm in the vast universe. “Everyone, please focus. We’re about to begin the observation,” the teacher’s voice sounded especially clear in the steady darkness. I stared at the huge screen, trying my best to understand the constellations and the paths of the planets that the teacher was explaining. Yet inside, a sense of unease kept rising.

My heartbeat began to quicken; a fine sweat appeared on my forehead, and my palms grew damp. I told myself this was just a routine observation activity, nothing to be nervous about. But my mind kept conjuring catastrophic scenes: What if I suddenly fainted here? What if my question was mocked by the teacher in front of everyone? I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself, but anxiety still churned in my chest.

The classmates around me started whispering to one another, discussing the names of the constellations. “Do you know Lyra?” a classmate beside me asked. “Yeah, I know it,” I answered reflexively, though I wasn’t very familiar with the topic. Afraid that my lack of knowledge would be exposed, I forced myself to stay calm, while my mind kept searching for ways to cope. Even my own words sounded somewhat muddled, and I couldn’t help but feel a trace of shame.

After the observation ended, I walked out of the planetarium, and night had already slowly spread across the campus. The cold crept in, and I instinctively pulled my coat tighter around me. On the way home, I kept replaying my performance during the observation in my mind, filled with worry and doubt. Were those whispers from my classmates talking about me? Why did I always feel I was not good enough in front of people my own age?

That night, lying in bed, I was still thinking about those questions. Anxiety seemed to cling to my body, impossible to shake off. “Why am I always so nervous?” My mind was full of self-doubt. Despite repeatedly trying to comfort myself, those uneasy scenes still filled my thoughts, replaying again and again. I hoped that one day I would no longer feel ashamed or uneasy in situations like this, but for now, that feeling still would not go away.

On a midsummer afternoon, sunlight filtered through the leaves and dappled the path in the middle school campus botanical garden. I followed my classmates to take part in a plant observation activity organized by the school. A gentle breeze brushed my face, carrying the fresh scent of grass and the dampness of the soil. I could hear my classmates talking and laughing, yet I felt an unexplainable tension.

“What do you think is special about this leaf?” the teacher asked. I tried hard to examine the leaf in my hand, searching for what made it special. But no matter how closely I looked, it was just an ordinary green leaf.

“Well, I think it has some unusual patterns on it,” I answered softly, my voice filled with uncertainty.

A thought flashed through my mind: if I got it wrong, would the teacher be dissatisfied? Would the other students make fun of me? I began to imagine myself looking utterly embarrassed amid everyone’s ridicule, my heart racing and my palms sweating.

My inner monologue churned restlessly: “Why am I always like this? Why can’t I just relax?” This was a long-standing unease I couldn’t shake. I felt as if my stomach were tied in knots, and my steps grew heavy.

After the activity ended, I dragged myself home in a heavy mood. That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the scenes from the botanical garden in my mind. I repeatedly analyzed the teacher’s expression, trying to confirm whether he really had been dissatisfied with my answer. I began to blame myself, feeling that I was too sensitive and that I had even ruined such a simple activity.

In the days that followed, that mood would not let go. Whenever I talked with my classmates, I would unconsciously relive that feeling of being scrutinized in the botanical garden. I became even more sensitive and even began to doubt whether I was not good enough or not smart enough. Gradually, this unease became part of my life, leaving me often anxious and flustered even in simple everyday social interactions.

In the classroom, the fluorescent lights hummed faintly, and the air was filled with the smell of chalk dust. We were discussing poster designs in groups, and I was in charge of the layout, but I always felt my designs weren’t good enough. My palms were a little sweaty, and my hand shook badly as I held the marker. I tentatively asked, “Do you think this layout is okay?” A classmate sitting to my left said impatiently, “Why do you look so unconfident? Don’t you think this design is a mess?” My brain seemed to short-circuit instantly; my face flushed, and my voice grew smaller: “Um, I can change it… you can make whatever changes you want.”

Several classmates beside me exchanged a glance and let out a quiet laugh. One of them said softly, “They’re always like this—always asking questions.” Those words felt like a needle stabbing into my head. I lowered my head and stared at my draft paper, my eyes beginning to sting, a buzzing filling my ears, not knowing how to respond next. I tried to look up and smile, but the corners of my mouth twitched a few times and failed. The person who had spoken added, “Can’t you really be a little more confident? It’s hard to work with you when you’re always like this.” That “always like this” completely broke me. My whole body went rigid, and many scenes flashed quickly through my mind: being disliked by the classmate sitting next to me in elementary school because I didn’t like speaking up, and last year, being laughed at by the whole class during a class meeting because I was so nervous I stuttered. To me, those memories felt like a nightmare happening all over again.

My stomach started to cramp, and the pain made me want to leave, but my legs felt nailed to the floor and couldn’t move. One voice inside me was shouting, “They don’t want to work with you at all! You must be such a failure!” While another part of me was desperately suppressing those emotions: “Don’t cry, don’t let them know you’re upset, or they’ll look down on you even more.” I thought about pretending to stay calm, so I forced out, “I’ll redo it. I won’t hold everyone up.” But my hand was already shaking so badly that I couldn’t continue drawing the lines. I could feel sweat sliding down my back, and my neck was damp and sticky too.

When the bell rang, I felt a wave of relief as I grabbed the poster and ran out, but the sound of their mocking voices kept echoing in my ears. It left me unable to calm down. That night, I lay in bed turning over and over, replaying the classmate’s expression and tone in my head again and again. I thought of countless ways I could have answered them, but all of them made me feel like I wouldn’t be able to express myself properly and might only make them laugh harder. A few days later, I started avoiding taking the initiative to talk to my group members. Every time I saw them, my heart would race and I’d freeze up like I’d been shocked.

Since that incident, whenever I have to work with others, I’m afraid I’ll hold everyone back or be disliked. I’ve gotten used to rejecting my own ideas in advance, just so no one can point out my mistakes. It’s like I’ve built a protective wall around myself, but inside that wall it has become even darker, leaving me constantly trapped in self-doubt and isolation.

Our math teacher stood at the front of the classroom and announced that we would be having group discussions today, the kind of activity that always makes me nervous. I was sitting by the window; the playground outside looked a little dim, and the sky seemed like it was about to rain. The teacher’s tone was calm, but I felt as if my ears were picking up some invisible pressure. I lowered my head and flipped through the textbook, not knowing how to deal with the groups that were about to be formed. The group list was announced soon after, and I was assigned to work with several classmates I wasn’t usually familiar with. My heartbeat began to quicken, and my fingers unconsciously twisted at my sleeve, while a faint, twisting pain rose in my stomach.

We gathered around a small table in a corner of the classroom and began discussing the problem. They put forward a few initial ideas, and some additional thoughts flashed through my mind, but the words got stuck in my throat. I worried that these ideas were too “stupid” and that I would be laughed at. “What if they think I’m dumb?” I opened my mouth several times and then closed it again. A boy glanced at me, his brows knitting slightly, and said, “Why aren’t you speaking? If you have an opinion, just say it.” His tone sounded a little blunt, but my mind immediately started racing: “Is he blaming me? Does he think I’m lazy or useless?” My face grew hot in an instant, my breathing became rapid, and my palms started to sweat.

To hide my unease, I forced myself to say, “I think your plan is a bit too complicated and might not be very easy to carry out.” My voice was very low, almost inaudible. “What do you mean, complicated? What exactly are you trying to say?” another girl asked impatiently. I tried hard to squeeze out a smile, but perhaps it only looked awkward to them. I started blaming myself again: “Did I say something wrong? Did I upset them?” My stomach pain worsened, and I felt my body stiffen like a stone.

That discussion ended quickly, but I felt as if I had been through a war. Over the next few classes, I kept replaying the expressions on their faces and the tones of their voices, repeatedly analyzing whether I had acted too foolishly. That night, lying in bed, my mind kept replaying the boy’s furrowed brow and the girl’s slightly irritated response. I even began imagining whether things would have been better if I had been put in another group. That thought felt like an invisible burden pressing on my chest, making it hard to fall asleep. The next day, although the group members showed no signs of dissatisfaction, I still carefully avoided interacting with them too much, afraid of saying something wrong again.

I stared at the blank sheet of paper on the table, and my palms started to sweat. The teacher had asked a few of us to design a poster together, and we needed to present it in half an hour. I suggested drawing a large title in the center with two smaller illustrations on the sides, so it would look more layered. But the teammate sitting across from me frowned. “Wouldn’t that be too ordinary? Every group does that. We need something more creative.”

My mind suddenly went completely blank, and the sounds around me seemed to stretch out. I tried hard to look up at the others, and they all seemed to be nodding in agreement. “Maybe she’s right,” I heard myself mutter softly. “Then do you have any better ideas?”

A boy immediately jumped in. “I think we could make it look like a newspaper front page. That would catch people’s attention.”

“Oh, that’s awesome!” the girl across from me added. “We could also use that coffee-colored background paper and make it look retro!”

The more they talked, the more excited they became, and their voices gradually drowned out the sound of my own heartbeat. My face began to burn, and a strong wave of shame rose in my throat. I felt like everyone’s eyes were on me, even though they weren’t. I forced a smile to cover my awkwardness. “Uh, then you decide.”

For the next ten minutes, I hardly spoke at all. I just listened mechanically as they talked. But my attention wasn’t on their conversation at all—it kept replaying what had just happened in my head. Was I too ordinary? Was my idea really that boring? Why couldn’t I come up with something better? Did everyone think I was useless?

I only realized how hard I had been gripping the pencil when it snapped in my hand. I quietly hid the broken pencil in the drawer, afraid others would see how embarrassed I was. At the same time, sweat soaked my back, and my head felt a little swollen.

Finally, it was time for the presentation. Our group went up to the front, and a few people stood there speaking confidently, while I stood off to the side, arms tightly crossed over my chest, forcing myself to smile. A few classmates in the audience were whispering, and I instinctively felt they were making fun of me. In my line of sight, the teacher had also frowned slightly. Was she disappointed in my performance?

After the presentation, the teacher came over and said briefly, “You have a good idea, but your teamwork could be better.” When I heard that, my heart skipped a beat. Was that a hint that I hadn’t cooperated well? Was she blaming me for not contributing more?

When I got home, I went straight into my room and quickly shut the door, locking it. My mind kept replaying every conversation and every detail from the day like a movie. I even imagined my classmates talking about me after school: “Why is she so ordinary? She barely has any presence.” Then I bit my lip hard, and a self-blaming, nauseating feeling welled up inside me. Sitting at my desk, I scribbled and drew on paper, trying to design something better than a “newspaper front page,” but no matter how I drew, I still felt like I was just a complete failure.

Sunlight slanted in through the window, bathing half the desk in a warm yellow glow. I sat in the chair, with a pile of old photo albums spread open on the desk, along with a few scattered photos. I gently turned them with my fingers, and the paper gave off a faint rustling sound. Some of the photos along the edge had curled up, and when I touched them, I could feel the roughness of their corners. Occasionally, the back of a photo would have a bit of dust on it, and I would lightly flick it away. The dust drifted through the shaft of sunlight, like tiny golden particles floating in the air.

Some of the photos showed familiar scenes. I saw one of myself as a child playing on a slide in the park, wearing a little red jacket, smiling brightly. I remembered that moment was on a spring weekend, with Mom standing nearby holding a camera, urging me to pose. I turned to another photo, one showing me and several cousins gathered around a birthday cake. The candles on that cake were burning brightly that day, and one of my younger cousins was secretly dipping a finger into the frosting, while I stood nearby staring at him. The photo had clearly captured that instant of interaction between us.

“What are you looking at?” Mom’s voice came from the doorway. I turned around and saw her carrying a plate of freshly cut fruit. “Just these old photos. I wanted to see what I was like as a kid,” I replied. “Ah, these photos are still here. For a while I thought they were lost.” She smiled and set the fruit plate on the desk. “It’s nice to go through them at a time like this, isn’t it? No need to rush—just take your time.” She patted my shoulder, then walked off to another room. I picked up a slice of apple and bit into it, my mouth filling with a sweet, crisp taste.

I kept looking through them. One photo of a family dinner made me pause. In the picture were many faces, some familiar and some strange. Everyone was gathered around a large round table, covered with dishes, and the whole scene felt especially lively. There was no sound in the photo, but I seemed to hear the laughter and the clinking of bowls and chopsticks, and could even catch a vague smell of the food. I tried to recall in my mind what we had eaten that day, but I couldn’t remember at all.

After finishing the entire album, I put the photos back in order, returned them to their original place, and then slid them into the corner of the bookcase. When I stood up, my legs were a little stiff from staying in the same position for so long, so I stretched, hearing a soft crack from my joints. The sunlight was still warm, and I couldn’t help glancing out the window again. On the street, pedestrians passed by from time to time, and the shadows on the lawn swayed gently with the breeze. I felt a kind of ordinary quiet, as if the whole afternoon could pass like this, plain and calm.

By the next day, I was no longer deliberately thinking about the photos I had gone through, but the subtle warmth they had brought still seemed to linger a little, leaving me with not much resistance as I faced a full day of schoolwork. Even though it was just an ordinary afternoon, I still felt that it was somehow a little special.

The sunlight on the lawn was bright and warm, golden rays filtering through the leaves and casting mottled shadows. I sat on the grass, surrounded by the laughter and teasing of my classmates and the occasional breeze, the tips of the grass gently brushing my fingers. That day we had a group activity, and the teacher wanted us to do an impromptu performance within our groups. Hearing that, my heart instantly sped up, and it felt as if every sound around me was amplified. Each breath I slowly exhaled was tinged with tension. “Come on, everyone line up and get ready to begin!” the teacher’s voice rang out, interrupting my thoughts. A classmate beside me nudged me with his arm. “Are you okay? You look a little nervous.” His concern made me even more uneasy. I forced a smile, but inside I couldn’t help rehearsing the worst possible outcome. Facing everyone, what was I supposed to do? What if I made a mistake...

As the line slowly moved forward, I felt my palms begin to sweat, and my stomach seemed to churn. When it was finally my turn, I stood up, feeling my legs tremble slightly. The lawn was soft and uneven, as if reminding me I might fall. I tried hard not to think about those negative images. “I can do it, I can do it.” But just as the teacher waved a hand and the signal to begin sounded, my mind went completely blank.

“Ah!” I stumbled by accident and nearly fell. Soft laughter rose around me, and my face burned red-hot. I quickly steadied myself and tried to find words to save the situation. “Sorry, I...” Before I could finish, my voice caught in my throat, and I was so embarrassed I didn’t know how to go on.

That brief performance seemed to stretch on endlessly. I could feel my heartbeat pounding so hard it seemed about to burst my eardrums. When it was finally over, as I walked back to the line, my legs felt as heavy as lead. Facing my classmates’ glancing looks, I kept my head down as much as I could, silently repeating all kinds of comforting words to myself.

That night, the whole thing kept replaying in my mind, like a rumination that simply wouldn’t stop. Each recollection came with a stab of pain in my heart. “Why am I like this? How embarrassing.” Lying in bed, I tried to think about how I could improve next time, even though my heart was filled with fear of the next time.

Over the next few days, I still felt uneasy, always worrying whether my classmates would tease me about it. During casual chats between classes, whenever I heard their laughter, I couldn’t help wondering whether they were talking about me. That feeling of unease lingered like a shadow, impossible to shake off.

Outside the classroom window, the sky grew dark and overcast, and distant thunder rumbled on and off. There was a stifling dampness in the air. I sat by the window, one hand gripping my textbook tightly, the other continually scraping my fingernails along the edge of the desk. I knew I was being questioned—the teacher had just called my name, and all eyes were on me. I cleared my throat, my heart pounding like a drum, trying to force out a complete sentence, but my voice was so soft I could barely hear it myself. A boy in the front row turned around and chuckled under his breath, and the girl beside him covered her mouth and snickered. In an instant, I felt my face flush hot, as if I had become transparent, mocked and scrutinized by everyone.

The teacher frowned, then after a brief pause said in a somewhat impatient tone, “Who can hear you when you speak so softly? Speak up!” Her words stabbed into my skin like needles, and my body instinctively tensed. I tried to answer again, my lips trembling with nervousness, but my voice was still not loud enough. My ears began to burn, sweat slowly trickled down the back of my neck, and my stomach felt as if it had been clenched in a fist; the pain made it almost impossible to concentrate. I lowered my head and stared fixedly at the desk, not even daring to look at the teacher’s face again.

“This is really troublesome!” The teacher turned to the other students and continued asking questions. I felt like a scrap of waste paper thrown into a corner, my fingers picking at the wood grain beneath the desk, my nails nearly digging in. The teacher’s words kept replaying in my mind, even with the contempt, displeasure, and disgust I imagined in her tone. Over and over, my chest felt crushed under a heavy stone, and even breathing became difficult. This shame and anger intertwined like a pot of boiling water, bubbles rising one after another, impossible to stop. I kept telling myself, “They must think I’m useless. The teacher thinks so too. I’ll never be liked.” Another laugh came from the back row, and I couldn’t help thinking: it must be directed at me.

When the bell rang for class to end, I was almost the first one out of the classroom. Outside in the hallway, the damp wind hit my face, yet I felt my breathing grow even heavier. I leaned against the wall, gripping my phone tighter and tighter until my knuckles ached faintly. Scenes from the past flashed before my eyes—being criticized, being laughed at, speaking too softly, expressing myself poorly—like a huge whirlpool pulling me downward. I even began blaming myself: Why can’t I be a little braver? Why do I always mess things up? Is there something wrong with me? This relentless self-questioning nearly drove me out of control.

That night, I lay in bed unable to sleep until very late. Every time I closed my eyes, the scene from class kept replaying like a movie. I listened to my own heartbeat, growing faster and faster, my chest tightening more and more, as if I were trapped inside a space that kept shrinking. The next morning, my stomach was still faintly aching. When I ate breakfast, even the bread tasted bitter; with every swallow, it felt as though a lump of cotton were blocking my throat. When I got back to school, I began deliberately avoiding the teacher’s gaze, and even chatting with classmates became more cautious, afraid of being laughed at or having yesterday brought up again.

After school, two friends and I decided to go sit in the park. There weren’t many people there, and the winter sunlight filtered through the thin clouds, falling on us with a faint warmth. We found a bench and sat down, with a rustling thicket beside us. The friends talked about things at school, and I chimed in from time to time, feeling fairly good.

“I heard the math competition is about to start again,” one of them said. “Have you signed up?”

“No, I’m terrible at math,” I replied with a smile, feeling a little self-deprecating.

“You should still give it a try. You never know, maybe you can do it,” the other friend encouraged me.

Hearing that, I suddenly felt a bit uneasy. Even though he meant well, I kept feeling as if he was implying that I wasn’t good at studying. My heart began to race, my palms grew slightly sweaty, and I tried hard to calm myself down.

“Uh, I think I’ll pass,” I tried to answer lightly, though my voice was trembling a little.

He went on, “Actually, you could try getting some tutoring. Maybe you’d catch up.”

That sentence instantly sent me into anxiety. Did he think I was hopelessly bad? Was I always holding everyone back? A string of questions started flashing through my mind, and I felt a knot of pain in my stomach.

“You don’t need to keep reminding me. I know I’m bad!” I suddenly raised my voice, my tone impulsive.

My friends looked a little surprised. They hadn’t expected me to react like that. I immediately realized I had overreacted, afraid they would be angry or stop liking me.

An awkward silence filled the air, and even the rustling of the shrubs seemed to stop. I lowered my head, thinking about how to make up for the situation.

“Sorry, I’m fine. I’ve just been a little stressed lately,” I forced out a smile, trying to ease the tension.

They looked at each other and then laughed a little, and the atmosphere finally relaxed somewhat. Although my friends didn’t seem to take it to heart, I still felt uneasy, with a voice in my head continually blaming me.

That night, after I got home, I lay in bed, replaying the afternoon’s conversation over and over. The feeling lingered, and I began to wonder whether I was being too sensitive. It took several days before I slowly stopped thinking about it, but that uneasiness still bothered me from time to time.

The classroom lights shone brightly on our desks. It was an ordinary English class when the teacher suddenly announced a surprise speaking test. My heart immediately started racing, and my palms grew sweaty. I thought, This is so sudden—I’m not prepared. Behind me, I could hear classmates whispering. I tried to listen to what they were saying, but it was all drowned out by the anxiety filling my mind.

The teacher began pacing back and forth across the classroom, her heels making heavy sounds on the floor, which made me even more nervous. “Everyone needs to come up and say a few sentences about your favorite activity,” she said. My stomach twisted painfully, and I even felt a wave of nausea. I tried hard to suppress those feelings, thinking I should describe my awkwardness first and foremost; at least that way, I wouldn’t be knocked down by other people’s mockery.

When it was my turn, I stood up, feeling my legs go a little weak. My mouth seemed not to obey me either. I tried to open it, but I felt like an idiot. “Um, I… I like reading.” My voice was so faint I could barely hear myself. The classroom was silent, and I could hear my own heartbeat.

The teacher nodded, seeming to encourage me to continue. Around me, some classmates were fiddling with pens, others were chatting softly, and I felt as if all eyes were on me. I tried to remember the last book I had read, but my mind was blank. All I could do was repeat mechanically, “Books are interesting. I read all kinds of books.” My voice grew smaller and smaller.

The teacher let me sit down, and I felt completely drained. As I returned to my seat, my hands and feet began to tremble. I kept my head down, pretending to organize my backpack to avoid making eye contact with anyone.

After the bell rang, I quickly left the classroom, and the cold wind outside hit me in the face. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself down. After school, I hid in my room, repeatedly replaying my performance in my mind, even imagining classmates gossiping behind my back about how awkward I had been. That night, I tossed and turned and couldn’t fall asleep.

Over the next few days, I remained restless, worried that something like this might happen again. I kept rehearsing different topics in my head and trying out various ways of speaking, but every time I thought about speaking in front of others, my heart would start racing. Even though the teacher never brought up a similar test again, I still felt troubled. A few days later, the anxiety gradually faded, but it still lingered beside me like a shadow.

The morning sunlight poured through the classroom windows onto the desks, but my mind was clouded with dread. Today was the math quiz, and the classroom was so quiet that only the soft rustle of pencil on paper could be heard. Every sound made my heart race, as if each one were reminding me: you cannot make a mistake. I looked around, and my classmates were all bent over their papers, focused and composed, as if everything were under control. Someone sneezed, but it seemed not to disturb anyone’s train of thought; everyone quickly sank back into their own calculations. “Don’t be nervous, you can do this,” I whispered to myself, trying to let those words echo in my mind to ease the anxiety that kept rising. Yet the more I told myself that, the more sweat broke out in my palms, more and more of it. My heartbeat seemed to keep time with the second hand, even a little faster than it.

I wiped my palms on my sleeves, trying to grip my pencil tightly and write the first number on the blank page. But for some reason, every formula looked like unfamiliar characters, with nothing connecting them to me. My stomach began to churn, and an ominous feeling settled over me. I looked up at the clock on the wall; its hands ticked on, mercilessly pushing time toward the end. Suddenly, the teacher’s footsteps broke the silence. “Ten minutes left, everyone, make the most of your time.” His voice was calm and steady, but to me it sounded like the tolling of a judgment bell.

“It’s over. I won’t finish at all,” I muttered inwardly, and scenes flashed through my mind of being scolded by the teacher and mocked by my classmates. I began to attack myself: “Why didn’t you review earlier? You’re such a failure, always like this, never good at anything.”

When the bell rang, I mechanically handed in my paper, my heart filled with helplessness and shame. Every cell in my body seemed to scream: “You’re such an idiot.” I dragged my exhausted body back to my seat, while my classmates began excitedly discussing the quiz, and all I wanted was to disappear from their sight. That night, I tossed and turned in bed and barely slept at all. I kept replaying every detail of the quiz, magnifying every failure into an unbearable boulder.

Over the next few days, I became especially sensitive. Every time I heard even a stray mention of math, I felt as if someone were mocking me. Although I knew it was just my imagination, I still couldn’t control the feeling. When chatting with friends after school, I didn’t even dare bring up the quiz, afraid they would be the next to notice my shortcomings. “Maybe I should try to believe in myself and not always think of the worst outcome.” That was what I kept reminding myself that night, though it wasn’t easy to do.

The abandoned corner behind the playground always felt a little desolate. The ground was pitted and uneven, and at the edges there were a few clumps of wildly overgrown weeds that rustled softly underfoot. The club performance was coming up soon, and we needed a temporary place to rehearse. The class monitor chose this spot, saying it was quiet and no one would disturb us. I stood at the front of the line, my heart gradually racing, my palms already damp. “Don’t mess this up, don’t mess this up!” I kept telling myself over and over.

It was my turn to go on. I took a deep breath, walked nervously to the center position, and started to pose. My old sneakers scraped against the tiny gravel underfoot, distracting me so much that I couldn’t help thinking, “What if they think my movements are clumsy? Should I change into another pair of shoes?” Just as I was thinking that, I was already losing the beat of the music. In my panic, I missed my footing, slipped, and fell flat on the ground.

Everything went silent for three seconds, then a burst of laughter erupted around me. I was lying on the ground, my face burning—I couldn’t even tell how badly—and my mind was in chaos. “They’re all laughing at me. Do they think I shouldn’t have come to this performance at all?” My muscles were so tense they were nearly cramping, and the laughter in my ears seemed amplified, impossible to stop. I struggled to prop myself up, my knees stinging painfully. Looking down, I saw that a large patch of my school pants at the knee had been scraped open, and beads of blood were slowly seeping out.

“Hey, are you okay?” a teammate came over to ask, the laughter in their voice impossible to hide. I nodded and immediately stood up, pretending nothing was wrong. “I’m fine, I’m fine. Let’s keep going,” I said with a forced light laugh, but inside I was already boiling over. My hand inside my sleeve clenched into a fist, my nails nearly digging into my palm. The music started again, but I seemed frozen in place, my body stiff as the scene of my fall kept replaying in my mind.

At last, rehearsal was over, but my face still felt hot. All the way there, I kept my head down, afraid to see anyone’s smiling face again. How could they laugh so easily? Had all the effort I put in practicing at home until two in the morning after evening study yesterday been for nothing? When I got back to the classroom, I hid in the back row, spread my book open and pretended to read, but I didn’t take in a single line. My head was full of words like “embarrassing,” “failure,” and “damn it.”

When I got home, as soon as my mom opened the door, she noticed my knee. “What happened?” she asked. I mumbled, “I fell.” Just as I was about to slip quickly into my room, I heard her ask with concern, “What’s going on? Did you fall by accident?” I held back my tears, but the anger in my heart quietly started to surface again: “Would she think I’m clumsy too?” I brushed her off with a few casual words, closed the door, and collapsed onto the bed.

That night, I lay there fully dressed, with the scene of me falling over and over again replaying in my head. It felt like I could still hear that burst of laughter, as if it were stabbing straight into my nerves. Every time I replayed it, a sharp pain shot through my heart, and my stomach began to feel faintly sour. The next morning, when I saw the scab on my knee, I still couldn’t stop myself from cursing at me: “How can you be so stupid!”

The classroom walls were covered with colorful paintings, and the air was filled with a faint smell of paint. Today was the art class competition, and everyone was energetically preparing their work. I sat by the window, sunlight spilling across the desk, the white paper glaring a little in the light. My heart was racing, my fingers kept rubbing the paintbrush, and all I could think was that I absolutely must not make a mistake this time. 

The teacher came over and stopped beside me, examining the painting I had just started. I tried to stay calm, but inside I felt like a volcano about to erupt, ready at any moment to spew out lava of anxiety. “Hmm, the colors are used well,” she said, nodding slightly before walking away. I stared at her back, trying to read every subtle shift in her tone. “Is she just brushing me off? Does she think I’m not painting well?” These thoughts kept repeating in my mind.

I began to feel a tightness in my stomach, and my sweaty palms were slick and slippery. The paintbrush slipped from my hand and fell to the floor. I bent down nervously to pick it up, while the voice inside me kept blaming me: “This is awful. Why can’t you just be normal?”

The classmates nearby were whispering, and I always felt their eyes drifting toward me, but every time I looked up, they would lower their heads again. I kept painting, yet in my heart I had already rehearsed the worst possible ending: when the teacher announced the winners, everyone would cheer, and I alone would be overlooked. 

After the bell rang, I packed up my art supplies and quickly slipped back into a corner of the classroom. My classmates were excitedly discussing their own work, but I couldn’t join in. I wanted to ask for their opinions, but I was afraid they would give me answers I didn’t want to hear. To avoid that possible embarrassment, I chose silence.

When I got home, my confidence in my painting had vanished completely, and I kept feeling that the teacher’s praise might have been nothing more than politeness. I kept replaying her tone and expression in my mind, endlessly speculating. That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t calm my heart; the tension in my body kept me tossing and turning. The next morning, my stomach still hurt a little, and the unease hung over me like an invisible shadow.

Although the classmates gradually talked less about the competition, I still felt as if I were carrying an unresolved knot in my heart. Every time I thought about that painting competition, I couldn’t help blaming myself for being so sensitive and so full of self-doubt.

The classroom was filled with a mingled smell of disinfectant and rust. The teacher had just handed out the samples for the microscope experiment. I sat in the third row of the lab, with a black microscope and several cell slides on the desk. A tightness began to twist in my stomach, and that familiar pressure spread through my whole body. I wasn’t very good at hands-on experiments, and I always felt like the dumbest one in the class, especially in science. The teacher’s footsteps echoed through the room. My fingers stiffly held the microscope, too afraid to press down hard in case I broke it.

“Everyone, pay attention. The nuclei should be very clear and purple. If you can’t see them clearly, the aperture may not be adjusted right!” the teacher’s voice came from the front of the room. I lowered my head to look at my sample, only to find a blurry shadow in my field of view. I couldn’t see any purple nuclei at all. I couldn’t help swallowing hard and looked up to glance around. The other students all seemed to be working smoothly, and some had already started recording data. A sharp pain stabbed at my heart, and my breathing grew rapid.

The student beside me whispered, “Why still haven’t you seen it? Hurry up and adjust the aperture.” His tone wasn’t exactly harsh, but it landed on my ears like a heavy blow. I blurted back instinctively, “I know, I’m adjusting it!” But in truth, I had no idea what I was doing wrong. I fumbled frantically with the knobs on the microscope, but accidentally let the slide slip and heard a sharp “snap.” In that instant, it seemed as if all sound had been sucked away, and the whole world consisted only of the teacher turning to look at me. My face instantly burned, and my palms began to sweat.

“What happened?” The teacher walked over, looked down at the broken slide, and frowned. I was so panicked I could hardly breathe. “I... I didn’t hold it steady...” My voice was so faint it was like a mosquito’s buzz, sounding even less confident to my own ears. “Be careful next time. These slides are pretty expensive. Don’t waste them,” she said. Her tone wasn’t severe, but it was enough to make words like “this is bad” and “I’ve disappointed everyone again” spring up in my mind. I forced myself to nod, then quickly bent down to clean up the glass shards on the desk. When the back of my hand brushed against a fragment, a sharp sting shot through it, but I had no time to care.

“Seriously, do you know how much those slides cost? What a pain. You had to make it like this.” A voice from nearby wasn’t loud, but it hit my ears with pinpoint accuracy. I didn’t look to see who said it; my shoulders stiffened at once, as if nailed in place. I kept telling myself, “Don’t cry, don’t cry,” but my emotions spread like a flood released from a dam. I lowered my head and pretended to write in my lab notes, though the graph paper before my eyes had already blurred into a canvas streaked with water stains.

Finally the bell rang. I packed up my things quickly and rushed out of the classroom with my head down. The hallway was crowded with people coming and going. I stood against the wall, trying hard to calm my pounding heart. My fingers brushed the broken skin, and it hurt a little, but I didn’t care at all. All I could think was that I must have looked like a complete failure just now.

After school that day, I went home, tossed my backpack onto the floor, and locked my bedroom door. I didn’t want to hear my parents ask about what happened today, and I didn’t want to say much either. The scene of everyone watching me clean up the broken pieces on the floor kept replaying in my head, tightening my chest again and again. I lay on the bed staring at the crack in the ceiling, and tears began to 흐 out before I knew it. It wasn’t until midnight that I finally drifted off in a daze, still thinking: if I had been more careful then, would I not have been so embarrassed?

The spotlight on the stage cast my shadow onto the floor. I stood there, my palms slightly damp with nerves. The air was thick with the smell of dust and old props, carrying a sense of age and neglect. Today was our drama club rehearsal, and I really wanted to make sure my lines were correct before going onstage.

“Hey, that last part—did you move to the wrong mark?” the team leader asked me in a flat tone. Hearing that, my heart gave a hard thump, and my face instantly flushed. Her tone felt somewhat cutting, and I couldn’t help wondering whether she had something against me. “No, no, it’s just that I... might have remembered it wrong,” I forced out a slight smile, trying to hide my unease.

She nodded, but I still felt as if her gaze was reproachful. A scene immediately flashed through my mind of her whispering to the other members. I knew it was absurd, but I couldn’t stop myself from thinking it. I tried to steady my breathing, but my heart kept racing.

After rehearsal ended, I walked out of the theater, and the sunlight made me feel a little dizzy. I hurried under a large tree, where the cold wind blew past and cleared my head somewhat. Sitting beneath the tree, I replayed the scene over and over in my mind, trying to find hidden meanings in her tone. “Does she have some kind of resentment toward me?” That question kept echoing in my head.

That evening, when I got home, I sat down at my desk. Spread across the table were various magazines and homework I hadn’t finished yesterday. I tried to focus on my assignments, hoping to ease the anxiety in my heart, but the notification sound from my phone interrupted my thoughts. It was a group message from the drama club, where the leader praised everyone’s performance and suggested we practice more. “Is this a hint directed at me?” I couldn’t help returning to that question again.

A few days passed, and I still couldn’t completely let go of the knot in my heart. Every time I saw her post in the group chat, I would instinctively tense up, worried that I had done something wrong again. I started avoiding eye contact with her, and whenever such thoughts arose in my mind, it felt as if a knot were tied in my stomach. Even when she wasn’t paying attention to me, I would feel inexplicably lonely because of these thoughts.

Although even now I’m not sure whether the team leader really meant to criticize me, this experience made me realize that I always overinterpret other people’s tone and expressions. Perhaps I need to try to relax a little in moments like these, or ask for clarification in time, so I don’t get trapped in my own assumptions.

I’ve realized that this habit of ruminating and attacking myself causes me a lot of pain, but I still haven’t found a good way to break free from it.

The classroom air was thick with the smell of oil paint, and the walls were covered with vivid student artwork. The teacher asked us to take turns presenting our paintings, and my heart began to race, my palms growing sweaty. I glanced at the students standing at the front; they were confidently explaining their work, earning wave after wave of applause. I couldn’t help but worry: if my painting wasn’t recognized, what would that mean?

When it was my turn, I carried my easel to the front of the classroom, feeling the gazes of everyone slice across my skin like sharp knives. “This is my piece,” I said, trying my best to keep my voice from trembling. “I wanted to express the loneliness of life in the city.” As soon as I finished, my stomach started to twist painfully.

The teacher stepped closer, frowning slightly. “The composition of this painting is thoughtful, but the color choices seem a bit too heavy.” My cheeks flushed hot all at once, as if every pair of eyes were scrutinizing my failure. I nodded, forcing myself to resist the urge to turn and run.

The classmates began whispering. I heard someone murmur in a low voice, “Those colors are really depressing.” Though it was said quietly, it stabbed at my ears like a needle, instantly triggering the self-attack in my mind. “They think my painting is bad. If I can’t do this well, then what am I good for?”

After the last student finished showing their work, everyone started putting away their art supplies. I quickly packed mine up, trying not to meet anyone’s eyes. Questions in my heart crashed over me again and again like furious waves: “Are they thinking I shouldn’t keep painting at all?”

As I left the classroom, a friend gently patted my shoulder and smiled at me. “Hey, don’t take it too seriously. The teacher’s advice can help you improve.” Even though their words were so warm, my thoughts were still swallowed by negative emotions, and I could only nod mechanically in response.

That night, I lay on my bed tossing and turning, replaying everything that had happened in class over and over, doubting whether I really had the ability to keep painting. I couldn’t shake the shame in my heart, and I kept feeling as if I had too many flaws. My friend’s comfort echoed repeatedly in my mind, but it seemed unable to penetrate my self-doubt.

A few days later, when I picked up my paintbrush again, that suffocating feeling was still there. But I tried hard to apply the teacher’s suggestions to a new piece, hoping that maybe I would find my own colors.

I walked into the school library, and through the large windows I could see the gloomy sky outside. The air carried the comforting mixed scent of old books, paper, and ink. The library was so quiet that only the occasional rustle of turning pages could be heard. Standing between the shelves, I felt anxious inside.

While choosing a book, I couldn’t help imagining the worst-case scenario: what if I picked the wrong book and the librarian laughed at me? What if I made a mistake with the borrowing procedure and was reprimanded? So I kept checking the book’s classification labels and barcode, making sure I hadn’t made a mistake. My heartbeat began to quicken, and I felt a slight sweat forming on my forehead.

The librarian glanced at me, and I immediately and reflexively interpreted her expression as displeasure, as if she already knew I was about to make a mistake. By the time I got to the borrowing desk, my palms were already sweating. “Could I borrow this book, please?” My voice sounded smaller than I had expected. The librarian smiled as she took the book and gave a slight nod. While she processed the borrowing, I began to ruminate over every moment I had ever made a mistake, bitterly thinking: why do I always imagine these tragic scenes?

After the borrowing was completed smoothly, I leaned on the counter and slowly exhaled, feeling some of the tension in my body ease. But when I left the library and walked home, I still couldn’t help reflecting: was she really impatient with me? Did I really seem that awkward? That night, as I stayed up late, my mind echoed with one unnecessary self-attack after another, repeatedly asking myself why I was like this. I knew it was foolish, yet I couldn’t stop the cycle.

A few days later, the aftereffects of this anxiety and self-reproach gradually faded, but I still hadn’t completely broken free of the loop. I realized that whenever I thought of that borrowing incident, my heart would still race and my palms would grow hot. When I went to the library again, I couldn’t help rehearsing in advance, trying to reduce the risk of falling back into that self-attacking pattern.

The lights on the stage were a little blinding. I stood in the center, my feet seeming nailed to the floor, sweat running down my forehead. The teacher encouraged me from below the stage: “Don’t rush. Take a deep breath. Go slowly.” But no matter what I did, I couldn’t remember the next line. I could hear the murmuring in the audience and the rustling of paper, and they blended into an irritating buzz in my ears. I thought to myself: if only the floor would crack open and let me crawl into it. Below the stage, the other students’ eyes were on me, and my cheeks burned. It was an indescribable sense of embarrassment and shame, magnified infinitely under those gazes. My stomach suddenly began to twist in pain, and I could feel my heartbeat speeding up, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. “Do you want to do it yourself, or do you need help?” the teacher’s voice came again. I swallowed and tried hard not to let my voice tremble. “I… I’ll try.” Every word that forced its way out of my mouth seemed to drag a heavy tail behind it. Even so, I still managed to recite the lines haltingly, my tone somewhat stiff. After the rehearsal ended, I dragged my heavy steps off the stage. The sky had already begun to darken, and a breeze brushed my face, but the lingering tension still left my palms damp. Sitting on a long bench at school, I replayed what had just happened in my mind, repeatedly asking myself: Why did this happen? Why can’t I ever remember my lines? To me, this was a personal flaw, a defect that could not be remedied. That night, after I got home, I lay in bed tossing and turning, and the scene from today kept flashing through my mind. Even after a few days had passed, whenever I thought about that rehearsal, a wave of unease and shame would still sweep over me. The other students didn’t seem to care, but in my mind, it was like an eternal torment, impossible to escape.

At lunchtime, I sat with a few friends at a long table in the school cafeteria. The place was buzzing with voices, and the clatter of plates and silverware blended together into a noisy symphony. I absently poked at the spaghetti on my plate with my fork, but my thoughts had drifted back to a conversation from just moments before.

About five minutes earlier, I had overheard Friend C say to Friend A across from me, “She probably doesn’t really get this joke.” When I heard that, my heart sank and my stomach twisted unpleasantly. I started to wonder whether C was talking about me, because just before that, they had told a joke I didn’t understand. I tried to recall the joke, but I still couldn’t figure out what was funny about it. At that moment, my mind was filled with all kinds of possible interpretations: Were they making fun of me? Or did they think I was slow?

“Are you feeling okay?” Friend B suddenly asked, tapping my shoulder with concern. “Huh?” I came back to myself and realized I had put my fork down. “Oh, I’m fine.” I forced a smile and immediately looked down, avoiding eye contact with the others. I could feel my face getting a little hot, and my heartbeat had quickened.

“Really, you’re okay?” B asked again, sounding a bit uneasy.

I nodded. “I’m just a little tired.” I tried hard to steady my voice so it wouldn’t tremble.

They kept talking about other things, and I halfheartedly followed along, chiming in once or twice, but my attention remained stuck on that ambiguous remark. The cafeteria air was thick with the smell of fried food, which now made me feel slightly nauseous. Even so, I kept trying to force a smile, hoping they wouldn’t see through me.

After returning to class, I fell into a spiral of overthinking. Were they really talking about me? Why did I always feel so distant from other people? Thinking back on my usual conversations with C, it didn’t seem like she had meant anything against me. Maybe she had just been speaking casually.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed the day’s events in my mind. I felt a little regretful that I had let myself get trapped in such baselessguess and anxiety. Maybe I should try to trust my friends more and stop immediately jumping to negative conclusions about myself. The next morning, I decided to talk to C and see whether it had all just been my misunderstanding.

Over the next few days, my mood gradually settled down. Although I still sometimes became overly sensitive about small things, I began trying to view them with a calmer mindset.

There is always a particular smell in the music room—the scent of old wooden piano stands mixed with chalk dust, and the slightly heated air that comes from a dozen people squeezed together. The piano sounds on and off: someone is testing their voice, someone is turning pages, and the noise spreads like a net, trapping me inside. The teacher has already stepped onto the conductor’s podium and is waving us into position.
