A classmate sitting next to me heard me, turned around, and said in a teasing voice, “You’re not the only one here, don’t make such a fuss.” His tone wasn’t exactly mean, but to me it felt like a heavy blow.

“I just want it a little quieter,” I replied softly, but inside I was full of irritation and unease. I could feel the heat rising in my face, as if everyone was looking at me and thinking I was the troublemaker. My eyes began to sting, and that familiar feeling of anxiety filled my nose.

At that moment, my inner monologue became unbearably loud: Why am I always so sensitive? Why do other people’s simple words always hurt me? I hate this feeling, hate the helplessness of being unable to control my emotions. Tears welled up in my eyes, and I hurriedly lowered my head, trying to hide my vulnerability.

I quickly gathered my books and notes and practically fled the library. The air outside was cold and fresh. I took a breath and tried hard to calm my racing heart. Yet the tension in my body did not completely disappear, and even my steps felt heavier than usual.

For several hours after getting home, I was still unsettled. I kept thinking back to what happened in the library, chewing over the conversation and my own reaction again and again. I felt ashamed of my sensitivity. Why do I always overreact like this? Tossing and turning in bed, I feared being mocked and gossiped about when I returned to school the next day. I kept reminding myself to learn to be strong, to learn not to be driven by my emotions. Yet these self-reminders seemed futile. Even so, I still tried to meditate briefly in my room, hoping to calm myself down a little.

That night, I remained restless in bed until the early hours of the morning, finally drifting off into a dazed sleep. My dreams were filled with all kinds of blurred scenes, yet there was always a sense of being isolated. Still, I knew I had to learn to face situations like this, because they are part of my life, and also the darkness in my heart that I must eventually step out of.

In the classroom, sunlight filtered through the windows and cast dappled patterns of light and shadow across the desks. Our class was holding a group discussion, and the teacher had assigned us a topic about environmental protection. All around me was the hum of my classmates talking, along with the occasional burst of overlapping laughter. Sitting in the group, I felt somewhat out of place.

The student next to me was pouring out his ideas nonstop, his voice even drowning out the low buzz in the classroom. I tried to cut in and share my thoughts, but every time I spoke, he would interrupt me and continue with his discussion. A wave of unease began to rise in me, as though something were churning in my stomach.

“Maybe we could start by talking about reducing plastic use?” I finally found a gap to slip in a sentence.

“Yes, but I think we should focus more on reusing resources…” He immediately took over the topic and kept talking, as if my suggestion wasn’t even worth mentioning.

Did the way he said that mean my idea was really that bad? Self-doubt surged through me. I began to feel a little angry at his attitude, but more than that, I felt discouraged. I couldn’t help glancing sideways at the other students’ expressions, trying to find any sign of approval or disapproval of my suggestion in their faces. But they all seemed more interested in what he was saying.

My heartbeat quickened, and I could feel sweat in my palms. Every time I tried to speak again, it felt as if my throat were blocked. I didn’t dare interrupt him anymore, afraid I would be even more openly ignored or mocked. My thoughts spiraled: Did they all dislike me? Did they think everything I said was nonsense?

The bell rang, and the meeting ended. I quickly gathered my things and wanted to leave the classroom as soon as possible. On the way from the classroom to the hallway, I felt as though I were shrouded by an invisible shadow, unable to let go of the scene that had just played out, turning it over in my mind again and again.

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t stop thinking about the discussion. I kept replaying my classmates’ expressions and tone of voice, blaming myself over and over for not being more confident when I spoke. Before the bonfire party began, my classmates and I sat in a circle on the grass, feeling the crisp autumn air. The firelight reflected on our faces, warm and gentle. The backstage lighting was dim, and the air was thick with the mingled scent of sweat and tension. I sat in a corner, gripping my sheet music tightly, my mind in chaos. The classroom is always noisy. During breaks, almost all the students are chatting and laughing loudly. They exchanged glances, and one classmate said with a smile, “Nothing, your note-taking style is pretty special—kind of an artistic creation!” Though the smile looked friendly, I couldn’t hear any warmth in it; all I felt was a hidden malicious meaning behind the words.

“I just wrote them that way so they’d be easy to look at,” I hurried to explain, my voice carrying a trace of haste even I could hear. I forced myself to stay composed and lowered my head, flipping through my notes again, but their laughter kept echoing in my ears, almost like mockery. That phrase kept replaying in my mind: “An artistic creation!” Each word was like a small knife, carving tiny wounds into my heart.

My hand began to grip the highlighter nervously, and sweat slowly seeped into my palm, making it slightly slick. I noticed my heart beating faster and a slight heaviness in my chest. I tried to breathe in, but it felt as if the air were blocked in my throat. Suddenly I felt my face growing hot; maybe I was already blushing. I murmured softly, “Why are they always like this? Why is their laughter so harsh?” Then I started blaming myself: “Was I really not good enough? Are these marks really that childish?”

After the break ended, I realized I hadn’t absorbed any of the rest of the lesson at all. My mind was a tangled mess, filled with echoes of those conversations and their expressions. I kept rehearsing all kinds of possible scenarios in my head: What if they laughed at me again later? What if other classmates also thought my notes were strange? When I got home and packed up my schoolbag, I saw the notes again. The more I circled, the more upset I became, until I finally closed the notebook. The next day in class, I chose to sit near the window, hoping to reduce that group of classmates’ attention. I felt a bit like someone avoiding a battlefield, yet at the same time I kept pushing myself inwardly: “Why can’t you just be tougher and fight back? Are you really that weak?”

The classroom lights were always a little harsh, the white fluorescent lamps bleaching the desktops into a blank glare. I sat in the back row, a thin layer of sweat beading in my palms. As they discussed my task, I kept feeling a restless tension hanging in the air. Did he think I wouldn’t do well? Or did he simply not want me involved at all? The seats around me were quiet, with only the occasional chirp of birds drifting in from outside, and that silence made my own heartbeat sound especially clear. I couldn’t help lowering my head to look at my task sheet, and the more I looked, the more I felt like an impostor.

A few minutes later, I heard a classmate beside me say to the group leader, “They seem a bit uncertain.” My heart lurched violently, and my breathing immediately grew rapid; my face burned as if on fire. What did that mean? Had my performance already made them doubt me? I wanted to pretend I hadn’t heard it, but the next second the group leader turned to me. “You’re okay, right? If it feels awkward, we can adjust it.” His voice seemed even gentler than before, but all I felt was as if a needle had pierced my brain. I heard myself answer instinctively, “I’m fine, I can do it.” I spoke so quickly that even I thought it sounded unnatural.

When I walked out of the classroom, I felt the pressure in my chest hadn’t eased at all; if anything, it had grown heavier. The sunlight at the end of the hallway seemed blinding, and I held my backpack tighter, as if clutching my only line of defense. That afternoon, everyone else seemed especially happy, but I was immersed in my own whirlpool of thoughts. At dinner, I heard my parents talking about my studies. Their tone was casual, but I always felt it carried a faint trace of disappointment. The food on my plate grew colder and colder, and the stomachache came back.

A few days later, we had another group discussion. I worked hard to finish my part and even organized some extra materials in advance. The group leader was very satisfied with my work; he even told me, “You did really well, more meticulous than I expected.” That sentence should have made me breathe a sigh of relief, but instead I fell into another mental trap—did “more meticulous than I expected” mean he had really thought I wasn’t capable before? I still couldn’t fully trust other people’s evaluations. That careful, defensive mindset seemed to have become my shell, and I didn’t dare take it off, afraid of being seen through.

The classroom lights were a little harsh, and the shadows of the trees outside the window swayed gently in the wind. A few classmates and I sat around the desks; the group discussion had just begun, and the atmosphere was somewhat tense. Anna spoke up: “Why don’t you look at it from another angle?” Her voice was calm, but I caught a hint of doubt and contempt. Right then, images of being mocked in the past flashed through my mind, and I felt as if I were cornered, powerless to fight back.

To avoid seeming too passive, I replied firmly, “I don’t think there’s any difference; that angle doesn’t really mean much.” I tried to sound confident, but my voice was trembling slightly. At that moment, my chest felt tight and painful, as if I were being bound tightly, unbearably uncomfortable. Then another student in the group, David, chimed in: “Anna’s idea is good; we can try it.” In an instant, I felt isolated, and a panic of abandonment rose in my heart. The classmates in front of me seemed to be exchanging glances, intentionally or not, as if I were the one who didn’t fit in. I bit my lower lip and tried hard not to look too embarrassed.

When the class bell finally rang, it sounded louder than usual. I quickly packed up my bag, wanting to leave this suffocating place as soon as possible. In the hallway, I felt a dull pain in my stomach, as if a heavy stone were pressing down on it. I walked with my head down, afraid of running into anyone I knew, but Anna caught up with me and patted my shoulder. “Don’t be so nervous; we’re just discussing things.” At that moment, I felt a little better, but I still couldn’t completely let it go.

When I got home, I lay on my bed and closed my eyes, but I kept seeing the expression on Anna’s face when she spoke. A voice inside me kept asking, “Why am I always so sensitive?” I kept replaying every sentence and every expression over and over, trying to figure out exactly what I had done wrong.

The next day, when facing Anna and the other classmates, I felt a bit at a loss, and I still felt uneasy inside. I forced myself to smile, as if that could hide the panic in my heart. Over those next few days, I began avoiding group discussions, always feeling that I would embarrass myself again. I started to wonder whether I was really suited for this kind of teamwork, because the feeling of not being accepted just would not go away.

The school sports meet was not only a moment to showcase athletic talent, but also a stage for my anxiety. I stood at the edge of the playground, the wind rustling the leaves, sunlight filtering through them and scattering patches of light on the ground. I tried to control my breathing, but my heart was pounding faster and faster, as if it were about to leap out of my chest. My palms were already slick with sweat, and my stomach was twisted so tightly that I could hardly stand upright. At that moment, the 100-meter sprint was underway. I watched the other competitors getting ready on the track, their faces full of focus. I tried hard not to think about the possibility of failure. But a voice inside me kept blaming me: “If I lose, it’ll be so humiliating. What will everyone think of me?”

“The race is about to start. Are you ready?” A classmate passed by me and patted my shoulder.

“Mm, I’m ready.” I forced out a smile, but deep down I couldn’t help asking myself: Am I really ready?

The moment the starting gun fired, I sprinted forward desperately, yet I felt as if I were sinking into a swamp. My leg muscles were tense, my breathing grew rapid, and it felt as though I had run ten kilometers instead of ten meters. Beside the roar of the wind in my ears was the thunder of my own heartbeat. Countless scenes of possible failure flashed through my mind: falling, being mocked, being isolated. Each image made me more uneasy. By the time I crossed the finish line, my result was far from satisfactory. Standing beside the finish line, I felt utterly disappointed, and a lonely sense of being abandoned.

After the race, I walked alone to a large tree at the edge of the playground and closed my eyes to feel the breeze around me. My inner voice kept blaming me without end: “Why is it always like this? Why can’t I control my emotions?” These thoughts were like invisible hands, mercilessly tearing apart my confidence. I sat under the tree, picking at the grass with my fingers, trying to find the suppressed calm buried inside me.

In the days that followed, my mood remained low. At home, I kept replaying that unchangeable moment over and over, my heart unbearably heavy. Even in class, I was trapped in this mood, often worrying whether every word from the teacher carried criticism. It wasn’t until the next day that my classmates, unintentionally comforting me, said the competition was just part of the process and told me to face it more lightly. I realized that perhaps no one was truly interested in my failure, and that I didn’t need to worry so much about what others thought.

Gradually, I began to accept my sensitivity and anxiety, seeing them as an inseparable part of myself rather than a disgrace. Although those uneasinesses still lingered in my heart, I found that I was slowly becoming capable of coping with these feelings, without letting them affect my hopes for the future or my efforts toward it.

Class had just let out, and my hand slowly pulled back from the teacher’s desk, still trembling slightly. The fluorescent lights overhead stung my eyes, and I did my best to avoid meeting anyone’s gaze. Even though I had tried my hardest to act natural, I could still feel a burning sensation on one side of my head — that was the classmates on my left whispering. That night, I couldn’t sleep no matter what. The lamp by the bed cast my shadow onto the wall, and I stared fixedly at that twisted silhouette. The sunlight in the hallway slanted through a crack in the window, leaving several ghastly white patches on the tiled floor. I was carrying my textbooks to the classroom when, suddenly, a low conversation came from behind me, mixed with laughter. I couldn’t make out the words, but that laughter was like a fine needle, precisely piercing a place I had been trying to ignore.

My steps grew heavy at that moment.

My fingers unconsciously tightened around the edge of my textbook, my knuckles going a little pale.

“Yo, why are you wearing that outfit again?”

My stomach dropped violently at that second, and heat rushed to my face almost at the same time. A thin layer of sweat broke out on my forehead, and my heartbeat suddenly quickened by two beats. This was the kind of scene I feared most—being singled out in public, and in the hallway, with people everywhere.

I heard myself say, “What’s wrong with this outfit? I like it.”

My voice trembled more than I expected, as if it were coming from somewhere very far away.

TA laughed, and a few people beside TA laughed too. I wanted to leave, but my legs seemed nailed to the floor by something.

Then I heard myself say, “If you’re so good at judging clothes, why don’t you become a designer?”

TA paused for a second, then spread TA’s hands and wore a smile I couldn’t quite read: “Didn’t expect you to be this emotional.” Someone nearby said softly, “Don’t mind TA, let’s go,” and then they turned and left.

I stood there motionless, the floor beneath my feet feeling as if it had lost its support. I even started regretting wearing that outfit, regretting walking down that hallway, regretting speaking up to fight back.

Even if friends greeted me, I only nodded or said “yeah.” I didn’t want to give anyone another chance to pick at me, and I didn’t want people to think I was emotionally unstable.

But that feeling didn’t disappear because of it. It just stayed in a different form—like that blinding patch of light in the hallway. If you don’t look at it, it’s still there.

The classroom windows trembled faintly in the wind, and the gray, overcast sky outside made everything feel oppressive. The teacher stood at the podium and called out, “Next group, it’s your turn.” My heart jolted violently, almost jumping out of my chest. My palms were already drenched with sweat, and my fingertips were numb. I took a deep breath and walked to the front with my group members. When the projector turned on, our prepared slide appeared on the screen, and I could hardly focus my eyes. A scene kept flashing through my mind: me standing in front of everyone, stumbling over my words and saying the wrong thing, not knowing what to do, while the people below looked at me with contempt. A low voice came from behind me. “Relax. Didn’t you prepare?” I nodded and pretended to be calm as I walked to the speaking position.

“Our group’s topic is the cyclical role of ecosystems, focusing mainly on the ecological balance of wetlands.” My voice was much sharper than usual, and I could even hear a slight tremor in it myself. At the same time, my gaze swept across the classroom. Most people had their heads down, playing with pens or straightening their notebooks, but there were still a few pairs of eyes fixed on me. A thought popped into my head: Do they think my voice sounds weird? Have they already started laughing at me secretly? Just then, I heard a girl in the front row whisper something to the person beside her. An alarm went off in my head: She must be talking about me.

When it was my turn to explain the role of the food chain, speaking became even harder. I tried to steady my breathing. “Don’t rush, take it slowly.” The content on the screen was already very familiar, but my mind began to go blank. Suddenly I jumped to an unrelated point and felt that my explanation might be more complicated, smarter, something that could impress everyone. I wanted to seem less ordinary. So I said a long stretch of words, but the more I spoke, the more wrong it felt. The teacher’s brows furrowed slightly, and my throat felt blocked, as if the air couldn’t pass through smoothly. A soft laugh came from the back row. I wasn’t sure if it was directed at me, but in that moment I believed it: they were laughing at me. I even felt the muscles in my arms stiffen, and my shoulders began to tremble slightly.

The teacher sighed softly and interrupted me. “Hold on, something here doesn’t seem right.” She began correcting my mistakes. My face burned as if it were on fire, and I lowered my head uncontrollably, trying to make myself as invisible as possible. I wanted to hide, like a snail retracting into its spiral shell, as long as I could avoid those gazes. But my eyes still involuntarily swept over a few classmates—some wore a contemptuous expression that said “just as expected,” while others absentmindedly fiddled with their pens. Yet even their indifference made me feel as if I had been ignored.

When the bell rang to end the presentation, I almost stumbled back to my seat. From where I sat, my deskmate was looking down and fiddling with a rubber band. He asked me quietly, “Are you okay?” That simple question stirred something inside me, and tears almost fell. I held them back with difficulty, only nodding and muttering, “I’m fine.” But my hands kept twisting the pen cap, as if trying to vent all my energy.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the moment I answered incorrectly, like an endlessly looping video that couldn’t be turned off. I even began to doubt myself—why had I tried so hard to seem smart, why couldn’t I just be simpler? For the next several days, I avoided talking much with the group members in class, afraid of any judgment about my performance. As I silently reconstructed that scene in my mind, trying to imagine a flawless version of myself, that sense of pressure still would not go away.

The sunlight dappled the sparse shade of the trees on the playground. I stood among a group of classmates, feeling as if a thin sheet of ice lay beneath my feet. I had just tried to tell a joke, thinking it would make everyone laugh, but instead there was only a brief silence. That silence felt like a sharp needle stabbing into me, filling me with an uncontrollable panic.

Then a boy suddenly laughed and said, “What kind of joke is that? So awkward.” He repeated what I had said in a deliberately exaggerated tone, mimicking my manner of speaking. A few classmates nearby started laughing too. Their expressions didn’t seem malicious, but in my head a fire had already exploded. My face burned instantly. The laughter in my ears sounded like countless flies buzzing, and I could only freeze there, like a puppet pinned in place.

I wanted to explain that I hadn’t meant to say it so strangely, but the words got stuck in my throat and wouldn’t come out. I even started to wonder whether I really was stupid, unable to even tell a joke properly. But at the same time, a deeper shame surged up: I felt they were mocking me, not just my joke, but my entire person. I began to overanalyze their looks, their laughter, and even the classmates standing off to the side who hadn’t joined in—I felt sure they must all be silently looking down on me.

“Ha, why are you blushing so much?” Another girl noticed my reaction. There was no malice in her tone, but the words cut through my facade like a scalpel. I touched my face and sure enough, it was hot as a furnace. I forced a smile. “It’s nothing, maybe it’s just the heat.” But she didn’t let me off the hook. I didn’t know what to do. The laughter grew sharper and sharper, and there was only one thought in my mind: run out, leave this place. Like an animal cornered against a wall, I suddenly muttered, “Forget it. Have you laughed enough yet?” Then I turned and left in a hurry.

All the way home, my stomach felt twisted tight, and the scene kept replaying in my head. Did I seem especially fragile? Would they think I was weird, useless? Every laugh in my mind became sharper, more vicious. I even began to suspect that they didn’t really like me at all—that they were only pretending to be friendly on the surface, and that this time they had finally found a chance to make fun of me.

After I got home, I felt completely deflated. I lay on my bed and stared at the ceiling. The words “Why are you blushing so much?” echoed over and over in my head, and my face seemed to stay hot for a long time. I wanted to message a close friend, but I worried she would think I was complaining or overreacting. That night, I kept wondering whether everything would have turned out differently if I had smiled more naturally, or simply not told that joke at all. The next day, my heart was still tight with unease, and I didn’t even dare meet those classmates’ eyes, afraid of reading “disdain” or “contempt” in them. Even though no one brought it up, I still felt that that humiliating moment had already been etched into their memory.

The wooden floor of the dance rehearsal room glowed softly in the sunlight. The air was filled with the warm scent of sunshine and a faint smell of sweat. Outside the window came the noise of campus life; from time to time, classmates passed by laughing and chatting, but the concentration inside drowned out all those sounds. The teacher stood in front, guiding us through the movements for the stage performance we were about to take part in. I stood in the middle of the line, trying to keep up with the rhythm of the music.

I worked hard to swing my arms, but my footwork was always just a little off. The teacher’s gaze occasionally swept over me, making my heart race, and fine beads of sweat gradually appeared on my forehead. I heard my partners whispering, as if every word was about my terrible performance. It felt like a direct blow to my heart, and I began to nervously bite my lip, trying to calm myself down, but it had almost no effect.

“Can we try again? Everyone, keep the beat in mind, and please make the movements cleaner and sharper,” the teacher said, coming over and pointing me out specifically. The words echoed in my ears, pressing down on me like an invisible weight. I forced myself to throw myself back into the music and tried hard to stay with the rhythm. But inside, I kept turning over the thought of how humiliating it would be if I failed. The mirrors around the rehearsal room reflected my panicked expression, as if they, too, were mocking my awkwardness.

When the music started again, my movement lagged by half a beat, and my foot slipped, nearly causing me to fall. At that moment, my heart pounded even more fiercely, as if someone were constantly drumming beside my ear, and my chest felt heavy. I couldn’t help but ruminate again on my earlier mistake, and the teacher’s disappointed expression appeared in my mind. A spasm tightened my stomach, as if I had just swallowed a bitter medicine.

Finally, the class bell rang, and I let out a slight sigh of relief, sitting weakly on the floor. Other students passed by me, yet hardly anyone noticed I was there. A sense of disappointment and shame swirled inside me, and I felt that I had become a complete laughingstock in this rehearsal.

That night, the scene in the rehearsal room kept replaying in my mind, like an inescapable nightmare. I kept asking myself why I couldn’t have done better. It wasn’t until several days later, when I still couldn’t shake off that thick, oppressive anxiety, that I realized this might not have been a failure of the performance at all, but rather my own harsh demands on myself.

This feeling made me uneasy at every rehearsal that followed, always worrying that I would make a mistake again. I began to be exacting with myself in every detail, hoping that at least next time I wouldn’t disappoint the teacher again.

When the sunlight streamed through the rehearsal room windows and fell on the floor, I stood in the rehearsal room with the other members of the choir. The air was filled with a faint smell of chalk and slightly damp wooden floors. The conductor stood at the front, waving her baton. My heart was pounding so fast, like a deer being chased. I tried hard to look at her face, hoping to catch any sign of approval for our performance from her expression. Yet I always felt that she was frowning, the corners of her mouth turned slightly downward.

“This won’t do. Everyone, let’s do it again—from the beginning,” she said.

My temples throbbed, and my palms started to sweat. Had I just sung the wrong note? Was my voice too loud?

“Don’t be nervous. Relax a little,” the classmate beside me whispered.

I nodded unconsciously, trying to calm myself down. Yet a voice in my head kept echoing: If I mess this up, will she stop letting me perform in the future? Or will everyone in the choir know it was my fault?

As the music started again, I tried to focus and keep up with the beat. But my thoughts wandered uncontrollably to the conductor’s expression, and her seemingly displeased face made my chest tighten once more. I felt my stomach begin to churn, as if a stone were pressing down inside it.

“Relax, take a deep breath,” I told myself in my mind.

I tried to stop thinking about those negative things, but they were like uninvited guests, intruding mercilessly. After rehearsal ended, I hurriedly packed up and left the rehearsal room, my heart still pounding violently. My face felt hot, as if everyone were staring at me.

Why am I always like this? I kept blaming myself inwardly. Why can’t I be as confident as everyone else?

That night, I hid in my room and refused to come out, worrying whether the next rehearsal would be just as awful. Over the next few days, I kept thinking about the conductor’s face that day, repeatedly imagining possible disastrous outcomes. Even when I was walking down the school hallway and saw a fellow choir member, a mere glance from them would make my heart race, afraid they might bring up that rehearsal.

Sunlight filtered through the balcony’s glass and fell on my legs, warm and cozy, but not scorching. A slight coolness drifted in from the wind outside, just enough to balance the heat of the sun. I sat on the balcony chair with a thin blanket over my legs, holding a novel in my hands. The pages gave off a faint papery scent, and I always found that smell especially soothing. From the residential complex below came little fragments of sound: children chasing and playing, their shouts, and the faint clink of a metal buckle on a dog collar as someone walked their dog.

As I turned the pages, I would occasionally look up at the window. In the greenery below the building, several small flowering trees had been planted, and their pale lilac petals swayed gently in the wind. I tried to focus back on the story in the book, but I kept getting distracted. I found myself wondering whether the protagonist was having things a little too easily—how could his luck be that good, time and again? Wasn’t it a bit unrealistic? But then I thought I was overthinking it. It was only a novel; wasn’t it enough that the author wrote it well and made it enjoyable to read?

On the balcony, only the sound of the wind and the rustle of my turning pages remained. I suddenly remembered that this morning, while Mom was brewing coffee, she’d said it might rain in the afternoon, but now the sky was even bluer than it had been in the morning. I set the book aside, leaned slightly toward the window, and looked up hard for any sign of clouds, but the sky was clear and almost entirely free of white clouds. I thought Mom must have misread the forecast; this kind of sunny weather probably wouldn’t let up until evening. So I sat back down and kept reading, thinking that if it really did rain this afternoon, it would probably be nice and cool, but for now this was fine too. The sunlight gave me a very comforting sense of steadiness.

After reading for a while, I realized I was getting hungry, probably because I hadn’t eaten much at lunch. I closed the book and set it on the arm of the chair beside me, then stood up, dragging the blanket with me. The coolness beneath my feet from the balcony tiles was noticeable, and I couldn’t help curling my toes. When I returned to the living room, I faintly caught the lingering smell of cooking oil and fumes from lunch in the kitchen, so I casually opened the window to air things out. Then I went to the fridge and looked around, taking out two pieces of sweet potato cake Mom had bought yesterday. I took a bite, and the sweet, sticky flavor immediately filled my mouth. While chewing, I heard the microwave beep as the milk finished heating. I walked over, took it out, and carried it back to the balcony, settling once more into my chair.

The balcony returned to its original quiet, with the soft rustle of the wind lifting the edge of the blanket and the increasingly distant sounds from the residential complex below. I read while sipping the milk, feeling as though this afternoon could go on for a very long time—long enough for me to forget that time even existed.

In the dance room at school, I was taking part in our class dance rehearsal. The mirrors all around reflected everyone’s figures, making the whole space feel especially spacious. Music poured from the speakers in the corner, its rhythm strong, accompanied by my classmates’ springing steps. The floor was smooth and hard, and I could feel the slight vibration when my feet touched the ground, transmitted through my dance shoes into my body.

“Everyone, please adjust your formation, let’s do it again!” the teacher called out loudly, her voice overpowering the music, and my heartbeat seemed to quicken along with it.

I tried to concentrate, but anxiety kept lingering in my ears. When dancing, I was always afraid of being laughed at or criticized, even though I knew most people didn’t care at all. Sometimes, a careless glance or a laugh, I would overinterpret it as criticism of me.

I secretly told myself, “If I don’t dance well this time, everyone will be looking at me and think I’m a joke.” This thought kept circling in my mind, leaving me no time to care about the graceful fluidity of the dance moves.

The music kept playing, and I tried hard to sync my movements with it, but every time I did a turn, I could feel sweat sliding down my back. I couldn’t help worrying whether these subtle bodily reactions would become the focus of others’ attention.

The whole day went by, and I still couldn’t fully immerse myself in the dance. After rehearsal ended, the teacher said to us at the dance room door, “You all did well today, keep it up!” I felt a little relieved, but still couldn’t help wondering whether her words really included me, or were simply meant to comfort everyone.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying every detail of the rehearsal over and over. My heartbeat was still racing, and a vague discomfort remained in my stomach. I even began to rehearse the embarrassing scenes that might happen in the next class: missing the beat, falling to the floor, everyone’s eyes gathering on me... This pattern of self-attack seemed to be protecting me in advance from possible humiliation.

A few days later, I found myself becoming more silent in class, avoiding bringing up dance class. When talking with friends, I couldn’t help repeatedly checking whether they truly had no dissatisfaction with me or whether they were annoyed by me. The shadow of anxiety still refused to fade.

In the rehearsal room, the mirrors on the wall reflected the shadows of our running figures as the teacher played the accompaniment over and over on the electronic keyboard. I stood near the corner, gripping the hem of my clothes. The formation was counting down to my side; it was my turn to perform that solo dance segment. I took a deep breath and suddenly felt as if a lump of ice had formed in my stomach, my fingers cold too. I had practiced this many times just now, and each time there were some details that weren’t perfect, like not fully pointing my toes when landing, or not controlling my balance in the spin. The teacher had said to make it more natural, but why were my legs still so stiff, moving slowly and in a mess?

“Come on, let’s go through that section again.” The teacher’s voice was gentle, but it sounded a little distant to me. I walked to the center in front of the mirror, and the classmates around me all stopped and stepped aside. I could feel their eyes on me, a little pricking. I started stepping and turning, trying hard to keep my footwork on the beat of the music. Just as I was turning the third circle, my foot slipped, and my body drifted away from the position I had planned. I hurried to adjust my weight and continue, but everything was already completely off.

“Stop for a moment.” The teacher pressed a key, and the music cut off abruptly. “Your weight shifted just now, and the rest of the formation couldn’t follow.” Her tone wasn’t harsh, and there was no blame, but my face quickly grew hot, as if something had been brutally torn open. I nodded and said, “Okay,” then quickly stepped back to the side and took a big sip from my water bottle. The water went down my throat slowly, as if reminding me of my mistake just now.

A classmate muttered quietly, “They’re always like this, making the rest of us rehearse several extra times.” The voice was very soft, but it was right by my ear. I didn’t know who said it, or whether they had said it by accident, but that “always” felt like a sharp needle prick. I lowered my head and stared at the floor, pretending I hadn’t heard it, but my mind was already starting a chain reaction: did they all think I wasn’t up to it? Did they wish even more that I wouldn’t take part in this performance?

“Are you okay?” my friend came over and asked me. I shook my head, then immediately added, “Was I really that bad? Did everyone… think I was dragging them down?” She frowned and said, “No, you’re overthinking it.” But I searched her expressionless face for a few seconds and couldn’t find anything that would truly reassure me.

After rehearsal ended, I walked out of the classroom. It was already dark, with only a few streetlights on, casting the shadows on the ground into long and short shapes. My palms were covered in sweat, and I gripped the water bottle tightly, feeling that if I loosened my hold, I would fall apart. With my head down, I went into a small convenience store outside the school gate and casually picked a bag of chips, wanting to eat something to ease the anxiety churning in my stomach. When I got home, I didn’t dare bring up rehearsal with my parents. I just sat at my desk in a daze, the classmate’s whispered “always” echoing in my ears. That night, I lay in bed staring at the ceiling, turning over several times and unable to fall asleep. I kept thinking that maybe if I performed a little more confidently, they wouldn’t think I was a burden.

Before the game began, I stood by the basketball court, feeling a gentle breeze brush against my cheeks as the sun was just about to peek out from behind the clouds. It was the school’s annual basketball tournament, and I had been chosen by my classmates as a reserve player. That brought me a little comfort, but far more than that, I felt uneasy. There was some noise around the court; I could hear my classmates cheering and the sound of shoes scraping across the floor. The game was about to start, and every player was doing their final warm-up, all looking full of fighting spirit.

I thought to myself, “What if I can’t catch the ball properly, or make a mistake on the court? Will I be laughed at?” That thought made my stomach clench and my heart race, and my whole body began to feel a wave of tense heat.

A teammate patted me on the shoulder and smiled, saying, “Come on, you can do it.” I gave a slight nod, though I still doubted whether I could handle the role. The referee’s whistle sounded in my ear, and the game officially began. I watched every move on the court, trying as quickly as possible to analyze and understand the next strategy.

Suddenly, a teammate passed the ball to me. I instinctively reached out to catch it, but the ball slipped from my fingertips. I froze for a moment and watched it roll toward the edge of the court. My heart beat even faster, and I could almost feel my teammates’ gazes gathering on me as my mind went blank. “How could this happen?” That instant seemed to stretch out endlessly. My face began to burn, and my palms kept sweating.

“It’s okay, keep going!” I heard the teacher’s encouraging voice from the sidelines. Even so, I still felt a deep sense of self-blame, repeating to myself over and over, “I really am such an idiot.”

The game continued, and I worked hard to adjust my mindset so that the small mistake wouldn’t affect the rest of my performance. A few minutes later, I actually caught a pass and successfully passed the ball to a teammate. That made me relax a little, and my heartbeat gradually steadied.

When I got home, I lay on my bed, still replaying every detail of the game in my mind, especially the moment the ball slipped from my hands. Even days later, I would occasionally think of that moment, worrying whether some classmates had formed a bad impression of me. At the same time, I secretly looked forward to doing better in the next game.

Today our class had dance rehearsal in the school dance studio. The studio was dimly lit, with only a few pendant lights illuminating the whole room, and the air was filled with the smell of old wooden floors and sweat. I stood in front of the mirror, trying to remember the dance steps the teacher had just demonstrated. “Kid, make your left-turning movement a little smoother,” the teacher reminded me from the side. I nodded and tried again, but every time I waved my arms and turned around, I felt my movements becoming stiff. My heartbeat began to quicken, and fine beads of sweat appeared on my forehead. I told myself that if I tried one more time, I would definitely do better. Every time I turned and saw myself in the mirror, feeling ashamed of my mistakes, a surge of negative emotions and memories churned in my mind. I imagined myself making a fool of myself on performance day because of stiff movements, standing frozen on stage. “That turn you just did was already pretty good, don’t worry,” a classmate beside me comforted me. I forced a smile, but I couldn’t shake my unease. I always felt that there was a veiled criticism of me hidden in their words. As the rehearsal continued, my stomach began to ache faintly. “Why am I always like this?” I complained to myself, trying to relax. That night, after returning home, I sat at my desk, replaying the afternoon rehearsal over and over in my mind. I tried to analyze my classmates’ expressions and the teacher’s tone, wondering whether they were talking about me behind my back. I forced myself to prepare for the next practice, mentally reenacting the details of the movements again and again. A few days later, dance rehearsal started again. I still felt nervous, but I tried not to overreact. I worked hard to focus my attention on the music and the dance steps, hoping my body could move with the rhythm and loosen up. The teacher smiled and encouraged me, “You did much better today, keep it up!” This made me feel a little relieved, but deep down I was still afraid of making mistakes again. Although unease and anxiety filled every rehearsal, I was still determined to keep trying. Because I knew that no matter the outcome, the act of trying itself was progress.

During music class, sunlight streamed through the classroom windows and fell across the desks, reflecting a faint halo of light. The teacher told us to divide into small groups to discuss the upcoming music showcase. I stared at the whiteboard, trying not to pay attention to the whispers around me. As soon as the group discussion began, I felt a little uneasy, my palms slightly sweaty. We decided that I would be in charge of the piano part, but I kept suspecting they were only humoring me. The sheet music in front of me was clear, yet I found it hard to concentrate.

“You’ll play the piano, okay?” a classmate turned and said, in a calm tone.

I nodded, but I couldn’t suppress my nervousness. “Of course.” As I said it, my throat felt a little tight.

The classmates beside me began discussing the arrangement of the other instruments, but I couldn’t help focusing on every word they said, trying to detect any hidden criticism or dissatisfaction. When I heard them talking about the difficulty of the piece, my heartbeat began to quicken, as if every word in my ears carried enormous pressure.

“Are you sure you’ll be okay?” another classmate asked again.

I instinctively nodded, trying hard to stay calm. “No problem, I’ll be ready.” But in my mind, many uneasy scenes surfaced: if I made a mistake during the performance, what would everyone think? Would my error affect the entire presentation?

After the discussion ended, I kept ruminating over the conversation, replaying each expression and tone, trying to find the source of my unease. Later, when I got home, I kept feeling a tightness in my stomach, as if worry were twisting inside my body. That night, I tossed and turned in bed, replaying everything that had happened during the day, and the anxiety in my heart only grew harder to shake off.

The next morning, I looked a little haggard, and my thoughts were still stuck on the group discussion. I checked the sheet music again, taking it out to practice over and over, hoping to ease my inner unease with a flawless performance. However, during the repeated practice, my fingers often stiffened, and the doubts in my heart would not go away. I even began to question my own ability, thinking I might become a burden to the group and cause the whole performance to fail.

A few days later, when I returned to class, the group members gave feedback, encouraging me to keep working hard and saying they believed in my performance. I knew it was just an ordinary group performance, but my heart still felt uneasy, as if it could collapse at any moment.

The classroom was a little dim, with several textbooks and notebooks scattered across the desks. Outside the window, a fine rain was falling steadily, and the air was filled with a faint smell of earth and the fresh scent of paper. A few classmates and I sat together, having a discussion after class. “I think this problem should be solved like this,” Xiaoli said, pointing to her own answer. I looked carefully, but felt something was off. “Isn’t that right? Shouldn’t this formula be used like this?” I picked up a pen and tried to explain my point on the blackboard. Just then, I noticed Xiaoli’s brow furrow slightly, and her tone seemed a little displeased. “You’re always like this. Why do you always have to argue with me?” she said.

My heart suddenly sank, and my pulse quickened, as if a heavy stone were pressing on my chest. My face felt hot, and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my forehead. “I just wanted to help. There’s no need to get so upset,” I heard myself say, but my voice already carried some tension and unease. I began to wonder whether there was something wrong with the way I handled things. Why was it always so hard for me to communicate smoothly with others? Had I done something wrong again? A sudden wave of panic awakened the fear of abandonment I had once felt, as if they were all drawing away from me.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying that scene over and over, feeling that I had been misunderstood. My heart was still beating a little fast, and my stomach ached faintly, as if my body were resisting this unpleasant memory. I considered whether I should apologize to Xiaoli the next day, but I was afraid she would reject me again. The darkness around me seemed to swallow my thoughts, and I couldn’t stop blaming myself. The next day, I found that I couldn’t concentrate in class, with the conversation between us repeating endlessly in my mind. Every time she turned around, I instinctively avoided her gaze, afraid she still held resentment toward me. It wasn’t until a few days later that this tension eased somewhat, but I still avoided speaking up in after-class discussions, afraid of making the same mistake again.

The sun was so blinding that I could barely keep my eyes open. The sandy dirt of the playground rustled under our feet, its sound irritating in a way that set me on edge. Everyone was preparing for the basketball game that was about to begin, while I felt sweat drip down my palms along the grooves of the basketball, my heart filled with wave after wave of unease. Something seemed wrong, but I couldn’t say what. That oppressive feeling reached its peak when the captain walked over. He patted my shoulder. “Why are you so nervous? You’d better contribute something this time.” My heart suddenly sped up, my whole body tensed, and in an instant my face burned red, as if I had been exposed in front of everyone. 

My teammates were joking with one another, and the easy atmosphere made me feel out of place. I opened my mouth to explain something, but a powerful fear suppressed my voice. “Will they think I’m useless? If I fail, will they abandon me?” These thoughts crashed over me one after another like waves. I stiffly followed them through warm-ups, hearing nothing but my own heartbeat, along with the occasional sneers by my ears. 

The game began, and all I could hear were the spectators cheering and the squeak of sneakers against the floor. I chased after the basketball with all my might, feeling like a puppet soaked through with sweat, my hands and feet no longer under my control. Not long after, one mistake gave the other team a point. I nervously glanced at my teammates; their faces were full of blame and disappointment. “It’s over. They definitely don’t want me anymore.” I thought despairingly, my stomach twisting as sweat broke out on my forehead. I wiped it away hard, as if I were wiping away my self-respect too. 

After the game, everyone gathered in a circle to sum things up. I hardly dared look at their faces, keeping my head down and staring at my shoes. The captain’s voice came to my ears: “We need to do better next time. Someone has to step up this time.” I knew he was talking to me. After everyone dispersed, I was left alone on the court. The sunlight gradually softened, and the evening breeze, carrying the smell of earth, brushed across my face. I felt powerless, tears streaming down uncontrollably. “I really shouldn’t have come to this game,” I let myself sink into that sense of defeat. 

The next day, I hesitated over whether I should apologize to my teammates, but in the end I chose silence. A few days later, the matter of the game gradually faded, but whenever I thought about that period, I still felt uneasy and embarrassed. Although no one blamed me for what I had done wrong, that feeling of being abandoned and blamed lingered for a long time.

I was sitting by the window in the library, and raindrops kept pattering against the glass, making a crisp rhythmic sound. Outside the window, the gray-white sky looked especially dull. I liked this corner; it was usually quiet, making it ideal for me to work with my head down. But this time, my attention was interrupted.

“How do you think we should handle this project?” a classmate asked me. He was sitting opposite me, a classmate I didn’t know very well; we didn’t usually talk much. My heart skipped a beat, and I immediately felt a trace of unease. His voice was gentle, but I always felt that it hid some kind of expectation, and I couldn’t understand his question right away. “I think... maybe we can try analyzing the problem from different perspectives,” I said, trying to keep my voice steady.

But he frowned, seeming dissatisfied with my answer. “That’s not specific enough. Can you explain a bit more?” he urged. I felt a tightness in my stomach, and the discomfort made me wonder whether I had missed something important.

I looked at him, trying to read more from his expression, yet afraid that my interpretation might be wrong. Under the table, my fingers lightly pinched my arm, helping me focus. I tried to think of a better answer, but my mind was in complete chaos.

“We could first look into previous cases and see which approaches were effective,” I finally said, and at that moment I caught a faint musty smell in the library, perhaps because of the rainy weather. I noticed that my voice was a little shaky, and I didn’t know why I was so nervous.

“Okay, that sounds good.” He finally nodded, seeming to accept my suggestion.

Only after he turned and left did I realize my palms were already sweaty, and my heartbeat gradually began to settle. When I looked around again, I saw that the rain had eased off; only a few scattered drops were sliding down the window. That small discussion made me realize that I always seemed to pay too much attention to other people’s attitudes toward me, even to hints that weren’t really important.

That night, after I got home, I lay in bed with that conversation repeatedly running through my mind. Although I knew the other person had meant no harm, I still felt overwhelmed by unease. I kept imagining different versions of the conversation, wondering whether things would have been different if I had been a little more confident.

Over the next few days, whenever I passed the library, I couldn’t help but think of that afternoon’s scene. But I kept telling myself that it was only a small episode in life, and I should try to learn from it rather than remain immersed in that uneasiness.

The corridor was noisy with voices, and the various footsteps made by shoes striking the tiles rose and fell all around me. My palms were covered in cold sweat, and even my shoulders had stiffened with nerves. I clutched the letter I had spent all night writing, rehearsing over and over in my head what I would say in a moment. I kept telling myself it would be fine, that it would be over in at most a few minutes, but my heartbeat was so fast it felt like it would leap out of my throat. I kept repeating his name in my mind, fighting desperately to suppress the urge to turn and run.

He finally appeared, carrying a backpack and walking with his friends. I called his name, my voice trembling uncontrollably. He turned to look at me, with a hint of surprise on his face. The friends beside him stopped too, and no one seemed intent on leaving. I gathered my courage and said, “Can I speak to you alone for a moment?”

He said, “Just say it here.” His tone sounded casual, but the people around us suddenly fell silent, as if waiting for a show. I could feel everyone looking at me; my face was burning, and my fingers trembled so hard on the letter paper. What should I do? I can’t back down.

“I… wrote you a letter.” I handed it to him. He glanced down, then took it. I don’t know whether he truly hadn’t noticed, or whether he deliberately opened the envelope slowly in front of everyone and pulled out the neatly folded sheet inside. He read it with a frown, then looked up, a faint smile lifting the corners of his mouth—a smile that stabbed into my heart like a blade.

“What does this mean?” His voice wasn’t loud, but it was enough for everyone nearby to hear. I froze, not knowing how to answer. He held up the letter as if displaying some kind of trophy. “Do you like me?”

Someone nearby let out a quiet laugh, and another said, “Wow.” I heard myself say, “Y-yes.” My voice was so soft I could barely hear it myself, but he across from me raised his eyebrows. “Sorry, I’m not interested in you.”

Those words hit me like a blow, stunning me completely. I didn’t know where I had gone wrong. I thought writing a letter was a safe and dignified way to do this, but why had it turned out like this? I stood there, feeling the air around me press in from all sides, every pore stinging as if pierced by needles. Tears welled in my eyes, but I bit down hard and refused to cry. I could only nod and say, “Okay, I understand. Sorry for bothering you.”

After saying that, I turned and left, no longer caring whether I bumped into anyone. The ground felt like cotton under my feet, and my arms and legs barely obeyed me. My stomach twisted tightly, and each step felt like I might throw up. Run, hurry and get away from there—that was the only thought in my head. I ran to a corner of the school rooftop and crouched down, and the tears I had been holding back finally came pouring out, unstoppable.

That night, under the covers, I kept reliving his incredulous expression and the laughter of the people around us. I started blaming myself—why had I written that letter? Why had I been so foolish as to think he would take it seriously? I dug my fingernails into my palm, as if only pain could briefly pull me out of the swamp of shame. Even after things gradually died down over the next few days, I still didn’t dare meet the gaze of any classmate, always feeling that they must be laughing at me.

The piano in the classroom began to sound tentatively as the teacher played the notes softly, setting the key for our opening chorus. I stood near the window, sunlight falling at my feet, a little glaring but without warmth. I lowered my head and stared at the sheet music in my hands, feeling as if a heavy stone were pressing down on my chest. The more I tried to sing well, the more my mind went blank. Around me were the scattered humming voices of my classmates; a few had already gotten into the rhythm, their voices clear and confident, while I felt as if something were stuck in my throat. Whatever came out would surely sound harsh and awful.

“Alright, everyone sing the first two lines again, but pay attention to pitch!” The teacher looked at us, his tone seemingly casual, but I could hear the patience wearing thin beneath it. One thought echoed in my head: Is he talking about me? Does he think I sang the worst?

Just then, the girl beside me turned and whispered, “Your pitch sounds a bit off.” My face instantly burned, as if I had been slapped hard. I murmured “thanks,” but I couldn’t stop the overwhelming shame flooding my mind. She meant no harm, so why did every word feel like rejection?

The music started again, and this time we had to follow his piano from beginning to end. “I mustn’t go off-key, I mustn’t...” My palms began to sweat, and my fingers, gripping the sheet music, were slipping slightly. At first I managed to keep my pitch more or less steady, but by the second verse I suddenly realized my voice didn’t quite fit the melody, so I sang even more cautiously. In the end, the softer I tried to sing, the less I could hear myself, until I finally fell completely silent.

“Stop for a moment!” The teacher’s voice cut through the chorus. He stood up, bent over with one hand on the piano lid, and looked at us. My heart shot up into my throat, and my whole body went stiff. Was he about to call me out in front of everyone? I didn’t dare meet his eyes; I just stared at the lyrics on the sheet music, unable to make out a single word.

“There’s nothing wrong. Just relax a little more, don’t force it too much.” He went on to say a few words of encouragement, but they only made me feel worse. For a moment, I pictured him patting other students on the head with a smile, while I was always the one left unnoticed.

After class, I stayed in the classroom with my sheet music and didn’t leave right away, replaying that moment over and over in my mind. Was the chorus stopped because of me? Did my classmates’ faces show impatience, or had they simply not noticed at all? I couldn’t even remember whether I had actually gone off-key in that section. Maybe they had heard it and were secretly laughing at me in their hearts.

I rubbed my temples, feeling a sharp pain in my stomach, as if a finger were stirring inside it. Laughter came from outside the classroom, and I could tell they were talking about the weather, but my mind automatically produced another interpretation: were they outside laughing at me? Thinking that way, I became even less willing to face them outside.

It wasn’t until dusk fell and I heard the cleaning lady mopping in the hallway that I hurriedly packed up and fled the classroom. Along the way, it felt like everyone passing by was talking about me, and my chest was so blocked it felt stuffed with cotton. Once I got home, I locked myself in my room and pretended to study, but I didn’t dare make a sound. I even thought that I would surely embarrass myself in the next exam, and that the teacher was already disappointed in me.

For the past few days, whenever I saw the music homework, my heart would start racing, and even hearing others hum made me feel unbearable. At night, I sat on the edge of my bed flipping through the sheet music, trying to sing it, but each time I would only open my mouth before giving up again.

The classroom was filled with tension, and sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains, casting dappled patterns of light and shadow. I stood on the podium, clutching my speech tightly, my palms already soaked with sweat. The judges sat in the front row, their expressions stern. I cleared my throat, trying to calm myself down. “Honorable judges and fellow students, hello everyone.” I began my speech, my voice trembling a little. More than once, I felt as if I were about to forget my lines. My heart pounded like a drum, and my fingers trembled slightly. When I saw one of the judges frown faintly, my heart sank. Was he dissatisfied with my performance?

I struggled to continue. Whenever I paused slightly, the classroom became eerily quiet. I could hear my own heartbeat echoing in my ears. With every sentence I spoke, I wondered whether they would be captivated or find it utterly dull. Suddenly, I noticed some classmates seemed to be whispering to each other, and a wave of anxiety surged through me. Were they mocking me? I tried hard not to think about any possible negative judgments, and did my best to go on calmly.

“I hope everyone can gain something from this speech,” I concluded, forcing out a smile. After stepping down from the stage, my legs were so stiff I could hardly walk. As I sat back down, I felt a spasm in my stomach. The judges began discussing my performance, and my heart was racing wildly, with a buzzing in my ears. The classroom bell rang like salvation, and the speech contest was finally over.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed the scene over and over. I recalled every expression on the judges’ faces and every whispered remark from my classmates. I wondered whether they were disappointed in me, whether anyone had any recognition for me. Unable to stop myself, I checked my phone for the expected time the results would be announced, but the more I looked, the more uneasy I became.

A few days later, the results were announced, and I got a decent placing. But that brought me little comfort. What I truly couldn’t shake was my harsh self-criticism and my overinterpretation of others’ reactions. Even after everything was over, I still doubted whether I had done well enough.

The cafeteria was always filled with all kinds of sounds: the clatter of plates, the chatter of students, and the hurried footsteps of the cooks. I stood in line, facing a long row of students waiting for lunch. The aroma of food filled the air, but it did nothing to ease my irritation. The line was moving too slowly; every second felt like an hour, and I felt as if my stomach had already pressed against my back.

I lowered my head and stared at the tiles on the floor, one square after another. I couldn’t help thinking over and over: “When will it be my turn? Why does waiting in line always take so long!” Suddenly, I looked up and found that the student next to me was looking at me too. Was he laughing? Or had the corners of his mouth just lifted a little?

“You think the line is really slow too?” I asked tentatively, hoping to get some comfort from his reply. “It’s all right, there are just more people today.” His tone sounded relaxed, but I felt there was something in his words. That feeling brought a certain unease, making my heartbeat a little faster.

My thoughts began to churn rapidly: “Did I do something wrong? Is he making fun of me?” The uneasiness in my heart spread quickly through my body like waves of heat, and sweat silently slid down from my forehead. I rubbed my palms hard, trying to calm myself down.

At last, the line moved forward a little more, and my mood eased somewhat. By the time I finally got my lunch, nearly twenty minutes had passed. I found a seat by the window and tried hard to focus on the food in front of me instead of what had just happened.

But even so, that feeling of unease and embarrassment still would not go away. A few minutes later, that student actually sat down beside me too. “Are you okay? You seemed a little nervous just now,” he asked casually.

“I’m fine,” I quickly shook my head, though I couldn’t help but reflect on how I had overreacted. “I’m just a little hungry.”

That night, lying in bed and thinking about what had happened that day, the more I thought about it, the more I felt I had been making a fuss over nothing. Maybe he was only showing normal concern, and I had overread the expression on his face. I told myself, “Next time, I need to stay calm and not think so much.” Even so, I still couldn’t help wondering whether he would see me differently when he met me the next day.

A few days later, I ran into that student again in the hallway. He smiled at me, and I made an effort to smile back. Although there was still a little embarrassment in my heart, at least I could feel that things were not that bad.

Sunlight streamed through the glass windows into the music classroom, shining on the piano keys and making them especially bright. The teacher stood at the front of the room, scanning us with an expression I couldn’t quite read. “Today, let’s try improvising,” he said with a smile, but to me that smile carried some ominous undertone. My stomach tightened, my palms began to sweat, and my heartbeat quickened. “You go,” he said, pointing at me. I forced myself to stand up, feeling the air around me grow heavy.

“Damn it, what should I say?” I thought frantically. The other students were all looking at me, as if expecting something interesting or at least not too awful. “Relax, it’s okay, it’s just a small exercise.” The teacher’s voice echoed in my ears, but I still couldn’t calm down.

“Fine, let’s begin,” I muttered to myself, trying to force a smile. Taking a deep breath, I picked a melody at random in my head, but my fingers started trembling on the keys. I tried hard to feel the flow of the notes, but my mind was completely blank; I couldn’t think of anything. The melody stumbled out beneath my fingers, and every note made me feel more embarrassed.

The classroom was utterly silent, as if everyone were holding their breath. I could hear my own heartbeat, as though my inner vulnerability were laid bare before the whole world. My face burned, sweat slid down my forehead, and my back was damp with it.

When the last note finally ended in a strained finish, the whole world fell silent again. I sat back down stiffly, trying not to look at the curious or sympathetic eyes around me. “Well done,” the teacher encouraged me. “Improvisation is about being brave enough to try and step outside your comfort zone.” But I knew he was only trying to make me feel less embarrassed.

That night, after I got home, I kept replaying what had happened in class. My stomach ached faintly, and my mind was filled with a sense of failure. I kept blaming myself for being so nervous, for not being able to perform well, for always feeling so inadequate.

Over the next few days, whenever I thought about that music lesson, I felt as though I were trapped in an invisible cage; with the slightest movement, all my anxiety and fear would surge out. I knew I needed to become stronger, and maybe next time I would handle such a challenge better.

There was never enough space on the desk. My physics textbook, notebook, and the cup of milk tea I had just bought occupied a big chunk of the right side, while my deskmate’s math test paper and calculator kept inching over toward me. I looked at the paper pressed right up against my elbow, and anger started to rise in me. “Can you stop pushing your stuff over here all the time?” I finally said in a low voice, trying to keep my emotions in check. She looked up at me, her expression calm but with a hint of impatience in her eyes. Her voice was slightly raised. “I don’t have enough room here. Should I put my things on the floor?”

My heartbeat immediately sped up, as if some heavy weight were pressing down on my chest. I forced myself to take a deep breath, but my eyes uncontrollably kept drifting to her side of the desk, trying to figure out: was she really short on space, or did she just want to crowd over here? I could hear my classmates roughhousing in my ears, louder than usual. The air was filled with the salty smell of sweat mixed with textbook paper, and the whole classroom was buzzing restlessly.

“I didn’t say you had to put them on the floor, but at least don’t push them over to my side, right?” I tried to keep my tone calmer, but my hand had already unconsciously nudged my own physics book a little farther to the right, making a small open space. She raised her eyebrows, then kept writing on her test without even looking up, as if she hadn’t noticed my concession at all.

At that moment, my stomach gave a slight twist, as if someone had tied a knot inside it. “Is she deliberately ignoring me?” That thought almost immediately flashed through my mind, followed by a surge of humiliation at being dismissed. A voice inside me was shouting to argue with her, but another part of me reminded me that this was only a small matter and not worth causing more trouble. I stared at her pen, watching her forcefully write line after line of formulas, and one question after another of doubt and resentment welled up in my mind: “Is she doing this on purpose? What did that look just now mean?”

Ten minutes later, the bell for class break rang. My tense shoulders suddenly loosened a little, and my deskmate packed up her things and stood up to leave. She said nothing, not even leaving me a glance. I sat there in a daze, my mind in total chaos. Around me were classmates’ laughter and chatter, desks being pushed back and forth, and my hand pressed against the physics book, the spot already sticky with sweat. It took several seconds before I slowly stood up. As I packed my things away, I couldn’t help thinking: “Am I being too sensitive and making a big deal out of nothing? But her reaction really was too cold...”

After I got home, the matter was still circling in my mind. I sat at my desk reviewing physics, but I kept replaying her expression and tone from that moment over and over. That feeling of being looked down on was like a tiny fish stranded on the beach, slowly draining away all my energy. Even before bed, my stomach still ached faintly.

The air in the laboratory was thick with the smell of chemicals, and sunlight streaming through the window cast mottled shadows across the tabletop. I sat beside the lab bench, facing what seemed like a simple chemistry experiment: mix two reagents and observe the color change. Silently, I kept repeating the teacher’s instructions to myself, but my hands wouldn’t quite obey me and were trembling slightly. In the lab, my classmates were talking in low voices, with the occasional soft laugh and the clinking of test tubes. I lowered my head, feeling as if all their eyes were turning toward me.

“You’re not doing it right. Why don’t I do it for you?” The classmate sitting opposite me suddenly leaned over and said. Her tone sounded joking, but I couldn’t help shivering inside, and I almost couldn’t lift my head. “It’s okay, I can do it,” I hurriedly replied in a low voice, trying to hide the unease on my face.

A voice kept echoing in my mind: if I fail, everyone will laugh at me. Why can’t I even handle this simple little experiment? I wanted to cover my ears and stop listening to the sounds around me. My stomach began to churn, and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my palms. I tried hard to concentrate, but my heartbeat felt as if it were about to leap out of my chest.

At last the experiment was finished, but the result was not ideal—the color change was somewhat blurred and indistinct. I bit down hard on my lower lip, replaying every step in my mind and repeatedly wondering where I had gone wrong. Although the teacher didn’t criticize me specifically, I still felt my face growing hot, as if I were being scrutinized by an invisible gaze.

“Just be more careful next time. Everyone has a first time, after all,” said a classmate who usually got along well with me, trying to comfort me. Her smile was kind, but at that moment I didn’t dare meet her eyes. I only nodded, still wondering whether she was implying that I really was terrible.

That night, lying in bed, I thought about what had happened today, and my stomach started aching faintly again. I kept imagining the expressions on the teacher’s and classmates’ faces when they saw me fail, and it felt as though the sound of laughter from daytime was echoing in my ears once more. The next morning, I almost didn’t want to go to school, afraid of facing my classmates’ whispered conversations and the possibility of being laughed at again.

But after a few days, the incident with that experiment gradually faded away in class, as if it had never happened. No one mentioned it again, and I finally felt relieved, thinking that I had at last gotten through it. I told myself that next time I had to be much more careful and never make the same mistake again.

I stood on a woodland path, surrounded by dense trees, with occasional shafts of sunlight slipping through the leaves. All around me was a murmuring hush as my classmates discussed the natural science lesson the teacher had just given. Above us, a squirrel darted quickly from one tree to another; I could almost feel the tiny patter of its feet and the soft rustling of branches and leaves. The teacher’s voice seemed farther and farther away in my ears, while my thoughts were pulled elsewhere. As the teacher began asking questions, my heartbeat quickened and my palms grew slightly sweaty. I tried hard to remember every detail I had read earlier in the textbook. “What do you think about the shape of this leaf? What is special about it?” he asked one of the students, and my heart sank at once, because I knew I might be next. Although I was not unfamiliar with this knowledge, expressing my thoughts in public always made me feel more nervous than ever before.

“It looks like a dandelion seed,” the student beside me answered, her tone firm and confident. I tried to steady my breathing, telling myself this was only a simple class discussion. Yet familiar images kept surfacing in my mind: losing focus, giving the wrong answer, and then the awkward silence and curious looks from my classmates. I was terrified of that feeling of being noticed. A quiet laugh came from nearby, and my stomach suddenly tightened, as if a heavy stone were pressing down on it, impossible to describe. Just as I strained to focus on the teacher’s continued explanation, my mind began rehearsing every possible worst-case outcome: being mocked, being isolated, even being too afraid to come to class again.

That night, lying in bed, I still could not shake off the tension from the day. I kept wondering whether I was too sensitive, whether I always overinterpreted the atmosphere around me, whether I always made a mountain out of a molehill. Though I knew these reflections would not truly solve anything, I could not stop blaming myself. Perhaps tomorrow I would be braver and at least try to speak up in class and share my thoughts, instead of merely standing aside and watching in silence, refusing to let other people’s opinions control me. Even a small change might help me become less afraid of being ignored and rejected.

When the library doors are pushed open, there is always a faint smell of paper mixed with the scent of disinfectant. The air is a little cool, probably because the air conditioning is set too low. My friend and I go in one after the other; she keeps her head down, looking at her phone, while I look around, scanning the library’s situation for the day. In fact, we come here almost every weekend, and I suppose that counts as a kind of understanding between us. The librarian at the entrance glances at us but says nothing else. Maybe she already recognizes us and won’t ask that familiar question, “Did you bring your ID?” anymore.

“Should we go to the second floor today? I think it’s quieter there,” I say softly.

“Sure, but I need to find a novel first.” She looks up at me briefly, then heads straight to the literature section. I follow behind her, catching sight of many familiar titles along the way, and somehow feel a sense of comfort, as if these books have become part of my life. She picks a novel with a flashy cover, while I take a book on psychology, titled The Logic of Emotions.

We find a corner on the second floor and sit down there, next to the window. Sunlight filters through the glass and casts a soft pattern of light and shadow on the floor. Sitting in the soft chair, I open the pages; the small print appears before my eyes, yet there is a quiet pull that keeps me reading. She is buried in her novel, occasionally turning a page with a delicate rustling sound. I can feel the atmosphere of the library enveloping me, the distinctive scent of the pages mingling with the sunlight, making it impossible not to relax.

“Look at this part—it’s so funny,” she suddenly says, looking up and pushing the book toward me. She points to a passage describing something absurd, and I laugh too, though very quietly, afraid of disturbing others. “This author really has a wild imagination,” I say, then lower my head and continue reading my book.

Until after three in the afternoon, we hardly spoke, each immersed in our own world. Now and then I would look up at the window and see children playing in the square in front of the library, with young parents standing nearby watching them, occasionally breaking into smiles. I don’t know why, but scenes like this always make me feel peaceful.

When I was reading a section about ways to regulate emotions, my thoughts paused for a moment. The book mentioned the phenomenon of over-interpretation, seeming to describe some familiar feeling. I stared at that sentence for a long time, sensing a faint and strange resonance in my heart, but I couldn’t quite put my finger on what it was. Maybe it was because this week’s school life had left me a little tired; some of the teachers’ words always seemed to carry deeper meaning, though they might not mean anything at all.

In the evening, we closed our books, packed up our things, and prepared to leave. “How was the book today?” she asked me.

“Pretty interesting,” I nodded.

“Then let’s come again next week and choose something different,” she said with a smile, then walked out of the library with me. The air outside was much warmer, with that special sense of leisure unique to the weekend. I felt my steps becoming lighter too—perhaps it was just that these few hours of quiet had made my heart smoother as well.

That night, I opened my notebook and wrote down some random impressions about emotions, about the children outside the window, and about those patches of light and shadow. I don’t know whether these feelings were profound, but at least they made me feel a little warm.

The air in the classroom seemed more stifling than usual. The afternoon sunlight streamed through the windows and fell across my desk, making my eyes sting. I sat at the round table for our group discussion, holding a pen and pretending to jot something down, but my mind was already completely blank.

“So, we’ve unanimously decided that you’ll summarize this part.” The group leader looked at me and slightly lifted her chin. I wasn’t sure whether I sensed a trace of impatience in her tone, and I also couldn’t tell whether that sentence was a suggestion or an order. I realized I had apparently missed the key part of the discussion just now. “Huh? What?” I blurted out instinctively, my voice trembling a little from nerves.

“This part—you’re in charge of summarizing it,” she repeated, with what seemed like a faint smile on her face, but to me that smile felt more like mockery.
