The other few people also looked at me; someone lowered their head to flip through a book, someone else pressed their lips together. My stomach suddenly felt tied in knots, my palms began to sweat, and the sweat on my back clung to my school uniform, making me even more uncomfortable. A voice inside me was shouting: Do they all think I’m useless? Do they think I don’t belong in this group?

“Oh, okay, I’ll give it a try,” I said stiffly, forcing out a smile, but my voice was still as faint as a mosquito’s buzz. I picked up my pen and stared at the blank notebook, as if expecting it to write the answer itself.

At that moment, one group member muttered under his breath, “Hope this goes smoothly this time.” His voice was very soft, but I heard it clearly. I couldn’t even be sure he was talking about me, but in that instant I felt my face flush all at once, as if I’d been slapped in the face. Was he implying that I’d done badly before? Was he saying I was holding up the progress?

I barely heard the rest of the discussion. My mind was filled with those murmurs and the looks that were cast my way. I tried hard not to dwell on it, but my heartbeat kept speeding up, and my chest felt unbearably tight, as if something were blocking it. Even when I forced a smile and nodded along, I still felt like I was embarrassing myself in front of everyone.

After the discussion ended, I was the first to rush out of the classroom. I went to a corner of the hallway, leaned against the wall, and panted, gripping my school uniform sleeve tightly with my fingers. The sounds and expressions from the classroom swirled in my mind like echoes. The more I thought about it, the more I felt that I had done badly, and the more I felt that everyone was laughing at me. Why do I always mess things up? Why can’t I just act like a normal person?

That night, after getting home, I opened my notebook again and wrote down everything that had happened today, even trying to analyze every word the group leader and the other members had said. I recalled their tones and expressions, trying to find more clues to prove that my own judgment was correct, but the more I thought about it, the more I felt like a complete failure. I kept asking myself: Why does it turn out like this every time? Is there really something wrong with me?

The next day, I really didn’t want to face my groupmates again, but I still went to school, bracing myself. All morning, I avoided making eye contact with those few members, and even when answering their questions, I kept my voice very low. My mind was still replaying yesterday’s scenes, like an old movie that couldn’t be stopped.

Walking down the school hallway, I kept my gaze fixed ahead, my ears filled with the noise of students chatting after class. It wasn’t until I saw her—my former best friend—that the familiar wave of anxiety surged back. She was laughing and talking with a group of classmates, apparently not noticing me at all. Her laughter seemed magnified in my mind, as if every note were mocking me. My heart raced, and I could feel my palms starting to sweat.

“Hey,” I said as I walked up to her, filled with doubt and unease. She turned around, froze for a moment, then smiled. “You seem really busy lately. You hardly ever contact me anymore.” I tried to make my tone sound casual, but there was still a trace of blame in my voice. She clearly noticed it, and her smile stiffened instantly.

“Oh, I... schoolwork has been pretty busy,” she said, running a hand through her hair, her eyes shifting uneasily.

In that instant, the defenses in my heart collapsed. The feeling of being abandoned was so intense that I began to doubt whether every one of her actions and expressions was hinting that our friendship was already over. “Too busy to even reply to a message? Or do you just not care about our friendship anymore?” My voice trembled slightly, and I suddenly felt as though I were standing on the edge of a cliff.

Her expression gradually shifted from surprise to anger, and the curious glances of passersby fell on us. I felt even more pressure and humiliation. “It’s not like that! I just...” she tried to explain, but I could no longer listen. The torrent inside me swept away the little reason I had left, and I heard my own sharp voice echoing through the hallway.

For the next few minutes, we argued fiercely, her voice rising with her emotions as well. My face burned, my breathing quickened, and my stomach felt heavy, as if a huge stone had settled in it.

After the argument ended, I stood there frozen. The people in the hallway gradually dispersed, leaving only me alone, facing the empty corridor and the emptiness in my heart that I couldn’t shake. My heartbeat was still racing, my fingers trembling slightly as I tried to calm my agitated emotions.

That night, lying in bed, I tossed and turned, my mind replaying the argument from earlier over and over again. Regret and self-blame wrapped tightly around me like two enormous hands. I began to wonder whether I was really worthy of having friends, or whether I was simply a flawed person who always made a mess of everything.

A few days later, I tried to contact her and sent an apology, hoping to mend the relationship. Her reply was brief and distant, and it stung like I had lost a part of myself. That fear of abandonment surged back once again, and I realized that although I didn’t want to admit it, I was still deeply trapped in it.

I stood by the beverage vending machine in the gym, and the line was moving forward as slowly as a snail. My palms were a little sweaty. Sunlight slanted in through the windows, making the floor gleam, but it was heating up my back. I couldn’t help sneaking another glance toward the front of the line. Two girls were standing by the machine, chatting on their phones, not the least bit in a hurry to choose a drink. I felt as if a ball of fire were burning in my stomach, and my heartbeat seemed a few beats faster than before. I began weighing whether I should just walk over and remind them, but I was also afraid they’d roll their eyes or say something nasty.

“Could it get any slower?” I heard a boy behind me mutter softly. His voice wasn’t loud, but it was definitely clear enough. I turned my head slightly and caught him frowning, his eyes seeming to seek my agreement. I didn’t respond. I just lowered my head and pretended to check my wallet. Honestly, I had no desire to form some kind of “revolutionary friendship in the line” with a stranger, because I didn’t know whether it would turn into an argument.

At last it was my turn. I quickly pressed a few buttons and chose the orange juice I knew best, and then it felt as if a stone in my heart finally dropped away. The machine clicked, the orange juice fell into the slot, and when I reached for it, I realized my fingers were a little cold. I grabbed the drink and didn’t dare linger by the line, practically fleeing out of the gym, still feeling damp across my back.

Back in the classroom, I took a sip of the orange juice. It still tasted like the usual sweet-tart flavor, but this time it somehow seemed a little bitter going down. I kept replaying the boy’s expression in my head—did he think I should have said something too, to hurry the line along? Or did those girls think I was a coward, someone who didn’t dare stand up for her rights, because I stayed silent? These little thoughts tormented me until the evening self-study session ended, and only then did I start to feel a little less awful.

The next morning, when I passed the gym, I had a strange urge to take a detour, but then I felt that would be a bit unnecessary. I told myself that what happened yesterday was only a trivial matter—no one would remember it, and no one would care. But I still felt a faint uneasiness in my heart. In front of the gym entrance, I took a deep breath and hurried into the teaching building.

The classroom was filled with rustling sounds as the teacher wrote a math problem on the blackboard. I stared nervously at the podium, my palms starting to sweat. The teacher called my name and asked me to stand up and explain how to solve the problem. I tried hard to remember, but my mind was a mess. My heartbeat sounded like a drum, pounding through my body one beat after another. The eyes of the whole class were fixed on me, and an invisible pressure hung in the air. I could hear the soft snickering of the students in the front row. “Go on, say it,” the teacher urged. My lips were dry, and my voice was weak and unsteady: “I... I don’t know.” At that moment, the classroom was so silent it felt suffocating, and the muffled laughter that followed stabbed into my heart like needles.

“How embarrassing,” I blamed myself inwardly, my cheeks burning as if all the heat in my body had gathered there. I sat down in a panic, head lowered, not daring to look at anyone again. Every second dragged on so slowly, and my stomach felt knotted, with a dull ache spreading through it.

When the bell for class dismissal rang, I hurriedly packed my bag, wanting to escape that suffocating place. In the hallway, my steps were quick, but an inner voice kept echoing: “Why am I always so useless? They must all be laughing at me.” I couldn’t help but think back to all the similar situations in the past; every mistake felt like a new wound carved into my heart. I felt utterly ashamed and frustrated, as if I had been abandoned alone on a deserted island.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to fall asleep. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw the classmates’ mocking laughter and the teacher’s disappointed gaze. The next day, I delayed going to school for a long time, afraid of facing them again. I rehearsed countless times in my mind the scene of myself being laughed at, and the more I thought about it, the more hopeless I felt.

After a few days, I began avoiding speaking in class. I often pretended I was taking notes, while deliberately avoiding eye contact with the teacher and my classmates. At night, I stood in front of the mirror practicing over and over, trying to improve the way I spoke, but the fear and shame in my heart never truly faded.

The classroom lights were a little dim and yellowish, and the glass by the window was coated with moisture, faintly reflecting the darkening sky outside. The debate competition was starting in half an hour, and my group members and I were gathered around a table near the front, urgently discussing the final points of our speeches. The air was thick with the smell of draft paper, and everyone’s discussion mixed with the low murmurs of other groups nearby, making the classroom feel slightly noisy.

“We need to make our position clear, or the audience will think our response is weak!” said the boy sitting next to me in a somewhat louder voice. His tone sounded a little rushed, as if he were subtly blaming someone for not preparing enough. I lowered my head and looked at the draft on my desk, a wave of unease rising in me. I kept feeling that his tone was directed at me. “Does he think I missed something important again? Do they all think I’m not capable enough?” In my mind, I immediately replayed the previous few meetings. I remembered them seeming to frown at some of my suggestions, and now that I thought about it, maybe they had been thinking I wasn’t professional enough.

“What do you think?” another girl sitting in front turned to ask me. I jerked my head up and found everyone’s eyes on me. My heart sped up, the tips of my ears grew hot, and my palms began to sweat, yet my mind was blank. The air felt thick, and breathing became difficult. Feeling guilty and uncertain, I lowered my voice and replied, “I think... maybe... we could start with the relevant data.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I regretted them. How worthless that sounded! My face felt like a furnace, and I no longer dared meet anyone’s gaze, staring instead at the pen on the desk.

“Yes, data is important.” Another girl nodded and added, “We can first list the supporting evidence, then summarize it into a strong conclusion.” Her voice was very calm, but I still felt a chill. Was she saying that just to ease my embarrassment? Why wasn’t anyone else speaking up? Were they silently thinking I was terrible? I tried hard to steady my breathing, but my stomach had already started to cramp, and I could only press it gently with my hand.

The discussion continued, and I felt myself gradually being pushed to the edge. The voice in my head grew louder and louder: “What I just said was really childish, wasn’t it? Was it not going to be taken seriously at all? They all think I’m a burden, don’t they?” I even began to suspect they might directly have someone else speak in my place. The tension in my body grew stronger and stronger; my shoulders and neck felt as if they had been tied up, and my fingers unconsciously tightened around the pen.

In the end, the discussion was over, and I didn’t even speak once more. Everyone split up to prepare their own parts, and I walked to the window to calm myself down. The cold glass touched my fingers, as if offering a slight comfort. I stared at the dark, heavy sky outside, filled with self-blame and shame. During the competition, I performed at the bare minimum, trying hard to control my speaking pace and expression, yet I felt my clumsy voice squeezing out of my throat, every word seeming to be put on trial. After the competition, I didn’t even dare make small talk; I hurriedly packed up my things and left.

After I got home, I lay on my bed, unable to stop my thoughts. My mind replayed every detail like a movie, obsessing over whether I had dragged down everyone’s efforts. I clearly could have answered the other side’s questions much better, but there was nothing I could do to change it now. My stomach still ached dully from time to time, so I curled up under the blanket, hoping to fall asleep as soon as possible and forget all of it, but the boy’s urgent voice still echoed in my head, lingering long after.

I stood on the stage in the school auditorium, looking out at the densely packed students below, so nervous I could almost suffocate. The lights shone down from above, illuminating every glance with piercing clarity. I could hear quiet conversations and a few soft laughs by my ears, and a wave of fear of being mocked surged through me. My palms began to sweat, my throat went dry, as if an invisible hand were tightly gripping it. “I won’t mess this up. They won’t laugh at me,” I kept telling myself, hoping to calm the anxiety flooding in.

“Come on, you can do it,” a classmate beside me said softly. I nodded, but the unease in my heart only grew stronger. I began to wonder whether he was truly encouraging me or just being perfunctory. When it was my turn to speak, I could hear my heartbeat quickening. I stiffly walked up to the microphone, my fingers unconsciously clutching the script. The words I had not yet spoken kept turning over in my mind, as if I could already foresee myself mispronouncing every single one. I tried to swallow, then finally began. “Hello everyone, today I want to share with you...” I tried to keep my voice steady, but there were still a few moments when it trembled slightly.

By the third paragraph, I felt a sharp cramp in my stomach, like a clenched fist striking me hard. A thought even flashed through my mind: “What would happen if I fainted here?” and the situation instantly felt a little out of control. My lips began to tremble, as if confirming my inner doubts about my own ability. I heard my voice catch for a second or two, and immediately a wave of self-attack surged through my mind: “How can you be so useless? Everyone is watching you make a fool of yourself.” At that moment, a teacher below the stage gently said, “It’s okay, take your time.” I nodded slightly and did my best to keep going.

After the speech ended, I walked off the stage stiffly, my mind filled with embarrassment and regret. I hardly dared look anyone in the eye, afraid I would see disappointment or ridicule. The whole afternoon, I was immersed in my own inner monologue, repeatedly reviewing every detail of the speech. That night, lying in bed, I was still overwhelmed by feelings of failure and shame, my mind full of the faint laughter from below the stage and the students’ gazes. When I woke up the next day, I decided to go to my teacher first thing in the morning to confirm whether he was truly not angry, and to ask whether he had any criticism of my performance. I found that I was always seeking affirmation from others to dispel my inner self-doubt; even a mild word of comfort could make me catch a glimmer of security.

The moment the test tube hit the floor, it felt as if my brain had been hit with a pause button. Glass shards scattered everywhere, flashing with a cold light, and my hand was still frozen in midair. The tongs I had been holding the test tube with suddenly felt impossibly heavy. I heard a brief gasp from the classmates around me, then the sound of chairs scraping back, followed quickly by the teacher’s voice: “Be careful, there’s broken glass over there!” It carried a note of urgency and warning. I nodded mechanically, my heart already pounding so fast it felt like it might burst through my chest. My face burned in waves, as if every gaze around me were piercing into my back.

“Are you okay? Did you cut your hand?” A girl came closer, her tone much gentler. I think she was only being polite. But I couldn’t help imagining that she was mocking me in her head for not even being able to handle a simple lab procedure. “I’m fine.” My voice was as dry as a wind blowing out of the desert. I lowered my head, trying hard to avoid everyone’s eyes. The glass shards on the floor seemed to be accusing me of my clumsiness, and my stomach began to twist with a dull ache.

The teacher brought over a broom and dustpan and didn’t say much more, only quietly saying, “Don’t move so fast next time.” That reminder stabbed into my heart like a needle. I nodded desperately and hurried to help clean up the fragments, but my fingers trembled so badly on the tongs that I could barely control them. I knew that in truth no one was really paying that much attention to me, but in my mind it was as if a concert had started, with every negative comment shouting at full volume: “How can you be so useless?” “Everyone’s watching you make a fool of yourself!” “Who would still want to be in a group with you after this?” The voices grew louder and louder, almost crushing me.

The faint smell of disinfectant in the lab had once made me feel safe, but now it felt pungent and suffocating. I heard classmates nearby whispering, “Wow, it dropped the moment they touched it.” “Maybe the tongs weren’t held steady?” Their tone carried no malice, but I still felt as if each word were a heavy blow landing on my chest. I tried to pretend I was focused on the equipment on the table, tried to pretend I couldn’t hear them, but my hearing had become terrifyingly sharp. Even the slightest snicker felt magnified tenfold. I began to feel sweat all over my body, and my palms were so slippery I could barely hold the tongs.

That night I sat alone in my room, replaying the scene of the test tube falling over and over in my head, like an old film reel stuck on repeat. I could even hear the sound of the glass shattering again and again—the sharp cracking sound of something bursting from within—which once more tightened my stomach into a knot. I imagined myself walking into the lab the next day, and wondered whether the teacher would look at me with disappointment. If something like this happened again, would people really laugh out loud this time? My mind felt trapped in an endless pit; every attempt to climb out became another round of attacks against myself. I wondered if I would never be able to do these things properly.

A few days passed, and I avoided alltake the initiative socializing, spending even the breaks sitting at my desk in a daze. I tried my best to ignore my classmates’ greetings because I was afraid they would bring up what happened in the lab. Even when they didn’t, I still couldn’t stop stealing glances at their expressions, trying to find any possible hint—was someone still talking about how clumsy I was? But in reality, the “attention” toward me had long since disappeared from their minds, and those malicious stares were nothing more than the phantoms conjured by my own inner demons.

Outside the window, the sky was overcast and gray. Fine raindrops struck the glass, leaving long streaks of water behind. The classroom lights were a bit harsh, reflecting off the desks in a pale, glaring white. I sat at one end of the long table, frantically sorting through the papers in front of me. The air was filled with my classmates’ laughter and discussion, each syllable piercing my ears like needles. I tried hard to focus on the materials, but the sweat on my palms made it impossible to hold my pen steady.

“Next, please come to the front and put on the microphone to prepare your speech.” The judges’ teacher’s voice came from the podium. As soon as I heard it, it felt like I’d been whipped by a sharp voice, and I couldn’t help straightening my back. It was my turn. When I stood up, I could clearly feel my legs were stiff, my steps unsteady, like I was walking on cotton.

The few seconds it took to walk to the podium seemed stretched out infinitely. I could feel everyone’s gaze burning against me, my back feeling as if it had been scorched by a hot iron. I told myself to keep looking straight ahead, but low snickers kept drifting into my ears, as if they were aimed at me. Had someone already criticized my posture for not seeming confident enough? Or did they think I was dressed too casually today? I unconsciously tugged at my hem, only to feel even more awkward all over.

Standing in the center of the podium, I gripped the microphone tightly, my fingers trembling slightly from the force. But the first sentence I spoke came out with a faint quiver. This was bad. I shouldn’t be like this, my mind raced. My gaze inadvertently swept across the judges’ faces; one teacher was lowering his head to take notes, and the corner of his mouth seemed to curl slightly. Had my opening been too plain, making him think I wasn’t professional enough? In an instant, countless scenes flashed through my mind: the judges complaining over tea about some contestant’s poor performance in this selection round, everyone exchanging knowing smiles when that person’s name was mentioned, and me becoming the butt of the joke.

My stomach clenched, and I hurriedly adjusted my breathing. “Next, I’d like to analyze three important aspects of this debate topic.” I went on, but suddenly realized I couldn’t remember one section of my argument no matter how hard I tried. I had clearly recited it countless times just back in my seat—how had it evaporated now? I could feel the judges’ gaze sliding over my shoulder. I looked up instinctively and saw another judge raise an eyebrow. He’s dissatisfied with me, I concluded quickly. It was as if a bucket of cold water had been splashed onto my face; my whole body went cold, but sweat had already started beading on my back. My clothes clung to my skin, wet and sticky.

“So, my point is this…” My voice involuntarily rose, only to tremble at the end. I hurriedly finished my speech, even forgetting the closing remarks I was supposed to say, and then lowered my head and quickly walked back to my seat. Sparse applause sounded here and there, and I felt as if I were in a dream, the sound distant and dim. The moment I sat down, my limbs went weak, yet my heart was pounding so hard it felt like it might burst.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed the afternoon scene over and over in my head. Why had my opening been so flat? Did the judges’ expressions mean I had lost my chance? If I had prepared a little more thoroughly, would everything have been different? It felt as if a stone were pressing on my chest, and the more I thought about it, the harder it was to breathe. I tossed and turned, unable to sleep until after midnight. When I woke the next day, my eyelids were badly swollen, but my thoughts were still stuck in the unfinished rumination from the day before.

During the break, we sat in the classroom. The group discussion had just ended, and I was feeling anxious. Around me was a noisy buzz—desks and chairs scraping, a few people laughing and chatting about something—but all my attention was on the discussion we’d just had. I held a pen and drew circles on my scratch paper, yet my mind kept replaying the same fragments over and over: what I said, their expressions, their tone of voice. When the group leader wrapped up at the end, he glanced at me and simply said, “Mm, not bad.” I nodded and smiled at the time, but doubts filled my mind. What did he mean by that? Was he just brushing me off, or was it genuine approval? Was there something cold in his eyes? Did he think I performed terribly? 

My palms were already a little damp, and the pen pressed harder and harder against the paper. I started reviewing my performance frame by frame, like an interrogation video. Was I speaking too quickly? Was my voice a little shaky? I clearly thought I had prepared for a long time, but suddenly I began to wonder whether the examples I chose were too ordinary. I started to regret not picking a more impactful story. Why didn’t they respond to my joke? Or was I never supposed to say those lighthearted things in the first place? Was that person’s tone really just “not bad”? Was it praise, or criticism? 

“What are you spacing out for?” A student from the neighboring group tapped my desk and pulled me back from my thoughts. I looked up and forced a smile. “Nothing, just doodling.” He said, “You did pretty well just now.” I nodded quickly, but I didn’t quite buy it. Why did he say “pretty well” instead of “great”? Did “pretty well” actually mean just so-so? Was he only trying to comfort me? I even started to suspect that maybe he thought I talked too much, so he deliberately said something nice to brush me off.

My stomach started to feel a little unsettled, as if a stone had been shoved inside. I didn’t want to talk to anyone anymore, so I lowered my head and kept drawing circles. At that moment, I didn’t even know what I was drawing—I just needed something to do to escape the doubts flooding into my head. When I spun my pen, my fingers were damp, and I felt an indescribable sense of suffocation, as if someone were standing beside me, staring at me and smiling the whole time.

A few days later, those memories would still resurface. Sometimes when I was washing my face, or when I saw the group leader walk past in the hallway, I would involuntarily start thinking about that discussion again. How exactly had he judged me? If I had been less impulsive and spoken in a more composed way, would I have earned more recognition? But I knew I shouldn’t keep dwelling on such a small thing, so I kept telling myself that “not bad” might really have been nothing more than an ordinary comment, with no deeper meaning at all. Those words calmed me a little, but my mind would still drift back from time to time, as if trapped in a vague memory.

I walked into the school science lab. The cold, gloomy weather outside seeped in through the windows, and the air was filled with a faint smell of disinfectant. I took a deep breath and silently cheered myself on. The lab tables were covered with all kinds of equipment, and the teacher was explaining today’s experiment up front, with the sound of the cold wind howling constantly outside as background noise. I stared at the teacher’s lips, trying hard to keep up with every word, but my mind kept flashing with scenes of what might go wrong.

The child sitting next to me gently nudged me. “Hey, are you okay?” I nodded, trying to appear calm, but my heartbeat was silently speeding up, and my palms were sweating. I was always afraid I would make a mistake and then be publicly called out by everyone, so I often harshly criticized myself several times beforehand in my mind. The teacher handed out some reagents, and I took them carefully, my fingers trembling slightly, my gaze falling on the transparent liquid. I wiped the sweat from my forehead with the back of my hand, trying to make myself look more normal.

After the experiment began, everyone around me seemed so confident, carrying out each step with ease. When I used the dropper to draw up the reagent, I could feel the stiffness in my fingers and the uncontrollable trembling, as if any mistake could lead to serious consequences. “Don’t make a mistake, don’t make a mistake,” I kept telling myself over and over. Suddenly, a little liquid splashed out of the mouth of the reagent bottle and landed on the lab table. I froze instantly, my heart pounding wildly.

“Be careful, it’s okay,” a classmate reminded me at just the right moment. I forced out a smile, but shame and panic surged through me. I felt a dull ache in my stomach, as if all those emotions had erupted in this tiny mistake. For the rest of the time, I was especially careful with every step, afraid of making another mistake.

When the experiment was over, I put away the equipment, trying not to look too embarrassed. As I left the lab, the wind outside was still bitterly cold, and I shoved my hands into my coat pockets, trying to find some warmth. That night, lying in bed, I replayed every detail in my mind, repeatedly blaming myself for not being able to perform better. A few days later, I still kept thinking back to that moment of embarrassment and fear, feeling as though I always did my worst when it mattered most.

Even in conversations with friends, I would sometimes recall the scene in the lab, with a faint sense of self-reproach weighing on my heart. I realized that my fear of failure and rejection was so strong that every small mistake was magnified into a disaster in my mind, becoming a shadow I could not escape.

I stood in the school lobby, waiting for the extracurricular activities to begin. Crowds had gathered here, and the air was filled with the mixed smell of earth and sweat. The clock on the wall ticked, reminding me of the slow passage of time. I gently tugged at my backpack strap, feeling the pressure on my shoulders intertwined with unresolved anxiety. The room was noisy with voices; I heard several classmates nearby talking about yesterday’s game, their voices rising and falling, as if they were trying to pierce through my mind. A girl said to her friend, “Do you think they’ll win?” Her friend replied, “I don’t know, but I really hope they do.” I didn’t join their conversation, just listened in silence. Yet somehow I began to feel nervous, and my heartbeat gradually quickened. Just then, my stomach started to ache faintly, as if reminding me of the anxiety that surfaced from time to time. Why is it always like this? I felt as if I were trapped in a whirlpool of unease, with no way out. The lobby floor was cold, and footsteps rang out clearly, making it seem as though everyone else was more at ease than I was. I did my best to calm myself, trying to focus on the small notebook in my hand. When I opened it, I saw the plans written inside, each one a trace of my efforts. I looked out the window, hoping to find a moment of peace, but the overcast sky dashed that hope. That was just how I was—always unconsciously making things more complicated, as if every detail were telling me a prophecy of failure. Again I felt the self-attack inside me, that familiar voice telling me I wasn’t good enough, not smart enough. I gripped the notebook tightly, trying to use the tangible feel of reality to resist the storm within. The activity finally began, and the noise gradually faded. I followed the crowd into the activity room, feeling the warm light spill down from overhead. That warmth eased my unease, allowing me to relax a little. After the activity ended, I went home in a much better mood. That night, I sat at my desk, trying to concentrate on my homework. Though I was still somewhat restless, I adjusted my emotions by writing down tomorrow’s plans. The next morning, when I woke up, I felt calmer and had a new sense of anticipation for the day ahead. I told myself not to overinterpret what others thought, and not to worry about failure all the time. Slowly, I learned to find a peace of my own deep inside.

On a crisp autumn night, the school astronomy club organized a stargazing event. After school, I hurried to the school’s back courtyard, where a crowd had already begun to gather. A thin moon hung in the sky, surrounded by faint tree shadows and the soft whisper of the wind. There was a hint of chill in the air, reminding me that autumn had truly arrived. The astronomy teachers were busy calibrating several telescopes, while the students nearby were whispering excitedly about the constellations we might see tonight.

“Come on, it’s ready!” an excited voice broke my thoughts. One of the teachers who had come to greet us led us toward a huge telescope. I felt a mix of nervousness and anticipation, my palms sweating uncontrollably.

“This telescope is special—you can see Saturn’s rings through it,” the teacher said with pride. I carefully tiptoed and looked through the lens. I held my breath, my heartbeat seeming to thud in my ears. When I finally adjusted the view and saw that distant planet with its beautiful rings, my breath caught, and I felt an indescribable joy and calm.

“Wow, it’s beautiful—did you see it?” a classmate beside me exclaimed. I nodded, though countless words seemed to surge within me at that moment, all of them pressed down by the awe of that instant.

I stood there as the surrounding sounds gradually blurred away, leaving only a silent exchange between myself and the universe. My fingers lightly touched the telescope’s cold metal, feeling its weight and strength flow into me. The wind behind me gently swept by, carrying the rustle of autumn leaves, as if accompanying the vastness of the sky.

When the event ended and everyone began leaving in small groups, I walked home through the night, the campus shrouded in darkness and distant starlight filtering through the tree shadows. I closed my eyes, and Saturn’s image still lingered in my mind, as if I could still feel the shock of glimpsing the boundless universe.

When I got home that night, I kept spacing out a little, constantly replaying the wondrous sight I had seen through the telescope. It was as if the whole world had become different. Deep in my heart, I said to myself: maybe I can, like those scientists exploring the universe, find my own star. Lying in bed and looking at the night sky outside the window, I felt an exceptionally healing sense of fulfillment, as if the starlight from light-years away were shining through the window into my heart, illuminating a quiet peace I had never known before.

After school, my friends and I went to the coffee shop we often visited near the school. The shop was always filled with the faint aroma of coffee mixed with the scent of sweets, which made people feel relaxed. I ordered a hot chocolate. The warm cup in my hands felt very comforting. The four of us sat at a long table by the window, and sunlight streamed through the large glass panes onto the table, adding a touch of warmth to the cold winter day.

The conversation went on as usual. One friend mentioned an embarrassing incident, and everyone laughed lightly. But I couldn’t help thinking of an embarrassing moment of my own. Perhaps driven by an irresistible desire to join in, I casually said, “Do you think I said something wrong that day?”

One of my friends smiled and said, “You really do worry too much; no one would mind.” Though her tone was light, my heart sank at once. I kept feeling as if her words were criticizing me for being too sensitive. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, my face grew a little hot, and my palms started to sweat. “Do I really care so much about these little things?” I silently questioned myself.

To avoid making things awkward, I forced a casual smile and tried to change the subject: “Have you all been anywhere fun lately?” The others began sharing stories about their weekends, while I kept turning the earlier conversation over in my mind. Whenever I recalled those small exchanges, I couldn’t help wondering whether my friends were really as unconcerned as they seemed.

That night, after I got home, I still couldn’t shake the anxiety that simple remark had triggered. I kept mulling it over, wondering if they thought I was too sensitive, or even that I was always ruining their good mood. I felt uneasy all evening.

A few days later, during a break between classes, I quietly observed the friend who had called me a worrier and noticed that she showed no signs of anything unusual. She chatted with me just as she always did, and everyone was still laughing and joking together as usual. That made me feel a little relieved.

Although the matter had hardly affected our relationship in any substantial way, the discomfort caused by that small misunderstanding lingered on, becoming one of the slightly bitter memories in my heart.

The air in the lab was always filled with a mingled smell of chemical reagents, and the daylight outside the window was somewhat dim. I stood in front of the lab bench, arranging various glassware and reagent bottles. The teacher was explaining the experimental steps in a slightly hurried tone, while the students around me were talking softly. I, however, was only focused on my own part and had barely even heard the teacher’s final reminder.

When I carefully poured the reagent bottle containing sodium chloride solution into the graduated cylinder, my hand suddenly trembled uncontrollably. The bottle tilted, and the liquid spilled out sharply, splashing onto the lab bench and my sleeve. I froze for a few seconds, feeling my face flush hot all at once, and it seemed as if I could hear the sharp intake of breath from the students around me. Someone said softly, “Why are you so careless?”

“Sorry, sorry!” I hurriedly grabbed tissues to wipe it up, but the spilled reagent spread far beyond what I could manage. My hands began to tremble slightly, and the teacher’s warning just now flashed through my mind at high speed: “Be sure to work carefully, or there may be danger.” I began to criticize myself as harshly as possible: “How can you be so stupid, not even able to pour a reagent properly! Everyone must think I’m a burden!”

The teacher quickly came over, his tone still fairly calm, but I felt that every word he said was pointing directly at my mistake: “Stop the other steps first and clean up the area around you.” I nodded hard, my lips pressed tightly together, my heart jolting as if pushed by an invisible hand, and I was almost unable to focus at all. I could even feel sweat beginning to form on my forehead, and the grip of my hand on the tissue became tighter and tighter.

My deskmate whispered, “It’s okay, it’s not serious.” But when I heard this, it felt as if she were comforting a hopeless failure. I forced out a smile, lowered my head, and continued wiping up the reagent, only to find that my hands could no longer control my movements very well. Even wiping had become messy and laborious. A faint cramping pain appeared in my stomach, and a familiar voice of self-attack echoed in my mind: “You’re always this stupid, always disappointing people.”

After the experiment ended, I silently packed up my schoolbag, almost without the courage to look anyone in the eye. After I got home, I took off my wet sleeve and, while washing it, kept replaying that moment in the lab over and over again. I remembered the teacher’s expression, the students’ murmurs, and my own trembling hands, as if I were facing a trial. When I lay in bed at night, I still could not stop the replay of this “disaster” in my mind, like a loop button being pressed again and again. I even began to doubt whether I was suited for this course at all. If this was only a beginner’s experiment, did that mean I was simply incapable of handling more complex study?

A few days later, I avoided standing in the center position at the lab bench and deliberately chose a spot near the edge, trying to keep myself away from the spotlight. I found that I had begun silently overchecking every experimental step, repeatedly confirming whether each one met the teacher’s requirements. Before every action, I had to take a deep breath, trying to suppress the tension inside me. I even rehearsed every step in advance, but even so, the shadow of fearing failure again still would not go away.

The rehearsal room was filled with the noisy sounds of instruments, with voices intertwined in a somewhat chaotic blend. We were getting ready for the final rehearsal for the upcoming campus music festival. I sat beside the drum set, drumsticks in hand, eyes fixed on the score, but I still felt that something was off. The band conductor walked over, patted my shoulder, and said, “Could the drums be a little softer? They seem to be drowning out the other parts.” I nodded, but my heart started racing, my palms grew slightly sweaty, and the drumsticks began to slip a little.

“Why is it always me who makes mistakes?” That question kept circling in my mind as I tried to stay calm, but a sense of shame had already begun to grow inside me. To keep the others from seeing the unease on my face, I lowered my head and mechanically adjusted the volume, afraid of being called out again.

A few measures later, the guitarist suddenly stopped playing and frowned at the conductor. “Some parts are still too loud. I can’t hear my own notes.” In an instant, I felt the blood rush to my face, panic rising within me. “Is he talking about me? Or does he mean some other part?” Every word felt like a stab of pain I could hardly bear. The conductor only looked back at me and said nothing, but that glance made me feel utterly uncomfortable.

“It’s okay, don’t think too much,” I kept telling myself, but a dull ache began in my stomach, and that familiar tension mercilessly spread through my body. Throughout the entire performance, I felt like I was walking on thin ice, terrified of making another mistake. Whenever my classmates chatted and laughed, I always felt they were talking about me, and the slight upward curl of their mouths seemed tinged with mockery.

After rehearsal ended, I quickly packed up my instruments, wanting to escape this suffocating place. Only after I stepped out of the rehearsal room and felt the cool wind on my face did I begin to calm down a little. My mind kept replaying what had just happened, and every look and every tone of voice felt like a detail under a magnifying glass, making me unbearably sensitive.

That night, lying in bed, I kept thinking over everything that had happened during the day, unable to control the way I analyzed every sentence and every expression. I kept blaming myself for always overthinking and not doing well enough. The next day, on my way to school, I even considered quitting the music festival, but I tried to convince myself to give it another shot; maybe things wouldn’t be that bad.

A few days later, I took the initiative to talk to the band conductor and clear up the misunderstanding. He told me that everyone was actually nervous, and they just wanted to perform better. That conversation helped me feel a little better, but I knew this sensitivity and unease wouldn’t disappear easily.

Our group walked out of the gym, sweat soaking through my T-shirt. The last rays of the setting sun spilled over the field, and the orange light seemed like a warm veil. The volleyball team practice had gone on longer than usual, and I could feel every muscle in my body protesting. Just a moment ago, I had mishandled a crucial ball, and the whole team lost the scrimmage because of my mistake. Although no one blamed me, I could feel my teammates’ gazes, an invisible weight pressing on my heart.

“It’s okay, you’ll do better next time.” The captain patted my shoulder and said with a smile. But that wasn’t what I thought at all. I unconsciously lowered my head and pretended to tie my shoelaces, really just trying to hide the embarrassment on my face. I knew I shouldn’t care this much, but that mistake kept replaying in my mind like a movie that wouldn’t stop.

I could feel my heartbeat getting faster and faster, sweat seeping into my palms, and even the fingertips gripping the ball were slightly cramped. Laughter from my teammates filled my ears, yet all I could hear was a voice inside me: “How many more times are you going to mess up?”

After practice ended, I walked home. The cherry blossom trees along the road swayed gently in the breeze, and petals occasionally fell onto my shoulders. I looked down at the ground, thinking about my mistake just now. If I had been more focused, more careful, would it have gone wrong? A strong sense of self-attack surged up inside me, and I began to doubt whether I was really suited to be on this team. That same unchanging worry and unease returned, like a cloud that refused to go away.

The next day, I still came to school carrying that feeling. Throughout the morning classes, I couldn’t concentrate and could only mechanically copy down what the teacher wrote on the board. Even at lunch, I couldn’t help but keep looking at my classmates’ expressions, guessing whether they were still thinking about yesterday’s mistake. “What’s there to worry about? It’ll pass,” a friend said to comfort me.

But I still couldn’t manage a relaxed smile. There was always a sense of unease in my heart, as if some hidden mockery was about to come crashing down. I knew I shouldn’t be troubled by such seemingly small things, but that was just how I was: rehearsing negative outcomes felt like an endless loop that I couldn’t stop.

A few days later, I finally tried talking to the coach. He patiently told me, “Everyone makes mistakes. What matters is learning from them. I believe in your ability—that’s why I chose you.” Those words gave me a sense of relief, and although the unease deep inside me didn’t disappear completely, at least I knew that someone believed in me.

Sunlight streamed through the classroom windows of the school, and I sat in a classroom with several other classmates, preparing for an upcoming academic club event. The air was filled with the smell of cleaning agent from recently mopped floors, and the chalk marks on the blackboard looked especially glaring in the sunlight.

After more than ten minutes of discussion, Classmate B joked, “Isn’t this plan of yours a bit too detailed? I don’t even have time to finish reading it.” He laughed somewhat helplessly, and the others laughed along with him. My heart tightened, and the pen I was holding suddenly stopped moving. How could this be? I had clearly spent several nights on it.

Unease began to churn inside me: was he implying that I hadn’t done a good job, or that all the effort I had put in was meaningless? Thinking of this, my heartbeat quickened and my palms began to sweat. The other classmates seemed not to notice my reaction and continued discussing other matters.

“Maybe I just didn’t grasp the key points...” I muttered self-mockingly, trying to ease the tension inside me. However, B suddenly turned serious: “Hey, that’s not what I meant. We just think it doesn’t need to be so detailed; you should focus on the important parts and not sweat the small stuff.”

I nodded, but inside I was enveloped by an indescribable sense of hurt, as if every word were stabbing into my heart like a needle. That feeling of being abandoned came back again, and it made me deeply uneasy.

On the way home, I walked alone along the school path. The cool breeze blowing toward me helped me clear my head a little, but the voices in my mind kept replaying what had happened today. The more I thought about it, the more I felt as if I had done everything wrong. At dinner, my mother asked, “Why are you not very happy today?” I could only force out a smile: “It’s nothing, I’m just a little tired.”

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my heartbeat still racing. Thinking back to Classmate B, the stomach pain started again. How did it end up like this after all? In the long night, I repeatedly replayed the conversation from the day, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt I should confirm in person how to improve my plan, yet I was unable to break free from the emotions of self-doubt that overwhelmed me.

A few days later, I finally gathered the courage to talk to Classmate B. In the end, he said very casually, “Oh, I was just joking. It really wasn’t a big deal. I think you did a pretty good job.” His reaction surprised me a little, and at the same time I felt relieved, and my heartbeat gradually calmed down. Although this uneasy feeling always appears without reason, I realized that perhaps some things are not as serious as I thought.

I sat in the corner of the classroom, surrounded by noise as my classmates chatted and joked with one another. Sunlight streamed through the window onto the floor, forming a bright patch. I was flipping through my textbook, trying to find a little reassurance before the upcoming exam. Then a classmate I usually got along well with came over and said with a smile, “Hey, have you been kind of antisocial lately?” His words echoed in my ears, as if they carried some hidden meaning. My heart tightened, and it felt as though the entire classroom had grown heavy with tension. Why would he say that? Had I done something wrong?

I replied, “No, not at all. I’ve just had a lot going on lately.” Even though I tried to make my voice sound casual, panic had already begun to spread inside me. The classmate smiled, patted my shoulder, and went back to chatting with others. I stared at the textbook on my desk and suddenly found the words inside hard to understand. My heartbeat sped up, and my palms began to sweat slightly. The noise of the classroom became blurred, as if the whole world were slowly receding into my self-doubt.

I began to replay every detail of the past few days: Had I been too guarded in some conversation? Had I been so focused on my own things that I ignored others? My stomach twisted painfully, as if a stone were pressing down on it. I tried to concentrate, but that question kept appearing in my mind: “Am I antisocial?”

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning. The question still wouldn’t leave me alone. I imagined all kinds of possible outcomes: Did everyone think this? Would people be talking about me behind my back tomorrow? I felt as if I were trapped in a circle I couldn’t escape, able only to keep imagining the worst. I felt ashamed, because being this sensitive made me seem so fragile.

A few days later, I tried to take the initiative and talk with my classmates, to join in on the topics they were discussing, as if that could prove I hadn’t lost my social skills. I told myself I had to be more positive and not let fear control my actions. Yet every time I tried, there was always some uncertainty in my heart. Even when they smiled at me, I still couldn’t fully be sure whether there was really anything wrong with me.

Inside the club activity room, the midday sunlight slipped through a gap in the curtains and fell across the table, and the dappled light and shadows gave me a slight sense of relief. I sat in a chair, staring at the debate materials on the table, trying to calm the tension inside me. “This time, you’ll be the main speaker for the opposition,” the club president said to me in an encouraging tone, but I felt my shoulders grow heavy at once. My heartbeat began to quicken, and I felt my palms dampen slightly with sweat. Why me? What if I say something wrong? What will everyone think of me? These thoughts spun wildly in my mind.

The atmosphere in the room felt lively because of the club members’ discussions, but I could only hear my own inner voice. The conversations by my ears became blurry, as if separated by a layer of water. I tried hard to focus, and a classmate beside me handed me a bottle of water. “You look a bit nervous. Have some water,” they said. I nodded, trying to force out a smile, but my facial muscles felt stiff.

Deep down, a voice kept repeating: You can’t embarrass yourself. You can’t let them see you fail. I began recalling the last debate, repeatedly wondering whether I had behaved inappropriately. My breathing grew rapid, and it felt as if there were a knot in my stomach. I tried to take deep breaths and force myself to calm down.

When the debate officially began, I stood up, but my body felt even heavier than I had imagined. Every step felt as though I were walking on cotton, slightly unsteady. I heard my own voice echoing through the room: “Regarding the other side’s argument, I have some rebuttals...” My voice did not sound as firm as I had expected.

During the debate, I kept watching the reactions of the other side and the audience, trying to catch every possible negative signal in their expressions and postures. Whenever I saw someone frown or lower their head, I would start reflecting on whether something had gone wrong in my performance. My heartbeat grew faster and faster, and every word felt unbearably heavy.

In the end, the debate was over. I sat back down, feeling relieved, but an unease still lingered in my heart. Afterward, the club president came over to comfort me: “Don’t worry, you did great.” I should have felt reassured by those words, yet the doubt and anxiety inside me still clung tightly to me.

Over the next few days, I kept thinking back to that debate, repeatedly wondering whether I had really performed that well. Even at night, I couldn’t fall asleep, tossing and turning as I recalled every detail from that time. The sense of defect within me and the fear of being abandoned further weakened my confidence. I kept telling myself it wasn’t a big deal, but I couldn’t escape the torment of anxiety.

I realized that I couldn’t keep attacking myself preemptively. Maybe all of this was just the result of my overinterpretation, but the anxiety in my heart kept me from escaping this cycle, trapping me in my own thoughts again and again.

I was standing in line at the school cafeteria, surrounded by the hum of conversation, the clatter of trays, and the smell of fried food in the air. I was holding a tray in my hands, but my palms were already damp with nervous sweat. I saw a few classmates I got along well with standing by a table not far away, chatting animatedly. They must have seen me too, but they didn’t wave me over.

I felt like my stomach had knotted itself into a tight ball, and my mouth had gone dry. I forced out a smile and tried to act as if nothing was wrong as I walked over, but the sound of my heartbeat was already drowning out the cafeteria noise. As I got closer, their conversation suddenly paused for a moment, then continued, but in much lower voices. I heard one of them say quietly, “She’s here again.”

“What do they mean? Are they talking about me?” That thought immediately filled my mind. I stood stiffly beside them, feeling as if something inside me had suddenly collapsed. Their eyes swept over my face; someone managed a strained smile, then quickly looked away. My head felt as though it had been pricked with needles, and I could almost hear my breathing getting faster.

“What are you all talking about?” I tried to keep my tone natural, but my voice was still shaking a little. For a moment, several of them looked at one another, and one of them said, “Oh, nothing, just some random stuff.” Then they quickly changed the subject again. I stood off to the side, feeling like an extra piece of a puzzle, as if I didn’t belong there at all.

“As expected, they’re deliberately excluding me.” The thought cut through my mind like a blade, and all at once images of every time I’d been ignored or mocked flooded back. The tray in my hands seemed to grow heavier and heavier, and my stomach began to ache dully.

“Forget it. They don’t care about you at all.” I kept telling myself over and over, but tears still welled up despite me. I lowered my head, quickly turned and pushed through the crowd, set my tray aside, and hurried out of the cafeteria in a panic. The wind outside was cold, and it stung my face a little, but I couldn’t tell whether it was the wind or my tears.

“Why can’t I just be as relaxed as everyone else? Why does it always have to end up like this?” Sitting in a corner, I wiped away my tears and blamed myself. But no matter how hard I tried to convince myself, that feeling of being rejected was like vines, climbing tighter and tighter until I could hardly breathe.

By the time I got back to the classroom, the last period was about to begin. I still kept my head down as I sat at my desk, trying not to look at anyone. That night, lying in bed, I replayed their expressions and tone of voice in my mind, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt like a joke. I kept asking myself: “Why did they look at me like that? What did I do wrong?”

A few days passed, and I still didn’t have the courage to speak to them first. I started avoiding the familiar places as much as possible so I wouldn’t run into them again. Even when they later tried to talk to me a few times, I would only give a quick nod in response. I was afraid they would say something even more hurtful. A voice in my head kept echoing: “They’ll abandon me and laugh at me sooner or later; I’d better leave first.”

It was an ordinary afternoon. I was chatting and laughing with my friends in the long corridor at school. Sunlight streamed through the windows, casting a soft golden glow across the floor. We teased one another and talked about the chemistry quiz that had just ended. Yet my heart felt strangely heavy. Suddenly, I heard one friend quietly say something to another. My heart immediately began to race, and it felt as though a chill had rushed up my back. “Are they talking about me?” The thought flashed through my mind.

I laughed a little awkwardly, trying to turn my attention back to the conversation, but the low voices from before kept echoing in my head. I began to watch their expressions closely, trying to find any clues. “Did I do something wrong?” That inner voice started to swell. I saw one of them gently shake their head. My heart pounded wildly, and I soon felt sweat seep into my palms.

“What are you talking about?” I asked cautiously, trying to make my voice sound relaxed. “Nothing in particular, just the way the new teacher teaches,” a friend replied in a calm tone, but I could clearly sense him glance away slightly.

My emotions churned, and I felt my stomach tighten. Would they make fun of the little things? Would they think I was too sensitive? These thoughts kept circling in my mind. To hide the fear slowly creeping over me, I nodded as if nothing were wrong.

After school, I sat on the edge of my bed, replaying the conversation from earlier that day. The anxiety of being abandoned surged up in me again. Fear of separation made it hard for me to sleep, so I kept thinking about whether anything similar had happened before. I began to recall, one by one, the events that had left their marks on my heart—those inadvertent smiles, whispered conversations, and faint sighs.

I wrote these feelings down on a piece of paper, listing them one by one, including that sense of loneliness and helplessness. Doing so seemed to let me breathe a little easier. I let out a long sigh and looked out through the window at the dark night sky, trying to find a trace of peace.

That night passed in repeated brooding until my awareness gradually blurred. In the days that followed, I became even more sensitive, constantly trying to verify whether they truly cared about me. Several times I wanted to ask directly, but I was afraid it would only lead to more misunderstanding.

This anxiety shadowed me everywhere, making me carefully scrutinize every movement and every word, afraid that a single misstep would be like cracking the ice beneath my feet. Although I knew this sensitivity would only add to my worries, at the time I clearly could not pull myself away.

Biology class was held in a sunlit conservatory. Sunlight poured in through the glass windows, making the room bright yet glaring. The air was filled with the scent of plants, along with a faint damp smell of earth. I sat in a seat near the window, one hand propping up my textbook, the other rubbing my fingers under the desk. The teacher was enthusiastically explaining the principles of photosynthesis, his voice echoing through the classroom, every word seeming to hammer into my brain.

“Next, let’s ask a student to explain the function of chloroplasts.” As soon as the teacher finished speaking, my heart clenched. My mind was like a hive full of irritable bees, buzzing nonstop, completely unable to calmly review what I had just heard. I lowered my head and stared at the words in my textbook, trying to look focused.

The teacher seemed to be searching for a target, and I could feel his gaze sweeping across the class. I prayed he wouldn’t call on me; my fingertips had already started to sweat. “You there, by the window... yes, you.” It felt like the sky had fallen. I could hear my own heartbeat, racing as if I were in a competition. Slowly, I raised my head, feeling the eyes of the whole class converge on me, each gaze pricking my skin like needles.

“Uh... chloroplasts... uh...” Something seemed to be blocking my throat, and my voice was so dry I could barely hear it myself. My mind was in chaos, and I couldn’t remember a thing from what I had just heard. My face heated up at once; sweat began to form on my forehead and palms, and my whole body stiffened like a stone. The more I forced myself to speak, the more my mind went blank.

The teacher frowned slightly and gently prompted, “It’s okay, take your time. Think about the relationship between chloroplasts and photosynthesis.” I nodded, but those words only made me feel more ashamed. I even started to wonder whether they were mocking me in their hearts—was it because they thought I was stupid? Or because I was always this fragile, so easily defeated?

“Chloroplasts... uh, are... um, are...” I finally forced out a few words. Before I had even finished, a student in the front row raised her hand. “Teacher, may I try?” Her tone was relaxed, even carrying a faint friendly smile. But to me, that smile seemed to hide some kind of pity or superiority.

“Alright, then you answer it.” The teacher turned to her, and I let out a relieved breath, but what followed was a deep sense of humiliation. I kept my head down, staring at the textbook on the desk, too afraid to look up. I heard the student answering fluently, her voice clear and confident, in stark contrast to my stammering.

After the bell rang, the student beside me asked quietly, “Are you okay? You don’t look so well.” I shook my head and forced a stiff smile. “I’m fine, just a little nervous.” My stomach felt as heavy as if it were filled with lead, and my chest ached with a dull tightness. On the way home from class, the wind was cold, but my back felt chilled from the sweat of nerves. I kept replaying what had just happened, growing more and more frustrated the more I thought about it. Why am I always this fragile? Why can’t I even answer one simple question properly?

That night, lying in bed with my eyes closed, the looks from the teacher and my classmates kept flashing through my mind. I told myself over and over that I must never be like that again next time, but deep down I knew clearly that I would still be just as nervous next time, and I would still be unable to put my thoughts into words.

I was sitting in a corner of the school reading room. Outside the window, the leaves swayed gently, and sunlight spilled across the table, casting mottled shadows. The room was filled with the faint musty smell of paper, reminding me of old books that had never been opened. In this quiet atmosphere, I felt my heartbeat gradually quicken. Today, our task was to complete a group discussion about a literary work, and it put me under an inexplicable pressure, as if every topic were waiting for me to make a mistake.

I tried to open the discussion first, but the other students didn’t seem willing to respond to my suggestion. “What do you think the theme of this book is?” I asked softly, gripping the edge of the table with both hands, trying to calm my nerves. No one answered me, and I began to feel my cheeks burn, as if all eyes were focused on my mistake.

“Maybe it’s about growing up,” one student finally replied, but then he quickly turned to discuss it with another student. In their whispers, I felt as though I were isolated on a tiny island, lonely and helpless. I tried to keep smiling and nod, but inside, a sense of abandonment welled up. It surged over me like a tide, gradually pulling me into a cycle of self-attack. “They must think I’m stupid. Why am I always like this?” I silently blamed myself.

My stomach started to cramp, as if an invisible hand were gripping it tightly. Every time my mind drifted, my body’s reactions reminded me—reminded me of my fear of being rejected. I began absentmindedly fidgeting with the pen in my hand, trying to shift my attention. Even so, I kept ruminating on my classmates’ cold attitudes, repeatedly imagining the worst possible outcomes.

After the discussion ended, I walked out of the reading room. The world before my eyes seemed blurred, as if I were trapped in a tunnel full of shadows. That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t shake the tension inside me; in my mind, my classmates’ faces and that heartbreaking scene kept circling round and round. A few days later, my mood was still fluctuating, and the occasional self-attack had begun to feel normal. I decided that next time, I would definitely find a way to relax myself—for example, by preparing the course material in advance, so I wouldn’t fall into such an awkward situation again.

The walls of the art classroom were painted in all kinds of colors, and each painting seemed like a story. I was intently adding the final details to my own work, full of anticipation and hoping the teacher would notice how much care I had put into it. The classroom was peaceful, with only the occasional soft sound of a paintbrush rubbing against the canvas. I liked this place and felt it was like a safe harbor for me. Here, I could temporarily forget the things that troubled me and focus only on creating.

Beside me, a classmate suddenly said, “I think your painting is a bit too dark. Maybe you should add some brighter colors?” His tone was not malicious, but I immediately felt my heart race and my face grow hot. “Is he implying that I’m not good at this?” “Why would he say that? Am I doing really badly?” My inner monologue began to question myself over and over, and anxiety gradually took over my thoughts. Although I tried to hide my unease with a weak laugh, it was useless.

I tried not to dwell on my classmate’s words and continued moving my brush across the canvas. But my fingers were slightly trembling, my strokes started to become unsteady, and the colors before my eyes seemed to be mocking my incompetence. I felt restless, my palms sweating, my neck stiff, and even a faint stomachache rising from deep inside.

After art class ended, I hurried out of the classroom, wanting to find a place to calm down and sort out my tangled thoughts. I sat down on the school playground, hoping the cold wind would ease my mood a little. Laughter and chatter from other students filled my ears, but to me those sounds seemed like a dream far out of reach. My mind kept churning over what that classmate had said, repeatedly wondering whether I really was not as good as others.

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning, unable to sleep. My thoughts kept lingering on that moment in the art classroom, and my mind kept replaying my classmate’s comment, while I seemed to hear the classmates’ whispers in my ears. I kept doubting my abilities and imagining how others judged me. Although the next day I tried to look at my painting again with fresh eyes and tried to accept my classmate’s suggestion, the shame and unease inside me still surrounded me at all times, making it hard to break free from those negative emotions.

After school, a few friends and I decided to go to a nearby café and hang out for a bit. When we walked into the small café, the air was filled with the rich aroma of coffee and the scent of freshly baked desserts. We found a seat by the window, where sunlight streamed through the glass and onto the table, making it feel warm and cozy. After ordering drinks, we started talking about recent movies. One friend said, “Have you seen that newly released sci-fi movie? It’s getting really good reviews.”

I jumped in right away: “I have. The visuals were definitely stunning, but I still felt the plot was a bit far-fetched.”

Another friend disagreed: “I think the plot is great, especially the twist at the end. It was really surprising.”

Hearing that, I suddenly felt a little uncomfortable. Why is it always like this? Every time I voice my opinion, someone comes along to challenge it. My heart started racing, and my palms were a bit sweaty. To avoid seeming too serious, I forced a casual smile and said, “Maybe I’m just too picky.”

But in fact, it bothered me deeply. Was I always overthinking things and being too sensitive? I couldn’t help but start reflecting on the way I spoke and what I said, worried that I might have made it seem like I was just picking a fight again. My friends kept talking about other parts of the movie, but I was already distracted, occasionally clutching my coffee cup and feeling the heat from it seep into my fingertips as a way to calm myself down.

“Are you okay? You seem kind of distracted,” one friend noticed something was off.

“I’m fine, I just suddenly remembered I still have some homework to finish,” I said quickly, making up an excuse, while thinking to myself: am I too concerned with what others say? Why do I always feel so uneasy?

On the way home, I still felt a bit down. Even though it was just a minor disagreement, no matter how hard I tried, I could never quite let things go in moments like this. After I got home, I did some homework to distract myself, but that slight discomfort still wouldn’t go away. Lying in bed, I kept replaying today’s conversation, trying to figure out whether I had said something wrong.

A few days later, I gradually put the matter out of my mind, and my friendship with them wasn’t affected by it. Still, this little clash reminded me once again that I need to learn not to care so much about every disagreement. Maybe I should try to understand and accept more different viewpoints, instead of always wanting everyone to be on the same page.

On the ceiling of the gymnasium, the sound of raindrops striking the roof echoed through the entire space like an endless whisper. In the rain-soaked air there was a smell mixed with plastic flooring and wet clothes. I stood in a corner of the gym, surrounded by classmates who, like me, were sheltering from the sudden downpour. The court was divided into several sections: a few students were practicing basketball shots, while some sat on the floor chatting with one another. I leaned against the wall, trying to shield my jacket with my backpack, and I could hear my own heartbeat in my ears, beating so fast it felt as if it might burst out of my chest.

Just then, I noticed a few classmates gathered not far away, whispering to one another. Every now and then they would glance up in my direction, then lower their heads and let out soft laughs. I tried hard to tell myself they were probably talking about something unrelated to me, but I couldn’t help wondering: were they talking about me? Did I look ridiculous in what I was wearing today? Or were they mocking how disheveled and embarrassed I had looked when I first arrived at the gym? My hands began to sweat uncontrollably, and I felt a sharp pain in my stomach, as if an invisible hand were gripping it tightly.

“Are you okay?” A gentle voice interrupted my thoughts. I turned around and saw one of the boys from my class, concern showing in his eyes. “You look a little pale. Are you feeling unwell?”

“I-I’m fine,” I stammered, trying to force out a smile, but to me it looked uglier than crying. “Just a little stuffy.”

“Oh, that’s good. If you need any help, just let me know.” He nodded with a sincere smile, then turned back to continue talking with the others.

The moment his words ended, I felt a brief sense of relief, only to have it replaced by another kind of unease. I kept replaying what he had said—“If you need any help, just let me know.” Was he implying that I was incompetent and needed to rely on others? Or was he simply being polite?

Thoughts like these were like waves with no end, one after another. I kept searching for changes in their expressions and details in their words, hoping to find evidence to support my irrational fear. The temperature inside the gym gradually rose, and the dampness in the air made my head feel heavy and stuffy. I shut my eyes tightly, trying to calm myself down, only to find my hands trembling slightly.

That night, when I got home, I still couldn’t settle down. Even though I was in a warm room, the disturbing fragments of that conversation still wouldn’t leave my mind. Unconsciously, I kept constructing worst-case scenarios, imagining how others looked at me with contempt. In my sleep, the sound of rain continued, like a background track on repeat, intertwined with the anxiety in my heart.

The rehearsal room was lit by a somewhat dim yellow light, and the chandelier on the ceiling gave off a faint hum. I stood in the second row, following the conductor as we practiced a classic choral piece. The air was filled with the distinctive smell of the wooden floor, lingering along with the notes. My lips trembled slightly as I tried to remember the pitch issue the teacher had just corrected, so I wouldn’t make the same mistake again, but my mind felt wrapped in fog, my thoughts hazy.

“Second row, third one, stop for a moment!” The teacher’s voice suddenly rose, and at that instant my heart clenched. It felt as though my feet had taken root in the spot, unable to move. Then her gaze swept over and landed precisely on me. “Your entrance was too low just now; adjust it in the next measure.”

A faint murmur and a few low chuckles drifted around me. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw a classmate in the front row slightly turn her head to look at me. My face burned at once, as if I had been laid bare before everyone. I lowered my head, trying to hide my unease, but the sour, bloated sensation churning in my stomach and that inescapable shame had nowhere to run. “What should I do? Do they think I never should have joined the choir? It must be that.” My mind felt like a reservoir on the verge of breaking, rehearsing every possible mockery and rejection.

The next section of rehearsal began, but my voice seemed stuck, unable to keep up no matter what. I realized my palms were already soaked, and even my arms had started to tremble slightly. The teacher’s gaze swept over again, and this time she was clearly frowning. “Second row, third one, raise your voice a bit more and adjust the pitch!” Though her tone wasn’t harsh, it felt like hammer blows striking my eardrums. I braced myself and nodded, forcing out a sound: “Sorry.” But even to my own ears, the apology sounded unconvincing.

Rehearsal finally ended. I quickly packed my things, trying to avoid everyone’s gaze. But just as I reached the door, the classmate in the front row said softly, “You sang pretty well today. That part wasn’t a big deal, so don’t take it to heart.” Her tone was sincere, but another meaning surfaced in my mind: “Is she deliberately comforting me because she feels sorry for me?” A deeper wave of shame surged up, almost leaving me unable to respond.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning. The rehearsal room scene replayed endlessly like a movie—the teacher calling me out and correcting me, the voices and gazes around me, and that classmate’s low remark. I even began to doubt whether I was truly suited to be in the choir, whether I was holding everyone back. I wanted to give up, but I was unwilling to, and the conflict inside me kept me awake all night. The next morning, my eyes were red and swollen, but I still decided to go to practice. I had to prove that I wasn’t that bad, even if that proof was more for my own peace of mind than for anyone else.

I stood backstage at the school concert, surrounded by busy classmates and teachers. The sounds of instruments being tuned filled my ears, and from afar came the noise of the audience filing in. My palms began to sweat, and I tried hard to steady my breathing. I kept worrying that I would make mistakes on stage, and the worst-case scenario kept replaying in my mind—if I forgot the lyrics or sang off-key, the audience would laugh, and I would become everyone’s joke.

“Hey, why are you so pale?” A classmate beside me suddenly noticed my unease and sneered, “Don’t be nervous, no one’s going to notice a nobody like you.” His tone stabbed into my heart like a needle. I lowered my head, trying not to look at his face.

I was filled with shame and fear, feeling as though I were isolated in an endless darkness with nowhere to escape. “I must be a complete failure. If I embarrass myself on stage, everyone will surely distance themselves from me, maybe even stop talking to me.” I kept attacking myself relentlessly, because only then did I feel somewhat safe, as if hurting myself first could spare me harsher criticism from others.

My stomach began to cramp, my heartbeat sped up beyond control, and my fingers trembled violently. I tried to take a deep breath and tell myself to focus, but the snickering and dismissive looks still kept echoing in my mind.

After the concert ended, I hid in a corner, imagining what would happen if I ruined everything that night. My mind was filled with images of failure. I repeatedly sought reassurance from people I trusted, asking whether they thought I had done well and whether they were upset with me. The next day, I was still anxious and uneasy, worrying whether everyone was talking behind my back about my mistakes, unable to stop myself from replaying every detail.

A few days later, my emotions were still unsettled, my mind heavily churning with memories of that day. Even when someone praised my performance, I still suspected it was only polite consolation. I was afraid of being abandoned, afraid of becoming a joke in everyone’s eyes, and I always felt that I could never truly be accepted.

The wooden floor faintly held a damp, slippery chill. Outside, rain struck the window glass, making a dense but uneven rustling sound. The fluorescent lights in the activity room were a bit harsh, casting a particularly cold, hard sheen over the debate club’s table. The moderator cleared their throat. “Next, please have the second speaker for the affirmative side begin.” I stood up and felt everyone’s gaze lock onto me like searchlights.
