I gripped the note card in my hand; my palm was already slightly damp, but I still tried to make my voice sound organized. “Honorable judges, opposing debaters…” Before I even finished, I suddenly realized I hadn’t actually caught the key point of what the previous opposing debater had just said—my mind was blank, as if beyond the drawn curtain there were only a black hole. The sound of the rain in my ears seemed louder, mixed with the roar of my heartbeat. I forced myself to continue, but the next four or five sentences came out broken and disordered. I saw one of the judges lower their head to write something in the notebook, while another frowned slightly. I quickly scanned the expressions of the club members; some were looking down at their phones, while others had a vaguely indescribable, complicated look in their eyes: were they embarrassed for me, or simply indifferent?

My voice trembled a little as my intonation rose toward the end. I clearly knew that if I kept hesitating, I was only dragging things out, but once the words slipped out, that stabbing feeling of “I may have said something wrong” made me even more at a loss. “Thank you, everyone,” I tried to keep my voice low as I wrapped up, but it still carried fatigue and nervousness. I quickly sat down and felt even the wooden surface of the chair was soaked through with coldness. My teammate sitting beside me said softly, “You didn’t have to talk that long just now.” The tone wasn’t harsh, but that sentence felt like a needle stabbing into my chest. My heart sank, and I had the intuition that this time I might have dragged down the whole team’s performance.

The surrounding discussion grew noisy, and the moderator then announced the next segment. I tried to tell myself this was all just normal practice, nothing worth taking so seriously, but that self-comfort felt like wrapping a scorching piece of iron in a wet tissue—completely useless. I lowered my head to look at the note card in my hand and found that the writing had blurred because of the sweat in my palm. My mind began replaying every sentence I had just said, like watching a repeated recording. Should I have started with a shorter statement? Should my tone have been firmer?

After I got home, I kicked off my wet shoes at the entryway and hung my coat on the rack by the door. Sitting in my room, I opened the draft I had casually brought back, only to find myself somewhat resistant to those neat lines of text; a wave of irritation and frustration rose again in my chest. I pinched the bridge of my nose, thinking about whether there might be a chance tomorrow to explain or make up for it, but soon I quietly set down the pen in my hand. The past few hours felt like a pointless farce gone through in a frenzy—no matter how hard I practiced, whenever it was truly time to step up, there always seemed to be an invisible force pulling me down. That night, I tossed and turned, wondering whether no one had even noticed how nervous I was, maybe everyone was only paying attention to their own performance… but that kind of self-directed consolation didn’t make me feel much better.

Sunlight seeped in through the gaps in the curtains, slanting across the tabletop and making the drawing paper feel almost blinding. I kept my head down in silence, sketching lines on the poster draft with a pencil, trying as hard as I could to look focused and hide the nervousness inside me. The classmates’ laughter echoed all around, occasionally mixed with hushed comments. I didn’t dare look up, always feeling that those whispers were directed at me.

“Wouldn’t the title look better if it were a little bigger?” The girl sitting across from me suddenly spoke, pointing at the words on my drawing. I froze for a moment, then looked up in a panic. “Mm, I’ll adjust it.” After saying that, I hurriedly lowered my gaze again and stared fixedly at the paper, my heartbeat starting to quicken. Her tone wasn’t especially harsh, but for some reason I felt as if she was displeased with how I’d done it, and I even began to doubt whether my drawing skills were too poor.

“Should this color be a little darker?” Another voice came from behind me—it was another classmate. She seemed to have glanced at my drawing by accident and casually offered a suggestion. My hands suddenly started to tremble; sweat kept beading on my fingertips around the pen, and it felt as if a needle had pricked my heart, with a faint ache spreading inside. “‘A little darker’ means it looks really bad, doesn’t it? Is she indirectly expressing dissatisfaction?” My inner voice churned uneasily.

I nodded and said softly, “Okay, I’ll try.” But in reality, my mind was in complete chaos. The tip of the pen tapped the paper twice, yet I couldn’t draw anything. I was afraid that if I kept drawing, it would only look worse. I really didn’t understand why I had taken on this part of the work.

Someone nearby was laughing. I couldn’t hear what they were discussing, but that laughter made my heart sink. “Are they laughing at me? Is it because my poster looks so bad?” I could no longer concentrate. My ears were filled with noisy sounds, as if every word had something to do with me. I even felt my face start to burn, as if it had been set alight, and a buzzing wind sounded in my ears.

“Are you okay?” A male classmate suddenly came over and asked gently. His gaze swept over my drawing paper, as if he wanted to see what was going on. “I’m fine,” I quickly forced out a smile. “I’m just not very satisfied with this part of the design.” “Oh, then do you want me to try drawing something?” As he spoke, he took out a different colored marker and motioned that he could help. I stared at the first line he drew and couldn’t stop my thoughts from surging. “Does he think I can’t draw at all, that I’m not even capable of holding a pen? Should I leave this club?”

I murmured my thanks, pushed the paper aside, grabbed a bottle of water, and left the classroom quickly. The warm sunlight was shining on the corridor floor, but all I felt was a chill shaking through me, as if I had been caught in a silent rainstorm. I went to the restroom, splashed cold water on my face, and braced both hands against the sink to steady myself. My pounding heart finally calmed down, but it was replaced by a deep frustration: “If only I were a little better at drawing, then everyone wouldn’t look at me like this.”

After that day, I took the poster home, ready to redraw a perfect version. I told myself that next time I would never let myself be so embarrassed again. But even so, the sounds and expressions from that afternoon kept magnifying over and over in my mind, making me feel that they really were looking down on me.

In the club room, a bare incandescent bulb hung from the ceiling, casting a harsh glare. The walls were covered with posters from various debate competitions, and the space felt stuffy with the windows shut. I sat near the door, clutching a debate speech tightly in my hands, my fingertips turning white from the pressure. The air was filled with the voices of my classmates discussing things—speaking quickly, their tones laced with argument. I tried to focus on my own script, but an uncontrollable sense of nervousness kept rising inside me.

“Do you really think this point is okay? I don’t think it fully holds up.” One classmate suddenly raised his voice, glancing at me with what seemed like a look of doubt. I jerked my head up and felt everyone’s attention converge on me. My throat tightened; my words seemed stuck there, but I still forced out a few sentences: “I… I think from this angle, it can be supported.” My voice was very soft, and I wasn’t even sure whether anyone had heard me clearly.

“Your argument is too weak. If the judges catch this point, we’ll get a low score.” The classmate continued to challenge me, his tone growing sharper and sharper. I lowered my head and began scribbling random lines on the paper with my pen, trying to hide my unease. My heart raced, my stomach started to ache faintly, and my whole body seemed wrapped in a tense force, making even breathing difficult.

“Take it easy. They’re just expressing their opinion,” another gentle voice interjected, but hearing the words “take it easy” only made me feel even more ashamed. Why did everyone think I needed to calm down? Did I really seem that bad? Memories of similar moments from previous activities flashed through my mind—every time I was questioned, every clumsy response I gave, replayed like scenes from a movie. I forced myself to look down at the script, but the words gradually blurred into meaningless symbols.

The argument in the room went on, voices piling up together like a wall of sound crashing toward me. Suddenly, I felt I couldn’t stay any longer. I stood up and excused myself, saying I needed to use the restroom, nearly stumbling in my haste. The cold air of the hallway hit me in the face. I braced myself against the wall, trying to steady my nerves, but the heaviness in my chest felt like a huge stone pressing down on me. In the restroom mirror, I looked at my own face—pale and disheveled. The faucet dripped softly. I cupped cold water in my hands and splashed my face several times, trying to wake myself up.

After returning to the club room, I tried to make myself as inconspicuous as possible, avoiding becoming the center of attention again. For days after the activity ended, whenever I closed my eyes, I could still picture that classmate’s expression and tone when he questioned me, like a sharp arrow stabbing straight into my nerves. I even began to obsess over whether, if I had been more confident back then, things might not have turned out this way. But no matter how much I reflected, the answer always escaped into a haze of fog.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning. The scene from the activity kept reappearing in my mind like a spinning kaleidoscope. I tried to comfort myself, telling myself that everyone gets questioned sometimes, but that self-comfort was as thin as paper, unable to withstand even the slightest wind before my emotions were torn apart again.

The hotpot restaurant always has a strangely sticky warmth to it, perhaps because the steam from the pot mingles with the scent of spices and fills the air. I held the menu, my eyes fixed on the spicy red broth options, but my finger drifted to the mushroom broth. My friend urged me from beside me: “Hurry up and choose, or the waiter’s going to leave.” I quickly said in a low voice, “Sorry, let’s do this one—the mushroom broth.” The waiter took the order quickly, and as the pot began bubbling, we started picking up our first slices of beef rolls. The ingredients in the pot were vividly colored, the aroma of the red broth drifted far away, and the surrounding chatter mixed with the pot’s “gurgle, gurgle” sounds. I felt that this atmosphere was comforting.

“Which university are you planning to choose? Have you submitted your applications yet?” the friend sitting opposite me suddenly asked. My chopsticks froze in midair, and the tofu I had just picked up nearly fell back into the pot. I answered cautiously, “Not yet, I’m still thinking. Maybe I’ll go with something I’m interested in.” In truth, I had no idea at all. I felt like I wasn’t good at anything, and I didn’t know whether I would regret my choice afterward.

“What are you interested in?” she asked, smiling at me, her tone carrying a hint of teasing. I hesitated for a moment and swallowed. “Maybe it’s... writing something, or painting, that sort of thing. I don’t know if that can make money.” A faint unease began to rise in my chest, and I suddenly worried she might laugh at how impractical I was. She lowered her head and swished a slice of lamb in the broth, not pressing the matter further. Instead, she said lightly, “Doing something you like is pretty good. Even if it doesn’t make money, at least you’ll be happy.”

After hearing that, I was stunned for a while, and I stirred the fallen piece of tofu around in the pot with my chopsticks, feeling as if the air had grown tense again. I wanted to say more, but I didn’t know how to respond, and my thoughts suddenly became a mess. That confusion wasn’t really because of the topic itself, but because the contrast between her easy tone and my heavy mood was so stark.

Later, we started talking about one of the strange things our teacher had done at school, and the conversation quickly turned lighthearted. I gradually let go of that inexplicable tension from earlier and started laughing with her. When she imitated the teacher’s exaggerated way of speaking in class, I even laughed so hard I nearly burned my mouth on the hot tofu.

After dinner, we walked out of the restaurant together. The air by the street was cool, carrying a mix of greasy smoke and earthy smells, yet it also felt real. She waved goodbye to me at the intersection, and I waved back, but I still couldn’t help repeatedly thinking about our earlier conversation. When I got home, I opened my notebook and tried to write something, but my mind was blank—only the steam from the pot and her words kept echoing over and over: “At least you’ll be happy.”

The classroom fell silent, with only the occasional rustle of turning pages and the scraping of chairs. I sat gripping my pen at the round table, while the classmates across from me stared at me with eyes that were not as friendly as usual. And in the discussion just now, my viewpoint seemed not to have been acknowledged—or, more precisely, had been silently ridiculed. His earlier words still echoed in my ears: “Maybe you haven’t quite figured out the logic yet?” Although it sounded like advice, the raised eyebrow and slightly lifted corner of his mouth, which should have been an ordinary expression, now cut through my heart like a knife. My palm around the pen began to sweat, and I could no longer hold it steady.

I tried to put on a disdainful expression, pretending I didn’t care at all. Just as I was thinking about how to disguise my discomfort, the girl beside me added, “Yeah, I think your approach is a bit convoluted.” My stomach suddenly tightened, as if someone hadfiercely punched it with a fist. I wanted to say something, but the words got stuck in my throat. The only thought echoing in my mind was: “They’re mocking me; they think I’m stupid.”

“Do you want to explain your idea again?” the boy continued. This time his tone sounded calmer, but all I could hear was a faint challenge. I felt everyone’s gaze shooting toward me, hot like stage lights, leaving me nowhere to hide. My fingers began tapping nervously on the table, my heartbeat so fast it felt like it was about to burst through my chest. I tugged at my sleeve and wiped the sweat from my forehead, trying to cover it up.

“Um, actually what I meant was...” I began, but my voice came out much smaller than I expected because I couldn’t control the trembling. I managed to say a few sentences, speaking faster and faster, as if trying to race away from some kind of judgment. Sure enough, their expressions grew colder and colder, and an unspoken rejection seemed to fill the air. I hurriedly finished my explanation and no longer looked at their faces.

After the activity ended, I walked alone along a path on campus. It had gotten a little darker, and the streetlights cast a dim yellow glow. I looked down at my footsteps, my mind replaying the scene over and over: his tone, her expression, my voice and my pauses. Why hadn’t I spoken more firmly then? Why am I always so sensitive, always hearing ridicule and rejection in other people’s words? These questions kept snowballing in my head.

When I got home, I put my backpack on the chair but didn’t want to open it. I tried playing a mobile game for a while, but the colors on the screen looked glaringly bright, and the sounds irritated me. In the end, I chose to sit on the edge of the bed in a daze, my heart filled with a shame I couldn’t shake off. Those looks and tones pressed down on my chest like a dark cloud, and all night I felt like I couldn’t breathe properly. The next morning, when I woke up, my body still felt stiff, and the first thing that came to mind was last night’s scene—did they really think I was a failure?

At the start of the group discussion, I was sitting in the corner of the classroom, my palms already sweating. The sunlight outside was glaring, and a sharp beam of light fell straight onto my desk, making my notebook look almost blindingly bright. I couldn’t help but lower my head, afraid that others would notice how stiff I was sitting.

The teacher asked us to break into groups to discuss the topic, and I was grouped with three classmates, one of whom was a very outgoing girl in the class. I always felt that she didn’t like me, even though she had never shown it clearly. I listened carefully to their discussion, but my mind had already drifted far away. I was trying to guess whether they were unhappy with my silence. I even thought they had already labeled me in their minds as someone who didn’t fit in.

Suddenly, the outgoing girl turned around and asked me in a somewhat hurried tone, “Why aren’t you saying anything? We need your thoughts.” I froze, as if I’d been struck in the chest by an arrow, and it suddenly became hard to breathe. My head was in chaos, and the sound of my heartbeat drowned out everything around me. I quickly apologized, my voice as faint as a mosquito’s: “Sorry, I don’t know how to say it.”

Another group member then added, “We don’t have much time, okay? Don’t drag this out.” For some reason, that sentence hit me like a heavy hammer to the chest. I felt my face burning instantly, as if someone had stripped me naked in public. I said, “Sorry, I’ll think about it.” But their expressions had already convinced me that I had been judged as the one holding everyone back.

I tried to join in the discussion that followed, but found that my voice was trembling and my sentences were stumbling, like a grade school student reciting a text. They didn’t interrupt me directly, but I could see that they had already lost patience. I noticed that my pronunciation wasn’t clear enough, my voice was too soft, and my comments were off-topic. My stomach began to cramp violently, and for a moment I even felt like I was going to throw up my lunch.

At last, the outgoing girl frowned and said, “Fine, then we’ll just do it ourselves.” Her tone was light, but it cut through my mind like a blade. I nodded and didn’t dare say anything else, lowering my head and pretending to look at my notebook, hoping everyone would ignore me.

At that moment, I began replaying every sentence from earlier in my mind, even scrutinizing my own expressions over and over. I ruminated on every failure and felt like nothing more than a complete burden. I kept thinking that if I had performed better back then, maybe they wouldn’t have been so disappointed; maybe I could have felt even a little more valued in their eyes.

That night, I lay in bed with the stomach pain still unresolved. I closed my eyes but didn’t dare fall asleep, because the memories kept flooding back again and again. The words “Why aren’t you saying anything” kept echoing in my ears like an alarm. I began to classify myself as a “burden,” an identity I could never escape.

The next day, I wanted to explain myself to the group members, but as soon as I saw them, I backed away. I was afraid of leaving them a bad impression again, and even afraid that they would listen to my explanation only halfheartedly. I spent the entire morning keeping my distance from them, and only dared to hurry out of the classroom when class was over.

The classroom felt a little dull, and the homeroom teacher was urging everyone to come up with ideas for a class activity. I was sitting by the window, sunlight spilling across my desk, twirling my pen cap around my fingertips. I struggled for quite a while before finally summoning the courage to raise my hand.

“I think we could organize a class debate competition. It would be interesting, and it would also help everyone practice their speaking skills,” I said, trying to sound confident, even though my heart had already started racing.

As soon as I finished, the classroom fell silent for a second. Then someone laughed—it was Chen Yu, sitting in the back. He said, “A debate competition? How many people in our class do you think can actually debate? Sounds so boring.”

His tone sounded casual, like he was just making a joke, but the thought instantly flashed through my mind: Was he targeting me? Someone next to him chimed in, “Yeah, it feels a bit nerdy. We should do something more relaxed, like a sports day or something.”

I could feel the heat rising in my face. I lowered my head slightly, my gaze falling on the small circular patch of sunlight on the desk. My left thumb traced circles on the tabletop without me even realizing it, and all kinds of intense emotions surged up inside me: Did they think I was someone who didn’t fit in? Did they think I was weird? Was it because I always seemed too nervous that they felt I couldn’t blend in?

“No, that’s not it. Debate competitions can have lots of interesting topics...” My voice came out almost forced, and it trembled a little halfway through, like I was defending myself. I heard the homeroom teacher speak up: “That’s actually a pretty good suggestion. We can refine it further. Chen Yu, and everyone else, please think about it more.”

But that didn’t make me feel any better, because I always felt like her tone was only to save my face. Besides, it was obvious that most of the class had little interest in a debate competition. I pretended to write in my notebook, but I wasn’t really writing anything at all—I was just moving the pen across the paper. Every few seconds, I felt a tight knot in my stomach, as if something had grabbed hold of it.

After the class meeting ended, I walked back to the dormitory, and that “so boring” kept echoing in my ears. A completely inappropriate thought even popped into my head: Did they not even need me to take part in these discussions?

That night, sitting on the edge of my bed, I scrolled through social media and saw photos and videos of debate competitions posted by other classes. The sense of disappointment in my heart grew even stronger. I told myself I shouldn’t care so much about this, but the more I suppressed it, the more Chen Yu’s words kept replaying in my head. His tone, his expression—they were magnified in my mind to an absurd degree. I felt as if a stone was pressing on my chest, making it hard to breathe.

Two or three days later, I began to avoid speaking up in class meetings. I always felt that anything I suggested might be questioned or simply ignored. I told myself that next time, I’d better not do anything so stupid.

I walked along the school hallway, and through the window I could see the shadows of the trees swaying in the wind outside. For some reason, the sunlight today seemed especially glaring, gently striking my face and making me feel slightly dizzy. Chemistry lab was about to begin, and I had to hurry into the lab. As I opened the lab door, a pungent smell of disinfectant rushed toward me, mixed with a faint scent of paint that had not yet dried. I found my lab station, and several classmates were already getting ready beside me. “Remember to handle the reagents carefully. This experiment is very important,” the teacher’s voice came through the microphone. My palms began to sweat, and my heartbeat gradually sped up. Why do I feel especially nervous today? Did I forget some important step? Is some disaster brewing? The whispering of my classmates in my ears made me feel even more uneasy. “Are you okay?” the classmate standing beside me asked softly. I forced a smile. “Yeah, I’m fine, just a little nervous.” What I really wanted to say was: I’m afraid of making mistakes. I’m worried that a slip-up will disappoint everyone. As the experiment went on, I tried hard to concentrate, carefully working between the reagent bottles and beakers. But just as I poured the reagent into the beaker, my wrist jerked, the bottle hit the edge of the table, and the reagent bottle was instantly knocked over, with a few drops splashing onto my hand. My heartbeat suddenly shot to the limit, and I felt a tightness in my stomach. I quickly wiped it with a tissue, trying to cover up the mistake. In that moment, the worst images flashed through my mind: the reagent corroding my skin, a bad reaction spreading across the whole room. The teacher walked down from the monitoring station to check on me. “It’s okay. Calm down first, and rinse your hand with water.” His tone was calm, but it struck me as especially harsh, as if announcing my failure. I felt a burning flush of shame on my face, while inwardly blaming myself for being so careless. That afternoon, I kept replaying that scene in my mind, endlessly magnifying the mistake, my heart filled with frustration and anxiety. Even after several days, every time I walked into the lab, I would involuntarily think of that spilled bottle and worry that I would make the same mistake again.

The classroom windows were being pelted by rain, and the sound of it echoed through the room along with the teacher’s lecture. I sat in the corner, surrounded by the familiar photography equipment—cameras, tripods, and stacks of photography books, the air faintly scented with paper. The teacher waved a roll of film in his hand and announced that today’s assignment was to take a series of photos on the theme of “loneliness.” My heart began to race, pounding in my ears like a drum. 

“You have two hours to go out and photograph scenes on campus that represent loneliness, then come back and share your work,” the teacher announced. As everyone began whispering to one another and picking up their cameras to set off, I stood up and felt a cold sweat slide down my spine, my clothes clinging tightly to my skin. I was always worried that my work would not meet others’ expectations, and this theme made me especially uneasy.

I slowly left the classroom and wandered through the rainy campus, trying to find inspiration. Raindrops hit my umbrella with a rustling sound, but my thoughts were as tangled and chaotic as the endless rain. From time to time, I murmured to myself, “Something’s going to go wrong, something’s going to go wrong.” But I knew I needed to turn those worries into motivation, because backing away would only make me even more anxious.

In a corner behind the library, I saw an abandoned basketball hoop, surrounded by overgrown weeds, the rim hanging precariously. I was deeply drawn to the scene. That desolate loneliness seemed to resonate with something deep in my heart. I lifted my camera and tried to adjust the angle, feeling my hands tremble a little. Even though I was still filled with fear of failure, I forced myself to focus on the image in the viewfinder, and little by little, my breathing steadied. With every press of the shutter, my heartbeat seemed to gradually sync with the mechanical click of the camera.

After the assignment ended, I returned to the classroom with a mixture of anticipation and unease. The rain was still falling, making the whole room feel especially gloomy. Everyone began showing their work, and when it was my turn, my palms started sweating again. The projector enlarged my photo, and the room fell silent at once. Every time I saw others staring at my work, my stomach felt as though it had been tightly clenched.

“This photo conveys a very unique sense of loneliness,” the teacher said with a slight nod. Hearing those words of approval, the tension in my heart eased a little, like warmth breaking through a curtain of rain.

When class ended that afternoon, I felt an unprecedented sense of relief. Although I was still uneasy about my performance, at least I had bravely taken that step. Over the next few days, I occasionally took out that photo to admire it, reaffirming my own ability, and that small burst of confidence helped me perform better in my future creative work.

The air in the classroom seemed stuffy all the time. I sat by the window, with the other three members of my group beside me. Just now, the teacher had assigned a group discussion project and asked us to work together to give a short in-class presentation. The sunlight outside was glaring. My notebook lay open on the desk, my palms were a little damp, and the pages seemed to have curled slightly. I tried to regulate my breathing and told myself it was just a simple task, but my heartbeat still began to quicken. I felt as if I were completely exposed before everyone, as though everyone was watching me. Would they think I was incompetent?

“Then let’s start assigning tasks,” said the boy in the front row first. His voice was low but crisp. “Who will be in charge of researching?”

“I can,” I said, raising my hand. For some reason, my throat felt tight, and my voice was much softer than usual.

He nodded. “Okay. And who will make the slides?” he continued.

The girl beside him chimed in. “Ah, I’ll do that. I’m pretty familiar with slides.” She smiled as she spoke, sounding relaxed, but I felt as though there was a slight chill in her tone. Was she implying something? Was she dissatisfied with my choice to handle the research?

“Then I’ll take care of the rest of the presentation,” said another boy. After speaking, he glanced at me, and my heart sank. Why was he looking at me? Did he think I would hold the group back? Was he doubting my ability in his mind? I wanted to say something, but my mouth was dry; I could only lower my head and scribble aimlessly in my notebook.

“Do you think that’s okay?” the boy in front suddenly asked me. His tone was flat, but I could hear scrutiny in it. “Okay, it should be fine,” I hurriedly replied, speaking so fast I could barely hear myself. “Is it really okay? I think the research part is pretty important.” His expression was very serious, but my mind had already begun churning with images of myself messing everything up: not finding suitable materials, missing the deadline, failing to produce results, and even dragging down the group’s grade.

After the break-time discussion ended, I returned to my seat and felt that even the uniform pressed against the back of the chair was damp with sweat. When I realized that, I felt unbearably embarrassed. However I looked at it, it all proved that my nervousness and lack of confidence had been laid bare.

That night, I spent three hours organizing the materials, trying to find the most authoritative information from various academic websites and books. But every time I wanted to share something in the group chat, I would hover over the send button and repeatedly check it two or three times, afraid that I might post something inaccurate or unprofessional and cause problems for the whole group. I even sent a brief message: “The materials should be okay, right? If anything seems off, please let me know.” They replied quite quickly, all saying “It’s fine” and “Pretty good,” but that still didn’t make me feel at ease. All that remained in my mind were the thoughts they never voiced: maybe they had long since felt my performance was insignificant.

The next day I brought the materials to class, still uneasy. With every step toward our group’s seat, I kept pondering the expressions they made when looking at me. Was I being too casual? Were they implying something? The group presentation went very smoothly, and everyone clearly raised no objections to my materials, but my heart still could not calm down, as if a string were constantly pulled taut. I don’t remember what everyone said after the group discussion ended; I only remember asking myself for a long time afterward: why can’t I be more composed than other people?

After school, the classroom was much quieter than usual, and everyone was tidying their bags in twos and threes, getting ready to go home. The setting sun outside the window bathed the room in gold, warm light spilling over the desks, but I felt my stomach churning over and over, and a thin sweat had broken out in my palms. Our homeroom teacher had just announced that we were going to have an impromptu class meeting because of issues with the campus environment, and asked each of us to share our thoughts. When it was my turn, everyone turned to look at me. I squeezed my fingers hard, trying to control the turmoil inside me. “Don’t mess up, don’t mess up.” I kept telling myself.

I stood up, bracing one hand lightly on the desk, cleared my throat, and began to speak. “Um… I think we could organize more… um, volunteer activities, like cleaning the classroom, which would help improve the relationships between classmates…” My tone gradually became unnatural, and my voice grew softer and softer. Just then, I heard a soft laugh from the corner, apparently from the class’s most lively boy. My ears instantly burned hot; my voice trembled even more, my palms started sweating, my mind went blank, and I couldn’t even remember where I had left off.

“Am I going to be laughed at? Do they think what I said was stupid?” These thoughts flooded into my head wildly. I tried to stay calm, but my voice was already shaking so badly that even I could hear the obvious weakness in it. “They can tell at a glance that you’re nervous. How embarrassing!” My knees seemed to be trembling, my throat felt blocked, and my tongue would not obey me. I blurted out something random: “Uh, anyway… that’s my opinion.” Then I hurriedly sat down.

I lowered my head and pretended to organize my notes, hardly daring to glance at everyone’s expressions from the corner of my eye. My heart was pounding like it was about to burst out of my chest. My throat felt dry, and all my attention was focused on that laugh just now and on what expressions my classmates might have had. “Why am I always such a loser? Why can’t I even do something as simple as speak up? They must think I’m completely useless…” That feeling surged through me like a flood, instantly washing away the rest of my thoughts.

After the class meeting ended, I mechanically packed my bag and followed behind the last student as I left the classroom. I stayed far behind, not wanting to squeeze in among everyone else. Every time I heard people whispering in front of me, I felt as if they were talking about me. “Are they making fun of how I performed just now?” That thought lingered like a shadow.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying those humiliating few minutes in my mind, and I could even clearly hear my trembling voice and that soft laugh. I buried my face in the pillow and couldn’t help biting my lip hard, trying to calm myself down, but the more I tried to stop thinking, the clearer the images in my head became. I was unable to sleep for nearly the whole night, and only at dawn did I finally collapse from exhaustion.

The next morning, my stomach still felt awful, and even walking into the classroom made my heart race. I deliberately picked a seat by the window, avoiding my classmates’ eyes, and silently opened my book. But no matter how hard I tried, I couldn’t focus. As soon as anyone started talking to each other, my brain would automatically assume they were discussing what I had said yesterday. “They must be laughing at me, right?” That thought tormented me like a spell, leaving me almost unable to breathe.

Sunlight poured through the bookstore’s large windows, casting a scatter of delicate light and shadow across the wooden floor. I set my backpack down by my feet, gently pulled out a chair, and sat in the reading nook by the window. There weren’t many people here; the air carried a faint scent of paper, along with a hint of malted sweetness—perhaps from someone who had ordered a latte by the counter. I glanced up at the bookshelves, where the colors of the spines interwove in a quiet, orderly way.

I opened a novel I had picked at random. Its cover was pale blue, and the edges of the pages were a little fuzzy, clearly from being handled many times. The print was too small, and I frowned slightly, bringing the book closer in an attempt to adjust my focus. After reading a few lines of the introduction, I began to get drawn in; I hadn’t expected the story to be so captivating. But after two or three sentences, my mind abruptly drifted away again. I suddenly wondered whether the ending of this book would be like others I’d read before—always too idealized, as if written especially for people who prefer to escape reality.

A young couple nearby was chatting quietly about something, and my attention was briefly drawn to them. Their laughter was soft, as if they were sharing a little story they both knew well. I wanted to hear more clearly, but it felt a little impolite, so I turned my gaze back to the book. Yet something in me had loosened, and I felt as though I were in some kind of gentle background noise, completely at ease.

I pulled the chair closer to the table and leaned over it to prop up the pages, only to find that my arm brushed against some rough, chalk-like marks. My heart gave a jolt—had I gotten my clothes dirty? I looked down to check, but thankfully there was no trace. I gently brushed off the powder and forced myself not to get distracted again, continuing to read. Then the rustling sound of the pages as I turned them felt oddly soothing, as if it added a little rhythm to the quiet world around me.

Every time I turned a page, I couldn’t help glancing out the window. On the street outside, a few students in uniforms passed by, backpacks on their shoulders and milk tea in their hands, laughing and talking as they walked. I found myself thinking of my own school days; sometimes it felt as though everything had moved too fast, and before I had time to hold onto anything, time had already rolled onward. I frowned, trying to shake off these emotional thoughts, and lowered my head to read another page.

By around noon, more people were moving about the bookstore. Some carried a few books to the cashier to pay, while others quietly shifted their chairs closer to the places with more sunlight. I straightened up and stretched, realizing my body had become a little stiff, but my mind was unexpectedly calm. It was as if, in a space like this, all the things I needed to deal with, all the details I kept worrying over and over, had been sealed off outside.

Later, I closed the book, put it back where I had found it, dusted myself off, stood up, and picked up my backpack. As I left the bookstore, I looked back once more. Through the glass window, the view from outside—the light and shadows layered over the bookshelves—looked like a tiny secret hideout, unreal in a strange way.

Outside the music classroom window, sunlight spilled across the floor, casting mottled shadows. The air inside carried a faint wooden scent. The other group members were nearby tuning their instruments, and in the background I could hear the soft strumming of a guitar. I stood in the corner, my palms damp with nervous sweat, my heart seeming ready to jump out of my chest. Silently, I thought to myself: “If only I could never have to go on stage.”

“Are you ready?” a classmate in my group asked me softly. His tone seemed casual, but I felt a surge of pressure, afraid that he expected too much from my performance. I nodded, yet instinctively looked down at the floor, trying to avoid his gaze. In truth, I didn’t feel ready at all.

When the teacher announced that our group was going on stage, my stomach tightened at once, as if gripped by an invisible hand. I felt my breathing quicken, and it seemed as though all I could hear was the pounding of my heart. I followed the others onto the stage, trying hard to pretend I was calm, but in fact every step felt unsteady, as if I were walking on cotton.

We began to play, and I could feel my fingertips gliding over the keys. But nerves kept me from concentrating, and I made mistake after mistake. It was as if I could hear a voice deep inside me saying: “You never should have come to this performance. Now everyone knows how bad you are.”

After the performance ended, everyone stepped down from the stage. A classmate beside me patted my shoulder and said comfortingly, “It’s okay, we all make mistakes sometimes.” His voice was very gentle, but I couldn’t find any comfort in it; instead, I only felt even more shame. I gave a slight nod and forced a reluctant smile.

Back in my seat, I felt as though all my strength had been drained away, and I only wanted to find somewhere to hide. In my mind, every mistake from the performance replayed over and over like a stuck videotape that wouldn’t stop. My stomach still ached faintly, probably from being too tense.

That night, lying in bed, my thoughts still refused to settle. I thought that if I could have recognized my inner anxiety earlier, perhaps I would have been able to handle these situations better. The next day at school, I ran into the classmate from my group, and he told me that they all thought I had done well, and that I was simply being too hard on myself. The tightly strung cord in my heart seemed to loosen a little, but the feeling of self-reproach still would not go away.

I slowly walked into the orchard behind the school. The air was filled with a faint fragrance of fruit, and sunlight filtered through the leaves, scattering mottled patterns of light and shadow on the ground. I liked this place; although few people came here, it always gave me a sense of calm. Stepping on the thick layer of fallen leaves, I could hear the branches swaying softly, and occasionally a bird would fly past, its chirping bright and pleasant.

“Why did you come here?” A classmate saw me as they passed by and asked loudly.

“I just wanted to pick a few apples,” I replied, turning back with a slight smile.

The orchard’s apple trees were laden with fruit, the apples bright red and gleaming with an enticing color. I reached out and carefully picked one, holding it to my lips. A little bit of soil was still stuck to the peel, giving off a natural fresh scent. When I bit into it, the sweet juice instantly filled my mouth, making me feel utterly satisfied. At that moment, it seemed I had forgotten all my troubles, focusing only on the fruit before me and the peace of the present.

My heartbeat seemed to slow here, and my gentle breathing, along with with the autumn breeze, seemed to ease the tension in my body as well. I couldn’t help thinking of a recent exam; I had felt I hadn’t done well, and I kept turning over the answers to those questions in my mind. But standing here, it seemed those worries were carried away by the wind too.

I picked a few apples and put them in my bag, planning to take them back and share them with my friends. Who knew whether they would also like the fragrance of this orchard? Though I sometimes felt I was overly sensitive, always worrying whether others might be angry or dissatisfied, this time I hoped to bring them some happiness.

After a while, I slowly walked out of the orchard and returned to the school building. The autumn wind brushed my face, as if reminding me that life holds so many beautiful moments, and there is no need to stay tense every moment of the day. That night, lying in bed, I could still feel the orchard’s quiet stillness. That place seemed to have become a haven for my soul, allowing me to catch my breath now and then amid a tense life.

At lunchtime a few days later, I shared those apples with my friends, and their laughter gave me a simple kind of happiness. Though the worries weighing on my mind would not disappear right away, at least in that moment I felt a touch of warmth and comfort.

The studio lights were harsher than usual, filling the air with the chemical smell of paint. My palms were sweaty, and my fingers kept trembling around the brush. No matter how I adjusted it, the shadow on that painting’s face never looked right; every revision only made it feel like it was mocking my incompetence. I tried to take a deep breath, but it felt as if a stone were pressing down on my chest, making it impossible to breathe. A few classmates nearby were whispering to each other, and one of them glanced at me by accident. My heart immediately started racing, and a roaring rang in my ears. They must be laughing at my work—or at me. I stole a side glance, and it really did look like they were smiling, the corners of their mouths seeming to say, “How pathetic.”

“The shadow on this—would it be better if it were a little deeper?” someone suddenly came up beside me and broke my train of thought. It was Li Ming, always so confident, with work that was often praised by the teacher. Though his tone carried a hint of hesitation, it felt like a needle stabbing into me. “I know how to paint it!” I blurted out, my voice rising almost to a shout. He froze for a moment, then smiled. “Just a suggestion, no need to react like that.” His tone sounded like he was backing down, but I felt as if he were mocking me. My face burned, and my ears were hot.

“Do you think you’re so great? I don’t need your advice!” The words were out before I could stop them, and I immediately regretted them. The classmates around me fell silent in an instant, as if everyone’s gaze had converged on me. I could feel their stares pricking my face like needles. My fingers clenched the brush so tightly that my nails dug into my palm. I desperately held back useless tears, but my throat felt stuffed with cloth, and my breathing turned rapid.

Li Ming frowned, turned, and walked away, while I completely lost control. The conversation I’d just had began replaying in my mind. Was he laughing at me behind my back right now? Or going to tell others that I’d lost my temper? Why was this painting so awful? Why was I always like this, disappointing everyone?

The atmosphere in the studio gradually returned to normal, but I felt as if I had been cut off from the world, floating on some deserted island. My stomach started cramping, and cold sweat slid from my neck down my back. I stood up and hurried to the restroom. The moment I closed the door, I finally broke down and cried out loud. Tears poured out like a burst dam, blurring my vision. Looking at myself in the mirror, I muttered curses under my breath: “You’re such a failure. Why do you always mess everything up? Who would ever like you?”

That night, I never went back to the studio, and I never finished the painting. I lay in bed, staring at the ceiling, my thoughts scattered like spilled oil paint. Over and over, I kept wondering why Li Ming had come over to say those things to me. Was he trying to embarrass me? Or had he really not cared, and was I just imagining it? Then I thought about how the other classmates might see me—would they think I was moody and impossible to get along with? Those questions never left me for a single moment, and it wasn’t until three in the morning that I finally managed to close my eyes.

The stage lights were so blinding that I could hardly open my eyes, and the heat from the spotlight made me feel sweat slowly running down my back. The background music started, and I knew this was my cue to begin dancing. The whispering of the audience below gradually faded with the music, but my heartbeat began to grow even more rapid and unsteady. I could feel the tension in my stomach like a tangled knot. I kept telling myself in my mind that everything would go smoothly, but fear still lingered stubbornly in my head.

At first, everything went well, and I danced in time with the music. But in the instant of a turn, I suddenly lost my balance, stumbled underfoot, and an overwhelming wave of shame surged through me. Someone in the audience gasped, and all I could hear in my head was a voice repeating over and over: You failed. The performance went on, and I tried hard to keep a smile on my face, but I realized that every movement was starting to feel unfamiliar and stiff. I could hear someone in the audience speaking in low voices, and I couldn’t help wondering if they were talking about my mistake.

“Are you okay?” After the performance, my friend came over to ask me. I nodded, trying to hide the turmoil inside with a smile, but I knew the trembling on my face had given me away.

“I was really terrible...” I said in a low voice, my tone full of disappointment and self-reproach.

“No, you tried your best. It’s okay,” she comforted me, but I still couldn’t shake that intense sense of inadequacy.

On the way back to the dressing room, I kept replaying my mistake just now, every turn, every beat running over and over in my mind. The sweat in my palms had not subsided, and my back had gone stiff with anxiety. When I got to the dressing room, I sat on the bench, feeling the chill of the plastic beneath me, and tried to force myself to calm down. But that uneasy voice in my heart kept reminding me: “Everyone will remember your mistake.”

That night, when I got home, I lay in bed, and the patterns on the ceiling were so familiar I almost had them memorized. Thinking about the criticism I might face the next day made me toss and turn, unable to sleep. The next day, I walked into the classroom with a nervous heart, closed my eyes, listened to the whispers around me, and silently prayed that I could get through the day without being laughed at.

But after a few days, I realized that my classmates hadn’t paid much attention to my mistake that day. In fact, a few friends came over to ask about the details behind the performance. I finally realized that maybe I had been taking things too seriously; perhaps in their eyes, it was just a small accident.

People moved back and forth in the hallway, and sunlight slanted through the windows onto the floor. My shoes made a faint squeaking sound on the floor where light and shadow overlapped. My best friend and I stood at one end of the hallway, and the surrounding noise seemed far away, leaving only our voices echoing in my ears.

“You’re always like this, making such a big deal out of every little thing!” Her voice was full of impatience and anger. Those sharp words pierced my heart like arrows. I felt my cheeks grow slightly hot, my heart race, and my palms begin to sweat.

“I’m not! I’m just worried...” My voice trembled with anger and nervousness, and before I could finish, she cut me off.

“You always think the worst of everything, like the whole world is against you!”

Those words were the last straw. My stomach suddenly cramped, and the pain was so sharp I could hardly stand. I tried hard to hold back my tears, feeling as if something had clogged my throat. What echoed in my mind was the sense of disappointment I had always thought she would understand.

“I didn’t mean it. I just...” I said indistinctly, lowering my voice to the very minimum, afraid anyone else might hear.

“But you have to change, or I don’t even know whether we can still be friends.” Her final words struck my heart like a heavy hammer.

I stood frozen, watching her walk away, sunlight outlining a faint halo around her. I remained there in the hallway, feeling as if the world had suddenly become empty, my heart filled with a vast sense of hollowness. Only a few seconds later did I realize that people around me had begun to cast curious glances my way, which made me feel even more ashamed and helpless.

For the entire day, I was distracted, constantly replaying the argument in my mind. That feeling of being deeply misunderstood and abandoned was like a nightmare, tightly wrapped around me, impossible to shake off. When I got home that night and lay in bed, I found I couldn’t fall asleep, and my tears soaked the pillow.

A few days later, even though we tried to reconnect, that rift still stuck in my heart like a thorn that couldn’t be removed. I began to doubt myself, thinking that maybe I really was too sensitive and impossible for everyone to tolerate.

In the school hallway, the afternoon sunlight spilled across the windowsill, while I stood in the middle of the passageway, my ears filled with the laughter of classmates in the corridor. Everything around me seemed blurred by the pounding of my heart, and cold sweat had already broken out in my palms. My close friend was standing with me, a smile on his face, when he casually made a joke: “Your hairstyle really looks like a bird’s nest today!” I froze at once, as if pricked by a needle. The tightly held feeling of inferiority was suddenly triggered, and scenes of being excluded kept replaying in my mind.

I forced out a faint smile. “Are you saying I’m ugly?” My voice trembled a little, and my heart started aching in waves, as if those words had struck my deepest fear. “No, I was just speaking casually.” He hurried to explain, but I could sense there was not much sincerity in his tone; he just wanted to end the awkward moment quickly.

I said nothing, only felt a surge in my stomach, as if I were about to throw up. The warning of “being abandoned” kept echoing in my mind, and that scene flashed before my eyes again and again: my flaws magnified by everyone, and in the end, I would be cast aside. That thought filled me with unbearable shame and fear. “I have something to do; I’m leaving first.” I tossed out the words hurriedly and rushed toward the restroom.

In front of the mirror in the restroom, I stared at my reflection, my mind filled with chaotic voices. “Are you really that awful? Will they all leave you?” I asked myself in the mirror, but got no answer. A sour ache rose in my heart, and tears began to flow uncontrollably. Even here, I still felt there was nowhere to escape.

After a long while, I calmed down and decided to distance myself from him; that feeling of being mocked seemed to drag me back into the abyss. I thought to myself, “Rather than wait for them to abandon me first, I should leave first.” That night, I sent a text message: “Sorry, I’m feeling a bit unwell today. I may need some time to calm down.”

A few days later, I could still feel the impact of that incident. Although his texts and calls showed concern, I could never fully let it go, and the feeling of being dismissed in my heart never truly faded. Whenever I thought about it, my stomach would twitch, and even my hands and feet seemed to grow cold.

In the days that followed, this sense of abandonment and defectiveness often accompanied me in silence, always ready to burst forth at the most unexpected moment.

The morning sun bathed the entire sports field in light, and the air was filled with the fresh scent of grass. I stood at the starting line for the 100-meter dash, surrounded by classmates who were both nervous and excited. In my ears were the teacher’s words of encouragement and my teammates’ cheers, as if the whole world were waiting for this moment to arrive. “Are you ready?” the PE teacher asked from beside me. I nodded, but inside I was in turmoil. My heartbeat quickened, and my palms grew slightly sweaty, afraid that I might make a mistake in the race. When the starting gun went off, I tried my best to take off, but my uneasiness made my legs feel as heavy as lead. As I ran, I could hear my breathing grow rapid and my throat tighten. Halfway through the race, I suddenly stepped on the foot of the person beside me, instantly lost my balance, and fell to the ground. The noise of the sports field was immediately drowned out by the sound of my fall, and everything before my eyes seemed to sway. “Are you okay?” The teacher and classmates quickly gathered around, trying to help me up. But all I wanted was to hide, to disappear from this embarrassing situation. I forced a smile, while shame and self-reproach weighed on my heart like a huge boulder. After leaving the track, I sat at the edge of the field and watched the other competitors keep running. Why am I always so clumsy? Why do I never run well? My inner monologue churned on and on. I felt the cold wind brushing my cheeks, and there were no more cheers in my ears. I felt abandoned, left alone in a sea of mistakes. Even after the sports meet ended, I still couldn’t shake the shame brought on by my mistake. When I got home, I hid in my room, replaying the fall over and over again and blaming myself harshly. That feeling lasted for several days, and I could even see that moment in my dreams. My heart was filled with unease, unable to bear the doubts and fears about how others saw me. But in truth, no one blamed or accused me except myself. Perhaps I need to learn to accept even those imperfect moments.

Today, the debate club’s activity room seemed especially busy. Sunlight streamed through the blinds outside the window and fell across the tables, casting alternating bands of light and shadow. I sat at one of the tables, surrounded by stacks of debate materials and notes, absorbed in my own world. The room was filled with my classmates’ discussions, and the mixed, fragmented sounds would sometimes make it hard for me to concentrate. My heartbeat began to quicken, a reaction I always had, along with that familiar stomach pain. I imagined the interschool debate that would take place tomorrow, and all sorts of possible mistakes kept flashing through my mind. My teammates were excitedly discussing strategy, while I could not suppress my worry that my performance would drag the whole team down.

“Hey, how’s the preparation going?” a classmate beside me suddenly asked, her voice encouraging. I forced out a smile. “Still working on it, I’m worried I’ll forget my lines.” My voice was slightly trembling. “You won’t. You’ll be fine,” she continued, trying to comfort me. I nodded, but the anxiety in my heart did not ease.

Looking out the window, even the warmth of the sunlight made me feel an indescribable unease. My habit of catastrophizing small things filled ordinary days with unnecessary tension. “If I make a mistake in the debate, it won’t just be embarrassing.” I kept turning it over in my mind, replaying all those embarrassing moments from the past one by one. My palms were slightly sweaty, and I could hardly hold my pen steady.

While my teammates practiced and discussed strategy, I would do my best to hide my fear. I knew they needed a solid backup, and I couldn’t be the one who let everyone down. But whenever the discussion turned to me, I felt as though all the attention in the room was focused on me; my throat tightened, and my voice nearly caught in my throat. It was as if I could sense the hidden criticism in my classmates’ words and catch a trace of doubt in their eyes.

After the activity ended, I went home still weighed down by my mood. That night, I kept dwelling on everything bad that might happen, and it was past midnight before I finally closed my eyes. When I woke up the next day, the debate was about to begin, and my emotions still had not eased; the physical tension returned again. As I stepped into the venue, the air seemed to carry a stifling, heavy atmosphere. I tried to steady my breathing, but my heartbeat remained rapid.

This experience had a profound impact on me. Although it did not turn into the worst-case scenario, it made me realize that I always overinterpreted other people’s reactions and subtle hints. I feared being abandoned, rejected, and mocked, and these fears drove me to become increasingly anxious in public.

The moment the rooftop door shut, my heartbeat had already sped up, like uncontrolled drumming. The air was filled with a metallic chill, mixed with a faint smell of tobacco and a trace of the morning sun that still lingered. It was a secret gathering organized on the spur of the moment by a few classmates, and after only a few hours of preparation, I had actually agreed to go. By the railing on the rooftop, a few scattered figures stood whispering to one another, with bursts of laughter drifting over now and then. I hesitated in the corner, staring blankly at the rust covering the railing.

“Hey, why are you standing over there?” A familiar voice startled me. I quickly turned around; it was a classmate, looking at me with his head slightly tilted. His tone wasn’t overtly provocative, but I instantly felt an undertone of sarcasm. Was he implying I didn’t fit in? Was he secretly laughing at me for not having any friends? My face began to burn, sweat beading on my forehead, but I tried to force a calm smile. “Nothing, the wind is more comfortable here.” My voice sounded a little stiff, even to my own ears, and I found it strained.

He didn’t press the issue, only shrugged and walked away. I let out a sigh of relief, but my heartbeat still hadn’t returned to normal. Snippets of conversation kept drifting into my ears, as if someone were saying, “They’re always like this, not very talkative,” or “Isn’t that a little weird?” My mind immediately began to simulate scenes of them talking about me behind my back, even automatically filling in details that definitely had never happened. “Do they think they’re really aloof?” “Do they hate our group?” Those words scratched at my nerves like a cat’s claws, and my stomach began to ache faintly.

I gripped the railing tightly; the iron felt cold and hard, but I still felt powerless. I felt as if I were standing in the center of a stage, yet there was no script for me to perform, and no spotlight was meant for me. One classmate came over and handed me a bottle of water, apparently not noticing my awkwardness. “Have some, don’t stand so far away.” Her voice was flat. When I took the bottle, my hand trembled slightly, and even the fingers she had extended seemed to brush against me with a faint touch.

Gradually, night fell, the laughter around us dwindled, and everyone seemed to start leaving as well. I finally relaxed, as if I were surfacing from deep water. I quickly ran down from the rooftop, feeling even my footsteps were too loud. My heartbeat shifted from rapid pounding to a heavy thud, but it never fully calmed down. After I returned to the dorm, it took me a long time to calm myself. That night, the pain in my stomach never eased, and I kept feeling as though their laughter was still echoing in my ears.

Over the next few days, I kept replaying those conversations in my mind, again and again guessing every possible judgment they might have formed about me. This exhausting cycle left me almost unable to concentrate, and I always felt as though a voice inside kept asking over and over: “Was my behavior disappointing?”

I was backstage at the school arts festival, getting ready to go on stage. This was a performance we had rehearsed for weeks, and everything needed to be perfect tonight. The scene around me was hectic: the stage lights were bright and glaring, and the crew moved back and forth, adjusting microphones and the set. My palms were sweating as I stood at the back of the stage, my heart racing, with hushed conversations and the sound of music being tuned in my ears. I tried to take deep breaths, hoping to calm my nerves.

“Are you ready?” A classmate smiled as she came close to me, her voice drowned out by the noise backstage. I nodded nervously, though I was full of uncertainty inside. “We’ll go up together, don’t worry.” She gently patted my shoulder. Her smile made me feel a little more at ease, but it also made me realize how little confidence I had in myself. I began to keep thinking over and over about what would happen if something went wrong, and my thoughts came flooding in like a tide.

Standing backstage, in the flickering light, my inner monologue kicked in. Why were so many people coming to watch our performance? What if I forgot my lines on stage, or messed up the choreography? I could feel my stomach knotting, as if an invisible hand were stirring it. I tried to fight the feeling, only to find it useless. To keep myself from losing control, I kept attacking myself in my head: Why are you so useless? Why do you always end up making yourself this anxious?

The performance began, the music started, and the piece we had rehearsed for so long unfolded step by step. I moved to the center of the stage in time with the beat, the lights enveloping me, the heat on stage seeming to burn my skin. I could feel the audience’s eyes on me, as if everyone were watching me. My breathing became rapid, my heart raced, but I still forced myself to complete every movement.

After the performance, I sat alone in a corner backstage. People around me were cheering and congratulating one another, yet I felt unable to fit in. I could only manage a forced smile, while inside I still felt tightly wound. Hours later, when I got home, exhausted in body and mind after a day of stress, I still tossed and turned the next morning, replaying every possible mistake and detail from the performance.

Although everyone said the show was wonderful, I still felt that I hadn’t done well enough, and I often fell into self-doubt. The aftereffects lingered for days, and whenever I closed my eyes, the scene on stage would play back in my mind.

As the spring air drew nearer, the temperature in the classroom gradually rose, and the stuffy air carried a faint smell of sweat. Outside the window, the glaring sunlight spilled across the floor, casting mottled patches of light and shadow. Today was the school’s annual photography competition, and all the entries had been placed at one end of the classroom, waiting to be judged. I stood in front of my own work, my heart churning restlessly.

“This piece is really good, with a clean, crisp composition,” said a classmate beside me. I looked up and gave her a forced smile. “Thank you,” I replied, though a voice inside me seemed to object, “She’s only being polite.”

My gaze returned to the photo. It was a shot centered on slanting sunlight filtering through tree branches, the light falling through green leaves and scattering into tiny specks of brightness. But in my eyes, every detail of the picture seemed to expose my flaws. “The edges of the leaves aren’t sharp enough, and the handling of the light is too crude.”

My heartbeat began to quicken, and sweat beaded on my palms. My stomach felt tied into a knot, and my mind was filled with self-blame and denial. Other participants gradually arrived, excitedly discussing their works, their eyes full of anticipation. Afraid that others might notice my unease and lack of confidence, I unconsciously lowered my head and pretended to straighten the hem of my pants.

“The competition is about to start—are you ready?” another participant came over and teased. I nodded in response, but my voice was so faint it was almost inaudible. “What about you? I’m really looking forward to seeing your work,” I said, forcing myself to sound composed and trying to appear calm.

As the competition went on, the judges walked around one by one, stopping in front of each piece to examine it carefully. My heart pounded as I feared their eyes would linger too long on my work and reveal flaws I couldn’t see. I gently brushed the dust off the photo with my fingers, trying to make it look flawless.

After the competition, several classmates gathered together to discuss each other’s work, and I unconsciously joined in. Though I tried hard to take part in the conversation on the surface, inside I couldn’t help but keep replaying the judging process over and over. “They must have dismissed my photo completely.”

That night, lying in bed, the light and shadow in the photo kept flashing through my mind, as if mocking my lack of confidence. A few days later, the results were announced, and my work had not won any prize. Although it was not surprising, I still felt a wave of disappointment, as if my deepest suspicions and unease had been confirmed.

During that week, I kept replaying the competition in my mind, repeatedly examining my work and questioning my abilities again and again. I began to handle my creations with even greater caution, afraid of facing that feeling of not being acknowledged once more.

On an autumn afternoon, the sky was overcast and gray, as if covered by a thin curtain of clouds. I walked along the edge of the city and came to an abandoned old train station. The walls were covered in green moss, and the ground was littered with old newspapers and broken wine bottles. There was no human chatter, only the occasional sound of the wind echoing in my ears. My feet stepped on the yellowed ties, making creaking sounds, as if the station itself were telling me its story.

“How did you get here, kid?” A man who looked like the station’s old caretaker stepped out of the shadows, sounding mildly surprised. My heart tightened, and countless possibilities flashed through my mind—would he not let me stay, would he call the police because I’d trespassed into an abandoned place? “I just came to look around out of curiosity. It seems to have some history,” I replied stammeringly, trying to make my voice sound steady.

My mind was in chaos. Somehow, I kept feeling that every second someone was watching me, judging me. My heart raced, my palms began to sweat, and the clothes on my back gradually grew damp. My stomach churned uneasily. I silently blamed myself for always coming to these forgotten places, for always being so out of place.

The caretaker shrugged and slowly turned to walk deeper into the station. I let out a breath and looked around. The whole environment seemed as though time had frozen. Weeds grew wildly on the platform, and a few stray cats were lazily basking in the sun not far away. The wind carried the smell of rust and dead leaves, as if telling of the desolation here and the endless waiting.

I sat down on a worn-out bench and stared blankly at the tracks in the distance as they wound away and disappeared from view, as if they were leading me toward an endless void. I thought of those vague memories. Whenever I felt abandoned by the world, I would always run to a corner like this, as if loneliness were my only companion.

After I got home, I still felt shrouded by a heavy mood, as if the ghost of the old station had followed me all the way. That night I couldn’t sleep, and the scene of the train station kept replaying in my mind. A few days later, at school, I still couldn’t concentrate, as if the whole world had left me behind and only I remained on those yellowed ties, listening to the never-ending wind.

The lighting in the costume room was dim, and the air was thick with the stale smell of old fabric, faintly pungent. My fingertips trembled slightly as I tried to fasten the costume buttons, but the rough loose threads kept snagging. I could feel a thin sweat breaking out on my forehead, my heartbeat fast and irregular like a drum. From behind the curtain came my teammates’ voices: “Hurry up and get ready, it’s almost time to go on!” I tried hard to suppress the discomfort in my body, but found I couldn’t focus.

“Why aren’t you changed yet?” The club leader poked her head in, her tone urgent and somewhat impatient. I lowered my head and didn’t dare meet her eyes, stammering, “The buttons… the buttons are stuck.” She frowned, but apparently had no time to probe further, and tossed out, “Get it sorted quickly. Formal rehearsal starts in ten minutes.”

I clenched my teeth, and the worst images had already started flashing through my mind: if my clothes weren’t fastened properly when I went on stage, would everyone laugh at me? Would someone think I was slowing things down? Cold sweat slid down my back. I seemed to hear my breathing grow rapid too, while all the outside sounds reaching my ears blurred into a haze.

My inner voice screamed like an alarm: I’m a troublemaker, always dragging everyone down. Why did I mess up something so simple again? Those recurring thoughts made my chest feel prickly, and my stomach started to churn. Discomfort and shame washed over me at the same time. I even briefly wanted to run away, imagining leaving the room, leaving all this embarrassment behind.

In the end, my roommate Xiaoli came in and found me in my predicament. “What happened? Are the buttons stuck?” Her voice was calm and slightly concerned. I nodded, forcing back the moisture in my eyes. “Let me help you.” She came over, and with practiced hands quickly fixed the problem; the buttons were finally fastened.

I lowered my voice to thank her, but the guilt inside me surged even more violently. On one hand, her kindness warmed me; on the other, I felt deep self-reproach for my own incompetence. Head down, I asked, “Am I really such a bother?” not even daring to meet her gaze. She shrugged. “It’s fine. Everyone has moments when they’re flustered. It’s nothing serious.” Her tone calmed me a little, but that sense of shame still lingered in my mind like an unshakeable shadow.

During rehearsal, I tried hard to focus on my character’s lines, but the stiffness and unease in my body kept pulling my attention back to what had just happened. I was afraid that under the stage lights I looked especially unnatural, afraid that everyone present was constantly scrutinizing my movements.

After rehearsal ended, I quietly packed up my things, wanting to be the first to leave. But Xiaoli stopped me again. “Don’t take it too much to heart. Next time we can come earlier, and you’ll have more time to prepare.” I nodded, my voice faint. “Okay… yeah, okay.” But deep down, I started questioning her words again—were they only meant to comfort me? Had she perhaps already grown tired of my slowness and mistakes? That inner debate kept me tossing and turning all night, and when I woke the next day I still felt completely drained.

This little episode weakened my confidence once again, as if an invisible hand had pushed me back into that familiar whirlpool of loneliness. As I kept replaying the details, I tried to analyze my own behavior, only to find myself sinking deeper and deeper, even beginning to dread every rehearsal that lay ahead.

The air in the rehearsal room carried a faint smell of dust, and sunlight filtered through the blinds, casting mottled patches of light and shadow. I stood in the third row of the choir, leaning slightly forward, my palms sweating from nervousness. I kept my eyes fixed on every movement of the conductor on the podium, afraid of missing even a single beat. Today was our final joint rehearsal for the upcoming musical performance, and the teacher seemed especially stern.

“Watch the rhythm, watch the rhythm!” The conductor waved his arms, his voice carrying an unquestionable force. I tried hard to keep up with his tempo, but as his gestures quickened, so did my heartbeat, as if the blood in my whole body were being pulled along by every movement he made.

The choral voices echoed through the room, and the harmonies woven through the melody flowed smoothly like water. Yet when I noticed the conductor frown and slightly turn his head in my direction, my heart suddenly sank. Had I done something wrong? I immediately began to review every note and every tone I had just sung, trying to figure out what mistake I might have made.

“You, the kid in the third row, once more.” His gaze briefly locked onto me, and though his voice was not loud, it sounded like thunder in a tin can to me. In an instant my cheeks burned hot, as if pierced by countless eyes. My mind churned with every possible way I might have gone wrong, fearing he would point out my shortcomings and make me the center of attention, which was exactly what I could least bear.

I felt a spasm in my stomach, and my fingers began to tremble uncontrollably. I tried to calm myself, taking deep breaths and convincing myself that it was only a small misunderstanding. “What’s the problem?” I asked myself as I sang, my mind filled with doubts.

The rehearsal continued, and the conductor’s tone did not change; he simply glanced casually over each person. But in my heart, it felt like a huge accusation. I could almost hear my own heart pounding wildly, like a dense drumbeat striking against a marble floor. All I could hear was his repeated “Remember the key points,” while my thoughts kept circling around fears of being abandoned and making mistakes.

After the rehearsal ended, I did not leave right away. I stood in the empty rehearsal room, trying to sort out what had just happened. I still wasn’t sure whether I had really done anything wrong; just that look and that one sentence were enough to make me anxious and unsettled. I looked down in frustration at my own hands, rubbing my thumbs over and over, using this gentle form of self-soothing to calm the turmoil inside me.

That night, after returning home, I was still immersed in what had happened during the day. Sitting at my desk, I tried to recall every detail of the rehearsal, even unconsciously mimicking the conductor’s gestures, hoping to find out what had gone wrong. I kept questioning myself over and over in my mind, wondering whether I had truly let other people’s trust down.

“Maybe I’m just overthinking it; he wasn’t targeting me.” I tried hard to convince myself, but the sense of inadequacy would not go away. That night, I hardly slept well at all, and the fragments of that scene kept replaying in my mind, like a one-person show that had yet to end.

The homeroom teacher assigned a group discussion task in class, and we divided into groups of four or five. I gathered with several classmates from my group around a table, discussing ideas for the project topic. Everyone casually brought up their own thoughts. When it was my turn to speak, I swallowed nervously and tried to act natural, talking for two minutes about my viewpoint. I tried my best to express myself clearly, but after I finished, one classmate across from me raised his eyebrows and said, “Oh, that idea, hmm, it’s okay, I guess.” I froze for a moment, and my mind immediately exploded. What did he mean by “it’s okay”? Was he just brushing me off, or looking down on my opinion? Was he implying that I was boring? My thoughts started racing nonstop, wondering whether I had said something wrong or was just too mediocre and had disappointed everyone.

The conversation continued, and the other classmates brought up new ideas, but I was completely unable to focus. I could hear their voices, but they seemed blurred like distant buzzing, while all my attention was consumed by my inner monologue: “Does he hate me now?” “Am I holding the group back?” My heart was pounding so hard it felt like it could jump out of my chest at any moment. I could feel my cheeks burning, my forehead beginning to sweat, and my palms getting damp. I put my hands under the desk and clenched my fists tightly, trying to suppress the trembling in my fingers.

After the discussion ended, we dispersed and returned to our seats. I lowered my head and walked back to my place, feeling stiff as if the whole class was watching me. After sitting down, I opened my notebook, but found my hand almost wouldn’t obey me, and I couldn’t write at all. The teacher started lecturing, but I couldn’t take anything in. The scene from just now kept replaying in my mind over and over—the raised eyebrows, the words “it’s okay, I guess”—like a thorn stuck in my throat that I couldn’t shake off. Every time I thought of that moment, my stomach felt vaguely twisted with pain, leaving me restless and unsettled.

That night, after I got home, I lay on my bed staring at the ceiling. There was no sound around me, but my head was still full of noisy self-reproach. I even began to wonder whether the other groups had all spoken much better than I had, and maybe I was just a boring, useless person. Those thoughts weighed on me so heavily that I could hardly breathe, and tears started falling unconsciously.
