I tossed and turned, unable to sleep, constantly thinking about whether those classmates would be disappointed in my performance when I went to school the next day. Would they no longer want to listen to me speak? These thoughts swirled around me for the entire night, impossible to dispel even with my eyes closed.

The next day, I forced myself to stay alert in class, but I still couldn’t focus. When the teacher called on me, I answered haltingly, feeling as though I had only proven my own inadequacy even more. That sentence, that expression, seemed to hang in my heart and refuse to leave.

Sunlight streamed through the balcony glass, bringing a warm, tactile feeling with it. In front of me, the coffee cup gave off a faint wisp of heat, and the subtle aroma of coffee drifted into my nose from time to time. I adjusted the recliner to a half-reclined angle, holding a novel in my hands, trying to immerse myself in it. In the background, I could vaguely hear a neighbor’s child laughing and the television playing commercials, and occasionally the low rumble of vehicles passing back and forth below.

The feel of the paper as I turned the pages always helped calm me down a little. The novel was about a fugitive, but my attention kept coming and going. As I read the words, I couldn’t help getting distracted by everything on the balcony. Some of the plants by the railing had yellowing leaves, and I thought they should probably be watered, but I couldn’t be bothered to move. The breeze carried a slight chill, so I pulled the blanket up over myself.

My phone buzzed with a text notification. I picked it up; it was a message from a friend: “Free this weekend? Want to go eat hot pot?” I stared at the screen for a few seconds, hesitating a little. I really wanted to go, but then I suddenly remembered how I always felt awkward and never knew what to talk about. I replied, “Sure,” but in my mind I had already started rehearsing possible conversation topics for then. I came up with a few reasons to ease my nerves, like talking about books I’d been reading lately or asking about their new plans. I always have mixed feelings about this kind of socializing—both anticipation and anxiety.

I had been lying there for less than half an hour when the cramped space of the small balcony began to make me feel a little stifled. I stood up and stretched my shoulders, feeling stiff. The plot in the book had just reached its climax, but it left me somewhat distracted. I looked out at the world beyond the balcony; downstairs in the residential complex, people were out walking, and two cats were crouched by the flowerbed. I suddenly felt a bit bored, wanting to do something else, but not knowing what to do.

As the sun slowly moved toward the other side of the building, I felt the angle of the sunlight change, and the warmth on my body gradually faded. I slowly put the book away, finished the coffee, and stood on the balcony for a few minutes, staring at the gray, hazy sky in the distance. After that, I went back inside, turned on the computer, and listened to a few songs at random, wanting to find some new stimulation for myself. For dinner, I casually cooked something simple, just like on any ordinary day.

The music was deafening, my head felt swollen, and the air was filled with a mixture of sweat and cheap perfume. I stood at the edge of the crowd, holding a glass of orange juice, pretending to be relaxed at the party, but in fact my shoulders were already as stiff as stone. I stared at the dance floor ahead, trying to look like I was enjoying myself, while in my mind I was counting every word I had said—had I just smiled too awkwardly at Xiaoya? Had she noticed my nervousness? My chest began to tighten, and even breathing became difficult.

“Hey, why are you standing so far out here? Afraid we don’t welcome you?” A Liang pushed through the crowd and came up to me, joking with me. There was a hint of a smile at the corner of his mouth, and his voice carried a touch of drunken laziness. I froze; my heart seemed to be frozen too, beating sluggishly in my chest. Only one phrase echoed in my head—“Afraid we don’t welcome you.” Why would he say that? Did he think I was a nuisance? Did everyone not want me here? Did I look too out of place?

“I... of course I’m not afraid.” As soon as the words left my mouth, even I thought they sounded weak and hollow. He laughed casually a couple of times, turned to chat and joke with others, and didn’t spare me another glance. I stood there blankly, the orange juice in my glass growing cold. My heart began to race, my palms broke out in fine beads of sweat, and I gripped the cup tightly as if I were holding a slippery block of ice.

I couldn’t help thinking of many similar scenes: being mocked by classmates in elementary school for wearing old clothes, being ignored at a birthday party while others took photos with their friends... Were all of those true? Had I never really been accepted? A dull stomachache slowly crept in, and I felt like I could hardly stand.

Several familiar faces gathered not far away, and laughter drifted over. “I know what you’re laughing at!” My voice suddenly burst out sharply, carrying a surge of uncontrollable anger and shame. The people around me stared as the crowd fell silent. A Liang looked baffled. “What’s wrong with you? We were just talking about something else...” His tone held no malice, but his gaze felt like a needle stabbing into my heart.

My face began to burn, and my ears rang with a buzzing sound. I ran out of the house; the cold night wind outside, damp and chill, seemed as if it wanted to tear my skin apart. I ran while gasping for breath, tears blurring my vision. I felt like the whole world was laughing at me, talking about me behind my back. I had become a monster, a lonely monster that could never be loved.

That night I sat on a bench in the neighborhood for a long time, until deep into the night. My stomach still hadn’t stopped hurting, and my hands were still shaking. I listed countless reasons for “why nobody likes me,” trying to convince myself that this was simply the truth. But those reasons only made me feel more powerless, more ashamed. In the end I went home, locked myself in my room, and didn’t even dare look at myself in the mirror.

The activity room of the photography club was eerily quiet. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains and spilled across the table, casting mottled patches of light and shadow on the back of my hand. I sat in the corner, my fingertips still sticky with traces of glue. Spread out on the table was my work—a photo collage portraying the clamor and loneliness of a crowd. I had chosen my favorite piece, but now, standing in front of it, the senior didn’t seem very interested in my work at all.

He turned to look at me, one eyebrow lifting slightly, and said slowly, “This theme feels a bit overused, doesn’t it?” My heart suddenly clenched, as if something had grabbed hold of it. I tried to steady my breathing, but my chest tightened more and more, as though there wasn’t enough air to go around. I nodded vaguely, but not a single word came out.

A classmate beside me murmured, “I think it’s still pretty unique. The collage part is really well designed.” The senior shrugged and said, “Maybe. But it’s not very original. Try thinking of more creative themes next time.” As he went on to comment on the other students’ work, I was already completely unable to concentrate. I stared hard at the piece on the table, and the only words echoing in my mind were, “not very original.”

Deep down, I could feel that familiar sense of frustration and shame rising up. Why did I always feel like my ideas were as bland as stagnant water? Why was there always a trace of impatience in the senior’s expression? It seemed I really wasn’t suited for this kind of artistic thing—why had I even joined the photography club? My thoughts churned endlessly, each one like a sharp shard stabbing into me.

My palms started to sweat, and I unconsciously gripped the chair beside the table. The joints in my fingers tensed until they ached. I didn’t dare look up, afraid of meeting anyone’s eyes. The discussion around me gradually blurred into a humming background noise. My stomach began to cramp slightly, as if my whole digestive system were protesting my tension.

After the activity ended, I quickly packed up my work, put it into the tube, and hurried out of the room. The moment I stepped outside, I felt as if a mountain had been lifted off me. I took a deep breath, and the air suddenly felt fresh again. With my head still lowered, I walked all the way to a small grove of trees behind the teaching building. There weren’t many people there. I leaned against a tree and slowly sat down, trying to calm myself.

That night, I kept turning over the senior’s comments and my own reaction in my mind. Every time I closed my eyes, the image of that collage and his raised eyebrow flashed before me. I tried to defend myself in my head, telling myself, “It was just a group critique, nothing major,” but then I thought maybe he’d lost confidence in me and would never seriously look at my work again. By 2 a.m., I still hadn’t managed to calm down, so I got up, opened the tube, and laid the collage back out on my desk.

The next morning, I decided to take the tube back to the photography club and put the piece in the cabinet. I told myself that if I kept avoiding things, I might never make any real breakthrough in art. I’m still not sure whether that decision was the right one, but at least next time the senior criticizes me, I hope I can stand in front of him and respond calmly instead of lowering my head and staying silent.

The stage lights were so bright they made me feel a little dizzy. The chatter around me was noisy, as if I were wrapped in a thick cloud. I stood in the center of the stage, my palms damp and trembling slightly, with a hunch that everything was going to go wrong. The background music started, and I tried hard to steady my breathing and focus on my lines, when I heard someone nearby mutter, “Why are they always like this?” It wasn’t loud, but it clearly pierced my ears. My heartbeat instantly quickened, and it felt as if a huge rock were pressing down on my chest.

“Say that again?” I asked my classmate almost instinctively, my voice shaking. “Nothing, I just wanted to remind you not to forget your lines,” my classmate explained with a frown, in a calm tone. “Oh,” I let out two awkward laughs and kept staring at the script in my hands, where every letter seemed to be wobbling. A suffocating wave of unease surged up inside me. Did they all think I was useless? Were they all talking about me behind my back?

My stomach began to ache faintly, as if it were being squeezed again and again. I clenched my fists so tightly that my nails almost dug into my palms. Rehearsal after rehearsal, I was always this nervous, and yet I kept messing things up. Even in this occasion full of laughter and anticipation, deep inside me the echo of unease still lingered. I could feel sweat running down my back, my throat tight and blocked, my body as though it were sinking into icy water.

After rehearsal ended, I dragged my heavy steps out of the auditorium, while my classmates were still enthusiastically discussing every detail. I forced out a smile, but the muscles in my face felt unbearably stiff. When I got home and lay on my bed, the scenes from the day replayed over and over in my mind, as if a voice were repeatedly insisting: “You’re just not good enough, never good enough.”

The next day, I still walked into the classroom with a heavy mind. My classmates’ small talk made me feel out of place, and I began to doubt myself, even wanting to avoid everyone’s gaze. Every smile, every nod in conversation, felt like I was desperately performing a one-person show. At home, I kept thinking: Were they all pitying me, or even laughing at me behind my back?

A few days later, I made up my mind to take the initiative and ask the classmate who had spoken to me the day before. “That day, did you mean that I performed badly?” I asked her, gathering my courage. “Of course not. We all know you were just a bit nervous. Don’t overthink it,” she comforted me softly. I nodded slightly, but the unease in my heart seemed only to deepen. That fear of being “abandoned” would not leave me, like layer upon layer of shadow shrouding me.

The backstage lighting was dim yet harsh, and the metallic glare reflected from the long row of chairs made me feel hot and uneasy. I stood beside the black curtain, my palms sweating; several times I squeezed a tissue until it was soaked and then threw it away. Today was the class speech contest rehearsal. I had already prepared my script many times, but when it was my turn, it still felt as if my throat were blocked. “Relax, you can do it,” the class monitor said, patting my shoulder. His tone was very light, but I felt a hint of contempt in it, as if he were saying, “Even though you’re nothing special, there’s no need to worry too much.” I lowered my head and looked at the script, my heart already beginning to race, each beat feeling like it was about to leap out of my chest.

I began my speech, my voice trembling from the very start, pitched a little higher than usual. I could feel that some of my words were not being pronounced clearly, but what made me feel worse was seeing the students in the front row glance at one another, the corners of their mouths lifting slightly. My mind instantly fell into a chaotic analytical mode—were they laughing at me? Did they think my tone was odd, my voice awkward? Even though I was still reciting the script, my attention had completely gone off track, and my hands began to tremble uncontrollably.

At last I finished all the paragraphs. I heard a smattering of applause, almost certainly just polite applause. Walking back to the row of chairs, I felt unsteady, as if everyone’s gaze were criticizing me. After I sat down, the classmate next to me turned and asked, “Did you revise the script? It seems a little different.” His expression looked normal, but I immediately felt as if he were implying that my script wasn’t good enough, wasn’t clear enough. I nodded vaguely and didn’t dare say anything. His words began replaying in my head like an audio recording, over and over, searching for hidden meaning.

The physical reactions were becoming more and more obvious too. My stomach felt twisted into a knot, my palms kept sweating, and sitting there, my back felt as stiff as a plank of wood. I began to lower my head and flip through the pages, pretending to check the details again, but inside I kept blaming myself for not controlling my voice properly, for why my expression had been so stiff. I even started wondering why I had entered this competition at all—was it just to embarrass myself?

Later, after I got home, I shut myself in my room and lay on the bed, not wanting to move. What kept flashing through my mind were that moment when the classmates looked at each other and those polite rounds of applause. It felt exactly like being publicly rejected, yet there was no clear evidence for me to convince myself. That evening, while scrolling through social media, I saw that several classmates had posted photos of the stage, but none of them mentioned my name. I even started to think: was my speech so mediocre that it wasn’t even worth bringing up? That feeling of being overlooked made me even more anxious, and even the stomach pain wouldn’t go away. The next morning, I was still hesitating about whether to keep participating in the competition, until the class monitor messaged me: “If you’ve revised the script, I can help take another look when you have time.” I instantly felt a wave of embarrassment, and self-doubt surged back up. I could only reply with a brief “Okay.”

On an early autumn night, the air carried the scent of earth and withered leaves, with a hint of coolness slipping into my collar. I sat under the shed in the small courtyard, beneath a windbreak my dad had pieced together from wooden boards and old cloth. Insects chirped on and off all around. Stars hung sparsely in the sky, and my fingers pressed the strings as I practiced that F chord over and over again—my index finger barring the fret, always causing one or two strings to sound dull and muffled.

I knew I was making slow progress. Slower than others who had started around the same time. That thought was like a thorn; when things were quiet, it hurt the most.

Suddenly, barking burst out from the neighboring yard, sharp and continuous. My fingers froze on the strings.

My heart started racing.

“Is it because I’m playing too badly?” The thought came faster than I could suppress it. I took a deep breath and told myself not to overthink, to focus, to focus on the smoothness of switching chords. But my palms were already sweating, and the feel of my fingertips against the strings had turned sticky. I strummed again, and the sound fell apart, like an untuned radio.

Then the neighbor’s window opened.

The neighbor leaned out and said in a voice neither high nor low, “You’re playing pretty well, but it’s a bit noisy. We’re trying to sleep.”

The window closed.

I stood frozen, forcing out a smile and nodding.

They were gone, but their words stayed behind and began growing in my mind. “Playing pretty well” — was that just politeness? “A bit noisy” — did they actually think it sounded terrible, but didn’t want to say so directly? Was there a hint of impatience in their tone? I replayed those few seconds again and again, trying to find the real meaning in the intonation. My stomach tightened faintly, as if something were slowly twisting it.

I looked down at the guitar. It lay quietly in my arms, unaware of everything.

I tried playing a little more, but my fingers wouldn’t cooperate; I pressed the wrong frets, and the strings let out a harsh screech. I put the guitar down, not even sighing, just sitting there, feeling as though something inside me was slowly leaking away.

I went inside very early that night. Lying in bed in the dark, that “a bit noisy” kept turning over in my head. Had they been annoyed for a long time already? Did everyone around me think I shouldn’t keep going? I turned the question over and over, and the more I thought, the bigger it grew, until it seemed to cover the whole bed.

A few days later, I went to my guitar teacher and brought it up—casually, with understatement, but I said it. They smiled and said the volume could be adjusted, that everyone went through this stage, and it wasn’t a reason to quit.

I nodded and said, “Yeah, I know.”

But what I really felt was this: I had taken a perfectly ordinary complaint from a neighbor and forced it into a judgment. Mixed into that sense of relief was a little shame—not because I played badly, but because I had frightened myself again.

I’ve carried this sensitivity with me for a long time. It makes me overvalue every detail, translate every sentence into the worst possible version. I hate it, but it is also part of me, sitting quietly beside me, and every time I pick up the guitar, it is there.

The world behind the stage curtains always feels especially tense and hurried. The lights are blinding, and the air is thick with the scents of perfume, sweat, and heavy makeup. I stood backstage, my hands habitually clutching a small prop shaped like a compass, my palms sweating and my fingertips trembling slightly. Around me, there were footsteps and hushed conversations, along with the occasional burst of laughter, all of which only made me more uneasy.

“Ready?” the director’s voice sounded in my ear, and I jumped, almost dropping the prop in my hand. I hastily replied, “Pretty much.” My voice sounded sharper than I had expected. I could feel my heartbeat quicken, as if it were about to burst out of my chest.

My fellow cast members were all busy adjusting costumes and props. I tried to focus on the play that was about to begin, but my mind seemed trapped in a bind, unable to function properly. Then I heard someone say, “I hope this technical issue doesn’t act up again.” Those words stabbed into me like a sharp needle, and instantly the worst possibilities flashed through my mind: the stage lights suddenly going out, the audience’s eyes turning toward me like arrows, and me trembling awkwardly under the spotlight, isolated and helpless.

“Don’t think about it too much. It’ll go smoothly,” I silently told myself, but even I couldn’t believe it. My heart was still racing like mad. I felt a twist of pain in my stomach, as if anxiety were gradually spreading within me. To ease that unease, I took a deep breath, but the air still felt suffocating.

“Don’t worry, you can do it,” a fellow cast member said, patting my shoulder in an attempt to encourage me, but it only made me feel more like my anxiety was a burden.

A few minutes later, the lights finally stabilized, and a bell rang out, signaling the start. My scene was about to begin. Time seemed to stretch out, countless thoughts spinning in my head. Every step felt like treading on thin ice, and the image of myself making a mistake kept replaying in my mind. My sweaty palms nearly slipped the compass out of my grasp.

When I finally stepped onto the stage, the moment the lights hit me, I suddenly felt as if all my defenses had been stripped away. The lines caught in my throat, and I almost thought I had lost my voice. Time stopped in that instant. I struggled to recall the script, and only then was I able to force the lines out word by word.

After the performance, I practically fled back backstage, my heart pounding, my palms covered in useless, anxious sweat. And yet, instead of the criticism I had expected, I was met with praise and my fellow cast members’ smiles. The self-attack that had been building inside me was gradually covered over by this unexpected affirmation.

A few days later, when I looked back on that night, I realized that although I had felt such fear and unease, the version of me that had held on was stronger than I had imagined. I came to understand that in certain moments, I was not alone, and that trusting others was also a way to receive support.

The rustling of paper filled the air, and the editors’ desk was piled high with various proof sheets. I stared at the computer screen, repeatedly adjusting the layout of the article. I habitually bit my lower lip, with a persistent unease churning inside me. The atmosphere in the editorial department was a little tense; everyone was racing to finish copy for the next issue of the school magazine, and the air was mixed with the mechanical hum of the printer and the clacking of keyboards.

“Little one, we may need to change this picture. The date printed on it is wrong,” the chief editor reminded me softly by my ear. I suddenly looked up, my heart jolting, as if I could hear an undertone of reproach in his words. My heartbeat quickened, my palms sweating, and I hurriedly explained, “That’s impossible. I’ve checked it many times already; the date is definitely correct.”

The chief editor frowned, as if he wanted to say more. Sensing his attitude, I immediately grew anxious: “If there was a problem, why didn’t you tell me earlier? Everyone’s wasted time now!” I heard how sharp my own voice sounded, and instantly felt embarrassed and regretful.

The other colleagues looked over this way and lowered their heads slightly, their conversation becoming softer. I felt my cheeks burning, thinking, “Do they think I’m not fit for this job at all? Are they secretly laughing at me again?”

As my emotions grew more and more strained, my back was soaked with sweat, and my stomach ached dully as if it were being clenched. A strong urge to run away surged up in me, and images of being abandoned flashed through my mind, as though any mistake would make everyone keep their distance from me.

I forced myself to calm down, trying to preempt the other person’s possible criticism with self-attack: “I’m just an idiot who always makes mistakes. Maybe I should never have been put in charge of such an important task.” Yet instead of making me feel better, this only made the panic in my heart grow further.

When the chief editor pointed out the date to me, and it was indeed my mistake, my heart sank to the bottom instantly. I felt a tremendous sense of shame, as if I had been exposed in front of everyone around me. I needed to say something to salvage the situation, but I couldn’t even remember where to begin.

“I’m sorry. I’ll fix it right away,” I forced out through gritted teeth, my voice so soft it was almost inaudible. The chief editor’s expression immediately softened: “It’s okay. Just be careful next time.”

That night, when I got home, I still couldn’t calm down. Lying in bed, I tossed and turned, with only my stammering voice in the editorial department and my colleagues’ gazes echoing in my ears.

A few days later, I returned to the editorial department and decided to learn from this experience, no longer allowing small mistakes to trigger an out-of-control storm inside me. I reminded myself that failure does not mean being abandoned, and mistakes do not have to be defended against with self-attack.

In the debate club activity room, sunlight from outside streamed through the slats of the blinds, casting bands of light and shadow across the tabletop. The room was quiet, with only the faint rustle of turning pages audible. Several classmates and I sat around the round table, with a few debate reference books and stacks of notes scattered across it. The air carried a faint smell of ink, as if every molecule were reminding me how important today’s discussion was.

“What do you think of this argument?” asked the classmate sitting across from me, looking up with a hint of anticipation in their voice. I steadied myself, my hand unconsciously gripping the notebook on my lap, yet I could still feel my palms growing damp. My heartbeat quickened, as if each beat were deepening the unease in my chest. My own hesitant voice echoed in my ears—if I said something wrong, would everyone criticize me?

“Um… I think it’s okay, but we may need to add some real-world examples, otherwise it won’t be persuasive enough.” I tried to keep my voice steady, though it sounded more like an attempt to hide the anxiety in my heart. I glanced at the vice president sitting nearby, and she was nodding slightly, apparently agreeing with my opinion. That made me feel a little more at ease.

“Then I’ll go look up some new data and combine it with a few cases,” she continued, her tone light, seeming to bring a bit of ease to everyone. At that moment, my mood eased slightly as well.

As we continued discussing, I couldn’t help but keep watching everyone’s reactions, searching their faces for the slightest expression, trying to decipher their true feelings about what I said. This habit sometimes left me utterly exhausted, because I knew I was always overanalyzing things, worrying about being rejected and dismissed. The tension in my shoulders never fully went away, as if an invisible stone were pressing there.

After the discussion ended, I walked out of the activity room alone. The sunlight was so bright it made me squint. As I walked toward the library, I felt somewhat drained and unsettled. I kept replaying the conversation from earlier in my mind, trying to examine my performance and find possible flaws and mistakes. I kept thinking I should have said things better, expressed myself more clearly.

That night, in my dorm room, I flipped through books related to debate, with a cup of hot coffee beside me. The faint aroma of coffee filled the room, easing my nerves a little. I knew I had to become more confident, but realizing that didn’t mean I could change right away. The words on the pages blurred from time to time, and I closed my eyes, trying hard to calm myself. The next day, I appeared in the activity room with my thoughts reorganized, ready to face a new discussion.

On the basketball court, the glaring lights bleached the floor white, and the air still carried a faint rubber smell. I stood off to one side of the crowd, a little awkwardly watching the other students gather around the instructor. They were discussing how to divide up the filming duties for the promotional video, but my mind kept replaying one sentence over and over. “Do you really need to stand in the front? That doesn’t seem quite appropriate.” The words carried an almost imperceptible tone of contempt that I caught sharply, like a thin needle pricking my ear. The speaker was a boy who had always been fairly confident; he had said it offhandedly, but to me it exploded silently like a bomb, stirring up a wave of self-doubt.

I had only been following the teacher’s instructions, standing in the camera position to practice an opening move. The moment I heard those words, my stomach seemed to tighten, and my hands clenched into fists without my even meaning to, fingertips pressing hard into my palms. A sharp pang shot through me, and my mind immediately launched into a catastrophic inner monologue: Did the others also think I wasn’t suited for it? Did they think I was doing terribly? Were they secretly laughing at me behind my back? A sense of shame quickly spread through my body, and I even began to feel as though my sweat glands had become overactive; the dampness on my back and palms made me afraid to touch anything in the classroom again.

The teacher’s voice pulled me back to reality. “Come on, a few of you try standing in front and cooperate a bit so the movement looks smoother.” I had no choice but to squeeze back into the group and stand in that spot again. My chest felt heavier and heavier, as if a giant stone were pressing down on it. The boy next to me glanced at me again, and his expression made me feel picked apart. He then added a few more words: “Hey, it’s fine, just do your best and try.” On the surface it sounded reassuring, but I could tell it was a more subtle kind of perfunctory dismissal.

My brain exploded again, my heartbeat sped up, and even the sensation of the chair’s edge felt far too sharp, as if it had been magnified dozens of times into discomfort. I could almost hear my breathing growing deeper and more rapid, while the friction of sneakers against the floor as the other students moved around the scene grated on my nerves more with every second. By the end of the filming, my movements were stiff and awkward, and I missed the timing several times. The instructor furrowed his brow slightly but didn’t say much. When it was over, the boy even half-jokingly said to me, “You might need to practice more next time.” His tone stirred up an urge of self-attack that I couldn’t shake off; I involuntarily lowered my head and forced a smile at the corners of my mouth to hide something.

That night, after I got home, I was still turning the scene over and over in my mind. I kept trying to recall whether I had really performed that badly, whether everyone had noticed my mistakes. I even stood in the bathroom, staring at my expression in the mirror, trying to rehearse how I might respond next time. I regretted not explaining or pushing back on the spot, yet I was also afraid of seeming too sensitive. Sitting on the edge of my bed, I tossed and turned all night, my mind churning with those glances and fragments of words. When I woke up the next morning, my eyes were still heavy, and my stomach ached faintly again—I knew this whole thing probably wouldn’t pass so quickly.

On a cold winter day, the heater in the studio seemed to be having some trouble, and the air felt chilly. I rubbed my hands together, thinking that maybe after school I should buy a pair of gloves from the little shop beside the school. The walls of the studio were covered with students’ painting exercises, and the atmosphere felt a bit oppressive, mainly because we were discussing the theme of our graduation project, and no one was willing to speak up easily.

“Why don’t we... do a series about the modern city?” I tentatively broke the silence, deliberately avoiding everyone’s eyes.

“The modern city?” A male classmate looked up at me, his tone tinged with doubt, then muttered, “Isn’t that too ordinary?”

I felt my ears grow hot, and my heartbeat quickened, as if my heart were trying to break through my chest. I desperately wanted to hide my unease, but the hand holding the watercolor brush betrayed me; my fingertips trembled slightly. I quickly searched for arguments in my mind, trying to defend my suggestion, but other than what he had just said, I couldn’t think of anything.

Another person added, “Actually, the modern city is a pretty broad theme, but wouldn’t it be a little too hard to express? It also involves real-life scenes and the like, so the workload might be a bit heavy.” He spoke very cautiously, but hearing that made my heart sink even further. Did even he think my suggestion wasn’t worth trying?

“Actually, I think we could dig deeper, for example by focusing on certain architectural styles...” My voice grew softer and softer, and my confidence faded bit by bit.

“Could we consider some themes that feel closer to people’s hearts? Like youth, emotions, or family?” Another girl spoke from the corner, earning a few words of agreement. I felt as if I had been excluded; the surrounding conversation began to press my thoughts down even further. Suddenly, I felt clumsy beyond measure. It was clearly just a discussion in the studio, but it felt to me like I was going through a public trial.

“What do you all think?” The group leader glanced at me. Seeing that I remained silent, he continued asking for everyone else’s opinions. I should have said something, but what was there to say? Those thoughts seemed stuck at the back of my throat, impossible to get out.

Later, the discussion shifted in a more specific direction, and my suggestion had long been carried off to the horizon. I lowered my head, pretending to be busy drawing something, my gaze falling into the shadow cast by a plaster statue on the table. The sweat in my palm made the watercolor brush slippery.

When the discussion was nearing its end, the atmosphere relaxed a little. Everyone began putting away their art supplies, and the follow-up plans were basically finalized. I stole a glance and found that everyone looked normal, as if they hadn’t noticed my embarrassment at all. Yet my stomach was tied in knots, and half an hour later, when I walked out of the studio, my hands were still ice-cold.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed clutching a pillow, the entire scene in the studio replaying over and over in my mind. From the moment I spoke to every response, I kept analyzing it repeatedly: Was my explanation unclear? Was I being too presumptuous? Should I never have spoken at all? It was only deep into the night that I finally drifted into a daze, yet the next morning, that scene surfaced again on its own, like a jammed videotape, forcing me to relive every detail of the moment again and again.

The gallery’s white walls made my paintings seem especially out of place. The exhibition hall was filled with the soft sound of footsteps and people speaking in low voices. The air carried a cool scent mixed with paint and metal, as if every breath reminded me of how little presence I had. I stood in front of a work hanging in the very center, trying to smile at everyone who passed by, but it seemed no one ever truly stopped to look at my piece. A wave of discomfort washed over me; a dull pain began in my chest, and my heartbeat quickened against my will.

“Is this yours?” a stranger’s voice came from behind me. I turned around and saw a middle-aged man staring at the work. “Yes, I created this,” I replied, my tone somewhat tense.

He nodded, but quickly turned away without saying anything else about my work. I felt my face growing hot, and my palms began to sweat. I felt as though I had been left behind in a vast wilderness, alone before the art on the walls, which seemed to mock the effort I had poured into them.

A surge of unbearable shame and disappointment rose in me. I muttered to myself, “Why is no one willing to stop? Is my work really meaningless?” I could not stop these self-attacking thoughts; they were like blades piercing my heart, leaving me in endless pain.

After the event ended, I hurried out of the gallery. The freezing wind outside was like merciless lashes striking my face. The lights on the street were glaring and cold, as if silently criticizing my failure. My stomach twisted, accompanied by waves of fear and anxiety.

That night, lying in bed, I closed my eyes and could still see the empty exhibition hall and those paintings no one cared about. The next morning, I woke up still weighed down by my mood, replaying the disappointment from the night before, feeling that I could no longer face such occasions. Over the next few days, I repeatedly turned down invitations from other friends to attend similar events, afraid of experiencing that pain of being ignored again.

The art exhibition was held in a small gallery on the outskirts of the city. The space was relatively cramped, with the walls painted a deep blue, giving off a quiet, tranquil feeling. Raindrops tapped slowly and steadily against the window glass, making a faint but continuous pattering sound that lent the place a subtle sense of loneliness. The air was filled with the faint smell of oil paint and wet earth, as if I had just stepped into a space meant to heal the soul. I stood in front of my painting, gazing through the glass window at the gray sky outside, feeling a bit uneasy.

“This painting is really interesting,” a man said behind me. His voice was deep and carried a certain detachment. “Your use of color is very bold.”

I turned around and saw him studying my painting intently. He looked like an art lover, and there was a kind of confidence hidden in his casual attire. He turned back to me and smiled slightly. “Are you a painter?”

“Sort of,” I replied nervously, my heartbeat quickening and my palms starting to sweat. I worried secretly that he would see any flaw in the painting, or overlook the effort I had put in over many days.

His comment made me a little pleased, but it was followed by even deeper anxiety. I began to chew over his words repeatedly in my mind, trying to find any hidden hint of disapproval. My stomach began to ache slightly, as if warning me of some unease. I kept rehearsing the worst-case scenario: what if his smile was merely polite rather than approving? What if he actually thought my work was childish and ridiculous?

“You convey a strong emotion through your colors,” he continued, pointing to a detail in the painting. “It reminds me of some old Impressionist works.”

Though my heart was still racing, my thoughts were already entangling themselves around these words of praise, trying to find a sense of security in them. I forced out a smile in response to his compliment, while still unable to stop the urge to attack myself. Now and then, echoes of past scornful remarks rang in my ears, and those shameful words seemed to push me forcefully toward the abyss of self-doubt.

That afternoon, I felt like a lonely traveler lost in the rain. Even after leaving the gallery for several hours, I still felt his voice lingering in my ears. At night, lying in bed, I kept going over every detail and every sentence, filled with doubt and anxiety.

Over the next few days, I repeatedly revisited my painting, and from time to time I thought about those words that might have contained negative judgment, in a defensive sort of way. The experience at the exhibition made me even more uneasy about my own work, as if every brushstroke were hinting at my flaws.

The walls of the music club’s rehearsal room were painted light blue, and sunlight streamed in through the large windows, making the room almost too bright. We were preparing for next month’s school anniversary performance, and the room was filled with the sounds of various instruments. I stood beside the piano, my stiff fingers cautiously testing out the melody on the keys.

“What’s wrong with you today?” the club leader asked, leaning slightly toward me, his voice somewhat drowned out by the guitar. “You don’t seem quite yourself.”

“I... I might be a little tired.” I tried to keep the tremor out of my voice and kept staring at the sheet music, hoping to look more focused.

My heart was beating much faster than usual. I could feel sweat beginning to gather on my forehead, and my stomach felt tightly knotted and uncomfortable. I had been worrying that I would make mistakes during the performance. I couldn’t let everyone down, and I couldn’t let myself look foolish. My mind kept replaying every failure from the past, as if each effort were only reminding me of them.

We began practicing a new piece, and the band’s sound gradually blended together. My fingertips moved across the piano keys, but I could feel that my motions were somewhat stiff. The others in the band seemed fully immersed, while I was trapped in my own worries, unable to escape.

“That section was good. Everyone, let’s do it again,” the leader said. Hearing his voice made my heartbeat speed up once more. This was the part I was going to play at the school anniversary. I was afraid I would make a mistake, afraid of being blamed, afraid of being left behind.

After rehearsal, I packed up my instrument, my fingers still trembling slightly. The other members were discussing next weekend’s publicity work, but I didn’t dare join in. I only listened from the side, afraid of missing any detail. I kept thinking: would they think I wasn’t good enough? Would someone be talking behind my back about my performance?

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mind full of everything that had happened during the day. I couldn’t fall asleep. When I was alone, I always felt even more isolated and helpless, as if the world had been reduced to the sound of my anxious heartbeat. A few days passed, and my mood still hadn’t fully recovered. From time to time, I would imagine myself embarrassing myself on the day of the school anniversary. Even at other times, I often felt tension in my body, and the fear of this performance would not go away.

The café was lit somewhat dimly, and the air was filled with the aroma of roasted coffee beans, a scent that felt especially pungent when I was on edge. People around me were whispering, while inside I was caught in a silent storm. My friends sat around the table talking about trivial school matters, but my attention kept being held by one small incident. Just now, by the restroom door, I happened to overhear a few friends talking about something, and I clearly heard the words, “She’s really too sensitive sometimes.” I wasn’t sure whether they were talking about me, but a sharp pain shot through me, as if a cold dagger had pierced some old wound.

When I returned to my seat, my friends were still laughing and chatting. Even so, I still couldn’t shake off what I had just heard. I sat down, forcing down the panic inside me, and asked, “Who were you just talking about?” My tone, without my meaning it to, sounded anxious and stiff. They froze for a moment, exchanged glances, and then one of them said, “Oh, we were just talking about class stuff, nothing special.” I grew even more uneasy, feeling that they must be hiding something.

“Really nothing? I think I just heard... some things.” My voice was almost trembling, and my heart was racing so fast that my chest felt tight. I looked at their faces, trying to read something from their expressions, but everything was only vague speculation. Their smiles now seemed like a cover-up, and I immediately felt unbearably lonely. “Do you think we were talking about you?” another friend asked half-jokingly. I was instantly mortified; my face burned, my palms were sweaty, and I nodded at a loss for what to do.

They all laughed, and someone patted me on the shoulder. “Don’t overthink it, we were just chatting.” But those words felt like feeble reassurance, making me doubt myself even more. I began to dwell on my own embarrassing moments, replaying in my mind scenes of them possibly being dissatisfied with me. My stomach started to tighten, and I couldn’t even hold my coffee cup steadily, as if all my unease had come crashing down at once.

After leaving the café that day, I walked home alone, the noise of the street ringing in my ears. The lights from the shops on both sides flickered through my blurred vision, yet I felt especially cold and desolate. When I got home, I kept thinking about the possibility that they were actually unhappy with me, repeatedly turning over every one of their words and every glance. The sense of inadequacy welling up inside me would not let me rest.

Over the next few days, I didn’t dare take the initiative to contact them, afraid that the faint sense of distance would be further confirmed. I even began to question my own value in this friendship, and felt utterly lost about the future.

The stage lights blazed uncomfortably onto my face, and the air was thick with the scent of foundation and the warm breath of the crowd. I stood before the microphone, clutching the draft of my short story in both hands. My palms were drenched, cold sweat sliding down my spine, and I could even feel the discomfort of my clothes clinging to my skin. “Next is our original literature sharing segment,” the host’s voice came through the speakers, bright and cheerful, as if they had not noticed my stiff expression at all. “Please welcome the next creator—let’s give them a big round of applause!” Scattered applause broke out from the audience below. I took a deep breath and told myself, “Keep reading. Don’t look at the audience. Pretend they don’t exist.”

I began to read the script. The first few lines went fairly smoothly. Although my voice was a little dry, I tried hard to keep my tone steady. But just as I reached the first turning point, I heard a muffled laugh from the audience. It was very soft, but it stung my eardrums. “What are they laughing at? Did I mispronounce something, or do they think my story is ridiculous?” I kept reading, but my mind was full of all kinds of possible mockery: “They probably think the plot is stupid, right? Is someone cursing me in their heart for being overly dramatic?”

As these thoughts flashed through my mind, my stomach began to twist, as if it had been knotted into a ball. I tried to adjust my breathing, but the more I inhaled, the more constricted my chest felt. Finally, when I finished the last sentence, I quickly looked up, bowed, and then practically fled the stage. By then, the applause from below had already thinned out, and I could even hear people whispering. I couldn’t resist eavesdropping on one sentence: “It’s still a bit deliberate, not very sincere.” In that instant, my mind buzzed like shattered glass, the sound of cracks mingling together. I clenched the hem of my clothes, my nails already digging deep into my palm.

Backstage, I hid in a corner, my heart still pounding wildly, as if it might burst through my ribs. I tried to calm myself, repeating in my mind over and over: “This is just a presentation. No one cares about my work; they’re just talking offhandedly.” But those words couldn’t convince me. “Do they really think I’m insincere? Is this criticism of me?” I started going over every sentence and every plot point in the manuscript again and again, trying to find the part they might have mocked. The more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt, and I even began to doubt the passion I had once felt while creating it: “Maybe it really was too melodramatic. It wasn’t worth showing at all.”

That night, after I got home, I tried to open the manuscript and revise it, but every time I read a few lines, the whispers and laughter echoed again in my head. My fingers hovered above the keyboard, yet I never typed a single word. In the end, I closed the manuscript and went straight to bed. Although I felt utterly exhausted, the voices inside me still refused to stop once I lay down. I tossed and turned repeatedly, trying to find a way not to feel so helpless, but in the end I found nothing. It was only around dawn that I finally drifted into an uneasy sleep.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves and scattered across the grass, while a gentle breeze brushed my cheeks, bringing with it the fresh scent of grass. A few friends and I found a shady spot in the park and spread out a large picnic mat. Everyone brought some homemade food and placed it in the middle. Looking at those colorful little treats, we couldn’t help but admire everyone’s cooking skills. Not far away, the sound of children’s laughter drifted over on the breeze, filling me with a sense of inner peace.

“Your cake is so delicious. How did you make it?” one friend asked curiously.

“Actually, it was pretty simple. I just followed an online tutorial, and I didn’t expect it to really work,” I replied with a smile, lowering my head a little bashfully.

“You have to bring this again next time we get together!” another friend said eagerly.

So we ate and talked about interesting things in our lives. We shared little recent stories with one another—someone talked about a funny customer they met at a café, and someone else shared a great movie they had recently watched. As time passed, the sun warmed our bodies, as if time itself had stopped.

I lay half-reclined on the mat, feeling the coolness brought by the breeze, surrounded by my friends’ laughter and chatter. I closed my eyes and enjoyed the simplicity and beauty of the moment, a sense of contentment rising in my heart. There was no anxiety, no worry—just the simple act of living in the present. That feeling flowed through my body along with the breeze and the laughter. I could feel my heartbeat growing steadier, my muscles relaxing slightly, and an unconscious smile lingering on my face.

When the sun was about to set, we all began to pack up. My friends said goodbye reluctantly and promised to have another gathering like this as soon as possible. On the way home, I felt happy and relaxed inside.

That night, lying in bed and recalling the day’s little moments, I could still feel that easygoing atmosphere. I realized that sometimes these simple and joyful moments are the ones most worth cherishing in life. When I woke up the next day, I still felt that peace and contentment, as if yesterday’s sunlight were still shining in my heart.

The sign on the glass door was stained orange by the setting sun. As soon as the door opened, a wave of cool air hit me, carrying a faint milky sweetness. I walked into the ice cream shop with two classmates, and while they eagerly discussed all kinds of flavors ahead of me, I unconsciously lagged behind, feeling a little unsettled. The server behind the counter smiled and asked, “What would you like?” They each ordered a strawberry sundae and a matcha snow cap. When it was my turn, I hesitated for a moment and finally ordered the most ordinary vanilla ice cream.

We sat down by the window, where we could see pedestrians hurrying past the street corner outside. I scooped up a little ice cream with a small spoon and put it in my mouth; it was cool, and the sweetness melted across my tongue. They started talking about the latest school gossip. One of them said, “Did you hear? That chemistry teacher actually deducted points from the whole group!” I nodded and chimed in, “Yeah, that’s really too much.” But when they began discussing some classmates’ private arguments, my stomach started to tighten a little, as if something had gently twisted inside it. I worried that my opinion might upset them, but I also felt out of place for not joining in.

“What do you think?” one of them suddenly turned and asked me, with an expression that was half curious and half encouraging. I froze for a moment, then hurriedly said, “I think... there are probably two sides to this.” When I finished, I noticed they each just gave a soft “oh” and then continued their own conversation. I felt as if I’d been stung. I thought what I said was wrong, but I didn’t know how to continue.

“Do you think this kind of topic is boring?” the other one asked suddenly, her tone light, though I seemed to hear some dissatisfaction in her words—or maybe she was just trying to confirm something. I quickly waved my hands and said with a smile, “No, not at all. I think it’s pretty interesting.” But even as I said it, I thought it sounded stiff. My heartbeat sped up a little, I felt slightly sweaty between my shoulder blades, and I gripped the small spoon too tightly, until my knuckles turned pale.

They didn’t seem to notice and kept talking about other things. The ice cream in my mouth was almost melted, but I ate it very slowly, as if I were afraid the sound would disturb them. I tried to tell myself, “It’s fine, it’s fine,” but I kept replaying my answer from earlier in my head, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt that I looked unnecessary, awkward.

By the time we left the ice cream shop, it was completely dark. The streetlights were on, and the signs of nearby stores were flashing. I followed behind them, trying hard to find an easy rhythm. Their laughter was bright and clear, but it felt distant to me. I wanted to join in, but I always felt like I couldn’t keep up.

After I got home, I hastily finished dinner, then curled up in my room and scrolled through videos on my phone to distract myself. But whenever the screen dimmed and my shadow appeared in the black glass, I couldn’t help thinking, “Did I do something wrong? Do they think I’m boring?” These questions were like background music that kept bothering me, and it was only very late that they slowly faded away.

I sat at the small table in the school broadcast room, facing a heavy old-fashioned microphone, with walls covered in posters and old cassette tapes. The light overhead was somewhat dim, and the air was filled with the mixed smell of old paper and plastic. The room was well soundproofed; I could only hear the faint sound of my own heartbeat. Nervously, I stared at the script in my hands, sweat seeping from my palms and making the paper slightly damp between my fingers. I began to feel uneasy about the recording session that was about to start. Taking deep breaths, I tried to steady my emotions.

The classmate sitting across from me began adjusting the equipment, and a faint crackle of static came through the headphones. “Don’t be so nervous, kid. It’s just a normal recording,” he said with a smile. I managed a weak smile, but inside, waves of unease were still churning. My stomach seemed tied in knots; every thought brought a dull ache, and the discomfort distracted me.

“Alright, you’re ready. Let’s begin,” he said, gesturing for me to start. Suddenly, my own voice filled my ears, and I tried to open with the tone I had practiced before. “Welcome to today’s campus broadcast, I am…” Yet with every sentence, I seemed to hear the flaws in my own voice, as if every slight shift in pitch could be magnified endlessly and judged.

A few minutes later, I finished the recording, and my heartbeat gradually calmed. Just as I was about to relax, he suddenly said, “Hmm, not bad, but some parts sounded a little nervous. It would be better if you were more relaxed.” Though his tone was gentle, my heart tightened at once, and I felt judged and dismissed. That simple comment kept echoing in my mind, as if warning me that I hadn’t done well enough.

After leaving the broadcast room, I was met by a chill breeze, and my skin felt slightly stiff from tension. On the way home, I couldn’t stop ruminating over my performance, replaying every small mistake from the recording. That night, I lay in bed, but my thoughts were still lingering in the broadcast room, and the knot in my stomach still hadn’t eased.

A few days later, the comment was still troubling me, and I kept wanting to prove myself again. In front of my other classmates, I tried to act unconcerned, pretending that the remark hadn’t affected me. But only I knew that it was like a needle, constantly pricking my heart, filling me with awe and fear every time I took part in an activity in the broadcast room.

I stood downstairs by the dorm building. The dim yellow streetlamp cast my shadow on the ground, making me look all alone. The night air was damp and cold, the moisture soaking through my coat. I could faintly smell the plants in the bushes not far away, and my fingers were shaking from both the cold and my nerves. I had just had an argument with my roommate, and the sound of her slamming the door as she left was still echoing in my mind. I had lowered my voice and argued with her, but in the end I still couldn’t help saying something too harsh: “Do you just think I’m really annoying? Have you guys long since stopped wanting to live with me?” Her face darkened all at once. She didn’t answer, only said coldly, “You should know that yourself.” Then she turned and left. I stood there, feeling completely emptied out.

“Have they been putting up with me all this time? Have I never been likable?” Thoughts like these rushed in wildly, almost making it hard to breathe. I could hear my own heartbeat, fast and heavy. My stomach hurt as if it had been clenched in a fist, and there was even a nauseous feeling to it. I looked down at my toes, trying to calm myself, but the more I tried to settle down, the harder my heart pounded. The cold wind brushed across my face; I covered my face with my hands, but my palms had already started to sweat, sticky and damp.

“Why do I always mess things up? Why can’t I just be normal?” These words kept looping in my mind. I knew my sensitivity made them impatient, but I just couldn’t control it. The scene of the argument replayed over and over: the look she gave me as she frowned, her impatient tone, and that line that kept pounding at my heart, “You should know that yourself.” Know what? Know that I’m just a burden? I felt like I had fallen into a bottomless black hole, and the harder I tried to break free, the deeper I sank.

Someone passed by not far away. Their laughter sounded incredibly distant to me, even a little piercing. I didn’t dare look up, only pretending I was invisible. I didn’t want anyone to see how miserable I looked. I even felt that if a passerby glanced at me one more time, they might realize I was a failure. I looked around, and there wasn’t a single place that felt safe enough for me to hide. It felt as if I had been abandoned, truly abandoned.

In the end, I still went back to the dorm. My roommates were already asleep. In the darkness, I quietly climbed into bed, pulled up the blanket, and buried my face in the pillow. Then the tears started flowing uncontrollably, as if a valve had been opened. I bit my lip with all my strength, afraid of making a sound, afraid of being heard. In my head, I replayed the conversation from the evening again and again, analyzing every word she said, breaking down every expression on her face, trying to figure out what she really meant. But all I seemed to find was one conclusion: they really didn’t like me.

The next day, I woke up at 6:30 in the morning, my eyes so swollen that I didn’t even dare look at myself in the mirror. My head felt heavy, as if I were still trapped in yesterday’s black hole. I put on my coat and went to wash up, pretending not to care, but when my roommates got up, none of us said a word. That silence felt like an obstacle frozen in the air—impossible to get through and impossible to escape. Silently, I warned myself to try not to say anything offensive to them, but that careful restraint made me feel suffocated.

In the café, the place was buzzing with chatter, and the rich aroma of coffee filled the entire space. My friend and I sat by the window, looking out at the nonstop traffic and the gloomy sky. We ordered coffee—he got a latte, while I chose a cappuccino—and steam rose in the air. I stirred the coffee in my cup with a spoon, watching the milk foam sway slightly. We talked about a recent movie, and I couldn’t help but complain a little: “I really think the ending was so boring—there wasn’t a single surprise.”

My friend smiled, took a sip of his coffee, and said, “But I think that’s exactly what makes the director clever. In real life, how many things are really surprising?” His tone was relaxed and low-key; clearly, he had no intention of arguing with me.

My heart tightened a little, and my pulse quickened. I wondered if I was being too harsh. I looked at his expression, trying to tell whether he was angry, but he only raised an eyebrow slightly. I quickly adjusted my attitude and said with a smile, “Maybe I’ve just been in a bad mood these past few days. Everything feels off somehow.”

Just then, a cold draft rushed in from the entrance, and I couldn’t help shivering. I shrank back a little in my chair. The surrounding conversations gradually turned into a background hum, and I stared at the surface of my coffee, feeling somewhat uneasy.

“Are you okay?” my friend asked suddenly, his tone full of concern. I looked up and immediately realized I might have been a bit too sensitive.

“I’m fine. Maybe it’s just the gloomy weather—it makes me a little down,” I said. Afterward, I felt a bit silly, but I didn’t know how else to explain that inexplicable mood.

The conversation continued, and we shifted to lighter topics. Although that slight discomfort in my heart hadn’t completely gone away, I tried my best to ignore it. After leaving the café, the cold wind immediately swept over me. I pulled my coat tighter and seemed to feel a little more at ease.

That night, lying in bed, I was still thinking about the conversation with my friend. Though it had only been a small episode, it left me feeling a little guilty. I thought I might really need to learn not to be so sensitive, not to let little things upset my mood so easily. The next day, I could still feel that slight unease, but I also knew this was a normal reaction for someone like me. Gradually, perhaps I would be able to handle feelings like this better.

When I walked into the library, the lamplight on the desk quietly spilled across the thick carpet, and the air was filled with the smell of old books. The faint rustling of turning pages and the occasional cough intertwined to form a unique kind of tranquility. I had mentally prepared myself for this quiet time, hoping to use it to escape everything disturbing around me. Yet when I found a secluded spot in the corner and sat down, the moment I looked up, I saw a familiar figure walking toward me.

“Hey, how are you?” Her voice broke the silence. I looked up and tried to force out a smile. “Hey, long time no see.” My words were a little stammered, and my heartbeat began to quicken. My inner monologue started to surge, just as it had years ago when I shyly spoke to her.

We started talking. She chatted about some recent events, her voice gentle and her face smiling. However, my attention was not entirely focused on what she was saying; it was distracted by the sound of my own heartbeat. I could feel my palms beginning to sweat, and my stomach aching faintly, as if anticipating the worst. Whenever she mentioned a mutual friend or a shared memory, scenes of possible awkwardness would instantly replay in my mind.

“Do you still remember that outing we took? I really wish we could have another chance like that.” Her voice carried a note of nostalgia, while I felt a wave of unease. I quickly replied, “Of course I remember. That was really fun.” The faint crackle of static in the phone was especially noticeable in our silence, as if reminding me of the countless unspoken details. She tilted her head slightly, watching my expression, while I tried to keep smiling, my feet repeatedly rubbing back and forth under the table, trying to divert my overly focused attention.

After the conversation ended, I watched her leave in a hurry, disappearing into the shadows behind the bookshelves. My heartbeat still had not settled, my body was somewhat stiff, and I tried hard to steady my breathing. When I turned back to the book in my hands, I found the words blurred and unclear.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying every moment of our conversation. I quietly blamed myself for my awkwardness, well aware that this tendency toward overinterpretation and catastrophizing had always troubled me. Yet I also knew these feelings did not arise without reason; they stemmed from my deep-seated fear of being overlooked or misunderstood. A few days later, I wrote down these feelings in my notebook, hoping that in the future I could face similar situations more calmly.

The classroom was empty and deserted, with only uncollected colored paper and chairs piled haphazardly in the corner. A faint floral scent still lingered in the air, carried by the bouquets the parents had brought earlier. The graduation ceremony had only just ended, and the classmates were still outside taking photos together. But I was holding my phone, staring at a message on the screen, my mind in complete disarray.

“You’ve misunderstood, haven’t you?” The screen showed a short message from a friend. My hand holding the phone was trembling slightly, and the screen felt slippery from the sweat in my palm. I unconsciously bit my lower lip, feeling the sting of my teeth pressing into it, but it was nothing compared to the bitter ache welling up in my heart.

Two minutes earlier, I had seen her whispering with several other classmates at the classroom door, and I had clearly heard one of them mention my name. “She’s just like that—too sensitive.” The sentence cut across my eardrums like a sharp knife. Though it wasn’t loud, it was amplified endlessly in my mind. A scene formed rapidly in my head: they were standing there judging me, discussing the things I hadn’t done well enough, maybe even sneering at me in secret.

“I knew she never took me seriously.” Blaming her in my heart, I quickly left the crowd and returned to a corner of the classroom, curling up on a chair. The feeling in my chest—as if it had been torn apart—grew stronger and stronger, as though something were squeezing my heart and making it hard to breathe. I could feel my stomach starting to ache faintly too, as if it had been clenched in a fist.

My phone vibrated again. I looked at the screen; it was still her message: “Are you angry? I really didn’t mean it.” Seeing the words “didn’t mean it,” I became even more convinced of my suspicions. She must have been saying bad things about me just now. I could feel my eyes heating up, and tears, embarrassingly, began to rise. I instinctively wiped them away, but the more I wiped, the more tears came.

“It’s fine.” I typed the two words quickly on the screen and pressed send. Then I immediately threw the phone into my bag, as if it had turned into a piece of burning hot iron. I lowered my head and stared at the floor, feeling a huge wave of shame rise in me. Why was I always so prone to overthinking? Why did I always assume that whenever others mentioned me, they were talking behind my back?

Even after I got home, I still couldn’t calm down. During dinner, when my family asked why I hadn’t taken photos with my friends, I gave a vague reply: “Nothing.” I retreated to my room, buried myself under the blanket, and closed my eyes, but no matter what, I couldn’t sleep. Her words echoed over and over in my ears: “She’s too sensitive...”

A few days later, she tried to explain what had happened that day, saying those words weren’t directed at me at all. I nodded and pretended not to care, but in my heart I had already put up a wall. It was no longer possible to trust her the way I had before. I told myself it wasn’t that I was too suspicious—it was that other people simply weren’t worth trusting.

Raindrops tapped gently against the window, and the gray sky made everything seem heavier. Sitting in the school study room, I could hear the rain outside blending with the ticking of the clock. In weather like this, I always feel oppressed, as if an invisible stone were pressing on my chest. My friend was sitting across from me, holding a thick novel in her hands, looking completely absorbed. My mind kept drifting to our recent conversations, replaying every detail that might have been overlooked.

“How have you been lately?” she suddenly looked up and asked me. Her tone sounded a little casual, but I couldn’t help feeling a jolt of nervousness. My heartbeat quickened without me even realizing it, as if I had to give a reply from the depths of my soul. My palms grew slightly damp, yet my back remained chilled by the weather.

“Pretty good, I guess, just that the weather is awful,” I tried to keep it light, but my voice may have betrayed a hint of trembling. She frowned slightly, as if thinking about something, which made me uneasy. Had I said something wrong? Was she dissatisfied with my answer just now?

In my mind, I began overanalyzing every expression on her face, even wondering whether she had some dissatisfaction with me. I couldn’t ignore the vague anxiety in my heart, and I started blaming myself for always reacting so strongly. Memories of similar situations came back to me—I always worried excessively over the smallest things.

“Don’t you like weather like this?” She put down the book in her hands and took on an interested expression.

“It’s okay, really. I just didn’t sleep well last night, so I’m a bit tired.” I adjusted my posture, trying to look more relaxed.

“It’s fine, relax a little. I think cloudy days have their own beauty too.” She smiled. I clung to her smile as if it were a lifesaving rope, and my heart calmed down a little. There was no reproach in her eyes, and that made my taut nerves loosen somewhat.

That afternoon, I returned to my room, and the sound of the rain in my ears gradually became a comfort. I began to realize that I often fell into self-blame and panic over even the tiniest things. And this time, my friend didn’t question me because of my unease.

Sometimes this kind of weather is actually quite nice, giving me a chance to reflect on my own sensitivity. I turned my attention to the droplets disappearing on the windowsill, and my mood gradually settled as the rain washed away that tense feeling. That night, when I went to sleep, it was still raining outside, but I felt a little more at ease inside. The next morning, the rain was still falling in a steady drizzle, but it seemed that I had also found again the quiet sense of peace that had once been soaked by the rain.

The glaring sunlight spilled over the rooftop iron railings, while cold gusts of wind swept across in waves, carrying the dry chill unique to winter in the distance. I stood here not to enjoy any scenery, but to calm the heart in my chest that felt ready to explode. I glanced down at the wrinkled draft paper in my hand, on which a few cue words were scribbled messily, but I could no longer make them out. My brain seemed frozen by the wind, completely blank. In the first class of the morning, the teacher suddenly announced that each student had to give an impromptu share during the class meeting about a social hot topic, and I had drawn the third turn to speak. This sudden task made my stomach twist painfully in an instant. 

“How are you? Nervous?” A voice came from behind me, startling me so much I almost crumpled the draft paper into a ball. My classmate Awen poked his head out through the door and stood beside me. He looked at me with an expression I couldn’t define, and dozens of possible meanings flashed through my mind in an instant. Was he mocking me? Did he think I couldn’t do it? Or was he actually just as nervous, pretending to be relaxed? “Yeah, I’m okay, I guess...” I said awkwardly with a small smile. Awen tapped the iron railing. “Honestly, just say whatever. It’s fine. Anyway, nobody remembers who said what.”

Did he really think that? Or was he implying that I’d definitely make a fool of myself? I tried to read something from his face, but he quickly lowered his head to look at his phone, the corners of his mouth carrying an indifferent smile. That smile felt unbearably glaring to me, even more piercing than the winter sunlight. I tightened my grip on the draft paper, my fingernails nearly digging into my palm. I gritted my teeth and muttered inwardly: Even if I speak a bit worse, at least I prepared seriously, not like someone who acts like it doesn’t matter at all! 

The bell rang, and I had no choice but to go downstairs with Awen back to the classroom. As the class meeting just began, the teacher called on me to get ready. I sat there, my heart beating so fast that my ears were almost buzzing. I felt as if every classmate was secretly watching me, those gazes pricking my back like countless tiny needles. 

“Next, the third student...” When the teacher’s voice fell, my body seemed to flip a switch, and I stood up mechanically, clutching the draft paper as I walked toward the podium. My footsteps sounded especially loud in the silence, as if each step were announcing my unease. 

The moment I stepped onto the podium, my throat felt blocked by something. Facing dozens of familiar faces below, I couldn’t think of a single word from those ordinary topics. I looked at the expressions on my classmates’ faces; some were looking down at their phones, some were whispering, and some had the corners of their mouths slightly raised, seeming to suppress laughter. It felt as though someone was pointing and whispering behind your back, maybe thinking, “She’s definitely going to be embarrassed.” “Oh my God, why can’t she say anything?”

Those few seconds of silence felt like a century had passed. I forced myself to breathe, then began to read out the contents on the draft paper in a halting, recitation-like tone. My voice sounded both dry and stiff, and with every sentence I spoke, cold sweat seemed to squeeze out from my palms, soaking the paper in my hand. I could feel the skin at the roots of my ears burning hot, my scalp tense, my neck rigid as if it had been fixed in place. 

At last I finished reading, bowed, and hurried back to my seat. When I returned, the classmate beside me whispered, “Not bad, actually. Better than me.” I didn’t respond, just lowered my head and fiddled with the pen in my hand, while inside my mind was already in turmoil: Did he really think it was good, or was he just comforting me? My back was soaked in cold sweat, and I felt utterly drained, my head full of how many words I had misread just now, how many times I had paused, and what the others might be laughing about. 

After class, I deliberately stayed a little longer, waiting for everyone to leave before I went, because I really didn’t want to face their gazes anymore. That night, I lay in bed staring blankly at the ceiling for who knows how long, replaying every expression on their faces one by one. I kept trying to remember whether Awen had been laughing at me. Maybe he had just been thinking about something else. But if he really was laughing at me, then hadn’t I completely humiliated myself today? My mind spun like a perpetual-motion machine until the alarm rang, and only then did I realize I didn’t even know when I had fallen asleep.

On a sunny afternoon, our group discussion took place in a corner of the library. Sunlight streamed through the windows onto the tabletop, and the shadows of the pages danced across the wooden desk. I sat at one end of the table, facing three classmates. The discussion was about a simple sociology project, but I always couldn’t help but see it as a challenge.

“We can analyze this issue from different perspectives,” one classmate suggested, his voice clear and confident. I nodded in agreement, but inside, the seeds of anxiety had already begun to grow. His tone made me uneasy, as if he were implying that my earlier ideas were not comprehensive enough. I began to doubt my own contribution.

“Well, I mean, should we focus on the social significance of these cases?” I cautiously offered my view. As soon as the words left my mouth, my heart started beating faster, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. The surrounding silence made me even more nervous; I could hear my breathing becoming quicker.

Another classmate replied, “Yes, that makes sense, but we need more specific data to support it.” Her gaze was calm and focused, but I immediately interpreted it as a challenge to my point.

“Did I say something wrong?” I asked anxiously, my cheeks starting to burn, my stomach aching faintly. My thoughts spun rapidly, and past mistakes surfaced one by one, as if mocking my present incompetence.

She smiled and shook her head. “It’s okay. I just hope we can find more information to back it up.”

I tried to smile back, but the self-criticism inside me still would not stop. Why was I always like this? Always so sensitive, always overanalyzing what others said. The discussion continued, and I struggled to stay focused, but the feeling of being excluded would not go away.

After the discussion ended, I walked alone along the path back to the dormitory, the conversation replaying in my ears. I could not shake off the guilt and shame that had suddenly pressed down on me. The evening breeze brushed gently across my face, and the leaves rustled softly, yet I felt no peace at all.

“Calm down, everything will be fine,” I whispered to myself. But such self-comfort only made it harder for me to trust myself. I wandered around the dorm for a long while, unable to let go of the details of that group discussion, repeatedly wondering whether I was disappointing in others’ eyes.

A few days later, I was still brooding over that discussion, but my classmates’ attitudes had not changed in the slightest. Gradually, as other classes and projects moved forward, that intense unease began to ease, though I still felt confused about my own personality.

The atmosphere in the classroom was tense and silent, with several fluorescent lights bathing the whole room in a stark, white glow. Outside the window was a clear blue sky, and sunlight slid across the glass, casting bands of shadow on the floor. I sat in the last row, anxiously staring at the teacher in the front. She was holding a student’s paper and pacing in front of the lectern. I could feel beads of sweat gradually breaking out on my forehead.

“This argument is somewhat weak in its reasoning,” the teacher said, looking up and sweeping her gaze across the classroom before finally resting it on my side. I instantly held my breath, feeling an invisible pressure squeeze my chest. Her words echoed in my mind, each one seeming to harshly criticize my own paper. “She must be talking about me.” I kept chewing over the thought in my head, and my heart began to race. “I must have messed up.”

The classmates beside me were talking softly. I tried to listen to what they were saying, but it felt as if a thin veil had fallen over my ears, blocking out all sound. I could feel my palms starting to sweat, and my stomach beginning to cramp. I kept repeating to myself: “Will she think I’m stupid? Will she give me a very low grade? How am I supposed to explain my point of view?”

“What do you think of this point?” the teacher’s voice continued as she looked toward my side. Startled, I sat up straight, clutched my notebook, and began to stammer out my thoughts. My voice sounded smaller than I had expected, and a sense of helplessness began to spread.
