After I left the classroom, my head was still buzzing. On the way from the classroom back to the dormitory, I kept replaying what had just happened, like reliving a nightmare I refused to admit. I blamed myself, feeling that I simply couldn’t fit into this academic environment. “I really am just not good enough. Everyone else can answer so easily—why am I so stupid?”

That night, I lay in bed in the dorm, staring at the shadows wavering on the ceiling, while the faint sound of my roommate’s breathing drifted by my ear. The inability to fall asleep came over me again, and past mistakes, other people’s expressions, and even the judgments I had imagined replayed over and over in my mind. I kept asking myself whether they really thought I wasn’t good enough, whether that glance from the teacher had truly shown disappointment in me. Several days later, I was still afraid of that speech. It had become a shadow of unease in my heart, and I became even more cautious in every class.

I realized that perhaps I should learn to let go of this habit of overinterpreting other people’s expressions and hints. Even though I was still anxious deep down, I told myself that maybe I could try once not to assume, and instead try to get feedback from reality rather than from my imagination.

In the classroom, sunlight streaming in from outside cast dappled shadows across the desks, and the clock on the wall made a faint ticking sound. The professor was introducing today’s group discussion topic up front, and I sat by the window, trying to focus. Everyone in the class was whispering to one another, and the air was filled with the faint scent of laundry detergent. I could vaguely feel my stomach starting to cramp slightly, a common reaction when I’m nervous.

After the discussion began, my group formed a circle. In situations like this, I always try to hide my presence, afraid of saying something wrong and disappointing others. One classmate in the group suggested what seemed like a good direction, and after hesitating for a moment, I decided to try voicing my own opinion: “This direction is good, but could we also consider another angle?”

I noticed a change in the expression of one boy in the group. He frowned, his tone slightly impatient: “Isn’t that not really the main point we’re supposed to discuss?” His voice seemed amplified several times in my ears, and my heartbeat instantly sped up. My cheeks grew slightly warm, and my palms began to sweat. Had I said something wrong? Would they think I was stupid?

I nodded and apologized softly: “Oh, maybe I misunderstood.” But the inner monologue in my head kept blaming me relentlessly: Why can’t you be more careful? How did you not understand what he meant? For the rest of the discussion, I became much quieter, mechanically echoing the opinions of those around me, while still thinking about the awkward moment from before.

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning without being able to fall asleep, my mind replaying the scene from the day over and over. The boy’s slightly impatient tone haunted me like a spell. “If only I hadn’t said that then,” I blamed myself silently, feeling that I was always so impulsive. Why couldn’t I think more before speaking? This self-doubt made me feel unbearably ashamed, as if the whole world were watching me make a fool of myself.

A few days later, I still couldn’t help feeling a bit down in class and didn’t dare speak up on my own, fearing I might cause unnecessary trouble again. Although no one mentioned that incident again, the burden in my heart had not disappeared.

I was sitting in a café near the university, surrounded by the rich aroma of coffee beans, which put me slightly at ease. On the table was an unfinished latte, and it was nearing evening; the sky outside the window was gradually darkening. The class I had just finished left me feeling tired, but what worried me more was the conversation I was about to have with my friend. We had agreed to meet here, hoping to clarify some things that had been troubling me lately. When she walked in, I noticed her expression was a little tense, and my heart sank. I immediately began replaying our most recent argument, and my heartbeat gradually quickened.

After she sat down, we started talking about trivial things, yet I could feel the tension between us. “Are you okay?” she asked, and it struck a nerve. I tried to act unconcerned. “I’m fine, just a little tired lately.” In truth, deep down inside, I had been churning with thoughts, wondering whether that argument had caused irreparable damage to our relationship.

I tried my best to seem calm, but under the table my hands were clenched tightly, sweat seeping from my palms. I finally gathered the courage to ask her, “Are you still upset about what happened that day?” She looked up at me, her brows knitting slightly. “I think we both need some time to cool off,” she said, with a hint of hesitation in her voice.

Those words felt like a thorn piercing my heart, instantly triggering my fear of being abandoned. I began to overinterpret every expression on her face, as if searching for the slightest sign that she was about to push me away. I could feel shame rising within me, and this unease almost drove me out of my mind. I tried to suppress these emotions, but a dull ache had already begun in my stomach.

After the conversation ended, I mechanically walked back to the dorm, feeling completely hollowed out. That night, I lay uneasily in bed, repeatedly thinking over what she had said, and the sense of defectiveness in my heart grew stronger and stronger. Even days later, I was still obsessing over that conversation, hoping to find some unnoticed clue. I kept checking whether she was truly angry, and that left me trapped in a whirlpool of anxiety.

In hindsight, I realized that my preemptive self-attack was nothing more than a way to protect myself from getting hurt again, but it only made my relationships with others more strained.

The final exam was finally over. I sat in a college classroom, the clock on the wall ticking, bright sunlight shining outside the window. I looked at the room full of people; they were talking in low voices, along with the faint sounds of desks and chairs scraping as they moved. My palms began to sweat, and my heartbeat gradually quickened. Although the exam was over, my mind still could not settle down. I tried to chat with the classmate next to me about something trivial, hoping it would ease my tension. She said, “This year’s exam questions felt a bit tricky. They’re always like that.” I nodded, but inside I felt uneasy. Was I the only one who thought the questions were hard? Were my answers not good enough? These questions rippled through my mind like pebbles tossed one after another into water.  

I tried hard to recall the mistakes I had made on the exam—the multiple-choice question where I chose A instead of B, the essay question where I didn’t list all the examples. Every mistake looked like a flaw under a magnifying glass, unnaturally clear and magnified. I wondered whether I might not have passed at all, and my mind began rehearsing every possible worst-case scenario. I twirled my pen between my fingers, yet I couldn’t focus on anything. My muscles were tense, and my stomach ached faintly, as if warning me of the disaster to come.  

After a while, my friend sat down beside me and asked how I felt about the exam. “Pretty okay,” I answered, forcing myself to stay calm. “Do you think you’ll pass?” she asked. I felt a heavy thud in my chest, as if every word she said were exposing the anxiety inside me. I smiled, doing my best to hide my emotions, and replied, “I hope so.” She nodded and went on talking about other things, while I remained deeply uncomfortable.  

That night, lying in bed, I struggled to fall asleep, thinking that the exam results might affect my future and cause me to miss out on important opportunities. I carried all my unease into every dream, and when I woke up, I still felt heartache. Over the next few days, I kept replaying the exam in my mind, guessing how the teacher might react while grading the papers. Whenever the exam came up in conversation, I would instinctively avoid it, afraid that others might mention my possible mistakes. Even weeks later, when the grades were released, I still checked my transcript repeatedly, afraid of missing even the slightest detail or error.

The lights in the conference room were a little too bright, and I sat at the edge of the round table, my palms slightly damp with sweat. Facing my classmates, I felt an indescribable tension. Everyone was discussing our project plan, and the atmosphere was relaxed yet full of energy. Each person was sharing their ideas, but I still hadn’t found the courage to speak up. My heart was racing, as if everyone could hear it.

“Why don’t we try approaching it from this angle?” the girl across from me said softly, her eyes full of anticipation. I nodded in agreement, but a trace of unease flashed through my mind. My proposal still hadn’t taken perfect shape; if I said something wrong, would everyone think I was ignorant?

When it was my turn to present my thoughts, I took a deep breath. “I’m thinking maybe we could add some research so we can better understand user needs.” My voice was a little shaky, and louder than usual. The brief silence in the room made my heart beat even faster.

A boy responded, “Your idea is good, but we may not have enough time.” His tone was calm, and I should have felt understood, but instead I shrank inward. Why couldn’t he just say it was good directly? Was he indirectly questioning me? In an instant, the idea that I had been “abandoned” took over my thoughts. I began to ruminate on what he had just said, afraid I had missed some important explanation.

After the meeting ended, my body still felt tense, and my stomach was somewhat unsettled. When I stood up, my legs felt weak. I quietly gathered my things and waved goodbye to everyone. Several classmates warmly invited me to lunch, but I found an excuse to turn them down. I was afraid of these social situations, afraid of having to keep smiling all the time even when I was churning inside.

Back in the dorm, I sat on the edge of my bed, replaying the meeting in my mind over and over. Was my proposal really that bad? Or was I just being too sensitive? I felt increasingly powerless, and anxiety hung over me like a heavy cloud. To distract myself, I opened my laptop and kept refining our project plan, hoping it would ease my inner turmoil.

A few days later, I decided to talk to that boy directly and find out what he really thought. That night, he told me, “Actually, I think your suggestion was great. I just wasn’t clear when I spoke because I was thinking about our limited time.” Those words made me feel instantly relieved, but they also led me to deeply reflect on my own sensitivity. Why do I always mess up these social interactions?

Night fell, and the dorm room lights cast a soft glow over the desk. I sat at my desk, trying to focus on the document on the screen. Yet my roommate’s words kept echoing in my mind. “Do you think this project can be completed smoothly?” He had only asked casually, but it stirred up endless ripples in my heart. I couldn’t help wondering: was that a sign of doubt? Did he lack confidence in my ability to deliver this project?

We had a brief conversation: “Do you think this project can be completed smoothly?” I replied, “It should be fine, as long as we all do our best.” He nodded. “I hope so.” His tone sounded a little uncertain.

As time passed, I became increasingly restless. My heartbeat seemed to quicken with anxiety, my palms began to sweat, and my stomach tightened. I found it hard to sit upright, my thoughts spinning over and over. I tried to hide my emotions, but the worry inside me kept growing. I began to obsessively replay our conversation, trying to figure out the exact meaning behind his tone.

Tossing and turning in bed all night, I couldn’t fall asleep; those anxieties haunted me like ghosts. The next day, sunlight from the dorm window filtered through the curtains, yet I still hadn’t slept a wink. My roommate had already left for class, and I lay staring at the ceiling, my mind filled with unanswered questions. At that moment, I felt utterly exhausted, my whole body heavy and drained.

A few days later, I gathered the courage to ask my roommate what he had meant that night. He looked puzzled. “I was just asking casually; there wasn’t any special meaning,” he said with a light laugh.

Afterward, I realized that it was perhaps my overreaction and overinterpretation that had trapped me in this baseless anxiety. Still, the sleepless night lingered in my mind for a long time. Even so, understanding the problem brought me a little relief.

I sat in the study area on the rooftop of the library. The sky had just begun to darken, and the light had taken on a faint yellow tint. The table was made of pale gray metal, cold to the touch, with a few faint scratches on its surface. I spread out my notebook, biting on my pen as I looked through the textbook, trying to focus despite the irritation building in my chest. Next to me, a pair of students were talking in low voices, apparently discussing some group assignment, but their voices drifted into my ears from time to time, making it hard to settle down. The chair beneath me wobbled a little, and without thinking I pushed the floor with the tip of my shoe, trying to steady it, but it still gave off a faint creaking sound.

“Hi, do you come here to study often?” A sudden voice pulled me back from my thoughts. I looked up instinctively and saw a strange boy standing across the table, holding a thick reference book, a polite smile on his face. My heart instantly sped up, like the reflexive jolt of being suddenly shouted at. “I, I…” Before I could even finish speaking, I could already feel my cheeks burning hot, and my mind was racing to find the right answer. “Um... occasionally, I guess.” I finally forced out a few words, though my voice was trembling a little.

“Oh, I’m here for the first time. Seeing you here alone, I thought maybe you’d know the rules around here.” He kept smiling, his voice low and slow, as if he was afraid of startling me. But I was already completely tense, my attention scattered into countless pieces: Was he scrutinizing me? Was he just asking a question, or did he have some other purpose? If he kept trying to chat forever, how was I supposed to refuse? Did he think I looked easy to bully? I even felt like simply breathing at the same time as him was making it hard to breathe.

“The rules? There aren’t really any special rules, I guess. Just don’t talk too loudly.” I tried to make myself sound casual, but my voice was still a little shaky. I felt like my back was soaked with sweat, even though there was no air conditioning on the rooftop and it wasn’t particularly hot. I pressed my hands against the tabletop, my fingertips cold and slightly trembling.

“Oh, I see. Then... then thank you!” He looked a bit hesitant, as if he had sensed my unease. He gave an awkward laugh and turned to leave. I secretly let out a breath of relief, lowered my head, and stared at my textbook, trying to make some notes on the page, but my hand still trembled unconsciously, and the pen tip slipped into a curved line. Several minutes passed before my heartbeat gradually calmed down, but in my mind those few sentences kept replaying over and over. Was I being too rude? Would he think I was weird? Or was he just...?

That night, I packed up early and left the library. Even after I returned to the dorm, I still couldn’t settle down. The face and voice of that unfamiliar boy kept appearing in my mind, every detail of his expression as clear as if it had been etched into memory. I even began to feel annoyed with myself—why was I always unable to handle situations like that naturally? Why did everyone else seem so relaxed and at ease, while I always felt like there was danger lurking?

I stood in the center of the campus gallery, surrounded by all kinds of works. The oil paintings hanging on the walls looked especially vivid under the lights. I had been watching people’s reactions to my painting, my heart racing and my palms sweaty. A boy stopped in front of my painting and frowned slightly, as if he were studying some detail in it. I felt a wave of unease: had he noticed a mistake in my painting? In fact, this painting had made me incredibly anxious from the very beginning. I always felt that my skills were not mature enough, that I couldn’t paint what I wanted to express in my heart. After the exhibition opened, I stood among the crowd, trying to smile and respond to everyone’s comments, but deep down I still felt uneasy. The soft rhythm of music drifted from all around the gallery, yet it did nothing to calm my nerves; instead, it made me even more sensitive. Later, I heard a couple whispering in front of my work: “Look, isn’t something about this place a little strange?” I immediately held my breath, trying my best not to speculate about what they meant. I always overanalyze every tiny expression and every word. In my mind, the most likely negative comments kept replaying: “Is this painting not as good as I imagined?” “Am I not suited to be an artist?” In this whirlpool of self-doubt, my throat tightened, as if a stone were stuck there. Hours later, the exhibition ended. I walked out of the gallery feeling drained, the smell of oil paint still lingering at the tip of my nose. That night, I lay on my dorm bed, my mind filled with all the flaws I believed I had. My heart was still beating too fast for me to sleep, and my stomach even felt a little knotted. The next day, I tried talking with my classmates about the exhibition, but I found that I always criticized myself first, as if that would keep them from criticizing me. This defense mechanism was my way of protecting my fragile self-esteem. A few days later, I decided to contact that boy and wanted to hear what he really thought. His reply was unexpectedly warm: he said that a certain detail in the painting reminded him of a childhood experience, and it was completely not the criticism I had imagined. This small exchange eased my anxiety a little, but I knew I still needed to learn to accept the imperfections in my work.

I stood downstairs by the dormitory building, stepping on the wet tiles as the patter of rain drowned out the surrounding noise. The damp, chilly air carried the pungent smell of earth, and now and then a cold gust slipped into my neck, making me involuntarily hunch my shoulders. The overcast night sky looked as though it were covered by a gray-black curtain, and my mood was just as oppressive.

The scene from the day kept replaying in my mind: the professor staring at me in class, saying in a low but sharp voice, “You’re late again. I hope this is the last time.”

That word again—“again”—stuck into my chest like a needle. I could hardly keep listening to the rest of the lecture. Every subtle glance from my classmates, every cough or sound of pages turning, felt like they were all judging me. I sat at my desk, my fingers trembling, the tip of my pen frozen over the blank notebook, unable to write a single word. Only when the class bell rang did I hastily pack my things and flee the classroom. But the professor’s words, and those looks around me, were like brands that could not be erased.

At that moment, I stared at my reflection in the puddle by my feet. My face was pale, but red veins showed in my eyes. I didn’t know how to make this suffocating feeling go away. Two voices were fighting in my head: one blamed me, saying, “How could you be late again? You’re really useless, only good at disappointing others.” The other tried to defend me: “The alarm didn’t go off! And what the professor said wasn’t that serious anyway—everyone has already forgotten it!” But I knew these excuses didn’t hold up at all. Every one of them sounded so weak and powerless.

The rain sounded like a lullaby, and before I knew it, my feet carried me toward the campus path. As I walked, raindrops splashed onto my pant legs, and the dampness crept through the fabric onto my skin, yet I paid it no mind. The streetlights along the road cast a dim yellow glow, their blurred reflections swaying in the puddles like my emotions, uncertain and restless. As I kept walking, I suddenly felt a cramp in my stomach—a familiar sensation. Whenever my anxiety reached its peak, my body always reminded me through pain.

“Can I stop and catch my breath?” I whispered to myself. My voice trembled, even choking up a little. Looking around, I spotted a small stone bench not far away, so I went over and sat down. The rain grew a little heavier, and dense tapping sounds fell on the leaves beside me. A chill quickly spread from the bench to my thighs, and I subconsciously rubbed my arms. Still, that tight knot inside me remained.

“Why did it come to this?” I asked myself inwardly. I didn’t really want to be late; I just couldn’t wake up because of insomnia. And wasn’t my insomnia caused by worrying about all those messy little things in life? It seemed as though every time I was running myself ragged just to prove how useless I was. Even sitting here, I could still feel the professor’s gaze on me tomorrow. I could even hear what he might say—and all of it made me feel as if I had truly become a failure.

In the rain, time slipped by quietly. I don’t know how long passed before the cold finally brought me back to reality. When I looked up, the rain had gradually stopped. Only droplets slid from the edges of the leaves and struck the ground with a ticking sound. I took a deep breath and caught a faint fragrance of earth, along with the peaceful scent of everything being washed clean by the rain. I understood that life might just be like this—sometimes battered by the outside world, and sometimes made even more painful by our own cruelty toward ourselves. But tonight’s rain seemed to remind me that no matter what, the air after rain is still so fresh, and life goes on.

By the time I got back to the dorm, it was almost midnight. I took off my rain-soaked jacket; my hair was wet and clung to my cheeks, and my body gave off a damp smell. My roommate looked up at me. “It’s raining and you still went out?”

“Yeah, I wanted to walk around.”

He shook his head and handed me a towel. “Don’t catch a cold. Go to bed early.”

I took the towel and murmured my thanks. That night, my dreams were still filled with scenes from class, but when I woke up, they didn’t seem quite so unbearable anymore.

The warm yellow light in the dormitory reflected on everyone’s faces, making the room feel especially intimate. They huddled together, chatting about campus gossip, while I sat in the corner. The sweetness of the drink in my cup churned my stomach. I tried to join the conversation, but their pace seemed too fast, as if they were deliberately excluding me. Then I heard one roommate say, “You’re pretty quiet—you don’t mind us overlooking you, do you?” In an instant, my mind went blank with a boom. Was it a joke? Or did they really think I was a nuisance? I gripped my cup tightly in the corner, my palms starting to sweat.

“What do you mean by that?” I heard my own voice sound strange to me—sharp and uneasy. She froze for a moment, then laughed and said, “Ah... nothing by it. It’s not like we’re targeting you.” But her smile looked so fake. Was she hiding something? As I thought this, I could feel my heartbeat growing faster, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. My throat went dry, and my fingers began trembling uncontrollably. I set the cup on the table because I was afraid I’d drop it.

“Am I really that annoying?” I heard myself press on, my voice almost a shout. “Do you think I’m weird?” I saw them exchange glances, and the air felt thick and still. My mind was flooded with scenes from the past when I’d been isolated, and memories of rejection surged over me like a tide. I thought of high school, when no one wanted to sit with me during breaks, and of being mocked as a child for being too sensitive. The roommates in front of me now looked just like those people.

“Hey, don’t overthink it. We’re just joking,” another roommate said, trying to smooth things over as she patted my shoulder. But the gesture made me feel like she was pitying me, like she was throwing me a bone. “I’m really that obnoxious, aren’t I?” My voice was shaking, tears already welling in my eyes. They began to look flustered. Someone murmured, “That’s a bit much, isn’t it? Are you being too sensitive?” The words stabbed into my heart like needles.

I stood up, my throat tight, feeling dizzy. “Forget it. I’m interrupting you guys.” I rushed out of the dorm, leaving their murmurs behind me. I didn’t know what they were really saying, but my mind was filled with nothing but, “They must be so annoyed with me,” and “They definitely think I’m too weird.” The wind in the hallway was cold. I hadn’t put on a coat, and all I felt was the chill on my shoulders and neck.

That night I couldn’t sleep, lying in bed and replaying that moment over and over. I started blaming myself—why was I always like this? No matter where I was, I always took jokes as attacks and always made things spiral out of control. My stomach hurt all night long, and I felt beyond help. This loneliness and shame seemed to cover me like a thick veil. I tried to tell myself, “They didn’t mean it,” but another voice said, “There’s something wrong with me.”

The classroom was dimly lit, with the projector’s blue glow cast onto the whiteboard. I stood beside the podium, and I didn’t know when my palms had started sweating. I had just finished a five-minute presentation, and my face was probably still stuck in a tense, forced smile. The walk back to my seat seemed especially long; each step felt like it was landing on a sheet of paper, so light that I couldn’t even tell whether the floor was really there. My teammate was sitting in the last row. She always looked so relaxed, leaning back in her chair, completely out of sync with the atmosphere in the front. She glanced up at me, and the corner of her mouth seemed to twitch slightly. “I think you were a bit too nervous. Your voice got really soft in the second half. The beginning was okay, but overall you didn’t seem confident enough.” Her voice was calm, without any deliberate tone, but my mind immediately turned into chaos. In an instant, my stomach clenched as if something had grabbed it, and then it started to feel sour. The wet, sticky feeling on my palms became even more obvious. I didn’t know how to respond, so I could only force a smile; my throat was so dry I couldn’t squeeze out a single word.

After I sat down, the surrounding voices became a hazy layer of background noise. The teacher continued commenting on other students’ presentations, but in my head there was only her voice, replaying over and over like a recording. “Too nervous,” “voice too soft,” “not confident enough”—those words seemed to carve themselves into my mind, and the more I thought about them, the harsher they sounded. Did she think I was awful? That I couldn’t even handle the content I was supposed to present? Would the other students have the same impression? I even started to wonder whether the applause just now had been nothing more than polite courtesy. I felt like a clown, exposed under the lights with all my flaws on display.

“Are you okay?” another teammate asked me softly. I hurriedly nodded, even trying hard to force a smile, because I was afraid people would notice how much those words had affected me. But my heart kept racing faster and faster, and sitting in the chair made me feel as if I were tied down; I could only mechanically flip through my notebook and pretend to be listening to the comments that followed. I began to think: if she thought I did poorly, why didn’t she tell me earlier, or help me a bit? The growing resentment and self-blame tangled together, and I started blaming myself again for being too sensitive. The feeling left me unable to breathe properly, and even my breathing became shallow and rapid.

That night, when I got back to the dorm, I burrowed into my blanket, and that sentence still lingered in my ears. I tried to recall every detail of what I had done, even replaying my tone and movements during the presentation. Lying in bed, I started worrying that tomorrow’s group discussion would turn into a criticism session, and that they might think I was completely not worth working with. In the middle of the night, I kept debating whether I should send them a message first and admit my shortcomings, but I was afraid of being seen as weak. In the end, I did nothing, and instead played out countless versions of the conversation in my head. I even felt like I was slowly heading toward an unsolvable disaster, and all of it had started with just that one sentence.

The air in the studio was thick with the scent of oil paint, and sunlight streamed through the window onto the floor, adding a touch of warmth to the entire room. I stood before the canvas, brush in hand, feeling my heartbeat quicken in my chest. I had come here to complete my first oil painting, and at that moment, every choice of color, even every brushstroke, made me incredibly nervous. The teacher walked over, his gaze lingering on my canvas for a moment before he asked, “Are you okay? Do you need any help?” His voice was gentle, but I couldn’t help overanalyzing it, feeling as if he were implying that I wasn’t doing well enough. “I... I just want to try something different,” I stammered, while inside I was in turmoil, surrounded by a strong sense of abandonment and defectiveness. I began to feel like an unqualified actor, trying to find my role. My heartbeat sped up, fine beads of sweat appeared on my forehead, and my stomach felt uneasy; that sense of unease seemed ready to swallow me whole. To calm myself down, I tried to focus on expressing the colors, yet with every stroke I questioned: is this the result I’m really after? After a while, the other students in the studio began talking, and I seemed cut off from their conversation, hearing only the inner voices endlessly pulling at me. Finally, in this anxious self-talk, I chose to leave a bold red mark on the canvas. Then I felt a slight tremor, as if the whole room were asking me: What are you doing? Almost in order to stop myself from being questioned, I instinctively began to attack myself preemptively, hinting inwardly that failure was to be expected. That night, when I returned to the dorm, the scene in the studio was still echoing in my mind, and I ruminated over and over on whether I had chosen the wrong color. Although the painting was not yet finished, I felt as if I had already gone through a long mental journey. In the days that followed, I kept recalling the expressions on the teacher’s and classmates’ faces, sinking myself deeper into anxiety through overinterpretation, and even beginning to doubt whether I was suited to continue creating like this.

The light on the wall fell across the table, bathing several faces in a soft yellow glow. We were sitting around the small table in the dorm, with snacks and drinks on it, all of us laughing and talking about the trivial things that had happened during the day. At the time, I was holding a cup of cola, listening to a friend tell a funny story about class, and everyone burst into laughter. The atmosphere was lively. Suddenly, I heard someone half-jokingly say, “You always overthink things like that; you’re going to wear yourself out.”

In an instant, it felt as if something had pricked my heart, and a wave of unease surged up. “What does that mean?” I thought instinctively, as self-doubt began to spread. My cheeks started to burn, my heart raced, and the cola in my hand suddenly felt heavy. I felt helpless and isolated amid their laughter, as if all eyes were on me, scrutinizing every reaction I made.

“Are you okay?” the friend sitting beside me asked, her tone kind yet tinged with curiosity. I forced a smile. “I’m fine, just a little tired.” I lied, hoping to conceal how I really felt. Yet deep inside, a voice kept echoing: “Yes, I always overthink things. I’m always causing trouble.”

After the gathering ended, I lay on my dorm bed, replaying that remark over and over in my mind. I kept reflecting: “Am I really too sensitive? Do others think it’s exhausting to be around me?” My heartbeat remained erratic, and I felt weak and irritable all over. It was as if all my strength had vanished, leaving only the fear of being abandoned and isolated.

The next day, I still couldn’t concentrate in class, and everything seemed even heavier. The teacher was saying something at the podium, but I was just staring at the blank page in my notebook, my palms sweaty and my mind in complete disarray. I was afraid my classmates would notice how off I was, and even more afraid they would look at me with contempt.

For the rest of that week, I uncharacteristically didn’t want to eat with my friends, always finding excuses to stay alone. I tried to calm myself down, but a voice inside kept reminding me how out of place I was, how easily I could be disliked. Every time I walked past them, I seemed to feel an invisible wall separating me from them.

A few days later, I finally couldn’t hold back any longer and called a close friend late one night, hoping to confide my worries in her. She comforted me gently: “We all like you. You don’t need to overthink it.” Her words warmed me, but the shadow of unease still lingered. I knew in my heart that this wasn’t a problem with my friends; it was my own trauma at work.

The café was brightly lit, and the table was covered with the books and notes we were using for our discussion. The aroma of coffee filled the air, stirring nerves that were already a little frayed. I sat among my friends, trying to concentrate, but I kept thinking about the feedback on our last project. The professor had said we needed to organize the structure better, and that sentence kept echoing in my mind. I always couldn’t help interpreting it as criticism rather than constructive advice. My heartbeat seemed to quicken with my thoughts.

“I think we could cite that new study here,” I heard one of my friends suggest, her voice gentle yet firm. I nodded, trying to keep up, but my mind kept circling back to the professor’s comment, missing the details of the conversation. “What do you think?” another friend asked me, and my heart tightened at the sense of all eyes turning toward me. “Uh, I think—” I stammered, and before I could finish, a familiar fear began to spread. I was very aware that I might say the wrong thing and be seen as incompetent. My palms were slightly sweaty, and my stomach churned.

“Actually, we may…,” I began, but before I could finish, another friend cut in: “Don’t get too caught up in the details—we need to look at the big picture.” The faint impatience in his tone sent my mind sinking rapidly. Was he dissatisfied with my work? Was I always the one dragging everyone down? These self-attacking thoughts came rushing in like a flood.

At that moment, I forced a smile. “Oh, of course.” I tried to make my voice sound relaxed. But as they continued discussing, I still couldn’t let go of what had just been said. While my friends were planning the next steps of the project, my mind kept replaying every word I’d said. My heart was beating so fast it felt like it might burst out of my chest, and I sat there quietly, trying not to seem flustered.

The next morning, I sat staring blankly at my computer screen, completely stuck. The conversation at the café kept flashing through my mind, and I suddenly wondered whether I should talk to my friends about what had happened yesterday. But the thought of being seen as overly sensitive and fragile made me pull back again, leaving me to wrestle with it in silence. The scent of coffee, my friends’ slight laughter—all of it started to blur.

A few days later, I finally gathered the courage to text the friend who had sounded impatient yesterday: “Do you think there’s something wrong with how we’ve divided up the project? I always worry I may not be doing well enough.” The reply came quickly: “Not at all. A lot of the time I think you’re great. It’s just that sometimes we all need to focus on the main point.”

That made me feel a little more at ease, though I still instinctively wondered whether they were only being nice out of politeness. But at least it meant I no longer spent the whole night replaying that conversation.

The spotlight at the center of the stage flickered on and off, the light beam swaying in the air as if restlessly searching for its own focus. I stood at the side of the stage, gripping a stack of freshly completed stage design sketches so tightly that the edges of the paper bit into my palm with a faint sting. My eyes kept sweeping over the classmates gathered in discussion at center stage. I couldn’t yet make out their voices, but my heart was pounding like a drum. I tried hard to take deep breaths, attempting to suppress the rising unease in my chest.

“Next one, you—your drawings?” The classmate in charge of organizing the discussion waved at me, signaling me to come up. I seemed to be walking on cotton, yet I had no choice but to step forward; every muscle in my body was so tense it felt like a puppet’s. I handed over the design sketches, forcing myself to calm down. “Actually... this layout is based on the script and the overall style concept. Um, take a look.” My voice trembled, and the last syllable was almost inaudible.

They studied the paper for a while. Quiet. Terrifyingly silent. I felt as if the whole world had been swallowed by that silence, as if time itself had frozen. I started wondering whether my design was just too terrible. Were these lines too messy? Was the theme not clear enough? “They must be disappointed in my design, maybe even think I didn’t put any thought into it,” I thought to myself, my stomach tightening into a knot of anxiety.

“The... color palette is okay, but this pillar design of yours doesn’t quite fit the plot, does it?” one classmate finally said, pointing to part of the sketch in the lower right corner. I stared at his lips as he spoke, as if every word were a hammer striking my head. What did he mean? Did he think I was stupid? Or that I was simply unreliable? Or was he mocking my design? I felt my cheeks starting to burn, and a buzzing rang in my ears.

“The part you mentioned... actually, it’s an important point in that scene. I was hoping the lighting could come down from there to create a contrast between light and shadow...” My voice grew smaller and smaller, as if something were pressing down on me, making it hard to breathe. The classmate who had spoken frowned slightly, and my heart lurched; alarms went off in my head at once. He must think my explanation is awful, maybe even boring. Was he holding back laughter at me?

“I can revise it again. I know it may still not be very mature.” I hurried to add. I spoke quickly, afraid I’d be interrupted halfway through. After I finished, I didn’t even dare look at them. I lowered my head and stared at the floor, like a child who had done something wrong, waiting for judgment.

“It’s okay, we can all work on it together,” one of the classmates said, glancing at the others. “We’re still in the adjustment stage, so just take itslowly.”

I nodded, forcing out a dry “Mm.” Then I quickly went to sit off to the side, pressing my back tightly against the chair as if I could use that to keep my weakening body upright.

For the next several hours that afternoon, I kept replaying the scene over and over, trying to analyze everyone’s expressions and tones of voice. I couldn’t help wondering: would they say behind my back, “She’s too much trouble, and she’s not reliable at all”? Or that I wasn’t suited to be part of this project? Those thoughts were like stubborn weeds, impossible to uproot no matter how hard I tried.

That night back in the dorm, I lay face down on my bed, hugging a pillow, feeling utterly exhausted yet unable to sleep. Later, a classmate sent me a message saying, “Let’s work hard to improve together, don’t put too much pressure on yourself.” I stared at the screen for a long time before hesitantly replying, “Mm, thanks.” But I still felt a weight hanging in my heart, worried that she was only saying that to comfort me. Even the next morning, my shoulders still felt heavy, as if last night’s thoughts had crushed my whole body.

The lights in the music composition room were dim, the walls were lined with acoustic materials, and the air carried a faint musty smell. In the stillness, the only sounds were my barely audible breathing and the occasional distant laughter and chatter of students outside. Whenever I heard laughter, my heartbeat quickened, as though the happiness of the outside world had nothing to do with me. I sat in front of the electronic keyboard, repeatedly pressing the keys, trying to find inspiration to finish this semester’s music composition project. The melodies I usually loved flowed through my headphones, but today they seemed to have lost their usual magic. My fingers on the keys began to sweat slightly, as if the keys had become sticky and never quite dried. Every note in the composition process made me feel as though I were facing a formidable enemy; questions kept surfacing in my mind: “What if they don’t like my work? If the quality isn’t good enough, will it affect my grade?”

My roommate once encouraged me, saying, “You just need to relax and do whatever feels right. Don’t worry about what others think.” But those words felt incredibly light in my ears, seemingly too weak to withstand the heavy pressure from within. I knew music was the purest form of expression, yet I always felt that my own expression was far from perfect. With every note I played, my unease deepened. The fear that I wasn’t good enough, the feeling of being looked down on or abandoned, weighed heavily in my chest. To stop these emotions from spreading, I began mentally simulating all kinds of possible presentation scenarios, even imagining how my classmates would judge me on the day of the presentation. Every imagined look, every possible criticism, made me feel worse.

As time passed minute by minute, my stomach began to ache with anxiety, as if it were being constantly twisted by an invisible pressure. I suddenly stood up and walked to the window, trying to let the fresh air clear my overly tense mind. The autumn breeze gently brushed my face, bringing with it the rustling sound of leaves. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself, but the turmoil inside me remained. One of my roommates suddenly pushed the door open and came in. Smiling, she said, “Why did you come so early today? How long have you been here?” I forced a smile and replied, “Not that long, I just hit a bit of a creative block.” She patted my shoulder and said, “Don’t think too much. It’ll be okay.” Her brief comfort made me feel a little better, but the unease was still churning deep inside me.

After leaving the music composition room, I wandered through the campus at night, still hearing the unfinished melody echoing in my mind. That night, I could hardly sleep, repeatedly worrying whether my project would be accepted by my classmates. A few days later, my roommates seemed to sense my tension and invited me to a café to relax. As we talked, I gradually came to realize that perhaps no one would be as harsh as I was in judging these minor flaws.

Warm sunlight spilled across the balcony, and a gentle breeze brushed by, carrying a hint of early spring’s coolness. I sat in the wicker chair on the balcony, a freshly borrowed novel spread open on my knees. The crisp scent of the paper mingled with the earthy smell of the small potted plants on the balcony, making me feel refreshed and at ease. I opened to the first page and gradually became drawn into the story. Occasionally, the wind would turn the pages, and sunlight would scatter tiny specks of light between the lines. I softly pushed my hair aside and continued sinking into the world of the book.

Just then, the child next door was playing noisily in the yard, their bright laughter drifting over like wind chimes. I heard them chasing and playing, sometimes shouting words I couldn’t quite make out, but that simple happiness needed no language to be felt. “You can’t catch me!” one child shouted, drawing laughter from the others. I couldn’t help but smile a little too, remembering how carefree I had been as a child.

Sunlight fell on my arms, pleasantly warm, and a long-lost sense of peace rose in my heart as well. I closed my eyes and let the sunlight bathe me, feeling that faint warmth on my skin. My heartbeat slowed, and my breathing grew easier. I told myself to enjoy this pressure-free afternoon; it seemed I hadn’t relaxed like this in a very long time.

The muscles in my shoulders began to loosen, and I gently moved them, pressing my thumbs against my temples, trying to drive away the stress and unease that had surfaced from time to time in recent days. I lingered over the pages for a while, watching the words flow by as if they were part of the scenery around me, and my thoughts flowed along with them.

After a few hours, the sky gradually darkened, and I began to feel hungry. I closed the book and let out a soft sigh, content with this peaceful afternoon. Back in my room, I prepared to make a simple dinner. That afternoon of sunshine and books stayed with me, becoming a rare moment of calm in my college life.

For several nights afterward, I kept thinking of that afternoon on the balcony, trying to find similar peace in my daily busyness. I knew that although life would bring all kinds of challenges and pressure, there would always be simple and beautiful moments like this, reminding me to slow down and enjoy the present.

The table in the meeting room was covered with materials related to the club’s activities, and several members were discussing next week’s preparations with great enthusiasm. The setting sun outside the window stained the sky red, and warm light slipped in through the blinds, casting interwoven bands of light and shadow across the tabletop. I sat in my chair, flipping the pen in my hand over and over, but I just couldn’t focus. Halfway through the meeting, I finally decided to speak up. “I feel like I didn’t do a very good job last time. That proposal was put together a bit too hastily, and I feel like I held everyone back.” As soon as the words left my mouth, my heart sank sharply, as if I had fallen into a deep pool. All the strength in my body seemed to be drained away, my palms started to sweat, and I was so nervous that even the area behind my ears felt hot.

One of the boys looked at me and smiled. “It wasn’t that bad, really. Just be more careful next time.” But another interpretation immediately came to mind: he must think I’m terrible, right? Maybe he thinks I’m not suited for this club? I forced down the rising emotions in my chest and lowered my head to keep fiddling with the pen. No one responded, and I felt the air freeze in an instant, as if everyone were silently scrutinizing every move I made. The light in my eyes grew even harsher, and I could even clearly feel each joint of my fingers as I gripped the pen tightly.

“Actually, we all need to pay more attention to the details,” a girl said. She had always been the vice president of the club, and her tone seemed to carry a hint of reassurance. “Next time we can discuss things earlier and more thoroughly, and this kind of problem won’t happen.” I looked up at her and gave a tentative smile, but my eyes couldn’t help darting to the side. I vaguely saw another person lower their head and type quickly on their phone, and my unease immediately deepened: Was she complaining about me to someone else? Sending messages saying I’m always dragging everyone down?

My stomach began to twist in pain. I tried to adjust my posture and pretend I was paying close attention, but anyone could see that my palms were already damp. I started blaming myself. Why had I taken the initiative to admit my mistake? I could have just acted like nothing had happened and gone along with everyone else’s pace. Now I was only making my own shortcomings too obvious. I glanced out the window, where the red sunset was gradually swallowed by the dark purple night sky, and the fading colors somehow made me feel oppressed. The self-reproach in my heart was like scattered points of light, filling every corner and making it hard for me to breathe.

After the meeting ended, I left the room before anyone else. “It’s fine, it’s fine,” I muttered to myself in the hallway, trying to calm down. But my mind only grew more chaotic, replaying everything that had just happened, trying to analyze every expression and every tone of voice, even imagining how they might talk about me in private. “Do they think I’m not good enough, not hardworking enough? Will they start considering whether to kick me out?” The pain in my stomach didn’t ease at all; if anything, it got worse. By the time I reached the bottom of the dorm building, I could barely stand without leaning against the wall.

For the entire week, I was trapped in this matter and unable to pull myself out. At night, after the lights were turned off, I lay in bed with my pillow damp, replaying every sentence and every glance that had passed over me. In fact, there was no evidence to support these images, but I still couldn’t help believing them. Every time I thought about it, the feeling was like invisible claws tightening hard around my heart, making me more and more anxious. Later, I even began silently repeating those self-attacking sentences in my head, trying to preemptively lessen the blow of being actually rejected by others. This self-criticism gradually became my default way of thinking, and I found it hard to break free.

The awards ceremony was held in the school’s spacious auditorium, where the crystal chandelier overhead shimmered with dazzling light, as if it were determined to expose every trace of tension in my heart. I sat in the third row, clutching the awards program tightly in my hands. The music beside me was soft and melodious, yet it felt as oppressive as war drums. People around me were chatting in low voices, laughter echoing through the air. I forced out a smile, trying to blend into the joyful atmosphere.

When the awards segment began, I found myself repeatedly glancing toward the podium. My heart was already pounding wildly in my chest, and I worried that if anything unexpected happened, I would lose my composure. Sitting next to me was a classmate from the same group activity, who was also nominated for an award. She smiled at me and said, “Today you’re sure to have good luck.” Her tone was relaxed, but I still felt a faint unease. Did she really want me to win, or was she just being polite?

“I don’t know, I’m just a little nervous,” I replied, my voice slightly stiff from tension. Her smile vanished in an instant, and my heart sank. It felt as though I had deliberately created an awkward moment. I began overanalyzing her reaction, wondering whether she truly harbored hostility toward me or was dissatisfied with the award itself.

When the host announced the winner, my heart seemed to stop for an instant. As applause erupted around me, I realized that I had won, but what followed was not joy, only endless anxiety. “Why isn’t everyone happier for me? Did I do something wrong?” I kept asking myself inwardly. That unease caused a dull, silent pain in my stomach, and fine beads of sweat appeared on my forehead.

At the gathering after the ceremony, I tried my best to smile and talk with others, but every time someone whispered nearby, I couldn’t help wondering whether they were talking about me. After returning to the dorm, I lay in bed and still could not escape those negative thoughts. My mind felt like a tangled mess that couldn’t be unraveled. I opened my phone and tried to message that classmate to check whether she was okay and whether she had any issue with me. But halfway through composing the message, I gave up again. The voice of self-criticism pounded at me like a hammer, telling me it would be best not to ask.

A few days later, when classmates shared photos from the awards ceremony on social media, my anxiety surged again. Even over something so small, I still couldn’t help sinking into doubt and self-reproach. The lingering aftershock of these emotions left me exhausted, yet it followed me like a shadow.

The whirring of the potter’s wheel filled the entire classroom, and a low vibration rose from the floor, traveling up through the soles of my feet to my knees. I sat on a wooden stool, both hands covered in wet, soft clay. Outside the classroom window, the sky was growing dark. Yellowish light fell across the wheel in front of me, making the clay’s surface look like soft, sticky cream, though I knew it was much trickier than it appeared.

The instructor walked over and said softly, “Remember, keep your hands steady, control your pressure, and relax a little.” I nodded and replied, “Okay, I’ll try.” But my hands would not cooperate at all. My wrists felt stiff, and my fingertips were like springs with no tension control—impossible to tell light from heavy. The clay spun more and more off-center on the wheel, its edges beginning to rise and fall irregularly like surging waves.

“Don’t panic, take it slow.” The teacher’s voice was still echoing in my ears, but my heartbeat had already sped up. My chest felt tight and swollen, and a fine sheen of sweat broke out across my forehead. I wanted to correct the shape of the clay, but the harder I tried, the worse it got. The clay seemed to have a life of its own, wriggling free from my control, until the whole lump lost its balance and flew off, landing with a slap on the floor beside me and splattering mud all over my pants.

“Oh no, what happened?” A classmate beside me put down her work and handed me a tissue. She looked genuinely concerned, but my mind was already buzzing with only one thought: it’s over. They must think I’m clumsy, that I’ve caused trouble for everyone again.

“It’s fine, I can handle it myself.” I took the tissue in a hurry and bent my head to wipe at my pant leg, trying to hide the flush on my face. My fingers were still covered in wet clay, yet I could not wipe the stain off the pants no matter how hard I rubbed; in fact, the more I tried, the worse it got. When I used too much force, my fingernail even tore the fabric on my thigh, exposing a patch of red skin underneath. The small sting made my nose start to ache, and my eyes grew hot.

“Next time, try keeping your hands more relaxed. If you’re too nervous, the clay will think you’re being unfriendly,” the teacher said with a smile, joking as he bent down to pick the clay back up. He patted my shoulder. “This takes time. You have to try a few more times to find the feeling, so don’t rush.”

I nodded repeatedly, saying, “Okay, okay,” but my mind was filled with piercing voices: “Your hands are so clumsy, you might as well just give up and go back.” “You mess things up every time—how can you still have the nerve to come?” “They must be laughing at you, laughing because you can’t even do one thing right. Even the clay won’t listen to you.”

Forcing down the tight, breathless feeling brought on by my racing heart, I lowered my head and started over, only to find my fingers trembling slightly. The pressure changed from light to heavy and back again as they touched the wheel, and the clay collapsed and tilted in turns. The lump fell apart once more, and I simply slapped it hard onto the wheel, using it to vent my silent anger and shame.

When the bell for class rang, my work was nothing more than an ugly lump of clay, not even a complete cylinder. The other students began to stand up, put away their tools, and clean their desks, while I remained seated there, staring at the “failed piece” in front of me, motionless.

“It’s okay, take your time.” A senior student patted me and gave me a comforting smile. “Mine was even worse the first time. You’ll get used to it.”

“Mm, thanks.” I replied softly, but inside I felt that she was only trying to comfort me. After I got back to the dorm, I tossed the pants stained with clay spots carelessly onto a chair and lay on my bed, replaying every detail of the class over and over. How could my hands shake like that? Why couldn’t I even manage something so simple? If I went again tomorrow, would my classmates avoid me? Would they point at me and whisper?

That night, I couldn’t fall asleep for a long time, and I even began wondering whether I should ask for leave from the next pottery class. At least that way, I could avoid embarrassing myself again.

We had just finished a campus event, and everyone had arranged to meet at a nearby café to discuss the next project. The café was filled with the aroma of freshly ground beans, and outside a light rain was falling, blurring the world beyond the window. I sat in the corner, my tense mood making it impossible to enjoy my latte. My classmates were all talking among themselves, excitedly exchanging ideas, and the lively atmosphere made me feel out of place. One classmate suddenly turned to me and asked, “What do you think of this event?” His tone made me involuntarily wary. My heart raced, my palms began to sweat, and my throat tightened with nerves. I forced a smile and replied, “I think it’s pretty good, but there are some details that could be improved, like the music arrangement.” His brow furrowed slightly, and I immediately sensed that this might mean displeasure, which left me feeling helpless. “You mean the music wasn’t good enough?” he asked, making me even more nervous. Had I said something wrong? Was I being too harsh? These questions swirled in my mind. To hide my unease, I quickly added, “No, I just think it could be a little more perfect.” He shrugged, seeming unsatisfied with my opinion, then turned back to the others and continued the discussion. I felt excluded, as if I had been abandoned in this lively yet distant environment. My stomach began to ache faintly, and I couldn’t help wondering: if I performed better, would they be more willing to listen to my opinions? That thought made my heart twist with pain. After the event ended, I returned to the dorm alone, and the sound of raindrops hitting the window seemed to mock my inadequacy. Over the next few days, I kept replaying the conversation in the café, doubting whether I was really bad at communicating with others—why did I always feel like I said the wrong thing? This filled me with anxiety about the upcoming events, fearing that I would once again be misunderstood and ignored.

The photography studio in the afternoon felt a bit messy, with a faint burnt smell from the heating bulbs in the air and the soft hum of camera chargers. The warm yellow ceiling lights lit up the room as I adjusted the camera in my hands, trying to capture the interplay of light and shadow on the sculpture. After taking a few photos, I noticed a tiny scratch in the lens. This was my favorite camera—I couldn’t even bear to let a classmate borrow it, much less touch it. I had bought it with two years of savings. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, my palms began to sweat, and my breathing felt heavy. My ears seemed filled with lead, and I could hardly hear the sounds around me. Who had touched my camera? Was it some careless classmate? Or had someone deliberately damaged it? These thoughts surged up like a flood, leaving me no time to pay attention to my teammates’ conversation.

“What’s going on?” I muttered under my breath, and the boy sitting next to me heard me. Noticing my expression, he asked, “What happened?”

“Nothing,” I said, forcing an easy tone and trying to hide my inner panic, while quickly stuffing the camera into my bag. In my mind, a disaster had already begun to unfold. The names of every teammate flashed through my head, and I even started imagining them picking up my camera and casually fiddling with it when I wasn’t there, only to end up breaking it.

When the team leader called everyone together to discuss the next shooting plan, I stared at the floor, pretending to be deep in thought. In reality, my heart was still pounding like it might leap out of my chest at any moment. My fingers gripped my pant leg tightly, afraid someone would notice that I was losing control of my emotions.

“What do you think?” the team leader suddenly asked. The words were right by my ear, and only then did I realize everyone’s eyes were on me. It felt as if the air had instantly turned thick. I stammered, “Uh, I think we can add a side light.” Then I quickly lowered my head and pretended to organize the equipment.

Everyone seemed to pay no further attention to my odd behavior and continued discussing other things. I just mechanically went along with the flow, no longer taking the initiative to speak, yet deep down I couldn’t stop cursing myself: Why is this happening? Why am I always so easily flustered? Would they think I’m incompetent? Or that I can’t even handle basic teamwork?

Later, I heard them discussing whether they needed to shoot more experimental shots. Soon after, they started assigning tasks, and I was surprisingly not given any particularly important part. That made me instinctively feel that I had been excluded. Did they not trust my ability? Or was it because I had acted too strangely just now? These questions tormented me over and over like a swarm of ants crawling around in my head.

That night, I lay in my dorm bed, tossing and turning as I replayed everything that had happened in the studio. Even the slightest changes in tone and expression from my teammates were examined one by one as I tried to find the exact reason they were distancing themselves from me. I kept blaming myself for not staying calm on the spot, for not dealing rationally with the scratch on the lens. The rhythm of my heartbeat seemed to speed up in sync with my self-reflection, making it hard to fall asleep.

The next day, I went to the photography studio alone to check the camera, and found that the scratch on the glass surface was actually just a hair stuck to it—the problem wasn’t serious at all. I let out a long breath, but then felt a wave of shame, annoyed with myself for being so hasty and so neurotic for an entire afternoon. Even so, I still couldn’t help wondering whether my teammates had noticed how off I had seemed yesterday. So Itake the initiative sent a few messages in the group chat with suggestions about the shoot, hoping to regain some favor, but after sending them, I started regretting it again, thinking they might see me as someone just trying to get attention. That vicious cycle left me exhausted.

The stargazing event took place at the school’s astronomical observatory. The night sky was like a deep blue velvet, studded with countless twinkling stars. A cool wind gently blew past as I hunched my shoulders, tightened my scarf, and looked up at the entire sky, feeling both excited and a little nervous. Around me, I could hear my classmates talking as they used telescopes to observe different constellations. “Come look, there’s Leo here,” someone called out excitedly. I walked closer, wanting to join their discussion, and stood nearby listening as they described the positions and colors of the stars.

“No, this one—not that one,” a classmate said, pointing at the telescope. “You’re looking at the wrong place. Polaris is on the other side.” His tone was flat, but my heart began to race, as if others had discovered my ignorance and mistake. I immediately reflected on my behavior—had I been standing too close and interrupting their observation? Or should I not have joined the discussion so abruptly? My stomach clenched, and I pulled off my scarf to cool down, yet my palms were still damp.

I quietly stepped back a few paces and no longer took part in their conversation, simply looking up at the sky. “It’s really beautiful here. That star looks like it’s winking,” I murmured to myself, trying to shift my attention to the night sky. Worried that my classmates might dislike me, I tried not to let any obvious expression show on my face and worked hard to remain calm. Still, a small voice in my heart kept echoing: “Will they think I’m stupid? Should I not have come to this event?” These thoughts left me anxious and uneasy.

After the event ended, I walked down from the observatory alone. On the way back to the dormitory, even the wind in my ears seemed to echo the conversation from earlier. In the room, darkness enveloped everything, and I could only hear the rustling of my bedding as I arranged it. After I lay down, the scenes from the evening played over and over in my mind as I wondered what I could have done better. Was I always like this, overly concerned with what others thought? Or was I simply afraid of being isolated and ignored, a fear that made it hard for me to tell reality from imagination? With these thoughts, I tossed and turned until I gradually fell asleep in the early hours of the morning.

When I woke the next morning, I decided to look up some books about the stars and try to understand more about the activity I had participated in, hoping that next time I would no longer be misunderstood or feel unnecessary. As expected, the knowledge about astronomy explained in those books brought me sudden clarity, and I no longer dwelled on last night’s embarrassment. I felt a little relieved. I understood that I could reduce these anxieties by taking the initiative to learn more. Though I still felt a bit guilty, at least I was growing.

That afternoon, I had no plans.

I just walked and walked, and my feet took me to the north side of the city—to the old shipyard. I usually didn’t dare go out alone. My mind was always crowded with voices rehearsing all kinds of possible disasters. But for some reason that day, I went out.

The railway tracks emerged from the grass, overgrown with moss, like a spine flattened by time. I walked along the gravel beside them, each step making a faint rustling sound. It was very small, but so clear it felt as if it were meant especially for me. The air smelled faintly of sea salt, mixed with rust and damp earth. I took a deep breath, and something in my chest loosened just a little.

Seagulls were calling in the distance. I looked up. The sky was an unreal blue, with a few clouds hanging lazily there, going nowhere.

I walked over to the remains of an old ship and stopped beside it. The paint on the hull had peeled up in layers, like memories flaking away. Sunlight slanted across it, and the weathered patches reflected a soft glimmer. I stared at it for a long time, and for once my mind wasn’t thinking about anything.

“Not many people come here now. Be careful being alone.”

I jerked around. Someone in work clothes was standing a few steps away. Their expression was calm, their voice calm too, as if they had simply said it offhand.

My heartbeat instantly sped up by half a beat. I nodded and forced out a smile. “Thanks. I’m just looking around.”

They gave a quiet “Mm,” and kept walking.

I stood there, watching their back disappear around the corner of a workshop, their footsteps gradually swallowed by the wind. I started replaying those words in my head—what did they mean? Did I look strange? Or were they suggesting this place wasn’t safe and I shouldn’t be here? My palms began to sweat, and there was a slight tightening in my stomach.

Then I stopped.

I don’t know why I stopped. Maybe because it was too quiet here, so quiet that the voices of my usual self-torment sounded especially absurd. I found an old sheet of iron and sat down. My fingers touched the metal—cold, rough, real. I just sat there and did nothing.

Not far away, the water reflected the sky. A few dragonflies flew past my eyes, their wings transparent in the light like glass. I closed my eyes and heard the faint hum of machinery in the distance, heard the wind, heard my own breathing slowly become even.

My heartbeat came back. So did my stomach’s tension.

I don’t know how long I sat there. By the time I stood up and walked back, the sky had turned a yellowish hue.

That night, as I lay in bed, I wasn’t chewing over anything in my head. The image of the old shipyard just stayed with me—the color of rust, the smell of sea salt, the touch of the cold iron sheet. I thought that place asked nothing of me, judged nothing about me; it just stayed there, decayed and quiet.

Later, on several occasions, when I found myself spiraling over some detail again and starting to rehearse the worst possible outcome, I would remember the temperature of that iron sheet. Not to solve anything—just to remember it, and breathe a little more easily.

The classroom lights were so bright they made me a little dizzy—though maybe it was nerves. I clutched a printed copy of my speech, my palms covered in sweat, the paper crumpled slightly from how tightly I held it. My teammates stood beside me, and it was my turn to open. I took a deep breath and had just said the first sentence, “Our group’s topic focuses on social media and personal anxiety…” when, right after I finished, I heard a boy in the front row say something under his breath, as if he were laughing. I froze for a few seconds, but quickly pushed myself to keep going.

I tried hard to stare at a fluorescent tube in the back of the room and pretend I hadn’t noticed anything unusual. “Am I speaking too fast?” “Do they think my opening is boring?” Those thoughts buzzed in my ears like little insects, and my hands started trembling uncontrollably. When I turned the page, I heard the dry snap of paper rubbing together.

After I finished speaking, I went back to stand with my teammates, and the rest of the group gave their parts. I should have been focusing on listening to them, but my mind felt muddled, like water had been stirred up in it, and I could only keep replaying my own tone and expression, even checking over and over whether there had been any grammar mistakes. It felt like every glance from them was a grade, as if they were all thinking, “Their performance is a complete disaster.”

“Are you okay?” a teammate standing next to me asked quietly, lightly patting my arm at the same time. Only then did I realize I had my arms wrapped around myself, my shoulders shaking the whole time. “I’m fine,” I said with a forced smile, though my voice sounded unnatural. I felt a twisting pain in my stomach, as if I had eaten something bad. I lowered my head and stared at the floor, doing my best to avoid making eye contact with anyone.

A few minutes later, my teammates finished the presentation, and we all stood at the front to receive feedback. The teacher’s expression looked calm as he said, “Overall, the content was good, but the visuals of the PPT still need improvement. Especially the first title slide—it could be designed to be more eye-catching.” My face instantly burned, because that cover slide was made by me. I forced myself to nod and said softly, “Okay, teacher.” Then I heard a teammate quietly add, “Actually, it’s already pretty good. Don’t worry too much.” But I just kept my head down and didn’t dare look at his expression.

After class, I went back to the dorm and shut myself behind my bed curtain, my mind filled with the teacher’s words: “The title slide could be improved.” The more I thought about it, the more I felt like I had dragged down the whole group’s grade. “We prepared for so long—why did I still make a mistake?” “Are the other teammates blaming me in their hearts too?” My chest felt tight again and again, and my fingers would occasionally grab the bedsheet and squeeze it hard. I even took out my laptop and tried to redesign the cover slide, even though it wasn’t necessary at all, because the presentation was already over.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, unable to fall asleep, feeling like I had let everyone down. My stomach ached faintly, as if it were some kind of punishment for failure.

“Are you always like this?”

My roommate’s voice came from behind the bed curtain, carrying a chill I couldn’t ignore. My hands froze over the keyboard, and my heart sank at her words. Her tone was not a simple question, but something more like an accusation. I didn’t know whether she meant the water glass I had knocked over again or the fact that I had been late to our general education class that afternoon, but the words hit my ears like a bullet straight to the nerves. My breathing instantly quickened, and all at once my mind started replaying every expression and tone she had ever shown me. Had she already thought I was a burden from that day on? Had she long ago reached the limit of what she could tolerate from me?

“What do you mean?” I tried to answer calmly, though my voice was trembling. I could hear the anger and defensiveness in it myself, even a trace of desperation. My palms began to sweat, and the hand holding the mouse went numb. That uncontrollable tension made me feel as though I were standing on the edge of a cliff.

“Nothing,” she said, her tone calm, but that calmness made me even more uneasy. “I just think you’re too sensitive sometimes.”

Sensitive. That word felt like it had opened some bottomless pit. I suddenly felt there was nowhere to escape, my eyes stung, and my throat burned. She said “sensitive,” but what I heard in my mind was “trouble,” “burden.”

“Sensitive?” I tried to say something else, even forcing out a faint laugh to hide my irritation, but my voice caught in my throat and came out sounding like mockery. I didn’t mean to mock her. I just wanted to sound less pathetic. Sweat began to bead on the back of my neck, and it felt as though a taut rope had been tied around my stomach. Was I going too far? Were my sensitivities really becoming unbearable to them?

The whole room suddenly fell into an eerie silence, broken only by the faint ticking of the clock on the wall. I could feel her turn over on her bed, then say nothing more. And I remained frozen in front of the computer screen, the cursor blinking on and on. The air was filled with an indescribable heaviness, as if she had in some sense already given up on something, while I was left hanging alone over an imagined abyss.

I began repeatedly going over my roommates’ behavior toward me in the past. I didn’t know if it was just my imagination, but it always seemed like they talked to me less and less. Every time I tried to join their conversations, the atmosphere seemed to cool ever so slightly. A terrible thought suddenly occurred to me: perhaps they had never liked me at all, and no one wanted to say it outright. Had I always been seen as someone “too sensitive” and “too much trouble”?

That night I sat rigidly in my chair almost until morning, my mind replaying her words over and over: “Are you always like this?” I tried to convince myself not to read too much into it, but every time I closed my eyes, her tone and expression came back to my mind like a knife, exact to the last detail. My stomach cramped all night, and in the morning, when I saw my pale face and dark circles in the bathroom mirror, I even deliberately avoided leaving at the same time as my roommates, waiting until they were all gone before I stepped out.

Over the next few days, I found myself being careful about everything I did, even making sure not to make a sound while washing my cup. Every time they laughed and joked, I couldn’t help wondering whether they were talking about me. Even when they said nothing, it felt as if a voice in my head kept repeating the warning: “They’re already tired of you.”

The afternoon light slanted in through the studio window, casting a soft golden sheen over the photography equipment on the desk. I stood by the window, adjusting my camera settings and preparing for next week’s photography assignment. There was a faint smell of coffee in the room, coming from the small coffee machine in the corner, accompanied by the low conversations of a few busy seniors. Just as I was hesitating over the aperture value on my camera, a senior came over. He was wearing a black hoodie, his head slightly bowed. “What do you think of this composition?” He handed me a photo.

I looked at it; the composition was indeed quite interesting, but the colors felt a little too saturated. Carefully, I said, “Um, I think the colors are a bit... too strong?” My voice sounded rather faint in the room. Unfortunately, my words seemed to make the senior pause. He frowned slightly. “Oh? Really? I actually quite like this style,” he said, with a hint of defensiveness that was hard to detect.

My heart sank, and I began to regret whether my comment had been too abrupt. My heartbeat quickened a little, and I could almost feel a thin layer of sweat on my palms. Why was I always like this, so stressed by even a simple conversation? “Yes, I didn’t mean it in a bad way, it was just my personal opinion...” I hurried to add, but my voice was already trembling slightly. I was always afraid that my words might offend others, and I couldn’t even tell whether they really cared about my opinion.

The senior nodded and seemed to simply return to his work without saying much. But I was left drowning in endless self-reproach. To distract myself, I refocused on the photography assignment. As I adjusted the camera, my fingers felt stiff with nervousness. The conversation kept echoing in my mind, and those subtle shifts in tone seemed to mock my sensitivity and overthinking. And so, I spent the entire afternoon in a state of unease.

When I got back to the dorm that evening, I still couldn’t stop replaying the conversation in my head, imagining countless different ways I might have responded. The inner voice of criticism tormented me without pause, making it almost impossible to concentrate on anything else. The next day, I looked through several photography books in the library, trying to improve my understanding. In any case, I didn’t want to feel embarrassed again because of my lack of knowledge. Though I still felt uneasy, I knew that at least these efforts would make me feel a little better.

Sunlight streamed through the greenhouse’s glass roof, casting mottled patches of light and shadow among the green plants. The air was filled with the damp scent of earth and the fresh fragrance of vegetation. I moved through this lush greenery, hoping to find some inner calm in the embrace of nature. Suddenly, I heard the laughter and chatter of several classmates nearby as they discussed a recent experiment that had gone wrong. My heart tightened as I recalled the mistakes I had just made in class, and a wave of shame surged over me. “What do you think of my experiment?” came one voice. In an instant, my chest constricted, as if they were criticizing my shortcomings. I knew I was overreading the situation, but the feeling would not go away.

I tried to focus on the plants in front of me, my fingers gently brushing over a broad, velvety leaf, yet I could not completely shake the irritation inside. My heartbeat quickened, my palms grew slightly damp with sweat, and a dull ache began in my stomach. I quickly looked around, hoping to find a place where I could briefly relax.
