I walked to a corner where there was a small open area and sat down on a stone bench, trying to breathe deeply.

“You look a little unwell,” a gentle voice interrupted my thoughts. It was a classmate from horticulture, also in the greenhouse, and her voice helped ground me a little. “Oh, I’m just a bit tired,” I replied, trying to hide my inner unease. “Plants always help people relax, don’t they?” she continued.

I nodded, trying to convince myself of her words. We talked for a few minutes about plant care techniques and the growing habits of different plants, and in that moment my irritation and unease seemed to be temporarily dispelled by the warm exchange. I realized that I needed more moments like this to balance my anxiety and restlessness. The next day, I decided to reexamine the mistakes I had made in the experiment and try to solve the problem in a more rational way.

Although the emotional fluctuations of that day had not completely disappeared, talking with my classmate gave me some relief. As I faced those troubling issues again, I knew I would need to adjust step by step.

Raindrops tapped gently against the window, and the gray sky outside weighed heavily on my mood. In the ceramics classroom, the air was filled with the scent of clay mixed with dampness, and I felt a wave of unease. Although the weather was overcast, the indoor lighting was soft, and the yellow glow drifted gently across the walls. I sat at my workbench facing a large lump of clay, my heart racing and my palms beginning to sweat. I was always afraid I would do poorly, unable to shake off those feelings of being “abandoned.” The teacher came over, placed a hand on my shoulder, and said gently, “What kind of piece do you want to make?” I hesitated, my mind flashing through all kinds of possible failures. “I’ll give it a try, maybe a vase,” I replied softly, my heart pounding. The teacher smiled slightly. “Trust your instincts. I’ll be here to support you.”

I began kneading the clay, my fingers feeling its slick texture, as if I were touching something resistant. Images of failure kept surfacing in my mind; the vase collapsing and cracks appearing everywhere made me anxious. I tried to concentrate, but my fingers seemed disobedient, as though countless possibilities were warning me: this would be a disaster. “Stay calm, take it slowly.” The teacher was guiding other students not far away, but her voice gave me a sense of comfort. I tried to slow my breathing and focus on the clay before me, and my heartbeat gradually steadied.

As time passed, the shape of the vase slowly emerged. It was not perfect, its surface was uneven, and there were a few slight tilts. A strong urge to attack myself rose within me, and I almost wanted to knock it down and start over. But I stopped, closed my eyes, took a deep breath, and once again felt the clay in my hands and the slight resistance between my fingers. Even though I was somewhat dissatisfied, I tried to tell myself that this too was part of the process.

That afternoon, my vase was finally finished. Although it was not the ideal piece in my mind, I began to accept its imperfections. As I was leaving, the teacher came up to me and said with a smile, “This is a great start. Next time we’ll keep working on it.” I nodded, though inside I was filled with mixed emotions. Back in my dorm, I kept thinking about that vase, and I also began to realize that my own incompleteness was a normal part of who I was. A few days later, when I looked at the piece again, I understood that every imperfection in the making process was part of growth, no longer simply failure. Although my neuroticism made me sensitive and uneasy, every moment my fingers touched the clay was a new exploration, bringing unexpected comfort and relaxation.

The gallery lights were slightly dim, and the light slid across each piece, creating an atmosphere of mystery. The crowd spoke in hushed voices, with the occasional burst of soft laughter, while the air was filled with the scent of flowers and a faint fragrance of perfume. My heart was pounding, and my palms were slightly damp with sweat. I forced myself to stand among the crowd, pretending to be interested in some of the works on the wall, but in fact my attention was completely drawn to the exhibition nearby.

“What do you think of this one?” A classmate walked over and gently patted my shoulder. He was pointing at a brightly colored abstract painting, which looked exceptionally vivid under the soft lighting. I forced out a smile. “Pretty good—the colors are very striking.” Yet inside, I was churning: why was she always able to win everyone’s praise so easily, while I had to struggle with every detail?

“Do you have work on display too?” he asked, his tone seeming to hold a hint of expectation. I turned my head, trying to hide my anxiety and unease. “Mm, yes, over there, in that corner.” I practically squeezed those words out, and at the same time my heart tightened, as the tension surged back again.

A voice inside me kept questioning: Was my work really good enough to compare with everyone else’s? Or was it just being swallowed up by the shadows in that corner? Every time I felt I might be overlooked or not acknowledged, I would fall into this vortex of self-attack.

As time passed, I felt my stomach begin to clench, and my breathing became rapid. I moved myself to a slightly quieter corner, trying hard to calm down. To avoid more self-doubt, I kept telling myself over and over in my head: “This is just an exhibition, not the final judgment.”

When I returned to the dorm that night, that uneasiness refused to fade for a long time. I kept replaying the students’ behavior in the gallery, especially the expressions on their faces in front of my work. My nerves were stretched to the limit, and I seemed still to hear their possible whispers and hidden criticism in my ears.

A few days later, I received an email from the gallery organizers, with a summary of the exhibition and thanks to each participant. I saw that my work was mentioned as well, and that made me breathe a sigh of relief. However, deep inside, there was still a faint fear and a sense of dissatisfaction. To ease these feelings, I began constantly reminding myself: the meaning of creation lies in expression and growth, not in other people’s judgments.

I realized that no matter what the outside world thought, I needed to accept my own imperfections and find the joy in creating. Over the course of that week, I started trying new techniques and giving myself more creative freedom. Although the process was still full of challenges, I gradually learned to find moments of peace in creation and to accept my own vulnerability.

I stood downstairs by the dorm building, holding the unopened takeout bag in my hand. The wind felt a little chilly, and the plastic bag rustled softly. I stared blankly at my phone screen, feeling as if something had clenched tightly around my heart—she had just sent me a message saying tonight’s dinner plan was canceled.

“Sorry, something came up suddenly. Let’s make another plan next time.”

There were only two lines on the screen, but they pierced my chest like a thorn.

I kept rereading the message, trying to find hidden emotional clues in those few words. Did I do something to make her unhappy? Did she actually not want to eat with me? Just two hours ago, we were chatting happily on WeChat. She said she wanted to try that newly opened Japanese restaurant next to the dorms, and I immediately made a reservation. Now she was saying it was canceled. What exactly was this “something”?

“Maybe she never wanted to come in the first place, and just found an excuse,” one voice in my head said. Then another voice followed: “Isn’t it because you’re too annoying, always asking these unnecessary questions?”

Without realizing it, I tightened my grip on the phone. The screen sensed my fingerprint and lit up, then went dark again. A dull pain started in my stomach, as if a chill were roaming around inside. I wanted to text her back, but I didn’t know what to say. I only typed, “It’s okay, remember to invite me next time,” but I didn’t dare press send. Would she think I cared too much? Would she think I was pressuring her?

A couple walked past me, their laughter interrupting my thoughts. The boy said softly, “Don’t forget to buy drinks later,” and the girl smiled and nodded. Watching them walk away, I felt as if my existence itself was a joke. Why am I always so easy to abandon? Is there really something wrong with me? Every time it has to end up like this, every time I have to force myself to get through it alone. It’s just one canceled meal for someone else, but I’m acting like the sky has fallen.

My eyes suddenly stung, and tears welled up uncontrollably. I hurriedly turned and walked back into the building, the tears blurring the stair steps in front of me. I tried desperately to take deep breaths, but my throat felt blocked and no air could get in. When I got into the elevator, I leaned against the cold metal wall, my head bowed low. At last I pressed send. The short words “It’s okay” made me feel as if I were signing a document confirming that I had been abandoned. As if I were the one who needed to apologize. The elevator doors opened, and I mechanically walked back to the dorm, nearly putting the key into the wrong lock.

After I got back to the dorm, I felt weak all over, like a drop of water evaporating away. I sat on the edge of the bed and tore open the takeout bag. Inside was the packed meal box, faintly smelling of soy sauce. But I had no appetite at all. I stared at the bag for a while, then pushed it aside, while scenes and conversations from downstairs kept replaying in my mind. Was it because I was too proactive? Was it because last time, when it was her birthday, I asked too many questions while picking out a gift? Was it because... all kinds of possibilities flashed through my head one after another, like an endless trial.

That night, I didn’t eat dinner. I only drank a glass of cold water. The stomach pain grew worse and worse. I curled up on the bed, hugging myself, and with my eyes closed, I twisted this matter over and over in my mind. It was clearly just an ordinary canceled date, but in my world, it felt like a signal of farewell—a proof that “you are not important.”

The atmosphere in the self-study room was always tense. Fluorescent lights cast a faint white glow, and as time passed, the light outside the window gradually turned from pale gray to deep gray. I sat at a desk by the wall, my notes and textbooks spread across the tabletop, along with a cup of coffee that had already gone cold. There was a faint mixture of coffee and paper in the air, and the leaves outside the window swayed slightly in the breeze from somewhere nearby. From time to time, I could hear classmates speaking in low voices about their homework. I tried hard to concentrate, but the anxiety in my heart kept piling up layer by layer, like waves rising one after another.

Just as I was flipping through my textbook, someone came up to my desk. “When can you send me the data?” My friend’s tone made me tense up instantly. Though his voice was calm, it carried a hint of urgency, and I immediately interpreted it as him blaming me for being too slow. I froze for a moment; my heart started pounding, and my palms began to sweat without me noticing.

“I... I’m not trying to put it off. I’ve just been busy today, it’ll be ready soon!” My voice was somehow rushed, and the defensive tone in my words was so obvious even I could hear it. He seemed to pause for a moment, said, “It’s fine, just hurry up,” and then walked away. His figure disappeared at the end of the hallway, but I remained seated, dazed, replaying the conversation in my head. Was this my fault? Was I being too procrastinating? Was he angry? Would he start holding it against me? I felt as if something were pressing down on my chest, and my breathing grew quick and shallow.

I tried to force myself to keep looking at the notes in front of me, but I couldn’t make sense of a single word. The murmurs around me seemed to grow louder, as if every sentence was aimed at me. I began to wonder whether I was being too sensitive, too full of myself. Or was this no longer my fault—had I already delayed his progress? My mind kept rehearsing how bad things could get if he really was unhappy with me: would he tell other friends that I was unreliable? Would everyone refuse to work on projects with me from now on? Those thoughts kept snowballing, making me restless and unable to sit still.

To calm myself down, I took out my phone and opened our chat history, wanting to check whether his tone had really been off. But the messages all looked perfectly normal, and I still couldn’t trust my own judgment. After hesitating several times, I finally gathered the courage to message him: “Were you a little upset with me just now? I’m sorry, I really didn’t have time. Please don’t be mad at me, okay?” After sending it, I gripped my phone tightly and waited for a reply.

A few minutes later, he wrote back: “No, I wasn’t upset at all. I just needed to sort out the data quickly. It’s fine, don’t overthink it.” I froze for a moment, and after reading that message, all my anxiety vanished like a punctured balloon. I let out a long breath, my heartbeat gradually returning to normal, and the cold sweat on my back slowly dried. But then a new sense of shame followed—why was I always this sensitive? Always this tense? Always so afraid that others had something against me? At the slightest hint of a possible meaning, I would immediately spin out an entire disaster scenario in my head. That night, I could hardly focus on studying, constantly replaying my words and feeling a deep sense of helplessness and dissatisfaction with myself.

Over the next few days, I deliberately avoided that friend. Whenever I ran into him in the hallway, I would instinctively lower my head and walk faster, afraid he might ask me another question. I knew I was being childish, but I couldn’t control the urge to avoid him.

We stood downstairs by the dormitory building, and the bone-chilling night wind made me shiver nonstop. I clutched my phone in my hand, my fingertips already stiff from the cold and from tension, and standing before me was Xiaoqian, her face filled with anger and disappointment.

“I’m just caring about you! Why do you always take kindness as if it’s aimed at you?! I’m really sick of this!” There was a tremor in her voice, growing louder and louder, like a sharp knife stabbing straight into my chest. As I listened to her, a buzzing ringing instantly drowned out her continued accusations. My heartbeat sped up, as if a stone were pressing down on my chest, and no matter how I tried, I couldn’t breathe smoothly.

I forced myself to respond, but my voice sounded like it was squeezed out from the bottom of my throat. “I didn’t... I just thought... do you think I’m always dragging everyone down? Do you think I’m... very... very disgusting?” After the words left my mouth, I could no longer hear her reaction. All I could feel was the stiffness throughout my body and the blood rushing hotly to my face. This overwhelming shame made me want to flee immediately, but my feet were rooted firmly to the ground.

She sighed, and in an instant there was a hint of impatience in her eyes, even pity. “There you go again, attacking yourself all over again. It’s exhausting.” That sentence completely broke me. I stared at her mouth, watching every word she said seem to strike my very existence with force. In that moment, countless scenes flashed through my mind: being ostracized by classmates as a child, the image of a friend suddenly no longer contacting me in high school, all those memories of being abandoned rushing back like a tsunami.

My stomach twisted, and a sour, bitter feeling surged straight up into my esophagus. I felt my eyes beginning to water, but I held it back tightly, with only one thought left in my mind: I can’t let her see me cry. I lowered my head, wanting to leave quietly, but her voice sounded again: “You don’t even know what your problem is. You’re just immersed in your own world.”

I looked up at this friend who had once made me feel safe, and suddenly everything became unfamiliar. It was as if I had fallen into a bottomless abyss, the air around me pressing so hard that I could hardly breathe. I forced myself to say, “I’m sorry I make you feel this tired,” and then turned around, almost running back to the dormitory.

That night, I lay in bed, my whole body stiff from overwhelming tension, my leg muscles twitching now and then. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw her tone, her expression, and those words that made me feel worthless. I kept replaying our conversation from that day in my mind, trying to figure out exactly where I had gone wrong, why she saw me like this. My stomach still throbbed dully, as if a ball of fire were burning inside.

A few days later, I tried messaging Xiaoqian, but her replies were cold and perfunctory. I felt a profound sense of abandonment, as if I had lost a foundation that had been supporting me. I began to doubt our entire friendship, wondering whether it had ever been as solid as I had imagined from the start.

At dinnertime, I decided to cook in the communal kitchen of my university dormitory. The warm yellow light reflected softly off the white tiled walls. Holding a spatula, I watched the oil in the pan bubble cheerfully, crackling and popping. As I tried to flip the ingredients, I accidentally splattered some oil out of the pan, and the scorching liquid landed on my hand. In an instant, a sharp pain shot through my whole body; my heart raced and my palms broke out in sweat. The air was immediately filled with the pungent smell of cooking fumes, and my hand instinctively pulled back, the pain making my muscles stiffen. Turmoil began to rise inside me, and images of being defeated by pain flashed through my mind: my palm red and swollen, a searing heat like fire piercing straight to the bone. I harshly blamed myself—why couldn’t I ever be more careful? I felt ashamed of my carelessness. A classmate nearby stopped what they were doing and asked with concern, “Are you okay? Do you need to go to the infirmary?” I forced out a smile. “I’m fine, just a little burned. Thanks.” But inside, I couldn’t help imagining myself being taken to the infirmary, receiving a stern lecture from the doctor and attention from my classmates. I felt my face growing hot, and I wanted to flee from the place. However, the pain in my hand made it impossible to focus on anything else, so I had no choice but to carefully keep flipping the ingredients in the pan. “Did the oil splash on you? Are you okay?” another classmate asked. I quickly replied, “It’s fine, I already wiped it off.” Anger surged inside me—why did accidents always happen, as if I could never escape disaster? As I tried to forget the pain, I kept cooking, but after that moment of hesitation, I no longer dared to flip the ingredients so carelessly. After a while, I finally finished dinner, and the whole kitchen was filled with a delicious aroma. I let out a soft breath, wanting to relax my tense nerves. That night, lying in bed, the burning sensation in my palm still had not completely faded. Anxiety lingered in my ears. Though my body was exhausted, the scene in the kitchen kept replaying in my mind. A few days later, I began to feel a trace of fear toward using the stove, afraid of getting burned again.

The library was filled with the scent of books, and sunlight streamed through the shadows of the trees outside, dappling the tabletop. A few classmates and I had gathered together, ready to discuss this week’s assignment. Situations like this always made me a little nervous; even though they were familiar friends, I always worried I might say something wrong. Jenny was sitting across from me, flipping through her notes, the pages rustling in her hands.

“Looks like you all got this question wrong,” she said suddenly, glancing up with casual indifference. My heart tightened all at once, my pulse quickened, and a light sweat broke out on my forehead. Her words echoed in my ears, and I immediately started reviewing the details of how I had solved the problem, feeling a bit sick to my stomach.

“Really?” I forced out a smile, trying to look more relaxed. Before I could even react, another classmate began analyzing his solution, and the discussion among us rose and fell. My gaze drifted between them, but all I could hear was Jenny’s one sentence.

I tried hard to concentrate and keep up with their discussion, but the word “wrong” kept replaying over and over in my mind. My hands unconsciously clenched on my knees, and my nails dug into my palms, causing a slight sting. Afraid they would notice how uneasy I was, I lowered my head and pretended to leaf through my notes, while an inner voice kept questioning me: “Did I miss something? Was what I did really that bad?”

When the discussion finally came to an end, I felt a wave of relief, and my heartbeat gradually settled. As I left the library, I habitually looked back to make sure no one was following me with their eyes. That little check made me feel a bit more at ease. Back in the dorm, I sat on my bed and went through my answers again in my notebook, trying to figure out where I had gone wrong.

That night, while chatting with my roommate, I couldn’t help bringing it up. “Do you think that sometimes when our class discusses things, it can make people feel pretty uncomfortable?” I asked cautiously, hoping for a bit of reassurance. My roommate shrugged and joked, “Maybe you’re overthinking it.”

Those words put me slightly at ease, and I thought maybe I really was taking things too seriously; my emotions gradually settled down. The next day, I decided to focus on preparing for my other classes, so I could stop letting such a small matter affect my mood.

At night, the dorm lights always seemed a bit too harsh, and the computer screen on the desk kept flickering. I was so anxious about the upcoming assignment deadline that my palms were sweating, and I could hear my roommates whispering nearby. I pricked up my ears and heard them mention my name: “She’s always like this, too sensitive.” In that instant, my chest tightened and my breathing became rapid. I tried hard to breathe normally, but the feeling of my throat being blocked wouldn’t let me calm down.

“Are you talking about me?” I finally couldn’t help but interrupt them. The roommates exchanged glances, and then one stepped forward and said, “We just think sometimes you overreact.” My heart suddenly plunged into a freezing abyss. At that moment, I felt as if everything in me had been drained out of my body, leaving only the pounding of my heartbeat in my ears. My face started to burn, and my hands began to tremble slightly.

“I’m not overreacting,” I said, trying to keep my voice firm, but the unease in my tone betrayed me without a doubt. “Maybe you don’t like me, then I’ll move out.” The words burst out of me, and then I felt a wave of dizziness, as if I were about to be crushed by their weight.

“That’s not what we meant!” one of my roommates tried to explain, but I could no longer take it in. I only felt like an isolated stranger, and the fear of being excluded enveloped me in an instant. I hurried out of the dormitory; the air outside was icy and bone-chilling. Every step felt like I was running away from something—and more than that, from that ever-present shadow: the feeling of being abandoned.

I stood on the bench outside the dorm, my heart racing and my stomach cramping. The wind howled in my ears, and the whole world seemed to be tearing apart. I didn’t know where I was going; I just kept walking farther and farther away. Right then, I only wanted to hide and not face anyone.

The next day, I was still unsettled in class. The professor’s voice had turned into background noise, and the scene from the night before kept replaying in my mind. A few classmates cast concerned looks at me, and the pressure of being watched made me deeply uncomfortable. I began to wonder whether I really was too sensitive, or whether I truly wasn’t liked by others.

A few days later, I had a long talk with my roommates. Although they repeatedly insisted they meant no harm, I still couldn’t completely dispel the unease in my heart. The shadow of that night still loomed over me, like a crack that could never fully heal.

On Saturday afternoon, I decided to spend some time in the campus library. Autumn sunlight streamed in through the tall glass windows, bringing a warm and cozy feeling. I sat at a long table by the window, with several books scattered across it, and my gaze settled on one of them. The pages were slightly yellowed, and when my fingers touched them, I could feel a faint roughness.

The surroundings were very quiet, with only the occasional sound of pages turning and soft coughing. A boy walked past me, carrying a faint scent of laundry detergent, which reminded me of the times when clothes were drying on the balcony at home. It was a reassuring, familiar smell. I looked at the book in my hands, but my attention unconsciously began to wander as I observed the people around me.

Not far away, I saw a girl writing intently in her notebook, the tip of her pen making a rustling sound on the paper. She wore an expression of concentration that made me a little envious. “I should work harder too,” I thought, but then I was drawn to a fallen leaf outside the window. It swayed gently, like a dance in slow motion.

I tried to refocus on the book, but before long, the atmosphere around me stirred my thoughts again. My heartbeat was steady, my body relaxed, and the view outside the window was peaceful. At the same time, my stomach would occasionally make a soft growling sound, reminding me that I hadn’t eaten much for lunch.

Being in such an environment brought a kind of pleasant calm to my heart, as if everything were in a natural balance. No pressure, no tension, just the simplicity of the present moment.

That night, when I returned to the dorm, I found myself thinking back to that afternoon in the library. A simple sense of contentment made me smile. I told my roommate, “This afternoon in the library felt especially good, especially relaxing.” She smiled and replied, “Then let’s go more often. It’s such a great place.”

So over the next few days, I would occasionally think of that afternoon, and that sense of peace and contentment stayed with me for quite a while.

The rehearsal room was dimly lit, with only a few spotlights on the stage shining brightly. I stood in the center of the stage, guitar in hand, my heart pounding like a drum. A faint woody scent filled the room, coming from the stage’s wooden floorboards. I was preparing with several band members for next week’s festival performance. The drummer kept a steady beat, giving us a solid foundation. But just thinking about the rehearsal made my palms start to sweat, and the slick feeling only made me more nervous.

“Come on, everyone, get ready,” the conductor clapped his hands. “From the top.” I took a deep breath and silently repeated the chord progression in my head. The music began, and I started to play, trying not to look at the expressions on the other members’ faces. But before long, my fingers made a mistake on a very simple chord, producing a harsh, off-key note that broke the flow of the entire piece.

“Stop, stop, stop!” The conductor shook his head helplessly. “What happened?” I felt my face grow hot and lowered my head, too afraid to look anyone in the eye. “Sorry, I…,” I mumbled, my voice so soft it was almost inaudible.

“Are you okay?” the bassist beside me asked quietly. I nodded, but inside I was in complete turmoil. “How could I make a mistake in such a simple place?” I kept blaming myself. My heart raced, and my stomach felt tightly knotted with discomfort.

During the break, I walked alone out into the corridor outside the rehearsal room, trying to calm myself down. The clock on the wall ticked away, and I watched the hands move, trying to soothe myself with the rhythm. But it didn’t help; the self-reproach inside me seemed to grow even louder.

When I returned to the rehearsal room, I noticed the other members whispering among themselves, and their looks toward me seemed to carry more doubt. “Did I drag the whole band down?” Once that thought flashed through my mind, it would not leave.

After the rehearsal ended, I forced out a smile and said goodbye to everyone. Back at the dorm, exhaustion left my whole body limp. I flopped onto the bed, feeling tears welling up. “If I could do better, none of this would have happened.” Thinking this, I tossed and turned until, in the still of the night, I finally drifted into a dazed sleep.

The next day, I walked into the classroom with a weary expression, still haunted by yesterday’s mistake. One of the band members came over and patted my shoulder. “It’s okay, we’ve all been there. Just keep working hard.” Though those words comforted me a little, I was still worried I would make another mistake at the next rehearsal.

The cafeteria was buzzing with voices, and all around there was the clatter of plates and the murmur of conversation. The food on the tables gave off heat, mixed with the fragrance of seasonings. A group of us sat around a long table, and a few roommates were discussing last night’s party. My spoon moved through the rice as I nodded along from time to time.

“How did you like the music last night?” one of my roommates asked, her voice squeezing through the noise into my ears. I tried to smile, doing my best not to let her see that I was a little tense. “It was pretty good. I like that kind of rhythm,” I replied, though a faint unease lingered in my heart.

They went on talking about music, with the occasional burst of laughter. I listened to them discuss the lead singer of some band, but my mind kept drifting back to a conversation I had had with a friend last night. Something he had said carelessly made me read too much into it, as though every word were criticizing me. I knew it was only an illusion, but I still couldn’t help feeling excluded.

“The singer you just mentioned—I think his voice is really unique,” I said, forcing myself to join in, hoping to fit into the small group. Yet a faint discomfort welled up in my stomach, as if a little stone were stuck somewhere inside.

During a lull in the conversation, I wiped my forehead with a napkin and realized I was starting to sweat. I began to dwell on it: would they think I was boring or unnecessary? The thought clung to me. I didn’t dare look directly at their expressions, afraid I might catch a trace of impatience.

By the time lunch ended, everyone was still talking, while I felt my own voice gradually fading away, leaving only their laughter and chatter. I kept silent as if nothing were wrong, trying hard not to think about how out of place I must seem in front of them.

After lunch, I walked alone along the campus path. Sunlight filtered through the leaves and scattered across the ground, breaking the shadows into small pieces. I tried to relax and told myself it was only an ordinary conversation, nothing to overthink. Back in the dorm, I lay on my bed and stared at the ceiling, forcing myself to breathe deeply. Still, that subtle unease remained, and I thought maybe in a few days this embarrassment would fade away.

Over the next few days, I avoided going to the cafeteria with my roommates. Instead, I chose a quiet corner by myself and ate lunch in silence, occasionally glancing at the book in my hands. It made me feel safe, with fewer outside distractions and no one able to see the fluctuations in my heart.

In the café on my university campus, I often chose a corner seat where I could observe everything going on inside. That day was like any other: there weren’t too many people, and the air was filled with the aroma of freshly ground coffee beans, accompanied by the low hum of the machines, which made me feel somewhat at ease.

I ordered a cappuccino, and while I was waiting, I took out my phone to browse social media. But I couldn’t help looking up at the counter from time to time, where the staff were busy making coffee. I noticed one of them kept glancing in my direction. I felt a little nervous, and my instinct told me he might have some kind of resentment toward me.

“Your coffee is ready,” the staff member called out to me a few minutes later in a tone I interpreted as slightly impatient. I quickly walked up to the counter, my heart rate picking up a little—the feeling pounding in my ears like a drum. When I took the coffee, I deliberately watched his expression, trying to find some clue that would confirm my suspicion. But he remained very calm, showing no obvious emotion.

Back at my seat, I started reflecting on what had just happened: “Was I being too sensitive? Did he mean something by the way he looked at me?” These questions kept circling in my mind, and a wave of shame and unease rose in me. I picked up the coffee and took a sip; the warm liquid slid down my throat, easing my anxiety a little.

During the idle chatting that followed, I shifted my attention to my phone. But before I knew it, my gaze drifted back to the staff member. Every movement and expression of his became something I tried to interpret, and I kept wondering whether he had a bad opinion of me. I admit this was a bit ridiculous, but there was always a voice in my head saying, “Be careful, don’t make people think you’re weird.”

I spent the entire afternoon caught in this conflicted state of mind. Even when I left the café, my worries still hadn’t eased. As I walked back to the dormitory, the sunlight was especially glaring; I narrowed my eyes slightly and felt a bit of a headache. Maybe it was because I had been tense for so long that, without realizing it, my shoulders had also become somewhat stiff.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the afternoon in my mind. I felt somewhat helpless about my sensitivity, and also a little angry, wondering why I always made such a big deal out of nothing. Although I knew full well that I was probably overthinking it, I still couldn’t help speculating and interpreting. It took several days before I gradually let it go, but that inexplicable sense of shame still lingered in my heart.

The wooden chairs in the cafeteria had a backrest that was a little hard and uncomfortable. I kept biting into the pan-fried dumplings, which had hardly any broth, while listening to the sounds around me. The light overhead was a little harsh; its white glare made my eyes ache slightly. I glanced up at the classmate sitting across from me. She was looking at her phone and barely paying any attention to me. What had happened in class just now came flooding back again, like a thorn stuck in my throat.

“Your point earlier didn’t really hold up, did it?” A male voice surfaced from my memory—it was the boy sitting on the right side of the classroom. Leaning back in his chair, he had a slight upward curl at the corner of his mouth when he said it, as if with a hint of contempt. My face had flushed at once, as if something were blocking my throat, and I could only force out, “Oh, maybe.” Then I lowered my head and pretended to look at my notes. But my palms were so damp that even my pen felt slippery.

“It clearly wasn’t like that. He must think I’m a joke,” I kept repeating to myself. My stomach felt tied in knots, twisted so tightly it wouldn’t loosen no matter what. Why hadn’t I explained myself again then? I actually had my reasons, but the way he spoke made it impossible for me to argue back. Did he think I was ignorant? Or not worth taking seriously at all? The more I thought about it, the more frustrated I became. My mind churned like boiling water, replaying that scene over and over, until even his expression and tone seemed more and more exaggerated.

“Hey, are you okay?” The classmate across from me finally looked up and waved a hand in front of my face. I let out an “ah” and realized I was gripping my chopsticks so tightly that my fingers had gone a little white. I hurriedly set them down and took a sip of water to cover it up. When the rim of the cup touched my lips, it was actually a little cold. “I’m fine. I just can’t quite figure out what happened in class.” I forced out a smile, but my voice was so low it sounded less like a conversation and more like I was talking to myself.

She glanced at me and said in a lowered voice, “Don’t take it too seriously. I don’t think anyone’s really thinking about it.” I looked down at the pan-fried dumplings, darkened by soy sauce, and didn’t dare respond. But a thought surfaced in my mind: “How could they not care? He singled me out so obviously.” Whenever someone says “don’t mind it,” it feels like they’re telling me that the only reason this is worth minding is because I’m too inadequate.

After I got back to the dorm, I tossed my backpack onto the bed and then sat down at the desk, staring blankly at the computer screen. The title of the paper on the screen was blurred beyond recognition, and all my attention had been dragged back to that scene. It seemed as though I could still hear the words ringing in my ears: “didn’t really hold up, did it?” I tried repeating the sentence in different tones, trying to figure out what he meant. My heart was beating a little fast. My hand rested on the desk, and the coolness beneath my elbow helped clear my head a bit.

For the next few days, this incident still clung to my mind like dust. I even started avoiding eye contact with that boy. If he was sitting near the door in the classroom, I would deliberately take a detour and enter or leave from the other side. I knew I might be overthinking it, but this kind of thought was like a chronic illness, leaving me powerless to resist.

I was sitting in the corner of the library study room, with a thick textbook spread open on the desk and my notebook on the left filled with formulas and keywords. The air smelled faintly of disinfectant, with a hint of old paper as well. Sunlight streamed through the somewhat worn blinds outside the window, making the pages look a warmer yellow. I was trying to focus on the complicated theory in front of me, but the person in the seat to my right kept lightly shaking their leg, and that subtle vibration seemed to pass into my line of sight like a huge wave of interference.

Thump-thump, thump-thump — the rhythmic sound of their foot tapping the floor. The classical music playing in my headphones couldn’t drown out the buzzing background noise at all. I wanted to change the music, but I didn’t know what would help me calm down. A familiar sense of tension began to rise inside me, as if all my effort were being swallowed by this meaningless sound. I even started to wonder whether I wasn’t focused enough, or whether I simply shouldn’t be studying here at all.

I tried to take deep breaths, but every inhale felt a little tight in my chest, and my heartbeat inexplicably sped up. My palms began to sweat slightly, and the pen in my hand felt slippery, as if it might fall at any moment. I looked up at the classmate shaking their leg; they seemed completely unaware of the “disaster” they were causing, concentrating on taking notes. I hesitated over whether to speak up, but I was also worried about disturbing them or triggering an awkward conversation.

So I muttered to myself under my breath, “Could you please stop shaking your leg…” But I said it so quietly that it didn’t catch their attention at all. A sudden impulsive thought flashed through my mind: just get up and leave right now! But that was quickly suppressed by another thought: I’ve already been sitting here for so long, and I’ve organized so many formulas—would leaving be too irresponsible? That inner conflict made my stomach ache faintly too. I began blaming myself: why am I always so sensitive? Why can such a tiny thing affect me this much? Am I just too weak?

At last, I heard him gather his things and leave, gently pulling the chair back. With that final scraping sound of chair against floor, my heartbeat seemed to return to normal. Yet this relief didn’t make me feel completely at ease; instead, it made me even more anxious. What if something like this happened again next time? How could I become less easily disturbed by my surroundings? All afternoon, I kept imagining similar scenes, so much so that by later on I couldn’t remember what the content of the next few pages of the textbook had even been.

When I returned to the dorm that night, I still couldn’t help mentioning it to my roommate: “There was this person shaking their leg in the library today—it was seriously so annoying.” She smiled and said, “You care too much about these little trivial things. Just relax.” But I didn’t feel much lighter inside; instead, I lay in bed repeatedly turning over the tone of her words in my head, wondering if she thought I was being neurotic.

In the classroom, sunlight streamed through the window and slanted across the desktop, revealing the subtle expressions on everyone’s faces. I sat at the edge of the small-group discussion circle, watching the other students the whole time. Our task today was to discuss a topic related to social responsibility, and several classmates had already begun exchanging opinions intensely. A classmate beside me smiled and said, “What do you think? Tell us your thoughts.” He slightly raised his eyebrows, and I felt his gaze fall on me like a few beams of scrutiny, making my chest tighten at once.

“Oh, I think...” I began, but my voice trembled a little, my heart raced, and my palms grew sweaty. I tried to grasp something meaningful from the gaps in my mind, but suddenly it felt as if all my thoughts had vanished without a trace. The people around me began whispering to each other, and I was immediately flooded with a sense of rejection.

“Are you okay?” he asked with concern, his voice very soft. I nodded, my skin flushing slightly from nervousness. I told myself they must be laughing at me, thinking I wasn’t smart enough, not quick-witted enough. My chest tightened again and again, and I felt a little sick to my stomach.

“They must think I’m so incompetent,” I kept repeating to myself inside, quietly imagining all the negative judgments they might have of me. These thoughts spread rapidly through my mind like vines, almost swallowing me whole.

For the entire class, I kept trying to conceal my unease, pressing my lips together and pretending to listen carefully, when in fact I could no longer pay attention to the discussion at all. My attention was completely taken over by the anxiety and uneasiness in my heart, and my body was starting to feel exhausted from being so tense.

After class, I silently packed up my things, feeling utterly frustrated and ashamed. Back in the dorm, I locked myself in my room and kept turning over those words and expressions in my mind. That first night, I tossed and turned, wondering whether I had done something wrong, why I was always so anxious, and why I couldn’t be as natural and confident as everyone else.

Over the next few days, I kept replaying that scene over and over, wondering whether I wasn’t suited for such an environment. Even when spending time with friends, I became cautious, afraid that anything I said would invite more judgment. Every time I thought of that classmate’s gaze, I couldn’t help but tense up again and fall back into doubt about my own abilities.

In the classroom, the air carried a faint smell of dust, the formulas on the whiteboard hadn’t been fully erased yet, and sunlight slanted through the window onto the desk. I sat in the seat closest to the window, my palms already sweating, my knees trembling unconsciously. Today was our team discussion day, and the topic was how to optimize a solution to a social problem. I had spent a week designing a proposal, feeling that I could finally let everyone see my effort.

When I began explaining my plan, my voice trembled a little. I tried hard to sound confident, but I could clearly feel a tightness in my chest. “My proposal is based on population distribution data, and I suggest gradually implementing it from the city center to the suburbs…” I had barely said that before the team leader cut me off directly, his tone somewhat impatient: “This idea is too idealistic. It would be very difficult to put into practice and may not be realistic.” I froze for a moment, my face feeling slightly hot, and a strong wave of unease rose from my stomach.

The group members began whispering. I looked around and saw them exchanging glances; some frowned, others lowered their heads to flip through the materials. I couldn’t help sinking inwardly, and in my mind I kept repeating the team leader’s comment — “too idealistic.” Was I completely unqualified to propose something like this? Did everyone think I was stupid?

I tried to salvage the situation and added, “Actually, if we combine data from similar projects from the past few years, I think we can find some compromise.” But my voice sounded more like a plea than a confident explanation. The teammates continued to raise objections, discussing other possible directions, and never mentioned my proposal again.

My heart was beating faster and faster, the pounding seeming to roar in my ears. I lowered my head and stared at my notebook, trying to pretend I wascarefully record opinions, but in fact every stroke was just random scribbling. I could feel fine sweat forming on my forehead, and my back had started to get damp too, as if something were pressing down on me tightly.

By the time the meeting ended, everyone quickly packed up the materials. The team leader patted my shoulder and said flatly, “Next time you can try suggesting some more concrete directions.” That sentence stabbed into my mind like a needle. It wasn’t comforting at all; instead, it made me feel completely unimportant.

Back in the dorm, those glances and the team leader’s tone were still echoing in my head. I pressed the back of my hand against my forehead and found that I was a little warm. Lying on my bed and staring at the ceiling, I thought: Why do I always mess up these social situations? Are my ideas really completely worthless? I started looking back through my draft, but no matter how I looked at it, it seemed full of flaws and shortcomings.

Later, my roommate came back and saw me lying lifelessly on the bed. She asked what was wrong. I forced out a perfunctory “It’s nothing,” but deep down I really wanted her to ask one more question, yet I was also afraid that explaining further would make me seem overly dramatic. That night I hardly slept at all. My mind felt stuck, and every time I closed my eyes, the team leader’s expression and the looks from the other group members would appear.

A few days later, I still couldn’t summon the courage to speak up on my own in group discussions. I chose to sit off to the side, not joining the arguments, silently watching them talk. Inside, there was a faint sense of safety, but I also felt excluded.

Sunlight streamed through the large glass windows into the café, falling across the computer screen on the table and casting a faint glow. While I rubbed the warmth of my coffee cup and tried my best to concentrate, I was meeting with several friends today to discuss an ongoing creative project. The sound of the coffee grinder and the lively chatter of students filled my ears, and I could feel my heart racing, my hands becoming slightly damp with sweat. Waves of anxiety kept surging through my mind, as if every tiny mistake could plunge me into an abyss.

“What do you think of this opening?” one of my friends asked, turning to look at me. Her tone was calm, but I searched her expression for any sign of dissatisfaction or uncertainty. “Um, I think it might be better to add a little more background information,” I replied vaguely, while worries began churning inside me: was my opinion just meant to please everyone, or was it actually helpful?

My stomach tightened, as if responding to those emotions. I tried to change the subject and introduce some new ideas, hoping to guide the discussion in a favorable direction. “Actually, we could consider adding a character to strengthen the story’s sense of tension,” I suggested, trying to sound confident. “That might be a good idea,” my friend replied with a smile, which relaxed me a little, but still did not erase the unease deep inside me.

The discussion continued, and in my mind I kept playing out the worst possible outcomes, as if every potential mistake would be magnified without limit. My breathing quickened, and my palms tapped unconsciously against the tabletop. At that moment, my thoughts immediately turned self-critical: I shouldn’t have brought up such seemingly immature ideas. Am I just going to drag everyone down?

“For the ending, we still need some plot twists,” a friend’s words brought my attention back to the discussion. I tried hard to suppress the turmoil inside me and focus on thinking. “Maybe we could do it like this…” My voice grew steadier as I began to describe a fleeting spark of inspiration in my mind.

That night, I lay in bed thinking about the discussion. My heart was still troubled by embarrassment and anxiety. Although some of my suggestions had been accepted, I still felt uneasy, worried that I might be abandoned or ignored in future collaborations. A few days later, when a friend sent me a message to thank me for my input, I felt a wave of relief. Though the aftershocks had not completely faded, I knew that my contribution to the team was real and had genuine value.

We were sitting in a corner of the classroom, sunlight slanting in through the window and falling across the table in front of us. The table was covered with our notebooks and textbooks, looking a little messy. I tried to sort out my thoughts in my head, preparing to explain my point to the group members. My voice was a little shaky, perhaps because I had already been interrupted twice in a row before, and my heart was pounding like a drum. There was a boy in the group who always seemed relaxed and at ease, with a smile on his face that seemed to carry a kind of careless confidence. Propping his chin on his hand, he said lazily, “Well, I don’t think this really holds up. Look, there’s a flaw in the theory itself.” His tone was flat, but I could hear the rejection in it. Suddenly, it felt as though the air in the whole room had grown heavy, like an invisible wall pressing against my chest.

I tried to respond: “I think it can be understood from another angle, like…” Before I could finish, he cut in again: “But that still doesn’t solve the fundamental problem. Did you even read the reference materials carefully?” That sentence made me feel as if my wound had been laid bare in public. I heard slight laughter from a few others; though brief, it was enough to trigger a violent alarm in my mind. I instinctively felt they were laughing at my ignorance. I clenched my teeth and tried hard to keep my eyes on my notes, but my hands began to tremble uncontrollably. Isecretly glanced at the others’ expressions, hoping to find some comfort, but none of their eyes lingered on me.

“What do you think?” The boy turned to another group member, and this complete disregard for me felt like a declaration that my opinion had been worthless from the very beginning. My stomach tightened as if a hand had clenched it hard, a dull pain spreading through it. In an instant, memories surged up in my mind—stammering during a debate competition in high school, the flushed embarrassment when I said the wrong thing at a friend’s gathering and was laughed at… These images gripped me and kept me from focusing.

I lowered my head to arrange my papers, pretending to study them carefully, but in truth I just wanted to avoid their gazes. My mind was churning wildly: “I’m really so stupid. Why can’t I ever say things clearly? They must think I’m completely clueless. How did I end up like this?” The pressure in my chest kept building, as if I were sinking to the bottom of the sea. I tried to comfort myself, thinking maybe I could do better next time, but the voice inside immediately denied it: “You can’t do it at all.”

After it ended, I left the classroom with almost no conversation with anyone. My back was damp, probably from sweating, but I hadn’t noticed. When I returned to the dormitory, I forced myself to open my notes and reread the material, but every time I saw the words on the page, it felt like they were mocking me. I tried messaging a friend and told her about what had happened in class. She comforted me, saying, “Don’t take it too seriously. They may not have meant it that way.” But I still couldn’t help replaying their tone and attitude over and over. A few days later, I still couldn’t shake that unease, constantly feeling as though I had lost face in front of everyone.

The air was thick with the smell of fresh plaster, with the occasional scent of metal and plastic mixed in. The lights overhead were a little dim, and I sat in front of the workbench, trying to shape the clay in my hands into the form I had imagined. But my palms were starting to heat up, and sweat gradually soaked through my gloves, making each knead more difficult.

“Doing it this way today doesn’t seem to match the plan we discussed,” the professor’s voice came calmly. He stood beside my piece, staring at my handiwork. I lifted my head and met his eyes, immediately feeling my heart race. “No, I think maybe the direction of inspiration you mentioned yesterday was a bit vague, I was trying to—”

“I thought we had made ourselves very clear.” His voice rose slightly, seeming tinged with displeasure.

My stomach began to ache a little, and I could almost hear my heart beating faster in my ears. The professor’s tone gave me an unsettling sense of foreboding, the “what did I do wrong again” feeling I feared most, like the shame I had felt years ago after having my mistakes pointed out. I struggled to stay calm. “I just wanted to try a different style, because—”

“But that goes against the direction of your project.” His words were blunt, like a hammer falling and shattering the little confidence I had left.

My face began to grow a little hot. I quickly glanced at the other students; they were busy at their own tables and didn’t seem to notice our conversation. I tried to take deep breaths, attempting to suppress the anxiety surging up inside me, but the sound of my heartbeat still wouldn’t let go. My fingers unconsciously started rubbing the hem of my clothes, my mind filled with the frustration and self-reproach of “Why is it always like this?”

In the end, I chose to remain silent, hoping to calm myself by adjusting my breathing. Yet the unease in my heart kept rising like a tide, impossible to shake off.

When the afternoon class ended, I slowly left the workshop alone. The wind outside was a little cold, carrying the faint chill of autumn. The professor’s words still echoed repeatedly in my mind. I kept telling myself to stick to my original creative path, but the doubts of “What if he’s right? Am I being too arrogant?” kept eroding what little confidence I had.

That night, lying on my dorm bed, I went back through the creative notes I had written, hoping to find some inspiration or comfort in them. When I woke up the next morning, the subtle, persistent anxiety from yesterday afternoon was still lingering. I told myself that today I had to make my thoughts clear and not let him feel again that I wasn’t listening to his advice.

Sunlight streamed through the tall glass windows into the small auditorium, casting light across the stage. A faint smell of damp wood lingered in the air. I stood beside the stage, clutching my debate script, my palms already sweating. My heartbeat was abnormally fast, like a little hammercontinuously tapping inside my chest. “Can I really do this?” I kept asking myself. Last night, lying in bed, I had been agonizing over every word, worried my speaking pace would be too fast or too slow, terrified that the judges would think I was unprofessional. Every time I thought of it, my stomach would cramp with pain, and now that same feeling was tormenting me again.

“Don’t worry, you’re very well prepared!” The team captain patted my shoulder in a lighthearted tone. I forced out a smile. “Mm, thanks…” But in my mind, I immediately started analyzing her expression: was her tone really that sincere? Or was she just brushing me off so I’d hurry up and get onstage? Could it be that she didn’t think much of me at all, but didn’t have the heart to say it outright? These thoughts surged in like a tide, drowning out my reason.

“You’re next, get ready.” When a classmate reminded me, my hands were shaking so badly I could hardly hold onto the debate script. I was terrified of making a fool of myself onstage. I swallowed hard and had no choice but to summon my courage and step by step walk up to the stage. The seats below were arranged in two rows; the first few rows were occupied by classmates and judges, while the back rows were almost empty, the light flickering unevenly across the vacant chairs. I tried hard to suppress the pounding in my chest, reminding myself that all of this was possible and that I needed to prepare for the worst. But what if others laughed at me? What if my voice trembled? What if I gave it my all and still forgot my lines? These questions churned in my head, buzzing in my ears.

“You may begin.” The judge’s voice pulled me back to reality. I looked up and saw them staring at me. The light pouring down made it feel as though every pair of eyes was scrutinizing each one of my clumsy movements. My throat instantly went dry, and I could barely force out a complete sentence. But I had no choice but to speak: “Honorable judges, dear classmates…” My own voice seemed to come from far away, almost impossible to hear clearly. I gripped the pages tightly, my fingertips feeling the roughness of the paper, trying desperately to suppress the fear of being judged at any moment. I was like a mechanical puppet reciting the opening lines before finally finding the slightest rhythm.

I tried my best to keep my eyes on the script and not look at the watching faces below, but I still heard a few classmates in the back whispering. I immediately began imagining them evaluating my performance: “Is TA too nervous?” “Look, their hands have been shaking the whole time.” “No way—how could someone at this level make it onto the team?” My stomach tightened like a rubber band stretched to its limit, and my mind was almost blank; I forgot what came next. I swallowed, forcing myself to squeeze out the remaining lines. At that moment, all I wanted was to hurry down from that stage.

At the end, several judges nodded expressionlessly. After I stepped down, I walked to the side door of the auditorium. Light streamed in through the glass door, falling on the floor, and I felt the air grow so heavy it was suffocating. A classmate came over and said, “You did pretty well just now, don’t be too nervous.” Her voice seemed comforting, but all I felt was irony. Was she just brushing me off too? The entire morning, I kept replaying my performance over and over, studying everyone’s expressions and tones, worried I might already have left a bad impression.

That night, lying in bed, my mind was still endlessly replaying the debate like a videotape. I could hear the mistakes, see my trembling hands, and even the brief pauses when the judges spoke became something I clung to. I thought, if only I could do it over, I’d surely do better—but that thought only made it harder to fall asleep. Maybe they had already decided to choose someone else; how could they possibly choose me? My chest began to ache faintly again, as if a huge boulder were pressing down on it.

The glow of my phone screen was blinding in the darkness beneath the dorm building. I paced back and forth, my fingers sliding across the screen, yet I still couldn’t find the courage to press the call button. Her words from the afternoon kept replaying in my mind: “I feel like you’re too much trouble. You always need other people to comfort you, and it’s really exhausting.” Those words were like a sharp thorn, stabbing into my chest so painfully that I could barely breathe. My heart was racing, and I could even hear the sound of blood rushing in my ears. She was my best friend, and in every moment we had spent eating together, talking together, sharing secrets, I had never imagined she would feel this way.

At last, I pressed the call button. As soon as the call connected, I heard her cold tone. “What do you want to say again?” She used the word “again,” and I froze. Tears surged up at once, but I forced myself to stay calm. “I wanted to ask... are you angry? Did I do something to upset you?” Even as I said it, my voice sounded so humble that I could hardly stand it myself. “If I made you uncomfortable, I’m sorry.”

There was no softening in her tone. “I just feel a little tired. I’ve already said the same things to you many times before, so why can’t you change?” She seemed to sigh. “I really don’t think we’re suited to be such close friends.”

My heart sank at once, as if I had fallen into an abyss. I tried to explain, “But I just... I just wanted to make sure...” But halfway through, I suddenly felt utterly ridiculous. Make sure what? Make sure she still cared about me? If the answer was no, then what was I supposed to do? Her voice kept going on the other end, but I could no longer make it out. All I could hear was a buzzing sound, like the roar of a speeding train passing by.

After hanging up, I sat on the stone bench beneath the dorm building, my palms covered in sweat, even my fingers trembling slightly. It felt as if my throat were blocked by something, leaving me unable to speak, unable even to breathe properly. I crouched down and buried my head in my knees, trying to stop myself from crying, but tears still slid down the bridge of my nose. Occasionally I heard footsteps from inside the dorm building, and my first reaction was actually fear that they would see me crying and think I was pathetic.

All night long, I replayed every word she had said, turning over every detail of how I had interacted with her before, desperately searching for the source of her annoyance with me. Was it something I said when we went out to eat last week? Was I too dependent on her when we worked on assignments together? I even started examining every message I had sent her, every emoji, trying to find the reason for her coldness.

That night, I didn’t sleep a single minute, and my stomach ached faintly too. I began to regret making that call. Did doing that make her even more annoyed with me? But not calling her also left me restless, like a cat endlessly chewing on its own tail, unable to escape its anxiety no matter what.

For the next few days, I never contacted her first again. Whenever others mentioned her, I would pretend not to hear, but inside, I couldn’t stop wondering whether she had already told someone else what was “wrong” with me. That feeling of being abandoned was like a huge whirlpool, pulling me in until I could barely breathe.

The air in the classroom seemed a little still. Sunlight streamed in through the windows, illuminating the notebooks and scattered textbooks on the desks. I sat in the middle of the classroom, listening as the professor explained the details of the course project on the podium, while my mind was already spinning with all kinds of ideas. Suddenly, the classmate sitting next to me turned around and, with a slight frown, asked, “Could you share your thoughts?”

His tone was calm, but I sensitively caught the slight lift of his eyebrows in that instant. My heart tightened immediately, and countless possibilities flashed through my mind: Was he questioning me? Did he think I wasn’t good enough? My heartbeat began to quicken, and I took a deep breath, trying hard to steady the unrest inside me.

“Um, actually, I still haven’t fully figured out the direction of this project,” I said hesitantly, my voice seeming a little faint in the air. After I spoke, I felt a thin layer of sweat break out on my back, and my palms started to sweat as well.

He seemed a little surprised, nodded, and turned back to continue listening to the lecture. But I couldn’t calm down. I kept replaying our conversation in my mind, again and again, along with the microexpression on his face. Why had he made that expression? Did I do something wrong?

For the rest of the class, I barely took anything in. I just mechanically wrote unrelated things in my notebook. When the bell rang, I quickly gathered my books and pushed through the crowd, wanting to leave as fast as possible. However, just as I reached the classroom door, I looked back at him again. He was discussing something with other students, a relaxed smile on his face.

“You seem a bit nervous today. Are you feeling unwell?” A familiar voice suddenly sounded beside my ear. I turned around and saw another classmate standing next to me, asking with concern.

“I’m fine, I’m just thinking about something I can’t quite figure out,” I forced a smile.

That afternoon, after I returned to the dorm, my mind still couldn’t stop ruminating over my performance. I paced back and forth, reanalyzing every expression and every word the other person had said, but in the end I still had no answer.

A few days later, I saw that classmate again, and we began talking about the course project. He said, “When we discussed it last time, I was actually really looking forward to hearing your thoughts. You always bring a unique perspective.”

Hearing that, I didn’t know how to respond for a moment, and could only manage a strained smile. It seemed as if a heart that had been hanging in the air slowly settled, but what followed was shame over why I had been so sensitive. Had I been overreading everything? Should I trust myself more?

That night, lying in bed, I suddenly realized that perhaps my anxiety and unease stemmed more from my own uncertainty than from any real judgment from the outside world. Future attempts may require me to spend more time understanding rather than refuting.

I walked into the university library, where the air was filled with the faint scent of paper and ink. Sunlight streamed through the tall floor-to-ceiling windows, casting dappled patterns of light and shadow between the bookshelves. I was looking for a book on art history, silently thinking to myself, “I hope I can find it smoothly this time, without having to spend as much time and effort as last time.”

As I approached the shelves, I gently slid my fingers along the spines, scanning the letters to find the book I wanted. However, when I reached for one book, it suddenly lost its balance and, with a rustling of pages, fell heavily onto my foot. I couldn’t help drawing in a sharp breath as pain shot through my body. “Oh no!” I whispered, glancing around to see whether anyone had noticed. Embarrassment flooded me, and my cheeks flushed red.

A classmate nearby wearing headphones looked up at me. “Are you okay? Do you need help?” His voice was somewhat loud because of the headphones, and it seemed to draw the attention of a few classmates farther away. I forced a smile and tried to keep my voice steady as I replied, “It’s okay, thanks. I can manage.” But inside, I couldn’t help thinking, “Why is it always like this? Why can’t things just go smoothly once?”

I tried to calm myself and put the books back in place, but my palms were sweaty from nerves, and the books kept slipping a little. I felt my hands damp, my heart racing, as if every movement amplified my embarrassment and unease. In my imagination, someone was laughing at me: “So clumsy.”

“It’s okay, actually I run into this kind of thing a lot too,” the classmate said with a smile, seeming to comfort me.

I nodded. Though I said it was nothing, the pressure in my heart lingered for a long time. After hurriedly tidying the books again, I whispered my thanks, turned and left the shelves, silently praying, “I hope no one else noticed.”

Afterward, I sat in a corner of the library, trying hard to calm my flustered emotions and focus on the study materials in front of me. But I still felt somewhat anxious, unable to completely ignore the little incident no matter what. A few nights later, I tossed and turned in bed, replaying the scene in my mind, and couldn’t help blaming myself: “Why do I always make these little messes? When will I be able to act naturally?”

Even though it was just a small matter, it reminded me once again that there are always moments in life that make me uneasy and anxious, and I can only do my best to face them.

Sunlight filtered through the branches and dappled the campus path, bringing the feel of spring to the air. I strolled along that familiar walkway, the stone slabs beneath my feet reflecting a faint sheen. A breeze brushed my face, carrying the fresh scent of flowers and grass. In the distance came the laughter of students and the harsh squeak of sneakers on the basketball court. Yet I felt a bit restless inside, as if I were waiting for some vague and uncertain change.

My classmates were enjoying this afternoon on the lawn, their cheerful chatter lively and bright. Just then, I ran into a friend from my department. “Hey, long time no see!” He waved at me. I forced a small smile and replied, “Yeah, long time no see. How have you been lately?” He talked about his recent classes and mentioned some professor’s strange demands. I nodded in agreement, but inwardly I began to wonder whether he was implying something was off with me. Why was he telling me all this at this moment? I felt a slight discomfort in my stomach, as though a sense of tension were spreading.

The sun was gradually sinking toward the horizon, and the light grew softer. I could feel sweat starting to form on my forehead, and my palms were getting a little damp. I tried hard to hide my unease and kept talking with my friend, doing my best to seem natural. He chatted about some personal matters, and I tried to join in, but I kept worrying over that feeling of discomfort. Did this small talk mean he thought something about me? Why did I feel a little paranoid?

After the conversation ended, I continued wandering around campus, trying to relax. Before leaving, I said goodbye to my friend, and he said, “Don’t overthink it. Take it easy.” That made me pause. Had he seen through my anxiety? At dinner, I ate alone in the cafeteria. The surrounding voices gradually faded, leaving only the faint clink of utensils and the aroma of food. I tried not to think about what had happened during the day, but the unease still lingered.

A few hours later, lying in bed at night, I tried to replay the afternoon conversation. I thought maybe there was nothing special about it at all—perhaps I had simply read too much into his tone and expression. After a few days, my mood gradually returned to normal, and that uneasiness seemed somewhat unnecessary.

I pushed open the half-broken wooden door and stepped into the abandoned old-fashioned photo studio. The bell on the door rang once, as if surprised by my arrival. The air was thick with the scent of dust and photographic paper, as though telling of a former time of prosperity and warmth. The black-and-white photos on the walls had turned yellow, recording the smiling faces and tense poses of strangers. I gently brushed the dust off a table, revealing a pile of messy photo albums. When I opened one, inside were unfamiliar faces I had never seen before, their laughter seeming to echo in my ears. Why did these smiles make me feel such a sharp ache? “This photo looks so nice!” I once heard a friend say to me, but at the time I only thought he was brushing me off, and that feeling of being dismissed surfaced again. My heart began to race, and I found it hard to breathe, as if every smile were silently mocking me. The smiles in those photos involuntarily brought back my own embarrassment at gatherings, that sense of loneliness of being forgotten in a corner. From the edge of the table, I picked up a photo showing a little girl smiling at the camera. My unease began to turn into shame; her smile reminded me of my past, those moments of being misunderstood. “Did I do something wrong?” The voice in my head questioned me over and over, and I felt a dull ache begin in my stomach. I suddenly realized I was attacking myself, as if trying to preemptively stop the laughter in those photos from becoming real. I sat on the floor, trying to sort out my emotions, but that feeling of abandonment gradually overwhelmed me. I closed my eyes, as though wandering restlessly through old times. When I woke the next day, the shadow left in my heart still would not go away. Even though sunlight poured into the room through the curtains, my mood felt trapped in that photo studio, unable to break free. A few days later, the smiles in those photos would flash through my mind from time to time, and I kept telling myself that those smiles were only in a photograph; they did not negate my worth.

I stood in the dim darkroom, my goggles slightly fogged over, my fingers feeling a bit rough from being soaked in the developer. The air was thick with the pungent smell of chemicals, mixed with the humming of the ventilator on the wall. Orange safelight cast a soft glow, and I stared at the photographic paper soaking in the developing tray, while a buzzing roar filled my ears.

“Take it slow, it’s fine, don’t be nervous,” my classmate whispered beside me, trying not to distract me as I adjusted the exposure time. I nodded, but my palms started to sweat, my heartbeat quickening with each passing second; every step felt like walking a tightrope. Suddenly, my hand slipped, and the photographic paper slid into the developer, wrinkling at the edges in an instant. I hurriedly fished it out with the tongs, but it was too late—the carefully taken photo already had a blurred, smudged patch in it.

“Damn it…” I muttered, feeling as if I’d been struck hard in the chest, my stomach cramping along with it. “I ruined it. I knew I’d ruin it!” I slammed the tongs back onto the table, my fingers beginning to tremble.

“It’s okay, we still have other negatives,” my classmate’s voice came from beside me, cautiously comforting me. But I couldn’t take any of it in; all that remained in my head was one line looping over and over: “Everyone’s definitely going to think I’m useless.”

“Sorry… it’s all my fault,” I said in a low voice, my lips trembling, not daring to meet her eyes. “You must be disappointed, right? This could have been completely avoided…” The words were nearly swallowed in my throat, as if I were admitting my own incompetence.

“Really, it’s fine. Everyone makes mistakes sometimes.” My classmate’s tone was still gentle, trying to calm me down, but I only felt those words were hollow and perfunctory. The pressure in my chest was so heavy I could hardly breathe. My eyes began to sting, and I forced myself not to let the tears fall.

The physical reaction grew even more obvious. My palms sweated more and more, wetting the edges of my goggles, and I even felt a little short of breath. “I’m going out for some air,” I said quietly, quickly leaving the darkroom. Cold air hit me in the face, and I leaned against the icy wall of the hallway, covering my face with both hands, trying to calm myself down.

That night, lying in bed with my eyes fixed on the ceiling, I replayed again and again the way the paper had wrinkled, my classmate’s expression, and my own performance. “Why do I always mess things up?” “Will she badmouth me to others?” Those thoughts surged in like a tide, making my stomach ache in waves. Even though I tried to distract myself, I still ended up spending a sleepless night tossing and turning.

Early the next morning, I walked into the photography club room still full of guilt, only to see the photo I had thought was ruined posted on the wall. “We thought the way you handled that mistake was pretty interesting, and we were even discussing whether to make it a special exhibit piece,” my classmate explained with a smile. Hearing that, my eyes suddenly burned, and guilt and relief mixed together. “Thank you for believing in me,” I said softly. My voice was so nasal and faint it was almost inaudible, but she still nodded seriously.

The air inside the gallery was filled with the faint smell of oil paint, and colorful works hung on the walls. The lights shone on the surface of each painting, casting a soft glow. Although the surrounding chatter was noisy, I still felt a heavy pressure weighing on my heart. I stood in front of my own work, my palms slightly sweaty, while all kinds of possible bad reviews kept flashing through my mind.

Among the crowd at the exhibition, there was a middle-aged man—possibly a professor—staring expressionlessly at my painting. I caught the slight furrow of his brow, and my heart instantly sped up, like someone beating a drum. “He must hate this piece and think it’s worthless,” I thought, lowering my gaze to the floor beneath my feet, trying hard to calm myself down.

“Your work is very imaginative.” A gentle voice pulled me back from my thoughts. It was a petite female classmate, looking at me with sincere eyes. I forced out a smile, but the tension in my heart did not ease at all. “Thank you, but... I’m not sure others will feel the same way,” I heard myself reply softly, my voice almost swallowed by the surrounding noise.

She raised her eyebrows slightly, seeming as if she wanted to say something else to comfort me, but then a friend beside her pulled her away, leaving me alone to face that still noisy space. A dull ache came from my stomach, and I sighed to myself. I never enjoy situations like this. In my mind, all the failed and embarrassing moments from the past kept resurfacing, affecting every judgment I made in the present.

As the exhibition went on, I kept watching every viewer’s expression, trying to read what they thought of my work. “Why did he leave so quickly? Was he disappointed by this painting?” Even though I tried hard to free myself from this paranoia, the habit of overanalyzing seemed deeply rooted.

After the exhibition ended, I quickly left the gallery. Stepping out of the building, the cold air hit me in the face and made me feel a little more clear-headed. Although my coat couldn’t fully keep out the cold, I preferred staying outside. “Why can’t I just focus on creating instead of always worrying about what others think?” I chided myself.

The next morning, I was still uneasy about what had happened yesterday. Sitting in a corner of the campus café, surrounded by quiet conversation, my thoughts still would not stop. My coffee in front of me gradually cooled, and I realized I needed to make a change for the next exhibition. “No matter what, I should learn to slowly build trust in my own work.” I made up my mind that next time, I would trust my own judgment first, rather than the voices from outside.

The studio was lit with a dim yellow glow, and raindrops tapped against the windowpane like a monotonous drumbeat for the quiet night.
