The air was heavy with the smell of oil paint, along with a faint earthy dampness. I was the only one left in the studio; the other students had gone back to the dorms long ago. The clock on the wall pointed to 9:30 p.m. In another hour, the place would be closed.

Standing before my easel, I stared at the large unfinished canvas, the palette knife in my hand catching the orange light from the palette. My heart was full of unease: this painting was a bronze-themed piece for midterm work, but my mind was in chaos. The colors were wrong, and something about the composition felt off. I felt as if a block of ice were lodged in my stomach, and cold sweat seeped from my palms.

“Make it a bit deeper, cooler-toned, or I’ll get told again that it lacks depth,” I muttered to myself. Just as I reached for the indigo oil paint on the desk beside me, I failed to notice my elbow hitting the turpentine can at the edge of the table. In that instant, like a slow-motion scene in a movie, the can tilted slowly, then suddenly fell to the floor, spilling the clear liquid everywhere as it quickly flowed toward the canvas at my feet.

“Damn it!” I froze, watching as the paint on the canvas was diluted into a blurred stain. I felt my cheeks begin to burn, as if scorched by fire, and all I could hear was the rapid pounding of my heart. My fingertips went cold, as though I no longer had the strength to hold a brush. I crouched down and tried to soak up the liquid with a towel, but the bigger problem was that my painting was ruined, and only a few days remained before the assignment was due. In my mind, I could already see the teacher frowning, and hear my classmates whispering behind my back: “Why do they always hold everyone back, can’t even do their own assignment properly.”

Tears suddenly welled up, but I quickly wiped them away with the back of my hand, silently cursing myself: “Why are you crying? Crying won’t help. Why do you always mess things up? Can’t you be more careful?” I bit my lip and tried to steady my breathing. It felt as though a huge stone were pressing down on my chest, making even breathing difficult. How I wished someone would come comfort me and say things like, “It’s okay, you’ll figure it out.” But even if someone did, I knew I wouldn’t believe it.

“Calm down. Clean it up first, then think,” I told myself. Panicked, I pulled out a rag and cleaning solution and wiped at the oil stain on the floor. The rag was covered in a riot of colors, and my fingers were stained patchwork with them too. The air was filled with a sharp, pungent smell that made me cough. The rain outside seemed to grow louder, and the streetlight shining in from beyond the window cast a slanted glow that reflected dimly in the puddles on the floor.

It took me half an hour to clean up the floor, but the canvas was still a complete mess. I stood there blankly for a while, feeling tears rise again, and hurriedly grabbed a brush, mechanically smearing paint across the canvas in an attempt to salvage something. But my mind was completely blank—I had no idea how to fix it, and I didn’t dare stop. I was afraid that if I stopped, all that would remain was boundless self-reproach and despair.

Half the studio lights had gone out, and the administrator stood at the doorway reminding me, “Student, it’s time. We’re turning off the lights.” I nodded quickly, hastily packed up my paints and easel, and carefully rolled up the canvas. As I stepped out of the studio, the cold night rain struck my face, as if mocking my failure. That night, when I got back to the dorm, I didn’t sleep at all. The image of the paint can tipping over kept replaying in my mind, along with that heartbreaking instant when my painting was ruined. The stomach pain became even more pronounced, so I simply sat up and started thinking through which paints I still had left, and how I might start over tomorrow.

The sunlight fell on my face, warm and gentle. Sitting in the recliner on the balcony, I held a novel in my hands, its pages fluttering in the breeze. The air was filled with a faint scent of grass and trees, perhaps drifting from the plants in the courtyard. In the distance, I could vaguely hear birds singing, as if reminding me that the world was not merely this small patch of space before my eyes.

I turned to the next page and saw a line of dialogue between the characters in the book: “What do you think is the meaning of life?” The question made me pause slightly. I closed the book and lifted my head to look at the sky. Beneath the blue sky floated a few lazy white clouds, and I couldn’t help but start thinking about my own life. These questions always seemed to pop up suddenly and disturb my thoughts, like a leaf in the wind drifting back and forth, with no intention of stopping.

“Do you want coffee?” A classmate next door poked their head out, interrupting my reverie. I smiled and nodded. “Sure, let’s have some together.”

I got up and went into the kitchen, my heartbeat echoing softly with my footsteps. A rich coffee aroma spread through the air. I carefully poured the coffee into cups, then carried two steaming cups back to the balcony.

“What are you reading today?” my classmate asked casually while stirring the coffee. “Oh, just a novel, something to pass the time,” I shrugged and gave a brief answer. I felt a little ashamed, because this wasn’t a book I truly wanted to read—I had just picked it up to while away the hours.

The sun gradually shifted westward, and the light falling on us became softer and softer. We sat there quietly, looking at the sky, looking at the trees, occasionally sharing a thought or two. There was no special topic, no special plan—just enjoying the afternoon.

After finishing the coffee, my classmate went back to their room, while I stayed on the balcony and continued reading slowly. The sunlight began to feel a bit harsh, and I raised a hand to shield my eyes, only to feel a slight bead of sweat trickling down from my forehead. I let out a soft sigh, feeling everything grow slow and quiet, as if the whole world had sunk into the laziness of the afternoon.

That night, back in my room, moonlight streamed through the window onto the floor. I closed the book, feeling an indescribable sense of peace and contentment. The day seemed to have passed so gently, with nothingespecially remarkable happening, yet it was still a kind of relaxed happiness. The next morning, I still remembered the sunlight and warmth from that afternoon on the balcony.

The faint glow of the setting sun filtered through the studio window, casting a warm, pale-yellow hue over the entire room. The air carried the distinctive smell of paint, reminding me of the works I had completed here in the past. The canvas before me was almost fully lit by the sunset, and I held my brush, ready to add the final touch of color. Yet my heart was pounding hard, my palms slightly damp, making it difficult to focus on the details beneath my hand. Suddenly, I heard my classmates talking behind me. Though their voices were soft, I found myself unusually aware of them. One person said, “This color is a little strange.” My heart tightened, and I immediately began to doubt my choice. Another person chimed in, “But overall, it doesn’t look bad.” I tried to make myself focus on that positive remark, but the fastest thought racing through my mind was the worst possible outcome: would my work be judged the worst? My hand, which was brushing paint across the canvas, began to tremble, and the color spread into irregular shapes on the fabric. “It might be better if you adjusted it a little more,” that voice went on, and my face instantly flushed red, as if everyone could see every flaw in my painting. My heartbeat quickened, and my stomach felt tightly clenched. I stopped what I was doing, my body growing a little stiff. A wave of shame rose inside me as I thought, why am I always so sensitive? I reached for the palette beside me, but my fingertips accidentally knocked over the paint bottle. Blue paint spilled onto the floor, and I hurriedly stepped back. In an instant, only one thought remained in my mind: everyone will see me make a fool of myself. Behind me, a classmate said softly, “Be careful, don’t panic.” The voice was gentle, but it only made my face burn even more. “Sorry, I…” I replied in a low voice, almost drowned out by the other conversations. My chest ached a little, as if under some unbearable weight. I set down my brush and took a deep breath, but I still couldn’t calm the chaos inside me. I stood by the window, trying to find some comfort. The view outside came into sight: the sun was sinking, the sky turning a deep orange, and the branches and leaves of the trees in the courtyard swayed gently in the breeze, offering me a little solace. Only after a few minutes did I pick up my brush again and try to adjust my work. That night, when I returned to the dormitory and lay in bed, my heart still felt heavy. My thoughts kept circling that moment from earlier in the day, as if I were surrounded by an invisible pressure. I kept asking myself: why can’t I ever let myself off the hook? This sensitivity made me feel overwhelmed, and it was this fragility that once again pulled me into a spiral of self-doubt.

There is always a faint scent of books in the library, which makes me feel a sense of calm as soon as I walk in. But that afternoon was a little different; it seemed as if everyone was breaking the silence in their own way. I sat in a corner by the window, where sunlight barely filtered through the leaves and scattered across the desk in glimmering patches. My task was to finish an essay, but whispers kept drifting into my ears, and the rustling of pages grew louder and louder. “No, I have to focus,” I told myself, trying to ignore the sounds around me. Yet the harder I tried to shut them out, the more distinct those faint noises became, leaving me with an invisible pressure. My heartbeat seemed to sync with the ticking of the clock, pounding heavily in my ears.

“Sorry, could you please keep it down a little? Some people over there are discussing something,” I suddenly heard myself say, my voice louder than I had expected. The boy I had addressed looked up at me, offered a slightly apologetic smile, and nodded. However, he then continued speaking quietly with his friend. My face felt slightly hot, and I began to blame myself again, thinking I was making too much of a fuss. “Maybe I should put on headphones; that would help,” I thought. But I didn’t have any suitable headphones with me.

To keep myself from sinking into even greater anxiety, I turned my attention back to my laptop, trying to use the task in front of me to distract myself from the turmoil inside. The words on the page were somewhat blurry, and I had to squint to make them out clearly. “Sigh... still no good,” I muttered, beginning to feel my shoulders grow stiff and tense, while my palms started to sweat. To help myself relax a little, I decided to get up for a glass of water. When I reached the library’s water dispenser, the rushing sound of water finally drowned out those harsh whispers.

After drinking the water and returning to my seat, the surrounding noise seemed to have faded a little. I tried adjusting my posture, took a deep breath, and slowly let it out. A few minutes later, I finally began typing some words on the keyboard again, gradually regaining my writing rhythm. Although the environment wasn’t ideal, I tried to tell myself that this was only a minor interruption and that all the discomfort was temporary. Still, even after I returned to the dormitory that night, the noisy whispers continued to echo in my mind, and it felt as though a taut string had been left hanging in my heart the whole time.

A few days later, I decided to try studying with headphones again, so that at least I could reduce my sensitivity to the sounds around me.

I stood on the podium, facing the classmates and teachers below, my heart pounding in my chest like a drum. The classroom lights were harsh, making me a little dizzy, and I blinked hard, trying to calm myself down. A faint smell of whiteboard marker hung in the air, seeping into my lungs as I took a deep breath. I began my presentation, realizing that my voice was trembling, like a small animal shivering on a cold winter night. “Today I’m going to introduce the topic of…” I tried to stay calm, but the words seemed to slip out of my mouth beyond my control. One of my classmates muttered something in the audience, and I almost thought I could hear their contempt and laughter. Maybe they were saying I was doing badly, or maybe they simply didn’t care what I was saying. My palms started to sweat, and my glasses slid down my nose; I had to push them back up from time to time.

As I struggled to get back on track, I saw the professor frown, as if lost in thought. At once, I felt ignored and unacknowledged. “Sorry, I’ll repeat that,” I stammered, trying to gather my thoughts again. Yet the scattered thoughts in my mind made it hard to focus, and a slight cramp began in my stomach. Whenever I lost my way, I always thought of past failures or embarrassing moments, as if they were endlessly replaying in my mind. “Go on, don’t be nervous,” the professor said gently, but I couldn’t really take it in. My face began to burn, as if I were completely exposed beneath the spotlight, with nothing to hide behind. By the time I hurried through my final few sentences, I knew this presentation had not lived up to my expectations.

After it ended, I rushed away from the podium, the floor feeling a little cold beneath me. Back in my seat, I tried to steady myself, my fingers tapping unconsciously on the desk as I looked for an outlet. I couldn’t help reflecting on why I wasn’t good enough. Why did I always get so nervous? Why couldn’t I ever seem as confident as other people in public? When I got back to the dorm, I sat on my bed and closed my eyes in exhaustion, replaying my mistakes over and over in my head, thinking about how to avoid this happening again next time. I knew these thoughts wore me out, but I still couldn’t stop myself. In the days that followed, I could feel the lingering embarrassment surrounding me all the time; whenever I occasionally thought back to what had happened, my heart would start racing again.

Bright afternoon sunlight streamed through the gap in the dormitory curtains, slanting onto the floor and casting mottled patches of light and shadow. I curled up in the corner of my bed, my ears still echoing with a joke one of my roommates had made in the common room just moments before: “Oh, you’re always this tense. Relax a little.” Her tone had sounded light and casual, yet it stirred an uncontrollable wave of anxiety deep inside me. My heart raced, my palms grew slightly damp, and my stomach felt twisted into a knot.

“Was she hinting that I’m annoying?” I kept dissecting her tone in my head, trying to find hidden hostility in her smile. I tried to remember whether there had been a trace of impatience on her face, whether she had already had enough of me and wanted to get rid of living under the same roof as me.

“What’s wrong?” Another roommate pushed open the door and asked with concern when she saw the dazed look on my face. I looked up and forced out a faint smile. “Nothing, just a little tired.” In truth, my mind had already begun racing wildly, rehearsing the worst possible scenarios: Would they complain about me to other people? Had they already planned to dump me, this “troublemaker”?

“It’s okay. We all know you’re a bit sensitive, but nobody minds.” She sat down beside me and patted my shoulder. Even though her voice was gentle, my body still couldn’t relax; the pounding of my heart roared in my ears, and my muscles were tense like drawn strings. I lowered my head and stared at the floor, not daring to meet her eyes, afraid I would see any sign of disappointment or blame in them.

After a while, she left the room. The moment the door closed, I couldn’t help but replay scenes from earlier: the happy things we had done together, the times they had helped me through difficult moments. I knew they were good to me, so why did I always feel a fear of abandonment deep inside? Why was I always anticipating the worst outcome?

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t fall asleep. In the darkness, I listened to my roommates’ even breathing, yet I couldn’t bring myself to feel at ease. It always seemed as though there were an invisible wall between them and me, one that could crack open at any moment and swallow the little sense of safety I had left.

Over the next few days, I became even more cautious, afraid of crossing their boundaries. They seemed to notice my unease too, and from time to time tried to help me relax. But no matter what they did, I could never shake the possibility of being abandoned that kept circling in my mind.

I was sitting in a small meeting room of a university club, and through the window I could see the noisy campus scene outside. Only a few lights were on in the room, so the lighting was somewhat dim. A classmate sitting across from me was speaking, and we were discussing the preparations for our next event. She said, “I think there are some problems with the publicity strategy for this event. We need to reconsider it.” Instantly, I felt my heart race and my palms start to sweat. I began to turn her tone over and over in my mind—why did it sound a little dissatisfied? Was she criticizing me for not doing my job well enough? Did she have some complaint about me? My stomach suddenly felt as if it had been twisted, and the tension kept mounting.

I stared at the table, feeling a strong wave of shyness and unease. I remembered a previous mistake: I had been responsible for publicity at a club event, and because I hadn’t thought things through, some minor problems had arisen on site. I was terrified that something like that would happen again, and even more afraid that others would stop trusting me because of my mistake. In my mind, I kept rehearsing the worst possible outcome, and I could even imagine myself being isolated in the club.

The classmate went on, “Maybe everyone can offer some suggestions and see if there’s a better way to promote it.” Her eyes swept over me, and I immediately felt uncomfortable. I was desperate to explain myself, and even started attacking myself: “Actually, last time it was because I didn’t think things through. This time I can definitely do better. Maybe I should step out of this event—I don’t want to disappoint everyone.” My voice was trembling, and my heart was beating even faster. I knew I was overreacting, but in that moment, I couldn’t control the impulse.

“Why are you saying that?” another classmate sitting next to me said kindly, trying to comfort me. “No one is blaming you. We just want to brainstorm together. You’ve already done a very good job.” Her voice was gentle, but all I felt was growing shame, as if she were trying hard to cover up my flaws.

After the meeting ended, I dragged my heavy steps back to the dormitory. All evening, my mind was filled with self-blame and unease. I kept ruminating over the conversation in the meeting, trying to find the root of my failure. When I woke up the next day, everything still seemed unclear before my eyes, and my body remained exhausted from anxiety. I tried to pull myself together, but I couldn’t escape the fear of being abandoned and not accepted.

Although this scene is already in the past, the anxiety and shame that came with it still lie deeply buried in my heart, like an unhealed wound, ready to be triggered at any moment.

The rain was falling in drizzles outside the window, and the piano room’s glass panes blurred the view with raindrops. I was sitting at the piano, practicing a newly composed piece. My fingertips moved across the black-and-white keys, but my thoughts were long gone from the notes. From next door came a broken-up conversation; I could tell it was the teacher speaking with a student. They seemed to be discussing my piece—probably the assignment I had turned in last week. My ears instinctively perked up. Even though I told myself not to eavesdrop, curiosity and anxiety kept me from focusing on my playing, so I stopped and tried to slow my breathing to make out their voices.

“TA’s work is a bit emotional, with a pretty distinctive style, but technically it’s still somewhat immature.” The teacher’s voice blended into the rain. Those words stabbed into my chest like a needle. My hand tightened suddenly on the edge of the piano, my fingertips cold. “Emotional? Distinctive? Are those good or bad?” I kept chewing over the comment in my mind, the more I thought about it, the more wrong it felt, as if they weren’t discussing my assignment at all, but judging me as a person.

“Mm, I feel like TA really focuses on expression, but some parts are handled a bit too much,” the student said then. It was someone I knew, maybe an upperclassman from the club. I felt my stomach tighten, my heartbeat quicken, as if the air in the piano room had suddenly grown thick and every breath became difficult. Though there was no obvious malice in the words, they made me feel like I was sitting on hot coals; my palms began to sweat, and I didn’t dare move.

“TA’s note expression does have a very personal style,” the teacher added in a somewhat approving tone, but I couldn’t make sense of it at all. My ears seemed to turn into radar, pulling his words through the thick wall and filling my mind with negative speculation. I started remembering the tiny rhythm mistake I’d made when I played the piece before, and my self-reproach doubled instantly. “They must think I’m really amateurish, right?” Thoughts like that kept intruding, and my chest grew tighter and tighter.

I tried to keep playing, but my fingers wouldn’t cooperate; every movement was stiff, as if assembled mechanically. I couldn’t help imagining what the teacher and student would say if they walked into the piano room, replaying in my mind, over and over, how awkward I would look. I even began to feel as though they were watching me, as if I couldn’t shake those thoughts even though there was clearly a wall between us. “Calm down first,” I told myself, but it barely helped.

The rain grew more urgent, striking the window glass and forming dense white specks of water, draping the whole room in a gray haze. I let out a self-mocking sigh, silently stood up, closed the piano lid, and then sat in the chair in a daze. I knew that if I didn’t leave, I would stay trapped in that emotional whirlpool forever, but my legs felt as heavy as lead. I remembered that the teacher’s comments had included both praise and criticism, yet the critical parts seemed magnified countless times, pressing down on me until I could hardly breathe.

That night, lying on my dorm bed, I tossed and turned, as though their conversation were still echoing in my ears. All my emotions tangled together, making it nearly impossible to fall asleep. A few days later, when I tried practicing that piece again, their comments kept replaying in my mind. Even though I knew they hadn’t meant to hurt me, I still couldn’t get rid of the deeply rooted fear of being “judged.” That feeling left me both ashamed and unable to let go, repeatedly reminding me that my technique needed improvement, while I couldn’t help doubting whether I truly had the ability to continue down this path.

The atmosphere in the rehearsal room was tense, with everyone busy preparing for the upcoming performance. Sunlight slanted through the window, and the dappled patches of light on the floor swayed gently with the leaves outside. I was sitting by the piano, my fingers moving across the keys while my mind dwelled on what had happened during the group discussion that morning. The voices discussing notes and rhythm echoed in my ears, and I kept feeling that I had said something wrong, perhaps upsetting the others in the group.

“Kid, are you sure what you’re doing here is right?” the bassist suddenly stopped rehearsing and asked me, his voice tinged with doubt. “I think what you said earlier might have been a little off.”

My heart sped up, and a sick feeling rose in my stomach. Was he blaming me for not preparing properly? Was he dissatisfied with my contribution? “I think my part is fine. I handled it according to what we discussed before,” I said, trying hard not to let my voice tremble, hoping to sound more confident. Yet in my mind, the conversation from earlier had already begun replaying: Had I said something I shouldn’t have? Had I disrupted everyone’s rhythm?

Sunlight poured in from outside, but its warmth could not dispel the shadow in my heart. I began to sweat, and the beads of sweat slowly ran down my forehead. I knew I had once again fallen into a cycle of catastrophizing, with every negative possibility piling up in my mind. I wanted to control my reaction and keep my emotions from spiraling, but the way my fingers tapped on the keyboard gave away my unease.

After rehearsal ended, I hurried out of the room, the air thick with the distinctive wooden scent of the instruments. I wanted to find a quiet place to calm down, but the uneasiness in my heart was like a clenched fist that would not let go. That night I hardly slept at all, tossing and turning as I thought about the bassist’s words, which lingered like an inescapable echo, sending ripples through my mind over and over again.

The next day, I gathered my courage and found the bassist. “I think there may have been a misunderstanding yesterday. Can we talk again?” I tried to stay calm, and his smile made me relax a little. “Of course. We’re all just trying to make the performance better. Yesterday’s discussion was just a bit tense.” His attitude immediately eased my mind, and my heartbeat gradually returned to normal.

A few days later, during a rehearsal, I felt an entirely new sense of harmony. Though fears still lingered in my heart, I knew I was trying to change, trying to understand instead of immediately blaming myself. I realized that I needed more confidence and patience to face these misunderstandings and the tension they brought.

The ceiling lights in the café were rather dim. Through the floor-to-ceiling window, I watched the streetlights along the campus road come on one by one, while the figures outside swayed into blurry shapes. I stared at the ceramic mug on the table, absentmindedly rubbing the rim with my fingers. Across from me was my friend—we had known each other for two years, but at that moment she looked strangely unfamiliar. She was looking down, fiddling with her phone, the corners of her mouth turned slightly downward, seeming unhappy.

“Why did you suddenly stop talking?” I asked tentatively, my voice carrying a faint, unnatural tremor, even though I tried my best to sound relaxed.

She looked up at me, brushed aside a strand of hair that had fallen across her forehead, and said something that made my heart sink: “Nothing. Don’t overthink it.” Her tone was casual, but in that instant I almost felt as if her eyes were scrutinizing me, hiding some discontent she didn’t want to say out loud.

It felt as though something had suddenly crushed my heart, and my chest instantly grew so tight I could hardly breathe. I forced a smile. “Did I just say something wrong? If I did, tell me—I can change.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I felt a wave of shame. This repeated need for reassurance made me feel like a helpless child.

She shook her head, her eyes returning to her phone screen. “Really, it’s nothing. Don’t be like this.”

But I could no longer stop myself. My heartbeat sped up, my cheeks grew hot, and my palms broke into sweat. I could clearly feel a sharp, churning ache in my stomach. In my mind, every detail from moments ago kept replaying: the way she had lowered her head, the slight furrow of her brows, her light and dismissive “don’t overthink it.” It must mean something. Was she already fed up with me? Did she think I was clingy? Had I done something wrong? Did she not want to be friends with me anymore? I couldn’t say a single word, as if I were stuck.

I don’t know how much time passed before she looked up at me and said, “Why don’t we go?” I nodded mechanically and followed her out of the café. The evening wind was a little cold, carrying the grassy scent of the trees by the roadside, but my palms were still damp, and my heartbeat was like it had been locked inside an airtight box, pounding wildly. I wanted to say something, even just to make small talk about the weather, but my throat felt locked, and not a single word came out.

After we parted, I returned to the dorm. My roommate hadn’t come back yet, and I was alone in the room. I threw my bag on the floor and lay directly on the bed, staring blankly at the ceiling. Was she angry with me? Had I disappointed her? Maybe I really wasn’t good enough, which was why I always ended up annoying people. At that thought, a huge wave of shame washed over me like a tide.

That night I slept uneasily, waking up over and over. The next morning, I saw the message she had sent me: “I’m really sorry about yesterday. I got an email on my phone at the last minute and was a bit distracted.” The knot in my chest seemed to loosen a little, but I also felt that it was nothing more than an excuse. Was she really being cold because of that? Or… I couldn’t even tell whether all those details from last night had been imagined by me or had truly happened.

The campus café was filled with the rich aroma of coffee and the background murmur of quiet conversation. My heart was pounding like thunder, my palms began to sweat, and my stomach felt as though it were tightly clenched in discomfort. We sat at a small table in the corner, discussing the project that was about to be submitted. He said softly, “Why haven’t you finished your part of the analysis yet? It’s due this weekend.” His tone was calm, but it made me feel intensely anxious. I began to overthink his words, as if every word concealed hostility and blame. I replied in a low voice, trying to control my emotions: “I’m trying. I’ve already done a lot, but a few of the data analysis programs have had some problems.” Deep down, I was afraid he would see me as incompetent, because that thought unsettled me. My mind had already begun to rehearse the worst possible outcome: he would tell the other students, I would be isolated, and eventually abandoned. As the image grew more vivid, my fingers began to tremble. Suddenly, he said, “But you should have told me earlier. We could have solved it together.” Those words stung, because the fact that I hadn’t said anything sooner made me feel flawed, and I felt ashamed. “I’m sorry,” I quickly apologized, my voice trembling a little, as if bracing myself for reproach in advance could ease my anxiety. Outwardly, I seemed slightly flustered, but inside, it was an emotional storm, churning fiercely. Our conversation continued, and he proposed a solution. I nodded in agreement, even though the panic inside me had not yet subsided. That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, thinking about every detail of what he had said. I kept replaying the slight furrow in his brow as he spoke, wondering again and again whether it meant he was really angry, or disappointed in me. The next day, I spent a great deal of time on the project, eager to prove my worth, while the fear of being abandoned kept flooding back and driving me to work hard to make up for what I believed were my shortcomings. A few days later, I even took the initiative to talk to him about the project’s progress, to make sure there was no misunderstanding between us and to confirm that he really wasn’t angry.

The lighting in the conference room was rather dim. I sat at the end of the table, holding a pen in my hand and repeatedly tracing lines along the edge of my notebook. The table was piled with proposals, notebooks, and several cell phones. Voices overlapped as the meeting went on for more than an hour, with everyone offering suggestions for the event. At that moment, I felt my heart beginning to race, as if the air in the room had grown thin. I took a soft breath, trying to calm myself down. In the middle of the meeting, a classmate suddenly pointed at me and said, “Shouldn’t the part you’re responsible for have been done already?” His voice wasn’t loud, but it made me tense up immediately. I hurriedly opened my notebook and explained in a slightly trembling voice, “Actually, I’m still waiting for a key piece of data. That data may affect the arrangements that follow.” I saw him frown and whisper a few words to the person next to him. My heart sank, and I thought, “What did he mean just now? Have I disappointed everyone?” Whenever something like this happens, I always start needlessly wondering if there’s something wrong with me. I looked anxiously at my notebook, trying to find clues to solve the problem, but my mind was a tangled mess. My heartbeat suddenly sped up, and I felt a rush of heat rise from my chest to my face. I could even feel sweat starting to form on my forehead. After the meeting ended, I slowly packed up my things, feeling somewhat deflated, as if I could read criticism in everyone’s eyes. When I walked out of the conference room, I took a deep breath, and the cool air made me relax a little. That night, lying in bed, I thought about what had happened in the afternoon. I tossed and turned, unable to sleep, replaying over and over in my mind the tone of voice that classmate had used. I thought again, “Does he think I’m irresponsible? Should I prepare everything in advance next time?” In class the next morning, I looked a bit listless, still entangled in yesterday’s events. Your part was actually pretty good.” Hearing that, I finally felt a little more at ease. This small matter made me realize once again that I always overread other people’s words, often complicating simple things and even causing unnecessary trouble.

The café was dimly lit, and the air was thick with the rich smell of coffee. I was sitting by the window, while my friend across from me was looking down and stirring his latte. The clinking of cups on the tables and the low murmur of conversation from the table beside us blended together, making the whole café feel bustling and busy. I had just finished a class on artistic creation, and the professor’s discussion of personal expression was still echoing in my mind. I hesitated before saying to my friend, “I’ve been writing lately, but I feel like everything I write is too personal. People will think it doesn’t mean anything, right?” My voice sounded light and airy, but inside I was already tightly strung.

He looked up at me, frowning slightly. “Well, what you write is indeed a bit hard to relate to. I think maybe you need to focus more on social issues and stop writing about yourself all the time.” Those words were like a sharp arrow, piercing straight through my defenses. I forced a smile, trying to respond casually, but unease was already surging inside me. I stammered, “B-b-but I think personal experiences are also a form of genuine expression.”

“Genuine? Have you ever thought about whether your experiences are really that important? Not everyone cares.” He tossed out the words in what seemed like an offhand tone, then lowered his head and kept stirring his coffee, as if unwilling to delve any deeper into the topic.

My heart sank all at once, and my chest began to feel tight. I felt as if my whole body had been soaked in ice water, growing colder and colder. My cheeks burned, my palms started sweating, and even my stomach ached faintly. My mind began frantically running through all kinds of conversations. Was he hinting that everything I made was worthless? If even the people closest to me thought I was boring, what would others think of me? Had I failed completely? I started to explain in a stutter, “Actually… actually, my work is meant to express a kind of inner tension, I think… I think…” But then I stopped, realizing that my words were becoming less and less logical, more and more chaotic. He gave no response, just kept looking down and playing with his phone.

In an instant, the air seemed to freeze. I felt as if my very existence had suddenly become redundant. That feeling of abandonment surged up like a flood, pressing down on me until I could hardly breathe. I lowered my head and stared at the coffee cup on the table, but my eyes were already starting to sting. Suddenly, I had an impulse: better to attack myself first than wait to be ignored by someone else. Clenching my teeth, I summoned all my strength and said to him, “Maybe you’re right. What I write really doesn’t mean much. Maybe I’m not even a competent creator.”

That night, I sat on the edge of my bed, staring at my phone screen. He didn’t send an apology, and he never brought it up again. I tossed and turned, my mind full of his words: “Are your experiences really that important?” It was like an invisible hand, constantly tugging at my thoughts. I began to doubt whether all my efforts had been futile. I tried not to care, but I simply couldn’t. When I woke up the next morning, my stomach still hurt faintly, and my head was foggy, as if I had been completely drained.

That sentence became a thorn, deeply embedded in my memory, reminding me that no matter how hard I try, there will still be people who think I’m not good enough.

That afternoon, sunlight slanted through the floor-to-ceiling windows on the second floor of the library, casting a glare over the pages in front of me. I pressed down the corner of the book with my palm and slid my chair a few centimeters to the left, settling myself right at the edge of light and shadow—warm enough, but not so bright that I couldn’t keep my eyes open.

It was very quiet around me. The kind of quiet unique to libraries, not true silence, but all sound compressed into a low background hum: pages turning, the air conditioner droning, someone coughing softly in the distance. The smell of paper mixed with wood and dust was a little old, but I liked that kind of old.

I was reading a novel with my head down, and my heartbeat was steady. That surprised me a little.

Usually at this hour, I’d already be tallying which messages I needed to reply to tonight, how many words my draft for tomorrow was still short, whether the comment I posted last week had been screenshotted and mocked by anyone. But that afternoon, those thoughts all seemed to have wilted in the sun, lazily shrinking into some corner and not coming out to bother me.

“Can you make sense of this problem?”

The person next to me slid over an economics textbook, speaking very softly, their finger pointing at a derivation problem. I glanced at it, then shook my head, then nodded—I sort of understood, but I wasn’t sure I could explain it clearly. We leaned in and muttered a few quiet words to each other. In the end, they frowned and said, “Oh, I guess that’s how it is,” then took the book back and didn’t say anything else.

I stared at their profile for a second.

*Did they think my explanation was terrible?*

The thought popped up, and I felt my stomach tighten slightly. But then the sunlight shifted a little farther over, warming the back of my hand, and that thought was simply dried out and scattered. I didn’t chase after it. That was rare.

I lowered my head again and kept reading. The characters in the book were going through a crisis whose ending I wasn’t worried about at all, because I had already read the afterword and knew they survived. This way of reading, knowing the answer in advance, was a small privilege I gave myself—not everything has to be endured in uncertainty.

Later, someone handed me a cup of hot coffee. It was a classmate I knew, who smiled and said, “Bought it on the way.” I took it, feeling the warmth of the cup in my palm, and said thank you. We chatted for a few minutes about an elective course, and at one point mentioned a professor’s favorite catchphrase; both of us held back our laughter.

That was it. Nothing special happened.

The lights came on before I noticed, and the blue outside the window deepened. Somehow the sun had already left. I closed the book and realized I was a little reluctant to get up.

Back in the dorm, I made a cup of tea and sat by the bed, spacing out for a while. My body was a little lazy, but not the kind of laziness that comes after anxiety has drained you dry—it was the lazy of true relaxation. I opened my journal and wrote just one line:

*This afternoon, I didn’t think anything bad into existence.*

For me, that already counted as a kind of victory.

Sunlight filtered through the golden leaves and fell across the grass. I sat with a few friends on a patch of lawn on the university campus, surrounded by sounds of laughter and the rustling of autumn leaves. A hint of cool autumn air lingered in the atmosphere, as if reminding me that summer had already passed. We sat in a small circle, holding paper cups that gave off a faint warmth, chatting about trivial things. 

“I heard your project has been going pretty well lately?” a friend said to me, his tone relaxed, a slight smile on his face. I nodded, trying to stay calm, though my heart had already begun to beat restlessly. “Yeah, not bad, but I still feel like there are some parts that aren’t quite good enough.” After saying that, I instinctively searched their faces for tiny shifts in expression. 

The air seemed filled with a unease I couldn’t put into words directly. My friends’ expressions looked somewhat blurred in the interplay of light and shadow. I noticed that when one friend turned around to get something, the smile on their face vanished in an instant, and that made me start to worry. Did they think what I had just said was boring? Or did they actually not want me to be part of this gathering? 

My heartbeat began to quicken, each beat seeming to strike my chest. The growing chill in my palms reminded me that even though I was trying hard to stay composed, my body was still reacting on its own. I unconsciously tightened my grip on the paper cup, feeling the warmth of the cup’s surface gradually fade. 

“What’s wrong? You look a little nervous,” another friend’s voice interrupted my thoughts. Their concern made me feel a wave of warmth and reassurance. “Ah, it’s nothing, just a little tired.” I forced out a smile, trying to hide the unease inside me, yet the smile felt stiff. 

However, this unease stayed with me long after the gathering ended. Back in the dorm, I collapsed exhausted into a chair, my mind replaying the day’s conversation over and over. I began blaming myself without realizing it, wondering why I was always so sensitive, why I couldn’t just relax and enjoy the fun of a gathering. 

Over the next few days, I became even quieter, afraid I might say something inappropriate again. In class, I noticed myself deliberately participating less, simply observing others’ reactions in silence. 

These thoughts and feelings stirred ripples within me that I couldn’t ignore. No matter how hard I tried, I kept thinking back to that autumn gathering and those tiny expressions that might have been nothing more than my own overinterpretation.

The air in the classroom was faintly scented with chalk dust. My heart was beating a little faster, and my palms were slightly damp with sweat. I sat at my desk, with an open notebook in front of me, a pencil slowly spinning between my fingers. The professor had just finished a lecture on art history, and my mind was still echoing with the colors and lines of the paintings. The classmate next to me leaned over and asked softly, “What do you think of the way this painting is expressed?” Her smile was warm and friendly, and I immediately felt it was a good opportunity to share my opinion. I cleared my throat and tried to sound composed: “I think this painting uses contrasting tones to express the artist’s inner conflict.”

After hearing me out, she nodded, then said with a smile, “But I think that interpretation is a bit ordinary; it may need a deeper explanation.” Those words struck me like lightning. My smile froze, my heart started beating even faster, and I even began to feel uneasy. I started turning over her words in my mind, repeatedly examining her tone and expression, afraid that I had come across as too shallow or ignorant.

“Maybe I really said something wrong,” I began to blame myself. “Was she hinting that I’m not smart enough?” These thoughts made my stomach churn, sending a wave of tension through me. Although she showed no hostility at all, I heard a denial of me in her words.

I tried to keep listening to the opinions of the other students as if nothing had happened, but the voice in my head only grew louder. I struggled to suppress the chaos and keep from adding unnecessary embarrassment. Even so, my attention kept being pulled back to that brief exchange, turning it over again and again. “Maybe I’m just too sensitive,” I thought. “Why is it always like this? Why can’t I just accept other people’s comments?”

After class, I walked alone along the paths on campus, absently kicking at the little pebbles by the roadside. The sunlight that day was warm, but my mood felt as though it were covered by clouds. My mind was still circling around the conversation from class, as if it would never end.

Two days later, I ran into that classmate in the library. She walked over with a smile and chatted with me for a while. She didn’t bring up that discussion, nor did she show any sign of unkindness. I gradually realized that perhaps I had misunderstood her intention, and that she had no ill will toward me. This made me breathe a sigh of relief, though I still felt a little ashamed of my tendency to overinterpret things.

Over the next few days, I tried to remind myself not to overread every word and every expression, because sometimes people’s words contain no hidden meaning at all; perhaps it was only my own mind putting on a performance.

I sat in the deserted conference room, where the white meeting table was piled high with all kinds of documents and notebooks. A light breeze moved the curtains outside the window, and although sunlight filtered in, it could not dispel the chill in my heart. Our team was holding an important project discussion, and everyone was actively offering their opinions. My heartbeat quickened, and my palms had already begun to sweat, because I always worried that my suggestions would be dismissed or completely ignored.

“This approach may not be very suitable; we need to reconsider it,” the team leader suddenly interrupted me during our discussion, her tone seeming tinged with a hint of impatience. I immediately felt a wave of suffocation, as if an invisible hand were tightly gripping my chest. My cheeks began to burn, and the words on the documents before me blurred.

“Do you disagree with my suggestion?” I tried to stay calm, but my voice trembled involuntarily. “No, I just think we need more data to support it,” the leader replied. Her tone was calm, but I caught a subtle trace of weariness in her eyes.

At that moment, my thoughts began spinning rapidly, and scenes from the past—being cast aside and criticized—flashed through my mind. Friends ignoring my opinions at gatherings, colleagues treating me coldly and rudely in meetings; all these memories filled me with unbearable pain and shame. I began to imagine the worst outcome: they would give up working with me because of my incompetence, and I would be isolated once again.

The sound of my heartbeat roared in my ears, and a wrenching pain churned in my stomach. I suddenly stood up, gripping the edge of the table tightly in an attempt to steady my fraying emotions. “I know I always do things wrong, always disappoint everyone,” I said, my voice shaking, on the verge of tears.

“No one thinks that. We just want to make the project better,” a colleague tried to comfort me, but I had already sunk into extreme unease and despair. Tears streamed down my face uncontrollably as I frantically blamed myself, convinced that I was worthless.

The aftermath lasted for several days. I could barely take part in any social activities normally, and I became unusually sensitive and nervous. During that time, I kept replaying the meeting, even losing confidence in my own abilities. I felt I could no longer bear any negative evaluation. Every night, I ruminated on those negative moments, and the shadow of my emotions never seemed to lift.

The air was thick with stifling humidity, and I could smell the mingled scent of wood and sweat rising from the floor of the practice room. Several standing fans turned at a steady pace, yet they could not drive away even a trace of the heat. Just as I adjusted my chair and sat down, the conductor clapped twice: “Starting from measure sixteen, get ready!” Those words were like a cold wind, sending a chill down my back.

I tightened my grip on the bow in my hand; sweat had soaked my palm, making it so slippery I could barely hold on. I looked down at my score, and even though I had checked it countless times, my eyes still kept darting to measure 24—within seconds, I would have to play that hardest transition note. I knew I had made mistakes there in the previous rehearsals, the pitch always ending up either too high or too low, making everyone notice.

The tremolo in the violins began to layer over itself, gradually enveloping the entire rehearsal room. My gaze drifted across the score, but all the symbols seemed like some alien script, completely without logic. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself, but my heartbeat only grew faster, a buzzing filled my ears, even drowning out the other instruments.

“Hey, careful, you’re off the rhythm,” the classmate beside me whispered. Her voice was soft, but to me it sounded like a huge blow. I forced a stiff smile and nodded in thanks, but my fingers wouldn’t obey; out of control, I pressed the wrong note. The low, wrong pitch instantly broke away from the harmony of the whole orchestra, like a drop of ink falling into clear water, a spreading stain impossible to cover. I felt my face begin to burn, my breathing grow rapid, and the sheet music before my eyes turn blurry.

“Stop! Wait a second.” The conductor’s voice pulled me back to my senses. He turned to me. “What was that just now?”

“I’m sorry…” The words almost burst out of me, my voice trembling. “I wasn’t paying attention to the rhythm. I’m sorry…”

“Don’t rush this section; the rhythm is important. Try again.” His tone was calm, but it felt like a bucket of cold water poured over my head. I nodded and lowered my head to look at my instrument, only to find my fingers trembling slightly. My mind was filled with accusatory voices—“Why do you have to embarrass yourself like this?” “Everyone must have been dragged down by you.”

At that moment, a boy beside me gently patted my shoulder. “Don’t worry, just go slower. We’re all here.” I looked up at him, and he smiled at me. Though he probably meant well, I only felt my face grow even hotter, as if my weakness and incompetence had been seen through. Suddenly, I wanted nothing more than to put down my instrument and run out.

The music started again. When it was my turn, I tried to draw the bow slowly and forcefully, but my nerves made my movements rigid and awkward, and the strings produced a sharp, grating sound. I fought back the tears pooling in my eyes and thought, “Fine, so be it. I’m the loser they all think I am anyway—the harder I try, the more pathetic I look.”

After rehearsal ended, I hurriedly shoved my instrument back into its case, wanting to escape as quickly as possible. But then a girl came over to comfort me. “Don’t take it too seriously. We’ve all had days like this.” I nodded absently, forcing myself not to let the tears fall. However, just as I stepped out of the rehearsal hall, my nose stung and I stood in the corner of the stairwell, where my tears, disappointingly, slid down my face.

That night, I tossed and turned in my dorm bed, the wrong notes of that passage replaying again and again in my mind, each mistake magnified as if it were an indelible stain on me. I could even imagine my classmates discussing my performance. “Why did I come to this rehearsal?” “They must regret letting me join.” These thoughts pressed down on me like a shadow that wouldn’t go away, making it hard to breathe. It wasn’t until the faint first chirp of birds came from outside the window that I finally drifted into exhausted sleep.

The air in the studio was thick with a distinct blend of coffee and wires. The acoustic foam on the walls was a deep gray, and the leaves outside the window swayed in the breeze, making a soft rustling sound. I sat in front of the mixing console, one hand holding the headphones to my ears, trying to capture the subtle sense of loss in the music. The speakers beside me gave off a low, breathing-like beat, and I tapped the tabletop with my fingertips, trying to stay in sync with the rhythm. Suddenly, I felt my heart race, and sweat began to bead on my forehead. I gently set the headphones down and took a deep breath, trying to calm the uneasiness.

At that moment, my collaborator looked up at me, his brows slightly furrowed. His tone was both concerned and a little dissatisfied: “Are you okay? If something’s off, we can always do it again.”

“Mm, I just feel like this part might need a few changes, but I can’t quite put my finger on it,” I replied. But inside, my emotions were like an overturned paint palette, colors spilling everywhere: worry, anxiety, even fear. Would he think I was holding the whole project back? Would I end up being abandoned in the end?

To keep the anxiety inside me from taking complete control, I immediately turned to self-attack. “I’m really useless, always dragging everyone down.” This defense mechanism seemed to temporarily allow me to coexist peacefully within those four soundproof walls.

My body was reacting beyond my control; sweat from my palms soaked the wooden desk in the studio. I took a deep breath, and a faint cramp tightened in my stomach. I knew I had to face these inner demons and not let them affect this collaborative creation. I told myself, “Calm down, you can do this.” But the voice sounded so weak, as if it weren’t enough to comfort my sensitive nerves.

The studio lights began to shift subtly with the beat, dimming with a hint of warm orange. I worked hard to focus on the mixing console in front of me, trying to find clues in the audio waveforms to reconcile the mistakes. That focus temporarily pulled me away from self-reproach and back into the ocean of music.

That night, I returned to the dorm still preoccupied with how I had performed during the day. Lying in bed, I kept replaying my friend’s barely perceptible look of dissatisfaction and my own unreserved self-criticism. Going over those scenes again and again in my mind kept me awake all night, and it wasn’t until dawn that I finally drifted into a shallow sleep.

Over the next few days, I worked hard to pull myself out of the whirlpool of emotions. I kept listening to that day’s recording, hoping to learn something from it—maybe to confirm my inadequacy, or perhaps just to find a few directions for improvement. Though I was still uneasy inside, I decided I would communicate honestly with my teammates, so that every collaboration could take place in a spirit of joy and understanding.

On the big screen in front of me, a horror movie was playing. It was our school film club’s weekly screening. The room was dimly lit, with only the eerie blue glow from the screen illuminating the surroundings. I sat in a corner of the screening room with a few friends beside me. The sound effects in the movie were intense, and I could feel the low bass vibrations traveling through the seat into my body, making my heartbeat quicken unconsciously.

“Look at this shot, it’s really iconic!” a friend sitting next to me said in a hushed voice. I tried my best to respond casually: “Yeah, but it is kind of scary.” Even as I said that, my palms started to sweat, and I felt a chill on my back.

During the climax of the movie, I couldn’t help but close my eyes, but my mind kept playing out the worst-case scenarios. Had the others noticed how nervous I was? Would they think I was too weak? These thoughts tangled with me, and the rhythm of my heartbeat suddenly grew even more rapid.

After the movie ended, the lights came back on, and everyone began discussing the plot. Though I was surrounded by my friends’ laughter and relaxed conversation, I felt an indescribable pressure. “What’s wrong? You don’t look so good,” one friend said, patting me on the shoulder with concern.

“I’m fine, I was just scared,” I forced out a smile, but inside I was wondering whether they thought I was making too much of a fuss. I even began to ruminate over every detail from just now: had I reacted too intensely when I screamed? Would my voice have carried too far? These doubts kept looping in my mind, like replayed scenes from a movie.

I started to feel a sharp cramp in my stomach. This kind of physical reaction was familiar; whenever I felt stressed, it always showed up as promised. Wanting to calm myself down, I decided to go with my friends to the campus café, hoping the bustle of the crowd would ease the unease in my heart.

Sitting at the wooden table in the café, I unconsciously watched my friends’ expressions and tones, trying to judge whether they really thought I had acted oddly. “Actually, you’re pretty brave. Most people would have run at the sight of that kind of scene,” a friend joked.

“Really?” I couldn’t help asking, testing his reaction. He then added, “Of course it’s true. Don’t overthink it.” Even though his words were comforting, I still felt a hint of uncertainty in his tone.

That night, lying on my dorm bed, I kept thinking over what had happened during the day, trying to convince myself that nothing was that bad. When I woke up the next morning, the feeling still lingered, though as time passed it slowly faded into a faint shadow.

The café was bustling with chatter. Sunlight streamed through the large glass windows and fell across the table as I sat with a few classmates, drinking coffee and chatting. Notebooks and smartphones were scattered across the table, and the aroma of coffee filled the air. Every so often, I looked out the window at the busy campus outside. I took a sip of the slightly hot coffee in my hand, and the sweet taste of caramel dissolved in my mouth. One classmate casually brought up the recent course schedule and assignments. In a relaxed tone, he said, “Why haven’t you turned in last week’s report yet? You’ve got quite a procrastination problem, huh?”

Hearing that, my heart tightened and started racing. The coffee cup in my hand trembled slightly. I tried hard to keep smiling, but a wave of unease washed over me, as if the air had grown heavy. “Is he implying that I’m not taking this seriously?” I thought. Was there also some dissatisfaction in his tone?

I didn’t want to seem so fragile, so I forced a casual laugh and said, “Ah, it’s fine. Besides, the professor said to give us a little more time.” But deep down, my thoughts had already turned into raging waves, and I began to blame myself: “Why do I always wait until the last minute to get things done? What will others think of me?” I could feel my palms starting to sweat, and my stomach felt a little uneasy. Afraid of making a scene, I tried to shift my attention to other topics.

“Has the weather been changing a lot lately? Have you caught a cold?” I asked another classmate, hoping to move the attention away from me. He answered casually, and we started talking about the recent weather again. Although the conversation continued, I still zoned out from time to time, unable to stop thinking over that earlier remark.

A few hours later, we each left the café. After returning to the dorm, I lay on my bed, still replaying my classmate’s tone and expression in my mind, feeling as though I had been looked down on. That night, I tossed and turned because of these tangled thoughts, not falling asleep until the early hours of the morning.

When I woke up the next morning, my mood hadn’t improved; I was still haunted by yesterday’s conversation. It felt as if a heavy stone were pressing on my chest, making it hard to breathe. But within a few days, my emotions gradually settled, and those anxieties and self-reproaches seemed never to have existed at all, only drifting through my mind occasionally.

On Saturday morning, I decided to wait for a friend at the bookstore café on campus. Sunlight streamed through the large windows onto the tables, adding a bit of warmth to the already quiet shop. I sat by the window with a freshly ordered hot coffee in front of me, sending up a faint wisp of steam. The distinctive scent of paper and ink in the bookstore lingered at the tip of my nose, and the background music was a gentle piano piece, as if soothing my slightly uneasy mood.

The coffee tasted a little bitter, but in the calm of late morning, it felt strangely fitting. I softly flipped through the magazine in my hands, occasionally looking up toward the entrance. Suddenly, a voice broke the silence: “Is anyone sitting here?” I froze for a moment and saw a boy in a trench coat standing by the table. His tone was friendly, but I instantly felt a twinge of nervousness. “Oh, someone’s already coming. He’ll be here soon,” I hurriedly replied.

The boy nodded and turned to leave. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, and my palms began to sweat. I started to wonder whether I had misread the time and place we had agreed on, and I was filled with unease: what if I had gotten it wrong? I tried hard to calm myself down and took a deep breath, but there was no new message on my phone.

After a few minutes, I finally couldn’t resist and sent my friend a message: “Are you almost here?” Anxiety and unease made me keep checking my phone, but I still got no reply. Meanwhile, the café music shifted to a lively guitar tune, but that still couldn’t calm me down.

Not long after, my friend finally pushed open the door and came in, while I somehow looked a little embarrassed. “Sorry, someone just asked if they could sit here earlier, and I didn’t dare say yes,” I said awkwardly. “It’s okay, I said I’d be here in a little while anyway,” my friend replied with a relaxed smile.

This small incident left me feeling both relieved and a little at a loss. Even such a minor misunderstanding still made me uneasy. For the rest of the day, that faint tension would occasionally flash through my mind, and only gradually fade away after the weekend ended.

Raindrops wound their way down the window glass, and the recording studio lights were turned very dim, the bulbs giving off a faint warm yellow glow. I sat in front of the microphone, the sound in my headphones seeming sharper than usual, and every bit of noise the mic picked up made my nerves tighten. The others sat in front of the computer screen adjusting the tracks, and one classmate said softly, “Do you need to relax a little more? Your voice sounds a bit tense.” Although the tone of the words seemed calm, my heart sank all at once, as if pricked by a sharp needle.

“I’m not nervous, I’m just reading the way you asked.” I blurted out hurriedly, speaking so fast it was like I was building a wall of words for protection. The moment it left my mouth, I regretted it, feeling that I sounded argumentative rather than explanatory. I noticed the other person frown slightly, their lips pressing together, as if they wanted to say something but held back. That tiny movement was almost like opening a floodgate, and countless guesses surged through my mind in an instant: “Do they think I’m unreasonable? Do they not want to work with me at all? Will they never invite me to join the team again?”

My heartbeat gradually quickened, and the sound in my headphones seemed magnified several times over. The rain mixed with the hum of the recording studio’s computer fan, as if the entire space were mocking my unease. I tried to slow my breathing, but there was still a heavy stone pressing on my chest, and even swallowing became difficult. My fingers unconsciously traced lightly across the tabletop, like a lost person unable to find an exit.

For the next stretch of recording, I felt I had completely lost my focus; every word came squeezing out of my dry throat like parched scraps of paper. My mind kept repeating: “Was my reaction just now too much? Did I seem overly sensitive? What did he think of me?”

“Let’s take a break first. I’ll go get some water.” Another classmate stood up and walked to the door; the rain instantly rushed in, then was shut back out. The others began chatting softly about unrelated topics, but I didn’t dare join in, worried that the moment I opened my mouth I’d say something wrong. I forced myself to focus on the pen and paper on the table, pretending to check the script, but in reality I couldn’t get a single word in. My eyes kept fixed on the draft paper covered in markings.

After the break ended, I stiffened and kept recording, but my state had already gone completely off track. Later, when we finished work in the studio, my track was still the first to be deleted. They said, “It’s fine, it’s not your fault, it’s the equipment.” But in my heart I knew that was just a comforting line they were telling me.

When I got back to the dorm, I sat by the desk in a daze, my mind repeatedly replaying that “Do you need to relax a little more?” and my impatient reply. I even wrote the conversation down in my diary, over and over weighing whether I had said something wrong, whether I had made others think I was hard to work with.

The next morning, when I woke up, my stomach was still faintly aching and I had no appetite at all. I stood in the cafeteria holding an empty plate for a full five minutes, and in the end I still decided to leave. All weekend, I kept turning this matter over in my mind, and every time I thought of the look on the other person’s face, I felt like I was about to suffocate. I even started to think about never taking part in any recording projects again, afraid that such a scene might happen once more.

The café was so quiet that all I could hear was the low hum of the coffee machine and the occasional clink of cups. I sat by the window with an untouched latte on the table, the foam already collapsed into a thin film. I stared at it in a daze, my mind replaying the words my roommate had just said to me across the table. She had lowered her head and stirred her coffee, saying in a tentative, apologetic tone, “I think we’d be better off living separately.” The sentence was like a cold stone suddenly crashing into my chest; my breathing turned shallow at once, and my palms began to sweat. My first reaction was to laugh, but I could feel how rigid my face had gone. “Is it because I did something to upset you?” I asked cautiously, trying to keep my tone normal. She shook her head and avoided my eyes. “It’s not your fault. I just feel like… maybe living together isn’t really a good fit.”

My head was buzzing, as if it had been suddenly blocked off, and every word became blurry and meaningless. I couldn’t hear the chatter in the café, and I couldn’t feel the hardness of the chair back anymore—there was only that dull pain in my chest. Instinctively, I desperately tried to recall all the little things that had happened between us over the past few months, from the last time she invited me to hot pot to just a few days ago when we were laughing happily while talking about school events. What exactly had I done wrong? Or was it that what I had always thought was a “pretty good relationship” had actually just been my own wishful thinking?

“Do you think I’m really annoying?” I blurted out suddenly, not even giving myself time to think about the consequences. She froze for a moment, then looked up at me. “No, it’s just… sometimes you seem too concerned about other people’s feelings. I think it’s kind of exhausting.” The words hit like a violent hurricane, brutally tearing apart every defense I had tried to build inside myself. “So I really did make her uncomfortable…” I kept chewing over that sentence in my head, as if I were chewing something rotten, feeling more nauseated with every repetition.

I forced myself to stay outwardly calm, not wanting her to see my despair. “Alright, then let’s leave it at that.” I heard myself say it in a light, indifferent tone, as if I were an outsider speaking. She seemed to relax, a faint smile of apology but relief appearing at the corners of her mouth. “Mm, then I’ll move out in the next few days.” I nodded and lowered my head to stare at the latte until she got up and left.

After she was gone, my whole body went limp. A ring of sweat had soaked the chair armrest under my palm. I realized I was trembling slightly, my heartbeat racing as if it were about to burst out of my body, my stomach twisting painfully. I forced myself to take deep breaths, trying to calm down, but every time I inhaled halfway, her expression from just now, her tone, and those words—“too concerned about other people’s feelings”—would flash through my mind again. Back in the dorm, I locked the door and sat alone on the edge of my bed, burying my face in my hands. I tried to tell myself this was just a normal breakup in living arrangements, but I couldn’t stop the tears from spilling out.

Over the next few days, I kept catching myself watching her movements, wondering whether she was becoming closer to other friends, or whether she had more patience with other people than with me. Every time I saw her laughing and talking with someone else, it felt like a needle pricking my heart. I started doubting every relationship I had, feeling like everyone was only friendly on the surface while being utterly fed up with me inside. I even became afraid of interacting too much with other friends, terrified that they too would one day tell me, just like she did, that “it’s better to live separately.”

The air in the restaurant was filled with the mingled aromas of savory sauce and frying oil, while the hum of conversation and the clatter of bowls and chopsticks filled the entire space. I was sitting by the window, twirling a pair of disposable chopsticks in my hand. The spicy dry-pot on the table was almost finished, with only a little broth left, dotted with a few cilantro leaves and a sheen of red chili oil. Everyone was chatting animatedly, sharing little anecdotes from the club event earlier that day. Then, out of nowhere, someone half-jokingly said, “That suggestion of yours today was really kind of ‘artist thinking’—we regular people just can’t keep up.” A few people burst out laughing.

The laughter was like a fuse igniting instantly; my face flushed at once, and my heartbeat quickened. I forced a smile and pretended not to care, but my mind had already started racing: “What do they mean? Are they mocking me? Do they think I’m weird? Did I say something else that made me seem unnecessary?” The neon lights outside the window flickered irritatingly bright, but I didn’t dare look away, because it felt as if the moment I took my eyes off the table, everyone would immediately start talking about me.

I lowered my head and picked up the last slice of potato from my plate, pretending to chew seriously, but I couldn’t taste a thing. A vague sense of discomfort began building in my stomach. I switched chopsticks to my other hand and realized my palm had already grown a little damp with sweat. I couldn’t help blurting out, “Actually, I just thought... that plan might be a bit more creative.”

“We know,” the person across from me said lightly with a blink, “you’re overthinking it, aren’t you?” It sounded like consolation, but to me it felt more like confirmation of what I had just feared. I forced a smile, nodded, and said, “Maybe.” But inside, everything was churning: “What do you mean? Did I really overthink it? But they were clearly laughing at me—they don’t understand me at all.”

After the meal, I was the first to stand up and say I’d pay the bill. When I stood by the counter, I could clearly feel the heat in my ears, as if an invisible pair of eyes were still fixed on me. When I swiped my card, my hand was actually trembling slightly. The moment I stepped out of the restaurant, the cold night air hit me in the face. I took a deep breath, but my chest still felt tight, as if a stone were pressing down on it. I told everyone, “I’m heading back first,” and left quickly without waiting for a response.

After returning to the dorm, I immediately rushed into the bathroom, turned on the faucet, and splashed my face with cold water. In the mirror, I looked pale, with a few droplets still on my temples. I stared at myself in the mirror, and my mind roared like a tide: “Why did you say that explanatory remark? Obviously, the more you explain, the more it seems like there’s something wrong with you. But if you hadn’t said anything, would they really think you’re stupid? Why did they call it ‘artist thinking’? Is it because what I make is too unrealistic?” One “why” after another wrapped around me.

That night I tossed and turned, and it felt as if I could still hear their laughter and the words “you’re overthinking it.” When I got up in the morning, my head felt heavy, and there were dark circles under my eyes. I tidied my hair in front of the mirror and whispered to myself, “Forget it, stop thinking about it. Next time, just say less.” But even saying that, I knew I would probably end up in a similar situation again—I just didn’t know when.

I stood in the center of the ceramics studio, trying to shape the clay into the form in my mind. Outside, raindrops gently tapped against the windowpane, creating a peaceful background hum. The room was filled with the damp scent of earth, reminding me of playing with mud in the courtyard as a child on rainy days. Yet the calm in my heart was shattered by rising anxiety. As my fingers moved over the clay, my heartbeat quickened, and sweat slid down from my temple. I was always afraid of ruining my work, and that worry clung to my chest like twisting vines.

Nearby, my classmates were speaking quietly. I heard them mention my name, and my nerves tightened instantly. “I think their piece is a bit… unbalanced,” one classmate whispered.

“Really?” another chimed in. “A little, maybe, but perhaps that’s their style.”

My heart sank with a jolt, as if someone had squeezed it hard. The word “unbalanced” kept echoing in my mind, growing louder and harsher. Why did I always think the worst? Did they think I could never do anything well? My vision blurred, but I forced my head up and pretended to stay focused on the pottery in my hands.

“It’s okay, I just need more practice,” I told myself, trying to offer a little comfort. But that comfort always felt so weak and powerless.

The clay in my hands refused to change the way I wanted, and I felt my fingers beginning to tremble slightly. It was as if a voice in my head was whispering to me, “Give up. You can’t do it.” I desperately wanted to prove that voice wrong, but it felt so real that it almost made me believe it.

After class ended, I left the studio, carrying a self that kept replaying everything under my umbrella. I kept thinking about my classmates’ comments, and it felt as though waves of self-doubt were surging up inside me. I couldn’t even imagine how I would face the next ceramics class.

That afternoon, I spent a long time in the library looking up information about ceramics, trying to immerse myself in that atmosphere of learning to ease my inner unease. I told myself that with more practice I would surely improve, but whenever I thought of my classmates’ eyes on me, a heavy feeling rose in my chest. A few days later, I returned to the ceramics studio. A new day, a new attempt—I told myself that this time would be different.

The university’s plant greenhouse is a place I often go. It is filled with all kinds of plants, and the air is infused with a faint, fresh scent of earth and greenery. That day, when I stepped into the greenhouse, sunlight streamed through the glass walls onto the floor, creating patches of dappled light and shadow. I love the dappled patterns formed by the sunlight and the leaves; they look like a living painting.

That day, the greenhouse was very quiet, with only the soft sound of water coming from the irrigation system. I stopped beside a huge fern and studied its leaves closely. The lush green fronds seemed to be telling the story of nature. I reached out and gently touched the soft edges of the leaves, feeling a hint of coolness and moisture. My mind, too, gradually grew calm.

“These plants look so full of life, don’t they?” the greenhouse attendant asked as he walked over.

“Yes, they’re beautiful,” I replied, noticing the friendly smile on his face.

“This place is really peaceful,” I continued. “Every time I come here, I can forget some of my worries.”

He nodded and then went back to his work. In this little oasis, I needed to do nothing at all, only enjoy nature’s tranquility. I strolled along the path, admiring the various plants, some of which were even blooming with tiny flowers in bright, charming colors. Occasionally, I heard the buzzing of insects, as if they were singing hymns of praise for these plants.

My heart was filled with peace and contentment, free of any troubles or worries. Although classes and assignments were weighing on me and leaving me a little breathless, in this place I seemed able to set all that pressure aside, and everything felt far away.

When I left the greenhouse, I felt light in body and cheerful in spirit, as if I had just undergone a spiritual cleansing. The fresh scent of the greenhouse still lingered in the air, and I couldn’t help taking a deep breath, letting myself be fully immersed in that moment of tranquility.

In the days that followed, I found myself becoming more peaceful. Even when faced with the pressures of coursework, I could still respond with a smile. The quiet stillness of the greenhouse seemed to become part of my mind, giving me a small space to breathe amid busy university life.

The lights in the studio were scorching hot. I stood behind the camera, glanced through the lens, and felt a throbbing pulse at my temples. The model had already struck her pose, wearing a bright red gown, the hanging tassels swaying gently in the fan’s breeze. The assistant team members were whispering nearby, and I knew very well they were watching me. I was too slow; they must be mocking me. I swallowed, gripping the camera with both hands and pretending to adjust the focus. In truth, my hands were shaking, and I just couldn’t get the focus right. My mind was in chaos, thoughts scattered like a tangled ball of yarn, impossible to sort out.  

"Are you done yet?" A deep voice came from behind me. It was one of the boys on the team, and there was a hint of impatience in his tone. I jerked upright, my ears suddenly burning hot, as if set on fire. I turned to look at him, trying to tell whether he was blaming me. His expression was ordinary, but the corner of his eye seemed to lift slightly. I guessed that was a sneer.  

"I... I’m adjusting the lens a bit more. Just wait." My voice was so soft it was almost inaudible. He sighed and went back to the computer, continuing to check the photos with another team member.
