My stomach began to churn, and as the acid rose, more voices flooded my head— they must think I’m overwhelmed, that choosing me as the main photographer was a mistake. My palms grew sweatier and sweatier. I grabbed a tissue to wipe them, but it was soaked almost immediately. I kept wiping, yet the camera kept slipping as if it could fall from my hands at any moment.  

Another team member came over and said softly, "Why don’t I try taking one?" Her voice was gentle, but my ears rang instantly, and I felt every bone in my body vibrating. I glanced at her face and caught that faint smile at the corner of her mouth, thinking it was pity—she must be so disappointed in me that she had to step in and save the situation herself. I shook my head at once, nearly bumping into the light stand beside me.  

"No, no, I’ll shoot it. I can do it." My voice came out more hurried and weaker than I had expected. She sighed lightly, patted my shoulder, and said nothing. I looked at the model, and she seemed a little impatient too. I heard the voice inside me shouting: You’re really a mess! Always like this—always screwing up at the critical moment, always letting everyone down!  

A sharp pain stung the back of my hand. I looked down and saw that my nails had dug into the flesh. I forced myself to breathe deeply, forced myself to look at the lens. I pressed the shutter, but the photo came out ludicrously blurry—so blurry that even the model’s outline was indistinct. My face burned, my breathing turned rapid, and I almost hurriedly turned around and handed the camera to the team member beside me. "You take it instead. I... I’m going to adjust the lighting." I tried my best to sound calm, but my voice still shook.  

After several hours, the shoot finally ended, and my hands had been trembling the whole time. Back at the dormitory, I curled up on the bed and cried uncontrollably. I struggled several times, but still couldn’t fall asleep. The same images kept replaying in my mind: the model’s expression, the impatient murmurs, and my own embarrassing mistakes. The next day, I barely had the courage to look at the photos they had sent. When I opened the chat again, I was still wondering whether they had a problem with me—that thought lingered all week, impossible to shake.

The light in that corner of the library was a little dim, and the white desk lamp on the table cast a soft glow. I was sitting in a chair, my notebook and several papers spread out on the desk, my notes covering every blank page in dense writing. My roommate was sitting across from me, her brow slightly furrowed, as if she wanted to say something but hesitated. She set down the marker in her hand, then said quietly, “What you wrote is a bit too complicated. It’s hard for us to keep up with your train of thought.” Her voice was very soft, but those words hit my chest like a hammer. My ears started to feel hot, and a prickling sensation spread through me.

“Oh, do I?” I gave a tentative laugh, trying to hide my tension. My voice actually sounded a little shaky. She went on to explain, “It’s not that it’s bad, it’s just a little roundabout—maybe it would be better if you were more direct?” Her tone wasn’t offensive, but my heartbeat had already become erratic. I felt my stomach tighten, as if a hand were squeezing it from the inside. I nodded and turned my attention back to my notebook, only to find that I couldn’t make sense of a single word.

My mind started racing, replaying scenes from the past like a movie: Had I been too pushy during group discussions? Or was my way of expressing myself really that hard to understand? My eyes moved back and forth over the writing on the desk, while the sentence she had just said kept repeating in my head: “What you wrote is too complicated.” I began ruminating over how I had behaved in the study group as a whole, wondering if I had given people the impression that I was “full of myself.”

“Sorry, I’ll change it.” I heard myself say in a low voice. She just nodded and said nothing more. I tried to pick up my pen and keep writing, but my fingers were trembling slightly, and the pen left a few messy marks on the paper. I felt as if the space around me had suddenly grown smaller, and even the low hum of the air conditioner made me unusually irritated. In the end, I decided to clear my desk and leave the library early.

That night, I lay in bed, still turning those words over in my mind. I kept replaying the expression on her face as she spoke, carefully trying to tell whether there was a hint of hidden sarcasm or dissatisfaction in her tone. I even started to wonder whether my other friends saw me that way too, but simply didn’t want to tell me. I tossed and turned unable to sleep, my head like a spinning top that wouldn’t slow down. I felt a crushing sense of shame, as if some hidden flaw in me had been exposed. The next day, I forced myself to take the initiative and talk to my roommate, simplifying some of my notes before sending them to her. She didn’t seem any different and even praised my revisions a little, but the self-doubt inside me wouldn’t go away. I started speaking less in the study group, trying to avoid drawing similar criticism.

The sound of rain beat against the windows, and the entire self-service laundromat was thick with a damp smell. I stood in front of the washing machine, with a faint sense of unease in my heart. The roar of the machine echoed through the cramped room, and my pants dripped onto a stool nearby. I should never have walked over in the rain. I opened the washing machine door, and a rush of warm air and the scent of laundry detergent hit me, but what I saw made my heart sink: the white T-shirts that had once been spotless were now tinted a pale pink. In an instant, I remembered the moment I’d made the mistake—I had somehow failed to notice that I’d thrown in a red sock too.

“What is wrong with you?” I muttered to myself, tugging at my wet clothes, my tone tinged with unconscious self-blame and frustration. Immediately, I thought of the consequences: next week’s event, and no suitable white clothes left to wear. My heartbeat began to race, as if I were in a small-scale heart marathon, and my palms started to sweat uncontrollably.

A little girl waiting beside me for a machine glanced at me curiously. “Did your clothes get dyed?” she asked with concern. “Yeah, and the kind that can’t be saved at all,” I replied with a wry smile. She nodded, then lowered her head and went back to scrolling on her phone.

I put the stained clothes into a plastic bag and sighed, thinking about how so many similar little mistakes had happened lately. I realized I’d been too anxious, always worrying that trivial things would spiral into unsolvable problems. When I walked out of the laundromat, the rain had eased somewhat, and I opened my umbrella casually.

Back in the dorm, I collapsed onto the bed, listless, still replaying the stained T-shirt in my mind. I couldn’t help blaming myself for not being more careful. I was always like this, treating small things as though they mattered terribly, as if every mistake were a denial of my own worth.

That night, I decided to call my mom. On the other end of the line, she comforted me in a gentle voice. “Everyone makes mistakes. What matters is how you face them,” she said. Lying in bed and staring at the white paint on the ceiling, my unease gradually gave way to the comfort her words brought me.

Over the next few days, I browsed online for many ways to cope with anxiety and tried to figure out which things were truly worth worrying about. I also told myself that the stained clothes were just a small mistake, and that they didn’t represent me as a person as a whole. Thinking this way helped me relax a little.

My mood slowly settled down, and I realized that even in life’s little detours, I could learn something important, such as how to deal with anxiety better. In the days that followed, I decided to try pausing briefly before doing anything, giving myself more time to think and observe, rather than immediately falling into worry and self-reproach.

The podium seemed somewhat radiant to me, glaring unusually hot across the entire classroom. There was a strange smell in the air, a mixture of the subtle heat given off by the projector and the faint dusty scent of the old curtains. The teacher stood at the podium looking at us and announced a temporary assignment: everyone had to choose a topic and give an impromptu speech. I felt as if my heart had been violently seized, beating several times faster than usual, and cold sweat began to seep into my palms. I quickly looked around at the other students’ reactions; some seemed quite calm, while others were frowning slightly. I wondered whether they were as panicked and flustered as I was.

“Let’s start with you,” the teacher said, his gaze sweeping across the class before finally settling on me. I swallowed, my throat dry. “Uh, I think, I think I’d like to talk about time management.” My voice sounded far more stammering than I had expected, which made me even more uneasy. “Time is our most precious resource, and we need to learn how to use it effectively...”

My mind was in chaos, my thoughts like scraps of paper whirled up by the wind, unable to find the right words to organize my ideas. I struggled to stay calm, trying to cover up the weakness in my speech with exaggerated gestures. “You see, my problem is...” An inner voice kept echoing in my ears, as if telling me, “You can’t do it. You’re going to fail.”

My whole body felt intensely tense, sweat running down my temples. My voice began to tremble a little, and in my ears, besides my own voice, there seemed to be the whispering of other classmates and a faint undercurrent of anxiety. Just as I was about to finish, my fingers unconsciously clenched the edge of the podium’s support. I could feel them aching slightly from the force, but that pain also seemed to give me some invisible support.

When I finally finished and returned to my seat, my mind was still shrouded by the tension from moments before. My heartbeat had still not slowed, and my body felt half emptied out. For the rest of the time, I listened to the other students’ speeches, yet I still could not calm down; even the sound of the projector in the air seemed especially harsh. The unease in my heart was like a source of noise, continually disturbing my inner world.

After the speeches ended, I walked out of the classroom with heavy steps. The cold autumn wind blew in my face, instantly making me feel a little more awake. Several days later, I could still feel that invisible pressure, as if every time I stood before a crowd, I would involuntarily recall the embarrassment of that moment. For that reason, I resolved to practice more and try not to be so nervous and uneasy when speaking next time.

On a weekend afternoon, I sat in a small café near campus. Sunlight streamed through the large windows and spilled across the table, warm and gentle. The coffee on the table was still steaming, and the air was filled with its aroma, accompanied by the occasional hum of the coffee machine, creating a cozy atmosphere. People around me talked in low voices, their words like background music—sometimes clear, sometimes fading into the blur.

I opened my notebook and tried to focus on the course materials, occasionally looking up at the window to see the leaves swaying lightly in the breeze. Outside, pedestrians came and went; the street was quiet, and only the faint sound of footsteps could be heard. I felt my heartbeat slow, as if everything had sunk into the laziness of the afternoon. I gently stirred my coffee, watching tiny swirls form in the liquid.

Suddenly, my friend sat down across from me. She smiled and said, “Why aren’t you at the library?” I shrugged. “It’s quiet here, and the coffee is good.” We chatted about trivial things—classes, and recently released movies. She mentioned a film she was really looking forward to, and I promised to go see it with her next time.

After she left, I continued reading. The surroundings felt like a comforting shield, keeping the clutter of the outside world at bay. Now and then, random thoughts would flash through my mind—how I should write the next paper, whether I had fully absorbed what the professor said yesterday—but they only brushed past and didn’t linger long. I adjusted my posture and felt the firmness of the chair against my back, as if reminding me to stay focused.

The café door opened and closed, bringing in a hint of cool air, and I pulled my coat tighter around me. Time passed slowly, and my attention gradually settled on the words in front of me. The afternoon slipped by unnoticed, and by the time the sunlight began to soften, I finally realized how much time had passed.

After returning to the dorm, I still felt calm. A few nights later, thinking back on that peaceful time made me feel that even amid busyness, there are moments of quiet worth cherishing.

Raindrops pattered against the dormitory windows, and the air was thick with the damp scent of earth. I sat in a corner of the common room, the clock on the wall ticking away, its sound mingling with the drizzle outside and leaving me somewhat uneasy. A few newly made friends joined me at the table, and we discussed the progress of our project. Though I tried to seem relaxed and natural, the anxiety inside me kept growing.

“How have you been lately?” asked a girl sitting across from me, her voice gentle and kind. Yet I always felt there was some hidden meaning in her gaze. Was she implying that I had been doing badly lately? I forced myself to suppress that thought and replied, “I’m okay, just a little busy.” At that moment, I felt my heartbeat quicken, and my palms began to sweat.

The conversation went on, and the others began talking about the difficulty of the course and the urgency of the project. I tried to join in, but I kept worrying that I might say something wrong or be misunderstood. “I think this project is too difficult; I’m afraid we won’t be able to finish it.” I tried to voice my concerns, but immediately regretted it. Did I sound too pessimistic? Would they think I couldn’t handle the project?

“Maybe we can divide the work and cooperate, so the pressure won’t be as great,” the boy beside me said. His words made me feel relieved, but then I started overthinking again: why did he say that? Was it because he thought I couldn’t finish it on my own? I tried to focus on the topic, but I still couldn’t shake this habit of overinterpreting everything.

A sharp pain rose in my stomach, a sign of anxiety, and I tried to find an excuse to leave the scene. “I need to go look for some materials; it may take a while,” I told everyone, hastily standing up. As I left the lounge, I could feel my shoulders twitching slightly from the tension.

Later, I sat alone in the library, repeatedly replaying the earlier conversation in my mind. I felt annoyed and ashamed of my tendency to overanalyze, yet I still couldn’t control it. Even days later, I was still thinking back on the details of that meeting, worried that I might have unintentionally left them with a bad impression. Every time I thought of it, I felt a wave of heartache and exhaustion.

In my interactions with them, I had always tried to hide my vulnerability, but the fear deep inside me remained like a shadow. I longed to change this situation and had tried to adjust my mindset, but I always failed. I needed to find a way to face these challenges, rather than avoid or magnify them.

The dorm room lighting was a little dim and yellowish. I sat at my desk, the glow from the computer screen harsh on my eyes. In my ears were the low voices and soft laughter of my roommates, and the air was thick with the tension of the approaching final exams. I knew they were going out tonight to relax, but I had no time to pay attention to that, because I had an important speech to prepare for tomorrow. My fingers tapped against the keyboard as I tried to organize my chaotic thoughts into words people could understand. But a kind of unstoppable panic welled up inside me, and I kept feeling like I wouldn’t be able to handle the challenge ahead.

“Hey, are you still working on that?” My roommate’s voice interrupted my thoughts. She walked over to my desk, carrying a bag full of snacks. “Do you want to come with us and unwind a little?”

“No, I still have to prepare my script.” I forced out a smile, hoping she would understand and leave me alone for a while. But she didn’t leave.

“You’re going to drive yourself crazy like this. Isn’t it just a speech tomorrow? How hard can it be?” Her tone was casual, but it unintentionally struck at my most vulnerable spot.

My face suddenly flushed hot, my heart began racing, and my hands started to tremble slightly on their own. “You don’t understand! This is very important to me!” I looked up at her, somewhat exasperated, my voice laced with anxiety and a hint of anger.

“Oh, okay.” A flicker of confusion crossed my roommate’s face. She shrugged and said nothing more, turning and leaving the room.

I stared at her back as it disappeared through the doorway, overwhelmed by a sense of being misunderstood, of grievance and loneliness. The room suddenly fell silent, with only the ticking of the clock on the wall accompanying my heartbeat. I took a few deep breaths, trying to calm the turbulence inside me, but my emotions remained as uncontrollable as a tide. My stomach cramped, and sweat slowly began to seep from my forehead.

A few hours later, I finally finished my speech, shut down the computer, and leaned back in my chair, my whole body consumed by exhaustion. Even so, that uneasy feeling still lingered like a shadow. That night, I tossed and turned in bed, the argument with my roommate replaying over and over in my mind.

The next morning, when I stood at the podium and began my speech, everything went smoothly, but I still couldn’t help thinking back to the argument from the night before. I realized that my sensitivity and nervousness often made me misunderstand other people’s kindness, and also added unnecessary friction to my relationships.

The bright fluorescent lights in the classroom were glaringly harsh to me. I sat in the front row, my palms slightly damp with nervous sweat. At last it was our turn for the group presentation, and I felt as if my stomach were being tightly clenched, completely unable to relax. I heard one of my groupmates say in a low voice, “Let’s go.” There was a hint of impatience in their tone. I hurriedly stood up, trying to hide the panic inside me, but I could feel my legs going a little weak.

When I stepped up to the podium, I looked at the dozens of eyes in front of me, and my heartbeat suddenly became extremely fast. One of my teammates began introducing the project background, and I stood on the right side with the microphone in my hand. When it was my turn to speak, I took a deep breath, trying to make my voice sound steady, but my lips trembled slightly. “Uh... hello, everyone. I’m the member in our group responsible for data analysis...” As soon as the words left my mouth, I realized my voice was shaking a little, and I even paused.

As I started explaining the data charts, a thought suddenly flashed through my mind: Would they think I had prepared terribly? Was I explaining this too stupidly? My gaze swept over the classmates below the stage. Some were looking down at their phones, and others were whispering to each other. I suddenly felt as if something were blocking my throat, so I quickly lowered my head to look at my PPT and stopped looking up. I could feel my face burning red, and even my ears were getting hot.

After finishing my part, I quickly stepped back to my group and watched the audience’s reaction out of the corner of my eye. They applauded, but the applause sounded somewhat scattered. I almost instinctively interpreted this as, “They’re only being polite; they don’t really recognize us.” One of my groupmates said softly to me, “You did pretty well just now.” I nodded, but I didn’t believe it. I felt they were probably just trying to comfort me, not speaking sincerely.

After the entire class ended, the students gradually dispersed. I sat alone in the classroom packing my things, replaying the presentation over and over in my mind. The more I thought about it, the more I felt that everything had gone wrong: my voice wasn’t steady enough, my eye contact was evasive, and my content wasn’t clear. I even began to wonder whether I simply wasn’t suited to speaking in front of others at all. My stomach started to ache again, as if responding to my self-reproach. I lowered my head and stared at my notebook, my fingers unconsciously gripping the edge of the book tightly.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, unable to sleep. Those scattered rounds of applause kept echoing in my head, along with the looks from my classmates that I interpreted as impatience. I even mentally redesigned the entire presentation, thinking that if I could do it again, how I would adjust my pacing and how I would make myself seem more confident. But these thoughts only made me more anxious, as if they were reminding me of how awful I had been.

A few days later, the score for that group presentation came out, and we got a pretty good grade. But when a classmate said, “Actually, we did quite well,” I still couldn’t make myself truly believe it. I stubbornly continued to think that it was only because the teacher had shown mercy that we received a high score, not because I had done well enough.

The soft lights of the art center fell gently on the paintings on the walls. I stood before an abstract work, glancing around from time to time, taking in the busy atmosphere of the exhibition opening. The wooden floor creaked beneath my feet, the air carried a mix of paint and cleaning agent, and the sounds in the gallery blended into an anxious hum. I was sure I could hear everyone whispering, repeatedly speculating in my mind whether anyone was talking about me. Suddenly, a classmate came up beside me and pointed to the painting on the wall. “What do you think of this piece?” he asked. His voice seemed a little uncertain, and I couldn’t help wondering whether I had misread something.

“I’m not really sure; I think it’s pretty good,” I replied, trying to keep my voice steady and natural. Yet deep down, waves of tension kept rising. My heart sped up, and my stomach began to feel slightly unsettled. I forced a smile, trying to hide my unease, but sweat still slid uncontrollably down my forehead.

He said nothing more, only stood there quietly. In the silence, I began to fear that he was disappointed in my opinion, that he might think I lacked an appreciation for art. My thoughts spun rapidly, and every worst-case possibility surged in like a tide. Just then, I heard him chuckle softly and say, “You’re always so careful; there’s really no need.”

His words spread through me like a shockwave. “I just…” I wanted to respond, but the words seemed hard to get out. I silently blamed myself for being so fragile. So I immediately changed tactics. “Sorry, I’m just a little nervous.” This was the preemptive self-criticism strategy I often used in our interactions, so the other person wouldn’t discover my flaws.

After our conversation ended, I walked to the buffet table and took a drink. Every step felt heavy; I could feel the muscles in my legs starting to tighten and ache. In the rim of the glass, I saw my somewhat pale face and felt ashamed of it. The sight only deepened my anxiety, so I left the noisy crowd and found a corner to stand alone.

That night back in the dorm, I kept ruminating over what had happened during the day, unable to escape the conversation replaying in my mind. I went over my classmate’s words again and again, trying to reinterpret every word, looking for any hidden criticism or rejection, which only made me doubt myself more. Even days later, I was still churning over those emotions in my mind. Faced with every interaction, I became increasingly sensitive, unable even to tell whether someone was truly displeased with me.

The classroom lights were a little harsh, and the incandescent bulbs seemed to be constantly expanding and contracting before my eyes. Our group was doing one last rehearsal for the graduation defense. Everyone else looked relaxed, and I was the only one who felt every nerve in my body taut like a drawn bow. When it was my turn to speak, the material I usually knew so well seemed to have been pulled clean out of my brain. I stumbled over my words and even got the data wrong. After I finished, I subconsciously glanced at everyone’s expressions. Their faces were undeniably stiff.

“You really need to get more familiar with your part,” one teammate said with a frown, his voice not loud but clear enough. “Otherwise there’s no way this will pass.”

I forced out a smile and nodded, but I could feel my stomach twisting into a knot. My heartbeat suddenly sped up, as if it were about to break through my chest. I lowered my head and stared at my fingers on the table, not daring to look at their expressions again. The voice inside me was louder than their criticism: “Do they think I’m dragging everyone down? Do they think I’m terrible? Have they already regretted letting me join?”

They moved on to discuss the next part, but I couldn’t take in a single word. My head was filled with a buzzing noise, as if countless people were all criticizing me at once. My palms started to sweat, my breathing grew shallow and rapid, and my temples throbbed painfully in waves. I kept telling myself that it was fine, that everyone just wanted the project to be better. But that little bit of reason was quickly drowned out by a stronger voice: “They must be talking behind your back about how unreliable you are. They’re probably thinking they’ll never work with you again. Look at the way they’re looking at you—that’s obvious disgust!”

After the rehearsal ended, I made up an excuse that I needed to organize the PPT and stayed behind in the classroom. The moment the door closed, tears welled up at once. I slid down to the floor with my back against the door, wrapped my arms around my knees, and curled into a ball. Waves of self-blame kept crashing over me, like knives stabbing into my chest: “What’s wrong with you? You even messed up such a simple task.” “They must think you’re a natural-born failure.” “You ended up being hated by the group in the end, didn’t you?” Each thought was like a snowball rolling downhill, growing bigger and bigger until it crushed the air out of my lungs.

That night, I hardly slept at all. In my mind, that teammate’s words and their expressions kept replaying over and over again. When I saw them the next day, I deliberately put on a smile to hide the turmoil inside me, but the voice in my head kept telling me: “They’re just being polite to you. Don’t let the surface fool you.” This made me speak cautiously, afraid of provoking any further dissatisfaction. Even when they smiled and praised me for improving, I still couldn’t fully believe it and instead felt that it was just part of their politeness.

Sunlight filtered through the sparse leaves and spilled onto the ground, the flecks of light like tiny golden specks gently drifting. I walked slowly along the park’s cobblestone path, my steps lightly tapping against the stones. The air was a little damp, and every so often I could catch the faint smell of grass and the light, fishy scent drifting from the little lake not far away. All around me, I could hear children’s laughter from time to time, along with dogs barking and the swish of leashes moving through the air. My hands were in my trench coat pockets, and my fingertips touched something hard and small: a key ring I had absentmindedly left in my pocket when I went out that morning.

Ahead of me, not far away, I saw a young mother crouching down to help her child adjust the red shoelaces on their little shoes. The child stood there, swaying one ankle while watching the pigeons in the sky, letting out a giggly “kekekeke” laugh. I stopped and leaned against a thick plane tree beside me. Its bark was a little rough, and when I reached out to touch it, my fingers felt its cool, coarse texture.

“The weather’s nice, isn’t it?” A voice came from a bench not far away. I turned and saw a boy sitting there reading a book. He was wearing a gray hoodie and holding a thick book in his hands, the pages making a soft rustling sound. When he saw me look over, he nodded, as if to confirm that I had heard him. I hesitated, then smiled and nodded back without saying anything. He didn’t continue either, and simply turned another page with focus, looking as though he was thoroughly enjoying the afternoon.

I looked down at my toes and realized that my shoes had somehow stepped in mud, and some of it had splashed onto the cuffs of my pants. I crouched down and rubbed at it with my hand. Though I got some of it off, my fingertips were left dirty too, sticky and somewhat uncomfortable. I stood up and looked around, spotting a small fountain not far ahead, and decided to walk over to wash my hands. The cobblestone ground beside the fountain was slightly damp, and droplets of water reflected a little glimmer in the sunlight. I bent down and turned on the tap, cupped some water in my hands, and carefully cleaned the mud from my fingertips. The cool sensation quieted my heart a little too.

After drying my hands, I sat on the low wall beside the fountain and tilted my head back to look at the sky. There were hardly any clouds in the blue expanse, and the wind stirred the leaves with a soft rustling. I felt, rarely, such peace in my heart, free of all the little scattered emotions that usually surrounded me. After sitting there for a while, I looked down at my watch; it was already nearing evening. I stood up, put my hands back in my pockets, and felt the key ring again. I remembered that on the way home I needed to stop by the supermarket to buy some eggs and milk, so I slowly headed toward the school.

On the way back, I passed a cluster of shrubs covered in small yellow flowers and couldn’t help stopping to look a little longer. The fragrance of the blossoms wasn’t strong, more a natural, fresh scent mixed with a faint earthy smell. The sounds around me seemed to quiet down all at once, leaving only the sound of the wind passing through the leaves. In that instant, I felt as if I had become one with the whole world. It was only for a few seconds, but that feeling was wonderfully comforting.

The chairs and desks were stacked in the corner of the classroom, and the light from the incandescent bulbs was a little blinding, casting mottled reflections across the floor. I had deliberately chosen this empty classroom; it was probably the most secluded one in the school, because I needed a place where no one would disturb me so I could focus on practicing tomorrow’s speech. From outside the window, I could occasionally hear the wind rustling through the leaves. In the room, apart from the sound of me flipping through the pages of my script, it was almost frighteningly quiet.

My palms were sweating a little. I wiped them with a tissue, then crumpled it into a ball and tossed it aside. Standing on the podium, I cleared my throat. “Hello everyone, I am…” Before I could even finish the sentence, I felt my voice was so light it sounded like a joke, not steady enough. I have to be more confident, I told myself. So I tried again. This time it was better, but after only a few lines, I got stuck on the data table I had to explain. Deep down, I regretted taking on this topic. Why had I chosen something so complicated? If I didn’t present it well, would people surely laugh at me in their hearts? Maybe even the teacher would be disappointed in me, or think I didn’t deserve a high grade at all. I started sweating all over, and my fingers unconsciously twisted the edge of the script.

“Again,” I whispered to myself, trying to steady my emotions. I took a deep breath, but my chest felt heavy, as if a stone were pressing down on it. Even when I was just facing empty air, I could feel an invisible pressure, as though more than a dozen pairs of eyes were fixed on me, waiting for me to make a mistake. My hands wouldn’t stop trembling, so I gripped the edge of the podium tightly, trying to steady myself.

“Your data analysis section has some problems. Make the explanation clearer.” Suddenly, those words from my teammate after class today rang in my head. His tone had been very calm at the time, but in my ears it sounded like a knife. I recalled his expression—was there a hint of disappointment, or… disdain? My heartbeat sped up, and my ears were filled with pounding thuds. I tried hard to calm down, but my chest felt tight and uncomfortable, as if I couldn’t get any oxygen.

I tried shifting my attention to the script, quickly scanning a few lines, only to find my mind completely blank. I pressed my temples, trying once more to start from the beginning. “Hello everyone, I am…” My voice was so soft that even I felt ashamed of it. I couldn’t help thinking: how could a voice like this possibly be convincing? Scenes instantly flashed through my mind—the teacher frowning, classmates lowering their heads to laugh, the awkward silence of the whole room.

“Forget it. I’m really terrible.” I sat back down in my chair and stared blankly at the floor. Suddenly, my nose felt a little sour, my eyes grew hot, and then tears began streaming down my cheeks. I wiped them with my sleeve, only making my vision blurrier. Why is it always like this? Why does everything feel bottomless, like I’m about to be swept away by my own incompetence?

It was probably about an hour, or maybe longer, before I finally pulled myself out of that emotional abyss. The late-night classroom was so quiet that even my sniffles seemed to echo off the walls. I got up and went to the bathroom to wash my face. The touch of cold water felt like it had reconnected some switch in my body. When I returned to the classroom, I spread the script out on the desk again. This time I didn’t stand on the podium, but sat in the front row and began reading in a lower voice. I told myself that I didn’t have to be perfect the first time; if I practiced more, maybe it would get better… maybe tomorrow wouldn’t be so bad.

Sunlight from outside streamed through the library’s huge floor-to-ceiling windows, casting a soft golden glow along the edge of the desk. I was sitting in a corner on the second floor of the library, in a row of seats near the plants. On the desk in front of me were my water bottle and a thick book, and beside them my scattered notes—several sheets of A4 paper covered with irregular arrows and symbols that even I could barely decipher. It wasn’t that I couldn’t understand the content; it was just that after a while, my notes would seem so messy that I wouldn’t know where to begin reviewing.

The pages had a slight dryness to them, and when I turned them, they made a faint rustling sound. When my fingers brushed along the edge of the book, I could feel the tiny roughness of the paper fibers. Not far away, someone coughed softly, followed by the sound of a chair being moved. I looked up instinctively and saw a boy in a gray sweater carrying his books toward the shelves. His footsteps were light, but the friction of his shoes against the floor still seemed amplified in this quiet space. I quickly turned my gaze back to the book, afraid of being noticed, though I was also a little curious about what kind of books he was reading.

When I lowered my head to the book again, I found my attention drifting. The sunlight fell across the pages, and the words seemed almost too bright, making me feel slightly dizzy. I closed my eyes for a moment, absentmindedly turning the water bottle on the desk, feeling the coolness of the bottle’s surface. I took a sip; the warm water slid down my throat, and I suddenly realized my stomach felt a little empty, as if it was nearly time to be hungry. I looked up at the clock on the wall—it was almost five. I had actually been sitting there for three hours.

I heard the sound of someone beside me unzipping a backpack. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw a girl take a sticky note pad out of her bag and bend down, apparently tidying something up. I quickly lowered my head again, feeling that I shouldn’t be curious about what other people were doing. But those small sounds and movements, together with the faint wind outside stirring the leaves, seemed to hold my attention more than the complicated academic papers on the book pages. I suddenly drifted off for a moment, thinking, why can some people always stay so focused? Am I just too easily affected by my surroundings?

A faint unease rose in my heart, like a voice reminding me: “You’ve wasted too much time just because you were distracted.” But that thought didn’t last long. I took a deep breath, turned to a new page in my textbook, and tried to force my eyes to focus directly on that academic definition. I ran my finger slowly along the lines, making myself read it sentence by sentence.

After a while, my phone screen lit up, and I glanced over to see an alarm reminder. The light on the desk had dimmed a little too; the sun was starting to move toward the corner of the wall, and the shadows of the trees outside were swaying across it. I decided to pack up and leave, to change my surroundings and perhaps find something to eat to fill my empty stomach.

When I got up, I instinctively tidied the desk and straightened the chairs around me. Those small actions made me feel a little calmer, as if I had just finished a small ritual. When I stepped out of the library entrance, a chill wind hit my face, carrying a faint earthy scent, and only then did I feel fully pulled back into reality.

Sunlight slanted in through the window, and the air was filled with the aroma of coffee. I sat in the corner of the café, my fingers gripping my coffee cup tightly, feeling the warmth in my palm. Li Lin sat across from me, her expression somewhat impatient. We had originally agreed to meet here to discuss plans for our graduation trip, but the conversation quickly veered off course. “Why are you always like this?” Li Lin finally blurted out, her brow slightly furrowed. “Every time we plan something, you always think of the worst possible outcome first.”

My heart suddenly constricted, my chest feeling as if it were being gripped by an invisible hand. My heartbeat quickened, and a bit of nausea rose in my stomach. I looked at her, trying to find even a trace of gentleness in her face, but her expression was only serious.

“I just want to avoid trouble,” I muttered in defense, though even to myself my voice sounded unconvincing. Li Lin sighed, raising her voice a little. “No one wants trouble, but life is full of uncertainty. You can’t always be so negative!” I felt my face start to burn, tears welling in my eyes, while my mind was in complete chaos. I knew she had a point, but I couldn’t suppress the fear inside me. I was afraid our plans this time would turn into a disaster, afraid she would distance herself from me because of it.

“Maybe you’re the one who wants to leave.” The words slipped out of my mouth, and I almost didn’t know how I had said them. Li Lin froze. After a moment, she frowned, her tone carrying unmistakable disappointment. “How can you think that? I’ve always been here.” Her voice reached my ears as if it were coming from far away. I had no strength to argue, my heart filled with the panic of abandonment. My palms were sweating, my nerves were taut, and my body felt as if it were about to fall apart.

Li Lin stood up and gathered her things. “Maybe we should both calm down.” She left the café, leaving me sitting there alone. I watched her back disappear beyond the door, and my heart sank to the bottom. I stayed in the café for a long time by myself, trying to sort out my thoughts, but I still couldn’t calm down.

That night, I barely slept, repeatedly replaying the argument from the afternoon in my mind. I tried to message Li Lin, but I was afraid she wouldn’t reply. A few days later, things between us were still awkward. I tried hard to mend them, but the unease in my heart still wouldn’t let go.

I was holding a psychology reference book in my hands as I slowly made my way into the second-floor reading room of the library. Sunlight streamed in through the windows and fell across the long wooden tables; it should have been a perfectly suitable afternoon for studying. The air carried a faint smell of disinfectant, and every so often there was the soft rustle of turning pages, making the place feel very peaceful. But my mind was anything but calm.

I walked along the rows of tables, scanning each seat, trying to find an empty one. Every seat was occupied; everyone had their heads down, focused on reading or typing, and no one noticed me looking for a place to sit. I kept telling myself not to worry, that I would definitely find somewhere, but my heartbeat still quickened, and my palms began to sweat a little.

“There should be empty seats in another room, maybe,” I tried to comfort myself, but at the same time I couldn’t help thinking—what if I can’t find one? What if I’m accused of taking someone’s seat? In my mind, I began to picture myself being chased away, and even other people’s expressions, half mocking and half reproachful.

Finally, near the wall, I saw what looked like an empty spot at a table. I hurried over, only to find a notebook on the chair; it was clearly already occupied. I bit my lip and felt a little disappointed. Just as I was about to turn and leave, a girl sitting nearby looked up at me and said, “Are you looking for a seat?”

“Yes, I am.” My voice was so soft I could barely hear it myself.

“Oh, someone’s sitting here.” She pointed at the notebook. Her tone was very flat, but I felt as if there was a hint of helplessness or impatience in it. I froze for a moment, then quickly nodded. “Ah, it’s okay, it’s okay. Sorry to bother you.” I almost stumbled backward in a panic, feeling my face grow hot.

After standing there for a few seconds, I decided to give up and turned to leave the reading room. Only when I stepped into the hallway and breathed in the air there did I realize I had been feeling somewhat short of breath. I kept blaming myself over and over in my head: Why did I walk over there? I clearly saw the notebook—why didn’t I just give up from the start? That must have seemed so rude. That girl’s look just now must have meant she thought I was stupid, or that I was bothering her. My stomach suddenly felt as if someone had clenched it tight; it was sour and a little painful.

I dragged my feet to the bench at the end of the hallway and sat down. There was no table here, but at least it was quiet. I took out the reference book and pretended to read seriously, but my mind kept replaying what had just happened. That “someone’s sitting here” kept echoing in my head. I tried to comfort myself that it was only a small matter and there was no need to think too much about it. But I was still tired; my shoulders felt stiff, and even leaning back in the chair, I couldn’t relax.

That night in the dorm, my roommate asked why I hadn’t gone to the study room with them. I made up a casual lie, saying I had something to take care of outside and it was too late, so I couldn’t be bothered to go. That night, I hardly read at all; my mind was full of that girl’s voice and expression from the afternoon.

The classroom lighting was dim and yellowish, and most of the students had already left. Only the people in our group were still seated together in the back row. Scattered across the desk were several notebooks, sketches, and a few project proposals already covered with revisions. There was still a faint smell of curry lingering in the air from someone’s lunch. My notebook lay open in front of me, but I had spent longer staring at it than writing in it.

“Revise this part again,” the team leader said quickly, with a hint of impatience. “You’ve already delayed things a lot on your end before.” She didn’t look up, twirling a pen in her hand, her eyes drifting among the others. I froze for a moment, feeling heat rise from the back of my neck, my face growing warm. “I already revised it in the direction you said before. Why is it still not okay?” I tried to keep my voice steady, but after hearing that, the team leader only nodded and didn’t spare me another glance.

“Mm, but this time the key points need to be highlighted more clearly. If you have any questions, just ask me directly.” Her tone was still casual, but I kept feeling there was some reproach and dissatisfaction hidden in it. Those words stabbed me like a needle, tightening my chest and leaving my palms slick with sweat. I couldn’t help lowering my head and pretending to flip through my notes, though in reality I couldn’t focus at all. I kept wondering whether her tone just now had been deliberate. What did “you’ve already delayed things a lot” mean? Was she implying that I hadn’t done well enough, or even dragged down the whole group? And why hadn’t she even looked at me—was it because she simply disdained speaking to me directly?

The other group members kept discussing, but their voices grew more and more indistinct, as if separated from me by a layer of smoke. It felt as though I had suddenly become an outsider, with everyone’s gaze and words skirting around me. My stomach began to hurt a little, as if an invisible hand were twisting it. I wanted to join in, but I felt that whatever I said would be wrong; yet staying silent made it seem as if I really did have a problem. Caught in this double bind, I was almost suffocating. I could only grit my teeth and try my best to look absorbed in my notes.

“Are you okay?” the classmate sitting beside me asked softly. There was a hint of concern on her face, but all I felt was shame, as if some inappropriate emotion of mine had been exposed. “I’m fine, I’m just thinking about something,” I forced out. Then I made myself lift my head and pretended to listen carefully to what the others were saying. But my mind was in complete disarray, and I couldn’t remember what they were talking about at all.

After returning to the dorm, I threw my backpack onto the bed and sat at the desk, staring blankly for a long time. The team leader’s words and tone kept replaying in my mind. Was I really the one with too many problems? Had she already been dissatisfied with me in her heart for a long time? The more I thought about it, the more irritated I became. I opened and closed my notebook repeatedly, and even after the dorm lights went out, my thoughts were still wandering around that dim yellow classroom.

The classroom was dim, with only a few pendant lights casting a soft yellow glow. The walls were covered with various students’ sketches and oil paintings. I stood in front of my own work, filled with tension and unease. The silence before the critique made me feel even more pressured, as if all eyes were fixed on me.

“Next, please have this student introduce your work.” The professor stood at the podium, speaking in a steady voice. I could hear my heart pounding wildly in my chest. Taking a deep breath, I walked over to my piece, my palms slightly sweaty, my voice trembling with nerves. “This is my reflection on the city at night, trying to use the contrast of color and light and shadow to express... uh...” My mind suddenly went blank, and my words broke off.

The students sat behind their easels, turning their heads to look at me. A few were talking in low voices. I shouldn’t have been able to hear them, but it felt as though those conversations were lingering in my ears, as if they were discussing my painting. I couldn’t help but overinterpret every expression on their faces, as if every glance was a sign of contempt and rejection for my work.

Fear spread rapidly inside me. “Did I say something wrong? Why is everyone looking at me? Is my work really that bad?” These thoughts surged up like waves, making it almost impossible for me to focus. My heartbeat quickened, and it felt as though a heavy stone were pressing on my chest. By then, I noticed my cheeks growing hot, sweat trickling down my forehead. The professor’s gaze put even more pressure on me, my mouth was dry, and I could only continue speaking mechanically.

“When I created this painting, what I wanted to express was...” Struggling to gather my thoughts, I forced myself to keep explaining the concept and the story behind the work. The room seemed to grow even quieter, but that silence only made me more uneasy, as if everyone were waiting for me to make a mistake.

After finishing my introduction, I managed to force out a smile and return to my seat. The moment I sat down, my exhausted body sank into the chair, the muscles that had been tense like a drawn bow finally loosening. Although my heart was still racing, it was a little steadier than before.

That night, I couldn’t stop thinking about the critique from earlier that day. I replayed my performance in front of my classmates over and over, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt like a joke. Going over every possible mistake and awkward moment, as if I absolutely had to find an error before I could feel at ease. That feeling wrapped around me for the entire night, and even when I woke up the next morning, I could still clearly feel the lingering unease.

Even several days later, the fear of being judged and not being accepted still lingered in my mind. Whenever I encountered even a slightly similar situation, it would tug at that taut nerve.

The bare bulb overhead buzzed incessantly, and the whole discussion room had a damp, dusty smell. I sat in the corner while the other three people in the group were gathered around the table, discussing the final photography project plan. I suggested using the camera to capture inconspicuous little scenes in the city, like an abandoned park bench or a faded wall. “This could reveal the fragments forgotten by life,” I said, stressing the ending as I tried to sound confident.

“Hmm… it’s a bit ordinary, isn’t it?” The classmate sitting across from me looked straight at me, her tone carrying a subtle distance. Suddenly the air seemed to grow heavy, and I found my eyes drifting to the tabletop as I pretended to lower my head and flip through my notes. “I think we should still shoot something with more conflict, like social protests, or marginalized groups,” she continued.

My face began to burn, and my heart raced, as if blood were rushing into my ears. “Is she hinting that my idea is boring?” I kept asking myself over and over. I could feel the tension in my stomach, that familiar stabbing pain pricking in like fine needles. I tried to keep my composure on the surface and replied softly, “Oh, um, maybe. Your ideas might be more engaging.” The tremor I couldn’t hide in my voice made me even more ashamed.

Another male classmate beside me chimed in, “Yeah, photographing protests will definitely have more visual impact.” He didn’t look at me, and seemed even to be deliberately avoiding any exchange with me. I began to feel completely cut off from the discussion. I wanted to leave, but I was afraid that would make me seem too sensitive.

“So we’ll go with this plan. Is everyone okay with it?” the group leader asked, scanning each person. I nodded, though my throat felt blocked by a stone and I couldn’t even speak. At that moment, I felt like an insignificant shadow, unable to contribute anything at all.

After leaving the classroom, I walked down the dim corridor, the words “ordinary,” “boring,” and “uncreative” echoing in my head. Those words hammered at my self-esteem like mallets. I harshly scolded myself: “Why am I so useless? Why can’t I ever come up with good ideas?” That loop left me feeling breathless.

When I got back to the dorm, I didn’t even turn on the light and went straight to bed. The crack in the ceiling seemed to mock my failure. My phone buzzed; it was a message from my roommate: “What’s wrong? You look like you’ve been hit hard.” I didn’t reply, afraid that whatever I said would sound overly dramatic. Lying there, I started replaying tomorrow in my head, imagining everyone talking about that discussion, maybe even judging my incompetence behind my back. I knew this speculation was probably just my own overthinking, but I couldn’t stop.

The next morning, I woke up still feeling a heaviness in my chest. After several rounds of inner debate, I sent a message to the group leader: “The suggestions from yesterday’s discussion were actually pretty good. I also agree that the protest theme is more impactful, and I hope I can do my part to help with this plan.” As I sent the message, I both hoped she could sense my effort and feared she would think I was just trying to please her.

In a college dormitory, under soft lights and surrounded by music, I stood at a small gathering with several familiar classmates around me. The air was thick with the smell of beer and chips, which made me feel a little uneasy. I tried to join in their laughter, but unease kept surging inside me.

“You look a little tired today,” a friend said casually. Her tone was light, but my heart instantly clenched. I immediately wondered whether she was implying that I looked bad or didn’t fit in. I strongly wanted to defend myself, yet I was afraid I was being too sensitive. I forced a smile and said, “Oh, maybe I just didn’t sleep well last night.” But inside, everything had already begun to churn.

The music picked up, and people started chatting happily about classes and plans. My heartbeat grew faster and faster, like drumbeats vibrating in my chest; I was sweating, my palms damp. I tried to steady my breathing, but my stomach still cramped in waves. Images from the past surfaced in my mind—times when I had been excluded, when friends had kept their distance.

“What’s wrong? You don’t look too good,” another classmate’s voice cut through the noise. I could no longer keep pretending to be fine. “I’m really okay,” I said quickly, then turned and walked out to the balcony. The air was cold, and the night had blanketed the campus. I needed a place to catch my breath, away from those potential criticisms and rejections.

Standing on the balcony, tears streamed down my face, though I knew they should not have been there. I felt ashamed—why did I always overreact like this, and why could a simple remark trigger such panic? I replayed their tone over and over, trying to figure out whether they were really mocking me. I was always worried about being abandoned, always afraid of not being accepted.

A few days later, I was still on edge, even though my friends had no idea what had happened that night. Every time I walked into class and saw them, I couldn’t help but watch their expressions and movements, afraid they might have any negative judgment of me. Even when they acted as they always did, my mind was still filled with unease and doubt.

The next day, I tried talking to one of my friends, wanting to confirm that I had simply overinterpreted everything that night. “You weren’t angry that night, were you?” I asked, holding my breath. She looked a little confused. “Of course not. Everyone was having a great time that night.” This time, her tone did not comfort me, because my heart had already lost its way in the shadow of that night.

I stood on the podium at the front of the classroom, clutching several printed pages of my thesis abstract in my hand, feeling as if my palms were already soaked. The classroom lights were too bright, making my vision a little dizzy; the low conversations and whispers from the students around me were like an invisible net of thorns, wrapping around every nerve in my body. My advisor sat in the center of the front row, his hands clasped on the desk, his expression stern. I tried to take a deep breath, but it felt as though my breath had caught in my throat, and I could only gasp like a fish. I looked down at my draft, while my mind kept echoing the advice my advisor had given me earlier: “Keep the logic clear, and don’t go off-topic.” But my heart was pounding like a drumstick, and I couldn’t make sense of any clear logic anymore.

The moment I opened my mouth, my voice trembled slightly, and I could tell even I could hear it. I tried to explain in a steady tone, but halfway through, I suddenly realized I seemed to have misquoted a theoretical model, one that was completely inconsistent with the framework in the previous paper. I froze and stole a glance at my advisor’s face, only to see his brow seem to furrow slightly, the corners of his mouth tightening even more. I felt as if someone had brutally squeezed my stomach, the pain rising from deep inside and pressing against my chest. One thought burst through my mind: “It’s over, he’s angry.”

I barely managed to finish explaining the model, my voice sounding almost drained of strength. After I finished, my advisor cleared his throat and said, “What theory are you basing this on? It doesn’t match the model you cited at all.” His voice was calm but blunt, like a needle stabbing into my skin. I reflexively began to explain: “Maybe I remembered it wrong... I checked...” But before I could finish, he cut in directly: “If you’re this unsure, why are you using it as a core argument? You haven’t even met the most basic standards of rigor in your logic.” That last sentence felt like a verdict, and my face burned red instantly. I heard a faint cough from the back row, and someone said something under their breath; though I couldn’t make it out, my mind automatically filled in words that might have been mocking me. The pain in my stomach almost became a cramp, and my vision darkened in waves.

When it was over, I stood there frozen until my advisor reminded me to return to my seat. On the way back, I felt as if the gazes around me were needles stabbing into my back, and I even began to wonder if people were staring just to see how embarrassed I looked. I couldn’t take in a single word of the rest of the defense; I just mechanically stared at the paper in my hands, while the same thought kept echoing in my head: “How could I be this stupid? I made a fool of myself again. Why do I always mess things up!” By the time I walked out of the classroom, it was already dark, but I felt as if I were completely exposed under the bright lights of a courtroom, with nowhere to hide. I walked to the dormitory and called a friend, hoping to confide in someone, but when the words reached my lips, all I said was, “It’s nothing, I was just asking casually.”

The next morning, I woke up with my stomach still aching faintly, and my mind was filled with the same embarrassment and shame. I kept replaying my advisor’s expression, and even reconstructed my classmates’ reactions in my head: had those coughs been mocking how stupid I was? I wanted to go explain myself to my advisor, but I was afraid he would think I was just making excuses for my mistake. The more I thought about it, the more I felt I was beyond saving.

The laundry room downstairs in the dormitory always hung with a damp, detergent-like smell, and the buzzing of washing machines never seemed to stop. I stood at the doorway, feeling a little uneasy. There were quite a few more people in line than usual. I gripped the basket full of clothes tightly, mentally counting how many people were ahead of me. I silently blamed myself: why hadn’t I come earlier? Now I could only stand here and wait. The person in front of me was busily stuffing clothes into the washing machine, their movements looking a bit clumsy, and that made my irritation flare up.

“How much longer is this going to take?” I couldn’t help muttering under my breath. The girl beside me seemed to hear me and turned around with a somewhat impatient expression. I hurriedly lowered my head, my heart starting to race, my face feeling a little hot. Had I been too loud? I hoped she wouldn’t think I was targeting her, and that worried me a little.

I looked around, trying to distract myself. Posters on the wall promoted water conservation, and a small pile of unused laundry bags had accumulated in the corner. I felt trapped, as if I could hardly breathe. I kept telling myself it was only laundry, nothing to make a fuss over, but that uneasiness just would not go away.

At last it was my turn. I quickly walked over to the empty washing machine and stuffed my clothes in, my hands trembling slightly from nerves. I took a deep breath, pressed the start button, and as the machine began to run, I finally felt a little calmer. At last it was taken care of.

Even after I returned to the dorm, I was still somewhat restless. Even though it was over, the anxiety I had felt while waiting lingered in my mind. That night, sitting at my desk trying to focus on studying, my thoughts kept drifting back to how I had acted in the laundry room. I began to reflect on why I felt so uneasy over something so small. Maybe it was because I always felt like I wasn’t calm enough in front of others.

After a few days, that uneasy feeling gradually faded, but I still occasionally remembered the awkwardness of that moment and my own reaction. I told myself that next time I should be more composed, not so eager to prove myself, and hopefully do better.

We sat down in a small, cozy café. The wooden table carried the aroma of coffee, and the air was filled with the sound of beans grinding and soft music. My friend looked at me, her eyes full of expectation and curiosity. She asked, “Do you have any new creative projects lately?” I hesitated for a moment, my heart suddenly racing, my palms slightly sweaty. I replied, “Actually... I have a few ideas, but I’m not sure I can do them well.”

My friend smiled and said, “Share them with me. Maybe I can help.” I began to describe my ideas, but my voice grew quieter and quieter, and I felt that these ideas were more childish than I had imagined. Her serious attention only made me feel more pressured. The voice inside me kept reminding me: your ideas aren’t good enough; everyone will think you’re useless. That sense of being fundamentally flawed began to surface. I forced a smile, but my stomach tightened.

After listening, my friend offered some insights, her voice gentle yet firm. “I think these ideas have a lot of potential, but maybe you could try making the third one more concrete; it might be more appealing.” Her advice was practical and fair, but I couldn’t help overanalyzing it, wondering whether she really believed these projects had a future. Why didn’t she praise me? Was she saying this only so I wouldn’t be disappointed?

I nodded, pretending to think it over carefully, but inside I felt increasingly discouraged. To hide my unease, I quickly added, “Actually, a lot of the time I also feel these ideas aren’t very mature. Maybe I’m just not ready yet.” My friend looked at me with concern and said, “Take it slowly, and don’t put too much pressure on yourself.” Her tone was gentle, but in my mind her suggestions kept echoing. It was as if there was another meaning behind every sentence. Had she already lost confidence in me?

That night back in the dorm, I lay in bed, replaying the conversation with my friend over and over in my head, as if the café’s background music were still echoing in my ears. I tossed and turned, my heart still racing, and the whispers of the other people in the dorm seemed unusually loud. On that sleepless night, my thoughts kept spinning, and I began to doubt my own abilities, even blaming myself for ever sharing such immature ideas. How did it come to this? Could it be that I simply couldn’t do it at all?

When I woke up the next day, I felt dazed and groggy. Although my friend’s advice had come from kindness, I was tormented by my own unease and self-doubt. A sense of abandonment lurked faintly in my heart, making me feel that no matter how hard I tried, it was all too futile.

In the studio, sunlight filtered through the window and fell in patches across the floor. I sat in front of the easel, surrounded by silence, with only the faint sound of the brush sliding across the canvas. Looking at the unfinished oil painting, I felt a wave of unease rise within me. The room was filled with the smell of paint; that heavy, oily scent put me slightly at ease, yet at the same time it felt oppressive. My heartbeat began to quicken, my palms gradually grew sweaty, and the brush in my fingertips became less steady. I kept thinking: “What if I can’t paint it as well as I hoped? Will people think I’m not good enough?”

I recalled my teacher’s comment on my work: “The color combination is very distinctive, but it would be better if the details were handled a bit more delicately.” That sentence echoed over and over in my mind, like a reverberation, aggravating my already taut nerves. I stopped painting and tried to smooth out my thoughts with my hand, but my mind didn’t loosen at all. I heard someone quietly enter the studio; it was a classmate coming to pick up some art supplies nearby. He turned and smiled at me, saying, “Your painting is very good. You’re just always too hard on yourself.”

“Mm, I just want it to be better,” I replied with difficulty, not daring to look up and meet his eyes, afraid he would see the uncertainty in them. I felt a cramp in my stomach, and the physical reaction brought on by the pressure left me somewhat at a loss. I lowered my head, almost in a posture of self-protection, silently telling myself, “Keep painting, don’t let negative thoughts take up any more space.” My ears were filled with those self-attacking voices: “You’re not going to succeed, give up.” With those thoughts, I gripped the brush even more tightly.

I kept reminding myself of how others saw me, and that expectation felt like a burden. The canvas before me became a huge challenge, as if mocking my lack of ability. I tried once again to adjust my mindset and turned my gaze out the window, hoping the scenery outside would give me some inspiration. After a while, I began to feel a trace of relaxation, and my thoughts were no longer so tightly wound. I picked up the brush again and tried boldly coloring in the parts of the picture I had been hesitating over.

“How are you planning to revise your work this week?” my classmate asked me.

“I’ll try changing some of the layout and hope for a different effect,” I answered, trying my best to sound calm. After the conversation ended, I felt a little better inside. At least I was no longer fixating on the earlier comments, but instead looking ahead to the future possibilities of the work.

That afternoon, when I finally left the studio, I carried with me some unresolved confusion and unease, but also a degree of self-comfort. Back at the dormitory, under the light, I continued thinking about how to further refine the piece. Whenever negative emotions tried to invade, I made a conscious effort to force myself to focus on the painting itself. Over the next few days, I came to realize that although these self-attacks on my own abilities could not disappear completely, they also pushed me to explore more deeply the ways of artistic expression.

The lights were as white as an operating room in a hospital. I sat on one side of the table, my palms sweating, but I kept them pressed down and did not wipe them. The classmate across from me was presenting her revised design proposal. She spoke quickly and in an even tone, pausing occasionally as if waiting for our feedback. I took a deep breath, trying to focus on her explanation, but the voice in my head only grew louder: “She’s talking so fast—does that mean she doesn’t want me involved?” My stomach twisted a little, and her voice sounded as if it were coming from far away on the subway. I nodded from time to time, pretending I was following perfectly.

When it was my turn to present, my fingers were trembling. The images on the screen suddenly looked terrible: the colors clashed, and the typography seemed clumsy. I became even more convinced that the whole room was full of eyes judging me. My voice was much softer than usual, even slightly unsteady, and I felt sure they could hear it. Just after I finished the first slide, a classmate blurted out, “Isn’t this color scheme a bit too bright? And the spacing between the text seems off.” His tone was so casual, but it felt like a heavy hammer striking my heart. He said it so directly—was he dissatisfied with me? Did he think I was just not good enough? My mind started racing with these questions.

“Um, that’s what I was thinking, but maybe we can adjust it a bit.” I forced out a smile, yet it felt as if I were wearing a stiff mask over my face. My hands grew wetter and wetter, and it seemed as though everyone nearby could see my discomfort. I even felt that some people were exchanging glances in secret; my reaction was like a complete farce. After that, everyone continued discussing, while I became even quieter. Whenever someone offered an opinion, I instinctively assumed they were hinting that I lacked ability.

After the discussion ended, I walked out of the library. It was already getting a little dark, and the cool air made me instinctively pull my coat tighter around me. My heartbeat still hadn’t fully settled, and my mind kept replaying that classmate’s criticism: “Too bright, the text spacing is off.” I even began to question whether I was suited to continue designing in this field. To escape that sense of helplessness, I planned to email my advisor for some guidance, but then I hesitated for more than ten minutes, worried that I would seem too incompetent.

The next day, I saw the classmate who had made the criticism in the classroom. He took the initiative to greet me and said, “The design yesterday was generally pretty good; just tweak the colors a bit and it’ll be fine.” His natural tone stunned me for a moment. I nodded, but I didn’t dare say much. Inside, I thought: so he wasn’t trying to dismiss me after all, but why do I so easily fall into that feeling of being rejected?

My God, overcast days always seem to have a way of making people feel especially oppressed. This part of the city’s south side always looked particularly desolate, especially when the weather was dark and gloomy. That day I walked along the long riverbank, the air faintly carrying a smell of rust, and the towering silhouette of the old shipyard gradually came into view. Those giant rusting hulls lay silently by the water, as if telling the story of time’s mercilessness.

“Hey! What are you doing here?” I suddenly heard a deep, slightly hoarse voice. I turned around and saw an old shipworker in a thick coat. He stood not far away, looking alert. “Oh, I’m just... taking a look around,” I replied nervously, my heartbeat inexplicably quickening, worried that I had wandered somewhere I shouldn’t have been.

“It’s fine, just don’t get too close to the hulls. Be careful,” he said, waving his hand, seemingly no longer concerned, then turned and walked toward a pile of old tools. I stood there, feeling an indescribable tension. My heart was pounding like a drum, and my palms began to sweat. It felt as though some shadow were chasing me, those persistent fears and unease.

I tried hard to calm myself and looked around, wanting to steady my thoughts. The shipyard here had long been forgotten; aside from the old shipworkers who came by occasionally to inspect the place, almost no one ever came. Near the water, I noticed a tattered rubber boat, its color so faded it was barely recognizable. I gave it a light kick, and the hull bobbing in the water swayed, as if making a silent protest.

“What a ruin,” I muttered to myself, feeling a trace of pride in my own boldness or fearlessness, yet the fear inside kept surfacing. “What if one day I’m forgotten like them too?” Thoughts like that surged through me like water, making it impossible to keep my footing.

That night, I left the shipyard with a heavy heart. On the bus ride home, my hands were still trembling slightly, as if some invisible force were churning inside me. When I woke the next morning, that tension still hadn’t gone away. It was like an inescapable shadow that could swallow my reason at any moment. The feeling lasted for several days; every time I closed my eyes, I saw those abandoned giant ships, silent and so lonely it felt like there was nowhere to run.

“Maybe I should be a little braver,” I said to myself a few days later. “I need to learn to live with that unease, instead of being overwhelmed by it.” The old shipworker’s words still echoed in my ears. His presence seemed to remind me that facing these abandoned things didn’t require so much fear—only that I find my own balance.

When the wind brushed my cheeks, I realized the rooftop was colder than I had imagined. An empty can by my feet rolled slightly, making a faint clatter before disappearing into the shadows. I hugged my arms tight, trying to tuck my hands into the pockets of my hoodie, but the chill inside me didn’t ease at all. I looked up, and the city lights formed a blurry halo, tinting the distant sky a grayish yellow. The stars were almost impossible to see.

“Why does it have to be like this?” I muttered to myself. This afternoon, I gave a presentation in class about my latest project. Yet just as I held my breath and finished my final point, only scattered applause came from below. I saw my advisor frown, then give that unreadable smile. When I noticed him lingering too long on one slide of my PPT, I realized it was the data analysis I had hurriedly put together last night after staying up late. I had made all sorts of mistakes out of exhaustion, but I thought no one would really scrutinize it. But when he spoke, his tone was unusually slow and measured: “This data of yours seems a bit questionable, doesn’t it?” Those words brought the whole room to silence.

I lowered my head and left the classroom in a hurry, not even waiting for the question session afterward. My stomach lurched as if it had flipped over in midair, followed by a burning sensation. As I idly spun the key ring at the classroom door, I noticed a few classmates whispering in the corner, occasionally glancing my way. I could hear my own heartbeat—thump, thump—so loud it seemed as if others could hear it too. I forced myself to look straight ahead, yet my steps felt like they were sinking into cotton, drifting endlessly toward an empty void.

So I escaped to the rooftop of the laboratory building. Hardly anyone ever came here at this hour; it was so quiet that only the wind remained, along with the occasional car horn from below. I kept replaying my advisor’s tone, the looks on my classmates’ faces, and the sound of my left fingernails scraping against the table—that delicate yet grating friction. It felt as if someone had hit fast-forward in my head, replaying the scene over and over, each time adding more humiliating details. It was as though those expressions grew clearer, those tones sharper, and even the remote control I was pressing seemed to warp.

“Why can’t you just do it properly? Why is it always like this!” This time, the voice did not come from anyone else—it was forced out of my own throat. I shouted into the dark sky, but the echo was quickly carried away by the wind. The moment I finished yelling, my face went numb, followed by a scalding rush of tears. I sank to the ground, buried my face in my knees, and tried to shrink myself into the smallest shape possible. Just then, I heard someone downstairs open a door, and footsteps gradually receding. I held my breath, my heart nearly in my throat, terrified of being exposed in my humiliating flight.

I stayed there until several of the streetlights below had gone out, until my fingers had gone stiff from the cold wind, and only then did I slowly stand up and prepare to leave. Back in the dormitory, I climbed into bed as fast as I could, wrapping the blanket around my whole body. The glow from my phone screen shone on my face, reflecting my swollen eyes. The next morning, I still couldn’t bear to look at myself in the mirror, and the afterimages of those looks and words still hadn’t faded.

Sunlight streamed through the floor-to-ceiling windows onto the wooden desks in the classroom, as the professor continued his lecture and the slides on the screen flickered with fragments of knowledge. I sat by the window, taking notes as I listened. The classmates around me were whispering, and I felt somewhat uneasy, always sensing that they were talking about me. The professor posed a question and invited us to discuss it in groups. Three other students and I formed a group and sat together sharing our views.

“Do you think this theory can explain this phenomenon?” the girl next to me asked in a tone I couldn’t quite read. My heart raced, and I felt a slight sweat in my palms. Her tone sounded like she was questioning me, so I began to reflect on what I had just said, wondering if I had made a mistake somewhere. I tried to stay calm and replied, “I think this theory may have limitations in certain situations, but...” Halfway through, I felt a tightness in my stomach.

My voice trembled a little, and the girl simply nodded without pressing further. The noise all around left me somewhat at a loss, as if every laugh was mocking my ignorance. The professor came over to our group and asked if we had any new perspectives to share. I knew this was an opportunity, but that voice in my head was again warning me: “What if I say the wrong thing? What will they think of me?”

“We think this theory may need to take into account more variables, such as socioeconomic factors,” I finally said, trying to make my voice sound confident. The professor smiled slightly and nodded in agreement, but I quickly interpreted that smile as a kind of benevolent charity. Was his expression one of approval? Or did he think my remarks were insignificant?

After class, I hurried out of the classroom, feeling as though every glance was scrutinizing me. I quickened my pace, wanting to shake off this embarrassment as soon as possible. Back in my dorm, I lay on the bed, my heart still beating a little fast, a lingering discomfort still churning in my stomach. I kept replaying the conversation just now, ruminating over every detail, trying to identify the awkward moments and avoid making the same mistakes next time. That night, I repeatedly replayed the classroom scene in my mind, wondering whether the classmates’ tone had really been hostile, or whether I was simply too sensitive.

A few days later, it seemed that I had gradually let go of that discussion, but deep inside, the shadow of self-doubt still surfaced from time to time, as if it were part of my personality. I knew this kind of repeated doubt would not truly help me grow, but in that moment, I could not control my thoughts.

I stood backstage at the university theater, surrounded by a din of noise and a tense atmosphere. Around me, classmates were busily preparing for an improv performance. Light from the theater seeped through the gaps, and the stage lights looked especially dazzling. I was drawn to that bright light, yet I didn’t dare go onstage. The upcoming performance made my heart race and my palms sweat. I repeatedly checked my lines, anxiously imagining the worst possible outcome.
