Suddenly, I heard someone calling my name: “Hey, are you ready?” I nodded, but I didn’t dare meet their eyes. My mind kept churning: Was I not prepared enough? Was I going to embarrass myself on stage? These thoughts were almost impossible to bear.

My classmates were whispering nearby. “Do you think we should tweak this part a little?” They began discussing it, but I was oblivious to what was being said around me; all my attention was fixed on my own lines. I tried hard to concentrate and ignore the unease. My stomach began to ache faintly, as if a gust of wind were swirling inside it. The sweat on my palms kept soaking the paper in my hands.

“Hey, don’t worry so much. Just be a little more confident.” A classmate beside me gently patted my shoulder. Their tone was kind, but all I felt was even greater pressure. This kind of self-attacking seemed unable to stop. I kept telling myself that I would be rejected, that I would be abandoned, that I couldn’t control these thoughts.

Finally, it was my turn to go onstage. I took a deep breath, trying to calm the fear inside me. I swallowed every trace of unease as if that alone could slow my heartbeat. My steps were heavy, as though I were carrying a thousand pounds beneath my feet. I stepped onto the stage, facing an audience in silence. The lights shone on my face, and my body began to tense up as if it were a drawn bowstring.

That night, after my performance ended, I lay in the dormitory and replayed every detail of the stage in my mind. Self-blame and self-attack followed me like shadows, impossible to shake off. A few days later, I was still immersed in the aftermath of the event, constantly ruminating over how I had performed and doubting whether I was good enough.

The lights in the classroom were somewhat glaring. I sat in the front row, gripping my pen, waiting for the professor to begin today’s discussion. The air carried a faint scent of disinfectant, and the desktop was smooth and cold. Uneasily, I looked around at my classmates; their faces were blurry, as if they had become unreal in the light. The professor started asking questions, and I tried to focus, but there was always a voice in my mind urging me to answer. At last, I decided to raise my hand and speak, yet my palms started sweating and my heartbeat quickened.

“I think the application scenarios of this theory are not very reasonable because...” I tried hard to keep my voice from trembling. As soon as I finished speaking, the classmates turned to look at me. Suddenly, a boy named Jack interrupted, “What’s new about that? You can find this viewpoint with a casual search online.” His tone was casual, but in my mind, all kinds of possible subtext flashed by instantly, as if a door had opened and inside were those ignored and inadequate memories.

I lowered my head and looked at the desk, trying to hide my embarrassment and shame. An inner monologue began to ring out: “Does he think what I said is worthless? Is he mocking me?” Each thought felt like a nail, piercing my mind over and over. I started ruminating over my words, trying to find where I had gone wrong. My muscles gradually tightened, and my stomach began to feel a little upset, as if it had been clenched. The whole classroom became blurred in my ears, and Jack’s face kept growing larger in my mind.

After class, I walked out of the classroom. The sunlight was so harsh that I didn’t dare open my eyes, and my mind kept replaying what had just happened. I began to doubt whether I was suited to taking part in such discussions, whether I should keep my mouth shut. Back in the dorm, I tried to look for classmates’ opinions on social media, but found nothing. So I messaged my roommate, “What did you think of my comment today?” She replied, “It was fine, don’t take it too seriously.” But I still couldn’t feel reassured; that sense of being abandoned seemed to cling tightly to me and would not fade.

A few days passed, and that unease gradually subsided, but whenever I faced class, I still couldn’t help checking other people’s reactions. Jack’s remark left a mark in my mind, reminding me to be cautious and not make the same mistake again. I began avoiding speaking in class, afraid I would be rejected in the same way again.

This experience made me realize that I always overinterpret other people’s comments, magnifying negative possibilities to the extreme while ignoring many positive signals. What I need to learn is not to let other people’s casual remarks affect my self-confidence.

Sunlight streamed through the café’s glass windows onto the tabletop, and fine dust drifted in the light. I sat by the wall at a not-too-large table, just big enough to hold a thick reference book and my notebook. Beside me was a cup of hot cocoa topped with whipped cream, with a slight sticky trace of cream along the rim. I liked watching the cream slowly melt; it felt a bit like the flow of time. It wasn’t noisy around me, only a few people were talking softly. Now and then, the sound of a waiter’s footsteps came from the wooden floor, lightly appearing and fading away. I stared at the page, trying to memorize a formula, but my mind drifted on its own. This formula had been covered in today’s class, but I had already forgotten how it was derived. Back then, the teacher had said, “This part won’t be too complicated,” but to me it felt so complicated that it gave me a bit of a headache. I lowered my head and flipped through my notes, trying to find the class record from that time, only to discover that I had written down just a few words, nowhere near enough for me to understand it again. My heartbeat quickened slightly, and my chest felt a little tight, but soon it loosened again. I told myself that today was only for review, and I didn’t need to remember it that firmly. I looked up at the window, where several students were riding bicycles past, the sunlight on them looking especially warm. I felt my tension gradually being diluted by the atmosphere around me.  

A waiter in the café walked over and asked softly, “Would you like the cocoa reheated?” I shook my head and said, “No, thank you.” She nodded, smiled slightly, and turned to leave. I noticed that her uniform was neatly pressed, and her shoes were also clean white. I felt a little envious of how capable and efficient she seemed; lately, I’d felt as if I were stagnating. I thought of how, when I got up this morning, I had hesitated for more than ten minutes before deciding which sweater to wear today, and that hesitation made me feel a bit incompetent. I shook my head, lowered it again to read, and forced myself to focus. After a while, I finally read through the derivation of the formula again. It was still somewhat vague, but at least I felt that I was making an effort.  

Around four o’clock, I packed up my bag and prepared to leave. When I stepped out of the café, the cool breeze brushed gently across my face, briefly making me forget the fatigue of studying. The path from the café to the dormitory was lined with many ginkgo trees. It was late autumn now, and a layer of fallen leaves had already gathered on the ground; each step made a faint rustling sound. The sound of my shoes on the leaves felt leisurely, completely different from the anxiety I’d felt a few hours earlier about studying. After returning to the dorm, I put the reference book back on the shelf and casually turned on some light music on my phone, letting myself relax completely.

Sunlight streamed through the window and spilled across the floor. I sat in the chair on the balcony, holding a novel in my hands. This was my favorite way to enjoy my time. Before me was a campus lush with greenery. I could hear the rustling of leaves gently swaying and the occasional birdsong drifting from afar. A breeze brushed across my cheeks, bringing a touch of refreshing coolness that made me feel even more relaxed.

“Hey, what are you reading?” A classmate leaned over from the neighboring balcony and asked.

I looked up and smiled in reply. “A novel. I just started reading it recently, and it’s pretty interesting.”

“You look so relaxed. I’m jealous,” he said with a laugh, then went back to his own balcony.

“That’s the beauty of the afternoon—you can take your time and enjoy it,” I murmured, returning to the pages.

I immersed myself in the story, feeling the joys and sorrows of the characters. Although I was on a college campus, with graduation still some time away, my worries about the future seemed to melt away in such tranquility. The sunlight seemed to have a kind of magic, soothing the restlessness in my heart and letting me temporarily forget those lingering tensions.

My heartbeat was steady, my body relaxed, and every breath was filled with the scent of sunlight. The breeze lightly stirred my hair, like a friendly comfort. I realized how fortunate I was to be able to enjoy this moment of peace in such a comfortable setting.

After some time had passed, I sat in the chair and closed my eyes to rest for a moment, feeling the warmth of the sun. The book lay quietly on my lap, as if waiting for me to open it again. I savored the moment and did not want to break the harmony. College life can be extremely stressful at times, but in this very moment, I felt incomparably calm.

A few days later, I still remembered that peaceful afternoon on the balcony. I realized how important such moments were to me, and they became my secret little trick for coping with stress. I decided that whenever I felt too overwhelmed, I would give myself time like this to relax and truly enjoy the quiet, beautiful moments in life.

I stood in the corner of the classroom, staring at the mottled gray patterns on the floor, feeling my breathing grow shallower and shallower. The defense for my graduation thesis had just ended, and it kept replaying in my mind over and over, especially my advisor’s comment: “This paper is far too disorganized; it shows no rigor at all.” His tone was very flat, yet it was like a dull thorn slowly piercing my chest. I could feel everyone in the classroom focusing their gaze on me, like countless invisible needles pricking my skin until it went numb. At that moment, I didn’t even dare to look up at their expressions. I could only force out a smile and say in a low voice, “Thank you for your guidance, teacher.”

After the bell rang, I pretended to be looking for something in my bag, not wanting to talk to anyone. Everyone else was standing around in small groups chatting in the classroom. I couldn’t make out what they were saying, but the occasional laughter that drifted over made me feel as if it were aimed at my failure. Li Ran passed by me, carrying a faint scent of perfume. He paused, as if he wanted to say something to me, but in the end he only said, “Don’t take it too much to heart.” I was stunned for a few seconds before nodding, but in my mind countless thoughts were racing—was he really comforting me, or just brushing me off? Or did he think my performance was so awful that he didn’t even want to stay a moment longer?

“Don’t think about it, don’t think about it...” I told myself inwardly, but those images still kept spilling out uncontrollably, like a basin of dirty water poured into my brain. I began to think back to the rehearsals a few days earlier, when my classmates had still praised my PPT for being well made and hadn’t questioned my content much. I suddenly felt deceived. Had they known about my problems all along, but no one wanted to say anything, even waiting to watch me make a fool of myself?

My stomach started to ache faintly, and my palms became sticky with sweat. It was as if there was some smell in the air that made me dizzy and lightheaded—I couldn’t tell whether it was the chalk dust from the classroom or the smell of my own nerves. I shoved my books into my backpack in a panic, thinking I had to leave this place quickly. But just as I was putting the backpack on, I heard Zhou Lin’s voice from the other side: “Did she just cry?” My left arm muscles suddenly tightened, as if a layer of skin had been peeled off me in public. I tried hard to tell myself she wasn’t talking about me—that maybe it was a coincidence, maybe it was just my imagination.

I ran all the way back to the dormitory and almost collapsed onto my bed, drained of all strength. The dim light on the ceiling reflected in my line of sight, like a shadow shrouding my mind. I kept replaying the scene just now, staring at my advisor’s expression, savoring my classmates’ reactions, guessing what they were really thinking. Would they think I was useless? Would they be whispering about me behind my back? And would they not even want to talk to me anymore after this?

The next day, I had originally planned to go find my advisor to discuss revisions to the thesis, but after my phone alarm rang three times, I still couldn’t get up. Lying in bed, my stomach clenched tightly, I kept turning over the thought: if my advisor wasn’t satisfied, would graduation even become a problem? But how could I go face him and listen to criticism again? In the end, I only sent my advisor a text message, briefly saying, “Thank you for your suggestions yesterday. I will revise it carefully,” and then spent the entire afternoon barely managing to write a few lines of revision ideas.

The windows of the study room let in the faint light of autumn. It was so quiet that one could hear the soft rustle of every page turning. I sat in the corner, trying to focus on the book in front of me, but my thoughts were like the dead leaves drifting outside the window—unable to settle. I looked around, and everyone else, absorbed in their own work, seemed wrapped in a kind of peace I envied. Yet my heart was racing, and sweat was slowly dampening my palms. The boy sitting in front of me suddenly turned around; his gaze swept over me, then immediately returned to his notes. I instinctively lowered my head, trying to avoid any eye contact, because that split second of attention made my stomach clench, as if my disguise had been stripped away in public.

“What’s wrong?” a friend asked softly. She was sitting right beside me. Her voice was so gentle, yet carried a concern I couldn’t ignore. I forced out a smile, trying to make myself look less terrible. “Nothing, I’m just a little upset,” I lied, because I knew that even if I explained, she still wouldn’t really understand. I could hear the tremor in my own voice, as if I had just finished running.

The leaves outside the window rustled. It should have been a comforting sound, yet it felt like a mockery of the unease inside me. I felt myself gradually fading from everyone’s sight, becoming transparent, like an unimportant brick in this building. I tried to remember why I had come here, why these days filled with anticipation had slowly been hemmed in by invisible walls. A wave of bitterness washed through me, and it felt as if I had been misunderstood and forgotten from beginning to end.

“If you keep spacing out like this, you’ll fall behind in your studies,” she reminded me again. But I knew that what was falling behind was not just my schoolwork, but also the sense of security that had collapsed deep inside me.

When I left the library, it was already dark. I dragged my feet heavily, feeling as though each step landed on an unbearable loneliness. The moment I stepped out the door, a strong urge to turn back surged in my chest, but I knew nothing would change because of it. The next day, when I woke up, I could still feel last night’s emotions with nowhere to go, unable to free myself from the confusion in my thoughts. Every time I thought of that afternoon, there was still an unmistakable heaviness in my chest.

A few days later, I grew cold toward my close friend, as if silently resisting some hurt she may never have even realized she caused. This instinct for self-protection was like a ridiculous self-fulfilling prophecy, gradually pushing me toward a bottomless abyss of isolation and helplessness.

The lights in the conference room are always a bit glaring, and today they seem even worse. Sunlight outside streams through the blinds, forming stripes of light that mingle with the fluorescent bulbs inside, making everything feel harsh on the eyes. The air in the room is stuffy and warm, and the hum of the air conditioner sounds like a constant buzz, as if hinting at the machine’s age. I find it hard to focus; my heart speeds up slightly, I feel a touch of sweaty dampness, and the whispers of coworkers nearby seem to grow clearer and clearer. “The AC doesn’t seem to be working very well. It’s really hot in here,” one colleague complains. I nod, silently hoping the meeting will end soon.

I can’t help thinking that if the room were cooler, I might be able to concentrate better. As the meeting goes on, I hear the leader explaining the new project requirements, which makes me a little uneasy. Though the requirements aren’t complicated, I’m always afraid I’ll miss some detail or misunderstand an instruction. Her tone isn’t particularly stern, but I start overanalyzing every word she says. The slight furrow in her brow makes me wonder whether she’s dissatisfied with my earlier work. Even though she doesn’t mention me directly this time, I still feel a wave of unease.

My stomach starts to twist with tension, a common reaction when I’m anxious. I try to ease the discomfort by taking deep breaths, but it only helps a little. “It’s okay, it’s just a simple update, nothing major will happen,” I tell myself silently, trying to reassure myself.

After the meeting ends, I walk out of the conference room, and the cool air hitting me head-on slightly lifts my mood. All afternoon, I keep ruminating over the details of the meeting, especially the things I might have missed. The next morning, I decide to get to the office early so I’ll have time to review the project documents carefully once more. I tell myself that although these small things won’t really affect the bigger picture, I still can’t afford to be careless.

The air in the conference room was still stifling. The projector screen on the wall flickered, data charts taking up half the display, while the host went over the problems in our proposal one by one. I sat in the corner, trying to make myself invisible, but the noisy thoughts in my head came one after another, hemming me in tightly. Suddenly, the manager’s gaze landed on me. “Why has the budget gone over so much in this section? You’re in charge of this part—can you explain?” His tone wasn’t harsh, but it made my back tense at once, as if I’d been struck by a current. My heart started pounding wildly, my palms turned sweaty, my stomach tightened, and I could even feel my fingertips trembling slightly. I tried hard to steady my breathing and told myself it was just a normal question, but my lips were so stiff I could hardly open them.

“When calculating the budget, I may have made a mistake in one of the allocations… but it can be adjusted later, and it won’t affect the final result,” I answered carefully, my voice so low it was almost inaudible. The manager frowned. “This kind of problem should be avoided in advance. You need to follow up on these details earlier—you can’t always fix things after the fact.” My colleagues’ eyes all turned toward me at once, like needles pricking my skin. I couldn’t help but start magnifying their expressions, trying to guess from the subtlest changes in each face: Did they think I was incompetent? Would they no longer want to work with me because of this? Did making another mistake mean I really wasn’t suited for this job?

In that instant, I felt a huge wave of shame explode in my chest. I looked down at the notebook on the table, trying to find something to focus on, but my vision had gone blurry. I tightened my grip on the notebook’s edge, my fingers gradually whitening from the pressure, yet I still couldn’t stop the rising tension. The manager kept talking, but it had become background noise; my ears felt blocked, and all I could hear was my own heartbeat.

When the meeting ended, I almost fled the conference room. The hallway was quiet, footsteps echoing hollowly. I pressed hard at my temples, but my stomach still ached faintly, as if a stone were weighing it down. I tried to tell myself it was just a small mistake, nothing serious, and that they probably wouldn’t even remember it, but that reassurance lasted less than a few seconds before the thought “they must be talking about me behind my back” threw me off again. I imagined myself being isolated, everyone on the team disappointed in me, and in the next meeting they might simply leave me out of the proposal altogether.

That night, I tossed and turned without sleep, the conversation from the meeting and the manager’s expression replaying over and over in my mind. My stomach pain kept getting worse, and I even wondered if I should go to the hospital. I took out my notebook and tried to check the budget again, hoping to prove that I wasn’t completely useless, but even when the numbers were fine, I still couldn’t calm the feeling of being rejected. Over the next few days, I deliberately cut back on talking to my colleagues; whenever someone laughed in the office, I wondered if they were talking about me. A week later, I finally gathered the courage to proactively speak with the manager about the specific budget adjustment plan, and he merely nodded, with no sign of dissatisfaction. The matter seemed to have long since passed at the company, but every time I walked past that conference room, I would unconsciously hold my breath. That moment when everyone’s eyes were fixed on me felt as if it had been burned into my muscle memory, impossible to truly erase.

Early in the morning, the air was filled with the aroma of fresh bread and coffee. I stood by the breakfast cart at the entrance of the company, watching the sun slowly rise, its glare making me squint slightly. The streets around me were full of pedestrians hurrying past, their footsteps mingling with the roar of car engines, all accompanied by the breakfast cart owner’s cheerful greetings.

“How sweet would you like your coffee today?” the owner asked enthusiastically. I took the steaming paper cup, my heartbeat quickening slightly, my palms already beginning to sweat. I couldn’t tell whether it was from the heat of the coffee or the unease in my heart. I couldn’t help but think again about what had happened yesterday—that accidental mistake in the office, when I sent an important document to the wrong place, leaving me spending half the afternoon apologizing and fixing things in embarrassment.

A coworker walked over, smiling faintly and nodding at me. “Good morning. How are you feeling today?” His tone was casual, but to my ears it seemed to hint at something. I forced a smile. “All right... but I’m a bit nervous. Do you think everyone is still angry about that document?”

He laughed. “You’re overthinking it. Don’t worry, it was nothing.” I tried to reassure myself, but I still felt a vague unease in my heart. Especially after he turned and walked away, I stared blankly at his back and began replaying our conversation over and over.

Restless inside, my stomach started to cramp, and my fingertips trembled a little. I knew these physical reactions were because I was once again overanalyzing, going in circles over something small. Everything here made me feel stiff and uneasy. I suddenly wanted to find an excuse to escape this situation for a while.

At last, before I even entered the office, my mind was already surging like waves—I imagined my coworkers losing trust in me because of yesterday’s incident, and I even rehearsed a near-apocalyptic work disaster in my head, though reason told me it was nothing more than fear I had created myself.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed every detail of the morning, and then launched into a preemptive self-criticism session. “Why did this happen again?” I blamed myself. “Why can’t I ever control these emotions?” I spent a long night tossing and turning, telling myself that the next day I must work hard to become better and avoid making similar mistakes again.

Only after going through all this inner and outer turmoil did I realize that I had to find a balance—not be overwhelmed by my own sensitivity, and also not attack myself because of overinterpreting others. When I walked into the company gate the next day, I told myself to try listening more and thinking less, and to let go of those unrealistic worries.

Colorful lights flickered, and the whole room was filled with lively music. I held a glass of juice and stood in the corner, taking in everything around me. My coworkers were chatting and laughing, all seeming so relaxed. I knew this gathering was a good chance for me to make connections, but I still couldn’t control my nerves. After taking a sip of juice, my palms began to sweat. Just then, I noticed my supervisor walking toward me. The lights swayed slightly, and a friendly smile was on his face. “How’s the party?” he asked. I nodded and managed to force out, “Pretty good.”

He went on, “I saw your recent project report. You did well, but there are still some areas that could be improved.” His tone sounded relaxed, but my heart suddenly tightened. Countless thoughts flashed through my mind at once: Did he think I wasn’t doing a good job? Was he criticizing me in a roundabout way? How should I respond? What should I say so I wouldn’t disappoint him?

“Thank you, I’ll work harder,” I replied haltingly, trying to keep my smile from looking stiff. Yet my heartbeat sped up uncontrollably, and a sharp knot formed in my stomach. I felt my cheeks growing hot, and I wished I could find a hole to crawl into.

My supervisor nodded and continued talking with other coworkers. But my thoughts could not calm down. Every word kept echoing in my mind, and I even began to read into every slight expression on his face. Had he just frowned a moment ago? Did that mean he was disappointed in me?

After the party ended, I walked home alone, the evening breeze gently lifting my hair. I kept going over that conversation again and again, and the unease in my heart would not go away. Was it really as I thought? Or had I once again overinterpreted what others said?

After I got home, I opened my laptop and tried to distract myself with work, but I was still full of regret and helplessness. That night, I tossed and turned and could not fall asleep. A few days later, I worked even harder, hoping to make up for any shortcomings through my performance. But whenever I recalled that conversation, I always felt an indescribable heaviness and unease in my heart.

Sunlight filtered through the branches of the early spring trees and spilled down around us as my friend and I strolled along a path in the city park. The weather was pleasantly warm, and everyone seemed awakened by the gentle sunlight. Around us were children’s laughter, the fluttering of pigeons’ wings, and, not far away, an old man playing the accordion, the notes drifting off with the wind. In the air, one could faintly catch the fresh scent of grass just mown, mixed with the sweet aroma of ice cream in the hands of a couple nearby.

“Don’t you think today is especially nice?” my friend asked, shielding his eyes from the sun with one hand. I nodded, feeling the warmth flow down from above. “Yeah, it’s rare to have such good weather. I really don’t want to stay indoors.” We continued deeper into the park, the gravel path beneath our feet rustling softly from time to time.

I felt a wave of ease in my heart. There was no pressure from work, and for the moment I had set aside my worries about the future. Everything at this moment seemed so simple and beautiful. “Sometimes I really wish life could stay this simple,” I said casually.

My heartbeat was steady, my steps light, and my whole being seemed to melt into the harmony of this spring day. Now and then a breeze brushed past; I pulled my scarf tighter and felt the cool touch of the wind lightly graze my cheeks.

“Don’t worry, there’ll always be a way to solve things.” My friend’s reassurance was always so plain, yet so effective. I nodded.

Later, we sat down on the grass. Beside us was a small lake, its surface glittering in the sunlight, with a few ducks swimming lazily back and forth. I watched them, and it seemed that all the anxiety in my heart was carried away by the water.

By the time we left the park, the sun was already beginning to set, and the sky had taken on a layer of orange radiance, filling my heart with a sudden, unaccountable peace. That night after I got home, I was still savoring those simple moments. The balcony window was half open, and the evening breeze carried the scent of earth. I leaned back on the sofa, drinking tea, and felt a calm I had never known before.

I stood in front of the projector screen in the conference room, my palms so damp they seemed ready to seep water, gripping the remote tightly and doing my best not to let it slip. On the screen were the data and proposal I had spent two full days putting together. I tried hard to keep my voice steady, but my throat was so dry it felt tight. Every time I misspoke or paused awkwardly, I could sense the subtle change in everyone’s gaze—was that just my imagination, or were they really mocking me inside? When I said the last word, I finally let out a breath of relief and hurried back to my seat. After the meeting, the team leader came over and said to me, “Pretty good, but next time you could focus on the key points a bit more.” The expression on his face as he spoke was impossible for me to read—it was neither praise nor criticism. His tone was perfectly ordinary, but I immediately felt that the “pretty good” in his words was just a polite formality, a courteous way of reminding me that I had failed.

After I got back to my desk, my thoughts poured out like an out-of-control waterfall. “Focus on the key points a bit more”—what did that mean? Was he saying my content was too empty and everyone had wasted their time listening? Or was the proposal completely worthless, merely a presentation in form only? I stared at the computer screen, pretending to revise a document, but in fact my mind was filled with the team leader’s expression and tone replaying over and over. “What do you think?” The supervisor suddenly called my name. I felt as if I were standing naked under a spotlight, with everyone watching me. In a panic, I replied, “Uh, I think maybe… maybe the parameter part could be optimized.” My voice trembled with nervousness. I knew what I said was very vague, sounding like an echo thrown into a hollow well. A coworker stepped in to explain the details of my proposal, their tone carrying polite correction, while my face burned as if pressed against a scorching stove.

After the meeting, I sat at my desk, surrounded by the sound of keyboard clicks and people talking, yet I felt as if I were sealed inside a glass dome. I went over every word my supervisor had said again and again, trying to confirm whether he was actually dissatisfied with me. I pored over every expression, every tone from earlier, and in the end came to the conclusion that they were all hinting I wasn’t good enough. They just weren’t saying it outright.

That night, lying in bed, my mind was like a noise trapped in gears, being pulled apart over and over. “If I worked harder, maybe it wouldn’t be this bad,” I kept thinking, again and again, until well past midnight, my palms still damp and cold, my stomach feeling as if a block of ice were pressing down on it. In the end I forced myself to close my eyes, but the images in my mind kept replaying the embarrassing moments from the meeting.

The light in the conference room was blindingly bright, and there was an indescribable heaviness in the air. My palms were already sweaty, as if I had just washed my hands; it was always like this—I would start sweating whenever there was a meeting. I sat in the third row, trying to make myself as inconspicuous as possible. But the more I tried to disappear, the more it felt as though everyone’s gaze could see straight through my back. When my supervisor walked in, my mind buzzed. The second before, I had been trying hard to remember the key points of the report; the next second, everything went blank.

“You—who wrote this proposal?” My supervisor’s voice was utterly emotionless, like a slab of ice. She looked straight at me, her eyes like knives. “Uh, I wrote it.” My voice was so faint it felt like a mosquito’s buzz, and I even wondered whether she had heard me clearly. But she had. I saw her eyebrows lift slightly, as if confirming her guess.

“What kind of quality is this? It’s wildly wrong, completely unprofessional.” She flipped open the report, pointed to a table, and began listing the logical problems one by one. I wanted to explain, but the words were stuck in my throat. In the end, all I managed was: “I may have missed some details. I’ll... fix it.” My heart was pounding like a drum, and my stomach hurt as if someone had clenched it in their fist.

“Details? This isn’t a detail issue. It’s an attitude issue. How can you be so careless?” Her words lashed at me like a whip. I heard some colleagues lower their heads and quickly leaf through their notes; it was obvious they had already fallen into the role of spectators. Images of all the times I had made mistakes flashed through my mind—the times I was called into the principal’s office as a child, the times I was scolded by my parents for being useless. At that moment, they seemed to be magnified and scrutinized over and over again. I felt like a complete and utter failure.

After the meeting ended, I didn’t leave right away. I hid in the company bathroom, shut myself in a stall, and turned on the faucet to cover up the sound of my sobbing. Crying, I kept blaming myself desperately: How could I have done so badly? Why couldn’t I even complete such basic work? Should I not have come here? Was I simply not suited for this career?

A few days later, I resubmitted the revised proposal, but I no longer had any expectations for my supervisor’s feedback. I felt deeply exhausted, and the words “attitude issue” kept echoing in my head, as if they had been carved into my chest. I started trying to avoid my supervisor, deliberately sitting in places where she wouldn’t notice me, and even cutting back on how often I spoke up. I felt like some kind of outcast who could be exiled at any moment, forced to keep my presence as small as possible.

Outside the window, the sky was a dull gray, and a fine drizzle tapped lightly against the glass, leaving the air faintly damp and cold. The office lights looked somewhat pale. I sat down beside the conference table, feeling my body unconsciously stiffen a little. Through the glass walls of the meeting room, the surrounding noise seeped in faintly, and several colleagues were discussing the latest project progress.

“We need to finish this first draft by next week,” the team leader said, his voice clear and firm. I wrote the deadline in my notebook, but inside I began to churn, worrying whether we could deliver something satisfactory on time.

At that moment, the leader’s gaze swept across the room and briefly settled on me. “How’s your part coming along?” he asked. His tone was ordinary, yet it made my chest tighten. In an instant, I felt my heart pound hard, and my palms began to sweat slightly.

“I’m working on it. It should be done on time,” I replied, trying to keep my voice calm. Yet deep down, a foreboding thought quickly surfaced: what if I don’t do well enough? Will they be disappointed in me? Will my mistake affect the whole project?

The meeting continued, and everyone began discussing other topics, but I found it hard to refocus. One colleague suggested an adjustment to the design plan, and another quietly agreed. But in my mind, the leader’s question and my lack of confidence in answering kept replaying over and over.

“We can make some minor adjustments to our design direction in this area,” a colleague’s voice pulled me back into the meeting. I forced myself to stay engaged and join the discussion, but every time our eyes met, my heartbeat would quicken. I started to wonder whether they were implying that I should be doing more.

At last, the meeting ended with everyone giving reluctant nods. I let out a sigh of relief, but my body still felt tense, like a taut string. Back at my desk, I looked at the design draft on my computer screen. My fingers moved over the keyboard, but I slipped unconsciously into rumination, repeatedly replaying the conversation from earlier. I tried hard to convince myself that this was nothing more than an ordinary meeting, yet the fear of being cast aside still would not go away.

All morning, I couldn’t fully calm down. Whenever a colleague walked past, I would instinctively watch their expression, trying to catch any sign of displeasure or dissatisfaction. At lunch, I didn’t even have much appetite. As usual, I just nibbled on a sandwich while repeatedly rehearsing in my mind how I should present myself more impressively at the next meeting.

That evening, when I got home, night had already deepened. I brewed a cup of hot tea and curled up on the sofa, trying to sort out my thoughts. My body and mind felt exhausted, yet I still couldn’t fall asleep. The next day, I still felt tense inside, and I resolved to further improve my part of the work, hoping to gain some recognition and ease my mood a little.

The office was so quiet that only the sound of the air conditioner could be heard. I sat in front of my computer, with the quarter’s data materials spread out before me. My fingers trembled slightly on the keyboard as I tried to organize my thoughts and put together a perfect report. My heartbeat was like a drumbeat, rapid and uneven, accompanied by waves of discomfort in my stomach. There was an important meeting today, and I had to present the progress of the project I was responsible for. My boss often pointed out problems mercilessly in meetings, and thinking of his sharp words made my forehead start to sweat.

“How are you doing with the prep?” a colleague came over and asked with concern. I forced a smile and said in a louder voice than intended, “Just a little more, it’s almost done.” In reality, I felt trapped in a maze with no way out. Every data point seemed to be drawing closer to my boss’s criticisms, as if saying, “You’re not good enough.”

I repeatedly adjusted every detail in the report, as though every number and every explanation could become a source of ridicule. To ease my tension a little, I swallowed a sip of coffee, but it only made me more anxious, as if my stomach might turn at any moment. I became overly sensitive to my colleagues’ whispers and the occasional glances they cast my way, constantly fearing that they had already seen through my incompetence and lost trust in me. Again and again, I rehearsed the worst-case scenario in my head: my boss suddenly pointing out my mistakes in the meeting, everyone’s disappointed looks leaving me too ashamed to face them, being isolated in the department, and then being forced to resign.

Even so, I pushed myself to keep working, preemptively blaming myself in my mind: “How could you be so stupid? If this goes on, you’ll be fired.” This self-attack seemed like my umbrella—dark, yes, but able to shield me from even greater blows from the outside. Eager to confirm that my report was perfect, I checked every detail over and over until there was no more time.

The meeting went on longer than I had imagined. My heart raced, and every time I spoke it felt like a challenge to my limits. I could feel my voice trembling, and I could feel every pair of eyes on me. Even so, I stubbornly managed to finish the report. After the meeting ended, I completely relaxed, and exhaustion surged over me like a tide.

“Good job!” my boss unexpectedly smiled at me, and I was so surprised I almost forgot how to respond. This brief affirmation eased my emotions a little, but it was soon eroded by the anxiety and doubt in my heart: maybe he had just said it casually, maybe he was only being polite. With these conflicting feelings, I spent the next few days repeatedly replaying every detail of the meeting, afraid I had missed any potential criticism.

My hands gripped the steering wheel tightly, trying to suppress the restless pounding of my heart. It was already dark, and I was sitting in an underground parking garage, able only to vaguely hear the rumble of cars passing overhead. My breathing echoed in the dim parking lot, and the air, mixed with the smell of motor oil and concrete, made me feel suffocated. “Can you wait a moment? I’ll be there soon,” the business manager had said on the phone just now. Inside me churned a familiar panic, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that I had made some irreparable mistake. I kept replaying today’s meeting, wondering whether I had missed something in my performance. Maybe I had said something wrong, or perhaps my proposal seemed too thin or too idealistic. I was afraid he would reject me, even take this opportunity away from me. It felt as if an invisible hand were constantly stirring my stomach, leaving me nauseous and dizzy. The car began to heat up, sweat started forming on my forehead, and I kept denying my urge to roll down the window. “What are you waiting for?” came the manager’s voice from behind the suddenly opened car door, startling me. My muscles tensed instantly. “Hello,” I said with a forced smile, “I just wanted to confirm how today’s proposal went.” “Mm, it was okay, but I think you could make it more concise,” he said, his eyes seemingly drifting across my face. I nodded slightly, but my heart seemed to fall into an abyss. His words felt like a denial of my ability, and despite having analyzed his tone countless times, I still felt uneasy. I hurriedly promised, “I’ll revise it. I’ll optimize it again. There are indeed some parts that need to be thought through more carefully.” I was eager to criticize myself before he could do so more harshly. Even afterward, I still couldn’t shake the feeling of being dismissed. That night in bed, I repeatedly replayed every word he had said, and even remembered similar situations from before, when I had been blamed. I felt unbearably ashamed, as if every effort I had made had become meaningless. The next day, I tried to break through this mood with a new proposal, updating and checking it again and again, hoping to win his approval, but the fear in my heart still could not be completely dispelled.

The conference room was filled with tension, and the projection on the white wall displayed the final slide of the project I was responsible for. I could feel eyes fixed on me; every face looked slightly solemn, as if waiting for a verdict. The air carried a faint scent of coffee and paper. I tried to press my fingers against the sheet of paper to steady my trembling. I had just finished presenting the last part of the project and said to my boss and colleagues, “This is the plan I believe can bring the company the greatest return.”

Then came silence, a few seconds that felt as long as centuries. At last, the boss spoke. “This plan doesn’t seem mature enough, especially the market research part.” His voice was low and forceful, like an alarm bell ringing deep inside me. I forced a smile, though I could feel the muscles in my face beginning to tense.

My heart raced, and I could almost hear my blood rushing in my ears. “Did I make an unforgivable mistake?” I asked myself silently, as my emotions began to churn. The conference room lights were blinding, and I felt dizzy, with a strong wave of nausea rising in my stomach. I tried to defend myself. “In my research, I found some trends that may help with the decisions ahead.”

The boss seemed unimpressed and continued, “What we need is reliable data. Guesswork is meaningless.” Those words were like cold water poured over my heart, leaving me feeling deeply powerless and humiliated.

When the meeting ended, I lowered my head and gathered my things, wanting to leave that suffocating space as quickly as possible. As I walked out of the conference room, I felt a chill sweep across my skin, as though even the air itself were mocking my foolishness and failure.

That night, I lay in bed thinking over every detail, my mind filled with self-criticism. “Why can’t I do things well? Am I naturally a failure?” I kept turning these questions over and over, my mood sinking into an abyss I couldn’t escape.

Over the following week, I was extremely cautious at work, afraid of making another mistake. The only way to ease my anxiety was to keep working overtime, hoping to prove my worth through my tasks. Yet the shadow of doubt and self-blame never lifted, and every night left me unable to sleep.

The lighting in the conference room was a little harsh, and the white tabletop reflected a cold glare. Everyone was quietly flipping through the documents in their hands, and the atmosphere felt somewhat oppressive. I took a deep breath and forced myself not to pay attention to the dampness in my palms. I knew people would be watching me, waiting for me to speak. Cold air from the vent on the right side of my seat brushed against my back, making it feel chilly, yet sweat had started to bead on my forehead.

When I finally gathered the courage to put the proposal in my hands on the table, my voice was actually trembling a little: “This is the content marketing plan I put together. I think we can start from users’ emotional needs…” As I spoke, I flipped the PPT to the first slide. My eyes swept across my supervisor’s face; she showed no expression, just looking at the screen.

“This idea… isn’t it too idealistic?” she interrupted me, her tone carrying a kind of disappointment I found hard to explain. I froze instantly, as if an invisible hand had clenched my heart, and the sweat on my palms became even more noticeable. I tried to argue, “I think approaching it from emotional needs would be more compelling…” but she shook her head. “We’ve already tried similar strategies, and they didn’t work very well. We still need to be more practical.”

The conference room remained silent, but it had grown colder. I could feel everyone’s gaze on me—some sympathetic, some distant. I sat there stiffly, my scalp tingling, as if I had been nailed to the chair. My supervisor then looked toward the next colleague and signaled for him to speak. I knew I had already been brushed aside. But those words—“too idealistic,” “didn’t work well”—kept pricking at my mind like tiny needles. Why was this happening? I had clearly prepared for so long, and I truly believed this proposal had value.

When I left the conference room, I almost mechanically gathered my things. The air conditioning was still cold, but my neck and arms were burning. I walked quickly down the hallway with my head lowered, avoiding eye contact with anyone. By the time I got back to my desk, it felt as if my stomach had been twisted into a knot; I couldn’t tell whether it was nervousness, hurt, or shame. I wanted some water, but my hands were shaking so badly I couldn’t even hold the cup steady.

For the next few hours, I could barely concentrate. My supervisor’s words played over and over in my head like a recording on repeat: “Too idealistic,” “not practical,” “ineffective.” Was I really that incompetent? Was I simply not suited for this job? I started criticizing myself again and again, even recalling past mistakes, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt I never should have come here in the first place. I secretly opened my email and began writing an apology letter to my supervisor. But halfway through, I deleted it.

That night, I went to bed early, yet I couldn’t fall asleep no matter what. I stared blankly at the ceiling as tears streamed down uncontrollably. I thought again about middle school, when I had been criticized by a teacher for missing a tiny detail in my homework. That feeling of being dismissed had apparently been buried in my body all along, never truly gone. Was everything I did destined to be rejected?

A few days later, I finally gathered the courage to ask my supervisor for specific feedback on the proposal. In a flat tone, she told me that my idea wasn’t bad, it just needed more data to support it. I nodded, but in truth I could still feel that frustration and self-doubt clinging to me like a layer of glue that was impossible to peel away.

On a weekend afternoon, the whole room was filled with a lazy kind of sunlight. I moved my chair out onto the balcony, where the sun landed right on my face and knees, and that warm feeling made me a little drowsy. Beside me was a cup of coffee, brewed casually with the coffee machine at home. It didn’t really taste that good, maybe a bit weak, but I could still catch a faint aroma of roasted beans—a scent mixed with a slight sourness. I ran my finger lightly around the rim of the cup and felt that the edge of the ceramic was a little rough, probably from being chipped before. I looked at the sky outside the balcony: blue, pure like a huge canvas, not a single cloud in sight.

I picked up a book from beside me. Its cover was teal, and the paper felt a little rough to the touch. I glanced through the table of contents for a while, but I couldn’t remember why I had chosen this book. Maybe I had bought it on a whim during a trip to a bookstore. I flipped open a few pages and tried to get myself into reading mode, but my mind kept drifting to other things. For example, the email my boss sent me yesterday, where he wrote “looking forward to your update” in the last line. The tone was perfectly normal, but I kept wondering if he was actually pressuring me. Had my progress this week already left him somewhat dissatisfied? I shook my head and tried to push those thoughts away.

The wind brushed past the balcony railing, making a faint whooshing sound. I stretched out my legs and put my feet on the small tea table by the balcony. The sunlight slowly climbed onto the tops of my feet, warm enough to feel almost hot. Feeling a little thirsty, I picked up the coffee and took a sip, only to find that it had already gone cold, and the taste had turned somewhat bitter. But I had no intention of getting up to heat up another cup. So be it. After all, the taste didn’t matter.

From time to time, children’s laughter floated up from downstairs in the apartment complex. I didn’t know whose kids were chasing and playing around. Their voices were sharp and bright, carrying an unhidden kind of joy, as if adding a bit of elasticity to the air around them. I felt an indescribable wave of envy, as if their laughter were some kind of freedom, something I had already forgotten how to have.

It wasn’t until a passage in the book suddenly led to an amusing sentence that I realized I had actually smiled without meaning to. The smile was brief, but it seemed to make my body feel a little lighter. I closed the book and felt that I’d probably had enough sun, so I got up and went back inside. When I came in, I glanced at the mirror and saw that my hair had been sun-dried into a messy, sticking-up state, as if a gust of wind had blown through it. That made me feel oddly self-conscious, but I didn’t really care much.

At dinner, I stir-fried some shredded potatoes on a whim, ate while watching a show, and felt that the day had passed quite pleasantly. Although I didn’t really have anything especially worth recording, I still felt a little more relaxed inside.

The sky had already begun to darken, and the streetlights had just come on, casting a warm orange glow. I had just left the office, my head still a little foggy. Today’s work had felt as if my thoughts were wrapped in something sticky, making everything I did feel slow and powerless. A cool evening breeze brushed past me, and before I knew it, I had wandered from the little alley by the street into the plaza. There was an open-air flower shop there, one I had rarely noticed before. Its lights were a soft white, giving the surrounding plants an unreal, hazy look.

I moved a little closer. The owner was an elderly woman, bent over and tidying up a bonsai plant. Looking at the neatly arranged pots, I couldn’t help wanting to step closer. The air was filled with a faint scent of earth and plants, mixed with the cool dampness often carried by the evening wind. It smelled strangely healing. I crouched down and gently touched a succulent leaf. Its thick, cool texture made me pause, almost dazed. The woman looked up and smiled at me, her expression gently kind.

“These plants are all pretty easy to care for. Just looking at them when you have time can make you feel better,” she said, her voice as gentle as the flower shop lights. I nodded, though I felt a little nervous, afraid that saying too much might bother her. I lowered my head and pretended to study the leaves of a pothos plant. My mind was a little blank, but in a very comfortable way. It seemed as if all the irritability from the whole day had been absorbed by these quiet plants.

“Do you like growing these plants?” she asked casually.

“Mm... I want to try,” I replied softly, amused even by how illogical my own tone sounded.

In the end, I chose a very ordinary hanging spider plant. Its leaves were long and slender, as if they could sway at any moment in the wind. She handed me a card covered with care instructions and said, “Look at it more when you have time, and remember to water it.”

“Thank you.” I carefully held the spider plant with both hands, as though carrying something precious, and slowly walked out of the flower shop.

On the way home, I noticed that my breathing had become much steadier, and my steps were no longer so hurried. The traffic and crowd noises in the distance were still loud, but at that moment they seemed very far away. The spider plant’s leaves swayed gently, as if speaking to me in the wind. I felt a faint, subtle kind of happiness, as though the empty spaces inside me were being filled little by little with something soft. After I got home, I placed the spider plant by the windowsill and watched its green leaves glimmer faintly in the light. That feeling of ease and calm made me sleep especially soundly.

When the elevator doors closed, I realized the deputy manager from my department was standing right across from me. He was a composed man, usually unsmiling, and whenever people mentioned him, they always described his strictness with a kind of awe. My heart suddenly sped up, and my hand gripping my bag strap was already damp with sweat. The air was quiet, with only the low hum of the elevator in motion. A rich perfume lingered in the air, carrying a faintly sharp sweetness. I quickly weighed my options in my head: should I greet him? He was looking at the elevator buttons, his face showing no change at all. I hesitated for a few seconds, and in the end chose to lower my head and stare at my shoes.

“Morning.” A single, simple word suddenly came out of his mouth. By the time I looked up, it was already too late; I could only stammer out a vague, muddled sound: “Uh... good morning...” and then immediately looked down again. From the corner of my eye, I seemed to catch him frowning slightly. In that instant, it felt as if my stomach had been tightly clenched, producing an unbearable stabbing ache. I began replaying the scene over and over in my head, trying to confirm whether I had really upset him.

When the elevator doors opened again, he stepped out without looking back. I stood there until the doors were about to close again, then hurriedly stepped out. On my way to my desk, my mind was already filled with accusations at my own reaction: “How could this happen? Why can’t I be more natural? That voice just now—did it sound especially stupid?” My hand stiffly held the mouse, and before I knew it, I had already started replaying that less-than-thirty-second scene. It felt as if I could hear my own voice echoing harshly, and see the deputy manager’s face, faintly marked with impatience. The more I dwelled on it, the more certain I became that I had unquestionably left him with a terrible impression.

For the entire morning that followed, I couldn’t truly settle down to work. Every time I heard someone passing in the hallway behind me, I would instinctively judge whether the deputy manager was coming. That tense feeling made my scalp prickle, and the faint burning sensation in my stomach never went away. I even began imagining that during today’s meeting, he might sharply criticize one of my reports, or that tomorrow I might be placed on a performance review list.

By lunchtime, I ran into a coworker I was fairly familiar with, and cautiously brought up what had happened in the elevator. “Ah, you’re just being too sensitive! He doesn’t care about that at all,” she said with a laugh and a wave of her hand, as if it weren’t even worth discussing. I nodded in agreement, but I felt no relief at all. Her offhand attitude only made me feel more ashamed—why did I even want to check what others thought of me? Why couldn’t I just be normal?

After I returned to my seat, I forcefully suppressed the endless rumination about whether the deputy manager was dissatisfied with me, trying to focus on my work tasks, but every time a new email notification popped up on the screen, my fingers would tremble slightly. That night, even after I got home, I still couldn’t calm down. I even kept straining my ears to hear whether my phone vibrated, whether he had sent some critical email. I realized that perhaps my problem wasn’t just an awkward moment in an elevator, but rather a mindset in which, whenever I sensed someone might be judging me negatively, I would collapse inward as if facing a major crisis.

The conference room lights were harsh, and the white fluorescent glow hit the tabletop so directly that it made my eyes sting. I was sitting against the wall, my palms already sweating, but I tried to wipe them on my sleeves and pretend I was calm. The supervisor’s voice suddenly rose an octave, his tone like a knife stabbing at me: “This proposal was yours to approve. How could you overlook such an obvious mistake?” My brain buzzed as if a huge gate had been thrown open, and all the embarrassing, shameful memories surged in at once. I tried to explain: “I... I understood at the time that the client’s requirement was...” Before I could finish, the supervisor cut me off. “The client’s requirements are basic. Don’t make excuses. This is directly your negligence.” The air around us seemed to freeze. The other colleagues looked complicated; some lowered their heads to check their phones, others stared at me expressionlessly. I subconsciously swept my eyes over their faces, trying to catch any sympathy or support, but all I felt was indifference and distance. I began to wonder whether they had long been dissatisfied with me, just waiting for a chance to bring me down completely. My stomach twisted in pain, as if a hand inside it were constantly kneading and turning, and my heartbeat sped up so much that I felt dizzy. My hands and feet went cold, and I even briefly wondered whether I was about to faint. I said softly, “It’s my fault. I should have noticed.” But my voice was trembling, sounding like a hysterical defense. The supervisor said nothing more. My face burned, and my whole body felt as hot as if I were sitting in a furnace. I suddenly realized it was all over. They would think I was an unreliable colleague, a failure. I started blaming myself for why I had submitted that proposal, why I was always so disastrously wrong. I couldn’t help picturing it in my mind—all my colleagues discussing my failure behind my back, the supervisor having long planned to use this mistake to weaken my position. After the meeting ended, I stood up stiffly and dragged my heavy feet back to my desk. My fingers trembled as I turned on the computer, trying to keep working, but my eyes were fixed on the document title on the screen, unable to take anything in. After work, I walked alone down the street, and though the night wind brushed past me, I felt a bone-deep chill. I kept replaying every word the supervisor had said, until even his expressions and tone became sharper and sharper in my mind. I began to doubt whether I was really suited for this job, or even for any team at all. I felt like a hidden liability, someone who would hold everyone back, and sooner or later someone would demand that I leave. That night, I barely slept, endlessly rehearsing scenes of myself being fired or openly isolated by my colleagues.

The lights in the conference room were too bright, stinging my eyes so badly I couldn’t fully open them. Everyone was looking down at their laptops or phone screens, and a faint smell of coffee hung in the air, but it did nothing to ease the tense atmosphere. I sat in my seat, my palms sweating so much they nearly dampened the tabletop, my heartbeat so fast it felt like my whole chest was trembling.

My supervisor’s voice suddenly rang out, calm in tone but sharp as a needle with every word. “Why was yesterday’s project proposal such a mess in format? You didn’t even check it carefully, did you?” As soon as he finished speaking, I felt everyone’s gaze turn to me at once. My stomach twisted violently, and only one voice echoed in my mind: It’s over, I’m in trouble, everyone knows I made a mistake.

I tried to explain. “I checked it several times yesterday, maybe it was the template…” But before I could finish, he cut me off: “Don’t make excuses. Templates don’t just get messed up on their own. Look at your colleagues’ proposals, then look at yours—if this isn’t a problem of attitude, what is it?” I heard my coworkers’ quiet whispers. Though I couldn’t make out the words, I was sure they were talking about my failure.

My face burned hot, and I wanted to flee from my seat immediately. Images flashed through my mind—my supervisor’s gaze growing colder and colder, my team members starting to distance themselves from me, and even getting fired. Every scenario pointed to one conclusion: I wasn’t worthy of trust.

As my supervisor kept criticizing me, my neck and shoulders grew increasingly stiff, as if pinned in place by an invisible force. My fingers gripped the edge of the table tightly; my palms were already soaked and even a little slippery. I didn’t dare look at anyone’s expression, and could only stare at the water glass on the table, imagining it could block out everything outside.

After it was over, I trudged back to my desk, completely unable to remember any details of the walk. Once seated, I opened my computer like a machine and tried to revise the proposal, but I couldn’t focus no matter what I did. I replayed my supervisor’s criticism over and over, every word seeming etched into my mind. I started blaming myself—how could I make such a mistake? How could I be so stupid, so useless? Throughout the afternoon, I kept rehearsing the possible consequences in my head: Would someone report me up the chain? Would my supervisor soon stop trusting me?

That night, I lay in bed with no sleepiness at all. In the darkness, the sound of my heartbeat was unusually loud. I could even smell the sweat on my clothes, mixed with a slightly sour odor. When I closed my eyes, my supervisor’s expression appeared again, and I suddenly felt he was right: no matter how hard I tried, I was always flawed. At that moment, I simply couldn’t shake that thought, and I even began to doubt whether continuing to work was meaningful at all.

The afternoon sunlight streamed through the café’s floor-to-ceiling windows and spilled across the tabletop, casting mottled patterns of light and shadow on the wooden surface. A few coworkers and I sat around the table, with several cups of coffee and some desserts scattered here and there. The café was filled with the aroma of coffee, and from time to time we could hear the hum of the espresso machine and the crisp clinking of cups.

“What do you think of this project?” Xiaolin, sitting across from me, asked in a tone that seemed casually offhand. I tried hard to keep smiling, but my heart suddenly began to race, and my palms started to sweat.
