Two people nearby were speaking softly, and every so often a few clear phrases drifted over, like “It seems like this café changed its beans” or “I think you should try that online course; it seems pretty reliable.” Their voices were the kind of background white noise that somehow made me feel at ease. I looked up in their direction; one was wearing a dark coat, the other a red scarf, but the details didn’t stay in my mind for long. I started trying to sort out the structure of the report again, changed the title of the first section to “Project Overview,” and then listed a few short phrases as subheadings.

My attention briefly settled back into the document when someone accidentally bumped the back of my chair. I turned around and saw a waiter carrying a tray. He quietly said, “Sorry,” and I instinctively replied, “It’s okay.” Right after saying that, I suddenly felt like my voice had been a little louder than necessary. Did that make me seem a bit impatient? But he didn’t seem to care much; he turned and went back to the counter. I shook my head, trying not to let these tiny details keep occupying my mind, and turned my gaze back to the screen. For a full hour, I wrote less than 300 words on the “Project Goals” section intermittently. Progress was slow, but at least it hadn’t come to a complete halt.

Before leaving, I bought a slice of chocolate cake at the cashier as dessert for dinner. On the way home, the sky gradually darkened, the streetlights slowly came on, and there was a slight chill in the air. As I waited at the traffic light for those few seconds, I suddenly remembered my state of mind in the café earlier and realized it really wasn’t that much of a problem. I just tend to overthink things a little, but these small interruptions hadn’t affected my overall plan. I decided that once I got home, I would keep working on the rest of the report, and to my surprise, I even felt a faint sense of anticipation for the work ahead.

Sunlight filtered through the dense leaves and dappled the ground with patches of light and shadow. This team-building event was held in a forest not far from the city, and the air was filled with the scent of grass and damp earth. My coworkers and I were dressed in lightweight athletic wear and walked along a forest path. Not far away, I heard birds singing, and this natural background music made me feel somewhat at ease. Suddenly, the team leader at the front announced the start of a group game: we had to pair up, cross a small stream, and find a hidden target item according to clues. Her voice rang out especially clearly in the woods as she said, “You need to trust each other and work together in sync.”

I immediately felt my palms grow slightly sweaty, and my heartbeat quickened involuntarily. My coworkers quickly formed pairs, but I hesitated. In the end, a colleague who always seemed calm and composed in daily life came over and asked me to join him: “Want to team up?” I nodded and forced out a faint smile.

We walked along the path beside the stream, but I couldn’t help thinking through every detail of his tone. Was he only asking out of politeness? If I became a burden, would everyone be unhappy if we lost the game?

We began crossing, with the stream gurgling beneath our feet. I clenched my teeth and tried hard to keep up with his pace. Suddenly, he stopped ahead and looked back with a hint of helplessness. “Watch your step. There’s a slippery slope here.” I immediately grew tense and asked anxiously, “Is it because I’m holding you back that you can’t keep your speed up?” He froze for a moment, then laughed. “How could that be? Let’s go together.”

My face instantly burned, and I had no choice but to lower my head, my eyes nearly brimming with tears. We continued forward, and I tried not to think about what had just been said, but inside I was in turmoil. I always seemed to catch this fear of being abandoned without meaning to; like an old scar, it would split open with the slightest friction.

After we returned to the meeting point, I saw the other coworkers laughing and chatting, sharing what they had gained from the activity. My colleague came over and gently patted my shoulder. “Well done. Next time we’ll be even faster.” I nodded, not knowing what to say.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed my colleague’s “How could that be?” over and over in my mind, feeling an indescribable mix of shame and relief. The next day, I still walked into the office with unease, trying to remind myself not to overinterpret other people’s words. Maybe he had just been joking at the time, but those subtle, uncertain emotions still lingered in my heart, making me feel utterly tormented.

Around the office desk, the sound of keyboards clicking and quiet conversations rose and fell; sunlight streamed through the window and fell on the carpet, creating patches of dappled light and shadow. I was focused on the project report on my screen, feeling a slight sweat on my forehead and my heartbeat quicken. Leaning over the documents on my desk, I tried to sort out my thoughts, but my mind kept replaying a message a colleague had sent me earlier that seemed unfriendly.

“Are you sure about doing it this way?” The colleague across from me looked up, her voice coming through my headset. My heart tightened as I kept mulling over her tone, feeling that she seemed slightly displeased. “Yeah, I think this plan might be more suitable,” I replied cautiously, trying to hide my unease.

She frowned a little, but I interpreted it sensitively as a challenge to me. I kept calculating what she might be thinking: Did she think I wasn’t capable enough? Or did she have some bias against me among the other colleagues? My stomach began to ache faintly, as if warning me of a potential conflict.

“I’m not trying to question it; I just think this timing may not be ideal,” she said. I had wanted to handle it lightly, but I couldn’t help feeling defensive. “I understand, but this plan has already been discussed many times, and I believe it’s the best solution,” I said, struggling to stay calm, while inwardly I was uneasy, afraid of being rebutted in public and afraid of making a fool of myself with unclear reasoning.

It wasn’t until she sighed and turned to the other colleagues that I realized I might have overreacted. The discussion in the meeting room now seemed especially clear, and my attention was drawn back to the conversation among the others, though my thoughts were still circling around that earlier exchange.

After work that day, I kept replaying the conversation on the way home, trying to find clues in the small details about who was right and who was wrong. The unease in my heart wouldn’t go away, as if I were enveloped by an inescapable cloud. Thinking of those unsettling remarks, I kept blaming myself for being too sensitive.

The next day, I decided to talk to her proactively. Though I was still a little nervous, I didn’t want the misunderstanding to continue. We met in the hallway, and I said softly, “About yesterday’s discussion, I was thinking maybe we could look at it from another angle.” She smiled slightly and said frankly, “Understood. I think we’re both trying to make the best possible preparation for the project.”

This calm exchange put me at ease. Back at my desk, the gloom in my heart seemed to have been dispelled somewhat; although I still felt uneasy, I sensed the power of a slightly eased relationship.

The lunch break in the office had just begun, and I decided to go downstairs to buy a cup of coffee. The elevator took me down to the first floor, and I walked toward the automatic coffee machine in the corner of the company lobby. The afternoon sunlight slanted in through the glass wall, and I squinted as I felt its faint warmth. The air was filled with a subtle coffee aroma, and I stood in line waiting. A coworker ahead of me was also waiting for coffee; he seemed to be in a good mood, with a smile at the corners of his mouth. I greeted him with a smile and said, “How’s work going today?” He turned around, looked at me, and frowned slightly. “Hmm, it’s okay, I guess, but I’m a bit tired.”

When it was my turn, I pressed the button a little nervously, and the machine started working with a clacking sound. I felt my heartbeat seem to speed up a bit, and my palms were slightly sweaty as I kept telling myself not to mess it up. “I hope I won’t forget to add sugar today,” I joked half-seriously to the coworker in front of me. He shrugged. “You’re always like this; you should pay more attention.” His words made me feel a little uneasy, and I forced a smile.

After getting my coffee, I stood aside and stirred the mixed liquid. The warm coffee cup gave off a comforting heat in my hands, which made me relax a little. After taking a sip, I found the sweetness just right and couldn’t help taking another. “What do you think of this coffee machine?” I asked my coworker, hoping to find something to talk about. He shrugged. “It’s all right, I guess. At least it’s better than the one in the office,” he said flatly.

When I returned to my desk, I felt somewhat uneasy. Even though it was only trivial small talk, I always tended to overthink things, with a vague worry in my heart about whether I had said something wrong. This uncertainty often stayed with me and bothered me a little. Looking up at the blue sky outside the window, I tried to distract myself, but my mind kept circling back to the conversation from earlier.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mind replaying the small incident from the afternoon over and over. Although I knew I was just being overly sensitive, whenever I thought about that coworker’s words and attitude, I couldn’t help but blame myself for how I had expressed things. When I saw him the next day, I was still a little tense, but he didn’t bring up yesterday’s conversation again, and I felt somewhat relieved. Perhaps this was just a small ripple in my life, and I needed to learn how to handle details like this better.

On a weekday evening, I carried my bag out of the company and took the subway to a small pottery workshop on the edge of the city. The sign at the door was hand-painted, the letters a little crooked, yet it gave off an easy, warm feeling. As soon as I pushed the door open, a faint damp clay smell rushed into my nose, along with the subtle scent of clay being dried by a wood-fired kiln. Several students’ works hung on the wall—some immature, but full of personality. The soft yellow light inside fell gently across the tables, weaving light and shadow into a quiet atmosphere.

I chose a seat by the window, where I could see the sky growing darker and the streetlights in the distance slowly coming on one by one. I sat down and lightly touched the materials on the table with my fingers. The clay was soft and moist, with a cool, earthy feeling. The teacher came over and asked with a smile, “What would you like to make today?” I wasn’t quite sure. After hesitating for a moment, I answered, “I want to try making a cup, something simple.”

At the beginning, my fingers actually felt a little tense when they touched the clay, as if I were handling something fragile. Under the teacher’s guidance, I gradually steadied my hands and placed the clay in the center of the wheel. When the wheel started up, it gave off a low hum, and the vibration traveled from my fingertips into my palms. I carefully adjusted the shape of the clay, feeling a bit of damp friction at my fingertips and the fine, slightly rough texture of the earth. The teacher occasionally stood nearby to remind me, “Use a lighter touch. Keep your hands steady. Don’t rush.” Her voice was gentle, which helped me relax a little.

When the wind blew in from outside the window, I felt a faint sheen of sweat on my forehead. The concentration made me forget time, and even the pile of trivial matters at work. I gradually pulled out the beginnings of a cup shape. It wasn’t very smooth, but you could already tell what it was supposed to be. I felt a little excited, yet also somewhat uncertain, as if afraid it might suddenly collapse. During the final shaping, the clay slowly became firmer, and my fingers grew slightly numb, as if I had been holding something tightly for a very long time without letting go.

The teacher came over to take a look and said with a smile, “For your first time, this is already very good. Want to try glazing it?” I nodded and took the cup over to the kiln. Through the half-open kiln door, I could feel the heat of the fire rushing toward me, and my face grew slightly warm. The glazing process was slow, and the moment the color was brushed on, I suddenly felt as if I were coating some kind of emotion with a protective film.

By the time the cup was finally fired, more than two hours had passed. I picked it up and found the glaze a little uneven, but overall it looked acceptable. On the way home, I carefully packed the cup into a box, afraid it might get knocked around on the road. That subtle sense of accomplishment slowly seeped into my heart, like a small lantern quietly lighting the way.

When I finally got home, I put the cup on the table and poured in some water to see if it leaked. It didn’t; the cup held the water perfectly. That made me smile. Although it wasn’t perfect, it was already the product of my own hands. In the days that followed, whenever I saw this cup, I felt a strange sense of peace, as if it were reminding me that some things don’t have to be perfect—just truly existing is enough.

The stage lights gradually dimmed, and the surrounding audience began to lower their voices. With a faint breeze, I could smell the damp scent rising from the grass. In my ears were the soft, hushed murmurs of people talking among themselves; some deliberately kept their voices low, but they were still clearly audible. I looked up at the sky. As night approached, it had taken on a deep blue hue, with a few stars flickering uncertainly.

When the actors came on stage, the crowd fell silent at once. I was sitting in the third row, with a view that let me clearly see their expressions and body language. This play had been recommended by a friend, who said it was an experimental avant-garde piece and very creative. I was somewhat resistant to this kind of event myself, always worried that I might not understand it properly or that my reaction would be lacking, but I couldn’t refuse because of my friend’s recommendation. Not long after it began, the actors started guiding the plot forward with exaggerated movements and highly metaphorical lines, and I found myself gradually unable to keep up with the rhythm. A tense feeling slowly crept up inside me.

“What do you think this plot is alluding to?” I turned and asked my friend beside me in a low voice. She smiled faintly and said, “Hmm, maybe it’s a satire of reality?” Her tone sounded relaxed and matter-of-fact, but I immediately sensed a kind of perfunctory indifference, or perhaps dismissiveness. My heart suddenly sped up, and sweat seeped into the palms of my hands. Had I asked a particularly stupid question? Did that make it seem like I completely failed to grasp the deeper meaning of the play?

Halfway through the performance, the actors posed an open-ended question and invited the audience to join the discussion. Responses rose one after another around us; my friend also raised her hand and spoke clearly and coherently, earning a round of applause and approval as soon as she finished. I sat in my seat, my legs stiffly crossed, my back pressed into the chair from tension. My mind raced, trying to piece together a “smart” answer. But every time I came up with an idea, another voice in my head immediately poured cold water on it: “That’s too superficial.” “Will people laugh at you?” “If someone argues with you, how will you respond?” In the end, I stayed silent, my fingers gripping the edge of the chair tightly.

After the performance, my friend turned back and asked what I thought. Her gaze was gentle, and she wore a smile, but I still instinctively felt that there was some kind of expectation hidden in that smile, perhaps even a trace of concealed sarcasm. “It was pretty good, I guess, just a little deep,” I said softly, trying to keep the tremor out of my voice. She nodded. “Yeah, that style really isn’t easy to understand.” A simple reply, yet it felt like a thorn piercing my mind — was she implying that I didn’t understand the play at all? Was she subtly suggesting that I simply didn’t have enough appreciation?

That night when I got home, I lay in bed turning over and over without being able to sleep, replaying again and again the scene in which I had not spoken up. I blamed myself for being too cowardly and for missing the chance to show myself; then I kept imagining that if I had had the courage to raise my hand, how much more perfectly I could have answered. My chest tightened in waves, and my stomach ached faintly as well. I sat up in bed to drink some water, but it didn’t ease the anxiety inside me.

Over the next few days, I began avoiding talking to that friend about the play. Even when she brought up related topics, I would unconsciously steer the conversation away, afraid she might mention my reaction that night. Deep down, there was always a voice blaming me: Why are you always like this? No matter how hard you try, your sensitivity and hesitation keep holding you back.

The lights in the conference room always felt a bit harsh, especially when I was already nervous. I sat in the middle of the room, surrounded by my colleagues. Our manager was talking about this month’s goals, and my heartbeat quickened; it almost seemed as if I could hear the air moving around me. I adjusted my chair and felt a slight pressure against my back. Today it was my turn to report on a project’s progress, and I silently rehearsed my remarks in my head.

“Next, let’s hear about your progress,” the manager said, pointing at me. I stood up, cleared my throat, and began presenting my slides. My voice sounded a little dry, and without thinking I pinched the cuff of my sleeve. The first slide appeared, with a pale blue patterned background and somewhat small text. A trace of unease suddenly rose in my mind: “Will they be able to see it clearly?”

My colleagues’ eyes gathered on me, and I could feel my palms beginning to sweat slightly. Someone in the audience coughed softly, and I instinctively took it as a sign of dissatisfaction with me, my cheeks immediately growing warm, as if they had been lightly licked by flames. I continued my report, trying to keep my pace steady.

“Here, we ran into some technical issues, but I believe there will be a solution soon,” I said. After saying this, I lifted my eyes and quickly swept across everyone’s expressions, catching some subtle, barely noticeable changes. My mind raced, trying to interpret what those expressions meant, but I soon suppressed those thoughts again. “Just finish what you’re saying,” I reminded myself.

After the presentation ended, I looked toward the manager. He nodded in approval, and only then did I relax a little and sit back down. The meeting continued, but my thoughts seemed to remain stuck in those few minutes just now.

Back at my desk, the text on the computer screen seemed especially glaring, and my mood was somewhat complicated. I kept feeling that my performance hadn’t been very good, that I must have said something wrong somewhere. But I couldn’t recall any specific details, only a vague sense of unease.

That night, lying in bed with my eyes closed, the scene in the conference room surfaced again in my mind. Those uneasy feelings lingered like a breeze that wouldn’t die down, accompanying me as I drifted off to sleep.

A few days later, I realized that everyone seemed not to care much about that presentation, and everything around me carried on as usual. That made me feel a little more at ease, though I still faintly felt that next time I must do better.

The poetry reading was held in a small arts center in the middle of the city. As I strolled in, a night breeze and the faint scent of flowers came toward me. The lighting in the hall was dim, and the walls were covered with works from different artists, creating a feeling that was both rich and slightly oppressive. My heart raced as I looked at the faces of the audience; they were whispering to one another, with soft laughter occasionally drifting through the room. I kept rehearsing in my mind what it would be like once I got onstage: what if I spoke too fast, too quietly, or forgot my lines? These thoughts kept circling endlessly in my head.

At last it was my turn to go onstage and recite. My steps felt heavy, and my throat tightened as if someone were squeezing my chest. I walked up to the stage and stood in front of the microphone, trying to steady my breathing, only to find that my palms were already sweating. I began to recite, my voice echoing through the sound system, yet I still doubted whether I was speaking clearly enough. I kept watching the audience’s reactions; some were talking, while others stared at me with no discernible expression. I felt uneasy inside: did they dislike my work? Did they think my recitation was dull and uninteresting? My stomach began to ache faintly.

After a round of applause, I returned to my seat, filled with frustration and shame. I tried hard to recall every detail from the stage and reflected repeatedly on whether I had made any mistakes. My heartbeat was still rapid, and it seemed as though I could hear the flow of my own blood in my ears. After the event ended, I went with a few friends to a nearby bar for drinks and couldn’t help asking what they thought of my performance. “You did very well,” a friend said. “You just seemed a little nervous.” I nodded and smiled, yet I was still frustrated by my own nervousness.

Over the next few days, I kept replaying when and why I had felt so helpless, my heart full of unease and fear. I felt powerless in the face of my sensitivity and anxiety, unable to completely break free from them. Whenever I thought back to the scene of the recital, I always felt hollow inside, as if I had lost something important. I began to question my abilities and my worth, and I feared having to face such public situations again. In the end, I decided to try recording everything in writing, hoping that through writing I might find a way to release and relieve myself.

Outside the little theater on the street corner, a spring breeze brushed across my face as I waited for the doors to open. Warm sunlight spilled over the road, but my palms were slightly sweaty. I had been looking forward to this experimental theater performance for a long time, and a mixture of unease and anticipation stirred inside me. I took out my phone and scrolled through messages, but I couldn’t fully focus, only mechanically swiping the screen. At last, the theater doors opened and people began filing in. The ticket checker’s smile made me relax a little. “Welcome, hello,” she said softly. I nodded in response, trying hard not to look so nervous. 

The lights were dim. I found my seat, and as I sat down, I noticed someone familiar beside me. It was another creator from our school. A wave of unease rose in my heart as I remembered our disagreement at the last club event. “What a coincidence,” I said quietly, forcing a smile. He nodded, his gaze drifting restlessly toward the stage, offering no reply. That coldness made my heart race, and my stomach felt tightly clenched. 

The lights in the theater gradually dimmed further, and the music began. I tried to concentrate on the stage as the actors started performing. But the sound effects were a bit harsh, and the lighting onstage kept shifting unpredictably, making it even harder for me to focus. The repeatedly recurring scenes and faint lines of dialogue left my attention drifting. I began to reflect on that unpleasant conversation between us, anxiety tightening inside me. I kept turning over his reaction just now in my mind: “Did I say something wrong? Is he still angry?” I scrutinized every glance and every subtle expression, as if the scrutiny beyond the play itself had become a kind of self-judgment. These thoughts made me unconsciously grip the armrest of my seat; my fingertips touched the cold metal, and I felt a faint sting. All of this only made me more anxious. 

After it ended, I hurried out of my seat and decided to linger a little longer before leaving, hoping I might get a chance to talk with him. Outside the theater, a spring breeze mixed with the scent of flowers swept toward me, and I could hear other audience members talking nearby. I tried to calm the turmoil inside me and waited by the exit. At last, he emerged from the theater’s shadows. 

“The performance was pretty good,” I tried to start a conversation. He hesitated slightly, his gaze unfocused. “Yeah, some of the ideas were quite original.” His tone was still flat, and I gave an uneasy smile, trying to keep the conversation going. 

When I got home, I still felt heavy-hearted. That night, I kept wondering whether I had done something wrong, trying to piece together a reasonable explanation to ease the unease inside me. I tossed and turned in bed, feeling as though I were struggling in an endless ocean, until dawn finally came and I drifted into a drowsy sleep.

The office in the afternoon always makes people drowsy. After typing out my last email at the computer, I shut it down, picked up my backpack, and went straight to a newly opened café near the company. I had heard that its décor was very interesting, and that there were several unique pour-over coffees on the menu, so I wanted to check it out.

When I walked in, the brass bell on the door gave off a crisp sound. The interior was lit with warm yellow light, and the grain of the wooden tables and chairs looked richly textured. I caught the scent of freshly ground coffee beans mixed with a faint woody aroma in the air, which made me feel very relaxed. A staff member in a dark green apron smiled and said, “Welcome.” I nodded slightly and asked casually, “Which pour-over coffee do you recommend?” She recommended beans from Ethiopia, saying they had citrus and floral notes. I ordered that cup and found a seat by the window.

Outside, the sky was gradually darkening. Pedestrians along the street hurried by, but inside the shop there was a different rhythm. Every table had a small lamp, and the soft light fell across the tabletop. I looked up and saw a couple talking quietly, occasionally smiling at each other; in the corner, someone wearing headphones was bent over a laptop, typing. I thought this shop seemed to have really found its niche, like a little harbor from the storm. I took out a notebook I’d left unused for a long time, opened to a blank page, and began writing down ideas and notes that usually came to mind.

When the coffee was brought over, I noticed the cup was interesting too, made of an irregular ceramic with a warm, pleasant feel in the hand. I took a sniff and, sure enough, caught a hint of citrus fragrance. When I tasted it, it was a little sour, but very clean. Before long, soft jazz began playing in the café, with a somewhat hazy saxophone accompaniment. I suddenly realized that I hadn’t sat alone like this, taking in my surroundings, for a very long time. Most of the time, I was either rushing through work or at home sinking into endless chores and rumination.

After I’d written a few pages of notes, night had fully fallen. I looked up at the window, where the glass reflected the café’s interior; the warm yellow lights seemed even cozier in the darkness. Time had passed quickly, but I didn’t feel restless at all. I finished the coffee in my cup, stood up, nodded to the staff member, said, “Thank you, it was delicious. Goodbye,” then turned and left the café. A cool breeze blew in outside, and I felt much more awake.

After I got home, I put the notes on the table and flipped through them casually. Although the content was still scattered, I felt as though I had captured some interesting ideas that I could continue to develop. That state of mind gave me a subtle sense of fulfillment and calm.

I walked into the office, and sunlight poured in through the window. The desk was already piled high with documents. I thought to myself that I had to get all of these files printed out today. The office was filled with the sounds of activity, with the phone ringing and the clatter of keyboards rising and falling all around. A faint aroma of coffee lingered in the air, and I took a deep breath, hoping the day would go smoothly. Suddenly, my printer started flashing a red light and making urgent beeping noises. My heart sank, and a wave of anxiety washed over me in an instant. I moved closer to the printer, trying to figure out what was wrong. I pressed every button and checked every connection. “What’s going on?” I muttered to myself, my palms starting to sweat and my heart racing. It seemed as if the printer was working against me; every time I thought I had solved the problem, it would start stopping again for no reason. I began to wonder whether I had accidentally changed some setting while organizing the files yesterday. And so my mind started turning over last night’s events, wondering if I had been too careless. Xiao Wang from the office came over and smiled slightly. “Need any help?” I looked at him, embarrassment rising in me, and replied a little hastily, “No, no need. I can handle it myself.” In truth, I secretly hoped he would help me, but my words preemptively rejected his offer. Xiao Wang shrugged and left, and I felt somewhat disappointed, and also a little annoyed with my own reaction. Just as I was struggling to fix the malfunction, the phone rang again. I answered it, and it was a client calling. I tried to make my voice sound natural. “Hello, please hold on. I’ll handle it as soon as possible.” After hanging up, I took a deep breath toward the printer and told myself to stay calm. I rubbed my shoulders, trying to relax my muscles. I spent the whole morning wrestling with this little problem. Finally, just before noon, I found the cause: a paper jam. I let out a long sigh, and instantly the air around me seemed lighter. At noon, I had coffee with my coworkers in the kitchen. I like these little office breaks, when everyone chats about everyday odds and ends. I mentioned the printer problem from the morning, and Xiao Zhang said with a smile, “Next time you run into a problem, come find me. I’m a printer repair expert.” I laughed too, and the tension and unease in my heart seemed to be peeled away a little. When I got home from work that evening, I felt much more relaxed. Lying in bed that night, I realized today’s troubles hadn’t affected me for very long at all—it was just a small episode.

At lunchtime, my colleagues and I walked into the fast-food restaurant near the company. The place was noisy with voices all around, and the clatter of plates and utensils came and went. The smell of fried chicken filled the air, and my stomach began to rumble in response. The line was long, and I started to feel a little irritable, with a slight sweat breaking out on my forehead. I chatted with my colleagues about the morning’s work strategy, trying to make the time pass more quickly.

"I think we should try another approach; it might be more effective," one colleague suggested. I nodded in agreement, but another colleague disagreed.

"No, I don’t think that would be better; it could backfire," she said, with a somewhat firm tone. My heart tightened, and I worried that this small discussion might turn into an unnecessary argument.

"Maybe we can try it first and then decide which is better?" I interjected, trying to ease the tension, my heartbeat quickening and my palms growing a little sweaty.

After getting our lunch, we found a corner and sat down. Just after taking a bite of my hamburger, I couldn’t help saying again, "Actually, everyone’s ideas are good; they just need to be brought into alignment in terms of direction."

No one responded, and the atmosphere became a little quiet. I lowered my head and stared at the fries in my hand, thinking over and over: Was I talking too much? Would they think I was meddling? These thoughts made me feel somewhat at a loss.

After lunch, we each returned to our desks. I opened my computer and tried hard to focus on the work in front of me. But fragments of the conversation kept lingering in my mind. I realized that perhaps it had only been a minor disagreement, nothing worth making a fuss over, yet I still couldn’t help overthinking it.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mood in a tangle. I tried to convince myself that disagreements at work were normal and that maybe everything would be back to normal tomorrow. A few days later, when I discussed things with my colleagues again, they all seemed to have forgotten that little incident. But I knew that this small sense of anxiety could come back at any time.

Sunlight streamed through the glass windows of the company building, refracting into a blinding glare. The people in the office seemed used to it, but I found it somewhat uncomfortable. The afternoon air was stifling, so I decided to go to the rooftop garden to get some fresh air. As I climbed the stairs, each step was accompanied by an increasing heartbeat; for some reason, I felt uneasy. Pushing open the door to the garden, a breeze mixed with the scent of flowers and plants greeted me. I took a deep breath, trying to calm the restlessness inside me.

There were only a few coworkers there whom I didn’t usually interact with. I sat on a wooden bench near the edge, gazing at the city skyline in the distance. Just then, I heard someone calling me. Looking up, I saw my supervisor walking toward me with several colleagues. They had also decided to come out and relax.

“Hey, why are you hiding here all by yourself?” my supervisor said to me with a smile. I gave an awkward smile in return. “Oh, I just came out for some air. The weather really is stifling.”

“How about helping us settle a debate,” my supervisor continued. “We were just discussing next month’s project goals. Do you think Zhang’s strategy is better, or Li’s?” He said it in a half-joking tone, but I found it a little harsh, perhaps a test of me.

In an instant, sweat slid down my forehead, and my palms grew damp. I felt my heart pounding as if it were about to jump out of my chest. A voice inside me began to speak: “Is this hinting that I’m not proactive enough about the project? Or that I’m not involved enough in the team?”

A wave of intense self-doubt washed over me, yet I forced out a few words, “Um, they both have good ideas. I think combining them might work better.” My supervisor glanced at me, nodded slightly, and then turned the conversation to the other colleagues.

Throughout it all, my stomach tightened, as if a heavy stone were sinking inside it. The clock on the wall ticked on, with only half an hour left until that important presentation. I gripped the mouse tightly and realized my palms were already soaked with sweat; the dampness only made me more nervous. A coworker’s voice came from beside me: “Are you ready? Don’t blow it—this is the key battle for our team.” My heart sank, and my pulse began to race, each beat seeming to warn me of the disaster that might be about to unfold.

“Good luck!” He patted me on the shoulder, but all I felt was a chill across it, and when he left, he left me alone with my fear of failure. I quickly flipped through the slides, telling myself over and over that I knew the content by heart, yet the unease in my chest would not go away.

By the time I was in the conference room, more than a dozen pairs of eyes were fixed on me, and the air was thick with subtle pressure. I stood in front of the projector, my fingers trembling slightly when they touched the mouse. “Hello everyone, I’m…” My voice echoed through the empty room. But my inner voice kept questioning me: “They’ll realize I’m not good enough. They’ll be disappointed.”

About halfway through, I felt a dull pain begin in my stomach, and beads of sweat slid down my back. The content on the slides seemed to blur before my eyes, and I struggled to stay focused, determined not to fall apart in front of everyone. Suddenly, I heard quiet conversations, and it felt as though they were criticizing and mocking me. Though it was only an illusion, it quickly shattered my fragile defense.

When the presentation ended, I forced a mechanical smile and thanked them, then hurried out of the conference room, filled with shame and regret. In the bathroom mirror, my face was as pale as paper, and my hands clutched the edge of the sink as I tried to calm myself down. My heart was still pounding furiously, and I felt as though I were fighting an endless battle.

On the way home, the noise of the streets made me even more unsettled, as if every sound were urging me to reflect on today’s failure. The whole evening, I kept replaying those embarrassing moments, unable to stop myself from feeling disappointed in who I was.

A few days later, I could still clearly feel that sense of helplessness, as if I were trapped in some kind of mire, sinking deeper the more I struggled. I tried to make up for it by working even harder, but the sense of something being fundamentally wrong with me followed me like a shadow, constantly eroding my confidence.

The fluorescent lights in the conference room were a little harsh on the eyes, and the air inside felt somewhat stuffy with more than a dozen people in the room. I sat at the edge of the meeting table, my heartbeat picking up uneasily. I always felt as if my coworkers’ eyes were on me, even though most of the time they were looking at the presentation slides. The project manager was explaining the progress of the project, and her voice seemed amplified in my ears, making me even more nervous.

“Next, we need to discuss the strategy for the next phase,” the manager said, then let her gaze sweep over us. My stomach suddenly tightened, and I had a bad feeling. The brief silence in the room made me realize that I was supposed to speak, but my mind went blank; all I could hear was the beating of my own heart.

“I think we should consider increasing our social media promotion,” I finally said, my voice slightly trembling. After speaking, I sneaked a glance at my coworkers, and their reactions made me even more uneasy.

“Social media?” one of the more senior coworkers said, his tone tinged with a hint of skepticism. “But according to our market research, the target customer base is mainly concentrated in offline channels.”

At that, my throat went dry, and the sound of my heartbeat grew clearer in my ears. My cheeks felt hot, as if everyone were scrutinizing my suggestion. I was afraid they would think I was unprofessional, or even laugh at my unrealistic idea in their hearts.

“I just think we could try a different approach,” I said, trying hard to keep my voice steady, though inside I was already berating myself over and over for not having prepared a better reason in advance.

The meeting went on, and I could hardly concentrate anymore. My mind was full of the conversation from just now and their reactions. I began to doubt my own ability: Why was I always unable to express my opinions confidently? Why did I always feel as though others were judging me?

At lunch, I sat alone in the company break room, the air filled with the aroma of coffee. I stared at the coffee cup in my hand, my thoughts in chaos, and my palms were actually slightly damp with sweat. Although it was over, the self-doubt and shame in my heart still would not go away.

That night, lying in bed, I thought about everything that had happened that day. I began to blame myself for always overanalyzing other people’s reactions, for always caring so much about what others thought. Even so, I still couldn’t stop these thoughts, as if they had become part of my life and could never be shaken off.

A few days later, my coworkers were still as friendly to me as ever, and they did not look down on me because of that meeting. That gave me a quiet sense of relief, but at the same time I realized that my unease came from a sense of inadequacy inside me, and that I needed to work hard to overcome it.

Sunlight streamed through the window and fell across the conference room table, while the scent of coffee filled the air. The team was discussing a new project. Sitting in my chair, I felt cold all over and my heart was racing. I tried to sort out my thoughts in my head, preparing to bring up an idea I believed was good. Finally, after a moment of hesitation, I spoke: “I think we could try another approach; it might be more effective.” My voice sounded faint, almost as if I were asking for something.

After I finished, the leader merely glanced over at me and then continued discussing the suggestions others had made, as though mine had never existed. My stomach began to tighten, and tiny beads of sweat appeared on my forehead. I looked around, trying to find support in my colleagues’ expressions, but they all seemed occupied with their own thoughts, and no one noticed my unease.

“Regarding this issue, I think...” the leader went on, completely ignoring my suggestion. I felt as if I had been placed inside a transparentcover, my voice erased and my presence stripped away. I began to wonder whether I really shouldn’t be here. A strong sense of shame welled up in me, as if I had been rejected in front of everyone. I thought of all those past failures and embarrassing moments, and it seemed as though they had all come back to mock me.

After the meeting ended, I walked out of the conference room feeling down. The air in the office grew heavy, and every step felt like I was dragging heavy shackles. I returned to my desk and tried to keep working, but my thoughts remained trapped in the scene from moments ago. Even simple tasks became hard to continue, and I felt powerless.

That evening, I sat on the sofa at home, my mind endlessly replaying the scene from the morning’s meeting. Those moments of being ignored and dismissed kept tormenting me, leaving me unbearably lonely. I began to worry about work the next day, afraid that I would encounter the same situation again. When I tried chatting with friends, I still couldn’t shake off that sense of loss.

After a few days, with the support of other colleagues, I slowly began trying to raise my suggestion again and found some positive feedback. That lifted me a little. Although self-doubt was still there, I began to realize that it was only my deeply rooted fear.

Five minutes after I sent the email, my phone screen lit up with a new message—it was a reply from the client. They mentioned that several pieces of data above didn’t match. My heart sank, and sweat had already begun to bead in my palms. “What happened? I clearly checked it three times before sending the email. If there’s a problem here, won’t I have to do it all over again?” I frantically searched my mind for possible mistakes, but my eyes stayed fixed on the email body on the computer screen, too afraid to look away, and my breathing grew shallow.

My supervisor, carrying a cup of coffee, walked by behind me and casually said, “The client has given feedback on some issues. Move quickly and get it sorted.” His tone didn’t sound especially emotional, but I somehow felt deep dissatisfaction. “As expected, this time it must be my carelessness. Am I simply not capable of handling this job?” My stomach tightened as if it had been grabbed, and the text on the computer screen was already starting to blur.

With trembling hands, I typed on the keyboard and reopened the email attachment. The date format was wrong—my mind was instantly filled with self-reproach: “So it was such a low-level mistake! If even something like this can go wrong, am I just not suited for this role at all?”

It took me ten minutes to fix the spreadsheet, but I still didn’t dare click “Reply.” My anxiety had spread into an indescribable sense of pressure; my shoulders were stiff as stone, and my heartbeat kept quickening. Again and again, I pictured the client’s disappointment over the spreadsheet error and my supervisor’s impatient expression. I even began imagining that my supervisor might directly criticize me, or even threaten to fire me. “No, if I get reprimanded, how should I respond? How should I apologize to calm them down?” I repeatedly rehearsed in my mind the wording for defending myself and apologizing.

At last, I gathered the courage to send the corrected file, along with a sincere apology. Watching the send button turn gray, I closed my eyes and took several deep breaths. But that relief didn’t last long. For the rest of the time, I kept mentally simulating how the client might react after seeing the apology—some reactions cold and distant, others a helpless sigh.

That night, I lay in bed unable to fall asleep. The details of the day played over and over in my mind like a movie on loop—the smell of the printer, the spreadsheet on the computer, the wording of the client’s email, all constantly intruding on my thoughts. I even began imagining how I would tell my family if, in the worst-case scenario, I were reassigned or even dismissed. The next morning, my stomach ached faintly. I didn’t want to eat breakfast, but I forced myself to swallow some bread. Soon after, the client’s reply made me sigh in relief—they very politely accepted my corrected file, but one sentence gave me pause: “Please pay attention to the details next time.” Somehow, that sentence seemed to carry hidden blame and belittlement, and I fell back into self-criticism, repeatedly wondering how I could improve so I wouldn’t disappoint others again.

The meeting room was dazzlingly bright, bright enough that the floating dust could almost be seen. I sat in a seat near the door, both hands gripping the edge of the conference table, my fingertips already turning slightly pale. The leader stood at the head of the table, waving a proposal in her hand, and that proposal was the one I was responsible for. Her tone was cold and precise, every sentence seeming to dissect the flaws in my heart. Suddenly she raised her voice: “How could such a mistake happen? Did you do the basic checks?” My stomach spasmed, as if being tugged by a hook. Just as I was about to explain, she pressed on sharply: “This isn’t a personal issue, it’s an attitude problem!”

The surrounding silence was like a vacuum, broken only by the brush of a few people lowering their heads to take notes. I could feel my colleagues’ gazes; they didn’t look directly at me, yet they were all caught up in a tacit act of watching. My face began to burn, my breathing became broken and uneven, and my heartbeat pounded against my eardrums. By the time her last sentence landed, my mind had already fallen into chaos: Did she no longer trust me? Did she think I wasn’t good enough? Was she waiting for me to resign? I tried to tell myself this was just criticism, but another voice kept whispering: everyone knows you’re a failure.

At last I gathered the courage to say, “This issue was indeed my mistake. I’ll make adjustments and optimize it so that next time it won’t—” Before I could finish, she cut me off: “It’s not a matter of next time. The key is that your attitude right now is very disappointing!” Her eyes were icy, as if every needle prick were declaring my irredeemability.

My palms were already starting to sweat, but I didn’t dare wipe them,can only let the dampness make my grip feel slick and unstable. Every face before me blurred; all I could hear was the nonstop roar of my heartbeat. After the meeting, when I walked back to my desk, my steps were almost unsteady, as if I were treading on loose sand.

That night I lay in bed, unable to fall asleep no matter how I turned. I replayed her words “very disappointing” over and over, as if chewing repeatedly on a bitter pit. I felt as though I had been exiled to a lonely island, with everyone watching my struggle from afar. I began to doubt whether I was suited for this job, even wondering if my abilities had been fooling me all along. I tried to confide in a friend, but swallowed the conversation back down, afraid they would think I was exaggerating. The stomachache lasted all night, making me almost wonder at one point whether I needed to go to the hospital for a checkup.

The next day at the company, I deliberately avoided making any eye contact with my leader and just completed my tasks mechanically. I even didn’t dare go to the break room, for fear of running into any colleague. I felt cut off from the group, like a lost bird flying without direction; even when faced with a smile, I worried whether contempt was hidden behind it.

The humble little tailor shop at the street corner made me stop in my tracks. On the glass display window was a yellowing sign that read: “Clothing repair, alterations, mending.” I pushed open the door and was met by a strong smell of thread ends and a faint oily scent, mixed with a trace of mildew from old fabric. The shop was tiny. On the left stood a wooden worktable piled high with cut fabric; on the right was an old-fashioned sewing machine, even its spool pins flecked with rust. Several rows of colorful thread spools hung in the corner, and the weak sunlight filtering in from the window made them look especially vivid. I lowered my head and touched the cuff of my coat. The tiny hole and frayed threads made it look worn with age, but I still couldn’t bring myself to throw it away. After all, it had accompanied me through many cold winters.

A skinny old tailor came out from a small room in the back. Wearing a pair of reading glasses slid down his nose, he smiled and asked, “Need something repaired?” I held up the cuff and said, “Could you mend this for me?” He took the coat, felt the hole with his fingers, and nodded. “I can fix it, but the thread color may be a little off.”

“No problem. It doesn’t need to be perfect,” I said with a smile.

He spread the coat out on the worktable, used a mottled pair of scissors to snip off the loose threads, then skillfully drew out a spool of dark gray thread. I stood nearby, watching his fingers thread the needle with fine, practiced movements. Each stitch quietly sank into the fabric, occasionally making a faint rustling sound. I could hear the occasional creak of the machine’s wheel turning, and the tailor shop clock’s ticking every few dozen seconds.

I felt strangely calm, even a little reassured. That sense of peace came from the quiet of the place and the old tailor’s focused movements. I couldn’t help imagining: how long would this kind of craftsmanship still be needed in this fast-paced city? Decades from now, would there still be people willing to mend clothes instead of throwing them away at a whim?

“What kind of work do you do?” the old tailor suddenly asked, after a flurry of needle and thread.

“I do content creation,” I replied a little awkwardly. “You know, writing things, filming things…” My voice gradually trailed off, because whenever I mentioned my job, I always felt it wasn’t quite “real.”

“Oh, young people all do that kind of thing,” he said without asking further, and went back to mending.

Standing there, I felt a flash of self-mockery and helplessness. His response seemed both honest and ruthless, but I did feel a little relieved—at least I didn’t have to struggle to explain how hard or meaningful my job was.

After a little over ten minutes, he looked up and said, “It’s done.” I glanced down and saw a quiet line of gray stitches lying on the cuff. Though the thread color didn’t perfectly match the original fabric, it had a kind of casual, plain beauty to it. I paid for the repair and left the tailor shop, only to find that the sky had already taken on a faint orange tint.

That night, after I got home, I held the repaired coat and felt as if I were looking at a piece of pieced-together memory. I thought that carefully mending broken things, whether clothing or everyday life, seemed to give them a new meaning. A few days later, while on a filming job, I wore that coat, and the patched cuff became a strange kind of presence—like an embellishment, yet also like some hidden mark.

The office pantry always carried a faint, damp aroma of coffee, along with a faucet that seemed to be dripping almost constantly. That noon, I walked in with my own mug, planning to make a cup of instant coffee to wake myself up. The pantry window faced the alley beside the company, where delivery riders would occasionally hurry past. The hum of motorcycle engines mixed with the footsteps of passersby and drifted in through the open window, becoming a broken, intermittent background sound.

“Do you think this month’s task assignments are fair?” My colleague Xiao Li stood beside me, holding a freshly brewed cup of black tea, and asked with a probing look on his face. His voice was low, but with a kind of sharpness that seemed deliberately restrained. I had just picked up a packet of instant coffee, and the moment I heard that, my nerves tightened at once.

“Mm... I guess so. I think they’re all about the same.” I tried to answer as naturally as possible, but I couldn’t hide the slight tremor in my voice. I stole a glance at him; the corners of his mouth seemed to pull down a little, and he lowered his head to stir his tea. “Oh, but I think the project you got should be more complex—it must be more stressful,” he added.

My heart started pounding faster, as if I had just run up a flight of stairs. My stomach also began to tighten faintly, with a subtle ache. I suddenly realized that what he might have meant was—I wasn’t capable of handling complicated tasks, or that I wouldn’t do them well. In my mind, yesterday’s project meeting flashed by instantly, and it seemed like I had been rambling incoherently during my comments; even some colleagues had exchanged subtle glances a few times. I couldn’t help replaying those scenes, wondering if everyone thought I wasn’t professional enough.

“Actually... I think it’s a bit difficult too.” I hurriedly added, trying to soften his impression of me, but as soon as the words left my mouth, even I thought they sounded somewhat timid and ingratiating. I even began to wonder if I looked too weak—whether that would deepen his negative impression of me.

Xiao Li didn’t reply, but he looked up at me, and a hard-to-read emotion flickered in his eyes. Was it contempt? Or simply thoughtfulness? I couldn’t tell at all. Maybe I was overthinking it, yet I was already overwhelmed by a sense of being dismissed. I quickly poured hot water into the coffee and ended the conversation.

But after I returned to my desk, that anxiety didn’t subside; instead, it gradually tightened every string in my mind. Every word my fingers typed on the keyboard felt heavy. Xiao Li’s words were like an invisible thorn, repeatedly prodding my doubts about my own abilities. “The tasks are complex,” “more stressful” — those phrases kept echoing in my head. I even started to wonder whether I wasn’t suited for this job. Would there come a day when, because of a few small mistakes, everyone would no longer be able to trust me?

In the days that followed, I kept thinking back to that conversation in the pantry, trying to decipher his tone and word choice, even mentally simulating his impression of me. I became increasingly cautious at work: I checked every email twice before sending it, and even my tone when speaking with colleagues grew overly careful, afraid of saying something wrong and leaving yet another bad impression.

As the elevator doors slowly closed, I squeezed in just in time. There was only one other person inside: a middle-aged man. He was wearing a dark gray trench coat and carrying a briefcase, staring straight ahead. I pressed my floor button and stood in the corner with my head down, trying hard not to look at him. A faint mechanical hum filled the elevator, and the air carried a light smell of tobacco and metal. The man’s shoes brushed against the floor with a slight creak, which sounded a little harsh.

My gaze couldn’t help drifting to my reflection in the corner. My hair looked a bit messy, and my face seemed slightly oily. Was I looking especially disheveled? I quickly pulled out my phone and used the reflection on the screen to tidy myself up a little, my heartbeat inexplicably quickening. Just then, the man suddenly reached toward the floor buttons, apparently to check his floor. I subconsciously shifted aside, but my movement was a little too hurried, and my shoe sole made a sudden tap against the floor. I felt embarrassed by my own reaction, and at the same time wondered whether he thought I was uncomfortable, or assumed I was uneasy because of what he’d done.

“It’s a bit cold today,” he said suddenly, his voice low and hoarse, as if he had just rushed back from outside. My mind went blank for an instant—was he talking to me? After a two-second pause, I managed a strained smile and said, “Yeah, it’s gotten colder lately.” My tone sounded very soft, and a little weak. As soon as I said it, I immediately started replaying my own words in my head, feeling like I might have sounded too cold. Maybe he’d think I was being rude? Or should I have said a little more, maybe talked about the weather forecast or something?

The elevator kept rising, the indicator lights ticking upward slowly. I could hear my own heartbeat thudding, and my palms were starting to sweat. I tried to relieve my tension by lightly pinching the edge of my bag with my fingertips, but somehow my hand posture only seemed even more awkward.

When the elevator stopped at the floor he had pressed, he gave a slight nod, which counted as his goodbye. I had originally wanted to say “bye” or “take care,” but after my lips moved slightly twice, I still made no sound and only watched him leave. The elevator doors slowly closed, and in an instant there was only me and my reflection left. The whole space became especially quiet. I stared at my own eyes and noticed that the hair at my temples had already fallen down, blocking part of my view.

When I got home, I turned on the light, set my bag down on the sofa, and the scene in the elevator kept replaying in my head. Why am I always so awkward? I let out a silent sigh, went to the kitchen to get a glass of water, and tried to calm myself down. I took out my phone, opened a messaging app, and wanted to chat casually with a friend, but then found I didn’t really have anything in particular to talk about. In the end, I just leaned back in my chair and absentmindedly scrolled through videos for a few minutes.

That stranger’s voice, the color of his trench coat, and the words “It’s a bit cold today” kept lingering in my mind like background noise. Though it had only been a very brief encounter, I kept mulling it over, as if I had overlooked some important meaning.

Just after the sun had set, the sky took on a soft hue somewhere between blue and orange. I walked slowly along the park’s main path, passing a few joggers here and there and pairs of people out for a stroll. The air still held a faint warmth from the sunlight that had soaked the grass during the day. I raised my coat collar; winter nights always came with a chill that felt a little abrupt, but it didn’t make me uncomfortable.

The gravel path beneath my feet looked uneven in the moonlight, and I noticed the faint crunch of my shoes pressing down on the little stones. The slower I walked, the clearer that sound became. I tried to lengthen my breathing, like the people running, keeping my breath and steps in sync as much as possible. Fallen leaves on the ground were gently stirred by the wind, occasionally brushing against my pant legs.

“Wow, so beautiful!” Two little girls ahead of me stopped and pointed toward the lake on the right. I followed their gaze and saw the surface of the lake smooth as a mirror, reflecting the glow of the tall streetlights, with a few ducks drifting lazily near the shore in the distance. I didn’t stop, just looked a little longer.

For some reason, lately I’ve kept feeling as if my head were stuffed full of all sorts of messy thoughts. Even though my time off work is my own, it still feels as though I’m being chased by some elusive emotion. Today’s work hadn’t really included anything especially difficult, but when I was writing emails just now, I kept wondering if the wording I used was still a little too impolite. Would my supervisor think I wasn’t professional enough? Everyone says to relax, but I’ve found that those three words—“relax”—are truly hard to do.

When I came near an empty bench, I hesitated, but kept walking. Stopping always feels a little unnatural; it’s more comfortable to keep moving. In the distance, I could hear accordion music coming from somewhere, the melody lively and tinged with something fairy-tale-like. I pictured the player as perhaps an old man in a rough wool coat and a knit cap, or maybe a student practicing in their spare time. The sound came and went, incomplete, but it still made me feel a little lighter.

As I passed a row of benches, a boy was tossing a ball to play with his dog. His dog didn’t seem very interested, just lying there lazily, its tail swaying slowly. He looked up and noticed me watching, and gave an absent-minded smile. I nodded and walked on past.

Just before I reached the park entrance again, I stopped, slipped my hands into my pockets, and looked up at the sky. The night had grown deeper; only a few stars were visible, but it felt as if the whole sky were relaxing. I finally let out a long breath, and my shoulders loosened a little too. Nothing special had happened, but it seemed those trivial little thoughts from before weren’t so intense anymore. I even felt that what to have for breakfast tomorrow might be more important than the wording of today’s emails.

After I got home, I opened my computer but didn’t rush to work. Instead, I casually made myself a cup of hot tea, leaned back on the sofa, and scrolled through my phone, reading the chatty messages friends had sent. The wind outside the window was soft, and I felt like I had finally found a bit of peace again.

The lights in the university activity room were dim, and the decorations on the surrounding walls gave the space an artistic atmosphere. A faint smell of paint and ink drifted through the air. On this ordinary Friday afternoon, I was taking part in a small script reading and performance session organized by the club. Sitting on the slightly worn wooden chair, I was filled with unease and anxiety.

The friends around me were enthusiastically discussing their roles, while I held the script in my hands and read the densely packed lines. The voices around me seemed to grow farther and farther away. I tried desperately to concentrate, but images of failure kept surfacing uncontrollably in my mind. I imagined myself stumbling through the reading, my face flushed red as everyone silently laughed at me.

“Hey, how are you feeling?” asked a classmate sitting beside me, wearing a gentle smile. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, as if a gust of wind had knocked me off balance.

“Uh, I’m a little nervous,” I forced out a smile, trying to seem more relaxed.
“That’s okay, we’re all like that. Just do your best.” His voice was soft yet firm. Still, I remained uneasy, afraid that my performance would disappoint everyone.

While waiting for things to begin, I felt my palms growing damp, and a dull ache started in my stomach. My thoughts involuntarily drifted back to the past, to similar occasions when I had lost the ability to speak because of nervousness. This fear and guilt were like invisible chains, binding me tightly.

As the activity began, it was my turn to go on. I took a deep breath and stood up, feeling my knees tremble slightly. I tried to walk steadily to the front, script in hand, attempting to meet the eyes coming toward me. Drawing a deep breath to suppress those anxious feelings, I began reading my part, and all I could seem to hear was my own trembling voice.

After the reading ended, I returned to my seat, but the tension in my heart had not completely faded. From time to time, I wondered whether I had missed any important lines, and whether anyone might be laughing at me in their heart. I tried to push these thoughts away and listened to the other students’ readings, hoping I could use that to calm myself down.

After the event ended, I returned to the dormitory still feeling unsettled. Over the next few days, I kept dwelling on my performance, replaying the details again and again, hoping to find something worth improving. This kind of rumination left me exhausted, but it seemed unavoidable.

The next day, I decided to try relaxing and told myself that these small mistakes were simply part of learning, so that this anxiety would no longer affect my performance in club activities.

The moment I walked into the office, I could feel that familiar pressure quietly building. The air was filled with the aroma of coffee, and I headed for the automatic coffee machine downstairs, hoping a strong cup would ease my anxiety. However, my colleague was standing by the machine, trying to troubleshoot it and seeming a bit impatient. When I went over to greet him, he looked up at me, and his expression seemed somewhat complicated.

“Good morning. Is the coffee machine acting up again?” I asked in an attempt to sound casual, hoping to ease his irritation.

“Yeah, that’s right. Anyway, this is the second time today.” His tone was a little heavy, with a hint of annoyance.

My heart started racing, as if I had been gripped by some unease in an instant. I wondered whether I had disturbed him, or whether my greeting had made him uncomfortable. I lowered my head and tried to focus on the coffee machine’s buttons, but the voice inside me would not quiet down.

My palms began to sweat, and my nervousness kept intensifying. To keep the awkward silence from dragging on too long, I tried to keep the conversation going. “Hopefully we can get through today smoothly. This machine always breaks down at the busiest times.” I tried to keep my voice steady, but I couldn’t help raising it a little.

He seemed to hear me. After a moment of silence, he spoke again, but his tone was stillcold and indifferent. “Yeah, it’s really annoying. I hope it gets fixed soon.”

I forced out a smile and quickly left the machine with my coffee. But inside, I was already churning, replaying the conversation in my head and analyzing every word and sentence to death. Had I said something wrong? Was his displeasure because of me? My stomach began to ache faintly, as if I could not stop this self-attack.

When I got back to my desk, the coffee in my hand felt scorching, and I could hardly enjoy it. Every interaction with a colleague seemed to become a trigger for my anxiety, as if the air were filled with rejection and dissatisfaction. I spent the whole day in that mood, my heart as heavy as a stone.

A few days later, this incident was still echoing in my mind, even though it had only been an unintentional misunderstanding. I finally decided to ask that colleague about it, hoping to clarify things and apologize for any offense I might have caused. To my relief, he said he hadn’t felt uncomfortable at all and instead thanked me for my concern. The weight I’d been carrying finally lifted, though I still couldn’t completely shake off the unease.

This experience made me more determined than ever to challenge my tendency to overinterpret and catastrophize. Every random exchange should not become a source of panic. I have to learn to find balance in the complexity of social interactions.

On a winter afternoon, with the cold wind biting through me, I wrapped my scarf tightly around my neck and walked into the Museum of Modern Art in the center of the city. The museum’s heating washed over me, and the warm air carried a faint smell of plaster. My friend and I had agreed to meet here to see an art exhibition we had been looking forward to for a long time. In the hallway, the smooth floor gleamed under the dim yellow lights, the exhibits were neatly arranged all around, and the walls were covered with masterpieces by great artists. I was full of admiration for these works and eager to share my excitement with my friend.

After waiting for ten minutes, my friend finally arrived. I forced a smile, trying to ease my own slight tension. My friend gave a small nod, but his tone sounded cold: “You’re here.” My heart tightened, and my pulse suddenly quickened. I couldn’t help wondering whether I had done something recently to upset him. We walked side by side toward the exhibits, but inside, our inner monologues seemed to be at odds: “Did the message I sent yesterday make him misunderstand?” “Why is he talking like that?”

Standing before a huge abstract painting, I found myself focusing involuntarily on my friend’s microexpressions. Perhaps it was only a fleeting smirk, but I interpreted it as a veiled reproach. Anxiety spread rapidly; my palms began to sweat, and I felt a dull ache in my stomach. At that moment, my friend seemed to notice that something was off about my expression and asked softly, “Are you okay? You look a little strange.”

“I’m fine,” I managed a smile. “I’m just a bit tired and didn’t sleep well.” My voice trembled slightly as I tried to conceal my inner panic.

As the exhibition continued, I remained captivated by the works, but my mind was in turmoil and I couldn’t fully immerse myself. I kept thinking about how I should talk to my friend, whether I should apologize face to face. But with no clear clues, I ultimately had no choice but to stay silent and continue viewing the exhibition.

As the exhibition was nearing its end, my friend suddenly suggested stopping by a nearby café. Although I was still uneasy inside, I reluctantly nodded in agreement. In the warm aroma of coffee, I finally couldn’t hold back and asked the question that had been weighing on me: “Did I do something to make you unhappy?”

My friend froze for a moment, then laughed. “No, not at all. I was just really tired today, so I probably seemed a bit unenergetic.” His answer made me feel utterly relieved; the heavy stone in my heart gradually fell away, and the tension in my body slowly eased.

After I got home, I was still thinking about it. Although all the misunderstandings had been cleared up, the anxiety and unease deep inside still remained. I reminded myself not to be so sensitive next time, but I also knew it was almost an instinctive reaction, hard to resist. That night, I tried my best to relax and filled my mind with music. A few days later, I began to try interacting with friends more naturally in social situations, doing my best not to overinterpret things anymore.

The thunder on the rainy day was low and relentless as I sat in front of my office computer, waiting for an important video conference. The light in the office was dimmed by the gray rain clouds outside the window. The coffee cup on my desk was still steaming, and a faint coffee aroma lingered around me, trying to soothe my tense nerves.

The number of participants on the computer screen kept increasing, and the time inched closer to the scheduled start. My heartbeat gradually quickened, and fine beads of sweat gathered in my palms as I gripped the mouse tightly. I couldn’t help muttering to myself: “Please don’t go wrong, please don’t go wrong.”

After the meeting began, everyone’s avatars appeared on the screen one by one, and the leader’s face looked especially stern. My stomach started to feel uneasy, and the slight bloating made me restless. The meeting went relatively smoothly until it was my turn to present—then something terrible happened: the network connection suddenly dropped, and the screen was left with nothing but a lost signal icon.

“What’s the problem?” the leader’s voice came through, carrying a suppressed urgency. I couldn’t stop myself from tensing up; my body stiffened like a stone, and the buzzing in my ears mixed with my heartbeat, as if forming some strange symphony.

“I’m trying to reconnect,” I replied, striving to keep my voice steady. The signal icon on the screen turned into a spinning circle, as if mocking my helplessness. I could feel my colleagues holding their breath, waiting for me to fix it quickly.

Finally, the network came back, and I rescreen-shared my presentation. My fingers were so tense I nearly pressed the wrong key. I thought I would be met with criticism or reproach, but my colleagues typed a few “You can do it” messages in the chat, using simple words to support my confidence.

After finishing the presentation, I forced out a smile, and the tension in my body eased a little. The leader’s voice was softer than before, saying the meeting could continue. My heart finally relaxed halfway, but the other half was still knocking at my consciousness, reminding me of that brief loss of control just now.

When the meeting ended, the rain still lingered, and I sat in my chair recalling my performance. A wave of shame rose in my heart, and I felt deeply dissatisfied with my own sensitivity and flustered reaction. I knew this would be a scene replayed over and over in my mind for the next few days.

That night, I returned home with both body and mind exhausted, while the rain continued tapping against the glass outside the window. I brewed a cup of tea, trying to use its warm aroma to pull myself out of that terrible day. Although it was all over, the unease and shame that still lingered in my mind kept reminding me that there was still so much I needed to learn and grow from.

On a bright afternoon, I stood at the edge of the rooftop garden at my company, holding a folder in my arms. A gentle breeze brushed past, bringing the fresh scent of mint from the garden. I looked around and saw everyone chatting in the teams they had formed, with laughter and conversation intertwined all around me. My supervisor came over, patted me on the shoulder, and said with a smile, “Relax, kid. This is a team-building event, not a job interview.” I managed a strained smile, but inside I felt as if I were being squeezed tight. My heart began to race, my palms grew sweaty, and a knot tightened in my stomach. Situations like this made me extremely uneasy; I worried that I wouldn’t perform well enough and would become the subject of other people’s gossip.

I tried to fit in with a team and joined the discussion they were having. Yet all I did was nod mechanically, while a voice inside me kept questioning: “Do they think I’m weird? Am I completely out of place?” I kept overanalyzing their microexpressions and tone of voice, and even the slightest change made me uneasy. I even started ruminating over my past mistakes, as if every embarrassing moment were mocking me.

A coworker tried to reassure me: “Don’t be nervous, it’s fine.” But that only made me more sensitive, and I began attacking myself, with the thought repeating in my mind: “I’m just a failure.” I was overwhelmed by a deep sense of abandonment, afraid that if I didn’t do well enough, they would no longer want to work with me. During the event, I could hardly focus on anything; my anxiety made my thoughts chaotic.

After the event ended, I sat alone in a corner of the garden for a while as the noise around me gradually faded. My heartbeat slowly settled down, but the shame and self-blame still lingered. In the days after I got home, that feeling hung over me like a shadow, and whenever I tried to focus on work or anything else, those anxieties and doubts would keep surfacing in my mind.

This event made me realize just how strong my neurotic tendencies are, especially in team settings. I can’t stop attacking myself preemptively, all just to ward off outside criticism. It leaves me utterly exhausted.

A gentle breeze brushed the plants in the company’s rooftop open-air garden, and sunlight filtered through the leaves, casting dappled patterns on the ground. We were holding an impromptu brainstorming meeting here, and the surrounding greenery and blue sky made the moment seem calm. Yet inside, tension surged like a tide. The supervisor’s voice echoed in my ears: “We need a breakthrough idea for this project.” I sat on a small chair in the corner, my palms beginning to sweat slightly. I had already pondered the details of this project countless times. Even so, I couldn’t help worrying that my ideas would be rejected.

My colleagues gradually shared their opinions, and the discussion intertwined in the air. My eyes moved back and forth among them, trying to find reassurance or approval in their expressions. But all I saw were focused faces; no one noticed my inner panic. At last, it was my turn to speak. I took a deep breath and tried to keep my voice steady: “I think we could consider making some bold color choices in the user interface, for example...” Before I even finished, my heart had started pounding wildly, loud as a drum.

The supervisor nodded slightly, signaling me to continue. I hurriedly explained my design ideas, outlining my rough concept. Yet images kept flashing through my mind of the other person frowning or rejecting them. A few strands of hair were blown onto my face by the wind, and I couldn’t help reaching up to brush them aside, only to find that my hand was trembling slightly.

After the meeting ended, I stood up from my chair almost in relief, my legs feeling a little weak. My colleagues left in pairs and trios, while I slowly walked to the edge of the terrace and looked far out at the city skyline. The tension in my heart seemed to ease somewhat under the sunlight, but the feeling of always being overlooked and misunderstood still lingered.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to sleep. I replayed my performance in the meeting in my mind, worrying whether I had already left a bad impression on my supervisor. Every time I thought about those details, an invisible pressure seemed to close tightly around me.

Over the next few days, that tension still rose up from time to time, especially when I saw my colleagues discussing the project’s progress. I kept imagining possible failure, repeatedly asking myself, “Do they think I didn’t do well enough?” This constant inner torment left me utterly exhausted.

When I left the office, the sky had just begun to darken, and the streetlights were coming on one by one, washing the sidewalk in a warm yellow. The air was a little cool, but very clean, carrying a faint scent of earth mixed with fallen leaves. I carried my bag and walked home at an unhurried pace, the soles of my shoes making a soft tapping sound against the ground. Now and then a car passed by, the tires rolling over the road with a low, gentle hum.

I wasn’t thinking about anything. For me, that was actually pretty rare.

At the corner there was a small flower shop, and every time I passed it I felt it had some indescribable warmth. Today the flower stands were filled with bright bouquets, and I couldn’t help stopping. The owner was an elderly person who looked up at me with a smile and asked, “What would you like to buy today?” Their voice was soft, carrying a calmness that didn’t require any reply. I looked around carefully and chose a bouquet of pale pink carnations, their petals soft, as if they might melt in my palm at any moment.
