I handed over a banknote, and the owner gently placed the change and the flowers into my hands. Those hands were thin and bony, but steady. I thanked them and continued homeward.

Walking along with the flowers, I suddenly felt a trace of lightness in my heart. I lowered my head to look at the carnation petals and couldn’t help touching them with my fingertips; they were so delicate it was almost impossible to see any flaw. I suddenly realized that I had bought this bouquet for no reason at all—just because it was pretty, so I bought it. For someone like me, who usually has to ask, “Should I do this?” before doing anything, this tiny impulse felt like a small crack, letting something slip through.

There was none of that usual tightness in my chest. I stopped to make sure—yes, there really wasn’t. Normally, when I walk on the street, my mind is always rehearsing every possible way things could go wrong: whether I said something wrong in today’s meeting, whether the wording of that tweet might seem strange, how much is left before tomorrow’s deadline. But at that moment, all those voices were quiet. All that remained was the tapping of my shoes and the faint scent of the flowers in my hands.

There weren’t many people on the road. A child sped past me on a scooter, leaving behind a trail of laughter you could hear. I glanced at the shop window beside me; the glass reflected a blurry version of myself, along with the bouquet in my hands. In that moment, I didn’t try to analyze what the image meant. I just looked at it, then kept walking.

When I got home, I put the flowers into the small vase in the living room and placed it in the center of the table. The warm yellow light from the lamp fell on the petals, making them look almost unreal. I took a photo and sent it to a friend, and they replied, “So pretty.” That was it—nothing more. I sat on the sofa and spaced out for a while; there were no particular images in my mind, and even the annoying worries I usually had seemed to sink for the moment into some unreachable place.

That night I fell asleep earlier than usual, and more easily too.

The next morning, when I passed through the living room, I looked down at the carnations and could still catch their faint fragrance. I stood there for two seconds without thinking about anything, just standing. Then I went to pour myself a glass of water and began a new day.

During the company’s lunch break, I was the only one on the terrace. A gentle breeze brushed across my face, carrying the coolness of early autumn. In the distance, the city skyline stretched out, while sunlight filtered through the clouds and cast golden patches of light across the terrace floor. In my hand, I tightly held the project proposal feedback my supervisor had just given me, the lines full of sharp insight and merciless criticism, leaving me chilled to the bone. The murmur of the city drifted in my ears, the roar of car engines mingling with a faint hum of noise from afar; these sounds seemed like background music to the unease in my heart.

My supervisor’s words kept echoing in my mind: “The ideas here aren’t innovative enough. Have you considered other styles?” His tone was flat, yet it sliced through me like a dagger, plunging me instantly into a deep sense of frustration. I began to ruminate over past details, remembering every decision that might have been flawed. Why hadn’t I thought of a better solution? Why hadn’t I anticipated these problems in advance? These questions entangled me, making it impossible to break free.

My heartbeat quickened, and I could almost feel the pounding in my chest; cold sweat broke out in my palms. I tried to take deep breaths, trying to calm the turmoil inside me, but the harder I tried, the more tears surged uncontrollably into my eyes. I was afraid of being abandoned, of being seen as an unqualified employee, and I felt inexplicably ashamed of my own sensitivity.

“Are you okay?” A familiar voice came from behind me. It was my colleague, speaking with concern. She came over to my side, saw the proposal in my hands, and said softly, “Don’t take those comments too much to heart. They just want us to keep improving. You’ve done really well already.” I forced out a smile, but all I could feel was how fragile it was.

That night, lying in bed, I was still turning over every detail of the proposal again and again. The voices in my head churned relentlessly, leaving me almost unable to fall asleep. In the end, I decided to review the entire plan again the next morning and rethink and redesign it from a fresh perspective. Although I still felt uneasy inside, at least I had a plan of action.

A few days later, I submitted the revised proposal to my supervisor again. This time, he gave me positive feedback and even envisioned some possibilities for collaboration. Although thinking back to that day still caused a dull ache in my heart, I learned not to let those negative emotions completely crush me, and to try to turn that feedback into motivation to move forward.

The lights on the street looked a little dim and yellowish, and there was a faint chill in the air—the feeling of deep autumn was already obvious. I had just gotten off work; by the time I walked out of the subway station, it was already completely dark. The leaves on both sides of the street were falling, and every now and then the wind would blow some of them over to people’s feet. My coat was a bit thick, but I still felt somewhat cold. I didn’t want to rush home, so I slowly walked along the familiar street. There were few pedestrians on the road, and from time to time I could hear the “beep beep” of a checkout register from the little shop across the way, as well as the occasional “buzzing” of electric bikes passing by. These sounds didn’t bother me; instead, they made the quiet street feel a little more alive.

I came to the mouth of a small alley, where there was a familiar convenience store. The light at the entrance was especially bright, in stark contrast to the dim street. I paused for a moment, thinking about whether I should go in and buy something, but I didn’t feel like moving, so I kept walking. My footsteps echoed on the wet brick pavement, and that soft “tap-tap” made me feel a little relaxed. I began to think randomly about things—whether dinner should come with an extra bowl of soup, whether I should find time over the weekend to buy a desk lamp, or buy a few more books I hadn’t read yet.

On the right was a barbecue stall, and when the smell drifted over, I felt a little hungry. I heard the stall owner chatting with a customer: “Everything’s getting more expensive lately; even meat costs more.” The customer casually replied, “But your food still tastes great.” The stall owner laughed and said, “As long as I make enough to live on, and have plenty of repeat customers, that’s enough.” I smiled quietly to myself. Heaven knows whether that was just the owner’s usual routine, but the customer seemed pretty happy after hearing it. I stood there for a while but didn’t buy anything, just kept walking and looking at the storefronts of every shop within sight along the street. Orange-yellow light spilled from the windows of the shops, like a simple portrayal of life itself.

“Did I miss something?” That thought suddenly popped into my head. I didn’t mean anything by it; it was just an occasional feeling, maybe because I saw the busy people on the street and felt as though I were a completely different kind of existence from them. I didn’t feel especially lonely, but rather a plain, simple sense of contentment. Life is like this: a little chill, a little quiet, and some disconnected, fleeting moments. Surprisingly, I didn’t feel the slightest irritation, as if I were wrapped in all that gentle light and sound.

By the time I got home, it was almost seven. I hung up my coat and poured myself a glass of warm water. The house was very quiet; a few lights were on in the windows outside, and I could hear people downstairs chatting softly. I sat on the sofa and spent a while scrolling through the news on my phone. The news felt far away, but that didn’t make me uneasy. I just sat there quietly, spacing out, and then suddenly remembered the barbecue stall from my walk. I guessed that if it were a little later, it might already have been full of customers. I didn’t have any emotional reaction; I just thought that the stall owner seemed pretty good at business.

The long table in the conference room was covered with memo pads and proposal documents, and the air was filled with a mix of coffee and tension. Outside the window, the gray, overcast sky was somewhat oppressive. I sat by the window, my palms slightly sweaty, my heart racing, constantly worrying that my remarks would be rejected. Other colleagues were whispering to one another; I couldn’t make out what they were saying, and I couldn’t help wondering whether they were discussing my last proposal.

Finally, it was my turn to speak. I cleared my throat and tried to make my voice sound less shaky. “I think we could add an interactive segment to the celebration to make attendees feel more involved,” I said. When I finished, I stared at the papers on the table, avoiding eye contact with my colleagues, afraid of finding any sign of disapproval in their expressions.

“That’s actually a pretty good idea. How do you think we should implement it?” my supervisor asked in a tone I couldn’t quite interpret. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, as if it might burst out of my chest at any moment. I tried to calm myself down. “I think we could design some fun little games, or have everyone share a short story related to the company,” I added hesitantly.

After hearing me out, the supervisor nodded. “Hmm, we can discuss this further in detail.” Although he offered no clear praise or criticism, I still felt relieved.

After the meeting ended, I quickly left the conference room and stepped into the hallway, feeling a slight dizziness and a churning unease in my stomach. I needed a glass of water to settle myself. Back at my desk, I kept replaying my remarks in my mind, constantly blaming myself for not having prepared more thoroughly. All day long, I remained in this anxious, ruminating state, wondering whether my colleagues were discussing my performance behind my back.

That evening, when I got home, I still couldn’t soothe that faint sense of self-reproach. I collapsed onto the sofa and stared at the ceiling, my mind filled with worries about my future work: if my supervisor thought my idea was too immature, would I be labeled as incompetent? To keep myself from sinking deeper into a spiral of negativity, I wrote down my thoughts in my journal, trying to record the details of the day’s events in hopes of finding a way to calm myself.

This week, I noticed that my colleagues seemed, intentionally or not, to avoid mentioning that meeting. The fear of being excluded rose up in me again, though I also understood that this might just be a sign of my own oversensitivity. To keep myself from turning inward with self-attack, I decided to actively take part in the upcoming celebration preparations, hoping to improve my state of mind through action and results.

The meeting had just ended, and my coworkers swarmed into the break room to refill their coffee cups. When I went in, there was only one last packet of green tea left. I hesitated, wondering whether it was worth grabbing it or whether I should turn around and go to another floor to find something to drink. While I was looking down, torn, I vaguely heard someone behind me say, “Some people are always so quiet, like they’re invisible. I really don’t know how to communicate with them.” The voice was so light it sounded like a careless complaint, but all at once I felt as if something in my heart had been struck. Were they talking about me? I quickly turned to look, but the two coworkers had already gone, leaving only an empty corner behind.

My hand froze, my heart started pounding faster, and my stomach seemed to knot up. My mind immediately flashed back to the moment I had spoken up in the meeting just now. Was it because I’d said so little that they thought I didn’t fit in? Or had they been watching me all along, seeing how nervous I seemed, and then discussing my flaws in private? Fine beads of cold sweat began to break out on my forehead, and my palms turned clammy. The break room around me felt narrower and narrower, the air as if it were thickening, making it hard to breathe.

“What are you looking for?” My manager suddenly appeared at the door, pulling my attention back. I hurriedly set down the tea bag and forced out a smile. “Oh, just looking around. I need some water.” But I could feel how stiff the smile was, like a mask. He paused for a second, frowned, and then turned to get his coffee. I instantly started attacking myself—why was my reaction so awkward? Why did even a normal conversation feel so forced? Did I make him think I was weird? And when I thought back to that comment about being invisible, the shame almost crushed me.

I hurried out of the break room and returned to my desk, but my mind never stayed on work; it kept replaying the sentence I had just heard. During lunch, a friend texted to ask if I wanted to go to an exhibition together this weekend. I stared at the screen for a long time before replying, “Let’s decide this weekend.” For the entire afternoon, I kept going over the details of my interactions with coworkers in the meeting, hoping to find some shred of evidence proving that their “invisible person” comment wasn’t aimed at me. But no matter how I looked at it, I felt I hadn’t done well enough.

Even after I left the office, I kept turning over that remark in my mind, my emotions rising and falling, and I even began to wonder whether I should keep trying to fit in with this team. I felt irritated and powerless, like I was trapped in a maze of my own making with no way out. That night when I went to bed, my stomach began to ache faintly, as if reminding me that this day had been full of unanswered self-examination.

The atmosphere in the conference room was tense. Everyone sat along the long table, each of them flipping through the planning documents in front of them. Low rumbles of thunder rolled past outside from time to time, seeming to echo the tension in my own mind. I could feel a slight dampness on my fingertips, my heartbeat quickening, and a faint discomfort beginning in my stomach. I tried hard to concentrate, but one sentence my supervisor had just said kept flashing through my mind: “The direction of the project needs to be reconsidered.” That sentence stirred up a deep sense of anxiety within me. His tone had been calm, but I kept probing for hidden meaning behind it. Had I not done well enough? Was he disappointed in me?

My coworkers began discussing some adjustment plans, their voices overlapping, and I tried to join in, but the noise in my head was far too loud. I watched my supervisor’s expression; he was frowning slightly. I even suspected that he was blaming me. I worked hard to suppress my unease, trying to look as though I was engaged, but deep inside I kept imagining scenarios in which I would be fired.

The voices around me grew more and more distant, and even the lights in the conference room seemed to dim. Sitting there, I felt as if I were trapped in a vortex with no way out. My supervisor was saying something to another colleague, and I immediately assumed they were discussing my mistake. That thought gradually drove me into despair. To protect myself, I began preemptively criticizing myself in my head: “I’m not good enough. I’m going to fail again.” This voice grew stronger and stronger, leaving me unable to argue back.

When the meeting ended, I walked out of the conference room, and the thunder was still rolling. That night, I repeatedly replayed what had happened in the meeting, and my anxiety did not subside. On the way home, the bitterness of the coffee seemed especially strong, and I couldn’t help but keep reflecting on my performance. This unease and self-blame continued for several days and even affected my sleep. When I finally gathered the courage to speak with my supervisor, he said the change in the project’s direction was not directed at me personally, but was a decision made from the overall situation. Only then did I realize I had overinterpreted his words.

Although I felt somewhat relieved, I still felt ashamed and powerless, because this habit of overinterpreting and attacking myself had become my default response. I knew that if I didn’t control it, it could continue to affect my performance at work.

The lighting in the conference room always had that unnatural white tone, making my eyes feel dry and stinging. The pen in my hand traced circles on the notebook without my even realizing it, while I kept silently rehearsing the key points of my presentation. When it was my turn to speak, I stood up, cleared my throat, and tried to make my voice sound as steady as possible, but my heart was pounding so fast it felt like even my eardrums could feel the vibrations.

“Our preliminary data for this month... um, shows...” My voice suddenly caught, and I could feel my face flush hot all at once. The room fell briefly silent, with only the soft rustle of pages turning and the faint creak of a colleague in the front row shifting in their seat. I swallowed and tried to continue, only to find that the clearly logical sentence I had had in my head had shattered into pieces, like a puzzle scattered apart. I forced myself to go on: “Um, this shows that our target... um, is still 10% short.”

The supervisor sitting in the front row looked up, lifting his gaze from the documents and over to me. His expression held a hint of confusion, or perhaps what I thought was confusion. He asked, “Why is this data so far off from last month’s forecast?”

I tried hard not to keep staring at him, but found my eyes involuntarily settling on the faint crease between his brows. I started explaining aimlessly: “Maybe it’s because... the users... we... overlooked some variables.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I regretted them, because they sounded exactly like I was making excuses. I noticed the colleague beside me lower their head, and I couldn’t tell whether they were holding back a laugh or focusing intently on taking notes.

My palms were already sweaty, and the notebook paper felt a little slick. I hurriedly ended my remarks, pushed my chair back into place, and kept my head down, not daring to look at anyone. My stomach felt as if it had been twisted; a sour, bloated ache made me feel like throwing up, but I knew I had to hold it in.

After the meeting ended, I didn’t leave with my colleagues. I pretended to tidy up in the conference room until they were all gone. Standing alone in the empty room, I stared at the last slide on the projector screen, berating myself over and over: Why didn’t I prepare more? Why couldn’t I even answer one question properly? What would they think of me? They must think I’m useless.

When I got home, I flung myself onto the sofa, trying to blank my mind, but those scenes kept replaying like a movie. I even kept recalling the supervisor’s expression, trying to read from every glance and subtle movement whether he had been disappointed or impatient. The more I thought about it, the worse I felt. In the end, I simply opened my laptop and started working, trying to cover up those thoughts, but every few minutes that stabbing pain inside me would still suddenly surface, as if I had been fiercely pricked.

Sunlight streamed through the clear blue sky onto the giant wall we had gathered around. The air was thick with the pungent smell of spray paint, along with a faint chemical scent from paint thinner. I gripped a can of spray paint so tightly that my palm was already soaked with sweat, the damp, cold sensation making me uncomfortable. I stood quietly to one side, watching the people around me chatting and painting with enthusiasm and ease, while my heart churned like beans in a boiling pot, beating wildly.

“You could add a bit of yellow in that corner for contrast—what do you think?” A young designer from the partner team suddenly turned around and smiled at me. His tone was perfectly calm, but my heart instantly tightened, as if he were saying I hadn’t done well enough. “Uh, I…” My face burned, and I hurriedly stammered, “N-no need, I think... maybe it’s enough already...” My voice was as faint as a mosquito’s buzz, the end of the sentence almost drained of strength. The other person seemed to freeze for a second, then nodded and turned back to continue working.

“Does he think I’m being uncooperative? Does he think I’m too arrogant to listen to his advice?” Such thoughts kept flashing through my mind, growing bigger and bigger like a rolling snowball. I stared at the spray cans on the ground, viciously blaming myself inside, feeling that my reaction had been terribly immature. I even started wondering whether the whole team would think worse of me because of it. A vague pressure spread through my chest; I took a deep breath, only to find that even breathing felt a little difficult.

Before I knew it, the sunlight had become blinding, shining so directly that I could barely keep my eyes open. I walked to a corner of the workshop, anxiously twisting the hem of my clothes in my hands, rubbing it again and again until the joints of my fingers began to turn white. I stole a glance at the designer; he was at the other end of the wall and didn’t seem to be paying attention to me anymore. But the sour unease in my heart had not lessened at all. All I could hear was the hissing sound of spray paint in my ears, like a mocking echo, making me feel even more out of place.

Time seemed to have frozen, but in reality not much had passed when the designer came over again. “Is this your first time participating in something like this? Don’t be nervous—paint however you want. There’s no right or wrong here; it’s all about your creativity.” His voice was gentle as he handed me a can of spray paint, and lightly tapped the can in my hand, which I had already squeezed so hard it was misshapen. “But this color is actually pretty good. It might work really well on the edges.”

I gave an awkward smile and forced out a “thank you” as I took the spray paint he handed me. I nodded, trying not to dwell on the embarrassment from just now. The sweat in my palm made the can unusually slippery, so I held it even tighter. When I stood in front of the wall again, my gaze fell on that blank corner. My mind was still a mess, but I could only mechanically begin spraying. My wrist ached a little from the force I was using, but the intermittent pain instead gradually calmed me down.

After it was over, I awkwardly packed up the tools, trying to avoid making eye contact with him. As he was leaving, he lifted the can in his hand and smiled, saying, “Looking forward to your next piece.” I nodded, but didn’t have the courage to reply. After he left, I let out a long sigh and slowly crouched down with my back against the wall. I still felt uneasy, repeatedly thinking about how badly I had performed. I even worried that he might tell his superior about my poor showing, affecting future cooperation.

That night, I couldn’t sleep. My mind was filled with his slightly hesitant gaze and that phrase, “Don’t be nervous.” Lying under the covers, I quietly clenched my fist and made up my mind that next time, I would definitely try to be more natural—whatever happened, at the very least, I must not panic like that again.

The basement lights were always dim. I dragged my slightly weary steps into this temporary document archiving space. The air was thick with the smell of yellowing paper, mixed with a faint mustiness that made one want to hold one’s breath. Around me were stacks of cardboard boxes marked with dates, and in the corner stood several layers of rusty metal racks, on which file folders were piled in a chaotic mess, as if they had been casually discarded. This time I had been assigned to sort through some old documents that were about to be destroyed. Unfortunately, it seemed no one else wanted the task. I lowered my head and looked at the list in my hand, trying to make sense of it all.

Just as I opened a heavy cardboard box, a yellowed folder slipped out, and the photossandwich; clip inside scattered onto the floor. I crouched down and picked up one of them. It was an old photograph showing a group of office workers with bright smiles, with our company’s early meeting room in the background. The white border around the photo had already turned yellow, as if time had coated it with a mottled halo.

“Huh, you haven’t started sorting yet?” My supervisor’s voice came from the doorway. I jumped and quickly stood up, the photo in my hand nearly falling. “I’m still looking for the files marked on the list. I’ll start right away.” I forced out a smile and slipped the photo back into the folder. The supervisor didn’t seem to care about my expression; he just nodded and left.

But my heartbeat began to quicken, and I could hear the flow of my own blood in my ears. Hesitantly, I opened the folder again and found several old logs and an early employee handbook. These long-forgotten records, their handwriting seeming to carry some unfinished story, faintly bore an indescribable weight. A thought flashed through my mind: are these people still at the company now? Are they still smiling? Or have they already been swallowed by time amid larger waves?

My stomach suddenly felt as if it had been clenched, and a dull pain began to creep in, while my palms grew slightly damp. I forced myself to close the folder, put it back into the box, and only then did I suppress the complex emotions that had begun to rise. I told myself these were just some old, meaningless things, nothing worth connecting to any self-pitying feelings.

A few hours later, the task was finally over. As I walked out of the basement, I tried to take a deep breath, but the heaviness in my chest still would not dissipate. Through the glass door, I could see that it was already completely dark outside, and the city lights reflected as blurred points on the rain-wet ground. I wanted to leave immediately, yet for some inexplicable reason I felt that certain moments of this day would stick in my heart forever. When I got home, I threw myself onto the sofa, but I couldn’t stop thinking about the photo of that group of smiling faces. Or rather, I was afraid that one day my own face would become just such a yellowed record forgotten in a folder, waiting to be dealt with at random—that was the image I feared most at this moment, even more than any other unease.

The lights in the banquet hall were flickering, and beneath the crystal chandelier was a bustling crowd, with faint music flowing through the air. I clutched the champagne flute in my hand, feeling somewhat uneasy. Although the surrounding noise and laughter were constant, I felt as if I were standing alone on a deserted island. Many of my colleagues were gathered in small groups chatting, while I lingered at the edge, trying to find the right opportunity to join their circles.

As I wandered around, I noticed a smiling colleague who seemed to be admiring a painting hanging on the wall. I gathered my courage and walked over. “This painting is really nice, isn’t it?” I tried to start casually.

She turned and seemed a little surprised. “Yes, the colors are very vivid.” Her tone was calm, but I somehow felt it was a little forced.

“What do you think?” She looked at me, seemingly waiting for my reaction.

“Uh, I think it has a unique way of expressing emotion,” I replied, though I was panicking inside. Was this a sign that she wasn’t interested in me? Had I said something wrong?

My heart raced, and my palms began to sweat. The music around me suddenly seemed harsh. “Oh,” she seemed unaware of my inner turmoil and continued, “I heard you’ve been planning a new project lately?”

“Yes, that’s right.” I tried to keep my voice from sounding too nervous. “Do you have any suggestions?”

She nodded slightly. “Actually, your ideas have always been very creative.”

“Really?” I suddenly felt a wave of warmth in my heart, but immediately began to doubt whether she was being sincere. Was this a polite compliment or a genuine one? For a moment, I didn’t know how to respond.

After a while, she was called away by other colleagues to join another conversation, and I stood there, replaying our exchange over and over in my mind. I overanalyzed every word, worrying whether I had behaved appropriately. The champagne bubbles rose gently in my glass, while all I felt was a churning in my stomach.

That night, I hardly ever truly relaxed; I was constantly caught in a state of anxiety and tension. In the end, I made an excuse that I wasn’t feeling well and left the reception early.

After I got home, I felt utterly exhausted, both mentally and physically. Even after several days, that uneasiness was still affecting me, and I kept replaying that conversation in my head, analyzing every detail, every word. Why am I always so sensitive?

This experience made me more aware that I need to handle feedback in social settings more rationally, and try to accept my occasional small mistakes and imperfections.

I was standing on the green terrace of the company rooftop, surrounded by the laughter and chatter of my colleagues. A gentle early-summer breeze brushed past me, and I raised a hand to smooth my hair, which had been blown into disarray. Although this team-building event was meant to strengthen friendships and cooperation among coworkers, I had been taut with nerves the whole time, afraid that any movement or word of mine might be misunderstood. I had always wanted to fit in, but the tension deep inside me kept rising.

“Hey, let’s go do that team game together!” one colleague called out to me. I nodded and tried hard to force out a smile.

After the game began, I noticed one colleague frown slightly for an instant. Though it lasted only a moment, I immediately began to overanalyze it: Was it because I hadn’t performed well enough earlier? Had I said something wrong? My heart started racing, and I felt sweat gradually seep down my back. To hide it, I turned around and pretended to look at the greenery along the edge of the terrace, but in my mind, that fleeting expression kept replaying over and over.

After the game ended, everyone gathered together to talk about what had just happened. I tried my best to join the conversation, but I kept brooding inwardly over that colleague’s expression. “Are you worried about something?” a colleague beside me suddenly asked, apparently noticing my unease. I froze, panic flaring in my chest. “Oh, no, I’m just a little hot,” I replied with a smile, though the tightness in my stomach only grew worse.

When the event was over, I returned to the office. That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t stop thinking over those tiny details. Why did that slight furrowing of the brow unsettle me so much? Why did I always feel I wasn’t good enough, afraid of being abandoned? My heart refused to calm down, even deep into the night.

Over the next few days, I became even more attentive to interactions among my colleagues. Whenever their tone changed even slightly, I would start analyzing whether it was because I had done something wrong. This overinterpretation made it hard for me to focus at work, and I kept falling into cycles of self-doubt. Every time I walked into the company, I felt discomfort in my stomach, as if it were foreshadowing another wave of anxiety to come.

The murmur of voices from the stairwell led me to a temporary art exhibition set up downstairs at the company. The decor was simple, with a few warm spotlights shining on the works hanging on the walls. I took a deep breath, my palms already slick with sweat. Two of my own design drafts were on the right side of the exhibition—pieces eliminated from the last client proposal—but my supervisor said they could be displayed to “build some courage.”

I stood in front of those pieces of mine, catching sight of a few colleagues chatting not far away out of the corner of my eye. One of them was Sister Li from the marketing department. I heard her lower her voice: “This design style seems a bit outdated. Clients don’t buy into this at all anymore.” There was no doubt her gaze was directed at my work. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, and the ringing in my ears began.

“Are they talking about my work? They must be.” I struggled to suppress the urge to turn and leave, but found my legs as heavy as lead and unable to move. I stared down at my shoe tips, pretending I hadn’t heard anything, but in my mind a disaster movie was already playing out. At tomorrow morning’s meeting, would Sister Li tell my supervisor that my work was a joke? Or would the whole department think I was a useless burden?

When someone passed by and brushed my shoulder, my stomach clenched into a knot. “Sorry!” I blurted out, my voice trembling a little. The person just smiled and softly replied, “It’s fine.” But my face was already burning, as if the whole world had seen my embarrassment.

“Are you being a little too sensitive? Why assume they were talking about you?” My rational mind tried to rein in my emotions, but to no avail. I felt completely exposed under the bright lights, like a clumsy actor waiting for the audience’s ridicule at any moment.

A few minutes later, I finally managed to move, trying to escape this suffocating space. But for some reason, a feeling of unwillingness surged up inside me again. I was afraid of criticism, but even more afraid of being ignored. If I left now, wouldn’t that be the same as admitting defeat?

I forced myself to go back to my work and summoned the courage to ask a colleague, “What do you think of this design?” She looked up and said, “I think it’s pretty good, actually. Quite distinctive. Though the colors could probably be adjusted a bit more.” I nodded in agreement and tried hard to force out a smile, but inside I felt like a shattered mirror, chaotically reflecting the words “quite distinctive.”

After I got home, I kept replaying that whispered criticism, convinced they had been targeting me. I lay in bed all night unable to sleep, and the sharp pang in my stomach made me realize I was probably just anxious again. The next morning, I got up listlessly and silently vowed: I would never let my work appear in public again. But deep down, a stubborn unwillingness was clearly resisting that decision.

On an early summer afternoon, I walked out onto the company terrace, sunlight spilling between the city’s skyscrapers. I always felt like I was a small part of this city, yet somehow still out of reach. Standing at the edge of the terrace, I looked down at the streets below, where cars moved silently like flowing rivers, while faint noise drifted over from afar. A wave of tension rose in me; the slight frown on my leader’s face during the last meeting had left me uneasy. I always overinterpreted these small expressions, worrying that I might have done something wrong.

My phone rang. It was a message from a coworker: “What did you think of the last proposal? Any feedback from the boss?” I gripped my phone, my palms a little damp. I tried to reply: “The boss hasn’t said anything yet. It should be fine, I guess.” But the unease that followed the silence in that meeting kept echoing in my mind. I quickly turned and left the terrace, heading back to the office. The air was thick with the smell of toner from the printers, mingled with the voices of coworkers chatting nearby.

“You don’t look too good. Is something wrong?” A coworker in the conference room looked at me thoughtfully. My heart raced, and my face felt hot. “No, I’m just a little nervous.” I forced out a smile.

When I got home that evening, the scenes from the meeting were still swirling in my mind. I began to think back on the past, on misunderstandings and mistakes caused by my over-sensitivity. I resolved to start learning how to better control my emotions and avoid letting unnecessary anxiety affect my work performance.

The office was already empty, leaving only me sitting alone at my desk, facing the computer screen. The preparations for the year-end party had already ended in a noisy bustle during the day, and the air still carried the plastic smell left behind by burst balloons. The coffee beside me had long since gone cold, and its strong bitterness made it hard to swallow. My supervisor’s words kept echoing in my mind: “Your recent performance still needs some more effort.” I kept chewing over that sentence in my heart, as if it were a saw blade slicing through every nerve.

“Why are you still here?” My colleague Xiao Zhang peeked in from the doorway, sounding slightly surprised. I forced out a smile. “Mm, just organizing some things. You go on ahead, don’t wait for me.” “Okay, see you later.” Xiao Zhang closed the door, her footsteps fading away, while I kept staring at the papers on my desk, increasingly convinced that my supervisor’s words were meant to criticize my string of mistakes.

My heart began to beat irregularly; I felt a faint, dull pain in my stomach, and my palms were starting to get clammy. The documents on the desk blurred before my eyes, and the barely audible voice in my mind kept asking, “Am I going to be fired soon?” “Am I simply not qualified to stay here?”

I forced myself to stand up and walked to the window to get some air. Outside was the city on the verge of nightfall, neon lights breaking into mottled patches of color. Taking a deep breath, I tried to tell myself, “Maybe he was just encouraging me. I don’t need to always think so negatively.” Yet the anxiety and unease inside me seemed to keep churning without pause.

Back at my seat, I began to imagine a scene in which my supervisor was disappointed in me—his cold expression, his ruthless words, even the things he might say echoed in my head. It felt as though I had no way to stop this cycle of self-reproach and fear, repeatedly convincing myself, “It must be my fault. Why can’t I ever do better?”

Finally, in the midst of this self-entanglement, I made a decision: I needed to ask my supervisor directly what he meant, instead of endlessly speculating and assuming. So, with my heart racing, I dialed the number. “Hello, boss? I’ve been a little uneasy about today’s performance. When you said I should ‘put in more effort,’ did you mean you were planning to adjust my position?” On the other end, my supervisor’s voice carried a hint of confusion: “Oh, that was meant as encouragement for you to perform even better, not as a negative evaluation.” Hearing this, my heartbeat gradually calmed, as though a gentle breeze had softly wiped away the cold sweat on my back.

That night, when I got home and lay in bed, holding my phone, I kept thinking about that conversation. A heavy stone in my heart slowly lowered, and I began to reflect that maybe I needed to learn to be a little kinder to myself, instead of living in constant anxiety. A few days later, the party was held as scheduled, and amid the holiday fireworks, I took my first taste of the sweetness of self-acceptance.

Anxiety surged toward me wave after wave, preventing me from falling asleep.

A few days later, I finally ran into him in the office. After swallowing nervously, I gathered my courage and walked over. “About last time... I hope you didn’t misunderstand. I wasn’t questioning your proposal.”

“Oh, no problem. I understand what you mean,” he said with a relaxed smile.

At that moment, the stone that had been hanging in my heart finally fell away. I realized that I always overinterpreted other people’s offhand remarks, and it was only because I wasn’t confident enough in myself. Even a conversation the other person didn’t care about at all could trigger a complete storm in my mind. I decided to try my best not to complicate little things anymore, but this change was still a daunting task for me.

The office lights today seemed a little harsh, casting long shadows across the conference table. A few of us sat around it, making final preparations for tomorrow’s important project presentation. After the meeting ended, I sat alone by the table organizing the materials, trying not to think about those embarrassing details. The surroundings gradually grew quiet, and the night outside the office slowly settled in. The daytime noise faded from the air, but it felt heavier instead. I took a deep breath, trying to dispel the restlessness inside me.

The next day, I did my best to appear professional during the presentation, though I still felt uneasy inside. To my surprise, everything we had prepared was approved without issue, and I even received praise from my supervisor. Even so, I kept telling myself: “Thank goodness nothing went wrong this time. I stood in the company lobby waiting for the meeting to end. Sunlight streamed in through the huge glass windows, casting itself across the polished marble floor. That night, I lay in bed at home, repeatedly replaying every detail of the day. I tried hard to reflect on whether I had been too sensitive, whether I had overread my colleague’s intentions. I walked into the small shop downstairs from the company building and gently pushed open the glass door, making the bell on the door ring with a crisp sound. The rain softly tapped against the library’s windows, and the air was thick with dampness and the smell of rotting paper. Suddenly, my phone vibrated, as if reminding me that the real world still existed. Opening it, I found it was from the project manager, and the message was simple and direct: “The project has failed. The client has decided to withdraw funding.” Those words seemed to strike a sensitive nerve. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, sweat began to form on my forehead, and my stomach churned. The rain kept falling, as if urging me to leave this place. Several days later, I was still feeling the heavy pressure brought on by the failure. Every time I closed my eyes, the scene of failure would appear in my mind. The stage lights cast mottled shadows backstage through the curtain, and the music from the main venue drifted into my ears. I pretended to be busy organizing the materials in my hands, but my head had already started racing, trying to work through every possible misunderstanding and consequence.

“Hey, are you okay?” At that moment, a colleague I was more familiar with patted me on the shoulder. I was startled by the sudden contact, my muscles tightening instantly. I froze for a second before reacting, forcing out a smile. “I’m fine, just a little nervous.”

The launch event went ahead as scheduled. Standing backstage, all kinds of worst-case scenarios flashed before my eyes, and I even rehearsed in my mind how I would be criticized and surrounded by disappointment if my presentation went wrong. Why didn’t I do better earlier?” These thoughts played out in my mind like a self-directed drama, and my stomach began to ache faintly.

After the event ended, I sat alone at my desk, filled with anxiety and unresolved tension. Even after several hours, I still couldn’t shake the feeling. The old printer in front of me made its squeaking mechanical noise again; it had jammed more than once. The office air was filled with a faint smell of ink and the heat radiating from electronic devices. I put my hand on the printer and felt its slight vibration, yet no paper came out.

“The data is, uh... based on the results of the previous market research... I reorganized it...” I tried to stay composed, but when I met the manager’s slightly skeptical gaze, my voice grew softer and softer.

“I think this model isn’t accurate enough. Maybe Xiao Yang can help add something?” The manager turned to Xiao Yang.

“Oh, I think her overall idea is worth referencing. But maybe here, you added some assumptions, which led to deviations in the results.” Xiao Yang’s tone was light and casual, but I felt as if a heavy hammer had struck me hard inside.

For the rest of the meeting, I forced myself to remain calm and didn’t say another word. I merely nodded mechanically, pretending to listen attentively. Inside, however, it felt as though I had sunk into a swamp, and I could feel everyone staring at my mistakes. After the meeting ended, I practically fled back to my desk, and behind me I heard Xiao Yang and another colleague speaking in low voices. Someone seemed to laugh.

I turned off my computer screen and lowered my head to stare at the keyboard, the table on the screen that had been called out for errors flashing repeatedly through my mind. “Why didn’t you check it again?” “Will the manager think I’m unprofessional?” “Is Xiao Yang making fun of me behind my back?” These thoughts hit me like a flood.

When I got home that night, I curled up on the sofa and kept reopening the proposal on my laptop. The more I looked, the more I felt the details were incomplete, and my mind filled with the words “failure.” Unconsciously, I even began to feel that the manager had already lost trust in me. Even when ordering takeout, I found myself thinking, “Does the delivery rider think I ordered too late?” That night, my sleep was extremely light, and I kept waking up in the middle of the night, my dreams filled with the conference room scene.

The next day at the office, I deliberately kept my head down as I passed Xiao Yang’s desk, feeling her gaze sweep over me. I couldn’t help wondering whether she was still holding a grudge over my performance yesterday.

The clock on the wall ticked steadily. The office was brightly lit, yet the air was thick with tension. I sat on one side of the performance review table, the documents spread out before me, my palms slightly damp with sweat. Across from me was my supervisor, his expression stern and focused. I tried to stay calm, but my heartbeat quickened uncontrollably.

"Over the past year, your ideas have had some merit, but the implementation of certain projects has not been ideal," my supervisor said in a tone I found hard to read. He went on to list my shortcomings point by point, and my ears began to ring; every word felt like a needle piercing my heart.

An inner voice couldn’t help but surface: Were they making me the scapegoat for the failure of that project? Was I not good enough? Had they wanted to push me out all along?

I unconsciously tightened my fists, my nails nearly digging into my palms. My heart raced, my stomach tightened, and a wave of loss and unease quickly washed over me.

I didn’t want to be misunderstood like this. I wanted to explain, but in my nerves my voice came out faint: "I know there were some problems with that project, but I did my best and tried many new approaches. It’s just that the results weren’t very satisfactory..."

My supervisor frowned slightly and said in a calm yet unyielding voice, "We all know effort doesn’t always lead to results. What matters more is the outcome, not the process." At that moment, it felt as if my heart had sunk to the bottom of a well, as though the whole world was denying my worth.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, tears flowing uncontrollably as the day’s conversation replayed again and again in my mind. Had everyone lost confidence in me? Would I be abandoned?

Even after several days, I still couldn’t shake off the gloom. Every time I thought about that review, I felt waves of pain, as if my existence and all my effort had been stamped with a huge label: "invalid."

I felt lonely, like standing on the edge of a cliff, ready to fall at any moment. Yet I didn’t want others to see my vulnerability, and I didn’t want to admit how helpless I felt. I knew I had to work hard to become better, but the fear and sense of failure never seemed to leave me.

The rain pattered against the iron railing, as if keeping time for my heartbeat. I stood in the garden on the company rooftop, surrounded by wet plants, their leaves covered in droplets that seemed to be silently telling their own stories. Though the night was already deep, the sound of the rain made everything feel unusually clear. I could smell the damp earth in the air, mixed with the fresh scent of rain, as if the city’s noise had been temporarily washed away. Above me, the waterproof canopy rustled softly in the wind, and I pulled my coat tightly around me.

“Why haven’t you gone home yet?” a coworker’s voice came from behind me. I turned around and saw him standing at the doorway, rainwater sliding off the edge of his umbrella. “I… just wanted some quiet.” I forced a smile, my voice mostly drowned out by the rain. We stood under the eaves, and he looked at me as if trying to read the expression on my face. “If you need anything, just let me know,” he said. Then he gently closed the door, leaving only me and the night.

I sighed, a tremor rising in my heart. In the meeting room earlier that day, the boss had criticized my project a great deal, and I kept replaying those words in my head like a stuck tape, over and over again. I had put so much effort into it—why did I still get such a result? These questions tangled together and weighed so heavily on me that I could hardly breathe.

My heartbeat was as fast as the raindrops, and the muscles in my back began to stiffen, as if they dared not relax. I walked to the railing, trying to steady my breathing, while rainwater ran down my forehead and the cold seeped into my skin.

Going back to my desk to keep working was impossible; I could no longer face those files and data. Instead, I kept questioning myself again and again: “Why do I care so much about what others think? Why do I always feel like I’m not doing well enough?”

That night, all my sensitivity was amplified, like a pressure cooker about to explode. I sat on the wet floor, with echoes of embarrassing moments and past mistakes ringing in my ears. Self-doubt hovered over me like an invisible shadow, impossible to drive away.

The next morning, the sky was still overcast. I returned to my desk and typed rapidly on the keyboard, as if the rain from the night before had washed away some of my frustration. Though there were still knots in my heart that had yet to be untied, I decided to take the initiative and bring up my suggestions for improvement at the next team meeting. I began to realize that accepting imperfection is also part of growth. Rather than passively enduring it, it would be better to face it head-on; perhaps turning it into momentum would bring new opportunities. “I can do it.” I whispered to myself, as if bringing the long rainy night to a close.

The air in the shop seemed to carry a faint heat wave, leaving me drenched in sweat. When I walked into the instrument restoration shop, the walls were covered with all kinds of antique instruments, some only half restored. The air was thick with the mixed scent of wood and old leather, accompanied by the clatter of tools, each sound seeming to remind me of the trial ahead.

“You came at just the right time,” the owner said, wiping down an old violin. “Take a look at these—can you help restore them?” I nodded and walked over to a workbench, where an old harp sat, its strings coated with years of dust. I tried to focus, to put all my attention on the restoration. Yet with every pluck of the strings, my heart began to race, my palms grew damp with sweat, as if every eye in the room were on me.

“That’s not right,” the owner’s voice suddenly rose. “You need to be more careful—you can’t be so careless.” The words pierced my ears like needles, and my stomach began to ache. I looked down at my hands, feeling as though there was nowhere to escape, as if all I wanted was to vanish from that room at once.

“I’m sorry, I’ll try again,” I stammered, my voice so faint it was barely audible. The muscles all over my body began to tense, filled with shame and a sense of inadequacy. I took a deep breath, trying to calm the turmoil inside me. I kept trying, but with every pluck of a string, that pattern of self-attack kept looping again and again. “Why do I always mess things up?” The self-doubt echoed repeatedly in my mind.

“You seem very nervous. Is this a bit beyond your ability?” the owner asked, his tone unmistakably skeptical. I could feel the heat rising in my face, as if my whole self had been laid bare in broad daylight. It felt as though a thousand-pound weight was pressing down on my shoulders; I wanted to run, yet had to keep standing there.

A few hours later, I stepped out of the shop, and the air outside seemed even heavier. I struggled to breathe, replaying the scene over and over in my mind, trying to understand what had gone wrong. Even after I got home, those words still echoed in my head, filling me with an endless sense of defectiveness and fear of being abandoned.

Over the next few days, I kept reflecting on my work performance, doubting whether I was truly suited for the job. Even when I tried to rest, I couldn’t calm my mind, always worrying that I would be seen as incompetent. Whenever I touched an instrument, my heart would race and my palms would sweat, as if that criticism could come crashing down again at any moment.

Standing in the archive room in the company’s basement, I stared at row after row of dust-covered folders, my heart filled with unease. The only window on the wall was blocked by heavy iron bars, and the faint light that came through cast mottled shadows on the floor. The air was thick with the smell of old paper and mildew, and I could hear my own heavy breathing echoing in the narrow space. “Why are you down here alone, and why did they assign you this kind of task again?” a coworker’s voice came from behind me. I turned around and forced a smile. “I’m just helping out temporarily. It’s nothing serious,” I replied, though I could faintly feel myself being isolated. Once upon a time, situations like this always made me feel rejected, as if every assignment to some task on the company’s fringe were a secret hint. Standing here, I felt a deep unease, as though the whole world had left me behind and I was facing everything alone. “Are you okay? You look a bit pale,” the other person asked. I shook my head and tried to make my voice sound natural. “I’m fine, just a little tired.” In truth, it wasn’t just tiredness; the feeling of being abandoned was slowly spreading inside me. I could feel my heartbeat speeding up, my palms starting to sweat, and a cramp twisting in my stomach. I tried to keep going through the files, but with every page I turned, the anxiety grew stronger. Gradually, all kinds of catastrophic scenes began to build up in my mind. I wondered if, should I fail to fit in with the team, I might really be fired or completely pushed out. That intense loneliness left me almost unable to breathe. I pretended to check the files, but I couldn’t take in a single word, only turning the pages mechanically, trying to hide the turmoil inside me. After saying goodbye to my coworker, I returned to my desk and kept replaying every sentence from our conversation, afraid I had said something wrong. That night, I tried to shift my attention to other things, but the shadow of being shut out never left my mind. Every time I closed my eyes, that lonely feeling surged back, even making me doubt whether I truly had any presence in the company. The fear I couldn’t shake made me feel ashamed, but I couldn’t escape it.

The sea breeze arrived first, one step ahead of my thoughts.

It was a Saturday afternoon. Sunlight pressed the surface of the sea into shards of broken gold, shimmering piece by piece. I took off my shoes and stepped into the sand. It was warm, with a dull, almost tearfully soft feeling. My toes sank in and then pulled free; with each step came a faint scraping sound, as if something were being slowly smoothed over. The waves were unhurried, one rolling after another. In the distance, a seagull cried twice, then fell silent. The air smelled of salt and some indescribable fishy sweetness. I took a deep breath, and something in my chest loosened.

I didn’t know what I was waiting for.

Usually I’m always waiting—waiting for the next blade in the comments, waiting for a reply that a collaborator has delayed too long, waiting for the screenshot of something I said wrong on a livestream to be blown up. I’m used to rehearsing every little thing in my head into the worst possible version, like an obsessive script editor, endlessly revising the ending, each time making it more miserable. But that afternoon, the rhythm of the waves was more patient than my anxiety. Again and again they came ashore, without judgment and without expecting an answer.

A child ran over, clutching a little beach shovel, squatted down beside me, and started digging a hole with great seriousness. After digging for a while, they looked up, their eyes bright as the reflection on the sea, and asked me, “Is the sand here especially fun?”

I froze for a second.

Normally, in that second, I would have started analyzing—was the child mocking me for standing there blankly as an adult? Was anyone nearby watching? Did I look strange? But that day, that second was only a second, and then I said, “Yes, it’s very fun. Dig carefully.”

The child smiled and lowered their head to keep digging.

I stood there, feeling my heartbeat go flat. Not suppressed flat—truly flat, as if something was gently supporting it from within. My palms weren’t sweaty, and my stomach didn’t have that familiar tight knot. I closed my eyes and listened to the waves, the wind, the sound of sand being scraped by the shovel. Nothing was collapsing.

I stayed there until the light began to turn orange.

On the way home, I didn’t immediately take out my phone. For me, that was almost abnormal. I just walked, still feeling the sand’s warmth at the bottoms of my feet, even though it had long since fallen away.

That night, I made tea and sat on the sofa without opening a single work group chat. I just sat there, thinking about that sea, thinking about how seriously the child had dug their hole, thinking about those few minutes when the wind blew over and I didn’t think about anything at all.

In the days that followed, things started piling up again. Deadlines, falling numbers, a caption that had been misread. I began rehearsing again, ruminating again, searching for thorns again in other people’s words. But sometimes, in the instant when anxiety was just beginning to rise, I would remember that sea, and remember that moment when my heartbeat had gone flat.

It wasn’t a cure. Just proof—proof that I, too, could simply exist without collapsing.

In the damp air, a stale, long-unopened scent lingered. I slowly pushed open the creaking wooden door and stepped into this gallery that had been abandoned for years. Dust floated in the air like a sheer veil, and through the broken glass windows, the hazy light cast a dim glow over the mottled paintings on the walls. I could faintly hear the howl of the sea breeze outside the window, as if telling the stories this place had once held.

I stood before an old abstract painting, and the intricate lines on it made me feel unaccountably irritated. Unbidden, my recent works came to mind, and I always felt they lacked some kind of spirit. This thought kept swelling, bringing with it endless criticism; the voice of self-reproach in my heart grew sharper and sharper: “What on earth are you doing? Why are you never satisfied with yourself?”

My heartbeat began to quicken, and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my palms. Every breath seemed to tug at an ache deep inside me. Ashamed of these endless emotions, I tried hard to calm everything down. At that moment, my footsteps echoed through the empty gallery, and I unconsciously walked toward an old painting of a television set, on which was reflected a gaze from times past.

“Maybe some things are simply destined never to change.” As soon as that thought surfaced, it was swallowed by a stronger wave of panic. “If I keep going like this, even they will leave me, won’t they?” I kept rehearsing the worst possible outcome, and that voice deep inside continued to whisper in my ear, leaving me no room to catch my breath.

“What are you seeking here?” A sudden voice jolted me out of my thoughts. I turned around and saw, in a corner of the abandoned gallery, a blurred figure tidying up a pile of scattered paintings. “Maybe I just wanted a place to sit quietly for a while,” I answered as calmly as I could, though the unease inside me was still churning.

“Sometimes, the creative process is nothing more than an endless conversation with oneself. People always miss the dialogue with themselves.” His voice seemed to carry an echo, striking a corner of my heart. I stood there, not knowing how to answer. In that moment, a warm yet moving feeling filled my heart. Perhaps I needed to learn to accept impermanence and imperfection.

When I stepped out of the gallery, thin rain mixed with the wind beat against the windows. A chill swept over me, and it seemed that with these cold gusts, my thoughts gradually settled. Over the next few days, I tried to remind myself to face these emotions, no longer fear them, no longer avoid them. Although the anxiety I felt whenever I created was still there, I was a little more forgiving toward myself.

That day, I had an unusual conversation with myself in the abandoned gallery. Though it did not completely solve my anxiety, the comfort I felt in that moment made me realize that on the road of creation, accepting my own imperfections is also part of moving forward.

The afternoon sunlight streamed through the small carriage window, filling the air with a sense of history, perhaps mingled with the scent of old wooden floors and metal. I sat by the window; the coffee on the table had already gone cold, the rising steam long since dissipated, leaving only a thick black liquid gently swaying in the cup. Now and then I picked up the spoon to stir it, while summoning all my strength to focus on the manuscript before me. But my mind seemed occupied by a tiny voice, echoing the waiter’s words from moments ago: “If you don’t need anything else, you can settle the bill.”

I remembered his expression when he said it as clearly as if it were happening now. The corners of his mouth lifted in a forced smile, but there was unmistakable impatience in his eyes. My heart sank. Had I upset him somehow? Was it because I’d sounded too abrupt when ordering the coffee? Or had I been expressionless when I looked at him just now?

The more I thought about it, the worse I felt. My stomach tightened as if an invisible hand had clenched it. I tried to tell myself that maybe I was overthinking it, or perhaps he was just in a bad mood today, and it had nothing to do with me. But that self-comfort was almost immediately interrupted by another voice: “If it’s not your fault, whose fault could it be? He was cold to you because he has a problem with you.”

I couldn’t help letting out a soft laugh, tinged with bitterness. I always felt like a little boat drifting with the current; when the winds and waves of the outside world came, I was as light as a leaf, pushed this way and that without control. Thinking back to the conversation just now, I even began to doubt my own memory. Had he really not looked impatient? Or perhaps my reaction made him think I was the kind of customer who disliked being disturbed?

Looking at the sky outside the window as it gradually darkened, I felt a slight sheen of sweat forming on my forehead. Even though the carriage had air conditioning, I could feel my heartbeat speeding up, and my palms were damp with sweat. Had other customers nearby seen what had just happened? Would they think I was difficult to get along with?

At that moment, the bell at the door rang, and a set of footsteps approached. I straightened my back instinctively, my heart rippling with even greater unease. The waiter brought over a glass of water and set it on my table. “I noticed you hadn’t touched your cup just now, and it might be because the weather is too hot. Please have some of this cold water.”

I froze for a moment, my gaze moving from his hand to his face. This time, his smile seemed genuinely warm, and his eyes no longer had the same distance as before. Had I really misunderstood him???

“Thank you...” I lowered my head, not daring to look at him for long, but the tips of my ears were already beginning to burn. He nodded and turned to leave. I stared at the glass of water, the rise and fall of my chest gradually evening out, but my mind remained a tangled mess. Did he think I was a weirdo, someone who fretted over even such a small thing? After drinking a few sips, the coolness slid down my throat. I tried hard to reassure myself, yet I still couldn’t stop thinking about it.

By the time I got home, it was completely dark. I closed my notebook, having written only a few hundred words all day. I lay on the sofa, closed my eyes, and once again recalled the waiter’s expression, then kept simulating all sorts of possible scenarios in my head. Guilt and shame intertwined in my heart like two ropes; the more I struggled, the more suffocated I felt. At one in the morning, I picked up my phone, opened a search engine, and typed in “how to overcome social sensitivity.” The cold light of the screen stung my eyes, and a trace of mocking thought drifted through my mind again: You’ve lived 41 years, and something this small is still bothering you. How regrettable.

Sunlight streamed through the café’s floor-to-ceiling windows, casting shifting patches of light and shadow across the table. My team members and I sat around a large wooden round table, with the aroma of coffee and the faint smell of baking filling the air. They were discussing the creative direction for a new project, and everyone seemed energized. But to me, it was as if a layer of frosted glass had been placed over my ears; only broken, blurry fragments of sound seeped through, words like “more impactful” and “young users will like it.” Nervously, I held my pen so tightly that my palms sweated, and the damp feeling made me unconsciously dot the page a few times.

“What do you think?” someone suddenly asked. I looked up and found every gaze fixed on me, glaring like spotlights until I almost had to squint. “Ah, I think…” My voice felt as dry as a brittle leaf, with a slight tremor in it. I offered some vague ideas, like “maybe we could make it simpler” or “how about trying brighter colors.” But almost immediately, I noticed the few seconds of silence in the air. The noise in the room seemed to grow louder all at once, like waves surging from every direction and drowning me out.

“Hmm, we can try that, but it might not really fit the brand tone,” said a young member of the planning team, with a polite smile. His words were like a needle stabbing into my mind. I knew he meant no harm, but those words had already started looping in my head: “Was what I said not deep enough? Was it too superficial?” My stomach began to ache faintly, as if a hand were clutching my organs. I didn’t know whether my expression had changed noticeably, but I could feel myself struggling to keep calm.

For the rest of the discussion, I hardly said anything at all, just sat there nodding, occasionally murmuring a muffled “mm” or “right.” My attention was fixed on my fingers, absentmindedly fiddling with the cup handle of my coffee. Time stretched out long and heavy, every second seeming to confirm that I had already fallen behind. I felt as though my presence had become some background element that could be ignored.

After the meeting ended, I walked out of the café. The air outside was a little cool, carrying the slight dampness unique to autumn. I hurried toward the parking lot, as if trying to shake off the humiliation of being watched just moments before. On the drive home, a light pop song played on the radio, but I had no mood to hum along. The conversations from the meeting kept circling in my head, like a moth trapped in a room, crashing wildly into everything. I began to wonder whether I was no longer suited for this job, or whether they had long ago considered me an unnecessary piece of the puzzle and simply never said so.

A few days later, I started deliberately avoiding messages from team members. Even the thought of going back to the café for another meeting made my palms sweat for no reason. I told myself it was only a passing mood, but deep down I felt an unfathomable loneliness and unease. It was like the shame I felt as a child when a teacher called me out in class and criticized me, and I walked back to my seat with my head down—only now it was more hidden, and far harder to escape.

I sat at a small table in the corner of a café, sunlight slanting through the window and spilling across the wooden tabletop. The air was filled with the aroma of coffee and freshly baked pastries. Outside the window was a busy street, where the sounds of traffic and people occasionally drifted in, contrasting with the soft music inside the shop. The chair across from me was empty, a disturbing reminder of what had happened not long before.

I had arranged to meet an old friend here. We had known each other for years and used to talk about everything, but recently we had drifted apart because of some misunderstandings. When she came in, I immediately noticed a subtle change in her expression, a flicker of tension and displeasure. “Hi,” she said simply after sitting down.

“Hi,” I replied, trying to look calm. My heart was beating faster, and my palms were starting to sweat. We ordered coffee, and she kept tapping her fingers on the table. “How have you been lately?” I tried to break the icy silence.

She frowned slightly, her eyes flickering, “Okay, just really busy with work.” Her tone unsettled me, as if something unsaid were weighing on her mind.

“I feel like there’s been some misunderstanding between us,” I said cautiously, anxiety rising in me like a tide. Her reaction immediately made my heart clench.

“Maybe,” she looked up and gave a forced smile, but it never reached her eyes. “I just feel like this relationship has become a little exhausting.”

The words struck me like a bolt from the blue. I held my breath, feeling my stomach twist. Exhausting to her? Was it because I was too sensitive, always blowing small things out of proportion? I wanted to explain, but I was afraid the more I said, the worse I would make it.

“If you’re uncomfortable, we can talk about it,” I tried to stay calm, though my voice rose slightly without my meaning to. Several nearby customers began to notice this corner.

She shook her head. “Sometimes I feel like you keep chewing over little things from the past, and it’s stressful.”

Her words were like a sharp thorn driving straight into my heart. My sense of inadequacy was instantly triggered. “I just don’t want to lose you as a friend,” I blurted out almost helplessly.

She sighed, lowered her head, as if weighing something. “I know that’s how you feel, but I need some space,” she finally said.

Every word she said felt like a heavy stone pressing on my chest, and I felt powerless. “Oh, okay,” I replied, my voice so low it was almost inaudible.

She nodded, as if having made up her mind, and stood up. “Sorry, I have to go.”

Watching her walk away, my eyes grew wet, and my heart still would not settle. The smell of coffee became pungent, and the music turned unbearably harsh. A few days later, I found myself still repeatedly replaying that conversation, blaming myself for every possible mistake.

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning and unable to sleep. The sense of helplessness and fear of being abandoned in my heart hung over me like an inescapable shadow. I was always this sensitive, and it had caused me to lose an important friend.

The old train station echoed with a hollow reverberation. I stood beside the overgrown tracks; the ground was slightly damp, and the air seemed to carry a faint smell of rust. Several wandering musicians were assembling their instruments. Broken guitar notes mingled with drumbeats, forming a strange rhythm. Sunlight streamed through the shattered windows onto the tiled floor, casting irregular patches of light and shadow. My heart began to race, and I watched the surroundings uneasily. This scene reminded me of some kind of loss, even abandonment. One of the musicians turned around, smiled at me, and said, “Hey, want to join in?” I smiled hesitantly and shook my head. My mind told me this was a safe environment, but my body was starting to tense up, my hands slightly damp with sweat. I struggled to stop myself from imagining the worst-case scenario, such as someone suddenly barging in and interrupting the performance, or me embarrassing myself while taking part.

The performance began. The guitar gently unfolded and blended with the drumbeat, flowing like a stream. I stood to the side, trying to let myself merge into the music, as if searching for some kind of comfort. I closed my eyes and tried to regulate my breathing to the rhythm. My heartbeat steadied somewhat, but there was still an uneasy feeling in my stomach. After a while, the musicians began singing a song I wasn’t very familiar with, and the lyrics seemed to mention loneliness and hope. I realized that my sensitivity to these themes had stirred some inner emotion.

By the end of the performance, I felt my body loosen a little, yet my mind kept ruminating on past embarrassing scenes, which made me uncomfortable. The musicians put away their instruments and said to me, “Thanks for coming to listen. We’ll be back here again soon.” After leaving the train station, I still felt a heaviness in my heart. A few days later, the memory would occasionally surface, reminding me of the tangled emotions in that music, quietly and persistently affecting my mood. In the creative work that followed, I tried to turn these feelings into material, hoping to find some kind of release through artistic expression.

The air in the bookstore was thick, and the old wooden floor gave off a faint woody scent. I wandered aimlessly among the shelves, my fingertips brushing across row after row of books. Even on such a quiet afternoon, I still couldn’t suppress the restlessness in my heart. Muffled jazz drifted from the radio, masking the murmurs of conversation. Yet my heartbeat quickened against my will.  

Near the entrance, I saw a seemingly intimate young couple speaking softly about a novel. “Don’t you think what happened to the protagonist is tragic?” the girl said in a low voice, a trace of worry showing between her brows. I stopped in my tracks, an all-too-familiar fear rising within me. “Yes,” the boy replied, “but that kind of loneliness is something we can all feel, right?”  

Before he had even finished speaking, my stomach clenched violently as if struck by a heavy blow. That word—loneliness—rang in my mind like an alarm, shaking me so badly I could no longer think. Panic at being abandoned seized my heart in an instant, as though their words were some sort of omen about my own fate. I turned away and pretended to browse the magazine in my hands, trying to find a little comfort in it.  

“Are you all right?” a store clerk suddenly came over and asked gently. I was startled by her words, and the magazine nearly slipped from my hands. “I’m fine, thank you,” I said, forcing myself to stay calm and trying to smile, though I could feel the corners of my mouth trembling. At that moment, my heart pounded like a drum, fine beads of sweat broke out on my forehead, and my palms grew slick.  

When I left, the sunlight blazed down on the street, dazzling and dizzying, and my steps grew unsteady. In the corner of my eye, I saw my reflection in the shop window outside, pale beyond recognition. My mind was filled with the other person’s casually spoken words, playing over and over again. Why is it always like this? I tried hard to drive away these intrusive negative thoughts, but it felt as though I were trapped, unable to break free.  

Back home, I lay in bed, unable to fall asleep. The exhaustion of the whole day and a sense of shame washed over me like a tide. I wondered if every emotional fluctuation always looked so awkward and ridiculous. I kept replaying that scene in the bookstore, rehearsing countless possible responses in my head, none of which made me feel any better. That night, I wrote myself a reminder: “Stop overinterpreting other people’s unintentional attitudes, and shift your attention in time.”  

In the days that followed, I had to confront those ruminating thoughts. The couple’s words and emotions in the bookstore were like a dark ocean, with towering waves bringing unease and endless worry about the future, but I knew this was merely a projection of something within me. These feelings of unease and fear are inborn; even if I don’t want to admit it, I still have to learn to live with them.

The aroma of the coffee seemed sharper than usual. My fingers twirled around the rim of the cup, the friction barely audible, yet to me it sounded like noise from a loudspeaker. I lowered my head and stared at the wood grain on the table, trying to distract myself with those tangled lines and cover up the restless waves inside me. The café before me was a place I knew well, but today’s atmosphere was like a gray overcast sky—heavy and so stifling it was hard to breathe.

“Have you been a little too sensitive lately?” the person across from me said. It was my friend of more than twenty years. Her voice was not loud, but it felt like a sudden blow to my eardrums, and my chest tightened at once, as if someone were holding me too tightly without giving me a chance to relax. I lifted my head, trying to find comfort in her expression, but all I saw was a trace of indifference.

“I... I just wanted to make sure about a few things,” I said softly in defense, though I knew full well how weak and powerless it sounded. In my mind, it was as if a floodgate had been opened; the texts from the past few weeks, the unanswered calls, the perfunctory tone—all of it came rushing back. This hadn’t just started recently, had it? Maybe it had been earlier. Had she been impatient with me for a long time? Did she... already feel that I wasn’t worth keeping this relationship going?

“Do you really not know how exhausting you are?” she went on. Her voice never rose, but it landed like sharp droplets of water, striking the most fragile part of me. “Every time I talk to you, I have to be so careful. The moment I say something a little off, you start overthinking, and it’s really exhausting.”

My scalp prickled as I listened, and it felt as though someone hadfiercely struck my temple. I struggled to keep my expression under control and not let tears spill out, my fingers clutching at my sleeve so hard my nails nearly dug into my skin. Her mouth kept opening and closing, but my ears seemed to have lost their function; the rest of her words turned into a vague hum. Only one sentence kept echoing in my head: “Are you really that unlikeable?”

“I... I’m sorry.” When I forced those words out, my voice was nearly trembling. But after I said them, I realized my back was already drenched in sweat. My stomach twisted violently, leaving me with a sour, swollen feeling that made me want to vomit.
