I didn’t even dare look up at her reaction; I only stared fixedly at the swirl in my coffee cup, the slick sheen on the surface like a projection of my chaotic thoughts.

“I’m not asking you to apologize,” she sighed. “I just think maybe we need a little distance, really.” After saying that, she lowered her head and started checking her phone, clearly no longer willing to continue the conversation.

I don’t know how I managed to end that conversation. It was only when I stepped outside that I realized it had started to drizzle. The cold wind brushed across my face, and only then did I notice my cheeks were wet, unable to tell whether it was rain or tears. The road beneath my feet seemed to float in midair. I stared at the streetlights in the distance, my mind in complete chaos, with only one voice telling me: “She’s gone. She really is going to leave.”

When I got home, I curled up under the blankets and looked through her chat history on my phone again and again, telling myself again and again not to look anymore. But I couldn’t stop. In every line, I could find traces of her dissatisfaction with me. The stomach pain didn’t go away; instead, it made me let out a faint groan. That night, I lay awake until dawn, my mind endlessly replaying her words and that indifferent face.

The autumn sunlight slanted across the street, and my steps followed the dance of fallen leaves as I slowly walked into the independent bookstore on the edge of the city, one I loved dearly. The outside walls of the shop were a warm orange, and inside stood row upon row of old bookshelves, the air filled with the scent of paper and a faint aroma of coffee. I passed through the narrow, alcove-like aisles, my fingers brushing over the spines of the books, imagining the unexplored worlds hidden behind them.

“Welcome. Can I help you?” The shop owner peeked up from behind the counter and asked with a smile. I shook my head, trying to focus on the books before me, yet I couldn’t shake the heaviness in my heart. My recent creative block had left me unbearably anxious, and I urgently needed a place where I could think in peace, undisturbed.

I found a seat by the window and sat down. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains, warm against my body. I opened a book, trying to immerse myself in it, but my thoughts kept leaping around. “If this new work still fails to receive a good response, will my creative career come to an end here?”

My heartbeat quickened, my palms gradually grew damp, and a sharp pain began twisting in my stomach. I closed my eyes tightly and took deep breaths, trying to relax my body, but the negative thoughts in my mind pulled me in like a vortex. Suddenly, everything around me felt unreal, as if I were merely an onlooker watching my own life slip away.

The afternoon slowly deepened into dusk, and I was still sitting there, no longer able to tell time passing. In the end, I closed the book, clenched my fist hard, and tried to encourage myself. “I can’t be defeated like this,” I whispered to myself. “I have to find a way to make all of this meaningful.”

After that day, I began setting aside time every day to come to this bookstore. In that moment of solitude, I came to realize that I needed a place to escape, a place to sort through the anxiety and unease I couldn’t express in the outside world. Though the difficulties of creation still remained, at least in those brief moments, I found a place within myself to rest.

The air was filled with the fresh scent of wood shavings, and a ray of sunlight slipped through the crack in the window and fell across the floor. I stood before the carving bench, gripping the carving knife tightly, trying to carve the image in my mind into this block of oak. At that moment, the only sounds in the room were the ticking of the wall clock and my own heartbeat, yet a sense of unease hung over me. I always felt as if every tool in the room, every piece of wood, was scrutinizing each of my movements.

“Do you think this is okay?” My colleague across from me looked up and asked softly. I forced a smile and said, “Hmm... not bad, I guess.” But inside, I kept doubting my own words. I stared at the half-finished carving and the more I looked at it, the more I felt it was far from the image in my imagination. My palms began to sweat, and the fingers holding the knife started to tremble.

“Calm down, don’t be too nervous,” I told myself, forcing my attention back to the work at hand. Yet the voice in my mind kept reminding me of past failures, of those pieces that had never been successful. The sound of my heartbeat grew louder in my ears, as if it were trying to drown out everything else.

Although I tried hard to focus on the details of the carving, anxiety kept growing inside me. Every time I closed my eyes, those once-rejected works appeared before me, those moments at exhibitions when no one paid them any mind. I couldn’t shake this torment; it was like an invisible chain, binding my soul tightly.

That evening, I sat at home, still unable to stop thinking about that piece of wood and about the struggle in the studio that day. Even though I told myself to rest for a while, the restless thoughts in my mind kept me from doing so. The next day, I still walked into the studio carrying the fatigue of a sleepless night.

A few days later, one morning, sunlight once again streamed through the window onto my workbench, and I realized I had been avoiding facing my self-doubt all along. I decided not to let these thoughts keep hijacking my creativity. Even though fear still remained in my heart, I began to consciously accept imperfect works and see them as a necessary part of the path to growth.

The light from the incandescent bulb stabbed into my eyes and fell across the wooden desk in front of me. Several sketches and a laptop lay scattered on the desktop. The studio wasn’t large, and the air was thick with the mixed smell of coffee and paint. It was a little stuffy and hot. The clock on the wall ticked steadily, and every second seemed to make me more uneasy. I sat in the chair, nervously rubbing my hands together, trying to steady my breathing, but my stomach felt knotted tight, aching faintly. The collaborator across from me was staring at his phone, occasionally glancing up at me with a somewhat impatient expression.

The criticism in his tone was impossible to miss, and it made my heart race. “What logic was your feedback on the last version based on, exactly?” he finally said, his voice low but oppressive. “We’ve already been delayed for two weeks. We can’t keep going like this.”

My throat felt blocked, and after a long while I managed to force out a sentence: “I thought the direction last time had drifted a bit off the theme, so I adjusted it again...” My voice was astonishingly soft; even I could barely hear it.

His brow was tightly furrowed, and his tone made no attempt to hide his irritation. “But some of those changes were completely meaningless! Do you know that? The client was actually more satisfied with the original version!”

Those words hit my chest like a sledgehammer, and my breathing instantly quickened. My cheeks grew hot all at once, and my ears buzzed as if all my blood had rushed to my scalp. I tried to explain: “But... but at the time I thought...”

“You thought?” he almost cut me off, his tone clearly more agitated. “Couldn’t you at least have communicated in advance? These changes really wasted everyone’s time!”

My palms began to sweat, and countless images flashed through my mind at lightning speed—my teacher pointing at my homework as a child and saying I was “careless,” my mother looking at my exam paper in disappointment, even a scene from years ago when a client rejected a collaboration because my idea had been turned down. All of it felt like knives slicing through my chest, making my breathing even more rapid until I could hardly get a full sentence out.

I lowered my head and stared at the sketches on the desk, where the lines before my eyes seemed to twist into a tangled mass. Perhaps because I was afraid of being attacked again, I spoke first: “It’s my fault. I shouldn’t have made changes to the design on my own. You can put all of today’s losses on me...”

He let out a sigh, as if he still wanted to say something, but in the end he didn’t. He just waved a hand. “Forget it. Let’s just say I never said anything this time.”

As he turned and left, I was still sitting motionless in the chair, as if nailed there. Tears welled up in my eyes, and I bit down hard, forcing myself to hold them back, telling myself I absolutely could not cry in a situation like this. But the moment the door closed, the tears still slid down involuntarily, hitting the papers on the desk and blurring the ink.

That night, after I got home, I collapsed onto the bed, curled up tightly with my knees pulled to my chest, and tears streamed uncontrollably from the corners of my eyes. I went over the conversation from the day all over again, the words “wasted everyone’s time” replaying over and over in my mind. It felt as if a huge stone was pressing on my chest; I had trouble breathing, and my stomach cramped in waves.

Over the next few days, I barely slept properly. Every time I closed my eyes, the scenes from the day replayed before me, and that inescapable sense of shame tormented me. I started to wonder whether I simply wasn’t suited for this job. Whether all my collaborators saw me as a burden. When the phone rang, I didn’t even dare answer it, afraid of hearing the other person’s disappointed voice.

Standing in the empty glass factory, I could feel the floor beneath my feet trembling slightly. The place was nearly abandoned, but I always managed to find places like this to shoot my videos. Sunlight poured in through the broken windows, forming thin shafts of light, and fine dust floated in the air, adding a touch of mystery to the whole scene. A magpie flew over my head, accompanied by the distant rumble of traffic outside the window, while my camera kept rolling. Suddenly, I heard a noise and the lens jolted sharply. In an instant, a wave of heat rushed to my face, my heart raced, and sweat ran down my back. I quickly checked the camera and found that the tripod had not been secured properly, ruining the entire shot. I stomped my foot in frustration, feeling a sharp ache in my stomach, while a strong sense of shame welled up inside me.

"How could this happen?" I muttered to myself, my voice echoing through the empty space. I took the camera off the tripod and wanted to start over, but the feeling of unease still wouldn’t go away. Deep inside, a voice began whispering: Was I simply not suited for this job? Was I going to fail again and again? Just then, I heard my phone ring. It was my partner calling. He asked how the shoot was going, and I did my best to keep my voice from trembling as I replied, "Oh, it’s okay, there were a few minor issues, but I’ll take care of them."

He encouraged me, saying, "It’s fine, don’t be too nervous. Take your time." But my mind remained unsettled. I kept replaying the mistake over and over, imagining how my career might be affected if this shoot failed again. In that state, I could hardly focus on the work ahead. My muscles were tense, and my whole body felt stiff. The warmth of the sunlight made me feel hot, but the anxiety inside me was like a cold wind creeping in.

After the shoot, I went home and almost immediately opened my computer to review the footage. Sitting in front of the screen, I reached up to knead my shoulders, trying to ease the tight muscles, while the shaky image kept replaying in my mind. In the end, I tried editing the usable clips, forcing myself to believe that this mistake would not completely bring me down.

A few days later, I slowly began to accept the mistake, though every now and then I would still think of that trembling image when I closed my eyes late at night. My heartbeat gradually settled, and although I still felt uneasy whenever I thought about it, I knew I had to keep moving forward. Even if filming in an abandoned glass factory failed, I still had to keep trying.

The lights in the conference room felt unbearably harsh. Standing in the middle of the room, the script in my hands seemed much heavier than usual. Every time I looked up, I saw a ring of faces shrouded in shadow around the conference table, and the expectant looks in their eyes made me feel extremely uncomfortable. The only sounds in my ears were the ticking of the clock and the occasional rustle of papers being turned. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself. The moment I spoke, my voice was actually trembling: “Uh… this year’s revenue growth…” My voice was faint, and being watched by so many people made my palms start sweating, while a cold sweat gradually broke out on my back. At every pause, I worried I wouldn’t be able to go on. When the presentation slides changed, the charts flashing on the screen left me momentarily dazed; the numbers seemed to be dancing, reminding me of many unachieved goals and imperfections. I couldn’t help imagining everyone judging me in their minds: “Why is he so nervous?” “He’s still speaking at this level?”

A colleague sitting across from me suddenly interrupted my thoughts. “Can you explain the reason for this quarter’s decline?” His voice wasn’t loud, but in my mind it rang like a warning bell. “It’s… well, the market has changed a lot…” I tried hard to suppress my unease and organize my words in response. Yet an inner voice kept circling: “I’m not good enough. Have they lost confidence in me?”

After I finished speaking, I collapsed back into my seat, my heart still pounding. The feeling of icy hands and feet never really faded. All I could do was instinctively lower my head and fiddle with my phone, trying to avoid whatever glances others might cast my way. In my ears were the voices of other colleagues continuing to speak, but I couldn’t focus at all. My mind kept replaying every sentence I had just said, and every pause felt so obvious, so terrible.

That evening, when I got home, exhaustion came over me like a tide. The bedroom was so quiet that only the faint hum of the fan remained, surrounding me on all sides. I lay in bed with a heavy heart, still thinking about the impression I had left in the meeting. “Do others all think I did terribly?” That thought made it hard to fall asleep. I tossed and turned, unable to calm down for a long time. The next day, even while drinking my morning coffee, I still felt a dull ache in my stomach, and the nervous agitation lingered for a long time.

A few days later, a colleague greeted me in the hallway. “Your last performance analysis was good. Want to chat sometime?” That unexpected feedback made me pause slightly, and the tightly stretched string in my heart loosened a little, giving me a sense of relief.

I was sitting in a familiar café in the city center, holding a warm cappuccino in my hands. The air was filled with the rich aroma of coffee, and soft jazz played in the background. It was a place I visited often, and its warm lighting always gave me a sense of comfort. When my partner Kevin walked in, I noticed that his expression was somewhat serious, and he seemed to be missing his usual smile.

“Hey, hi,” I greeted Kevin, trying to ease the atmosphere with a light tone.

“Hello,” he replied, his voice slightly low.

We began discussing the new content creation project, but I quickly found that he responded only lukewarmly to my suggestions. From time to time, he furrowed his brow, and those slight changes in his expression made my heart race, stirring an inexplicable unease in my chest. Kevin’s words made me feel as though he was dissatisfied, and I quickly slipped into a spiral of self-doubt.

“Do you think these ideas aren’t good enough?” I finally couldn’t help asking.

Kevin looked at me with a conflicted expression. “No, it’s just that I think these directions might need more market research.”

Hearing this, my palms began to sweat, and my stomach tightened. Worried, I had to grip my coffee cup more firmly. I started to doubt my own ability. Maybe I really wasn’t capable of completing this project? Maybe I really wasn’t suited to my current role?

In just a few minutes, my mind had already staged a terrifying drama about failure. I thought of past plans that had not come to fruition because of anxiety, past mistakes that I had worried over again and again. All of it resurfaced now, as if mocking my incompetence.

“I’ll consider your suggestions more carefully. Thank you very much for your feedback.” I forced out a smile, hoping that this somewhat formulaic remark could hide my inner turmoil.

Sitting by the café window, I could see pedestrians coming and going outside. Compared with the crowd, my disappointment seemed so insignificant. After saying goodbye to Kevin, I took a deep breath, trying to calm my racing heart.

On the way home, I couldn’t help but keep replaying the entire conversation in my head, silently blaming myself for my mistakes. Maybe I should have noticed these issues earlier? Maybe I was reading too much into Kevin’s attitude?

A few days later, I tried to calm down and take a fresh look at that meeting. I decided to do more market research and, combined with Kevin’s suggestions, readjust the plan, trying to turn this setback into an opportunity for growth.

The bench on the balcony looked especially comfortable, so I spread a blanket over it, as if I were creating a little corner of my own. Sunlight filtered through the half-drawn curtains and poured in, its warm glow turning the blanket a soft yellow. In my hands I held a collection of essays, its cover a deep blue—the kind of quiet, profound color that always put me at ease. I opened the book, and the pages carried a faint woody scent, softened further by the warmth of the sun. Now and then, when I turned a page, the paper made a subtle rustling sound, like a tiny whisper.

“Aren’t you cold?” I heard my husband call from the living room. His voice held a trace of concern, yet not the slightest hint of intrusion. I looked up and replied, “No, it’s just right here.” He said nothing more, simply settled back onto the sofa and continued watching his movie.

Back in the book, I came across a passage about the author strolling alone on the beach, feeling the wind and the grains of sand against their skin. I suddenly felt a little dazed and unconsciously ran my fingers over the wooden surface of the bench. The grain of the wood was cool to the touch, but the sunlight gave it a certain warmth, creating a strange balance between my fingertips. I thought of my work—the drafts I revised again and again, yet still always felt were flawed. That feeling of never quite reaching the edge of perfection was like my fingers tracing the bench’s uneven wood grain.

I paused and looked outside. Beyond the balcony was a cluster of old residential buildings, and in the small courtyard below stood an old locust tree, its leaves swaying gently in the breeze like a slow song. From time to time, children’s chasing voices drifted up from the neighborhood, mixed with loud shouts and laughter. Listening to those sounds, I felt as if life were an accordion, with all kinds of notes woven together. Sometimes there were high, bright notes; sometimes, a quiet melody. At that moment, I felt my own melody was soft and unhurried.

When I turned to the next chapter, I noticed the author writing about self-doubt, and I suddenly felt a little dazed, as if my heartbeat had slowed by half a beat. I didn’t feel much intense emotion, only quietly wondering whether I was always making a mountain out of a molehill, always overthinking the details. I tried to let those scattered thoughts drift away as naturally as turning a page, but they only continued to float in my mind, like those leaves swaying in the wind.

As time slowly passed, I closed the book and stood up to stretch. The reflection on the glass window let me see my own blurred shadow, and I even noticed a strand of my hair fluttering slightly in the breeze. I walked to the kitchen and poured myself a glass of water. The cool touch of the glass pulled me a little away from the warmth of the sunlight. Dinner still hadn’t started, but I felt that life is made up of such gaps and pauses—not something that needs to be overfilled, nor something that requires one to deliberately search for meaning.

Over the next few days, I found that I seemed to have consciously or unconsciously remembered the wooden bench on the balcony—its texture, its warmth in the sunlight. These elements would surface from time to time in my mind, bringing with them a peace that was hard to put into words.

Sunlight streamed through the large windows and spilled across the gallery, while a faint scent of paint lingered in the air. I stood before an abstract painting, feeling nervous about this exhibition. It was my work, and it was undergoing an initial internal review. A colleague beside me said, “The colors in this painting are very bold, but don’t you think the overall composition is a bit messy?” Her voice was gentle, but unease immediately welled up inside me. “Messy?” I thought, my heart beginning to race, every hair on my body standing on end. My stomach churned, as if the lunch I had just eaten was protesting.

“Uh, do you mean I didn’t control it well?” I asked cautiously, trying to keep my voice calm. She smiled. “No, no, that’s not what I mean. It just feels like maybe you could think a little more about it... Of course, that’s only my opinion.”

Her smile did nothing to reassure me; instead, it made me even more uneasy. “Is she implying that I’m not professional enough?” a voice in my head kept asking. Over the next few minutes, she continued analyzing the strengths of the piece and the areas that might be improved, but I seemed unable to take in a word she said, able only to keep chewing over her remark about the “messy composition” in my mind.

I could feel my palms starting to sweat, my heart pounding somewhat out of control, and I had to shove my hands into my pockets to keep it from showing too obviously. To hide it, I nodded slightly and chimed in from time to time, but my attention was no longer on what she was saying; it was completely taken over by the anxiety inside me.

When she finally stopped talking, I felt a wave of relief. She patted my shoulder and said with a smile, “I believe you’ll do better.” That left me feeling powerless, as if I were expected to correct some mistake, rather than simply receiving advice. I forced out a smile and thanked her for the feedback.

That night, I lay in bed, the moonlight outside the window casting a soft glow on the floor. Yet inside me, thoughts roared like wild grass. These comments may have been nothing more than well-intentioned suggestions, but the shadow of criticism still lingered in my mind. My stomach cramped painfully, as if countless little bugs were crawling around inside. I began to doubt my abilities, worrying that in future presentations I would be criticized just as harshly by peers and audiences, or even rejected.

Over the next few days, I tried to take another look at my work, making an effort to view her suggestions with a calm eye. Although I had been interpreting every brushstroke through a lens of self-doubt, I also slowly began to accept my imperfections. A week had passed, and I found that I no longer cared so much about my colleague’s criticism; instead, I tried to find a direction for improvement in it.

The concrete floor beneath my feet was a bit damp and slick, and the air was filled with the mixed smell of engine oil and rust. In the bicycle repair shop, a dim yellow bulb barely illuminated a pile of discarded parts in the corner. I was standing beside an old bicycle, trying to figure out why the chain had jammed. “This bike’s chain is badly worn and needs to be replaced,” I heard the mechanic say in a low voice. He had his back to me, focused on fiddling with a battered bicycle. I wasn’t entirely sure about what he said, because I had a deep emotional attachment to this bike and always felt it could still be used. “I think we can try oiling it first,” I countered, struggling to suppress the anxiety in my heart.

“Sure, but it might not work well.” He turned his head slightly and shot me a frown. My heart began to race, and my palms grew a little sweaty. “Then let me try first,” I insisted, handing him the lubricant in my hand. He shrugged, as if he didn’t want to say anything more, and I took the chance to move closer and began gently rubbing the chain with oil.

Throughout the process, I kept sneaking glances at the mechanic’s expression, afraid he might read displeasure into it. He only occasionally let out a muffled grunt or two, while I concentrated fully on the stubborn chain, as though focusing only on the challenge before me could ease the unease in my mind.

Outside the repair shop, the street carried the distant sounds of passing vehicles’ engines and the murmurs of pedestrians. These noises blended in my ears into a kind of background hum, creating an almost imperceptible pressure around me. The chain finally loosened a little, and I breathed a sigh of relief, but the tension inside me had not eased in the slightest; I still doubted whether he truly minded my insistence.

That night, back home, even after I was sitting on the sofa, my thoughts kept returning to that moment in the day. Over and over I wondered: Was he mocking me in his heart? Did he think I was just an ignorant fool who didn’t know the trade? I did my best to suppress this recurring line of thought, yet before bed I couldn’t help fiddling with the phone by the bedside, trying to search online for little tips on chain maintenance, hoping to prove my method tomorrow.

In the days that followed, I still found myself thinking about it from time to time. Although it was unlikely to cause me lasting distress, a faint sense of unease would always rise with my thoughts, prompting me to reflexively check whether I had done something wrong.

There was a faint scent of wood in the air, drifting into my nose along with the early-summer breeze. I walked down an alley piled with carved wooden items, the path beneath my feet uneven and pitted, with the occasional broken wood chip crunching underfoot. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the old tiled eaves overhead, casting dappled patterns of light and shadow on the ground. The wooden stalls around me were filled with handcrafted birdcages, old cabinets, and even some rough models of ships. I thought to myself that this might be a good place to look for inspiration for a new piece.

Walking aimlessly, I was drawn to a set of wooden carvings at one stall—several lifelike little horses, each frozen in what seemed like a single, leaping moment. I bent down and gently pointed at one of the running horses, asking, “Are these carvings handmade? How much are they?”

The stall owner was a middle-aged man with a gray-streaked beard. He was bent over repairing another wooden item and didn’t look up at me, only replying coldly, “See for yourself.”

My face immediately flushed, as if I’d been doused with cold water. My heart tightened all at once: “Does he think I can’t afford it? Or that I don’t look like someone who would buy anything? Does he think I’m just wandering around idly?”

Unease quickly took root in me, and I began to feel that everything had gone wrong. The quiet alley no longer felt serene and charming; its silence became suffocating. I looked up and saw a few people talking by another stall not far away, glancing at me from time to time. Suddenly, I felt like an extra person, completely unwelcome. I awkwardly stood up, a thin layer of sweat forming on my palms, my chest growing tight.

“I should have just pretended not to notice this stall from the start,” I thought. “Why did I have to ask about the price? If they really think I can’t afford it, isn’t standing here just humiliating myself?” I felt a wave of embarrassment, as if the whole world were laughing at me.

I hurriedly got to my feet and headed for the stalls farther away, as if trying to escape. My fingers gripped the strap of my backpack tightly, and the sweat in my palms made it slippery and clammy, so I wiped them hard without thinking. I muttered to myself, “Why are you so useless? You can’t even ask a simple question! Can’t you stop being so sensitive?!”

But the voice of reason soon came back: “Maybe he just didn’t hear you clearly. Maybe he’s not good at talking to people.” Yet the more I thought that way, the more it felt like I was making excuses for myself. The tide of anxiety gradually washed over my reason, and I quickened my pace, almost running as I left the place.

When I got home, I tossed my bag onto the sofa and went straight into the bedroom, closing the door behind me. My heartbeat was still a little irregular, and a dull ache had begun to creep into my stomach. Leaning against the headboard with my knees pulled up, I started replaying what had just happened. “Was my voice too soft? Did my expression make him think I didn’t really want to buy anything?” These questions spun around in my head like a carousel, and my mood sank lower and lower.

After letting myself calm down for a while, I decided to write something to sort through my emotions. I opened my computer and tried to record how I felt that day, but after a while I realized that writing wasn’t helping much either. I began blaming myself for always being so fragile, for caring so much about other people’s reactions. In the end, I simply shut the laptop, pulled the covers over my head, and went to sleep. When I woke up the next day, I still felt uneasy, but compared with the helplessness I’d felt before, I was much better.

The wind brushed past the broken glass windows; the old tracks of the cable car station were streaked with rust, and the breeze carried a faint dampness. I stood inside an abandoned cable car station, camera in my arms. The ground was covered with scattered pine needles and gravel, and the wooden planks beneath my feet gave off a faint creak as I moved. This place had once been a local tourist attraction, but now no one came here anymore. I had deliberately chosen this area as today’s shooting location, only to find the atmosphere far colder and more oppressive than I had imagined. The silence around me was so deep I could almost hear my own breathing, and it made me even more tense.

In the corner sat an old cable car, its door half open, as if inviting me inside. I hesitated for a moment, then walked over anyway. The rustling sound of my shoes on the pine needles suddenly tightened every nerve in my body. I stepped into the cable car and found the seats covered in dust, while the mottled ceiling showed specks of rust. I tried adjusting the aperture and focal length on my camera, aiming the lens at the tracks outside, but no matter what I did, I couldn’t find a composition I liked. A strong unease suddenly welled up inside me: “Why does my photography always feel like it’s missing something? Have I already run out of creativity?”

I tried to make excuses for myself. “Maybe I’m just not in the right state today. Maybe the setting itself just isn’t interesting enough.” Such thoughts flashed through my mind, only to be shattered by another sharp inner monologue: “No, the problem is that my vision is flawed. I’m simply incapable of capturing this hidden beauty. Maybe I never should have chosen this path.” In an instant, the voice inside me grew louder and louder. I even began to wonder how I had ever believed I would take good photos today.

Just then, my phone vibrated. I glanced down—it was a message from a collaborator: “How’s the progress? Any new material to share?” That brief message was like an alarm bell, reminding me of how urgent time was. My hand suddenly trembled slightly, and I nearly dropped the phone. A cramp tightened in my stomach. I swallowed, trying to steady my emotions, but anxiety had already spread through my whole body. I felt as if every beat of my heart was speeding up. “If I can’t even take a decent photo today, what will they think of me? Will they think I’m just a fake creator?”

I leaned against the cable car door, trying to catch my breath, but the empty station offered no comfort at all. In the end, I chose to leave the cable car and sit on the cement steps beside the platform. The gray sky seemed to press down on my shoulders, and my mood was so heavy it felt like it might crush me. I tried opening my camera again and reviewing the few photos I had taken earlier. Each one disappointed me more the longer I looked at it. A phrase from the previous week’s collaborator kept replaying in my head: “The images feel a bit thin, lacking narrative.” Those words were like needles, pricking at my self-esteem again and again.

That night, after returning home, I hid in my study and repeatedly went through the material I had shot that day. It was not until late at night that I finally managed to pick out a few images I was somewhat satisfied with and sent them to my collaborator. The reply came quickly: “They’re okay, but could you try to present the sense of story more deeply?” I stared at those words, feeling as if this were the final straw that broke the camel’s back. My stomach tightened again, and it felt as though something was clamping tightly around my head. I threw the phone onto the bed and let out a long sigh, feeling as if I had failed completely—not only in this assignment, but in my entire creative career.

The night at the edge of the city always carried an indescribable chill and desolation, and the abandoned old ice storage facility was especially so. The patchy frost on the walls looked even colder in the shifting moonlight. The air inside was piercingly cold; I pulled my coat tight, trying to fend off the biting chill. With each soft footstep, anxiety gradually spread within me.

“Are you sure you can handle this project?” A colleague’s doubts still echoed in my ears, and he seemed to question my creative ability. “Of course, I’ll get it done,” I replied quickly, trying to hide my unease. But at that moment, the question would not leave my mind.

“Why choose here?” I asked myself. Perhaps it was to stay away from people; I had always felt that I could find inspiration in such a lonely place. Yet my heartbeat sped up uncontrollably, as if protesting my choice. Every time I felt this unease, I wondered whether I was being too impulsive and catastrophizing things.

I stopped in a corner of the ice storage room and closed my eyes, trying to calm myself. “How could there possibly be inspiration in a place like this?” I asked myself silently, doubting whether I had been too idealistic in hoping to find inspiration here. The cold tightened my muscles, and I began to wonder whether this project was beyond my capabilities.

Although anxiety surrounded me like ice, I tried to concentrate, listening to the faint sound of the wind by my ear, as if it might offer some kind of revelation. “I can’t let them down. I can’t,” I kept telling myself, unable to tell whether I was encouraging myself or attacking myself.

When I left the ice storage room, I found that my hands had gone numb from the cold, my skin slightly red. On the way home, I began to think about whether I should talk with the team and ask for their help. The sense of helplessness in my heart made me realize that creating alone was not the only way, yet I was still afraid of being rejected.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to fall asleep. The next morning, I decided to try sharing my ideas with the team and break free from my inner fear. Though still nervous, I no longer felt alone, and I began to think that perhaps things were not as bad as I had imagined.

I stood in the middle of the conference room, the bright lights around me making me feel a little dizzy. The colleagues seated all around were looking down at the files in their hands; some were whispering, others said nothing. I tried to steady my breathing, but my heartbeat kept racing faster and faster, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. Sweat silently ran down my forehead and dripped onto the collar of my shirt. I knew I should start speaking, but it felt as though something wasblocking my throat, and I couldn’t make a sound.

“Are you okay?” the colleague sitting next to me asked softly. “You look really nervous.”

I forced out a smile and nodded, but a wave of uncontrollable shame surged up inside me. I cleared my throat and finally began to speak, but my voice was so faint it was almost inaudible. As I struggled through my report, I could feel every pair of eyes on me; those tiny snickers and impatient expressions stabbed at my nerves like needles.

“Could you please explain this part in more detail?” the moderator suddenly interrupted, his tone impatient and cold, as if questioning my ability. I tightened my grip on the report in my hands, my fingertips turning slightly white, while sweat slid down my forehead again. It felt as though I had been abandoned by everyone in a place with no way out, and could be judged at any moment as a joke for being incompetent.

“This part is indeed a bit complicated; I’ll explain it in more detail later,” I stammered, my voice trembling uncontrollably.

The meeting seemed to drag on forever, every minute and second stretched endlessly. I could feel the cramping in my stomach growing worse as my tension intensified. By the time the meeting finally ended, I was almost staggering out of the conference room, hurrying to the restroom, desperate to find a place where no one could see me. Standing at the sink, I looked at myself in the mirror: my face was pale, my expression dazed. I closed my eyes and took a deep breath, trying to calm the trembling in my body. A faint smell of disinfectant lingered in the air, the only scent that offered me even a little comfort.

That night, I lay in bed turning over and over, unable to sleep. In my mind, every detail of the day’s meeting replayed again and again—every moment of embarrassment and awkwardness, every tiny expression seeming like a denial of my ability. I kept thinking about what I had done wrong, why I was always so sensitive, why I couldn’t be as composed as everyone else. A few days later, my colleagues seemed not to care, but I still couldn’t shake the feeling of being isolated.

The wooden floor of the piano shop creaked underfoot, carrying a sense of age and bringing a smell of wood and polish that filled the air. Morning sunlight filtered through the blinds and spilled over the vintage pianos, casting a warm glow. I stood before a grand piano, gently pressing the keys, trying to catch a melody long since lost.

“You play really well,” the owner’s voice came from behind me, clearly appreciative. I turned around, and he was smiling at me.

“Thank you. I haven’t played in a long time,” I replied somewhat self-consciously, while complex emotions began to churn inside me. Compliments like that often left me at a loss, as if they would vanish in the next instant and leave me alone with my loneliness.

Unconsciously, I touched my palm, which had become slightly damp; my heartbeat quickened, as if that one sentence had been some kind of omen. I began to consider what others might be thinking, a habit too deeply rooted to shake. “Does he think I’m showing off on purpose?” “There should be someone better here—I shouldn’t come here to show off.”

“Really, it’s good,” he repeated, as if trying to dispel my doubts. His words did not fully put me at ease; instead, they made me even more uneasy. I smiled and nodded, but my facial muscles were tense, my smile stiff.

After a while, I continued walking among the crowded display stands in the piano shop, touching one instrument after another. With each approach, their histories seemed to whisper in my ear, and those voices made me feel both familiar and frightened—they intertwined with my inner unease, leaving me nowhere to escape.

“If you’d like, you can play here a bit longer today,” the owner said with a smile. “We don’t often have someone this skilled come in.”

I nodded lightly, a flicker of unease crossing my mind: “Does he want me to help attract customers?” Then I realized I was overthinking again. Anxiety spread through me, and I instinctively looked around, as if expecting loud accusations and ridicule to come from somewhere.

That night, I lay in bed, replaying my experience at the piano shop. My heartbeat was still a little fast, and I tried to calm my emotions. Although the owner’s praise seemed insignificant to others, it stirred layer after layer of waves within me. All night long, I couldn’t forget what he had said, always feeling that there was some unnoticed implication hidden in it, or some deeper meaning.

When I woke up the next day, my mood was still somewhat low. Every step into the piano shop seemed magnified countless times, forming an unbearable burden in my mind. I decided to write down these feelings, hoping that the words on the page could sort out some clear answer.

In the afternoon at the workshop, the air was filled with the distinctive scent of wood. I was debugging the new machine, my hands still covered with sawdust that stung slightly when it brushed against my cheeks. These details always relaxed me, but today was different, and my heartbeat carried a trace of unease. Last night, I dreamed about the new project and woke up drenched in sweat. Now, standing before this colossal machine, I couldn’t help recalling a colleague’s joking remark: “Hope things go a little more smoothly this time.” It had been said offhandedly, yet I remembered it clearly. “Do they really want me to fail? Why do I always feel like I’m not good enough?” These questions echoed in my mind again and again.

“Hey, you look a little nervous today,” a colleague said casually as he passed by. I forced a smile. “It’s nothing, I just want to get the machine running as soon as possible.” He nodded and went back to his own work. I stared at his back, feeling an inexplicable sense of loss. Was it because of his comment? Or because of my own lack of confidence?

With all kinds of noise invading my mind, I tried hard to concentrate, but my fingertips had already started to tremble slightly. Whenever anxiety hit, this uncontrollable feeling became especially intense. Taking a deep breath, I forced myself to think about the next step: check the power connection, adjust the workpiece’s position. But my hands still shook involuntarily, and I couldn’t make them settle down.

The afternoon sunlight streamed through the workshop windows and spilled onto the floor, bright enough to be a little dazzling. I walked over to the window, trying to shift my attention, but the feeling of being abandoned wouldn’t go away. It was as if any tiny mistake would become the center of others’ attention, waiting to be magnified at any moment.

By evening, the project had finally made some progress. I worked out how to program the machine and came up with several improvement plans, feeling slightly relieved. Although I wasn’t sure whether these efforts would be noticed, I had at least done my best. On the way home, I was still troubled by my colleague’s comment. The moment I closed the workshop door, I decided that next time I would definitely do better.

At the project demonstration a few days later, everything went smoothly, which brought me relief and made me realize how overly sensitive I had always been. This experience made me feel that perhaps I wasn’t a failure in other people’s eyes after all, but rather that the shadows within had been whispering in my ear all along.

I stood in this dim hat-making workshop, with cold air slipping in through the crack under the door, carrying a biting chill. The walls of the room were mottled and peeling, and all around were piles of fabric, molds, and dust-covered unfinished hats. A bare incandescent bulb hung in the center of the ceiling, casting a faint light. The stale smell of leather mixed with damp fabric filled the entire space, stinging my dry nasal passages. The people around me all seemed unusually relaxed; they gathered in twos and threes, chatting softly, while I kept rubbing my scarf, as if that would make me warmer.

A middle-aged man walked up to me with a smile, holding a strangely shaped hat. He handed it to me. “What do you think of this one? I just tried changing the brim.” His smile was casual and confident. I took the hat, my hands awkwardly gripping the edge. The fabric was a little rough, wool with slight pilling, and I could feel that the stitching around the corners wasn’t quite even. I forced a smile: “It’s quite inventive, very unique.” The words had barely left my mouth when I felt my tone sounded too fake, like rusted metal scraping against itself. “Did he think I was being perfunctory? Will he think I don’t understand design at all?” My mind started racing, and my eyes drifted restlessly.

He nodded and walked away without saying anything else. I breathed a sigh of relief, only to find my palms already damp with sweat. I began rubbing my hands hard, staring at the floor without meaning to. Soon, I noticed a young female designer chatting and laughing with a few people in the distance. Her gestures were elegant, a composed smile on her face, while the others listened attentively and nodded frequently. I suddenly felt as if I were especially out of place, like a decoration that had been put somewhere at the wrong time. In my mind, their conversation seemed to turn entirely into talk about me: “Why is she so quiet? Is she unprofessional?” Those thoughts stabbed into my chest like needles. I even suspected they might exchange glances when I wasn’t looking, hinting that I was a joke.

“You look a bit tired. Is it because it’s not warm enough in here?” A gentle voice interrupted my thoughts. I looked up and saw a middle-aged woman nearby, sincerity in her eyes. She handed me a cup of hot tea. My hand trembled slightly as I took it. “Thank you, I... maybe I’m just a little nervous,” I replied softly, feeling my cheeks beginning to burn. She smiled. “Actually, I’m a little nervous too. You know, whenever you face so many unfamiliar people, it always takes a bit of time to adjust.” Her tone was relaxed, which brought me a little relief, but I still had some doubts in my heart: was she really comforting me, or was she subtly reminding me that I was acting too strangely?

After the event ended, I stood alone outside waiting for a car, the cold wind lifting my hair. I kept replaying the details: the expression on the middle-aged man’s face when he handed me the hat, the body language of those people as they talked and laughed, the tone of that woman’s voice. These scenes looped through my mind like a film, while my brain repeatedly scrutinized every word I had said and every move I had made. Was something off? Did someone think I was being too deliberate? These questions were like an endless vortex, dragging me into a bottomless anxiety.

When I got home, I hung the hat on the coat rack. Even though I was exhausted, my mind still wouldn’t slow down. When I woke up the next morning, my first thought was still of the previous day’s event. Even so, I felt a little relieved; at least that woman’s comfort kept me from completely unraveling.

The kitchen light was a little too harsh, the incandescent bulb buzzing faintly. I could hear the faucet dripping, drop by drop, into the sink. I set the coffee cup in my hand down on the table with a thud. My partner was scrolling through something on their phone again, not even looking up. The emotions I’d been holding back suddenly exploded like a kettle boiling over. “Do you even care about me? You didn’t hear a word I just said, did you!”

He looked up, frowned, and said irritably, “What’s wrong with you now? I was just looking at my phone for a minute. Can you not be so sensitive? Does everything have to revolve around you?”

Those words stabbed into my chest like a dagger. I felt my face start to burn, my ears ringing, my heart pounding faster, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. Stammering, I said, “It’s not being sensitive—you just don’t care about me at all! Do you think I’m a nuisance, so annoying that you can’t even be bothered to listen to one complete sentence?” My voice trembled as I nearly lost control of my emotions.

He sighed, threw down his phone, and stood up with his hands on the table. “If you want to put it that way, there’s nothing I can do. Should I kneel down and beg you before you’ll be satisfied? Do you even know whose fault this really is?” His tone was harsh and cold.

Every word he said hit my defenses like a bullet. My stomach clenched as if it had been struck hard, the sour ache making me feel sick. Tears surged up uncontrollably. I bit my lip to keep from crying out, but my voice was already shaking. “You don’t understand me at all. You keep making the same mistake, ignoring me again and again!”

He muttered something about me “making a scene,” then slammed the kitchen door and stormed out. The door sent a gust of air through the room, gently stirring the curtains. I stood there, stiff as stone, my pounding heart feeling like it might tear me apart. The moisture in the air mixed with the bitter smell of coffee, making me nauseous, as if something invisible were pressing down on me, sinking me into a place where I could barely breathe.

I don’t know how long I stood there. All I remember is eventually sitting on the sofa, staring blankly at the floor. The conversation kept replaying in my mind, every line laced with thorns. I began to wonder if maybe something really was wrong with me. Was I really a burden, someone no one could stand? But those thoughts only made me feel more ashamed, more desperate to run away. I kept blaming myself and even felt I didn’t deserve to be treated well by anyone.

That night I couldn’t sleep at all. I tossed and turned until my pillow was soaked with tears. The next day, my head still felt as heavy as lead, and the knot in my chest had not eased at all. I felt completely abandoned. Even though he hadn’t truly left, I still couldn’t shake the loneliness, as if I had been cut off from the whole world.

Walking into the small patchwork shop on the corner, the little bell hanging at the door chimed softly, as if welcoming me into this warm haven. The shop was quiet and cozy, with colorful patchwork works hanging all over the walls. The air carried a faint scent of lavender, giving off a gentle sense of comfort. I wandered between the shelves, feeling the texture of each piece of fabric—soft or rough, delicate or heavy. An employee came over and smiled, asking, “Can I help you? We just received some new fabrics.” I nodded, trying to focus on choosing fabrics instead of my drifting thoughts.

“These fabrics are beautiful,” I said to the employee.

“Yes, they’re from our winter special edition. Customers often come specifically to pick them out.”

I smiled, while an indescribable sense of loneliness began to rise in my heart. Every time this feeling came over me, it was as if I were standing in an empty wilderness, abandoned in an unknown corner. Waves of anxiety spread through me; I couldn’t help but feel my heartbeat quicken, and the palm holding the fabric started to sweat. “These patchworks are really special, aren’t they?” I tried to keep the conversation going to hide the turmoil inside me. The employee nodded kindly and continued introducing other fabrics.

In that brief exchange, I felt an unease I couldn’t shake off. I was always too sensitive, overanalyzing a simple sentence or an offhand smile. A voice inside kept asking whether I was truly liked, whether I was being judged, whether I was being rejected. I used harsh self-criticism to suppress these anxieties, reminding myself again and again that they were unreasonable. That same circular logic left me both ashamed and helpless.

“Thank you, I’ll take a little more time to look around,” I said politely, ending the conversation and continuing to wander through the shop. My heartbeat gradually calmed, and my tense muscles began to loosen. That night, I still couldn’t shake off the lingering loneliness, as if a cloud had wrapped itself around me, no matter how hard I tried to break free.

The next day, I decided to write, to record this experience and hope to process the unease inside me through creation. A few days later, when I reread those words, I realized that my feelings were not unique, but emotions many people experience. Writing transformed those chaotic thoughts into something I could contain, giving me a certain degree of relief.

The smell of rust and machine oil hung heavy in the air, like some old matter that could not be dispelled. The repair shop was tiny—so tiny that from the doorway I could take in the whole place at a glance: parts and scattered scraps of fabric piled on the tabletop, the window glass coated with a layer of dust, and the afternoon sunlight forced its way through that dust, falling in mottled patches on the floor. A wall clock ticked slowly on the wall, tick, tick, each sound seeming to remind me: you are still here, and you still haven’t dealt with this.

I set the sewing machine on the counter, my fingers absently rubbing the corners of its body. I had bought this machine at a secondhand market, thinking at the time that it had the texture of an older era, suited to some creative project. Now it had broken down here, like a silent rebuttal: what made you think you could use it properly in the first place?

The mechanic came over and tapped the tabletop lightly with his knuckles, his tone calm. “The movement’s badly worn. It may not be repairable. Some parts will need replacing.”

At those words, my stomach lurched downward.

I heard what “may” really meant, and what “parts will need replacing” meant: more money, and a longer wait. I said awkwardly, “Could you try repairing it first? I… have a limited budget.” As soon as I said it, I wanted to take it back. That pause, that “I…,” exposed too much. I looked petty in front of him, strapped for cash, like someone who couldn’t even pick the right tool.

He said nothing more, just nodded and started fiddling with the machine.

Silence settled in. Standing beside him, I began interpreting that silence. Did he think I was troublesome? Was he calculating in his head that this job wasn’t worth taking? Did he have some unspoken dissatisfaction with me? I knew I was imagining things, but those thoughts were like weeds—pull one batch out and they’d grow right back.

I tried to shift my attention and stared at the old-fashioned sewing machine posters on the wall. The people in the posters were smiling easily, their postures relaxed, creating a strange mismatch with the shabby condition of the shop. Suddenly I felt that I was also part of that mismatch—not belonging here, nor belonging to that ease. Memories began to surface: rejected commissions, the way a collaborator’s tone shifted when they said, “It doesn’t quite fit the style,” the words from a comment section that I had chewed over again and again for days. Memory, like a tide, quietly crept over my ankles.

“Try pressing the pedal.”

The mechanic’s voice pulled me back. My palms were already sweaty. I took a deep breath and stepped down. The machine did not respond. I bit my lip, trying to keep my expression within normal limits, not letting him see what was happening inside me. He looked up at me, as if he wanted to say something, but in the end he didn’t speak.

“We’ll need to order the parts. Probably about a week’s wait.”

I nodded, thanked him, and asked about the cost, hearing a kind of humility in my own voice that I didn’t like. When I walked out of the shop, the sunlight on the street hit my face directly, and my eyes inexplicably stung. In my mind I kept repeating that sentence: you can’t even get the thing you work with to function.

That night, I sat on the sofa for a long time and did nothing. The mechanic had shown no dissatisfaction the whole time; I knew that, but that “knew” couldn’t suppress those guesses at all. What exactly had that glance of his meant? Sympathy? Impatience? Or nothing at all, just an ordinary glance?

I kept dissecting that look until it lost all meaning, and then regained all its meaning again.

When I went to bed late that night, my heartbeat was still echoing in my ears, like the clock in that shop: tick, tick, unable to stop.

Frost on the glass window blurred the dusk outside into a patchy orange-purple mass, and my fingers tapped lightly on the tabletop while my heartbeat thundered in my ears. The air in the old spray-paint workshop was thick with a strange chemical smell, mixed with the cold, dry scent of winter, sharp enough to make you involuntarily hold your breath. My collaborator sat across from me; the screen of his laptop was still lit, showing the proposal framework he had just shared. His voice remained as flat as before: “I think this visual style of yours will make the audience feel it’s too emotional. You know the trend now—rationality and restraint are what’s mainstream. Maybe we should adjust it?”  

My stomach clenched all at once, as if a cold hand had seized it. I forced a smile, trying to hide my discomfort: “Really? I actually think being emotional can make it more relatable. That’s the direction I’ve always wanted to try.” As the words came out, I could almost hear the disgustingly lack of confidence in my own voice, like a small animal flapping its wings without enough strength to fly. He looked at me for two seconds, his expression barely changing: “Mm… think it over yourself. The final result is what matters most to us.”  

After saying that, he got up to get some water, his footsteps making a faint clacking sound on the concrete floor. I had nowhere to rest my gaze and could only stare at the sketchbook spread open in front of me. The ideas and drafts I had painstakingly accumulated now looked like childish doodles. I felt my cheeks begin to warm slightly, and something in my chest seemed to be swelling, forcing my breathing to quicken. My mind started chewing over the same thoughts again and again: was he implying that I wasn’t capable enough? Did he think I was dragging the whole project down? If so, why not say it outright? Why communicate with me in such an indifferent tone?  

My fingers mechanically flipped through the pages of the sketchbook, but without realizing it, I turned them faster and faster until the sound of a page tearing broke my motion. I froze, looking at the tiny torn piece of paper hanging from the edge of the notebook, swaying as if mocking my clumsiness. The sensation in my fingertips carried that thin, rough texture, yet my heart felt as if someone had squeezed it hard. I couldn’t help muttering to myself, “Useless.”  

Less than a minute later, he sat back down at the table and said flatly, “Let’s leave it at that for now. We can discuss it further tomorrow.” I nodded and squeezed out a “Okay, see you tomorrow” so softly that I could barely hear it myself. When he left, the workshop door slammed shut too abruptly with a harsh bang, and my shoulders jolted almost reflexively. My eyes inexplicably grew hot. I quickly turned to stare at the workshop’s old wall, where the remaining patches of spray paint and mottled cracks seemed to reflect my mood at the moment.  

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, my stomach still aching faintly. I kept questioning my choices—was I simply not suited to creative work? Or was I just not good enough, always driven by emotion and always disappointing others? Those thoughts clung to me like a nightmare; even when I finally drifted off into a daze at three in the morning, my dreams were still a blur of darkness and gray.

The wind slipped through the cracked seam of the window and into the lighthouse, letting out a low whimper. I stood on the small platform on the third floor of the lighthouse, my feet covered in thick dust mixed with the pungent smell of sea salt. The railing around the platform was already covered in rust; when I touched it, it felt cold and rough. I tried to adjust the angle of the camera to capture the battered ship outside the window, but the lens kept shaking and I could never get it into focus. The photographer came over, and his always-cold tone made me even more nervous. “Still not adjusted? Do you need help?” His voice was like the sound of a hammer striking iron, cold and direct. I immediately felt a sting of being scrutinized, rising in my throat like a mouthful of hard water that I couldn’t swallow. “No, I can do it.” I heard my own voice, dry and stiff.

But the shaking of the lens became more and more obvious. My palms started to sweat, and my forehead felt slightly damp too. I tried to wipe it with my sleeve, but that only spread the sweat farther onto my arm. I could hear my heartbeat growing heavy, like a broken mechanical clock, while in my mind I kept rehearsing the worst possible scenario—he would point out my mistake in front of everyone, everyone there would think I was utterly incapable, and I would become, in an instant, the failure under everyone’s gaze. I could even see their expressions: slightly furrowed brows, mouths carrying the faintest trace of mockery.

He was still standing beside me, looking down at the camera screen, a faint frown appearing between his brows. I couldn’t help asking, “Is something wrong?”

“You forgot to adjust the aperture,” he said, his tone like a helpless explanation to a beginner. Heat rushed to my face, as if I had been exposed in public, and I began to attack myself. “How could I make such a basic mistake?” “He must think I’m unprofessional now.” “Am I just not suited for this kind of activity?” My thoughts were like wild horses broken loose, galloping madly and crashing into every obstacle. I desperately tried to excuse myself, even saying, “Maybe the light here is too unstable.”

He didn’t respond. He simply lowered his head, readjusted my camera, and then left directly. I watched his back, my throat aching as if blocked by a stone, the corners of my mouth turning slightly bitter. I could almost hear my inner voice repeating over and over: “Is he disappointed in me? Does he think I’m dragging everyone down?”

By the time I left the lighthouse, it was already evening. I walked alone along the shore, the sand and gravel making a faint rustling under my feet. The sunset at the horizon was breathtakingly brilliant, red and purple interwoven like an artist’s brushstrokes. I tried to gaze at it, but I couldn’t feel true quiet. The conversation in the lighthouse kept replaying in my mind, every detail magnified, as if a painting were being brought closer and closer without end. I even began to fill in the photographer’s possible inner words with my imagination: “How can someone be this stupid?” “We can’t let her come next time.” My chest ached faintly, and my stomach began to cramp. When I got home, I didn’t want to say anything. I just made myself a cup of tea with hot water, crouched in a corner of the kitchen, and drank it silently, trying to calm my racing heart.

A few nights later, I looked through my camera and found that the shot I had taken was unexpectedly good—the lighthouse window ledge and the distant coastline came together in a perfect composition. I let out a long breath, but there was still a trace of bitterness in my heart. Could the photographer see that too? I wasn’t sure, and I had no way to confirm it.

We sat in the dim living room, the night outside silent and still, with a few stars faintly twinkling. The light inside wasn’t bright, but it was enough to illuminate every corner I didn’t want to face. My palms were sweating, feeling like a thin layer of sticky moisture that was almost about to drip off. My heartbeat quickened unconsciously, and I felt a wave of unease. From the eyes of the partner sitting across from me, I seemed to catch a hint of dissatisfaction. “You know, lately you’ve been using the same excuses to avoid the problem.” My partner’s words echoed through the room, and my breathing began to quicken. “I’m not avoiding it,” I retorted forcefully, my voice louder than I expected. “I just… have my own thoughts.” Even so, I could clearly hear the unease and guilt in my own voice. My partner was silent for a moment, then shook their head. “Sometimes I feel like you’ve never even thought about our future.” Those words were like a needle, pricking the fear hidden deep inside me. I couldn’t help feeling a chill rise from the soles of my feet and spread through my entire body. “I think about it every day, but I have my own confusion too.” I nearly shouted it out, and then came endless silence again. My fingers tapped nervously on my knees, trying to cover up the panic that was about to burst from deep inside. I often felt as though I were walking along a narrow path, with a cliff right beside me, where even the slightest breeze could push me over. After a long while, my partner sighed, and it was a sound of disappointment. My stomach twisted painfully, and I knew my fear was not unfounded. I wanted to salvage something, but my lips wouldn’t move; I could only silently endure the pressure coming from all sides, as if the walls were closing in on me. “I don’t know how to say it, but I really need some time to sort things out.” I forced down the trembling in my voice and said to TA. “Maybe we both need some time to think things through.” TA stood up and walked toward the door, the sound of their footsteps echoing in my mind. I didn’t move, frozen like a statue, able only to watch TA grow farther and farther away. The door closed softly, and the room was left with only the ticking of the clock. I sat there in a daze, my thoughts in a tangled mess, feeling as though my heart had been hollowed out. That night, I barely slept at all, repeatedly turning over TA’s words in my mind, every sentence like an accusation against me. I couldn’t help but think: if TA no longer needed me, where would I go? This fear of abandonment consumed me deeply, until at dawn, in utter exhaustion, I finally fell into a hazy sleep.

When I pushed open that heavy glass door, a smell mixed with sawdust and paint hit me in the face, leaving me slightly dizzy. The light of the setting sun filtered through the carved window frames and fell across the counter in a quiet, warm yellow. I stood in front of the counter, where a freshly framed painting sat before me. The grain of the wooden frame was smooth and refined, carrying a classical charm. The owner lowered his head to jot something in the ledger and clicked his tongue in admiration. “This painting is rather special,” he said. He looked up, glanced at it again, and added, “Though the style is a bit… well… distinctive.”

I froze for a moment. “Distinctive?”

He looked at me, then lowered his head and continued writing, as if he hadn’t noticed my reaction. He casually added, “Of course, that’s a good thing, but maybe it won’t be very popular.”

My stomach tightened, as if gripped by an invisible hand. I forced a faint smile at the corners of my mouth. “Really? Well, I think I’m pretty satisfied with it.” The words had barely left my lips before my mind began churning. That phrase “may not be very popular” kept echoing in my head, and I couldn’t stop reading into the subtext. Did he think my work was too strange? Or was he implying I should cater to the market? Was I being too self-indulgent?

My mind was like an old projector, endlessly replaying scenes from the past: a judge once frowning at my work at an art exhibition; a collaborator telling me my creations were hard for the public to relate to; and the sparse comments visitors left after an exhibition—“a bit niche, hard to understand.” These voices mingled together into a surging flood of emotion, while I stood there rooted to the spot.

“Hey?” The owner’s voice pulled me back to reality. He handed me the bill. “Cash or card?”

I lowered my head and fumbled for my wallet, my hands shaking so badly that several bills slipped to the floor. I hurried to crouch down and pick them up, my ears burning, as though everyone in the shop was watching me. When I stood up, the skin on my knee had scraped against the table leg and stung slightly. I took the frame, nodded stiffly at the owner, and said, “Thanks.”

As I turned and walked out of the repair shop, my heart was pounding like a drum, and my breathing had grown rapid. The afterglow of sunset still hung on the horizon, but it looked blinding, like a sky lit by fire. The edge of the frame pressed into my palm, and that rough wooden texture made me uneasy. On the way home, I kept replaying the conversation in my head, trying to decipher the owner’s real meaning: was “distinctive” praise, or a veiled criticism? And why did I always care so much about what others thought?

After I got home, I placed the frame on the table, but I had no energy to admire it. I sat in a chair, staring blankly at the ceiling, my mind a tangled mess. That feeling of being questioned lingered like a shadow, refusing to fade. Hours later, when I finally went to sleep, the texture of the frame’s edge remained as vivid as if it had been carved into my memory, even my dreams tinged with a sour unease. Over the next few days, I still couldn’t fully immerse myself in any other creative work, always feeling as though I were under a huge magnifying glass, where even the slightest flaw would be magnified beyond measure.

I walked along the edge of the city to a forgotten place: an abandoned old brick-and-tile factory. Around the brickworks grew patches of golden wild grass, swaying gently in the breeze and rustling softly. A distinctive smell hung in the air, a mix of dusty old bricks and the fresh scent of wild grass. I liked coming here to look for inspiration, because the quiet made me feel at ease and allowed me to escape, if only for a while, from the trivialities of everyday life.

As I walked through the familiar, rundown brick factory, sunlight streamed in through the broken windows, casting crisscrossing shadows on the floor. I was absorbed in watching the changing patterns of light and shadow, wondering whether I might capture something special today. Suddenly, something inconspicuous caught my attention: a seemingly solid brick covered in moss. I wanted to get closer for a look, but my foot caught on some hidden weeds, and I lost my balance and fell heavily to the ground.

“Ow!” I cried out involuntarily, my voice echoing through the empty brick factory. I braced myself on the floor and slowly got back up, my lower back muscles aching a little from the impact. My heart raced from the accident, and I could feel it pounding violently in my chest. All around me was silence, broken only by the sound of my breathing and heartbeat.

“This is my own fault,” I blamed myself inwardly. I knew perfectly well the ground here was uneven, yet I still let my guard down. Though I wasn’t seriously hurt, I still felt a twinge of frustration; the minor mishap had interrupted my reverie. I brushed the dust off my clothes and continued walking carefully through the brick factory.

Several hours passed, and I still hadn’t found any particular inspiration. On the way home, a light breeze brushed my face, and I felt a chill. Though a little disappointed, I told myself that next time I would be more careful and wouldn’t fall so badly because of a moment’s carelessness.

After I got home, I took a hot bath, hoping to relax my muscles. Though my body ached a little, I still tried to write down what had happened today so I wouldn’t forget it later. Lying in bed, I felt drowsiness creeping over me, and the brick factory’s distinctive smell seemed to linger in my nose as I slowly drifted off to sleep.

I was sitting in the café corner of a bookstore, with sunlight streaming through the window onto my table, warm and bright. Across from me sat an old friend, and we were drinking the new coffee she had just recommended. Soft music played in the background, accompanied by the rustle of turning pages and the occasional quiet conversation. She was talking about a recent trip she had taken, and I was listening intently.

“You know,” she said, with a hint of excitement in her voice, “I think the most important thing about traveling is the experience. Photos can only capture the surface. I even think that if you don’t take photos, you can focus more.”

I nodded, but a trace of unease flickered in my heart. “But sometimes photos help us remember those precious moments. Every time we look back at them, it feels like going back to that time.”

She smiled slightly and continued, “But sometimes we’re so busy taking photos that we miss the chance to enjoy the moment itself.”

I felt my heartbeat quicken, my face growing a little hot, and my hands unconsciously tightened around the coffee cup. I wondered if she was implying that I wasn’t doing well enough. I began to recall the photos I had taken on previous trips, wondering whether I had overlooked something because I was too busy taking pictures.

I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself. “Maybe,” I said, trying to sound indifferent, though I still felt a faint sense of unease and shame.

For the entire afternoon, I remained somewhat tense, my body feeling faintly tired. Her words kept echoing in my mind, as though every sentence she had spoken was dissecting my flaws. I couldn’t help but keep thinking about what her words meant.

After our chat ended, I went home. The room was quiet, with no disturbances at all. I sat at my desk and flipped through that travel album, feeling a bit heavy-hearted. Those images should have made me feel happy and nostalgic, but at that moment, they were mixed with a trace of weary self-doubt.

Over the next few days, I would occasionally think back to that conversation, reflecting on how to balance experience and recording it. I began to notice my own sensitivity to judgment and to examine more fully how this emotion affected me.

The streetlights flickered on the road, and from far away came the sound of car horns. With both hands in my coat pockets, I slowly walked along the familiar road toward home. The cold wind hit my face, making me shrink my neck and pull my scarf tighter, feeling the soft touch of the yarn against my chin. The orange-yellow lights from the convenience store by the roadside spilled warmly onto the ground, red promotional posters were pasted on the glass windows, and silhouettes moved back and forth inside. The stuffy heat from just leaving the office finally faded away; my body was only slightly chilled, and my steps carried a relaxed, unhurried rhythm.

Soft background music played in my headphones. I couldn’t remember when I had added it to my playlist, but it seemed oddly fitting, blending naturally into this quiet evening. From a nearby alley came a few bursts of excited laughter from young people. A few blocks away, there was also the buzzing sound of machinery from some construction work, but it wasn’t harsh. Now and then the wind passed through the branches, making irregular rustling sounds. There weren’t many people on the main street; occasionally I brushed past a few, all of them hurrying along, some looking down at their phones, others carrying large shopping bags. I couldn’t help thinking, “They’re probably thinking about going home too, right?”

When I passed a bakery, I stopped. A wave of sweet fragrance drifting out from inside distracted me a little. My reflection appeared in the window glass; perhaps because I’d walked for a while, my cheeks were slightly flushed and my eyes a little blurry, maybe from the warm streetlight. I stood there for a while, debating whether to go in and buy something to eat. In the end, I shook my head and kept walking. I didn’t want bread; it was just that the scent made me feel a little content. I thought to myself that perhaps this too was a kind of happiness: even smelling an overly sweet smell could ease the mind.

When I reached the entrance to my residential complex, I happened to run into my neighbor, Auntie. She was carrying two bags of groceries and holding her little grandson’s hand with the other. “Just got off work?” she said with a smile, looking to be in a good mood. “Yeah. You bought so much food?” I replied, intending to help carry something for her. Who would have thought the little boy would suddenly break free from her hand, shouting, “I want candy! I want candy!” as he ran toward the little shop. I watched as Auntie chased after him helplessly, and she called back to me, “Go on home quickly. This child is too much!” I smiled slightly and nodded. Watching her run off that way, I started walking again and continued home.

When I reached my front door and took out my key, my nose felt a little sour—maybe from the cold wind I’d been exposed to while walking. After I went inside, I set down my bag, took off my heavy coat, and the warmth from the heating hit me at once, making my body feel somewhat lighter. I made myself a cup of hot tea and sat on the sofa, spacing out for a while. Outside the window, I could still hear the faint wind. I stared at my reflection in the glass and suddenly felt a little dazed, as if I had become one of those hurried figures outside on the street, carrying packages. The contrast between the quiet of home and the noise outside created a strange sense of balance, leaving me feeling relaxed both mentally and physically.

I didn’t do anything special that night. While listening to music, I organized my work plans for the next day and flipped through a few pages of a book I’d just bought. Some of the sentences in the book were quite interesting, and I couldn’t help stopping to take a few photos of the pages with my phone, thinking I might use the content someday. I can’t quite say what’s so good about this calm, ordinary kind of day, but it simply feels comfortable—perhaps because there are no upheavals, no out-of-control emotions, and no moments when you desperately need to escape.

At two in the afternoon, the light on the balcony was just right.

Not the kind of harsh white light, but a lazy warmth tinged with gold. I dragged the wicker chair to the spot closest to the railing, so the sunlight could fall fully across my legs. In the air was the oily smell of someone’s cooking from downstairs, mixed with the coffee I had just brewed—a dark roast, with bitterness arriving first and the sweetness slowly following after, leaving a faint trace of sweetness at the root of my tongue. I set the cup back on the table and heard the soft click of porcelain against the glass tabletop, and thought the sound was lovely.

The book was flipped to around page eighty-something, the one I had put off finishing for more than half a year. I usually always had reasons to set it aside—messages to reply to, drafts to revise, data to watch refresh. Today there was nothing. My phone lay facedown on the table.

A pothos leaf in the corner of the balcony was pushed by the breeze, then bounced back. I looked at it for a while without thinking about anything.

This state was rare for me. My mind usually refused to stop—whether someone in the comments section of a video had said something, whether the client I worked with last week had sounded a little cold in their reply, whether I had said something wrong at some event.
