Those thoughts were like programs running constantly in the background; I couldn’t shut them off, only pretend not to hear them. But that afternoon, it was as if they had temporarily lost signal.

“You’re here.”

The child was standing at the balcony door, holding up a sheet of drawing paper. The sunlight came from behind them, blurring their outline a little, but I could see they were smiling.

“I drew you, and me, and the sun.” They handed me the paper. The crayon lines were crooked and uneven: two round heads, a big sun overhead, its rays drawn with great force, the color rubbed beyond the edges.

I took it and looked at it for a long time.

“What color is the sun?” I asked.

“Orange,” they said. “Because today’s sun is orange.”

I didn’t answer right away. I just placed the drawing on my lap and looked up at the real sun—it really was orange through the thin clouds. They had noticed something I had missed.

They sat down beside me and asked what I was reading. I said it was an adventure story. They went “oh” and didn’t press further, just leaned back in the chair and basked in the sun with me.

We didn’t say much. The breeze came again, and the pothos leaves swayed once more.

That afternoon I didn’t check my phone, and I didn’t think of anything that needed worrying about. My stomach was calm, my heartbeat steady, my palms dry. For me, all of that counted as some kind of achievement—my body hadn’t betrayed me, hadn’t suddenly sounded an alarm in a moment of peace.

That night, lying in bed, I thought of that drawing. The orange sun, the two round heads.

I don’t know whether that counts as happiness, but I do know those two hours were real. It wasn’t calm I was performing for myself; nothing was truly collapsing.

That was enough.

The air was thick with the stale smell of ink, and my fingers gently brushed a rusty printing press. Sunlight filtered in through the broken windows, casting mottled stains of oil across the floor. My throat felt dry, as if I were wrapped in a scent from decades past. A pile of old newspapers beside me drew my eye, and I crouched down, carefully turning open those yellowed pages. The paper was rough and brittle, liable to crumble at the slightest force. Every front page seemed to carry the memory of an era, and some of the content even formed a strange connection to my life when I was young, such as an interview with a certain writer. I had just graduated then and had once imitated that writer’s style in a few essays that went nowhere. “In truth, maybe I never truly belonged to any era.” The thought suddenly darted through my mind, followed by a spasming pain in my stomach. I felt a little unwell, as though the weight of my body were no longer under my control, and sweat slowly crept up my forehead. I stood up, trying to shake off the entanglement of my emotions, but the rust-covered machine before me seemed to lock me in like a cage. I thought I heard someone sneering in a low voice: “Do you really think you can leave anything behind?” That voice was far too familiar; it always appeared at the loneliest, most helpless moments. I closed my eyes and took a deep breath, trying to steady my heartbeat, but failed. “Are these newspapers even more meaningful than I am? At least they remembered something.” I bit my lip, feeling like an intruder in history, utterly out of place here. In the end, I lacked the courage to turn to a second newspaper. I turned and left, returning to a corner untouched by sunlight, colder there, and in some sense making me feel safe. A few days later, I was still thinking about the rust on that old printing press and the contents of those yellowed newspapers. They were like a mirror, forcing me to face the lingering shadows within myself.

A cold wind squeezed through the cracks in the window, bringing with it a musty smell and a stifling dampness. The light was dim, as if someone had draped a filter over the entire room. I was wearing a heavy coat, but the bone-chilling cold still seeped up through the gaps in the floorboards, shooting straight to the soles of my feet. Scattered on the floor were broken spindles and faded balls of thread, lying there like abandoned children, covered in dust. I swept the flashlight beam around and saw that a yellowed production schedule was still tacked to the wall; the messy handwriting on it had already become blurry and unreadable. I couldn’t help but imagine the workers who had once been busy here—machines roaring, yarn spinning at high speed, the blackboard on the wall filled with orders and progress charts. Now there was only a deathly silence, as if everything had been swallowed by time.

I walked up to a huge sock-knitting machine. It was covered in rust, and when I touched it, it was actually a little cold. I didn’t know how many pairs of socks it had once produced at its peak, but now it had become a pile of scrap metal. I tried pressing the switch on it, but there was no response at all. I let out a self-mocking laugh and lowered my head to fiddle with the balls of thread on the floor. Suddenly, I thought I heard footsteps behind me—the sharp clack of leather shoes hitting the floor was especially jarring in the empty space. My heart suddenly tightened, as if it had stopped for an instant, then began pounding wildly.

“Who’s there?” My voice sounded weak and trembling, as if it had been frozen. I strained my ears and held my breath, but the surroundings fell silent again, as if the sound had been nothing but my imagination. I felt my heart hammering in my chest, and my stomach began to cramp as if an invisible hand had clenched it. I swallowed hard, my mouth full of the rusty taste I had just inhaled. The flashlight suddenly flickered, and I jolted, the beam wobbling across the ceiling, making everything look even more terrifying.

“Shit, calm down, calm down!” I cursed myself inwardly, telling myself it was just the old building being structurally unstable, maybe the wind had moved something. But my legs wouldn’t obey me; they had gone stiff, as if I were sinking deep into the dust on the floor. I didn’t dare turn around, afraid of seeing something I shouldn’t, and I even began to keep an eye on the escape route out of the corner of my eye.

There was another sound, this time even more obvious! I turned around, and the beam of light landed on a broken chair in the distance. The chair was tipped over to one side and swaying slightly. I couldn’t hold back any longer and shouted, “Is anyone there?!” My voice echoed through the factory, and the only answer was the echo itself. The next second, I took off running, my shoes repeatedly stepping on loose floorboards and producing a series of creaking sounds.

Running out of the factory and breathing fresh air made me feel a little dizzy. I leaned against the wall and gasped for breath, still hearing the frantic pounding of my own heart in my ears. The surroundings were dead quiet—no people, no cars, only the whistling wind passing through the factory. I pulled a crumpled pack of tissues from my pocket and wiped the cold sweat from my forehead hard, my hands still trembling slightly.

After I got home, I brewed a cup of hot coffee, trying to calm myself down, but the swaying chair and the echo of footsteps kept replaying in my mind. I knew I might have been overinterpreting those sounds; maybe it really had been the wind, or perhaps a rat. But an uncontrollable wave of fear and shame still surged up in me—what was I afraid of? Why was I always like this?

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, over and over recalling that sound of footsteps and my reaction. I even started to wonder if something was wrong with me, why I always imagined the worst. Was I really the only one like this?

I sat in a corner of the living room, clutching my cup, the surrounding chatter noisy yet muffled as if separated by a pane of glass. I listened to my sister’s voice coming from the other end; her tone was light and casual as she chatted with everyone about childhood. “Back then, you were always so sensitive, always thinking everyone disliked you. In fact, you were just scaring yourself,” she said. As she spoke, I saw the corners of her mouth lift slightly, and in that moment it felt as if everyone’s gaze had landed on me. My face burned, as though I had been stripped naked and stood before everyone. “I never did that!” I retorted almost on instinct, my voice sharper than I had intended. The living room fell silent in an instant, the atmosphere freezing like cold air. I saw my father lower his head to fiddle with his phone, my mother let out a soft sigh, and my sister raise her eyebrows at me. “You’re still like this now—anyone says a couple of things to you and you think you’re being singled out.” There was a trace of sarcasm in her tone that I couldn’t ignore. My stomach twisted into a knot, and my palms began to sweat. My heart raced, and the buzzing in my ears almost drowned out what she said next. I don’t remember what I said, only that my sister’s face grew colder and her words became more direct. “You’re always like this, turning the most ordinary things into the sky falling. How is anyone supposed to talk to you?” Her tone was tinged with barely concealed annoyance. I felt my throat tighten, as if an invisible hand had gripped it. I suddenly stood up and slammed my cup down hard on the coffee table. “Don’t pin every problem on me! Whether when I was a child or now, none of you has ever truly understood me!” My voice trembled, and my eyes burned hot. I rushed into the bathroom, regardless of how they reacted outside. After closing the door, tears surged out of me at once, but I didn’t dare make a sound; I could only let them fall silently. Leaning against the bathroom wall, memories from childhood kept flashing through my mind—the birthdays that were ignored, the moments my sister mocked me, those afternoons when I stood alone in the corner of the classroom. Those scenes were blurry yet vivid, like old film, each frame stabbing at my chest. I began to doubt myself: had I been the one creating problems all along? Was I really the one destroying every relationship? By the time the gathering ended, I silently took my bag and left without saying goodbye to anyone. For the next few days, I didn’t reply to any of my sister’s calls or messages. I didn’t dare touch them; I was afraid her words would shatter the little sense of security I had left. This incident weighed on my heart like a boulder, nearly making it hard to breathe.

I stood in the basement of this city’s old public library, surrounded by yellowed bookshelves, with the air carrying a mix of the scent of paper and a faint mustiness. The lighting was dim and somewhat stifling. Old posters were pasted on the walls, and I could even feel their corners curling slightly. Beside me, the librarian was guiding me as I sorted the old bookshelves for a volunteer activity.

She said softly, “You can start from here and arrange the books by category.” I nodded, my heart inexplicably beating faster, my palms beginning to sweat slightly. I struggled not to let my panic show, but I couldn’t help thinking: if I messed up, would I be rejected or criticized? Every book on those shelves felt like a heavy brick. I tried to move them steadily, yet from time to time I felt my fingers stiffen with tension.

In my mind, I kept previewing the worst possible outcome like a movie: all the books falling, the librarian scolding me, and then being expelled from the volunteer activity. This catastrophic imagination gave me a dull pain in my stomach. I secretly glanced at her expression; she was simply focused on the work at hand, with no sign of displeasure.

I silently repeated a spell to keep calm, doing my best to continue arranging the books. Yet time seemed elusive. Every time I shifted my posture, I could feel the muscles in my back tightening like strings. Every few minutes, my fingers would unconsciously rub against each other, trying to relieve my anxiety.

After about half an hour, she checked her watch and smiled faintly. “You’re making good progress. It’s about time for a break.” Hearing that, a huge weight finally lifted from my heart. I let out a soft breath, trying to appear more relaxed, and the tension on my face gradually eased.

However, just when I thought I could relax a little, she spoke again: “It seems a few books are in the wrong categories. Could you help me reorganize them?” My heart started racing again, and I could only preemptively attack my own role in my mind to avoid possible criticism. I quickly apologized, my voice trembling: “Sorry, I’ll check them again.”

That night after I got home, the experience at the library still knotted itself around my thoughts. Although the staff had been friendly, I fell into prolonged introspection, repeatedly weighing every detail and trying to find possible mistakes. For several consecutive days, I kept reliving that basement in my dreams, the phantom sound of reproach echoing in my ears, making it hard for me to sleep.

Deep down, I knew it was nothing more than my fear of rejection and my sensitivity, but I still couldn’t completely shake it off.

The space beneath the railway bridge was open and quiet. Now and then, a breeze would drift by, and I could hear the sound of car tires passing overhead, mingled with the occasional birdsong. The gravel under the bridge was a little rough, and I lightly kicked at a small pebble with my foot, while inside I was sinking into deep anxiety over a project at work. It felt like an invisible burden was pressing on my chest, making my breathing a little tight. As if the whole world were bearing down on me, forcing me to solve problems that seemed impossible to resolve.

“How have you been feeling lately?” a partner had asked me in a meeting earlier that day. His expression was so calm, yet in that calm I sensed a hint of hidden tension. His tone made me wonder whether it was a veiled criticism. I struggled to stay composed and replied, “Other than being under some pressure, I’m actually okay.” After that, silence fell again.

My inner monologue kept surging: “If this project fails, will I be blamed? If he’s disappointed in me, what should I do?” My heart began to race, fine beads of sweat gathered at my temples, and my stomach tightened. Moments like this always made me feel as if I could be abandoned at any time, and this time I even played out a scene in my head of being isolated and ignored by everyone.

I paced back and forth beneath the bridge, occasionally lowering my head to study the rails, worn down by time. The wind carried a faint smell of rust from the abrasion of steel, reminding me of those cold, steel-like business negotiations and ruthless competition. Each step hovered over the uncertainty of the future, and I seemed to hear an alarm sounding in my heart. I knew my sensitivity often made things more complicated, and this time I was facing an unavoidable pressure.

While my thoughts were still tangled, I heard my phone vibrate. The call was from a colleague, who only wanted to confirm details of a report. The tone on the other end was kind, which put me slightly at ease. Yet after hanging up, I still couldn’t shake the heaviness in my heart and could only keep wandering aimlessly beneath the bridge, like a version of myself trying to escape reality.

That night, lying in bed, my body still tense, I kept replaying the conversation from the meeting and the facial expressions I had overinterpreted. A few days later, I decided to be honest with my team members about how I was feeling, trying to find relief from that sense of oppression, like the dry stones beneath the bridge, worn away naturally by time, finding my own ease and freedom.

In the hall of the exhibition, the walls were covered with illustration works of all styles, their vivid colors dazzlingly bright and overwhelming to the eye. I walked slowly, the carpet soft beneath my feet, while the air carried a faint, fresh scent of sandalwood. In my ears were the quiet voices of the crowd chatting; occasionally someone would comment on a certain piece, and I tried to catch every word, attempting to infer their true intentions.

“What do you think of this painting?” a bystander suddenly asked.

I froze for a moment, my heart instantly racing and my palms beginning to sweat. “Well, I think... it’s very creative,” I stammered, though inside I was full of uncertainty and began to question whether my judgment was professional enough.

In front of a landscape painting, I stopped. The lush greenery and shifting light and shadow in the work reminded me of some long-ago beautiful summer day. At that moment, I began an internal struggle, thinking about how I would present such details if I were the one creating it. Yet soon I fell back into doubt—did I really have the ability to reach that level?

Suddenly, I felt a strong pain in my stomach, as if tension had turned into an invisible hand twisting inside it. I tried to take deep breaths, hoping to ease the discomfort a little, but my heart was still pounding violently. I remembered the shame I had felt in the past when I performed poorly in similar settings, and that fear of being judged came flooding back.

“Everyone’s looking forward to your work,” a colleague’s voice came from behind me, carrying encouragement, but to me it felt like an invisible pressure. I forced myself to smile and reply, “Thank you, I’ll do my best.” But after saying that, my mind was filled with scenes of failure I had already played out in advance.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying every detail of what had happened at the exhibition in my head, especially that line—“Everyone’s looking forward to your work”—which kept echoing over and over. On that sleepless night, I felt trapped in an inescapable cycle, utterly exhausted.

A few days later, I still couldn’t help but revisit my work, repeatedly checking whether it was good enough, while also worrying that the audience would criticize it. Although I hoped to draw new inspiration from it, anxiety and nervousness never seemed to leave me.

I sat at my desk, and the dim lamplight cast my shadow onto the wall, where it seemed to be mocking me. I was preparing to release a new work. Yet the anxiety in my heart was like an invisible hand, gripping my throat tightly. I took a deep breath, trying to steady my heartbeat, but everything was slipping out of control. The words on the computer screen blurred, and I began to doubt whether these things were even worth showing. The few emails I had received earlier still weighed on my mind, making me increasingly uneasy. Their words pierced my heart like needles: “Are you writing something boring again?” 

At once, I felt a cramp in my stomach, and fine beads of sweat broke out on my palms. I examined my work over and over, not even sparing the punctuation marks, afraid that any detail might become ammunition for others’ criticism. Then the phone rang; it was the editor from the publishing house. “We’re arranging the release for tomorrow. Are you ready?” Her voice sounded so calm, while I could only manage to answer on my end of the line, “Of course, I’m ready.” 

I hung up, and my inner monologue surged like a flood: Did I deserve these expectations? Would people think these works were utterly boring? I even began to imagine the disappointed expressions and voices after the release. The wind outside seemed to repeat those taunts, and I felt my heart race, my hands and feet go cold. I thought of those failures and embarrassing moments from the past, as if they were playing out right before my eyes again. 

Unable to endure this torment, I rushed out the door, hoping the fresh air would calm me down. The cool night breeze brushed across my face, and my tension eased a little. Walking down the street, I found myself unconsciously kicking at the pebbles underfoot, while my mind kept spinning: What if no one likes my work? Would all my efforts have been in vain? 

That night, when I got home, my emotions were still in complete disarray. Even though I was exhausted, I couldn’t fall asleep lying in bed, and I kept thinking over and over: If everything fails, how am I supposed to face it? Panic and shame intertwined, and I could hardly break free from them. The next morning, at the moment of release, I felt as if I had been thrown onto a runaway roller coaster, with no idea where the end was. A few days later, I kept refreshing the page to check the feedback. Positive comments gave me a little reassurance, but I always magnified the critical voices; they echoed again and again in my mind: Was I really that bad?

Sunlight filtered through the lush leaves in the park, casting dappled shadows across the grass. A few friends and I sat around a picnic blanket, enjoying the rare pleasant weather. The air was filled with the aroma of food—grilled chicken wings, sandwiches, and the fresh scent of fruit salad. I picked up a sandwich and was just about to take a bite when I heard one friend beside me say, “You always seem a little nervous in situations like this.” My heart gave a jolt. I paused, looked up at her expression, and saw that she didn’t mean anything by it—she had only said it casually.

“Yeah, I guess I am a little,” I replied with a forced smile, trying not to let her see my unease. Then my mind began churning as I tried to interpret the meaning behind her words. Was she saying that I was never relaxed enough in social situations? I tried to recall various scenes from the past, hoping to find the basis for her comment, but that only made me more anxious. My heart started racing, my palms grew sweaty, and a dull pain began to stir in my stomach.

The laughter and conversation around me suddenly became muffled. I felt as though I were sealed inside a transparent dome, able only to see people’s lips moving without hearing what they were saying. I desperately wanted to rejoin the moment, but it was as if an invisible force were pushing me farther and farther away.

“Are you okay?” another friend noticed something was off and asked with concern.

“Oh, I’m fine, maybe it’s just too hot today,” I replied dismissively, forcing out a smile. But an inner voice kept blaming me: “Why do you always mess up these simple situations? Why can’t you relax like everyone else?”

After the gathering ended, I walked home alone, replaying those words over and over in my mind: “You always seem a little nervous.” The spiral of self-attack seemed to consume all my reason. That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to sleep. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw myself embarrassing myself in all kinds of social situations, and my heartbeat remained too fast to calm down. For a full week, that unsettled feeling seemed like chains wrapped tightly around me, making me hesitate every time I had to attend a group activity.

The smell of the leather was strong, with a faint spicy note to it. The workshop was somewhat dimly lit, and the hanging lamp overhead seemed to be a favorite of the older generation of craftsmen too—a white incandescent bulb with a yellowish glow that filled the whole room with a sense of quiet. The tabletop was crowded with all kinds of tools, bottles of paint, and a hide that was in the middle of being pieced together, giving off a strange mixed odor. The air was slightly cool, but my palms were sweating.

“You can try cutting it yourself, just follow the white line and don’t use too much force,” said the bearded master across from me, smiling as he looked at me. His voice was deep, but his tone was gentle. Normally, such a kind instruction should have made me feel at ease, but my stomach began to tighten uneasily again.

I picked up the heavy little knife, my fingers slightly stiff from nervousness, and the blade almost slipped out of my hand. “Just don’t damage the leather, or you’ll have to start with a new piece,” he said lightly, but I sensitively caught a faint upward curl at the corner of his mouth. I started to wonder whether he thought I was clumsy, or whether I simply wasn’t suited for this kind of meticulous work.

“I’ll try not to ruin it,” I said, my voice a little shaky, deliberately keeping it soft, almost as if I were muttering. But inside, everything was in chaos, like an alarm going off: “What did that smile just mean? Is he implying I’m too clumsy? Or does he think I should just give up?”

The blade moved along the white line, but because I was so tense, when I cut one spot, the leather suddenly tore into an irregular gash. In an instant, my palms were drenched, as if they had been squeezed underwater. “Oh no!” I whispered, quickly putting the tool down.

The master leaned in slightly to take a look and shook his head. “It’s fine. Beginners are like this.” He said it very casually, as if comforting me, but my ears heard something more in it. “So, in his heart, does he really think I’m just a talentless outsider?” My heartbeat quickened, like noisy drums pounding nonstop against my chest.

“Maybe forget it. Perhaps I really’m not suited for this…” I blurted out hurriedly, trying to hide my embarrassment, but as soon as the words left my mouth, I felt extremely awkward, even a little childish. “Why not? Failure is perfectly normal. Give it another try,” he said in a very calm tone, but in my head a chain of scenes began to emerge: would he turn around and discuss my mistake with the other apprentices? Had he already decided in his heart that I belonged in the category of people “not worth training”?

For some reason, my stomach felt increasingly uncomfortable, even starting to ache faintly. I felt as if I were trapped in an invisible net, unable to escape the self-reproach and shame. After that, I mechanically finished a few simple cuts, my technique awkward and my movements stiff, completely sinking into a tense state of “just don’t make mistakes.”

When I got home, I felt as if I had been completely drained, my legs weak and sore. Sitting on the sofa, I didn’t even have the strength to take off my coat. My mind kept replaying the master’s tone of voice, his expression, and even every syllable of the words “failure is normal.” I began to wonder whether I had been too conceited, or whether I simply shouldn’t have tried to do this at all.

Yet that night, I suddenly remembered the gentle expression on his face when he handed me the tool. Maybe he really was just trying to encourage me? Although this tiny possibility was far from enough to dispel my shame, to some extent, I felt that small bit of warmth had helped calm my emotions a little.

Sunlight streamed through the large windows onto the floor, and the scent of wood shavings filled the room. I stood in an abandoned woodworking workshop on the east side of the city. All around me were piles of discarded furniture and tools; though their owners were long gone, these objects still seemed to be telling stories of the past. I tried to focus on examining the old wood carvings, but unease quietly crept into my heart. I could hear my heartbeat growing fast and heavy, and sweat gradually began to bead on my skin. In the silence of that space, I could clearly hear the sound of my own breathing, and feel each heartbeat thudding in my ears. Then a voice came from behind me: a young woodworking apprentice had come by to take a look at these old tools. He smiled at me and asked, “Do you like these antique pieces of furniture?” I nodded, not knowing how to respond. Worst-case scenarios began playing out in my mind: a hanging beam might suddenly fall, or an old iron nail might pierce the sole of my shoe and stab my foot, with no one there to help me escape. I tried desperately to stop my thoughts, but past mistakes and embarrassing moments kept echoing back, eroding my mood. A dull ache started in my stomach, and the discomfort made me want to flee. I desperately tried to hide my anxiety and told myself I was just overthinking. The apprentice continued explaining the history of the furniture, and I forced a smile in response, trying my best to seem natural. “These once belonged to a famous craftsman. He was someone who truly cared about details,” he said. I tried to touch a piece of wood carving with my hand, but my fingers felt stiff, which made me even more ashamed. I felt like an outsider, unable to understand the true meaning of this space. There was a sense of age and decay in the air of the workshop that left me feeling a trace of abandoned loneliness. Even as I tried to convince myself that everything was perfectly normal, I couldn’t shake this feeling of insecurity. That night, I lay in bed still feeling my heart racing and my stomach unsettled, and the aftershocks of those emotions lasted for several days. I couldn’t help but reflect on why I was always so sensitive, and why an old workshop could make me so anxious.

At first, the atmosphere at the dinner table was relaxed. The restaurant was lit with a dim, warm glow, and the air was filled with the aroma of grilled meat and sauce. I held my chopsticks and picked up a freshly sliced piece of steak, pausing with it near my mouth without eating, because the conversation beside me suddenly made me feel something was off.

Just now, my younger brother had laughed and mentioned my work: “You’ve been writing those things for so many years, and you’ve actually kept at it. I really admire that.” On the surface, there was nothing wrong with that, but there was a kind of mockery in his tone that I couldn’t ignore. The others laughed along too. Though it was a friendly laugh, it seemed to hide some sort of judgment.

“Kept at it? What do you mean?” I asked, trying to keep my tone light, but my chopsticks were clenched so tightly my fingers ached. My brother waved it off and said, “Oh, nothing. I just mean what you’re doing, how should I put it, doesn’t seem very stable.” In that instant, it felt as if something had slammed into my chest. My stomach tightened, and a wave of heat surged from my feet to the top of my head. I forced myself to sit up straight, but my heartbeat was already racing, and the buzzing in my ears drowned out everyone else’s laughter.

I lowered my head and stared at the steak on my plate, pretending to focus on cutting it, only to realize I didn’t even have the strength to press the knife down properly. My mind started spinning stories: Did they always think I was a failure? Were they talking behind my back, saying I was a loser? Or were they just too lazy to say it outright, believing I was destined to be the family’s “odd one out”? Why couldn’t even my own family truly acknowledge my choices? A huge wave of shame washed over me, and my hand suddenly trembled.

“I know what I do isn’t very stable,” I cut them off loudly, nearly slamming the knife and fork onto the table. “But I like it! You don’t understand at all what it costs to create!” The laughter at the table stopped at once, and several faces froze. My brother looked at me, seeming at a loss, the smile on his face turning into an awkward stiffness. He said quietly, “That’s not what I meant. Don’t be mad.”

“You did mean that!” My voice rose uncontrollably, growing sharper and sharper, and I could even feel my face flushing red, my eyes starting to sting. My stomach pain was getting worse and worse, and I felt as if I were being hung over a furnace and roasted. The scent in the air had become suffocating, and the grease from the steak and the sweetness of the sauce made me nauseous. “What I do is different, but that doesn’t mean it has no value! Do you understand that?”

In the end, I grabbed a napkin from the table and wiped my face, then stood up and threw out, “I’m going outside for some air.” I practically fled the restaurant. The night wind outside was cold, and the streetlights stretched my shadow long. I leaned against the wall, breathing hard, with only the sound of my own heartbeat in my ears. A huge sense of loneliness swallowed me, as if the whole world were mocking my helplessness. Every argument seemed to remind me that I wasn’t “normal,” that I wasn’t truly accepted. That feeling stung so much I wanted to disappear on the spot.

Over the next few days, I barely took the initiative to contact my family. My brother sent me a message explaining that he only thought I was very persevering and meant nothing else. I didn’t reply. That feeling of being dismissed seemed to have taken root in my mind, tormenting me over and over again.

In the basement, the air carried a faint musty smell, and a few bone-chilling drafts seeped out from the cracks in the floor and walls. I sat on a plain iron chair, my hands tightly clasped, nervously listening to the intermittent broadcasts coming from outside. The lights around me were dim, and the clock on the wall ticked on, as if time had frozen at that moment.

When the drill began, I was told to stay behind and make sure no one remained in the basement. Everyone else evacuated to the ground level according to instructions. Although I nodded and agreed on the surface, a wave of unease rose inside me: “Does this mean they don’t trust my ability, so they left me with this relatively simple task?”

My heart began to race, and my breathing involuntarily grew rapid. I heard the voice inside me echoing again and again: “Why am I the one left behind? Do they think I’m useless?” The thought kept circling, as if reminding me of the fear deep inside me of being isolated and overlooked.

Suddenly, urgent instructions came over the broadcast, telling us the drill was over and everyone could return to normal work. A few minutes later, footsteps sounded on the concrete floor above the stairwell, and the vibrations reached my feet. I tried hard to calm myself, repeating to myself: “It’s just a drill; everything was arranged.”

When I finally stepped out of the basement, the sunlight made me squint slightly. Outside, there was a crowd in disarray—some people were putting away the drill equipment, others stood in small groups chatting and laughing, yet no one seemed to notice my presence.

That night, lying in bed, my mind kept replaying the events of the day. When I closed my eyes, that cold, damp feeling from the basement came over me again. My stomach ached faintly, and my body remained tense with anxiety. I began to reflect: if I already felt this way in a drill, what if it were a real situation—would I really be at a loss? That thought brought an even deeper panic.

A few days later, I found a friend and confided in him about my unease. After listening to my account, he smiled faintly and said, “You know, sometimes being left behind isn’t because you’re not capable, but because you’re trusted—they believe you can handle that kind of situation.” Although this didn’t completely dispel my doubts, it at least made me begin to try looking at things from a different angle.

When I stepped into this abandoned toy repair shop, the old bell on the door gave off a faint jingle, probably because it had fallen into such disrepair over the years. The place was utterly silent, save for the wind that occasionally slipped in through the broken windows, stirring up the dust on the floor. I stood at the doorway and couldn’t help shivering; my heart began to race. I instinctively looked around again and again, making sure no one had followed me.

“It’s eerily quiet in here,” I muttered, trying to make my voice soften the loneliness of being here by myself. The corners of the room were piled with broken gears and splintered wood, and the air was filled with a stale, pungent smell of grease. A dull ache began to gnaw at my stomach, as if the unease and anxiety had found an outlet in my body.

“Are you okay?” I pretended someone was beside me, giving myself a little false companionship. I walked over to an old wooden toy and gently touched it, my fingertips lifting a thin layer of dust. I began to imagine what this place must once have been like, with children laughing here and toy repairmen busily mending the beloved toys.

An inner monologue surged up like a tide. I thought back to those moments in the past when I had been rejected and ignored, and the fear of those feelings returning rose up again. I did my best not to fall into the abyss of repeated memories, but those recollections were like the dust in the toy shop—impossible to shake off. “If I had worked harder back then, maybe it wouldn’t have turned out like this.” That thought had almost become an instinct.

“Maybe you should go back,” a voice said in my mind. I talked to myself in my head to ease the unease. I realized that although the place was dark and dim, I didn’t have the courage to leave right away. Something seemed to be keeping me there—perhaps it was a sense of kinship with those broken toys. My hand clenched unconsciously, and a faint tingling sensation slipped across my palm, reminding me of reality.

For several nights after leaving that place, I tossed and turned without sleep. Whenever I closed my eyes, those shabby toys and vanished laughter appeared in my mind, refusing to go away. “Why are you like this?” In the stillness of night, I began to question my own sensitivity and fragility, wondering how I could stop being driven by these endless inner dramas.

A few days later, those emotional fluctuations gradually eased, though they never disappeared completely. I resolved to begin a new creative project and weave this experience and these feelings into it. I realized it was time to strip those old memories from my heart and no longer let them become obstacles in my life. The day I walked into the abandoned toy repair shop left me feeling lonely, but it also made me more deeply aware that self-attack was a weakness I had to face.

Soft light spilled across the wooden floor of the hall, and the air was mixed with the scents of red wine and pastries. I stood in a corner with a glass of champagne in my hand, scanning the crowd around me. Some people were laughing loudly about today’s exhibition, while others were speaking in low voices. My stomach felt a little uneasy, as if it had been gently stirred. I tried to make myself look relaxed, but the champagne glass in my hand had already become hard to hold because of my sweaty palm.

A fellow artist came over and said with a smile, “Your work is very distinctive, especially the use of color. It’s truly unique.” His tone sounded casual, almost offhand. I froze for a moment, and my mind instantly churned through all kinds of possibilities: Was “distinctive” a compliment or a criticism? Was he hinting that my work was too unconventional? “Unique” sounded like praise, but why did it feel a little strange to me?

“Thank you,” I hurriedly replied, forcing out a smile, though I could feel my facial muscles stiffen. He continued, “Still, I think if there were a little more tension in how you express emotion, it might be better.” Those words felt like a thin needle pricking my chest. I nodded unconsciously, but felt my stomach tighten and my heartbeat suddenly quicken, as if someone nearby were beating a drum. I tried hard to control my expression and not look too obvious, but my fingers instinctively clenched the rim of the glass.

A debate quickly unfolded in my mind: Was he subtly criticizing me? Was my work really lacking in tension? If so, he must think it was wrong for me to create according to my own intentions. Could this exhibition really have been a failure? And if he told others, what would everyone think of me? My throat gradually went dry, yet I didn’t dare defend myself. I was afraid that anything I said would be interpreted as evasion or argument—and that would only make things worse.

After a while, I made up an excuse to go look at other exhibition areas and left the conversation, but in truth I only found a corner to stay in. His words kept echoing in my head, every single one amplified. What kept appearing in my mind was his expression: disdainful or casual? I replayed the tone and pauses in that sentence again and again, trying to find clues. My whole body felt heavy, as if my shoulders were being pressed down by something. By then, I could no longer remember much of the original conversation at the event; all my attention had shifted to my own worries.

That night, even after I got home, I still couldn’t shake off the scene. I sat on the sofa, staring at the dim yellow light in the living room, repeatedly thinking about those words, “the depth and tension of emotion.” I began to doubt whether my work really was missing something. Even though a voice inside me wanted to say, “Maybe he was just speaking casually; there was no deeper meaning,” that voice was always drowned out by self-attacking thoughts. I wrote pages of analysis in my journal, trying to find the root of the problem, only to discover that the more I wrote, the more it felt like proof of failure. Over the following week, I kept adjusting my creative direction, hoping to fill that so-called “tension.”

At the first light of dawn, I walked into the flower market on the west side of the city. The air was filled with the scent of damp earth and fresh blossoms. I wanted to buy some flowers to brighten up my room, hoping they would bring a little calm to my tense work life. Yet as soon as I stepped into the market, my heart began to race and my palms started sweating, which made me feel somewhat uneasy. Looking around, I saw colorful flowers in full bloom, with customers of all kinds weaving among them. I decided to buy some sunflowers, but when I passed the counter, the clerk’s expression made me suspicious.

“These flowers just came in this morning, and they look very lively,” the clerk said, with a hint of weariness I couldn’t quite identify.

I immediately started wondering whether I was dressed too casually, or whether she simply didn’t like the way I looked. I hurriedly gripped my bag tightly, feeling a knot of pain in my stomach, and tried to stay calm. “How much are these flowers?” I asked, trying to make my voice sound natural.

“Twenty-five yuan a bunch. If you buy more, I can give you a discount,” she replied, but her eyes drifted elsewhere. Instantly, I began to suspect that she was indifferent to me. Why wouldn’t she look at me when she spoke? I felt a sting of being ignored, as if everyone in the market could sense my sense of abandonment.

I decided to strike first to avoid being completely dismissed by her. “Do you think I’m not going to buy them?” I asked, my voice much sharper than I had intended.

The clerk gave me a slightly puzzled look. “No, I just meant that it would be more economical if you bought in bulk.”

I felt even more uncomfortable, my heartbeat quickening, my back damp with sweat. She must be mocking my poor judgment; I should leave this place. But I still felt unwilling to walk away like that. In the end, I bought two bunches of sunflowers, while my mind was practically in turmoil. After leaving the flower market, I kept thinking about what had just happened, and the unease in my heart lingered for a long time.

That evening, I still felt weighed down. Whenever I glanced at the sunflowers on the living room table, I was reminded of the awkward moment at the market. That sense of humiliation at not being taken seriously seemed to seep into every cell of my body. I inevitably began to reflect on myself, criticizing my own oversensitivity and anxiety. The next day, I decided that any future shopping would require thorough psychological preparation to prevent similar emotional swings from happening again.

The air was thick with the damp scent of wood, and many xylophones awaiting repair were piled in the corner. The dimness of the room made me uneasy, and the walls were hung with decorations made of old musical note patterns. I stood in front of the counter, trying to hide the anxiety in my heart. “This xylophone needs a complete adjustment, but there is still hope of repair.” The repairman’s voice was hoarse and deep as he examined the xylophone’s resonating box. I nodded, my heartbeat beginning to quicken, as if afraid things would turn out badly. The light in the room was dim, and I struggled to concentrate. “Do you think this can be fixed?” I asked, my voice betraying an involuntary tension. The repairman gently ran his rough fingers over the strings. “It will be challenging, but it should be fine.” His answer eased me a little, but there was still a faint twisting pain in my stomach. I felt trapped in an invisible pressure, as if even the air around me had grown heavy. The old clock on the wall ticked on, as though time itself were reminding me of each passing second. At that moment, a sense of loneliness rose within me like an incoming tide, and I could not shake it off. “Are you all right?” the repairman suddenly asked, a hint of concern in his eyes. I quickly replied, “I’m fine, thank you.” In truth, I was in utter confusion inside, as if there were nowhere to escape. My palms began to sweat, and I could hardly control myself. I pretended to inspect the scratches on the xylophone, while actually trying to calm myself down. After a while, I finally found an excuse to leave this oppressive space. However, the shadow in my heart did not fade even after I left the shop. In the days that followed, I kept thinking over the possibility of this repair, fearing that it would ultimately fail. The thought of possibly losing the chance to restore it made me even more anxious. It seemed that whenever I faced a challenge, I always hoped to attack myself first, so as not to be hurt by real failure.

Sunlight filtered through the broken window panes, casting mottled patterns across the workshop floor. This had once been a busy leather workshop, but now only empty rooms and peeling paint on the walls remained. A faint lingering scent of leather hung in the air, reminding me of all those fleeting moments from the past. With a camera in my hand, I tried to capture this perfect blend of emptiness and nostalgia.

The silence around me was so profound it felt unsettling. I could hear my own heartbeat echoing rhythmically through the workshop. Light footsteps broke the stillness, and my colleague came over and asked softly, “Are you okay? You seem a little distracted.”

“I’m fine, it’s just… this place makes me think too much,” I told him, trying to hide the stirring in my heart.

I turned my attention back to the task at hand, photographing the old tools around me and the scraps of leather left behind. But with every press of the shutter, I couldn’t help thinking back to unpleasant experiences from the past, as if these scenes were awakening some dormant memory.

“If these things could speak, what kind of stories do you think they’d tell?” my colleague tried to start another conversation.

“Maybe stories about being forgotten and abandoned?” I replied, my tone a little heavy.

After finishing this set of photos, I found a corner to sit in and tried to relax. Yet nameless anxieties crawled through me like insects. My heartbeat quickened, and beads of sweat began to seep onto my forehead. Even though the temperature around me was comfortable, I felt an inescapable chill.

I began to examine myself. Was I making things complicated again? Was my old habit acting up once more, letting the shadows of the past block out the sunlight of the present?

“Maybe these details aren’t that important,” I told myself, trying to respond to emotion with reason. I brought my focus back to the present and gazed at the photos I had taken, realizing that these images were not only about sorrow and abandonment—they also carried a sense of calm and history.

After that inner conversation, I finally felt a little lighter. I decided to break the silence and step out of the workshop. The sunlight outside was somewhat blinding, and a breeze blew toward me, scattering my thoughts and gradually easing the tension in my heart.

After leaving the workshop, I sat down in a nearby café and began sorting through the photos I had taken. Looking back at these images, I realized they were not merely records of an abandoned workshop, but also reflections of my inner state. As time passed, these photos might become part of my own growth, reminding me of the thoughts and emotions I once carried.

The next morning, after making myself a cup of coffee, I let the sunlight streaming through the window fall across the tabletop and began a new day’s work. At times, as I recalled my experience in the workshop, I came to understand that even if my heart was stirred, those feelings would eventually settle. And I, too, would find the strength to keep moving forward in the midst of that unease.

Sunlight streamed through the large glass windows onto the café’s wooden floor, and my friend and I were enjoying this lazy afternoon. The aroma of coffee filled the air. I lifted my cup and took a small sip; the bittersweet taste spread across my tongue. Sitting face to face with my friend, I listened as she recounted a funny incident that had recently happened at work. As she got more excited, she gestured wildly, her voice rising a little.

I smiled and nodded, replying, “That’s really hilarious! But I think this could be viewed from another angle.” I shared my thoughts, which were perhaps somewhat different from her perspective. Unexpectedly, her brow furrowed slightly, and a hint of displeasure entered her voice. “I actually think your idea is a bit too idealistic.”

At that moment, I felt my heart race, as if a rush of heat had surged up from my chest, and my cheeks began to burn. I tried hard to keep smiling, but I couldn’t help turning her words over and over in my mind. “Did I really say something wrong?” I kept replaying our conversation in my head, trying to figure out which word or point had upset her.

I realized my overreaction at that moment was irrational. Taking a deep breath, I tried to calm myself down. The café was noisy with people talking, my attention growing scattered, and my palms were slightly sweaty. I could only grip the coffee cup tightly to keep myself from feeling so nervous.

“Don’t take it to heart. I just think… well, maybe we see things differently,” my friend said, noticing my unease and trying to ease the atmosphere. I nodded, showing I understood. “Yeah, maybe my thinking was a bit extreme.”

When I got home, I was still mulling over the conversation. I sat on the sofa, next to cushions warmed by the sun, with background music playing on the TV. I thought I needed to let this little episode go and not dwell on it too much. But there was still a subtle uneasiness in my heart, like a wisp of mist hanging over the afternoon sunlight. A few days later, when we met again, that discomfort seemed to have faded, though I remained especially cautious about the details of what I said, always afraid of touching on something she might not like.

The studio curtains were half open, and sunlight spilled onto the desk as I continued editing a new video on my computer. Suddenly, my phone rang—it was a message from a friend. He said, “Do we have some kind of misunderstanding?” Those simple words made my heart tighten. My pulse quickened, sweat began to bead on my forehead, and I felt a knot forming in my stomach. “Misunderstanding?” I thought. Could it be that I said something wrong at the last gathering?

I hadn’t wanted to go to that gathering, but he insisted that he had some new ideas he wanted to share. I still remember the scene: music filling the air, dim lights, and a faint smell of alcohol drifting around. He smiled at me and raised his glass, saying, “You’re always so hardworking.” Yet at that moment, I suddenly felt a sharp sting in my heart: was that praise, or some kind of criticism hidden beneath it? I didn’t think it through, and simply responded mechanically, “Thanks, but I always feel like I still have a lot of shortcomings.” He just smiled then.

Thinking back on it, I began to wonder whether he thought I didn’t trust him enough, or whether I was always saying things to him at the wrong time. My cheeks felt warm, and my heart pounded even faster, as if it were about to leap out of my chest. I immediately messaged him back: “I feel the same way. Can we talk on the phone?”

During the call, his voice was very calm. “I just felt like you seemed a little uncomfortable last time. Did I say something wrong?” His tone put me at ease a little, but then my mind started racing again: was he actually not really concerned about my feelings, and just pretending to care? “No, it was my fault. I was probably overthinking it.” I apologized quickly, my throat tightening, afraid he might distance himself from me because of this.

After hanging up, I still didn’t feel reassured. The entire afternoon, I kept going over the details of our conversation, trying to figure out what might have caused a misunderstanding. Every time I thought of his questioning tone, it felt like I was being scrutinized. Even though I knew misunderstandings between friends weren’t serious, I still couldn’t shake my anxiety. That night, I barely slept, and the phrase “Do we have some kind of misunderstanding?” kept echoing in my head, as if it had become evidence used to accuse me of some flaw in my character.

A few days later, even though I met him again and tried to rebuild trust, I still felt uneasy inside. I was afraid that I would once again lose others’ trust and care because of some unintentional action.

It had been raining nonstop. The streetlights cast their glow on the wet pavement, reflecting a dim yellow sheen. I had just come out of the café, and the door hadn’t quite closed behind me; the noise and music inside spilled out through the gap. I could feel my hands trembling slightly, my fingertips damp and cold—I wasn’t sure whether it was rainwater or sweat from my palms. She and I had argued fiercely, and that sentence was still echoing in my ears. Almost shouting, she said, “You’re always like this! You’re so afraid of being rejected that you reject everyone else first. I’m really sick of it!” Her voice was sharp, like a needle stabbing into my eardrums. I stood there, staring at her stiffly, my face burning as if I had been slapped.

My heart was racing, and my chest felt like it was pinned down by a compressed block of iron; every breath felt heavy. I tried to respond, but my tongue had frozen, and all I could manage was an awkward, quiet, “That’s not what I meant.” But she didn’t stop. Her face flushed red as she went on, “Every time I try to talk to you about something deeper, you turn the issue into one of your disaster stories. Do you know how exhausting that is!” Those words struck at my core like bullets. I could feel a tightening pain in my stomach, like bent steel bars pressing into me.

“If you can’t stand me, then why do you keep coming to me?” I heard myself blurt out, my voice mixed with anger, hurt, and a trace of sadness. She froze for a moment, then shook her head, her gaze turning cold from hot with anger. “Maybe I really shouldn’t have come.” Then she picked up her bag, stood up, and left with a dry “See you next time.”

I sat there in the café, the surrounding noise pressing in like a tide, yet it all felt so far away. My eyes were fixed on the damp tissue on the table, while my mind kept replaying what had just happened. I even began to wonder what she meant by that last line—would there really be a “next time” for us to meet? Or was it just a polite phrase? The more I thought about it, the more I felt she was hinting at some kind of ending. My feet felt icy, as if all the warmth in my body had been drained away.

The rain beat against my umbrella as I staggered out onto the street, raindrops dripping from its edge onto my shoulders. I felt as if the whole world had abandoned me, or rather, as if I had pushed myself out of it. Did my friends feel the same way she did, secretly tired of me long ago? Were people only maintaining these relationships out of obligation, while I kept testing their limits? My mind began to rehearse the worst possibilities—she would talk to other friends about all my problems, and then everyone would gradually drift away from me. The cramping pain in my stomach grew worse. I stopped beside a tree, closed my eyes, and tried to breathe deeply, but my breathing only turned shallow and rapid, like a wheezing bellows.

When I got home, I took off my soaked coat and sank into the sofa. The cold dampness on my body made me intensely uncomfortable, but I couldn’t even be bothered to change clothes. My phone was still on the coffee table; several times I stared at the screen, wanting to message her and ask if she was angry, but the shame inside me stopped me. I was afraid she would reply with a cold “It’s fine,” or simply not reply at all. I started to feel like a hopeless failure—had my sensitivity and my overreactions long ago become exhausting to everyone? That feeling was like a thick veil covering my heart, pressing so hard on me that I could barely breathe.

When I woke up the next day, the pain in my stomach had eased a little, but that heavy mood still lingered like a shadow trailing behind me. I checked my phone and there was no message from her, which made me even more uneasy. I tried to cling to trivial little things to steady myself, but I still couldn’t shake off yesterday’s scene. I began to wonder if this was the end of all relationships: my sensitivity always wears people out, and then they leave me one by one.

I sat in the corner of a café attending a book discussion group. The book on the table was a literary work I had recently come to love, and around me sat several strangers, along with a moderator. The aroma of coffee filled the air, and the cups on the table made faint clinking sounds. My fingers rubbed absentmindedly along the rim of my cup, trying to calm my nervousness.

As the discussion began, the moderator asked, “What part of this book resonates with you the most?” I cleared my throat, straightened up a little, and shared, “I think the author’s portrayal of loneliness in the book feels especially real; it reminds me of a deep sense of self-doubt.” My voice was a little shaky. I could feel a few eyes turn toward me, but they quickly looked away.

A middle-aged man spoke next, his tone carrying a hint of disdain. “I think you’ve misunderstood the author’s intention. Loneliness in the book is something to be celebrated, not as negative as you’re making it out to be.” His voice was cold and hard, though his expression remained calm.

My heart suddenly began to race, and my stomach felt as if it had been clenched. I felt heat rush to my face, and my fingers stiffened. I quickly glanced at the expressions of the others, but most of them were simply nodding in agreement with him. A thought flashed through my mind: They all think I’m foolish, don’t they? They must be silently mocking how shallow I am.

I tried to respond, but my voice was trembling: “I’m not saying the author’s intention isn’t important, I just…” Before I could finish, the other person had already turned away and continued discussing with the rest. I bit my lip, forcing myself to hold back the urge to leave immediately. My mind began replaying the scene over and over, like a videotape stuck on repeat: his tone, his slight expression changes, even the look he had given me.

After the meeting ended, I quickly packed up and prepared to leave. There was still half a cup of coffee left on the table, but I had no desire to finish it. A woman sitting next to me said softly, “Actually, I think your point is quite interesting too. Loneliness really can be interpreted in different ways.”

When I heard her voice, my throat suddenly tightened. I nodded and managed a weak smile, but the feeling of shame still would not leave me. I muttered a vague thank-you, then quickly left the café.

That night, I lay in bed, turning over the whole discussion in my mind. The man’s dismissive image kept replaying there, and I tried to balance it with her affirmation, but failed. A few days later, I finallyorganizeed my reading notes on loneliness, trying to find the true grounding for my own perspective so that I could express it better next time.

The banquet hall for the company’s annual gala was glaringly bright, and the music from the speakers made the air feel hot and vibrating. I stood in the corner beside a long table, holding a glass of red wine; a thin film of condensation had already gathered on the outside of the glass. People flowed past in front of me, laughter and clinking glasses rising and falling in waves, like an invisible wall separating me from them. My eyes kept scanning the room, trying to find a familiar face, while at the same time praying no one would notice I was looking.

Before I went in, I had heard two coworkers in the elevator speaking in low voices behind me. I only caught the words “this color,” and their tone wasn’t particularly mean, but it still pricked my chest like a fine needle. My heartbeat thudded once, hard, then began to speed up uncontrollably. I lowered my head to look at what I was wearing today, and my mind had already started playing the worst possible version on its own: they were laughing at me, the whole department had noticed, only no one had said it to my face.

“Here already?” The department manager came over to my left with a drink in hand and smiled as he glanced at me.

“Yeah,” I forced out a smile. “You look very energetic today.”

He said, “Thanks,” then turned to talk with the coworker beside him.

It was that turning away. My brain froze for that second, then started replaying it over and over: was that look just now a little perfunctory? Was that smile polite or sincere? Or had he actually long since formed some opinion about me, and was only coming over to say hello tonight because of the occasion? I stood there listening to them talk about work, not taking in a single word, just staring at the wine glass in my hand, feeling it grow heavier and heavier.

I tried to shift my attention and walked over to a coworker I usually got along with. “What do you think of this year’s gala?” I asked.

“Pretty okay, I guess.” He took a dessert and turned to leave.

Three words. I stood in those three words for a long time. Had I asked something too boring? Had he long since been dissatisfied with me and was only now too lazy to hide it? My stomach started to ache faintly, as if something inside was slowly tightening. My face began to feel hot, my palms grew damp with sweat, and I switched the wine glass to my other hand, pretending to look at my phone.

In the end, I still left the hall and found a lounge in a quieter corner, sinking into a soft sofa. The noise outside blurred through a door, but the voices in my head grew even clearer. The manager’s turning away, the coworker’s three words, the unfinished sentence in the elevator—they lined up in my mind and replayed over and over, each time seeming more like proof than the last.

I forced myself to breathe deeply. I told myself: You’re overthinking it. The annual gala is just a formality anyway; nobody cares about these details.

But I knew it was useless. Those words were just cotton I used to plug up that voice, stuffed in for a while, only to be pushed back out again. That voice said: You shouldn’t have come. You don’t belong here, and everyone can tell.

When I woke up the next morning, my stomach still felt off. I stared at my phone screen for a long time, wondering whether I should send the manager a message explaining that I hadn’t really been involved in much interaction last night—but then I felt doing that would seem too deliberate, and would only confirm something. In the end I sent nothing, and just mechanically opened my email, dealing with one message after another.

Later, I saw people in the coworker group chat talking about the gala, posting a few photos from the event, with a string of lively replies underneath. I scrolled through all of it and didn’t find myself in any of them. I set my phone facedown on the desk and kept staring at the document on the screen, pretending that feeling of being left outside the door wasn’t rising up over me again.

The lights in the exhibition hall were bright, flickering with a slight glare. I stood before my own work, filled with anticipation, hoping to see people stop and admire it. Yet everyone seemed to hurry past, and very few paused to look closely. The air was filled with the noise of the crowd and background music, as if I had been pushed into an invisible corner, isolated and helpless.

“This painting is good, but nothing special,” someone whispered behind me. Though their voice was soft, it felt like they were stabbing me in the heart. I couldn’t help turning that sentence over and over in my mind, as doubt and unease kept welling up inside me.

I felt my heart race, my palms begin to sweat, and an indescribable discomfort churn in my stomach. I kept telling myself that art is subjective, and you can’t expect everyone to understand it. But this inner reassurance felt so powerless, and I still felt waves of suffocating embarrassment.

A colleague came over, patted me on the shoulder, and asked, “Are you okay?” I forced out a smile, nodded, and replied, “I’m fine, just thinking about some things.”

In fact, my mind was a complete mess. I thought of countless setbacks from the past, those failures I had once seen as my own, and other people’s indifference, gradually piling up into an invisible burden in my heart. Whenever that happened, the feeling of being “abandoned” would follow me like a shadow, entangling me and refusing to let go.

When the exhibition ended, I walked home alone. The night wind brushed against my face, and I felt a chill, my body trembling slightly. The words kept repeating in my mind, along with the image of my work being ignored. I wanted to dissect my own emotions, but found myself unable to break free.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my heart filled with deep exhaustion and disappointment. I began to question my own worth, feeling that I always failed to fit in, and that perhaps I really was, as they said, not enough to attract attention. I closed my eyes in the dark, trying to calm myself, but tears still slipped down silently.

A few days later, though the feeling had eased somewhat, it still returned quietly each night, keeping me from sleeping peacefully. I realized that this exhibition experience was only a continuation of countless times I had been overlooked in the past, and that this emotion always seemed to lurk in the corners of life, ready to sweep over me at any moment.

I sat in the dark corner of the movie theater, watching the flickering images on the screen. The room was filled with the musty, dusty smell peculiar to old cinemas, as if I had stepped into some other time. The emotional impact of the images made my heart race; my palms grew sweaty, and I remained in a state of unease. It was an old film I had once cherished in my youth, now being re-released, awakening many sealed memories within me. Beneath the shifting light and shadow, many things related to the past surfaced in my mind—why did the things that had once troubled me have to rise up again at this moment? To ease this anxiety, I tried to focus on the details in the film, listening to the dialogue beside my ear: “You can’t keep living in the past.” But those words did nothing to lighten the burden in my heart. I couldn’t help wondering: am I now more fragile than I was when I was young? I kept myself alert to avoid sinking into a meaningless abyss of emotion. As the light and shadow alternated, I faintly heard the soft conversation and laughter of the audience behind me. How could they enjoy this film so at ease? I thought, perhaps because they did not have such a deep emotional connection to it. These sounds disrupted my thoughts and filled me with a powerful sense of loneliness. After the film ended, I walked out of the cinema, and the night breeze gently brushed my face. I looked up at the sky, but my heart still could not settle down. The next day, this sense of loss still lingered in my heart, making it difficult for me to concentrate on creating. I began to see that my sensitivity had, to some extent, affected my relationship with my work. Through reflection, I realized that some emotions need time to wear away rather than being immediately resolved. In the days that followed, I tried to turn this emotional turbulence into new creative material, hoping to transform sensitivity into some kind of creative energy.

Sunlight streamed through the conference room windows, spilling across the table. The air was filled with the scent of coffee, and the slides on the computer screen flickered. Seated in my chair, I clasped my hands together, and a growing unease spread through me.

Halfway through the meeting, a colleague casually said, “Isn’t this a bit too detailed this time?” My heartbeat suddenly quickened, and my cheeks began to flush. “Is he talking about my part? Does he think I said too much?” I tried hard to keep my face expressionless, but my body had already started to sweat. I lowered my head and quickly scanned my notes, hoping to find something I could improve so I wouldn’t seem incompetent.

I heard another colleague reassure me, “Don’t mind it, we all understand the situation.” But my chest still felt tight, as if a heavy stone were pressing down in my stomach. I replied, “I just wanted to make sure everyone understood the background.” My voice sounded tense.

The meeting went on, but I couldn’t focus. Everyone’s face seemed to carry a subtle hint of criticism. I thought: if this really failed, wouldn’t I be letting everyone down and holding up the team’s progress?

After it ended, I exchanged glances with several colleagues in the elevator, feeling a wave of disappointment. I pressed them: “Do you think there’s something wrong with my part?” They shook their heads and said, “No, relax.” I forced out a smile, but already I was ruminating over every detail of the meeting, trying to make sense of their true attitude. Back in the office, I couldn’t stop thinking: Is this feeling of unease my own problem? Am I being too sensitive?

By evening, I was sitting alone on the sofa at home, the day’s conversation echoing in my ears. My body still felt slightly tense, unable to fully relax. A team review a few days later confirmed that my fears had been unfounded; everyone thought the presentation was rich in content, with nothing unnecessary. I finally breathed a sigh of relief, yet I still felt a bit of regret—why do I always overcomplicate things and read too much into them?

Sunlight slipped through the gaps in the curtains, casting a soft glow across the floor of my study. I sat in an old but comfortable leather chair, and the desk was piled with all kinds of papers, paints, and a few notebooks. The air carried a faint scent of paint, tinged with the weight of years gone by. I was carefully going through a stack of old paintings, preparing to pick out a few and see whether they might inspire me to create something new.

My fingers touched a slightly yellowed sheet of paper, and the pattern on it made me pause. It was an unfinished work, one I had almost no memory of. I stared at it, trying to recover the original idea from its faint outlines and incomplete lines. Gently, I brushed my hand over the paper, feeling the slight indentations of the brushstrokes, trying to piece together fragments of memory.

"What are you looking at?" my partner’s voice came from the doorway, and he was carrying two cups of steaming tea.

"Oh, just some old paintings," I replied, my voice a little hoarse.

He came over and handed me a cup of warm tea. The heat of the drink instantly eased the stiffness in my body from all that concentration. Then he glanced at the painting in my hand and said, "This one looks quite special."

My heartbeat suddenly quickened a little, and I couldn’t help feeling a pang of self-reproach. Why hadn’t I finished this piece back then? Was it because I lacked inspiration, or because I was too self-critical? I only remembered that I was often dissatisfied with my own work, always feeling there were flaws, as if no finished piece could ever be perfect enough.

"Maybe you could finish it?" my partner suggested, his words light as a feather, yet they stirred a faint ripple in my heart.

"Maybe," I answered softly, my feelings in a jumble.

The whole day, my thoughts were drawn to that painting. Images of myself painting back then kept surfacing in my mind, and I imagined what it would feel like to move the brush across the paper again. That night, I tossed and turned in bed, my mind busy with how I might complete the painting, yet a faint unease lingered, as though taking up an old work might bring back that same anxiety and self-doubt.

A few days later, I decided to pick up my brush again and continue the painting from where I had left off. I carefully mixed the colors, trying to preserve the original tones, while I could hardly suppress the anticipation and nervousness beating in my chest. With every stroke, I felt a touch of relief; perhaps the unfinished past could finally find rest through this completion.

The whole process felt like a journey of the soul. I was in conversation with my past, gradually finding a sense of peace. I realized that perhaps imperfection is not frightening; what is frightening is stopping creation out of fear of imperfection.

The air was thick with a stale dampness and the smell of rust, as if the entire water treatment plant were quietly rotting away. I stood on the moss-covered second-floor corridor, looking down at the shattered basin below, its bottom filled with black-green sludge. I had arranged to meet my collaborator here to assess the project’s filming locations. What had originally been a routine work arrangement had turned into an inescapable conflict.

“This place isn’t suitable at all.” He stood below me, his voice echoing through the empty factory building. “The lighting is this bad, and the structural support is unstable. Why would you think you could shoot anything good here?”

I tried to explain. “It has a very special atmosphere, that desolate, rusted texture—doesn’t that fit the setting of our story?” My voice sounded a little strained, almost ingratiating, but he cut me off mercilessly.

“Special? Desolate?” He shrugged. “You always go after this kind of unrealistic stuff. Do you even know whether the budget can handle it? It has nothing to do with practical considerations!”

Each word stabbed into my chest like a needle. I felt a dull ache starting in my stomach, and my palms began to sweat. I clenched the edge of my scarf, trying to keep up a calm front, but inside I was already seething with shame and anger. I didn’t answer his accusation, only looked down at the basin, where the sludge seemed to mock me.

Countless similar scenes flashed through my mind at once. Being denied, being questioned, being laughed at. I started overinterpreting every expression on his face. Were his eyes slightly narrowed because he thought I was stupid? Was that hint of a smile at the corners of his mouth meant to suggest my idea was absurd? My breathing grew shallow, and my heartbeat quickened.

“Have you even seriously considered what the team needs?” he pressed on, his voice turning deeper.

“I have considered it!” I shouted suddenly, my voice trembling a little. “Do you think making these decisions every day is easy for me? I’m not doing this for myself. I just—I just want to do things well!”

The factory’s echoes made my words sound even more helpless. I knew he wouldn’t understand, and I even doubted whether I truly had the ability to convince him. My legs felt weak, and I could barely keep myself standing. At last I fell silent, lowering my head and forcing my gaze to focus on the rust stains beneath my feet. Time seemed to freeze, the air as heavy as iron.

After the conflict ended, I was left alone in the abandoned factory, sitting blankly beside a corroded water pump. I began to ruminate over the entire conversation. Why was he so harsh with me? Was I really not good enough? Were my choices always wrong? That doubt snowballed, growing larger and larger until it crushed the breath out of me.

That night, lying in bed, my stomach pain grew worse. I kept replaying the argument, every word taking root in my mind. I felt like a helpless clown, mocked by everyone. Even my dreams were filled with oppressive images: the rotting basin, the piercing echoes, and that cold indifferent voice.

A few days later, I began to reexamine my choices, not to prove I was right, but to find some compromise that could avoid conflict. I even forced myself to imagine whether it would be easier to be accepted if I simply followed his opinion completely.

As I stepped into this antique bookstore, I was immediately enveloped by the scent of old books. The shop was tucked away in a narrow alley in the city, its exterior wall covered in vines. Crossing the threshold felt like passing through a tunnel of time; the fragrance of aged paper rushed toward me. The store was dimly lit, with only a few hanging lamps casting a gentle play of light and shadow among the shelves. The bookcases lined the walls, and the yellowed lettering on the spines seemed to whisper stories passed down through generations. Then the owner turned to me and said, “If you’re interested in antique books, there are some unique volumes in the basement.” I nodded softly in response, anticipation slowly growing within me.

Following the wooden staircase down, I found the basement air cool, and the flickering light illuminated rows of dusty bookshelves. My fingers traced over the worn covers of one book after another, and my heart fluttered uneasily, as if each one concealed an unsolved secret. At last, in the farthest corner, I found an old handwritten diary, so aged it was almost impossible to make out, with only a thin layer of dust over it. I crouched down and gently blew the dust away; the words revealed beneath made my pulse quicken.

“Whose diary is this?” I asked myself silently, opening the first page in the dim light. The handwriting was clear and familiar, recording some trivial matters from earlier years along with the author’s inner reflections. Between the lines lay a sense of loneliness and persistence. An inexplicable feeling of closeness rose within me, a resonance that seemed just beyond reach. A forgotten emotion welled up in my heart, and memories of failed attempts and unfinished works gradually surfaced in my mind, accompanied by a slight ache in my stomach.

“What did you find?” a softly spoken female customer asked from behind me, her voice like the whisper of antique books. I looked up at her, trying to hide my unease, and replied, “Just someone’s lost soul.” We smiled at each other, each of us searching for some kind of answer in this mysterious space.

The silence of the basement gave me a rare sense of peace. My fingers brushed over the pages, and my heart felt calm yet full. I realized that my emotions had been awakened, that I was in conversation with my past self, as if searching for the courage to face awkward moments in my creative work and the social missteps born of overinterpretation.

When I left the bookstore, I felt as though time had congealed around me, and my shoulders seemed burdened with untold stories. After returning home, the excitement I could not contain lingered for a long time without subsiding.
