A few days later, in the flow of inspiration that lasted several days, I began trying to create again, releasing those silent souls onto the page, hoping to find a new kind of expression and release in words.

The rain drummed densely against the window as I stood in an old book-and-decor shop in the eastern part of the city. Heavy antique books lined the wooden shelves on the walls, and the air was filled with the faint, pleasant scent of paper. I ran my fingers lightly over an old book whose cover had split open, and the pages made a soft rustling sound, giving me a strange sense of calm. Yet my mind was far from peaceful.

I had come here that day in search of inspiration. An important client had given a harsh critique of my recent work, saying my style was outdated, my pieces too emotional, and lacking force. I muttered under my breath, “Do they even understand art?” My heart began to race, and cold sweat broke out on my hands. I tried to tell myself that this was only one person’s opinion, not the truth, but those words kept echoing in my head, like hammer blows striking at my confidence.

The shop owner came over and smiled at me. “Need any help? We have some special collectibles here.” I forced out a smile. “Just looking, thanks.” He nodded and went off to attend to another customer. I noticed something off in his tone, as if he were implying that I was no longer welcome. I pinched the back of my hand hard, and the pain snapped me back to my senses. Maybe it was just my imagination—this habit of overinterpreting things had once again trapped me in endless self-doubt.

As time passed, I began to feel a bit queasy, even a slight stabbing pain in my stomach. I knew it was all a manifestation of anxiety, yet my whole body felt submerged in exhaustion. I walked to a corner of the shop, where there was a comfortable leather chair, and sat down to look around. The old hanging lamps above the bookshelves cast a dim yellow light, filling the room with a nostalgic atmosphere. I closed my eyes and tried to relax, but the client’s harsh voice still would not leave my mind.

On the first night after I got home, I lay in bed turning over and over, unable to sleep, thinking about how to prove myself to the client. I began planning new work, hoping to respond to or dispel the criticism. I had to prove that, whether to them or to myself, I had the ability to break through the obstacles and move further along the path of art. The next morning, I still felt a faint tension in my body, but I knew I had to face these evaluations squarely, turn them into motivation, and stop running away.

A few days later, I regained my confidence and threw myself back into creating, doing my best to make my work deeper and more vibrant. I realized that although those negative comments had stung me, they pushed me to look at my work from a new perspective and helped me grow through constant self-reflection.

That afternoon, sunlight lazily filtered through the café’s glass windows and spilled across my table. I was working on a laptop to meet a creative deadline, surrounded by soothing jazz and the occasional hiss of the coffee machine. The air was filled with the aroma of freshly ground coffee, which was deeply relaxing. I looked up at the clock on the wall, feeling a little anxious, but still determined to finish the article that day.

Just then, my phone vibrated. I picked it up and saw a new message from a coworker. He was asking about a detail in our last project, and his tone seemed a little impatient: “Is there still a problem with this part? Do we need to discuss it again?” Seeing the message, my heartbeat sped up and my palms began to sweat slightly; a wave of tension washed over me instantly.

Immediately, I started ruminating over the scene from our last meeting, remembering some of my suggestions for the project back then. Was he blaming me for not handling those parts well? Or did I make him feel that the project was falling behind? These thoughts came rushing in like a tide. I quickly replied, “I’ll recheck these sections and make sure there’s no problem.” With a bit of nervousness, I almost trembled as I hit send.

After a while, he replied: “Oh, I just wanted to make sure. There’s nothing major—don’t worry.”

While I felt relieved, my mind began another round of debate. Why am I always so sensitive, always overinterpreting what others say? Could it be because I’m not confident enough deep down, always fearing that I’m not good enough in other people’s eyes? I opened my laptop and tried to keep working, but that uneasiness never really went away. My fingers tapped weakly on the keyboard, and even my typing rhythm felt off.

In the evening, as I walked home, the cool wind brushed across my face and made my mood heavier. Nearing my front door, I decided to stop by the supermarket to buy some groceries. Standing in the produce section, I found myself unconsciously picking out a lot of comfort foods. Was I avoiding things, trying to fill that inexplicable sense of emptiness with material things? Suddenly, I realized that many things become complicated simply because I overthink them.

Back home, I sat at the dining table, my mind constantly replaying the conversation from earlier in the day. In fact, this was nothing more than the most ordinary communication between coworkers—why did I need to dwell on it like this? But my emotions didn’t seem easy to settle. That night, I spent some time quietly reflecting, checking my phone from time to time, repeatedly confirming his reply to make sure I hadn’t misunderstood.

A few days later, I gradually came to realize that when dealing with situations like this, I needed to be calmer and trust my own judgment more.

The lights in the conference room were a little harsh, and the air was mixed with the smell of printer ink and the bitter scent left behind by someone’s morning coffee. I sat near the door, because I always felt that if something came up and I needed to leave, this spot would be the most convenient. Everyone’s voices rose and fell, merging into a vague hum, but my attention stayed fixed on the framework drawn on the whiteboard. Today’s discussion was a key part of deciding on the new project. The proposal I had spent several sleepless nights preparing had just been briefly mentioned, but before I could finish speaking, the person in charge turned to a colleague on the other side and started discussing the next steps.

My cheeks began to burn, and sweat quietly broke out in my palms. Why was no one responding to my ideas? Was my proposal too mediocre? I felt as if a cold, hard stone had been stuffed into my stomach, and even breathing became difficult. “Do they think my abilities have declined? Do they not want me involved in this project at all?” The thought flooded into my mind like a tide.

“What do you think?” The lead’s voice suddenly interrupted my train of thought. I froze, realizing he was asking the younger designer across from him for their opinion, not me. I swallowed a dry mouthful of saliva, trying to calm the anger and humiliation rising in me, but my fingers kept fidgeting under the table. The words on the whiteboard blurred, and all I could hear was the pounding of my own heart. “Why is this happening? Have I really become worthless?”

When the meeting ended, I mechanically gathered my notebook and materials, still hearing the easy chatter among my colleagues. “Should we go pull him aside for a chat in the break room?” a voice in my head suggested, but my body had gone rigid. I worried that if I asked him what he thought of my proposal, he might flatly tell me it didn’t matter at all, and that would be even worse than this vague uncertainty.

When I got back to my desk, my shoulders felt as if they were weighed down by a thousand pounds, and they drooped on their own. Even as my computer screen lit up, I couldn’t concentrate. The fatigue in my body and the loss of control over my emotions filled my mind with accusations: Had everyone from the very beginning thought I wasn’t a competent colleague? Had they been waiting for me to make a mistake so they’d have a reason to push me out?

At nine in the evening, I finally dragged my exhausted body home. The clatter of dishes came from the kitchen, but my ears couldn’t register any comfort in it. When I switched off the lights and lay down in bed, today’s scenes played over and over in my mind like a movie on rewind. “Why am I like this? Why is it always other people’s unintentional actions that can drag me this deep?” At that moment, I felt an indescribable shame spreading from my throat to my chest, as if the vulnerability that an adult should have long since overcome had been laid bare, and there was nowhere for me to hide.

Sunlight streamed through the window of the old bicycle shop, and specks of dust drifted gently in the beam. The shop was filled with a faint smell of machine oil and rusted iron. I stood beside an old-fashioned bicycle, fiddling with the loose chain. From time to time, I could hear the sound of cars passing on the street outside. I tugged hard at the chain, my fingers smeared with black lubricant, feeling a bit sticky.

“Do you need any help?” the shop owner asked as he came over. He was an elderly man who always wore a gentle smile.

“No, I’m trying to fix it myself,” I replied with a smile, though I secretly hoped he might give me a little more guidance. I turned the pedals, feeling whether the chain moved smoothly.

“As long as the chain doesn’t come off track, you’re just about done,” he said softly in encouragement, then nodded and turned back to the counter to sort out some tools.

I continued focusing on the work in my hands, feeling my heartbeat gradually steady and my skin no longer damp. Repairing the bicycle made me temporarily forget the troubles and pressure in my life. Every adjustment made me feel like I was solving a small problem, and that sense of accomplishment was deeply satisfying.

The bicycle shop was quiet, with only the faint clinking of tools against the wooden floor. I thought to myself that I had to make sure this bike could ride smoothly. Occasionally a customer would come in, and the shop owner would greet them warmly, while I remained absorbed in my own little world, enjoying the brief calm.

“You look like you’re almost finished,” the shop owner said after a while, seeing me tighten the last screw.

“Yeah, just about,” I said, standing up and brushing the dust off my hands. I felt a small sense of accomplishment. “Thank you for letting me repair it here.”

“Not at all. You’re always welcome here,” he said, handing me a clean rag. I used it to wipe the grease off my hands, feeling especially relaxed.

When I left the shop, the sunlight was shining beautifully on the street, and the air carried a hint of warmth. After I got home, I put the greasy rag into the washing machine and sat on the sofa, feeling a wave of peace. The satisfaction of having fixed the bicycle made me feel that the afternoon had been truly meaningful.

A few days later, I rode the bicycle slowly around the neighborhood, a breeze brushing across my face and lifting my spirits. The repaired bike was light and smooth, and each pedal stroke made me love the experience even more. The memory of the repair shop made me realize that sometimes peaceful moments are also a luxury, one that puts the heart at ease and deserves to be cherished.

A weathered wooden sign hung above the exhibition hall’s entrance, its peeling paint revealing gray-white grain beneath. When I pushed the door open, the wood creaked. The empty air inside carried a faint smell of earth and rust. Sunlight streamed through the tall glass windows, falling on the rusted plows, the worn hand-cranked seeder, and a cutting machine, casting mottled shadows. I sat down on a worn leather sofa, holding a small notebook in my hand, trying to find inspiration for my new project. Silence hung in the air, and whenever my pen moved across the page, I seemed to hear the faint rustle of writing. A few staff members were preparing for a small lecture event, occasionally speaking to one another in low voices, their words drifting across the exhibition hall in indistinct fragments.

Just as I was lost in thought, one staff member looked up at me, pointed in my direction, and said to another, “They look pretty nervous. I wonder if they came to the wrong place.” I tried to pretend I hadn’t heard and kept my head down, writing on, but then my heartbeat suddenly quickened and my palms began to sweat. I felt as if I were exposed under a spotlight, even though almost no one in the exhibition hall was paying attention to me. I thought back to the last time I attended a book club, when someone accidentally knocked over my water cup. I apologized at once, even though I knew it wasn’t my fault at all. Did I look like someone who was always making a fool of themselves? Did they think I was a joke when they said that? Was everyone else secretly talking about me?

“Sorry, I may have been a bit rude,” I suddenly stood up and walked toward the two staff members, my voice colder than I expected. “I’m just sitting here for a while; I’ll try not to disturb your event.” Only after I said it did I realize my tone sounded as if I were blaming them, and they simply froze for a moment before waving their hands hurriedly. “Oh, no, no, that’s not what we meant! Please, make yourself comfortable. We were just chatting casually.”

The words “chatting casually” made my chest tighten. I didn’t know whether I felt more angry or ashamed. Had I really lost control over something so trivial? Or were they truly mocking me and just pretending to be innocent now? That thought stuck in my mind like a thorn, painful and hard to shake. I hurried back to the sofa, but I could no longer focus. It felt as though laughter filled my ears, even though the hall was so quiet you could hear the faint sound of the wind brushing against the glass. My thoughts spiraled, and I recalled countless similar scenes: those little details that had made me feel judged and ridiculed replayed in my mind like a movie. I knew this state of mind was ridiculous, but it was like being trapped in mud—the harder I struggled, the more I sank.

My chest tightened slightly, my stomach turned sour, and my head felt a little foggy. I took a deep breath and forced myself to stare blankly at an old shovel on the wall. Its wooden handle was cracked, but the metal part still glinted faintly, as if it had endured years of wind and frost and survived stubbornly. I tried to tell myself that this wasn’t such a big deal. Even if someone really did have opinions about me, it wouldn’t change my worth. I gripped my pen tightly and scribbled aimlessly in my notebook, trying to shift my attention back to my work.

After a long while, I heard the staff members’ footsteps gradually fade away; they seemed to be going to set up the event area. The exhibition hall fell back into silence, with only the occasional sound of wind. Slowly, I felt my heartbeat settle, and the heat in my face began to fade. I still wasn’t completely immersed in my writing, but at least I had some ideas. I sketched a few random lines and decided I would come back later to refine them.

By the time I left, dusk had already begun to fall, and the air was growing cold. I pulled my coat tighter around myself and headed toward the parking lot. On the drive home, I kept thinking about what had just happened, trying to convince myself not to take everything as an attack against me. Even so, the uneasy feeling lingered in my heart for a long time. Even that night, I kept thinking back to the comment that “they look pretty nervous,” imagining different ways I might have responded, my emotions rising and falling again and again.

In the early morning, sunlight filtered through the old windows and fell across the floor of the pottery studio, the air filled with the scent of clay. The potter’s wheel I was adjusting gave off a low rumble, a sound that always made me feel at ease. Yet the unease in my heart would not go away. I gently touched the clay with my hand; its slight dampness and silky texture briefly drew my attention back to the work in front of me. Just then, footsteps sounded at the doorway. I looked up and saw a friend from years ago. He smiled and said, “I never thought I’d run into you here.”

“I didn’t think you’d come here either.” I tried to suppress my surprise and keep myself composed. But inside, uneasiness began to churn: How would he see my work? Would he think all these years of effort had been meaningless?

He came up to my workbench and carefully examined the rows of neatly arranged new pieces. “These are really good. Looks like you’ve been making progress,” he said, looking up at me with encouragement in his eyes.

“Thank you.” I forced a smile, unable to tell what he truly meant beneath his words. Suddenly, my heart began to race, as if every beat were a question of my own ability. I could feel fine beads of sweat forming on my forehead, and the clay in my hands became unbearably slippery.

He seemed to sense my unease and spoke in a gentle tone about recent events. “Lately I’ve been trying out a new creative style, but the process hasn’t been smooth sailing either.” He shared his own progress, clearly hoping to ease my tension with his experience.

Our conversation gradually warmed up, and sunlight slowly moved across the clay beneath our feet, as if time itself were passing with it. As our talk deepened, my thoughts gradually settled, and my tense muscles were able to relax. “Sometimes, creating can be lonely, but if you keep going, there will be unexpected rewards,” he said.

We kept talking through the entire morning, and it was only at midday that he waved goodbye. I watched him walk away, my thoughts scattering in every direction. Though anxiety still came over me from time to time, I realized that it was precisely these seemingly insignificant gestures of support that gave me the courage to keep moving forward.

That night, I returned home, opened my laptop, and began to record my conversation with my friend and my own feelings. I discovered that deep inside, there seemed to be a voice reminding me that overinterpreting things and attacking myself would not change the facts; instead, it would only make me miss the chance to understand others. Over the next few days, I felt a long-lost sense of relief, as if I had gained one more source of support on the road ahead.

This exchange made me realize that when facing the many challenges of creation, the unnoticed support from those around me often gives me the greatest strength. And perhaps that support is the key I have been overlooking all along.

The chandelier in the restaurant cast a warm yellow light, with soft glints reflecting off the plates and bowls, while the air was filled with the aroma of sauce. I sat at the side of the table, my fingers unconsciously sliding back and forth over the knife and fork, trying my best to stay calm. Everyone was talking about my work progress, and the conversation gradually shifted from casual chatter at the start to pointed comments. My sister suddenly brought up a creative project I had mentioned before. She smiled and said, “But it seems like that project of yours still hasn’t really gotten anywhere. Isn’t it a bit too risky?”

A wave of heat surged from my stomach straight to my chest, and I felt my breathing quicken, the muscles in my face tightening. I forced a smile and said, “Yeah, some parts are still being adjusted.” Then I tried to steer the conversation elsewhere. But my uncle quietly added, “Sometimes, being too risky isn’t necessarily a good thing. It’s better to be more steady.” His tone didn’t seem malicious, but my mind had already started racing. Were they implying that I wasn’t rational enough? Did they think I was wasting my time? Did they think I wasn’t suited for this at all?

My hands clenched more tightly under the table, my palms already damp, and my breathing grew shorter and shorter. I forced out a smile and said, “Actually, the direction of this project is already clear, it’s just...” Before I could finish, Grandma interrupted me, speaking slowly: “You still haven’t settled down after all these years, and the family has always been very worried about you.”

At that moment, I heard a roaring sound in my head, and it felt as if I had been hollowed out. My heart pounded like a drum, my temples throbbed, and my stomach ached as if cut by a knife. I murmured, “So you think I’ve never been good enough, is that it?” The moment I said it, I knew I had lost control, but I could no longer stop. I stood up, and the chair scraped harshly against the floor. Everyone was looking at me, their eyes filled with surprise, confusion, and a hint of pity.

“I really don’t need you to keep reminding me of where I’m not good enough!” My voice was much louder than I had expected; I was practically shouting. I turned and left the restaurant, walking into the courtyard. The night air was freezing, and my hands began to tremble slightly. I leaned against the wall, trying to regulate my breathing, but found that my body wouldn’t cooperate at all, and my heartbeat still felt like a galloping horse.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying those words in my mind—“It’s better to be more steady,” “the family has always been very worried about you.” I couldn’t control my emotions, and tears slid down unconsciously like an unstoppable flood. A few days later, although I had outwardly regained my calm, every time I saw their expressions, I would instinctively feel that they were judging me, even doubting me.

Sunlight filtered through the balcony glass, gently spilling over my face. I sat in a chair, holding a book, while the plant in the corner of the room swayed softly in the breeze. In the air, I seemed to still catch a hint of the osmanthus fragrance drifting in from outside the window last night, filling me with a sense of peace and delight. In the quiet surroundings, the only sounds were the occasional cheerful laughter of children downstairs and the low rumble of cars passing in the distance.

As I turned the pages, I found myself often pausing to think about a certain idea in the book. Sometimes I would also lift my head and look out through the glass window toward the distant sky, where white clouds moved slowly, as if the world were gradually unfolding. I felt a rare sense of calm inside me, with a small flame of happiness burning in my chest.

Soon, my phone rang with a text from a friend. She asked whether I had any plans to go get coffee together today. I picked up my phone, looked at the message on the screen, and felt warmth in my heart. Then I replied, “Of course. When shall we meet?”

On such a quiet morning, I always feel inner peace. Even though I sometimes feel that the trivial matters of life are complicated and overwhelming, these moments make me realize the beauty in the ordinary. My heartbeat remained steady, as if it had blended into the rhythm around me. I couldn’t help wondering whether such a simple morning could offer me some comfort amid a busy life.

In the afternoon, my friend arrived as promised. We sat on the balcony chairs, enjoying the warmth of the sun. She drank coffee while we chatted about the small details of life and happy memories. This exchange made time slip by like flowing water—light and effortless, without feeling tedious. The sunlight gradually softened, and we both became immersed in the comfortable atmosphere.

That evening, thinking back on that relaxed morning, I felt a gentle warmth rise in my heart. Although there are many things in life that trouble me, these precious moments have taught me to cherish the present even more. My heartbeat was still steady, and I slept especially soundly, my heart filled with a tender anticipation for tomorrow.

The abandoned hat factory was thick with the smell of age; the air was filled with the scent of old fabric and dust. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the broken windows, slanting across the floor. I stood in the center of the workshop, and the old wooden floor beneath my feet gave off a faint creak. It was silent all around, and only the occasional sound of the wind made the space feel even lonelier. I gently touched the discarded hat rack beside me, and when my fingertips brushed the fabric, I felt its coarse texture. This had once been a vibrant place, but now only ruins remained.

Several dust-covered hats hung on the wall nearby, as if telling stories of the past. I couldn’t help walking closer and lightly straightening those crooked hats, yet an unnamed sense of regret and anxiety stirred within me. Why was I always like this, forever uneasy about the choices I had made in the past? These hats, like the failed creations of those years, had been forgotten in a corner. I thought of those rejected proposals and unfulfilled dreams, and suddenly a wave of suppressed emotion surged up inside me.

"Why did you come to this place?" My phone suddenly rang; it was a message from a friend. I hesitated for a moment, then quickly replied, "I just wanted somewhere quiet."

Although my friend seemed caring on social media, deep down I was somewhat doubtful whether that concern was genuine. Were they just asking out of politeness? I began to overthink the meaning of the message, and a feeling of being abandoned welled up inside me. My gaze unconsciously returned to those old hats, and for some reason I felt they were like silent witnesses, witnessing my panic and loneliness.

My heart started racing, my breathing became shallow and rapid, and my palms began to sweat slightly. I tried hard to calm myself and told myself, "It’s nothing, just an afternoon." But these self-soothing words seemed to have little effect, and my inner monologue grew more and more chaotic. Standing in the middle of the hat factory, I felt that my own situation was no different from these abandoned hats.

After leaving the hat factory, the aftereffects continued to haunt me. That night, I couldn’t stop ruminating over my past failed creations, afraid that the future would bring the same failures again. At home, I leafed through my old works, trying to find a little comfort, but my mind was still filled with unease and doubt about my own abilities. It was only a few days later that this mood began to ease slightly, though it still lingered. My experience in the abandoned hat factory forced me to reexamine myself and think about whether I would truly be able to overcome these troubles in the future.

The rain blurred the outlines of the entire city, and on the deserted streets only a few pedestrians hurried by. I opened my umbrella, and the puddles beneath my feet splashed with each step. Reaching an inconspicuous corner in the eastern part of the city, I found this abandoned old fabric shop. The sign above the door had faded beyond recognition, leaving only a few indistinct characters. Pushing open the creaking wooden door, I was met with the stale, sour smell of old cloth, along with a faint odor of mildew. The whole room was dim and damp, as if I had stepped into a place forgotten by time. Various fabrics were scattered across the floor; some had grown heavy with moisture and were covered in dust. Several outdated garments hung on the wall, their colors dull and lifeless. On a workbench sat a few unfinished fabric samples, their edges weakened by the erosion of time. I gently touched them, my fingertips sensing the subtle texture of the cloth, as if countless hands had once worked here in haste. My thoughts began to wander, imagining how these fabrics had once been carefully cut and the passion and creativity the designer had poured into them. Suddenly, I heard faint footsteps at the door. It was a passerby peering in, murmuring, “I never expected anyone to come to a place like this.” I nodded in response, though inside I was surprised by my own instinctive attraction to this place. After he left, the room returned to silence, leaving only the sound of raindrops hitting the ground. I closed my eyes and listened to this silence born from ruins, as if it were telling a story of reluctance and loneliness. My heartbeat seemed to match the quiet inside the room, stirring the raw spark of inspiration within me, and my desire to create seemed to awaken at that moment. Yet at the same time, I felt uneasy—could this attachment to the past lead me into an unconscious trap? A few days later, back at home, I was still repeatedly reflecting on the feelings that the fabric shop had stirred in me, and an unwillingness to part with the years gone by kept welling up in my heart. I began to pour this complex emotion into my work, hoping to use it to express the unfinished loneliness and nostalgia.

The air was thick with the damp smell of earth as I stood in an abandoned ceramic workshop on the northwestern outskirts of the city. Broken ceramic pieces were piled everywhere, and fallen tiles formed a chaotic pattern across the floor. I gently touched a shard of broken tile with my hand; the icy sensation sent a slight sting through my fingertips.

Hearing the wind in the distance, my thoughts seemed to be pulled back into the past.

“This place is really interesting,” my companion remarked.

“Yeah, it feels like exploring a forgotten castle,” I replied with some reluctance, though my heart was filled with unease.

I walked to a corner where unfinished clay pots were stacked. They stood quietly, as if waiting to be discovered. I began to imagine what these unfinished works might become. Some inspiration surfaced in my mind, only to be suppressed by an even stronger sense of loneliness. I had to admit that I felt a profound sense of inadequacy before these works.

Suddenly, my heartbeat quickened and a wave of tension hit me. I started sweating, groping around with my hands for something to lean on so I wouldn’t faint. That fear of being utterly isolated returned once more, as if the walls around me were closing in and making it hard to breathe. I struggled to steady my breathing, but every inhalation was accompanied by a sharp anxiety.

“Are you okay?” my friend asked with concern.

“I’m fine. It’s just that the atmosphere here makes me a little sensitive,” I said with a forced smile, though all I wanted was to leave.

The aftereffects continued when I got home. That night, I couldn’t fall asleep, and the scenes from the workshop kept replaying in my mind. I worried that I was being too sensitive, afraid that this anxiety would affect my creativity. Even after several days, I still couldn’t stop recalling that feeling of loneliness, and the deep sense of inadequacy in my heart would not fade.

But I also came to realize that perhaps this unease and sensitivity themselves are also a source of creativity, even if they cause me pain. I must learn to live with this feeling, rather than simply resisting it and turning on myself. Perhaps it is precisely this deep inner conflict that gives rise to the authenticity and resonance in my work.

On a winter morning, the cold air always makes me reluctant to leave my warm bed, but a healthy body requires persistence. Wrapped in a thick coat, I walked into the old gym in my residential complex. As soon as I entered, I was hit by the smell of sweat mixed with disinfectant. Although the equipment here is old, it has always been a good place for me to exercise. The environment is always filled with the clanging of machines, the sound of people panting, and the occasional burst of laughter.

I walked over to the treadmill I used most often. I turned on the power, only to find the display screen blank. I pressed the buttons a few times, but the machine gave no response. I immediately felt a little irritated: “Why is it broken again?” I muttered under my breath, trying to check the power cord, when a familiar voice came to my ear: “Hey, kid, is the machine on strike?” It was the gym administrator, who came over with a smile.

“Yeah, it’s acting up again. Honestly, every time I decide to work out properly, something always comes along to disrupt it.” I spread my hands helplessly, my tone tinged with inevitable frustration. He checked the machine a couple of times and shook his head as well, saying he was powerless to do anything. “Looks like it’s not planning to cooperate today.”

I sighed, and the thought that “persistence is useless anyway” began to surface in my mind, leaving me feeling disappointed. Thinking about how I had gotten up early only to have this small mishap throw everything off, my heartbeat quickened and my palms grew slightly sweaty, as if my body were uneasily reminding me that “today’s workout is ruined.”

“Maybe you could try jump rope?” the administrator suggested. “After all, moving around is always good for you.” I nodded. Though reluctant, I knew deep down that it was better to find an alternative than to give up.

So I picked up the jump rope from the corner and swung it, making it produce a rhythmic whooshing sound. Although it wasn’t as enjoyable as running, sweat gradually began to soak my forehead, and my mood improved a little.

Afterwards, when I walked out of the gym and the cold wind hit me in the face, I felt a sense of relief. Although the equipment malfunction had disrupted my plan, it didn’t make me give up my morning exercise entirely. My body still felt the comfort that comes after working out.

Over the next few days, I would think about this incident from time to time. Though it was only a small inconvenience, it seemed to remind me that there will always be unexpected setbacks and frustrations, and all we can do is, like today, keep facing them and solving them in a different way.

White ceramic dust drifted through the air, and sunlight streamed in through the workshop’s high windows, forming shafts of light. All around were unfinished ceramic pieces, rough yet full of the passion of creation. I stood off to the side, my heart racing, feeling the mounting tension in my chest. Those people—peers, artists, professors—were all chatting and laughing animatedly, occasionally using the clay in their hands to demonstrate their ideas.

“How is that piece you prepared coming along?” a young male artist came over and asked with a smile.

“Oh, I’m still refining the details.” I forced out a smile, though I was wondering whether the flicker in his eyes was hinting that my work wasn’t good enough.

My palms had already started to sweat, so I pretended casually to slip my hands into my pockets. The smell inside was a mix of damp earth and smoke from the kiln, with a faint cool scent of soil mixed in. At that moment, all of it felt less like an atmosphere and more like a heavy pressure, so overwhelming I could hardly breathe.

“When will your piece be ready to exhibit?” he pressed on.

“Probably soon. I’m trying my best to make it in time for this exhibition.” My voice trembled slightly. Though I tried to stay composed, the panic inside me had nowhere to hide. Deep down, I kept chewing over the same questions: What if I fail? What if they’re disappointed in my work?

These questions were like thorn-covered vines; the more I tried to break free, the more tightly they seemed to entangle me. I should have been confidently presenting my creation, but at that moment, all I wanted was to find a corner to hide in, out of reach of anyone’s gaze.

After the conversation ended, I tried to find a little comfort in a corner of the workshop, but to no avail. The other artists were eagerly discussing their own pieces, and the sounds of laughter and clay clashing against each other kept echoing through the room. I couldn’t help wondering whether those laughs were mocking my hidden fear.

I clenched my fists hard, trying to hide the dampness in my palms. I knew that as long as even one person showed dissatisfaction or an unintentional indifference, my self-esteem would be punctured like paper. It was truly unbearable, because it reminded me of all my past embarrassments and failures.

That night, after I got home, I couldn’t fall asleep. My mind was still haunted by those repeated exchanges of eye contact with others, by every detail of each conversation. The changes in expression, the subtle differences in tone—they kept replaying in my memory. My stomach cramped slightly with anxiety.

A few days later, although my colleagues’ misunderstanding had been cleared up through repeated confirmations, my mood still had not settled. Perhaps this was just who I was: perpetually sensitive and unable to break free from it, and this seminar undoubtedly pushed everything to the extreme once again.

I was sitting in the corner of the coffee shop, surrounded by the laughter and chatter of my friends. The table was covered with all kinds of desserts, and the rich aroma of coffee filled the air. My eyes kept drifting to the window, trying to hide my unease. My friends were talking about the latest trends, while I always felt I was falling behind in the conversation.

"How have you been lately?" A friend sitting across from me suddenly turned to me and asked with a concerned smile. My heart immediately began to race, and a slight sweat broke out on my forehead. "Pretty good, just busy with work," I replied as casually as I could, but inside I couldn’t help reflecting on my own work situation.

"I heard you ran into some trouble on a project before?" He said it lightly, but it made me squirm in my seat. I could feel my stomach tighten, and my hands unconsciously gripped the chair. Thoughts of those little work mishaps and mistakes came flooding back, and I desperately tried to shake them off.

"There were some challenges, but they’ve been resolved." I struggled to keep smiling, but in my mind, all kinds of negative scenarios had already begun to play out. Yes, I really had encountered difficulties on that project; poor communication among colleagues had put me in a difficult position, and those issues had nearly brought the whole team’s work to a standstill.

After the gathering ended, I walked home alone, habitually replaying my friend’s comment over and over in my head. Was he implying that I wasn’t trying hard enough? Or did I really seem a bit incompetent?

That night, I locked myself in my study, trying to fill the emptiness inside me with work. Moonlight spilled across the floor through the curtains, and my fingers mechanically tapped on the keyboard, while my friend’s words kept echoing in my mind. “How have you been lately?” That seemingly simple question now felt like a needle, piercing me.

Over the next few days, I still couldn’t shake off that unease. Whenever I tried to focus on a new project, those past mistakes and awkward moments always seemed to shadow me. I knew this kind of overthinking was just my own nervous tendency, but I couldn’t control it.

I started talking to my friends more often, hoping to gain a sense of security by constantly confirming how they felt about me. But in fact, I realized this wasn’t a long-term solution. A few days later, I decided to tell my friends about my worries directly so I could get the most honest feedback. Fortunately, their response made me feel relieved—I had simply been too sensitive.

The little talk stage in the bookstore was much brighter than I had imagined. A few warm-yellow pendant lights overhead blazed down on me, making the back of my neck itch a little, like the kind of itch you get when someone is staring at you. Hand-drawn posters were taped to the walls, showing the cover of the book I was signing today—the face on the paper looked so unfamiliar, like someone else’s. There were about twenty people in the audience; the atmosphere wasn’t exactly lively, but it wasn’t dead either. My palms were already damp, and when I signed, my fingers nearly slipped off the pen. I quietly rubbed my hand against my trouser leg, pretending it was just an unconscious gesture.

“What do you think was the biggest challenge behind creating that book?”

The question came from someone in a gray sweater. Their voice was low, but they spoke deliberately slowly, as if weighing every word. Their hands were folded across their chest, their lips pressed together slightly, giving off a subtle sense of detachment. I forced a smile and gave a more “official-sounding” answer: “Probably having to live with a lot of inner unease. Writing always feels like a kind of self-exposure.”

They followed up: “So as a professional creator, do you think that kind of ‘unease’ weakens the power of a work in some sense? After all, readers may be looking for a strong narrative, not vulnerability.”

When they said that, their gaze paused for a moment, as if it had deliberately landed on my eyes. Their tone remained steady, but it felt to me like hearing a whisper before a storm.

My heart suddenly sped up. Heat rushed to my face, as if a layer of skin had been stripped off me in public. Something in my stomach began to tighten, like a hand slowly curling into a fist.

*Are they implying that my work is too weak? Because of that review last month saying my storytelling was too emotional? Are they representing some unspoken judgment from more people?*

Those thoughts surged in like a tide. I tried to keep my expression calm, but one hand unconsciously clenched the fabric over my thigh. I smiled and said lightly, “I think vulnerability is actually part of strength. Human beings are complicated like that—without vulnerability, there’s no resonance.”

But even I could hear the defensiveness in my own voice. My speech sped up by half a beat, like trying to block a leak with my hands.

The host stepped in at the right moment to smooth things over. “That’s a very interesting point. Emotional complexity is exactly why so many people like your books.” The gray sweater nodded and said nothing more. I told myself: it’s over. But somewhere, something wasn’t over at all.

On the way home, I replayed that sentence over and over in my head. “Weakens the power of a work”—those words were like a thorn. The more I tried to pull them out, the deeper they dug in. Did they really mean harm? Or was I overreacting again?

I tried telling a friend about it. They comforted me and said maybe the person was just curious. But I heard “dismissiveness” in my friend’s tone, like a magnet drawing all my attention toward it.

Then, from somewhere, an older scene surfaced. Many years ago, during a classroom essay competition, a teacher had said I was “too emotional, not grand enough.” That sense of shame came back almost unchanged, pressing on my chest until I could barely breathe.

Over the next few days, I buried myself in revising the manuscript, but I kept feeling that every passage where I let my emotions show had turned into a weakness. I started cutting and rewriting, trying to make myself seem “more rational.” But with every sentence I deleted, it felt like some support was being pulled out from under me, leaving me hollow.

I knew what I was doing. I knew it was self-defense, preemptively striking at myself before anyone else could, so that at least the wound would be one I had made. But knowing it was one thing; my hand still kept deleting.

The chandelier in the restaurant cast a blinding light, and the aroma of the dessert left on the plates mixed with the smell of coffee, filling the air. I stood in the corner, clutching my phone in my palm and staring at the time on the screen. Everyone else was laughing and chatting by the table, their voices overlapping into a din that made it feel as though piercing noise was coming from every direction. “Come over here, we’re taking a group photo!” A voice cut through the commotion—it was my sister calling me. My heart suddenly raced, and a wave of panic surged up out of nowhere. I didn’t want to go over there. I didn’t want everyone staring at me. What if the angle I stood at was wrong? What if my smile looked stiff? What if they noticed how tense my eyes were? I could already picture my face in the photo, and compared with their natural smiles, mine would look like a foreign object forced into place.

“Did you hear me?” My sister raised her voice again, irritation showing on her face. I nodded and forced my steps to seem steady as I walked over to her. I stood at the very edge, but she pulled me to the middle and said, “Stand here. You’re part of this family, stop acting like an outsider all the time.” Her tone made my stomach knot up, and I could feel the heat rising in my face. “I don’t want to be an outsider, I just—” Before I could finish, she cut me off: “Stop making excuses. It’s just taking a photo. Why do you always have to make everything so complicated?”

It felt as though a stone had been dropped on my chest, and in the next second, all the pent-up emotions erupted at once. “I’m making it complicated? You always make me feel like I’m not good enough! I’m here, I’m with you, I’m already trying my best!” I was practically shouting. Everyone else in the restaurant stopped talking because of my voice. I saw surprise on my mother’s face and on the faces of several cousins, and even some confusion, as if they had never expected this scene to unfold.

My sister froze for a second, then said coldly, “What are you talking about? How have we made you feel not good enough? It’s just a photo—do you really have to act like this?” Her words stabbed into my ears like needles. I couldn’t help taking a small step back, and my hands began to tremble. I felt my stomach churning and my brain buzzing, as if my thoughts were spiraling out of control. Fragments of the conversation started swirling in my mind, and even her original call sounded like some kind of attack. I struggled to keep myself together and stop the tears from falling, but that feeling was about to break open like a flood.

After the photo was taken, I went straight to the restroom and hid there. I stared at myself in the mirror—my eyes were red, and my lips were trembling slightly. Her words kept repeating in my head: “Stop making it complicated.” I felt ashamed, blaming myself for exploding, for not being able to handle it calmly. But another part of me felt angry, feeling that she didn’t understand my struggle. This wasn’t just about taking a photo; it was about the way she treated me, always making me feel like something was wrong with me.

Even after I got home, I still couldn’t shake off that anxiety. That night, lying in bed, I seemed to still hear my sister’s voice in my ears, and my stomach ached faintly. I kept thinking over and over: did they already dislike me? Was I always going to make things awkward no matter how hard I tried? Before going to sleep, I looked at the group photo on my phone. Sure enough, my smile looked stiff, as if I had forced it out.

Under the gray sky, the air was damp, as if brewing a belated spring rain. I pushed open the wooden door, and my foot stepped on a loose floor tile, producing a faint sound. The room was dim, with only one or two weak beams of light seeping through the cracks in the window, falling across the center of the workshop like a lonely candle flame lit for this sleeping space. The air was thick with a complex scent: the sweetness of roses, the heaviness of musk, mingled with the dusty smell of years gone by. I instinctively held my breath, then gently inhaled again, as if this fragrance were a letter from the past, waiting to be opened. 

Scattered across the floor were glass bottles and test tubes, some already cracked, their dried contents leaving irregular marks on the boards, like chemical ghosts recounting their fate. I walked to the wooden shelves against the wall, which were lined with intact bottles of fragrance ingredients, their labels blurred by moisture. When I reached for one, the bottle felt cold, and my fingers brushed a fine layer of dust. I softly twisted off the cap, and a faint lavender scent drifted out, flooding my nose in an instant and making my heartbeat quicken involuntarily, as though an old melody were sounding in my ears. I remembered this scent; it reminded me of a spring night long ago—the first time I tried to make a perfume of my own, in a corner of a laboratory, filled with the stubborn passion of youth for the unknown. 

On a wooden table in the corner sat some worn perfumery tools: a rusted metal spoon, a small measuring cup, and a few yellowed recipe sheets with curled edges. I couldn’t help reaching out to leaf through them. Familiar chemical names rose before my eyes line by line like gentle whispers, awakening my memory of those ingredients. “The base notes should be deeper... or maybe add some amber?” I murmured to myself, as though I were back in some busy morning of the past, discussing an ideal fragrance with old companions, carried away by our enthusiasm. 

My footsteps echoed through the empty room, and I gradually felt a dull headache, perhaps because the scent in the air was too intense, or because emotions that had settled for too long were beginning to surface. Unconsciously, I pressed my temple with my hand, trying to steady my breathing, yet my chest felt heavy, as if a stone had been placed upon it. Suddenly, my shoulder was lightly struck by a wind chime hanging from the ceiling, and the thin metal bells gave off a series of delicate clinks. The sound left me momentarily dazed, and in my heart I seemed to hear a blurred conversation: “This is the most perfect scent of all!” It was the voice of a companion from my youth. 

I sat down in a rickety wooden chair, trying to calm my thoughts. A chill crept up the back of my neck, perhaps because the damp air in the room was slowly seeping through my coat. I carefully recalled the path I had walked over the years, and the confidence with which I once believed I could control everything now seemed to be peeled away layer by layer by these faint scents. The coldness of chemistry, the fragility of art, and the complexity of human hearts intertwined among these bottles and jars, like an unfinished movement of a symphony. 

That night, after I returned home, the complex fragrance still lingered in my mind, like an invisible hand constantly reminding me of my failure and my vulnerability. In front of the mirror, I tried to force a smile, but it was only in vain. I couldn’t help whispering to myself inwardly: “If only these fragrances could really seal time away—then they would not merely be a scent, but a door leading into memory.”

Sunlight streamed through the large windows of the old record shop, soft and warm across the floor. I gently pushed open the heavy wooden door, and the wind chime on it jingled, bringing with it a cozy atmosphere. The walls were covered with aging posters, and the air carried a faint smell of dust and vinyl—a place I often came to escape the noise.

“Welcome! Can I help you with anything?” the shop owner asked me with a smile from behind the counter. He was an old man with silver hair, his voice steady and warm.

“No, I’m just looking around. Thanks,” I replied, a strange anxiety rising in me, as if I didn’t know how to explain my own presence.

My fingers lightly brushed over one record cover after another, the faces of pop singers on them reminding me of songs that had once inspired me. My heartbeat began to quicken, and sweat slowly dampened my palms. In that moment, I found myself once again reflecting on the years of my creative journey, wondering whether I had truly captured that deep resonance of the soul.

“These old records always make people think of the days gone by, don’t they?” The shop owner looked at me, his eyes carrying a kind of understanding.

“Yes,” I answered softly, my thoughts drifting back to those years when I burned the midnight oil for my work. Back then, every effort seemed full of meaning, but now I was always filled with doubt.

“You know, many people come here just to look for some lost feeling,” the shop owner continued, as if he had seen through the unease in my heart.

I nodded, while an inner voice poured out like a river: Was I also searching for something lost? For the motivations I had abandoned myself, the ones that had once kept me going.

Uneasy footsteps echoed in my mind, and my legs trembled slightly as I tried not to seem hurried. “Maybe I need to find that feeling too,” I tried to respond lightly, but I couldn’t hide the tremor in my voice.

After leaving the record shop, I sat on a bench in a nearby park. Sunlight filtered through the leaves and fell on my face, its warmth easing some of my tension. After taking a few deep breaths, I realized I needed to face the motives behind my creativity again—the passion that had once made me lose track of time in front of a canvas. Though my heartbeat was still rapid, I felt a glimmer of new hope. Perhaps someday, I would find that pure joy in creating again.

That evening, I stayed for a long time at my desk at home, picking up my paintbrush, feeling a little lighter, as if a new door had opened before me.

I was standing by the art shelf in a bookstore, holding a heavy art album in my hands, its cover showing an impressionist-style seascape. It wasn’t crowded around me, and sunlight streamed in through the glass windows, the air seeming to carry a faint smell of paper and ink. A middle-aged man stood beside me, flipping through a photography collection. His glasses reflected the light from the shelf lamps, and I didn’t dare look at him for too long, afraid it would seem rude. But then he suddenly looked up and asked, “What do you think of this book?” His voice was low and casual, as if it were just a passing question.

I froze for a moment, my mind racing. Why was he asking me? Was he expecting a reaction from me, or was he just trying to start a conversation? I panicked inside, not knowing how to answer in a way that would sound insightful without being offensive. I tried to keep my tone controlled so it wouldn’t sound too tense: “Well… I think these photos are very emotional, but maybe a little too heavy.”

He said, “Oh, really? I actually think it’s pretty interesting.” His tone was calm, even carrying a hint of casual curiosity, but I still immediately felt uneasy. Was he implying that I didn’t understand art? Or did he think my answer was too superficial? My stomach began to tighten in waves, my fingertips grew a little sweaty, and the surface of the album felt slick in my hands. I forced a smile: “Maybe I just didn’t understand it very well. After all, I don’t have much experience with photography.”

He nodded and said nothing more, continuing to flip through the book. But inside my head, the voice had already started shouting: “Why did you say that? Why didn’t you just say you like it? He must think I’m stupid and just pretending to know about art!” My heartbeat noticeably quickened, as if all the surrounding noise had been amplified—the rustle of turning pages, the beeping sound at the nearby checkout counter, all of it seemed to mock my nerves.

I tried to shift my attention and kept looking through the album, but my eyes couldn’t focus at all on the colors and brushstrokes. My mind was full of fragments of the conversation just now: Did my voice sound natural enough? What exactly did he mean by “Oh, really?” Was he looking down on me a little? I secretly glanced at him; he had already picked up another book and seemed not to care at all about how I had acted. Even so, I still felt utterly embarrassed and wanted to leave that area as quickly as possible.

After leaving the bookstore, I walked to the café on the corner and ordered a hot latte. Sitting by the window, I tried to calm down. My brain refused to stop, replaying the scene over and over. I even started blaming myself: Why am I always so sensitive? Why can’t I just answer questions confidently? Does this mean I really don’t have any insight and am simply not suited to talking with people? Even after the coffee had gone cold, my emotions still couldn’t fully settle back down.

A few days later, while tidying up the bookshelf at home, I saw that art album lying quietly in the corner. Although I had bought it back then, I had only opened it a handful of times. I tried opening it again, telling myself that perhaps the book itself was more worth paying attention to than the anxiety from that conversation.

When I pushed open the wooden door, the hinges let out a sharp squeak. I walked quietly into the abandoned instrument repair shop on the corner. Dust covered the floor, and each step stirred up a faint cloud of particles drifting through the air. Light filtered through the scratched, mottled window glass, casting shifting bands of brightness and shadow across the floor and walls. The air carried the metallic scent of oxidation, mixed with the faint, tart smell of old wood.

On the left side of the shop stood a row of abandoned instruments: a battered piano in the corner, its lid slightly ajar, revealing ivory keys speckled with stains. I gently pressed one key, and a dull note sounded—short and hoarse, like a labored breath. Beside it was a violin with a broken string, its body marked by a deep crack that exposed the curved wood fibers inside. Near the workbench sat a rusty string bow, looking as though it had been left untouched for years.

“Hm… what are you looking for?” A hoarse voice suddenly came from deeper inside the shop. I jumped and turned around to see an elderly man standing behind the counter, a half-wiped oilcloth in his hand, his expression wary and helpless. “I’m just looking around…” My voice trembled slightly, and my heartbeat quickened at once, as if the squeak from the door had exposed my uninvited intrusion.

“No one comes here anymore. We closed two years ago. What you see now can’t be repaired by anyone.” His voice carried regret, but more than that, it sounded like the quiet relief of someone who had made peace with the past.

I nodded, suddenly feeling a dull ache rise in my chest. In my mind, I saw myself thirty years ago, when I first secretly saved up my small writing fee to buy an old guitar. It was a secondhand wooden guitar, thin in tone, yet warm in a way that obsessed me. I had practiced with it through countless late nights, and I had also played melodies on it that I was too shy to share with anyone.

“Can I try it?” I pointed to the piano that had been left there for years, trying to keep my voice calm.

“Suit yourself.” The old man spread his hands, then silently walked over and sat down in a chair nearby.

I slowly sat down in front of the piano and rested my fingers lightly on the keys. They were worn unevenly from use, but still cold to the touch. I managed to play a few notes, the melody broken and intermittent, like someone who had lost their memory trying to piece together a shattered language. The tail end of each note echoed through the room, like the reverberation of overlapping bygone days, carrying a lonely weight.

As I played, my eyes began to sting and my vision blurred. I closed my eyes and let my fingers slide across the keys, as if searching for a sound that had once been familiar but was long gone. It was a rhythm that belonged to me, to the fragments I had created in late-night solitude, to the days when I still believed in dreams.

When the last note dissolved into the air, I heard the old man let out a soft sigh. He stood up, nodded at me, and said nothing. I also stood, nodded back, and quietly left the shop. The wind on the street was a little cold, and I pulled my coat tight around me, while in my mind those melodies on the verge of being forgotten kept replaying again and again.

On the way home, my stomach throbbed faintly, perhaps because I had drunk too much coffee that morning. That pain intertwined with the heaviness in my heart, leaving me with an indescribable weariness. That night, I wrote down the unfinished melody in my notebook, though I knew I might never be able to play it all the way through again.

Sunlight streamed through the tattered curtains and fell across the floor, casting mottled patterns of light and shadow. The air was faintly scented with paint. I stood in the abandoned old watercolor studio, surrounded by a familiar silence, as if time itself had stopped here. A few faded paintings hung on the wall, covered in dust, and I couldn’t help thinking of the glory they must once have had. My heartbeat quickened, and my palms grew slightly damp—perhaps because the atmosphere stirred my longing to create, and my constant unease about my own abilities.

In one corner, I saw a table piled with clutter, with a few dried-up paintbrushes and an unfinished palette on it. I lightly touched the brushes with my hand, and the cold sensation made me pull back. Just then, I heard a few bird calls from outside, as if reminding me not to wallow in the past. Yet my thoughts stubbornly drifted to those works I had once published and that had been criticized, and a shame I could never fully shake rose in my heart.

“Is imagination like this,” I muttered to myself, “a source of motivation, or a burden?” My eyes moved to a painting on the wall—brightly colored, yet drained of life, as if telling a story of creation and forgetting. I took a deep breath, trying to disperse the negativity in my mind. The scene made me imagine that if I could work in such an atmosphere, perhaps it would inspire new ideas. But at the same time, I feared failure and the possibility of rejection.

My stomach tightened, as if reminding me of my doubts about my own abilities. I sat down on a rickety chair, closed my eyes, and tried to calm my restless mind. Preemptive self-attack was my usual strategy: if I could deny myself first, then others couldn’t deny me. That thought made me feel temporarily safe, but it also shut down any possibility of embracing new attempts.

After staying in the abandoned studio for a while, I decided to leave. When I stepped out, I felt a strange sense of relief, perhaps because I had finally begun to face the struggles within myself. That night, I tossed and turned, the studio scene replaying over and over in my mind. A few days later, I began to try a new project, and though unease still accompanied me, I knew this exploration and challenge were exactly what I needed to face.

Sunlight filtered through the café curtains and fell across the table, while the steaming coffee in my cup gave off a faint bitter aroma. Seated across from me was one of my closest friends from college, still wearing that familiar smile. Her voice rang especially clearly amid the noisy surroundings: “How have you been lately?” My heart instantly stirred, as if a gate to my memories had been opened. I tried to stay calm and replied with a smile, “Oh, pretty well—just busy with my creative work, and some little things in life.” But inside, I couldn’t help repeatedly pondering the meaning behind her words. Was she hinting at something?

My heartbeat quickened, and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my palms. Those old moments of self-doubt came flooding back—the countless times in college when I felt overlooked and misunderstood. That feeling of being abandoned surrounded me once again. She paused, looked at me, and said, “Actually, I’ve always thought you were very talented. You’re just always too hard on yourself.” It felt as if a taut string was hanging in the air; my stomach tightened, and an inner voice began to question: Why is she only saying this now? Was she hinting that I had never actually lived up to her expectations?

“Do you know? Back then, after we graduated, you suddenly seemed to disappear. Everyone missed you very much,” she continued, a trace of regret in her tone. My breathing grew a little rapid, guilt pressed on my chest, and the sense of social distance—whether initiated by me or forced upon me—became vivid again. I lowered my head and quickly took a sip of coffee; the bitterness, mixed with warmth, slid down my throat and gave me a moment of comfort.

“It was because I always felt I wasn’t good enough, and I was afraid of disappointing you all,” I finally admitted, my voice trembling slightly. “Actually, I don’t think anyone would be angry with you for that,” she said. There was no blame in her gaze, only a kind of warm understanding. I silently looked out the window, the sunlight stinging my eyes a little.

After leaving the café, my mind was still filled with our conversation. Back home, I lay on my bed, images of self-criticism from different periods flashing before my eyes: immature, timid, unable to face judgment. Even after a week, my heart still felt heavy, as if shrouded in mist.

I began to reflect that perhaps self-criticism does not truly protect me; instead, it only deepens my sense of isolation. In reality, no one harbored that kind of malice toward me, yet I still could never face them with confidence.

Sunlight filtered through the shabby blinds and spilled across the floor, while the air was thick with the smell of old paper. This abandoned stationery store had once been a place I frequented in my school days, but now it stood deserted, its floor covered in layers of dust and torn wrapping paper. As I walked past the familiar shelves, I couldn’t help but remember the times I had chosen pens and notebooks here.

Just as I was lost in those memories, I suddenly heard footsteps at the entrance. Looking up, I saw an old friend I hadn’t been in touch with for a long time. His appearance made my heart race, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. Panic surged through me as I struggled to steady my breathing. But my body seemed beyond my control, my heartbeat growing ever faster, as though I were trapped in a silent chamber.

“Hey, long time no see!” he said, his voice carrying a hint of surprise and warmth. We began talking about our respective lives. He mentioned his success and his family, while I only compared everything silently in my mind. Although his tone was very friendly, I couldn’t suppress my own nerves. I began to repeatedly interpret his expressions and tone, as if searching for some hidden sarcasm or contempt.

“Are you doing okay? And lately... how’s your work?” His question froze me in place, filling my mind instantly with past failures and frustrations. I forced out a smile, but my voice trembled slightly when I spoke: “Uh, pretty good, I’ve just been really busy.”

The tension in my body made my breathing feel heavy, and a wave of anxiety rose from my stomach and spread throughout me. We kept talking, but every pause in the conversation, every tiny shift in tone, would trigger my self-doubt. To break this tension, I quickly changed the subject.

That not-so-long conversation left a lingering impression in my mind. After leaving the stationery store, I kept replaying his words on the way home, filled with all kinds of assumptions: Was he really concerned about me? Was he secretly laughing at me?

That night, lying in bed, I thought back on the encounter. It felt as if I could still hear the sound of the breeze brushing over the paper inside the shop. Although I knew he probably meant no harm, my sensitive nerves always made me overinterpret things without realizing it. To calm my unease, I began attacking myself in my own mind, blaming myself for being so sensitive and immature.

However, after a period of inner struggle, I decided not to let these emotions keep draining me. That night, I wrote down these feelings, hoping to ease the pressure inside me through words. In the morning light a few days later, I finally felt a sense of calm. Perhaps that chance encounter was only a small episode in life, but it made me realize that my sensitivity could also become a source of inspiration for my writing.

I sat at the small table in my studio, the laptop screen in front of me displaying a newly released video. Around me was the familiar environment I knew so well, with all kinds of creative works hanging on the walls, and sunlight streaming in through the thin curtains from outside the window. I took a deep breath and prepared to see what the audience had to say.

As I browsed the comments, a glaring negative remark jumped out at me: “Your work is getting more and more boring. Have you lost your inspiration?” Those words were like a sharp needle, piercing my heart. My heartbeat quickened, my palms grew slightly sweaty, and a dull pain stirred in my stomach.

“Why is this happening?” I kept asking myself. Before I knew it, tears were welling up in my eyes. I turned off the screen, took a deep breath, and tried to calm myself down. But those words kept echoing in my mind: “Boring… no inspiration…”

A phone call rang, pulling me back from my thoughts. I answered it, and it was a long-time collaborator. Her voice was gentle and concerned: “Are you okay today? I noticed your video. It’s pretty good.”

I forced my voice not to tremble. “Yeah, I’m fine, just… the comments made me a little uneasy.”

She chuckled softly on the other end of the line. “Don’t take those comments too seriously. Sometimes people just like to nitpick, and your work always has room to grow.”

After hanging up, I closed my eyes and tried to think through what she had said. Maybe she was right; I shouldn’t let one or two comments affect my emotions. But that helpless feeling still hung over me. For the next few hours, I could hardly focus on anything else. I just sat on the sofa in a daze, my mind turning that comment over and over again.

By evening, with my mood a little calmer, I opened my computer and began to look at my work again with fresh eyes. The image in front of me no longer felt as harsh, and I started thinking about how to make some changes without losing my own style. A few days later, Iorganizeed my thoughts and made a new plan.

After a few days of reflection, I finally felt my emotions settle down. Though the impact was still there, I knew I wouldn’t give up easily this time. Whenever I’m criticized, I may feel discouraged right away, but it also becomes the driving force that pushes me to keep improving, reminding me that I need to step beyond my comfort zone.

Footsteps echoed through the empty hall of the puppet theater, and the intricate wooden floor groaned with each step I took. I pushed open the heavy, rusty wooden door, and it creaked as if protesting my arrival. The theater was dead silent, with only the sound of my breathing reverberating in the stillness. Faint moonlight streamed through the broken glass of the tall windows, casting a glow on a lone puppet on the stage, as if it were staring at me. The air was thick with the smell of old wood and dust, and I shivered involuntarily.

I couldn’t help but speak to the scene, asking softly, “How many audience members used to be here?” Of course, no one answered. I felt an incredible sorrow and loneliness rising from deep within me, that sense of being forgotten and excluded, like the rejection I often encounter in my creative work. I stepped onto the stage, and the puppet’s joints clacked lightly, like the beating of my own heart in the midst of inner conflict.

“Are you okay?” I gently asked the silent companion in my hands. In such an environment, I couldn’t help but start talking to myself, pondering those nightmare-like creative dead ends. I thought of the works that had been dismissed, the intentions that had been misunderstood, and my heartbeat quickened while my palms began to sweat. I hurriedly took a breath, trying to bring my thoughts back to the present.

I sat in a corner of the stage, trying to blend into the abandoned space. The clamor inside me echoed endlessly, and a sense of helpless isolation surged like a tide. I thought of the relationships that needed reassurance, of every tiny gesture and tone of voice that needed to be interpreted, and anxiety filled my entire chest.

Slowly, I pulled a notebook from my pocket and began recording what I felt in that moment. “Everything here is like a puzzle of my memories,” I wrote. “Broken and incomplete, yet hiding countless stories.” At that moment, it was as if I saw myself from another angle; all those stumbling moments in creation and in life became flowing images, flashing through my mind.

As I left the theater, I looked back at the stage, and the puppet seemed to still be looking at me. I said goodbye softly, and the long-lost calm in my heart gave the exhausted me a faint sense of relief. Back home, seated in a warm chair, I flipped through the notebook and thought about how to weave today’s feelings into my next work. Although my emotions were still unstable, I realized that it was precisely these imperfections and uncertainties that gave me the drive to create.

This experience may not immediately change my state, but I gradually came to understand that perhaps it is precisely this direct confrontation with my inner fears that can give me a reason to keep moving forward amid awkwardness and rejection.

The conference room lights were glaring, and the cold white light cast over the rough tabletop felt especially unforgiving. The air was thick with the smell of coffee and printer paper. When my fingertips touched the documents, they felt slightly damp—probably from the sweat in my palms. I tried to adjust my posture and told myself to look calm and credible, but my chest felt as if it were being gripped by an invisible hand, and my breathing grew rapid. The client spoke in a low, slightly skeptical tone: “Are you sure this plan will avoid the problems we had last time? We lost quite a bit of time.” His gaze swept over me like a blade. I tried to respond, but my voice started to tremble. “It was my mistake, I... I may not have fully considered the risks.” The moment I said it aloud, I felt completely drained, and my ears began to burn, as if everyone could hear the shame and panic in my heart.

Another colleague hurriedly took over, trying to ease the situation. “Actually, we can further optimize this part. Please rest assured.” His voice was steady and composed, in sharp contrast to mine. I lowered my head and looked at the draft on my notebook, the handwriting blurred as if floating in water, realizing that I could no longer regain the initiative. My heartbeat quickened until it seemed ready to burst through my chest, each beat reminding me of my own incompetence. The client was silent for a few seconds, then let out a soft sigh. “All right, I hope you can do better this time.” A trace of disappointment flickered in his eyes. When I caught that subtle emotion, my throat felt as dry as if it had been scraped with sandpaper.

As I left the conference room, my legs were weak and I could hardly take a step. I looked down at my shoes, trying not to meet the eyes of coworkers passing by, afraid that they were already silently judging me in their hearts. A dull pain began to gnaw at my stomach, as if a tiny iron nail were stirring inside it. I silently leaned against the wall in the hallway, feeling the weight of my body pressing down until I could barely breathe. When I got back to my desk and opened my computer, I found that my fingers could not focus on the keyboard at all. In my mind, that trembling answer kept replaying, like a never-ending loop.

That night, I lay in bed but could not make myself fall asleep. Every time I closed my eyes, I could see the client’s disappointed expression and my own loss of control in the meeting. I began arranging all sorts of possible conversations in my mind, imagining whether I could have salvaged some of the situation if I had been calmer and more confident. But each simulation only made me feel worse, because I knew it was an unchangeable fact. I tried to write down how I felt that day, hoping to find an outlet through words, but discovered that I could not even organize my thoughts into language. In the end, I could only stare blankly at the empty page of my notebook, feeling a profound sense of helplessness spread from the bottom of my heart.

The bookstore was filled with the mingled scents of paper and coffee. Soft lights shone on the bookshelves, creating a quiet yet lively atmosphere. I paused in front of a new book, thinking about the discussion earlier that day in the office. Suddenly, I heard someone behind me mention my name.

“I really don’t understand why she always makes things so complicated,” said a familiar voice—it was my colleague. She and another coworker were standing behind the next bookshelf, clearly unaware that I was here. “Have you heard about her new project? I think it’s a bit too melodramatic.” Their voices were perfectly clear, and my heartbeat immediately quickened, heat rising to my face.

“I guess that’s her problem. She’s always like this,” another voice chimed in. Their conversation stabbed at my heart, as if I were standing in front of them naked. I quickly lowered my head and pretended to browse the book in my hands, but in truth, I didn’t see a single word. My stomach clenched, my palms began to sweat, and my feet, planted where I stood, felt as if they had been nailed to the floor. The urge to flee and the desire to confront them collided fiercely inside me.

“Maybe we should tell her her work needs more positivity.”

“I don’t know how to make her less sensitive.”

A running monologue interrupted my already unsettled thoughts: what if they were right? Had I been disappointing everyone around me all along? A mix of anger and shame surged together, making it almost unbearable. In that moment, all my fears of abandonment and not being accepted awoke and filled my entire consciousness.

I desperately wanted to break free from this feeling and not be suffocated by the sense of being rejected. The morning sunlight was bright as I stood on the terrace atop the company building, gazing out at the city skyline. Through this reflection on the terrace, I began to realize that my oversensitivity and self-criticism were indeed hindering my growth. I need to try seeing things from the team’s perspective and learn to accept differing opinions instead of immediately feeling dismissed. This is a direction I need to keep working toward.

The warm yellow light in the café fell across the tabletop. The coffee in my cup had gone cold, and a ring of dried marks clung to the inside of the glass. When his gaze drifted to my left, a sharp pain went through me—was he growing tired of me? Did he think I wasn’t professional enough? Was he planning to cancel this collaboration? I began to suspect he was just brushing me off, and even wondered whether he had completely lost confidence in my ability to do the job.

I felt my emotions slip out of control in an instant. Memories of past failures started replaying in my mind—the scenes of others criticizing me, the self-blame and shame after being rejected—crushing me so hard I could hardly breathe. The next day, I rushed to check the footage, afraid that there might be any mistake that could not be remedied. Fortunately, most of the shots were fine, and I finally felt a little relieved. “I think the logic in this part needs to be adjusted, otherwise the audience may feel the transition is too abrupt,” I cut in, trying to keep my voice steady. But as soon as I finished, Xiao Li’s expression suddenly froze for a moment. Then he lowered his head and flipped through the materials in his hands, without responding right away.

My heart sank. Had I sounded like I was blaming him? I tried to recall my tone just now; my pulse started to quicken, and a little sweat broke out in my palms. I quickly added, “What I mean is that your idea is very inspiring, it’s just that this part might be worth refining a bit more. What do you think?”
