He looked up, his expression recovering some of its naturalness, and said, “Mm, I’ll go back and make some adjustments.” Though he sounded fairly calm, I still felt a hint of distance in his tone, as if he were a little unhappy. My mind started running wild: had what I said made him feel I didn’t respect his viewpoint? Or would he think I was trying to present myself as more professional?

For the next hour, I could hardly focus. Every time Xiao Li looked at me, I instinctively tried to read whether there was some hidden displeasure in his gaze. My stomach started to ache faintly, as if a knot had been tied tightly inside. My fingers tapped unconsciously against the edge of the table, but then I worried that this too would be misunderstood as impatience, so I forced myself to stop.

After the meeting ended, I said to Xiao Li, trying to sound relaxed, “Thanks for your patience today. I learned a lot.” He nodded and replied lightly, “Mm, let’s stay in touch by email.” His tone was as plain as could be, but in my ears it sounded cold. I forced out a faint smile and left.

When I got home, I took off my coat and collapsed onto the sofa, my mind replaying Xiao Li’s expression and that line, “Let’s stay in touch by email,” over and over. I started blaming myself: Why did I use that tone? Why couldn’t I have been more tactful? In that moment, my sensitivity felt like a floodgate that could never be closed, with every subtle signal from the outside world rushing in and drowning me. I even couldn’t help opening my computer, wanting to send Xiao Li a message to explain, but I was afraid it would seem too unnecessary. In the end, I closed the screen.

That night, the stomach pain kept me from falling asleep until very late, and I was filled with frustration. Over the next few days, I even felt resistant to the team chat, afraid that I would again cause misunderstandings because of my tone or wording.

The gallery lights were a warm orange, and several beams fell onto the photographic works on the walls, as if draping them in a soft halo. I stood before a piece titled “Flowing Light,” holding a glass of red wine, feeling the atmosphere to be subtle and somewhat unnerving. The low murmur of conversation from the crowd drifted to my ears from time to time, indistinct and muffled. I had originally hoped to take this opportunity to talk with some people in the field, but I didn’t have the courage to speak first.

Just as I was hesitating, the exhibition organizer—who was also the artist, a fairly well-known photographer—came over to my side. He smiled and nodded, a simple greeting. I quickly adjusted my tone, trying to sound composed: “Your work is very moving. I especially love the layering of light and shadow.”

He looked down at the piece, then said, “Thank you. But some viewers feel it’s too ‘perfect,’ and as a result it lacks a bit of emotional tension.”

Hearing that, it felt like I’d been pricked by a needle, and my fingers tightened unconsciously around the wineglass. My mind immediately started racing: Was he indirectly criticizing my taste? Did he think I wasn’t professional enough to like something so “superficial”? I forced a faint smile, but my heartbeat began to speed up, and I could even feel a slight flutter in my chest.

“Uh… maybe everyone experiences it differently. I was mainly drawn to the light and shadow,” I said, trying to keep my voice calm, though it seemed to tremble a little.

He shrugged with a casual air. “Maybe.” Then he walked over to another group of people who were praising his work. I stared at his back, and the gloom in my chest burned like a small flame, making my stomach ache faintly.

For the rest of the evening, I barely initiated a single conversation. The gallery grew more and more crowded, and the air was thick with perfume, red wine, and a hint of damp wooden floors. It felt as though a lump of lead were pressing down on my heart; no matter how I looked at the photographs, I felt as if they were silently mocking my ignorance. I began to wonder whether I was simply not suited to this circle at all.

By the time I got home, it was nearly midnight. I kicked off my high heels carelessly and collapsed onto the bed, but my mind kept replaying the photographer’s expression and his words about it “lacking emotional tension.” The more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt. My heartbeat still hadn’t fully settled, and my stomach had started to ache faintly. I even got back up, opened my laptop, and began looking up reviews of his other works, wanting to prove that I wasn’t entirely without judgment. But every praise-filled article and every analysis of his profound insight felt like a mockery of my own shallowness.

The next morning, my eyes were a little swollen, probably because I’d rubbed them too many times without realizing it in the middle of the night. I forced myself to take deep breaths, trying to let it go, but my stomach still felt a bit off. When a coworker later asked me what I thought of the exhibition, I just brushed it off with a vague answer and didn’t dare mention the phrase that had continued to gnaw at me.

Sunlight streamed through the tall windows, and dust on the floor danced in the beams. We were gathered in a small creative workshop in the city warehouse district, with all kinds of materials and tools scattered across the worktables. I sat on an old wooden chair, fiddling with an unfinished sculpture in my hands. The air was filled with a faint smell of paint. I noticed my colleague’s gaze seemed to signal me. “What do you think of this design?” she asked in a flat tone, but my heartbeat sped up and my palms began to sweat. My mind instantly churned through all kinds of possible interpretations, replaying them one by one like a disaster movie in rehearsal. “Did I design it terribly? Or does she have some other opinion of me?” I muttered to myself. I leaned forward slightly, and a fear of being rejected welled up inside me. “I think it’s pretty good,” I said, trying hard to stay calm, forcing a smile at the corners of my mouth, though my heart was still pounding like thunder. Her eyebrows lifted slightly, and my stomach suddenly tightened, as if I had sunk into an abyss. “Really? I thought maybe some parts might need adjusting.” Her tone was nothing unusual, yet I began to doubt everything I had said. After the meeting ended, I hurriedly packed up, making an excuse to go to the bathroom, when in fact I just wanted to escape this suffocating environment. The cold water from the tap brought me a little back to my senses. I stared at my somewhat pale reflection in the mirror, blaming myself over and over in my mind. Why do I always read into what others think? Why can’t I let go of my harsh judgment of myself? That afternoon, I couldn’t get back on track all day. Every time I tried to chat a little more with a colleague, the little drama in my head would start up again. On the way home after leaving the workshop, the setting sun stained the city skyline red, while my inner world remained bruised. When I woke up the next day, last night’s self-doubt, like water that hadn’t yet dried up, soaked my confidence once again.

The meeting room today was brightly lit, and the whiteboard on the wall was covered with the project workflow we had just discussed. I sat in my chair, with scattered documents spread out on the table in front of me, still preoccupied with a moment from the meeting. I heard a colleague say in a slightly serious tone, “This part needs more careful revision.” In that instant, I felt my heart race and my face grow hot, as if I had been directly criticized. I couldn’t help but wonder whether he was dissatisfied with my work.

After the meeting, I moved from my seat to the break room, hoping to find a quiet corner to catch my breath. The air here was filled with the smell of coffee, which helped me relax a little. However, my mind kept replaying that moment, my palms started to sweat, and my stomach began to ache faintly. A colleague came over and asked, “Are you okay? You don’t seem very happy.” I forced out a smile and replied, “I’m fine, I’m just thinking about how to improve the project.” He nodded and went back to getting his coffee.

I knew I should focus on how to improve the plan instead of dwelling on other people’s tone. Sitting there, with the sound of the coffee machine filling my ears, I tried to calm myself down. That feeling of being abandoned lingered in my mind, and I had to keep asking myself, “Is a colleague dissatisfied with me?” just to ease it a little. But the more I asked myself, the stronger my anxiety became. After a while, I tried hard to sort out my thoughts and told myself that he was simply expressing what the work required, not criticizing me personally.

Lunchtime came, and I tried not to overinterpret the matter. After finishing lunch, I returned to my desk and continued dealing with the mountain of tasks. After dinner, I brewed a cup of hot tea and sat on the sofa watching TV. That sense of disappointment had faded somewhat, but it was still hidden deep inside me. Over the past few days, I have unconsciously kept wondering whether I am being too sensitive, always overanalyzing other people’s words and tone, afraid that they may harbor any negative thoughts about me.

Morning sunlight streamed through the glass window onto the tabletop and the colorful plates laid out before us. My friend and I sat in a newly opened restaurant, taking in the buzz of conversation around us and the occasional roar of the coffee machine.

“This place’s pancakes are really delicious!” she said with a smile, holding a golden pancake in her hand as syrup slowly dripped down.

I nodded, chewing on a bite of sweet strawberry, but an undercurrent of unease rose within me. She went on, “Actually, I didn’t expect you to write something like this. It really feels very different from your usual style.”

My heartbeat quickened, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. Her tone was casual, but I couldn’t help analyzing her words. Did she think my work wasn’t as good as before? Or did she feel my style had become not good enough?

“Really?” I tried to reply in a relaxed tone, though a hint of tension still lingered in my voice.

“Yeah, maybe that’s just my personal opinion, so don’t take it to heart.” She shrugged and continued enjoying her breakfast.

I forced a smile and nodded, but anxiety had already spread inside me like wild grass. My stomach felt unsettled, as if I had eaten something too greasy. I thought maybe she had just mentioned it casually, but why did those words feel so heavy?

Even in that offhand conversation, I couldn’t help but ruminate, replaying what she had said over and over, like a looping scene playing in my mind. At that moment, I made myself take a sip of orange juice as if nothing were wrong, but the cold liquid seemed unable to cool the heat inside me.

The friction at the restaurant that morning seemed minor, but after I got home, I still couldn’t relax. Sitting in front of the computer, I kept turning her words over and over, trying to understand every subtle implication that might be hidden within them. My heartbeat sounded like the ticking of a clock, especially clear in the quiet room.

At night, I lay in bed, breathing deeply and slowly, trying to relax my taut nerves. Though it was only a slight discomfort between friends that had stirred up this inner turbulence, I’ve always been so prone to making small things complicated. It seems to be part of my nature, leaving me both conflicted and powerless.

The screen was divided into six sections, and the client’s face was in the upper-right corner. I had already been speaking for five minutes, trying to explain my design thinking. When I got to the key point, the client’s brows knitted slightly and the corners of his mouth drooped a little, as if he were struggling to hold back his dissatisfaction. I paused for a second, and my heart immediately sped up; it felt as if something were blocking my throat, and my voice began to turn dry and hoarse. “Does he think my proposal is too childish? Is this style completely out of sync with their company’s tone?” A tidal wave of shame surged up inside me. “Have I overestimated myself? Why did I take on this project? I knew from the beginning it was a bit beyond my abilities.”

I heard a low voice coming through my headset. “So, can we see roughly what the specific visual elements will look like?” The client’s voice didn’t sound overtly displeased, but I couldn’t help magnifying every pause and shift in tone. I hurriedly switched to the design draft presentation page, but for some reason the mouse kept missing its clicks. My palms were so sweaty I could barely hold onto it. “Hurry, hurry, don’t keep them waiting too long!” My breathing grew shallow, my face felt scorching hot, and I wished I could simply disappear from the video call.

The presentation page finally came up. I forced out a smile and said, “This design is still in the early stages of adjustment, but this will probably be the direction we’re heading in...” Before I could finish, the client gave a small nod. “Okay, we’ll take a look at this version first and discuss it further later.” I couldn’t read any emotion in his words, and all I felt was my heart suspended in midair.

After the meeting ended, the sound of setting down my mouse seemed especially harsh in the room. I stared at the screen, replaying the client’s expression over and over. What did that frown mean? Disappointment? Irritation? Or did he simply not care at all? Maybe it was just a habitual expression. “Maybe he’s thinking, how could this person be a designer? Their level is terrible.” I buried my face in my hands. My ears were buzzing, and it felt as though a block of ice had fallen into my stomach. This round of self-attack went on for two hours, until I realized I still had other work to deal with.

Three days later, I received the client’s feedback email. He didn’t mention any dissatisfaction; he even wrote, “I really like one of the design directions.” But even so, my heart still couldn’t settle down for a long time. I kept feeling that my level might only be barely passable, and that if there were a next time, he would definitely choose another designer and never come to me again.

As night fell, a small gathering on the company rooftop grew lively. Soft lights spilled across the floor, and the air was filled with the mingled aromas of barbecue and beer. I stood in a corner, holding a drink, while a gentle breeze brushed my face. The colleagues nearby laughed nonstop, and their enthusiastic chatter made me smile unconsciously. A few coworkers came over to me and started making small talk. “How’s the project going lately?” one of them asked. “Pretty well, I guess—just a few small issues,” I replied, a trace of unease rising in me. The possibilities hidden in her tone left me tense.

My heart began to race. I tried to listen carefully, but I kept worrying in my mind whether they were hinting that I wasn’t doing well. “You look a little tired,” another coworker said softly, patting my shoulder. “You should relax a bit.” In an instant, my heartbeat grew even stronger, and my stomach tightened. Was she saying that I had disappointed her? Looking down at the drink in my hand, I started blaming myself for always being so sensitive.

“Actually, I often feel like I’m under too much work pressure too,” she continued. My heart relaxed a little. Maybe she was just sharing her own stress, not hinting at my shortcomings. “We all do,” I tried to hide my nervousness. “It’s just that sometimes it feels overwhelming.” My shoulders were stiff, sweat quietly appeared, and I struggled to maintain a calm exterior.

After the gathering ended, I walked downstairs alone, still hearing those conversations echo in my mind. That night, I lay in bed unable to sleep. I carefully replayed every sentence, afraid my coworkers would think I was strange because of how I had reacted. The next morning, I decided to be extra cautious at work and avoid saying anything that might be misunderstood.

A few days later, I was still occasionally remembering that conversation. Although my coworkers never brought up my behavior at the party, I felt sad about my own excessive sensitivity and overanalysis. At the same time, I reminded myself to be more understanding and forgiving, and not let these tiny details control my emotions and behavior.

The air in the café was damp and slightly sticky, the aroma of coffee beans mingling with a faint smell of cleaning solution. I was sitting by the window, across from the representative of the partner company, who wore a pair of metal-framed glasses that reflected the light from outside. In front of me sat a latte I had barely touched; the milk foam had long since sunk, and the white froth around the edges looked feeble. I was clutching my notebook so tightly that I almost wrinkled the cover.

“Hmm, I feel like something’s obviously missing,” he said calmly, though there seemed to be a hint of dissatisfaction in his tone. He flipped through my design draft and paused on one page, his brow knitting slightly. In an instant, my throat tightened, as if someone had looped a thin rope around it. I forced out a reply: “What’s missing? Is it the content, or is the style inaccurate?” My voice was kept very low and sounded a little hoarse.

He paused for a second without answering right away. His fingers tapped lightly on the tabletop, his eyes still fixed on my draft. “Overall, it doesn’t quite feel close to the direction we discussed before,” he said slowly, but the words landed in my ears like a heavy blow. My scalp tingled, and a flood of chaotic thoughts surged through my mind: Had I misunderstood his requirements? Had I failed to express myself clearly enough? Or was he actually dissatisfied with my ability at all? Would this collaboration end here? Fear pierced my chest like a cold knife.

I nodded in response, trying hard to look as if I were accepting the criticism. Yet my gaze couldn’t help drifting to the subtle changes in his expression. The corners of his mouth were pressed low, and his eyes seemed a little darker too. What did that mean? Was he hinting at some more serious disappointment or discontent? My heartbeat quickened, and my palms grew clammy. I lowered my head and pretended to look through my notes, avoiding his eyes. I couldn’t let him see me falling apart right then.

“It shouldn’t be too much trouble to revise, right?” His tone was casual, but I caught a trace of coldness in it. I murmured a few responses, my voice trembling. He seemed to notice my tension, and his brow relaxed slightly, but I still felt a knot twisting in my stomach, to the point that I almost wanted to vomit.

After the discussion ended, I practically fled the café. When the wind outside hit my face, I realized my back was already drenched. I went to a bench on the corner and sat down, looking at the stream of people and traffic in front of me, while the draft notebook in my hands felt like a heavy stone. I began replaying every one of his expressions and every word he had said, wondering if they all hid deeper blame or criticism. Was I simply not suited to this project? If he still wasn’t satisfied with my final submission, would he cancel the collaboration outright? These thoughts coiled through my mind like venomous snakes, biting until I could barely breathe.

After I got home, I tried to sort through my drafts, opening them again and again, then closing them just as often. I even started to feel that all my designs were terrible and worthless. I grew angrier and angrier at myself—how could I make such an obvious mistake? How could I be so useless? That feeling lasted until after midnight. I tossed and turned without sleeping, replaying the conversation from earlier in my head, and tears kept welling up. Only after I had endured until dawn did I finally manage to close my eyes.

The café was lit with a dim yellow glow, and the air was filled with the scent of coffee. I sat by the window, my laptop open in front of me, the screen showing the proposal I had just finished organizing. I tried to make myself look confident, but my stomach was clenched tight. The other person seemed calm and composed, taking a sip of coffee while flipping through my proposal. “Hmm, we may need to adjust this part,” he said in an even tone, though the end of his sentence seemed to drag slightly, as if hinting at some dissatisfaction. My heart sank abruptly, and I felt as if I had been seen through completely. “What’s wrong with it?” I asked, trying to keep my voice steady, though my heartbeat had already quickened and my palms had started to sweat. He looked up at me, frowning slightly, as if hesitating over how to answer. “The content itself is fine, but some parts aren’t expressed concisely enough.” In that instant, my mind began frantically playing out disaster scenes: Was he thinking I wasn’t capable enough? Did he regret choosing me as a collaborator? Did he feel I was wasting his time? I nodded, pretending to accept the criticism calmly, but in fact my stomach had started to cramp in waves. I tried to hide it, quickly jotting down his suggestions with my pen, not daring to look up at his face. “Are you okay?” When I suddenly heard that, I froze for a moment, then looked up to see a hint of concern in his expression. I quickly forced a smile. “Oh, I’m fine. I was just thinking about how to revise this.” My smile was as stiff as plastic sheeting blown by the wind, and the look in his eyes seemed a little uncertain. After the discussion ended, I stayed in the café and didn’t leave, his flat words echoing over and over in my ears, especially the line about certain parts not being concise enough. I began to blame myself: Why do I always seem so unprofessional? Why am I never truly confident? I flipped through the proposal, trying to find the so-called “problem,” but the more I looked, the more I felt that what I had written was a complete mess. I even started to wonder whether this collaboration would end because of my performance. That night, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to escape the feeling of being deeply flawed after being judged.

The lighting in the conference room was always a bit too bright, stinging my eyes and making me feel even more tense. Today we were discussing the strategy for a new project, and everyone was enthusiastically sharing their opinions. The air was filled with the smell of coffee, yet it did nothing to ease my unease. I noticed that the colleague sitting across from me had a slight furrow in his brow, as if he didn’t agree with the suggestion I had just made. My heartbeat sped up involuntarily, and my palms gradually began to sweat.

“I think this strategy might involve some risks,” I said, trying to keep my voice steady. Even so, I could still feel a slight tremble. As soon as the words left my mouth, I unconsciously began ruminating over what I had just said, wondering whether I had misspoken.

The colleague said to me, “Your idea is pretty good, but we may need to consider other, more reliable options.”

I nodded, trying hard to stay focused, but an inner voice kept questioning me: Was he rejecting me? Did he think I wasn’t professional enough?

My stomach began to ache faintly, as if something inside it were churning. I glanced down at my watch; time seemed to be passing especially slowly. The meeting continued, and no one’s attention was on me, but I could feel my own presence being magnified infinitely.

“Don’t overthink it,” I told myself. Yet the self-criticism constantly surfacing in my mind would not let up. I realized that I had once again fallen into this pattern of preemptive self-attack, trying to criticize myself before being criticized by the outside world.

After the meeting, I returned to my office and tried to calm down. The view outside the window was just as usual, but in my eyes it looked somewhat blurred. After a few deep breaths, my heartbeat gradually returned to normal, but the feeling of unease still lingered.

That night, alone at home, I revisited the matter, trying to convince myself that it had only been a normal discussion. Yet self-doubt kept surfacing from time to time. I tossed and turned in bed that night, unable to fall asleep.

A few days later, I spoke with that colleague again. He brought up the meeting and said that, in fact, my viewpoint had been very insightful, only it hadn’t been explored further at the time. Hearing that, I felt relieved, but also a touch of regret. Why did I always fall into self-doubt so easily?

I was sitting by the window in a coffee shop, looking at the laptop screen in front of me. The proposal document I had just opened was blank. People moved back and forth on the street outside the glass window, but my attention was completely on the colleague sitting across from me at the table. In a tone I couldn’t ignore, he said, “Did you not get the point? I’m talking about the client’s needs.” His speech was a little fast, his expression irritated, and his eyes were fixed straight on me.

My stomach felt like it was suddenly being clutched tight. My breathing became heavy, and my hands began to sweat on my knees. I tried to keep smiling, but the corners of my mouth twitched stiffly, and my heartbeat grew faster and faster. I heard myself ask in a shaky voice, “So do you mean the direction I took is completely wrong?”

He frowned, his tone still not easing. “I’m just saying you need to think it through more carefully. Don’t always rely on your own ideas. The client needs a practical solution.”

At that moment, three scenes surged into my mind almost at once: the scene of me being publicly rejected by a client in a conference room, the sound of the whole class laughing when I was criticized by a teacher for not doing my homework well as a child, and the comment “This is too childish” that I once received after sending a sketch to a friend. These images rose like mountains of accusation, leaving me surrounded with no way out. I felt as if I were sitting in the dock, everyone waiting for my failure to be announced.

I tried desperately to bring myself back to the present, but my voice grew smaller and smaller: “Yes, yes, I didn’t consider practicality...” Then I quickly lowered my head and stared at the coffee cup. I could feel heat gathering at the corners of my eyes, but I held it back tightly and lifted the cup as if to drink. The bitterness of the coffee slid down my throat, but it irritated my stomach and made me feel even worse.

My physical reactions grew more intense. My hands began to tremble slightly, and my legs felt as heavy as lead, unable to move. A deep sense of shame made me want to flee, but I was also afraid that leaving would make him think I was even less professional. I tried to focus on the wood grain of the table, looking at the tiny scratches, forcing my breathing to slow down.

Seeing that I didn’t respond, he softened his tone a little. “You don’t need to be too nervous. I just want the proposal to be more practical. Don’t take my tone too seriously.” It sounded like comfort, but I could still sharply catch the impatience in his voice, as if he were urging me to fix it quickly.

When I left the coffee shop, my legs still felt heavy, each step like wading through mud. After I got home, the first thing I did was repeatedly turn over every word he had said, trying to figure out what he really meant. Did he not think much of me as a person at all? Had he already lost confidence in my ability? These questions tangled my mind into a dizzy haze. At night, I tried to sleep, but with my eyes closed, the words “Did you not get the point?” kept echoing in my ears over and over. It wasn’t until after midnight that I finally drifted into a dazed sleep, exhausted by the rumination.

The next morning, when I woke up, I still felt weak all over. I opened the proposal document several times, but it still felt like I had no clue where to start. That deep self-doubt hung over me like an unshakable gloom, making even every key on the keyboard feel heavy.

I was sitting by the window in a café, where the raindrops outside tapped softly against the glass, blurring the figures of passersby. The coffee on the table had already gone cold, and I had barely touched it. Sitting across from me was the person in charge on the client side, someone I had always been trying to please. I remember she was wearing a dark blue suit, holding a pen in her hand, marking up a notebook. Her expression was calm, but to me, her face looked as if she could announce my failure at any moment.

She had just finished speaking, and my ears were buzzing. She said, “We don’t feel that the idea you proposed really fits the tone we’re looking for. We may need to reconsider the direction of our collaboration.”

My heart lurched, and it felt as if a stone were churning in my stomach. I swallowed, but my throat felt blocked. I heard my own voice trembling. “So... is there something not good enough about my proposal? I can change it...” She looked up at me, her tone still even and unhurried. “It’s not a problem with you personally. It’s just that, after the team’s overall evaluation, we feel we may need a different direction.”

At that moment, it felt as if something had squeezed my chest, making it hard to breathe. She said it was the team’s overall assessment, but the only thought left in my mind was: they don’t want me anymore.

My fingers tightened subtly, and I felt the nails digging faintly into my palm. I tried to smile, but it felt like the muscles in my face were twitching. “I know that feeling. I must have done something not good enough.” I lowered my head, speaking faster and faster, trying to explain. She interrupted me. “There’s no need to blame yourself too much. This is just an adjustment in direction.”

I nodded, but her tone sounded perfunctory, like a polite refusal. I began to replay every detail from the past—the countless email exchanges, whether every word had been inappropriate, whether I had seemed too nervous at each meeting. I even started wondering whether the clothes I wore today had made me seem unprofessional.

My throat tightened, my palms began to sweat, and my body on the chair was stiff as a puppet. I looked down at the tabletop; on the rim of the cold coffee cup, there was still a trace of my lipstick. I heard her say, “I have to go. It was nice talking to you.”

She stood up, adjusted her suit jacket, and glanced at me. I could read the meaning of that gesture: she was ready to leave, while I was still trapped in her rejection. I forced myself to stand, my hands and feet trembling slightly, and said stiffly, “Okay, thank you.”

She turned and left, leaving behind a faint scent of perfume. I sat back down, and it seemed the rain was falling even harder, but in my mind there was only her retreating figure. I kept replaying her expression and tone, and the more I thought about it, the more I felt like a failure, even beginning to doubt whether my abilities would ever be enough to satisfy anyone else. That feeling lasted the entire week. Every time I thought of that scene, I could feel a heart-wrenching ache in my chest, like some kind of deeply painful sense of being abandoned.

Outside the window, a light rain fell at a slant, accompanied by a soft ticking sound. My friend and I sat by the window in a café, and the woman across from me seemed to be frowning slightly, as if she were dissatisfied with something. The aroma of coffee filled the air, and for a moment I fell into a daze; the coffee in my mouth tasted faintly bitter. I tried to break the awkward silence and joked, “What a perfect day to hide away in here.” But she only replied flatly, “Mm, yeah.” Her coldness made me uneasy, and my stomach seemed to start churning too, as if I were about to feel nauseous.

I rubbed my hands together nervously and felt a trace of sweat. Had I said something wrong? I started going over our earlier conversation, but found no clues. Carefully, I asked, “Are you okay? Did I say something wrong?” She looked up, seeming a little surprised. “No, I’m fine.” Her expression startled me, and I tried to read the meaning behind her words, but felt somewhat at a loss.

To hide my unease, I picked up my coffee cup. Steam rising from the rim blurred my vision, yet my heartbeat grew even faster. Nothing substantial seemed to have happened just now, but I still felt that something was off, as if a thin thread were slowly tightening. I awkwardly changed the subject: “How’s work been lately?” hoping to make the atmosphere a little lighter.

Her answers remained brief, and I began to wonder whether I had done something to upset her, or whether I had missed some signal from her. Thinking back to the times she had gotten angry over small things, I felt a vague premonition—was she thinking something similar now?

After we parted, I wandered aimlessly through the streets, rainwater leaving icy streaks on my face. It felt as though a stone were weighing on my heart, and I kept thinking about her expression and tone; many thoughts intertwined in my mind. In the darkness, the sound of rain grew clearer in my ears, blending with the dim yellow glow of the streetlights to become a faint but constant background hum.

The next day, I messaged her to make sure she really was okay, but all I got in return were the simple words, “I’m fine.” For the next few days, I often found myself replaying that conversation, beginning to wonder whether I hadn’t cared enough about her, or whether my overthinking and anxiety had worn her out.

The rain tapped softly against the window outside. I sat by the café window, trying to focus on finishing a new order for a client. Yet my mind kept replaying the conversation from that morning.

In a tone I felt was somewhat cold, the client had said to me, “This draft doesn’t feel like your usual standard. It’s a bit... casual.” Although she hadn’t explicitly expressed dissatisfaction, I felt a sharp sting rise in my chest, as if she were directly questioning my ability.

I instinctively nodded and said, “Mm, I understand. I’ll revise it.” After saying that, I lowered my head and wrote down the key points for revision in my notebook, though my fingers were slightly trembling. She went on to offer some specific suggestions, but I barely heard them clearly. All I remembered was that her expression seemed to contain a hint of dissatisfaction—or perhaps my mind had automatically filled in those negative details.

After leaving the meeting room, my stomach began to ache faintly, and I felt as though I had been wrapped in a damp, cold blanket. By the time I stepped into the café, mist from the rain was rising, and my thoughts were still stuck in that moment. “Why did she think my work was ‘casual’? Am I really not trying hard enough? Or have I lost my creative touch?” My inner monologue surged like a tide; the more I tried to suppress it, the more it overflowed. I even began imagining that she might already be discussing my “decline” with other peers, and that maybe she would no longer choose me in the future.

The warm coffee beside me brought me back to reality a little. I took a deep breath and tried to look at the file again from a fresh perspective. My heartbeat was still fast, my palms a little sweaty, but I forced myself to calm down. “This is actually normal feedback. She didn’t say she hated it; she just wants it to be better.” I tried to convince myself, though even I sounded pitiful.

However, that effort didn’t fully work. I thought back to similar moments in the past—when other clients had given me feedback on my work, I was always like this: overinterpreting their words or expressions, then attributing the problem to my own flaws. I hated myself for being so sensitive all the time, yet I couldn’t stop reacting this way.

A few hours later, the rain stopped, and I finally finished the revisions. When I sent the email, my fingers paused again, hesitating over whether I should add a line like, “If you have any other suggestions, please let me know.” Behind that simple sentence, however, so much unease was hidden in my heart, as if I were asking for forgiveness—hoping that she would not be disappointed in me.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the little incident over and over. I quietly blamed myself for being too emotional, yet I couldn’t help fearing whether the client’s reply would contain even more criticism. This cycle made me even more tense, and I even wondered at one point whether I should change the way I worked in order to escape this constant sensitivity. I didn’t know whether the problem was mine, or whether the creative industry itself simply demanded this level of psychological resilience.

The air was thick with the stale smell of cement, and a haze of dust drifted by in the wind. I stood in the middle of this abandoned old cement plant, surrounded by crumbling buildings and rusted equipment. The ground beneath my feet was uneven and pitted, so I had to move carefully, afraid of getting cut by the discarded metal frames. It was eerily quiet here; only the occasional flutter of a bird’s wings echoed in my ears, sounding unusually clear.

“Isn’t this place distinctive enough?” I muttered to myself, aiming the camera at the huge cement mixer in front of me, trying to figure out how to give the shot a sense of story. I had come here today to gather material for a new visual project, but no matter how I adjusted the framing, that inexplicable loneliness on the other side of the lens never went away.

Just as I was concentrating on the composition, hurried footsteps came from afar, and my heart tightened; the camera in my hand nearly slipped. I turned around and saw a worker wearing a hard hat crookedly walking toward me. “Hey, what are you doing here?” he asked in Mandarin with a strong local accent.

“Oh, I’m here to shoot some footage,” I said, trying hard to sound calm. “This place has such a unique charm.”

He frowned, looking somewhat puzzled. “It’s really dangerous. You’d better be careful. This place hasn’t been in use for a long time.”

“Thanks for the warning,” I replied, my heart still pounding hard, a faint sheen of sweat seeping out on my forehead. I went back to shooting, but the unease in my heart wouldn’t leave. I couldn’t help feeling that, in his eyes, what I was doing was so unreasonable and incomprehensible.

As time passed, the sun slowly began to set, tinting the sky with a dim orange-red glow. I packed up my equipment and prepared to leave. My palms were slightly sweaty, mixed with the dusty smell in the wind, making them feel sticky. I quickly headed toward the exit, as if something had taken root in my heart and refused to let go.

After leaving the cement plant, I accidentally stepped on a loose stone and twisted my ankle in pain. I squatted down, rubbing my sore foot, and looked up at this desolate place, a wave of helplessness at being isolated rising in my chest. All along, I had never been unfamiliar with this feeling, and yet I still couldn’t get used to it.

The next day, I could hardly focus on my everyday work, and the worker’s face and his slightly wary expression kept replaying in my mind. That feeling of being misunderstood was like a shadow covering my heart, lingering and refusing to disperse. I began to reflect on my choices, on why I was always drawn to these dilapidated places. Perhaps I had always been trying to find some unique meaning of my own through them, even though this effort was often misunderstood by others as a pointless obsession.

On a weekend afternoon, I decided to take a walk to the old stone carving workshop near my neighborhood. This place has been around for a long time, and in my memory, it has always been a quiet corner. As I stepped inside, I was surrounded by air tinged with the smell of lime, and as I breathed it in gently, I felt the cool touch of stone flow across my fingertips. Sunlight streamed through the half-open windows, casting warm shafts of light into the house. Scattered across the carving benches were several unfinished sculptures, while fine particles of lime drifted faintly through the air, seeming like dancing sprites in the sunlight. I looked around, and each piece seemed to have its own story—some fierce and hideous, others calm and serene—as if waiting for someone to uncover their secrets. Suddenly, I heard footsteps at the door, and a stout old man walked in. “Hello, do you like stone carving?” His voice was deep yet gentle. I nodded, trying hard not to seem nervous. “Oh yes, these sculptures are very interesting. I feel as if they have a life of their own,” I replied. He smiled slightly and went on, “Yes, every stone has its own unique voice. We just help them tell their stories.” I continued wandering through the room, pausing beside each sculpture, trying to understand what they were saying. Inside, I felt an indescribable calm; perhaps this immersion in art on a midday could bring me some comfort. My heartbeat was steady and slow, and my inner restlessness began to ease. My body felt relaxed, even quietly joyful. As I left, the old man said to me again, “Come by often—it always helps lift your spirits.” I smiled and nodded, leaving with a sense of peace and delight in my heart. In the days after that weekend, I would occasionally think of the old man and his sculptures. The tranquil atmosphere of the stone carving workshop gave me a brief respite from anxiety. That serenity continued to stay with me, helping me feel calm as I dealt with stress at work.

I was standing in an abandoned hand-made shoe workshop, with old leather scraps scattered across the floor. The air was thick with the smell of leather that had lingered for years, mixed with the damp stench of mold. Through the broken windows, the clouds outside were growing heavier and the light was fading fast. I was trying to shoot a short film, hoping to capture the decayed beauty and sense of history here. However, just as I began recording, the camera malfunctioned—the screen showed an “error code,” and it would no longer start. I panicked at once, my whole body tightening, my heart beginning to race, and a thin layer of sweat breaking out on my palms.

“How could this happen?” I muttered to myself, my voice echoing in the empty room. Unwilling to give up, I tried several more times: unplugging it, plugging it back in, pressing the power button again, but there was still no response. It felt as if a stone were lodged in my throat—heavy and suffocating—and all my plans seemed to be thrown into disarray in an instant.

From time to time, I could hear the whistling wind blowing through the damaged window frame, bringing with it a deep sense of loneliness. I crouched on the floor, staring intently at the camera in my hands, while my mind kept obsessively replaying the same thoughts: “I should have checked the equipment yesterday. Why am I so unreliable?” “If I upload this online, viewers will definitely think it looks rough and unprofessional—they might even unfollow me right away.” “My client already thinks I’m not professional enough, and now I’ve messed up again. What am I supposed to do?” Every thought felt like a hammer striking my heart, growing more and more painful.

A few minutes later, I sat down on a dusty table nearby, trying to calm myself. But my body would not cooperate; my stomach began to ache faintly, as if it were being tightened. I looked down at my clenched hands, my knuckles nearly white, and found myself feeling ridiculous: “You can’t even handle a piece of equipment—what right do you have to be filming at this level?” Those self-blaming voices kept circling around me. I pulled out my phone, hoping to send a message and ask for help, only to discover that the signal here was unstable. Unable to hold back my emotions any longer, I gritted my teeth, my eyes starting to sting and blur.

I tried my best to take deep breaths, hoping to calm down, but it was useless. In the end, I forced myself to stand up and walk toward the window; the moment my hands rested on the glass, I felt weak all over again. Outside, the shadows of the trees swayed in the wind, as if mocking my incompetence and failure. I began to imagine how the outside world would judge me if all of this were exposed. That familiar feeling of being “not worth it” and “not good enough” welled up once more.

When I got home, I couldn’t even focus on anything. The failed shoot replayed over and over in my mind, and I felt as though I was wasting time, that I had no value. The next morning, when I woke up, yesterday’s shadow was still hanging over my mind. I dragged my heavy body to try repairing the equipment again, but my fingers were shaking so badly that I could hardly hold the screwdriver, and my heart was filled with a painful, conflicted struggle over right and wrong, success and failure.

The café was filled with the afternoon’s bustle: machines roared, the clatter of cups and plates never stopped, and the air was thick with the rich aroma of coffee. My friend and I sat by the window, sunlight filtering through the curtains and spilling across the tabletop, casting a warm glow over both our shadows. I stared at the coffee in my hand; the foam was slowly dissolving, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that something was off. My friend asked, “Have you been working on anything interesting lately?”

I did my best to match his interest, describing a new idea, but after only a few sentences I caught a fleeting microexpression on his face—his mouth seemed to tighten slightly, and his gaze looked a little distracted. My heart sped up, a faint sweat breaking out on my forehead. My fingers tightened around the coffee cup handle until my knuckles turned slightly white.

“Is he not interested in what I’m saying?” I thought anxiously, and my inner monologue began to surge. “Is my idea too boring? Could it even make me seem stupid?”

He went on, “That’s a pretty creative way of thinking.” His tone sounded encouraging, but because of his earlier reaction, I only grew more doubtful. Did he really mean that? Or was he just saying it out of politeness?

I pressed my lips together hard, trying to hide my inner panic. I kept replaying every detail of the conversation, as if I could find some trace of his true attitude in it. My stomach clenched into a knot and a dull pain began to spread. The coffee smell in the air was no longer pleasant; instead, it carried a hint of bitterness, as if reminding me how much of a failure I was.

By the time I left the café, my body was still tense, as if I were suspended on a thin thread covered in thorns, ready to be pierced at any moment. My friend waved goodbye, and I smiled and nodded, but my steps were heavy as I headed out the door.

That night, lying in bed, my mind still refused to settle. I kept replaying the conversation from earlier that day, even feeling ashamed of every detail I might have gotten wrong. When I woke the next morning, I still felt drained, as though I hadn’t slept at all. One night a few days later, I finally realized that maybe I had been overanalyzing my friend’s reaction, but there was always a voice whispering in my ear: “You’re not good enough.”

Afterward, I sent my friend a message to confirm once again what he really thought of my project. Although he quickly gave me a positive response, for some reason, that unease still didn’t go away.

Raindrops tapped softly against the glass outside the window. I pushed open the door, and the wind chime on it let out a bright, crisp jingle that sounded especially abrupt. The lighting inside the shop was dim, as if only a few small spotlights were illuminating the wooden shelves where the fragrance bottles sat. Several mixed scents filled the air—some sweet and cloying, some cool and fresh—like a wind on a rainy day that couldn’t find its direction. I walked over to a small display table covered with scented candles, browsing the labels while trying out the fragrances. Each label was written very poetically, with names like “Pine Forest After the Rain” and “Beach at Dawn,” but all I felt was a kind of weariness, as if none of the scents could completely relax me.

The clerk was a young woman. She came over from the counter and asked with a smile, “Is there anything I can recommend for you?” Her tone was gentle, but it made my shoulders stiffen at once. My heart sank as my thoughts raced: Was I being too awkward just now, making her think I was going to waste her time? Or did my clothes make her think I wasn’t worth serving properly?

“I… I’m just looking around, thanks.” I tried to sound natural, but my voice came out a little dry. She didn’t walk away. Instead, she said softly, “We just got a new scent in here. Most people say it’s very soothing. You could try it.” With that, she handed me a small transparent glass bottle. My hand trembled slightly as I took it, and the cold touch of the bottle made me even more uneasy. In that instant, my heart sped up, my palms began to sweat, and even my stomach started to ache faintly. Would she think I was a troublesome customer? Or think I wasn’t going to buy anything at all, just wasting her time? The voice in my head was like a train with no brakes, crashing into my reason again and again.

I tried to smell it, and the faint click of the cap unscrewing tightened my nerves another notch. The fragrance was warm sandalwood with a hint of citrus freshness. I said quietly, “That’s a pretty comforting scent, thanks.” She nodded slightly, still wearing her professional smile. “Yes, this one is especially popular. If you have any other preferences, just let me know anytime.” Then she stepped back a little to tidy up the shelves nearby, but I still felt her gaze sweeping over me from time to time.

“She must think I’m really strange.” My mind quickly filled in countless things she might be thinking, each one laced with criticism. I could only lower my head and pretend to keep looking at the labels, but the words in front of me were becoming blurrier and blurrier. At last, I picked a medium-priced candle and hurried to the counter to pay. Only then did I realize my breathing had become irregular, and even my hand reaching for my wallet felt clumsy. When she took my money, she thanked me in a low voice, but there seemed to be something hidden in that tone… sarcasm? I didn’t dare think further and almost fled the shop with the bag in hand.

When I got home, I sat on the sofa and tossed the bag aside carelessly. I tried to steady my breathing, but her eyes, her tone, even her comment that the scent was “especially popular” kept surfacing in my mind. Was she mocking me for following the crowd? Or hinting that I had no taste? From afternoon until night, these thoughts circled over and over. Although I kept trying to reassure myself—she was just aordinary shop clerk, and had probably forgotten me long ago—the uneasiness still gnawed at my nerves, slowly fading only after the night grew deep and the world fell quiet.

The air was thick with a moist, slightly sweet plant scent, and the giant palm leaves all around drooped low in a lush green canopy. I exhaled softly, watching the white mist from my breath vanish quickly before me. This morning, the company had arranged a stress management workshop in a small indoor botanical garden in the city center. In the middle of the garden, a fountain bubbled continuously, and a faint sound of water drifted into my ears. Standing off to the side, I looked at the coworkers lined up ahead and behind one another, my heart uneasy.

“Hey, how are you feeling?” my colleague Xiao Li suddenly leaned over to me, his tone carrying a hint of teasing.

“Oh, I’m fine,” I forced out a smile.

“You look a little nervous. Don’t be scared—it’s just a workshop.” He patted my shoulder.

The moment his hand landed on my shoulder, I felt a chill sweep through me. My heartbeat sped up, and my palms grew sweaty. I began to doubt his intentions, regretting that I had shown even a trace of unease. Had I once again left them with a negative impression? I silently scolded myself: “Why can’t I be more composed? Why am I always so sensitive?”

The tropical plants indoors seemed to blur before my eyes all at once, and an uncontrollable tightening sensation rose in my chest. The faint light ahead felt as if it were being blocked. I subconsciously adjusted my breathing, trying to keep that familiar panic from completely taking over my mind.

The workshop leader began explaining the key points of stress management, but I couldn’t focus at all. All I could feel was the repeated tension in my chest. In my mind, I kept asking myself over and over: “Is he making fun of me? Did I do something wrong again?”

Time seemed to slow at that moment. The sounds in my ears gradually receded, until everything seemed to blend together. I began to pay attention to my breathing, trying to calm myself down. Xiao Li seemed to notice my reaction and joked half-seriously, “Hey, relax. Today we’re surrounded by nature!”

“Y-yeah, that’s right.” I tried to make my voice sound less shaky.

After the workshop ended, I walked alone to the rest area in the garden and sat on a bench, staring at the lush greenery before me as sunlight poured down through the glass roof, stirred by a gentle breeze. My heart was filled with disappointment and self-reproach. Why was I always so easily shaken? Those fears and unease twisted around my heart like vines.

That night, after I got home, I lay awake for a long time, unable to sleep, replaying Xiao Li’s words and tone over and over in my mind. I kept wondering: “Should I try to explain myself more proactively, or should I just ignore these uneasy feelings?”

This experience made me realize that I am overly sensitive to how others judge me, and I often overreact, even to the point of affecting my normal judgment. I need to learn to give myself more room when facing these moments, rather than constantly attacking myself. Perhaps this is something I need to work on improving in the future.

Sunlight filtered sparsely through the curtains and fell across the floor, while the autumn wind outside gently stirred them. I was standing in the center of my new studio, trying to figure out how to arrange the furniture and equipment. Unopened cardboard boxes were piled in the corner, holding all of my creative tools. It almost felt like I could hear the boxes rustling faintly in the breeze, as if impatiently urging me to get moving.

“Do you think this table is okay here?” my friend’s voice came through my phone’s speaker. She was helping me make design adjustments over a video call. “Maybe it would be better by the window?” she suggested. I bit my lip, my mind turning over all kinds of thoughts. By the window there would be more natural light, which would be a big advantage for filming. However, I worried that I wouldn’t be able to make better use of the space. My heartbeat began to quicken, and the rising anxiety left me feeling a little breathless.

“Hmm, I think maybe we still need to think about the background too,” I replied, trying to sound calm. My voice couldn’t hide my inner uncertainty; I wasn’t sure about anything. That uncertainty churned in my stomach.

“Don’t worry, take your time,” she comforted me, but my palms had already started to sweat. I’ve always cared too much about every detail, afraid of missing any possible mistake. I forced a smile at myself, hoping to ease the tension.

After hanging up, that unease kept echoing in my mind. Self-doubt began to surface: why couldn’t I even handle something this simple? I always lacked confidence, always felt that the outcome might not turn out as expected. And so I seemed to see the doubtful look on my friend’s face, worrying that she was only forcing herself to support me.

After several hours, I finally decided to move the table by the window, trying to trust that I could make the right decision. As night fell, the autumn wind battered the window even more strongly, and I felt the atmosphere in the room grow colder and more desolate. I stood in the center of the room, looking around, and felt my mood become a little calmer. The boxes were still unopened, but at least I had a rough layout.

That night, I sat on the sofa and used my laptop to record the thoughts and decisions from the day. Although anxiety was still there, I felt a small sense of satisfaction at my little progress. A few days later, I began filming in the new studio, hoping to turn it into a comfortable place for creating. The voices of self-doubt from the past gradually grew distant, and at least within this small space, I felt a sense of control.

The café was filled with the rich aroma of coffee, and soft music drifted through the background. I sat by the window, sunlight streaming through the glass onto the table. My palms were a little damp, and my heartbeat had quickened without my noticing. The editor across from me was going over my latest proposal. Her expression seemed somewhat hesitant, which made me increasingly uneasy. “I think there are some issues with this direction, and we may need to reconsider it.” Her words were like a gentle tap, yet they sent a wave of anxiety through me. I nodded and tried hard to appear composed, but in my mind I had already started to rehearse all kinds of possible failure scenarios.

“Where do you think it needs improvement?” I asked, my voice trembling slightly as I tried to hide my unease. “This part may be too sensitive, and the market response might not be very good,” she replied, her gaze cautious. A rush of heat rose in my chest, as if I had been lightly stung. “Is it because I didn’t write it well enough?” I kept asking myself. My shoulders felt tense, as though under an invisible pressure.

I tried to calm myself down, but the coffee cup in my hand accidentally tipped over, and the liquid quickly spilled across the table, splashing even onto the editor’s papers. I hurriedly apologized, fumbling to wipe it up with tissues. “It’s okay, it’s okay, it’s just a small accident,” she comforted me, her tone gentle. But I was filled with shame, feeling like an awkward clown.

After leaving the café, I wandered aimlessly down the street, replaying the scene over and over in my head. Why is it always like this? I’m always too concerned about what others think, too afraid of making mistakes. The feeling of being rejected surged within me like towering waves, crashing repeatedly against my confidence.

That night, I lay in bed and couldn’t fall asleep no matter what. All I could see were the editor’s furrowed brows and my own embarrassment when I spilled the coffee. An inner voice kept criticizing me: was I not good enough, why was I always like this? I imagined a perfect version of myself, and the gap between that longing and reality left me feeling utterly frustrated and helpless.

A few days later, I received an email from the editor with some specific revision suggestions, along with encouragement to keep refining it. The sense of frustration eased a little then, but I still felt tense, afraid of making another mistake.

The shop was filled with a rich fragrance. Candles were neatly arranged on wooden shelves, and the pale yellow light cast on the walls created a warm atmosphere. I gently pushed open the door, and the wooden floor beneath my feet gave a faint creak. I walked up to the display case, and a shop assistant came over with a smile. She asked softly, “Can I help you?”

“I... I’m just looking around,” I replied, but inside I was already starting to feel nervous. Was her smile sincere? Was she hinting that I should make my choice quickly so the sale could be closed?

My heartbeat gradually quickened, and my palms began to sweat, as if even the fragrance in the air had turned oppressive. I tried hard to steady my breathing, but my thoughts had already gone out of control. I started remembering a small mishap from the last time I was in a similar store: I had accidentally broken a ceramic jar and was severely reprimanded by the owner. Although the assistant in this shop looked kind, I couldn’t help imagining the worst outcome in advance.

“If you’d like, you can try those scents,” the assistant said again, her voice gentle. I noticed her glance at the slightly trembling scented candle in my hand, and I immediately felt that she might have noticed my unease.

“Okay, thank you,” I managed to say with a strained smile, then turned to carefully look over a row of exquisite scented candles, trying to distract myself. In my mind, I kept replaying her tone, trying to find any hidden signs of displeasure.

After browsing for a while, I picked a box of orange blossom candles and walked to the counter. “Um... I’ll take this one,” I said softly.

The assistant nodded slightly and wrapped it up skillfully. “This is one of our bestsellers. I’m sure you’ll like it,” she said, handing me the packaged bag with a smile.

I nodded. When she handed me the receipt after I paid, my fingers accidentally touched hers. In that instant, I immediately felt a wave of sweat rising up my back, as if afraid she might notice my tension. The brief contact made my heart pound like thunder. I quickly said goodbye to her and left the store, trying to keep myself composed.

After leaving the shop, I took a deep breath and slowed my pace, trying to calm the turmoil in my emotions. The assistant’s smile and tone kept replaying in my mind, and I continued chewing over those details, fearing I might miss some hidden trace of displeasure. The inner restlessness lingered for a long time, and even after I got home I was still repeatedly thinking back on the experience.

That night, I lit the candle, and the orange blossom fragrance filled the room. Although I knew I might have been overreacting, I couldn’t explain why such a simple shopping experience had left me so exhausted. I felt helpless about my sensitivity, yet powerless to do anything about it.

I was sitting in the conference room, the air filled with the faint smell of coffee and the plastic scent wafting from the printer. The walls were illuminated by white fluorescent lights, making the room feel harshly bright. As the meeting went on, I tried hard to focus on every word the speaker said. Then, all of a sudden, a colleague mentioned the project delay in a subtly dissatisfied tone.

"Do you know why the project has been delayed?" he looked straight at me, his voice carrying a hint of accusation.

My heart instantly began to race, and I could feel sweat starting to bead on my forehead. I struggled to keep myself together and avoid losing composure in front of everyone. Over and over, my mind echoed: "Are they blaming me? Do they think I’m incompetent?" Every muscle in my body tightened, and my stomach began to ache faintly from the stress.

I tried to explain the project’s progress, but my voice trembled with nervousness: "Actually, it’s because of issues with resource allocation, plus some external factors..." My voice grew softer and softer.

The colleagues kept discussing it as if my explanation hadn’t been heard at all. I felt increasingly isolated, as though they had lost trust in me. The meeting continued, yet in my mind I kept replaying what had just happened, believing I had made an unforgivable mistake. Whenever someone looked up at me, I couldn’t help feeling that they were evaluating my worth with a scrutinizing gaze.

After the meeting ended, I staggered out of the conference room, feeling utterly down. Sitting at my desk, the words on the computer screen seemed to be mocking me. Images of being abandoned kept flashing through my mind, as if all my colleagues were distancing themselves from me.

Hours passed, and I still couldn’t calm down. Even after I got home that night, I still couldn’t shake off every detail of the meeting. Even in my dreams that night, I dreamed of being rejected by the entire team and felt unbearably lonely.

A few days later, I made efforts to communicate, hoping to gain my colleagues’ recognition and understanding, yet the uneasy feeling never completely went away. Although I eventually discovered that I had not actually made any fundamental mistake, the wound inside had already formed, leaving me anxious in every meeting thereafter.

In the pottery studio, the air was filled with the scent of earth. The windows were half open, and a faint chill of early autumn drifted in from time to time. In the corner stood an old floor lamp, its yellow light spilling over my worktable and making the whole process seem calm and quiet. I carefully stroked the wet clay still spinning beneath my fingers, trying to shape it into a perfect vase.

The teacher slowly came over to my side, looked at my piece, and said, “This shape is already quite close. You have a good feel for it.” I smiled faintly, but the worry in my heart did not fade. I always doubted myself when it came to such delicate things, because I was too easily knocked down by the smallest mistake.

“Sorry, I feel like it’s not very good.” My voice was a little hesitant, afraid that anyone might hear the slight tremor in it. The teacher patted me on the shoulder. “Don’t put too much pressure on yourself. Just enjoy the process of making it.”

Part of me agreed with the teacher’s advice, but I couldn’t help thinking: What if this vase breaks? If I don’t do well, does that mean I’m just an average failure at creating things?

I began to feel nervous. The lump of clay in my hands seemed heavier than before. My heartbeat quickened, and my fingertips ached faintly from gripping too tightly. A series of possible disastrous outcomes flashed through my mind. I felt sweat break out on my forehead. Unlike the dampness of the clay, this was a moistness that made me uneasy.

“Maybe I’m simply not suited for this kind of delicate work,” I muttered to myself, trying to put down my tools and look at the others’ pieces. They all seemed so confident, and some of their vases had already been fired, gleaming with enchanting glaze.

On the way home, I kept replaying everything from the classroom over and over, even wondering whether I should keep trying this new hobby. At night, I sat on the sofa in the living room, gently rubbing my fingers and feeling the intermittent stinging pain. Before I knew it, I seemed to slowly recall the teacher’s words. Maybe I really should learn to enjoy the moment instead of tormenting myself endlessly.

A few days later, I walked into the pottery studio again, determined to set aside all those excessive worries and anxieties, and truly seek a long-lost sense of peace and joy among the clay. Perhaps I could also try to accept my imperfections and give myself a little more tolerance and hope.

The afternoon sunlight streamed through the large windows of the pottery studio, casting a warm glow on the floor, while the air was filled with the damp scent of earth. I looked around and saw all kinds of pottery displayed throughout the room, their outlines traced by the soft lighting. I walked to a workbench in the corner, where some clay and simple tools were laid out. Several other students had already started working, absorbed and confident in their creations, while I kept doubting myself inwardly.

“Would you like to give it a try too?” a middle-aged female teacher asked with a smile as she came over. She wore an apron, her hands covered in clay. I nodded and smiled, but felt my heartbeat quicken, my palms sweating involuntarily. I sat down and began kneading a piece of clay with my hands. It was cold and soft, with a strangely wonderful texture. I tried hard to shape it into the design in my mind, only to find that the clay would not obey my commands.

“Mm, like this—take it slow, don’t rush,” the teacher guided me beside. I nodded, yet felt fine beads of sweat forming on my forehead. My hands moved slowly under her guidance, but it still never felt right. I kept wanting to press harder, but I was afraid that one careless move would ruin the whole shape.

“See, pottery is a lot like life: don’t rush or panic, just carve it out slowly.” Her words were gentle yet firm. But in my mind, countless past failures kept surfacing against my will, each mistake like an impurity in the clay that could never be removed.

Sitting at the workbench, my thoughts became chaotic and scattered, repeating in my head: “I can’t do this; everyone will see me fail.” Amid the laughter and conversation of the other students, I felt like a little boat drifting alone, at any moment liable to be overturned. I tried to take deep breaths, but a sudden tightness in my stomach kept me from relaxing.

Then one student came over, glanced at my piece, and casually said, “Not bad.” Yet that simple remark made me instantly alert. I tried to read more into his words—the tone, the look in his eyes, whether they were full of mockery. I couldn’t help attacking myself at once: “Why can’t you just do better? Why care so much about what others think?”

After holding on for an hour, I finally made a crooked little bowl, its surface uneven and its rim jagged. Although I knew it was the best I could do, I still couldn’t suppress the shame and unease I felt. When I left the studio, my fingers still carried the warmth of the clay—that was the only sensation that made me feel at ease.

Back home, lying on the sofa, my feelings still would not settle. That night, I dreamed I was sailing on the sea, surrounded by huge waves. I struggled to keep the boat on course, but it still swayed unpredictably in the wind and surf. When I woke up, that sense of helplessness and uncertainty still lingered in my heart.

The lights were spilling down from above, a little blinding, and the air was mixed with the scents of champagne and incense. My palms were already sweating. I gripped a glass of red wine tightly, trying not to let it shake too obviously in my hand. All I could hear around me were voices—people talking, laughing, even the crisp clinking of glasses. But all my attention was fixed on the face in front of me. She was my friend, or at least, that was what I had always believed.

It was during a pause in the conversation when she suddenly frowned slightly and said, “Your work has felt a bit repetitive lately.”

I froze, as if her words were a blade of ice, stabbing straight into my chest. My mind immediately started racing. What did she mean by that? Did she look down on me? Was she trying to put me down by saying this in front of so many people?

I forced out a smile. “Really? Maybe I just haven’t had as much inspiration lately.” But every word I said felt scalding, as if it had been burned by fire. I tried hard to act indifferent, but the panic and shame inside me surged up like a flood. My face was hot, my ears were buzzing, and my stomach suddenly began to churn, as if I had swallowed a piece of raw meat.

The whole room became blurry and distant. Their laughter drowned out my heartbeat, or rather, my heartbeat was mixing with the laughter into a chaos of sound. I stared fixedly at her face, trying to find the emotion hidden in her expression. Was she really criticizing me, or was it unintentional? But the slight upward curve at the corner of her mouth looked, to me, like smugness and mockery.

“I just meant maybe you could try some new styles and things,” she added, her tone so light that it felt like a casual extra stab.

“Oh, I see.” I answered mechanically, then walked away with my glass in hand, my legs a little weak, like I was walking on cotton. Half of it was to get away, and the other half was to breathe. I rushed out onto the balcony. The cool wind hit my face, but my chest still felt tight.

“Why am I so useless?” The thought sprang up, and I wanted to smash the wine glass in my hand. God, I couldn’t believe I was making myself like this over such a small comment. But at the same time, another voice inside me was screaming: It’s not my fault, it’s hers—she shouldn’t have said that!

I leaned back against the balcony railing, fingers gripping the edge so tightly that my nails even felt a slight sting. The wind at my ears was a little cutting, but it couldn’t scatter the images churning in my head. I started imagining her talking about me in front of other people, all those possible looks, expressions, tones of voice, each one making my stomach ache more.

When I got home that night, I threw myself onto the sofa. The ceiling light was especially glaring. I tried opening my computer and writing something to distract myself, but all I could think about was her sentence and that expression on her face. I opened and closed the work software again and again; the cursor blinked on the document, as if mocking me. I wrote less than a sentence before deleting it again. In the end, I just hugged my knees and stared at the blank page until my eyes hurt.

Eventually, I shut the computer and lay down on the bed, trying to convince myself: “Maybe she just said it offhand.” But no matter how I tried, that blocked-up feeling in my chest still wouldn’t go away. I don’t remember how I fell asleep that night. I only know that deep self-loathing and fear lingered for days afterward, like a shadow that wouldn’t leave me alone.

The damp, chilly air carried a faint smell of old wood. The wooden floor beneath my feet swayed slightly, and every step produced a creaking sound. A few damaged chandelier cords hung down from the ceiling of the piano workshop, leaving the place nearly dark. The only shafts of sunlight seeped in through cracks in the wall, clearly outlining the drifting dust. Some discarded old pianos leaned quietly against the wall, looking like forgotten monsters. In the distance, the lid of one piano was open, and I could see its faded keys, with several strings already broken and bent. I found a spot, set up my tripod, and tried adjusting the lens angle to capture the desolation here, while also worrying whether doing so made it seem too deliberate.

My partner was ten minutes late. He messaged that he might need to wait a little longer, and I nodded, not knowing what to do. Irritation began to rise in my mind. “Why choose such a place? What if the footage doesn’t turn out well? Did I not prepare enough last night, and was my reference for the location too vague?” I did my best to keep my thoughts from turning negative, but it didn’t seem to work. I tried taking deep breaths, only to find the heaviness in my chest growing more and more oppressive. My right hand clenched the zipper of my jacket, and I noticed my palm had grown damp with sweat, my fingertips even tingling slightly.

From far away came a burst of hurried footsteps and a low voice calling my name. “Why is it so dark? You gave me a scare,” he complained, panting. “I should’ve brought a headlamp.”

“Are you okay? Is the shoot going smoothly?” His words caught me off guard, and I actually forgot to answer. I nodded, but my voice must have sounded very weak. “Yeah, more or less, but... we may need to figure out the lighting problem,” I said quietly, trying not to seem so tense.

“Okay, then let’s get started quickly, or it’ll be trouble once it’s completely dark.” He pulled out his gear and started working. I forced myself to stay calm, but the unease inside me only grew stronger. Countless self-blaming thoughts began to surface in my head: “Why am I always so unreliable? What will others think of me? This place is terrible—he’ll definitely think I chose the wrong location.”

Halfway through the shoot, the equipment suddenly malfunctioned and began emitting a piercing warning beep. In an instant, my self-blame surged over me like a flood. “It’s over. We definitely can’t film now. It’s all my fault, all my fault.” My head felt like it was rushing with blood, my chest grew tight in waves, and my stomach cramped with tension.

To fix the problem, I picked up the tool beside me and asked as calmly as I could, “Let me take a look at the camera and see what’s wrong.” But the moment my hand touched the equipment, I started trembling. I fiddled with it mechanically a few times, but still couldn’t find the issue. My throat felt agonizingly tight, as if someone had stuck a needle into it.

At last, he said softly, “Don’t worry. These things happen all the time. We can readjust the plan, and if we really have to, we can reshoot tomorrow.” Hearing that, I suddenly felt like crying, but I held it back and just nodded.

On the way home, I kept replaying the scene in my head, imagining over and over whether he had already lost trust in me. “He must think I’m terrible.” The pressure in my chest lasted until night. Even when I sat on my bed, I couldn’t stop thinking about today’s mistake. My stomach had already started to ache faintly, so I decided to drink a cup of hot water, hoping it would ease things a little, but it barely helped. In the end, I sent an apology text, saying today had been my oversight and that I hoped to make up for it.

The next afternoon, he replied, saying yesterday’s shoot had actually turned out pretty well and that some of the footage was already usable. That made me breathe a little easier, but I still felt that my performance had left a bad impression on him.

The air was filled with a faint scent of cinnamon and vanilla. I moved closer to the shelf, my fingertips lightly brushing the surface of a clear glass jar. Sunlight streamed in through the mottled window frame, casting shadows on the floor like some ancient symbol. I had long been saying I’d give a friend a unique gift, and today I had finally come to this independent spice shop. The atmosphere in the store was nice, with vintage wooden shelves lined with jars and bottles of all shapes and sizes. The clerk was a young woman with short hair, busy behind the counter blending spices. She looked up at me, then lowered her head and kept working. Suddenly, I felt that her expression seemed a little cold. Was it because I had stood in front of the shelf too long? Or had I somehow annoyed her the moment I walked in?

My heartbeat quickened all at once, and my palms began to sweat slightly. I told myself not to overthink, but all kinds of possibilities still sprang to mind: was it because I made too much noise when I pulled the door open just now? Or had I accidentally messed up her display? “Maybe I look indecisive, like someone who knows nothing about this, and that’s irritating.” I held the spice jar in my hand, but I didn’t dare take it to the counter to pay.

“Need any help looking for something?” Her voice suddenly came from behind the counter, flat and emotionless. I jerked my head up, my throat tightening, but without thinking I blurted out, “No, thanks, I’m just looking around.” My voice sounded somewhat stiff, and I wasn’t even satisfied with it myself.

She simply nodded and continued mixing spices. I could clearly feel the muscles around my shoulders and neck tightening, and my stomach seemed to ache faintly too. I lowered my head and glanced quickly at the jar in my hand, realizing it was a blend of lemongrass and rosemary—the exact scent my friend liked. Even so, I hesitated for a few seconds and put the jar back on the shelf. I secretly scolded myself for being too neurotic: why was I so sensitive to the tone and gaze of an ordinary shop clerk? But I really couldn’t convince myself that I hadn’t upset her.

In the end, I gathered my courage and brought the spice jar to the counter. “I’ll take this.” I tried to keep my voice calm, though I could still hear a slight tremor in it.
