She took the jar, wrapped it skillfully in kraft paper, and when she handed it back, she even smiled and said, “Thanks for coming. Come again next time.”

I forced out an awkward smile and hurried out of the shop, feeling that my back was already drenched. Back on the street, the cool autumn wind blew past, helping me calm down a little. But my mind kept replaying the clerk’s tone, her gaze, even that fleeting frown. I started to doubt myself—had I done something wrong somewhere? Even though I had already walked quite far, I still couldn’t help glancing back.

That night I gave the spice to my friend. She happily opened it and said it smelled amazing, so refreshing that it lifted her spirits. Yet I couldn’t feel happy at all. My mind kept replaying that clerk’s expression and the tone I had used when speaking. If I had been a little warmer, would she not have spoken that way? Or if I had been a little more confident, would I not have felt she was singling me out? I analyzed it over and over, and in the end I fell asleep with that dull, heavy ache in my chest. When I woke up the next morning, the first thing I told myself was that I needed to learn to let go of little things like this. But could I really do it?

The mottled bricks and stone on the walls, along with the sunset light filtering in through several worn-out windows, made the old warehouse seem mysterious and somewhat oppressive. Around me were all kinds of art installations—some hanging in midair, others looking as though they had grown out of the walls. The air was thick with the smell of old lime, mixed with the sharp freshness of paint.

The exhibition had drawn quite a crowd, and my ears were filled with conversation and footsteps. Everyone around me seemed to be chatting and laughing with ease, while I felt as if I were sealed inside an invisible bubble. I kept looking around, trying to find someone to talk to, but whenever someone’s gaze swept over me, I quickly looked away.

“What do you think of this?” came a low voice beside me. It was a tall man, pointing at a huge metal installation.

“Uh, it’s cool, really unique,” I replied awkwardly, while countless questions swirled in my mind: Was he genuinely interested in my opinion, or was he just looking for someone, anyone, to talk to?

Then he turned back to continue talking with his friend, and my heartbeat instantly quickened, sweat spreading across my palms. I gripped my bag tightly to keep my hands from shaking too visibly. Why couldn’t he ask me a few more questions? Did he think I was boring?

Standing amid the bustling crowd, I felt lonelier and lonelier. A sharp inner voice began to whisper: “You’ll never fit into a place like this. They can all see your flaws.” That only made me want to flee more, yet I somehow remained rooted to the spot.

I tried to take deep breaths and calm myself down, but my mind started replaying the moments of that conversation again and again, analyzing every expression and tone. I wondered whether I had said something stupid or seemed too nervous. My stomach began to churn, as if all my unease were gathering there.

Hours passed, and I still remembered the man’s indifferent expression the moment he turned away, as vividly as ever. It was like a thorn, driving deeper into my mind. That night, sitting at home, I imagined my performance over and over, trying to find clues that could help me become better, less likely to be overlooked.

Over the next few days, I carefully avoided crowded places, afraid of experiencing that sense of abandonment again. Even though I knew it might just be my own overinterpretation, I still couldn’t shake off that shadowlike feeling of shame.

I was sitting in a café, sunlight streaming through the window and falling across the table, the air filled with the aroma of coffee, soft music lingering in my ears. E was sitting across from me, her expression seeming somewhat displeased, which made me feel tense. We were discussing my upcoming new project, and I eagerly described my ideas to her. But when she spoke, her words came like an unquestionable judgment, striking straight into my heart. “Are you sure anyone will be interested in doing this?” she said with a frown. My heart sank abruptly, my breathing grew rapid, my heartbeat quickened, and fine beads of sweat emerged on my palms. “Does she think I’m incapable?” I kept asking myself, and an involuntary fear of abandonment welled up in my mind. 

I forced a smile and replied, “I think this will be a breakthrough, and it may attract a very specific audience.” My voice trembled a little, and even I could hear the uncertainty in it. But E continued, “I’m just worried you might be wasting your energy on something that isn’t worth it.” Her words echoed in my ears, as if an invisible wall had separated me from her. I didn’t dare look up at her; my gaze remained fixed on the coffee cup in my hands, my fingers gripping the handle so tightly that my fingertips turned white. 

“Am I really, as she said, destined to fail?” My thoughts began to churn, and countless images of being doubted and dismissed in the past surged up, like an endless vicious cycle. My stomach began to hurt, as if an invisible hand were twisting it tightly inside. “If even E doesn’t support me, how am I supposed to keep going?” my inner voice whispered in a choked sob. 

That night, I went home and curled up on the sofa, trying to find calm amid the chaos. The night outside grew deeper, and the occasional sound of cars passing drifted in from the street. I kept replaying E’s words, sinking into deep self-doubt. “Maybe I really am a hopeless failure.” I blamed myself inwardly, thinking, “Has she already lost confidence in me? Will she leave me like everyone else?” 

Over the next few days, I felt depressed, as if surrounded by invisible pressure that made it hard to breathe. Every time I thought about that conversation, it felt like a huge stone was pressing on my chest, leaving me breathless. I became even more afraid to take that step, worried I would be rejected again. I began checking my plan over and over, trying to find any possible flaw, but the more I looked, the more hopeless I felt.

The vibrations of the music came through the thin walls, mingling with the frantic beat of drums and electric guitar. I sat on a worn bench, surrounded by busy staff members darting back and forth, each clutching various pieces of equipment. The air was heavy with sweat and the heat radiating from the lighting rigs, making me increasingly uncomfortable. My mind kept projecting countless embarrassing scenarios, and my palms began to sweat without my realizing it, while my heartbeat drummed densely in my chest.

"Hey, are you ready?" came a voice from behind me. I looked up and saw a friend who was handling the sound for today. He looked at me with a perfectly measured smile. "Mm, I think so." But even as the words left my mouth, I felt unsure of myself. My friend patted me on the shoulder. "Relax, it's just a small show. Everyone's supporting you."

I forced out a smile, while in my mind I kept rehearsing the worst possible outcomes—microphone failure, forgetting the lyrics, dead silence from the crowd. I knew I should focus, but nervousness felt like invisible chains, winding around my heart, impossible to break free from.

The backstage lights flickered on and off. I closed my eyes, trying to calm myself, only to feel a familiar ache starting in my stomach—a familiar anxiety response. I took a deep breath and told myself I should act more professionally, instead of being so flustered and uneasy. When I opened my eyes again, my gaze was drawn involuntarily to my reflection in the mirror. I looked paler than I actually was, and the unease in my eyes seemed almost ready to spill over.

"You'll do great." I whispered the encouragement to myself again. Suddenly the music grew louder, and the blinding spotlight pierced through the thick curtains, signaling that the performance was about to begin. I struggled to my feet, tightened my grip on the instrument in my hands, and walked toward the edge of the stage. Behind me was the noisy backstage area; ahead of me was the stage, filled with unbearable tension.

That night, I ended up performing successfully, though the process was not as perfect as I had expected. At the end, the thunderous applause felt like a long-lost release, and I realized I had not been abandoned; perhaps it was because that applause carried understanding and acceptance. A few hours after I got home, I collapsed exhausted onto the sofa. The words and sounds from earlier in the day still echoed clearly in my mind, but my mood gradually settled. Looking back on the experience a few days later, I had to admit that although anxiety remained a difficult problem to resolve, it was, in any case, another experience that helped me grow.

The dim lights of the exhibition hall shrouded the entire space in a mysterious and eerie atmosphere. The air was thick with a damp smell, mixed with the scent of animals, which made me feel slightly uneasy. I wandered among the various display booths, carefully observing those reptiles—their scales glimmered with a faint light, and I could hear them scratching inside the glass enclosures.

“Do you like reptiles that much?” A staff member at the exhibition suddenly appeared beside me, his tone impossible to tell whether it was curiosity or sarcasm. I froze slightly, my heartbeat quickening, a faint unnatural flush rising to my face. “Uh, yes, they’re pretty interesting,” I managed to force out with a smile.

I could feel sweat sliding down my forehead, my palms growing damp. With every reply, I doubted whether my words were appropriate, whether they made me seem foolish or uneasy to others. I couldn’t help but ruminate over the conversation again, afraid of embarrassing myself in front of a stranger.

He went on, “These guys are actually pretty friendly; they won’t scare you.” I nodded, but I couldn’t stop the doubts surging inside me. This kind of polite small talk left me at a loss, and I quickly shifted my gaze, pretending to be captivated by a monitor lizard on display. It lay lazily on a rock, its black eyes staring at me without blinking.

When I left the exhibition hall, night had already fallen outside. Light spilled onto me from the far end of the street, bringing a little warmth. Still, my stomach ached faintly, and that embarrassed feeling of being misunderstood remained close behind me. To fend off this suffocating unease, I began harshly judging myself in my head: “Why is it always like this? Can’t you just be more confident?” I blamed myself inwardly.

The next morning, when I woke up, the reptiles and the staff member’s face were still lingering in my mind. I tried to shift my attention to the work project ahead, only to find that my thoughts were still tangled up in everything from the night before. Anxiety was like a sticky spiderweb, and I was just a little insect caught in it, struggling in vain.

Sunlight streamed through the carving shop’s window, falling across the workbench. I gently stroked a piece of wood I had just begun to carve, and the air was filled with the faint scent of wood shavings, which was deeply soothing. Yet my mood never truly eased; the pressure of anxiety made my stomach ache faintly. The shop owner stayed beside me, smiling as he watched the progress of my work. Soft background music flowed through the shop, but I could barely focus on the carving in my hands. “Have you tried this technique before?” the owner asked casually. I nodded and replied in a faint voice, “A few times, but I always feel like I’m not good enough.” I tried to keep my smile relaxed, but inside I was almost falling apart. Countless scenes of failure flashed through my mind at once: the carving turning out shapeless, being mocked by peers, being rejected by customers. I could even feel sweat in my palms, making it nearly impossible to hold the tool. Every slight change in the owner’s expression made me wonder whether I had done something wrong; before I knew it, I was tense, my heart racing, my fingers trembling nonstop. “Don’t worry too much about the details. Sometimes relaxing can lead to better results,” he said. I tried to take a breath, hoping to calm myself, but my hands remained stiff. The owner turned away to attend to other customers. I lifted my head and looked around at the carvings in the shop; those exquisite works of art made me feel that success was still far away. “How could I ever make something that good?” I asked myself silently. As I continued carving, the tool in my hand seemed to have a will of its own, and every touch against the wood’s surface made me feel insignificant. That night, when I got home, I lay in bed, still seeing the unfinished carving before my eyes. I involuntarily replayed every detail of the day in my mind, doubting my talent and worrying that I would not be recognized. That lingering sense of shame kept me tossing and turning for several nights. A few days later, I happened to see a post by the shop owner on social media. In a few brief words, he shared some beginner carving pieces he had seen in the shop that day, including mine. Although he did not specifically mention my name, those photos once again sent me into deep self-reflection, and the anxiety and tension in my heart surged back.

The lights in the conference room were a little harsh, and the files on the table were piled in a mess. I sat on the corner of the table with my notebook in my arms, my palms slightly sweaty. Right after my manager emphasized today’s topic, people started discussing it intensely. I tried to chime in, but several times I was pushed aside by colleagues with louder voices. I couldn’t help clenching the pen in my hand, feeling my palms grow sticky with sweat.

“I actually think we could try presenting it in a more relaxed way, like combining a short film with an interactive game. That might attract the audience better.” At last, I found a gap and voiced my idea, my voice sounding a little shaky.

No one responded. After only a brief second of silence, another colleague continued with his own idea. “Or we could directly use a set of data to make a cool animated chart, which would fit our brand style better.” A few people immediately laughed and chimed in, with an undertone I couldn’t quite make out, as if silently suggesting that my proposal wasn’t professional enough or wasn’t a good fit.

My stomach gave a sudden jolt, as if someone had twisted it hard. I sat there and forced a stiff smile to hide my disappointment. “But if we add an interactive game, it might actually be a bit risky...” I added quietly, only to be drowned out at once by someone else’s laughter. In that instant, I felt completely invisible, as if everyone were saying to me, why do you always bring up these childish ideas?

My thoughts started spiraling out of control: Did they think my ideas had no technical substance at all? Didn’t even bother responding? Was I really that terrible, looked down on by everyone? I struggled to suppress the urge to stand up and leave, placing my hands on my knees and trying to make my body seem more relaxed, but my shoulders stayed tense. I thought my face might be a little red, and I tried hard to pretend to flip through my notes, avoiding anyone’s gaze. My heart was beating too fast, and my ears were buzzing. For the rest of the meeting, I didn’t say another word, but my mind kept replaying what had just happened, speculating on how each person had judged me.

After the meeting ended, I rushed out as fast as I could, not even daring to make eye contact with anyone. Once inside the restroom stall, I finally let out a breath, but the tightness in my stomach didn’t lessen at all. I stared fiercely at myself in the mirror and began silently blaming myself: Why am I so invisible? Why do I always seem so unprofessional? Am I really not suited for this job?

That night, lying in bed, I still couldn’t let myself off the hook. The suffocating feeling and the shame of being ignored kept wrapping around me, like a tightening rope, coiling tighter and tighter. I couldn’t help thinking that if I were more persuasive, maybe everything would be different. In the end, I didn’t manage to fall asleep until two in the morning, and when I woke up the next day, my eyes were badly swollen.

I sat at my desk, the cold light from the computer screen stinging my eyes. The air was filled with the smell of coffee, but I had lost all appetite for it. The meeting was about to begin, and I flipped through the proposal I had just prepared. A sense of nervousness rose involuntarily, like an invisible hand squeezing my heart tightly. The conference room was full of my colleagues. The hum of the projector and the tapping of keyboards stood out especially sharply in the quiet room.

“What do you think of this proposal?” a colleague’s voice came from my left. I looked up and met her eyes; her gaze seemed to be appraising me, and I felt an inexplicable pressure. “Well, I think it could still be further optimized,” I replied, trying to control the tremor in my voice. The corners of her mouth tightened slightly, as if in faint disdain, and that instant felt like a needle stabbing the softest part of my heart.

“Does she think I did a terrible job? Is everyone criticizing me?” These thoughts spun wildly in my mind, growing louder and louder, almost drowning out everyone else’s conversation. The meeting continued, and the focus of the discussion shifted to the details of the proposal, but I was held captive by my own anxiety and the negative thoughts flowing endlessly through my mind.

“Can we talk about your thoughts?” another colleague asked me. My heart raced, fine sweat began to cover my face, and there was a tight knot in my stomach. “Of course, sure.” My voice was barely forced out of my throat, unable to remain steady.

For the entire meeting, I couldn’t concentrate. My muscles were so tense that I could hardly sit still, and my palms were sweaty. I kept feeling as though invisible eyes were watching me, examining every mistake I made. After the meeting ended, I mechanically gathered my papers and left the conference room, feeling a heavy exhaustion.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying my performance over and over. “If only I had been more decisive then, maybe they wouldn’t have questioned me.” A deep sense of defectiveness and fear of abandonment enveloped me. This feeling did not disappear in sleep; even in my dreams I was still being criticized and judged.

A few days later, I was still ruminating over every detail of that meeting. Although my colleagues later expressed support for me, I still couldn’t fully trust their goodwill. Every time I walked into the conference room, I would remember that feeling of being scrutinized and my own unease. It made me increasingly dissatisfied with myself, and I tried to counter this sense of defectiveness by constantly criticizing myself.

The museum’s lights fell softly over the canvases of every color as I stood before an abstract painting, surrounded by visitors speaking in low voices. The music in my ears was light and airy, seeming to form a harmonious backdrop with the artwork. I should have been in a cheerful mood, but in fact I was churning with unease, like waves of tide rising one after another. Now and then I caught snippets of other people’s conversations, and I strained to hear every word, afraid of missing something important. I’ve always been like this, afraid of missing some crucial piece of information. Suddenly, my friend E beside me said, “What do you think of this painting?” His tone seemed casual, but I instantly tensed up. My palms grew sweaty and my heartbeat quickened, as if I had no idea what to make of these abstract paintings. “Oh, I think it’s… pretty interesting, I guess,” I stammered, not daring to meet his eyes. E’s brows twitched slightly, and I started frantically wondering whether I had said something wrong. I silently blamed myself: why do I always put myself in situations like this? It seemed like this would never get better. I began to ruminate over my earlier conversation with E, trying to find anything that might have displeased him. The pressure in my chest grew stronger, and a dull ache started in my stomach. Many people continued walking around the gallery, discussing their own impressions, while I seemed trapped inside a shroud of tension I couldn’t escape. After a while, E patted me on the shoulder. “Relax a little. It’s just an exhibition; you don’t have to take it so seriously.” His voice was gentle, but hearing those words stirred up a wave of helpless shame in me. Even comfort felt like a hint that I was somehow always magnified in other people’s expectations. I gave an embarrassed smile, and he turned away to admire another piece. When I got home that night, I still couldn’t calm down. Every time I thought back to E’s expression and those hushed words, my stomach would tighten again. A few days later, I tried to analyze what had happened that day and reinterpret E’s reaction. Maybe I was just overthinking everything, I told myself. Next time, don’t be so nervous. And yet these emotional fluctuations would arrive so quietly, always catching me off guard.

The air in the bike shed carried a faint musty smell, and the green paint on the walls had peeled away, revealing the gray concrete beneath. I sat beside an old bicycle, surrounded by scattered tools and rusty bike parts. The sound of the wind mixed with the distant noise of the city, leaving me feeling a little lonely. I tried to focus on the notes in my hands. “Today’s creative discussion was very good,” I told myself. “But did they really like my ideas?” My heart began to beat uneasily, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. “Or were they just brushing me off, agreeing out of obligation?”

I kept thinking over everyone’s reactions in the meeting, remembering how the manager had frowned slightly before relaxing again as he said, “Interesting idea.” But I couldn’t tell what he really thought. The scenes kept replaying in my mind, like a movie on a loop. I tried to recall the expressions and tones of the others. “Was it support, or just indifference?” This made me restless inside. “Maybe I should have given up on these ideas long ago.” My heartbeat grew faster and faster, and a dull pain began to spread through my stomach.

“Am I okay?” I muttered to myself, trying to calm down, when I heard someone pass outside the bike shed. A voice called out, “Kid, what are you doing here?” It was an older neighbor from the community. “I’m sorting out my thoughts,” I replied, my voice tense. “This place doesn’t look very ideal,” he said, with curiosity and a hint of concern. “Yeah, it’s only temporary,” I said, forcing a smile.

When I got home that night, I still couldn’t shake the doubts from the meeting. I tossed and turned, feeling as if my mind were knotted up. “Next time, can I do better?” I thought, the question wandering through my mind. “Or am I simply incapable of making any difference?” That sense of helplessness made my shoulders feel even heavier. “Still, I should keep trying,” I told myself, trying to break free from this feeling of being overlooked.

A few days later, I was still uneasy about my ideas. Every time I thought about that discussion, my heart would race, but I tried to tell myself, “Now is the time to reorganize my thoughts; I can’t keep doubting myself like this.” So I found some new materials, read and reflected, and gradually let my mind settle down.

The light in the shop was dim. I held a vibrato harp in my hands, gently tracing the smooth wooden surface. The air was filled with the scents of paint, old wood, and a faint sweet-and-sour note, as if reminding me that this place had endured the years. In the corner, the owner was repairing an ancient ocarina. He looked up, swept me with his perpetually tired eyes, and then said in a low voice, “If you’re just here to look, forget it. That instrument isn’t for sale.”

“Oh, I…I’m just curious,” I stammered, my heart beginning to race and my face burning. I immediately realized I might have upset him—always like this, why do I always manage to annoy people?

“This isn’t a showroom; it’s a workshop.” His tone was flat as he turned back to his work. I tried to keep smiling, even as I could feel sweat running down my forehead, my back already soaked, my stomach twisting into a knot.

I wanted to say something to ease the awkwardness, but all the words stuck in my throat. All I could hear was my own breathing, quickening. “Sorry, I’ll leave right away.” My voice was so small it was almost drowned out by the shop clock’s ticking.

As I left the shop, my mind kept churning over the dismissive look he had given me, as if I had really done something wrong. I could even feel that gaze nudging me on the shoulder, telling me to leave faster. On the way back, the streetlights glowed dimly and the shadows stretched long, while I imagined every passerby was talking about how out of place and awkward I was.

That night, lying in bed, my thoughts kept replaying the scene from the afternoon. My inner voice kept blaming me: “Why are you always so out of place?” My heartbeat pounded like a drum in my ears, intensifying my anxiety, as if those sounds could drown out any criticism from outside.

A few days passed, and the incident was still lingering in my mind. I tried to turn my attention back to work, but the knot in my head remained. Every time I thought of the owner’s tone, I found myself involuntarily questioning my place in any interaction.

In the end, I decided to write a short piece about that experience, hoping it would help me work through those negative feelings. At last, my fingertips in front of the screen stopped trembling, as if words could untangle those runaway thoughts. Even though I knew I might still catastrophize small things, at least today’s unease could rest for a while.

The fish market was lively from early morning, the air filled with the smell of fish and a faint scent of sea breeze. The scales on the fish stalls shimmered in the morning light, like tiny fragments of pearls. I wandered through the market, admiring these creatures from the ocean. A bearded vendor was arranging his goods, while resonant calls rose one after another, marking the start of a new day.

I stood in front of a stall piled high with salmon, and the vendor greeted me warmly: “Want to take a look at some fresh salmon?” I gently shook my head and smiled, saying I was just browsing. “Today’s salmon is excellent, brought in from the harbor only last night,” he continued, as if I were already preparing to buy.

My gaze moved from the salmon to the sea snails and clams beside them, lying quietly in pale blue plastic boxes, sprinkled with a little seawater. I liked looking at these sea snails of all shapes and sizes; their shells bore beautiful patterns, like works of art created by nature. “If you like those, you can try making soup,” a middle-aged woman vendor said to me, her voice soft and kind.

I smiled faintly and told her I wasn’t very good at cooking seafood. “Then buy some and give it a try—they’re not easy to keep alive,” she said with a laugh, then went back to greeting other customers.

Standing in front of the stall, I felt an inexplicable sense of peace. The market was like a miniature ocean, with all kinds of sounds woven together, yet it didn’t make me anxious. My heartbeat remained steady, my body comfortable, as if this place had become a brief escape.

I kept walking and noticed a young boy in the distance busily hauling crates of fish. Sweat slid down his cheeks, but his expression was focused and content. “You work really hard,” I said to him. He stopped and smiled gratefully. “This is everyone’s livelihood. I enjoy it.”

The noise of the market was not a burden; instead, it felt like a gentle background hum, accompanying my wandering thoughts. After walking around for a while, I decided to leave. The sun had begun to break through the clouds, casting a golden sheen over the ground.

A few days later, I still found myself thinking from time to time about that day at the market. Although I hadn’t bought anything, the quiet of that morning and the mingling sounds had left me feeling relaxed. Memories like that temporarily pulled me away from busy life, painting a brief scene of comfort.

As dusk slowly fell, the abandoned amusement park on the outskirts of the city was shrouded in a dim golden light. Everything around was quiet, and the only sound was the occasional engine of a car passing in the distance. I walked there, my feet on the moss-covered ground, feeling the breeze brush against my face. The park’s equipment had long since rusted over; the swings swayed gently, as if still echoing with the laughter of children from long ago. In the air beside me was a mixture of rust and wet earth, which made me feel a trace of unease. At that moment, a thought suddenly crossed my mind: this place seemed like it could become the source of inspiration for my new work—a story about loneliness and fear.

“What do you think of this place?” Friend B’s voice broke my reverie. He stood beside me, looking around.

“A little eerie, but interesting, right?” I replied, while trying hard to suppress the tension inside me and appear relaxed.

At that moment, I noticed my heartbeat quickening, I was starting to sweat, and my palms were slightly damp. I kept worrying in my mind whether this place was too oppressive, whether we might run into trouble. I began to regret coming here, imagining the worst-case scenario: if someone suddenly appeared, would they mean us harm? I kept dwelling on the decision I had made earlier, trying to find a bit of reason amid my unease.

“Should we leave?” I asked. “This place feels a little unsafe.”

But Friend B just smiled. “That’s exactly what makes it so appealing—we’re here to find inspiration, aren’t we? There’s a story here.” His optimism stood in sharp contrast to my anxiety, making me feel somewhat uncomfortable. I tried to calm myself down.

I tried shifting my attention to the surroundings. The afterglow of the sunset tinted everything a soft orange, and an incredible sense of stillness began to seep into my heart. Although my body was still a little tense and my heartbeat slightly fast, I began to feel a strange sense of merging, as if wandering back and forth between different worlds.

That night, when I got home, I lay in bed still thinking about the abandoned amusement park. Excitement and unease were intertwined, and I felt I should write these thoughts down as soon as possible, afraid they would vanish by morning. A few days later, I began turning my impressions of the park into a story, trying to describe the interweaving of loneliness and fear. Although during the writing process that senseless fear often surfaced in my heart, the surge of inspiration gave me a measure of comfort.

A few weeks later, my work was completed, and the abandoned amusement park’s distinctive atmosphere became its central element. Although the process was accompanied by much anxiety, this experience also brought me closer to the emotional depth I wanted to express.

The chair was a little hard. I shifted my sitting position, but it didn’t ease the discomfort in my back. The coffee on the table had gone cold, and I tapped the cup wall lightly with my spoon, trying to hide my nerves. The editor sat across from me, flipping through my proposal, frowning from time to time. I couldn’t help staring at his fingers; every time he turned a page quickly, it felt as if my chest had been pricked by a needle. “This structure of yours,” he finally said, “I think it’s too complicated. It’ll lose the reader.” His tone was flat, but my ears caught a faint edge of sharpness. In an instant, a hundred possibilities flashed through my mind: Did he dislike my whole idea? Was I simply not suited to this project? Did my expression come across as childish?

“Mm, I understand what you mean,” I heard myself say, my tone even a little hurried. After saying it, I felt my face grow hot, as if I had betrayed myself. I actually wanted to argue with him, because I had spent a full two weeks refining this proposal and felt it had already reached its best state. But at that moment, I actually chose to give in.

He kept talking, and my mind began to drift. I stared out the window at the people passing by on the street, feeling a dull pain in my stomach. I wasn’t unfamiliar with this pain; it appeared every time I felt rejected. Suddenly I noticed that his gaze seemed to sweep past my shoulder before shifting to the tabletop. I abruptly realized he might be giving me a hint—was the way I spoke too hasty? Or did he think I wasn’t calm enough? My palms began to sweat. My eyes accidentally settled on the faint glint of his watch, and I even started examining its material, trying to ease my confusion.

“You’re okay, right?” His voice rang out again, seeming to carry a note of concern, but I felt even more ashamed. I bit my lip, forcibly swallowing the sourness rising in my eyes, and managed a strained smile. “It’s fine. I’ll adjust the structure again and give you a more streamlined version.” The moment those words left my mouth, I regretted them. Why had I yielded again? Why couldn’t I stand by my own viewpoint?

After the meeting ended, I mechanically gathered my papers and pen. When I walked out of the café, the air outside was a little cold, mixed with a faint smell of gasoline. I walked home with my head down the whole way, replaying the editor’s comments over and over in my mind, even magnifying his tone, his expression, and his gestures endlessly. I began to wonder whether I was simply not cut out for creative work, or whether this was a sign that I would be abandoned by the industry. After I got home, I lay motionless on the sofa. My heartbeat was still a little fast, as if I had just run a short race. I started blaming myself for being so incompetent, for always catastrophizing small things, yet being unable to stop and think. These thoughts lasted all night and even affected my state when I tried to revise the proposal the next day.

The morning air was especially fresh, and the cheerful chirping of birds came to my ears. I decided to go for a jog on the greenway in the community garden, hoping it would help clear my head. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the leaves and scattered across the ground in dappled patches of light and shadow. I could smell the mingled fragrance of the various flowers and plants in the garden, and beneath my feet was damp soil, softly touched by my running shoes. As I ran, my thoughts involuntarily drifted back to the new work I had published a few days earlier, which had not received the response I had expected.

“Maybe I should change direction.” A small voice began to whisper in my heart. My heartbeat quickened as I thought again of the silence after the release of my work, and of the goals I had not achieved. I had hoped the work would be understood and appreciated, but everything seemed to have become an unattainable luxury. Anxiety seemed to start churning inside me; my stomach felt tied in knots, and sweat was flowing not only because of the exercise, but also because of the unease in my heart.

A few days earlier, a friend had comforted me over the phone: “You’ve already done a great job. Don’t be so hard on yourself.” Yet I still felt uneasy, wondering if they were only saying that to make me less discouraged. Their words echoed in my ears, while another part of me kept attacking itself: “Why listen to comforting words? They aren’t real criticism.” I struggled to focus, hearing only the sound of my footsteps and my breathing.

As I ran, I kept trying to regulate my breathing, hoping to ease the tension in my mind and the discomfort in my body. I began to speed up, as if that would let me escape the lingering negativity in my heart. However, after the run ended, that heaviness did not disappear. When I got home, I was exhausted, yet my heart remained unsettled. That night, lying in bed, the unsatisfactory comments on my work and the silent feedback kept replaying in my mind.

A few days passed, and I was still thinking about it. Although my friends continued to support me, I knew the panic and sense of inadequacy deep down were still there. I needed to face them, not keep deceiving myself. I decided to take another look at the work, think about what could be improved, and remind myself not to lose myself in criticism.

The room was a little stuffy, perhaps because the windows were shut tight, or perhaps because there were too many people. The light from the chandelier overhead was somewhat glaring, and the shadows it cast made the person sitting across from me look especially cold and indifferent. He said, “I think this idea might be a little lacking in originality.”

Those words hit my chest like a blunt instrument. I forced up a smile, clutching the notebook in my hands, and answered casually, “Hmm, that makes sense. Maybe it could indeed use some more improvement.” But my voice trembled on the last word, and I could hear it myself. I made myself look up at him, only to find his expression was very flat, with no hostile intent at all. But so what? A voice had already started looping in my head: See? You’ve been found lacking again. Did you really think your idea would be recognized?

My hand unconsciously tightened around the edge of the notebook, my fingertips turning a little white. I felt my heart rate begin to quicken, pounding straight against my chest like when I was running. That familiar suffocating feeling was back; my throat was terribly dry, my stomach was cramping a little, as if gripped by an invisible hand. I glanced down at my shoes and noticed a little dust seemed to have rubbed onto the toes, and suddenly I felt an urge to leave immediately.

“Actually, I think your idea still has a lot of potential,” someone beside him added. Her tone was gentle, and she spoke more slowly, as if trying to give me an easy way out. But my mind was still buzzing, fixating on the word “lacking in originality” from what he had just said. “Not original,” not original, not original... Those three words seemed to echo in my ears, refusing to go away.

I kept nodding and smiling. “Yes, yes, I understand. Still, thank you for your suggestion.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I started regretting them again. Thank you? I was actually thanking someone for putting me down. What was wrong with me?

After the meeting ended, I almost rushed out of the room. When I got to the street, the night air was a little cool, blowing on my face and clearing my head a bit. I stopped at the entrance of a convenience store, hesitated for a moment, then went in and bought a bottle of ice water. The moment the bottle touched my palm, I realized my hand was still trembling slightly. As I unscrewed the cap, I thought: Why am I always so easily affected? Why can a single offhand remark from someone else make me feel so much shame and helplessness? Am I really that inadequate? Has everyone seen that my so-called creativity is just a joke?

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, unable to sleep. The seemingly indifferent face from the daytime kept flashing in my mind, and what he said replayed over and over. I even began to suspect whether he actually held some hostility toward me, whether there were conversations behind my back that I didn’t know about. Those thoughts clung to me like water weeds; every time I managed to catch my breath, they pulled tighter. It wasn’t until two in the morning that I finally closed my eyes in exhaustion.

The next morning, while brushing my teeth in front of the mirror, I stared at my own face for a long time. The person in the mirror looked fairly normal, but only I knew how chaotic I felt inside. I told myself that maybe that person had really just spoken offhandedly, and that it didn’t mean anything. But what about next time? If someone said something similar again, would I fall into that same embarrassment and unease all over again?

The coffee in the cup had already gone cold, but I still didn’t dare reach for it. Looking around, the bright chandelier and soft background music seemed to make everyone look relaxed, except me. I sat at the edge of the table, my palms slightly sweaty, my fingertips occasionally rubbing against my pants, trying hard to look focused. Another member of the team was describing the key progress of the project so far. In a flat tone, he said, “If this part could be a little clearer, it would probably be better.” My heart sank instantly, as if I had been gently pushed to the edge of a cliff. I wasn’t sure whether his tone was implying that my report wasn’t clear enough, or whether he simply wasn’t satisfied with my contribution at all.

“Do you mean my part isn’t clear enough?” I couldn’t help interrupting him, my voice a little rushed, sounding defensive even to my own ears. I saw him frown slightly, then say, “Oh, no, I just mentioned it casually. You’ve done a good job, no problem.” But that brief frown froze in my mind like a picture, and I began overanalyzing every angle of that one second. Was he actually just brushing me off? Did he secretly have reservations about my ability but not want to say it directly?

The meeting went on, but I could no longer truly take part. My mind began chewing over my interactions with this team over the past few weeks, every detail flashing by like a movie replay. “Have I been talking too much? Do I seem too self-important? Do they think I’m a nuisance?” I tried to refocus, but every time a team member’s gaze swept over me, I felt as if I were being scrutinized. My stomach began to ache faintly, and I quietly pressed my right hand against my abdomen, hoping to ease that strange tightness.

By the end, I forced a smile. “Thanks, everyone. Today’s discussion was very inspiring.” They all nodded, waved at me, and left. I stayed seated, my fingers unconsciously drawing circles on the tabletop, repeatedly replaying that line: “If this part could be a little clearer.” I even began to doubt whether I was completely suited for this job, whether I should take the initiative to step aside and let someone else do it better.

That night, I lay in bed, staring at the ceiling in the dark. The stomach pain was still there, and my mind had already started rehearsing the scene of the next team meeting. I even practiced a few times how to respond in a way that sounded confident but not offensive. I knew I was being too sensitive, but these thoughts were like the tide, impossible to control. The next day, I tentatively sent a message to that team member: “About the part you mentioned yesterday, I’ve started making careful adjustments. If you have any more suggestions, please feel free to let me know.” He replied quickly: “Really, don’t worry too much. You’ve already done very well.” I felt relieved, but that faint unease still lingered like a pebble under my foot, occasionally making me uncomfortable, yet leaving me unable to find a complete way to get rid of it.

The café was buzzing with conversation, and the coffee on the table gave off a rich aroma, yet it brought me no comfort. I was seated across from my partner, who was reviewing the creative proposal I had submitted. My heartbeat began to quicken, and a thin layer of sweat broke out in my palms, forcing me to pull my hands back under the table. I struggled to stay calm, but his furrowed brow and occasional sighs pierced my nerves like needles. “Can this really work?” he finally asked, his tone laced with doubt. My stomach tightened instantly, as if a flame were burning inside it. I kept turning over every word he said in my mind, worrying that he might be preparing to abandon me. 

I tried to respond, “I think this idea has potential, as long as we can—” However, he cut me off, his gaze growing sharper. “Are you sure this isn’t just another failed attempt?” My face flushed at once, and my ears rang. It felt as if a hammer had struck my heart, and all my negative memories came flooding back. I thought of every moment in the past when I had been criticized and rejected, and the fear of being cast aside surged up again. I began to doubt myself, wondering whether, as he said, I really had been failing all along. In my mind, I replayed over and over the scene of being abandoned by my partner, seeing myself sitting alone in the office, ignored by everyone. 

“You can’t keep doing this; you need to be more realistic.” His voice broke my reverie. I managed a strained smile, trying to hide the emotions on the verge of collapse inside me. My fingers kept rubbing the rim of the cup, as if that could give me a sense of security. By the time he left, I had hardly enough strength to stand, as though my body were pinned down by a crushing weight. I sat in the café for a long time, trying to sort out my tangled thoughts. On the way home, I kept replaying every word he had said and every expression he had made, trying to figure out where I had gone wrong. 

The next day, I still couldn’t shake that unease. I began to wonder whether I was suited for this job and whether I could keep going. My partner’s criticism and doubt lingered in my mind, like a heavy stone pressing on my chest. These past few days, I had felt the threat of abandonment at all times, afraid of being cast aside once again in some neglected corner where no one cared. I began attacking myself, blaming myself for not being good enough, not being smart enough, feeling that everything was my fault.

Sunlight poured through the large window behind the counter, filling the entire shop. I found myself in a space full of wooden furniture and worn fabrics. The air carried a faint pine scent, and every so often I could hear cars passing by across the street. As I walked into the store, I wandered casually through the cramped rows of furniture, touching the mottled surfaces and feeling the wood’s warmth and the roughness of the fabric. In my ears lingered the store’s gentle music, adding a touch of calm to the afternoon.

“Looking for anything special?” the owner said, lifting his head from behind the counter and asking me kindly. I froze slightly, yet a strange sense of unease welled up inside me. His smile made me feel unsettled, as if he were hinting that I should know something. “Uh, nothing in particular. I’m just looking around,” I replied, my tone carrying an instinctive caution.

I kept moving around casually, but I couldn’t help wondering about the deeper meaning of his words. Was he implying that I shouldn’t be wandering around here? Or did he think I was wasting his time? That uneasiness gradually spread, my heartbeat began to quicken, and a thin sheen of sweat formed on my palms. I tried hard to act naturally, but an inner voice kept urging me to look for something abnormal, even making me suspect that I was being watched. At that moment, I felt a slight twist in my stomach, and my emotions kept rising.

“We’ve got some new arrivals over here; you can take a look,” he said, pointing to a corner where several pieces of rather old-fashioned furniture were displayed. I walked toward the direction he indicated, hoping to shift my attention. A near-compulsive curiosity welled up inside me, trying to understand his intent. As my mind repeatedly ran through different possibilities, I began to wonder whether those pieces of furniture might have some hidden flaws. My gaze settled on an antique writing desk, as I tried to find clues in its weathered surface.

This interaction left me feeling somewhat self-conscious, and I even wondered whether his opinion of me was as negative as I feared. Afterward, I spent several days repeatedly replaying that moment, inexplicably feeling ashamed and embarrassed. Even a week after it was over, I still couldn’t stop ruminating on those feelings and the conversation, as if a tiny incident had become an inescapable shadow in my mind. I began to realize that this overthinking and self-criticism were nothing more than a reflection of my own unease.

I worked hard to respond to this emotion in a more positive way, and little by little, I began to understand my own overinterpretation, trying to reduce this psychological burden in the future.

I stood in the repair shop, watching various old bicycle parts neatly arranged on the shelves beside me. Sunlight streamed through the window, and the air was filled with the smell of metal. The clock on the wall ticked steadily, and I could hear the mechanic busily working in the workshop out back. The walls of the shop were covered with brightly colored posters depicting thrilling moments from different bicycle races. Beside me, an old sofa was piled with several worn magazines, the dust on their covers glittering in the sunlight. I looked down at the bicycle I had brought in, feeling slightly uneasy.

“Do you need any help today?” the mechanic asked, peeking out from the workshop with a smile.

“This chain seems to have a problem—it keeps making strange noises,” I replied, while my mind began imagining all kinds of complicated possible causes.

The mechanic nodded and came over to inspect the chain carefully. My heartbeat began to quicken. I could almost feel cold sweat beading on my forehead; every muscle in my body was tense, and my stomach twisted with a faint ache.

“It’s just a little loose. I’ll adjust it, and it’ll be fine,” the mechanic said easily, working skillfully on the chain.

Just a little loose? I questioned inwardly. How could it be that simple? What if it isn’t adjusted properly? Could the whole bike break down completely? In an instant, I pictured the worst-case scenario—the chain snapping entirely while I was riding, me falling to the ground, suffering serious injuries, maybe even needing to be hospitalized. My face went pale.

The mechanic turned back and looked at me, apparently noticing my tension. “Don’t worry, it’s fine. I deal with this kind of thing many times every day,” he reassured me, trying to help me relax.

“Oh, okay,” I forced out a smile, but I still felt uneasy, haunted by a lingering sense of defectiveness and the panic of being abandoned. I began attacking myself internally, questioning why I was always so anxious.

After adjusting it, he let the bicycle roll along the ground to test it again. “All right, give it a try,” he said softly, handing the repaired bike back to me.

A few days later, I still remembered that brief repair experience and kept replaying every movement the mechanic had made, always worried that I had missed something. I kept checking whether the bike was functioning normally, always afraid that the chain would have trouble again. I realized that my excessive worry had already affected my attention to other things, and that even in my dreams similar scenes kept appearing. I felt unable to escape the shadow of abandonment and defectiveness.

The lights were a little harsh, and the projector fan hummed incessantly. I stood on the other side of a long conference table, behind me a densely packed PowerPoint presentation. Eight or nine people sat below, their faces blurred and somewhat indifferent under the fluorescent lights. My palms were already soaked, but fortunately I could hold my notebook tightly with both hands and hide the fact that I was sweating.

“Overall, this direction is still pretty interesting, but...” A middle-aged man pushed up his glasses, drawing out the words. “But I feel like it seems to lack... well, a core highlight. Do you know what I mean?” His voice was calm and measured, but I felt the whole room go quiet, as if waiting for the verdict of that sentence.

My heart suddenly tightened, and my chest began to feel constricted. I forced out a smile. “So what you mean is, my idea isn’t very appealing, right?” I tried my best to make my tone sound natural, but my ears had already started buzzing.

He seemed a little surprised and frowned slightly. “No... I just mean maybe it could be further refined, for example, by making a core storyline stand out more.”

“Oh...” I nodded, but my mind was already in chaos. He thought I hadn’t done well enough, didn’t he? What did “refined” mean? Was it a vague, polite way of brushing me off?

A young girl sitting next to him took over. “Actually, I quite like your theme, but... um, I also feel that maybe the emotional buildup could be strengthened a bit?”

What did that mean? Could liking it and saying the emotional buildup was insufficient coexist? My face started to burn, and it felt as though my body had been pressed into a shell. My stomach ached faintly. I had a strong urge to apologize, even to admit outright that my idea was worthless. But I stood there, my legs as if nailed to the floor.

“Sorry, I may have... really not done my best.” My voice was a little hoarse, my throat dry and tight. The moment the words left my mouth, my eyes grew slightly wet, but I quickly lowered my head. “Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll make more adjustments.”

After the meeting, I fled to the restroom and sat on the toilet lid, burying my face in my hands. The conversation from just now kept replaying in my head like a movie. Their expressions, voices, and pauses were all magnified. I even felt that they must have thought I was a joke, that my work was terrible, but they just didn’t want to say it outright. The more I thought about it, the harder it became to breathe, and the worse the cramping in my stomach got.

That night, I lay in bed staring blankly at the ceiling. Every detail floated through my mind, like dull needles pricking my skin. Even knowing that what they said might have been well-intentioned advice, I still couldn’t stop myself from imagining the worst. Maybe they were only “pretending” not to be angry? If I performed even worse, would they stop even bothering to be polite on the surface?

The next morning, I tried to open that PPT again, but just one glance made my fingers go cold and my whole body tense up. I closed the computer again, took a deep breath, but there was still a knot in my stomach.

“Can’t you stop being so dramatic...” I muttered under my breath, as if scolding myself, but that feeling of shame still wouldn’t let go of me.

Walking into that battered old movie theater in the city center, the bitter wind outside bit through to the bone, yet I felt a familiar sense of comfort. The lobby carried the wooden scent of old spring-loaded seats, along with a faint trace of lingering perfume. The outdated posters on the walls and the dim lighting created the illusion of being transported back in time.

I found my seat, and the movie was about to begin. Sitting there, I could occasionally hear faint creaking from the joints of the chair. The audience in the front row was whispering; it sounded like they were commenting on the film, and I strained to listen closely. “What do you think this movie will be like?” said a deep voice. “I’ve heard it’s pretty good. I hope it won’t disappoint,” another voice replied.

The film started playing, and familiar images lit up the screen, but my mind drifted elsewhere. I began to recall those times I had spent in old movie theaters, especially the moments in social situations when I felt awkward and uneasy. A strange tension rose within me; my heart began to race and my palms grew sweaty.

“You should relax right now and focus on the movie itself,” I told myself. Yet my mind was crowded with scenes from the past: those moments when I had misunderstood others in conversation, countless times I had gotten lost in a smile or a glance. I blamed myself for always being too sensitive, for always overanalyzing in those moments.

In one part of the film, a character is misunderstood by friends and forced to leave alone, and that loneliness seemed to resonate with me. I could feel a slight knot in my stomach, and a wave of unease rose in my heart. That fear of being isolated and misunderstood churned within me. “They don’t really care about you,” a voice inside me declared, trying to protect me by warding off possible hurt through preemptive self-denial.

After the movie ended, I walked out of the theater into a gloomy sky and the same biting wind rushing straight at me. My mood was as heavy as the weather. I wandered aimlessly down the street, trying to let the cold wind scatter my restless thoughts. Yet that fear of abandonment still spread inside me like an inescapable shadow.

That night, I lay in bed for a long time, unable to fall asleep. Scenes from the movie and fragments of my own memories kept replaying in my mind. I couldn’t help wondering whether I really cared too much about what others thought and had neglected the beauty of being alone.

A few days later, I tried to sort through my emotions and decided to make these reflections part of my growth. After all, the past cannot be changed; all I can do is learn to accept my sensitivity and strive to find balance within it.

I stared at the design mockup on my computer screen, trying to adjust a few color combinations. The client was sitting beside me, his brow slightly furrowed. I had already revised it three times, but he still wasn’t satisfied. “What do you think of this version?” I asked tentatively, trying to sound confident. He was silent for a few seconds, then said softly, “Hmm… it still doesn’t feel quite right.” Those words felt like a needle piercing my chest. My stomach began to ache faintly, and my palms started sweating.

I couldn’t help wondering: was there something wrong with my design thinking? Did he regret working with me? Did he think I wasn’t professional enough? My heartbeat gradually quickened, and a buzzing began in my ears. I forced a smile and said, “Then where do you think it needs improvement?”

He pointed to a pattern on the screen. “This part feels a little abrupt. Maybe softer colors would be better.” His tone wasn’t particularly harsh, but I still heard criticism in it. In my mind, I had already started replaying scenes of him being completely disappointed in me: he would email me to say he wanted to end the collaboration; he would discuss my shortcomings with other designers; he might even mention my failure to others in the industry. All of these images left me feeling somewhat breathless.

“I understand, maybe my previous direction wasn’t clear enough.” I preemptively put the label of “wrong” on myself, even though deep down I wasn’t sure where the problem really lay. “I’ll make the adjustments as soon as possible.” As I said this, my throat felt tight and my voice came out dry.

After the meeting ended, I sat in my chair in a daze, the screen in front of me growing more and more glaring. I stared at the design draft, silently repeating what he had said, trying to infer his real intention. Was he dissatisfied with me? Was he indirectly expressing disappointment? Going over it again and again made my head throb, and my shoulders began to tense up unnaturally. I didn’t dare ask him directly whether he was satisfied, afraid of hearing an even more direct rejection.

When I got home that evening, I still couldn’t escape those thoughts. During dinner, my husband looked at me and asked, “What’s wrong? You seem a bit tired today.” I opened my mouth but couldn’t bring myself to tell the truth, so I could only say, “Nothing, just a bit bothered by work.” I felt an indescribable shame, as if I were incapable of facing the client’s concerns or calmly accepting the fact that I was being judged. I was afraid of letting him see my vulnerability, as if I were teetering on the edge of failure.

Over the next few days, I kept trying to revise the design, constantly thinking about whether “he would be satisfied,” yet I could never reach a conclusion. Every time I opened my computer to modify the proposal, I could feel my palms going numb, and I would have to stop now and then to rub my temples, trying to ease the tight pressure. Although the client ultimately accepted my revisions, the self-criticism and sensitivity throughout the process left me utterly exhausted.

Sunlight streamed through the café’s floor-to-ceiling windows onto the wooden floor, and the air carried a faint aroma of baking. I sat by the window, while the cappuccino on the table still gave off steam. Across from me, the editor was flipping through the draft I had submitted, her brow slightly furrowed. I stared at her movements, feeling as heavy as if lead had been poured into my chest, with a dull, intermittent pain tightening in my stomach.

She looked up and said, “In this section, are you trying to express some kind of metaphor? I feel it’s a bit obscure—readers may not easily catch your intention.”

My lips instantly went dry and tight, my heartbeat quickened, and my hands began unconsciously rubbing the cuffs of my sleeves. “Mm, yes, I wanted to make it a little more vague, but... I can make it more direct.” My voice sounded a bit rough; I could hear it myself.

Her tone was flat, devoid of emotion. “Also, this ending feels a little drawn out. It might be better to trim it a bit.” As she spoke, she marked up the manuscript.

My mind exploded at once. Did she hate my writing? Did she think I simply wasn’t suited to be a writer? Her brow was knitted so tightly—was I really that terrible? I tried to keep my expression calm, but my palms were already slick with sweat. I lowered my head and quickly took a sip of coffee, trying to cover up my embarrassment.

“Okay, I’ll revise these parts when I get back.” I replied mechanically, trying my best to avoid any words that might make my tone sound defensive. She nodded and made a few more marks elsewhere.

Throughout the entire process, the tightness in my stomach grew more and more obvious, like a cord being twisted tighter and tighter. I could feel the muscles in my face remaining stiff, not even daring to move the corners of my mouth much. Scenes from the past flashed through my mind: teachers criticizing my essays in middle school, professors’ cold evaluations in college—every detail only made me more convinced that this time too, I had failed.

After the meeting ended, the editor’s phone rang. She simply said, “Send it to me after you’ve revised it—don’t stress too much,” and then left. I sat there watching her back disappear, my mind filled with everything she had just said. I felt like a joke. Why did I always overread things whenever I was being evaluated? Why couldn’t I face even the slightest criticism calmly? It all felt like a cycle I could never escape.

That night, when I was revising the manuscript at home, I still couldn’t shake the feeling of being rejected. With every sentence I changed, I kept replaying her expression and tone, trying to find more hidden “clues.” This state made it impossible to focus, and I began blaming myself: “You really are a failed creator, unable even to handle ordinary feedback from someone else.” In the end, I didn’t finish until two in the morning, and my hands were trembling when I sent the email.

A few days later, the editor replied: “It’s been revised very well—much clearer than before. Keep it up.” She even included a smiling emoji. But I still didn’t feel fully relieved. That sour feeling of being dismissed seemed etched into my bones, impossible to shake off.

The lighting in the conference room felt a bit harsh, and the clock on the wall ticked steadily. A few colleagues and I sat around the conference table, lightly tapping our pens against the tabletop. The air was filled with a faint coffee aroma. Someone was flipping through project materials, and I unconsciously held my breath; my heart began to race, as if I were waiting for some unease to arrive. The project lead began explaining our new project. His tone was steady, and when he glanced at me, he smiled slightly. “What do you think of this proposal?”

I immediately felt a surge of tension, my palms starting to sweat, as if everyone’s gaze were fixed on me. I tried hard to keep my voice calm and replied, “I think some of the details may need further adjustment so that it aligns better with our goals.” I glanced at the colleague opposite me; her brow was slightly furrowed, and that made my stomach knot up. I suddenly began to doubt whether my suggestion was right. I started overthinking everything I had said, muttering to myself: “Did I say something wrong? Do they think what I said makes no sense?”

After the meeting ended, I walked out of the conference room, clutching the materials tightly in my hands, while my mind kept replaying the conversation again and again. I paced back and forth in the company hallway, trying to slow my heartbeat. “Are you okay?” A colleague gently patted my shoulder, and I jumped, quickly forcing out a smile. “Oh, I’m fine, just a little worried about the project’s progress,” I said, though I was thinking to myself: Did she notice my unease? Does she think I performed terribly? All afternoon, my stomach had been aching faintly, as if protesting my anxiety.

That night, lying in bed, I could still picture the conference room and hear my colleagues’ discussion. I kept going over every detail of the day and even began to question my own abilities. I knew I was always like this—overanalyzing other people’s reactions and taking everything too seriously, as if every slight gesture and tone concealed some enormous threat. The next day, I decided to get to the office an hour early and write down the improvements I had thought of. I wanted to be better prepared for the discussion ahead.

Although I still felt uneasy, I knew in my heart that this kind of anxiety and self-doubt was all too familiar to me. Sometimes I wondered whether I would ever be able to escape this cycle of sensitivity and self-criticism.

At sunset, I stood on the hilltop lookout at the edge of the city, gazing down over the entire metropolis. The buildings in the distance were tinted orange-red, and the clouds drifted slowly across the sky. I could feel a gentle breeze brushing my cheeks, and the rustle of leaves reached my ears. It was a moment that made me feel calm, yet inside I could not be at peace.

A gardener was carefully tending the flowerbed beside the lookout. He glanced up at me and gave a slight nod. “The weather’s really nice today, isn’t it?” he asked casually.

“Yeah, it really is,” I said with a grin, though my mind was elsewhere. I kept looking at the city, filled with doubts: Was my creative work really headed in the right direction?

I dimly remembered the comments I had seen a few days earlier, sharp and stinging. I always magnified those negative remarks, chewing over them again and again. My heart raced, my palms grew slightly sweaty, and a dull ache began in my stomach once more. Was I not good enough? Should I change? These questions pressed down on me like an invisible weight, making it hard to breathe.

“You look like you’ve got something on your mind,” the gardener said again. “Why not sit down and talk?”

I forced a smile. “Nothing, just thinking.” I turned to face him, trying to seem relaxed and natural, but inside I was being crushed by a sense of anxiety.

“Sometimes, calming down is what helps you find the answer,” he said, continuing to trim the plants as if everything were simple.

I turned the words over in my mind, then looked back at the city again. My mood was a little complicated at that moment—ashamed, yet wanting to run away. I realized that I always tended to attack myself first, simply because I was afraid of being rejected by others. Maybe I needed to trust myself more and give myself more support, instead of blaming myself over and over.

The next morning, when I woke up, I was still thinking about the gardener’s words. I decided to take a fresh look at my creative direction and try to turn that anxiety into motivation. I began listing some concrete small goals and making a plan, hoping to reduce pointless worry and self-criticism. These changes were not easy, but at least I was willing to try.

The street was already empty of pedestrians. A cold wind skimmed along the ground, stirring dead leaves into a whirl in the night. I stood before an old wooden door, the paint on its frame flaking away to reveal the dark brown grain beneath. The “Caution: Fire” sign on the door was barely hanging on, so rusted that only a few blurry letters remained. I pushed the door open, and it let out a sharp creak, as if protesting my arrival. The air was thick with the mixed smells of wood and paint, along with a faint, hard-to-identify stale odor, as though no one had set foot here for a very long time. The workshop floor was covered in sawdust and broken parts, and every step made a soft crunching sound. Several yellowed design drawings hung on the wall, their edges fluttering now and then in the breeze, the lines of the sketches seeming to silently tell of unfinished ideas.

“Is there really no one who can see these through to the end?” I murmured to myself, my voice echoing through the empty workshop. My gaze fell on a workbench in the corner, its surface crowded with tools: hammers, carving knives, sandpaper, and a few cans of paint that had already dried out. Beside the bench were several unfinished wooden toys, some with rough edges not yet smoothed down, their shapes seeming to suggest animals—a fox with a broken tail, a little rabbit with no ears, and a wooden truck missing half a wheel. I reached out and picked up the truck; the texture of the wood came through my fingertips, cold, hard, and heavy. A few carved marks on the body showed the maker’s attempts and effort, but in the end it had still been abandoned. “Maybe something more important forced them to leave,” a ridiculous thought suddenly popped into my head.

In the center of the workshop was also an old lathe, which looked as if it could no longer function properly. Its wheel was covered in dust and cobwebs, and some wood blocks beside the base had been carelessly discarded, scattered pieces that somehow formed a kind of disordered beauty. I stepped closer to the lathe and gently touched the wheel, as though imagining what it had looked like when it spun at high speed. A strange sadness suddenly rose in my chest; my heartbeat began to quicken, and my throat felt dry, as if something were lodged there. I closed my eyes, and in my mind appeared the image of myself at home beside my worktable, struggling to come up with ideas only to give up again and again. That sense of helplessness mingled with the workshop’s silence, making me feel no different from those unfinished wooden toys. My stomach also began to ache faintly, and I took a deep breath, trying to ease this sudden physical reaction.

“Hello, do you need help?” Suddenly, a voice came from the doorway. I opened my eyes sharply and saw a man in a dark coat standing there, a flashlight in his hand. He didn’t seem hostile, but I tensed up at once, my defenses kicking in immediately: “I just came in to have a look, it’s fine, thanks!” I regretted it as soon as I said it, my voice clearly tinged with panic. He nodded without saying anything, casually closed the door, and left. My heart pounded harder, my palms began to sweat, and countless scenes of being misunderstood flashed through my mind—would he think I had bad intentions? Or think I was an intruder? Those thoughts would not leave me alone, circling like a swarm of flies.

A few minutes later, I forced myself to calm down and tried to continue exploring the things in the workshop. In the end, I found a wooden board in a dark corner, with a nearly illegible sentence carved into it: “Unfinished does not mean failure.” I froze for a moment, my eyes suddenly growing a little hot. Holding the board to my chest, I let out a quiet sigh, as if some force had made me believe again that even in this silence, I could still find an answer of my own.

The next day, I began revising the piece in my hands with a strange new drive. At first, I was still full of anxiety, but the carving on that wooden board seemed like a spell, reminding me to embrace what was unfinished rather than run from it.

The lights in the wedding hall made me feel a little dizzy. People around me were smiling and talking, and the air was filled with the scent of champagne and flowers. I sat at the table, trying not to pay attention to my racing heartbeat and sweaty palms. A friend came over and said casually, “You look a little nervous today.” My heart sank. My intuition told me that this was not a simple expression of concern. “Why did he say that? Does he have a problem with me?” My mind began racing uncontrollably, my heart beating faster and faster, as if with each thud my chest hurt a little more. A few seconds later, I smiled and replied, “Oh, no, I’m just a little tired.” But the panic inside had already crept onto my face.

I noticed him standing with other friends, whispering about something, glancing over at me from time to time. My mind immediately started imagining all kinds of possibilities: “Are they talking about me? Do they think I don’t fit in?” My stomach twisted painfully, and my fingers clutched the tablecloth tightly. This feeling was all too familiar; in countless situations, I had felt this fear of being excluded and scrutinized.

Later, during the dance after the wedding ceremony, I tried to join their conversation, but my voice seemed to be drowned out by the music. They kept talking, and my presence felt thinner and thinner. “Is he deliberately ignoring me? Does he think I’m annoying?” I was nearly overwhelmed by these thoughts. “Maybe, in their eyes, I don’t matter at all.” A sense of helplessness washed over me, and I felt completely abandoned.

Standing there, feeling like an outsider, sweat had already soaked through my clothes. Unable to endure this hellish emotion any longer, I turned and left. On the way home, the city lights outside the car window blurred into a haze. In my mind, his words and their gazes kept echoing over and over. When I got home, I threw myself onto the sofa, and tears began to fall despite me. I blamed myself for always being so sensitive, for being unable to ignore these little details.

Over the next few days, I grew cold toward any greeting from my friends. I no longer wanted to reach out to them first, clumsily trying to prove that I didn’t care. “If I can stop caring, none of this will hurt me.” But the loneliness inside followed me like a shadow, with nowhere to escape.

I sat at the far end of the conference table in the office, facing a ceramic cup half full of coffee, releasing a faint roasted aroma. Outside the window, the breeze gently swayed the treetops, and my gaze couldn’t help drifting with the movement of the shadows, yet my heart was filled with an inescapable sense of tension. We were holding an important team meeting, and my task was to present the initial concept for a new project. As I began explaining, I heard the soft rustling of papers and quiet conversations between colleagues. My words echoed in the room, yet I noticed that some of my colleagues’ attention had already wandered elsewhere; they seemed to be discussing their own matters. My heart tightened in an instant, as if a cold current were rising from deep within me.

I strained to keep my focus and continued explaining the details, hoping for their approval and support. But when I saw one attendee impatiently looking out the window, a strong wave of self-doubt hit me. “Do they think my idea is childish?” This inner monologue kept repeating itself, like a form of self-attack. I tried to shake off the feeling, adjusting my tone so I would sound more confident, but my heartbeat only grew faster, each beat seeming louder than the last, even making my ears ring a little.

After the meeting ended, I sat at my desk and still couldn’t calm down. My palms were slightly sweaty, and my stomach felt unsettled. I couldn’t help replaying every detail from earlier, disgusted with my own sensitivity and overthinking. I could almost feel the fabric on the back of my chair rubbing against my back, but that comforting touch did nothing to ease the unease in my mind. Hours passed, and I still couldn’t resist checking my email, wanting to confirm whether the team had any feedback to prove whether my performance had been acceptable.

By evening, I received an email from my supervisor. He said my project had some interesting highlights but needed more detail. I felt a wave of relief, yet at the same time the pressure doubled. Although there was no explicit rejection, it still felt like a gentle refusal, as if it were conveying a message that improvement was needed. Days later, I could still feel the lingering aftermath of that unease, pushing me to reflect on and improve my proposal.

Under the gray, overcast sky, a fine rain fell without end. Raindrops struck my umbrella with a faint crackling sound. I walked into an abandoned steel-rebar processing factory in the northern part of the city. Around me were rust-covered machines and shattered glass windows, and the floor was covered with puddles. I was looking for footage to shoot, inspiration for a project. Just as I was lost in my own world, a surprised voice came from behind me: “What are you doing here?”

I turned around and saw my former colleague, looking awkward and surprised. “Oh, I’m here to film some footage,” I replied, trying to hide the turbulence inside me. My heart suddenly raced, and I could feel my face grow slightly hot. I remembered how he had objected to my proposal in a meeting; after that meeting, I received a lot of criticism.

“You’re still doing those creative projects?” His tone stung a little, reminding me of the doubts he had about me back then. I forced myself to keep smiling. “Yeah. What about you—how have you been?”

“Not bad, just incredibly busy.” He glanced around, seeming to want to change the subject. Strangely, I actually felt the tense hostility gradually ease, but the unease in my heart still would not go away.

My inner monologue kept churning. Was he mocking me, or was he concerned about me? I wasn’t sure. That sense of being abandoned surfaced again, as if even this space were conspiring to turn us against each other. I started sweating, my palms slick with moisture.

To ease the awkward atmosphere, I took the initiative and asked about how he had been. As the conversation deepened, our tone gradually softened. Little by little, I realized he meant no hostility; perhaps our misunderstanding was merely a projection of the past.

We talked for a long time in that silent ruin until the rain let up a little, and then he took his leave. I watched his receding figure, my heart full of mixed emotions. As I walked out of the factory, the air was thick with the smell of rust and wet earth, and my mood was complicated.

That night, I tossed and turned, unable to sleep. The scenes of today’s conversation kept replaying in my mind. I thought about our past collaboration, our past misunderstandings, and I began to doubt myself. I felt ashamed of my sensitivity, yet powerless to change it.

A few days later, I slowly came to understand that sometimes other people are not deliberately trying to hurt me; I am simply reading too much into their behavior. Perhaps I need to trust myself more, and trust others as well.

The lights in the conference room were a bit glaring, and my seat seemed particularly uncomfortable. The table was covered with all kinds of materials and notebooks, and the electronic whiteboard was filled with various proposals.
