The atmosphere in the room was a little tense, and everyone was waiting for my creative presentation. I began my introduction, my voice slightly shaky, but I tried to keep it steady. Just then, a colleague sitting across from me interrupted and asked, “Have you considered that this direction may not meet the client’s requirements?” His tone sounded as if he were only asking a question, but I immediately felt a wave of unease. I could feel my heartbeat quicken, my palms beginning to sweat, as if I had been suddenly pushed to the edge of a cliff by this challenge.

“Yes, I’ve considered that issue,” I replied, trying to keep my tone calm, but I couldn’t help wondering whether he was implying that I had overlooked something important. I continued explaining my idea, but in my mind, that sensitive nerve had already been tightened. I couldn’t stop replaying his expression—was there any hint of contempt or disdain? Every detail, every change in tone, was magnified in my head.

After the meeting, I walked out of the conference room with my mind full of doubts. Sitting at my desk, his words still echoed in my ears. I began to ruminate over the meeting, thinking over and over again: had I been too hasty? Had I missed something important? A wave of discomfort rose in my stomach, as if a stone were pressing on my chest. I knew I shouldn’t keep overthinking like this, but I couldn’t help it. It felt as though the meeting was a test of my ability, and I might have failed.

That night, I lay awake in bed, still fixated on the phrase “doesn’t meet the client’s requirements.” This doubt and anxiety were like vines wrapping around me, leaving me unable to escape. The next day, I decided to have a deeper conversation with that colleague. “I feel we should communicate more about yesterday’s meeting to make sure we’re aligned in our understanding of the project,” I told him. He looked somewhat surprised, but quickly nodded in agreement. I realized that he wasn’t as critical as I had imagined, and that made me feel a little more at ease.

This conversation made me realize that sometimes I may overinterpret other people’s reactions, even losing myself in my own assumptions. Over the next few days, I made an effort to listen more openly to my colleagues’ feedback, treating it as constructive advice rather than a personal challenge. This shift in mindset made me much more composed in the work that followed.

The café was buzzing with voices, and the air was thick with the rich aroma of coffee. I sat at a round table with several colleagues, trying to join in their conversation. Laughter and chatter rose and fell around me, and I worked hard to sound confident and at ease. When one coworker mentioned his new project, I smiled and chimed in. However, he didn’t seem very interested in my response and turned to chat with someone next to him instead. My heart sank at once, as if doused with ice water, and my whole body instantly tensed up. Why was his expression so cold? Had I said something wrong? I began replaying the conversation in my head, trying to find any mistake I might have made.

“What are you thinking about?” another coworker asked. “You seem a little out of it.”

“Oh, nothing. I was just thinking about my next project,” I said with a forced smile, hoping to hide the turmoil inside. But his attention made me even more uneasy; my heart raced, and my palms began to sweat. I kept telling myself to stay calm, but the anxiety clung to my heart like a vine, growing tighter and tighter.

I noticed a dull ache beginning in my stomach, a physical reaction that always seemed to appear when I felt uneasy. The conversation at the table went on, and their laughter and glances made me feel like an outsider. I desperately wanted to take part, but overanalyzing the subtle interactions between my colleagues only made me feel even more insignificant.

When I got home that evening, I sat alone at my desk, thinking about the gathering that day. My mood was still heavy, as if a stone were pressing on my chest. To ease the burden inside me, I began writing in my diary, recording my thoughts and feelings, though this kind of emotional release could not completely dispel my anxiety.

Over the next few days, I felt resistant to any social invitation. I knew I needed rest, so I spent more time alone at home, reading or listening to music to soothe my tense emotions. Even so, those replayed scenes from the gathering still flashed through my mind from time to time, like an alarm constantly reminding me that I wasn’t good enough.

The lighting in the conference room was a bit harsh. I sat at one side of the long table, surrounded by the faint scent of cheap air freshener, which made it hard to breathe. On the whiteboard were our plans; everything should have been so orderly, yet in my mind it was all a huge puzzle. I stood up to begin the presentation, but I kept running through the worst-case scenarios in my head: What if I got stuck halfway through? What if the client rejected us coldly?

When I got to the key part, I caught the client frowning. In that instant, time seemed to freeze. That tiny reaction spread through my whole body like electricity. My heart raced, my palms started sweating, and it felt as if every cell in my body was screaming to get out of that room. I forced myself to keep going, but my voice trembled involuntarily.

“This part of the budget seems... a little unrealistic?” The client’s question cut through my defenses like a sharp blade. I hurriedly replied with a smile, “Oh, of course, we can adjust it to make sure...,” but even then, a voice inside me kept warning: See? You messed it up again.

After the meeting, I sat at my desk, no longer paying any attention to the information on my computer screen. I started replaying every detail of the presentation, every possible mistake. Did I speak too fast somewhere? Did I choose the wrong example? Why did he frown? These questions circled in my mind over and over, like a vicious cycle.

Filled with an unbearable mix of regret and shame, I once again realized how much I overinterpreted other people’s reactions, yet I couldn’t stop myself from obsessing over those subtle changes. I thought back to several similar situations before, and my self-criticism felt like a ghost lurking in the shadows.

That night, I lay in bed tossing and turning, my stomach burning with anxiety, as if it were a punishment for my own incompetence. Even when the client’s email the next day said they were very interested and wanted to continue discussing the collaboration, the news did not immediately make me feel relieved. Instead, it stirred up even more doubt in my mind: Were they really satisfied, or were they just being politely dismissive?

It wasn’t until a week after checking in that I finally half-believed the collaboration might truly have a chance, and that I hadn’t simply overread every expression and tone from the client.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves and scattered across the ground, forming dappled shadows. Dressed in light clothes, I followed the familiar path to the vegetable garden near home. It was a quiet place, where the only sounds were the rustling of leaves in the gentle breeze, and the occasional chirp of birds. I crouched down to examine the tomato plants carefully; a few strands of sunlight were dotted across the leaves, and the green fruit still carried a bit of dew. I lightly touched the leaves, feeling their softness and warmth beneath my fingers.

Suddenly, the ringtone of my phone broke the stillness. I picked it up and saw a message from a friend jokingly asking when I’d be able to share some homegrown vegetables. I smiled and replied, “Wait until the next harvest!” After putting the phone down, I went back to thinking about this year’s planting plan, hoping for a better harvest.

“Looks like they’re growing well,” a neighbor said as he walked over from the other side of the vegetable garden and waved at me. “Yeah, I hope I can get some good results this year,” I replied. “If you have any extra, remember to save some for me!” the neighbor said with a smile.

Here, my heartbeat slowed and I felt all the muscles in my body relax. Facing the plants before me, my mood also grew calm. There was no work pressure, no complicated social cues; in this small world, I felt a rare sense of ease.

After returning home, I began looking up some gardening tips on my phone, hoping to improve in that area. In the evening, I sat on the sofa drinking tea and thinking back on the day’s experience. A sense of contentment rose in my heart. Though it was only a brief time in the vegetable garden, it brightened my mood.

A few days later, I could still easily recall the peace of that afternoon; that sense of steadiness found in nature seemed to have taken root in my heart, giving me something to think about even on busy days. No matter how hectic work became or how much pressure life brought, as long as I could make time to return to that quiet vegetable garden, it seemed everything would have room to soften.

The floorboards beneath my feet creaked, the wooden planks slightly warped, and the air was thick with a damp, moldy, dusty smell. This abandoned theater had long since lost its former glory; cracks in the ceiling let in a few ghastly shafts of light, casting them onto the red carpet piled with clutter. A few rusted iron chairs lay tilted in a corner, forming an eerie stillness with a worn-out mannequin on the stage. I thought to myself: why does a place like this still draw me here? Perhaps because its loneliness and desolation so closely resemble some part of my inner self.

I heard footsteps—each one striking my eardrums clearly. At first, I thought it was my imagination, but as the sound drew nearer, my stomach tightened and the buzzing in my ears grew stronger. I held my breath, lightened my steps, and tried to move toward an exit on one side. “It can’t just be me here, right?” The thought rang alertly in my mind as I looked around; the theater hall was empty, yet it seemed to hide some concealed presence. Then I heard a faint laugh, as if coming from far away. It was cold and brief, carrying a hint of mockery. My body froze instantly, my fingertips turned cold with tension, and my mind flashed through all kinds of possibilities like a storm.

“Is anyone there?” My voice trembled, stiff with all the strength I could muster. But in the theater, only my echo swayed back at me. “What are you doing here?” A low male voice came from behind me, so startling that my heart seemed to stop. As I turned around, I nearly tripped over the floorboards beneath me. Standing at the entrance was a middle-aged man in a dark sweater, his expression seemingly calm yet sharply watchful. I forced out, with great difficulty, “I was just… taking a look.”

“This isn’t a place for casual visitors.” His tone didn’t change at all, yet it made my hair stand on end. I began to explain in a panic, “I mean no harm, I… I was really just passing by.” He stared at me for a few seconds, then waved me off, signaling me to leave. He made no further move or threat, but my mind had already staged countless catastrophic scenarios: had he been watching me for a long time? Could there be other people waiting here? What if he had some other intention? I even began to imagine a headline: “Woman attacked in abandoned theater…” My knees felt slightly weak, and my hands unconsciously clenched the cuffs of my sleeves. My steps quickly carried me toward the door, but I never dared look back. The tight pain in my stomach had spread throughout my body.

When I stepped out of the theater, I finally heard the wind, bringing with it a little room to breathe, but my mind was still racing. In my ears, it seemed I could still hear that low voice, and that faint laugh echoing again and again. I sat on a bench at a bus stop not far from the theater, my palms covered in cold sweat, still unable to shake the feeling of being watched. My attention remained fixed on everything around me, afraid that the man might appear again. That night, lying in bed, I kept chewing over his gaze and those words, “This isn’t a place for casual visitors.” They kept turning over and over, like a hard candy that could not be dissolved.

A few days later, I still couldn’t fully let it go. Countless possibilities kept surfacing in my mind: had I exposed some flaw in myself? Why had he looked at me that way—was it as if he had discovered something? I even began to doubt why I had chosen to enter that place; was some part of my subconscious trying to invite disaster? Each question felt like a thorn piercing my heart, impossible to remove.

The air inside the piano factory was filled with the smell of old wood and dust, and I could feel a faint stinging in my nasal passages. The building was vast and empty; most of the glass in the floor-to-ceiling windows had broken, and sunlight poured through the gaps, casting irregular patches of brightness across the floor. I had my camera with me, trying to capture the contrast between light and shadow. These scenes made me feel that perhaps they could express some of the brokenness I felt inside. I remember my palms were constantly sweating, making the camera feel almost slippery in my hands. As I adjusted the aperture, I kept wondering whether this shoot could convey the emotions I truly wanted to express—the feeling of loneliness intertwined with unease.

Just as I was absorbed in making adjustments, a strange voice suddenly came from behind and to the side: “What are you doing here?” The voice was low and cold, like the dull thud of an old skylight falling to the ground in the piano factory. I spun around abruptly and saw a middle-aged man standing a few steps away. He was wearing an old gray jacket, and the wrinkled cuffs made him seem as dilapidated as the factory itself. His gaze swept over my camera and the backpack at my feet, as if silently questioning whether I belonged there.

My heart clenched. My first thought was: had I trespassed on his territory? Or been mistaken for some kind of dangerous person? I stammered, “I just wanted to take a few photos. This place has a lot of history.” But he remained expressionless and simply replied shortly, “This place isn’t safe. You’d better leave.” At that moment, it felt as if something heavy were pressing down on my stomach, and my breathing became rapid. Sweat slid down my forehead as I glanced around anxiously, trying to find any way out of this sudden predicament.

He didn’t press me further, but his gaze felt like a knife in my back, and I could even feel my shoulders involuntarily tensing up. I crouched down and quickly packed my gear, my fingers fumbling with the backpack zipper several times from sheer nervousness. I kept blaming myself: Why had I chosen such a remote place? Why hadn’t I checked in advance that no one would be disturbed? When I slung the bag over my shoulder and prepared to leave, the man said another flat remark: “Don’t come to places like this again. Be careful.” His tone was still calm, but it felt as if I had been sentenced for some unknown offense.

After leaving the piano factory, I walked several blocks and still couldn’t calm down. Every time I thought back to his indifferent gaze, I felt like an intruder, someone out of place. When I organized those photos at home, my fingers were still trembling slightly, and my emotions seemed to remain trapped in some corner of the factory. I wanted to delete the photos, but I couldn’t bring myself to do it, because they were proof of everything I had felt that day.

A few days later, when I recalled what had happened, I still felt deeply uncomfortable. I kept questioning whether what I had done was really inappropriate, and feared that others would see me as someone who shouldn’t exist. That anxiety kept me awake again and again, and I even began to doubt whether I could continue creating. Every night, when I closed my eyes, that man’s voice and gaze would involuntarily surface, like some kind of mark that could never fade.

Night had fallen over the city, and I wandered in front of the abandoned old movie theater in the northern suburbs. The weather was bitterly cold, and the air was filled with the dusty scent of bygone days. The dilapidated sign looked especially lonely in the moonlight. I pushed open the creaking wooden door, and a blast of cold air rushed at me, mixed with the mildew of old upholstery and the acrid stench of rotten glue. The crystal chandelier overhead had long since gone offstage, leaving only a few withered cords hanging quietly, as if waiting for a performance that would never come again.

“What are you doing here?” I seemed to hear someone whisper behind me. I was startled, only to find shadows and blank walls all around. My heart suddenly raced, my chest felt tight, and cold sweat instantly soaked my back. Every chair leg and every window frame in this place seemed to be chewing on the fear hidden deep in my heart. I carefully walked into the screening room, my footsteps sounding especially loud in the empty space. The stained, mottled graffiti on the walls was like those lingering, bleak moments from my memory.

I sat down in the deserted audience seats, and scenes of my own failures and embarrassments involuntarily began to play in my mind. In past collaborations, I was always worried that I wasn’t good enough, and I was even too hard on myself over the smallest things. Once, at an important project meeting, I misread a slide and was left speechless in front of everyone, my face burning red. These memories came rushing at me like a storm, too much to bear.

“Ah, if only then...” I stopped myself from continuing the self-reproach and tried to shift my attention. I tried hard to recall my successful moments, but I was surrounded by a huge sense of powerlessness. That frustration, along with my racing heartbeat and the slight spasms in my stomach, surged over me uncontrollably. To keep myself from sinking into the abyss, I began to look around.

The damaged screen looked bleak in the moonlight, and the narrow beam of light outlined the laughter and tears left behind by moviegoers from different eras who had sat here before. I told myself that perhaps they, too, had once felt something similar, yet still looked forward to the start of the next film. “Things will always get better,” I whispered to myself, trying to shake off the unease of the moment.

After leaving the theater, the wind was biting, but the fresh air made me much clearer-headed. I took a deep breath and felt the quiet of the night sky. I knew this unease might not disappear, but I was learning to live with it. In the days after I left, that experience hung over my heart like a heavy stone, prompting me to reexamine my relationship with fear.

During that time, I ruminated on the past less and less, and I worked hard to stop overinterpreting other people’s words. I told myself that setbacks were normal, and that what mattered was how to face them rather than avoid them. Although difficulties remained, I realized that I was growing through the process and becoming stronger.

Sunlight filtered through the autumn leaves and fell across the park bench. My friend and I sat at opposite ends of it, surrounded by children’s laughter and the rustling of fallen leaves in the breeze. The air carried a faint blend of earth and dry leaves, giving a sense of steadiness and warmth.

We were talking about a recent movie, and I mentioned that I didn’t understand one of the protagonist’s decisions. “I don’t think he should have done that. It just doesn’t fit his character at all,” I said, my tone tinged with a bit of excitement. My friend smiled faintly and waved a hand. “I don’t think so. That scene was well set up—it felt very real.”

His answer left me a little uneasy. My heart sped up slightly, and my palms began to sweat. Every time I disagreed with a friend, I always felt a bit tense, as if their disagreement were a rejection of me as a person. I tried to calm myself down, but I still couldn’t completely hide the small irritation inside.

I also realized that these minor frictions shouldn’t affect our relationship, yet for some reason I always cared too much about these subtle differences. “Am I always this strange in the way I see things?” I kept asking myself inwardly.

As my friend continued explaining his perspective, I forced a smile and nodded, but I couldn’t fully focus on what he was saying. My mind kept replaying the tone he had just used, carefully analyzing whether there was any hidden sense of disapproval or dissatisfaction. It was a habitual response; I always wanted to find some kind of reassurance, even in what might have been an unintentional expression.

“What are you thinking about?” His voice pulled me back from my thoughts. I quickly masked my slightly flustered expression and said, “Oh, sorry, I zoned out just now. I was just thinking your viewpoint is quite interesting, and maybe I need to think it over more carefully.”

After the walk ended, I made my way home alone, the autumn wind gently brushing my face. Though it was a small matter, a trace of unease still lingered in my heart. At dinner, that feeling still wouldn’t go away. Sitting at the table, eating a simple meal, I hoped this uneasiness would slowly fade in the simplicity of everyday life.

A few days later, when I saw my friend again, the first thing that came to mind was still that conversation. I told myself that everyone has the right to hold their own opinions, and perhaps that is part of life; I should be more relaxed and accepting.

The walls were covered with colorful paintings, and the air was filled with the faint smell of oil paint. I walked into the gallery, my heart full of an uneasy anticipation. I had thought today would be a good day—my work was finally going to be exhibited—yet I couldn’t shake the anxiety inside me. I heard a familiar voice; it was a fellow artist, smiling as she said, “You look a bit nervous today. Are you not used to this kind of setting?” In an instant, my heart sped up and my palms began to sweat. The word “nervous” made me feel as if everyone were noticing my unease. I stammered back, “Oh, maybe, haha. I’m always like this.”

She went on, “Your paintings look really interesting. I’m truly looking forward to seeing more.” Though her tone was friendly, what came to mind were the questioning voices from the past: “Can you really do it?” I felt a tightness in my stomach, as if an invisible hand had clenched it hard. Her expression seemed a little hesitant, and I began to wonder whether she was implying that my work wasn’t good enough. These thoughts surged over me like a tide, and while listening to her speak, I struggled to suppress them. I awkwardly steered the conversation toward her work, trying to avoid focusing on myself.

After the opening ended, I walked out of the gallery, and the evening breeze brought a touch of coolness. I sat on a bench by the street, the earlier conversation echoing over and over in my mind. My heart was still racing, and my back was damp with sweat. Though these were all shadows of yesterday, I still couldn’t shake the feeling of being abandoned, as if I had always been an outsider in this industry. After I got home, that sense of inadequacy followed me like a shadow, keeping me tossing and turning all night. I began to reflect on whether it was my fault, whether I hadn’t done enough somewhere. When I woke the next day, I decided to work even harder, hoping to prove myself through better work and make those doubts disappear.

However, these emotions often came back over the next few days, and countless times I found myself sinking into self-attack, feeling that I wasn’t good enough. Even when some friends came to visit and tried to encourage me, those feelings still couldn’t be easily erased. A few days later, standing on the rooftop in the sunlight, I told myself that accepting all the unease and doubt is part of being an artist. They may never go away, but I must learn to live with them.

I walked into an old woodworking shop in the southern part of the city, where the setting sun shone through the battered windows and colored the floor a golden hue. Around the exhibition, a faint scent of wood hung in the air, and it seemed the place still carried traces of the old workshop’s past. Although the atmosphere of the exhibition was light and lively, I found that I could not relax. My hands rubbed together unconsciously as I tried to ease the inexplicable tension. My heartbeat began to quicken, and a layer of cold sweat formed on my forehead. The theme of the exhibition was “Wood and Creativity,” and I should have felt excited, but instead my mind kept imagining one unpleasant outcome after another. Whenever someone walked past, I would suspect they were casting a critical eye over my work.

A middle-aged man came over, his gaze lingering on my piece. “Is this your work?” he asked, his tone seeming full of curiosity. I immediately grew tense, my voice even trembling a little. “Yes, it is my work. Is there a problem?” I overinterpreted his tone, assuming he had some dissatisfaction with what I had created.

“No, there’s no problem. I just think the design is very unique,” he said, offering a friendly smile. Hearing that, I let out a slight breath of relief. My heartbeat still had not returned to normal, but at least my emotions had settled a little.

Realizing my own reaction, I felt a trace of shame. I was always like this, habitually catastrophizing, even in situations where there was no danger at all. The tension in my body and the turmoil in my mind made it hard for me to fully enjoy events like this. I tried to savor every detail of the exhibition, but the anxiety within kept reminding me that this sense of calm was only temporary.

After the exhibition ended, I sat alone on a small stool by the entrance of the workshop, still chewing over the embarrassing moment in my mind. “Why am I always like this?” I muttered to myself, my voice barely audible. Thinking back on my self-attack, I felt a bitter sense of shame.

Even several days later, that feeling would still come back from time to time. Whenever I remembered the man’s friendly smile, I blamed myself for reacting with such unease. In my mind, the feeling of being abandoned kept surfacing, along with a sense of defectiveness that had nowhere to go. I knew I should be more relaxed, that I should trust other people’s goodwill, but it always felt hard to do.

I sat in a corner of the living room, surrounded by my family’s laughter and chatter, with the children running around on the floor and festive music playing from the speakers. The clock on the wall ticked away, yet every second felt as slow as an hour. I held a cup of coffee that had gone cold, tasting only its bitterness. I tried to join their conversation, but every time I opened my mouth, my words were drowned out by louder voices. Inside me was an uncontrollable sense of loneliness, as if I were trapped under a glass dome—able to see, but unable to hear.

“Are you okay?” I heard my sister say, smiling at me.

“I’m fine, just a little tired.” I forced a smile in return, only to find that my voice sounded oddly harsh. She nodded and turned back to join another conversation. My heart raced, my palms sweated, and my stomach felt heavy, as if there were a lump of ice inside it.

Why couldn’t they see me? Why did no one notice I was sitting here? Had I done something wrong? Or did I simply not belong here? These questions roared in my mind like specters from the abyss. I kept searching for answers in self-doubt, but the answers never seemed to appear.

After the gathering ended, I drove home alone, the streetlights before me blurring into a haze. I had to keep asking myself whether it was because I wasn’t good enough, not interesting enough, or whether there was some irredeemable flaw in me to begin with. The question stabbed at my heart like an awl.

The next day, I still couldn’t shake that feeling of being abandoned. I kept replaying the scene from the night before, clinging to every overlooked detail, even wondering whether they were talking about me behind my back. Again and again, I launched preemptive attacks on myself, imagining how boring and awkward others might think I was. My emotions surged over me like tides, impossible to calm.

When the door to the exhibition hall was pushed open, the hinges let out a sharp scraping sound that instantly drew the attention of the few people inside. I immediately felt awkward, as if I had burst in wearing a label that said “disturbance.” I lowered my head and pretended to be absorbed in a brochure by the entrance—though I hadn’t even clearly seen what was written on it. The lighting in the hall was soft, but somewhat dim. A few yellow spotlights shone on the map display cases, and the brass frames reflected faint points of light. The air carried a faint musty smell of aging paper.

I walked up to a wooden display stand covered with an eighteenth-century nautical map. The densely hand-drawn lines gave me an inexplicable sense of pressure. I tried to focus on understanding the markings, but my thoughts kept drifting to a couple standing nearby. They were talking in low voices, occasionally letting out a soft laugh or two. I glanced at them quietly, only to meet the man’s gaze. He looked a few years younger than me, and his eyes seemed to carry a kind of... contempt? Mockery? Or was it just a coincidence? I couldn’t tell at once, and there was no time to think it through. All I knew was that my cheeks were quickly heating up and my palms were beginning to sweat.

“Maybe I’m standing where they wanted to look at the map,” I blamed myself in my head. “Or maybe the sound when I pushed the door open was too loud? They must think I’m really rude.” To ease the awkwardness, I quickly stepped to the other side of the display case and pretended to keep looking at the other exhibits, but my heartbeat still wouldn’t calm down. I could hear my breathing growing faster, and I unconsciously tightened my grip on the strap of my bag.

After a while, a staff member came over and handed me a small booklet introducing the new exhibition. He smiled and chatted with me: “Are you interested in maps too? Actually, the stories behind these hand-drawn maps are especially interesting. A lot of the details are expressions of the cartographers’ personal feelings.” His tone was relaxed, even a little earnest. I nodded and forced a smile, but I barely heard what he said at the end. I could only mechanically reply, “Oh, yeah, it’s pretty interesting,” and then walked toward another display stand.

My mind kept replaying the expression on that man’s face. I started inventing his thoughts: “Look at her, standing there blocking the way and pretending to look at the map.” Or: “People who don’t know anything still come to exhibitions like this?” My stomach began to twist in waves, and my throat felt tight, as if something were lodged in it. I tried to tell myself that all of this was just my own imagination, but every effort felt like crashing into an invisible wall, making no progress at all.

About ten minutes later, I could no longer focus on any of the exhibits, so I hurried out of the hall. The wind outside was a little cold, and my fingers had gone stiff from clutching the bag strap so tightly. I stood by the street, watching pedestrians come and go under the streetlights, but my emotions still wouldn’t settle. After I got home, I replayed that man’s gaze over and over—magnifying it, analyzing it, guessing at it—until I couldn’t sleep deep into the night. The next morning, I could barely eat breakfast, and the thought circling in my mind was still: “Did I make myself disliked in the exhibition hall?”

A few days later, I finally mentioned it in casual conversation with a friend. She just laughed it off lightly: “You’re overthinking it. Maybe he didn’t even notice you.” But her words inexplicably filled me with a wave of shame—why am I always like this, tormenting myself without end?

Night fell, and I wandered along the streets on the east side of the city before finally stepping into an old camera shop. The store was filled with an antique atmosphere, and the air carried the scent of wood and photographic paper. The owner was an elderly man sitting behind the counter, amber light casting itself across his face.

“Hello, how can I help you?” he asked with a smile. I nodded, seeming a little unsure.

“I’ve recently gotten into film photography,” I said vaguely. “I wanted to see if there’s any suitable equipment.”

He gave a faint, contemptuous smile and said in a low voice, “In this day and age, it’s rare indeed for a young person like you to be interested in old cameras.”

Something in his tone made me feel uncomfortable. My heart suddenly began to race, and my palms started to sweat. I tried to act as though nothing was wrong, but inside I knew my face was already growing hot. Why would he say that? Was it meant to be belittling? Did I seem ignorant?

To cover up my confusion, I began pacing back and forth among the rows of cameras, pretending to study their labels intently. Yet with every step, I could feel his gaze from behind the counter. My breathing grew uneven, and my stomach churned.

At last, he could no longer hold back and said, “These cameras are things with stories behind them; they’re not meant to sit around as decorations.” His voice carried an implicit warning.

My heart sank, and I vaguely felt the scorn hidden in those words. I forced a smile, wondering whether it was really his tone or whether I was overthinking it. Not daring to ask anything else, I hurriedly thanked him and walked out of the shop.

After leaving, I wandered aimlessly through the streets, trying to calm myself down. That phrase, “they’re not meant to sit around as decorations,” kept echoing in my mind, and I kept questioning whether I really seemed shallow and ignorant in other people’s eyes. I began to preemptively blame myself: why was I always so sensitive? They were only a few careless remarks—why did I care so much?

When I got home, my emotions still hadn’t settled. I collapsed onto the sofa and closed my eyes, but all I felt was a wave of emptiness and anxiety. In the end, I decided to make myself a cup of hot tea, and the scalding touch of the cup helped ease my tense nerves a little.

Over the next few days, I tried not to think about that unpleasant night, but I still couldn’t help turning it over in my mind from time to time. The next day, I told a friend about it. She comforted me, saying, “Don’t overthink it. Maybe he just said it offhand.” Though her words brought me some comfort, the sensitivity and shame were still hard to shake off.

The café was crowded, and the air was filled with a strange blend of scents: the aroma of coffee mixed with the cloying sweetness of freshly baked cake. I kept my head down, stirring the coffee in my cup with a spoon, the foam already beginning to fade. I heard her say, “You’re always like this. You never listen to what I say!” The resentment in her voice jabbed at my ears like thorns. I suddenly looked up and saw her frowning, her lips pressed tight. I tried hard to stay calm, but it felt as if a giant boulder were lodged in my chest, making it hard to breathe. “I... I did listen to you!” I stammered in reply, though my voice came out sharp as shards of glass. Her frown deepened, her arms folded across her chest, her gaze carrying a trace of disgust I couldn’t ignore. In an instant, countless scenes flashed through my mind: Had she already decided not to see me again? Did she think I was beyond saving? Had she already begun to hate my presence? These thoughts swirled in my head like an unshakable cloud.

The low murmur of conversations around us and the roar of the coffee machine gradually grew distant; all I could hear was my own heartbeat, that heavy, piercing rhythm that made me feel on the verge of suffocation. I tried to explain, “I didn’t mean to, I just... I just want to know what exactly you’re blaming me for...” Halfway through, it felt as if something had clamped around my throat, and no sound would come out. She sighed, her eyes full of exhaustion. “You’re so sensitive, but you’ve never really tried to understand other people. Every time I say something to you, it feels like walking a tightrope. I’m really tired.” Those words were like a sharp knife driven straight into my chest. I froze, feeling my face grow hot, my breathing turn rapid, and my stomach twist as if someone had squeezed it hard. I stood up stiffly, the chair scraping loudly against the floor, and a few people around us turned to look at me. With my head down, I grabbed my bag in a panic, not daring to look at her expression. “Maybe you’re right... I’m sorry.” My voice sounded strange, and full of despair.

When I left the café, the sunlight was so glaring that I had to squint, but it did nothing to ease the pain inside me. I wandered aimlessly along the corner of the street, the faint scrape of my shoes against the ground making me feel even lonelier. Her words kept replaying in my mind—“Every time I say something to you, it feels like walking a tightrope”—and they kept stabbing at me again and again. I began to ruminate over every one of my actions: Had I said something wrong again? Was I really that hard to get along with? I felt like a broken machine, unable to function properly. My stomach throbbed faintly, my teeth clenched so tightly that my cheeks ached, yet I refused to relax my jaw. The memories I shared with her—our first movie in college, the trip we took together after graduation—suddenly felt like distant illusions, as if they could vanish at any moment.

When I woke the next day, my eyelids felt as heavy as if a thousand pounds were pressing down on them. I tried to remember how I had fallen asleep the night before, and realized the last image was her indifferent expression. I sat on the edge of the bed, lost in thought for a long time, my fingers mechanically tracing circles on the bedsheet, each movement like a confirmation of my own existence. There was no message from her on my phone, not even those perfunctory emoji stickers. I sank into a deep sense of defectiveness, feeling like someone unworthy of love, unworthy of acceptance, as if no matter how hard I tried, nothing could ever change that.

The banquet hall was filled with flashing lights and the sound of conversation, surrounded by colleagues and judges moving back and forth. Wearing the carefully chosen outfit I had picked out, my heart was already racing as I stood at the entrance. My palms were a little damp, and I kept mentally rehearsing scenarios in which I might be overlooked or judged unfairly.

Inside the hall, I tried my best to smile and talk with a few colleagues, doing everything I could to hide my unease. Yet whenever they frowned slightly or merely nodded, I could not help but start wondering whether they truly did not think highly of my work. I heard someone say, “Your work is pretty good, but it just feels like something is missing.” That sentence felt like a thorn in my heart; my stomach tightened as if waiting to be surrounded by even more criticism.

The ceremony was long and agonizing. As I sat in my seat and the host announced the winners one by one, I kept repeating to myself, “They definitely didn’t choose me.” When the final award was revealed and my name was indeed not there, the sense of abandonment and inadequacy swallowed me instantly. I fought hard to conceal the disappointment in my heart and did not show too much emotion, but my fingers began unconsciously picking at the edge of my seat.

“It’s okay, there will be another time,” a colleague beside me said softly to comfort me. I replied politely, “Thank you, I’ll keep working hard.” Though I tried to maintain a smile on my face, I had already sunk deep into self-denial and doubt. I kept rehashing every possible mistake and overanalyzing every implication in every word.

That night, I returned home with such a heavy heart that I could not stop attacking myself. I kept imagining the disappointed expressions others had at the awards ceremony. Lying in bed, my heart still raced, and I could not fall asleep. Even days later, I still could not shake off that shadow, and I even began to wonder whether I was truly suited for this path.

The memory of touch made me think of the texture of that outfit, mixed with the dampness of my palms and my pounding heartbeat.

A few days later, I sat in the studio, the sound of rain continuing outside the window. I forced myself to begin a new creation, but dark doubts and unease still lingered in my heart.

Outside the kitchen window, raindrops tapped softly against the glass, making a faint ticking sound. I stood by the kitchen counter, preparing the ingredients for dinner. Half the onion on the cutting board had already been sliced, and my eyes stung from the fumes. I quickly cut with the knife, trying to finish this unpleasant task as soon as possible. Just then, I suddenly felt a sharp pain and looked down to find that the blade had sliced my index finger, and bright red beads of blood quickly welled up. I hurriedly ran my finger under cold water; the icy water stung the wound, making the pain even more pronounced. I silently blamed myself: “I was careless again. I really should have been more careful.”

The kitchen was filled with the pungent smell of onion, mixed with the rich aroma of tomato sauce drifting over now and then, making my stomach cramp a little. While pressing the wound with a tissue to stop the bleeding, I continued with the preparations at hand. A notification sounded on my phone; it was a message from a friend. “Hey, want to come out for coffee today?” I hesitated. My finger hurt, but dark thoughts began to creep in: “Do they think I’m not very sociable? Should I go?”

Thinking back to the awkward scene at the last gathering, when I had said the wrong thing, my heartbeat seemed to quicken, and sweat began to gather in my palms. I tried to reassure myself that maybe this time would be different. I looked up at the window; outside was a gloomy scene, and the rain still hadn’t let up. In the end, I turned down the invitation, using my injured finger as an excuse to rest.

My mood was somewhat irritated by this small episode, so I simply turned on some music, hoping the melody would soften my uneasy feelings. Relaxing jazz echoed through the kitchen, as if the rhythm of the music had healed the whole space a little.

A few days later, though the wound had begun to heal, I still found myself thinking from time to time about that afternoon, about how sensitive I was to small things. I wrote in my diary: “Next time, I have to slow down—slower still.”

The next day when I woke up, sunlight was streaming through the curtains and spilling across my face. The wound was much better, and it seemed even that trace of irritation had faded with time. Though the dreary rain would come again, I knew that as long as I slowed my pace and was a bit more careful, the chance of cutting my finger would be smaller too.

The air in the conference room carried the faint woody scent of the new office. I sat in a corner of the rectangular conference table, with drizzling autumn rain outside the window. Raindrops tapped against the glass, and the ticking sound mixed with the occasional rustle of turning pages made the room feel especially quiet. My heartbeat quickened involuntarily, and I could faintly hear the rhythm of my own breathing. I kept flipping through the notebook in my hands, trying to make myself look focused and confident.

“Let’s discuss the preliminary plan for this project,” the project manager’s voice cut through the stillness of the conference room like distant thunder. Every time his gaze swept over me, I felt my whole body tense up. My palms had already started to sweat, and I discreetly wiped them on my pants as if nothing had happened.

As the meeting went on, I noticed a colleague sitting across from me slightly furrowing his brows and tapping the table with his fingers. I couldn’t help wondering if there had been something wrong with what I’d just said, or if I had missed something at some point. These thoughts surged in like a tide, making it hard for me to calm down.

“What do you think of this proposal?” the project manager suddenly called on me. I hurriedly looked up, my throat feeling as if something were blocking it. I forced myself to steady down and replied in a slightly trembling voice, “I think we could make some detailed adjustments based on the client’s feedback. That might be more helpful for moving the project forward.”

After saying that, I felt a wave of palpitations, as if the beating in my chest were about to burst through the wall. I quickly scanned everyone’s reactions, trying hard to read their expressions. But each face wore a mask I couldn’t penetrate, which made me even more uneasy.

After the meeting ended, I didn’t dare linger for long. The colleagues gradually dispersed, and the rain had eased somewhat, filling the air with the fresh scent of earth. I walked out of the office building, the view under my umbrella hazy and blurred. The doubt about my colleagues’ attitudes and my own performance still refused to go away.

When I got home, I was still thinking about the colleague’s furrowed brow and the manager’s slightly evaluative gaze. I tossed and turned in bed, replaying every detail of the meeting over and over, repeatedly chewing over the hints I seemed to have missed. The next morning, I could still feel that lingering worry and self-doubt in my heart, like the autumn rain that had yet to stop. In the end, I decided to take the initiative and talk to that colleague with the furrowed brow, to confirm whether this unease was merely my own overinterpretation.

The air in the restaurant was filled with a faint aroma of spices, making it hard not to be drawn in. Sunlight streamed through the gaps in the curtains onto the white tablecloth, and the silver cutlery on the table reflected a soft glimmer. I sat in my chair, feeling my back pressed tightly against it, my fingers unconsciously twisting the napkin. Today was a business lunch with an important client, and I knew how significant this meeting was, which only added to my pressure. A waiter approached quietly and asked, “What would you like to drink?” His voice was gentle, but for a moment I didn’t catch it clearly. I looked at the client across from me; he was looking down at his phone, expressionless. I felt a wave of unease, unsure whether he was uninterested in what I had to say or simply bored by the lunch altogether.

“Just a glass of mineral water, thank you,” I said, trying to keep my voice steady. As soon as the words left my mouth, my heart began to race, and beads of nervous sweat appeared on my forehead. At that moment, the client looked up and gave me a slight smile. “Actually, I don’t really drink much either. I’ve always felt that alcohol at lunch is a burden.” His words eased me a little inside, but I still didn’t dare let my guard down.

“Actually, I’ve always admired the creativity of your company,” the client said as he carefully cut the steak on his plate with a knife and fork. “Especially the project you worked on before.” Hearing this, I finally relaxed a little; so he didn’t have any personal objections to me after all.

“Thank you,” I replied, trying to hide my nerves. “That really was a challenging project.” Still, I remained drawn to every subtle expression on his face, unable to stop myself from overanalyzing every sentence.

When the main course was served, I couldn’t help but start doubting my performance. Was my body language not confident enough? Or was I speaking too slowly? These thoughts came flooding in like a tide, and I felt a bit of discomfort in my stomach.

“Are you all right?” the client asked with some concern. That only deepened my anxiety. I nodded quickly and forced a calm smile. “Everything’s fine.”

The rhythm of my heartbeat slowed a little, but I still couldn’t fully calm down. I blamed myself inwardly for always falling so easily into tension and unease. It was truly embarrassing to feel this way. Just then, the restaurant lights grew softer, and gentle background music began to play, as if telling me that I should learn to relax.

After lunch, we exchanged business cards and agreed on a time for the next detailed meeting. The moment I stepped out of the restaurant, warm sunlight fell on my shoulders, bringing me some comfort. That afternoon, I kept reviewing my performance at lunch, replaying the scene over and over in my mind, and began reflecting on my tendency to overinterpret things and the anxiety it caused.

Although the lunch ended fairly well, fatigue and self-reproach continued to haunt me over the next few days. I worked hard to steady my emotions, hoping that next time I could better control my feelings and state of mind.

The meeting had just ended, and I was sitting in the café downstairs from the company. The air was filled with the bitter aroma of coffee, and the sound of the grinder echoed in my ears. Today’s meeting had left me a little unsettled. The manager mentioned in the meeting that our team’s project was falling behind schedule, and I immediately grew nervous. My heart pounded like a drum, and sweat quietly crept onto my forehead. Although he didn’t point directly at me, I still felt that his gaze lingered on me for a moment, and that uneasy feeling wouldn’t go away.

“What do you think?” my colleague beside me suddenly asked. Her tone seemed a bit dismissive, and I instinctively thought she was questioning me. In that instant, my face burned as if it were on fire. Stammering, I replied, “I, I think we can catch up by next week.” My voice was so faint it was almost inaudible.

I kept blaming myself inside: why am I always so lacking in confidence? I began replaying every word I had said in the meeting, repeatedly dwelling on the possible mistakes and oversights in my mind. I could feel a knot twisting in my stomach, and my hands started to tremble slightly.

After leaving the company, I arranged to meet a friend. I needed to vent the irritation bottled up inside me. Not long after, she sat across from me, holding a cup of hot chocolate. “You look really tense. What happened?” she asked with concern.

“I don’t know, I just feel like something’s wrong,” I said softly, my voice tinged with helplessness. I described what had happened in the meeting and how I had overinterpreted my colleague’s attitude. After listening, she just smiled. “You always do this—you think about things too much. She probably just asked out of habit.”

Late that night, I lay in bed, still unable to shake the image of the meeting from my mind. I tried to tell myself that other people’s opinions aren’t always directed at me, and maybe I had just been overthinking things today. But this attempt to convince myself felt so weak and powerless.

Over the next few days, I tried to prove my worth by working hard. I told myself that next time I had to stay calm and not let anxiety control my emotions. Yet that version of myself, the one who couldn’t control her feelings, still left me feeling powerless.

Sunlight slanted through the glass window and fell onto the blanket by my feet. I dragged a chair out to the balcony and curled up in the cushioned seat, holding a book in my hands. The cover was blue, and the scent of the paper mingled with a faint warmth from the sun. I turned a page; the print was a little rough, as if I could feel its raised and sunken texture. From downstairs, voices drifted up from time to time, people chatting about a gym class, with laughter mixed in.

“Have you tried that new instructor’s class? I heard it’s really tough.”

“Seriously, I tried it once and couldn’t even lift my arms afterward.”

The wind outside gently stirred the potted plants on the balcony railing, and occasionally I could hear a distant car horn. I held the book and tried to keep reading, but my attention kept being pulled away by those sounds. I lowered my eyes to the text; my eyes felt a little dry. A passage in the book mentioned some theory in psychology. As I tried to make sense of it, stray thoughts kept slipping through my mind, as if trivial little things had suddenly bubbled up—for instance, whether the shirt I ironed yesterday had gotten a bit wrinkled, or whether the succulent on the balcony needed fresh soil.

My fingers unconsciously brushed along the edge of the page, and that slightly rough, subtle texture distracted me for a moment. Then my ears caught the faint sound of a cat jumping onto the windowsill. It stared at me, its tail sweeping elegantly across the railing. I reached out and rubbed the top of its head, and it let out a lazy purr, as if in response to my soothing. Suddenly, I found myself reluctant to let it run off, so I gently tapped my leg. It glanced at me, then really did jump down and curl up in the corner of the blanket.

The warm sunlight bathed my body, and I suddenly felt sleepiness creeping in. After a few pages, I became too lazy to turn them, and my eyes grew sluggish as well. My body slowly relaxed, and my stomach felt heavy, as if it were knotted up. I put the book down, leaned back against the chair, and squinted, feeling the sunlight tenderly wrap around my face. My breathing became even, but then everything started to feel a little too quiet—so quiet that I almost lost my sense of direction. In the end, I picked up the book again and tried to continue, but inside me was a faint emptiness—this kind of calm somehow did not belong to me.

After about half an hour, I finally left the balcony. I put the book back on the table and patted the cat on the head; it gazed at me lazily. I went to the kitchen to drink a glass of water, then stood by the window as the wind blew in and stirred my bangs. I stood there for a while, doing nothing and not even feeling inclined to do anything. It was as if my entire afternoon had been left blank all of a sudden.

The restaurant lighting was a little dim, casting a faint warm glow across the table. The atmosphere should have been relaxed; everyone had just finished a busy day’s work and was gathered around the round table to start ordering. People were laughing loudly, and the clink of glasses rang out from time to time, but my attention was completely drawn to a subtle detail. Just now, I had brought up a topic, but after glancing at me, my colleague Xiaolin’s mouth twitched slightly. She then turned away and whispered a couple of words to the person beside her. My head immediately started buzzing.

“Was she mocking me?” My heart suddenly began to race, and my palms started to sweat, as if even the air had become sticky. I forced myself to take a big gulp of iced water, trying to calm down. But those scenes kept replaying in my head: Xiaolin’s expression, the way she spoke quietly to someone else, and all those tiny possibilities—was my topic too boring? Was my tone too stiff? Or was it even that what I said made no sense at all?

“Do you want steamed fish, or hot pot?” Colleague Xiao Zhang across from me suddenly handed the menu to me. I froze for a moment, almost startled enough to drop it, but still managed to take the menu awkwardly. “Ah, sure, steamed fish is pretty good.” My voice sounded even drier than I had expected. It felt like someone glanced at me sideways, or maybe it was just my own imagination. I lowered my head and stared at the menu, feeling a knot in my stomach; I couldn’t make out the words on it at all.

For the rest of the time, I barely joined in everyone’s conversation. Even when I did, I chose my words very carefully, afraid that I might again be caught saying something ridiculous. And even so, I still felt like someone was occasionally looking at me, with some slight, unclear scrutiny in their gaze. I could even hear my own voice in my head: “Here it comes again, everyone probably thinks I’m an uninteresting person.” “Are you dragging down the whole team’s atmosphere?”

After dinner, I was almost the first to leave. Walking along the night streets, the wind made my face feel a little cold. I began to ruminate over the whole thing: where exactly had it gone wrong? If Xiaolin’s expression wasn’t directed at me, then who was it meant for? But if it was aimed at me, why do I always manage to pick up on it so easily? These questions were like a tangled ball of thread. Even though I was already exhausted and tired, I still couldn’t help picking at them, until I got home and realized my stomach pain had become even worse.

The next day, I was even more reserved. When reporting recent work progress to my colleagues, my little movements were especially frequent; I kept tugging at my sleeves and wringing my hands. Although my coworkers didn’t show anything obviously unusual, my attention always focused on their subtle gestures, as if every pause in tone and every change in expression carried some kind of targetted meaning. I knew this state was bad, but I really couldn’t control it. This feeling of being “captured” by micro-expressions and tone of voice seemed to have become part of my life.

Sunlight streamed through the café’s large windows onto the table. I sat there in a creative discussion, holding a coffee cup and feeling its slight warmth. I was nervous, even a little palpitating. The team members sat around together, discussing the next steps for our project. In my ears were the hum of machines and people’s quiet conversations. The air was filled with the rich aroma of coffee, one of my favorite scents.

I put forward a new idea, hoping to spark everyone’s interest. My voice trembled a little, because I always worry that others won’t agree with me. “I think we could try this approach; maybe it would bring some freshness?” I said, trying to sound confident.

My colleagues exchanged glances, and then one of them said, “That sounds a bit risky. Do we really need to do this?” His tone made me feel as if my idea had been rejected. My heart raced, and my face began to heat up, as though I were being stared at. I could feel my palms starting to sweat, and the coffee cup seemed to slip more and more.

I tried not to read too much into it, but my mind kept ruminating on times in the past when I had been criticized. Those subtle expressions, that slightly skeptical tone, all made me uneasy. Unconsciously, I started attacking myself: “Maybe my idea really is terrible. Why is it always like this?” I kept questioning my own abilities in my mind.

After the meeting ended, I walked out of the café. The sunlight was dazzling, and I squinted reflexively. On the way home, I kept wondering whether these criticisms meant I had been cast aside by the team, whether they no longer believed in my abilities. These thoughts surged over me like a tide, making me feel somewhat overwhelmed.

After I got home, I tried to calm myself down. A few days passed, and I still felt that my position in the team was somewhat shaky, but I began to try thinking about how to improve my ideas and find different solutions, rather than getting stuck in self-doubt. I realized I couldn’t dismiss myself because of one small setback; giving myself a little more time and space might bring new inspiration.

I was sitting in a corner of the coffee shop, with sunlight streaming through the leaves outside and casting dappled shadows. The air was filled with the aroma of fresh coffee, and my close friend was sitting across from me as we discussed a recently popular film. “I think the director’s handling in this movie is a bit too straightforward,” she said, her voice soft but her tone firm. In an instant, my heart raced and a slight sweat broke out on my forehead. Why is it always someone disagreeing with me? Was she implying that I wasn’t smart enough? My stomach started to feel uneasy.

To hide my discomfort, I quickly replied, “I actually think his straightforward style is quite interesting; it gives a very powerful impression. Don’t you think?” At the same time, I nervously stirred the coffee in my cup, and I seemed to hear the low conversations of the people around us and the gurgling of the coffee machine; every little detail made me irritated. In conversations like this, I always overanalyze every word and every expression of hers, worrying whether I had done something wrong or been misunderstood. She looked at me and smiled slightly. “I understand how you feel, but I just think he could have been more subtle.” Her voice was still so calm, and the tension in my heart eased a little.

This kind of minor disagreement was not the first time between us, and I also knew that in most cases she meant no harm. After I got home, I lay on the sofa, and the conversation in the coffee shop kept echoing in my mind from time to time. Although those words were only a slight difference of opinion, they made me feel uncomfortable. I often felt ashamed of this slight unease. Why couldn’t I simply accept differing views? After a few days, I tried not to ruminate over the conversation and tried to focus on other things, but occasionally that sense of uncertainty still surfaced. That night, I told myself to work hard at learning to accept different perspectives and not always think that others were rejecting me.

The crystal chandelier in the hall cast a soft, warm glow, turning the exhibition space into a sea of gold. A faintly sweet scent from the old wood lingered in the air. My gaze drifted over the display cases, but it kept wavering. In the center of the stringed-instruments section sat an old Viennese qin, intricately crafted, its carved patterns seeming to have been etched into the rings of time itself. I stood there, trying to make myself look attentive and natural. A middle-aged man in a dark wool coat leaned close to me and said quietly to his companion, “The value of these instruments, I’m afraid, can only truly be appreciated by an expert.” His tone sounded casual, yet it carried some underlying scrutiny.

My head felt as if it had been struck dully for a moment—“Is he talking about me? Does he think I look like an amateur?” My heartbeat suddenly sped up, and the sound of blood rushing filled my ears. I stood there stiffly, my eyes fixed on the qin, yet I could no longer hear the Baroque music playing in the exhibit area. My stomach tightened as if twisted, my palms began to sweat, and I unconsciously clenched the sleeve of my coat. Those few words seemed to turn into countless flying notes, circling incessantly around my ears.

“Are you okay?” A gentle voice suddenly interrupted my thoughts. I looked up to see a young volunteer standing in front of me. Her smile was warm, but I felt a faint embarrassment, as if she had noticed my discomfort. So I hurriedly nodded. “Oh, I’m fine, thank you.” But my voice came out especially dry. Even my tone sounded like I was trying to hide something.

The exhibition went on, but my thoughts had already been seized by that middle-aged man’s remark. I kept replaying the scene over and over. Had he looked at me when he said it? Was my expression too stiff? Had I stood there too long, making myself look unnatural? These questions spread like endless ripples, one after another, weaving in my mind into a huge net of anxiety.

On the way home, the orange streetlights along both sides of the road cast blurry streaks of light across the car window. I tried to tell myself that perhaps it had just been an offhand remark, or maybe it wasn’t directed at me at all. But then another voice whispered in my ear: “Maybe it was. But why would he mention ‘expert’? Do you really look like someone who knows nothing?” Tears rose unknowingly in my eyes, and I blinked hard, trying to force them back.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, feeling as though a heavy stone were pressing on my chest. I tried to use logic to overturn this unease, but every time my thoughts began to clear, they were interrupted again by those repeated images and ideas. For an entire week, this matter became background noise in my mind, impossible to shake off. I even began to wonder whether, under this emotional impact, I was still suited to continue working in the creative field. Was I too sensitive? Why did other people’s words affect me so deeply?

The floor of the dilapidated warehouse was covered with a layer of dust, and sunlight streamed through the broken windows, casting mottled patterns of light and shadow. I walked carefully through the silent space, camera in hand, filled with a mix of nervousness and anticipation. This was the location I had chosen for my new project. Though its decay made me uneasy, the sense of mystery and the weight of time also drew me in.

“Are you sure this is a good choice?” my partner asked softly from the side.

“I think there’s a very special atmosphere here,” I replied, trying to sound confident. Yet inside, all kinds of uneasy thoughts kept churning: What if the final work doesn’t turn out as expected? What if this place isn’t safe, and I’m putting everyone at risk?

With those thoughts, my heart started racing, and I even felt a little dizzy. My palms began to sweat, and the hand gripping the camera trembled slightly. I stopped and took a deep breath, trying to calm the anxiety inside me. At times like this, I always couldn’t help imagining the worst possible outcome.

“Hey, we can start now,” my partner’s voice pulled me out of my thoughts.

“Okay,” I forced out a smile and adjusted the camera to begin shooting. With every press of the shutter, I tried to stay focused on the task in front of me rather than letting those murky thoughts pull me off balance.

As the shoot went on, the warehouse’s stillness and the warmth brought by the sunlight gradually soothed me. The sound of the camera shutter became a rhythm, and I slowly immersed myself in it. Though the tension in my heart never completely disappeared, at least for that time, I found a trace of inner peace.

After a while, we finished shooting. My partner and I walked out of the warehouse, the sunlight on our faces bringing a long-lost sense of ease. Once home, I couldn’t wait to import the photos onto my computer and review them one by one. They weren’t perfect, but I had captured the feeling I had been looking for.

A few days later, I still found myself reflecting on the experience from time to time. Although the warehouse’s darkness and unease had shaken me, I also came to realize that only by facing these emotions could I find myself in my creative work. This shoot taught me to accept my own uneasiness and transform it into the driving force behind creation.

When the call connected, my hands were already soaked, and the phone case stuck to my skin, making me terribly uncomfortable. Through the earphones came the other person’s voice, deliberately lowered, yet unable to hide the impatience in his tone. “I really don’t understand your logic. Why do you always discover problems at the last minute?” he said. My heart jolted violently, and it felt as if a bucket of ice water had been poured into my stomach. I took a deep breath, only to find my voice trembling. “I already checked the whole process yesterday. You changed the file and didn’t tell me.” I could hear the urgency in my own attempt to defend myself, but the moment the words came out, I regretted them, because I could hear the weakness in them.

The other person paused, and that immediately made me start guessing what expression he had on his face—was he rolling his eyes? Or barely holding himself back from exploding? Then he replied coldly, “So? You’re saying it’s my fault?” Those words stabbed into my chest like an awl. I suddenly realized that once again I was shifting responsibility onto someone else, which had always been one of his grievances against me. And all I could do was stand helplessly in the mire of that conversation, trying to prove my innocence while unable to stop imagining that he had already decided, in his mind, that I had failed.

“That’s not what I meant...” I explained in a small voice, my fingertips beginning to go numb. I could almost hear my heartbeat, that thudding sound overpowering the volume in my earphones, while cold sweat started to form on my forehead. He on the other end of the line let out a sigh, as if he had completely run out of patience with everything about me. “Forget it. I don’t want to discuss this anymore. Handle it yourself.” Then he hung up.

The call cut off, and the room suddenly became frighteningly quiet. I stared at my phone, feeling as if a part of me had been hollowed out. My mind began rapidly replaying every sentence just now, every rise and fall in tone, trying to figure out exactly when he had completely lost faith in me. I sat in the chair, one hand supporting my forehead, my nails unconsciously digging into my skin. Those familiar thoughts surfaced again: Was it because I wasn’t good enough? Was it because I always messed things up that people thought I was useless?

I tried to breathe deeply, but the air wouldn’t come in. I ran to the bathroom and splashed my face hard with cold water, staring at myself in the mirror, my eyes already wet. I thought of all those broken relationships in the past—friends, lovers, even coworkers. No matter how hard I tried, it always seemed I could ruin everything. I hated myself. Why couldn’t I be what others expected? Why was I always so helpless?

That night, I turned off my phone and lay under the blankets, tossing and turning. Every time I closed my eyes, the other person’s tone before hanging up replayed in my head, like an alarm bell echoing constantly in my ears. I started calculating whether I should send him a message to apologize, or just write an email to try to salvage things. If I lost this collaboration, how was I supposed to face the projects that came next? Those thoughts surged in like a tide, crushing the breath out of me. In the end, I got up, turned on my computer, and wrote a carefully worded email, revising it over and over until three in the morning, before finally hesitating and pressing send.

I was sitting by the window in a café, sunlight spilling across the table through the glass, while a small speaker beside me played gentle jazz. The coffee cup beside my hand had left faint fingerprints. I had ordered a latte, but after just one sip, I found the warmth already gone. The client was giving his feedback on my proposal. He frowned slightly and lowered his head to leaf through the design draft I had handed over. “Hmm, this part feels a bit repetitive. It doesn’t seem very original.” His tone was calm, but in my mind, a warning bell was ringing. His words were like a blade, stabbing straight into my chest, and my breathing immediately became shallow and quick. “Re, repetitive? Not original?” My throat went dry, and my voice sounded slightly unsteady. I forced out a smile, trying to hide my inner panic, but under the table my fingertips had already clenched into a tight fist.

“We need something more distinctive. This direction still doesn’t fit our brand positioning well enough,” he continued. I nodded, desperately searching my mind for a way to push back, but I was also afraid that the more I explained, the worse it would get. I could hear my heartbeat growing faster and faster, my breathing becoming uneven, and a faint stabbing pain in my stomach. The words before my eyes gradually blurred; all I could see was the slight movement of the paper as he turned the page. “Okay, I understand. I’ll revise the direction.” I tried my best to keep my tone calm, but inside I had already fallen into a whirlpool of confusion and shame.

After I got home, I sat at my desk and stared at the design draft on my screen. The conversation from the café kept replaying in my mind, as if it had been burned deep into my memory. “It’s too ordinary. How could I make something this bad?” I kept blaming myself over and over, even feeling that I never should have taken on this project in the first place. I grabbed a pen and scribbled frantically on paper, trying to find something I could be satisfied with, but the more I drew, the more out of control it became, and every stroke made me feel worse. In the end, I threw down the pen and collapsed into my chair, feeling as though a certain rigid, chronic fatigue in my body had seeped all the way through me.

The next day, I forced myself to get up early and turn on my computer to start designing again. I tried to think about the client’s needs from different angles while also reviewing my own strengths, telling myself that no matter how embarrassing yesterday had been, today I had to keep doing something. Although my emotions hadn’t fully settled yet, I gradually found some of my normal creative rhythm again. When I resubmitted the proposal, I still felt uneasy, but at least I wasn’t on the verge of completely falling apart.

I was sitting in the corner of a café, the air filled with the rich aroma of coffee, while the voices around me blended into a steady hum. My friend sat across from me, excitedly sharing her recent work achievements. Her eyes were bright, her voice full, and I felt myself gradually being pushed to the edge. “What have you been up to lately?” she asked, and I immediately grew tense, my heart starting to race. I cleared my throat and replied, “Oh, I’ve been doing some content creation, nothing special.” She nodded and then went on with her story, as if my words were only a passing breeze. I tried to keep smiling, but inside I was filled with unease and self-doubt. Why do I always feel ignored? Am I not good enough?

I noticed myself beginning to overanalyze every microexpression on her face, trying to find signs that she was dissatisfied or uninterested. Her brows furrowed slightly, and my heart sank at once. I started wondering whether something I said had gone wrong. My palms were a little sweaty, and the tension spread through my stomach. I made an effort to respond positively, pretending to be calm, but inside I was already ruminating. Did she think I was boring? Would this meeting leave her with a negative impression of me?

We talked about other topics, and I responded distractedly, afraid I might say the wrong thing. When she mentioned our mutual friend, I felt ignored once again. “She said on the phone that everything’s fine and that she’s been doing pretty well lately,” my friend said. I nodded, but the heaviness in my heart only grew more pronounced. Is my presence just too weak? Am I always being forgotten? I began imagining myself being abandoned, and the thought brought a sharp ache, as if I had lost other people’s recognition of me.

When it was time to say goodbye, I forced out a smile. “Let’s hang out again next time.” She smiled back, but I still couldn’t shake that sense of disappointment. As I walked out of the café, night had already begun to fall, and the lights on the street glowed a warm yellow. I tried to recall the details of the meeting, but realized with alarm that I had mostly been catastrophizing. Back home, my thoughts kept spinning, repeatedly playing out the worst possibilities. I lay in bed, filled with unresolved worries, exhausted and powerless. A few days later, I still couldn’t help sending her a message to make sure she really wasn’t angry. She replied, “Of course not, you’re overthinking it.” I felt relieved, but also ashamed all at once. Why am I always this sensitive?

In a café I often go to in the city, rain was falling in a light, steady drizzle outside, blurring the view on the glass window. I sat by the window with a cup of hot coffee in my hands, enjoying the aroma of the coffee beans mixed with the damp smell in the air. The gentle music in my ears drowned out the sound of the rain outside, but I still felt a little irritable. I kept staring at my phone screen, checking the message from my friend, who said she was almost there, but the appointed time had already passed. My mind started wandering—had something happened to her? Or did she not want to come after all?

Just as I was running through all sorts of possibilities in my head, the café doorbell rang. I looked up and saw her finally walk in, wearing an apologetic expression. Her coat was a little wet, and raindrops were falling onto the floor. As soon as she sat down, she said, “Sorry, there was terrible traffic on the way.”

“It’s okay,” I replied, trying to keep my tone light. In truth, I was a little annoyed, but I also realized it was my own nervousness at work. My heartbeat quickened a little, and my palms grew slightly sweaty.

We ordered some snacks and talked about recent life and work. She told me some amusing things that had happened at the company, and I smiled and said, “Looks like you’ve been doing pretty well lately.” But inside, I couldn’t help wondering if she was hinting that I should face life more positively.

“What do you think?” she suddenly asked. I froze for a moment, distracted by my own self-criticism just now. “Oh, I think it’s good,” I hurriedly adjusted myself and rejoined the conversation.

As we talked, I noticed that I kept repeatedly trying to read her tone, afraid I might miss some hint of dissatisfaction or unhappiness. Yet throughout the conversation, her smile and relaxed manner put me much more at ease. We talked about a movie we were going to see that evening, and I let down my guard and began to genuinely enjoy the meeting.

That night when I got home, I washed my face in front of the mirror and could still smell the coffee. My mood had already eased quite a bit. I realized that my overinterpretation and the unhappiness in my heart were all irrationally triggered by a fear of being abandoned. Although this emotion always surfaced unconsciously, I understood that it wasn’t the whole truth—just my brain’s habitual reaction.

A few days later, I sent my friend a message suggesting we meet again next week, and there was a little less anxiety in my heart and a little more anticipation.

The café air was filled with the aroma of baking, and sunlight streamed through the windows onto the tabletops, casting warm patches of light. A friend and I were sitting in a corner; she was looking down and fiddling with her phone, while I stirred the cappuccino in my cup with a spoon. As I stirred, the milk foam rose, circling around and around, making me feel somewhat uneasy inside. Soft music drifted into my ears, and the conversations around us seemed to blur together. I tried my best to relax, but I still couldn’t help feeling my heartbeat quicken.

“Do you know,” I said, “I think we should get together like this more often.” I spoke while trying hard to find the right words, not wanting to seem awkward in conversation. She looked up, smiled slightly, and nodded in agreement.

“But,” she went on, “the project you mentioned last time, I think it may still need a little more time to be polished. Otherwise, we might run into some trouble.”

Her tone was casual, but a string of possibilities suddenly flashed through my mind: Had I not done well enough before? Did she think I wasn’t professional enough? I gave a stiff smile, feeling a wave of regret and my stomach beginning to turn a little.

“Mm, maybe,” I replied unconsciously. Although I felt somewhat unhappy, I still did my best to keep up a calm outward appearance. The warm light in the room seemed to become somewhat glaring, and I could feel my palms sweating slightly, barely suppressing the urge to argue back immediately.
