The topic quickly shifted to everyday trivialities, and I listened absentmindedly, trying not to let my emotions show. She seemed to notice my unease and asked softly, “Are you okay?”

“I’m fine. Maybe I’m just overthinking it,” I said with a smile, hoping this response would bring the subtle tension to an end. She patted my shoulder, showing understanding and support, and I felt a little relieved inside.

After leaving the café, a breeze carrying the fresh scent of plants from the street came over me. Although the emotional turbulence in my heart had subsided, I still couldn’t help replaying the conversation over and over in my mind, trying to find where I might have gone wrong, or whether she had really been hinting at something. It left me feeling somewhat tired, as if these thoughts had never stopped.

The next day, thinking back on it, I felt that perhaps it had only been a trivial little matter. I told myself not to overinterpret casual remarks from friends next time, but deep down that sensitivity still remained.

Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains, casting a few slender beams across the study floor and mottling the stacks of manuscripts and magazines with light. The air carried the faint mingled scent unique to wooden furniture, and the old books on the shelf gave off a musty fragrance of aged paper. I sat by the desk, where several yellowed notebooks and an old laptop lay. As my fingertips turned the pages gently, I could feel the rough texture of the paper; the edges of each page curled slightly, making them seem marked by time.

I picked up an old draft. Its title had been written in black marker, the handwriting somewhat sloppy. “This article was submitted to a magazine back then, but it was later rejected,” I murmured to myself, not even sure why I remembered it so clearly. I flipped to the last page, where the reviewer’s comments were printed at the bottom: “The theme still needs further refinement; the presentation is too subjective.” Those words made my chest sink slightly, as if a sore spot had been prodded again. But then I shook my head gently, trying to tell myself that it was all a long time ago and not worth dwelling on anymore.

The desk lamp beside me was an old model repaired last year, with a small crack in the lampshade. I pulled open the drawer and took out a fountain pen; the barrel was still smooth and warm to the touch. I began listing some possible themes in my notebook anew: one about the loneliness of the city at night, another a reflection on internet culture. I muttered to myself, “These themes still sound a little vague—maybe it would be better to approach them from a different angle?”

The chirping of cicadas drifted in from outside, monotonous yet especially clear. I was a little distracted and turned my gaze out the window, where I saw a few sparrows hopping on the balcony railing. Their feathers were somewhat tousled, as if they were struggling against the midsummer heat. Suddenly, I felt a slight tightening in my stomach, perhaps because I had sat all morning without moving much. I stood up, walked to the kettle, poured myself a glass of water, and tasted a faint coolness in it.

In the corner of the study stood an old upright fan. I switched it on, and the mechanical hum began. The breeze brushed across my face, and I felt myself gradually relax, as though I could shake off the vague tension from before. I sat back down in my chair and sorted the scattered drafts into categories, putting them into a folder. Throughout the whole process, I tried to keep my attention focused and not let the unnecessary self-doubt in my mind spread unchecked.

Time seemed to pass quickly. The floor clock ticked on, and it was already nearing evening. I stood up and pulled back the curtains; the light became gentler, the shadows indoors slowly receding, while the sky outside took on a faint orange hue. An inexplicable sense of calm arose in me, like the small accomplishment that comes after finishing a task. It might not have been spectacular, but it gave me a solid, reassuring sense of security.

That night, I drank a cup of mint tea and didn’t touch the drafts that had already been filed away. The room was quiet, and the fan was still turning. I stood on the balcony and watched the sky gradually darken, while a trace of unease in my heart slowly dispersed like that. It was just an ordinary stretch of days, a peaceful time.

I wandered alone along the streets in the center of the city. Neon lights flashed by the roadside, and the air was filled with a mix of coffee and the greasy smoke from street stalls. I was afraid my comments weren’t accurate enough, and I even began to wonder whether they were truly listening to my opinion. I noticed that one person’s gaze seemed rather serious, and I couldn’t help but start ruminating over past embarrassing moments caused by speaking inappropriately. I struggled to control these emotions, while a faint fear in my heart crawled upward like vines. Time passed quickly, and before long, my friend began introducing her other works, giving me a chance to try hard to relax.

When I left the exhibition, my feelings were somewhat complicated. After returning home, I kept reflecting on my performance in the gallery, wondering whether I had said anything awkward. A few days later, I saw my friend’s post on social media. She happily documented the exhibition and mentioned the lively discussions there, which gave me a little comfort. Although anxiety often lingered in my heart, with my friend’s support I was able to gradually let go of those unnecessary worries.

I stood in the center of the new bookstore, the walls around me still being plastered, the air thick with the pungent smell of gypsum and building materials. Sunlight poured through the enormous glass windows onto the floor, where light and shadow intertwined like a half-finished painting. The irritation in my heart kept growing, as if every corner were mocking my unease. The construction foreman walked over and handed me a progress report. “This section of the wall needs to be adjusted again, otherwise it will affect the overall result.” His tone was polite, but I couldn’t help tensing up at it, as if he were implying that I had made some serious flaw. “Are you sure?” I asked, my voice higher than I expected, carrying an unconscious defensiveness. My heartbeat quickened, and fine beads of sweat broke out on my forehead. The foreman gave a slight nod. “Yes, it needs to be redesigned.” His answer filled me with a deep despair, like a rising tide, and I could hardly breathe. In my mind, I began to dwell on several recent misjudgments, as if each one were mocking my clumsiness. I thought of the construction delay last month caused by a budgeting mistake; back then, I had also wanted to strike first by attacking myself, to avoid even greater shame. I felt a slight cramp in my stomach, and my hands involuntarily clenched the report. “We’ll handle it as soon as possible, please rest assured,” the foreman continued, trying to comfort me. Yet my inner monologue kept questioning me: “What if this mistake causes the entire project to fail?” My chest gradually tightened, and my breathing grew rapid. After leaving the bookstore, I drove home and tried to calm myself by organizing the bookshelves. Hours passed, yet the smell of plaster still seemed to linger at the tip of my nose. Over the next few days, I repeatedly checked the construction plans, hoping to find what had been overlooked. I dared not relax for even a moment, fearing that I would make another mistake in front of others. Every late night, I struggled to fall asleep, my mind revolving around worries about the project’s outcome. I kept confirming what I had done right and what I had done wrong.

Sunlight poured through the café’s floor-to-ceiling windows, as if it were trying to heat the entire floor. I was sitting by the window, with the Americano I had just ordered beside me, steam rising straight up. The aroma of coffee was fragrant, but all I could feel was my stomach churning. She was sitting across from me, my proposal document spread out in front of her. She read it while frowning, and with every tightening of her brow, it felt like a needle stabbing my heart.

“I think there’s a problem with this part,” her voice was clear, even a little harsh. “The idea is good, but it doesn’t quite fit the target audience, does it? And this section of the text probably needs to be more concise.”

I tightened my grip on the coffee cup, trying hard to stay calm. “Mm, I see what you mean. Maybe I wrote it a bit... all over the place.”

She looked up at me. “It’s not that it’s completely bad. It just seems a little unstructured at the moment. And also... well, the overall framework needs to be clearer.”

“The framework needs to be clearer?” Countless voices suddenly flooded my mind. Did she think I wasn’t professional enough? Was she implying I wasn’t capable? Was she... I could feel my heartbeat speeding up, my palms breaking into a sweat. I stared at her lips moving, but I couldn’t hear what she said next.

“What do you think?” Her tone sounded casual, but in my ears it sounded like the order of an evaluation. I jolted back to attention, realizing I had drifted off, and hurriedly answered, “I... I think you’re right. I’ll...” The words caught in my throat, and I didn’t know how to continue.

The coffee wasn’t as hot anymore. I mechanically picked up the cup and took a sip, the bitterness making my stomach even more unsettled. I nodded, pretending to take her comments seriously. But as my hand wrote in the notebook, my mind kept repeating, over and over: She thinks you’re not good enough, doesn’t she? Maybe she already regrets working with you.

An hour later, she left. I sat there motionless, staring blankly at the now-cold coffee. I kept chewing over her words, even just the one phrase she used to describe the problem—“the structure isn’t very clear.” I started asking myself: have all these people realized I’m not actually as smart as they think? Does my idea really have any value? Have I been pretending all along?

It felt as if my heart had been wrapped in a thick layer of ash. I began thinking back to all those moments when I had been rejected, like a psychological film that refused to stop. That feeling trapped me until the café waiter came over to remind me they were closing.

When I got home, I collapsed onto the sofa and opened the proposal document. Her comments were clear and straightforward, but I was stuck in the mud of self-attack and couldn’t move. I kept thinking: if I revise these parts, will she be satisfied? If she isn’t satisfied, does that mean I really am incapable?

When I woke up the next day, my eyes felt sore. Even though I tried hard to calm myself down, a faint self-doubt still lingered in my mind. I looked at the computer screen; the document was still on last night’s page, the cursor blinking, as if mocking my incompetence.

I was standing in that semi-open restaurant, holding a cup of coffee that had already gone cold. Around me, people were chatting; the tables were covered with snacks and drinks, and the warm yellow light fell across everyone’s faces, making them all look relaxed—everyone except me. My stomach had already started to ache faintly, and my palms were beginning to sweat, but I still forced out a smile and pretended to be intently listening to what the people around me were discussing.

“Your recent project is pretty interesting,” I heard a peer say to me. I looked up at him; he was a creator I had followed on social media before. His tone seemed casual, but my mind exploded with a bang. Was he putting me down? Was he implying my content wasn’t good enough? Or was he testing my reaction?

“Mm… it’s okay, just some ordinary creative work,” I replied softly. My throat felt clogged with something, my voice so hoarse I could barely hear myself. “But traffic has been a bit low lately.” I didn’t know whether I was saying this to myself or trying to save face.

“Oh, you really do need to improve a bit more.” His words seemed to hit a nerve. I froze in place, staring at the expression on his face—a faint smile, as if he were teasing me, or perhaps just giving friendly advice. I fought back the sudden pounding of my heart and tried to look unaffected, but a voice inside me was screaming: “He’s belittling you! They all look down on you!”

What happened next seemed driven by pure instinct. I heard myself raise my voice and say, “Maybe you think you’re better than me, but at least my content was made by me alone, not thrown together by a team.” My voice wasn’t loud, but the people around us all fell silent. He looked at me, his expression stiffening. “I… didn’t mean it that way.” His voice also dropped, and I stood there at a loss, as if I had spent all my strength.

The air instantly turned heavy, and my face burned bright red. The few people nearby exchanged glances, then lowered their heads and went back to drinking, pretending nothing had happened. My heart was pounding so hard it felt like it might burst out of my chest, and the ringing in my ears made it nearly impossible to hear anything around me. I picked up my bag from the table, lowered my head, and hurried toward the exit.

The moment I left the restaurant, a cold wind hit me in the face, but it did not calm me down. My mind kept replaying what had just happened. Why did I say those things? Why couldn’t I hold it in? Did he think I was crazy? What would the others think of me? I crouched at the entrance to the alley, my stomach twisting in so much pain it felt knotted into a ball, and tears began to stream down despite myself. A passerby glanced at me, and I immediately stood up, pretending I was fine.

When I got home that night, I curled up in the corner of the sofa, phone in hand, but I didn’t dare log into any social media app. I was afraid to see whether they were already talking about me in their feeds. That feeling of being isolated was just like when I was a kid and my classmates would deliberately ignore me. I stayed awake until dawn, endlessly replaying every detail of the night and blaming myself over and over—if only I had shut up earlier, none of this would have happened.

The restaurant was filled with the sounds of conversation and clinking tableware, and the chandelier overhead cast a gently swaying warm glow. The eight of us were seated around a long table, and most people were enthusiastically discussing the networking event we had just attended. I could feel my heart pounding against my chest, as if it might burst out at any moment. Sweat slowly began to bead on my forehead, and my hands turned cold. “Are you okay? You seem a little unwell,” said colleague A beside me, gently touching my hand. Halfway through the meal, I finally couldn’t bear it anymore. I stood up and said to everyone, “Sorry, something came up at home, I have to leave early.” I could feel their eyes on me, but I didn’t dare meet them. When I got home, I collapsed onto the sofa and tossed my phone aside. My mind kept circling the same thoughts: Why do I always get misunderstood by everyone? Am I really not good enough? I started deliberately checking my colleagues’ social media, trying to confirm whether they had said anything behind my back, but found nothing.

A few days later, I didn’t even dare go have lunch with everyone, afraid of hearing something similar again and being forced to wonder whether I wasn’t accepted. Every time I thought about that conversation that night, I couldn’t help but feel like a failure, unable even to handle basic social interactions properly.

I felt the air in the studio was as thick as fog, pressing down on me until I could barely breathe. The clock on the wall ticked away, as if mocking my nerves. The coffee cup on the table gave off a faint warmth, while my palms had already begun to sweat and tremble slightly. My partner had just thrown out a harsh remark, and the coldness mixed into his tone cut me to the quick: “You’re always like this. Why do you always have to imagine the worst?”

Inside, I was full of anger and shame, as if an old wound had been torn open in public. Knowing full well I shouldn’t react that way, I still couldn’t help but strike back first: “If you would just listen to me seriously instead of criticizing me all the time, maybe we’d work together better!” I could feel my heartbeat quickening, a buzzing ringing in my ears. I kept telling myself not to lose my composure here. I struggled to hide my vulnerability, as if my body no longer belonged to me, rigid yet betraying my unease.

The cold glint in my partner’s eyes made me feel there was nowhere to hide, as though I were nothing more than a useless piece of trash. “Fine, suit yourself. You never can change how others see you, can you?” Every word he said was like a blade stabbing into my heart. I fought desperately to hold myself back, not letting tears burst from my eyes, while my mouth tasted the bitterness of sweat.

After the argument ended, I sat motionless in my chair, staring at the painting on the wall, feeling an inexplicable emptiness inside. I thought of many similar scenes from the past, those feelings of being abandoned lingering like a shadow. That night, back home, I collapsed onto the sofa exhausted, replaying every detail of the argument. I began to doubt my own abilities, to wonder whether I was even worthy of respect. I tried to write down what had happened that day, hoping that putting it into words would ease my unease, but that cold voice still filled my mind.

A few nights later, I still couldn’t shake off the shadow cast by that argument. Every time I closed my eyes, those piercing words echoed in my ears. I began to feel intensely anxious about future collaborations, terrified of going through that same feeling of being abandoned and questioned all over again.

It was already very late at night. The street outside the window was almost completely silent, with only the occasional flash of headlights passing by. I sat at my desk, my fingertips gradually growing cold on the keyboard. The only light in the room came from the computer screen, its glow casting a harsh glare on the wall. My partner had just told me over a video call that he was dissatisfied with my work, his tone slightly impatient: “Can you think more about the direction of this project? We need content with more impact.” I nodded and smiled, trying to keep my voice relaxed. “I’ll adjust it again. No problem.”

But after I hung up, my heartbeat suddenly quickened, as if something were pressing down on me. My fingertips tingled, my body broke out in an uncontrollable sweat, and my stomach churned. I kept replaying every detail of the conversation, my heart aching faintly. Was he losing patience with me? Had I made another mistake? These thoughts circled endlessly in my mind.

“Why am I always like this...” I muttered softly, trying to use my voice to wake myself up a little. I began rummaging through past failures in my mind, and all the embarrassing, disappointing moments came flooding back one after another, so vivid they seemed magnified under a lens. I couldn’t bear this intense panic, and I didn’t even dare look at the computer screen anymore.

I took a deep breath, trying to calm the turmoil inside me, but the rhythm of my heartbeat still refused to settle. I rocked back and forth in my office chair, and tears slipped down involuntarily. I wanted to talk, but I didn’t know who to confide in, as if there were no one in the world who could understand me. Suddenly, I sprang up, walked to the balcony, and opened the window to let the cold air hit me full in the face. The chill eased my confusion a little, and only then did the thoughts in my mind gradually begin to subside.

A few days later, I was still hiding in this apartment, continuing to work on the project. I gave myself more time and tried to revise it again and again, but the unease inside me still would not fade. I knew this state would last for a while, and I also understood that I would continue to feel anxious and afraid of every comment and piece of feedback. Every late night felt like a moment witnessing my own flaws, and all I could do was hide this vulnerability as best I could and keep moving forward.

When the glass door swung open, I was enveloped by the aroma of coffee beans. Sunlight poured through the floor-to-ceiling window by the café, and the clock pointed to two in the afternoon. I saw the client seated across from me—wearing a dark blue suit, elegant in manner. I had already read his profile three times, so familiar with it that I could even recite his past interviews, yet that didn’t make me feel any more confident. My palms were already soaked with sweat, and I was afraid he would notice when I shook his hand. As my heart raced, I took a deep breath, trying to make myself look calmer.

“Hello, I’m…” Before I could even give my full name, he had already stood up and given a slight nod. “Hello, please have a seat.” His voice was low and composed, which only made me more flustered. I felt like my own voice was trembling; I kept licking my chapped lips, trying hard not to let my eyes dart around.

Once we got to the main topic, he asked some questions about my creative background. I bit down hard on the inner edge of my lower lip, trying to avoid pausing for too long, but I also ended up adding too many details in places that weren’t appropriate. For example, when he said, “This is a unique and promising angle in the market,” I instinctively replied, “But I haven’t fully verified the data for this part yet, so there may be issues…” As I spoke, I realized my tone sounded like I was undermining myself. He paused, looked up at me, and only after a brief silence did he continue.

Throughout the entire process, I kept trying to read some sign of approval from his micro-expressions. Did the slight twitch at the corner of his eye mean dissatisfaction? Was he looking down to reply on his phone because he no longer wanted to listen? The more I thought about it, the more confused I became. It felt as if a dozen voices were shouting at once in my head, making it hard to focus. Halfway through, he mentioned something that needed further revision. I hurriedly replied, “Okay, I understand this part isn’t good enough yet. I’ll adjust it again.” The moment those words left my mouth, I began to blame myself, feeling like I had come across as completely incompetent.

In the end, he briefly summed up the meeting: “Thank you for your time. Let’s stop here for today. I’ll think it over some more.” Then he got up and left. I watched helplessly as his figure disappeared through the doorway. It felt as if something was pressing hard on my chest, and I didn’t even have time to ask how I should follow up next. My stomach felt vaguely sour, and I knew anxiety was at work again.

After I got home, I kept replaying every word and every detail from today. Especially that line—“there may be issues”—it looped through my mind dozens of times, and the more I thought about it, the more humiliating it felt. I couldn’t help but open my phone and send him a brief apology message, but before sending it, I spent another twenty minutes repeatedly revising the wording. Although he had said, “Thank you for your time,” I kept wondering whether that was just a polite rejection. Until late at night, my mind still circled around questions like “Where did I do badly?” and “What is his true evaluation of me?” unable to stop.

The lights in the conference room were a little glaring. I sat on one side of the long table, clutching my notebook tightly with both hands. Inside was the content concept proposal I had spent a week preparing. My supervisor sat across from me, his gaze calmly sweeping over the projection screen. The whir of the desktop computer’s fan was especially harsh, and every time I spoke, the air in the room seemed to grow heavier.

“Hmm, isn’t this part a bit too idealistic?” my supervisor finally said. His voice was low, but his tone remained flat. “Have you considered the cost? And the difficulty of execution.” As he spoke, he flipped through my document. I nodded, my lips dry, trying to explain my design logic. But my speech suddenly sped up, like flooring the gas in a traffic jam, and I even became somewhat incoherent. His brow furrowed slightly, and cold sweat broke out in my palms.

“I understand what you’re trying to do, but we can’t take on too much risk with this project,” he said at last. The task list on my computer screen blurred into a haze, and my heartbeat was still racing, like a small animal cornered against a wall. I tried to calm myself down, but that feeling of being rejected held me in a vice, leaving me breathless.

I began avoiding taking the initiative to talk to him, afraid of feeling that same sense of frustration again. Every time project discussions came up, I forced myself to prepare even more, but at the same time I was afraid that I still wasn’t good enough, afraid that others would discover my shortcomings.

I was staring at the coffee cup on the table, the warmth of it still lingering on my fingertips, yet my body felt as cold as if it were soaked in ice water. My friend across from me frowned and said quietly, “Why would you think that? I didn’t mean that at all.” Her words struck my chest like a blunt blow, and all the air seemed to vanish at once. Every night, I tried to calm myself, but my mind kept ruminating over these trivial details. For several days, I couldn’t shake off the inner doubt and unease, desperately needing to know whether my behavior had truly annoyed anyone.

I sat on the sofa in the corner. The café wasn’t brightly lit, but the wooden tables and chairs, along with the little potted plants scattered around, created a warm atmosphere. Several abstract paintings hung on the wall opposite me, and I stared at one chaotic splash of colors, thinking it looked exactly like my mood at that moment. My palms were sweating. Although the fingertips of my right hand were wrapped around the cup, even the chill of the iced latte couldn’t bring my temperature down. “He’s only five minutes late; it’s no big deal,” I kept telling myself, but my heartbeat only grew faster, as if it were about to pound through my chest.

He finally arrived, taller than I’d imagined, wearing a very formal suit, which instantly made me feel out of place in my jeans and loose sweater. He smiled and said, “Sorry, traffic on the way.” I nodded, not knowing how to respond, while only one thought echoed in my head: “Do I seem unprofessional enough?”

He ordered a single-origin pour-over, then sat down across from me and started talking about the project. I tried to keep smiling, but my attention kept drifting to little details. His brow would occasionally furrow slightly, and it felt like being pricked by a needle. “Does he think my proposal isn’t good enough?” My breathing became shallow and quick, and my hand began to unconsciously pick at my nails.

“Didn’t you fail to take the target audience’s needs into account here?” He pointed to a slide on my PPT. His tone was very flat, but to me it sounded like unvarnished criticism. I nodded instinctively, then quickly added, “Yes, I didn’t think it through enough. This part still needs to be adjusted.” My voice was a little shaky; even I could hear it. I forced out a smile, but the muscles in my face felt frighteningly stiff.

I hardly relaxed throughout the whole process. He kept asking questions, and my answers grew shorter and shorter, until I even started repeating myself. A slight cramp in my stomach made me feel even worse. Several times I tried to sneak in a deep breath, but no matter what I did, I couldn’t calm down.

At the end, he said, “You can make some adjustments when you get back. I’m looking forward to your revised version.” His expression didn’t seem malicious at all, but I still couldn’t help adding, “I’ll do my best to revise it. Next time I definitely won’t disappoint you.” Hearing that, he froze for a moment, then politely nodded and walked out.

I picked up the iced latte, now completely melted, and took a sip. The coffee had turned unbearably bitter. I began replaying the entire conversation in my head, over and over, fixating on the image of him frowning, while his voice seemed to repeat every word from earlier in my ears again and again. “Did I leave a bad impression?” “Will he think I’m completely unreliable?”

That night I barely slept at all. I went over the proposal from beginning to end several times, finding something wrong on every page, revising it again and again, only for it to seem worse the more I looked at it. My stomach pain gradually worsened, and it wasn’t until dawn that I finally drifted into a daze and fell asleep. When I woke up the next day, I felt completely drained, with dark circles under my eyes and a throbbing head.

Over the next few days, I kept trying to convince myself that he wasn’t actually that put off by my proposal, but whenever I remembered his expression, it felt as if an invisible hand had clamped around my heart. I even started worrying: would he put me on a “never work with again” list?

When I walked into the gallery, my heart was pounding. The walls were covered with the work I had poured my heart and soul into over the past few months, and the white lights shining on each painting made them stand out all the more. While I tried to keep smiling, I kept rehearsing the worst possible outcomes in my head, imagining someone criticizing my work. Among the crowd moving back and forth, I noticed a couple stopping in front of one of my favorite paintings, speaking to each other in hushed voices, their expressions utterly unreadable. Though I couldn’t hear what they were saying, I could almost feel their disappointment and dissatisfaction. My stomach began to ache faintly, and my heartbeat quickened a few beats.

“Your work has a very personal style,” came a familiar voice from behind me. It was one of my friends. “But maybe the style is a little too distinctive?” Her words drifted lightly, yet landed on my chest with the weight of a stone. I forced out a smile and replied, “Is that so? I thought it would be a bit more accessible.” But inside, a little theater had already begun to play: I saw everyone nodding along with her criticism, each painting seeming so out of place.

After a while, my palms were sweaty, and my breathing started to quicken as well. I made an excuse that I needed some fresh air and stepped out onto the terrace, hoping to get away from the tension inside. The night breeze brushed gently across my face, and I kept trying to tell myself that everything was fine, but the unease in my heart lingered like some stubborn shadow that would not go away.

After the exhibition ended, I went home and lay in bed, still unable to calm down. My mind kept replaying my friend’s comment, as well as those conversations I couldn’t hear. I began to question myself: Was I really too self-centered? Did no one actually like these paintings?

A few days later, my emotions had settled a little, but that inner unease still crept in from time to time. I read a book about art, trying to find new inspiration, and made an effort to convince myself to accept diverse opinions. Even so, I couldn’t help linking this experience to past failures, repeatedly dwelling on those possible shortcomings.

The cold wind hit me full in the face, and I pulled my scarf tighter, but the biting chill still seeped through my coat and struck my skin. The gathering had just ended, and I was walking home with a group of friends, the neon lights along the street flickering with a cold glow. I could hear my friends chatting and laughing beside me, but their voices seemed very far away. My mind kept replaying the little details from the dinner table over and over.

“You’ve been kind of quiet today,” one friend suddenly turned and looked at me, with a hint of probing in their tone.

“Nothing,” I forced out a smile. “I’m just a little tired.”

In fact, I wasn’t tired. I just couldn’t ignore what had happened earlier. From the moment we sat down, I noticed that one friend—we had known each other for ten years—had hardly said a word to me the whole time. They were only talking to others, and even the occasional glance in my direction carried a kind of coldness I couldn’t describe. It made me feel like I was invisible.

“Are they mad at me?” The thought pierced me like a needle, and my heart started racing. I tried to recall our recent interactions, afraid I might have said something offensive without realizing it. But no matter how I thought about it, I couldn’t find a reasonable answer.

In the middle of the gathering, that friend stood up to go to the bathroom. As they passed by me, they only said, “Excuse me,” in a tone without a trace of warmth, a kind of almost mechanical politeness. That made me even more certain that the problem had to be me.

On the way home, I couldn’t help asking, my voice a little sharp: “Can I ask you all something? Do you think I did something wrong today?”

A few people froze. One friend hesitated before saying, “No, not at all. It was fine. Why are you asking all of a sudden?”

“But I feel like you all were... like you didn’t really want to talk to me.” My voice trembled a little, and though I tried to suppress it, my anxiety still showed through.

“Are you overthinking this?” another person said with a smile, waving it off. “Everyone was acting normally. Why wouldn’t we want to talk to you?”

“Don’t brush me off.” I suddenly raised my voice, feeling as if my chest were filled with some heat I couldn’t release, and tears surged up uncontrollably. “Do you all find me annoying? Do you not want to be friends with me anymore?”

The air went instantly quiet. Everyone stopped walking and looked at me with expressions mixed with shock and helplessness.

“No one thinks that!” one friend finally broke the silence. “Why do you always have to make such a big deal out of the smallest things? It’s really hard to respond to that.”

The words stabbed into my chest like a knife. I stood there awkwardly, feeling like a complete failure. My vision blurred, and my nose was filled with the dusty smell carried by the wind. I muttered “Sorry,” then turned and jogged away.

When I got home, I locked myself in my bedroom, leaving the lights off, just sitting on the floor with my knees pulled to my chest. Tears kept falling, and my breathing trembled slightly. I kept replaying those words in my mind, every one of them like a heavy blow. “Always making a big deal out of small things”? Is that really what I’m like? I stared at the cold wall, my stomach churning violently, feeling myself sink, unable to stop.

A few days later, I hardly dared to reach out to those friends first, afraid that my behavior that night had completely ruined everything. When they sent me messages, I only replied with a few perfunctory emojis, afraid they would see how uneasy I was. Deep down, there was always a voice reminding me: they’re only contacting you out of obligation; they don’t even want to see you.

The shop was filled with the smell of old wood and a faint scent of paint. My fingers lightly glided over the keys of an old piano. The owner, a somewhat haggard middle-aged man, was chatting idly in the corner. I tried playing a few melodies, but the tension inside me was like a taut string; my heartbeat quickened and my fingertips grew slightly sweaty. I always felt as though the owner’s gaze was sizing me up, and a voice in my head began to question, “Am I disturbing them? Will my playing be looked down on?” “Do you like this piano?” The owner’s voice interrupted my thoughts. He came out from behind the counter, smiling warmly. “Uh, yes, but I’m not sure whether its tone suits me,” I replied, unconsciously lowering my head, my voice becoming faint and hesitant. The owner went on, “Its tone is very unique; many musicians speak highly of it.” I nodded, trying to focus on the keys, yet uneasy thoughts began to surface in my mind: “Am I drawing too much attention here? If I can’t play beautiful music, what will they think of me?” I strongly felt a slight cramping pain in my stomach, and this discomfort forced me to stop playing for a moment. The owner seemed to notice my unease and gently patted my shoulder. “It’s okay; music always needs to be felt slowly.” His tone was gentle, trying to calm my inner anxiety. I managed a smile and looked up. “Thank you, I’m just not in the best shape today.” The owner’s tolerance made me relax a little, but that lingering sense of abandonment still followed me like a shadow. That afternoon, after I left the music shop, I kept replaying our interaction in my mind. Walking home, the noise of the street made me feel a little exhausted, and I began to blame myself for always falling into this kind of needless tension. At night, I sat on the sofa trying to relax, vaguely aware of the tightness in my shoulders; the fear of being rejected still would not leave me. A few days later, I began to try soothing my emotions by immersing myself in music, hoping the rhythm of the music would carry my anxiety away.

The rain gently tapped against the window as I sat in a conference room chair, facing a group of colleagues. The lighting in the room was soft, but my heartbeat was steadily quickening. I connected my laptop to the projector and began presenting my creative proposal. Although I tried hard to stay calm, a sense of unease surged deep inside me, as if every slight expression and movement from my colleagues were judging me. My voice echoed in my ears, too rushed, and I kept asking myself: would they approve of my proposal?

When I introduced a new design concept, I noticed one colleague frown slightly. Though it might have been nothing more than his habit, I could not stop imagining that he was rejecting me. “Do you think this color combination is appropriate?” My voice had nearly lost its confidence, and I silently worried that my choice might not be well received. “Hmm, isn’t it a bit too bright?” he replied. My stomach instantly tightened, as if his words had just negated all my efforts.

I strained to continue the presentation, yet I kept slipping into rehearsals of failure in my mind. My palms were already sweating, and I discreetly wiped them on my pants several times. In the end, as I wrapped up, I tried to seek affirmation and asked, “What do you all think of this plan? Would anyone like to offer any further suggestions?” My voice still carried unease.

After the meeting, I returned to my desk feeling as though a damp cloud was pressing on my chest, lingering without dispersing. Sitting down in front of my computer, I began to ruminate over every detail of the presentation. I kept replaying whether I had been too nervous, whether I should have responded better to that colleague’s question. That night, lying in bed, with the rain still falling softly outside the window, I could not fall asleep. Was the situation really as bad as I thought? If the proposal were not adopted, what would I lose? Such worries kept washing over me, and I could not break free from them.

A few days later, the company officially announced that my proposal had been accepted, and the leadership highly praised my creativity. This made me feel somewhat relieved. Although things ultimately turned out well, I began to realize that when I am tense, I tend to overinterpret things and end up constraining myself. I need to learn to trust myself and not let negative signals that may not even exist hold back my progress.

In the dimly lit bar, warm yellow light fell softly across the mahogany tabletop, and the air was filled with the mellow scent of alcohol and a faint trace of tobacco. In my ears, an impromptu jazz performance was playing; the gentle saxophone blended with the deep bass, as if drawing me into another dimension of time. I sat in a corner by the window, while the headlights on the street outside flickered like stars. I lightly ran my hand over the cold glass in an effort to relax.

“Do you like this kind of music too?” the stranger at the neighboring table asked softly, his voice sounding unusually gentle against the background music.

“Yes, I’ve always liked it,” I replied, trying to make my voice sound calm and natural. Yet in that instant, a trace of unease seized me, and I worried whether my answer had been appropriate, whether it might have left the other person with some bad impression. The other person smiled faintly and turned back to focus on the stage.

My heart began to race, my emotions like a wild horse breaking free. I started to replay the conversation over and over, feeling that perhaps my voice hadn’t sounded confident enough, or my smile sincere enough. My pulse quickened, my palms grew sweaty, and I felt my stomach tighten, as if a tiny mistake kept magnifying in my mind, turning into yet another story of being rude.

The music continued, but I could no longer focus on it. I frowned, my hand tightening unconsciously, my fingertips tracing the smooth glass. Fine beads of sweat seemed to form on my forehead, and the warmth inside the room began to feel suffocating. I tried to control my breathing and make it steady again.

“It’s okay, it was just a polite greeting,” I kept telling myself inwardly, trying to pull my thoughts back to reality. That brief exchange replayed in my mind countless times, until the music stopped and I realized the performance was over.

When I stood up to leave, I caught a glimpse of the stranger smiling and nodding at me. I returned a somewhat stiff smile, still silently asking myself over and over, “Did he really just want to make friendly conversation?”

Once outside the bar, the autumn night breeze met my face and carried away some of the anxiety in my heart. The shadows under the streetlights looked like walls built from countless fragments of imagination. I quickened my pace, trying to shake off that lingering tension.

That night when I got home, exhaustion washed over me, but not a trace of sleepiness came. I was still turning the evening’s conversation over in my mind, feeling powerless and ashamed. Trapped in the whirlpool of my thoughts, in the darkness, my tears fell quietly.

Over the next few days, whenever I thought of that scene, I would feel an indescribable sense of frustration and self-doubt, as if I had always been an ill-timed visitor in this city.

The air in the pottery classroom was thick with the moist scent of earth. In my ears, I could hear the low hum of the electric potter’s wheel, accompanied by the faint sucking sound of clay being wetted by water. My palms were damp, their touch a rough yet slick clay; I did my best to steady my hands, trying to shape the lump of mud before me into the elegant, symmetrical vase I had just seen in the teacher’s book. But the wheel spun rapidly, and my hands gradually lost their balance to the wet, slippery clay. Then, all at once, I let my guard down and the mud collapsed uncontrollably, the vase that had nearly taken shape turning into a twisted mass of mud.

“Uh…” I muttered under my breath, quickly pulling back my mud-covered hands and glancing around out of the corner of my eye. The others were all bent over, carefully working, and almost no one had noticed my mistake. But something in me felt as if it had been prodded; my heart instantly sped up, and my ears began to burn red, as though the entire classroom’s attention were fixed on this failed lump of clay. I hurriedly used my muddy hands to rub my face, trying to hide the panic inside me.

At that moment, the teacher came up behind me. He bent slightly to look at the collapsed clay, and the corner of his mouth seemed to twitch almost imperceptibly. “Need help?” he asked calmly, with no trace of reproach in his voice.

“No need, thank you, I just…” I quickly shook my head. Before I could finish, I realized my voice was trembling a little, so I stopped myself. Images flashed through my mind: the teacher returning to the front desk, quietly discussing me with a colleague, then unable to help laughing under his breath; after that, everyone’s eyes on me turning into a kind of undisguised mockery. They would think I couldn’t do anything right—how could I even mess up shaping a piece of clay? A wave of shame surged over me, my stomach giving a slight cramp. I tried to take a deep breath, but my breathing had already begun to turn faintly rapid.

“Don’t be too nervous. If the clay collapses, you can always start over,” the teacher said, patting my shoulder. “Take it slow. Enjoy the process.” With that, he walked over to another group of students.

I watched his back as he left, but in my mind the words “If the clay collapses, you can always start over” kept repeating over and over. Really? Was it that simple? My reason wanted to accept the comfort in those words, but my emotions were still wrapped in some indescribable tension, as if the failed clay had long since stuck to my face and everyone else was secretly laughing. I even began to suspect whether there had been a hidden trace of sarcasm in what he had just said.

After trying a few deep breaths, I put my hands back on the lump of clay. The familiar texture reached my fingertips again; the damp, cool earth wrapped around my palms, strangely calming. I closed my eyes briefly and tried not to look around, not to think about the eyes that might be on me. I gently applied pressure with my fingers, trying to shape the clay as shown in the book, afraid of wasting my effort all over again.

This time, I finally managed to awkwardly pinch out a small, crooked cup-like form. It was by no means beautiful, but at least it hadn’t collapsed at once. Looking at it, I suddenly felt a conflicting mix of emotions: a subtle, small sense of accomplishment intertwined with the shame that still lingered in my heart.

When I got home, I lay on my bed, my mind constantly flashing back to the moment the clay collapsed and to the teacher’s words, “If the clay collapses, you can always start over.” It replayed like a videotape, each time making my heart jump; it was as though that failed moment had been magnified countless times, impossible to let go of. The whole night, my stomach ached faintly, and my ears still seemed to hold the heat from earlier, never quite cooling down.
