I sat by the window in the café, sunlight streaming through the glass and spilling across the table, illuminating the coffee cup in front of me. The surrounding noise filled my ears: people’s conversations and the hum of the espresso machine mingled together. I struggled to focus. The friend sitting across from me was speaking enthusiastically about something. Her eyes were bright, and she kept chiming in with ideas about my work. “You really should give it a try; it sounds very creative,” she said. I nodded and smiled, but inside, it felt as if an invisible hand had clenched around my heart.

“Will it really be okay?” I muttered to myself. That unease lingered in my mind, mixed with a racing heartbeat and a slight sheen of sweat. I felt a discomfort in my stomach, and my fingers unconsciously toyed with the cup’s handle. It was all too familiar. Whenever I faced judgment or expectations, this feeling would always shadow me, as if rehearsing some kind of disappointment or rejection. I looked around, as though I could hear faint criticism or disdain directed at me from those around me. My friend’s voice gradually blurred at my ear, replaced by the doubts and anxieties churning inside me.

“What do you think?” she asked. I came abruptly back to myself, a trace of embarrassment on my face, and replied hesitantly, “Mm, I’ll think about it a bit more.” She patted my hand. “Don’t worry, you can definitely do it.” Her words were warm and firm, but to me they sounded as if they were passing through a thick layer of cotton, leaving no echo behind.

When we walked out of the café, the sunlight was still blinding. I looked up at the sky, feeling a little heavy in my chest. That evening, when I got home, my whole body relaxed, and exhaustion came rushing in all at once. I sat on the bed, thinking about the conversation from earlier, and kept mulling over my friend’s encouraging words. Why could I never believe them? A wave of self-blame and disappointment washed over me, and my stomach tightened painfully.

Over the next few days, I tried writing down some ideas in my notebook, but every time I picked up my pen, the letters dancing across the page seemed so powerless. My friend’s words still circled in my mind like a tiny insect, continually gnawing away at the little confidence I had left. “Can I really do it?” That thought kept returning, again and again, impossible to shake.

Rain streamed down the café window, and my fingers unconsciously drew circles back and forth on the tabletop. The air was filled with the aroma of coffee and baked goods, mixed with the damp scent of rain. I tried hard to stay calm, to make myself look composed, but my heartbeat was so fast it felt as if it were about to burst out of my chest. The person across from me turned their coffee cup, then suddenly said, “I think it might be better if we work separately from now on.”

I froze instantly, as if my mind had been shackled, all my thoughts stopping at once. A few seconds later, I found my voice again. “Why? Did I… did I do something wrong?” My words came out stammering, trembling slightly. Their expression was calm, as if they were deliberately avoiding any display of emotion. “It’s not your problem. I just feel our collaboration directions aren’t quite aligned, and if we keep going, it may affect both of our development.”

That single sentence hit my chest like a heavy blow. I forced out a smile and nodded. “Okay, I understand what you mean.” But in truth, every word felt like a blade scraping across my throat. I subconsciously began to replay everything—had yesterday’s message sounded too cold? Had the suggestion I made last time seemed too forceful? The more I turned those thoughts over in my mind, the worse they became, until I was almost suffocating.

“Do you really think it’s about direction? Or… is there some other problem?” I tried to stay calm, but my tone was already tinged with anxiety and unease. The other person sighed. “It really is a matter of direction. Don’t take it too seriously; this kind of thing is normal in collaborations.”

His words didn’t comfort me. Instead, they made me doubt even more. A thought began to surface in my mind: “It’s because I’m not good enough, isn’t it? I must be terrible.” My stomach tightened, my fingertips went cold, and I could even feel sweat beading in my palms. I knew I should end the conversation, but my mind seemed locked, desperately trying to cling to something, anything, to salvage the situation.

The conversation finally ended with a round of polite goodbyes. I sat in the café while the rain still drizzled outside the window. His words, “not aligned in direction,” kept echoing in my head, but I still couldn’t make myself believe they were true. A voice kept repeating in my ear: “He must think you’re a hassle, afraid you’ll drag down his development.” I felt short of breath, my breathing turning rapid, and I even grew a little dizzy. I sank into my chair, trying to suppress that feeling of being abandoned.

That night, I lay in bed turning over and over, my mind full of his calm expression and those words—“normal,” “don’t take it too seriously.” They pierced my chest like needles. I began to blame myself: “Why did I have to ask so many questions? Why couldn’t I have seemed more easygoing?” That sense of shame made it hard to breathe. Even days later, I was still repeatedly replaying every detail of the conversation, trying to find the real reason. The decision to end the collaboration felt like a rejection of me, a direct denial of my worth.

The restaurant was bathed in soft light, with a small pendant lamp over the table casting a warm yellow glow. The glass outside the window was covered with condensation, obscuring the city’s neon lights and making the room feel even quieter. Across from me sat the editor from the publishing house, still holding the menu in his hand, his hair slightly disheveled. The sound of him flipping through the menu seemed a little hurried, as if tinged with impatience. A few seconds later, he looked up and asked me, “How about steak? Or is there something else you’d like?”

“Steak… sounds good.” I answered quickly, then added, “But I have a mild allergy, so… maybe we should check the ingredients?”

“Oh.” He nodded and lowered his head to keep looking at the menu. Yet my mind was already racing. “Does he think I’m troublesome? Does he dislike how picky I am?” I clenched the napkin in my hand, a thin layer of sweat beginning to seep into my palms, my fingertips even going slightly numb.

A few minutes later, the server came over to take our order. Without asking me, the editor directly ordered two of the same steaks, along with a bottle of red wine. I didn’t dare say much. My heart was beating fast, almost drowning out the jazz music beside my ears. I secretly scolded myself inwardly: “What’s wrong with you? Why didn’t you just make it clear? He must think you have no opinions at all!”

When the steaks were served, the aroma from the plate mixed with the scent of red wine and rushed toward me, but my stomach was twisted into a knot and I had no appetite at all. I cut into the steak, trying to keep a smile on my face, while listening to him talk about adjustments to the direction of the recent manuscript. But his tone seemed to grow more and more exacting, and even carried a hint of coldness.

“This section would be better if you rewrote it. The plot feels too mediocre,” he said. His tone didn’t sound accusatory, but my mind immediately began to dissect it frantically. “Too mediocre? Does that mean I’m not suited for this industry at all?” A shadow of self-doubt instantly swept through my thoughts.

I tried to respond: “Um… is it because the logic isn’t clear enough, or the language isn’t engaging enough?” As soon as I said it, my voice sounded even more cautious than I had expected. He paused for a moment, waved a hand, and said, “Neither. It just needs some more impactful phrasing. Don’t be too nervous.” But his smile didn’t seem fully relaxed, and even more questions exploded in my mind: “When he says don’t be too nervous, is he implying that my panic is already written all over my face? Do I really look that unprofessional?”

The whole meal felt filled with an invisible battle. I felt my stomach twitching, the sweat in my palms had gone cold, and my body seemed frozen, unable to relax naturally. By the end of the meal, I had barely tasted anything; the entire process was mixed with self-reproach and the anxiety of trying to make up for it.

When we left the restaurant, he looked relieved, as if satisfied that the meal was over. But I felt a deep emptiness, as if all of this had only deepened my doubts about myself. After I got home, I kept replaying every word he had said. Did he think I was completely useless? Was “don’t be too nervous” his way of being tolerant, or just resignation? I lay in bed, staring at the ceiling, unable to fall asleep for a long time.

The next day, I pulled up last night’s recorded notes, trying to review things rationally, but I still couldn’t stop an inexplicable sense of shame. It felt like a stain that couldn’t be washed away, lingering in my heart and refusing to fade.

Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains and spilled into the living room, while the air was filled with the aroma of coffee and freshly baked cookies. A few of us sat around the sofa, talking about our recent lives. Birdsong came from outside the window, accompanied by the occasional passing car, and I tried to relax. But my brain always seemed to have a switch ready to turn calm into tension at any moment.

My friend was enthusiastically describing a new project, her tone full of excitement. Suddenly, she turned to me. “How’s your recent work going? Any new ideas?” she asked with a smile, but the slight lift of her brows felt like an invisible challenge. I felt my heartbeat gradually quicken, and my palms became slightly sweaty.

“Um, it’s been okay lately, but sometimes I don’t know how to break through the bottleneck,” I replied, trying to stay calm, though faint ripples of unease had already begun stirring inside me.

She went on, “You’ve always been so creative, don’t worry too much.” It was a kind reassurance, but I felt a hint of reproach, as if I were being reminded that I still hadn’t lived up to my own expectations.

The voice inside me grew active: “Maybe she thinks I’m not working hard enough. Maybe she thinks I’m not improving at all.” These thoughts swirled in my mind, and I tried not to let them show on my face.

I smiled and nodded. “Yeah, I’ll keep trying.” But the voice of self-doubt inside me only grew clearer.

Not long after, the gathering ended. I walked home alone, replaying that conversation over and over in my head. Maybe it was because the weather was gloomy that I felt even heavier, as though the sky itself were responding to my mood. I couldn’t help reflecting: “Why do I care so much about what others think? Why do I always feel like I’m not good enough?” These thoughts echoed along with the sound of raindrops gently tapping against my umbrella.

The next day, I decided to ask her out for coffee. I needed to make sure whether she really had any dissatisfaction with me. Our conversation was relaxed, and her smile once again made me feel relieved.

“I truly appreciate every project you’ve done. You have to believe in yourself,” she said without hesitation. I realized that maybe I had been overthinking everything. That reassurance lifted a weight from my heart, and I could finally focus on my creative work in peace.

This experience taught me that the self-doubt and unease within often come from my own overinterpretation. Although I can’t completely eliminate those thoughts, at least I can slowly learn to tell which ones are phantoms I’ve created myself.

The weeds by the railway tracks had grown as tall as a person’s waist, as if they wanted to swallow up the entire station’s history. The air was thick with the smell of damp earth mixed with rusted iron, and when the cold wind blew through, it carried a faint trace of gasoline. I stood in front of a shabby repair shed, its paint peeled away until only mottled traces remained, and the glass window in the middle had cracked into a geometric pattern. I hadn’t brought an umbrella. The cold wind brushed my face, numbing the tip of my nose, and I kept both hands tightly shoved into my coat pockets. The ground beneath my feet was covered with broken old bolts and scattered wood shavings; I accidentally stepped on one, and it made a sharp “click,” gratingly accusatory, as if criticizing my carelessness.

When I went inside the shed, a few dim yellow beams of light filtered through the broken skylights, and the air smelled of the corrosion of old steel. I tried to take out my phone to snap some photos, but my fingers were trembling a little, and the result on the screen only left me dissatisfied. I felt that the images I had captured could not convey the desolation of the place, nor could they contain the emotions I wanted to express. This failure gave rise to a sharp self-doubt within me: “Why can’t I capture this feeling? Is my work really just not that good?”

In the corner of the shed stood a lonely bench, covered in dust, its wooden parts cracked into fine splinters. When I sat down, the whole bench swayed slightly, and I tensed up, afraid it might suddenly collapse. I tried to jot down some creative ideas, but the pen in my hand felt as heavy as lead and refused to write smoothly. “If other people saw these thoughts, would they think I’m childish?” The idea came out of nowhere, like a knife stabbing into my mind, and I began to doubt myself. This creative project had once filled me with anticipation, but now it felt like a heavy burden, pressing down until I could hardly breathe.

Suddenly, several rustling sounds of metal sheeting being blown by the wind came from outside the door, making my heart race and my breathing quicken. I felt a faint pain in my stomach, a few drops of cold sweat broke out on my forehead, and my palms began to grow damp. I tried taking a deep breath to calm myself, but the voice in my head kept mocking me: “You never should have come here. Your work is nothing but cheap imitation.” This preemptive self-attack seemed like the only way I could protect myself from greater blows, but at the same time it plunged me deeper into shame.

The atmosphere in the shed made me increasingly uneasy. When I left in a hurry, my mood felt as if it were being dragged along by a heavy iron anchor. Stepping back out into the cold wind, I instinctively hunched my shoulders and trudged back along the tracks. When my foot slipped on a sleeper, I nearly fell; my heart lurched, but I no longer even had the energy to curse myself for being clumsy. After I got home, I sat at the desk sorting through the photos I had taken, trying to find a few angles worth keeping, but every time I moved on to the next image, I couldn’t help scrutinizing the details. I fell into a ruminative loop, hating my own imperfection while refusing to stop.

A few days later, I still hadn’t managed to emerge from the shadow of this creative experience. Even when writing, I felt that every sentence I wrote was exposing my shallowness to others. I began trying to avoid any topic related to this project, but deep down it still ached faintly, as if there were a gap there that could never be mended.

The gallery was softly lit, with brightly colored paintings hanging on the walls. People spoke in hushed voices in the room, accompanied by the low melody of music. I stood before an abstract painting, its lines and patches of color seemingly layered together at random, yet somehow creating a strange harmony. Although I often felt tense in my heart, art always let me forget my unease for a while and immerse myself in an atmosphere full of creativity.

A well-dressed lady approached; she was a friend of the painter. I quickly straightened my back, trying to appear relaxed and composed. “Do you like this painting too?” she asked with a smile. I nodded, my heart beating a little faster, afraid I might say the wrong thing. “Yes, I think the colors are very striking.” I tried to make my voice sound confident, but before I had finished speaking, her smile seemed to freeze for a moment.

In an instant, my mind was flooded with all kinds of possible interpretations. Maybe what I said was too superficial? Would she think my taste was lacking? I felt a pang of panic, my palms growing slightly damp. That smile seemed to pierce straight into some corner of my heart, awakening my fear of being overlooked and misunderstood.

“Sorry, I have to go find my friend,” she said, then smiled and said goodbye. Her leaving left me deeply frustrated, and a strong sense of shame washed over me. I blamed myself inwardly for failing to seize the moment to connect. I barely managed to move to another painting, trying to conceal the turmoil inside me.

That night, the air in the gallery seemed even more stifling, and I felt a pressure in my chest. I tried to talk to the people around me, but every attempt made me more uneasy; the slightest change in expression or glance was magnified in my mind into outright rejection. It was as if I could see others whispering to each other, and I was filled with a premonition of being excluded. I tried hard to hold back my emotions, but my hands could not stop trembling slightly.

After I got home, I lay in bed, replaying that smile and the moment of departure over and over in my mind. Under the covers, my heartbeat still would not settle, as if I were being driven by an unshakable sense of loss. For days, these feelings of self-doubt and helplessness lingered, troubling my life and my work. When I looked back at those paintings, I began to think that perhaps the problem was not the expression I had seen, but my understanding and interpretation of it.

Even though this experience made me uneasy, it also gradually made me realize how much my sensitivity had affected the way I viewed social interactions. I need to learn to face others’ reactions with a calmer attitude, let go of my habit of overinterpreting, and approach the many possibilities in life with an open mind.

The long corridors of the hospital always make people uneasy. The white walls reflect the harsh light, and the occasional sound of soft footsteps or opening doors breaks the stillness. I sat on a plastic chair, the cold touch seeping through my thighs and making me shiver slightly. In my ears were the low hum of the air conditioner and distant voices, as if all of it were part of an endless whispering. My palms began to sweat, and with every heartbeat it felt as though my chest was being struck hard.

On the wall opposite me hung a slightly faded landscape painting; the lush forest scene could not soothe the anxiety in my heart. I picked up my phone and absentmindedly scrolled through the news, but I couldn’t focus at all. My mind kept replaying all the bad news the doctor might say.

“The next one, you can go in,” the nurse’s voice pulled me back from my wild thoughts. I stood up, feeling my legs a little numb, as if trapped in the helplessness of the deep sea. When I walked into the consultation room, the doctor’s smile gave me a brief sense of reassurance, but only for an instant.

“Is there anything to be concerned about?” the doctor asked gently. I forced myself to stay calm and tried not to let my voice tremble. “I’ve been having stomach discomfort lately. Maybe it’s work stress. I’m a bit worried.” Even though I knew I often turned minor aches and pains into major problems, I still couldn’t shake the unease.

The doctor examined my stomach, pressing it lightly, as if touching a piece of fragile porcelain. The slight discomfort in my stomach mingled with the shadow in my mind, leaving me a little dizzy. I swallowed my nerves and listened to the diagnosis.

“Nothing serious. It could be too much stomach acid. Just watch your diet recently,” the doctor said simply. I nodded, doing my best to convince myself that it all didn’t matter, but the anxiety in my heart still stubbornly remained.

When I left the hospital, it was a breezy afternoon outside, sunlight filtering through the leaves and scattering mottled patterns on the ground. I walked home, trying to steady my breathing, but my heart was still racing a little, as if a stone were pressing down on my chest.

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, fragments of the day flashing through my mind: the doctor’s smile, the hospital corridor, the sound of my own heartbeat. I prayed that the tension would fade with the passing night, but the worries stayed with me like a shadow. Over the next few days, I tried hard to adjust my diet and told myself everything was fine, but the occasional stomach discomfort still made me uneasy.

The studio lights were glaringly bright, mixed with the hum of equipment and the murmured whispers of a few people. I struggled to stay focused on the task at hand. The creative project I was in charge of was shooting its final few scenes, but my stomach felt as if a stone were pressing down on it, aching faintly. The air-conditioning was weak, and the air carried the smell of plastic from the lamps burning slightly hot, mixed with the milky scent of a few people’s lattes, making me feel a little irritable.

A photographer walked over and asked me in a voice that seemed gentle but carried impatience: “Are you sure this background color is okay?”

I froze for a moment, my mind immediately spiraling into overdrive. Why was he asking that kind of question? Was he dissatisfied with my arrangement? Did he think I wasn’t professional enough? My face started to flush, my heartbeat quickened like drumbeats, colliding with the rhythm of the flickering lights to create a suffocating sense of anxiety. I bit my lip and forced my voice to sound calm: “Yes, it should be fine.” But as soon as I finished, another assistant said in a low voice, “Actually, trying a darker tone wouldn’t be a problem.” My stomach twisted hard again, like an alarm had been triggered.

I kept replaying the expressions on their faces in my mind, trying to decipher whether they had a negative opinion of me, as if every decision I made was being magnified into impatience by the slightest glance or tone. Intense unease pulled my thoughts into a haze, and the inner monologue in my head roared without pause: “Did I really overlook something? Will they think I’m an amateur? If something goes wrong this time, will I completely ruin my reputation?” This feeling was like a sharp thorn, forcing me to start doubting my own judgment.

A few minutes later, the shoot smoothly moved on to the next stage, but I still couldn’t relax. My fingertips trembled slightly as I desperately tried to hide the unnatural expression on my face. While adjusting the props, my eyes met the photographer’s again, and I seemed to be able to directly sense that slight, subtle hesitation on his face. My anxiety flared up once more; the slight sweat caused by my arm movements made me uncomfortable, and the poorly air-conditioned room slowly turned into a suffocating little box.

After the shoot ended, I sat on a plastic chair outside the studio. The city noise outside the window had begun to settle into the night, but my mind was still occupied by one hint after another. I kept dissecting the tone of those questions, the photographer’s expression, and the assistant’s suggestion, as if I were pacing around inside a cage I had created myself, unable to break free and return to normal no matter how hard I tried. The next morning, when I woke up, I found that my mind was still quietly replaying that scene, carrying with it an inescapable sense of shame and unease.

The sound of raindrops striking the window was especially piercing in the quiet studio, as if it were setting the mood for my state of mind. I sat in front of the computer, unable to focus on the work before me; my heartbeat quickened, a slight cold sweat broke out on my forehead, and my stomach ached faintly. The argument with my collaborator kept echoing in my head. His words—“Maybe we shouldn’t keep working together”—were like a sharp blade piercing my heart. I tried hard to recall every part of our conversation, trying to figure out what he truly meant, but all the details pointed to the same conclusion: he was going to abandon me.

“Can’t you understand my position?” I heard a hint of desperation in my own voice, but even more so, helplessness.

“I’m not saying we should stop collaborating. I just think we need to reassess things,” he said in a calm tone, yet with a kind of distance that sent a chill through me.

My mind instantly churned. All the effort and hopes of these years seemed about to come to nothing. I felt tension in my chest, as if a huge rock were pressing down on it, making it hard to breathe. The worst-case scenario kept flashing through my mind: losing my job, losing my income, being looked down upon. I began to repeatedly think over every mistake I had made in the past, wondering whether this outcome had been destined all along.

“If that’s what collaboration is like, then forget it,” I blurted out, springing up from my chair. My voice was louder and more urgent than I had expected, and in my words there was a kind of preemptive self-attack, hoping to protect myself from further hurt.

The other person fell silent for a moment, then sighed. “Maybe we both need to calm down.”

I turned and walked out of the studio. The rain immediately soaked my shoes, and the icy drops struck my face, blurring my vision. I didn’t want to admit it, but the overwhelming sense of defectiveness had already surged up within me, as if shouting that I was so unworthy of trust and cooperation. My whole body was rigid, and rain mixed with tears streamed down my cheeks.

All night I agonized over the conversation, turning it over again and again, imagining every possibility, none of which ended in anything but loss. When I woke the next day, my eyes were still swollen, and my throat was hoarse from the emotion of the day before. Even so, I still couldn’t escape that fear of abandonment and the shame, feeling my vulnerability laid bare for all to see. The notification light on my phone flickered faintly, but I still didn’t have the courage to check it; some intuition told me it wasn’t a message I wanted to see.

I stood beside the worktable in the pottery classroom, my palms already slightly damp with nervous sweat. The air around me was faintly moist, carrying the soft earthy smell of clay. Gentle piano music played in the classroom, and one student was discussing glaze choices with the teacher, while I tried to focus on the clay form on the wheel in front of me. When my fingertips touched the wet clay, a chill shot up through me, making my hand jerk, and the clay form on the wheel tilted at once. I panicked and started trying to adjust its shape with my hands, but the more I tried to correct it, the worse it seemed to get. My heartbeat grew faster and faster, and the back of my ears began to burn. My mind went blank with a sudden roar, flashing back to previous mishaps and the expressions on my classmates’ faces when they glanced sideways at me. My stomach felt as if something were clutching it, aching faintly.

“Are you okay? Do you need help?” a classmate beside me asked with a smile, but I felt as if those words were some kind of mockery. The voice in quotation marks seemed to echo loudly in my ears, as though everyone in the room had heard my embarrassment. I lowered my head and looked at the piece in my hands, still horribly crooked. I forced myself to hold back the anxiety inside and managed a strained smile. “It’s fine, thanks,” I said. But deep down, countless thoughts were twisting together: They already know I’m a failure, don’t they? Do they think I shouldn’t have signed up for this class at all?

In the end, while I was trying to salvage the clay form, I accidentally used too much force, and it fell from the wheel and shattered into several pieces. The cracking sound was especially harsh in the quiet classroom. In an instant, I felt as if all eyes had gathered on me, though in reality only a few people looked up. At a loss, I crouched down to pick up the fragments, my face burning like fire. I started berating myself: “How could this happen? You can’t even do something this simple?” That self-attack surged up like a flood. I wanted to pretend it didn’t matter, but my body betrayed me: my hands trembled slightly, my heart raced to an uncomfortable degree, and I even felt dizzy.

The teacher came over and said softly, “Don’t worry. This is all part of learning. You can try again.” I tried to nod, but I didn’t even have the strength to answer. My ears were filled with the sound of my own heartbeat, and beneath my feet it felt as though I were standing on clouds, a suspended sense of unease that kept me from calming down.

That night, after I got home, I stared blankly at the cup on the table, and the moment the clay form shattered kept replaying in my mind. “Why can you even mess up a pottery class?” I muttered to myself. This rumination went on all night; even when I closed my eyes to sleep, I could once again feel the piercing sound and those eyes in the classroom. I began to wonder whether I shouldn’t continue taking the class, yet I also felt that quitting would only make me feel more like a failure. A few days later, though I was still struggling inside, I took my materials and went to the classroom, determined to try again.

Sunlight streamed in through the large living room window, warmly settling over the wooden floor and sofa. I sat in the corner of the sofa with my feet crossed up on the coffee table, a book open on my lap. On the coffee table sat a cup of freshly brewed jasmine tea, its faint fragrance rising gently with the steam. I don’t like drinking tea after it has gone cold very much, so every few minutes I’d take a small sip; as the tea slipped down my throat, it carried just the right hint of sweetness and bitterness. The book in front of me was a collection of essays, light and easy to read, with a few pieces that were quite interesting, though none of them made me laugh out loud or feel especially moved. I simply turned the pages quietly, watching the words flow past my eyes like a shallow little stream.

Now and then, I would look up at the window. In the park downstairs, someone seemed to be walking a little dog, and from far away I could hear a few short barks, with children’s laughter as a backdrop. I noticed that the potted plants on my balcony looked a bit yellowed and dry, and I made a mental note to water them later. Then my gaze fell back to the page. Beside the text were a few illustrations, their lines simple yet full of character, which made me drift off a little. I wondered if the artist had also once sat in some quiet place, calmly drawing those lines?

For some reason, I suddenly realized that my hands were a bit cold, probably because of the air conditioning. I rubbed them with my other hand and, at the same time, pulled the thin blanket from the sofa over my legs. The fabric of the blanket was somewhat rough, but the warmth made me feel a little more comfortable. Then I touched my face; it seemed a little cool too. After taking a sip of tea, the warm liquid felt reassuring on my tongue.

I picked up my phone and checked the time. It was past four in the afternoon. A message from a friend popped up on the screen; she had sent a photo of her cat. I opened it and took a look—it was a white cat with gray stripes, sprawled out asleep in a comical position. I smiled, replied, “So cute,” then yawned and put the phone back on the coffee table.

The tea was nearly gone, with just a few wet flower buds left at the bottom of the cup. The angle of the sunlight had changed a little, no longer reaching the sofa; the patch of light had shrunk to one corner of the wooden floor. I squinted, and the book had turned to some page in the middle, but I no longer knew exactly what I was looking at. I seemed to be simply staring at the page in a daze, letting myself sink into the quiet. Nothing particularly special happened. I suddenly felt a little hungry and wondered whether I should order takeout later or make something simple for dinner.

That Sunday afternoon passed like that—without any excitement, and without any particular happiness—everything peaceful, like a lake with no ripples. I wasn’t even sure whether I was truly enjoying that silence, or whether I had simply grown used to living this way.

The green world of the botanical garden surrounded me, and its vitality was truly refreshing. I sat in the spacious glasshouse, where sunlight streamed through the glass onto the floor, and the air was filled with the moist scent of earth and the fragrance of various plants. I chose a seat near the front so I could watch the lecture more clearly.

The speaker was a young man who looked very confident, his words fluent and passionate. “Each of us can contribute to environmental protection.” His voice echoed through the spacious room, resonating with me, but at the same time making me begin to doubt myself. Could I really do something like that?

I tried hard to focus, but as the lecture went on, my palms began to sweat and my heartbeat quickened. From time to time, I felt that some of his points seemed to imply that I lacked environmental awareness. Was everyone judging me? I looked around at the others; they all seemed to be listening carefully, with thoughtful expressions on their faces.

After the lecture ended, I hesitated before walking up to talk with him. Imagining that I might be ignored, I criticized myself in advance. “Excuse me, how can we better practice environmental protection in city life?” I tried to make my voice sound confident.

The speaker smiled slightly. “That’s a very good question. Actually, there are many opportunities in the city, such as reducing plastic use and choosing public transportation.” His answer was direct, and I felt a wave of shame, as if my question had been too basic. I thought to myself, was this the simplest advice he could come up with? But I still forced a smile. “Thank you for your advice.”

When I left the botanical garden, the unease in my heart had not faded; instead, it grew stronger. On the way home, I kept going over that conversation and my own reactions, feeling dissatisfied with myself. Why couldn’t I be as confident and self-assured as the speaker?

That night, I tossed and turned in bed, the conversation replaying over and over in my mind. I began attacking myself, believing that I wasn’t good enough, not smart enough, and would never be able to stand on the same level as those passionate people. Even a simple conversation made me anxious and uneasy.

A few days later, I tried recording my practical thoughts and plans about environmental protection in a notebook, hoping to ease the endless confusion and self-doubt in my heart. It also made me realize that even when I feel inferior in the face of excellent people, instead of attacking myself, I should try to find actionable directions from their advice.

The lights in the conference room were a little too harsh, stinging my eyes until they ached. I lowered my head and looked at my notebook, desperately trying to focus on the draft on my screen instead of what a coworker had just said with skepticism and an undercurrent of force: “This concept may not be novel enough. Should we dig a little deeper?”

“I just wanted the idea to be as unique as possible,” I said, my voice sounding even more rushed than I expected, almost shaky. My fingers fidgeted with the pen cap, and the feeling of my nails pressing into the plastic gave me a brief sense of comfort. But I could still feel my stomach twisting as if it were being clenched, aching with pain.

“Sure, but I think the market may not be very receptive to this direction. Should we try something that’s closer to mainstream aesthetics?” Another coworker, leaning back in his chair, added casually. His tone was light, but it sliced through my defenses with the precision of a small knife. My thoughts began to spiral. Did he think I was unprofessional? Did he think I was wasting everyone’s time? Had they already decided in their minds not to use this plan, but were too embarrassed to say it outright? Or were they hinting that I simply wasn’t suited to stay on this project team at all?

“So what you mean is, my proposal is terrible?” I blurted out, my voice rising an octave and turning sharp. I almost regretted it immediately, because everyone had gone quiet, all eyes turning toward me in unison, carrying a mix of surprise and uncertainty.

“That’s not what I mean, don’t misunderstand,” the other person quickly said, waving his hands in explanation. “I just mean maybe we can look at it from different angles.”

“Yeah, that’s what discussion is for. We can talk it through,” another coworker chimed in, trying to sound gentle. But my neck was still burning, and there was a buzzing in my ears. My face felt as if it had been set on fire, growing hot and red. I lowered my head and tried hard to control my breathing, but my heartbeat only got faster and faster, like a treadmill turned up to the highest speed. A lot of “maybes” flooded my mind: maybe they were already mocking me in their heads, maybe they would talk about me and laugh at me after the meeting, maybe...

After the meeting ended, my hands were still shaking as I packed my things. I couldn’t get the backpack zipper closed, and I yanked at it hard, almost breaking it. I shoved my laptop in carelessly, pretending I was fine, and quickly left the office.

Back in my rented room, I collapsed into a chair and stared at the ceiling, replaying the conversation over and over in my head. Had I overreacted? Did they think that as an adult, I’d lose control over emotions just because of a little criticism? How could I be so stupid, unable to even handle a bit of questioning? The more I thought about it, the more useless I felt, and before long tears were streaming down uncontrollably.

At the morning meeting a few days later, I deliberately brought a revised proposal, trying to prove that I really could do it. “I adjusted the direction a bit. Do you think this is better?”

After flipping through a few pages, the team lead nodded. “This does fit the theme better.”

Only then did I finally feel a little relieved, but the stinging emotions and self-doubt hadn’t completely disappeared. They were like air bubbles trapped underwater, ready to rise and burst at any moment.

Carrying my bag, I walked into this newly opened bakery. The first thing that hit me was a rich aroma of freshly baked bread, mixed with a faint scent of coffee, warming the bitter morning air outside. I saw the newly renovated wooden cabinets lined with freshly baked croissants and Danish pastries. Outside the glass window, the sky was still dim, and the gray-white morning light filtered through the bright windows onto the tables and chairs.

I walked up to the counter, intending to order a latte. Just then, a stranger’s voice sounded behind me. “Is this your first time here too?” I turned around and saw a strange man smiling at me, holding an exquisite pastry in his hands. His voice carried an unusual note of enthusiasm, and it stirred up an inexplicable sense of tension in me.

“Mm, yes,” I forced out a smile, my heart racing. My mind began to churn uncontrollably with all sorts of possible consequences: was he sizing me up? Did I look somehow out of place? I struggled to keep my expression steady, but my palms were starting to sweat.

“The puff pastry rolls here are especially good. I recommend you try them,” he continued casually, seemingly not noticing my unease. I nodded and reluctantly took the menu he handed me, silently trying to shake off the thoughts in my head.

“Thanks, I’ll try them,” I replied. But my body did not move at all, afraid any motion would make me look nervous and ridiculous. The cashier at the counter was smiling and waiting for me to make a choice, yet I hesitated, not knowing what to do. The stranger noticed my tension and kindly patted me on the shoulder. “Relax. Everyone has their first time.”

Those words jolted me, as if I had been exposed in an instant. I could feel my face growing hot. I lowered my head, quickly ordered a coffee, and hurried to a corner seat, trying as much as possible to keep my distance from the people in the shop.

After sitting down, my stomach churned. Perhaps it was because of my inner unease, which now seemed even more pronounced. That feeling of anxiety at being watched had never fully faded; instead, it grew stronger at this moment. I didn’t know why such a simple conversation could make me feel so out of control, so acutely aware of a sense of danger pressing in on me. While sipping my coffee, I tried hard to calm myself, but my thoughts remained in turmoil.

That night, lying in bed, I replayed everything that had happened during the day. I felt ashamed of my sensitivity and overreaction, yet I could not stop it. The stranger’s friendliness was nothing more than an ordinary social gesture, but in my mind I had turned it into an adventurous journey. Over the next few days, I found it difficult to shake off the emotional turbulence, afraid of encountering a similar situation again, and for no reason at all, trapped in a cycle of unease.

The air was thick with the aroma of coffee and freshly baked bread, and the crisp clink of cups against the table was as usual, but I could barely hear anything anymore. My eyes were fixed tightly on the face across from me, and the only thing echoing in my ears was what he had just said: “You’re always so extreme.” Those words stabbed into my heart like a needle. I forced the tremor out of my voice and shot back, “Extreme? I’m just trying to avoid mistakes as much as possible, to keep from disappointing our audience! Is that wrong too?”

He frowned and looked at me, as if struggling to suppress some emotion. “But the way you are just pushes me into a place where I can’t even breathe. Do you think everyone is as sensitive to every comment as you are?”

My stomach clenched, as if something inside it were churning. I knew my face must look awful right then; my palms were already damp with sweat, and I could even feel the fine beads of perspiration on my forehead. Why was he looking at me like this? I only wanted us to do better. He was the one who was sometimes too casual—why was it suddenly my fault?

“I just want us to be more rigorous. Didn’t you see how many people were questioning our sources in the comments under our last video?” I gripped the edge of the table so tightly that my voice had already started to tremble. “Those people may be few, but they could influence many more. They could ruin us.”

He turned his head away and let out a soft sigh. “You don’t understand at all. Your reaction to those comments goes far beyond what’s actually necessary. Sometimes I really feel like you care more about what they said than about what we actually did.”

My heart started racing. His words struck my heart like a hammer, over and over. “So you think I’m dragging us down? You stopped wanting to work with me a long time ago, didn’t you?” The words burst out of me, and I could almost hear the sharpness and desperation in my own voice.

He looked up at me, frowning, as if he wanted to say something, but in the end he only threw out one sentence: “I’m not blaming you, but maybe our partnership should end here.”

In that moment, time seemed to stop. My ears began to ring, and scenes from the past three years we had worked together flashed rapidly through my mind. From the initial excitement to the later arguments, everything was like a movie playing in fast reverse. I wanted to say something, but my throat felt blocked, and nothing came out.

After that, he stood up, picked up his bag, and turned to leave. I sat there with my palm still pressed tightly against the tabletop. The cold sensation came through, yet I felt feverish all over, my heart pounding as if it were about to leap out of my throat. The stares of the people around me pricked into me like needles, as if everyone were watching me make a fool of myself. I lowered my head and stared at the crack along the rim of the coffee cup. The churning in my stomach grew stronger, nearly making me vomit.

That night I couldn’t sleep. I tossed and turned in bed, replaying over and over the words he had said. “You’re always so extreme…” Each repetition felt like a knife carving into my chest. I began to question myself: was there really something wrong with me? Was I hard to get along with? Or did he just want to get rid of me? I wanted to confide in a friend, but I was afraid others would side with him and think it was my fault. In the end, I said nothing at all, just stared blankly out the window until the first ray of dawn pierced my eyes.

The rhythmic clatter of keyboard keys echoed through the room, while the rain outside gently tapped against the windowsill. I had thought this afternoon would be perfect for writing. The light from the screen was a bit harsh; I squinted at the last paragraph, yet no matter how hard I tried, I couldn’t find words I liked. I took a breath, my shoulders tightening inexplicably, as if something were pressing down on them. Just as I was trying to refocus, a mosquito buzzed past the window and swept straight by my ear. I shivered and suddenly felt a strange itch in my ear. I waved my hand, trying to drive it away, but it stubbornly refused to leave.

“Damn it!” I couldn’t help cursing under my breath. I raised my hand and flailed at the air, but kept missing. The mosquito’s buzzing rang repeatedly in my ear, as if mocking my inability to stay calm. My heartbeat began to quicken, and my palms grew slightly damp. I grabbed a book and stared at several possible corners of the room, trying to find where it was hiding. But the light in the room was dim, and the little thing seemed to blend into the background. I stared for several seconds before finally giving up.

“Forget it, just ignore it,” I tried hard to convince myself, turning my gaze back to the screen. But I found that my train of thought had completely broken. The sentences that had just been in my mind had now vanished without a trace, like smoke. I had no choice but to start reading again from the first paragraph, only to become more and more dissatisfied the further I read. I clicked around with the mouse, deleting here and changing there, and the logic I had wanted to adjust only became more and more jumbled.

Suddenly, the sound of the mosquito rang in my ear again. This time I almost sprang to my feet on reflex, and the book in my hand slammed onto the desk with a loud thud, shaking the teacup and splashing out a few drops of water. I forced myself to calm down and muttered, “It’s okay, it’s okay. It’s just a mosquito.” But inside, a spark of anger was still flickering, as if this wasn’t just a mosquito, but the embodiment of an entire day of writing failure. I turned my chair toward the desk, shoved my hands into my hair, and rubbed hard.

After several years of silence, the mosquito never showed up again. I stared at the screen, feeling the air in the room grow stifling and uncomfortable, like that sentence I could never write was stuck in my throat. I shut the window tightly, afraid that some unwelcome visitor might fly in again, then sat back down and forced myself to delete that paragraph and rewrite it. “Calm down—you can’t possibly make it worse than this, right?” The thought was a little self-mocking, but it eased my frustration a little.

Time passed bit by bit, and finally I finished a short passage that at least didn’t look too terrible. Still, I couldn’t quite let it go. I stared blankly at the screen until my stomach suddenly reminded me that I had already missed lunch. I closed the laptop, feeling a faint dizziness rise from the back of my head. I told myself I was probably just tired; a bite to eat would help.

The gallery was crowded, and the air was filled with the mingled smells of oil paint and perfume. I stood in front of an abstract painting, trying hard to make sense of it. A murmur drifted over from nearby, and I couldn’t help but prick up my ears. “This painting is actually quite shallow, with no depth at all,” I heard someone say. My heart raced, my face burned, and I couldn’t help wondering if they were talking about the painting I was looking at. I kept replaying that sentence over and over, and a wave of shame and unease surged through me, as though my mask of ignorance had been stripped away.

I turned around and happened to meet the gaze of an acquaintance. He gave a slight smile and came over to greet me. “What do you think of this painting?” he asked. Preoccupied with trying to steady my emotions, I stammered, “I’m still thinking about it. I’m not sure.” His smile froze for a moment, and his eyes flickered over my face. I began to wonder if I had said something wrong, and the heat in my face became harder and harder to bear.

I silently blamed myself for always being so anxious. I wanted to quickly change the subject, but not a single word would come out. All I could feel was my heartbeat pounding in my chest like a drum. Cold sweat ran down my back, and my palms started to sweat too; I quietly wiped them on my sleeve. Why was it that I always messed things up?

The gallery lights shone on me, and it felt as though I were being stung from all sides. I faintly sensed that everyone else was looking at me strangely. Though I knew that was unlikely, the feeling would not go away. In the end, I found an excuse and hurriedly cut the conversation short, turning and fleeing that area.

Afterward, I stood in a quieter corner, endlessly brooding over the embarrassment from before. I kept turning that sentence over in my mind, trying to pin down its exact meaning and intent. I began to feel ashamed of my own sensitivity and cowardice, and my mood sank to the bottom. To cope, I decided to go to the restroom and calm down.

Standing in front of the mirror, I stared at myself and tried to wash the heat from my face with cold water; only then did my heartbeat gradually settle. Even so, the anxiety in my heart still would not go away.

A few days later, I was still thinking back to that scene in the gallery. That ever-present fear of being exposed lingered in my mind, making me even more cautious in dealing with every little thing in life, afraid of embarrassing myself again. Yet I also realized that perhaps those whispers were nothing more than a result of my overthinking. Slowly, I began trying to find a tenuous balance within those emotions, reminding myself not to catastrophize every small thing.

The gathering took place in a dim yet cozy café. Sunlight filtered through the blinds and fell across the wooden table. I could feel the warm texture of the tabletop, while the hiss of the espresso machine and my friends’ laughter filled my ears. I held a cup of hot coffee in my hands; with each sip, the warm liquid slid into my mouth, bringing a brief sense of comfort. Yet the tension inside me refused to fade. I kept wondering whether they would notice my anxiety. I was trying to join in the conversation, but I still felt like an outsider.

“What have you been busy with lately?” a friend asked me with a smile. His tone was relaxed, but I heard criticism hidden beneath it. “Am I being too boring lately?” The thought quickly swirled through my mind. Forcing a smile, I replied, “Oh, I’ve been working on some new projects, trying out different things.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I immediately realized my answer was too vague and not interesting enough. My heart rate suddenly sped up, I felt sweat beginning to form on my forehead, and my stomach ached faintly from the nerves.

The gathering went on, and everyone talked about their own lives, but my thoughts were a mess. Why was I always so sensitive? Did my friends think I wasn’t good enough? Thoughts like these surged in like a tide. I desperately tried to calm myself, yet I was afraid they would notice my unease. I had to pretend that everything was normal.

As I struggled to stay calm, another friend asked softly, “Are you okay?” That question put me on high alert, as if she had seen through me. I forced a laugh and said, “Of course, I’m fine, just a little tired.” Conversations like this made me feel deeply embarrassed, as if the whole world were watching every reaction I had. I lowered my head and stirred my coffee, once again checking whether everyone was dissatisfied with how I was behaving.

When I got home, I collapsed onto the sofa, physically and mentally exhausted. That night, I replayed those conversations over and over in my head, anxiously thinking about what I had done wrong. My mind was filled with endlessly magnified self-doubt, and even falling asleep became difficult. Over the next few days, I found myself returning to those scenes from time to time, afraid that the next time I attended a gathering, I would go through the same tension again.

A few days later, I finally decided to examine those thoughts again. I realized that the criticism I imagined hidden in my friends’ words was mostly a product of my own assumptions and anxiety, rather than their true intentions. Although I felt somewhat relieved, the fear of being abandoned still lay deeply rooted in my heart.

The gallery was abuzz with conversation, and the walls were hung with all kinds of artworks. Brilliant lights shone on the oil paintings, reflecting a dazzling array of colors. My own work was placed in a rather inconspicuous corner, surrounded by small clusters of viewers talking in low voices. My heart was racing; I had a slight sheen of sweat on my forehead and sticky palms. I strained to catch snippets of conversation, hoping to find some positive comments to offset the anxiety in my mind. Just then, I heard a male visitor beside me say to his friend, “This painting’s concept is a bit clichéd. I wonder if the artist has hit a creative block.”

In an instant, it felt as though someone had clenched my heart, and my breathing quickened. I turned around and saw that they were staring at my work. Although I pretended to remain composed and walked over, that phrase kept echoing in my mind: creative block. Was that how everyone felt? I smiled at them and said, “Thank you for your feedback. Could you tell me where I need to improve?”

He looked at me, then gave an awkward smile. “Oh, nothing. We were just chatting.” I struggled to keep smiling, while inside a tide of self-doubt was surging.

I went on a few more steps, and a familiar colleague approached me, smiling as he asked, “How do you feel about tonight’s response?” I tried to answer naturally: “Pretty good, I guess. There are always places to improve.” But tension and shame rushed over me like a tide; I could feel my cheeks burning and a knot twisting in my stomach.

That night, until the exhibition ended, I kept up a formulaic smile, trying to conceal the humiliation and resentment inside. When I got home, I collapsed onto the sofa, thinking over the words I had heard during the day. I kept magnifying those remarks, even beginning to doubt my own ability as an artist. I tossed and turned, wondering whether I could have avoided that embarrassment if I had responded better at the time.

When I woke up the next day, I was still immersed in the emotions from the night before, as if caught in an invisible net. I decided not to go to the gallery for the time being. I knew that wouldn’t solve the real problem, but deep inside I was gripped by an intense, almost desperate sense of helplessness. I had always wanted to prove myself, but this negative feedback had brought me down in an instant.

For a full week, I could hardly pull myself together. I held the paintbrush in my hand but didn’t know where to begin, repeatedly wondering whether things would have been different if I hadn’t gone to the exhibition that day.

I stood in the corner of the conference room, sliding my fingertips back and forth across my phone screen, trying to hide the cold sweat on my palms. The room was full of people talking in low voices, and my ears were flooded with all kinds of sounds—high heels clicking on the floor, the coffee machine gurgling, and occasional bursts of laughter. Each laugh made me tense up all at once. My new work had only been online for a few days, and today’s meetup was my first time facing feedback from my peers. The snacks on the table gave off a faint lemon scent, but my stomach was clenched by an invisible hand; I had no appetite at all.

A fellow creator walked over, picked up my portfolio and flipped through it, then looked up at me. “Some parts are pretty interesting,” he said lightly. Though his tone was calm, I caught a momentary hesitation in his eyes, as if he were trying to find a less direct way to express disappointment. I forced a smile, while a voice in my head immediately started screaming: “Interesting? So it’s not good enough? Or is it terrible? Does he think I don’t understand the basics at all?” My face burned, and I stared at the floor as a strong sense of shame spread through my body.

“Sorry, maybe some parts still need adjusting. I haven’t been in a great state lately.” I rushed to get ahead of him, saying this in a self-deprecating tone, hoping to defuse whatever harsher criticism he might have had. “You don’t need to apologize. I was just saying it casually,” he said, then turned to chat with someone else. I looked at his back, and anger and hurt surged up in an instant. “Casually? Just casually? Then why say it at all? Does he think I need other people’s comfort? Or is he looking down on me?”

As the meeting went on, I shrank further into the corner, my back pressed against the cold wall, trying to recover from that stinging feeling. But every voice in discussion sounded like it was mocking me, and even the occasional glance from someone made me feel as though I had been seen through. I sat in the last row, the tissue in my hand soaked through with sweat. I couldn’t concentrate on a single presentation; all I could do was replay that sentence over and over: “Some parts are pretty interesting.” It lurked in my mind like a ghost, making me feel that my work was worthless and that my own flaws had been laid bare as well.

When I got home, my head was pounding, and my empty stomach felt as if it were burning. I collapsed onto the sofa, my phone still on the comments section of social media. I kept scrolling through netizens’ remarks endlessly, magnifying every mildly neutral phrase in an attempt to find proof that my work really wasn’t good enough. Sometimes I even felt that even praise like “not bad” was just a perfunctory response. I poured myself a glass of water, but when the rim of the cup touched my hand, my body actually trembled involuntarily, as if responding to the tension inside me.

When I woke up the next day, my head still felt heavy. I opened my computer and deleted some content from the work page, trying to make it look more perfect. I even thought about giving up my upcoming creative plans, feeling that I wasn’t suited for this industry. But I still couldn’t bring myself to let go, always thinking that if I tried a little harder, maybe others wouldn’t judge me with such an ambiguous word as “interesting.”

On the dining table were still several half-eaten dishes, and the soup in the pot was gradually growing cold. I leaned back in my chair, holding a cup of slightly cool oolong tea, and in the fragrance of the tea I could faintly catch the scent of the garlic shrimp on the table. The living room window was wide open, warm sunlight pouring in, and the air was still mixed with a faint fresh plant scent—the smell from the new potting soil I had changed for the houseplants that morning.

My friends sat around the table, chatting slowly. Xiao Lin was seated by the window, head down as she scrolled on her phone, occasionally looking up at us. “Look at this video, it’s hilarious!” she suddenly said with a laugh, holding up the screen. On it, a kitten had its head covered by a plastic bag, awkwardly bouncing around on the floor. Everyone laughed a few times, and A-De even imitated the kitten with an exaggerated gesture, almost tipping his chair over.

“Ugh, I’ve been insanely busy lately.” A-De picked up his chopsticks and poked at the shrimp shells on the plate. “Just talking about that Wednesday project earlier—I’m totally exhausted.”

“And you still got through it, didn’t you?” Xiao Lin glanced at him, her tone a little teasing. “Over all these years, haven’t you complained about plenty of projects?”

“Exactly,” I chimed in casually, though my voice sounded a little distant. I wasn’t sure if anyone noticed. I wasn’t really paying full attention; my eyes drifted involuntarily to the tea stain at the corner of the table, and I was thinking that I should wipe it off with kitchen cleaner later.

“Hey, were you zoning out just now?” A-De suddenly looked at me. Although his tone was half-joking, I still felt a bit nervous.

“Huh? No, not at all!” My voice rose a little higher than usual, and then I quickly added, “I was just thinking—could that project you mentioned earlier maybe be tried with a rapid-iteration approach?” Actually, I was just tossing out something loosely related to work, but it seemed to work pretty well. A-De didn’t ask any further. He just nodded and said, “Mm, that makes sense. Maybe we can try doing it that way sometime.”

Everyone kept chatting, and I tried to relax, taking a sip of tea. The warm liquid slid down my throat, making me feel a little better. Suddenly, Xiao Lin turned to me and asked, “Got any new inspiration lately? It feels like you haven’t posted any new work in a while.”

“I have some ideas, but they’re still in development and not fully sorted out yet.” I set down my teacup, trying to look natural. “Maybe something will come out in a while.” In truth, I hadn’t made any real progress, and the question was a little awkward for me, but in this easygoing atmosphere, I could still manage to brush it off.

Before I knew it, evening had arrived, and everyone began clearing the table. A reddish-orange sunset hung on the horizon, its light streaming through the window and spilling across the floor in a warm golden glow. When my fingers touched the edge of a plate, I felt a slight dampness—the trace left by the soup. The sound of running water came from the kitchen, where Xiao Lin was washing the dishes, and A-De tied up the trash bag and placed it by the door. I stood by the table clearing away the leftovers, listening to my friends laughing and talking, and felt my inner self slowly grow soft and peaceful as well.

After everyone left, I sat alone on the sofa and drifted off for a while. There was still some unfinished oolong tea on the coffee table, with tea leaves sparsely floating on the surface. I suddenly realized that, at some point, this kind of Saturday had become routine for me. Although life seemed plain at first glance, this kind of time also felt quite precious.

Sunlight streamed through the window onto the tabletop, and the hum of voices in the café distracted me a little, but my eyes stayed fixed on my laptop screen. Everyone was gathered around the table, and we were discussing a new creative project. It was supposed to be a relaxed brainstorming session, but I remained tense the whole time. After everyone had spoken, it was my turn. I took a deep breath and tried to look calm, though my palms were already damp.

“I think we could try a more narrative approach, like designing the user experience as a journey through a story…” Before I could finish, the colleague across from me suddenly raised his eyebrows and cut in, “That probably wouldn’t work very well. We seem to have tried something similar before, and the results were mediocre.” His tone was flat, but in that instant, it felt like I’d been doused with cold water in front of everyone.

My mind went blank. For a few seconds, it seemed as if all sound had vanished. I could hear my own heart pounding, and my fingers froze over the keyboard. Was my suggestion stupid? Did everyone think I wasn’t professional enough? Was he implying that I shouldn’t have spoken at all? “He’s dismissing me.” The thought surged up like a wave, and I couldn’t even hold it back.

“Uh… really? Maybe I remembered it wrong,” I said, unconsciously making fun of myself as I lowered my head and pretended to edit my notes. “Don’t get me wrong—I just think this route may not be very cost-effective, and we can talk it through more deeply,” the colleague added. I could tell his tone had softened, but my mind had already staged an entire elaborate drama: he might just be brushing me off, and everyone else might think I was holding the team back. In my ears, his follow-up came across as a veiled criticism.

By the end of the meeting, everyone else looked relaxed, chatting with one another or lining up for coffee, while I felt cold all over, as if I had just come through a battle. I mechanically said goodbye to everyone and walked out of the café alone. When I reached into my pocket for my earphones, I found them tangled into a knot. I muttered a curse under my breath, as if blaming myself, or perhaps this chaotic world.

Back home, lying on the sofa, I replayed the scene over and over. “What exactly did he mean? Was I being too sensitive? Should I be more confident?” That kind of self-review went on for hours, until late at night, when my stomach began to ache faintly, as if protesting the cruel internal beating I was giving myself. I opened a draft that needed revision, trying to distract myself, but the words on the screen only made me feel even more powerless. Could I have done better? Or did they actually not care at all how well I did?

When I woke up the next morning, I stared at the ceiling, trying to comfort myself a little. “Maybe he really was just giving his opinion, and it wasn’t aimed at me.” But as soon as that thought surfaced, it was interrupted by the familiar voice saying things like, “You’re really not that good.” My stomach still ached faintly, as if reminding me that yesterday’s brief but intense sense of frustration had not ended.

The restaurant’s lights seemed brighter and more glaring than usual, and the surrounding conversations intertwined into a noise that made it hard for me to concentrate. The pasta on my plate had already gone cold, and I had barely touched it. Xiao Li, the colleague sitting next to me, was chatting with another coworker about something, and their laughter felt like it was piercing my eardrums. “Why aren’t you eating?” Xiao Li suddenly turned to me, his tone carrying a hint of teasing. When I heard that, a wave of heat rushed up my chest, and my face instantly burned.

“Oh, I… I’m just not very hungry,” I replied, my voice so low it was almost inaudible. I tried to put on a careless expression, but inside I was already beginning to churn. Did they think I was deliberately avoiding the conversation? Had my silence already upset them? Or was Xiao Li just asking casually, and I was overthinking it again?

For the rest of the time, I was completely unable to focus on anything being said at the table, and could only nod mechanically in agreement. Every exchange of glances between them felt like a deliberate signal to exclude me, and I even felt that several of Xiao Li’s laughs carried some kind of meaning aimed at me. That familiar, deep shame rose again, like a hand gripping me tightly and making it hard to breathe.

My stomach began to clench, and I could feel sweat seeping out from my back. I kept trying to tell myself this was just my habitual neurotic reaction, but that voice surfaced again: they must be mocking me in their hearts, thinking I don’t fit in, thinking I’m a failure. What kind of person barely eats at a gathering? Isn’t that just a weirdo?

I had thought I could force myself to hold on until dinner ended, but when everyone suggested taking photos, I completely lost control. Xiao Li raised his phone and said, “Come on, stand a little closer, don’t look so stiff.” That word, “stiff,” pierced through my last shred of disguise like a needle. I felt as if my entire body had been exposed, as though everyone were staring at my flaws. I suddenly stood up, my tone turning sharp: “What exactly do you mean? I’m stiff? Do you think I’m especially ridiculous?” The words burst out of me, and everyone at the table froze.

The air seemed to solidify. I couldn’t even understand why I had said that, and all I felt was my heartbeat racing so fast it seemed ready to leap out of my chest. I saw Xiao Li’s expression change; he seemed to want to explain something, but I was already dizzy, as if the whole scene were spinning. I didn’t wait for them to say anything. I grabbed my bag and left.

When I got home, I sat on the sofa, feeling as if my body had been emptied out. My mind was filled with the expressions on their faces and Xiao Li’s final words: “That’s not what I meant…” I kept dissecting his tone, wondering whether he really had just been joking, and whether I had once again misunderstood him. But if it was a misunderstanding, then what would they think of me? Would they think I was emotional, immature? I replayed the entire incident over and over, even starting to doubt whether I had broken down crying loudly in the restaurant. That endless questioning kept me awake nearly all night.

A few days later, I ran into Xiao Li at the company. He tried to strike up a conversation, but after I mumbled a few vague responses, I hurried away. I didn’t dare face him, and I didn’t dare face the shadow left by that dinner.

The sky outside the window was a leaden gray, and cold winds howled through the streets. I sat at a long wooden table in a small screenwriting workshop, surrounded by other passionate creators. The room was filled with the aroma of coffee, and the walls were covered with vivid screenplay posters. My notebook lay open on the table, and I could hear the rustling of paper all around me. The mentor was reviewing everyone’s work one by one, which filled me with an inexplicable sense of tension. My heartbeat gradually quickened, and cold sweat quietly seeped out on my back.

“You’re next. Tell us about your script,” the mentor said with a slight smile, gesturing for me to begin. Under the friendly gazes of the others, I cleared my throat, tried hard to control my pounding heart, and began to talk about the inspiration for my script. I could feel my voice trembling, but I still tried to remain calm.

The mentor nodded and began offering his feedback. He mentioned that my plot development was a bit too loose and that the characters’ motivations were not clear enough, which required deeper thought. His voice was gentle, but I felt every word like a thorn, piercing straight into my heart. “You might want to think more about the characters’ backgrounds; that could give the story a deeper meaning,” the mentor suggested.

At the sound of his voice, memories of my own awkward and failed moments began replaying in my mind. I thought of the proposals that had been rejected for not being good enough, the moments when I had been ignored in meetings. It was as if I could hear those mocking voices, even though the room was completely quiet. I began to doubt my abilities, and a voice in my heart seemed to repeat over and over: I’m terrible.

I felt my stomach tighten, and it seemed as if my heart were about to leap out of my chest. My face grew hot, even though the heating in the room was just right. To hide it, I lowered my head and pretended to write down the mentor’s suggestions in my notebook. But I couldn’t write a single word; I merely went through the motions of taking notes.

That night, after I got home, I lay in bed, and the mentor’s voice still echoed in my head. I kept replaying every word he had said, trying to find details that could be improved. The noise in my mind kept me from sleeping, and it was only in the early hours of the morning that I finally drifted into exhausted semi-consciousness.

When I woke up the next day, I still felt the gloom of the previous day lingering in my heart. Dragging my heavy body along, I decided to take a walk in a nearby park. The cool air and the birdsong in the morning made me feel a little more relaxed. A week later, I revisited my script, determined not to dwell on self-doubt anymore, and began revising it according to the feedback from that day. Though the process was slow, I gradually felt the tension in my heart ease.

The light on the balcony was that kind of white that doesn’t glare, as if it had been filtered through something first, falling on the pages of the book and on the back of my hand, warm but not hot. The woven pattern of the rattan chair pressed into my back, and I didn’t move; instead, I felt that slight discomfort make me even more certain that I was truly sitting here. Someone passed by downstairs, their footsteps so light it was as if they didn’t want to disturb anyone. A breeze slipped in through the gaps in the balcony, carrying a faint earthy scent—the smell of the small flower bed downstairs, I guessed.

I’d bought the book a few days earlier. It was about how a person finds their center again amid the fragments of life. I opened it, read a few lines, and then stopped.

Not because I was distracted—it was because I realized I wasn’t distracted.

That realization made me pause for a moment.

Usually at this time, my mind would already have started running through rehearsals: would next week’s pitch meeting get rejected, did that video with the bad numbers mean my direction was fundamentally off, and that thing I said to a friend three days ago—did they reply slowly because I’d said something wrong? These thoughts usually ran in the background like programs I couldn’t shut off, and I didn’t even know when they started. I only knew there was always something pressing against my chest.

But today, those programs seemed to have been suspended for the moment.

“Not going out for a walk today?” The person I lived with poked their head out from the living room, speaking casually, just asking in passing.

“No,” I said. “It’s nice here.”

They nodded and withdrew.

I waited a second, and out of habit I started trying to analyze that nod—did they think I was lazy, or that I was avoiding socializing? Then I heard myself say inwardly: enough, stop thinking.

I was a little surprised even by that thought.

I lowered my head again and looked at the book. The sunlight shifted slightly and landed on my profile; I narrowed my eyes but didn’t dodge it. The character in the book was going through a kind of rift I knew very well—wanting peace, yet always shattering it with their own hands. When I read that passage, my heart did jump slightly, not with anxiety, but more like the feeling of someone suddenly calling my name.

I closed the book and put it on my lap, just sitting there.

I wasn’t thinking about anything. Or rather, some thoughts drifted by, and I watched them drift past without reaching out to catch them. The sun warmed me until I broke into a slight sweat; my back grew a little sticky, but I still didn’t move. A child was running downstairs, their laughter broken into little fragments, already very faint by the time it reached up here.

That night, we made dinner together and talked about what we’d each been reading. Nothing particularly special, and there was no awkward silence either.

For several days afterward, I would occasionally think back to that afternoon. Not because something had happened, but precisely because nothing had happened. I had just sat there, bathed in sunlight, with no disaster, no rehearsals, no mistakes to review.

That alone was enough.

I’m not very used to admitting this, but that day I really did feel that, for the time being, I didn’t need to fight with myself.

The exhibition hall was filled with the scent of clay, mixed with a faint earthy fragrance in the air. I paused at the entrance, trying to steady my racing heartbeat. The lighting here was soft, and the walls were hung with carefully crafted ceramic works by artists, each in different forms and rich colors. I gently ran my fingers over the exhibits, feeling their roughness and warmth. Yet I couldn’t stop my mind from catastrophically imagining these beautiful pieces suddenly shattering under my touch. My stomach tightened, and I began to blame myself, feeling that I shouldn’t be so uneasy.

“Don’t worry, these works are quite sturdy,” came a deep, warm voice. I turned around and saw an artist smiling at me. His gaze was calm and steady, which put me slightly at ease.

“Thank you, I’m just a little nervous,” I forced out a smile, ashamed of my unease.

“Are you interested in ceramics?” the artist continued to ask.

“Yes, but I don’t know much about it,” I replied, my voice slightly trembling, worried that he might be annoyed by my ignorance.

“You can try to feel it with your heart instead of trying to understand it,” he suggested.

I nodded, trying to relax my shoulders, and carefully observed those colorful ceramic works, attempting to sense the serenity they exuded. Although I still found it hard to fully relax, I was glad that I hadn’t fled this place because of my anxiety.

That afternoon, I had brief conversations with several visitors at the exhibition, trying to change my habit of overinterpreting other people’s expressions. Although the physical tension didn’t disappear completely, I found that by constantly reminding myself to enjoy the present moment, I could gain some relief. When I left the exhibition, my mood seemed to have improved and was no longer so heavy.

A few days later, I made an effort to remember the artist’s words, taking “feel with your heart” as my new way of facing anxiety. When I encountered similar emotional fluctuations at home again, I tried not to judge the potential danger of everything, but instead to focus on the beauty of things themselves.

Today’s sunlight was especially dazzling, and the air still carried a faint warmth. I strolled through a small secondhand book market in the eastern part of the city, a place I visited from time to time. There weren’t many people, and the aisles between the stalls were a little narrow, with old newspapers spread over the ground. A faint fragrance of books and the scent of paper lingered in the air around me. I took a light breath and felt myself relax a little.

The stall owners greeted me warmly. I nodded back and wandered unhurriedly from one stall to another. A somewhat worn hardcover caught my eye; it was a novel I had always wanted to read but had never bought. I carefully pulled it out from among a pile of books, unable to contain my delight, and opened its yellowed pages, gazing at the traces of old times hidden between the lines.

“Do you like this one?” the stall owner asked with a smile. He was a kindly old gentleman with neatly combed white hair.

“Yes, I haven’t seen it in a long time,” I replied with a smile as well, feeling my heartbeat quicken slightly, perhaps from excitement, or perhaps because I found a kind of comfort in such simple exchanges.

I continued wandering through the book market, occasionally stopping to browse a few magazines or art albums, enjoying this undisturbed time.
