Sunlight filtered through the awning above, casting mottled patterns of light and shadow over the bookstalls and the ground. A breeze passed by from time to time, bringing a refreshing coolness. I closed my eyes and felt the intertwining bustle and stillness around me.

“You seem very happy today,” came a familiar voice. It was an auntie stall owner I often ran into here.

“Yes, this place always lets me find little surprises,” I replied softly, my heart filled with a comforting sense of contentment.

When I left the book market, carrying the old book I had bought, I felt utterly relaxed and satisfied. On the way home, the vendors along the street were busy packing up their stalls, and the city’s noise seemed gentled by the afternoon sunlight. I didn’t know why a simple book market could make me feel so peaceful. Perhaps it was the sense of being out of step with time, allowing me to temporarily forget the disturbances of the outside world.

Sitting quietly at my desk at home, I began to read the book carefully, my fingertips sliding over the pages and feeling their roughness and warmth. Reading drew me in completely, and the anxiety in my heart seemed to dissipate along with it. The plot was as captivating as I had hoped, and the guilt and unease I felt toward the past seemed, in that moment, to be gently brushed away by the power of the words.

Over the next few days, I often thought of that book, and of that afternoon spent at the book market. Though it was just an ordinary day, it gave me a long-lost sense of peace and freedom, and I wanted to treasure that feeling and not let it be buried beneath the trivialities of life.

Gray clouds hung low over the entire city. The air still held the dampness of rain, mixed with some indescribable moldy smell. I pushed open that battered iron gate, and the creak tore through the silence of the whole building like a sneer. The abandoned telephone exchange building was peeling apart in sheets, exposing its gray-white concrete beneath. The floor was covered in a thick layer of dust, with a few crumpled scraps of paper and old circuit boards scattered here and there. The moment I stepped inside, a chill spread up from the soles of my feet. My footsteps echoed through the emptiness, each one seeming to announce: I’m the only one here.

In the corner stood an old telephone switchboard, its bulky metal casing covered in rust, the dial stopped on some number that no one had ever returned to zero. I reached out and touched it. Cold. Rough. At that very moment, for some reason, the call from last week’s client suddenly flashed through my mind — their tone was impatient, almost sighing: “This plan is too naive. Redo it.”

I pulled my hand back.

Something felt like it was pressing down on my chest, dull and heavy, leaving me unable to speak. I lowered my head and stared at the dust on the floor, and my mind began to take the same familiar path: Why is it always like this? Why is nothing I make ever good enough? Once that thought found a crack, it kept pouring out. Back in college, when I entered a competition, a judge had casually said, “It’s still not mature enough.” I hid in the bathroom and cried for nearly an hour. I thought that feeling was long gone, but now it had come back intact, as if it had never left.

I slowly slid down the wall, my back pressed against the cold concrete, my palms already damp with sweat. My stomach began to clench, again and again, and my heartbeat quickened too; I could feel it pounding heavily in my chest. I tried to take deep breaths, but it didn’t help. My gaze drifted aimlessly over a row of broken windows, the shattered glass faintly reflecting the last bit of light outside. A few gray pigeons flew past the window, the flapping of their wings drifting in, like some lonely rhythm.

Then I heard myself say in my heart: What if I’m doomed to never be good enough?

I had asked myself that question many times, but each time there was no answer, only a deeper sense of falling. I knew what would happen next — I would start attacking myself, using the harshest words, slandering myself before anyone else could, as if that could lessen the pain of being rejected. “Anyway, failing isn’t surprising. Anyway, that’s just how I am.” I gave a bitter smile in my mind, but I hadn’t expected my eyes to suddenly burn; tears surged up and I couldn’t hold them back at all.

I sat there without moving.

Outside, the sky grew darker and darker, and the darkness slowly swallowed the entire space. I don’t know how long I sat there. It was only when I could barely see anything anymore that I braced myself against the wall and stood up, wiping my face roughly with my sleeve. When I reached the iron door, I turned back for one last look at the switchboard — it just stayed there, broken, unwanted, its dial frozen on a meaningless number. I couldn’t explain why, but I suddenly felt a strange sense of closeness to it.

When I got home, I didn’t sit down. I walked back and forth through the room for a long time. That night I hardly slept at all. My mind kept turning over work, direction, those moments of being denied, like a loop with no exit. Lying in bed, my stomach was still aching faintly, and my heartbeat sounded especially clear in the darkness, as if reminding me: the problem is still there, the answer still hasn’t come, but time won’t stop and wait for me to figure it out.

The lights were dim and yellow, and in the air there was a faint smell of old wood and damp carpet. I stood in a small corner backstage at the theater, clutching the printed copy of my poem, my fingertips trembling slightly. From the stage outside, the readings rose and fell in tone, and every burst of applause felt like a reminder that many accomplished creators had gathered here, while I was nothing more than a timid outsider. I forced myself not to look at the busy figures of the staff, but in my ears kept echoing a line from their whispered conversation just moments before: “TA looks a little nervous. I hope TA doesn’t make a mistake.” That sentence stabbed into my ears like a needle, instantly making my heart race. My palms began to sweat, the manuscript grew slippery, and I could barely hold on to it.

“The next one—are you ready?” A staff member in charge of ushering approached me, sounding a little hurried. I nodded hard, but the words seemed stuck in my throat, unable to come out in a clear reply. “Good luck, you can do it!” she encouraged me in a low voice, yet I keenly caught the sound of her hurried footsteps as she left, as if she didn’t really believe her own words. My stomach began to ache faintly, as though gripped by an invisible hand. As I adjusted my breathing, I walked toward the stage, my legs heavy as lead.

Standing beneath the lights, the audience below was in darkness, and I could barely make out the few people in the front row. My throat tightened, but I still mechanically recited the first line: “On this night, raindrops strike the window, each sound like a knock on memory’s door…” My tone was stiff and my voice dry. Someone lowered their head and whispered to another; I strained to catch a glimpse of their expressions, but I couldn’t tell what they thought. A strong voice suddenly flashed through my mind: They must think I’m terrible. Why did I even come to this kind of event?

The more I thought this way, the stronger my physical reactions became. The stomachache grew more obvious, and my fingers began to tremble slightly, uncontrollably. But just as the rhythm in the next section eased a little, I actually heard one or two soft “mm” sounds—like someone was listening carefully. Somewhere in my heart, the tiniest thread of hope appeared, and I tried to hold on to it. But then I ruined another word in a breath, and that hope was struck down again: someone in the audience let out a faint laugh. In an instant, my face felt so hot it was almost burning, and a thin sheen of sweat broke out on my forehead. My mind rapidly replayed those disaster scenarios: they would definitely talk about me after the event, laugh at me, and even other attendees would pass it along to one another, saying, “Why did TA even come? TA doesn’t deserve to be here at all!”

At last I finished the final section. Standing on the stage, I stiffly said, “Thank you,” then fled toward the backstage in a panic. My heart pounded like a drum, my whole stomach twisted into a knot, and in my ears the hallucinated murmur of people below still filled the air. A staff member handed me a cup of water. I thanked her and took a few gulps, yet it felt as though the rim of the cup was knocking against my teeth. This sense of embarrassment made me strongly question why I had signed up in the first place. I even wanted to leave immediately, but I still dragged my heavy steps back to the audience seats.

The next few readers continued performing on stage, but I didn’t hear a single word. My mind kept replaying every moment of my own mistake and its possible consequences. I didn’t dare look at the people around me, and I even didn’t dare think about why they could applaud and smile so naturally. Later I finally couldn’t bear it any longer and left early. After I got home, I sat slumped on the sofa and looked through my phone. They hadn’t sent any feedback—no criticism, no comfort either—and that silence only made me more panicked: were they already talking about me behind my back? That anxiety lasted a full three days, and every time I thought of it, my stomach would ache faintly. I even decided that I would never try reading my own work aloud again.

The open-air art exhibition was held in a small square in the center of the city, filled with vibrant, colorful paintings. I stood before one canvas, depicting a weathered old house. Its delicate brushwork and use of color stunned me, as if I could hear the roof tiles softly humming in the breeze. People in the square chatted and laughed, and the air was filled with the scent of coffee and fresh paint. Beside me, the artist was enthusiastically explaining his creative vision to the audience. “Don’t you think the tranquility in this kind of scene helps people settle their minds?” I nodded, feeling a trace of unease. My heartbeat quickened, and my palms slowly grew damp. Every brushstroke in the painting seemed to question my own artistic ability.

I whispered to myself, “Can my work have this kind of power?” I had torn my own paintings to pieces countless times, never daring to show them to anyone, afraid they would see the flaws in my heart. The artist turned and asked me, “Do you paint too? I hope I’ll have a chance to see your work.” I forced out a smile. “Yes, but I’m still learning.” The unease in my heart swelled rapidly, as if I could be exposed at any moment.

When I left the exhibition, my stomach ached faintly, as though my body were protesting the anxiety rising within me. A light breeze brushed my cheeks, but it did nothing to ease my tension. I kept replaying the conversation in my mind, trying to find any hidden criticism in it. Before long, a fine rain began to fall, soaking my coat. The cold raindrops made me feel a little clearer, but I remained restless inside. After returning home, I sat at my desk and tried to look at my paintings again, yet my thoughts were overwhelmed by an unending flood of negative ideas.

Over the course of the following week, I kept thinking about the paintings at that open-air exhibition and the artist’s words, turning every detail into ammunition for self-attack. I began to doubt every one of my creative impulses and ideas. A week later, I finally forced myself into the studio and picked up my brush again. Though filled with fear, I knew I couldn’t keep hiding forever; the sound of the brush moving across the paper was the only thing that could give me even a little peace.

I stood at the podium, my sweaty palms pressed against my note cards. The lights in the room were blinding, so white it was hard to breathe. I looked at the dozens of blurred faces below, trying to find a friendly expression to steady myself. My voice trembled slightly because I was speaking too fast, but I told myself to hold on until the last slide. When the presentation ended, there was a scattered round of applause. I forced out a smile, took a deep breath, and mechanically said, “Thank you, everyone.”

My advisor came up to me; he was the host of the event. In a low voice, he said, “Everyone, does anyone have a question for our speaker? If not, I’ll ask one.” His gaze swept over me with an expression I couldn’t decipher. I froze for a moment, my heart pounding so hard it felt like it might leap out of my chest. Then he asked, “Do you think Claim P really applies under this topic? It sounds like your argument is somewhat lacking.”

I heard myself stammering, “Um... maybe... maybe I didn’t explain this point clearly enough. I...” A feeling of suffocation washed over me, as if the air had turned into thick, sticky gel. I couldn’t tell whether there was disappointment in his eyes, but that uncertainty stabbed into my skin like needles. People were talking quietly in the audience, and my ears started buzzing.

After the event, my advisor came over, nodded at me, and said, “Overall, not bad, but you can refine your logic a bit more when you get back.” Those words struck my fragile confidence like an invisible hammer. I mechanically said, “Okay,” then lowered my head to gather my things, not daring to look at him again.

On the ride home, streetlights flashed past the window like golden wounds. His words kept replaying in my mind: “You can refine your logic a bit more when you get back.” My interpretation grew more and more extreme: Did he think I was completely incapable? In his eyes, was I a failed student? Had the flaws in my proposal that day already made him sick of me? The tightness in my stomach became more and more pronounced. I pressed a hand over my lower abdomen, but the physical discomfort couldn’t ease the self-attack in my head.

When I got home, I didn’t even eat dinner. I shut the bedroom door, curled up on the bed, and opened my phone, trying to find more interviews with my advisor or reviews of his work to figure out what standards he held students to. I even searched social media to see whether he had posted anything about today’s event, even a single trivial comment. Nothing came up. Lying in bed, I imagined again and again him returning to his office and saying to the other advisors, “How is she so fragile?” Imagining these scenes made my chest ache faintly.

The next day I tried to focus on reviewing the slides, but every time I flipped to that page, I couldn’t stop thinking of his expression and tone. I started to doubt whether I still had any right to keep creating, and I even felt afraid of the next lecture I had signed up for. These feelings lasted until the team meeting a week later, when I gradually began to ease back into the rhythm of work.

The banquet hall was filled with laughter and joy, and colorful lights flickered all around as everyone basked in delight. Soft music drifted through the air, but I felt an inexplicable tension. I looked around, trying to catch the expressions on everyone’s faces and guess what they were thinking. When my eyes met those of an old friend I hadn’t seen in a long time, my heartbeat suddenly quickened, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. I forced out a smile, and she nodded in return as a greeting.

“Long time no see,” she said, walking over to give me a hug. At that moment, I caught the scent of her perfume—sweet yet sharp, as if it were awakening the unease deep in my heart.

“Yeah, it’s really been a long time,” I tried to make my voice sound relaxed, but inside I was full of caution. We had been very good friends a few years ago, but later, because of some misunderstandings, our relationship became strained. I had always wondered whether she still held some old grudge against me.

She wore a perfectly measured smile, but I sensed a touch of distance. I began to reflect on my own mistakes, wondering whether it was something I had done unintentionally that had upset her. In my mind, I kept repeating those possible missteps, and couldn’t help feeling waves of heartache.

“How have you been lately?” she asked, and I noticed a hint of uncertainty in her tone.

“Pretty good, busy with some new projects,” I replied, speaking a little too quickly, afraid she would notice my inner turmoil. I felt a flush of sweat; my palms were sticky, and I hurriedly stuffed my hands into my pockets so she wouldn’t see.

After exchanging a few polite words, she left to find other friends. I stood there feeling as though all my strength had been drained away. I tried to remember whether anything in my behavior had been inappropriate, but the more I thought about it, the more ashamed I felt. Every one of her words echoed over and over in my mind, and I worried whether she still harbored resentment toward me.

After the banquet ended, I returned home, my mind full of fragmented memories. That night, I kept replaying the arguments and misunderstandings we had once had, terrified of being misunderstood and abandoned again. When I woke the next day, I felt powerless and downcast, wondering whether I was truly worthy of trust and love. Before falling asleep that night, the moment of that embrace kept reappearing before my eyes, leaving me unable to sleep all night, with a faint ache in my chest.

The air was thick with the chill of frost. I pulled my scarf tighter and stepped through the observatory gates. The lobby was dimly lit, with only a few warm yellow wall lamps illuminating the astronomical exhibits on the walls. A few people were speaking in low voices, not noticing my arrival at all. The silence around me was so profound I could feel my own heartbeat in my ears, and that familiar sense of tension began to surge. I kept my head down and moved forward, trying to find a corner to stand in, but the creaking of the floor drew a few people’s attention. “Hello, are you here for the stargazing event?” A staff member walked toward me, smiling. I nodded hard. I opened my mouth, but found I couldn’t say anything, so I could only hold out the event QR code on my phone screen to her. She glanced at it and said, “Okay, please go inside. The telescope area is on the second floor.” I thanked her, but my voice felt as faint as a mosquito’s buzz. Without realizing it, I lowered my head and quickly headed for the stairs.

The stairs were a bit steep. I gripped the handrail and made my way to the second floor, feeling as though my steps would never quite steady themselves. I tried to use the light from my phone screen to confirm where my feet were, while the illusion that everyone was staring at me settled over me. In the room on the second floor, several telescopes had already been set up, and the glass dome was slowly opening to reveal a sky full of stars. People clustered around the telescopes, excitedly discussing Pluto’s orbit and identifying constellations. I stood by the door, my palms beginning to sweat, and my wool coat seemed to have grown several times heavier. I glanced at the faces in the room; their unfamiliar expressions suddenly made me feel out of place. Their words seemed to carry an invisible message: why did you come here?

“You can see Venus from here. You should try it,” one participant turned to me and said, pointing at a telescope. I froze for a moment and instinctively shook my head slightly. “No need. I’m just looking around.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I felt my face start to burn, as if scorched. I unconsciously tightened my grip on my sleeve, trying to look composed, but the shame of being seen through was almost unbearable. I just wanted to escape the scene, yet I didn’t want to appear like a loser. So I kept standing there, pretending to focus on the sky outside the window, even though my mind was already in complete chaos. My stomach began to ache faintly, my fingertips turned cold, and my toes curled inside my boots as if nailed to the floor. I even wondered whether I would be able to take a step and leave.

After the event ended, I was almost the first to leave. I stepped outside the entrance and breathed in a few mouthfuls of cold air, but I still couldn’t calm the thoughts that had been thrown into disarray by my nerves. On the way home, I kept second-guessing my behavior: why did I refuse that telescope? Why didn’t I try to talk to others? Would they think I was strange? Worries flooded my mind like an unstoppable torrent, and by midnight I was still lying awake, replaying every detail and every line of conversation, even the creaking of the stairs seeming to mock my cowardice.

The bookstore door gave a soft jingle as I pushed it open and stepped inside, the wooden floor creaking faintly beneath my feet. The air was mixed with the smells of coffee and paper, and the gentle lighting spilled across the bookshelves, casting long shadows. “Welcome,” a young clerk said, glancing up at me before lowering his head again to continue tidying the shelves. I nodded and walked toward the literary section in the corner, looking for a book about narrative techniques. My fingers brushed over row after row of book spines, the cool touch calming me somewhat, but then the murmuring beside my ear began to distract me. Someone was whispering in hushed voices; I couldn’t make out what they were saying, yet it made me uneasy, as if it were about me.

“Can I help you?” the clerk’s voice suddenly came from behind me. I turned around and forced out a smile. “Ah, no, thanks.”

He nodded, but then looked at me again and added, “You seem a little tense. Is everything okay?”

That sentence was like a stone dropped into water, instantly stirring up the calm in my heart. Was I acting too strangely? Why would he say that? Had my behavior just now been so odd that it made him suspicious? My heart started racing, and my cheeks burned hot. I stood there stunned for a moment, then said as casually as I could, “Oh, no, I’m just... uh... a little distracted.”

I quickly looked away and pretended to be choosing a book. But his words had already lodged in my mind like a thorn, impossible to pull out. Every time I moved to the other side of the shelf, I could faintly hear him talking with a coworker in low voices. I couldn’t be sure whether they were talking about me, but that uncertainty nearly drove me crazy, as if all the eyes in the room were fixed on me. My stomach cramped, my palms began to sweat, and even the feel of the book cover turned sticky.

After forcing myself to endure it for a while, I finally picked out a book and headed to the cashier, silently praying it would be over quickly. When I swiped my card, my hand trembled slightly as I signed. The clerk looked at me again. I quickly gathered my things and walked out of the bookstore with my head down.

By the time I got back onto the street, it was already dark. The cool autumn wind blew over me, as if reminding me that I had finally escaped that suffocating place. I clutched the book and, instead of going home, sat down at a small plaza nearby. I kept replaying the conversation in my head, over and over again. That “you seem a little tense” line echoed in my ears, magnified a hundred times. I started blaming myself—why had I acted so strangely, why couldn’t I have been more natural? Had the clerk thought I was a difficult customer? Yet another part of me tried to comfort myself: maybe he had just been casually checking in, and it didn’t mean that much at all.

That night, I went home and lay in bed unable to sleep, obsessing over it again and again. The next day, even after getting up, I still felt uneasy, and I even wondered whether I shouldn’t go to that bookstore again, so as to avoid running into another embarrassing situation like that.

Sitting on a park bench, I looked around me. Sunlight filtered through the leaves, casting dappled shadows. Children were cheering and playing at the nearby playground, their laughter drifting over with the breeze. Occasionally passersby walked in front of me, most of them looking down at their phones or talking with the people beside them. I tried hard to relax, but a faint unease kept twisting around my heart, like a shadow I could never quite escape. A woman pushed a stroller past me, and the baby’s giggles made my mind calm a little.

An elderly couple on the bench beside me was speaking in low voices. Though I couldn’t make out what they were saying, I could feel a warmth andtacit understanding that had settled over them through the years in their expressions and soft laughter. A wave of bitterness rose in my heart. Why was I always moved by such small things? “These people all seem to be living well; maybe they don’t have so many worries,” I told myself. I couldn’t help feeling disgusted with myself. Such thoughts were truly unreasonable and unnecessary.

A dog barked somewhere nearby, and I tensed up instantly. My heart suddenly raced, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. Looking around, I realized it was just a small dog chasing a squirrel, with its owner anxiously calling after it. “Hey, be careful, it runs fast!” someone nearby said with a laugh, reminding the owner.

I took a deep breath and tried to get my heartbeat back to normal. I tried to focus my attention on other things. The scent of flowers in the park drifted over with the breeze, carrying a reassuring calm. I closed my eyes and, while breathing in, silently repeated, “Everything is fine. Everything will be fine.” This simple act seemed to ease the tension in my stomach.

After I got home, my mood gradually settled. That evening, I thought back on my time in the park and even felt a little comfort. The next day, I slipped back into my usual routine, though I would still occasionally think of that afternoon on the bench, and the baby’s laughter in my ears.

The studio was filled with the earthy scent of clay. Sunlight streamed through the window and spilled across the floor, bringing a soft warmth to the whole room. I sat at the table, my hands covered in mud, trying to sculpt a complex piece. It was a project I had always wanted to do but had never dared to start. The thoughts of failure that kept circling in my mind rolled in like stubborn shadows, accompanying every friction of my fingers against the clay. “Will it turn out too ugly?” I wondered as I watched the piece slowly take shape. My heartbeat began to quicken, a few beads of sweat formed on my forehead, and my palms grew damp.

“You’re doing great. Keep trying,” the teacher in the classroom said as she walked over and stopped beside me, gently encouraging me. Yet all that remained in my mind was the voice questioning myself: “Is it really good, or is she just trying to comfort me?” Images of past rejections and criticisms flashed through my mind, and my stomach began to churn. I tried hard to control my breathing so that excessive tension wouldn’t ruin the piece.

Around me, the other students were busy at their own workstations, their clay constantly changing shape in their hands. What filled the classroom were their quiet conversations and the occasional bursts of laughter. My ears, however, were unusually sensitive, and I kept feeling as if someone were whispering about my work. An uneasy, prickling feeling spread through my heart. I began to recall those moments when I had been judged before, and a headache slowly started to set in.

“What style do you want it to have?” the teacher asked, interrupting my thoughts. She looked warmly at my work. Her gaze held sincere curiosity and encouragement. I tried to suppress the panic inside me and replied, “I want to try a new style, but I’m not sure whether I can succeed.”

“Trying is a kind of success,” she said with a smile.

My heart was touched again by those words, and a warm current washed some of the fear away. Still, a sense of shame I couldn’t shake pressed on my chest, as if it were a flaw waiting to be discovered. “Maybe I’ll never be able to do it perfectly,” I thought. “Why not give up sooner?” But my hands kept sculpting, even though my heart was still uneasy.

When I left the classroom, the sky outside had gradually brightened. Although my mind was still somewhat muddled, with too many fragments of past failures flashing through it, I still felt a little unburdened relief. I decided to try this new project again. Even though I was still uneasy about whether I could succeed, at least I had not allowed fear to completely take over.

Over the past few days, I would occasionally think back on this experience and imagine what different choices I might have made if I could do it over. But whenever such thoughts arose, I tried to bury them beneath action and told myself that this was part of growth.

The second floor of the bookstore had been turned into a small event space. On the long wooden table sat a few scattered books and several cups of hand-brewed coffee that were still steaming. To make the speakers stand out more, the organizers had deliberately placed a tall floor lamp on one side, and the light made my eyes ache a little. I clasped my hands together, my nails lightly scraping my palms, and kept glancing at the time on my phone screen, my heart beating a little too fast.

“Don’t be nervous,” said the woman sitting next to me in a low voice. “Relax. You just need to say a few things later; we’re all here to support you.” Her tone was easy, but I felt as if there was some hidden pity in her gaze. My ears suddenly grew hot. “Actually, no need to support me. I’m just talking casually...” I lowered my head and rubbed my palms together, my voice so soft it was almost inaudible.

When it was my turn to speak, I stood up and tried to make my voice sound steady. “I... I’m an independent creator. Um, I mainly make content about... uh, relationships.” I could feel myself speaking faster and faster, while my tongue seemed increasingly out of my control; a few words even came out slurred. I glanced at the few people seated across from me. One or two of them seemed to be whispering to each other, their expressions flashing with a hint of hesitation. I immediately felt a chill run down my back, as if I were standing under a giant magnifying glass, every detail of me being infinitely enlarged. “Uh... anyway, I’m very honored to be here sharing my creative experience with everyone.” I hurriedly finished, sat back down, and gripped the edge of my chair tightly, my palms already damp with sweat.

After the salon ended, people began chatting in small groups. Some came over to greet me, saying my speech was genuine and full of emotion. I forced a mechanical smile and nodded stiffly, but in my mind I kept replaying the moments when I had stumbled over my words, as well as the whispers and expressions of those people. The woman who had been sitting next to me came over again and patted my shoulder. “You did fine. Don’t worry too much.” I squeezed out a reluctant “Thank you,” but inside I felt she was just placating me, comforting a child who had just made a mistake.

When I got home, my stomach felt uncomfortable, as if it had knotted into a ball. I poured myself a glass of water and sat on the sofa, going over every detail from earlier: Was my tone too nervous? Was my speaking too fast? What exactly had those whispering people been saying about me? Did they think my content was too shallow? Did they think I had no right to stand under that lamp? More serious scenes began to emerge in my mind—would they think I was a joke? Did the organizers regret inviting me? The more I thought about it, the more chaotic it became, and I felt as though I were about to be swallowed by those emotions. At one point I even wanted to message the organizers and tell them not to invite me again in the future, but in the end I held back.

When I woke up the next day, my temples were still faintly throbbing. I hadn’t been able to sleep at all last night; my mind was full of those embarrassing scenes, and it was only at dawn that I forced myself to close my eyes. That day I hardly did anything. I just kept going over every detail of that salon, trying to figure out whether I had really done badly, or whether there was anything I could do to make up for it.

The rental room was eerily quiet at night, with only the occasional rustle of wind through the leaves outside the window. I stared at the computer screen, trying to concentrate on the unfinished creative project. The only sounds in the room were the tapping of the keyboard and the occasional flipping of manuscript pages. I felt exhausted, my shoulders ached, and my fingers were a little stiff. Just then, my phone vibrated, and I saw a message pop up from the client: “Please be sure to send me the latest draft by tomorrow.” My heart suddenly raced, and my palms began to sweat. I thought, There’s no way I can do that—I’m not ready yet. I can’t let them down, but I’m worried I won’t be able to finish on time. I began to run through every possible consequence in my mind if I couldn’t deliver the manuscript: the project being canceled, the client no longer trusting me, the team’s dissatisfaction......

I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself, but my stomach began to ache faintly. I kept reminding myself that I had to keep working, that I had to complete the task, so I sped up my typing, trying to drive away the anxiety inside me with faster movements. Although it was already late, I called a colleague, hoping to get some support from them.

After the call connected, I said cautiously, “Hey, sorry to bother you so late. Do you have time to talk?” The other person seemed a little tired as they replied, “Of course. Are you okay?” That simple concern made me feel a little better.

I told him about the client’s message and my worries. He paused for a moment, then said, “Take it easy. Let’s think of a solution together. Maybe we can adjust the priorities or simplify some of the content.” His advice made me feel warm and encouraged. I kept turning those ideas over in my mind, trying to shift my perspective in hopes of finding a better solution.

After hanging up, my tension eased a little, but my heart was still beating somewhat fast. I knew I needed rest, but anxiety drove me to keep working. So I continued sketching out ideas on the draft paper, trying to make the most effort I could within the limited time.

A few days later, I finally completed the manuscript and handed it to the client. The tension and unease of this period also seemed to ease with it. That night afterward, although fatigue still weighed on me, I was able to fall asleep peacefully, with dreams flickering with anxiety slowly fading away.

Colorful lights shimmered overhead in the venue, and the artworks hanging on the walls were illuminated by the lighting, making them even more striking. Around me came the low murmur of people talking and bursts of laughter, but I was focused only on the coffee cup in my hand, trying to conceal the unease inside me. My palms were sweaty, and my heartbeat was gradually quickening. My attention was interrupted by a colleague’s voice; he was standing not far away, discussing the details of a project. I tried hard to make out their conversation, but their voices seemed as if they were submerged underwater, blurred and indistinct. “The project is progressing pretty well, thanks everyone for your hard work. We’re very confident about this plan,” another colleague replied, sounding full of enthusiasm. Yet in my mind, one question kept echoing: Why didn’t they mention me? Did I not do well enough? These questions reverberated in my heart like rolling thunder. My stomach began to ache faintly. Flashes of various mistakes ran through my mind, as if reminding me that I had never truly belonged to this team.

I paused, trying to force a smile, but it felt like tugging at a taut mask. I walked toward them and reluctantly squeezed into the conversation. “What do you think of this concept?” A colleague suddenly turned to me, apparently noticing my arrival. I froze for a moment, and all my anxiety gathered into a single point. I heard myself answer in a somewhat hurried tone, “Oh, I think... maybe some details still need to be adjusted.” I didn’t have the courage to say what I really thought, fearing I would be seen as nitpicking. The other person nodded, but I caught a trace of impatience in his eyes—or was that just my imagination?

With my unease coiling around me like vines, I found an excuse to leave that suffocating circle and stepped out onto the balcony. A faint smell of tobacco lingered in the air, and it made me feel slightly more at ease.

That night, I lay in bed, replaying the afternoon’s conversation and still feeling a heaviness in my chest. I began to doubt whether I was really suited to stay on this team any longer. Could it be that, just as I suspected, they were all hiding something behind my back? I tried hard to focus on my breathing, attempting to calm the pace of my heartbeat.

A few days later, I received an email with project updates from the last seminar. I saw those familiar names again. Yet to my surprise, the email mentioned some of the improvements I had raised at the meeting. I felt a slight sense of comfort; perhaps I had misunderstood. Or perhaps what I was worried about wasn’t that serious after all. But that small comfort did not last. New unease and self-doubt soon followed.

Sunlight streamed through the large windows of the conference room, casting a bright glow across the floor and illuminating the day. I sat beside a table piled with snacks and coffee, surrounded by my colleagues. The air was filled with the aroma of fresh coffee, and the room rang with everyone’s laughter and conversation. It was a team-building event hosted by the company, and the atmosphere seemed relaxed. Yet my nerves were stretched taut, like a string pulled to its limit.

In the meeting room, I tried to take part in a discussion about how to improve team collaboration efficiency. I looked at the colleague sitting across from me, and she seemed to give an absent-minded frown at what I had said. Instantly, I felt a wave of unease; my heart rate jumped, and my palms began to sweat. “Does she disagree with me? Did I say something wrong?” These thoughts swirled through my mind like a whirlwind. I forced myself to keep smiling and pretended to be confident.

“What do you think of this plan?” asked the colleague beside me. His voice pulled me back from my endless self-doubt. “Oh, I think it’s pretty good, but maybe we could…” I struggled to keep the tension out of my voice, while inside I was filled with fear of being rejected.

During lunch break, I went up to the rooftop of the office building, hoping the fresh air would calm my chaotic mind. A gentle breeze passed over the rooftop, bringing a touch of coolness. I closed my eyes and tried to steady my breathing. “She probably didn’t mean anything by it; maybe I’m just overthinking,” I comforted myself, but the unease in my heart lingered like a stubborn illness, impossible to shake off.

After returning to the office, I couldn’t help opening my computer and searching online for ways to improve my social skills and better interpret my colleagues’ reactions. I realized that overanalyzing other people’s microexpressions had become a habit. Though I kept trying to persuade myself not to care so much, an inner sense of inadequacy would appear from time to time like an invisible shadow, reminding me that I seemed to fall short in some way.

A few days later, that colleague came over and said softly, “Your suggestion that day was really good. I hope I’ll have another chance to hear more from you next time.” I was stunned. It turned out she hadn’t been put off by my proposal at all. In that moment, a huge sense of relief washed away all the tension from before, and I realized that sometimes I really was overly sensitive.

Over the next few days, I would occasionally think back to that experience. Although my emotions had surged like a tide at the time, I now understood that my excessive worry about social awkwardness had actually come more from deep within—from doubts about my own self-worth.

Fragments of colored glass were scattered across the workbench. Sunlight passed through the workshop’s large windows and refracted onto the floor, casting brilliant patches of light. I stood in front of the bench, looking at a stained-glass pendant that was still unfinished, cutting the glass with tools I had not yet mastered. The small knife in my hand trembled slightly, and the metallic feel of the tool made me feel cold and unfamiliar. I could smell a sharp acidic odor drifting through the air—that was the chemical scent released during glasswork. I could not help holding my breath to avoid inhaling too much of it. Beside me, the instructor watched my movements and occasionally offered guidance: “Slow down. Keep your pressure even. Don’t rush.” His voice was calm, but the pauses in his tone made me feel anxious, as if he were indirectly expressing dissatisfaction with my skills.

“Is this okay if I cut it like this?” I asked, looking up and trying to confirm whether I was doing it right.

The instructor nodded, but did not say much in response. I immediately started overinterpreting his expression, feeling that he was disappointed in me but unwilling to criticize me directly. My heart began to race, as if the glass in my hand were mocking my clumsiness. I kept cutting, but because I was too focused, I did not notice the blade drifting off its original path. The glass suddenly cracked with a snap, and the misplaced piece fell to the floor with a crisp sound. “Ah!” I could not help crying out, and the eyes of the other participants immediately turned toward me.

My face quickly grew hot, as if a spotlight were shining on it. I hurriedly crouched down to pick up the shards, and my finger accidentally brushed against a sharp edge, drawing a drop of blood. “Careful!” The instructor quickly handed me a bandage. As I took it, I could feel the sting in my finger, and I could also hear my own heartbeat clearly, each beat pounding like thunder in my ears. I began blaming myself. “Why can’t I do better? Why is this so embarrassing? They must be laughing at me in their heads.”

I forced out a smile, trying to hide my embarrassment. “It’s fine, I was just too impatient,” I said, but my voice sounded weak, and even I thought it was false. The instructor patted my shoulder. “Don’t be nervous. Everyone makes mistakes when they first start learning. Just try a few more times and you’ll get it.” His tone was relaxed, meant to be comforting, but I heard a hidden criticism in it: “Everyone makes mistakes when they first start learning”—those words stung me, and I felt as though I had become a negative example for everyone, the “failed demonstration” that would be remembered.

On the way home, I kept replaying the workshop scene in my mind, over and over, along with the moment the glass shattered and the glances that had been cast my way. Every time I thought of it, my stomach twisted painfully, and the muscles in my neck tightened. I even began to wonder whether I should just give up on these kinds of experiential activities altogether, to avoid repeating the same mistake.

A few days later, I was still bothered by what had happened. I even posted a status on social media, obliquely expressing that I was “feeling down.” Although friends tried to comfort me in the comments, it did nothing to ease my self-criticism. I started avoiding mentioning that day’s experience, and even deleted the workshop advertisement from my favorites. That unfinished glass pendant became a scar in my mind, constantly reminding me of my own imperfection and my awkwardness in being different.

I walked into an old secondhand bookstore in the southern part of the city. The bell on the door rang softly, and the air was filled with a blend of the smells of paper and coffee. The shelves were packed with all kinds of old books, giving the feeling of traveling through time. I walked slowly along the shelves, my fingers lightly brushing the spines, feeling the rough texture of the paper. Suddenly, I heard someone calling my name. Looking up, I saw a former industry acquaintance from many years ago. He waved and motioned for me to come over. My heart began to race, and a wave of anxiety surged up: we hadn’t been in contact for a very long time—could he be upset with me about something? “Hey, how have you been lately?” he said with a smile, his tone seeming relaxed. But I couldn’t relax; I kept feeling that there was some dissatisfaction hidden behind his smile. “Pretty good, just a bit busy,” I replied, while thinking to myself: does he think I’ve been deliberately distancing myself from him lately? We stood beside a worn-out novel and struck up a conversation. Throughout the exchange, I kept interpreting every one of his words, trying to find any hint of displeasure in his tone. “How’s work been lately?” he asked. I thought, why is he suddenly asking about that? Is he hinting that I’ve overlooked how important he is? My stomach began to tighten, as if a stone were pressing down on it. We talked for a while, and he seemed to have no dissatisfaction at all, but I still couldn’t feel at ease, always sensing there was something between the lines. While he was speaking, I watched his eyes and every subtle change in his expression, trying to determine whether he was truly satisfied with my response. We stood there together as the bookstore gradually grew quiet, leaving only the ticking of an old clock. I couldn’t help thinking: if he is angry, what should I do? Apologize in advance? But would that make me seem too sensitive? After the conversation ended, I left as if nothing had happened, walking across the bookstore’s wooden floor and feeling the heaviness in every step. That night, my anxiety kept growing, and even as I slept I couldn’t stop thinking: was he actually angry or not? That unease lasted an entire week, and only after I repeatedly confirmed that he wasn’t angry did my mood finally settle down a little.

Sunlight slanted through the broken station roof, casting a warm yellow glow over the ground. I stood in this abandoned train station, with only the sound of wind moving through it all around me. In the distance, the occasional sound of cars driving by reminded me that I was still at the edge of the city, not completely cut off from the world. The silence here made me feel at peace, yet faintly uneasy. Why is my heart always filled with turmoil? I tried to take a deep breath and calm myself, but unease surged in like a tide. My heartbeat began to race, and a thin layer of sweat gathered on my palms. What flashed through my mind was the scene from my most recent project failure: that time in the conference room when my proposal was mercilessly criticized by my boss. Even though I tried to stay composed, I still couldn’t shake the feeling of being rejected. I told myself it was fine, but deep inside, those negative signals kept looping over and over. It was eerily quiet here. I walked along the cracked rails, which were covered in rust, as if reminding me of the passage of time. I heard a voice in my heart: “What if I fail again this time? Should I stop chasing my dream?” I knew such self-attack was pointless, but it still followed me like a shadow, bringing even greater emotional blows. In my ears, I seemed to hear the roar of a train passing over the tracks, even though I knew it was only my imagination. In such a lonely place, I tried to talk with my truest feelings. Perhaps this was a chance to look at myself again and make adjustments. I began to realize that I had been overanalyzing other people’s hints, often turning small things into catastrophes. Just then, my phone rang. It was a message from a partner inviting me to take part in a new project. In that instant, my mood shifted from extreme tension to a faint excitement, as if I could see sunlight shining back into reality. I couldn’t be sure this project would succeed, but I knew I could no longer let past failures hold me captive. That night, after I got home, I began preparing for the new project. Inspiration kept bubbling up in my mind, and my fingers flew across the keyboard. A few days later, I met with my partner to discuss it. Though I still felt a trace of unease, what I felt more strongly was anticipation and hope. I realized that when facing uncertainty, daring to try is the best way to keep yourself from being troubled by a sense of abandonment.

In the late autumn evening, I stood inside this abandoned clock factory, the air faintly tinged with dust and metal. Nearly all the windows near the top of the building were broken, and a few streaks of orange-red sunset slipped through the gaps, casting mottled patterns on the walls like cracks in a dried riverbed. I held my camera close in my coat, trying to keep it away from the drifting dust. The factory was spacious, but the emptier it felt, the less I could calm down; it was as if every sound was quietly amplified, even my footsteps carrying a suffocating weight.

My shooting team consisted of only two people—me, and a lighting assistant I had found at the last minute. He was standing off in the distance, trying to adjust the angle of the reflector. “Could you be quicker?” I heard myself call out at him, my voice tight. He seemed to hesitate, then moved even more carefully. “Okay, I’m almost done,” he said, with a puzzled tone.

I pressed the camera’s power button, only to find that the screen never lit up. I kept trying to restart the device, but all I heard was an abnormal clicking sound from the battery compartment. “No way...” My heartbeat suddenly quickened, as if the air in the whole factory had frozen. For a moment, I really wanted to smash the equipment. I told myself not to panic, but by then every worst-case scenario was already playing out in my head: the project failing completely, the client terminating the collaboration, my professional credibility being thoroughly questioned.

The lighting assistant hesitated as he walked over. “How about I take a look?” he said. I instinctively pulled the camera tighter against me. “No need!” I blurted out, my voice sharper than I had expected. I knew he was only trying to help, but I felt an indescribable shame—I didn’t want anyone to see me in such a mess, and I even felt that his initiative was implying I was incompetent.

My fingers ached slightly from pressing the buttons too many times, and my body had started to sweat from the constant tension. I felt a dull pain in my stomach, like a thin needle slowly pricking me. I wanted to escape from that place, yet I was also terrified that if I left, I would never have time to finish the shoot.

In the end, I took a deep breath and tried to calm myself down. I slowed my movements, used my tools to check the battery compartment’s contacts, and found that the battery was simply making poor contact. I reseated the battery, and the device finally powered on, the screen returning to normal. I forced out a smile and said to the assistant, “We can start.” He nodded, though there was still some concern in his eyes.

That night, after I got home, I still felt unable to fully settle down inside. Sitting on the sofa, I kept going over my reaction, feeling that I had simply overreacted to a minor problem. I thought back to how it had felt in the factory, as if the whole world were watching me make a fool of myself. That shame made it impossible to control myself. I tried writing some journal entries, recording what had happened, hoping to find at least a little relief.

Warm sunlight spilled onto the balcony, and a gentle breeze brushed past as my friend and I sat beside a small wooden table, cups of hot coffee in our hands, gazing at the blue sky in the distance. I could smell the rich aroma of coffee mixed with the faint fragrance of jasmine from the flowerpot. We talked about work progress and the occasional amusing stories we’d heard about friends. Smiling as she spoke, she said, “You know, Xiao Li has actually started learning how to cook. I can’t believe it!”

I couldn’t help but freeze for a moment, then laughed and said, “Wasn’t he always living on takeout? Looks like he’s finally come to his senses.” I took a small sip of coffee, feeling the warm liquid flow down my throat, and a quiet sense of contentment rose within me.

The sunlight on my face made me squint slightly. A few little birds chirped cheerfully not far away, and their sounds left me feeling unusually relaxed. Then we started talking about the TV drama we’d recently watched. My friend said, “Have you watched Those Years? The plot reminded me of us back in high school.”

I nodded, a hint of nostalgia stirring in my heart. “Yeah, it’s a bit exaggerated, but those little crushes and misunderstandings were actually pretty real,” I said with a smile, feeling as though time had returned to those carefree days.

After that, we fell silent for a while, each of us enjoying the peace. I unconsciously felt myself relax; my heartbeat was slow and steady, every part of my body easing as I listened only to the rustling of leaves.

“Actually, afternoons like this are really rare and precious,” my friend suddenly said with emotion.

I nodded, looking at the lush greenery before me, my heart wrapped in a warm feeling. “Yeah, those little joys in life are important too.”

We kept talking for a while longer, then she stood up to leave. I walked her to the door. As we said goodbye, she gently patted my shoulder and smiled, saying, “Come over for coffee again next time.”

I smiled in reply. By the time I closed the door, the sun was already hanging low in the sky, and the house was filled with the special warmth of afternoon light.

That evening, I brewed a cup of tea and sat on the sofa, savoring the afternoon in my thoughts. Lights outside the window had begun to sparkle on one by one, and the quiet of the house made me feel full inside. I realized that these ordinary moments are, in fact, a precious luxury. A few days later, my friend sent me another message, inviting me to her place next weekend. She had also bought a new coffee machine and was ready for me to try it.

Soft, gentle light spilled over the wooden bookshelves of the independent bookstore, and the air was filled with the faint scent of books and freshly baked coffee. Raindrops tapped lightly against the large glass windows, their sound delicate and rhythmic. On this drizzly evening, I came to the bookstore for a new book launch event. The store was small, but every corner was filled with warmth and a cultural atmosphere. Pushing open the door, I saw people gathered in the open space at the back, new books laid out on the table, and the author beside them, speaking with readers.

I took a cup of coffee and stood by the wall, my gaze drifting over the bookshelves from time to time and then returning to the author. His voice was gentle, and his words were full of passion for his work and insight into life. When I heard him talk about the chapter on exploring the self and overcoming inner fear, my heart began to race, and my palms started to sweat. That familiar sense of anxiety surged up in an instant, accompanied by a slight stomachache.

Suddenly, the author walked up to me and asked with a smile, “Do you have any thoughts about this book?”

I tried hard to suppress my unease and forced myself to appear calm. “The part about self-exploration in the book really impressed me. It sometimes makes me think of some of my own experiences.”

He nodded. “We are all searching for ourselves, and we all have many expectations of ourselves. Sometimes the greatest challenge is not letting fear hold us back.”

His words seemed to strike a sensitive chord deep inside me. I forced a smile in response, yet I could feel my heart pounding violently in my chest. I knew I was overanalyzing every one of his words unnecessarily, and the constant tension in my body made me feel almost suffocated.

After the launch event ended, I quickly fled the crowd and walked out of the bookstore. The drizzle shimmered under the streetlights, and I felt a little cold, but my emotions were still churning inside. When I got home, the fine rain was still pouring outside the window. I sat on the sofa, the author’s words and my own behavior echoing over and over in my mind. Overwhelmed by a strong sense of shame and self-reproach, I began to ruminate on whether I had seemed unconfident in the conversation, whether others would think I was strange. The voice inside kept questioning me: why am I always so sensitive, why is this anxiety always so hard to shake?

These past few days, I have tried to shift my attention to other things, but a lingering heaviness remains in my heart. I keep finding myself unconsciously recalling the scene in the bookstore, repeatedly scrutinizing every reaction and detail, waiting for the moment when I will no longer be trapped in such an emotional vortex.

Dim streetlights scattered across the quiet road, and I pulled my coat tighter as I walked over the damp, cold ground toward that remote old warehouse. A handmade poster was taped to the door, telling me this was the place for tonight’s small screening. As I raised my hand to knock, a thought suddenly popped into my head: what if they say my name isn’t on the list? My palms were already sweating, even though the temperature had dropped so low that my nose was red from the cold. After the door opened, a girl in a loose sweater smiled and said, “Welcome, you’re a participant, right? Your name?” My voice trembled as I gave my name, then, as if trying to make up for it, I lowered my head and added, “I hope I didn’t get the time or place wrong.” Her smile never changed. “Everything’s right. Don’t worry.” But my neck was stiff as stone, and I could only nod mechanically.

Quite a few people were already inside. All the light came from a few low-wattage hanging lamps, glowing warm yellow and casting shadows on the red brick walls like an old painting. I looked around and saw the seats arranged loosely in a circle, with people chatting in small groups. I instinctively looked for a seat in a corner, my heart beating faster and faster: if I sat in the back row, would people think I was unfriendly? If I sat in the front, would they think I was being too deliberate? The buzzing in my head started circling nonstop, and my stomach ached faintly too.

Just as I was frozen in place, a boy waved at me. “Hey, there’s an empty seat here. You can come over.” I moved over mechanically and sat down. As I caught sight of the smile at the corner of his mouth, my heart suddenly stung: was he inviting me over only because he thought I looked too pitiful standing there? My throat tightened a little, but I still forced out a smile. “Thanks. Did you organize this screening?” I tried to make small talk, but my voice came out high and anxious. He shook his head. “No, I just came because a friend recommended it.” Then he leaned back lightly in his chair, as if completely unaware of my nerves.

Once the movie started, I still couldn’t focus at all. The images on the screen should have been captivating, but all I could do was keep replaying whether my tone had sounded too strange or my expression not natural enough. The more I thought about it, the more unsettled I felt, until I could no longer even hear the dialogue in the film. To hide the chaos inside, I pretended to watch attentively, but my hands were already gripping my knees tightly from tension.

After the film ended, everyone started discussing the plot enthusiastically. I glanced down at my phone and saw that it was already late, so I hurriedly stood up to leave. The boy who had asked me to sit nearby turned to me and said, “Are you leaving? The discussion is actually pretty interesting.” I froze for a moment and instinctively said, “Oh, no, I just… suddenly remembered I still have some work to take care of.” As soon as I said it, I started blushing, and even my ears burned hot. He nodded without saying much, and I quickly turned and left, only feeling a thin layer of sweat from nerves on my back.

That night, after I got home, I lay in bed but couldn’t sleep at all. Every conversation and tiny interaction tangled through my mind like a tightly woven net. I even began to wonder if when he said the discussion was interesting, he was really implying that I should have stayed, and that I had messed up again. When I woke up the next day, my eyes felt sore and my head was foggy, but that unease still lingered, making it hard for me to concentrate all day long.

Sunlight streamed through the clear glass windows onto the café’s wooden tables, filling the entire space with a warm glow. I sat in the corner, my fingers typing rapidly on my laptop keyboard, trying to finish an important project before the deadline. In my ears was the occasional hum of the coffee machine, and the clock on the wall ticked steadily. Suddenly, I received a message from my best friend: “We need to talk.” Instantly, my heart started pounding out of control. Had I done something to upset her? I began recalling every detail of our last meeting—had I said something wrong? A sense of panic I couldn’t shake rose in my chest, and my stomach began to twist. I replied, “Is something wrong?” trying to keep my tone as calm as possible. The message on the screen read: “I feel like you’ve been a little distant lately.” That sentence hit me in the chest like a heavy punch, and I had no idea what she meant. Had I done something that made her feel ignored? Or had I failed to be considerate enough somewhere? “Sorry, I’ve been really busy with work lately,” I typed back quickly, trying to explain. “Did I do something wrong?” At that moment, some of our past arguments flashed through my mind, as if each one had started because I overinterpreted her words. Deep inside, a sense of abandonment kept rising. “Is she going to end our friendship?” The possibility made me shiver. “No, I just think we could stay in touch more,” she replied, and I felt slightly relieved, though anxiety still lingered like a shadow. Fine beads of sweat formed in my palms; the sounds around me seemed to vanish all at once, leaving only the silent exchange between me and the screen. We decided to meet over the weekend to talk things through. The moment I put down my phone, I remembered how I always attacked myself first, just to avoid being blamed or rejected by others. The next day, in a sunlit park, we finally met. When I saw her, I was as nervous as ever. I asked, “Are you okay?” She smiled and nodded, reaching out to hold my hand. “I’m not angry. I just think we need more time together.” Her words wrapped around me warmly, gradually easing some of my anxiety. I realized that I always overread things because I’m sensitive to rejection, but this time, I was willing to try to believe what she said was true, rather than the abandonment I had imagined. A few days later, during a work break, I sent her a short message: “Thank you for helping me understand. I’ll try to relax.” I felt a new sense of calm in my heart.

The afternoon sun filtered through the shadows of the trees, scattering over the lake’s rippling surface, where mandarin ducks floated in pairs. I sat on a bench by the lake, holding a newly bought diary, trying to jot down some ideas that had suddenly surfaced, yet my mind was as muddled as if stuffed with cotton. I twirled the pen in my hand for what felt like ages, but there were only a few scribbled lines on the page. “This is awful. I still can’t write anything—it's been three days already.” I let out a heavy sigh, silently reminding myself that this was normal creative blockage, but I still couldn’t help blaming myself for being so incapable.

Behind me, I heard a couple talking. Their voices weren’t loud, but I could hear every word clearly. “Look at her, sitting here all alone. How lonely.” The woman’s tone was casually teasing, while the man gently chimed in, “Yeah, she looks kind of pitiful.”

My body stiffened, as if countless tiny needles had pricked my heart. I pretended to keep writing, but my hand was trembling slightly. “They don’t know why I’m alone. They don’t know what I’ve been through.” My heartbeat quickened, and my ears grew hotter and hotter. I could feel my cheeks must be red as ripe tomatoes. Breathe in, breathe out—I told myself not to care, but in my mind, that phrase, “how lonely,” kept replaying over and over.

“Yes, how lonely.” I repeated to myself, my eyes suddenly stinging. Self-mockery and shame surged up like a tide. I thought about my recent creative slump, my growing distance from friends, and the restrained expressions of my coworkers when I kept making mistakes at work... “Maybe I really am a failure, which is why I’m always like this.” Somewhere in my heart, a corner seemed to be whispering with ridicule.

The pen in my hand nearly dropped to the ground. I hurriedly tightened my grip and wiped at my eyes with my hand to hide it. On the lake, the sunlight still gleamed brilliantly. A cool autumn breeze blew by, carrying away some of the scent of branches and leaves mixed with a faint hint of moisture from the water. My stomach twisted faintly, as if someone had lightly punched it. Right then, all I wanted was to leave—to escape the couple, to escape this place that made me feel so embarrassed and vulnerable.

I forced myself to stand as if nothing had happened, shoved the diary into my bag, and walked away quickly. The faster I went, the more breathless I became. I didn’t stop until I had made it out of the botanical garden. Sitting on a stone bench outside the park, I opened my phone and scrolled through social media, trying to distract myself, but that sentence still lingered in my mind. It was just a casual remark from strangers, yet it felt like a needle piercing straight through me.

That night, I threw myself into work, downloaded a bunch of new materials, and looked through them again and again, trying to find fresh inspiration, but I still couldn’t focus. In the middle of the night, my eyes began to burn, and I finally couldn’t hold back my tears. Waves of frustration and dejection kept churning in my heart. “Why can’t I stop caring so much about what others say?” I kept asking myself, again and again, but there was no answer.

A few days later, I gathered my courage, opened that diary, and wrote down the emotions of that day in full. The moment I finished, I felt a little lighter, but I also knew that feeling wouldn’t last; soon enough, it would come surging back again. I only hoped that next time, I could be less harsh with myself.

The gallery was buzzing with voices, and my works hung on the walls, each painting emitting a faint, dazzling glow under the lights. Yet my heart felt as if it were caught in a whirlpool, pounding unbearably fast. The air was thick with the familiar scent of canvas and paint, and the soft music in the background only made me more uneasy. Standing beside me, my partner wore an expression that was impossible to read, and it left me deeply unsettled.

“What do you think of our exhibition?” he asked, and I noticed a slight furrow in his brow. My mind immediately began to race. In my ears, that simple question turned complex and cryptic. I couldn’t tell whether his tone was sincere; it felt as though every word hid some kind of meaning. I froze for a moment, then blurted out, “What do you mean? Do you think I didn’t do a good enough job?”

He was clearly caught off guard by my reaction and let out a sigh. “That’s not what I meant. You misunderstood.”

But my emotions were already out of control, my heartbeat accelerating like a frightened bird trapped in a cage. My cheeks burned, my palms began to sweat, and my whole body was tense, like a bow drawn to its limit. I couldn’t help shouting, “I know you’ve always thought I’m not good enough. You’re always hinting that I might ruin everything!”

His expression shifted from confusion to resolve. “What are you talking about? That’s all in your head!”

Our argument drew the attention of the people around us, and I could feel their eyes gathering on us. A wave of shame washed over me, almost suffocating me. Deep inside, the shadows of abandonment and inadequacy surged up like a tide.

After the argument, I hurried out of the gallery and stood in the night air, the coolness of it hitting my face. I thought of the expression on his face just then, and a wordless sense of guilt rose in me, mixed with anger. I curled up in a corner, and the paper scraps fluttering in the night sky reminded me how absurd my loss of control had been. That night, my anxiety kept me awake until dawn.

The next day, I couldn’t shake the gloom in my heart. I kept replaying every detail from the day before, chewing over those harsh words again and again. I didn’t know how to face him, and I was afraid of feeling that pain of rejection once more. Only several days later did we finally speak again with cold, distant attitudes; though he said he understood, I still carried a deep sense of guilt and unease, unsure whether our relationship could ever return to what it had been.

I sat in the studio at home, my fingers tapping rapidly on the keyboard. The wind outside echoed through the night sky, and the light in the room was dim, but bright enough to illuminate my desk. I was absorbed in my writing when my phone suddenly buzzed, interrupting my train of thought. I picked it up and saw a message from a friend: “Your recent articles are too emotional; they’re a bit exhausting to read.” My heart tightened as if pricked by a needle. My thoughts were thrown into disarray, as though I had been cast into icy water.

“Really?” I replied, trying to sound casual, but inside I was panicking. My friend quickly answered, “Yes, but that’s just how I feel. Don’t take it too seriously.” At that moment, the computer screen in front of me flickered, and the text blurred. My stomach began to ache faintly, and my heartbeat quickened. Even though I knew my friend probably meant well, my mind kept racing, imagining whether she was truly disappointed in my work, whether what I had written was really flawed.

I put down my phone and tried to keep working, but my fingers just couldn’t move smoothly across the keyboard. I kept thinking: why am I always like this, so easily struck in the heart by a single sentence from someone else? I recalled those moments in the past when I had been criticized, and the feeling of not being accepted surged up like a tide and drowned me. I muttered to myself, “Am I really that incapable?”

My body began to sweat, my palms sticky. I stood up and walked to the window, trying to breathe in some fresh air, but the cold wind only made me feel more uneasy. I knew I should calm down and not let these emotions control me. Yet the feeling was too intense, as if some invisible force had seized my heart. I paced in front of the window, trying to shake off that unease, but it clung to me like a shadow.

Only after quite a while did I sit back down in my chair and try to face the screen again. However, my friend’s words kept echoing in my mind. I repeatedly checked whether I had made any mistakes, desperately trying to recall her tone and figure out the hidden meaning behind what she might have really meant. Even so, my mood remained heavy, as though a stone were pressing on my chest, making it hard to breathe.

Over the next few days, I couldn’t help but ruminate on these emotions, remembering countless moments when I had overinterpreted something small and fallen apart. Even when I was sleeping, I would think of it; even in my dreams, that comment kept repeating. I knew I needed to let it go, but knowing was not enough. The sense of being flawed remained in my heart like a giant boulder.

The air carried a faint scent of coffee, but at that moment the smell only made me dizzy and nauseous, as if a hand were gripping my stomach tightly. The fluorescent lights in the conference room were almost too bright, making my eyes ache. Everyone was seated there, their gazes more or less fixed on me. I heard the project manager’s voice, laced with impatience: “Did you not read last week’s documents? You got this key part completely wrong.”

“I...” My voice was trembling, and my palms were already soaked with sweat. I tried to remember whether I had really overlooked something, but my mind was blank. My heart was pounding so fast that it felt as if my ears were stuffed up, and the sounds around me suddenly became hazy. All I could hear was my own words echoing in my ears: “I shouldn’t have missed anything... I clearly checked it several times.” But in the room, those words sounded unbearably weak, like nothing more than an excuse.

“We’ve all wasted an entire week because of your mistake,” the manager went on, and there was no longer any trace of probing in his voice—only a cold judgment. I glanced around at everyone else’s faces and saw some looking down at their laptops, while others deliberately avoided my gaze. I stared at the pen on the table, feeling my face burn as if it had been seared by fire. Someone coughed softly, and that sound landed on my heart like a heavy blow.

Suddenly, images flashed through my mind—when I was a child, a teacher in the classroom pointed out my mistake while explaining a problem, and all my classmates whispered to one another; in college, during a group discussion, my proposal was dismissed with a casual remark, leaving the room dead silent. My hand gripping the pen was trembling, while my other hand absentmindedly rubbed the hem of my clothes, my fingertips feeling the rough friction of the fabric.

“Sorry, I... I’ll check it again.” I finally spoke, my voice so low I could barely hear myself. And then that familiar voice in my head started up again: “You always mess everything up. They must think you’re incompetent.”

After the meeting, I quickly packed up my notebook and left the conference room almost as if I were fleeing. The stream of people in the hallway made me feel even more suffocated. Everyone seemed to be watching me, even though I knew that was just my imagination. I ran into the restroom, shut the stall door, and collapsed onto the toilet lid. My breathing grew rapid; it felt as though a stone were pressing down on my chest, and my stomach was churning violently. I tried desperately to control my breathing, but the humiliation spread through me like poison.

“They must be talking about you behind your back.” The same voice kept repeating itself. I lowered my head and stared at my hands, my fingers trembling slightly. I dug my nails hard into my thigh, trying to calm myself down, but tears suddenly welled up without warning.

That night, after I got home, I lay on the sofa and kept replaying the scene from the meeting over and over. Every face, every sentence, even that smell of coffee refused to leave me. I tried to write down a review of the day, but the words in front of me suddenly blurred. I set down my pen, covered my head with both hands, and had only one thought in my mind: maybe they really will find someone to replace me.

On Saturday afternoon, I was strolling through the western outskirts of the city when I happened upon a small mushroom cultivation laboratory. The lab’s walls were light gray, and several charts introducing different mushroom species hung on them. The air was thick with the damp scent of earth, mixed with the fresh aroma unique to mushrooms. Inside, a staff member was arranging rows of plastic containers, each filled with mushrooms of various kinds.

I stood hesitating at the door for a moment, then stepped forward. “Hello, may I ask if it’s open for visitors?” I asked tentatively.

“Of course. Is this your first time here?” the staff member replied warmly.

“Yes, I’m especially interested in mushroom cultivation,” I answered, while feeling a trace of unease, worried that I might sound too awkward.

The staff member began explaining the mushroom-growing process, and I tried hard to stay focused. Yet in my mind, a faint discomfort kept flickering through the conversation, as if I were afraid that if I spoke poorly, the staff member would think I was too inexperienced. My heartbeat began to quicken slightly, and my palms grew a little sweaty.

“These mushrooms need specific temperature and humidity conditions, which you can see here,” the staff member said, pointing to the charts on the wall.

“Yes, I’ve read some books about mushrooms before, but I don’t have much hands-on experience.” I wanted to seem more knowledgeable, but I was also afraid of coming across as not smart or interesting enough.

At that moment, I noticed the staff member seemed to pause, a hint of helplessness appearing in their eyes. I began to wonder whether I had said something wrong, or whether I had behaved in some way that was inappropriate. My heartbeat quickened, and I tried taking deep breaths, hoping to calm myself down.

For the rest of the visit, I tried to focus on the mushrooms themselves rather than on the staff member’s reactions. Gradually, my heartbeat returned to normal, and I began to enjoy the lab’s fascinating sights and information.

That evening, after I got home, I still couldn’t help replaying the conversation over and over, questioning whether I had been too nervous, too concerned with other people’s reactions, or even made myself seem ignorant. After a few days, that uneasiness slowly faded. I tried to tell myself that it had only been an accidental conversation, nothing that could have been made much better, and that everyone has their own blind spots in knowledge.

I walked along a path carpeted with fallen leaves, a gentle breeze brushing my cheeks and bringing a hint of chill. The abandoned weather station before me was built in the early twentieth century; now it was covered in rust, with vines crawling over the walls, giving it a desolate air. I pushed open the creaking wooden door, and sunlight streamed through the broken windows, casting mottled shadows on the floor. A few pigeons startled into flight, their wings beating out a noisy echo. The room was thick with the smell of mildew mixed with rust, and I frowned.

I wandered aimlessly, my shoes crunching softly through a thick layer of dust. An old desk was piled with moldy files and instruments, and I rummaged through them casually until I unexpectedly found an unopened letter. That made me stop. On the envelope, in scrawled handwriting, were the words: “To a future meteorologist.” My heartbeat quickened, and my palms began to sweat. After a moment’s hesitation, I finally opened the envelope.

The paper had yellowed, and though the writing was blurred, it was still legible. I read it line by line; the letter brimmed with a love for meteorological work and a longing for the future, full of passion in every sentence. Suddenly, I realized that the writer was the old colleague I had once worked with, who had died in an accident a few years earlier. I froze. The handwriting on the page seemed to be speaking to me of a past that could never be continued and opportunities that had been missed. “If one day I am no longer here, I hope my passion can live on,” she wrote. I felt a sharp ache in my chest, and tears welled up uncontrollably.

My thoughts surged out like a flood breaking through a dam, with countless memories and regrets interwoven. I began to question myself: Was I too insensitive?
