Had I never given enough weight to her enthusiasm and hopes? I even began to doubt whether my own career obsession had any real meaning. My heart pounded violently with anxiety, and my stomach felt as if it had been clenched by an invisible hand, aching in pain.

A few hours later, night fell, and the temperature grew even colder. I returned home, still haunted by that letter. I kept thinking over every word my old colleague had written, and those words kept stirring up worries and pain deep inside me. That night, I tossed and turned and could hardly sleep. A few days later, I got back in touch with some old colleagues, hoping to share this memory and remember the past together. Perhaps that would help ease the unease in my heart, even if only a little.

The air was thick with the rich aroma of coffee, and the wooden tables and chairs still seemed to hold a faint roughness from wear. I was sitting by the window, having just ordered a latte, holding the cup in both hands in an attempt to hide my nerves. The gathering had already started ten minutes ago, and everyone was standing in a small circle, taking turns introducing themselves. I tried hard not to listen to changes in people’s tones as they spoke, but my mind kept involuntarily catching all kinds of details—for example, when one person paused slightly halfway through a sentence, was he concealing irritation?

Then it was my turn. I took a deep breath, looked up, and said in a trembling voice, “Hello everyone, I’m a freelance creator, mainly working on short writing and video content. I’ve recently been trying to—” Before I could finish, I heard a soft laugh from someone on my right. Though it was very quiet, in my ears it swelled into a volume loud enough for the whole room to hear.

In that instant, it felt as if someone hadfiercely twisted my stomach. My hands began to tremble uncontrollably, and my fingertips nearly dug into the ceramic ridges of the cup. My scalp tingled, and my face started to burn. “Do they think I’m putting on airs? Or that my work is boring?” My voice gradually grew quieter, until even I could barely hear it, and I hastily brought my remarks to an end.

“Nice to meet you,” a man on my left picked up the conversation and added with a smile, but I could hardly take in the tone of his voice. I kept replaying that laugh in my mind, over and over. Was it a malicious mockery? The person’s expression and movements began replaying themselves in my head, like a video that refused to stop.

For the rest of the time, I hardly said a word. I just nodded and smiled mechanically, and I barely touched my latte, afraid that I might slip and spill the cup in front of everyone. I noticed that the edge of a menu on the table had curled up, and I couldn’t help reaching out to smooth it flat with my fingers. It seemed that only by doing these mindless actions could I briefly pull my attention away from the chaos in my thoughts.

Before the gathering ended, the host came over, patted me on the shoulder, and asked with a smile, “How did you enjoy today?” My throat tightened instantly, and I forced out a smile. “It was good, thank you.” Then I quickly grabbed my bag and left. As I walked out of the café, I found my steps a little unsteady, as if each step were sinking deeper into the mud of my own mind.

When I got home, I lay on the sofa staring at the ceiling, replaying the scene over and over in my head. Why did that person laugh? Were they talking about me behind my back? I ran through possible conversations in my mind again and again, even beginning to blame myself for not preparing a better self-introduction in advance. It wasn’t until two in the morning that I finally fell asleep amid the confusion.

Pushing open the glass door, I stepped into a secondhand furniture store on the edge of the city, filled with the smell of old wood and the marks of time. The shop was packed with all kinds of furniture—tables, chairs, bookshelves—some even exquisitely carved, as if they carried some distant history. As I searched for a suitable chair, I could feel the wood grain in the floor lightly brushing against the soles of my shoes, and around me I heard the low voices of other customers talking inside the store.

I stopped beside an old chair, drawn to its curved armrests and faded red upholstery. I reached out and touched its wooden surface; it was a little rough, but warm. Just then, a clerk—a middle-aged man wearing round glasses—walked over and asked in a flat tone, “Are you looking at this chair?”

“Mm, yes. This chair looks pretty good,” I replied, trying to sound natural. But when he then added, “This chair is pretty old. It might not be especially comfortable. You might want to look at the newer ones next to it,” my heartbeat suddenly quickened. Was he implying that my taste was terrible? Did he think I was being too casual in my choice? An invisible pressure suddenly rose in my stomach, as if I were falling into some kind of abyss.

“No, no, this one is fine. I just like old things like this,” I added almost instinctively, the words coming out so quickly that even I could hear the anxiety mixed into them. I vaguely felt that my voice was a little too hurried, even awkwardly at odds with the clerk’s calm tone. He nodded, smiled faintly, and left without saying anything else. But I could feel my face growing hot, and my palms beginning to sweat slightly.

I kept wandering around the shop, trying to steady my emotions, but the conversation kept replaying in my mind. Was he thinking I was weird? What did that smile mean? Was it sincere, or just perfunctory? Those thoughts swallowed my attention like a whirlpool, and even my steps became disordered. The furniture before my eyes gradually blurred, and I even forgot that I had come to buy a chair for my studio.

In the end, I decided not to buy anything there, and as I was leaving I hurriedly thanked the clerk once more. He responded politely, but I still felt that my own tone sounded unnatural, as if I were trying to prove something.

After I got home, I spent the entire night replaying that moment in my mind. I sat on the edge of my bed, eyes closed, trying to analyze his words rationally, but each time I failed to escape that feeling of being dismissed. That emotion was like a cloud that refused to disperse, lingering over my heart. It took several days before I finally calmed down, but the incident became another small scar in my inner life.

The repair shop’s windows and doors were somewhat old and worn, and the blue paint on the exterior walls had peeled and faded, giving off a faint smell of rust. A row of neatly arranged tools hung inside, with every wrench and screwdriver placed in perfect order. I pushed my broken bicycle in, its flat tire dragging limply along the ground. The shop was so quiet I could hear the ticking of the wall clock, and there was also a slight smell of lubricating oil in the air. A middle-aged mechanic was standing by the workbench repairing another bike. He looked up at me and asked simply, “What seems to be the problem?”

I instinctively felt a bit uneasy, and the words in my mouth came out clumsily: “Um… my bike… I think the tire is leaking air… and the chain gets stuck a bit when I ride.” I heard my own voice sound slightly tense, even a little shaky, and immediately started berating myself inwardly: Had I said too much? Or did I sound too uncertain? The mechanic gave a brief nod and motioned for me to bring the bike over for inspection.

As he checked the tire and chain, he asked, “How long have you had this bike? Have you been getting it serviced regularly?” My heart suddenly began to race, as if this ordinary question had touched something inside me. I started wondering whether some careless ride had caused today’s problem, and a sense of guilt arose, as though I had failed in my responsibility toward the bike. I stammered, “It seems like it’s been a long time since I… really serviced it.” He nodded without replying directly.

I stood off to the side, my palms gradually growing sweaty, feeling like a grade-school kid who had done something wrong. That feeling made me involuntarily pay attention to every expression on the mechanic’s face—was he blaming my carelessness? Did he think I didn’t understand bikes at all? As he frowned and examined the chain, countless possible criticisms raced through my mind, and I even thought up ways to respond. If he really criticized my poor maintenance, should I make fun of myself first, or just admit my mistake outright? My stomach began to ache faintly, and my shoulders tensed up.

At last the mechanic said, “The chain needs oil, and the tire needs air, but overall it’s not a big problem. It can be fixed.” Hearing that, I felt a little relieved inside, but I still sensed some hidden criticism in his words. Was he tactfully saying I’d neglected maintenance? Or was he simply stating the facts? I overanalyzed every word, while secretly hoping he would finish quickly so I could leave this uncomfortable place as soon as possible.

The repair took about half an hour. I tried to fake the appearance of standing there casually, but inside I kept replaying my behavior, wondering whether I had done anything wrong. He occasionally asked technical questions, and I always paused a moment before answering, afraid my responses would sound foolish or unclear. A cold draft blew in through the crack in the door, and goosebumps suddenly rose on my arms, but I didn’t dare touch them, worried it would make me seem inattentive.

After the bike was fixed, I paid and pushed it out of the shop. Sunlight filtered through the leaves and scattered across the ground, the sound of the wheels rolling accompanying my steps. I was still brooding over the mechanic’s tone and expression, trying to figure out exactly how he felt about me—was he indifferent, or only mildly displeased? All this overthinking gave me a splitting headache. That evening, after I got home, I kept thinking about today’s conversation, even blaming myself for not being more natural, for always being so sensitive, and sometimes I even imagined that if I were more confident and spoke more appropriately, the outcome might have been completely different.

When I pushed open that heavy glass door, the little bell on it gave a clear jingle, a sound that seemed to pierce the cold, silent air. I wrapped my coat tighter around me and stood inside the shop, watching the dim yellow pendant lights above cast shifting shadows across the wooden floor, while a faintly sour chemical smell rushed into my nose. I set my crossbody canvas bag on the counter and carefully handed the clerk a roll of film I had just finished shooting. It was an old-fashioned film development shop, with the counter stacked full of yellowing envelopes of all kinds, trying to look neat, but an air of clutter still filled every corner.

“Could you please develop this film for me? Is there any way it could be a little faster? I’m kind of in a hurry lately.” My voice carried a trace of unease, as if I were afraid of disturbing someone. The clerk looked up and glanced at me, and that look suddenly made me feel an inexplicable tension. He nodded, his tone flat: “The fastest would still be two days. The machine’s been acting up lately.”

After saying that, he lowered his head and fiddled with the film equipment. I froze for a moment, and immediately a wave of disappointment and panic rose in me. Was he dissatisfied with me? Did he think my request was unreasonable? I hurriedly added, “Ah, that’s fine too, no rush, no rush at all. Take your time!” But his response was only a calm “Mm,” and he didn’t look at me again.

My heartbeat started to speed up, and it felt as though I could even hear the sound of blood pounding against my eardrums. I felt as if my focus had suddenly shrunk into a tiny circle: had I sounded too eager just now? Did he think I was a hassle? I rested my hand on the edge of the counter, my fingertips trembling slightly from nerves, while my palms began to grow damp with cold sweat. I lowered my head and pretended to straighten my backpack, but in my mind I kept replaying the conversation over and over, like a broken tape recorder. Had I sounded too blunt? Was my voice too loud? I really had no sense of boundaries—wasn’t I just an annoying person?

“Just fill out the processing form and leave it here,” his voice suddenly rang out, startling me. I nodded, but in my panic I grabbed the wrong pen, and I felt even more awkward, my handwriting on the form turning crooked and messy. I even thought: maybe he’s already laughing at me in his head, “How can this customer not even fill out a form?” Thinking that way, my stomach began to ache faintly, as if a block of ice were pressing down on it.

After I finished filling it out, I hurriedly handed the form over and turned to leave the shop. The moment the glass door closed behind me, I felt as if a thousand pounds of eyes were chasing after me. Walking along the street, I suddenly felt completely unable to escape the conversation from just now. Every line, every detail was magnified endlessly, as though etched deep into my mind. Was I overthinking it? But what if he really was unhappy with me? That kind of rumination kept me from concentrating on anything for the entire afternoon. Even after I got home, I kept staring at the sloppy writing on the development slip, my heart full of shame.

It wasn’t until I woke up the next morning that my mind loosened up a little, but when I thought about having to go back to pick up the film, that uneasy, anxious feeling quietly crept back up in my heart and would not go away.

Sunlight spilled across the balcony, warm and soothing, making one feel drowsy and lazy. In front of me were several pots of succulents I had planted, looking fresh and succulent under the sun. My friend and I sat in bamboo chairs, each holding a cup of warm green tea, gently savoring its faint fragrance. I could feel the steam rising from the teacup brush lightly against my face, bringing a touch of comfort.

“Today’s sunshine is so nice—it’s really a good day for tea,” my friend said with a smile.

I nodded and replied, “Yes, weather like this makes you feel much brighter inside.”

The gentle aroma of the tea mixed with the earthy scent of the plants on the balcony, creating a special kind of tranquility. I leaned back slightly in my chair and enjoyed the peace of the moment. “How’s work been lately?” I asked casually.

My friend gave a small laugh, his fingers lightly turning the teacup. “Not bad—just a bit busy. We’re launching a new project next week.”

“That sounds great, but make sure you get some rest too,” I said with concern.

My friend nodded, took another sip of tea, and turned his gaze toward the blue sky in the distance. Sunlight filtered through the leaves, scattering dappled patches of light and shadow across the ground. I followed his gaze, my mind drifting empty in that moment.

At that time, my heartbeat was steady, my breathing soft and slow, and every cell in my body seemed to be saying, “Live in the present.” A breeze swept gently across the balcony, bringing a hint of freshness, like a whisper from nature itself.

As the tea gradually cooled, I felt the subtle temperature difference on the teacup and held it softly in my palm, bringing a sense of warm comfort. Such an afternoon was calm and serene, without noise or tension.

After a while, my friend stood up and stretched his slightly stiff body. “I have to go. Let’s have tea together again another day.”

“Sure, you’re always welcome,” I said with a smile, seeing him to the door and watching him leave.

Left alone, I sat back down on the balcony and continued drinking the now lukewarm tea, savoring the pleasant time I had spent chatting with my friend. A few days later, I still felt that this little gathering on the balcony had given me quite a lot of relaxation and peace.

The glare from the screen stung my eyes slightly. I sat on the sofa, holding my laptop, trying to find the most relaxed position, but my body was stiff as if bound by invisible ropes. The sound in my headphones rose and fell, especially my supervisor’s voice, which sounded like it carried some kind of restrained criticism, every word seeming to nail itself into my eardrums. “Is there something wrong with the direction of this copy? Why does it feel like it goes against the brand’s tone?” he asked.

I froze at once, my fingers constantly picking at the edge of the sofa, as if that could help shift my attention elsewhere. My mind was a mess, as though black ink had been spilled everywhere. How was I supposed to explain this? Had I misunderstood his earlier instructions?

“It’s my fault. I probably don’t understand the brand’s core well enough,” I said before anyone else could, my voice so low I could barely hear it myself.

My colleague, Xiao A, quickly added from the side, “Actually, we discussed this once before. Wasn’t it that TA didn’t update and adjust it in time?”

Those words stabbed into my chest like a dagger. My heart raced, and heat rushed from my chest to my cheeks; my ears were almost burning. Why did she have to say that? Was she doing it on purpose? Or did I really seem irresponsible to everyone?

The supervisor coughed softly, but didn’t comment. Instead, he moved on to the next topic. The tension in my back seemed to loosen a little, yet at the same time I sank even deeper into a bottomless sense of frustration.

I kept replaying the conversation in my head and said to myself, “Why didn’t you report progress more often? Right, you should have asked him if there were any other requirements earlier.” But that feeling of being watched by everyone couldn’t be ignored. It was as if, in this team, I was the most useless one, and they were only being polite by not saying it outright. I wanted to say something to defend myself, but I was afraid it would be taken as shirking responsibility.

“It’s okay. We’ll pay attention and adjust the direction next time,” the supervisor finally concluded. It sounded casual, but I felt there was tremendous weight hidden behind it. The end-of-meeting notification sounded, and I stared at the screen, unable to bring myself to click the exit button. Cold sweat clung to my back, sticky and nauseating. I took a deep breath, but there was still a stone lodged in my chest.

That night, I stared at the ceiling, replaying the scene over and over again. Why had my colleague said something like that? Did she think I didn’t deserve to be in this team at all? Would they one day decide to kick me out? Even the supervisor’s cough, I slowed down and examined again and again in my mind, as if trying to decode whether there was disappointment hidden in it. I wiped the corner of my eye with the back of my hand, only to realize tears had been streaming down without my noticing. Thinking of the supervisor’s last words, “We’ll pay attention and adjust the direction next time,” I could almost hear myself screaming inwardly: “Next time? Will I even have a next time?”

The next morning, the emotions were still surging like a dammed-up river. Every time I thought of that “Wasn’t it that TA didn’t adjust it in time,” my stomach seemed to clench. I made myself a cup of hot water, but I couldn’t drink it. By noon, while working, I found myself unable to resist opening my email, wanting to write a detailed apology to the supervisor, explaining the whole sequence of events, but in the end I deleted it, because I didn’t even know whether that would only make things worse.

Raindrops battered the rusted tin roof, making a monotonous yet rhythmic pattering sound. I stood on the wooden floor of the passageway, the air around me thick with moisture and carrying the smell of old wood and earth. The camera in my hands seemed much heavier than usual. I tried adjusting the tripod angle, but no matter what I did, it just didn’t feel right. The splashes of rain bounced on the ground, and I forced myself to focus on filming this scene, yet my mind remained a total mess.

“No, this angle has no spirit at all. It’d be better not to film it.” I muttered to myself, my voice echoing in the empty platform, jarringly like an added noise. I looked around to make sure no one had noticed me, but a voice inside kept mocking me: “How embarrassing. Why are you even filming this kind of thing?”

A man came over holding an umbrella. He was tall, wearing a dark gray long overcoat, his steps slow but steady. His face was hidden beneath the shadow of the umbrella, but from the sound of his footsteps as he passed, I could tell he must have noticed me. I started to feel uneasy. My palms were sweating around the camera, and the metal body grew slick in my grip. Did someone think I was weird? Setting up a tripod in the rain to film water splashes—could they think I was secretly filming them?

The man suddenly stopped, standing less than five meters away from me. He tilted his head slightly, and his gaze seemed to sweep over me. I tried hard to tell myself that maybe I was just being too sensitive; perhaps he was only trying to avoid the rain and had stopped here. To hide my unease, I lowered my head and began checking the camera lens cap, pretending to be very busy.

“Rain’s coming down this hard, and you’re still filming here?” His voice drifted over through the rain.

I froze, then hurriedly looked up at him. His face was now clearly visible, a little haggard, with an expression mixed with curiosity and doubt. “Yeah,” I forced out a smile. “It feels kind of artistic in this rain.”

He nodded, said nothing else, and continued toward the other end of the platform. I let out a breath of relief, but my stomach felt like it had a block of ice inside, aching with cold. Had that conversation just now been too awkward? There was something strange in his expression—did he think I was up to something unspeakable?

The rain kept falling. I looked at the footage on the camera screen, and the raindrops and station scene, once so vivid, now seemed meaningless to me. I began replaying the look on the man’s face as he passed, once again wondering whether he thought I was strange. I even couldn’t help asking myself: did this little video have any meaning at all? What did it even mean to say the rain felt “artistic”? Thinking about it now was almost laughable.

By the time I got home it was already eleven at night. The rain had long soaked through my coat, and the chill seeped through my clothes into my bones. I trudged into the bathroom and let hot water wash over my freezing body, but the man’s gaze still refused to leave my mind. Why had he spoken to me? Was it because I looked especially odd? Or too attention-grabbing?

The next day, while cleaning my interview equipment, I reviewed the footage from that day. The images really were beautiful beyond criticism—the raindrops flowed like a galaxy under the dim yellow lights. I should have been satisfied, but inside I felt an indescribable exhaustion. A thought suddenly jumped into my head: was I the only one interested in this kind of beauty? If I posted it, would people mock it as worthless?

I turned off the screen and stared blankly out the window for a long time. Only after the sun had climbed into the sky did I finally make up my mind to edit the video and put it out anyway. No matter how others saw it, at least I had a reason to keep going.

Sunlight filtered through the café curtains and fell across the wooden tabletop. My friend and I sat in a corner, with two half-empty coffee cups on the table, while the air was filled with a faint aroma of freshly baked goods. Soft music mixed with the chatter of other patrons, making the whole place feel especially cozy.

"How have you been lately? Is work going well?" my friend asked.

"Pretty good, just that sometimes I feel a bit stressed," I replied. In truth, I felt somewhat uneasy, worried that I hadn’t met expectations.

"Mm, it’s normal to feel stressed—you’ve always worked so hard," she said with a smile, her tone seeming to carry a hint of dismissal. For a moment, I wondered if she was implying that I should relax a little.

"I just feel... that sometimes I overthink things and am afraid of making mistakes," I said, my voice slightly subdued.

My friend nodded and went on, "But sometimes it’s important to relax a little, isn’t it?" Her voice was gentle, yet it made me feel as if I were being blamed.

I forced myself to keep smiling, but inside I began turning her words over and over in my mind. Was I being too tense? Was she suggesting that I should change something? These doubts kept circling in my head, like endless rumination. Suddenly, I felt my heartbeat quicken slightly, and my palms grew damp.

"How about we go exercise next week? It might help relieve stress," my friend suggested.

"Sure, exercise really does help," I agreed, while secretly doubting whether I could truly reduce this inner anxiety through exercise.

As the afternoon sun gradually faded, we left the café. After I got home, I still felt somewhat upset, sensing that something in our conversation had stung me. That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the scene from the afternoon. My friend’s words seemed to keep reminding me: was I being too sensitive? I realized that I always interpreted other people’s kindness as criticism.

The next morning, after waking up, I tried to let go of those excessive thoughts. I changed into some light workout clothes and planned to enjoy the exercise my friend had suggested. I found that when I focused on my body’s movements, the anxiety inside me slowly began to dissipate, and I seemed to start feeling a little vitality and ease.

The afterglow of the setting sun streamed in through the bookstore’s large glass windows, casting a warm golden sheen over the wooden shelves. I casually picked up a hefty photo book and turned to a page about Nordic winter landscapes. The snowy expanse in the photo stretched endlessly, and the aurora in the distance flowed through the night sky like silk. Beside it was a description, the printed characters crisp and clear: “These lights are the product of the interaction between solar particles and Earth’s magnetic field, and their beauty arises from a cosmic inevitability.” I gently touched the paper with my fingers; its surface had a slightly rough texture.

Soft background music played in the bookstore. I didn’t know what piece it was, but the melody woven from piano and strings left me a little dazed, as if I had fallen into some strange dream, or perhaps returned to those evenings in childhood when I watched the sunset. I felt myself wrapped in an inexplicable calm, with only the sound of turning pages around me and fragments of low conversation from a few people not far away.

“How about this one?” a voice suddenly sounded beside me. I turned my head and saw a man talking to his companion, holding a book whose cover was filled with plant illustrations. They laughed and chatted for a few moments; I couldn’t hear clearly, but their relaxed tone somehow rubbed off on me. I suddenly realized that my shoulders seemed less tense, and a slight sense of ease spread from the back of my neck.

“Maybe I should buy a photo book like this too?” The thought flashed through my mind, but I quickly dismissed it: “Even if I bought it, it would probably just sit on the shelf and rarely get opened.” Thinking of that, I couldn’t help but let out a quiet sigh, lowered my head, and continued flipping through the book in my hands.

My body felt a little weary. Coming to this bookstore after work was actually a spur-of-the-moment decision. After standing for quite a while, my legs had begun to ache. I changed my posture and leaned slightly against the shelf for support, slowing the movement of my fingers as I turned the pages. My eyes were on the photographs, but my mind suddenly drifted.

I remembered a comment I had seen a few days ago, saying that people nowadays spend so much time on screens, yet rarely truly read printed books anymore. I stared at the photo book in front of me and felt that sentence seemed to apply to me as well. Oddly enough, at that moment I didn’t feel any particular shame or self-reproach; instead, I thought about it with a calm sense of detachment, as if I were looking at a notebook unrelated to me.

After standing there for a while, I decided not to dwell on it anymore. When I put the photo book back in its place, the soft rustle of the pages sliding past was oddly pleasant. I casually leafed through a few more books, but in the end I left the bookstore empty-handed. The sky outside was already completely dark, but the streetlights glowed warmly, and the wind was gentler than I had expected. Walking part of the way home, I found myself beginning to look forward to tomorrow.

Such moments of peace are always fleeting, but today it seemed like I didn’t need any more than this.

On a bright, sunny afternoon, a small open-air garden in the company’s backyard was gathering a few colleagues. Lush green plants and a little fountain gently flowing in the distance created a peaceful atmosphere. My palms were breaking out in fine beads of sweat, my heart was beating faster and faster, and in my mind I kept replaying the moment I was about to step up. Although it was only a small impromptu speech, I still could not calm myself.

I heard my colleagues laughing beside me. “Hey, are you ready? Don’t be nervous—everyone here is one of us.” Their tone was relaxed and easygoing, as if they didn’t sense the unease in my heart. I took a deep breath, trying to steady my heartbeat, but my stomach still felt uncomfortable, as if an invisible hand were squeezing it.

When I stepped onto a small platform, my eyes swept over my colleagues’ friendly faces, expectation in their eyes. I forced a calm smile, cleared my throat, and began speaking. I could feel my voice trembling slightly, my throat dry. Even though I had rehearsed many times, deep down the thought kept surging up: Would they think what I’m saying is awful?

“Actually, today I want to share some thoughts about our future project.” I struggled to keep my focus on the topic, trying to shake off those uneasy noises. But the harder I tried, the more those tangled emotions within me bubbled up, and I could almost feel my heart pounding hard against my ribs.

For some reason, I suddenly paused for a moment, and my mind went completely blank. The quiet in the room made me even more panicked, and sweat gradually soaked through my back. I forced myself to stay composed, catching the slight nods of my colleagues below the stage out of the corner of my eye; some friends even smiled and silently cheered me on.

“Sorry, I’m a little nervous…” There was a trace of embarrassment in my voice, but it also gave me a chance to breathe a little. Finally, I managed to deliver the rest smoothly, even trying to crack a small joke. Only when I saw everyone laugh did my nervousness ease a little.

After the speech ended, I stepped down from the platform. Though my legs felt a bit weak, my mood gradually relaxed. Colleagues came over to pat me on the shoulder and praise me: “You did great, don’t worry.” Some of the weight in my heart was lifted, but I also kept replaying every detail from earlier, trying to figure out where I might have gone wrong.

That night, lying in bed, my thoughts were still immersed in the scene from the afternoon. I could still feel the heat on my face, and I was indeed a little unwilling to let it go, but exhaustion soon pulled me into sleep. A few days later, although I still had lingering fear in my heart, my colleagues’ friendly encouragement gradually made me feel that I was not alone in the team.

The projector in the conference room hummed softly, and my PPT was stuck on slide seven. I stared at the chart on the screen, feeling my scalp tighten, while out of the corner of my eye I saw my boss lower his head to flip through a file. Then he looked up and frowned. “Tell me, how was this strategy proposal validated through research?” His voice didn’t rise; it was even quite calm, but my mind exploded. My ears buzzed, and all I could hear was my own heartbeat. My body went rigid, like a stone.

“Uh... because time was tight, we used a small sample for a preliminary test...” My voice trembled, as if I were forcing the words out from the bottom of my throat. As soon as I finished, I saw a flicker of impatience in my boss’s eyes. “So your conclusion is based on an insufficient sample?” His frown deepened. It felt like I’d been punched in the stomach; pain shot through me instantly.

The room was very quiet, so quiet that it made me even more uncomfortable. I could feel several pairs of eyes on my back, like needles. Someone coughed softly, and that sound only made me more anxious. Why wasn’t anyone helping me explain? Why was no one saying anything? I had clearly discussed this proposal with everyone, clearly... Then I suddenly realized that maybe they also thought I had messed up.

“Boss, actually...” I tried to explain, but my voice was so small, like a thin thread, easily cut off by his next question. “If this is based on such weak data, doesn’t that mean our entire plan may have problems?” His words were like a heavy hammer, and I found myself at a complete loss for words.

My face was burning, my palms were sweaty, and I could even feel the sweat on my back sticking to my shirt. I tried to take a deep breath, but it felt like I was choking, and I became even more short of breath. I stared at my hands, my nails digging into my palms, yet I felt numb, nothing at all. In my head, there was only one voice repeating over and over: “It’s over. I’ve disappointed everyone again. He must think I’m not professional enough, that I’m holding things back.”

The meeting finally ended, and I practically fled back to my seat. The whole day felt like I was living in the shadows. I went through every page of the PPT, trying to figure out what had gone wrong, but my mind was a mess—blurred and hazy, as if I couldn’t even make out the words. After work, a colleague squeezed out a “Go home and rest early,” and my embarrassment only deepened. What did he mean by that tone? Was he implying that I was terrible today?

That night I couldn’t sleep at all. The scene of my boss questioning me kept replaying in my mind—the furrowed brow, every word like a knife stabbing into my heart. My stomach hurt so badly I could only curl up on the bed, and all that kept coming into my mind was, “Why do I always fail like this?” “Who could still like someone who’s always messing things up?”

Sunlight slipped through the gaps in the curtains and gently spilled onto the balcony, where my friend and I sat in bamboo chairs, enjoying this rare moment of leisure. The sky was so blue there was hardly a cloud in sight, and a light breeze brushed past, carrying a faint fragrance of flowers. Beside us sat a small tea table, topped with a pot of freshly brewed green tea, its aroma drifting softly through the air.

I held the teacup in my hands, feeling the warmth of the tea flow through my fingertips, while I heard my friend ask casually, “How’s your work been going lately?”

I smiled and replied, “Pretty well, just that sometimes inspiration suddenly runs dry.”

He nodded and smiled reassuringly. “You can’t rush inspiration. Take it slow—no need to worry.”

Sunlight bathed us, and I closed my eyes. Through my eyelids, the light turned the world a warm orange-red. I realized I hadn’t relaxed and talked with a friend like this in a long time, so I raised my head and looked at him. “You know, sometimes I feel like I’m trying so hard to catch up with something, but I don’t even know what it is I’m chasing.”

He turned his face slightly; the sunlight fell across it, and he frowned a little in thought. “Maybe we’re all searching for a kind of inner peace? But sometimes peace is actually right beside us—we’re just too busy to notice.”

His words moved me. My heartbeat steadied, and the slight sense of urgency in my heart seemed to disappear all at once. “Yeah, maybe that’s exactly it.” I slowly took a sip of tea. The warm liquid spread through my mouth, bringing with it a familiar sense of comfort and calm.

Time slipped by quietly, and the sky gradually shifted into a gentle yellow. My friend stood up and stretched. “I should head back. Let’s come drink tea again next time.”

I nodded, saw him to the door, and watched him leave, a faint sense of contentment rising in my heart. In that moment, everything seemed simple and beautiful.

As night fell, I returned indoors, still thinking about our conversation that day. That unhurried way of talking made me realize that sometimes, the beauty of life lies in these unnoticed moments and in simple companionship. The next day, I continued with my work, but with a little more peace and anticipation in my heart.

I sat in the corner seat of the conference room, my backpack at my feet, my palms slightly sweaty. The walls were covered with everyone’s creative sketches, and sunlight streamed in through the windows, but the whole room still felt oppressive to me. I stared at my notebook, its pages filled with messy scribbles. The manager had just finished speaking and said everyone should take turns sharing their ideas. I was fifth in line, and my heart began to race; the buzzing in my ears grew louder and louder.

“Next is your turn,” I heard the manager say in a calm voice. I took a deep breath, stood up, and forced myself to speak: “I... um, I designed a concept themed around a lighthouse, symbolizing hope and a sense of direction...” My voice caught, and suddenly my throat felt tight, my stomach starting to ache faintly. A few people below seemed to be talking in hushed voices, and my mind immediately began to speculate: Were they laughing at me? Did they think my concept was cliché?

“And then?” the manager looked at me. I jolted and realized I had blanked out for a few seconds. “Oh, then... um...” My thoughts were completely scrambled, and everything I had rehearsed beforehand suddenly vanished. I looked at everyone’s expressions, which seemed to grow more and more impatient. Someone was lightly tapping the table; someone else was looking down at their phone. The manager stared at me, his brow slightly furrowed.

“Forget it, go sit back down. Next,” he said softly, but each word struck me hard. As I sat back in my seat, it felt as if all the blood in my body had frozen. An almost unbearable shame surged up inside me, and I kept my head down, avoiding eye contact with anyone. My palms were completely wet, and the stomach pain had become even more intense.

“That was such a failure,” a voice in my head said. “Why are you always like this? Why can’t you do well for once?” I clenched my notebook tightly, trying to distract myself. I didn’t hear a word of the speeches that followed; all I could hear was my own heartbeat, pounding like a drum.

After the meeting ended, before I could even move, the manager patted my shoulder. “Don’t take it too seriously. It’s normal to get nervous sometimes.” His tone was gentle, but I couldn’t hear any comfort in it; instead, I felt a hint of sympathy, even disappointment, in his eyes. I nodded, not daring to say much, and slung my bag over my shoulder before heading out the door.

When I got home, I flopped onto the bed without turning on the lights. All evening long, I kept replaying the scene from the meeting in my head. I began to magnify every detail: the manager’s expression, my coworkers’ small gestures, my own tone and posture. All of it seemed to prove one thing—that I wasn’t good enough, smart enough, or professional enough. The feeling twisted my stomach into even greater pain. That night, I barely slept at all, tossing and turning while blaming myself over and over in my mind.

I sat in the corner of the coffee shop, looking around. The artwork on the walls made the place feel especially warm, and as a creator, I was filled with mixed feelings about my own work. Today was a small sharing session for my pieces; I was looking forward to it, yet anxiety lingered at the back of my mind. The rich aroma of coffee drifted through the air, briefly distracting me, but my heartbeat remained rapid.

A friend walked over, looked at my work, and after a slight frown said, “Hmm, it’s pretty interesting.” In an instant, my heart sank. I couldn’t help but guess at the subtext: “Interesting” meant it wasn’t good enough, didn’t it? I fixated on that fleeting microexpression on his face, as if it had already proven that I had failed.

I tried to calm myself down and recall his tone, but memories of my own past failures and embarrassing moments kept surfacing in my mind. I felt my stomach tighten, cold sweat beading on my forehead. I forced a smile and asked, “Really? What do you think could be improved?” trying to confirm his true thoughts without giving anything away.

Then he continued, “Maybe you could add a few more details; it would be more engaging.” I nodded, but in my mind I began magnifying that suggestion, imagining my shortcomings being exaggerated into a laughingstock for others. I felt like a tiny insect trapped inside a transparent glass ball, with everyone watching every move I made.

After the sharing session ended, I sat on a bench outside the coffee shop, feeling the evening breeze brush past me. I still couldn’t calm down; his words kept replaying in my mind. Nearly half an hour passed before I realized I had fallen into an endless loop of self-criticism, trying to find every possible hint of negativity in what he had said.

The next day, I tried to look at my work again, seeking something constructive in my friend’s advice instead of focusing only on the potential criticism. This time, I decided to break through my own defenses first, to admit in my heart that even with flaws, I could still improve. Although I still felt uneasy inside, at least I had begun to realize that I didn’t need to turn every tiny implication into a trigger for self-attack.

The steaming hotpot sat in the center of the table, sending up wisps of steam, while the aroma of chili oil drifted through the air. I sat at the edge of the table, holding a pair of wooden chopsticks, feeling their warmth travel to my fingertips. My friends were all gathered around, laughing and chatting, the atmosphere relaxed and cheerful. With a soft click, I used my chopsticks to pick up a large shrimp and place it into my bowl. In that moment, everything felt especially simple and especially satisfying. A friend beside me said with a smile, “You’ve eaten a lot today!” I laughed too, my face a little flushed. “The hotpot broth here is just too good—I can’t help it.”

Listening to everyone’s conversation, I occasionally joined in. The topics ranged from the movie we’d recently watched, to amusing things at work, to future plans. As the friends kept talking, someone suggested taking a trip: “Let’s go traveling together next month and relax a bit.” As soon as those words were spoken, a wave of warmth and longing welled up in my heart, as if I could already feel the fresh air and unrestrained freedom of the journey.

“That’s a good idea,” I agreed, imagining every moment I would spend with my friends. The room was filled with our easy voices, and all the busyness and anxiety were cast aside for the moment. I felt as if I were surrounded by warmth. My heartbeat was light and steady, and my stomach felt pleasantly warm, as though everything was running smoothly in an orderly way.

My phone in my hand vibrated. I picked it up and saw a message in the work group chat, but I didn’t open it. The laughter around me and the bubbling sounds from the hotpot drowned out the phone’s vibration, and I only wanted to immerse myself in this moment. My friends kept chatting enthusiastically, while I picked up a thin slice of meat and dipped it into the sauce bowl, letting it soak completely in the garlic sauce.

That night, after saying goodbye to my friends, I walked home along the streets in the night. The glow of the streetlights shone on the ground, stretching the shadows long. My heart was filled with a peace and contentment that words could not describe, as if I were simply enjoying every moment of life.

When I woke up the next morning, I still felt that same sense of joy and ease. On the balcony, I made myself a cup of hot tea. Sunlight spilled across the floor, and a faint aroma of tea filled the air. I took a deep breath and felt that even breathing was so reassuring.

Sunlight poured down through the broken panes of glass, and the mottled patches of light and shadow tangled wildly on the floor. I stood at the greenhouse door, my fingers trembling slightly as I pushed open the rusted iron gate. A pungent smell of dampness hit me at once, mixed with the stench of decaying plants. I couldn’t help frowning, but I had come this far; turning back seemed even more shameful. My foot stepped onto the moss-covered concrete floor, the sole slipping slightly, and I hurried to steady myself against the shelf beside me. It had once been lined with seed pots, but now only a few yellowed leaves and some clumps of moldy soil remained. I felt a slight constriction in my stomach, as though seized by some indescribable embarrassment.

“There doesn’t seem to be anything special here,” I muttered, then quickly stopped, as if afraid of hearing myself. A few birds flew past the broken skylight, the sound of their wings beating the air especially clear in the silence. I tried to focus on those sounds, hoping they would drive away the unnecessary thoughts rising in my mind, but with little effect. Fragments of memory began to surface—those moments when I had given up halfway through in public, those looks that made me feel judged, every detail surging over me like a tide. I stood in the center of the greenhouse, with no one around, yet I still felt an invisible gaze scrutinizing every move I made.

I tried to take a photo to record the place. After all, I always felt that creators needed to keep material on hand. But the image on the screen discouraged me: the cold tones, the chaotic scene, absolutely nothing like the “aesthetics of loneliness” I had imagined. “Forget it, there’s nothing worth photographing,” I said softly, though I wasn’t sure whether I was saying it to myself or to the greenhouse. My fingers began to feel hot, as if protesting this failure. I put my phone back in my pocket, and my heartbeat quickened in my chest, each beat seeming to remind me that I was “wasting time.”

“Why are you always so useless? You can’t even take a decent picture.” My inner voice turned sharp. I imagined someone suddenly bursting in, accusing me of sneaking into the place with bad intentions, or someone seeing the photo I uploaded and mocking it for having no artistic value. A wave of self-disgust rose within me, and my stomach seemed to twist with pain. I drew a breath, trying to calm myself, but the sunlight still stabbed painfully at my eyes, and the wind in my ears grew increasingly annoying.

When I finally stepped out of the greenhouse, the cold air made me feel a little better. I walked along the path, my footsteps echoing softly. “You don’t need to prove yourself every time,” I tried to tell myself, but even that sentence sank like a stone into my chest, leaving only silent ripples behind. After I got home, I put the camera on the table and didn’t touch it for the rest of the day. I didn’t upload any photos either; I just tossed and turned in bed, trying to find some “meaning” in the visit.

“Maybe no one needs to know,” I muttered to the ceiling, my voice so low even I could barely hear it. Outside the window, the leaves drifted down, as if mocking my inaction.

Sunlight streamed through the window onto the floor of the antique restoration shop, and the air was filled with the scent of wood and a faint trace of paint. I stood inside, looking at those objects weathered by time, and images flashed through my mind of these antiques once being cherished by someone. The shop’s owner, an elderly man with a head of white hair, was carefully restoring an antique chair. My heart grew uneasy, as if the antiquity and prosperity of these objects made me aware of time rapidly slipping away from me. He looked up, saw how tense I still was beside him, and smiled, saying, “Sometimes antiques are like people—they need patient care and love.” I gave an awkward smile. “I think sometimes I need that kind of care too.”

Here, I felt a tightness in my chest, my heartbeat quickening from time to time, as if keeping pace with the passage of time. I couldn’t help asking myself whether I, too, was slowly losing my luster like these objects. The owner began explaining the restoration process in detail, how he used delicate techniques to bring each antique back to a state close to its original form. My palms began to sweat, and my mind was filled with doubts about my own creative career. I couldn’t help wondering whether my work could withstand the test of time, whether it too could be treasured like these antiques.

The shop’s quiet atmosphere made it impossible for me to escape those voices within. Until the owner said, “Every crack has its own story.” Those words seemed like a soft hammer striking the depths of my heart. I began to feel a tightness in my stomach, as if I wanted to flee from such thoughts. On the way home, I kept reflecting on whether my work was as worthy of restoration as these antiques.

That night, lying in bed, my mind was still filled with these scattered thoughts. I realized that my fear of time and my self-doubt were so real, and that these emotions continued to affect me over the next few days. I decided that in my future creative work, I would try to acknowledge my own vulnerability more, rather than constantly attacking myself just to avoid being rejected by others.

The air in the community farmers’ market was filled with the fragrance of fresh fruits and vegetables, along with the occasional warm scent of toasted bread drifting by. Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the canopy and scattered across the pavement in mottled patches of light. I walked slowly, feeling the faint vibrations beneath my feet with each step. I lingered for a long time in front of a stall selling organic vegetables, drawn in by the rows of vividly colored carrots and tomatoes arranged neatly in order. The vendor was a smiling middle-aged woman, her face flushed red by the sun. She greeted me warmly: “Young one, today’s tomatoes are especially sweet.”

“They do look really good,” I replied, feeling relaxed and cheerful. In chatting with her, I learned that they were all grown in her own garden, without chemical fertilizer, using only natural fertilizer. “You can eat them with peace of mind,” she said. Her eyes reflected satisfaction and pride.

I reached out toward a pile of carrots, feeling the subtle texture of their skins against my fingertips. All around me, the noise swelled and receded: vendors’ enthusiastic calls mingled with people’s conversations, forming a vivid scene of everyday life. I suddenly realized that I had spent longer in this market than I had expected, yet every minute felt worthwhile.

Leaving the vegetable stall, I walked toward the fruit stand, where bright, tempting cherries and strawberries were on display. As I leaned in, a sweet fragrance rushed toward me, leaving me slightly intoxicated. A warmth flowed through me, and my heartbeat became calm and rhythmic. The vendor was a somewhat shy young boy, who smiled at me and said, “Try one—these were just picked, and they taste amazing.”

Carefully, I picked up a cherry and put it in my mouth. The juice burst instantly across my tongue, perfectly balanced between sweet and sour, seeming like the best expression of a fresh morning. I grinned and gave him an appreciative smile.

After finishing my shopping, I walked past the market entrance with the fresh ingredients on my back. The sunlight shone on my forehead, warm and gentle, filling my whole body with a joyful energy. I did not hurry home; instead, I sat down on a park bench outside the market, looking at the passersby coming and going, my thoughts calm and at ease.

In the days that followed, whenever I thought back on that trip to the market, I felt peace and warmth. There was no unease or tension at all, only a simple, pure moment in life.

A cold draft crept in through the gap under the door, mingling with the aroma of coffee and baked brownies. I sat in the corner, head down, scrolling through my phone for something or other while half-listening to my friends chat casually. Every now and then the conversation would turn to me, and I’d respond mechanically with a few words before looking back down and pretending to be busy. I couldn’t quite figure out why, but over these past few get-togethers, I seemed to always be unable to keep up with everyone else’s pace. The laughter was clearly loud and lively, yet it felt like a transparent wall, keeping me on the outside.

“You don’t seem very happy lately. Is work too busy?” A friend across from me suddenly looked up and said in a soft, probing tone. I froze. My first thought was: why is she saying that? Was I doing such a terrible job that even my posture looked unnatural? Or was she implying that my negative mood had already become unbearable to everyone?

I forced out a smile. “I’m fine, I guess. Maybe I’m just a bit tired lately.”

“Oh, then maybe you should exercise more to relieve some stress? We run into each other at the gym every day!” she said with a smile.

Her tone was casual, but my mind immediately started racing. They see each other at the gym every day? Then why have they never invited me? Am I not sociable enough? Have I already left them with the impression that I hold everyone back? Was her question just now also hinting at the same thing? The more I thought about it, the more my heartbeat seemed to spiral out of control, and my face began to burn.

“I’m going to the restroom.” I stood up, barely holding back the tremor in my voice, feeling my vision blur. I walked unsteadily to the bathroom and splashed cold water on my face, but the panic inside me would not subside. Why am I always like this, always hearing criticism in other people’s words? Why do I put on an act of being fine when I can’t even fool myself? Did they really have a problem with me? Had I actually done something wrong?

My body started protesting too; a dull pain began in my stomach, and my palms were slick with cold sweat. I started breathing rapidly, feeling all the strength drain out of me. I even felt as if those laughs, those glances, had turned into mockery, replaying over and over in my head. I couldn’t go back anymore. I just wanted to escape.

When I returned to my seat and picked up my bag, my friends were all looking at me with puzzled expressions. “I just remembered I have something to do, so I have to go first,” I explained as calmly as I could, though inside I desperately wanted to disappear right away. Their gazes pricked at my back like invisible needles. I didn’t wait for a reply and walked straight out of the café.

The cold wind outside hit my face hard, and those few lines of conversation kept echoing in my mind. “Do they think I’m unnecessary?” “It was clearly meant to be kind, but I just can’t stop feeling like she’s openly dissatisfied with me...” I walked home like a deserter, my mind in complete disarray, my stomach twisted tight like a wrung-out rag, my body trembling slightly from the cold and my hurried steps.

That night, I lay in bed trying to calm myself down, but my mind kept replaying those scenes and voices. My friend’s tone, the expression on her face—was that subtle disdain after all? Or was I just too sensitive? I kept guessing, kept blaming my own nerves, but the more I thought, the less I could stop. At two in the morning, the stabbing pain in my stomach finally made me get up to take some medicine, and I swallowed it almost in tears. In that moment, all I felt was that I was incapable of handling relationships between people normally, yet I also longed desperately for someone to tell me that I wasn’t such a terrible person.

The walls of the recording studio were covered with thick black soundproofing material, and faint streetlight filtered in through the window. I sat on a stool with the microphone in front of me, headphones wrapped around my ears, as if the world had been reduced to just my voice and the mechanical echo. I took a deep breath, adjusted the height of the mic, and prepared to begin recording this episode of the podcast. Along with a faint hum of electrical static, I could hear my own heartbeat, as if underscoring my nervousness.

“Today we’re exploring anxiety in the creative process,” I began, my voice trembling slightly. “Many creators may overanalyze external feedback in their work...”

I suddenly stopped, a wave of unease flashing through my mind. Would they think I was talking nonsense? Would anyone feel that what I was sharing had no value? I began to doubt whether anything I was doing now had any meaning. It felt as though my insides were tightly bound by ropes, leaving me unable to breathe.

I forced myself to continue. “Even a small detail can trigger endless reflection on our part...”

My voice fell silent, and the studio was left with nothing but stillness and the faint sound of equipment running. My heartbeat quickened, and I felt fine beads of sweat break out on my forehead. My stomach began to ache faintly. I wanted to pause the recording and change the topic, but a voice inside told me that if I stopped now, I might never be able to keep speaking.

Suddenly, footsteps came through my headphones, and the sound engineer pushed open the half-closed door. “Are you okay?”

“I’m fine, just a little stuck,” I said with a strained smile.

“If you need, we can adjust the recording schedule,” he suggested, concern on his face.

“Thanks, I may need a little time,” I replied softly, as a wave of guilt spread inside me. I wondered whether I was being too sensitive, or whether the sound engineer had already begun to lose patience with me. Was the quality of my program really not good enough? These thoughts churned uncontrollably in my mind.

Back at the microphone, I tried taking deep breaths, hoping to calm myself down. Closing my eyes, I tried to picture a calm and confident image in my mind. But there was always a voice reminding me that all my efforts might be futile.

That night, after leaving the studio, I wandered alone on the street. The cold wind brushed across my face, bringing stabs of pain. I tried to recall the recording process and how many places could have been better. I listened to a clip on my phone and found that, without realizing it, I had expressed my views in a questioning tone, worried that listeners would think I was being negative.

Over the course of that week, I kept replaying that recording in my mind, and the anxiety in my heart had still not faded, as if it were constantly reminding me of my inner unease and fear. I felt ashamed of my sensitivity, yet I could not shake off that persistent doubt.

The venue was brightly lit, filled with the sounds of people talking and laughing. I stood among a group of creators, holding a glass of red wine, trying to fit into their conversation. Yet a sense of unease gripped me tightly; my heart began to race, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. The stylishly dressed woman was speaking animatedly about her success, and everyone around her was nodding in agreement, but I found it hard to blend into that atmosphere.

She looked at me and asked with a smile, “Have you been working on anything new lately?” I froze for a moment, then forced out a smile. “Ah, I’ve been doing some small projects recently, nothing special.” As soon as I said it, my cheeks started to burn, and a wave of self-doubt surged through me. Why couldn’t I speak about my work as confidently as she did?

The conversations around me continued, as if I were being left out. I tried to make myself look interested, but in reality my thoughts were drifting away. “Will they think I’m not qualified to be standing here at all?” I wondered to myself, my heart pounding violently.

Time seemed to slow down, and my stomach began to feel unsettled. I wanted to find an excuse to leave as soon as possible. But running away would only make me seem even more out of place, so I told myself to calm down. Turning around, I tried to join another group’s conversation. A young man talking about the latest creative ideas caught my attention. I cut in and said, “That idea sounds really interesting. Could you tell me more?” However, he only gave a perfunctory nod and then went back to laughing and talking with the others.

At that moment, I felt as if I were standing outside an invisible barrier, with all the sounds and smiles drifting away from me. Forcing a smile, I thought that perhaps this was not the kind of place I should have come to.

A few days later, I still couldn’t shake off the embarrassment from that night. Every time I thought back to the party, I could still feel the sweat in my palms and my racing heartbeat. A friend asked me how the night went, and I brushed it off by saying, “It was okay, but they’re all really impressive. I felt a bit inadequate.” Although I tried to hide it with a casual tone, the self-doubt deep inside me still refused to go away.

The air in the early morning carried a hint of chill, a coldness that seemed able to cut straight through my coat. As I walked into that small independent cinema in the city center, the wind chime by the entrance swayed gently, letting out a faint jingle that stirred an inexplicable tension in me. The cinema was very quiet, with only a few vintage movie posters hanging on the corridor walls, blurred by the dim yellow light.

“Hello, there’s a screening starting in half an hour. Can I help you book a ticket?” the ticket clerk asked kindly. I nodded, trying to conceal my anxiety. It was my first time at this theater, and everything around me felt unfamiliar, making me somewhat uneasy. “Was he being cold toward me? Did I do something to make him unhappy?” These questions spinning in my head always left me restless.

Sitting in front of the screening room, I tried hard to relax. But I noticed that the person beside me deliberately avoided eye contact. That small gesture made my heart sink, and my pulse suddenly quickened, like a heavy hammer pounding against me. “Did I do something that makes people dislike me?” Once that thought surfaced, my pulse surged like a raging tide. My muscles tensed slightly, my palms began to sweat, and I could only barely keep my hands clasped on my knees.

After the movie started, the plot gradually drew me in. But I still found myself distracted from time to time, and the murmurs of the people around me made me even more sensitive, afraid I might miss something. “Are they talking about me? Do they think my behavior is strange?” I thought in terror, and because of that I could not focus on the screen in front of me.

By the time the film ended, I still hadn’t fully shaken off the tension. As I followed the crowd out of the auditorium, the cold wind outside hit me again, and the biting chill woke me up a little. On the way home, amid the noise of traffic on the streets, I recalled what had just happened and couldn’t help feeling regret and shame. “Why do I always overread other people like this? Can’t I just be simpler?” I felt powerless before my loss of control.

That night, I lay in bed, my thoughts still in disarray. I kept trying to tell myself to calm down, not to think about the embarrassment I had felt at the movies during the day, trying to convince myself that it was all in my imagination, nothing more than my own overthinking. And yet my heart still raced, like aftershocks that kept striking without ever fully settling.

A few days later, I still couldn’t completely let it go, and there remained an unresolved knot in my heart. After talking with a friend, I tried to analyze my feelings at the cinema from a more rational perspective, trying to sort out the reasons for that unease. Though the process was difficult, I knew I had to face the distress caused by this habit of overinterpreting things, so I wouldn’t be tormented by similar situations again.

Stepping through that tightly shut, heavy wooden door, I heard the clear jingle of the bell on it, as if reminding me that I had entered another world. The air inside the shop carried a mixture of dust and old paper, mingled with an unfamiliar herbal scent. The walls all around were stacked with all kinds of old records, lined up neatly in row upon row—from bands to solo artists, from classics to avant-garde, everything was there. The covers of the vinyl records were old and yellowed, and the softly undulating music flowed slowly from the turntable in the corner, low and slightly raspy, as though telling stories of the past.

“What are you looking for today?” The shop owner gave me a faint smile. He was sitting behind the counter, gently wiping a record with his hand. His gaze made me tense up, and my heartbeat began to quicken involuntarily. “Uh, I’m just looking around,” I replied quickly, my voice rising a little without meaning to.

That familiar unease in my heart spread once again. “Does he think I’m not sincere if I’m not buying anything? Will I be seen as an unnecessary disturbance?” As I flipped through the record covers, I couldn’t help but blame myself and wonder if I was interrupting his normal work. Every time the shop owner lifted his head, every slight furrow of his brow, seemed to hint at something, making me feel even more uneasy.

I tried taking a few deep breaths, but my hands were faintly sweaty, and tiny beads of perspiration had begun to gather on my forehead. A dull discomfort in my stomach ached faintly, as if resisting this baseless tension.

“These records are really nice. Do you have any recommendations?” I forced out a smile, hoping to ease my discomfort while not seeming rude. The shop owner smiled faintly, set aside what he was doing, and pointed to a corner. “Over there are several recently arrived batches of classic old songs. You might find something you like.”

I nodded and walked over, doing my best to hide my unease, and began browsing through those records. As I went deeper into the stacks, I tried to let the music and those seemingly unremarkable covers lead me into another state of mind, searching for messages that could bring inspiration.

When I left the shop, I was carrying a record with a simple cover yet full of stories, and as I stepped out the door, that melody that had moved me was still echoing in my mind.

Back home, I gently placed the record on the player and sat quietly on the sofa to listen. Although the experience had made me nervous, the music seemed to soothe my anxiety. I knew I had to learn not to overinterpret other people’s gestures and expressions. Over the next few days, I immersed myself in my creative work, striving to make that beautiful melody a part of my piece.

The gray-blue evening light filtered through the blinds on the wall, casting a hazy yellow gloom over the entire first floor of the record store. I stood before the wooden shelves against the wall, my fingers gliding gently over row after row of album covers—the soft plastic texture and the occasional faint rustle gave me a strange sense of comfort. The air was thick with the smell of old wood, along with a faint trace of vinyl’s distinctive scent, faintly mixed with a hint of coffee, probably brewing behind the counter by the owner. I tried to focus on choosing an appropriate record, but my attention kept flickering like the wick of a candle.

A melody of rock music drifted softly from the store’s speakers, brisk in rhythm yet faintly oppressive to me. As I hesitated over whether to pick a classic album from the 1970s, I caught sight, from the corner of my eye, of a young man passing by from the other side of the shelves. He wore a maroon wool coat and held a record catalog in his hand. As he passed me, he gave a slight nod and a smile. I instinctively smiled back, but my body stiffened a little, and my heartbeat instantly quickened.

“Why did he smile? Was I in his way? Or did I make some weird expression?” My mind, like a tape recorder switched on, kept replaying these inner monologues over and over. I couldn’t help stealing a glance at his back; he had already turned toward another row of shelves and seemed not to have noticed me at all. I bit my lip, feeling the muscles in my back tighten and my palms beginning to sweat.

To hide my unease, I pretended to be absorbed in browsing the records in front of me, but inside I kept involuntarily chewing over what had just happened. I began imagining all sorts of possible scenarios: did he think my clothes were inappropriate today? Or was I moving too slowly and bothering other people? For a moment, I was even certain that my smile must have looked horribly awkward, like a stiff mask.

“Need any help?” A gentle voice pulled me back from my thoughts. I looked up sharply and found the owner standing in front of me. He wore black-rimmed glasses, and his smile was faint but sincere. I hurriedly shook my head, trying to hide my awkwardness. “Ah, no, I’m just looking around.” I could hear my voice higher than usual, as if it were involuntarily leaking my anxiety.

After the owner nodded and walked away, the waves inside me still did not subside. I felt mortified, and even wanted to leave immediately. But the moment I turned, I realized that doing so would only make me seem even more suspicious—would other people think I was being weird?

So I forced myself to stay where I was, took a deep breath, and tried to calm myself by counting the records on the shelves. But the stifling shame spread from my chest to my cheeks like rising heat. I began to feel uneasy about everything here: the dim lighting, the stuffy air, even the music from the speakers sounded like it was mocking me. I steeled myself and picked a record I didn’t really like, then hurried to the counter to pay. The owner smiled and spoke to me, but I could hardly make out what he was saying; all I could think was, “Hurry up and end this.”

When I got home, I placed the record on the table but didn’t open it. I stared at it for a long time, my thoughts churning like a boiling pot of soup. It wasn’t really a big deal, and yet I couldn’t help replaying it again and again. “If only I hadn’t been so stiff.” “Would he think I’m some kind of strange person?” These thoughts were like inescapable echoes, growing louder the more I thought about them.

It wasn’t until the next morning that I finally calmed down a little, and even began to wonder if I was being overly sensitive. Even so, whenever I thought of that person’s smile, a trace of unease still rose in my chest, as if I had missed some important signal. The feeling was sticky, impossible to shake off.

On a bright, sunny afternoon, I wandered through the antique market on the western edge of the city. The stalls around me were filled with all kinds of unique antiques, some already coated in the dust of age. The air was thick with the scent of old wood and a faint mustiness. My fingers gently traced a carved wooden box, its intricate details so exquisite that I couldn’t tear my eyes away. Just as I was about to ask the price, a voice leaning in interrupted my thoughts: “Are you interested in this too?”

I looked up and saw the seller. He wore a pair of reading glasses and seemed to know exactly how interested his customers were. I nodded, trying to stay calm, but a ripple of anxiety began to rise within me. “This box is nice, but it’s a bit expensive,” he said, and in his tone there seemed to be a mix of expectation and probing.

My inner monologue sprang to life: “Is he trying to rip me off? Is this price reasonable?” In an instant, all sorts of worst-case purchasing scenarios flashed through my mind. I noticed what seemed like a trace of subtle cunning in his smile, which made me even more nervous; my heartbeat quickened.

“Could you give me a slightly better price?” I asked, my voice trembling a little, trying my best not to let him notice my unease.

The seller shook his head slightly. “This isn’t easy to find. It really is a good piece.” His tone left no room for refusal, which only made me feel more helpless. My heart beat even faster, fine beads of sweat began to appear on my forehead, and my palms grew damp. I fought down the urge to leave quickly and forced out a strained smile.

After the conversation ended, I was still standing in front of the stall, lost in self-reflection. This preemptive self-attack made me unbearably ashamed. Why couldn’t I just be more composed? At that moment, I began to blame myself for being so sensitive, replaying every detail of the conversation over and over in my head.

Even after I got home, I still couldn’t let it go. Sitting at my desk, I stared at the wooden box I had reluctantly bought, filled with conflict and unease. It was as if a small transaction had somehow turned into a storm within me.

Days later, the experience was still circling in my mind. I started searching online for similar antique prices, hoping to prove that I hadn’t been cheated. Even so, the anxiety in my heart still refused to fade. I kept trying to comfort myself that there was no need to dwell on something so trivial, but whenever I thought of the seller’s smile, my heart would involuntarily tighten.

The café was noisy with voices, and raindrops struck the window, blurring the scene outside. We were seated by the window, my hand tightly gripping a hot coffee cup as I tried to ease the unease inside me. Her face was full of displeasure, and she kept staring at me, as if waiting for me to come up with some explanation. She finally said, “I heard you turned down another collaboration project? If you keep going like this, you’ll lose a lot of opportunities.” Her voice was laced with disappointment and impatience, like a thorn being driven into my heart. I forced a smile, trying to soften the atmosphere. “I just want to think it through carefully before making a decision.”

But inside, it was a different story: my heart was pounding like a drum, beads of sweat kept breaking out on my forehead, and I felt a faint ache in my stomach, as if warning me that something terrible was about to happen. I didn’t want to disappoint her, and even less did I want her to abandon me. I recalled past relationships that had fallen apart because I was too sensitive and suspicious, and the unease in my heart began to ferment. She went on, “You’re always so guarded. No one will wait for you forever.”

Those words were like a bolt of thunder, nearly shaking me out of my ability to think. My mind kept circling around words like “abandonment” and “not being understood.” I was afraid she would leave me because I couldn’t change my personality. At that moment, I felt an intense sense of suffocation, and I had to say something. “I know I have problems, but I’m trying to change.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I regretted them; the pleading and self-blame in my voice made me feel humiliated. She looked at me, as if she wanted to say something, but then closed her mouth.

“I’m not trying to pressure you. I just hope you can be a little more proactive,” she said, her tone softening. But I felt that my vulnerability had already been laid bare. Whenever faced with the threat of losing something, I would always attack myself first as a way to protect myself. I lowered my head, staring at my reflection in the coffee cup, hoping that the liquid would swallow up all my unease. I desperately wanted to escape this suffocating conversation, but I knew I had to face it; otherwise, my life would never change.

That night, I lay in bed, thoughts surging over me like a tide. I kept replaying today’s conversation, wondering why I was always so uneasy. The next day, when I woke up, I felt waves of helplessness and couldn’t move. I knew this conversation had left a deep mark on me, making me realize the panic and helplessness I feel when facing relationships. I needed to find a way to confront these shadows in my heart.

On Friday night, I attended a party hosted by an old friend. The room was filled with people’s laughter and chatter, and music drifted softly through the air. I could feel the faint vibration of the floor, as if the whole room were swaying along to the rhythm. The lights on the walls were a little glaring, and the air was thick with the mixed scent of red wine and perfume.

I was standing in a corner of the living room, holding a glass of red wine, my heart beating a little fast. Out of habit, I scanned the room, looking for familiar faces. Just then, I noticed one friend whispering to another, then glancing at me, and the two of them burst into laughter. An immediate thought flashed through my mind: “Are they laughing at me?”

A wave of unease began to rise in me. “Are they talking about me? Are they saying my outfit today is too casual?” I kept asking myself inside, but I didn’t dare go over to check. I could only stay where I was, pretending to look around, while inside I felt like a bowl of mixed flavors had been knocked over—sour and bitter all at once.

Amid their laughter, I felt heat rising in my face, my palms beginning to sweat, and a stone-like weight pressing on my chest so that I could hardly breathe. The uneasiness grew stronger and stronger, and I started imagining all sorts of possibilities: “Did I say something inappropriate? Do they not like me at all?”

I tried to take deep breaths in an effort to calm myself, but those thoughts kept surging in like a tide. I began to realize I should do something, so I decided to walk over and ask what they were talking about. As I approached, they immediately turned around, looking completely at ease, as if nothing unusual had happened.

“What were you talking about just now?” I tried to make my voice sound relaxed, though I knew there was still a trace of tension in it.

“Oh, we were talking about someone’s recent travel plans,” one friend replied. Her tone was natural, with none of the hostility I had imagined.

I forced out a smile, feeling a wave of relief, but the shadow of self-doubt hadn’t completely vanished. I told myself I shouldn’t be so sensitive, yet the uneasiness lingered like a shadow.

A few days later, I still couldn’t help but replay that night over and over in my mind. “Why am I always so sensitive? Why do I always overthink?” I felt somewhat frustrated, but more than that, I felt dissatisfied with myself and helpless.

I know that this deep fear of being ignored and abandoned is rooted in my heart, and from time to time it stirs up trouble.

The lights in the conference room seemed harsher than usual, and the warm yellow glow spread across the tabletop as my palms began to grow damp. Three other team members and I were seated around the long table, surrounded by disorganized piles of documents that everyone kept flipping through. I tried to focus on my own task list, but my mind kept drifting back to their voices.

“We may need to revise this part, and your design still needs some adjustment,” one colleague suddenly said, turning toward me with a flat tone and glancing up at me. His brows were slightly furrowed, and I couldn’t help but start wondering, “Does he think my design is terrible?
