Is he really unhappy with me?” My heartbeat sped up at once, and it felt as if the heat in my face had risen by several degrees. I forced myself to reply, “Okay, I’ll revise it as soon as possible.” My voice sounded a little stiff, and even I thought it came across as perfunctory.

After he finished speaking, the others continued the discussion. My eyes stayed on my laptop screen, but I couldn’t make out any of the content. Over and over in my mind, I magnified his tone and expression, trying to figure out what had gone wrong: “Was there a problem with the draft I submitted earlier? Does the team think I’m a burden?” It felt as though a knot had formed in my stomach, tightening more and more the longer I thought about it.

After the meeting ended, everyone left one by one. I deliberately lingered at the end, pretending to tidy up the documents. Once everyone was gone, I finally sat back down in my chair, my head hanging weakly. I started criticizing myself: “Why do I always end up disappointing people? They must think I’m incapable. I’m not suited for this project at all!” My head felt as if it were being pressed down by a heavy stone, and my heart was filled with shame.

After I got home, I kept replaying every detail of the meeting, even standing in front of the mirror and imagining whether my expression had looked tense or even foolish at the time. I wanted to message that colleague and ask if he was dissatisfied with me, but I was also afraid of seeming too sensitive. Torn like that, I struggled for hours until, in the early morning, I finally drifted into an exhausted sleep.

The next morning, a colleague posted in the project group chat: “Yesterday’s discussion went really well. With a few changes, your design will be excellent.” When I saw those words, my chest suddenly felt lighter, but what followed was an even more complicated mix of emotions: why did I so easily fall into anxiety and self-blame? Why did I always imagine the worst? I tried to remind myself that it wasn’t such a serious matter, but this cycle of thoughts and emotions had already consumed far too much of my time.

The café lighting was a bit dim and yellowish, and the colors on the projector screen looked slightly distorted, though I could still make out the content of my slides. I stood beside the podium, holding a glass of water, trying to hide the sweat that kept seeping into my palms whenever I clenched my hand. Today was my first time sharing my creative experience at a small cultural salon like this, and facing dozens of pairs of eyes below me, I felt my stomach tighten. I told myself I was prepared enough, but that familiar pressure still weighed on my chest, like a stone pressing down there.

Halfway through my talk, a man wearing rimless glasses raised his hand. His voice was low and steady: “I’m curious, why do you say creative anxiety is a good thing? Isn’t it possible that some people can create very well without anxiety at all?” He had a slight smile at the corners of his mouth as he spoke, but to me it carried an unsettling challenge, as if he were questioning my viewpoint.

A tingling sensation ran across my scalp, and my heart suddenly sped up. I quickly replayed the slides in my head, checking whether I had said anything like that. It didn’t seem so, but I felt a strong sense of unease, as if my point had been misunderstood, or as if I had overlooked some logical flaw. I forced a small smile and replied in a light tone: “Well... maybe I didn’t explain it clearly enough. What I mean is... sometimes anxiety can push people to explore more deeply, but of course, that’s not a necessary path for everyone.”

He said, “Oh, I see,” then nodded and said nothing more. But I kept feeling that his gaze lingered on me a few seconds longer, as if he were evaluating whether my answer really held up. I continued with the rest of my talk, but half my attention remained stuck on that exchange. Had I answered too vaguely? Did he think my argument was untenable? Would the other audience members think I was contradicting myself?

Soon it was time for the Q&A. I glanced at the time on my phone and silently urged it to end quickly. Finally, when the event was over, scattered applause rose around me, followed by the sound of chairs scraping against the floor and the low hum of people talking softly. I hurriedly packed up my things and forced out a smile as I exchanged a few words with the audience members who stayed behind. But my mind kept replaying that man’s question and my response, like a cassette tape stuck in place.

On the way home, my reflection in the bus window looked blurry and tired. I leaned against the glass, watching the city lights flash by, while the engine’s rumble filled my ears and that familiar sour feeling welled up again. I began counting my “mistakes” from today: Was the topic I chose not deep enough? Was I not flexible enough in the interaction? Had I failed to understand the intent behind each question accurately?

That night, I lay in bed, too restless to sleep, my chest so tight I kept turning over. My phone screen lit up; it was a message from an audience member saying they really liked my sharing and learned a lot from it. I stared at those words over and over, but the tension in me only eased slightly. More than that, I felt a contradictory shame: why could I never fully trust other people’s affirmation of me?

The air inside the brick kiln was damp and chilly, with moisture mingling with the smell of earth surging toward me. I stood beside a tripod, the lighting equipment emitting a faint hum. The kiln’s vaulted ceiling arched overhead, and in the dim light, the moss on the walls looked especially vivid and green. Silence surrounded me; the only sounds were my own breathing and the subtle operation of the equipment. The floor beneath my feet was slippery, and I kept adjusting my steps to avoid puddles. In front of me was a newly borrowed camera. I tried to adjust the lens angle, but the screen suddenly went black. My heart tightened, and my fingers trembled slightly.

“No way, a problem already?” My voice echoed through the kiln, then was swallowed by the walls, sounding unbearably thin. I crouched down to check the power connection and found that the battery pack had come loose. Forcing down my irritation, I clattered around for a spare battery, only to accidentally drop it into a puddle nearby. I froze, my chest starting to constrict, my palms breaking out in a fine sweat.

“No, this has to be shot well, we’re almost out of time!” I stood up and forcefully slapped my head, trying to calm myself. Suddenly, the equipment let out another sharp beep. I stood rooted to the spot, feeling an uncontrollable emotion surging to the top of my head. My stomach had started to ache faintly too, and my breathing grew rapid, as if blocked. I flipped the camera screen over, trying to find the problem, but it seemed as if everything was deliberately working against me. I could almost feel my anger rising from deep inside. “Why is there always a problem? Why can’t I just finish this smoothly!” My voice rose as I unconsciously ground my teeth.

“Calm down,” I muttered to myself, but it did no good at all. I had to think of a solution quickly, or this shoot would be ruined for good. I took a deep breath and, bracing myself, opened my toolkit, my fingers rapidly searching for replacement gear. The surrounding stillness seemed to mock my embarrassment, and my footsteps echoed through the kiln like the echoes of countless failures. I called a friend, hoping to ask about the equipment settings, but the voice on the other end was the mechanical prompt, “Number unreachable.” I hung up, clenched my fists, and felt tears threatening to spill.

My inner monologue began to churn restlessly: maybe I shouldn’t have come today, maybe I’m just not cut out for this at all. A cool breeze blew in from the kiln entrance, and I shivered, realizing my clothes were already soaked through, the damp fabric clinging coldly to my back. I sat on the ground, gasping, trying to steady my heartbeat. A few minutes later, I finally found a spare power module and barely managed to get the equipment running again.

The shoot went on for an hour, during which my fingers trembled involuntarily and a thin layer of sweat broke out on my forehead. By the time I left the kiln, the sun had already set and the distant sky was growing dark. I packed the equipment back into the car, leaned against the window, and let out a long sigh, my head still aching from the tension. The dampness I had brought out of the kiln seemed to still cling to my clothes, as if my whole body were soaked in a heavy, chilly wetness.

After getting home, I collapsed onto the sofa and opened the camera to check the footage. Some of the clips were blurry, and the angle had drifted off in several shots. I closed my eyes and sighed heavily, the dull pain in my stomach still unresolved. I began to replay every detail of the kiln in my mind, every equipment problem becoming a reason for endless negative emotions to attack me. In the end, I opened my computer, deleted the blurry footage cleanly, and then tried to edit the remaining parts, doing my best to salvage this failed shoot.

On a summer afternoon, I felt anxious for no reason and decided to visit a small independent handmade fragrance shop in the southern part of the city, hoping to find some peace of mind. When I pushed the door open, a sweet scent filled the air. Various fragrance bottles were neatly arranged on wooden display shelves, and sunlight streamed through the window onto the floor, creating a warm play of light and shadow. I couldn’t help taking a deep breath, trying to relax.

There was only one other customer in the shop. She stood beside me, looking at a row of small bottles. I heard her say softly to the clerk, “Your fragrances always remind me of some beautiful moment.” That sentence stung a corner of my heart. I began to overanalyze her tone and expression, wondering whether she was implying that I had never experienced such a happy moment. My heartbeat quickened involuntarily, and my palms began to sweat. I wanted to leave, but I couldn’t make my feet move.

To hide my unease, I decided to ask the clerk for some information about the fragrances. “Does this fragrance have any special formula?” I asked. My voice seemed to tremble, and even my ears felt hot. The clerk replied gently, “This fragrance combines bergamot and lavender, and many customers say it helps them feel calm.”

I nodded, trying to focus on her explanation, but memories of my own social missteps and embarrassing moments kept surfacing in my mind. I thought of details I had repeatedly dwelled on—other people’s offhand expressions, slight sighs—things that had once made me wonder whether I was accepted. In order to protect myself from rejection, I often resorted to preemptive self-attack, and that defensive strategy kicked in once again at that moment.

I felt a dull pain in my stomach. This physical reaction always came uninvited, accompanying my anxiety and unease. I secretly blamed myself for always being so sensitive, yet I also knew that realizing this would not change anything.

That night, I couldn’t shake the experience. Even lying in bed, my mind kept circling back to the words I had heard in the fragrance shop. I kept asking myself whether I always exaggerated other people’s intentions, whether I was going further and further down this endless path of rumination.

A few days later, the aftereffects of that unease had eased somewhat, but the incident reminded me that although I kept trying to seek peace from the outside, a storm still lurked deep within me.

The workshop lights were always a little soft, with a faint yellow glow cast over everyone’s faces, making the room feel especially warm. Around me were quiet murmurs of discussion, with the occasional hum of the coffee machine in the background. I sat at one end of the long table, looking at the sketches scattered across the surface, feeling uneasy. Across from me was my colleague, talking about his ideas for the new project. When he paused for a moment, I chimed in, “What if we add some abstract elements—would that work better?” His response came quickly: “Hmm, I’m not sure that would suit our theme.”

His tone made my heart sink, and I couldn’t help wondering whether my suggestion was really out of place. My heart began to race, and my palms started to sweat. I lowered my head and pretended to flip through the sketches, while in fact I was trying hard to calm myself down. “Maybe I really don’t fit into this kind of team collaboration,” I thought to myself. My mind began replaying all the times in the past when I had been dismissed at work, and those embarrassing, disappointing memories surged back all at once.

Over the next few minutes, the discussion continued, but I felt as if I were trapped inside an invisible bubble, the voices sounding distant. That feeling of being left out made me incredibly anxious. My stomach ached faintly, something that always happened when I felt tense and uneasy. I tried to adjust my posture, hoping to look more relaxed and attentive.

After the workshop ended, I dragged my heavy steps to a nearby café, wanting a cup of hot coffee to calm myself down. The aroma of coffee lingered in my nose as I held the steaming paper cup and took a deep breath, hoping to ease my emotions a little. “Why am I always so easily overwhelmed?” I thought, blaming myself.

The next day, I sat staring blankly at my computer, thinking about how I had performed in the workshop yesterday. Although my colleague later messaged me, saying our ideas could be discussed further, I still felt it was just a polite response. I began looking through relevant materials, hoping to find some inspiration that could help me. I thought that if I could come up with better ideas, maybe I wouldn’t be dismissed so easily.

A few days later, once I had finally calmed down a little, I messaged my colleague and arranged to meet again to talk. Although I still felt somewhat uneasy, I decided I had to try at least once. After all, fear of failure couldn’t become an obstacle to moving forward.

I stood amid the crowd at the exhibition, with noisy chatter and background music filling my ears, and all around me were artworks rendered in vivid colors by the lights. The air was thick with the smell of oil paints. My mood was like that multicolored canvas—messy and disordered. At that moment, my colleague walked over, gently patted me on the shoulder, and smiled as she said, “What do you think of this painting? A rather controversial choice, isn’t it?”

I noticed a hint of doubt in her eyes. A voice in my head began to mock me: “She’s questioning your ability; she thinks you’re not professional enough.” My face started to burn, my heartbeat seemed to thud in my ears, and my chest tightened as if gripped by an invisible hand. I tried hard to keep myself under control and make my expression look relaxed and natural. “I think it’s bold, but it may take some time to get used to,” I replied, striving to keep my voice steady.

Even so, an intense inner self-criticism kept raging on. “Your answer just now was too superficial; she must be laughing at you in her mind.” I realized I was beginning to overread every microexpression from my colleague, as if the slightest flutter of her eyelashes could amount to a whole criticism session directed at me. My stomach began to ache faintly, and fine beads of sweat appeared in my palms.

“Are you okay?” she asked, and there seemed to be a touch more concern in her eyes. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, as if all the blood in my body had rushed to my face. I hurriedly nodded. “Of course, I’m just overwhelmed by these works.”

That night, lying in bed, I chewed over the conversation again, repeatedly examining the wording of every sentence I had said, every pause I had made. Anxiety always haunted me, and I felt ashamed of my sensitivity, yet I was always powerless to change it. As time ticked by, I lay awake, knowing that even a simple conversation at an exhibition could set off endless overthinking.

A few days later, I ran into that colleague again in the office. She greeted me briskly, seemingly unaffected by our previous conversation at all. In that instant, I realized that perhaps the things I had worried about had left no trace in her mind. That thought brought me a slight sense of relief, but I still felt helpless about my habit of overinterpreting everything.

The lighting in the venue seemed brighter than I had expected, and the rows of long tube lights on the ceiling felt like countless eyes staring at me. I stood at the podium, holding the freshly printed presentation script in my hands, the edges of the pages roughened from my repeated rubbing. I could hear my own heartbeat drowning out the low hum of conversation in the crowd, and even my breathing seemed unnaturally loud. I tried to keep my voice steady as I said, “I’m very happy to be here today to share my latest work with everyone.” As soon as the words left my mouth, my ears seemed to become unusually sensitive, trying to catch every detail from the audience’s reactions. Some people lowered their heads to flip through notebooks, some wore smiles, but soon their eyes moved back to the projection screen. I couldn’t tell what these reactions meant; they all seemed to hint at some underlying dissatisfaction or indifference.

The first few minutes of the presentation felt like a century to me. I followed the plan and showed each page of the work, trying my best to explain the creative background and design intent in the language I had prepared. The ever-changing images on the projection screen were reflected on the faces of the audience below, and I tried to stay focused on my own content, but I couldn’t help glancing at some people’s expressions. There was a middle-aged man in the front row, his brows slightly furrowed, spinning a pen in his hand—I began to wonder: did he think my work lacked depth? Did he think my creative direction was too superficial? Every detail seemed magnified under a microscope, and I couldn’t escape these intrusive thoughts.

After the presentation ended, it moved into the Q&A session. After a young woman raised her hand, she said bluntly, “I think your design is very interesting, but some of the details may lack logical consistency.” Her voice was clear and decisive, and every word seemed to pierce my nerves like a needle. I forced out a smile and replied, “Thank you for your suggestions. I’ll think more deeply about this part.” Yet in my mind, a storm erupted at once: what did “lack logical consistency” mean? Was she saying my work was terrible? Was she implying that I wasn’t professional enough? During the entire Q&A session, as I answered every question, I was arguing with myself over how many people had rejected me in their minds.

Afterward, I slipped out through the back door of the venue and walked into the café next door. After ordering a hot coffee, I sat in a corner, holding the cup in both hands and trying to use its warmth to dispel the tension in my body. I kept replaying the middle-aged man’s expression and the woman’s question in my mind, once again pondering their possible meanings, even feeling annoyed with myself for not responding more cleverly. The indescribable sense of suffocation in my chest remained, and I couldn’t help rubbing my temples. In the end, I opened my laptop and wrote down their feedback one by one, trying to sort out which parts were constructive and which might just be my own overactive imagination. Doing this helped me regain a little sense of control, but my emotions were still like a tightly strung violin string, with lingering vibrations yet to fade.

A few days later, I reviewed the entire sharing session again. I realized that, regardless of whether there had been negative feedback, it wouldn’t stop me from continuing to improve my work. I began proactively reaching out to several attendees to ask for further opinions, and that made me feel some of the power of connection again.

Sunlight filtered through the balcony’s glass door, casting a warm glow across the floor. The air was filled with a faint, pleasant fragrance, perhaps the scent of jasmine growing nearby. The chair on the balcony had been warmed by the sun, and I sat down with a book in my hands—a psychology work about inner growth. Around me was a deep quiet, broken only occasionally by the soft chirping of birds. In such an environment, I felt especially relaxed, as though almost no worry could intrude on my present state of mind. Turning the pages, I read the author’s analysis with effort, hoping to find sentences that might move my heart. Sunlight fell on the pages, bringing a warm stillness.

At that moment, the children of a neighboring family were playing downstairs, and their laughter reached my ears, bringing a sense of life and vitality. I thought to myself how I wished I could be as carefree as they were, without having to worry all the time that one day I would lose these peaceful moments. But soon I was drawn back into the book, which was about how to recognize one’s inner patterns and how to face life’s challenges. I have always wanted to find answers, to find ways that could bring me closer to inner peace. Although I often feel anxious, at times I think that perhaps I am like the characters in this book, needing to slowly accept these complex emotions in order to truly grow.

As the sun gradually sank westward, the shadows lengthened across the floor, and I realized how quickly time had passed. I felt my heartbeat steady, without any excessive tension, my breathing easy and free. Everything around me seemed to tell me that such moments are precious and worth cherishing. Here there was no catastrophizing over small matters, no anxiety born of overinterpretation—only a conversation between me and the book, and the sun’s warmth. Setting the book down, I looked into the distance, and in my heart I said to myself that perhaps one day I would truly accept my sensitivity and no longer feel ashamed of it.

A few days later, I still remembered that sunny afternoon. Though ordinary, it was precisely this calm that made me feel a simple joy and a deep sense of fulfillment in life. I told myself inwardly that such moments are worth being grateful for, and that they are an indispensable part of my life.

The pottery studio door creaked open, and I was enveloped by the earthy scent rushing toward me. The clay was piled on the shelves, dry and rough. Outside the window, dark clouds hung low, and the shadows of the trees swayed in the wind. I walked to my workbench and gently stroked the unfinished ceramic jar before me. The repairs I had stayed up late making last night had clearly not gone as hoped—the cracks in the jar’s body were laid bare. The faint light streaming through the window fell on the jar like a flaw under a spotlight.

“Looks like you need some help,” a familiar voice said from behind me. I turned and saw the pottery teacher smiling, wiping the clay from his hands with a towel.

“Yes, I thought I could fix it myself,” I sighed, trying to hide my worry.

“Don’t rush. Take your time. Try to relax—it’ll be better that way,” he said, patting my shoulder.

I nodded. All I needed now was a little comfort. Trying not to let myself sink into excessive anxiety, I attempted to recall the techniques the teacher had taught me. Yet, before I knew it, my heartbeat quickened, and my fingertips turned cold. Every time I tried, I could feel an uneasiness in my stomach, as if it were a projection of the mind’s own unrest.

I kept at it, slowly repairing the cracks in the jar with relaxed, careful movements. Each attempt at feeling my way forward was accompanied by a fear of failure, afraid that a single tremor of my hand would damage it again. “Why do I always do such a poor job of these things?” a voice in my heart kept reminding me of my past mistakes.

The texture of the clay conveyed warmth through my hands, and the sensation at my fingertips gradually calmed me, yet the turmoil inside still churned. What should have been a relaxing pottery session had become a difficult task. My thoughts kept returning to the standards by which other works were judged, and to those negative criticisms.

“You don’t have to be so hard on yourself all the time,” the teacher said softly beside me, as though he could see through the struggle inside me.

When I left the pottery studio, I felt an indescribable mixture of relief and fear. That night, lying in bed, I kept reflecting on the experience, hoping that one day I would no longer fear these small failures. Perhaps these days, I truly needed more self-forgiveness. Over the next few days, I tried to avoid dwelling repeatedly on this failure and instead shifted my attention to future plans.

Even so, whenever I thought of the cracks in the jar, I still couldn’t help feeling a faint pang of unease. Yet a weak but steady sense of determination was also taking root in my heart, as if telling me that failure is not always the end.

Sunlight streamed through the stained-glass windows, casting dappled patterns of light and shadow. One evening, I sat in an old church on the edge of the city, waiting for a small concert about to begin. The air inside the church carried a faint scent of incense, and the wooden pew beneath me creaked softly. I kept shifting my posture, trying to avoid making any more noise. But every slight sound made my heart race, as if everyone around me were watching.

A couple sitting beside me was talking in hushed voices, their low tones blending with the murmurs inside the church. I couldn’t help leaning in to listen; though I couldn’t make out their conversation, I kept wondering whether they were talking about me. “Is it because I’m sitting too tensely?” I thought to myself, nervously rubbing my fingers together.

The concert began, and the music flowed gently, touching every corner of my heart. I tried to relax and breathe with the melody. But the occasional glances from that couple still made me feel painfully self-conscious, and I couldn’t help but start constructing all kinds of negative scenarios in my mind. Maybe they thought I shouldn’t be sitting there, that I looked out of place, or perhaps they had noticed my inner tension.

Before I knew it, sweat had soaked my back, and my breathing had become slightly uneven. The uneasy twisting in my stomach made me even more restless. I felt like I was about to lose control, so I pinched my thigh hard, hoping the pain would pull me back. I kept telling myself it was just overthinking, that my mind was playing tricks on me. Yet the fear deep in my heart—of being watched, of being judged—still would not go away.

When the concert ended and people began to stand up, I felt a wave of relief. My palms were still damp as I forced a smile to face the crowd around me. The moment I paused at the doorway, I wanted to take a deep breath; the fresh air, mixed with the coolness of early autumn, calmed me a little. On the way home, I kept replaying the scene, trying to analyze what exactly had triggered my unease. I couldn’t help worrying that this tendency to overinterpret things would affect future interactions with others.

When I woke the next day, the night’s anxiety still lingered. I opened my computer and began writing down everything that had happened the night before, hoping that putting it into words would help me sort out my thoughts. But chewing over those details again only dragged me into deeper self-reproach, as if I could never break free from these invisible shackles.

Sunlight streamed through the half-open gate onto the dust-covered floor, and I could smell a faint dampness and the tang of rust in the air. Before me lay a hush; only the occasional breeze swept through, stirring up small swirls of dust on the ground. I stood inside this long-forgotten glass factory, gazing at the once-brilliant machines, now reduced to silent giants. I had originally arranged to visit here with a friend today, but at the last minute she told me something urgent had come up and she couldn’t make it. I tried to convince myself it was no big deal, yet the disappointment in my heart slowly eroded my confidence. Did she have a problem with me? Had I done something to upset her? These questions kept circling in my mind, like those shards of glass that could never be pieced back together.

I gently ran my hand over the surface of an old machine, and the coldness of the metal instantly reached my fingertips. My heartbeat quickened, as if the ruin and decay of this place were silently accusing me of my own inadequacy. I often felt abandoned, left all alone on the sidelines, with no one truly caring about what I thought or felt. Just as I was lost in these emotions, my phone rang—it was a message from my friend, explaining that there had been an emergency at work.

“Sorry, I really didn’t mean to stand you up. Let’s make another date another day,” she wrote in the text.

Though the words were ordinary, I still mulled over every one of them. I replied to say I understood, yet deep inside I still couldn’t shake that feeling of being abandoned. The silence here stood in sharp contrast to my mood, as if the whole world were saying that I would have to spend the rest of the day on my own. I tried to relax and not cling to those vague and formless worries.

After a while, I decided to keep exploring the place, so I stepped forward and walked deeper into the factory. As I entered the darker areas, the surrounding smells grew stronger, with old cardboard boxes and decaying wood giving off a musty stench. I felt a wave of discomfort; my stomach began to ache faintly, but I did not stop. Even so, I still wanted to find what was special about this place. In my mind, I kept reminding myself that not everything can happen according to my expectations, and learning to accept what I cannot control is also a kind of growth.

That afternoon, I could not avoid questioning myself: what makes me so sensitive and suspicious all the time? Why do I always worry about being overlooked? These questions left me exhausted, but they also motivated me to want to change this state. That night, I thought seriously about these issues and wrote down my confusion and my thoughts in my notebook. Although I couldn’t resolve these emotions right away, at least it was a beginning—a beginning that allowed me to face the tension and unease deep within myself.

Sunlight slanted through the window lattice onto the wooden floor of the workshop, and the air was filled with the faint scent of paper and leather. As I gently pushed the door open, the wind chime on it gave a clear, ringing sound. The workshop owner, wearing reading glasses, looked up slightly and asked in a somewhat hoarse voice, “Are you here for theexperience?” I nodded, feeling both excited and a little nervous. The neatly arranged tools on the table drew my eyes more than once: a paper cutter, a flattening stone, needle and thread, and cover papers in various colors. I sat down and, under the owner’s guidance, tried to make a handmade notebook. At first, my fingers were stiff, and when using the paper cutter I was never decisive enough; the cut edges kept curling up. I heard the owner say from the side, “Don’t rush, take your time.” But his tone instantly made me tense, as if there were some hidden impatience in those words. I lowered my head silently, a strong sense of shame surging up inside me, and secretly blamed my own clumsiness: why couldn’t I even do something this simple? My palms began to sweat, the moisture seeped into my fingertips, and wet the paper. I tried to steady my breathing, but my heartbeat only grew faster, and my throat felt blocked. Carefully, I picked up the needle and thread to try sewing, but the thread kept knotting, and the needle tip left tiny red marks on my fingertips. I heard the owner walk over and say softly, “How about trying a different tool?” I gave a stiff nod, yet felt as if his words were hinting at my failure. After a few hurried attempts, I finally gave up on the needle and thread and switched to applying glue. The smell of the glue was pungent, making my mind even more chaotic. My hands began to tremble involuntarily, the glue went on unevenly, and the cover slipped, revealing the ugly bubbles formed after the glue set. I almost didn’t dare look straight at my work; it looked like a ridiculous joke. The owner came over, picked up the notebook I had made, and frowned slightly. “Hmm, you’ll need more practice.” Hearing that, I felt all the strength drain out of my body. I murmured “thank you,” quickly got up, and left the workshop, my back slightly damp with sweat from nerves. The afternoon sun was still warm, but my mood had plunged into a low point. On the way home, I tightly held the notebook in my hand, the owner’s words replaying over and over in my mind. “You’ll need more practice” became increasingly harsh, as if proving my incompetence. That night, after returning home, I placed the notebook on the table and stared at its mottled cover, feeling as though it were a glaring stain. I began searching online for bookbinding tutorial videos, trying to learn more, but every time I saw others’ practiced movements, I couldn’t help sinking into self-attack: why were others so excellent, while I was always so clumsy? This emotion lasted for several days, making me unusually anxious and even affecting my daily work efficiency.

Raindrops kept tapping against the glass outside the window, making a steady, gentle sound as I stepped into an abandoned photo studio on the edge of the city. The interior was dim, with only the pale yellow streetlights outside seeping in through the torn curtains, casting a faint glow. I searched for something that could spark inspiration, my fingers lightly touching the old photographs on the wall, their paper already yellowed by time. I ran my hand over an old photo taken last century; the people in it wore solemn expressions, which made me think of my own stress. “Maybe I can find the theme for a new work in these old photos,” I murmured to myself. Suddenly, I heard a faint sound from behind me, and my heartbeat instantly quickened. Sweat slid down my forehead. “Who would be here? Am I being followed?” I felt a tightness in my stomach, could hardly breathe, and began to wonder whether I had done something wrong. The memories of past mistakes and overlooked moments came rushing back. After struggling to steady myself, I walked toward the source of the sound, only to find that it was just the wind moving an old painting hanging on the wall. I gave a bitter smile at my own expense, and the tension in my heart eased a little. Amid the sound of light rain tapping against the window glass, I continued rummaging through the photos, trying to convince myself not to be so sensitive all the time. Just as I put the photo back on the wall, I noticed a card hidden behind it, with a few lines of text on it: “Every mistake in the past is the foundation of future growth.” Seeing this sentence, I fell into thought, as if somewhat moved. “Maybe I really should let go of the past and focus on the future I can create.” When I left the photo studio, I savored the emotions stirred up by those old photographs and decided to continue searching for creative inspiration the next day. Even though I still felt nervous, I also realized that I had to learn to turn these emotions into the drive for creation. That night, I wrote down my feelings in my diary and tried hard to avoid falling back into rumination about the past. Over the following week, I often thought back to this experience, trying to keep myself calm and focused on finishing the work rather than overanalyzing every detail.

On a chilly evening, the golden sunset poured through the broken blinds above the garage, casting mottled patches of light and shadow. I stood on a concrete floor stained with oil, surrounded by piles of rusted tools and worn-out car parts. The air carried the smell of engine oil, making it hard to breathe. I was busy setting up a crude filming space, fiddling with the tripod while still worrying about the reflector I had just adjusted but somehow still felt was at the wrong angle. A thought kept nagging at me: “What if there are extra reflections in the shot? Wouldn’t that look too amateurish?”

“Isn’t this too dark?” Xiao Zhang’s voice rang out beside me as he cautiously adjusted the angle of a floor lamp. I glanced up at the light, and even though this should have been something easy to handle, I blurted out in irritation, “Couldn’t you put a little more effort into it? How long have you been adjusting the same angle?” The moment I said it, I regretted it and felt a burning pain in my stomach. Xiao Zhang froze for a second, but he didn’t talk back. Silently, he kept adjusting the lighting.

The ground outside was already damp, and the air was thick with the promise of rain. The old garage door creaked as the wind made it sway gently. I endured the discomfort in my body while trying to comfort myself: this was just a short film, there was no need to be so meticulous. But when the words came to my lips, I still couldn’t stop myself from saying to Xiao Zhang, “No, the light here is too bright. Dim it a bit—do we have a warmer light source?” My fingers kept twisting the hem of my jacket.

“But the light color on this side has already been adjusted to the warmest setting,” Xiao Zhang said, with a hint of impatience in his voice. But he soon lowered his head and said no more, simply turning the light off to test it. I stood there, listening to the raindrops beginning to fall sparsely outside, holding back the sigh that wanted to escape my throat. Yet I knew full well that with a tone like that, how could anyone not get annoyed? I raised a hand to my forehead and found that I was already slightly sweaty. My chest felt blocked by something, and I couldn’t catch my breath. I didn’t know whether it was the stifling air or some kind of suffocation from within.

“Maybe we should take a break?” Xiao Zhang asked cautiously. I almost reflexively shot back, “If we take a break now, the light will be gone in a minute!” The words were out, and regret hit me again. Why could I never control myself? He was clearly just doing what I asked—why did I have to make the atmosphere so tense? Suddenly, a strong sense of shame overwhelmed me.

That night when I got home, I kept replaying the scene in the garage over and over. That tone that had slipped out of my mouth still lingered in my ears: “Couldn’t you be more careful?” I felt almost disgusted with myself, and at the same time I couldn’t stop blaming myself—you're always like this, either too sensitive, or too hard on people. I tried to relax by making a cup of hot tea, but my mind was still stuffed with memories, and even the steam from the cup couldn’t dispel the chill inside me.

It was past midnight when I was still lying in bed, unable to stop thinking: would Xiao Zhang be bad-mouthing me behind my back? Would the footage from the shoot be full of flaws? Thinking of the disappointed look someone might have if they saw the video in the future, I grew more and more panicked, and could only force myself to close my eyes and keep repeating, “It’ll be fine to deal with it tomorrow.” But the night remained hard to bear. With fragmented dreams, I woke again and again, my heart pounding so fast it felt as if someone were striking it hard.

I was recording a new video in the studio. Soft light fell across my face, and the camera beside me blinked with a red recording light. The whole room was quiet, except for my soft voice and the occasional hum of the video equipment. Just then, I noticed the camera screen suddenly go black, as if the machine had stopped working. I jumped up from the stool, my heart starting to race, feeling beads of sweat on my forehead. Was the equipment broken? Did that mean I’d have to start recording all over again? “Oh no, don’t do this!” I muttered, my voice nearly swallowed by my panic.

I tried to slow my breathing and began checking the power and connections. My hands were trembling a little, my fingertips feeling cold. At times like this, I always can’t help blaming myself—why do technical problems always happen at the most critical moments? How am I supposed to handle this? The room was filled with the sound of my heavy breathing, along with the squeaking noise of the equipment restarting. I finally got it rebooted, and the screen lit up again. I felt a little relieved, but the emotional turbulence still hadn’t completely faded.

I knew this malfunction might have been nothing more than a coincidence, but it felt like a snapshot of my life, making me think that every small mistake would push me toward the abyss. For the sake of the video, I had to make sure every detail was flawless, because what I feared most was the audience’s dissatisfaction and criticism. I sat back down in the chair and continued filming, narrating the content while constantly imagining how viewers would judge my work. Every time I stumbled, those critical words immediately flashed through my mind, as if someone were whispering in my ear: “You’re not good enough.”

The next day, I still felt a trace of tension and pressure, especially when checking the finished video. My heartbeat quickened slightly, and there was a dull, uneasy feeling in my stomach, but repeatedly confirming that the equipment was fine gave me some comfort. In the end, I published the video with a sense of relief and waited for the audience’s feedback. I knew I would continue down this path full of unease and criticism, because creation is just like that—you can never fully control it, and you can never completely escape anxiety.

Sunlight streamed through the workshop’s old glass windows, falling across the wooden floor. The air was filled with the faint scent of wool, accompanied by the rhythmic clatter of the looms. I stood in front of an old-fashioned weaving machine, staring at the tightly interlaced threads, watching the skilled craftsperson work with such ease that it felt as if every movement could trigger some out-of-control emotion inside me. I heard footsteps behind me. A young staff member came over and asked with a smile, “Can I help you?” Instinctively, I shook my head, my tone somewhat stiff: “No, thank you.” She paused for a moment, then walked away. In that instant, my mind began to churn: Did she think I was strange, hard to talk to? Was my tone just now too cold? Would she tell her colleagues I had a bad attitude? A string of questions kept snowballing until they weighed me down and made it hard to breathe.

I turned to leave, but then I felt that if I suddenly walked off, she would be even more convinced that my behavior was abnormal. So I forced myself to stay calm and pretended to browse a few knitted sweaters on the display rack, though I couldn’t take any of it in. She was talking to another staff member not far away, occasionally glancing back at me. I felt my face grow hot, and my steps became heavy. My mind felt like a tangled mess; my heart rate gradually sped up, and my palms began to sweat. I couldn’t stop my anxiety: She must be badmouthing me, right? Or mocking me? I became utterly convinced of all this, yet I didn’t dare confirm it, as if I feared my suspicions would be proven true. Thinking and thinking, I started to feel a dull ache in my stomach—the kind of physical reaction that always appears when I’m overly tense.

After about fifteen minutes, I finally gathered the courage to head for the door, when the staff member suddenly called out, “Sorry, did I make you a bit uncomfortable just now?” Her face showed concern. I stammered, “It’s fine, I just overreacted.” She smiled and said, “It’s okay. I only started here not long ago, so I’m still getting used to the job. I hope you like it here.” Her frankness instantly put me at ease, and I felt a wave of relief, but it was quickly followed by an overwhelming sense of self-reproach and shame. Why am I always like this, so on edge over nothing, even ruining a perfectly normal conversation?

After leaving the workshop, I felt a sense of emptiness and exhaustion. When I got home, I shut myself in my room and kept reflecting on my reaction, my mind full of self-blame. I began writing down what had happened that day, hoping to find some answer in it. As I wrote, I experienced a subtle emotional tide—both guilt toward myself and a sense of helplessness in the face of losing control of my emotions. That state lasted for several days, until I sealed away the memory and no longer dared to touch it.

The shop was filled with a mixed scent of metal and dust. The old fluorescent lights flickered with a cold white glow, and the walls were covered with worn-out wires and circuit boards. Tall shelves lined the space all around, packed with all kinds of small parts and tools. I walked up to a row of old CRT televisions and gently touched their chilly casings, as if I could feel the glory and busyness they once had. In one corner of the shop, the owner was busy at work, wearing reading glasses and studying a tiny part in his hand with the meticulousness of a craftsman.

I asked, “What can these old parts still be used for?” My voice echoed through the empty shop, making me feel somewhat awkward. Without looking up, the owner replied, “A lot of things can still be used for art installations, or for restoring old items.”

I nodded, a wave of tension rising in me, as if I were in a world cut off from everything else. My mind began rehearsing all sorts of possible failures and embarrassments. I felt I wasn’t qualified, and even thought that coming here to look for material was futile. My heart began to race, and my palms started to sweat, even though the shop wasn’t warm. I tried to calm my anxiety, telling myself these were all normal reactions, but the turmoil inside me only grew more obvious.

“If I bought this old radio component, do you think anyone would be interested?” I asked the owner tentatively, inwardly attacking my own idea and feeling like a troublesome child. The owner looked up at me and said flatly, “Interest is different for everyone. If you think it has value, then it has value.”

I took a deep breath, trying to make sense of those words, but I couldn’t help wondering whether he was implying that my idea was meaningless. On the way home, the streetlights were blurred, and the wind wrapped in cold, cutting and real. I kept replaying every detail and every conversation from the shop in my mind, feeling that I should have asked something else, or that I should have seemed more confident.

In the days that followed, I still couldn’t shake the shadow of self-doubt. Whenever I tried to create, those tense moments would surface in my mind, as if reminding me of the possibility of failure. In the end, I decided to write about these experiences in a short piece. Though I didn’t dare make it public, I gradually found a little peace of mind through the act of writing.

There were three laptops on the table. My coffee had long since gone cold, but I had absolutely no strength to reach for it. The partner sitting across from me was speaking. His pace was unhurried, but with every word he said, it felt as if needles were stabbing into my head.

“I think this proposal lacks practical viability. We may need to adjust the logic again,” he said calmly, even with a hint of patience.

But almost immediately, I felt my stomach clench, my heart start racing, and my palms unconsciously grip the edge of the chair under the table.

“Adjust it again?” I tried hard to keep my voice calm, but I could feel my lips trembling slightly. I couldn’t help interrupting him. “But we’ve already spent a month pushing this direction. Are you saying the whole idea is wrong?”

My voice seemed higher than I expected. Even a customer at the next table stopped talking and turned to glance over. I lowered my head and stared at the coffee cup on the table, my ears starting to burn.

“That’s not what I mean—” he tried to explain, but I couldn’t listen at all. His tone hadn’t changed at all, yet another voice had already started echoing in my mind: See, he doesn’t trust your ability to do the work at all. He thinks you’re inefficient and unprofessional. He must regret partnering with you, right?

Cold sweat broke out across my back, sticking damply to my clothes. I could still hear him continuing to say something, but I couldn’t take any of it in. My breathing grew rapid, as if the air itself had become thin. I gritted my teeth, and again and again I blamed myself: Why hadn’t I noticed these problems earlier? Why am I always so stupid?

“…Are you okay?” He suddenly stopped, looking at me with obvious concern. Only then did I realize my hands were shaking, and even my hurried gesture of waving him off was unsteady. “It’s nothing, I just…” I explained in a low voice, but even to my own ears it sounded unconvincing. In the end, I could only say weakly, “I’m probably just a little tired.”

The meeting ended hurriedly. When I carried my bag out of the café, the sunlight hit my face, but it felt painfully glaring. My mind started replaying the scene frantically: Did he think I was an emotional person? Did he think I wasn’t strong enough, not trustworthy enough? Every possible guess felt like a brick pressing on my chest. I walked faster and faster, and after I finally got home, I collapsed onto the bed and tossed and turned for hours without being able to sleep.

The next day, I reread our project documents and tried making a few changes. I felt that maybe part of the logic really could be improved, but that didn’t make me feel much better. I still couldn’t shake one thought: Was it already too late for this change? Had I already left an impression of unreliability in his mind? A few days later, our work progress returned to normal, but whenever I thought of that scene, my heart would tense up, as if one small mistake would be enough to make me lose this collaboration.

The air in the café was a mix of the bitter aroma of coffee beans and the smell of burnt cream. Outside the glass windows, the early winter sunlight fell on passersby’s heavy coats. I was sitting at a small table in the corner, across from a client, a somewhat domineering middle-aged man. He had just closed his laptop and was staring straight at me. “This proposal won’t do. It completely doesn’t fit our brand tone.” His voice wasn’t loud, but his tone was firm. The moment I heard that, it felt like something had suddenly clenched my stomach. My fingers tightened around the hem of my clothes on my lap. I nodded and quickly lowered my head to look at the laptop screen, trying to hide my expression.

“Do you have any other backup ideas?” he asked next. I looked up and tried to keep a faint smile on my face. “We could adjust the wording and make it more…” My voice caught. His expression seemed to say, “You don’t understand what we need at all.” I immediately felt my scalp tighten, a thin layer of sweat breaking out on my forehead, and my heartbeat became irregular, as if someone had hit fast-forward. All the answers I had prepared in my head seemed to disappear in an instant, turning into a blank void.

He continued, “Actually, we also asked other people to do some alternative drafts. Their directions are more appealing than this one.” Those words fell on my chest like a cold stone, making it hard to breathe. I didn’t know what my expression looked like at that moment, but I could feel my face growing hot, my palms sweating, even my ears burning. “If you feel we’re not a good fit, we can end it sooner…” My voice trembled a little, soft, almost like I was talking to myself. He waved his hand. “That’s not what I mean. I just hope you can be a bit more professional.”

In an instant, my mind filled with self-attacking thoughts: “I really am not professional enough.” Past failures flashed through me like old movie clips, replaying frame by frame. I guessed he must be regretting working with me and might already be planning to turn to someone else.

“How about we set up another meeting? When you get back today, try revising it again in the direction I suggested,” he said as he stood up. I forced myself to nod and said, “Okay, I’ll try again.” After he left, I sat there staring at the coffee cup on the table; the foam had completely dissolved. I reached out and touched the cup—the coffee was already cold, but my palms were still sweaty. I didn’t want to look at the faces of passersby, and I didn’t want to make eye contact with the waiter. It felt as if I were living in an isolated little compartment.

That night, I sat in front of my computer, staring at a blank document, my stomach aching faintly. All my thoughts seemed to sink into a swamp, impossible to bring into clear focus. I wanted to escape, yet I couldn’t stop replaying every detail of the day—his expression, his tone, my own reaction. Two days later, I finally revised it according to the new direction he had suggested. Although it was eventually approved, that sense of being “not good enough” stayed like a shadow, never quite able to fade away completely.

My footsteps made a faint creaking sound on the broken floorboards, and the air was thick with the musty smell stirred up by the dampness in the old paper. I pushed open the half-ajar wooden door, and what came into view were piles of scattered lantern frames; the narrow bamboo strips had begun to yellow, and the colors remaining on the cloth had faded into a dull blur. Light spilled in through the broken spots in the roof, outlining the dust hanging in the air. I unconsciously held my breath, afraid of disturbing this silence of decay.

“Maybe there’ll be some inspiration here,” I tried to say aloud to myself, but my voice died in my throat, and not even a whisper escaped. I walked up to a workbench covered in scratches, my fingertips brushing over the paint stains left on it, the texture rough and cold. A thought suddenly flashed through my mind: these lanterns must once have been made with such care, yet their moment of glory had long been forgotten. Would I be the same? Would the videos I had poured countless hours into also be completely forgotten after a few months?

I shook my head, trying to pull my thoughts back, but it seemed useless. Through the window, I heard scattered birdsong outside—only a few birds that had stayed behind at the end of autumn. I forced myself to lower my head and stare at the frame of an old lantern on the floor. Its shape was still full, but the edges had already gone moldy. I reached out to touch it, only to find a sticky layer on its surface, and I quickly drew my hand back.

“Why am I always so useless?” I muttered to myself, my voice a little hoarse. Suddenly, a comment from yesterday’s video popped into my head: “This episode has absolutely nothing new to it. Have you run out of ideas?” My chest immediately tightened with a dull pain, as if I’d beenfiercely punched. My fingertips moved absentmindedly in the air, as though trying to grasp something, but I caught nothing.

When I stepped on a loose floorboard, I lost my balance at once and my knee slammed hard into the floor. The sharp pain brought me back to my senses. I raised my knee to look; the pant leg had torn, and a few beads of blood were seeping through the skin. “What a mess,” I mocked myself through clenched teeth, only to realize a moment later that I actually felt like crying. I hurriedly lifted my head to look toward the window, afraid the tears would really fall.

On the way home, I walked more slowly than usual. Several of the streetlights around me were broken, and only the headlights of passing cars briefly lit the way ahead. In my head, I kept replaying that comment, repeatedly trying to decipher its meaning, wondering if there was some hidden malice I hadn’t seen. Maybe not just one person thought that way? Had all the viewers been disappointed in me? A faint cramping pain spread through my stomach, and I took a deep breath, trying to relax my shoulders.

When I got home, I placed the two old bamboo strips I had brought back from the abandoned lantern workshop on the table and stared at them in a daze for a while, then began looking up videos and materials about traditional lantern-making. “Maybe I could try making a video about lantern craftsmanship?” The thought brought me a little comfort, but it was soon swallowed by a greater unease: What if I didn’t do it well? What if people thought it was just more stale content? My mind seemed trapped by these two questions, unable to think of any practical next step.

When I woke up the next day, I found that my body was still tired, and my stomach still ached faintly. But I still tried to write down some ideas about the lantern theme. Even if it was only a few lines, it would at least count as a sign that I was making a little progress.

The sky reflected the gray-white clouds, and ripples of light spread across the sea. I wandered aimlessly, the wooden planks by the pier creaking under my steps, while the sea breeze carried a faintly fishy, salty scent. Nearby, two old fishermen were hauling nets, and the pungent smell of fish hit me full in the face; I turned away in mild disgust. Yet my mind kept replaying a phone meeting with a client from that morning. Although the other side’s tone had shown no obvious displeasure, those few pauses felt like needles stabbing into my thoughts. “Was I too long-winded?” “Do they think my proposal is too mediocre?” These thoughts kept circling in my head, making it hard for me to calm down.

I tried to take deep breaths, trying to convince myself not to think about it anymore. But every time I managed to comfort myself, another voice would push back: “But what if? Maybe they’ve already decided not to work with us, they just haven’t said so.”

The wind was a little strong, and I wrapped my scarf tighter, but inside I only grew more restless, as if a fire were burning in my chest. I wanted somewhere to sit, so I went to a bench at the end of the pier and sat down. My palms were already slightly sweaty, and my fingertips felt somewhat cold.

“Got a light?”

I froze for a moment and looked up. A young man wearing a knit cap was standing in front of me, a cigarette between his lips. That instantly made my nerves tense even more. He was wearing a wrinkled work jacket, and his whole body gave off a kind of careless, nonchalant air.

“I-I don’t have a lighter.” My voice trembled slightly from nerves. He just shrugged and said nothing more, turning and walking away.

“Did he think I was weird? Or was he actually angry, just didn’t show it?” This sudden little episode made me even more uneasy, as if I had exposed my flaws in front of a stranger too. A dull ache began to build in my chest; my heartbeat was fast and erratic, and it felt like I couldn’t breathe properly.

To steady myself, I forced my attention onto the scene before me: the faint sound of waves crashing against the pier, a ship slowly entering the harbor in the distance, its mast’s shadow swaying on the water. The fishermen nearby had already started tidying up their tools, speaking in low voices; their simple dialect sounded distant yet warm.

“What’s the big deal?” I tried to comfort myself. “He’s just a passerby. He won’t remember me.”

After a while, my heartbeat gradually calmed down, and the tightness in my chest eased. But it was replaced by a faint sense of loss. I realized that my life seemed full of these unnecessary little dramas. Why was there always a voice making me feel that others would care about these details?

Night slowly fell. In the distance, the lighthouse began to flash, and the lights on the fishing boats gradually appeared one by one. I left the pier with mixed feelings, and on the way home I still couldn’t stop myself from repeatedly overthinking the morning’s phone meeting and the little episode at the pier. I knew I should distract myself; I even tried listening to a few songs, but those scenes would keep popping back into my mind from time to time, like a broken CD inserted into my headphones, replaying on loop.

In the days that followed, I occasionally thought of that interrupted moment. I tried to laugh at myself for overreacting at first, but once the tension starts, it seems to become permanently embedded in memory. Sometimes, I really wish I could turn off this noise button that plays at any moment and let everything be completely, utterly quiet for a while.

Sunlight streamed through the tall windows into the workshop, and the air was filled with the faint scent of wood mixed with the fresh smell of paper. Scattered across several worktables were colorful paper crafts, and the walls were covered with vivid paper-cut decorations. I was seated at a large worktable, with sheets of thin green and yellow paper spread out before me. The soft music in my ears contrasted with the occasional sound of vehicles coming from outside the window.

“You can fold this into a lovely petal shape here,” a workshop instructor said with a smile, pointing beside me. I tried to pinch the paper into the proper shape, but accidentally left a noticeable crease in it. Kindly, the instructor said, “It’s all right. A little more practice and you’ll get it.”

I nodded with a smile, but a wave of unease instantly surged through me, and my fingers trembled slightly. I thought to myself, “Even if it’s just practice, why am I always so clumsy?” My quickening heartbeat made me feel a little dizzy, and a thin layer of sweat appeared on my forehead.

At the table next to mine, a middle-aged woman was chatting and laughing with her friend. “Look, I think this is really creative!” she said, pointing to her work, her voice gentle and confident. In that instant, I felt my own presence swallowed by their radiance.

“Am I too boring?” I couldn’t help asking myself. Thinking back on my creative journey over the years, I suddenly felt it was nothing but a collection of failures and embarrassment. My throat tightened slightly, and my stomach felt heavy, as if there were a stone inside.

In the afternoon, people gradually left the workshop, and only I remained, carefully trying new paper-folding techniques. The sunlight slowly faded, and my shadow stretched long, like the boundless darkness within me. I kept telling myself: this is just a simple experience, there’s no need to overthink what others think. But my emotions rose and fell like waves, impossible to control.

“You’re doing great, don’t get discouraged,” the instructor suddenly appeared beside me and gently patted my shoulder. I forced out a smile and pretended not to care.

That night, lying in bed, I repeatedly replayed my performance in the workshop, dwelling on trivial details, my mood swinging back and forth. “Why do I always care so much?” I couldn’t stop these unnecessary worries, and my emotions swept over me like a storm.

A few days later, I could still feel that lingering unease, and it even affected my focus on other creative projects. I tried writing about that day’s experience, hoping to find an answer in the lines, but the haze in my heart seemed not to have lifted at all.

On a winter afternoon, I walked alone into the abandoned train station on the southern outskirts of the city, the air carrying a faint smell of rust. Sunlight poured through the broken windows onto the floor, as if trying to warm this cold, history-laden space. Drawn in by the scene, I decided to take a series of photos here and look for inspiration for my new project.

On the platform, it was so quiet that only my footsteps and the wind could be heard. I took out my camera and began adjusting the focus. Yet an involuntary thought surfaced in my mind: “What if no one likes these works in the end?” That unease struck me like a sweeping cold wave, leaving my stomach tightening in waves.

Just then, I heard footsteps in the distance and looked up to see a person in a heavy black coat walking toward me. “What are you doing here?” he asked, his tone tinged with curiosity.

“I’m taking some photos and looking for inspiration for a project,” I replied, my voice slightly tense.

“Sometimes I like coming here to think too,” he said, then gave me an encouraging smile.

His presence made me feel less alone. My heartbeat gradually returned to normal; perhaps this was the reminder I needed: I didn’t have to bear everything by myself.

After he left, I continued to focus on shooting. Sunlight filtered through the cracked glass windows, carving the shadows as delicately as oil paintings on a canvas. I was full of anticipation for each composition, yet immediately swallowed by self-doubt. “Will these photos have any value? Will they be recognized?” My thoughts surged like a tide, nearly leaving me breathless.

The feeling of unease accompanied the entire shoot like a shadow. My heart would race at times, and cold sweat dampened my palms. In such moments, I often eased my anxiety through self-criticism: if others refused to acknowledge me, I would rather deny my own efforts first. It was a defense mechanism that spared me from sudden disappointment.

After leaving the train station, I went back home. Carefully, I organized the photos, repeatedly checking whether each one met the standard in my mind. The next morning, when I woke up, I was still wondering whether these photos could resonate with others, and that anxiety still lingered. Over the course of that week, I often dreamed of the stranger’s encouragement; behind that smile seemed to lie another kind of strength—the courage I had been searching for all along, the courage to face my own anxiety.

The air was thick with a warm, mingled scent, laced with the fresh fragrance of the grass and the smell of popcorn and barbecue drifting over from the snack stalls. I sat in a plastic chair in the back row, my left hand gripping the edge of the chair tightly, my right hand holding a cup of lemonade that had long since been drained, my palm sticky with sweat. Night had fallen, the stars were sparse, and on the huge screen was an experimental short film by an independent director, with erratic, shifting images and music that alternated between low and piercing. I had originally tried to focus on the film, but the low conversation of the two people beside me kept drawing my attention.

“Doesn’t she think she’s weird?” a deep male voice came from my right. Though it was a whisper, it still clearly slipped into my ears. I stiffened at once, my body straightening in an instant. Were they talking about me? When I entered just now, I accidentally knocked over a chair. Had I embarrassed myself?

“Yeah, she looks like she’s looking for a fight,” another voice chimed in, a young woman’s. My stomach suddenly tightened, and the lemonade in my cup seemed to turn into acid, churning in my gut. I barely dared turn my head to confirm who they were; I could only stare at the screen, but nothing entered my mind. “They’re talking about me, no doubt,” I frantically ran through the scene in my head. “It must be my expression, or maybe my behavior was too awkward!”

The shots in the film changed rapidly, light and shadow alternating across my face and hands, while my attention was completely hijacked by the whispers beside me. I pressed my temples, trying to calm myself down, but my heartbeat only grew faster, and in my ears there seemed to be nothing but the frantic pulse in my own body and the echo of those words. My chest felt as if a stone were lodged inside it; my breathing was shallow, my hands and feet cold. Again and again, the scene of the chair falling and people around me turning to look flashed through my mind, as if everything had been magnified under a spotlight.

“Are you okay?” someone in the front row looked back and asked softly. It was a stranger, a middle-aged woman, her voice carrying a hint of concern. I hesitantly nodded, my expression so stiff it was like I was wearing a mask. She gave an apologetic smile and turned back around. But I felt that her concern was nothing more than confirmation of how awkward I had been. I thought again of something a friend had once said to me: “You’re always too sensitive. No one is even paying attention to you.” But words like that could not explain my current embarrassment. The whole evening, I was immersed in a complex mixture of shame and self-attack.

After the movie ended, the audience gradually left. I walked alone toward the parking lot, my steps heavy, sweat soaking through my undershirt. The streetlights in the distance cast a dim yellow glow, illuminating a complicated whirlpool of emotions. Over and over, I replayed the two people’s conversation in my head, trying to find more details as evidence that I really was unlikable. I even dragged myself to walk more slowly, afraid of running into more acquaintances in the parking lot, being forced into a brief conversation, and then being disliked.

After I got home, I tried to open my computer and record how I felt that night, but I found my fingers so stiff I couldn’t type a single word. Those voices and images kept recurring in my memory, like a “movie” with a chaotic edit endlessly playing at the edge of my mind. I buried my face in my pillow and comforted myself that all of this was nothing more than my imagination, yet deep inside I still could not truly let it go. That night, I nearly couldn’t sleep, repeatedly analyzing whether what they had said was really directed at me.

In the café, the lighting was a little dim, and the air carried a scent mixed with coffee beans and slightly aged wooden boards. I sat in a chair in the corner, holding a warm cup of latte, the heat from the rim giving me a sense of comfort. A colleague sat across from me, wearing a dark suit, and looked more confident than I did. He was talking about a recent project and how efficiently his team had completed the work. Suddenly he turned to me, with what seemed like a hint of reproach in his tone: “What do you think? Are you used to this pace?”

My mind immediately went into a panic. What did that mean? Was he questioning my ability? Or was he dissatisfied with what I had mentioned earlier about my own project moving slowly? I instantly felt a slight tightness in my stomach, and my palms started to sweat. I forced out a smile. “Well, I think it’s pretty good, but it still depends on the team.” As soon as I said it, I suddenly felt that my voice sounded a bit dry, insincere, and even a little awkward. His expression didn’t change much, but I couldn’t help making assumptions: he must have been judging me in his head. Did he think I wasn’t capable enough? Or did he think I shouldn’t even be attending a gathering like this?

The conversation continued, but my attention was entirely on my inner thoughts. I kept replaying the expression and tone he had when speaking, trying to find any clue. Did he think I was dragging things down? Was I sounding too unconfident, making him think my opinion was worthless? I tried hard to adjust my posture so I wouldn’t look so stiff, but my hands were still clenched tightly on my knees, my fingertips even turning a little pale.

On the way home, I kept thinking about the conversation, replaying every detail over and over. The more I thought about it, the more inadequate I felt, and I even started to wonder why I had come to such a gathering in the first place. Anxiously, I unlocked my phone and sent a message to a friend: “Do you think I did really badly today?” My friend replied slowly. I stared at the time display on the screen, tapping my knee with my fingers. She finally wrote back: “No, not at all. You did pretty well. His tone didn’t seem particularly special, did it?”

I reluctantly accepted what she said, but inside I still couldn’t stop that magnified sense of shame. Over the next few days, I kept recalling that scene; even thinking about the dim lighting and the smell of coffee made my heart race. I tried to write something to distract myself, but my mind was still arguing over whether I had said something wrong. It wasn’t until a few days later, when I got some positive feedback in another online exchange, that I finally let it go a little. But the uneasy feeling still seemed to linger in the corner, waiting to emerge at any moment.

I sat in the private room surrounded by my coworkers. Their conversations rose and fell around me, mixed with the sharp clink of chopsticks against plates. I stared at a plate of tomato and scrambled eggs on the table. The rich aroma of soy sauce hung around the tip of my nose, but I had no appetite at all. A coworker on my right handed me a bottle of beer. I took it instinctively and whispered, “Thanks.” Then I quickly set it down in front of me, not daring to look up at him.

Not long before that, I had said something I thought was funny, hoping to ease the rather scattered conversation. I even curved my lips slightly, trying to look natural. But as soon as I finished, a coworker across from me showed an expression I couldn’t quite define—like a flash of surprise or disapproval. The corners of his mouth seemed to tighten, and then he lowered his head to pick up some food, without responding to me.

“Was I too awkward? Did they think it was embarrassing? Or did I say something wrong?” My mind seemed to hit fast-forward instantly. Almost reflexively, I started replaying the scene over and over. What did that expression mean? Was he secretly laughing at me? For the next full minute, I didn’t dare lift my head. The sounds around me seemed to drift farther and farther away, while only my heartbeat grew louder, as if someone were beating a drum right next to my ear.

“Why aren’t you eating? What’s the point of just staring at the dishes?” A coworker on my left suddenly leaned over and said that. I snapped back to reality and saw her face, carrying a hint of teasing amusement, though her tone was relaxed. “Ah... okay, I’ll try some.” I gave an awkward smile and picked up a bite of food, but I couldn’t taste anything.

For the entire second half of the gathering, I barely said anything, just nodded in agreement or occasionally let out a soft “mm.” I was afraid I’d say something else that might be misunderstood or make me look stupid. A kind of anxiety stung my chest like needles, dull and painful.

When I got home, I collapsed onto the sofa. Exhaustion hit me all at once, but my mind wouldn’t stop. I kept worrying over that coworker’s expression and tone. “Would he think I’m really stupid? After the dinner, are they all laughing about me behind my back?” My phone screen was lit up, and people in the group chat had already posted the photos. Everyone looked so happy. But I didn’t dare look too much, afraid I’d see something that would make me even more tangled up inside.

That night before sleeping, I made myself a list: from now on, try to tell fewer jokes at gatherings, and don’t try to show off; listen more and speak less, and observe everyone’s reactions; if the atmosphere feels off, change the subject in time. After I finished writing these down, I stared at the list and felt as if I had become a little safer—but also a little more constrained.

I was standing inside an indoor climbing gym in the center of the city. The afternoon sunlight streamed in through the large windows, and the colorful climbing holds on the wall were arranged in a scattered, orderly pattern, creating an unsettling sense of dizziness. The low murmurs in the gym and the faint scraping of ropes kept reminding me that this place was both quiet and full of challenge. Every time I came here, I could always feel that my inner world was as steep and uneasy as the climbing wall itself. I stared at that wall, the route on it looking both terrifying and tempting. The air inside the gym carried a mixture of chalk and sweat, which made me a little uncomfortable.

"Want to try this new route today?" the climbing coach said with a smile, pointing to a path near the window. The brief exchange made my heartbeat suddenly quicken, as if every word were testing my courage. I nodded in response, trying to make my smile look natural.

I began adjusting my gear, my palms already starting to sweat. Every time I climbed, my muscles would tense up, and my stomach would tighten in waves. I kept telling myself to pay attention to the position of each hold and to make sure my feet were steady. A sense of unease washed over me, and images of myself falling kept flashing through my mind. Why could everyone else climb so calmly while I was always so restless? I wasn’t the only participant in this activity, yet I felt as if I were fighting alone.

When I reached about halfway up, I heard another climber call out encouragement beside me: "Come on! You’ve got this!" His voice was strong and warm. I tried not to dwell on the thought of disappointing him and just kept climbing. When my fingers touched the holds, my fingertips felt the rough granules, while my other hand quickly grew slick with sweat. My heart was pounding in my chest like a drum, and each beat carried a mix of adrenaline-fueled thrill and fear.

By the time I reached the top, I struggled to keep the tension and embarrassment off my face. Looking down, the great height below me gave me a fleeting sense of superiority. I knew it was all only temporary, and that the climbing gear would safely take me back to the ground. Once I got down, my arms ached and my heartbeat gradually returned to normal. "That was great!" another climbing enthusiast nodded in approval. I forced a smile and didn’t dare meet his eyes, afraid he might see through my unease.

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying the climbing experience, and the faint soreness in my muscles reminded me that sometimes I could overcome my fears. A few days later, I found myself with a little more courage when facing other challenges. Although unease remained my shadow, I also began to believe that occasional moments of transcendence were possible.

I sat by the window in a café, my fingers absentmindedly tracing circles along the rim of my cup. Sunlight poured in through the tall glass windows, spilling over the wooden tabletop, making even the shadow of the coffee cup look soft, but my stomach felt as if it were tightly knotted with pain. The email on my phone screen sat there glaringly, and those few short paragraphs seemed to have brought my whole world crashing down. “After careful consideration, we have decided not to renew the contract.” Even “thank you for your cooperation” felt cold and distant. I read it three times over, and still couldn’t believe my eyes.

I took a deep breath, trying to force myself to calm down and ease the anger and fear that had hit me all at once. I tried to reassure myself: “Maybe it’s just a business adjustment. They probably aren’t targeting me personally.” But just as that thought rose in my mind, another voice surfaced: “A business adjustment? You’re someone they can discard at any time, aren’t you?” The pain in my stomach and the pressure in my chest grew stronger, and I felt a little breathless.

A waitress came over and gently asked, “Would you like some more hot water?” I froze for a second, and only after a moment did I realize she was speaking to me. I forced out an awkward smile. “No, thank you.” Her gaze seemed to flick toward the phone screen on the table, and I was instantly overwhelmed by an indescribable sense of shame.
