Had she seen that email? Did she think I’d been abandoned? Was she feeling sorry for me in her heart?

I instinctively looked down at myself and realized my fingers were tapping faster and faster on the tabletop, almost beyond my control. I picked up my phone and hurried out of the café as if escaping, the sunlight stinging my eyes. I stood by the sidewalk, hearing the sound of tires rolling over asphalt, the wind carrying the coolness of early spring, yet it made me break out in a cold sweat down my back.

In my mind, one image kept looping over and over—the contract being torn to shreds, all that trust turning into smoke. I began to blame myself: Was I not strong enough in the collaboration? Did I say something wrong in a meeting? Was I not “perfect” enough? My heart raced, as if countless eyes were watching me, each one judging me.

When I got home, I curled up on the sofa and opened my laptop, trying to find something work-related to distract myself, but every letter key seemed mixed with the word “failure.” I would type one character and delete one, unable to write anything. I didn’t fall asleep until late at night, and even then my dreams were full of the shadow of that email.

A few days later, I finally gathered the courage to open my computer and write a brief reply, thanking them for their cooperation and wishing them well in the future. The mailbox let out a soft “ding,” and my fingertips were still trembling slightly. I shut down the computer and stared out at the night beyond the window, but inside I remained unable to calm down for a long time. I understood that I was no longer their choice, and that this could no longer be changed.

I was sitting on a wooden folding chair in the last row of the workshop, my hands crossed on my knees, my eyes scanning the course slides on the projection screen. The room was filled with a faint smell of wood, perhaps drifting up from the floor beneath us. The host had just announced the start of the group discussion when the colleague beside me lightly tapped my arm and said, “Can our group talk about your idea first?” His tone sounded a little off, and I immediately felt a wave of discomfort, as if he were brushing me off—did he think my idea wasn’t good enough?

I tried to keep my expression calm and nodded. “Sure, let’s start with that.” My voice sounded a bit dry, and even I could hear the tension hidden in it. I picked up my notebook, flipped to a page I had written on earlier, and briefly outlined my proposal. When I finished, I looked up and glanced across the expressions of the group members. Their reactions seemed rather flat: someone was looking down drawing on paper, someone else was taking notes on their phone, and there was even someone sneaking a glance at a phone screen.

“Isn’t this a bit too vague?” the person sitting opposite me said. He pushed up his glasses, sounding as if he meant to be helpful, but I immediately felt as though a heavy block of iron had been shoved into my stomach. Was he being sarcastic? Was he actually hinting that my proposal was completely unreliable? My heartbeat quickened, a thin sheen of sweat appeared on my forehead, and the pen in my hand began to spin unconsciously. I quickly lowered my head to hide my complicated expression and blurted out, “Yeah, maybe. I’ll think it over some more.”

Throughout the discussion, I felt myself shrinking little by little, as if I were gradually being compressed from a whole person into an invisible point. I no longer took the initiative to speak, only nodding along occasionally. They didn’t seem to notice my silence, but I kept replaying the tone and content of those words in my head. Had I been too vague? Did they think I wasn’t capable, or even that I shouldn’t have come to this workshop at all?

During the tea break after the discussion, I hurriedly found an empty seat and sat down. Beside me was a plate of cake cut into pieces; it smelled sweet, but I had no appetite. I took out my phone and pretended to scroll through messages, really just to avoid making eye contact with anyone. Inside, my mind kept replaying, like a tape recorder, the tones and expressions that had unsettled me. I even began to wonder whether this was some kind of omen—that one day my abilities would be fully exposed to everyone?

On the way home, it was already completely dark, and the streetlights were faintly reflected on the wet ground. I trudged forward with heavy steps, but my mind never stopped. Did that colleague simply not think much of me? Did everyone think I was really unworthy? Once I got home, I set down my bag, leaned back on the sofa, and opened a notebook, hoping to write something to ease my nerves. But the moment I opened it, the scene from the discussion came rushing back, and a dull pain spread across my chest. I closed my eyes, took a deep breath, and told myself that maybe I was overthinking it. They might not have meant anything by it. But I still couldn’t fully believe that thought.

Over the next few days, I kept replaying the scene in my mind, imagining that if I had explained my proposal more clearly back then, perhaps all the reactions would have been different. Yet even with that imagined revision, I still felt a faint criticism lurking behind it, as if it could be exposed and used to humiliate me at any moment.

The air was damp with a salty tang, and the tide gently slapped against the wooden pilings beneath the pier, a low rhythm that made me involuntarily hold my breath. A rusted streetlamp flickered faintly not far away, and the occasional cry of a night bird broke the dead silence of two in the morning. I was bent over adjusting the tripod, checking whether the lens was pointed at the abandoned wreck of a boat in the distance. The night’s humidity kept fogging up the glass, and I tried to wipe the moisture off the lens with my sleeve, but my hand was shaking a little; the cold dampness spread from my fingertips to my elbows. I muttered under my breath, “Why is this so annoying!”

Footsteps suddenly sounded behind me—very light, but enough to tense every muscle in my body. I immediately held my breath, feeling my heartbeat quicken as a wave of panic surged up my throat. “Could it be the urban management officers? No, why would they even care about this place, or…”

“What are you doing out here so late?” a deep, hoarse male voice cut through my wild thoughts. I turned around and saw a thin, tall middle-aged man, wearing an old jacket and carrying a large canvas bag slung over one shoulder.

“Uh, I’m filming some footage,” I tried to sound calm, then added, “For a short film.”

“Oh.” He grunted, seemingly uninterested in my answer, and just stood there, staring at the wrecked boat for a while. “This place is cold, and you’re not dressed warmly. Don’t catch a chill.”

“Oh, it’s fine, I’m used to it.” The moment I said it, I regretted it—I actually thought my reply sounded like I was showing off! Did I sound too cold? Did he think I was being rude?

“All right, then. You get on with it.” He nodded, slung his bag over his back, and turned to leave.

I let out a breath and found my palms were drenched in sweat, enough to dampen the cool tripod. I subconsciously looked down at my jacket and saw that I really hadn’t dressed warmly enough, but what bothered me more at that moment was the conversation itself. I’m always like this, instinctively trying to guess whether there’s some hidden meaning behind every sentence. Was that man genuinely being kind, reminding me that I wasn’t wearing enough, or was he looking down on me for being here alone? Or maybe he simply didn’t care and was just making casual conversation?

A sort of pent-up frustration seemed to knot inside me, and I struggled to get back into filming mode, only to find my hands couldn’t keep the tripod steady at all. I tried to check the angle of the lens again, but my gaze kept drifting toward where the man had gone, until his figure was completely swallowed by the night.

After a while, the sea breeze picked up, making me shiver, and even my steps turned light and unsteady. I couldn’t help taking out my phone and scrolling through my chat history with my friends. I wanted to send them a message, ask what they thought about that conversation, or even ask why I always let myself get trapped in this kind of pointless anxiety. But I didn’t have any real reason to message them; my mind was blank, and my fingers hovered over the screen, not knowing how to ask without sounding so suspicious.

In the end, I put my phone away, quickly packed up the filming equipment, and hastily called it a night. I dragged myself home, my mind endlessly circling around thoughts like “Maybe what that man thought doesn’t matter anyway” and “Why do I keep making trouble for myself?” Yet I couldn’t help wondering whether choosing this line of work from the very beginning had been a mistake. When I got home, I didn’t turn on the lights and collapsed straight onto the sofa, feeling too drained even to take off my clothes.

When I woke up the next morning, my neck was a little stiff, probably because the sofa back was too hard. I stared at the gradually brightening sky outside the window, faintly feeling that last night’s frustration still ached somewhere deep inside me, yet I couldn’t find a way to fix it. The alarm went off; I turned it off and didn’t get up, just buried my face in the pillow.

Sitting in the corner of the office, I could feel the tension in the air around me. The incandescent lights on the ceiling flickered with a harsh glare, and I tried not to stare at them. My coworkers were all busy at their computers, occasionally speaking in low voices. This morning, I received an email marking the end of my involvement in a project. Although I knew there had probably been signs of it long ago, it still made my heart sink. All the work related to the project had come to an end, yet I still felt an inexplicable sense of loss.

"I heard you’re no longer on that project," one of my coworkers suddenly said behind me. I whirled around, my heart racing, feeling a little flustered. "Yeah, it was decided last week," I answered, trying to stay calm. My voice was trembling, and I could feel my palms starting to sweat.

"It sounds like you’re a bit disappointed?" the coworker continued, his tone seeming somewhat dismissive. I instantly felt offended, as if his words had pierced my heart. Was he implying that I’d been cast aside? Or had he seen some flaw in me? I struggled to rein in my impulses, but a strong sense of unease welled up inside me.

"No, I’m just a little surprised," I forced a smile, but the muscles in my face were so stiff they wouldn’t relax. My inner monologue began: "Why is this happening? Am I really not good enough?" I tried to convince myself of my own worth, but that thought was quickly swallowed by rumination over painful memories from the past.

After the conversation ended, I tried to focus on work, but no matter what I did, I couldn’t shake the feeling of rejection and the confusion in my heart. At lunch, I ate in the company cafeteria, surrounded by the aroma of food, but I had no appetite to savor it. That afternoon, after work, I went home, still unable to shake the sense of loss brought on by the conversation. My heart still seemed to be racing, and my stomach ached faintly. I thought about numbing myself with alcohol that night, but I quickly gave up the idea.

That evening, I sat alone on the sofa, my thoughts circling. My mind kept replaying the conversation with my coworker, trying to find clues hidden within it. Before going to bed, I realized that I was no longer worried about the project itself, but about whether I was truly worthless in my coworkers’ eyes. The next morning, I still felt somewhat uneasy, but I decided not to magnify the issue any further and instead focus on a new beginning.

Sunlight filtered through the narrow crack in the window and fell across the mottled dust on the floor. The air was thick with the smell of old wood, faintly mixed with rust. I stood in the center of the clock shop, looking around: grandfather clocks that had stopped moving hung on the walls, and broken gears and movement parts were piled all over the floor. Time seemed to have come to a standstill in this forgotten place, and I could hear my own breathing clearly.

“Aren’t you scared coming to a place like this alone?” my friend’s voice came from behind me, interrupting my thoughts. He was the only one willing to come here with me—after hearing that I was going to an abandoned clock shop, most people thought it was far too strange.

“No, it’s fine. It’s pretty quiet,” I replied casually, trying to look focused and keep him from seeing the slight tension in my heart. In truth, I felt my stomach tighten a little, as if an invisible rope were constricting my insides, and I could only take a deep breath to steady myself.

“Alright, I’ll take a look around up front first. Be careful,” he said before heading into the inner room. After he left, the quiet, echoing surroundings made me even more aware of the heaviness in the air. All I could hear was my own footsteps and the occasional creak of the wooden floor.

I groped my way toward an old counter covered with a white cloth and slowly lifted it. Inside were rows of faded watch cases, their dials covered in cracks. I couldn’t help reaching out to touch one of them; the icy surface sent a shiver through me. A thought suddenly flashed through my mind: what would I do if all these clocks were to start ringing at once?

“Maybe there’s no inspiration here at all,” a voice rose from somewhere deep inside me. I unconsciously bit my lip as images surfaced of how poorly the recent project had been progressing. The client’s feedback was full of doubts, the team was divided on several issues, and I was already close to breaking down. It all suddenly felt heavier, like several mountains pressing down on my chest, making it hard to breathe. A rush of heat surged from my stomach upward; I could feel the skin on my neck growing hot, and my temples pounding.

“Don’t worry, keep looking. Maybe I’ll find something.” I tried to calm myself, but that voice of self-doubt only grew louder: “You’re always like this. You can’t get anything done. Always fixating on weird things, so unrealistic. People must think you’re terrible.” I clenched the edge of the counter, my nails digging into the wood.

“Find anything?” my friend’s voice suddenly came from behind the door, and I jumped in fright, nearly dropping what I was holding. He poked his head out from behind the doorway, looking curious.

“Uh, not yet,” I managed a strained smile as I put the little clock back on the table. But inside, I was full of shame. I even began to wonder if he thought my idea was utterly boring. Was he disappointed in me too? Was he laughing at me in his heart as well?

“No rush, take your time. This place is actually pretty cool,” he said offhandedly before turning and leaving. I stared at his disappearing back, my eyes stinging terribly.

On the way home, we hardly spoke. Night fell, and the deep autumn scenery outside the window faded away in layers, as if those old clocks we had just found were being swallowed up by darkness. I could still feel the tightness in my stomach, and my chest felt blocked and uncomfortable. When I got home, I tried to sort through the material from today, but the voice of doubt kept circling in my mind. In the end, I picked up a notebook and started writing down how I felt today. I wrote about the smell of old wood in the air, I wrote about the moment my heartbeat quickened, and I wrote about how fear was suddenly replaced by shame, as if struck head-on. By the time I finished, I actually found a glimmer of creative inspiration in the words.

Even though it was already late at night and the palpitations had still not fully subsided, at least I felt a little comfort: perhaps none of this was entirely meaningless after all.

The light in the conference room was somewhat harsh. I sat at one corner of the table, which was piled high with all kinds of documents and draft paper. The editors were engaged in a lively discussion about the marketing strategy for my new book. I tried to speak up, but found that my voice was drowned out by everyone else, as if my presence didn’t matter at all. Across from me, a senior editor—a middle-aged man who always wore a stern expression—suddenly gave a contemptuous laugh. My heart sank instantly, and I kept replaying that smile in my mind.

“Sorry, I think that cover design may not be quite appropriate,” I finally mustered the courage to interrupt them, my voice trembling slightly.

A young editor replied casually, “We’ll consider it again.” But her eyes didn’t stay on me for even a second; instead, she looked at the others. I felt a wave of helplessness, as if all my efforts were being ignored.

My heart started racing, and sweat broke out in my palms. “They must think my work isn’t good enough, or that I’m not good enough,” my inner voice kept raging. A stabbing pain twisted in my stomach, and I unconsciously clenched my fists, trying to use the tension in my body to suppress the rising anxiety.

After the meeting, I felt my existence compressed into something utterly insignificant. When I left the conference room, I wandered the hallway for a while, trying to sort out my thoughts. But that deep-seated sense of defectiveness stayed with me like a shadow, impossible to escape.

That night, I curled up on the sofa, staring blankly at the ceiling alone, while my mind remained unusually active. “Why can’t they just listen seriously? Did I do something wrong?” My brain kept ruminating over every detail of the meeting, and the more I thought about it, the more it felt like everyone was trying to imply that I wasn’t needed.

When I woke the next day, I still felt uneasy. That sense of abandonment was like a lingering gloom, hanging over my heart. I began to doubt my abilities, and even felt intensely anxious and unsettled about the new book ahead. Although the morning sunlight streamed into the room through the curtains, it could not warm the coldness in my heart.

I once again made my way to the edge of the city, to that abandoned old painting workshop. Sunlight streamed through the mottled windows, illuminating dust-covered canvases and rusted easels. The air carried the scent of oil paint mixed with mildew, and from time to time I could hear the wind outside passing by, as if telling the story of the place’s former bustle. Today, I hoped to find some inspiration, though deep down a voice kept reminding me that perhaps I would gain nothing at all. Just as I was lost in these tangled thoughts, a stranger’s silhouette appeared at the doorway. He was a fellow artist, seemingly drawn to this place as well. We nodded to each other almost at the same time, as if we had reached some understanding without words.

“Are you here to look for inspiration too?” he asked, his tone lightly teasing. I replied, “Just dropping by to see this place—I thought I was the only one interested in it.” His smile put me somewhat at ease, but then I felt a familiar wave of anxiety rush over me: I wondered whether he was mocking my artistic ability. My heart began to race, my palms grew damp, and I tried to hide these reactions, forcing myself to appear calm as I showed him my work. “What do you think?” I asked, the tension in my voice barely concealed. He examined it carefully for a moment, then nodded slightly and said, “An interesting idea. Keep at it, and perhaps something wonderful will come of it.” Though it was praise, I could still feel that unease lingering.

After we talked for a while, he left, and I continued wandering through the silent space. As time went on, I kept replaying our conversation, trying to decipher whether there was some hidden meaning in his words. My stomach began to ache faintly, one of the signs of my extreme anxiety. That night, sitting on the edge of my bed, I was filled with the worst possibilities: did everyone think my work wasn’t good enough? Could I ever truly amount to anything? Feeling the weight of these questions, I kept sketching over the next few days, trying to prove that I was not incapable. Even so, I still could not escape the echoes of unease within me.

The drizzling rain pattered against the windowpane, playing a soft melody. I walked into a vintage record store on the east side of the city. The shop was filled with the distinctive scent of old records, mixed with a hint of damp air. The walls were covered with classic album covers from the 1960s and 1970s, colorful and vibrant. An old jazz tune drifted through the air, the low saxophone sounding plaintive and mournful. I leafed aimlessly through the records, my fingertips brushing the slightly rough covers, and a faint sense of nostalgia welled up in me.

“Hello, can I help you with anything?” The owner, a middle-aged man wearing a pair of heavy black-rimmed glasses, smiled at me.

“No, I’m just looking around.” I tried to stay calm, but inside I felt uneasy, as if I were afraid of seeming out of place here.

“We’ve got a few new arrivals on vinyl recently, all classic collectibles.” He pointed to a corner.

I walked over and looked at those covers, trying to appear knowledgeable and confident about music. “These are all pretty good, but I’ve actually been looking for an old record,” I said, immediately realizing that my voice was trembling slightly.

“Oh? Which one are you looking for?” He seemed interested.

“Uh, one by Fleetwood Mac, but I can’t remember the exact name at the moment.” The moment I said it, I immediately regretted it. A wave of intense shame and embarrassment surged through me. My cheeks felt slightly warm, my heartbeat quickened, and my palms grew a little sweaty.

“No problem, I understand. Could it be ‘Rumours’?” he suggested kindly.

“Yes, that’s the one.” I nodded slightly, trying to hide my inner panic, but I still couldn’t suppress the voice of self-doubt. This kind of doubt about my memory had almost become the norm. I always worried about embarrassing myself in front of others, and that feeling never seemed to go away.

This brief exchange made me realize how hard it was for me to relax and enjoy such a simple shopping experience. The emotional unease left me mentally drained. On the way home, I kept replaying the conversation in my mind, worrying that my impression in his eyes might already have been greatly diminished.

That night, I lay in bed, the sound of rain outside the window still unceasing. I closed my eyes, trying to calm the pointless anxiety in my heart. I knew I always magnified these tiny moments of embarrassment endlessly, yet for some reason I still couldn’t shake them off.

The café’s glass windows were covered with a thin layer of mist, making the people and streetlights outside look somewhat blurred. I sat by the window, looking at the steaming latte in front of me, occasionally rubbing the cup with my fingers to feel the warmth it gave off. Across from me was my friend, who was enthusiastically talking about amusing things that had happened recently at her child’s school. She spoke quickly, her voice a little louder than usual over the rustling background noise around us. I nodded, pretending to listen intently, but in truth I was a little distracted, my gaze drifting toward the window, trying to catch the vague outlines of passersby.

Suddenly, she said, “You know, sometimes I feel like you’re too sensitive. There’s no need to overthink so many things.” The sentence was like a silent arrow, passing through my defenses and stabbing straight in. I felt my throat tighten, and my hand unconsciously clenched the coffee spoon on the table. In a somewhat stiff voice, I forced out a few words: “How am I sensitive?”

She didn’t seem to notice my unhappiness and still laughed in a relaxed tone. “Like that thing last time—you kept saying you were afraid your boss had it in for you, but that wasn’t really the case. You were overthinking it.”

My heartbeat suddenly quickened, and a sense of shame at being exposed surged up from my chest. I could feel my face growing hot, and a slight prickling sensation crept up my neck. I lowered my head and looked at the coffee spoon in my hand, stirring the foam in the cup gently, trying to hide my unease. “Oh, really?” I replied lightly, trying my best to keep my tone calm.

But my mind wouldn’t stop racing, as if a switch had suddenly been flipped, and a stream of thoughts began pouring in: Am I really that sensitive? Has she looked down on me for a long time? Does she think I always make a fuss over nothing? If I argue back, will I seem even more sensitive? A feeling of tension quietly crept into my stomach, and my lower abdomen seemed to tighten slightly.

I made an effort to take a deep breath, then looked up at her, only to find her fiddling with her phone with her head down, with not a trace of reproach or displeasure on her face, as if what she had just said was only a casual remark. I suddenly realized that maybe she hadn’t meant any harm; perhaps I had simply gripped too tightly onto her words myself. I worked to steady my breathing, trying to pull myself out of that sharp emotional state.

A few minutes later, I turned to look out the window and saw fine snowflakes drifting down under the lights outside. Layer upon layer of white flakes covered the ground, like a kind of special stillness. After thinking about it, I still smiled and said to her, “Maybe you’re right. I really do overthink sometimes.” As soon as the words left my mouth, I felt the weight on my shoulders seem to lighten a little. She looked up at me, gave an understanding smile, and continued talking about something else.

A few hours later, I got home and sat on the sofa, watching the snow outside grow heavier and heavier. I thought back to that scene from the afternoon; the tension in my stomach had long since disappeared, leaving only a trace of self-mockery: I really should be too sensitive, but maybe that isn’t something completely unacceptable.

In the exhibition hall, a riot of colorful flowers came together to form a visual feast, while the indoor air was filled with a faint floral fragrance. I wandered through it, trying to find inspiration in these artistic botanical displays. Around me were the soft murmurings of people conversing, occasionally mixed with children’s laughter. I had long dabbled in garden design, yet always felt it still fell short of truly capturing nature. Standing before a booth called “Urban Oasis,” I studied its layout and design, silently admiring the designer’s ingenious concept. Just then, I heard the exhibition organizer talking behind me, her voice clearer than the surrounding noise. “This is one of our most prized works this year, and it has received extremely high praise from many creators,” she explained to a group of visitors.

In that instant, I felt a sharp pain in my heart, as if I had caught some subtext in her words—I had somehow been omitted from those “many creators.” Unconsciously, I began to dwell on all the moments in the past when I had been overlooked, on the experiences of unrecognized effort during long collaborations. My heartbeat quickened, my palms grew damp, and I asked myself: Was I simply not good enough? Why had my name not been mentioned? I decided to step forward, so I approached her and asked, “Hello, I’m very interested in this piece. Could you tell me more about it?” She gave a slight smile and glanced at me casually. “Of course, but this information is already recorded in detail in the exhibition brochure.” At that moment, my face began to burn, as though struck by her indifferent attitude. A thought flashed through my mind: Was she deliberately ignoring me? I suppressed the turmoil inside me, unwilling to show any weakness in front of the crowd.

A few minutes later, I was still standing in front of that booth, confusion and humiliation tangled together in my heart. Her dismissive attitude kept echoing in my mind. When I got home that night, my stomach felt faintly painful, as if a tight, unbreakable knot were turning over in my abdomen. I tossed and turned all night, even doubting whether I had lost my sharpness in creative expression. Over the next few days, I repeatedly replayed the conversation from the exhibition in my mind, trying to find the reason I had been overlooked and how I might better present myself. A few days later, I tried to write these emotions into a new work, as if through such creation I had found a kind of release and relief.

The coffee shop was filled with the rich aroma of coffee, and soft music drifted from the speakers in the corner. I sat by the window, with the client for this trip across from me. He was wearing a neat suit, looking at the proposal’s PPT with a grave expression, his fingers tapping lightly on the table. I could feel my palms starting to sweat; every meeting like this always made me nervous.

“I think this proposal is a bit unrealistic,” he said in a flat tone that seemed to carry a hint of impatience. “Is it possible to make some adjustments?”

“Oh, of course,” I replied immediately, speaking much faster than usual. My heart began to race, and I tried hard to steady my breathing. Yet a wave of unease crept up my spine. What exactly had I done wrong? Had I overlooked some detail?

I gave myself a moment to think. The words and diagrams before my eyes blurred together. I forced a smile. “Could you be more specific about which parts need improvement?” My voice trembled a little after I asked. I noticed my legs beginning to shake slightly, so I placed my hands on my thighs to steady myself.

The client frowned, and that slight change looked magnified many times over in my eyes. “I mean the budget and timeline in this section. It may need to be more detailed,” he said. “The current version makes it hard for me to explain things to my superiors.”

The pressure inside me surged, and I began to doubt whether I was truly capable of this job. Was I really not careful enough? Was my ability simply worthless to him? My stomach started to ache faintly, as if a clenched fist had landed squarely in my abdomen.

“Okay, I’ll provide a revised version as soon as possible.” I nodded, trying to make my voice sound more confident. This meeting made me feel like I was in a small boat that was constantly sinking, unable to control myself or the world around me.

After the meeting ended, I left the café. The wind outside brushed across my face, bringing a hint of coolness. My thoughts were still fixed on the tense conversation from earlier. Although the client had only expressed reasonable concerns, the core of my unease was still that fear of being discarded at any moment.

The next day, I was still anxious about the client’s evaluation, repeatedly checking every detail and worrying about getting stuck on some minor point again. This overinterpretation had followed me for many years, like an instinct I could not shake off.

The streetlights cast a dim yellow glow. I stood on the steps outside the café, the paper cup in my hand long since gone cold. I could feel a faint sticky dampness in my palm. Across from me was my partner, arms folded tightly across her chest, her expression taut, as if she were trying hard to keep her emotions in check. Her tone was unnervingly calm, yet it couldn’t hide the cutting cold beneath it: “I think it’s better if we end our partnership here.”

Each word stabbed into my heart like a needle. I forced a reflexive smile and answered as if nothing were wrong: “Oh, it’s fine. I feel like things have been a bit stuck lately too. Is there somewhere I haven’t done enough? We can adjust things again.”

She looked at me, her brows knitting slightly as if choosing her words. “It’s not that you haven’t done enough. It’s just that… the direction of our collaboration itself has a problem.” Her voice dropped a little, even carrying a hint of apology, but I felt as though someone had shoved me hard, leaving my back pressed against empty air, cold and trembling. I unconsciously lowered my head and looked at the ground. Thebroken gravel by the roadside and the damp soil seemed to sway in my eyes as blurred patches. What did “the direction has a problem” mean? Had she always thought everything we’d done was wrong? Was my way of thinking from the very beginning just a joke?

My throat was dry and tight, as if blocked, and I could only force out a few feeble syllables: “I… I don’t really understand what you mean.” In truth, I did understand. I understood perfectly. She was telling me that I had no value, that my efforts were meaningless, that I was a burden. Those thoughts rushed up instantly, and my stomach cramped as if it had been clenched in a fist. I gripped the paper cup tightly, hearing the faint sound of plastic tearing from the cup wall. She glanced at my movement, then let out a soft sigh. “Don’t take it too much to heart. We just want to be a bit more efficient.”

Those two words, “more efficient,” struck me like a hammer. In my mind, scenes of past arguments began to play automatically: what she had said then, the tone she used, even those subtle looks, all of them turned into accusations of my incompetence. I couldn’t make out what she said next. The sounds around me blurred into background noise, and only my heartbeat hammered at my eardrums like a drum. I forced myself to keep my expression steady, the corner of my mouth twitching stiffly as I said, “Then let’s leave it at that. I wish you the best.” I don’t know how I managed to say it; my voice sounded both dismissive and utterly exhausted.

She nodded, then left quickly. I stood there alone, feeling as if the entire street had grown cold. The iced coffee in the cup had melted into water, and the sensation through the plastic cup carried another kind of heavy chill. I barely managed to make my way to the car by the roadside. In the rearview mirror, my pale face and furrowed brow looked back at me. I started the car and drove home all the way, her words replaying endlessly in my head, trying to find what she had truly been dissatisfied with, trying to understand exactly what had made me unworthy of continuing the partnership. I spent three hours sitting at the desk, drafting and trying to analyze, but every time I wrote two lines I crossed them out myself, until the whole page was scribbled over again and again. In the end, all I felt was bone-deep exhaustion, but I still couldn’t sleep.

When I woke the next day, my stomach hurt even more, as if a stone were pressing down inside it. I didn’t even dare open any social media, afraid that I would see her already collaborating with a new partner, proving that her choice was right and that I was a complete failure.

On a summer afternoon, I stood in an open community square in the southern part of the city, taking part in a local mural-painting event. The afternoon sun slanted across the ground, and the smell of paint drifted through the air, making me a little dizzy. Around me was the rustling sound of brushes against the wall, occasionally broken by bits of conversation. I held a brush and tried to stay focused on my own work. Now and then, I would glance at the other creators nearby, watching their progress. It felt as though they all had some unspoken understanding and cooperation, while I seemed like an outsider.

“Can you help us mix the paint?” a voice called out. I turned and saw a young girl in a graffiti shirt smiling as she pointed to a bucket of paint beside her. I nodded and replied, “Of course.” But inside, I felt uneasy, worried that I might make a mistake even at such a simple task.

I busied myself beside the paint basin, trying to mix the color she needed. At the same time, my heartbeat quickened and my breathing grew slightly heavy. I have always been afraid of embarrassing myself in public, especially when someone is watching. My fingertips trembled slightly with nervousness, and the brush seemed out of control; before I knew it, paint splashed onto the ground.

“It’s okay, just be careful,” the girl comforted me in a gentle tone. I forced out a stiff smile, but inside I was deeply self-reproachful. Why could I never complete these simple tasks perfectly?

As the event gradually entered a break, people began gathering in small groups to chat. My gaze involuntarily locked onto a particularly lively little circle, and I secretly wondered whether they were talking about my earlier mistake. The laughter and conversation seemed to carry hints I couldn’t understand, which made me uneasy.

“You seem a bit distracted. Is everything all right?” one participant came over and asked. My expression must have already betrayed my anxiety. I nodded and said with a smile, “I’m fine, just a little tired.” But in my mind, I kept imagining the possibility of being excluded.

After the event, I went home and tried to calm my panicked emotions. My mood was terribly low because of the mistake at the mural-painting event, and I kept thinking about the negative judgments others might have made of me. The restless thoughts kept me from sleeping, until a message from a friend a few days later told me that everyone actually really liked having me there, and that finally made me feel a little more at ease.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves, cutting the ground before me into dappled patches of light and shadow. I stood in front of a stall at an antique market on the edge of the city, surrounded by the distinctive scent of old things, mingled with the smell of aged wood and brass. The stall owner was chatting and laughing with another customer; their voices were lost in the bustle of the crowd, yet I couldn’t help wanting to listen more closely. “This ceramic jar has been passed down since the 19th century—it’s truly a fine piece!” the owner said excitedly. My heart tightened a little, wondering whether that jar suited my taste.

I lowered my head and studied the small brass bell in my hand. It felt cold to the touch, yet oddly comforting. But an involuntary thought surfaced in my mind: if I chose the wrong thing, what would others think of me? That thought spread through me like a chill current, and my heartbeat quickened before I knew it, leaving me slightly sweaty.

“How about this one?” A voice pulled me back to reality, and I saw the stall owner looking at me kindly. I forced a smile, trying to hide my anxiety. “Well, I need to think about it some more,” I stammered, unwilling to admit my wavering. The owner didn’t seem to mind and simply nodded slightly.

A couple at the neighboring stall was quietly discussing an old music box they had found. The woman’s voice carried a faint sweetness and excitement, which made me feel an indescribable loneliness and unease. Perhaps I was paying too much attention to other people’s happiness and neglecting my own feelings. I clenched the brass bell tightly in my hand, as if only then could I suppress the restlessness in my heart.

After leaving the stall, I wandered aimlessly through the market, though my steps felt somewhat heavy. The air echoed with people’s conversations, children’s laughter, and that inescapable sense of nostalgia. I tried hard to relax, taking a deep breath, yet I could faintly feel discomfort in my stomach, as if an invisible hand were gently squeezing it.

When I got home, I sat on the sofa in the living room, unable to shake off the antique market scene from my mind. I tried to analyze the moment that had unsettled me, wanting to figure out exactly what had triggered such emotions. After a while, I realized that it was the desire to prove myself that had made me so uneasy.

A few days later, I still found myself thinking back to that scene at the market from time to time, but my emotions gradually calmed. In the end, I decided there was no need to overanalyze that moment of anxiety, and to attribute it to my own longing for perfection and approval. Whenever I thought of that brass bell, it also reminded me to accept imperfection and ease up on my concern for others’ judgments.

The lights shone harshly in my face, the camera was set up, but the atmosphere felt tense. In the studio, my coworkers and I were preparing to shoot an interactive short video, yet their expressions made me uneasy. Especially Xiao Liu—he stood behind the lights with his arms crossed and a slight frown. Was the idea I had just pitched too stupid? Did they think I was terrible but just not say it? I tried hard to focus on my lines, but inside, everything was a mess, like a box of paint had been knocked over.

“Do you think this angle works?” Xiao Li asked me. His voice sounded flat, but I immediately started imagining all kinds of possibilities: was he hinting that my performance was dragging everyone down? I forced a smile and said, “It should be okay, right? What do you all think?” I tried to use a smile to dispel any negativity they might be feeling, but the smile froze on my face, and no one responded. Right away, I felt my heartbeat quicken and my palms start to sweat.

Filming began, and I stared into the camera, starting my lines. But my voice sounded dry and weak, and I could even sense a trace of dissatisfaction in Xiao Liu’s gaze, as if he were saying, “That’s all you’ve got?” My stomach started to ache dully, like a small fist tightening inside me. Every time they adjusted the lights or made me pause, I felt as if I were being judged. Did they no longer want to work with me? Did they think I was worth nothing?

The shoot finally ended, and I forced myself to sound relaxed as I said, “Thanks for your hard work, everyone!” But the fatigue in my voice couldn’t be hidden. I hurriedly gathered my things, feeling like a child who had caused trouble and wanted to flee the scene. As Xiao Li passed by me, he said, “Thanks for your hard work. You did pretty well.” I froze for a moment, not sure whether he was just being polite. Then my mind split in two: part of me tried to convince myself that he was genuinely encouraging me; another part sharply doubted that I had only just barely met their lowest expectations.

After I got home, I sat in a chair and ruminated over the whole thing, as if replaying a film. I kept obsessing over Xiao Liu’s expression, Xiao Li’s tone, and my own performance. The more I thought about it, the more incompetent I felt, like an imposter afraid of being exposed. The stomach pain continued, and even after I drank a cup of hot water, it didn’t ease. That night, I slept very lightly, my mind full of their faces and those vague hints. The next morning, I even almost didn’t have the courage to check the edited video they had sent, fearing it would show traces of my anxiety all over my face.

The lights gradually dimmed, and only a few faint auxiliary lamps remained on in the livestream room. I sat in my chair, staring at the scrolling comments replaying on the screen, my heart still beating a little fast and my palms damp with sweat. The livestream had lasted two hours, and overall the audience’s response had been pretty good, but I kept fixating on one comment, reading it over and over: “The host didn’t seem to notice my question at all.” That line was like a thorn, lodged in my mind and impossible to shake. I remembered the question—it had popped up while I was explaining something—but worried that it would disrupt the flow, I looked away and chose to ignore it. But now, the more I looked at it, the more I felt how much of a failure I was. How could I let the audience feel ignored? Would they think I was an arrogant, cold person?

A colleague walked over and patted me on the shoulder, saying, “Don’t take it too seriously. That comment was probably just offhand.” I nodded and echoed him verbally: “Yeah, maybe I’m overthinking it.” But the voice inside me was screaming: How could it possibly just be offhand! They must really be dissatisfied. Otherwise, why would they type it out specifically? The more I thought about it, the tighter my stomach felt, as if it were being gripped by an invisible hand.

We had just finished the livestream, and we’d discussed a major topic, even adding a new interactive segment. Audience participation was high, but all that was left in my head was that one comment. Everything else had become background noise. I started replaying my own speech, analyzing it word by word and sentence by sentence, checking whether my tone had been off, or whether some part had been too fast and too perfunctory. My gaze drifted to the water cup on the table, and I picked it up for a sip. But the water had long since gone cold, and the icy chill as it hit my mouth made me shiver.

“Pretty much done, right? Shut down the equipment and get off work?” Another colleague was tidying up the livestream gear. I looked at him and nodded, but my hands didn’t move. I kept feeling like there was still something I hadn’t done properly, or some step I’d missed. In my mind, I kept hearing the faint “leave” sound from viewers exiting the livestream room; each time it rang out, it felt like something struck my heart. On the way downstairs to the parking lot, the air was thick with a mix of dust and machine oil. The night wind hit my face with a chill, yet I could feel sweat beading on my forehead. I held my stomach and still kept thinking: if that viewer really was disappointed in me, should I post an apology on social media? Or specifically address the issue before the next livestream?

After I got home, I couldn’t eat dinner. While repeatedly opening the livestream replay, I couldn’t stop myself from searching the comments section for more critical remarks. Even though many people had left praise and support, my eyes still automatically filtered toward the neutral or even slightly cold feedback. My head was dizzy and foggy, but I kept forcing myself to watch until midnight. The next morning, when I woke up, my stomach still ached faintly, as if reminding me that last night’s mistake had not been an illusion.

The soft lighting of the gallery fell across the walls covered with paintings, and I was standing before an abstract work, trying to interpret the chaotic patches of color. Not far away, I could hear the curator’s voice; he was discussing the meaning of the piece with another visitor. “This painting expresses the artist’s helplessness toward modern society,” I heard him say. Suddenly, my heart began to race and my palms started to sweat. I worried that my understanding of the work seemed superficial. “Did I miss something important? Will I look foolish?” These thoughts kept crashing through my mind.

I walked over to the curator and tried to join the conversation. “The choice of colors is very distinctive; it gives me a sense of deep unease,” I said. “Mm, that’s a common feeling,” the curator replied, and the subtle expression on his face made me uneasy. I began to suspect that my words might have sounded childish or ignorant. As he continued speaking, I noticed his brow furrow slightly, and I was suddenly flooded with a sense of rejection. “Are they laughing at me in their heads?” I thought.

To hide my unease, I hurriedly added, “Actually, I think interpreting art is a personal experience, and perhaps the complexity doesn’t need to be overanalyzed.” The curator did not answer right away, seeming to be thinking it over. I felt a dull ache starting in my stomach as anxiety surged over me like a tide. I desperately wanted to escape the space, yet I was unwilling to give up just like that.

After the event ended, I sat down at a nearby café, trying to calm myself. The shop was filled with the rich aroma of coffee, and the background music was soft. I picked up my phone and repeatedly checked social media messages, making sure the curator hadn’t posted any comments directed at me. Although I knew the chance was slim, I still couldn’t help doubting it. In my mind, I kept replaying the scene from earlier, imagining all kinds of misunderstandings and awkward conversations. My inner monologue was full of self-reproach: “Why am I always so nervous? Why can’t I be more natural?”

A few days later, I sat in my studio, recalling that conversation at the exhibition and reflecting on why I always overinterpret other people’s reactions. To that end, I tried to care less about others’ opinions when creating, and focus more attention on the work itself. I knew I couldn’t completely rid myself of this sensitivity, but perhaps I could find some comfort through creation.

I pushed open a half-closed wooden door and entered an abandoned puppet theater in the city’s southern outskirts. Inside was a dim gloom, the air thick with the scent of decaying wood and stale costumes. From time to time, eerie whispers seemed to rise from the walls, the soft murmur of wind passing through cracked windows. Scattered across the floor were broken stage props and snapped puppet strings, like fragments of forgotten stories. In the center of the theater, an old puppet stand stood alone, with puppets frozen in rigid poses; the colors painted on their masks had long since faded, and only their hollow eyes still gazed silently ahead. I stepped forward and touched the faces of those puppets that had once been alive, feeling the cold, roughness of the wood. My heartbeat quickened, my palms grew slightly damp, as if I had touched some indescribable vitality. “How much laughter did these puppets once bring?” I murmured to myself, trying to find traces of the past in these motionless objects. A dull ache began in my stomach, and a familiar anxiety rose within me, as though the theater’s silence were examining my inner self and forcing me to confront the creative anxiety that had long haunted me. The feeling left me frightened and ashamed, yet I could not escape it.

Later, I sat on a worn seat in the audience and saw several yellowed pages of a script scattered on the floor. I picked one up; on it, in scribbled handwriting, was a fragment of a puppet play script, telling a story of loss and loneliness. The script moved me deeply, and I fell into contemplation, as if those silent puppet performances were whispering unresolved secrets to me. A few days later, I was still feeling the aftershock of that depression and loneliness. I kept thinking about how to express, through my work, the emotions I had sensed in the puppet theater, and gradually an endless creative longing began to well up in my heart—a desire to give those motionless puppets new life.

I was standing in an abandoned warehouse, its walls covered with black-and-white photographs. The lighting was dim, and the air was filled with a stale dusty smell. Beneath my feet was rough concrete flooring, and from time to time I could hear the faint creaking of the metal supports in the roof, as if it might collapse at any moment. It was an underground photography exhibition, and a few strangers were speaking in low voices. I tried to lose myself in the works on display, attempting to interpret their deeper meaning.

The exhibition drew all kinds of people. Beside me stood a woman wearing a dark scarf, her posture seeming a little uneasy. I noticed she was looking at a photograph of a child sitting on a windowsill with a solemn expression. When I glanced at her absentmindedly, her eyes met mine. She frowned slightly, then turned a little away. My heart tightened, and I felt a wave of unease and shame, wondering whether she was displeased by how intently I had been looking at her—perhaps I had made someone uncomfortable again.

“This exhibition is really good today,” came a gentle voice from behind me. I turned around and saw a young male photographer talking with a friend. My heart began to race, and I felt as if his words were somehow directed at me, as though he thought I couldn’t truly understand the meaning of these works. I started to feel anxious, my hands growing slightly sweaty, and I could only keep adjusting my stance to hide my unease.

I kept ruminating over the interaction in my mind, a stream of possible misunderstandings flashing through my thoughts. Why am I always this sensitive? I tried to tell myself it was just my imagination, but I couldn’t shake the lingering sense of being rejected.

After the exhibition ended, I left in a hurry, and only after breathing the fresh air outside did I calm down a little. When I got home, I kept thinking over everything that had happened, trying to find factual evidence to prove that the woman hadn’t cared about my gaze, and that the photographer’s words were simply a comment on the exhibition.

A few days later, I was still thinking about that night from time to time, but as time passed, I began to understand this reaction better. That night, I set myself a small goal: to try not to overinterpret other people’s facial expressions, especially in unfamiliar settings. I wanted to remind myself that people’s reactions are usually not about me.

Sitting in my creative studio, I was surrounded by familiar visual elements: paintings of various styles hanging on the walls, drafts and tools piled on the desk, and a faint smell of paint lingering in the air. Sunlight streamed through the curtains onto the floor, feeling somewhat glaring. I was trying hard to finish a new project, but inspiration seemed blocked. My brush hovered motionless over the paper when I heard a colleague who had come to visit knock and enter, breaking the silence.

“Hey, how’s it going? How is the project progressing?” my colleague asked, his voice caring, though I could detect a hint of doubt. My heartbeat began to quicken, and I seemed to sense an attitude of challenge or scrutiny. “Pretty well, I’m trying some new things,” I replied, trying to stay calm, though unease began to surface inside me. I have always worried about how others perceive and judge me; even a simple question can make me feel as if I’m being examined under a microscope. My hands trembled a little as I gripped the brush tightly.

My colleague went on, “I thought some of the elements in your earlier drafts were pretty good; maybe you could dig into those ideas further.” His words brought back memories of several failed attempts in the past, immediately triggering doubts about my own abilities. I forced out a smile, but my stomach began to churn, and this physical reaction made me even more tense. I recalled several times when overanalyzing others’ comments had brought my creative work to a halt, and now it was happening again. Why am I always like this? Why can’t I just accept advice without speculating whether it means someone is rejecting me?

Afterward, I kept replaying the conversation in my mind, even overanalyzing my colleague’s expressions and tone. Had he lost confidence in my ability? Did he think my work wasn’t good enough? These thoughts made it hard for me to settle down and continue creating. Even after my colleague left, I remained trapped in a spiral of self-doubt, and the silence in the studio felt suffocating. I let out a soft sigh, feeling my shoulders grow heavy.

A few days later, I tried to get back into work mode, but found it difficult to focus. The shame in my heart and the fear of failure made every touch of the brush to the paper feel difficult. I began to question my creative responsibilities and even considered whether I should give up on the project. Late at night, I lay awake tossing and turning, and this continuing anxiety made it hard to fall asleep. Before going to bed, I decided to give myself some time; perhaps a break would help me regain inspiration and confidence.

The workshop’s door was left half ajar. I pushed it open gently, and a blast of cold wind nearly slammed it shut again. I braced it open with effort and stepped into this forgotten space. A strong smell of aged wood and machine oil hung in the air, with a faint trace of mildew. The light was dim, with only a few streaks of autumn’s fading glow slipping through the broken windows and falling across the dust-covered looms. I could hear my footsteps echoing through the workshop’s emptiness, each step seeming to land on some heavy sense of history. In the distance came a few faint sounds of wind rattling sheet metal, along with the subtle scurrying of rodents in the corner, and my stomach began to ache slightly.

I started by lightly touching the edge of a loom with my fingers. The cold metal made my palm tremble a little, carrying with it an inexplicable sense of awe. I tried to keep my breathing soft, not wanting to seem too tense in such a confined space. Suddenly, a sharp sound of something hitting the floor came from behind me. “Bang!” My whole body froze, and my heartbeat immediately turned frantic, like pounding gongs. I turned around, but saw nothing. Could there be someone else here? Or had the workshop, in some inexplicable state, somehow “come alive”? My mind instantly began constructing disaster scenarios: some unknown presence might be watching me, or the workshop’s severe structural damage could trap me at any moment.

I tried hard to steady myself and murmured, “It’s fine, just the wind, or maybe a window got blown open.” I wasn’t sure whether I was comforting myself—the sound of my voice was slightly trembling, with a faint, desperate hoarseness. I continued feeling along the edge of the loom, trying to drive away my fear through the sensation in my hands. At that moment, every step felt unusually heavy, as though each one was costing me immense courage and willpower.

Looking around, I found a broken wooden rod lying on the floor near a pile of abandoned yarn racks. Perhaps that was what had fallen just now. I bent down to pick it up, but the instant I touched it, it pricked my fingertip. “Ah!” I instinctively pulled my hand back and saw a drop of blood seeping from the split skin. At that moment, I seemed almost angry at my own stupidity—something so harmless, and yet I always managed to turn it into something so dramatic.

By the time I left the workshop, it was completely dark. The streetlights on the road cast a weak glow on the ground beneath my feet, yet I still felt as though I remained trapped in that dim atmosphere. Once home, I sat on the sofa and drank a few mouthfuls of water, trying to calm the horrifying guesses and panic-stricken images in my mind. Had this tendency to make a mountain out of a molehill already become part of my daily life? I kept reflecting, feeling that I had spent too much time rehearsing things that would never happen, and that these emotions only made my body more exhausted.

In the days afterward, I deliberately looked up some information about old weaving techniques, and even found a few materials online. They gave me a calmer, more rational understanding of that place. As for the panic that day, I still couldn’t fully let it go, but I at least came to understand that many times my fear did not come from the outside world, but from the shadows within myself.

The rain outside kept pounding against the window, filling the café with a continuous ticking sound. I sat by the window, holding a warm latte in my hands, feeling the warmth it passed into my palms. My friend sat across from me, enthusiastically sharing some of her recent travel experiences. I forced a smile and tried to focus on the stories she was telling, but the sound of the rain kept distracting me.

“Are you okay?” my friend suddenly stopped and asked.

“Oh, I’m fine. It’s just that the rain is making me a little annoyed,” I explained, giving a slight shrug.

“Why don’t we change the subject?” she suggested.

“Sure, that sounds good,” I agreed, feeling relieved.

As I listened to my friend talk about the amusing things she’d seen and experienced on her trips, I felt a trace of unease and irritability, even though the stories were interesting. A thought kept circling in my mind: “Why does it have to rain? If it were sunny, I’d definitely feel much better.” This helplessness toward the weather made it even harder for me to concentrate on the conversation at hand. My heartbeat seemed to fall out of rhythm with the cadence of the rain.

Just as I was trying hard to rejoin my friend’s conversation, a cold gust of wind suddenly slipped through the crack in the door, and I couldn’t help shrinking my neck. The dampness of the rainy day seemed to add another layer of gloom, and I could even smell the faint scent of wet earth mixed into the air.

After a while, I decided to go to the counter and buy a dessert to shift my attention. As I stood up and walked toward the counter, I could feel my muscles tensing slightly, even a little sore and tight. I adjusted my breathing, trying to relax.

This small bit of movement seemed to improve my mood a little. When I sat back down, picked up the dessert, and took a gentle bite, the sweetness blended with the bitterness of the coffee, unexpectedly creating a comforting balance. My friend looked at me and smiled. “Looks like dessert made you a little happier.”

I nodded, finally letting a truly relaxed smile appear on my face. That evening, when I got home, it was still raining outside, but my mood was much better than it had been in the afternoon. The next day, the rain stopped, and sunlight spilled onto the floor through the gap in the curtains. I felt a sense of relief, as if the smallest changes in the world could also change the scenery within my heart.

The museum lights had a faint bluish tint, and the air was filled with the smell of metal and plastic. I stood beside a huge flight simulator, looking at its complicated control panel, while the faint sound of children’s laughter drifted to my ears. They were gathered around a staff member, trying to operate a “Mars rover” model. I pinched my fingertips and felt that my palms were already a little sweaty. It was really too quiet here, and my mind was a complete mess.

“What do you think of this simulator?” one of the creative partners with me suddenly asked. I blurted out instinctively, “Honestly, it looks kind of cheap. It doesn’t really seem like a real spacecraft.” As soon as the words were out, I noticed the change in his expression. His smile faded slightly, and his eyebrows lifted a little, as if he were thinking about something.

“Oh, it’s okay, I guess. I think it’s pretty interesting,” he replied offhandedly, then looked down to fiddle with the device in his hands. I stared at him, and my mind immediately started churning: Did he think I was being too harsh? Or that I didn’t know what I was talking about? Had I ruined his mood?

My chest began to tighten, and my heart started beating faster. I felt short of breath, as if the air around me had suddenly grown heavy. I tried hard to pretend nothing was wrong and looked around casually, but everything in front of me seemed blurred. I lightly rubbed the knuckle of my thumb with my fingers, trying to distract myself, but it didn’t help much.

“Are you okay?” He suddenly turned back to look at me, his tone carrying a hint of concern. That made me even more uneasy. I forced out, “Mm, I’m fine, just a little distracted.” My voice sounded so stiff even I didn’t believe it.

For the rest of the time, I spent almost the whole visit smiling and nodding through the discomfort. Every time we passed an exhibit area, I struggled to think of something interesting and absolutely non-offensive to say to make the atmosphere feel more natural, but the harder I tried, the more awkward I seemed. Was he laughing at me in his head? Or did he think I was impossible to talk to?

By the time I got home, I was exhausted, and I was still thinking about that moment when he raised his eyebrows. I couldn’t help pulling out my phone to check his social media, trying to find any clue that would confirm my suspicion. I found a photo he had posted recently, captioned: “Some things need a little more tolerance.” My heart sank at once—he must have been subtly referring to me, right?

For the next full 48 hours, this “small matter” occupied my mind completely. I even began to speculate whether he would mention it to others and describe me as someone “always finding fault.” I blamed myself countless times in my head: “Why couldn’t you just keep your mouth shut?” I started drafting an apology message to him, but kept deleting it over and over, feeling that the more I said, the more it would seem like a guilty cover-up. In the end, I decided to pretend nothing had happened.

I was sitting by the window in a corner café, my laptop open on the table, a draft due today displayed on the screen. The light outside was lovely, with thin clouds covering the sky and the occasional ring of a bicycle bell drifting in from the street. The aroma of coffee gently surrounded me; it should have been the perfect atmosphere for writing. However, the problem was the person at the next table. A young man in a plaid shirt was typing at an extremely fast pace, the clacking never letting up. He seemed to be organizing an important file, focused and utterly unaware of his surroundings.

I tried to force myself not to care about the sound. “It’s just background noise, like the traffic outside—nothing to make a fuss about,” I told myself, while turning down my headphones, but no matter what I did, that sharp tapping kept piercing my ears and making it impossible to concentrate. I could feel a slight throb beginning at my temples, and my stomach also felt mildly unsettled.

“Take a deep breath and focus on your own work,” I kept comforting myself inwardly. I tried staring at the words on the screen, but my thoughts had already tangled themselves up like a mess of thread. I even started wondering whether, if I stood up and asked him to stop, it would lead to some awkward conflict. Would he think I was interfering? Or would he apologize and stop typing?

The tapping grew even denser, swirling around my ears like a whirlpool. In the end, I couldn’t help but take off my headphones and look up at him. He didn’t raise his head, looking completely absorbed in his own world. I opened my mouth, but the words got stuck in my throat. I even began to wonder whether I was being too sensitive—maybe other people wouldn’t think this was a problem at all. I froze for a few seconds, then lowered my head again, looking at my coffee cup and tracing circles along the rim with my finger.

At last, I decided to get up and go to the counter for another coffee, and while I was at it, try to shift my mood a little. The moment I stood up, I felt my heart beating a bit faster, as if I had just finished a marathon, and my palms were still slightly damp. I ordered a hot Americano at the counter, and while waiting for it, my body loosened up a little. I tried to redirect my attention to the sound of the coffee machine, and the hiss of steam along with the aroma of freshly roasted beans made me feel somewhat better.

When I returned to my seat, I found that the young man at the next table had already packed up and left; the keyboard noise was gone. I let out a sigh of relief and brought my attention back to the words on the screen. Though there was still a lingering aftertaste in my mind, at least I could now continue working in peace.

That evening, after I got home, I told a friend about this small incident. My friend smiled and comforted me, saying, “That’s just how cafés are—some noise is inevitable. Try sitting in a different corner next time; it might be better.” I didn’t say anything, but I was still thinking about why I was always so easily disturbed by little things like this. Even though I did finish the draft in the end, I still couldn’t shake a faint sense of dissatisfaction.

Sunlight streamed through the broken windows onto the metal fragments on the floor, and the mottled patterns of light and shadow swayed across the ground. I walked into this abandoned water purification plant on the edge of the city, the air thick with a mixture of rust and rotting wood. The place was eerily quiet, with only the faint sound of my dress shoes crunching on the dust. My heart suddenly began to race, as if someone were watching me from a corner. My palms started to sweat, and that tension made my whole body feel uneasy.

“This really is a strange place,” I muttered to myself, trying to comfort myself. But all kinds of unsettling thoughts kept flashing through my mind: “What if someone suddenly appears? What if something goes wrong?”

I tried hard to steady my breathing and kept walking, passing by old machines with rusty patches left by time on their metal surfaces. I stopped in front of an aged filter, as if I could hear the hum it had once made when it was working. It reminded me of a time during a project when I was criticized by a client for a small mistake. Back then, I felt abandoned by everyone, as if I were trapped alone in endless loneliness.

Suddenly, I noticed an old leaking pipe in the corner, with water droplets tapping lightly against the floor and forming a small puddle. “There’s still water here?” My heart skipped, and I felt even more uneasy for no reason. I moved closer to inspect it, my heartbeat pounding harder against my chest.

“It should be fine, right?” I tried to convince myself, but the fear deep inside still clung on. The camera in my hand slipped from my slightly trembling grip and made a soft thud. I crouched down to pick it up, and a pungent rust smell rushed into my nose, making me frown.

At last, I finished shooting the footage I needed and fled that dim, unsettling place as if escaping. The sunlight was still blinding, but this time its warmth helped calm me a little. Back in the car, I took a deep breath, and my heartbeat slowly began to settle. That night at home, I kept looking over the photos I had taken, yet my thoughts kept returning to that sense of helplessness and fear. I couldn’t shake them off.

The next day, I found myself staring blankly at my computer screen, my mind still trapped in the eerie atmosphere of the water purification plant. I knew I had slipped back into that pattern of catastrophic thinking, my heart full of worries, but I didn’t have the courage to bring it up with anyone. I could only bury those feelings deep inside.

The cool night breeze carried a hint of sharp chill, and the air was mixed with the smell of wet grass and rust. I walked into an abandoned chemical factory on the northern outskirts of the city. Most of the factory windows were already broken, the walls were heavily stained and peeling, and only a few dim yellow safety lights in the corners were still faintly flickering. I came here to look for new inspiration, a setting for a new video shoot. In the abandoned workshop, I could hear the creaking sound of my footsteps on the floor, as well as the faint noise made by stones occasionally falling. My heart raced, and my hands began to sweat slightly.

“Coming to a place like this alone, aren’t you worried?” I murmured to myself, hoping to ease my unease. My voice sounded especially out of place in the empty workshop. I began to recall my previous filming attempts, and the details of that project always made me anxious. My stomach throbbed faintly, and that familiar tension began to spread through my body. Any noise that might appear at any moment kept me in a constant state of strain. Thinking back on those unsuccessful shoots felt like missing one important opportunity after another. “If this fails again, what will happen? Will it be the same as before, with no recognition at all?” I tried to rehearse various possible outcomes, and scenes of myself being criticized and rejected kept flashing through my mind. This habit of attacking myself before seeing any results seemed especially active in this atmosphere.

So focused on anticipating failure was I that I barely noticed my phone vibrating. My partner’s voice came through the call: “Where are you? How are we going to arrange today’s discussion?” I quickly adjusted my mindset and tried to answer in a calm tone: “I’m thinking about some new ideas. I’ll get back to you later.” After hanging up, the connection to the outside world brought me a little comfort. But the aftermath lingered, and after I got home that night, anxiety was still lingering in my body. Whenever I thought back to the scene at the chemical factory, I would wonder whether I could really handle the challenges ahead. Over the next few days, I occasionally opened my computer to research related topics, always feeling that I needed a more complete plan to avoid repeating the same mistakes.

The air was thick with the stale smell of mold, mixed with the damp scent of earth. My shoe soles made a faint creaking sound against the floor, as if conversing with the quiet space. A few streaks of light leaked through the gaps in the damaged roof above, falling on the old machines covered in dust. Pale yellow moonlight spilled through the broken glass windows, and the crooked looms looked like abrupt metal monsters, exuding a sleeping stillness.

My heart was pounding. I clutched my phone tightly, trying not to make a sound. I had only wanted to escape the monotony of everyday life and find some strange place to shoot a few clips, but after entering this abandoned textile mill, an indescribable unease began to surround me. I gently adjusted my breathing and told myself, “It’s just an empty building, a shadow of the past. There’s nothing dangerous here.” Even so, my stomach still ached faintly, as if someone were gently kneading it with their fingertips.

Suddenly, a sharp crack came from my right, and my body stiffened reflexively. A few seconds later, I realized it was probably a bird flying off from the rusted iron bars, dislodging a loose piece of metal. I tried to let out a self-conscious laugh, but before it could escape, it was swallowed by the dry tightness in my throat.

“Maybe I should go back,” the thought began to circle in my mind, but I immediately pushed it away. “No, just stay a little longer. Find one more good shot, then take the last few pictures.” I kept inching forward slowly. Ahead of me was a row of toppled storage cabinets, with scattered scraps of fabric inside, their original colors completely eroded by dust and dampness.

My phone screen lit up, and a message popped up—my friend asking what I was doing. I stared at the screen unconsciously, my fingertips hesitating over whether to reply, but in the end I locked the phone. “If I tell them I’m here, will they think I’m crazy?” the thought flashed through my mind. “Why did I have to choose such a place? Why insist on coming alone?”

A cold sensation came from my palm, and I realized I had absentmindedly rested my hand on a rusted metal part of the machine beside me, my fingers slightly dampened by moisture. I quickly pulled my hand back. The icy feeling at my fingertips spread through my whole body, making goosebumps rise all over me. I looked around once more to make sure no one else was there, then forced out a faint smile. “Alright, let’s go. I’ve pretty much gotten what I came for.”

By the time I got home, it was already past midnight. My clothes clung to my body, and I smelled stale air and rust. That smell made me even more irritable. I collapsed onto the sofa and opened the photos I’d taken, scrolling through them, but found hardly any that I liked. Yet in my mind, scenes kept replaying of me being discovered on the spot, along with the image of my friends laughing at me—“Why do you always like to run off to weird places?” Suddenly, I wanted nothing more than to retreat into the dark, switch off my phone, and disappear completely.

The next day, I turned down a friend’s lunch invitation and made up an excuse about being too busy. I locked myself at home and repeatedly picked through and edited those photos, trying to uncover what I thought might be worthwhile work. I couldn’t tell whether what I felt was regret or guilt, only that it was like a pair of hands I could not touch, pushing and pulling at my chest, leaving me unable to steady myself.

The air was filled with the stale smell of paint, and a fine rain kept tapping against the window. I sat beside a workbench covered in paint. Everything around me seemed frozen in time. I gently touched the tabletop with my fingertips, feeling its rough texture, as if I were touching a forgotten time from the past. All that remained in my ears was the patter of rain, like tiny needles pricking at my heart one by one.

“Are you free today?” That message had been sent by that person this morning, and I still hadn’t replied. The phone had rung once half an hour ago, and I didn’t answer. At that moment, I felt my heartbeat quicken, as if an invisible hand had clutched my chest. Why didn’t I answer? Why didn’t I reply?

I blamed myself inwardly. “You’re always like this, always making simple things complicated.” I muttered helplessly to myself. That unread message still lay on the phone screen, like a spell that had sealed off all my actions.

“Maybe he’s angry,” a voice in my head hissed, “does he think I’m deliberately avoiding him?” That guess made my palms sweat, and my stomach churn as well. I tightened my grip on the paintbrush, trying to distract myself with the pain in my fingertips. But the unease inside me wrapped around me like a shadow, and I couldn’t shake it off.

“You’re always imagining things,” I started scolding myself again. “Someone like him, how could he possibly get angry over something this small?”

But those words of self-comfort didn’t help; instead, they made me even more terrified and uneasy. I began to remember those moments in the past when I had been misunderstood and abandoned, and that deep-seated sense of defect quietly came surging back. They wandered through my mind like ghosts, dragging my emotions down into the mire.

The rain suddenly grew heavier, pounding fiercely against the windowsill. I gasped, as if searching for a sliver of clarity in the air. But gradually, only one thought remained in my mind: “What should I do?”

“Maybe I can reply to that message.” That thought brought me a little relief, and I reached for the phone, but my fingers stopped in midair. I didn’t dare. I was afraid of being rejected or misunderstood once again.

That night, I tossed and turned, my thoughts in complete chaos, not daring to make even a simple phone call. Those old fears of abandonment surfaced again, intertwining with anxiety into a nightmare I couldn’t escape. The next day, when I woke up, the lingering unease in my heart was still with me, like an inescapable gloom.

Sunlight filtered through the curtains and spilled across the floor. The room was filled with the rich aroma of coffee. I sat beside the sofa, clutching my notebook tightly, a wave of unease rising in me. The sharing session had only just begun, and I could already feel my palms sweating and my heartbeat quickening. The people beside me were talking animatedly, and I tried hard to appear relaxed, but inside, my mind had already sounded the alarm.

I had to pay attention to other people’s reactions. A young man began by greeting me, “Are you responsible for the illustration presentation this time?”

“Yes, I am.” As soon as I answered, I immediately became alert for any subtle criticism in his tone, even though his smile seemed friendly. I started wondering what he really thought: Did he think there was something wrong with my work?

At that moment, another person joined the conversation. She showed great enthusiasm for my work. “Your pieces are truly captivating! The use of color is so distinctive.”

“Really?” I was eager to confirm what she truly meant. Even with praise like that, I couldn’t help but suspect it might just be polite lip service, and the muscles in my back tensed.
