The speaker’s voice echoed through the room as everyone listened intently. Yet I began to drift off, repeatedly replaying the conversation in my head, trying to find any possible negative meaning in it. After the exchange ended, my stomach felt a little unsettled, as if an invisible pressure were weighing on it.

After the meeting, I followed the crowd out of the room. The air outside was a bit cool, and I couldn’t help shivering. Although the conversation had been nothing unusual, I kept overanalyzing my own performance, worrying about whether everyone might misunderstand me. That night, lying in bed, I tossed and turned, my heartbeat still uneven. Whenever I thought back to their reactions, I felt anxious again, my mind circling one question over and over: Was that compliment genuine or not?

When I woke the next day, my phone showed that there were once again several anonymous comments, some of which mentioned yesterday’s sharing session. I tried to read them calmly, but a few negative remarks felt like a stab to my heart, and my self-esteem was hurt all over again. Although some comments were praising me, I still noticed the critical words first, as if they came with a magnifying glass, enough to unsettle my mood with a single sentence. The small confidence I had in myself seemed so tiny before these seemingly objective comments.

Warm yellow light spilled across the wooden tabletop of the café, and the air was thick with the rich aroma of coffee. The friend opposite me was slowly stirring her latte, a hint of hesitation on her face. My folder lay open on the table, containing the proposal for my newly launched project. I looked at her expectantly, my heart pounding harder with every second of silence, sweat sliding down the back of my neck. I tightened my grip on the coffee cup, the heat from its surface seeping into my palm, as if reminding me to stay calm.

At last, she spoke. “I think... this project may not be a good fit for me to get involved in.” Her tone was calm, but it landed in my chest like a dull hammer blow. A sudden buzzing rang in my ears, and the world seemed split into two spaces by a thin membrane. I gave a reflexive smile, but even I could feel how brittle and unnatural it was. “It’s okay, I was just asking casually.” My mouth moved mechanically, trying to hide my disappointment.

But my mind had already started racing, like toppling dominoes, uncontrollably playing out the worst possible scenarios. She didn’t support me—did that mean she looked down on my abilities at all? Had she already lost trust in me? Was there something fundamentally wrong with me, something that always let people down? Heat climbed up my cheeks, and my stomach felt as if I’d swallowed a whole vat of sour liquid, churning violently. I strained to catch any trace of meaning from her microexpressions, trying to find a deeper message behind her words.

“Don’t overthink it. I’m just really busy right now—I honestly can’t take on much,” she added, seemingly noticing my stiffness. I nodded, trying to make my expression look less defeated. I lowered my head and stared at my coffee; the foam on the surface had gradually dissipated, revealing a dark, murky liquid, like the shadow inside me that had been torn open. I didn’t dare look up into her eyes, afraid I might blurt out something intense and impossible to take back.

“Do you think I’m a terrible person?” The words were out before I could stop myself. As soon as I said it, I snapped my mouth shut, my heart seeming to stop for a moment. The air froze. She stared for a second before her face shifted into disbelief. “What? Why would you think that? What are you talking about?”

I lowered my head in embarrassment, my fingers mindlessly picking at the rim of the cup. My throat was so dry I could hardly speak, but the shame burned through my chest, like a living snake twisting inside. “Forget it, I was joking.” I forced out the words, my voice so faint it was almost inaudible.

On the way home, the night wind carried a hint of autumn and cut painfully against my face. I was exhausted, and the cramping in my stomach never eased. I kept replaying her face and her tone, as if searching for where I had gone wrong. My head ran through countless reasons she might dislike me, like an endless noise that would not stop.

All night long, I tossed and turned without sleep. When I woke the next day, my eyes were swollen, and I felt hollowed out. I decided not to bring up the project again, and not to contact her first either, though deep down I desperately wanted her to send me a message and tell me that I wasn’t as awful as I imagined.

I was sitting in my study at home. A light rain was falling outside, and raindrops tapped against the window with a soft, rhythmic sound. On the desk sat a cup of steaming tea, and the air was filled with a faint fragrance of tea. Just then, the notification sound for a new email on my computer rang out, and my heartbeat quickened a little.

“Hopefully this isn’t bad news again,” I thought to myself, opening the email with a bit of hope. The email was from a partner, giving feedback on my latest creative idea. I took a forceful sip of tea, feeling the warmth slide down my throat. The wording of the email was plain, even somewhat cold: “Your proposal is very creative, but at this stage our direction will not be considering similar collaborations.”

Just a few lines of text, yet they felt like a cold boulder pressing down on my chest. I stared at the screen, my eyes fixed on those words, as if trying to read some hidden emotion from them. I felt my chest tightening, and a dull ache began in my stomach.

“Do they think I’m not good enough? Is my idea really that bad?” The inner monologue kept echoing in my mind.

I stood up and began pacing around the room, trying to distract myself from the unease through movement. However, my footsteps echoed on the wooden floor, making me even more anxious, and sweat slowly began to dampen my forehead. Several times I wanted to reply to the email, but I didn’t know what to say.

“Maybe I should take the initiative and reach out, seem more professional? No, that won’t do. What if they think I’m being clingy? That would be even worse.”

Restlessness filled my thoughts. I bent over, bracing my hands weakly on the desk, and looked down at the cup of tea; it had already gone cold.

The rain grew heavier, and the tapping on the window became more frequent. I sat back down in my chair, took a deep breath, and tried to calm myself. “I should be used to this kind of thing, shouldn’t I? Not everyone will approve, and this isn’t the end of the world.” But deep down, that feeling of being abandoned still wouldn’t go away.

I opened my music player and tried to soothe the ripples in my heart with familiar melodies. A piano piece slowly flowed out, and it finally eased me a little. A few days later, I threw myself into my work, trying to showcase my abilities in new ways. Though I was still somewhat uneasy, I decided not to dwell too much on the rejection.

The morning sunlight streamed through the window, falling softly across the worktables in the pottery studio. Wearing a simple apron, I stood beside a table piled with various tools, my fingers caked with damp clay, carefully cradling the rough shape of a ceramic jar in my hands. The classroom was very quiet, with only the faint sound of wind drifting in from outside the window, occasionally joined by the low rumble of vehicles passing in the distance. At that moment, my heart was filled with an indescribable mix of serenity and anxiety.

“Don’t apply too much force, or the shape will go out of alignment,” the teacher beside me said gently. “Mm, I know, thank you,” I replied, smiling and nodding, though unease still throbbed faintly within me. Just moments before, I had accidentally pressed a slight dent into the jar. Though not serious, it was enough to make my heart race, and tension swept through my entire body in an instant. I kept checking it over and over, trying to smooth out the mark, while worrying that my attempts to fix it would only make things worse.

“Why is it always like this? It’s only a tiny flaw, so why does it make me so anxious?” I murmured to myself inwardly. It felt as though my heart was being gripped tightly, aching slightly; fine beads of sweat appeared on my forehead, and my palms grew damp as well. I took a deep breath, trying to steady my heartbeat, but with every breath I still felt a taut, constricting pressure.

“You seem to care a lot about every detail, but sometimes it’s okay to relax a little,” the teacher comforted me, apparently noticing my tension. I nodded, keeping a smile on my face. “Maybe it’s because I want to do it too well.”

By the time I finally adjusted the shape of the jar and gently set the clay down, my anxiety still had not completely faded. That night, after returning home, I still couldn’t help replaying the scene from pottery class that morning, repeatedly wondering whether I could truly let go of my obsession with perfection. Even then, every tiny choice I had made stirred waves of unease deep inside me.

A few days later, I tried using meditation to ease my tension. Sitting by the window, I closed my eyes and imagined myself standing in the pottery classroom, feeling the warmth of sunlight on my body, as if that small trace of unease were gradually being swept away, and a little of the calm in my heart had returned.

I sat beside the long table in the conference room, sunlight streaming through the curtains onto the tabletop. The air was filled with the aroma of morning coffee, and the projector’s faint glow flickered intermittently. The meeting was going smoothly until a colleague suddenly interrupted me mid-sentence. Her voice was sharp and forceful: “Isn’t this suggestion a bit too risky? We’ve tried similar approaches before, and the results weren’t ideal.” I felt a wave of embarrassment, my face instantly growing hot. “I just feel that our goals need more innovation and flexibility, to avoid staying stuck in the same old pattern,” I explained weakly, seeing her eyebrows lift slightly, as if dismissing what I had said. The other colleagues’ eyes drifted away, and for a moment the room was filled with awkward silence. My heart began to race, sweat seeped into my palms, and it felt as though a heavy stone were pressing down on my stomach. I tried hard to steady myself, but I could not shake a deep sense of abandonment. A voice in my mind kept repeating, “They don’t need me. They’re going to abandon me.” The feeling was like wildly growing vines, tightly wrapping around me. After the meeting ended, I stood alone in the restroom in front of the mirror, trying to regulate my breathing and calm down. The person in the mirror looked tense, with anxiety visible in my eyes. Hours passed, but my mood still had not improved, and I kept replaying that moment of doubt in my mind. That night, I couldn’t fall asleep for a long time, repeatedly dwelling on my flaws and shortcomings. Many memories flashed through my mind, and this sense of defectiveness felt like an inescapable mark. I began to question my place on the team, worried that I would be pushed further to the margins. A few days later, I noticed that I had become more sensitive, inclined to avoid one-on-one conversations with the colleague who had questioned me, afraid of facing her criticism again. I kept ruminating over this meeting, silently blaming myself for not responding better. Even when I tried hard not to think about it, the unease deep inside still would not go away.

The exhibition hall was filled with the scent of earth, and warm lights fell upon one exquisite piece of pottery after another. I looked around, my heart full of admiration for these works of art. Suddenly, a voice sounded behind me: “Beautiful pieces, aren’t they?” I turned around and saw a stranger smiling at me.

“Yes, they really are beautiful,” I replied, but a pang of unease rose involuntarily in my heart. What did his smile mean? Was he implying that my own work was inferior to what was on display? Doubts began to spread inside me, and my heartbeat suddenly quickened. I gripped my handbag tightly, trying to steady my emotions. “Do you make pottery too?” he asked next.

“Mm, yes, but I’m still learning. It’s not as professional as these.” I answered with a strained smile, but in my mind the worst-case scenario had already begun to play out—how would he judge my work? Would he point out that I lacked creativity? Fine beads of sweat had broken out on my forehead, and a dull ache began to build in my stomach.

After the exhibition ended, I went home and collapsed onto the sofa. His words kept echoing in my mind. How could I be so unsettled? Perhaps he just wanted to make friendly conversation, while I was always overinterpreting things. Shame and self-reproach intertwined in my heart, making it hard for me to calm down.

The next morning, I sat in my studio, still in a bad mood. I told myself that I had to control this oversensitivity. I took a deep breath and tried to focus on the piece in front of me. However, that simple greeting from the man still pricked at my heart like a thorn, making it impossible to concentrate. A few days later, I finally decided to take the initiative and email him, thanking him for his compliment and hoping to ease the anxiety in my heart.

I learned that even the simplest interaction can trigger unease, but more often than not, it is I who make things complicated. I need to learn to relax and not let my sensitivity ruin beautiful moments.

Warm yellow light cast soft shadows in the café, and each small wooden table held a bottle of dried flowers. I stirred my latte, now cold, the clinking of the spoon against the cup sounding like an amplified alarm, matching the persistent tightness in my chest. My friend, sitting across from me, smiled faintly and said, “Actually, sometimes you don’t need to care so much about what other people think. They may not judge you the way you say they will.” Her tone was easy, but my stomach clenched all at once. I knew she meant well, but those words were like a sharp knife, slicing open the most hidden part of my heart.

“Yeah, I know.” I nodded, trying to keep my voice steady. But what surged through my mind was another version of her words: I’m always too concerned, even overly sensitive. Have I made people think I’m hard to get along with again? In her eyes, am I just the kind of person who takes himself too seriously, is overly sensitive, and is a headache to deal with? These thoughts shot through my mind like a car with the accelerator floored, impossible to stop.

She kept talking about something, but my attention had already drifted. I heard the roar of the coffee machine, the laughter from the next table, and even felt the wood grain on the table digging into my palm. I gripped the handle of my coffee cup tightly, my palms starting to sweat slightly, the pressure in my chest growing worse. I felt like I should say something in response, but my mouth seemed sealed shut with glue, unable to produce a single word.

“Are you okay?” She looked up, concern in her voice. In an instant I felt even worse, as if the evidence of my breakdown had been caught red-handed. “Ah, I’m fine.” I forced out a smile. “Maybe I’m just a little tired lately.” Even as I said it, I could hear how shaky my voice sounded. I just wanted this conversation to end, but I was also afraid she’d think I was avoiding her.

“Why don’t we call it a day here?” Maybe she had noticed something was off. I nodded quickly. “Sure, sorry, I’ve really been a bit off emotionally lately.” As soon as I said that, my cheeks began to burn, and my heartbeat sped up even more. She smiled and said, “No worries, take care of yourself,” then stood up and said goodbye. I watched her walk out of the café, and suddenly a sense of lonely abandonment surged up inside me. I had been the one to suggest ending the meeting, and yet in that moment, I felt like the one being left behind.

Sitting across from the empty seat, I stared blankly at the coffee cup in my hands. The sounds around my ears seemed wrapped in a layer of mist, growing farther and farther away, until all that remained was my own inner monologue: Why do I always keep thinking about these things? Does she think I’m such a hassle? Why can’t I handle a conversation properly like a normal person?

That night, after I got home, the feeling of blockage in my chest still wouldn’t go away. I scrolled through my phone, trying to shift my attention, but those scenes and conversations kept resurfacing uncontrollably. Before bed, I even started imagining: if we met again next time, should I bring up what happened today myself, or act like nothing happened? But what if she really thinks I’m making a mountain out of a molehill? The arguments in my head kept me awake until three in the morning.

Sitting in the corner of the café, my fingers tapped lightly against the rim of the cup, as if trying to drive away the unease in my heart. The aroma of coffee filled the air, accompanied by soft music, but this comfort from the outside world seemed unable to ease the tension within me. I had arranged to meet my coauthor here to discuss the new project we were about to launch, and I felt both eager and anxious about it. She arrived ten minutes later than planned. The moment she pushed open the door, I saw her glance around before walking toward me. Her face wore a polite smile, one that I unconsciously interpreted as a kind of distance. “Sorry I’m late. There was traffic on the way,” she said in a light, breezy voice, like a plain latte. I nodded, trying to keep my smile from looking too stiff. “It’s fine, I just got here too,” I lied.

As we went through the project proposal, her words were full of professionalism, but to me they seemed to lack warmth. When she spoke about one idea, she said, “This is a good idea, but maybe we can be a bit more practical.” Those simple words sounded to me like criticism. I began to mull over what she had said again and again, and the taut string in my heart was pulled even tighter. My thoughts spun wildly like wheels out of control: Was she dissatisfied with my ideas? Did she think I wasn’t professional enough?

Even while talking with her, my inner monologue never stopped. I worked hard to hide my wavering, continuing to take part in the conversation and nod in response, while my heartbeat quickened and my palms gradually grew damp with sweat. I took a deep breath, trying to ease my tense nerves, but the twisting pain in my stomach cruelly reminded me that this anxiety was not easy to dispel.

We talked for about an hour and gradually settled some of the details. In the end, she smiled and said, “Thank you. I think we’ll work together very well.” Hearing that, I felt a little relieved. Though I wasn’t sure whether her smile was sincere, at least it showed that for the moment she had not clearly rejected me.

That night, lying in bed, I was still chewing over the conversation from the day. I worried about whether I had seemed too nervous at some point, or whether I had missed some detail that I should not have overlooked. Even so, I also realized that our collaboration was still continuing, and perhaps I was simply too sensitive, overinterpreting her attitude. That thought brought me some comfort. Although the unease in my heart had not completely faded, I decided to give myself a break and face it again tomorrow.

Over the next few days, I still found myself recalling that meeting from time to time, but I gradually learned to focus on the facts themselves rather than possible implications. Whenever I felt uneasy, I tried to sort out my thoughts so they would not stray too far.

The lights in the conference room were a little harsh, and the air was thick with the bitter smell of coffee, while I sat in my chair feeling like I was on pins and needles. Seated across from me was my team, and today’s topic was the direction of the new project. The discussion was lively, but all I could feel was that every sentence was scrutinizing me. When one colleague spoke, his expression seemed somewhat serious. He said, “I think there are some problems with this proposal. We need to think it over more carefully.” My heart suddenly raced, and my fingertips started to sweat. “Is he criticizing me? Is my plan not good enough?” I tried hard to suppress the panic rising inside me, but it surged up like a wave, engulfing my reason.

“What do you mean? Do you think my work has no value?” I blurted out almost uncontrollably, my voice sounding unusually harsh in the quiet conference room. Seeing everyone freeze, I immediately felt ashamed, as if they had already judged me incapable. My heart kept pounding, and a dull pain began to come and go in my stomach. I stared at the conference table, too afraid to look up at their expressions, and memories of being criticized again and again in the past surfaced in my mind, as if everyone were whispering about my failures.

My colleague tried to reassure me: “No one is doubting your ability. We just want to make the team better.” His tone was sincere, yet I was still struggling with the anxiety inside me. After the meeting ended, I quickly left, breathing hard as I walked into the bathroom. Looking at myself in the mirror, I could hardly see anything commendable—just a loser who could be abandoned at any moment.

That night, I lay in bed, tossing and turning, unable to fall asleep. The tide of emotions from the meeting still lingered in my mind, leaving me endlessly exhausted. The next day, I deliberately avoided the colleagues I might run into, afraid of becoming the target again. A few days later, I tried to throw myself back into work, but every time I walked into the conference room, that suffocating memory followed me like a shadow, reminding me that I could be denied and discarded at any moment.

Sunlight streamed through the tea house window onto the wooden tabletop, casting mottled patches of light and shadow. I sat there with a cup of green tea that had already gone cold in front of me. The person in charge of the publisher sat across from me, with a stack of documents on the table. He looked somewhat uneasy, his gaze shifting about. I felt a little unsettled, but I kept telling myself it was probably just a routine business conversation.

“We need to talk about our future cooperation,” he finally said, his tone heavier than usual. I nodded, trying to make my smile look as natural as possible. However, his next words suddenly made my heart race: “After internal discussion, we’ve decided to terminate our collaboration with you.”

In that instant, it felt as if the air around me had frozen, and the faint sounds in the room became piercingly sharp. I froze, my fingers unconsciously tightening around the teacup. Although countless questions and protests surged up in my heart, I could only manage to say, “Is it because of sales? Or is there a problem with the content?”

He shook his head, seemingly trying to soften the atmosphere. “It’s absolutely not your fault. We’ve simply decided to adjust our strategy, and this decision may be best for both sides.” His explanation sounded like a patchwork excuse, a total denial of my ability and worth. Immediately, that deep sense of abandonment welled up in my mind, as though all the rejections I had ever experienced were surging back over me at once. I had always tried to present myself as strong, but at that moment, all I wanted was to escape.

“I understand. Thank you,” I heard myself reply mechanically, my voice sounding both unfamiliar and distant. I struggled not to let him see my trembling fingers, but the turmoil inside me could not be concealed. My heartbeat quickened, my stomach felt twisted with pain, and fine beads of sweat began to appear on my forehead. Suddenly, it felt as though I had lost the support beneath me, as if I could collapse at any moment.

After leaving the tea house, the autumn wind hit me head-on, carrying a chill. I tried to steady my breathing and calm myself down, but his words kept replaying in my mind. My thoughts would not stop; I could not accept this sudden blow. No matter how much I told myself this was only a business decision, to me it felt like a profound betrayal and rejection.

The next day, I still felt weighed down. That sense of being abandoned lingered like a shadow that would not disperse. I began repeatedly reflecting on my work and career plans, trying to find possible shortcomings and ways to improve. Yet those thoughts were mixed with self-reproach and a sense of helplessness. Over the past few days, I had woken up more than once in the middle of the night, my mind repeatedly returning to that meeting, unable to pull myself free.

The door to the embroidery workshop creaked open, and cold wind slipped through the crack, gently brushing my face. I looked around; the walls were covered with old embroidery pieces, and the delicate patterns looked especially haunting and beautiful in the dim light. There were a few scattered spools of thread and torn pieces of fabric on the floor. I crouched down and touched the marks left by time; the rough texture rubbed against my fingertips, as if telling stories of the past. My heartbeat began to quicken, and sweat unconsciously gathered in my palms. I couldn’t help feeling that every detail was reminding me of unfinished work and the passage of time. Why had I come here? This place made me uneasy, as if I had stepped into some corner of my own heart, full of forgotten responsibilities and overlooked details.

“Are you here for inspiration?” The workshop manager broke the silence. His voice was low and gentle, carrying a reassuring rhythm. My gaze met his, trying to find an answer in his expression. “Yes, I’m looking for something... new,” I replied, my voice trembling a little, unsure whether I was speaking to him or to myself. He nodded and walked away, leaving me alone in this somewhat chilly space.

I tried to take a deep breath and calm myself, but with every inhale, it felt as though an invisible pressure was filling my chest. Every detail in the embroidery works was so exquisite, yet I was afraid I could never achieve such perfection. I began to dwell repeatedly on recent mistakes, from an email I hadn’t replied to in time to an important meeting I had missed. All these details kept swirling in my mind, as if trapped in a stagnant stretch of time.

The tension in my body gradually spread, and I had to sit down in a chair and close my eyes. In that instant, memories of the past surged over me like a flood, as if the unfinished projects and details were mocking my incompetence. Yet why keep tormenting myself? The loss and anxiety inside me rose and fell like tides, and I longed desperately to break free from this cycle.

When I left the workshop, the cold wind struck again. I only felt a chilling force tugging at my back. On the way home, I still couldn’t shake off that anxiety. The next day, when I woke up, I still felt the weight in my heart. The shadow of that workshop lingered in my mind for a long time, and every stitch of embroidery seemed to remind me of my pursuit of detail and my fear of mistakes.

It was like a performance I could not escape—everything seemed laid bare before my eyes. I realized that my pursuit of perfection had already turned into a never-ending anxiety. This made me even more distressed by my own sensitivity, afraid that I would never be able to accept unresolved matters. The embroidery workshop was like a mirror, showing me the truest reflection of my inner self.

Sunlight streamed through the wooden blades of the dilapidated windmill, casting dappled shadows across the moss-covered brick walls. I stood on an old floor mottled gray and green, camera on my back as I paced around. The air carried a mix of rotting wood and dampness, and now and then I could hear the wind passing through the mill, letting out a faint, mournful howl. I had thought I would fall in love with everything here, but standing in that empty space, it felt as if something were pressing down on my chest, so heavy I could hardly breathe.

I pointed my lens at a wooden ladder in the corner of the wall, where the sunlight happened to fall, like a spotlight on a stage. I adjusted the focus, trying to capture that moment of quiet. But my hands trembled against my will, and every photo I took came out blurry. I drew a breath, trying to steady myself, but a voice rose in my mind: “Who would want to look at these photos? Is this just another meaningless attempt?” My heartbeat quickened, and a thin sheen of sweat broke out on my palms. I put the camera down and shook my head hard, trying to shake those thoughts away.

But the voice did not stop. It grew sharper and sharper: “Aren’t you being too full of yourself? Who would care about an abandoned windmill? What an unimaginative subject!” I closed my eyes and took a deep breath of dust-laden air, trying to tell myself I was just overthinking. Yet in that empty space, I still felt as if countless eyes were fixed on me, scrutinizing every movement I made and every shot I took.

“Are you taking photos?” A man’s voice suddenly came from behind me, breaking my spiraling thoughts. Startled, I turned around and saw a young man standing at the entrance, dressed simply in jeans and a white T-shirt, a drawing board slung over his back. He looked at me with curiosity in his eyes. “Yes,” I stammered. “Just… taking a few random shots.”

“This windmill is really nice,” he said, walking over and glancing down at the photos on my camera. “Mind if I take a look?” Instinctively, I hid the camera behind my back. “Ah, they’re just random shots, not very good. No need to look.” He smiled and stepped back. “All right, up to you. But this kind of place really is pretty good for creating.”

His words made my face burn, as if he had seen right through me. It felt as though all my inadequacy and lack of confidence were laid bare in those photos. My stomach began to ache faintly, and I rushed out an excuse: “I still have something to do, I have to go.” Then I almost fled that place.

After I got home, I still couldn’t let it go. I opened my computer and kept scrolling through those photos again and again. The more I looked, the more lifeless and dull they seemed. I began to imagine: if others saw these photos, would they think my taste was too ordinary? Would they think I didn’t deserve to call myself a creator at all? That night, I hardly slept. My mind kept replaying my performance at the windmill, full of regret and shame.

For the next few days, I sat staring at those photos, several times wanting to delete them, not even daring to upload them to social media. It wasn’t until one night a week later that I sat alone at my desk and reorganized the shots from that day. I tried to pick out a few with the softest light, made some simple adjustments, and finally uploaded them to my personal portfolio page, adding a line: “Sometimes, the moment light breaks in is when you see yourself most clearly.”

That night, a photography blogger who had followed me for years commented: “This is your softest body of work yet. You can feel the gentle yet conflicted emotions behind the lens.” In the middle of the night, I stared at those words until tears blurred my vision.

Standing in an old woodworking shop, sunlight streamed through a half-open window onto the floor, sawdust lay scattered everywhere, and the air was filled with the distinctive fragrance of wood. Around me were all kinds of wooden furniture, casually arranged, as if hinting at the shop’s former bustle. I couldn’t help reaching out to touch an old wooden table, my fingers sensing the grain’s delicate texture and the marks left by time.

In this quiet, I suddenly heard whispers from the corner, where two craftsmen were talking. “Looking at them, they seem a little nervous,” one of them said in a gentle yet slightly appraising tone.

My heart instantly sped up, and my palms began to sweat. Were they talking about me? Had I done something wrong again? I quickly replayed my behavior from earlier, trying to figure out which actions might have seemed out of place. My mouth was suddenly filled with bitterness. Why is it that I can never relax, always feeling like an outsider?

“Are you okay?” A familiar voice sounded in my ear; it was the friend who had brought me here. His eyes were full of concern as he looked at me.

“I… I’m fine, just thinking about some things,” I forced out a smile, though I couldn’t help wondering whether he had seen through me.

“No need to worry, they were just talking casually,” my friend said, patting my shoulder gently in an attempt to comfort me.

“Thank you,” I replied, but the turmoil inside me took a long time to settle. Was I being too neurotic? Every time, I got this anxious over the smallest thing.

After saying goodbye to my friend, I walked out of the workshop alone. A light breeze brushed my face, bringing a sliver of comfort. But in my mind, I still kept turning over what had just been said, as if I needed to find some answer. I sat down on a bench by the street, trying to calm myself.

That night, I tossed and turned, unable to sleep. The scenes in the workshop kept replaying in my mind, and those whispered words echoed on and on. I tried to convince myself it had all been a misunderstanding, but unease surged in me like a tide.

A few days later, I gradually realized that I always cared too much about what others thought, often imagining things and reading too much into them; this destructive self-reflection left me exhausted. Perhaps I needed to learn to let go of some unnecessary worries and allow my mind to find true peace.

The sky was somewhat overcast, and the heavy clouds seemed to press down on my mood. I walked into an old, nearly forgotten video rental store in the southern part of the city. A faint musty smell filled the shop, making me feel as though I had stepped into a tunnel back to another time. The lighting was dim and yellowish, faded movie posters covered the walls, and rows upon rows of dusty videotapes lined the shelves. I gently brushed the dust off a tape with my fingers and looked at the blurred title on it.

Just then, the owner, a kind middle-aged man, came over with a smile. “Hello, can I help you?” he asked in a friendly, slightly expectant tone. I managed a forced smile in return, though inside I was tense with social unease. “I’m just looking around, thanks.”

I turned back to browse the other side of the shelves, and the uneasy feeling inside me began to build. I saw a tape labeled “Classic Comedy,” and immediately remembered how, years ago, I had told a terrible joke at a friend’s party. The embarrassment from that moment came rushing back like a tide. My heart raced, my palms grew sweaty, and my stomach began to churn.

“Are you looking for any specific movie?” the owner asked at just the right moment, interrupting me again. I was trying hard to control my breathing and keep myself from sinking deeper into embarrassment. “The past always makes people nostalgic, doesn’t it?” he said softly.

I nodded, trying to hide my panic. Yet the unease clutched at me like an invisible hand. I kept ruminating over those humiliating moments from the past, as if they were an inescapable fate.

When I stepped out of the shop, the air outside felt much fresher. I tried to take a deep breath and leave the tension behind. But like shadows, it wouldn’t go away; the small things that had been magnified in my mind still drove my heart to race. After I got home, I sat by the window, and the gloomy feeling lingered in my heart for a long time, as if it were quietly plotting the next storm in my mind.

A few days later, I thought back on what had happened in that video store. That brief social interaction and sudden sense of shame made me realize how often I am controlled by negative emotions. Even in simple everyday situations, I can’t help but rehearse the worst possible outcome. But I understand that this is me, and I need to find a way to accept it.

The café was bustling with conversation. I sat by the window, my fingers constantly rubbing the rim of my coffee cup, trying to calm myself down. Across from me sat my client, a stern-looking middle-aged man. He barely looked up at me, only staring at the documents in his hands. I tried to catch any hint from his expressions and tone, but he remained impassive, his voice flat. “This concept is quite creative, but are you sure it’s the best fit for our brand image?” he suddenly asked, looking up.

My heart immediately started racing, as if struck by lightning. “Well, I think we could start from the market needs of younger consumers, which could bring in some fresh energy…” I tried hard to keep my tone steady, attempting to explain my design logic. Yet my voice seemed so insignificant in front of him. He gave a slight nod, but no further response. The background music in the café remained upbeat, but to me it only seemed to deepen the heaviness in the air.

My mind was filled with self-doubt: Was my proposal not good enough? Did he think I was unprofessional? I couldn’t help but start ruminating on every similar situation from the past, all the mistakes I had made, all the clients I had lost, flooding back like a deluge and drowning out my thoughts. My palms began to sweat, my stomach churned, and panic rose inside me.

After a long silence, he finally said, “I think it’s worth trying. The data you mentioned is quite interesting; we hadn’t considered that before.” At that moment, I felt a wave of relief, but immediately fell into another worry: was he just humoring me?

On the way home, I kept replaying every word he said, every slight expression, even the faint crease in his brow when he drank his coffee. I couldn’t help feeling frustrated, afraid that I might face failure again in my career. That night, I read many books on brand strategy, hoping to find more inspiration and confidence.

A few days later, I received an email from him saying he was very satisfied with the proposal and looking forward to working together again. This put me somewhat at ease, but the unease in my heart never fully disappeared. I knew that this tendency to overanalyze and doubt myself was part of my personality, and perhaps I would never be able to escape it.

After I posted my new video, the notifications on my phone screen started flashing rapidly. The comments section felt like a battlefield, with all kinds of criticism pouring in, like invisible hands tightening around my throat. I could hear my heartbeat, each beat reminding me of some impending disaster. I sat at my desk, the cold glow of the screen reflected on my face, my fingers gripping the mouse so tightly that my knuckles turned white.

“Just look at your video. What a waste of time.” I clicked on one comment, and the harsh negative words stabbed into my heart like a knife. I could feel myself starting to sweat, while a low buzzing sound echoed in my head. I began to wonder if maybe I had really done something wrong.

My mind was in chaos. “Does everyone hate me? Did this video disappoint everyone?” Even when I tried to take deep breaths, my heart kept racing, and my stomach began to cramp.

Another comment came into view: “This kind of content is terrible, just as expected.” That sentence hit me like a hammer, bringing to mind those moments in the past when I had been abandoned, those times when I had been powerless to defend myself. I could feel my cheeks growing hot, and another wave of intense shame surged up inside me.

To avoid even harsher self-inflicted blows, I quickly closed closed the comments section. I buried my head in my hands, trying to block out everything from the outside world. I thought back to many years ago, when moments of embarrassment and failure had replayed in my mind again and again. Why am I always like this, always making myself suffer just to please others? It made me doubt my abilities, and whether I was really suited to be a creator. I realized that my sense of inadequacy was swelling, and these criticisms seemed like confirmation of what I had already feared deep down.

That night, I couldn’t sleep. Past moments of embarrassment and mistakes kept replaying in my head, and I kept going over other people’s words, trying to understand the true meaning behind their criticism. When I couldn’t fall asleep, I tried to distract myself by putting on music, but even those melodies felt grating.

The next day, I looked around like a ghost, utterly exhausted. I found that I didn’t want any contact with the world, and I even felt a trace of fear toward simple social interactions, afraid that in other people’s eyes I was no longer trustworthy or likable.

A few days later, as I gradually recovered from the flood of emotions, I realized that these criticisms were like a demon-revealing mirror, instantly exposing my deepest hidden fears. I resolved to face them and try to understand them in a healthier way.

A warm breeze brushed my face, and shafts of sunset light seeped through the cracks in the glass greenhouse. The mingled atmosphere of quiet and desolation made my heart tighten faintly. I stepped in carefully; the cracked glass panels reflected fragmented patches of light and shadow, and my shoes sank into the damp earth with a faint sticky sound. “This must have once been beautiful,” I murmured to myself, my voice echoing in the empty space, my throat a little dry. I kept walking, catching the faint scent of damp soil mixed with rotting plants, and a strange sense of familiarity washed over me. Perhaps this was some shattered projection of my inner self—I didn’t know.

Suddenly, my gaze came to rest in a corner: beside a rusty iron frame were several withered potted plants, and one of them still held a few half-green leaves, as if life itself were struggling desperately to survive. I crouched down to look; the moment my fingers touched a leaf, tiny fragments fell away. Yet I couldn’t bring myself to let go. I gently traced the remaining texture, and it reminded me of relationships I often tried so hard to salvage but could never control. “Why do things always erupt only at the very end?” That question surfaced faintly in my mind. I closed my eyes, my back tightening, as though some invisible weight were pressing heavily down on me.

“How did you find this place?” Footsteps came from behind me, and a brisk voice interrupted my thoughts. I stood up awkwardly—it was a community worker patrolling outside the greenhouse, wearing a uniform, his face slightly wary. “I just…” I looked down at the dead leaves and hid my hands behind my back, not knowing how to answer. He went on, “This place has actually been abandoned for years. People come in once in a while, but you know, it’s pretty dangerous.” I nodded and said, “Yes, I’ll leave right away.” He sighed and came over to tug at the plant’s iron support. “These things are all old; be careful.” Watching him, I couldn’t help thinking: “Am I just like the plant on that iron frame—only holding on at the surface, when I’ve already withered away?” My stomach suddenly clenched with pain, and I couldn’t tell whether it was emotion or a real physical reaction.

By the time I got home, it was completely dark. I sat in the middle of the living room, but no matter what I did, I couldn’t relax. In my mind, the withered leaves kept repeating themselves, their silent resistance carrying a faint mockery of me. I opened my computer, trying to strip away my feelings through writing, but with every sentence I typed, a wave of self-doubt rose up: “Is this really something worth expressing? Maybe it’s just an overly sensitive image.”

That night I barely slept. The pillow was damp, and the greenhouse scene kept echoing in my mind, a sense of helplessness wrapping around me like a giant net. The next afternoon, I picked up my pen again, trying to piece those emotions and images together into a story, only to find myself constantly worrying whether these broken fragments would be seen by others as meaningless venting. I stopped writing and stared out the window. The glass reflected my face, like a lingering shadow from the greenhouse.

Sunlight poured through the broken window onto the floor, adding a touch of warmth to the empty porcelain workshop. I gently pushed open the creaking door. The air was filled with the stale scent of earth and the smell of unfinished glaze, and unfinished pieces of porcelain were piled in the corner. I placed my hand lightly on a half-finished porcelain cup, feeling the rough glaze as my fingertips trembled slightly without my realizing it. I looked around, hearing only my own breathing echo through the hollow space. Each step seemed to declare my loneliness, and the sound of shattered shards of porcelain felt as though my inner self were breaking apart over and over.

Standing beside a long table covered with a jumble of ceramics, I tried to settle my mood into this chaotic stillness. Inside me, anxiety about the future and concern over unfinished work from the past were quietly intertwined. I asked myself, “If I discard every imperfect thing, will there come a day when I can no longer find even a trace of my own existence here?” Failures from the past kept resurfacing, like these unfinished works that could never be made whole. In the silence of that moment, I became acutely alert, as if this space were a true projection of my inner world.

Suddenly, I caught the faint musty smell of soil piled in the corner, and it reminded me of mistakes I had made over the past while and projects that had disappointed my partners. I recalled the critical remarks and furrowed brows, as if their disappointment had been whispering in my ear all along, growing louder and louder. My heart raced, my breathing grew shallow, and I felt a tightness in my stomach.

“This place seems to mirror me,” I said softly, an unconscious reaction that made the words slip out of me. In this abandoned workshop, I was astonished to realize that this silent environment seemed to reveal my body’s responses to me; sweat began to run down my forehead, and my heartbeat quickened even more.

For the rest of the time, I sat on the floor, staring at those worn ceramics, slowly coming to accept my mistakes and instability. A few days later, back home, I wrote this experience into an essay, trying to use words to understand my anxiety and unfinished creativity. I was still ashamed of my sensitivity, yet I came to realize that this was precisely where I should grow strong, healing through expression.

This experience led me to reexamine my place in the creative process, to accept imperfection, and to try to find a new starting point within myself through every failure.

At first light, I arrived at the abandoned warehouse. The walls were covered with wild, untended vines, and dust drifted through the air. My footsteps echoed in the empty space, leaving me with a sense of loneliness. The night before, I had received an email from senior management saying that the project I was responsible for had run into major obstacles and might not be able to continue. Images of past failures and moments of being rejected kept flashing through my mind, and I couldn’t stop myself from catastrophizing. A few birds were chirping outside the warehouse, but they did nothing to soothe the anxiety and panic in my heart. I felt a sharp cramp in my stomach, and my palms began to sweat, as if my whole body were protesting this helpless situation.

I called the project team members. “Everyone, we need to talk about the possibility that this project may be canceled.” There was silence on the other end of the line, followed by a few sighs. “Don’t worry yet. We still have time to make adjustments.” Their voices were comforting, but all I heard was helplessness.

I hung up and tried to take deep breaths, but my heartbeat still thundered like a drum. I asked myself: If this project really falls through, what am I supposed to do? All that effort would be in vain—would that mean my career is about to end?

I sat on the warehouse floor, leaning against the cold concrete wall, trying hard to calm myself down. By then, a stale, acrid smell filled the air, as if reminding me that this place had once been glorious, and now only decay remained. I told myself that perhaps this was like my own state of mind, filled with memories of past failures and being cast aside.

Later, when I left the warehouse, night had already fallen. I still couldn’t suppress that sense of unease, and I tossed and turned all night without sleeping. The next day, I decided to give myself some time away from work to think about how to face this setback and find a solution.

Over the next few days, I kept adjusting my mindset and worked hard to make myself stronger. I understood that no failure at work should define all of me. Though anxiety and fear still lingered, I began to try new ways of thinking and to face things more positively. The wounds of the past were still there, but I believed I could gradually find a way out.

The café was filled with the rich aroma of coffee and the soft sound of music. I held a warm cappuccino in my hands, feeling the slight tremble of the cup. Sitting in the corner, I looked around; everything seemed peaceful. My friends were talking animatedly, and I tried to join their conversation, but I felt uneasy inside, as if some uncertainty were lingering in my mind.

One friend suddenly mentioned her recent trip abroad, describing many fresh and interesting things. She looked at me and said, “You should try stepping out of these creative bubbles and seeing the outside world.” In that moment, it was as if someone had flipped a switch deep inside me. I felt my breathing suddenly quicken, my heartbeat speed up, and my palms start to sweat.

“I’m not sure that would help me,” I replied softly, trying hard to stay calm. Yet the inner monologue began to question myself relentlessly: “Is she implying that I’m lazy? Dismissing my efforts?” I tried to suppress that feeling, but I couldn’t stop traumatic memories of being abandoned and feeling incapable from rising up.

My body began to tense involuntarily, and I overinterpreted every subtle change in expression. I started reflecting on those times in the past when I had been overlooked, and the fear of rejection kept washing over me, impossible to escape. To keep these feelings from showing, I preemptively made a joke at my own expense, trying to cover up the turmoil inside.

“Haha, maybe I’m just used to this kind of lifestyle. Everyone has their own pace that suits them.” My voice was a little unsteady. A friend patted my shoulder. “It’s okay, relax.” Her reassurance made me feel a little better, but it still couldn’t completely erase the lingering anxiety.

After I got home, my mind kept replaying those words about “stepping out of the creative bubble.” Every time I remembered the conversation, my stomach felt uneasy, and an indescribable sense of loss lingered around me. I lay in bed, trying to calm myself, but deep down I was still unconsciously rehearsing all kinds of bad outcomes.

A few days later, I decided to message that friend, hoping to get more understanding and support from her. I wanted to confirm whether she was truly disappointed in me. Although her reply was full of care and support, I still felt a deep unease at the bottom of my heart.

I was standing in the activity hall, clutching the outline for the speech I had just given. The lights in the venue weren’t harsh, but the atmosphere made me feel suffocated. People gathered in small groups chatting, and the occasional burst of laughter stabbed at my eardrums like needles. I kept adjusting my posture, trying to seem relaxed, but my limbs felt as if they were filled with lead, so stiff that even moving looked unnatural.

One of my peers walked over and said in a low voice, “Your idea is very unique, but it’s a little immature.” My ears immediately grew hot, and I kept chewing over the words “unique” and “immature,” feeling as though they were a double-edged sword cutting through all my pretenses. I gave a stiff smile and said, “Thank you for your advice.” He responded with a hum, then turned away to talk to someone else.

I stood there motionless, my vision blurring, the sounds around me seeming sharp and chaotic. A strong wave of shame surged up from my stomach, accompanied by a racing heartbeat and sweaty palms. I kept replaying the conversation in my mind, his expression flashing before me—was it a hint of disdain? Or a smile tinged with pity? Why did he have to say that? Did he think I wasn’t qualified to be here at all?

“Are you okay?” Another event organizer came over and asked me. I forced out a smile. “I’m fine, I just suddenly feel a little dizzy.” He said, “Do you want to take a break? No need to be too nervous, everyone really appreciates your work.”

“Thank you, I think I should head out first.” I quickly brushed the topic aside, picked up my bag, and went straight for the exit. It felt as if people around me were watching me, or judging why I was leaving so abruptly. As I walked, every step felt like an escape.

When I got home, I threw my bag onto the sofa and collapsed onto the bed. My mind was filled with that assessment of “unique but immature.” I began to repeatedly examine what it meant: did he think I would never truly be recognized? Was everyone just humoring me? My stomach started to ache faintly, and I curled up at the head of the bed, hugging my knees, listening to the wind outside the window all night without being able to calm down.

The next day, I tried to open my laptop again and continue working, but I simply couldn’t focus no matter what I did. That sentence was like an anchor, pinning me in a whirlpool of shame that I couldn’t break free from. I began to doubt whether I was really suited for this line of work, and kept asking myself: Should I just give up?

In an abandoned printing factory, the air was thick with the stale scent of old paper. Amid that heavy sense of history, I slowly walked past the dust-covered machines, sensing the years when they had once bustled with activity. Scattered across the floor were broken printing samples; I stepped lightly over them, as if unwilling to disturb these sleeping memories. They seemed to tell countless stories from the past. When I reached a corner, I caught sight of an old diary out of the corner of my eye, its cover fallen off and its pages yellowed with age. I hesitated for a moment, feeling a little uneasy, but my curiosity compelled me to pick it up.

The moment I opened the diary, it felt as though I could hear my own heartbeat. Inside were the daily thoughts of an unknown author, filled with hopes for the future and helplessness toward the present. The words in the diary seemed to resonate with me in a strange way, as if they were speaking my own feelings. I quietly read these trivial yet genuine emotions, trying to find comfort in the words. Perhaps because I have always tended to catastrophize small things, seeing these words gave me an inexplicable warmth.

“What are you doing here?” A voice suddenly interrupted my thoughts. I snapped back to reality and realized it was the factory guard. I tried to explain myself, my tone mixed with unease and anxiety. “Oh, I was just looking around. Sorry for the disturbance.”

He glanced at me. “It’s been a long time since anyone came here. Be careful and don’t hurt yourself.” His voice was calm, but the unease in my heart did not lessen. I nodded to show I understood and turned my attention back to the diary. Though interrupted, I was still drawn to those delicate emotions. They seemed to have the power to ease my anxiety.

After leaving the factory, I still could not calm down. When I got home, I placed the diary on the table and stared at it, wondering: should I also record my own life, and release those uneasy, complicated emotions in written form? I began to feel ashamed of my sensitivity, yet at the same time I understood that it was something I could not change. So over the following week, I tried to change the way I faced anxiety, writing down my mood each night in a diary, hoping to find comfort and understanding in words.

This experience made me realize that even in ruins, one can find meaning of one’s own. Sometimes, when feeling lonely and anxious, perhaps we can find a missing connection in an unexpected place.

I was sitting in the conference room, surrounded by white walls, with the overhead lights a little too bright and the table covered with all kinds of documents and notebooks. A faint smell of coffee drifted through the air, and my palms were slightly damp. As we discussed the project, I felt my heartbeat begin to quicken. My colleagues’ voices filled my ears, sometimes clear, sometimes blurred. This mixed state made me uneasy.

“We should reevaluate this proposal,” one colleague said, her voice firm and confident. My heart tightened, and I wondered if the proposal I had put forward wasn’t good enough. Hearing other colleagues’ opinions in the meeting made me feel as if my suggestion was being scrutinized. I tried to smile, wanting to seem relaxed.

“I think we need to consider the budget,” I added next, trying to keep my tone calm. However, I began to mull over her expression again and again; she seemed a little impatient. Did that mean she disagreed with me? I felt a sharp knot in my stomach, my muscles tensing all over, and a slight sheen of sweat appeared on my forehead.

“It’s just a suggestion, of course, and we can continue discussing it,” I quickly added.

After the meeting ended, I slowly walked back to the office, my mind still filled with all the fragments from the meeting. My colleagues’ faces, their voices, and that moment of silence kept replaying in my head. I started blaming myself, wondering whether I should have seemed more confident or prepared more in advance. I walked over to the window and looked at the busy traffic outside, trying to calm myself down.

The next morning, I saw my colleagues’ feedback in my inbox. Some agreed with my proposal and offered constructive suggestions. This made me breathe a sigh of relief, as if yesterday’s self-doubt and anxiety had been unnecessary. But these experiences made me realize that overanalyzing other people’s reactions had become my habit, and that habit sometimes pulled me into an emotional whirlpool. I told myself that when discussing projects, I should focus more on the substance and not on other people’s microexpressions and tone of voice.

The office lights were glaringly bright. Everyone had gathered at a restaurant near the company after the year-end meeting, enjoying a steaming dinner. I was exhausted from spending the whole afternoon preparing my presentation, and my heartbeat still hadn’t settled down from the tension; from time to time, I felt a vague discomfort in my stomach. Not long after we sat down, my coworkers began chatting casually about today’s meeting and the approaching holiday atmosphere. The restaurant was filled with all kinds of sounds: clinking cutlery, low laughter and conversation, and faint background music.

A coworker sitting next to me suddenly turned and said with a smile, “Your presentation today was really profound—I almost couldn’t understand it.” His tone was lighthearted, but it suddenly made me tense up. My heart raced, and my palms began to sweat. I couldn’t tell whether he was genuinely complimenting me or implying that my performance hadn’t been good enough. I tried hard to recall in my mind whether my presentation had been too complex or whether I had made some mistake. “Really? Maybe I spoke too fast,” I managed to say with a forced smile, while internally I began to ruminate endlessly over those details.

I looked around; the other coworkers didn’t seem to notice this exchange and continued talking and laughing merrily. I felt surrounded by an invisible sense of isolation, as if the surrounding noise and laughter had nothing to do with me. I tried to adjust my posture, hoping to look a bit more relaxed, but my muscles remained tight and stiff. The words “profound” and “couldn’t understand” kept echoing in my mind, like a heavy haze blocking my thoughts and leaving me only able to respond mechanically.

“Actually, I think your analysis of industry trends was very insightful,” another coworker chimed in. “You should have confidence in yourself—after all, we all learned a lot from it.” Although her words eased me a little, I still wondered whether it was merely polite reassurance. All evening, I kept turning those conversations over in my mind, feeling an endless anxiety circling in my chest, while the tension in my stomach gradually intensified.

After I got home, I tried to relax with a shower. Warm water washed over my skin, but the effect of those words seemed hard to shake off, like a hidden sting that stayed with me. The next morning, I was still thinking about yesterday’s conversation, vaguely worried that it might affect how I was perceived among my coworkers. Although reason told me not to care too much, my emotions continued to churn.

A few days later, in another conversation with my coworkers, my presentation that day came up again, and everyone unanimously said they appreciated my unique analysis. Although this gradually improved my mood, I knew my tendency to overreact was still there, quietly triggering those old anxieties and unease at unexpected moments.

Soft light from the wall lamps fell over my work, as if trying its best to lend it some luster. I stood to one side, my hand clenched tightly around a glass of wine, but I could not calm myself. The guests around me stood in small clusters, speaking in low voices about something, yet all I could hear was a dull buzzing in my ears. I tried hard to relax, but their chatter gradually grew louder in my mind, like a noisy symphony I could not ignore.

“What do you think of this painting?” a well-dressed lady asked, turning to the gallery owner beside me.

“Well, it has a very distinctive style, though perhaps it’s a bit too emotional,” he replied, with what sounded like a hint of disdain.

My heart sank sharply, as if someone had struck it hard. I could feel my palms starting to sweat, and the slight trembling made it almost impossible to hold onto the wineglass. A voice of self-doubt began echoing in my head: They don’t like my work—does that mean I really have no talent? How could I be so foolish as to put it on display?

I tried to shift my attention elsewhere and took a deep breath, filling my nose with the mingled scents of champagne and flowers in the air, but it only made me feel more suffocated. I could not suppress the swelling emotions, as if the walls of the entire room were pressing in on me. While forcing a smile, I searched for somewhere I could breathe.

“It’s okay, they probably just didn’t appreciate how much effort you put into it,” a coworker passing by patted my shoulder, trying to comfort me.

I gave a stiff smile, though my stomach twisted painfully. I quickly slipped out through the side door and onto the balcony outside the gallery. The night air was cool, but it could not dispel the gloom in my heart. Leaning against the railing, my mind was a complete mess; all my doubts, shame, and anger tangled together. I closed my eyes, trying to force it all out of my head, but it only made the feeling sting more sharply.

After I got home, I locked myself in my room and could not fall asleep for a long time. Again and again, I reflected on myself, doubting my ability and my worth, as if I had returned to those times in my youth when I had been ignored and misunderstood. Over the next few days, I hardly dared to touch a paintbrush again, and even the sight of a canvas filled me with a helpless panic. Everything that happened that night felt like it had left an unhealable wound in my heart.

I had just closed my eyes on the sofa, the background music from the unfinished edited video still lingering in my ears. Suddenly, the ringing phone cut through the silence of the night. I froze for a moment and glanced at the clock: 2:12 a.m. My body stiffened as if electrocuted; a call this late had to mean bad news. I tried to reach for the phone on the table, but my fingertips were trembling and I couldn’t grip it properly. I pressed the answer button and cautiously said, “Hello?”

On the other end was my partner, who was also the planner on our team. His voice was unnaturally low, with a hint of hesitation. “Sorry to bother you at this hour,” he said. I forced a smile and tried to answer calmly: “A call in the middle of the night must mean something important, right?” In fact, my stomach had already begun to knot, and a vague unease was spreading like poison.

“Yeah, there is something I wanted to tell you in advance,” he said, his tone tentative and careful, which only made me more uneasy. “We’ve received a new collaboration opportunity, but the client specifically wants to change the creative direction. To be honest, they’d prefer to have... uh, another creator take it over.” His voice grew softer on the last few words, and I had to hold my breath just to hear him clearly.

I froze, my mind buzzing as if someone had suddenly snapped a steel wire. My heart began pounding wildly, as if it were about to burst out of my chest. I tried to take a deep breath, but my throat felt blocked, and air wouldn’t flow smoothly into my lungs. “Another creator?” I repeated, my voice almost trembling. He was silent for a moment on the other end, then said, “Yes, they feel your style might not fit the needs of their project and want to try a more aggressive expression.”

“I see.” I don’t know how I managed to say it. My tone sounded strangely calm, but my fingernails were digging hard into my palm, the skin stinging with pain. Yet the voice inside me was screaming: “See? They think you’re a failure! Everything you’ve worked for is being seen as ‘not good enough’!”

After the call ended, I stared at the ceiling and couldn’t sleep at all. My mind kept rapidly replaying every detail of our past collaborations, searching for where things might have gone wrong. I even thought back to a casual expression he’d had during a meeting a few weeks earlier—had it been hinting at this outcome all along? “Why didn’t he tell me earlier? Why did he have to hit me with this in the middle of the night?” I kept questioning myself, while also blaming my own sluggishness and incompetence. My stomach cramped violently again and again, and cold sweat had already soaked my back. I closed my eyes, but I could still hear my heartbeat clearly, heavy like one blow after another from a hammer.

The next day, I pretended nothing had happened and kept working, but inside I was bouncing around like a rabbit in panic. I opened the other party’s social media accounts several times, repeatedly studying his recent posts, hoping to glean more clues from them. Every few minutes, I couldn’t help checking my phone, expecting some additional explanation or clarification from him, but there was no message at all. I felt like an island left behind in the wilderness, completely without direction.

The glaring fluorescent lights in the office made my scalp tighten. I sat on one side of the conference table, fingers clenched around the edge. The editor handed me a printed manuscript with a sheet of densely marked revisions in red pen. I glanced at the slashes and circles, and my stomach immediately twisted into a knot. He began speaking in a calm tone, but with an undercurrent of indifference: “This part is too emotionally overstated. I suggest cutting some of the repetitive sentences, especially the last paragraph—it feels a bit melodramatic.” My throat dried instantly. I stared at the corner of his mouth, trying to catch that hidden trace of sarcasm or disdain. “I spent a lot of time polishing this section because it accurately conveys the character’s emotions—it’s important!” I heard myself snapping back, my voice quick and tense, while my heartbeat thudded faster and faster in my chest.

He didn’t answer. Flipping through the manuscript, he pointed to another mark. “And here, the narrative logic is a bit abrupt. Readers might find it confusing.” A wave of heat rose up my back, sweat sliding along the side of my neck. A thought flashed through my mind: Was he simply not acknowledging my ability at all? I kept arguing, my voice trembling. “I think the abruptness here is intentional. It’s meant to reflect the character’s anxiety.” He frowned and replied in a somewhat serious tone, “Of course anxiety can be shown, but the key is to make sure readers can keep up.” His gaze drifted toward the window, and I couldn’t help thinking: Has he already started to find me annoying? Does he think I’m too difficult to communicate with?

After the meeting ended, I almost rushed back to my desk, replaying the conversation over and over in my head. Every tone, every expression was magnified into a possible rejection. I could hear my own heartbeat pounding in my ears. The plastic armrest of the chair felt cold. I sat there with both hands gripping my knees, trying to calm myself down, but I couldn’t stop wondering: Is my work really that bad? Why do I always feel like I’m not good enough?

That night, lying in bed and staring at the gray blotches on the ceiling, my mind was like a recorder that wouldn’t shut off, endlessly replaying the editor’s furrowed brow. I began to wonder if I had been abandoned by this industry, if even he thought I was worthless. The burning sensation in my stomach made me toss and turn, and I didn’t finally drift off until two in the morning. When I woke the next day, my eyelids felt heavy, and those doubts were still echoing in my head. I even didn’t dare open my computer to check the feedback in my emails.

Outside the window, the sky gradually darkened, and the bookstore lights cast a warm yellow glow on the glass. I sat by the window seat in the bookstore, holding the coffee cup that had almost gone cold, my fingertips slightly chilled. The reading group that had just ended was still swirling in my mind—or rather, certain fragments and discordant sounds were still swirling there.

“I think this part of the analysis is a bit subjective; it’s more of an emotional impression, isn’t it?” That was said by a middle-aged man sitting across from me at the round table. As he spoke, he pushed up his glasses; his voice was not loud, yet it pierced my chest like a needle. I froze for a moment, then nodded in agreement. “Yeah, maybe that’s true.” But I could clearly feel my throat growing dry, and even my smile seemed forced.

After the meeting ended, I didn’t leave right away. I made up an excuse that I needed to sort out my things and stayed behind. In truth, I wasn’t sorting anything at all; I just needed some time to steady myself. That sentence kept echoing in my mind—“emotional impression.” His tone had been calm, but to me it felt like an invisible accusation, aimed directly at my flaw: not rational enough, too sentimental, even a little amateurish. My God, had he just implied that I didn’t really belong there?

My hands started to tremble a little, and even taking a breath felt stuffy in my chest. I looked out the window; passersby came and went in blurred silhouettes, each one hurrying along as if they were somehow more purposeful, more meaningful than I was. Images from similar moments in the past surfaced in my mind—those times when I felt riddled with flaws. Maybe I really was an overly emotional “outsider,” always hiding my inner unease, yet still seen through at a glance.

“Are you okay?” It was the bookstore clerk, someone I had become somewhat familiar with recently. She came over and asked in a concerned tone. I forced out a smile. “I’m fine, just want to relax a bit.” She didn’t ask any more questions and smiled as she returned to the cashier counter. Her thoughtfulness made me feel like crying for a moment, but these were my own emotions; I couldn’t let others see how fragile I was.

I clenched my teeth and told myself, “He’s just expressing an opinion. It has nothing to do with you.” But another voice deep inside said, “No, he’s right. Everyone can see that you’re hiding something. You’re the problem.” A slight spasm began in my stomach, as if something had twisted inside it, making me feel even worse.

It was only after I got home that night that I still couldn’t shake off what had been said during the day. I sat on the sofa, absentmindedly flipping through a novel, but I couldn’t read a single page. The repeated emotional blow had triggered an instinct in me: attack myself first. I wasn’t sure whether this self-attack was meant to vent my feelings or to get ahead of whatever criticism others might have leveled at me.

The next morning, my emotions had eased somewhat, but the exhaustion still lingered around me. I began trying to reexamine the whole incident—perhaps he really had just been expressing a normal opinion, rather than rejecting me personally. But this rational analysis was fleeting. I still felt a small “me” in my mind constantly reminding me, “Others can do it, so why can’t you?”

I walked into a small craft store in the northern part of the city. The air was filled with the mixed scent of wood and paint, creating a slightly heavy feeling. The shop was cluttered, yet full of creative energy: brightly colored yarn hung on the walls, and wooden boxes held all kinds of stone-carved figurines. As I wandered through the store, my heart began to race. Every time I saw some novel material, countless creative ideas flashed through my mind, only to be instantly dismissed by myself. “This could turn into a disaster. I might end up turning all these things into a pile of useless junk,” I muttered to myself.

“Can I help you?” The clerk, a smiling middle-aged man, came over and asked with concern.

“Oh, um, I’m looking for some materials suitable for collage.” My voice trembled slightly, worried I might say the wrong thing. “Those paints look nice, but I’m not sure I’ll be able to use them well.”

“Don’t worry. Collage is a great way to create freely. These paints are easy to use, so there won’t be any problem,” he explained patiently.

I nodded, trying not to overanalyze his tone, while my mind still churned with every possible scenario that could go wrong. “What if I buy these expensive paints and the work fails? Would the clerk think I wasted the good things he recommended? Would people laugh at me?” My stomach started to twist, and my hands clenched unconsciously.

In the end, I steeled myself and picked out some brightly colored paints and a few unique sheets of paper, placing them on the counter. When it came time to pay, I struggled to control my overwhelming anxiety, my palms starting to sweat. “Please wait a moment; I’ll get you a bag,” the clerk said kindly.

When I left the store, the cool autumn wind brushed against my skin, and my thoughts eased a little. After I got home, I neatly laid out the materials on my worktable, trying to sort out my ideas, but my heart was still racing. I took a deep breath and tried to believe the clerk’s words, telling myself: “There is no right or wrong in collage, only exploration.” A few days later, I finally began to create. Although every stroke still came with a racing heartbeat, I forced myself to keep going and did not immediately destroy the piece.

This experience made me realize that I am always immersed in fear of failure, but being willing to take a brave step despite the tension may bring unexpected rewards.

Sunlight filtered through the gauze curtain and spilled inside, dappled light and shadow falling across the floor. I gently pushed open the balcony door and felt a warm rush of air wash over me. There were several potted plants on the balcony; the pothos leaves gleamed in the sun, as if they had just been polished with oil. I dragged an armchair into the corner, where the sunlight was brightest and the place was also the quietest. The surface of the chair felt a little rough to the touch, but sitting down was surprisingly comfortable. In my hands was a novel, the text on the cover already somewhat faded. I had bought it a few years ago, but had never gotten around to opening it.

Earbuds in my ears, music flowed softly out—light instrumental music, with no lyrics, only a weave of piano and strings. Now and then I could hear car horns from the street in the distance, but that sound was quickly swallowed by the sunlight and the music. I opened the book and watched the words flicker across the page, but my attention kept drifting; every so often I would look up at the sky. Today the sky was a clear, vivid blue, with a few white clouds moving lazily across it like leisurely brushstrokes.

Random thoughts flickered through my mind: whether the cabinets at home should be tidied up, whether the beach in last night’s dream meant I’d been thinking too much about traveling lately. As I thought, I realized I had been stuck on the same paragraph for several minutes. I lowered my head and gave a self-mocking laugh, thinking that my concentration was still as poor as ever.

I kept turning the pages and finally began to be drawn into the story. The protagonist in the book was going through an adventure, while I felt that the breeze on the balcony was also a small adventure of its own. The wind gently toyed with my hair, a strand slipping across my cheek like sunlight teasing me. I put the book down and reached my hand toward the light, realizing that my palm was a little cool, in a strange contrast to the warmth of the sun.

After sitting for a while, the leaves of the plants seemed even greener, and I heard a few bird calls drifting in from afar, clear and brief. I couldn’t help taking off my headphones, wanting to listen closely to their voices. The birdsong mingled with the rustling of leaves like an arrangement by nature itself. I picked up my phone and took a photo of the balcony, where light and shadow and plants formed a tranquil scene. After taking it, I hesitated, and in the end still didn’t post it to social media, saving it only on my phone. In that moment, I felt that I didn’t need to share it with anyone; this brief peace was enough to satisfy me.

Before leaving the balcony, I pushed the chair back to its original spot and folded the page at the place where I had stopped reading. When I stepped back into the room, I felt as though my face still carried a lingering warmth from the sun. There was a faint lightness in my heart, like a note that had been gently soothed. Later, I made myself a cup of coffee and sat in the living room, glancing occasionally toward the balcony, where the plants and the play of light and shadow seemed still to be waving at me—as if this afternoon had not yet come to an end.

The wooden floorboards creaked softly beneath my feet, and the air inside the museum was filled with an indescribably stale scent—mixed with the faint metallic smell of rust and the musty aroma of old paper. I stood before a huge grandfather clock, its silver clock face reflecting the dim light, the intricate carvings blurring my vision.
