The tour guide’s voice came from afar: “This clock dates back to the eighteenth century and represents exquisite craftsmanship.” I tried to focus on the explanation, but the whispers around me and the occasional footsteps only made me more distracted, as if every sound were reminding me that my moment of self-doubt had already shown through.

A visitor walked up beside me, glancing from the camera in my hands to the grandfather clock. He said, “Are you a photographer? Your equipment looks pretty professional.” I hesitated, swallowed, and silently reminded myself to seem calm and natural. “Yeah, I am,” I replied, trying to keep my voice steady. But inside, my thoughts churned nonstop: He said I looked “professional”—did he really mean it, or was he just being polite? Had he noticed my lack of confidence while taking photos?

Then he asked, “How’s the shooting going today? Anything interesting?” My heart felt as though it had been tightly gripped, and my breathing quickened. For some reason, I felt a deep implication hidden in his words, as if he were questioning whether I had the ability to capture these beautiful scenes.

I forced out a smile: “It’s okay, I mostly take detail shots.” Then I turned and left. Behind me came his quiet farewell, but what filled my ears was the sound of my own racing heartbeat. My palms began to sweat, my stomach tightened slightly, and I wanted to escape that space without seeming too abrupt.

Later, I stopped in front of a glass case displaying antique watches. Inside, metal dials were set with tiny diamonds, and the hands were frozen at a single moment, as if eternally preserving their brilliance. I stared at the patterns on those watches, trying to quiet my mind, but suddenly a flood of self-reproach surfaced: Why couldn’t I have been more confident just now? Why do I always feel like I’m going to make a mistake? This inescapable unease kept grinding away at my thoughts like the gears of a clock.

Half an hour later, I finally left the museum. Morning sunlight spilled across the city streets, seeming to tell me it was all over, but my mood remained heavy. After returning home, I sat in front of the computer and imported a few photos from my camera, trying to distract myself with work. Yet when I looked at the compositions, my first reaction was to nitpick their flaws: this one was too dark, that one had too much clutter in the background. I found myself looking at the same photo over and over until my eyes grew sore. So I shut down the computer, put the camera back in the cabinet, and tried to take deep breaths, but the tightness in my chest wouldn’t go away.

Over the next few days, I kept replaying the visitor’s words, even thinking about his expression and tone. Each time I recalled it, I felt more like a failure, as if I were trapped in a maze I could never escape. In the end, I decided to send the photos to an editor I trusted and ask her to evaluate them. Her feedback put me somewhat at ease, but the shadow of self-doubt still surfaced from time to time, making it hard for me to truly feel calm.

Standing in that dusty old warehouse, I could feel the cold seeping into my skin from every direction. Faint sunlight streamed through the high windows in shafts of light, and the drifting dust added a mysterious, lonely atmosphere. I was looking for the perfect shot for my new short film, and everything here seemed made for that story.

As I adjusted the camera’s focus, a low voice came from behind me: “What are you doing here?” My heart raced. I turned around and saw a middle-aged man in a dark overcoat, expressionless, his gaze full of suspicion. “Oh, I’m filming a short here. I have permission,” I said, trying to stay calm, though my voice trembled a little.

The emptiness of the warehouse made every word he spoke sound even louder. He continued, “This isn’t a place ordinary people can just wander into. Be careful.” His words made me uneasy, and my heartbeat grew more intense. I could feel a thin sweat breaking out on my forehead, even though I was still wearing a heavy coat. Why was he saying this? Was it a warning, or a kind reminder?

“Okay, I’ll be careful. Thanks for the reminder.” I gave an awkward smile and watched the stranger turn and leave. His figure disappeared into the other end of the warehouse, leaving only silence behind. I kept thinking over his tone and expression, wondering if I had crossed some invisible line. I’m always like this, always taking things too seriously.

Standing there, I tried hard to focus on continuing the shoot, but I couldn’t help imagining all the things he might dislike about me. I could hear my own inner voice criticizing me: “You’re always like this. Why do you always put yourself in situations like this?” My stomach began to ache faintly, and I knew anxiety was to blame.

The shoot finally began to resume slowly. Amid the whirring of the camera, I tried to push away those uneasy thoughts. But when I stepped out of the warehouse and the cold wind hit me, I still couldn’t shake off that feeling of being blamed.

After I got home, I was still unsettled. Even though it was over, I kept thinking, “What if that man reports me?” That thought echoed in my mind often over the next few days. I replayed that scene over and over, examining every detail, trying to defend my actions. In the end, that anxiety weighed on me and made me decide to choose filming locations more carefully, so I wouldn’t run into a similar situation again.

I walked into a hidden old scrap-recycling yard in the south of the city, and the surroundings made me feel uneasy. Scattered across the gray concrete ground were all kinds of discarded materials, and the large open-air metal recycling bins looked rusty under the sunlight. A foul smell of metal mixed with paint hung in the air, making me frown. In the distance, I could hear the loud conversations of the recycling yard workers and the occasional roar of machinery, sounds that felt especially harsh to my ears.

I walked up to a worker who was unloading scrap, trying to ask about how the materials were sorted. “Hello, may I ask what standard these scraps are sorted by?” I tried to keep my voice calm, but the tension inside me somehow seeped into my tone.

The worker looked up, seeming a little impatient. “They’re sorted according to company instructions. Do you have a problem?” His words carried a hint of contempt, and in an instant I felt a wave of tension seize my heart. Instinctively, I began replaying the conversation in my head, trying to figure out whether I had done anything to offend him. My heartbeat quickened, a thin sweat broke out in my palms, and I struggled to keep myself from overexplaining.

“Oh, nothing, I just wanted to understand,” I forced out a smile, feeling even my facial muscles stiffen. After leaving the workstation, I kept thinking about what the worker had said. Why was he so cold? Had I seemed too nervous again?

For the rest of the day, I kept chewing over this simple exchange. Whenever I recalled the worker’s slightly provocative tone, my stomach would burn. Anxiety led me to imagine the worst possible scenarios, worrying that I might be mistaken for someone who didn’t know the rules or was simply being unreasonable.

Back home, I tried to calm myself by doing simple things, like reading books or listening to music, but self-doubt inside me lingered like an inescapable shadow. After a few days, I still felt unsettled, and I began to question my social skills, feeling that I always failed to handle these everyday interactions properly.

Although I tried to adjust my mindset, anxiety remained like a persistent fog, affecting my sleep and mood. That night, lying in bed and staring blankly at the ceiling, I realized that this habit of overinterpreting minor events had become part of my habitual thinking.

As the lights gradually dimmed, the murmurings in the audience faded with them. I sat in the middle of the third row, palms sweating, fingertips slightly cold. A peculiar scent filled the space, mixed with stage makeup and old wood. A suffocating sense of oppression rose in my chest. I had been clutching the program booklet tightly, my eyes fixed on every scene about to unfold. Onstage, the actors were nervously getting ready, the lights began to shift, and the music started. My heartbeat quickened, as if my heart were about to leap out of my chest.

“Is everything ready?” I asked the director sitting beside me in a low voice, a question I had already asked countless times. He gave a slight nod, his gaze fixed intently on the stage. To me, his silence seemed to carry some implied negation, and that negation was like a thorn stabbing into my heart. Those nonexistent tiny flaws seemed to mock me from the shadows. I let out a soft sigh, trying to calm myself down.

The lights suddenly became dazzling, and the actors began their dialogue. I tried hard to focus, afraid of missing even the slightest detail. The rhythm of the lines, the actors’ facial expressions, every tiny change was magnified in my mind, as if any small mistake would be scrutinized by the audience under a magnifying glass. “If this performance fails, what should I do?” My anxiety surged like a tide, and images filled with unease began flashing through my mind.

Just as I was brooding over it again and again, a slight burst of laughter came from the audience—the first laughter so far—and my stomach suddenly twisted. I began to let my imagination run wild: was the audience laughing because of an actor’s mistake? Was it because there was something wrong with the stage set? A sense of abandoned panic began to consume me, and I even felt my legs trembling.

The performance lasted about an hour and ended amid the audience’s enthusiastic applause. Only then did I realize my fingers had gone stiff from tension. I exchanged complicated glances with the director, seeming to confirm the success of the performance. A few audience members came over, smiling, to express their satisfaction, yet I still felt uneasy inside.

After I got home, I tossed and turned all night, unable to sleep. Although the performance had been a success, I still worried whether someone was criticizing it behind our backs, whether someone disliked it, whether someone didn’t approve. The next morning, I compiled the feedback on the show and saw that most people had given positive reviews, but my mood still couldn’t settle down; a trace of unease remained. I knew this feeling would not dissipate easily. It was part of my nature, constantly stirring up unnecessary worries in my heart.

I stood in the center of the abandoned old observatory, surrounded by the silent, huge dome. Dust floated in the air, and sunlight streamed through the dilapidated windows onto the floor, casting mottled patches of light and shadow. My task was to sort through the observatory’s records from the past several decades, even though the place had been unused for years. I leafed through a stack of yellowed archives, the paper rough and heavy to the touch. Occasionally, birds called outside the window, making the place feel even lonelier. After I had been working for a while, my colleague came over to me and seemed somewhat dissatisfied with my progress. He frowned and said, “You still haven’t finished organizing these records? We need to move faster.” Hearing this, my chest immediately tightened, and my heart began to race. It was as if someone were loudly accusing me in my ear; in an instant, I felt a fear of being abandoned and a sense of inadequacy. Anger and shame intertwined, making it hard for me to pull myself out of it. I tried to explain, “I’m doing my best to sort them faster, but the materials here are really too disorganized.” I could even feel my palms beginning to sweat slightly, and a tightness rose in my stomach. My voice sounded a bit shaky, though I tried to stay calm. The other person shook his head helplessly and turned to leave. The room fell silent again. My mind began replaying the conversation over and over, and the self-criticism deep inside me was quickly activated. I ruminated on my past mistakes and doubted whether I was suited for this job. Why am I always so sensitive? Why can’t I handle criticism from others with ease? That night, I lay in bed, thinking back on what had happened during the day, unable to calm down for a long time. It wasn’t until a few days later that I finally managed to comfort myself by saying that perhaps it had just been a misunderstanding, and that colleague had not been targeting me on purpose. Although I knew this way of thinking was not necessarily entirely correct, it at least eased my emotions a little.

Sunlight filtered through the leaves and scattered across the path as I strolled leisurely through the park. My feet sank into the soft grass, and the sound of birdsong drifted gently by my ears, making everything feel peaceful. But not long after, I heard a small dog barking incessantly nearby, its sharp, piercing cries cutting through the calm.

“Hey there, little one, stop barking,” I heard a woman say, clearly trying to soothe the dog. Yet that voice seemed to stir my unease even more, and I kept thinking: why don’t those people do something about their dog? It’s clearly supposed to be a relaxing afternoon—why should it be interrupted by this constant barking?

At that moment, it seemed my heartbeat quickened, and my palms grew slightly damp. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself and telling myself it was just a minor interruption, nothing worth getting upset over. But the irritation inside me rose like a small flame, hard to control.

I kept walking, hoping that putting more distance between myself and the noise would help me escape it. Instead, it made me focus on it even more. The more I tried to ignore it, the clearer it became. So I couldn’t help muttering to myself, “This is so annoying!”

After a while, things finally took a turn. The dog’s owner seemed to pick it up, and the barking gradually faded away. I could feel my tense shoulders slowly relax, and the irritation in my heart eased along with them.

On the way home, I was still thinking about what had just happened, wondering if I had been a little too sensitive—maybe there was no need to feel so disturbed by a dog’s barking. But for some reason I couldn’t explain, little things like this always seemed so important.

By evening, in the quiet bedroom, there was only the faint sound of the wind outside the window. Lying in bed, I thought back on that little episode in the park. I felt a bit helpless about my own sensitivity, yet I was also somewhat used to being this way. Perhaps instead of being hard on myself, I should be kinder to my own fragility, just as I would be with a friend.

The next morning, I still chose to go for a walk in the park. Not for any other reason, but because it was the brief moment of peace I had set aside for myself. Even if it was occasionally disturbed, it was still a quiet time I cherished.

Warm light spilled over the dining table, candlelight swaying gently, the air filled with the mellow aroma of red wine and the rich scent of steak. A few close friends sat around the table, laughter and conversation flowing nonstop, while I tried hard to adjust my expression and appear relaxed. Still, I couldn’t stop the faint undercurrent of tension. Every time someone looked at me with a smile, my heartbeat would quicken, my palms would grow slightly damp. Over and over in my mind, I kept asking: Do they really like me? Behind every smile, is there mockery I can’t see?

The gathering was in full swing when one of the usually quiet friends suddenly said in a light tone, “You’re always so sensitive. That’s really interesting.” His words sounded casual, but my eyes were fixed on his face, trying to read whether there was any sarcasm hidden in his subtle expression. My brain immediately jumped to the conclusion that he was implying I wasn’t good enough, and my cheeks began to burn, my heart pounding like thunder.

“I’m not that sensitive,” I shot back quickly, my tone a little sharp. The moment I said it, I regretted it, worried it would lead to deeper misunderstanding and hostility. I lowered my head and pretended to be deeply interested in the food on my plate, avoiding the looks they cast my way.

The voice inside me kept blaming me: Why did you say that? What will they think? Did you say something wrong again? Will they think I’m rude or too sensitive? The tightness in my stomach made it hard to keep eating, and in my mind a catastrophic drama of being isolated began to unfold: my friends leaving me one by one, me forgotten in a corner, becoming the subject of their conversations behind my back.

Even after that night ended, I still couldn’t calm down. When I woke up the next morning, I was still filled with anxiety and shame. Looking back on the conversation with my friends, I desperately tried to figure out what had gone wrong—whether I hadn’t done well enough, whether I had made them uncomfortable. Within a week, I tried several times to call that friend and explain, worried about losing the friendship, but in the end I stopped myself because I was afraid it would only deepen their resentment toward me. I made a promise to myself that next time we met, I would be more careful and avoid falling into such a situation again.

The plates on the dining table had already been cleared away, leaving only a few unfinished cups of tea. I sat on the living room sofa, the carpet beneath my feet soft yet suffocating. After the family gathering ended, my partner’s tone made me start imagining, beyond my control, whether he was unhappy with how I had acted. When he came over, I asked tentatively, “Do you think I talked too much tonight?” He paused, his expression looking a little tired. “It’s fine. You don’t need to worry this much every time.” In that moment, his tone pricked my heart like a needle. I kept turning over the meaning of that “you don’t need to worry this much every time,” and all kinds of scenes immediately flooded my mind: Did he think I was annoying? Did he think I had embarrassed him in front of others? Was he already tired of our relationship?

My stomach began to ache dully, my palms broke out in sweat, and my ears slowly grew hot. I stood up to take the teacups to the kitchen, but the cup in my hand slipped and nearly fell to the floor. He frowned and said, “Why are you always so careless?” That sentence struck down like a heavy hammer, and in an instant my mind replayed countless scenes from the past—plates I had broken, things I had said wrong in public, messages I had sent that were ignored. All of those images told me one thing: I really was someone who disappointed others.

I held back my tears with all my strength, but my voice was already choked with sobs. “I’m sorry, I really didn’t mean to. I know I always mess things up.” He looked at me, frowning, his tone cold. “Why are you always so tense? I was just making a casual remark.” But I could clearly feel his impatience, a feeling like an unstoppable current, violently washing over my chest. I wanted to explain, but I was afraid that the more I explained, the more incompetent I would seem; I wanted to calm down, but my heart kept racing faster and faster.

That night he went back to the bedroom early, leaving me alone in the living room. I sat there, the light from the chandelier glaring in my eyes, the faint cool fragrance of tea in the cup drifting into my nose, and the ticking of the clock on the wall sounding in my ears. Those sounds and sensory details made me feel as if everything around me was mocking my incompetence. I began to replay every detail of the argument over and over, wondering again and again whether there was hidden blame in what he had said. My mind became more and more chaotic, and I even began to doubt whether I was fundamentally unworthy of being loved.

The next morning, he asked if I wanted to have breakfast together. I replied softly, “No, I’m not very hungry.” Although he tried to seem calm, I felt some kind of disappointment in his eyes. I wanted to say something to him, but the thought of “what if he thinks I’m even more annoying” pressed down on me so hard that I couldn’t get a single word out. When I grabbed my bag and left, it felt like a knot had tied itself in my stomach, and I was indescribably exhausted.

The air was filled with the damp scent of earth as I wandered through a small pottery market on the edge of the city. The stalls around me were packed with exquisite ceramic pieces, colorful and shimmering softly in the daylight. I paused to watch an artist glazing a porcelain vase, their skillful hands inspiring admiration. Music from afar mingled with the sound of people talking, making this cloudy afternoon feel especially peaceful.

Just as I was immersed in the world of pottery, my phone vibrated with a message from a friend. We had arranged to meet at the market; she was always full of enthusiasm, as if she could always bring good cheer. However, a joking remark from her made me freeze in place: “Why are you always looking at these things? Are you trying to find some inspiration to fill a creative void?”

My heart instantly raced, my palms began to sweat, and I could feel my stomach tightening in waves. She may have meant nothing by it, but my mind spun relentlessly: “Yes, am I really lacking inspiration? Is my creative bottleneck that obvious? Is she implying that I’m falling behind?” These thoughts clung to me like a shadow, leaving me with nowhere to escape.

“Are you okay?” she asked with concern when I still hadn’t responded.

“Oh, I’m fine,” I managed a smile. “I was just thinking about my work.”

She nodded as if she thought nothing of it and continued telling me about her recent life. To keep her from noticing my unease, I forced myself to listen carefully, nodding in response with caution. But my mind had already drifted far away, and the sounds around me seemed muffled, as if separated by a thin veil.

After saying goodbye to my friend, I wandered alone among the stalls, trying to relax as much as possible. The pottery around me was beautiful beyond measure. I tried lightly running my fingers over their textures, feeling their unique touch, hoping it would calm me down.

When I got home, I sat at my desk with my notebook open before me, but I remained motionless. The blankness of the white page weighed on me even more, and that feeling lasted into the evening. When night fell, I lay in bed, repeatedly thinking over everything that had happened that afternoon. My emotions were like a roller coaster, never finding a point to stop.

A few days later, I decided to write down the experience, trying to sort out my inner feelings and fears through words. I realized that my friend’s words had only triggered my insecurity, and that the self-doubt buried deep in my heart was always searching for an outlet.

After reflecting, I told myself: I must face this unease, and stop avoiding it. The creative process is inherently full of challenges, and those challenges are precisely opportunities for growth. Just like the clay in a potter’s hands, only after repeated firings can it be refined into its most perfect form.

Sunlight spilled across the community garden, and I used my free time that afternoon to come here and trim a few potted plants. The scissors in my hand glittered in the light as I focused on the edges of the green leaves, catching the faint, pleasant scent of soil and plants now and then. The garden was quiet, with only the occasional breeze rustling the leaves. Suddenly, a familiar voice broke the stillness. “Oh, there you are!” My neighbor poked her head up from the flower bed next door. “You seem to have been really busy lately?” Hearing that, my heart sank slightly. Her words always made me feel a little uneasy, and I couldn’t help wondering whether she was hinting at something.

“Well, yes, a bit.” I replied, trying to keep my tone calm. But an inner voice kept turning it over again and again: Was she saying I didn’t have time to take care of these plants? Or that my contribution to the community wasn’t enough? My heartbeat began to quicken, as if that small question had stirred up waves in my chest.

“Your plants look nice, very neatly trimmed.” Her voice came again, sounding very friendly. I forced myself to smile, trying to suppress the urge to read too much into it. “Thanks, I’m just trying to make them look better.” My voice tightened slightly as I worked to stay composed. My hands were a little sweaty, and the scissors felt slippery in my palm.

After I finished trimming the last plant, I put away my tools, still feeling somewhat tense. That tension slowly faded with time, but left a faint aftershock deep in my mind. When I got home, I kept telling myself it had just been an ordinary conversation, and that my anxiety had been unnecessary. That evening, I opened a bottle of red wine and tried to relax in a more laid-back atmosphere. A few hours later, the unease had finally disappeared completely, and I realized that there probably had been no deeper meaning behind the conversation at all—that all that tension had been caused entirely by me.

The next morning, I decided to go back to the garden for a walk. This little community space always made me feel at ease, even if it occasionally came with a few ripples. Last night’s uneasiness no longer affected me. I took a deep breath and enjoyed the quiet that belonged to me.

I sat on the wooden chair in the studio, sunlight streaming through the half-drawn curtains and falling across the floor in mottled patches of light and shadow. My collaborator and I were discussing the creative direction of the new project. His voice was full of certainty, while my heart was filled with anxiety and unease. He looked at me and, with obvious impatience in his tone, said, “Why are you always so negative? We can’t keep moving forward at this pace.” His voice echoed through the room, mingling with the sound of my own heartbeat.

My heart raced, and my body felt burning hot, sweat beginning to gather on my forehead. I struggled to suppress the fear and shame inside me, but I couldn’t help remembering the times I had been abandoned in the past. Every time someone showed disappointment or dissatisfaction, I felt as if I were being shoved back into that helpless age again. “I’m just thinking we should keep the risks as low as possible,” I said weakly in defense, my body stiff as a stone.

“We can’t always be afraid of risk,” his voice seemed to be pushing my limits, and suddenly a surge of anger erupted inside me. “You don’t understand at all—I’m doing this for the good of the team!” I shot back loudly, my voice trembling a little. The moment the words left my mouth, I felt a wave of regret and self-reproach, fearing that such a retort would only damage our relationship further.

My stomach began to cramp, as if an invisible hand were tearing at it. I looked at him; expressionless, he silently watched me, intensifying my sense of defectiveness. “If this won’t work, then let’s each go our own way,” he said coldly. In that moment, it felt as if the whole world were collapsing. I felt my heart being tightly clenched, and breathing became difficult.

When he left, the door slammed shut with a dull thud, and I was left alone in the empty studio, numb with despair. I sat in the chair for a long time, not knowing how to face this situation. That night, I tossed and turned, unable to sleep, my mind replaying his words and his departing figure again and again.

In the days that followed, I fell into endless self-doubt, and every decision felt like an enormous struggle. I kept wondering whether I was really cut out for this line of work, and even considered giving it all up. But whenever I thought that way, a surge of unwillingness and sorrow welled up inside me, impossible to let go.

Sunlight streamed through the living room curtains onto the floor. My friend and I sat on the soft sofa, each holding our coffee cups, while the air was filled with a faint coffee aroma. Today’s topic was a movie we had recently watched, and I could hardly wait to share my thoughts. I liked both the plot and the performances, especially the emotional portrayal by the female lead, which moved me deeply.

“I think her acting was truly impeccable. She cried so convincingly in that scene,” I said.

“Really? I thought it was a bit too contrived, especially the ending. It kind of pulled me out of the movie,” my friend replied.

I felt a slight unease rise in my heart, and my heartbeat quickened a little. This was a movie I particularly liked, and my friend’s comment felt like a dismissal of my taste. I tried hard to push down my displeasure and wondered whether my own reaction was a bit too extreme.

“I actually think that kind of exaggeration just captured the character’s desperation perfectly. Maybe everyone feels differently,” I said, trying to sound casual.

My friend smiled and kept talking at length about another scene and his thoughts on the actor. As I listened, I felt that subtle uneasiness and dissatisfaction in my heart gradually spreading. I noticed myself starting to sweat, my palms growing slightly sticky, while I kept replaying the conversation in my mind.

I thought back to similar moments in the past, when I would often feel shaken and anxious over small things. Deep down, I blamed myself for always being so sensitive. Why couldn’t I simply accept differing opinions?

A few minutes later, I tried to change the subject and asked my friend about work recently, hoping to relax a little. He took the hint and began talking about some minor challenges he had encountered at work.

The afternoon continued in a friendly atmosphere. After my friend left, I lay on the sofa, thinking back over our conversation. Although I still felt a trace of unease, I realized that perhaps I was paying too much attention to other people’s opinions, especially on topics that weren’t all that important.

In the days that followed, this small disagreement did not have any deeper impact on our relationship. I told myself to learn to accept differing opinions calmly, and not to treat every disagreement as a rejection of myself.

Sunlight streamed through the café’s large windows onto the wooden tabletop. I sat in the corner, facing my laptop, trying to finish an article. The air was filled with the faint aroma of baking, along with the occasional clatter of machines. This was the place I came to work every week—familiar and safe—but today everything felt off.

The owner greeted me by the coffee machine. “You look a little stressed today?” His tone was light, but I caught a subtle hint of unease. My stomach tightened. In an instant, all kinds of explanations surged through my mind: Did I look too disheveled? Was the piece I wrote bad? Was he trying to say I’d been taking up this corner for too long? I forced myself to stay calm and replied, “Yeah, I’ve been a bit busy lately.” He nodded politely and turned to attend to other customers.

My hand hovered over the keyboard, frozen, not knowing how to continue. It felt as though the gears in my head had jammed. I thought back to the draft I had submitted yesterday and wondered whether I had left out some important detail. Had I used too many repetitive words? Was it simply impossible to make anyone satisfied? A thought began to repeat itself in my mind: “This is terrible. I messed up again.”

My stomach suddenly clenched, as if a rope were twisting inside it. I instinctively touched my chest and realized my heartbeat had quickened too. I picked up my coffee cup, trying to calm myself, but my fingers tapped sharply against the rim, betraying my nerves.

“Should this article be rewritten?” the voice in my head kept repeating. I started to panic, afraid that what I’d written was nothing but worthless paper no one would want to read. Sitting in the café, I still felt sealed off behind an invisible barrier, my thoughts churning within it, growing darker and darker.

After about half an hour, I finally summoned the courage to look over the draft again, but the questions in my mind still would not go away. I kept thinking about what the owner had said—was he implying something? Was he indirectly reminding me that this wasn’t a place for long-term work? I even felt like a failure, as though the slightest hint could make me think of rejection and abandonment.

By the time I got home that evening, my stomach was still aching faintly, and my emotions felt as if they were dangling from a rope, swaying back and forth. I tried to focus on making dinner, but I couldn’t resist taking out my phone to check my email again, afraid of receiving any criticism or a rejection notice.

The next morning, I woke up, sat on the edge of the bed with my head in my hand, and thought about the anxiety I had been unable to shake the day before. I had to find some way not to let a casual remark from someone else ruin my whole day. And yet I still felt that some things might be impossible for me to escape, like an invisible fate.

I was sitting at the desk in the studio, the clacking of keyboards sounding especially harsh in the empty room. The air was filled with the sour sting of cheap coffee and a faint chemical smell of drying paint, and my stomach ached dully. My partner stood by the window across from me, holding his phone; the blue glow of the screen reflected on his tightly furrowed brow. He suddenly spoke, his tone as cold and hard as ice: “Why did you post that Weibo? Did you think about how much impact this would have on our project?”

My throat felt blocked by a stone, and after a long moment I managed to force out, “I just wanted to express my thoughts... I never realized it would cause such a big reaction.” My voice trembled slightly, and I wasn’t sure whether he noticed.

“Thoughts?” He let out a sneer, turned to stare at me, his eyes full of disappointment and anger. “Do you know how many people have already started thinking we’re unprofessional? You’re going to ruin both our reputations.”

Every word he said pierced my skin like a nail, and my face instantly burned hot. I could feel sweat sliding down the back of my neck, yet my palms were icy. I lowered my head and stared at the notebook on the table; the writing was so blurred it seemed like a mass of accusations pasted all over it. “I didn’t mean to ruin anything...” I tried to defend myself, but my voice grew softer and softer, until it vanished into the air like a wisp of gray smoke.

He sighed, tossed his phone onto the table with a sharp clatter, and said, “I really think you’re extremely disappointing. We’ve worked together for so long—can’t you think a little more about the team as a whole?”

That sentence hit me like a slap across the face. Suddenly, countless fragments flashed through my mind: being publicly scolded by a teacher as a child, being rejected by a client face-to-face on a previous project, and all those moments that made me feel over and over that I was simply not good enough, not wanted. I heard myself screaming in my head, “He hates me. He doesn’t trust me at all.” My eyes started to burn, and I struggled desperately to keep the tears from falling.

“You think it’s my fault, don’t you?” I heard my own voice turn sharp all of a sudden. “You think I’m only thinking about myself? What about you? Have you ever asked how much pressure I’m under? Do you know how late I stay up every day?” After saying all that, I felt as if a stone were pressing down on my chest, my breathing becoming rapid, and even my ears started to ring.

He froze for a moment, but quickly recovered. “You think I don’t understand you enough? Have you ever thought that all these problems are really because of your sensitivity and selfishness?” His tone was as cold as a knife. I felt like my world collapsed in an instant.

When he slammed the door and left, only the dim light and the sound of my breathing remained in the room. I covered my face with both hands; my fingers were ice-cold, but my cheeks burned from the tears. I replayed our conversation over and over in my mind, thinking that every word I had said was full of loopholes, feeling certain that my outburst had only made him even more convinced I was difficult to work with. The more I thought about it, the tighter my chest felt, and my stomach began to cramp. In the end, I had no choice but to lean back in my chair and try to calm myself down.

That night, I hardly slept at all. My mind was filled with his last words: “sensitive and selfish.” I kept blaming myself in my head, feeling that he was right. I had messed things up again.

Over the next few days, I found myself completely unable to get into work. Every time I opened a file, I would think of his cold gaze and those piercing accusations. I started to wonder whether he was considering no longer working with me. Was my presence a burden to him? These thoughts kept circling in my mind, leaving my stomach in a constant dull ache.

The fluorescent lights in the conference room stabbed at my eyes, and the clock on the wall ticked away, each sound stretching my tension thinner. In front of me lay a proposal I had spent two weeks preparing, the edges of the paper already slightly curled from my repeated rubbing. I tried hard to stay calm, but sweat on my palms seeped through the pages and blurred the writing in my notebook slightly.

The editor-in-chief flipped through my proposal and said in a flat tone, “We feel this idea doesn’t really meet market demand.” His expression did not change at all, but I felt as if I had been nailed to the wall. His voice echoed in my ears like a heavy blow: “market demand.” In an instant, dozens of possibilities flooded my mind: Was I too personal in my writing? Did they think my aesthetic was outdated? Was it... was I simply not suited for this job? Almost immediately, I had already pictured myself getting fired—I was unemployed, a complete and utter failure.

I tried to argue back, but my voice trembled a little: “But I think this idea... it doesn’t necessarily have to cater to everyone. I believe it has value.” The moment I said it, I regretted it. I heard how anxious my tone sounded, even pleading. The editor-in-chief kept his gaze fixed on my face. He didn’t answer right away, but instead turned to the others. “What do you think?” he asked.

A few coworkers discussed it quietly, and in the end, one colleague I usually got along with fairly well said softly, “Sorry, maybe this direction really is a bit off.” She didn’t dare look at me, but her voice felt like a needle stabbing into my chest. I forced down the bitterness rising in me and nodded. “Okay, I understand.” But my heart was already churning. Why did she have to side with the editor-in-chief? Had she been laughing at me all along? Or... had she never considered me a friend in the first place?

My stomach started to cramp, as if a stone were pressing down on me until I could barely breathe. I struggled to regulate my breathing, only to find that every inhale came with waves of suffocating discomfort. My fingers were ice-cold as I clutched the proposal tightly, sweat even staining the paper. I could only keep my head down, not daring to look at anyone’s expression, afraid of seeing pity or mockery in their eyes.

After the meeting ended, I walked alone to the restroom and splashed my face with cold water. The person in the mirror looked haggard and miserable, and I even wondered whether I had clearly revealed my own vulnerability. That night, I sat on the sofa at home and stared at the proposal for a very long time, filled with shame and doubt. I began replaying every word from the meeting over and over, trying to infer their tones and expressions, and even the slightest smile made me think it might be a hint of my failure.

A few days later, I tried to reorganize my thoughts, but every time I opened the document, the scene from that meeting surged back into my mind. Those looks, those words, cut at my self-respect like knives. I knew my self-attacks had gotten out of control, but I had no power to stop those negative thoughts.

The bell at the repair shop door gave a soft ring as I arrived. Inside, the air smelled of old wood mixed with machine oil, carrying a strong sense of history. Various antique clocks and watches ticked quietly on the shelves, each telling its own story of the past. I was standing at the counter, waiting for the owner to come over, my heartbeat quickening. I had never studied antique clocks and watches in any depth, but at that moment I felt an inexplicable anticipation, perhaps hoping to seek some kind of understanding and connection through these old objects.

The owner slowly walked over. He was an elderly gentleman with a smile on his face. “How can I help you?” His tone was calm and unhurried, which put me slightly at ease. Even so, I couldn’t help overinterpreting his microexpressions, and anxiety began to rise in me. I worried that I might say something wrong at some point. “I just want to learn about the history of these clocks and watches, and whether they can be repaired,” I said, trying to sound composed, though my voice trembled slightly.

The owner patiently introduced the background of each clock and watch, his voice like an old radio broadcast. In an instant, I suddenly realized I was completely immersed in his story, as if I had entered a new time tunnel. Yet when his gaze turned toward me, I was suddenly tense again. Would he discover that I actually knew very little about these clocks and watches? I tried to defuse the unease with preemptive self-criticism, telling myself, “I’m just an amateur. It’s fine. I’m only here to take a look.”

He continued explaining the craft of repairing clocks and watches, and during that time I tried hard to stay focused, but doubts about myself kept surfacing in my mind. Why was I actually interested in these old things? Was it perhaps just a way to avoid real-life problems? My stomach began to ache faintly, and my palms grew a little sweaty. To hide the discomfort, I started nodding along and kept replying to the owner’s words: “Oh, I see.” It seemed that doing so would make me seem less ignorant.

After leaving the repair shop, my emotions were still unsettled. That afternoon, as I walked home, the city’s cold wind howled past me, and I couldn’t help hunching my shoulders. For the past few days, I kept thinking back to the scene in the shop, repeatedly mulling over every word the owner had said. Perhaps those clocks and watches weren’t that complicated after all; perhaps it was only my inner world that was complicated.

A few days later, I passed the repair shop again. The ticking of the clocks had not changed, but I no longer dared to step inside, afraid of exposing my ignorance once more. Whenever I passed by, I would quicken my pace, avoiding having to face the embarrassment of that day. I kept trying to tell myself that perhaps the world of clocks and watches was not the direction I needed to explore.

Sunlight filtered through the cracks in the curtains and fell across the desk, where I was bent over a new manuscript. That uneasy feeling in my heart had never gone away; it was as if something was about to happen. My palms began to sweat slightly. Just then, my spouse pushed the door open and walked in, looking at me expressionlessly. “We need to talk,” she said, her voice carrying a coldness I couldn’t quite make out.

My heart tightened, and I felt a churning unease in my stomach. “Oh? What’s wrong?” I tried to act indifferent, but my heartbeat was already quickening, as if it were about to burst out of my throat.

“I feel like we’ve never really communicated properly all this time. I feel very alone.” Her voice was calm, but those words were like a blade, thrust straight into the depths of my vulnerable heart.

I panicked instantly. All kinds of worst-case possibilities flashed through my mind: she was going to leave me; she must have discovered my flaws. My throat went dry. “Do you mean...” I hesitated, my voice trembling slightly. “Do you mean you want to separate?”

She sighed. “No, I just want us to have a proper conversation. Can you stop always thinking about things so negatively?”

Her words made my heart sink, and all the unease and fear I had tried so hard to hide suddenly burst forth. I felt the muscles in my legs tense, and my breathing grew faster and faster. In my mind, memories of all the times I had been abandoned began to surface for no reason.

“Tell me what I’m not doing well enough!” I nearly shouted, tears welling up uncontrollably.

She froze for a moment, her expression softening slightly. “No one is perfect. I just want you to stop putting so much pressure on yourself.”

I felt a wave of helplessness, as if I had been drained hollow. The sting of those words echoed over and over in my heart. Suddenly, I was overwhelmed by a deep exhaustion. I knew my sensitivity was unbearable to the other person, yet I still couldn’t break free of this deeply rooted fear. My whole body felt as if it were pinned down by a huge boulder, unable to move.

That night, I lay in bed with tears silently streaming down my face. Over the next several days, I kept dissecting every word she had said, savoring every expression on her face. I kept confirming whether she still cared about me, whether she still loved me. I knew it was painful and pointless, yet I still couldn’t stop.

That feeling of being abandoned, lodged deep in my heart, clung to me like a malignant growth and would not go away.

The color of the sky was gradually deepening, and the light of the setting sun stretched long across the horizon. I was walking alone beside the abandoned railway on the north side of the city. The tracks were covered with a thick layer of rust, and here and there a blade or two of withered grass poked up through the gaps. The air around me carried the smell of rust, mingling with the sound of gravel crunching beneath my feet, creating a distinctive silence. I looked up and saw several birds flying across the sunset-red sky, leaving behind a few brief cries. That familiar sense of loneliness surged over me like a tide; my heartbeat began to quicken, and sweat slowly seeped into my palms.

“What are you doing here all by yourself?” A strange voice broke my train of thought. I turned around and saw an old man wearing a hat. He was smiling slightly, carrying an old wooden box in his hand. His face looked strangely familiar, as if it had stepped out from some corner of my memory. “Oh, nothing, just taking a walk,” I replied with a forced smile, trying to hide the panic inside me.

“No one’s come to this place for a long time.” The old man set the box down on the ground and sat beside it. “When I was young, I used to come here often. I always felt the tracks had a mysterious attraction.” His voice carried a hint of nostalgia, which put me at ease, and I sat down nearby as well.

“Yes, it’s quiet enough to make you uneasy,” I said absentmindedly, voicing my own feelings. The old man nodded and stared into the distance without saying a word. A series of thoughts began to rise in my mind: if only I could face everything as calmly as he did. But a voice inside kept telling me that I was destined to be abandoned, destined to be overlooked. These thoughts made my stomach clench, as if turbulent currents were moving beneath a calm surface.

After a while, the old man stood up and gently patted my shoulder. “Even being alone has its own scenery.” He left me with that sentence, then disappeared into the glow of the setting sun. I sat there in a daze, my heart full of mixed emotions.

That night, after I got home, I still couldn’t calm down. Faint, blurry lights flickered outside my window. I stared blankly at the computer screen, my mind replaying the conversation from earlier in the day. I kept turning over the old man’s words in my head, deeply envious of his composure. In the end, I decided to try sorting out my emotions through writing. I opened a text editor, and the tapping of the keys echoed in the silent room. It was a process of release and self-reflection.

A few days later, I sent the article I had written to a friend, hoping she could give me some feedback. Her email came back quickly: “What you wrote is really honest—is this you?” Her affirmation surprised me a little. I had originally thought this encounter was just a trivial episode, but unexpectedly it gave me a chance to look at myself again. Repeatedly confirming my friend’s reply, I tried hard to make myself believe that none of this was a bad thing. Although it couldn’t completely dispel that sense of loneliness, it at least made me realize that when facing fear and unease, I was not entirely powerless.

The table was covered with delicious food, and the atmosphere seemed warm and cozy, but inside I was overwhelmed with anxiety. The voices of my family mingled with the children’s laughter. I tried hard to blend in, yet I felt completely out of place. I tried to join the conversation and talk about a recent creative work, but as soon as I spoke, my older brother cut me off. “Hey, kid, why are you always focusing on these vague, unreal things?” His tone was full of contempt. Immediately, alarm bells went off in my head; it felt as though a heavy stone had been pressed onto my chest, my heartbeat quickened, and my palms began to sweat. Why did he always look down on me like this? Why was I always treated as an odd one out?

I forced a smile. “I just think it’s pretty interesting. Maybe it could turn into something,” I added, trying to ease the awkwardness. But deep inside, anger was beginning to surge. Grandmother suddenly chimed in, “It’s fine, let’s eat first. Don’t talk about this.” I felt brushed off, as if they knew nothing about my efforts. I told myself that maybe I shouldn’t talk about my creative work in a setting like this, but I couldn’t suppress the feeling of being ignored and belittled.

After dinner, I slipped quietly onto the balcony. The cool breeze brushed my face as I tried to calm down. I wondered why these self-attacking thoughts always came uninvited. Why did I always feel unloved and unaccepted? Every time I tried to express myself, I was knocked right back down. My stomach ached in waves, and the laughter and chatter in my ears felt distant and grating.

My mother came over and asked softly, “Are you okay? Why aren’t you with everyone else?” I nodded weakly. “Nothing, I just feel a little tired.” But in my heart, I kept wondering whether she had seen through my vulnerability, and that vulnerability filled me with shame.

When I woke the next day, I still felt heavy, as if last night’s emotions had lingered in the air. I looked at myself in the mirror, questioning my worth and blaming myself for not being as confident as everyone else. Soon after, I tried to adjust my mindset and shift my energy back to creating, but the shadow of unease seemed impossible to shake. That night’s experience once again made me realize my role as the odd one out in the family, constantly struggling against a deep sense of inadequacy.

Amid the crowd, music pounded through the entire underground bar, and the dim lighting made everything around me seem blurry. The air was thick with the mixed smell of beer and cigarettes, adding an unspoken sense of unease. I tried to sit calmly at the bar, holding an untouched drink in my hand. An old friend I hadn’t seen in months had asked to meet me here, and I had thought it would be a relaxed and pleasant night. The noise around me only made me more anxious; my heartbeat seemed to quicken, and my palms began to sweat.

“Hey! Long time no see!” my friend’s voice came from behind me. I turned and saw him walking toward me, a sincere smile on his face. His appearance made me relax a little.

“Yeah, it’s been a while! How have you been?” I replied with a smile, trying to hide my nervousness.

We started talking, and with the music and voices blending together, I had to lean in to listen. As we talked, I caught some subtle shifts in his tone. He mentioned some past misunderstandings, and although his tone was casual, my thoughts were immediately pulled back to those unpleasant memories. I began to feel uneasy, and thoughts like “Is he still blaming me?” started running through my mind.

As the conversation went on, my stomach began to feel a little off, as if it had tied itself into a tight knot. I couldn’t help but start overanalyzing the subtext behind his words, repeatedly examining every detail he mentioned. Even after he changed the subject, I still couldn’t fully engage.

“Are you still listening?” my friend asked, looking at me with a puzzled expression.

“Oh, of course,” I answered at once, trying hard to seem attentive, but the anxiety inside me was spreading uncontrollably. I started to wonder whether I had lost the ability to talk normally with people, and worried that I might seem strange in his eyes, so I quickly added, “I just got a little distracted, sorry.”

We kept talking, but it felt like I was constantly attacking myself. That feeling of being abandoned and not accepted surged over me like a tide, and I struggled not to let it show on my face or in my voice. Every detail was magnified endlessly in my mind, and I was afraid of saying the wrong thing or making the wrong move. In the end, I couldn’t hold it in any longer and excused myself to the restroom for a short break, hoping to calm down.

When I returned to my seat, I felt a little more composed, but even so, the aftershocks of the night still echoed in my heart. The next morning, after getting up, I thought back on last night’s conversation and still regretted being too sensitive. I also realized that my reaction may have been somewhat over the top. I told myself that next time, I should handle situations like this more calmly and not catastrophize every little problem so easily.

When I pushed open the glass door of the snack wholesale market, the damp, chilly air came rushing toward me, carrying a mingled sweetness of candy. As I walked between the shelves, staring at the colorful packages, I felt an inexplicable restlessness, not knowing what exactly I was looking for. The gray concrete floor beneath my feet was a little slick, and with every step I could hear the squeak of my shoes rubbing against the ground.

As I bent down to pick up a bag of almond chocolate, a woman in a dark green coat suddenly turned sideways and bumped my hand. “Sorry,” she said quickly, hurrying away. Her voice was calm, but there was a hint of impatience in her eyes. A surge of heat shot from my chest to my face at once, as if everyone had seen my hand tremble and the chocolate nearly slip out.

“It’s fine,” I said, sounding a little stiff. She was already out of sight, but my mind began replaying that moment wildly: her movement, her tone, even her subtle expression. I couldn’t help wondering—had myaction made her feel I was blocking the way? Or had she simply not noticed me at all? Ah, maybe she thought I was deliberately standing there, in the way.

My heartbeat started to quicken, and it seemed I could hear echoes in my ears, as if all the whispers around me were pointing at me. “Take a deep breath, it’s nothing serious,” I told myself, but it did little good. I put down the chocolate, walked to the end of the shelf, and pretended to look at a few bags of spicy chips, just to use the movement to avoid people’s gaze.

“Want to try this?” A staff member suddenly appeared behind me, holding out a tasting plate with a piece of dried fruit. “Oh, thanks.” I took it, forcing out a faint smile, feeling my fingertips turn slightly cold. The dried fruit tasted pretty good, but I could barely taste it. After the staff member turned and left, I once again magnified her attitude without limit: her expression was neither warm nor cold—was she implying that I should act more naturally? Or was my smile so stiff that it made her uncomfortable?

My breathing growing rapid, I went to the checkout counter, grabbed a few items, and hurriedly paid. After leaving the market, the damp chill of the street seemed even more oppressive, and a faint ache began in my stomach. I stood by the roadside, staring at the shopping bag in my hand, and let out a tired sigh.

That night, I sat by the window lost in thought, my mind still replaying those details: the woman’s bump, the staff member’s expression, and whether I had seemed strange in the cashier’s eyes. I tried hard to convince myself that it was all just a trivial matter, but this catastrophic way of thinking seemed etched into my bones, impossible to dispel. I kept asking myself why every interaction with a stranger could sink me so deeply. This sensitivity made me feel ashamed, yet it was also like a mirror, forcing me to keep examining myself.

I was sitting in the corner of a cafe, my fingers lightly tapping on the table. Around me were the sounds of coffee beans being ground by machines, cups clinking together, and the indistinct murmur of people talking in the distance. The latte in my cup had gone cold, and the foam had settled to one side. My partner across from me had just finished sharing his new ideas for the proposal. “I think these parts still need major revisions; otherwise it’ll be hard to meet the objectives.” I froze for a moment and looked directly at his face. He didn’t have any particularly special expression; his tone was calm and natural, but I felt a chill quickly spread from my chest. I cautiously said, “But this part is the most crucial. Changing it might affect the overall style.” My voice still sounded composed, but inside I was already beginning to churn. Are you implying that I didn’t do a good job? Do you think I’m not capable enough? Do you regret working with me? These questions kept turning over in my mind like tiny insects, unable to settle.

His response made me even more nervous. “Style is certainly important, but market feedback is more important, isn’t it?” That last sentence struck like a heavy blow, quietly shattering my defenses. I nodded, pretending to be seriously considering his suggestion, but in reality my stomach had already begun to tighten and my palms were slightly sweaty. My gaze drifted past his coffee cup at the edge of the table, and I noticed that the moment he picked it up, there seemed to be a flicker of hesitation on his face for a second. What was that? Was it dissatisfaction with me, or concern? I tried to piece together his attitude from these details, but the more I thought about it, the more confused I became.

The whole conversation proceeded in an orderly way, but inside I was on a roller coaster. Several times I tried to interject, but then felt I was being too impulsive and stopped myself. In the end, my partner stood up to leave, and before he went, he handed me a sheet of paper with his complete revision suggestions for the proposal. “No need to decide right away. Take your time and think it over. We’ll meet again next week,” he said easily. I forced out a smile. “Okay, I’ll look at it carefully.” Yet in my heart I had already begun to question myself: Had I disappointed him? Did he think I was a nonconformist, unreliable partner?

That night, lying in bed, I kept replaying his tone, his expression, even every line of our conversation. In my mind, our interaction kept looping like I was trying to find where things had gone wrong. My chest ached from time to time, and my stomach felt as if it were soaked in sour liquid; I found it hard to fall asleep all night. The next day I decided to calm myself down and carefully reviewed his suggestions, only to find that many of them were reasonable changes. Even after a week had passed, I was still ashamed of how I had reacted in that cafe, but I also knew that this sensitivity seemed to be my instinct and was hard to completely change.

The air in the textile factory always seemed to carry a stale fiber smell. The cotton thread felt rough to the touch, rubbing against my fingertips. I was used to working here, facing the endless sound of looms turning day after day; the machines’ humming was like the murmur of the sea, washing over my thoughts again and again. Yet what I experienced today in the color-mixing room filled me with a sudden unease.

“What do you think of these two colors together?” a coworker asked, pointing at a piece of fabric. It was a challenge, and I had to reassess my own judgment. The room was dimly lit, making the colors seem subtle and complex. I felt a quiet sense of unease in my heart; a slight sheen of sweat began spreading across my palms, and my heartbeat seemed to quicken.

“I think... maybe not. Wouldn’t it be too harsh?” I replied hesitantly, uncertainty in my voice. My coworker frowned slightly, and I caught his doubt, but he said nothing, only nodded and went back to work.

My thoughts began to churn, and memories of those minor yet unforgettable mistakes from the past welled up in my mind. It was a mindset I couldn’t shake, one that magnified every detail and made every mistake feel intolerable. I stood by the window in the color room, looking out through the old glass at the gray sky pressing down over the city. Suddenly, I felt as if I were trapped in this endless grayness.

My inner monologue began to sting: “I’m doubting myself again—will I ever be able to trust my instincts?” I thought. “Could this choice eventually lead to being rejected by others?” My chest felt tight, and my breathing grew rapid, as though even the air was pressing down on me, leaving me unable to relax.

Afterward, I went home and sat on the sofa, still tormented by the question of color matching. The aftereffects wouldn’t fade; even on that quiet night, I still couldn’t calm the turmoil inside me. A few days later, that color scheme was accepted, yet I felt no relief. Instead, I was left with a persistent anxiety, the colors colliding in my mind as if foreshadowing more unease and doubt to come.

This incident made me realize that striving for perfection is an inescapable habit; overinterpreting every detail, even an unintentional hint, may only lead to more self-criticism. I tried to tell myself that occasional uncertainty should not be a reason for self-denial, but in such an environment, I kept testing that truth again and again.

Sunlight filtered through the gaps in the curtains and spilled across the floor. I sat at my desk, staring at the blank canvas before me. Several of my past works hung on the wall, and those long-finished paintings seemed to be silently accusing me. A wave of tension washed over me, and my palms began to sweat.

“What exactly do you want to paint?” I kept asking myself inwardly. In fact, when I first woke up that morning, I had been thinking about creating a special piece. Yet now I felt utterly empty and powerless. I turned on some music, hoping the rhythm and melody would awaken the wellspring of my inspiration, but every note in the song felt oppressive to me, quickening my heartbeat and making my breathing shallow.

“This painting has to be finished today. I can’t put it off any longer,” I told myself, my voice full of anxiety. I gripped the edge of the desk tightly, my fingertips turning slightly white, trying to force myself to focus that way. Yet, for some reason, memories of past failures kept surfacing in my mind: those returned drafts, those collaboration proposals that never received any reply. Each time I thought of them, my chest felt heavier.

My body’s reaction grew more and more noticeable. My stomach throbbed faintly, as if reminding me of my body’s overreaction to stress. I tried taking deep breaths, attempting to ease the tension a little, but my body simply would not cooperate.

Suddenly, the phone rang, pulling me back from my thoughts to reality. I picked up my phone; it was a curator from a gallery. “Hello, do you have any good works to exhibit recently?” His tone sounded casual, but it made me feel unbearably heavy. I stammered, “I... I’m still working on one.”

After hanging up, I stared blankly at the canvas. Every possible brushstroke seemed to be judging whether I was good enough, whether I deserved to keep doing this work. That night, I barely slept, my mind replaying those moments of failure over and over, making me doubt my own worth. Over the next few days, I spent a lot of time sitting before the canvas, trying to break through this bottleneck, my mood swinging between anxiety and calm.

Although the work was eventually completed, the unease in my heart never truly went away. A few days later, I finally decided to talk with some artist friends, hoping to seek encouragement and advice to help myself out of this low point.

The fine rain outside the window had wrapped this café in a faint, damp atmosphere, and a light scent of coffee drifted through the air. I was sitting with a few friends by the window, chatting and laughing. Suddenly, I heard one friend joking, “You’re always like this—when are you going to become a little more easygoing?” That joking remark echoed in the air. Although everyone else laughed along, I felt a wave of embarrassment, and my heart suddenly began to race. My cheeks grew hot at once, as if everyone in the café were looking at me. My palms started to sweat, and there was a tightness in my stomach. The sound of my friends continuing their conversation by my ears grew blurry, and all my attention focused on that one sentence.

“Is he unhappy with me? Am I being too cautious?” My mind began to churn uneasily. I tried hard to force a smile to hide my embarrassment, but I couldn’t help dwelling on those awkward moments from the past. I could feel my body stiffen, my fingers gripping the edge of my cup tightly in an effort to maintain an appearance of calm.

A friend across from me keenly noticed the change in my expression and asked softly, “Are you okay? Do you feel unwell?” I forced myself to steady down and replied in a casual tone, “I’m fine, it’s just that there’s been a lot going on at home lately.” My friends all nodded and changed the subject, but I still couldn’t let it go. That sense of being misunderstood and of doubting myself kept circling in my heart.

After the afternoon gathering ended, I walked home alone. The raindrops tapped gently against my umbrella, making a steady ticking sound. I kept thinking, “Am I really too tense? Why can’t I be as relaxed and natural as they are?” I felt ashamed of my sensitivity, yet I still couldn’t fully control my emotions.

That evening, after I got home, even though several hours had passed, those words were still lingering in my mind. I sat on the sofa, opened my notebook, and tried to write down these feelings, hoping to sort out my tangled emotions through words. Halfway through, I felt a wave of helplessness again: “Maybe that’s not what they meant. Am I overthinking this again?”

As time passed, my mood gradually settled. I came to realize that the ups and downs of these emotions were like this rain—they would pass soon enough. A few days later, when I met my friends again, I had already forgotten that joke. Maybe I should learn to accept myself more gently and with a little more ease.

I was sitting on the gray sofa in the studio, surrounded by the aroma of coffee and the warm golden sunlight streaming in through the window. The carpet under my feet was a little rough, and my fingers unconsciously twisted the hem of my clothes as I watched their expressions without giving anything away. A coworker across from me was speaking at length about her idea, her tone full of confidence. I forced a smile and nodded, but for some reason, it felt like a small beast was clawing at my insides. I kept feeling that there was a faint hint of superiority in her tone, as if she were implying that my idea had no value.

“I actually think this part could be adjusted a bit more, especially the logic here,” I said tentatively, my voice sounding somewhat dry. My heartbeat seemed to quicken, and a faint sheen of sweat began to appear on my forehead. My coworker turned her head, her eyebrows lifting slightly, and there seemed to be a brief pause before she said, “Mm, that could be considered, but for now we still lean toward the original approach.” Her tone sounded calm, but I felt my stomach tighten, as if someone had tied a dead knot there. I gave a reluctant nod, a smile tugging at the corners of my mouth, but inside, those familiar feelings of unease and doubt were already building.

“Actually, your opinion makes sense too, but we need to decide quickly,” she continued. Those words only made me more certain that perhaps my thoughts didn’t matter at all; they were just listening out of politeness. I forced myself to look like I was participating in the discussion, while my eyes quietly drifted to the documents on the table, pretending to flip through them to hide the turbulence inside me.

My mind rapidly replayed all those past scenes of being questioned and ignored, even dredging up old memories from college, like the time I answered a question wrong in class and everyone turned to look at me. “Maybe I really am not good enough.” That voice started echoing in my head. I took a sip of my coffee, now cold, and it tasted bitter and harsh, just like my mood.

After the discussion ended, I walked out of the studio, and the cold wind that hit me made me shiver. When I got home, I curled up on the sofa, my mind still replaying my coworker’s tone and expressions over and over, always feeling that some hidden message was concealed there. “Does she think I’m stupid? Or does she think I’m simply not worth it?” Those thoughts pulled me deeper and deeper like a whirlpool. The discomfort in my stomach was still there, and I could barely eat dinner, so I simply opened my laptop and tried to sort through the ideas for today’s concept again.

The next morning, I gathered my courage and messaged my coworker: “I still think the logic here could be adjusted a bit more. Here are some thoughts I reorganized.” The moment I hit send, my palms were sweating, and my breathing became rapid. She replied quickly, in a friendly tone: “Thanks for the suggestion, I’ll think it over carefully!” Seeing that message, I felt a little relieved, but I was still uneasy, always worrying that it was just a perfunctory response. Over the next few days, I kept a close eye on the project’s progress, afraid my opinion would be completely ignored.

The sunlight lazily spilled across the balcony; the afternoon was so peaceful. I sat in a reclining chair, looking up at the blue sky. There were only a few clouds, drifting along slowly as if wandering aimlessly. I held out my hand to feel the warmth of the sun, and the touch at my fingertips made me realize how real this moment was. Occasionally, birdsong drifted over from afar, like a kind of natural background music. I held a book in my hands; although I had read a few pages, I had not truly entered the story. At that moment, I only wanted to empty my mind and enjoy this brief peace. 

From time to time, voices from next door came from the balcony beside me; they seemed to be discussing their child’s recent exam results. “I think he should spend more time on math,” one neighbor said with concern. Another replied, “Yes, the pressure of education these days is no joke.” I did not pay much attention to what they were saying, only sensing the concern and responsibility in their tone. 

At that moment, my mind was relaxed, yet I couldn’t help but start to think. Life is like this book; sometimes we open it, trying to find where the story is headed, only to discover that we still have to slowly read each page to the end. I looked up toward the horizon, the sunlight falling on my face, bringing a warm feeling. My heartbeat seemed to slow, steady and at ease. I thought that although such days are plain, they are also a gift of life. 

After a while, I got up to brew a cup of tea. Steam rose up, and I caught a faint fragrance—the scent of tea leaves. The warmth of the teacup in my palm felt comforting. I took a light sip, and the mellow tea brought me inner peace. Time passed slowly, and I felt no urgency at all; such relaxation was truly rare. 

As the afternoon passed, I returned indoors, still feeling serene. In the evening, I ate a simple dinner and then watched TV in the living room for a while. The program was lighthearted, with nothing irritating or upsetting in it. By night, I lay in bed, thinking of the day’s calm and comfort, my heart filled with a steady sense of contentment. The next day, I still felt good, as though that leisurely afternoon had given me new energy and a new perspective.

The kitchen light was too bright, stinging my eyes until they ached. Standing by the sink, I scrubbed the dishes hard, sweat beading on my forehead, the joints in my fingers throbbing faintly. The argument we’d had over dinner was still swirling in my head. As I washed the dishes, I desperately tried to recall his microexpressions and tone, every pause feeling like confirmation of the suspicion deep inside me: was it me not being good enough again? Had I disappointed him again?

“Why are you always like this?” His voice came from the living room, flat as if he were talking about the weather. I set down the plate, turned around, and saw him sitting on the sofa, head down, fiddling with his phone.

“What do you mean, ‘always like this’?” My voice rose a few notches, trembling uncontrollably. “Say it clearly—what exactly do you mean?”

He looked up, frowning in confusion. “I don’t mean anything. You’re overthinking again.” Then he lowered his head and kept scrolling.

Those words hit me like a bucket of cold water. I felt myself lose my balance in an instant, my heart suddenly racing, my chest seized as if by a hand clenching hard around it. My mind started spinning wildly, trying to find any evidence that I wasn’t “overthinking.” I fought back the urge to cry and said in a low voice, “You’re always like this—indifferent to me, like I don’t matter at all.”

He looked up, a trace of exhaustion on his face. “I really don’t know why you have to make it into such a big deal every time. I’m tired. Really tired.”

At that moment, it felt as if I heard a huge crack tearing through my world. His words left me utterly isolated and helpless—not just an argument, but a verdict, a confirmation that I didn’t deserve to be understood, didn’t deserve to be cared about. I shouted, “Yes, you’re tired! Because I’m the problem. I don’t even deserve you thinking twice about me!” Then I rushed back into the bedroom and slammed the door shut.

Sitting on the edge of the bed, my stomach ached as if it were bound tight by ropes. Tears kept streaming down my face, and my mind replayed those cold tones and words over and over, each one cutting into my heart like a knife. I clenched my teeth, trying to steady my breathing, but the deeper I breathed, the more suffocatingly heavy my chest felt. Again and again, I started imagining in my head: if I weren’t here, would he be happier? Was every mistake mine? I began to doubt whether my very existence was a burden.

A few days later, I still couldn’t avoid returning to that night’s conversation, breaking down and analyzing every detail all over again. I tried to find some explanation that would make me feel a little better, but I still failed. Even after he later said, “That’s not what I meant,” my mind still chose to believe his original words—that was the real him, and he had seen through the real me.

The afternoon sunlight spilled across the floor through the shop windows as I wandered through this long-abandoned old craft store, where all kinds of handmade items were piled haphazardly around me. Whenever I drew near, the air carried a mixed scent of wood and old repair glue, which made me feel somewhat uneasy inside, as if every smell were reminding me of the history behind these objects. I gently brushed my hand over some of the wooden carvings on display; the touch of my fingers was cold and rough, making my heartbeat quicken slightly.

Just as I was focusing on an antique vase, a customer walked in. He wore a strange hat and let out a harsh laugh as he spoke quietly with the shop owner. I tried hard not to pay attention to their conversation, but suddenly I heard some comments about my work. “This thing is pretty interesting, but isn’t it a bit outdated?” he said in a tone I couldn’t tell was mocking or just casual.

A complex wave of emotions surged through me, and a faint sense of panic quickly spread. I began obsessing over his tone and expression; a little sweat broke out on my forehead and I felt a bit of stomach pain, and my anxious nerves immediately sprang to life: did he simply look down on me? Did he think my creations had no value at all? My inner voice kept pressuring me to imagine the worst. I couldn’t help but launch into self-attack, harshly criticizing myself, trying to deny my own worth before anyone else could.

“Are you okay, kid?” The shop owner noticed my unease and asked. That made me relax a little. “Ah, I’m fine. It’s just that these works make me a bit emotional.” I tried to hide my anxiety, but I couldn’t fully calm down.

That night, after I got home, I was still caught in a loop of rumination. I kept replaying the customer’s words, trying to interpret whether they were a challenge or a criticism. Even after several days, the heaviness in my heart and my self-doubt still hadn’t completely faded. I kept trying to convince myself that it was just an offhand remark from an insignificant customer, and that my work had its own unique value.

Although anxiety had affected me greatly, deep down I knew I had to keep moving forward in the face of these emotions. On the road of creation, there will always be uncertainty and challenges, but I should trust my abilities and strive to persist and grow every day of my life.

Holding that freshly washed bowl, I could feel the cold of the porcelain seeping from my fingertips straight into my bones. Drops of water fell into the sink one after another, their steady rhythm making me irritable. From the dining room came the faint sound of laughter, drifting in through the slightly ajar door like a language I could not take part in. I stood under the kitchen light, trying to slow my breathing, but my chest was already tightening, as if something inside me were slowly swelling.

“When are you actually going to do that thing you promised me before?”

The voice came from behind me, deliberately lowered, but carrying a kind of impatience I knew all too well. I didn’t turn around right away. The words “when are you” pricked precisely into some already inflamed place in my brain like a thin needle.

*TA is just asking about one thing. Just asking.*

But I had seen TA’s eyes. What was in that look—disappointment? Judgment? Or some conclusion that had already been formed, only spoken aloud today? My mind began to run on its own, like a machine I couldn’t switch off: Did TA already think I was unreliable? Did TA treat all my promises as empty words? Had TA already placed me in some irredeemable category?

“I… I’ll take care of it.”

I heard my own voice trembling, as if I were trying to plug a leak in a crack that was already flooding.

“When?” TA’s tone hardened, each word dropping separately.

My heartbeat suddenly went out of rhythm. A buzzing began in my ears, and my stomach lurched downward. I knew I had done something wrong, but I didn’t know where the edge of that mistake lay, or where to begin making amends.

“Don’t always be like this, okay?”
