By the time I heard myself shout it, it was too late to take it back. My tone was hurried, defensive, trembling with something even I found humiliating. TA froze for a moment, curled one corner of the mouth in annoyance, then turned and walked back toward the dining room.

I watched TA’s back disappear behind the door, and my legs suddenly went weak. I had to brace myself against the counter to keep from collapsing. My stomach kept spasming; the kitchen light became blinding, as if it were shining especially on the most pathetic part of me.

*What did you just say? What did you just say?*

I began replaying it frame by frame in my head—TA’s furrowed brow, the thin layer of chill in the voice, the curve of the back as TA left. I tried to find something in every detail that I could use to push back, but all I found were more pieces of evidence proving that I really was that kind of person: saying things and not following through, making promises and not keeping them, unable even to handle a small matter properly.

That night I sat on the sofa, a book open on my lap, not a single word going in. The machine in my head kept running, replaying that “when are you actually going to do it” over and over, each time clearer, heavier than the last. *TA probably stopped counting on you long ago. TA would probably rather go find someone else. What use are you, existing here anyway?*

I don’t know when I walked into the bathroom. In the mirror, my face was pale, my eyes swollen, like something used by someone and carelessly set aside in a corner. I stared at that face for a long time. I don’t know when the tears started, and I didn’t wipe them away.

The sounds from the dining room had long since stopped. The whole house fell quiet, leaving only me and the me in the mirror, staring at each other in the light.

The silent atmosphere of the church seemed to havesolidify from some moment in the past. Sunlight filtered through the broken stained-glass windows, scattering mottled patches of light across the floor and reflecting fragments of historical memory. I stepped carefully over the broken tiles and made my way toward the altar. This had once been a place full of life and hope, but now only silence and desolation remained. Standing in a corner, I looked around and felt an indescribable pressure settling on my shoulders. My heartbeat began to quicken, and I felt my breathing grow heavy. The church’s crumbling walls seemed to tell stories of abandonment, just like the fear deep within me. I muttered to myself, “Why did I choose to come here? What exactly am I trying to prove?”

This unease brought on intense self-doubt. I tried hard to steady my breathing and keep myself from falling into endless suspicion. Suddenly, I heard faint footsteps. Turning around, I saw an unexpected visitor. “Are you interested in this place too?” a middle-aged man asked me with a smile. The tension in my body spread from my shoulders, and his sudden appearance startled me. I immediately wondered whether he had come to drive me away or to criticize me for being here. Stammering, I replied, “Just taking a look around.” His gaze made me lower my head involuntarily, and I vaguely felt the heat rising in my face. “This place used to be so beautiful,” he said wistfully, his eyes returning to the far end of the church. I followed his gaze and felt an inexplicable sadness rise within me.

I suddenly realized that I always tended to catastrophize things, imagining the worst possible outcome. Deep down, I knew this was only a projection of an abandonment schema, and my sensitivity to separation and rejection made these processes feel far more difficult than they actually were. Back home, I was still lost in thought, and that oppressive feeling would not leave my mind. I began to question whether I should go to places like that, because they triggered the unease and rumination deep inside me. Even so, I also realized that it was precisely through such exploration and reflection that I was gradually able to understand myself, and even face the fears that left me feeling suffocated.

The afternoon sunlight squeezed through the gap in the curtains, laying a pale yellow band of light across the long table. The air carried the lingering scent of coffee, along with the intermittent mechanical hum of the printer — so faint, yet inexplicably irritating. I sat at one end of the table, trying to pin my attention to the agenda in front of me.

When the meeting reached the part about project progress, a colleague spoke up: “Oh, of course, this design looks very creative.”

It was that sentence.

My palms started sweating in that second. I didn’t move, but my whole internal system seemed to have had the alarm button pressed. Their tone—that “of course,” that pause—I rewound the sentence in my head, once, twice, three times. Was it sarcasm? Or was I just scaring myself again?

*If it was sarcasm, that means they’ve long thought there was something wrong with this plan. If they think there’s a problem, what about the others? If the whole team thinks so too, and no one’s just saying it…*

I forced myself to speak, keeping my voice as steady as possible. “Do you think these ideas still need some refinement?”

They paused. That pause was probably only two seconds, but in those two seconds I ran through every worst-case possibility.

“Oh, no, I just think it’s already very good.”

Expressionless.

That somehow made it worse. If they were sincere, why wasn’t there even a hint of a smile? Why was their tone so flat? I gripped the notebook in my hand tighter, my knuckles turning a little white. Something in my stomach tightened, like a piece of cloth being slowly wrung dry.

After the meeting, I walked into the hallway. The cold air from the air conditioner hit me, and only then did I realize my back was already a little warm. The hallway was quiet, and footsteps sounded especially clear against the floor. My mind hadn’t followed me out of that room—it was still back there, replaying that sentence over and over, repeatedly searching their expression at the time, trying to find some detail I’d missed, some piece of evidence that could make everything make sense.

*There you go again.* I said to myself inwardly. *You’re doing this again.*

But so what if I knew. Knowing didn’t stop it.

That night, the person I lived with glanced at me. “What’s wrong today? You look really down.”

I let out a sigh. I wanted to say it, but I was even more afraid that once I did, they’d think I was making a mountain out of a molehill—a colleague’s offhand remark, and what of it? So I only said, “There was a little friction at work. Nothing serious.”

I’ve used that line for many years. Its function is to close the door.

Over the next few days, that afternoon stayed in my shoe like a grain of sand—enough to not quite stop me in my tracks, but enough to make me feel it with every step. Occasionally, in some spare moment, I’d suddenly remember it, and then that prickling, unsettling feeling would return. I knew this was my old habit, knew I was using a vague sentence to prop up the skeleton of an entire disaster.

But being sensitive has never become easier just because you’ve seen through it.

In an old teahouse, the mellow fragrance of tea mingled with the scent of aged wood, filling the air. I sat at a small round table near the window, where the silhouettes of trees swayed outside in the dimming light, the scene growing darker as the sun set. On the table sat a steaming pot of green tea, the leaves unfurling in the glass pot. I gently stirred the tea with a spoon, while the low murmur of conversation from a few guests at the next table drifted into my ears.

Across from me sat a stranger, a middle-aged man in a dark coat, his face hidden in the smoky shadows. I wasn’t sure how he had started talking to me, but our conversation centered on a recent art exhibition. He spoke about his experience of visiting it, his words brisk and confident, while I could only nod mechanically in response.

“What do you think the metaphor of that piece is?” he suddenly asked, his gaze piercing through the tea mist and fixing on me.

My throat tightened, my heartbeat quickened all at once, and my palms began to sweat slightly. My thoughts grew chaotic in an instant, as if every word had been magnified endlessly, leaving me at a loss. I stammered, “Uh, I think... maybe it’s about the process of losing and finding again?”

His slight nod made me breathe a little easier, but then I sank into self-doubt again. Was he just politely agreeing? My mind, like an untamed horse, began rehearsing the worst possibilities: What if I had misunderstood everything he said? What would people think if I seemed ignorant?

On one wall of the teahouse hung an old-fashioned decorative painting, and dust beneath the frame shimmered faintly in the warm yellow light. I stared at the painting, trying to calm myself, but my bodily reactions were beyond control; the churning in my stomach only intensified.

The other person kept talking at length, while my attention remained fixed on every move he made, trying to discern his true opinion of me from his smile and tone.

Before I knew it, our conversation had ended. He got up and said goodbye, leaving only the tea set on the table and my endless thoughts behind. That night, after I returned home, I tossed and turned, replaying the conversation over and over in my mind, filled with regret and unease. Why was I always so tense and so powerless?

Several days later, the experience was still lingering in my mind. I began reflecting on the sources of my anxiety in social interactions, trying to ease it through meditation and deep breathing, telling myself that I didn’t need to seek perfection in every conversation.

Sunlight spilled across the café table. I looked up and narrowed my eyes slightly, watching the crowd passing by outside the window. The rich aroma of coffee lingered in the air, giving me a moment of peace. But when my partner began discussing the new project, my anxiety came flooding back mercilessly. “I think if we present it in this style, the audience might find it more interesting,” he said, his tone seeming to carry a hint of uncertainty. I gave a nervous smile, already turning over the meaning of his words again and again in my mind. Was he implying that my previous proposal wasn’t good enough? I tried hard to hide my unease, unwilling to let him see my vulnerability.

Although I did my best to focus on the discussion, a voice in my head kept reminding me: You’re not good enough—that’s what he means. My heart raced, and my palms grew slightly sweaty. That familiar tension left me feeling a little panicked. I bit my lip, trying to calm myself down. But in the end, I couldn’t help asking, “Do you think my proposal is bad?” He said, “No, I just want to see whether there are any other possibilities.” His tone was calm, but it felt as if my heart had been pricked by a needle.

I nodded, trying to accept that explanation, insignificant as it was. But the sense of something being wrong within me only grew stronger. Why was I always like this? Why did I always feel that others were dissatisfied with me? That feeling filled me with shame. I began to lose focus, replaying his comments about my proposal over and over, mindlessly linking them to rejection. My stomach started to ache dully, and a sense of helplessness spread from deep inside me.

Just then, the music playing in the café gradually grew louder—it was a song I had once loved very much. That familiar melody steadied me a little, as if offering silent support. I closed my eyes, took a deep breath, and tried to stop overthinking, reminding myself that this was nothing more than an ordinary collaboration discussion, and that I shouldn’t be so upset.

That night, after I got home, I still kept replaying that conversation. The anxiety and self-doubt intertwined, making it hard for me to fall asleep. A few days later, I wrote about the experience in my diary, hoping to find some insight in it. Though the turmoil inside me left me disappointed in myself, I knew this was also something I needed to face. To keep such emotions from affecting the next collaboration, I began looking for some psychological management methods, hoping that in the next project discussion, I would no longer be held back by this sense of unease.

The air in the meeting room was thick with the bitter smell of coffee. I sat in my chair, my body tense, my palms slightly sweaty. In front of me sat a familiar partner—we had worked together for many years. Even so, when he said in what I took to be an impatient tone, “Isn’t what you’re doing a bit inappropriate?” it felt as if my heartbeat suddenly shot up to my ears. The background white noise gradually faded away, leaving only his voice echoing in my mind. My breathing grew rapid. I stared at the pen on the table, trying to calm myself down.

“Why is it inappropriate? I think this plan is already perfect,” I shot back, my voice trembling, unable to hide the anger and hurt in it. He seemed not to notice the change in my emotions, and even completely ignored the effort I had put into this project all along.

In that instant, I felt a panic of abandonment. It wasn’t the first time I had felt this way. It was as if something had pierced deep into my heart, leaving me unable to pull myself free. Every potential criticism felt like a denial of my entire being. When his gaze passed over me and focused on the presentation screen, that feeling of being disregarded grew even stronger, as if the whole world had been reduced to me alone, isolated and helpless.

After the meeting ended, I almost fled the conference room. The cool air in the hallway blew toward me, and only then did I seem able to catch my breath a little. But the turmoil in my heart did not subside; instead, it grew even more intense. Sitting in my office chair, I kept replaying the scene in my mind, over and over, chewing on those words: “Isn’t what you’re doing a bit inappropriate?”

That night, I did not sleep at all. The sheets twisted in knots beneath me, and occasionally a car passed outside, its lights flickering faintly through the curtains. I stared at the ceiling, my heart full of resentment and disappointment. I kept asking myself, “Does he really not need me anymore?” “Did I do something wrong?”

The next day, I came to the office with heavy dark circles under my eyes. My whole body felt hollowed out, yet I still had to force a smile and face new tasks. At lunchtime a few days later, I still had not fully processed that conflict. I kept worrying that something like this would happen again, afraid that the whole team might abandon me. And this anxiety, together with my disappointment in myself, followed me like a shadow.

I walked into this small succulent exhibition on the northern outskirts of the city. The cold air carried a faint earthy scent, and the walls around me were covered with beautiful photographs of all kinds of succulents. There weren’t many people in the exhibition hall, yet I still felt a kind of commotion, as if those rustling whispers were endlessly echoing in my ears. My heartbeat seemed to quicken with it, as though every beat were reminding me of everything around me. I tried hard to focus on the exhibits before me, attempting to ignore those uneasy feelings.

Not far away, a staff member was explaining succulent care tips to several visitors. In a daze, I moved closer, only to stop again. “This plant needs sunlight and the right amount of water.” The staff member’s voice was gentle, yet it pricked at my nerves. I’m not very good at caring for plants, and those words inevitably brought back the memory of the last time I had killed a potted plant given to me by a friend. A wave of shame began to rise in me.

“Are you interested in succulents too?” Suddenly, an enthusiastic visitor greeted me. I froze for a moment. “Mm, yes, I like them quite a bit.” I forced out a smile in response, though inwardly I began to wonder whether I had been impolitely silent for too long just now. Would he think I was strange? Should I say a little more to hide my nervousness?

My mind churned with all sorts of thoughts as I continued to follow his conversation carefully. But no matter what the other person said, my thoughts kept drifting toward the expressions and movements of others, trying to infer what they really meant. My breathing grew rapid, and my palms broke into a slight sweat. At that moment, my stomach also began to ache faintly, something that always happened when I was nervous.

After the conversation ended, I hurried away from the crowd and went to a corner of the exhibition area. There were a few benches there, and I tried hard to relax, observing the colorful succulents around me, hoping to calm my mood. But in truth, my mind kept replaying the conversation, wondering whether I had behaved appropriately. “Did I say something wrong?” “Would he think I’m boring?”

That night, I tossed and turned, unable to shake the feeling of being scrutinized. Even though I knew perfectly well that it was just an ordinary misunderstanding, I still spent hours comforting myself, desperately trying to convince my inner anxiety that it was unnecessary. The next day, while pretending to be calm and getting ready for work, I could still feel the aftermath of that unease, as if it had left a faintly aching corner in my heart.

A few days later, I decided to revisit the matter in hopes of drawing some help and warning from it. I understood that it was nothing more than my habitual overthinking, and that visitor had probably long since forgotten our brief exchange. So I told myself to bravely accept occasional minor social setbacks, and to work hard at turning my attention back to the creative work that makes me happy.

The restaurant was warmly lit, and the table was filled with the dishes I had carefully prepared, their aroma drifting everywhere. My friends gathered together, smiles on their faces, and the atmosphere was relaxed and easy. My palms began to sweat, and a tide of unease rose in my heart, as if an invisible pressure were squeezing my chest.

“Hey, kiddo, have you got any new work lately?” a friend asked with a smile. I forced a smile on my face, but inside I was starting to churn. Every time I heard a question like that, that inner voice would surface: “They’re only being polite; they don’t care about my work.” “Things have been a bit stagnant lately,” I replied, my voice trembling slightly.

“Don’t be too nervous, relax a little,” another friend said, patting my shoulder with a smile. But all I felt was the pressure on my shoulder, and that heavy sensation made my breathing quicken. “I’m not nervous, just a little tired,” I tried to brush it off, but my heartbeat only grew faster.

They kept chatting and laughing, while my thoughts gradually drifted away. The laughter in my ears turned harsh, and I began to interpret every exchanged glance and every subtle expression, as if each one were hinting that I was unwelcome. I pretended to focus on fiddling with the cutlery, trying to hide my inner panic.

“Hey, what are you spacing out for? Cheer up tonight!” a friend teased, pulling me back to reality. In an instant, that humiliating feeling surged over me, and I couldn’t help thinking: “They’re mocking me. They really dislike me.” Tears welled up in my eyes. I forced a smile in response, but inside it felt as if I were being pricked by needles.

After dinner, I sat alone in the kitchen, awkwardly staring at a pile of unwashed dishes, feeling hollow and heavy inside. As I touched the cold plates, my hands trembled slightly, and tears slipped down despite my efforts. Deep inside, the wound of abandonment and defectiveness was touched again: “I’m really just a waste of time; they’re only humoring me.” That self-attacking voice echoed in my mind.

That night, I tossed and turned, replaying every moment of the gathering in my head, even hearing my own heartbeat, unable to sleep. The next morning, I still felt that pressure in my chest, as if I were carrying everything from the night before.

I began to think: perhaps I should keep my distance from friends and no longer risk approaching crowds, so I won’t once again feel that helpless loneliness and the pain of being rejected.

The meeting had just ended, and I walked into a nearby café with a few colleagues. The air was thick with the rich aroma of coffee beans. We sat by the window, sunlight spilling across the table through the glass, but I felt heavy all over. The table was covered with all kinds of desserts and drinks, yet I had little appetite. Everyone started chatting casually, and I forced a smile, trying to hide the turmoil inside.

“Have you been unhappy lately?” one colleague suddenly asked, in a tone that seemed caring but made my heart skip a beat. Immediately, I felt my pulse quicken and my palms grow slightly sweaty. I tried to cover my unease with a joke: “Ah, maybe the recent project has just been exhausting.”

“You seem a bit negative. Is everything okay at work?” another colleague added. The words stabbed into my heart like a needle, bringing back a familiar fear. A thought flashed through my mind: do they think I’m not capable of doing this job? Are they going to give up on me soon?

I held back my panic and said with a smile, “I’m okay, just a little stressed.” But my voice sounded shaky. I could feel the muscles in my face tightening, and my stomach felt knotted, aching faintly.

At that moment, another colleague suddenly changed the subject. I breathed a sigh of relief, but I still felt dizzy, as if I were trapped in a silent storm. My colleagues continued discussing work-related trivialities, while I had no mind to join in. I could only struggle to maintain the role of a participant, as if afraid that the moment I let my guard down, I would be abandoned completely.

When I got home that evening, I still couldn’t shake the fear from the afternoon—that feeling of being questioned and about to be abandoned. Lying in bed, in the dark, I could hear only my own heartbeat, still racing. I kept replaying my conversation with my colleagues, each word hammering again and again at my self-esteem. I even began to wonder whether I really wasn’t good enough, whether I was incapable of handling this job.

A few days later, I still couldn’t escape that low mood. Every time I saw those colleagues, my heart would race with fear that they might point out my shortcomings at any moment, as if waiting to hand down a verdict. I began to handle every email and every phone call with extreme caution, always worrying that some bad news was on its way.

I was sitting at my desk, trembling as I tried to reply to a business email, but every letter on the screen seemed to be dancing, and I simply couldn’t focus. The study door opened, and his footsteps were very light, like a gust of wind. He leaned sideways against the doorframe and said coldly, “Remember to close the background apps after using my computer. Don’t let it crash again.”

Those words felt like a needle stabbing into my chest. I whirled around and blurted out, “You think I’m that unreliable, don’t you? You have to remind me even about something small like that?” I heard my own voice, sharp and harsh, the end of it trembling so badly it seemed about to break.

He frowned, his gaze as if separated from me by a pane of glass. “I was just reminding you. I didn’t say anything else.”

“But that’s exactly what you meant!” I stood up, both hands braced on the edge of the desk, my fingertips pressing almost into the wood. “You’re always like this, impatient with everything, as if I never do anything well enough!”

He sighed, exhaustion seeping through his tone. “Are you overthinking again? I really didn’t say anything. That wasn’t what I meant.”

“You think I can’t tell?” I shot back. “Your expression, your tone, they’re all saying you look down on me!” I felt as if a ball of fire were lodged in my throat, burning so hard I could barely breathe. A wave of dizziness made me grip the back of the chair, my heart pounding as if it were about to burst out of my sternum. The buzzing in my ears made every word he said seem amplified.

“Stop taking everything personally, okay?” He raised his voice, his eyes turning cold. “I’m really fed up with this endless guessing and fighting! At this rate, can we still live together peacefully?”

“Are you blaming me? You think everything is my fault, don’t you?” My voice began to shake, and tears surged up so fast they blurred my vision. I blinked hard, trying to regain my composure, but the tears were like a broken dam—I couldn’t hold them back.

“I don’t want to argue anymore.” He gave me one last look, then turned and closed the study door. I heard his footsteps gradually fading away, growing heavier and heavier, until they finally disappeared into the living room.

The room suddenly became frighteningly quiet, leaving only the sound of my heartbeat and my ragged breathing. I collapsed back into the chair, my shoulders shaking uncontrollably, my stomach knotted tight. I clutched my arm hard, my nails digging into my skin, until a sting of pain made me come to my senses a little. “I ruined everything,” a voice kept echoing in my head. “He must be completely disappointed in me now. He’s probably already thinking about leaving me.”

That night, I tossed and turned, replaying every word he had said over and over in my mind, trying to find more hidden emotions and meanings in them. It was only when dawn was almost breaking that I finally fell into a dazed sleep, and in my dream he was standing at the edge of a bottomless cliff, turning to look at me once before disappearing into the thick fog.

When I woke the next day, the sun was already high in the sky. I stared at the ceiling, thinking back on last night’s argument, and another cramp twisted through my stomach. I tried sending an apology text: “I’m sorry, I overreacted last night.” But by evening, I still hadn’t received any reply. Outside, the sky grew dark, and the room was left with only the faint blue glow of my phone screen. My hand holding the phone was trembling slightly, and it felt as if a huge stone were pressing down on my heart, leaving me unable to breathe at all.

The gate to the swimming pool was still half open, and the rust on the sheet-metal door looked even more mottled in the dim moonlight. As I stepped into the lobby, my feet crunched over shards of broken tile, making a sharp, grating crack. The hollow echo in the distance made me uneasy. The air was thick with a damp, moldy smell, like fabric forgotten for years. The place reminded me of swimming lessons I used to look forward to as a child, but now there was only silence and decay. I walked over to a ruined changing area, hoping to take a few photos; inspiration seemed to be here. The moment I raised my phone, I heard some faint footsteps, as if someone were stepping on broken tiles. I immediately held my breath and listened closely. Besides my heartbeat, there was also a faint rustling sound, coming and going. I tried to tell myself it was just the wind blowing through damaged curtains, but my body had already tensed on its own, and I gripped my phone so tightly that my fingertips ached slightly.

“Is anyone there?” My voice rang out through the empty pool hall, only to be swallowed by silence after a moment. I wanted to run, but my legs felt weak, as if they were stuck to the floor. I recalled that when I first came in, I might not have noticed whether anyone was following behind me, and in my mind a scenario flashed by in a split second: what if it was a thief, or... something worse. I quickly looked around. The peeling tiles covering the walls and the ceiling dotted with black stains looked like some oppressive beast, leaving me breathless.

Hearing another rustling sound, I finally decided to move. I hurried across the hall, and my elbow accidentally scraped against a nail on a wall corner, sending a searing pain through it. I didn’t even dare stop to check; I could only run faster toward the exit. Every muscle in my body was taut and hard, and my stomach hurt as if it were being squeezed. I rushed to the door, only to find that the handle on the sheet-metal door would not turn. Then I remembered that when I came in, it had already been hanging half open. I had no choice but to slam into it with my shoulder. The metal door let out a grating screech. When I burst out of the pool, I found the outside deserted, with only the summer night breeze moving the shrubs by the roadside.

Even after I got home, I still didn’t feel safe. I kept checking whether the windows were shut and whether the door was locked. I repeatedly looked through the photos on my phone, but found no suspicious shadows or faces. Lying in bed, my mind was still haunted by imagined footsteps. That rustling sound seemed to keep echoing in my ears, impossible to shake off no matter what I did.

As I stepped into the old post office, with its heavy sense of history, my mood grew as quiet as the place itself. Yet deep down, I still could not suppress my tension. In this meeting with the art collector, I knew it would be a difficult conversation. The old stamp display cases on the wall glowed faintly, exuding a certain nostalgic air. Several old magazines were laid out on the benches in the hallway, and the faint, fresh scent of paper lingered in the air.

“The work you brought is interesting,” the collector said slowly, with a hint of caution in his tone. I immediately wondered whether he was implying something, whether he thought my work wasn’t good enough. My heartbeat quickened at once, and my palms began to sweat. I tried to stay calm, but the tension in my body kept rising.

I replied, “Thank you. I hope it conveys the unique perspective I’m trying to express.” My voice trembled slightly, and I prayed he hadn’t noticed.

I went on explaining my creative ideas, trying to find a comfortable rhythm in the conversation. But every time the other person raised his eyebrows slightly or gave a soft sigh, I couldn’t help magnifying those details in my mind. I imagined the worst-case scenario: that he would dismiss me, refuse to work with me, and I even began to doubt whether I was capable of continuing to create.

As the conversation went on, my heart raced, my whole body was tense, and there was a faint, dull ache in my stomach. I had to keep reminding myself inwardly to focus on the exchange in front of me, rather than letting my anxiety lead me astray.

After leaving the post office, I walked back to my studio. The weather outside seemed to sense my mood as well; dark clouds slowly rolled in. I sat down at my worktable, replaying the conversation from the day. Every expression and every tone from the other person kept running through my mind like a nonstop film. I began to ruminate on my mistakes, repeatedly weighing whether what I had said was appropriate.

A few days later, the collector emailed me to express his recognition and interest. I felt a tremendous sense of relief, as if the heavy burden in my heart had finally been lifted. However, I still remembered the tension and unease I had felt in the post office that day, a feeling that could be triggered again in every important conversation in the future. This experience made me realize that no matter what external judgment I face, my sensitivity is always too intense—and that is the challenge I need to confront.

The lights in the conference room were a little harsh. I sat in the center of the table, surrounded by my colleagues. The new project proposal I had spent the entire night preparing was now laid out before everyone. As I began to explain my idea, my heartbeat gradually quickened and my palms started to sweat. I could feel everyone’s attention on me, which made me even more uneasy. My voice trembled a little, though I tried hard to stay composed. One colleague suddenly interrupted: “This part may not be very realistic. Do we need to reconsider it?” I forced a smile and replied, “Of course, we can adjust the details.” But inside, a wave of shame and self-doubt surged up. Why do I always mess these things up? Images flashed through my mind of them discussing my incompetence in private.

After the meeting ended, my colleagues left one by one, and I sat there alone, thinking about the conversation just now. Remembering every expression and every word they had said, I kept replaying my own remarks over and over. For some reason, I always felt criticism hidden in their eyes. My stomach began to twist in pain, as if protesting my constant mental torment. I lowered my head and took deep breaths, trying to calm myself, but it was no use.

A few days later, I still couldn’t shake off these feelings. After work, I went home and tried to distract myself by reading. Yet the words on each page blurred before my eyes, and my mind remained filled with the scene from the meeting. Unable to concentrate, I closed the book, and my anxiety only grew stronger.

While having dinner with my family, I tentatively asked what they thought of my colleagues’ opinions. My family comforted me, saying this was a normal part of work and that I should accept different viewpoints. But I found it hard to see this as encouragement; I still felt I wasn’t good enough. That night, I tossed and turned, imagining different solutions and trying to avoid facing similar questions again. Even so, I still couldn’t escape the fear deep inside me—the fear that I would be abandoned because I couldn’t meet everyone’s expectations.

The restaurant was dimly lit, with waiters moving between the tables, the clatter of dishes mingling with people’s laughter. The gathering was already halfway through when a colleague serving as host suggested playing a quiz game to liven up the atmosphere. Although I forced a smile and nodded, my palms had already started to sweat. I looked down at the glass on the table; tiny droplets of condensation clung to its surface, as if I could feel the chill seeping into my fingertips.

“Come on, the next question is for you!” the host said, pointing at me in a half-joking tone. In that instant, everyone’s eyes turned toward me, and I could feel my pores tightening under my skin. I looked up and saw a few people wearing teasing smiles. I tried to pull at the corners of my mouth and act relaxed, but my voice still trembled involuntarily: “Sure, what’s the question?”

He asked a professional question about our latest project. I actually knew the answer, but at that moment my mind went completely blank. All I remembered was that the end of his sentence seemed drawn out a little, and I even started to wonder whether he was deliberately trying to embarrass me. My heartbeat suddenly quickened, and I unconsciously clenched the tissue in my hand. Several past situations like this flashed rapidly through my mind, stinging me like tiny needles.

“Uh... I can’t remember, sorry.” Even I could hear the apology and embarrassment in my tone. A colleague at the same table let out a soft laugh, and I immediately caught the sound; my heart tightened violently. “Are they mocking me? Or was it just a coincidence?”

Then another colleague smoothly supplied the answer, and the whole table resumed its lively discussion as if the little interruption had never happened. I lowered my head and stared at the remaining piece of beef on my plate, trying hard to keep a calm expression on my face, but my stomach had begun to feel vaguely unsettled, as though something heavy were pressing down on it.

When the gathering ended, I made up an excuse and left early. The moment I stepped out of the restaurant, a cold wind hit me, and I realized my shirt back was already soaked with sweat. On the subway ride home, I kept replaying the conversation over and over. “Why was I so useless? It was something I knew so well, yet my mind went blank.” “When that person laughed, did they think I was stupid, or did they assume I was slacking off?” These thoughts grew heavier and heavier, like a dark cloud pressing down on me until I could hardly breathe.

That night, lying in bed and staring at the ceiling, my mind was still turning over that one moment again and again. Every time I closed my eyes, I could see those half-real, half-fake smiles. It was already past two in the morning, and though I tried not to think about it, the harder I tried not to, the more chaotic my mind became. I grabbed my phone and started scrolling through the news, but even the headlines made me uneasy, as if danger and ridicule were everywhere in the world.

When I got up the next morning, my head felt heavy, and my stomach was still faintly aching. My face in the mirror looked dull and gray, with darker and darker circles under my eyes. I still had to go to work, I thought; otherwise, people would think I was even stranger.

I was standing in an abandoned ceramic workshop in the northern suburbs of the city, the air thick with the smell of damp earth and leftover glaze. Most of the workshop’s windows were broken, and a few shafts of sunlight slipped through, cutting across the dim space. Everything was silent except for the sound of my own breathing and my footsteps echoing softly on the floor. Suddenly, a strange voice broke the silence: “This place is pretty interesting, isn’t it?” I turned around and saw a man standing in the corner, wearing a friendly smile, but I immediately became alert inside, my heartbeat quickening noticeably and my hands beginning to sweat slightly.

“Yeah, it is kind of special,” I replied, trying to keep the tension out of my voice, thinking I should stay polite so things wouldn’t get awkward. He continued, “I’m here shooting some footage. The atmosphere here feels really unique.” I nodded, but in my mind all sorts of scenarios had already started flashing by: what if he had some ulterior motive? What if what he was saying was just an excuse? How should I respond? My tension kept rising, and my stomach felt unsettled.

“I’m here gathering material too,” I tried to make up an excuse. “The history of this place is really fascinating to me.” He said, “Yes, I heard this place used to produce a lot of famous ceramic pieces.” His words put me slightly at ease; at least we had something in common. As the conversation continued, I began to feel as though I were trapped in an invisible social net, constantly analyzing every one of his movements and expressions, guessing at his possible intentions.

I caught sight of the camera in his hand, and then a wave of unease came over me: what if he took pictures of me? What if those photos were misused? I quickly changed the subject. “What kind of things are you mainly filming?” He described some of the projects he was working on, and his words didn’t seem aggressive, so I relaxed a little. However, deep inside, that sense of unease still hadn’t faded.

After I got home, I was still unsettled by the conversation with him. An uncontrollable urge made me keep replaying the exchange over and over, as if every detail needed to be examined again. I started searching online for the history of the abandoned workshop, hoping to find some clue that would put my mind at ease. A few days later, I still couldn’t completely shake off the discomfort brought on by that encounter, but I realized that the anxiety of talking to strangers comes not only from fear of the unknown, but also from magnifying one’s own flaws. Gradually, I began to try to accept that unease and prevent it from affecting my mood.

Sunlight poured through the café’s large windows onto the wooden floor, and the air was filled with the rich aroma of coffee. I sat in a corner by the window, glancing at the clock on the wall from time to time. “Why isn’t it ready yet?” I muttered to myself, casting a sidelong look at the waiter. They seemed busy handling a pile of takeaway orders. Gradually, my palms began to sweat a little, and my heartbeat also sped up slightly. I felt somewhat helpless about this mild anxiety of mine, yet whenever this happened, it always seemed to follow me like a shadow.

I had already flipped through the magazine on the table several times, but my attention kept drifting to the lingering scent of coffee and the quiet conversations around me. At the table to my right, two young men were discussing a newly released game, their voices rising and falling. “We can play together when we get back,” one of them said with a smile, apparently not noticing the fact that I was still waiting for my coffee, and my impatience grew a little more.

“Your coffee is a little delayed. Would you mind waiting five more minutes?” the waiter asked politely. I managed a forced smile and nodded. In truth, I wanted to say, “Can’t it be faster?” But the kindness in his tone made me hold those words back. I could feel my shoulders tensing up, and I began gently massaging them with my hands, trying to relax.

At last, the waiter brought my coffee over. I caught a faint vanilla scent rising with the steam and let out a slight sigh of relief. For the rest of the time, I lowered my head and sipped the coffee in small mouthfuls, watching the pedestrians coming and going outside the window as my irritation gradually faded with time. After leaving the café, I strolled along the street, the breeze brushing across my face, and my mood turned cheerful.

That evening, I kept reflecting on the waiting experience at the café that day. “Why am I always so impatient?” This small incident made me realize that I was prone to losing patience over even a little waiting and uncertainty. I felt ashamed of this sensitivity, because I wished I could be calmer and more relaxed. Over the next few days, I tried to remind myself to be more patient in similar situations and not let small things affect my mood.

The air in the gallery was faintly scented with clay. Soft yellow light spilled down from the track lights on the ceiling, illuminating rows of exquisite ceramic pieces. Some had glazes as smooth as mirrors; others were rough and richly textured. I looked down at a uniquely shaped teapot and ran my fingers over the slightly raised patterns on its surface. My fingertips brushed the tiny grains left behind after the glaze had been polished, cool and coarse. I heard footsteps approaching behind me and turned to see L, one of the curators of this exhibition.

“What do you think of this?” I asked, pointing at the teapot, my voice tinged with anticipation. To be honest, I was a little nervous. L had always been someone I greatly admired, and I had recently taken part in some curatorial work. I had hoped to use this opportunity to talk with her and explore the possibility of working together in the future. She glanced at the teapot and replied flatly, “Hmm, it’s okay.”

I froze. My mind instantly went into overdrive. “What does she mean? Does she think my taste is off? How could she say only ‘it’s okay’—that’s so unlike her.” I couldn’t help recalling her cool reaction two months ago during an online meeting when I presented a design proposal. Had she been dissatisfied with me ever since? Did she think I wasn’t capable enough? Did she think I didn’t deserve to be part of her project?

As I tried to answer these questions, my stomach suddenly began to cramp, and a familiar wave of discomfort rose in my chest. I did my best to hide my emotions, but my body betrayed me; my palms even started to sweat—in the cool spring night! I tried to keep smiling, but I was sure I looked stiff.

“Are you okay? You look a little off,” L said. I quickly shook my head. “I’m fine, maybe I’m just a bit tired.” Hearing that only made me feel worse; I couldn’t help wondering whether she had noticed something. I hurriedly changed the subject, gave a few perfunctory replies, and then excused myself to look at other exhibits.

For the rest of the evening, I could barely bring myself to care about the ceramics that had originally interested me. My mind kept replaying the scene, chewing over her “it’s okay” again and again, trying to find more clues in it. Had I been too enthusiastic just now? Or was my question too amateurish, making her think I wasn’t qualified to take part in such a conversation?

When I got home, I was still unsettled. The discomfort in my stomach and the turmoil in my head tangled together, leaving me sleepless all night. The next morning, clutching the last bit of hope, I opened my phone to see whether L had posted anything on social media that hinted at mocking my taste. Instead, I found a post from her—a photo of that very teapot, captioned: “The beauty of details, I love its natural texture.” At that moment, my feelings were incredibly complicated. Regret and embarrassment flooded me—I had overreacted to every word she said again. Why had an ordinary interaction left me spending the entire night berating myself over my insecurity? I took a deep breath, and the guilt and self-reproach slowly receded, replaced by a sense of fatigue and emptiness.

“Forget it. I’ll try again next time,” I muttered to myself, while in my heart I had already begun quietly rehearsing the next time I would speak to her.

When I entered the old bookstore tucked away at the end of the alley, the wind had already turned sharp. The air was thick with the smell of aging paper, mixed with the distinctive scent of a damp wooden floor. I saw the owner sitting behind the counter, reading a thick dictionary; without looking up, he pointed toward the wooden staircase leading down to the basement. The store was dimly lit, and the stairs were wrapped in shadow. The wooden handrail felt cold and slightly rough under my touch. My nerves tightened at once, and I felt as if I were slipping into some abyss of unknown depth.

The basement light was very faint, with a yellow-white bulb flickering overhead, carrying a sense of some distant era. Tall bookshelves stood all around, the books arranged haphazardly yet full of charm. Looking around, I noticed a middle-aged man standing by the shelves, head bent over a travel journal whose cover had already yellowed. His eyes suddenly swept toward me, and he gave me a friendly smile. I felt awkward and instinctively lowered my head to avoid eye contact, while thoughts churned rapidly in my mind: “Why is he smiling at me? Does he think it’s strange that I’m alone? Or did my behavior just seem rude?”

I moved to another bookshelf and pretended to focus on choosing books, but my fingers were shaking uncontrollably. I could hear my heart pounding, and my stomach began to ache faintly. This kind of tension always came for no reason, and I had no way to control it. I heard the soft creak of the wooden floor beside me; the man shifted position and leaned closer in my direction, and I immediately felt as if the air had grown thinner. I started sweating heavily, pressing the back of my hand against the cold bookshelf, trying to ease the heat in my body.

“Do you like books like this too?” the other person suddenly asked, his voice gentle and his face smiling.

“Yes... yes.” I answered flustered, my voice trembling with nervousness. Alarm bells were ringing in my head: “Is he trying to make conversation? Is he about to sell me something? Or am I being targeted?”

He pointed to the old book in my hands and said with a touch of relaxed enthusiasm, “This is a good book; the author’s writing is very powerful.” I forced a smile and looked up in response. But immediately, more frightening thoughts surged through my mind: “Is he being sincere? Or just being polite? Or is this book actually very obscure, and am I even choosing books this badly?”

Not wanting to talk to him any longer, I hurriedly took the book and turned to head for the counter upstairs. The more afraid I was of facing him, the heavier my steps became. By the time I reached the counter, my hands were nearly weak with fatigue, and I almost dropped the book. “How much is this book?” I asked the owner softly, my voice hoarse from a tight throat. When I paid and left the bookstore, the cold wind hit my face, but I felt a wave of relief, as if a drowning person had finally touched air.

After returning home, I lay on the sofa looking at the book. The smell of the pages brought me some comfort, but in my mind the stranger’s expression and tone kept replaying again and again. I began to reflect: “Have I been overinterpreting other people’s kindness all along? But what if someone really is judging me? Would pretending to be natural be better?” Then I scolded myself for my cowardice: “Why did I avoid that person? Why couldn’t I have been more open and talked to him a little more?”

That night, while complaining about my own social helplessness, I repeatedly imagined how I should behave more normally if I ever encountered a similar situation again. In the sleepless dark, the time on my phone screen kept changing, but my emotions remained trapped among the basement bookshelves, unable to break free.

I pushed open the rusted iron door and stepped into the backstage area of the abandoned little theater. Dim light filtered weakly through the broken windows, falling onto the floor as dust danced in the air. For some reason, this place gave me an inexplicable pull. Everything around me was so quiet it felt as though I could hear the echo of my own heartbeat. I stood in a corner, on a faded carpet that made a rustling sound beneath my feet.

“This place is kind of creepy, don’t you think?” a friend once said to me, but I didn’t respond. Even though, deep down, I did somewhat agree, I was always deeply drawn to these mysterious, desolate places.

The footsteps seemed to keep echoing, as if each step were announcing my arrival. I walked deeper into the backstage area, gently touching the abandoned props and sets with my hand. The tips of my fingers felt cool, and the touch stirred a faint unease in me. It seemed as though every object had its own story, and every plank of wood retained secrets from the past.

“Why am I always drawn to places like this?” I kept asking myself. The silence and loneliness of these places seemed to answer the fragility within me. When I brushed my hand against the wall, a stale, moldy smell rushed toward me. My heartbeat began to quicken, as if each beat were reminding me of the instability of this place.

At that moment, my phone vibrated, breaking the brief silence. “Are you okay?” It was a message from my partner. I hesitated before replying, “I’m fine, just want to be alone for a bit.”

I continued wandering in the shadows, each heartbeat seeming to magnify the emptiness and stillness of the space. Unconsciously, I began to recall moments from the past—those mistakes I had made in my own creative work, and the shame I had never spoken of. It felt as though an invisible rope inside me was slowly tightening, leaving me unable to breathe.

In a place like this, any slight sound felt huge and abrupt. My back had gone rigid from tension, and the tightly clenched muscles made it almost impossible to relax. Without realizing it, my hands had curled into fists, my nails digging into my palms with a faint sting.

That night, I didn’t stay in the theater for very long. When I stepped outside and breathed in the air beyond it, my tense mood eased somewhat. Back home, I tossed and turned in bed, unable to settle my thoughts. All those memories and emotions intertwined in my mind, lingering and refusing to leave. When I woke the next day, my heavy eyelids and exhausted body reminded me that this burden in my heart needed time and a way to be released.

On a sweltering summer afternoon, sunlight streamed through the battered windows and fell onto the floor, while dust drifted slowly through the air. I was in an abandoned wood-carving workshop on the edge of the city. The place was in complete disarray, filled with unfinished sculptures and scattered tools. I could smell sawdust mixed with damp air, and every now and then I heard the faint sounds of wood expanding and contracting in the heat. My heartbeat was a little faster then, and my palms had started to sweat, as if it were always like this every time I came here.

I stood in the corner, staring at a piece of wood in front of me. My mind was filled with voices, constantly questioning my abilities, as if eager to undermine my confidence. I tightened my grip on the carving knife and tried to begin. Suddenly, I heard myself whisper, “Can I really do this well?” Then an unpleasant memory surfaced. I remembered that at the last exhibition, the audience seemed unimpressed with my work. Those subtle furrowed brows and slightly disdainful expressions kept replaying in my mind. I began to wonder whether, in their eyes, my work was insignificant.

Suddenly, someone appeared at the doorway: the workshop’s old owner, who often came by to check on its condition. “Need some help, kid?” His deep voice interrupted my thoughts. “No, I’m just a little lost,” I replied, trying to conceal the turmoil inside me. The old owner nodded and turned to leave, leaving me alone with those tangled thoughts. I kept recalling my past mistakes, afraid that my sensitivity would once again become a laughingstock.

My stomach began to ache faintly, a common reaction when I was anxious. I took a deep breath, trying to calm myself down and continue carving the wood. The sound of the blade cutting across the wood was like a comfort, easing my mood a little. But whenever I made a bit of progress, those negative signals in my mind and the fear of being abandoned would surge back again.

That night, I went home and lay in bed, still feeling conflicted. On one hand, I kept trying to convince myself that this was just part of the creative process, a stage of self-doubt I had to go through; on the other, I couldn’t stop worrying about whether I would be able to break through this barrier. The next morning, I decided to go to the workshop again, hoping I might find some answers there.

Over the past few days, I’ve tried to adjust my mindset and care less about what others think. I know I have a habit of catastrophizing small things, but this time, I hope I can find a trace of calm amid these complicated emotions. After all, artistic creation itself is a challenge and an exploration of the inner self.
